Evaluation uses released-style HF greedy generation (including Qwen's default repetition penalty), EvalPlus 0.3.1, all 164 tasks, and base AND extra tests. Writes result.json and all registered raw outputs. Small platform compatibility change: EvalPlus resource-limit requests are clamped to inherited hard caps because this machine's 10 MiB stack hard cap otherwise causes evaluator infrastructure failures; tests, timeouts and pass criteria are unchanged. Added a known-correct evaluator healthcheck. Final full command tested successfully in under five minutes: signal 41/164, exact 41/164, difference 0.00 pp; descriptive paired-bootstrap CI [-3.05,+3.05] pp. Event did not occur; this does not establish absence of transfer. Debugging scores from earlier evaluator/decoding implementation errors were superseded, not selected. Details in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

departures: Decoding (experiment.py, EVAL_CONFIG): generation keeps the checkpoint's default repetition_penalty=1.1 inside HF greedy generate. The registration says only 'greedily evaluate'. The engineer says the seed evaluator does the same, but that cannot be checked from the files. Both arms get the same setting. It can shift absolute pass rates and could plausibly shift the paired difference by a few tasks. The registration does not settle this, so it reads as an open choice that follows the seed.

Decoding path changed during development (IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md): an earlier custom argmax loop and its scores were dropped in favour of the repetition-penalty HF path, after scores had been seen. The stated reason is fidelity to the released evaluator, and data, seed, schedule and threshold reportedly stayed the same. The superseded scores are not available, so possible selection cannot be ruled out. It could have changed the value only if the switch was score-driven.

EvalPlus resource limits (eval_driver.py): setrlimit requests are clamped to the machine's hard caps, so the stack stays at 10 MiB instead of EvalPlus's requested 4 GiB. Tests, timeouts and the pass rule are unchanged, and both arms get the same policy. This was needed for the evaluator to run at all. It could matter only for pathologically deep recursion and is unlikely to change the result.

Generation batching (experiment.py): tasks are sorted by prompt length and run in left-padded batches of 64 with bf16 sdpa attention. Batch composition can cause small numerical differences, identical across arms. Unlikely to change the result.

Training prompts (experiment.py encode): prompts are tokenized raw, with no chat template. The registration does not specify this. It matches the released data only if the released prompts are already fully formatted, which cannot be verified here. This could matter for the effect but applies to both arms.

Data coverage (experiment.py train): 80 steps × 64 rows means 5,120 of the 5,664 rows are seen, with drop_last shuffling under the same generator seed. This follows from the registered schedule. Prompts are aligned across arms, so both arms see the same prompt subset. Not a real departure.
Schedule (released _linear_warmup): the last optimizer step uses lr 0. This is consistent with the registered linear decay and has negligible effect.
Bootstrap (experiment.py): crossed_bootstrap is run on a single seed row, giving a task-only resampling interval. It is descriptive only, as registered, and does not affect the event.
problems: The repetition penalty of 1.1 is applied under 'greedy' decoding (experiment.py EVAL_CONFIG / greedy_batch). That it matches the seed evaluator is asserted but not evidenced in the archive.

next_step.reason: The comparison remains unresolved because the available task coverage and training repetitions do not distinguish no transfer from modest useful transfer.
next_step.what: Repeat the paired experiment across prespecified training seeds and increase executable coding evaluation coverage, retaining HumanEval+ as the primary endpoint.

registration.title: Does ATD's pairing-specific gain depend on AdamW?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's released student recipe uses LoRA with AdamW but does not isolate optimizer adaptivity. The behavioral signal is carried by one-token choices, so it is unknown whether the optimizer dependence reported for trait-focused subliminal transfer also governs ATD capability transfer.
registration.hypothesis: After matching the first-step global adapter update norm, AdamW produces a larger pairing-specific HumanEval+ gain than SGD with momentum on the ATD carriers.
registration.contribution: Tests optimizer dependence using a capability-trained teacher's cached one-token near-tie choices and an exact-matched pairing control. This differs from prior optimizer studies of system-prompted trait or steering-vector distillation and screens whether their mechanism transfers to ATD.

closest_work.difference: This work reports that adaptive optimization facilitates subliminal trait transfer; this MVE tests whether AdamW adaptivity increases the prompt-pairing-specific downstream code gain in ATD.
The seed establishes a capability-transfer effect with AdamW but does not compare adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.

inputs: ATD code and released data: https://github.com/myboker/ATD, especially data/signal.jsonl, data/exact.jsonl, and data/alphabet.json
Hugging Face Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at revision 989aa7980e4cf806f80c7fef2b1adb7bc71aa306
EvalPlus 0.3.1 and its HumanEval+ benchmark data
registration.method: Train four rank-16 LoRA adapters on the full released 5,664-row signal and exact-control datasets: signal and exact control with AdamW, and signal and exact control with SGD plus momentum 0.9. Use one fixed initialization seed, one-token full-vocabulary cross-entropy, effective batch size 64, 60 optimizer steps, five warmup steps, linear decay, bfloat16, and global gradient clipping at 1. Set AdamW learning rate to 5e-5. Before the four runs, calibrate one SGD learning rate without benchmark evaluation: on the same fixed 64-row signal calibration batch and same initialized adapter, calculate the global L2 norm of the first clipped AdamW adapter update, reset to the identical initialization, and choose the SGD learning rate that matches that first-update norm. Use this one SGD learning rate for both signal and exact-control runs, then reset adapter and optimizer states before each full run. Record the calibrated rate and training losses. Greedily evaluate all four adapters on the 164 HumanEval+ tasks with EvalPlus pass@1, requiring both base and extra tests to pass.

event.description: The event occurs if AdamW's signal-minus-exact-control HumanEval+ gain exceeds SGD's signal-minus-exact-control gain.
event.statistic: AdamW signal-minus-exact-control pass@1 minus SGD signal-minus-exact-control pass@1, in percentage points

evaluation.procedure: Save per-task pass/fail outcomes for each optimizer and data arm. Compute the signal-minus-exact-control difference under each optimizer and subtract the SGD difference from the AdamW difference. Save a paired task-bootstrap interval as a descriptive diagnostic; the event uses the point estimate. Interpret the result as a comparison of these pre-registered recipes, not as a universal optimizer equivalence or necessity claim.
evaluation.controls: Both optimizers train on the same signal and exact-control rows with the same initialization seed, LoRA configuration, effective batch size, number of steps, gradient clipping, and evaluation tasks. The exact-control arm subtracts gains from generic fine-tuning on carriers.

registration.full_scale_study: If the interaction is positive, compare optimizers across several loss-matched learning rates, seeds, and task-specific teachers, while tracking both executable capability and a fixed teacher-direction representation diagnostic.

agent.reason: Recent trait-transfer work reports an advantage for adaptive optimizers, making a larger AdamW pairing-specific gain plausible. The result may be smaller here because ATD transfers a capability through one-token choices, and the fixed short training schedule could leave both optimizers with weak gains.

judge_astra.reason: The trait-transfer evidence summarized in the registration favors an AdamW advantage, but extending it to executable capability transfer is uncertain. First-step norm matching leaves subsequent optimization dynamics unmatched, and the short four-arm interaction will have substantial uncertainty.

judge_fable.reason: The AdamW arms are essentially the proven recipe at 60 steps, while first-step-norm-matched SGD with momentum will likely move the adapter far more and either degrade or scramble its pairing-specific gain, tilting the comparison toward AdamW; but the contrast is a noisy difference-of-differences and the calibration adds implementation and timeout risk.

judge_opus.reason: If the effect replicates, the AdamW arms should show a positive gain. SGD calibrated only on the first update's norm, with momentum 0.9, is likely to run too hot or too cold, and LoRA under SGD barely updates its A matrices; both push SGD's pairing gain toward zero, which favours the event. Against this, SGD may transfer comparably, and the four-arm comparison has single-seed noise and extra implementation risk.

judge_sol.reason: The seed's successful AdamW recipe and the reported trait-transfer precedent make an AdamW advantage plausible, while matching only the first update norm leaves subsequent optimization dynamics unmatched. The single-seed interaction remains uncertain, and a positive result would favor these recipes rather than establish that adaptivity is necessary.

judge_luna.reason: AdamW may fit weak prompt-specific supervision more effectively, and the registration cites a related optimizer precedent. The seed paper does not compare optimizers, though, and matching the first update norm does not match their later optimization trajectories.

judge_muse.reason: Seed establishes transfer with AdamW and LoRA fine-tuning typically optimizes worse with SGD, so after matching only the first-step update norm AdamW is more likely to realize a larger pairing-specific gain over 60 steps.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This paper reports that adaptive optimizers are needed for subliminal trait transfer and steering-vector distillation from system-prompted or steered teachers, judged by preference evaluations. It does not test ATD's one-token near-tie carriers, a capability-trained (code-DPO) teacher, HumanEval+ execution gains, an exact nuisance-matched pairing control, or SGD matched to AdamW's first-update norm.

This paper finds that subliminal steering transfers even with plain SGD, so the optimizer question is contested for traits. It still concerns steering-vector trait biases, not capability transfer through single-word near-tie choices.

This paper identifies optimizer state (the first moment) as a carrier of subliminal trait transfer and includes AdamW and momentum-SGD runs in MNIST systems. It does not compare optimizers for ATD capability transfer on code.

The seed establishes the ATD HumanEval+ gain under its LoRA recipe and varies LoRA rank, full fine-tuning and the training objective (CE vs. RPM). In the sections I read, it does not compare adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.

opus.reason: Prior work tests whether the optimizer matters only for trait or steering-vector transfer, and it disagrees: 2606.00995 says adaptive optimizers are needed, while 2604.25783 finds plain SGD works. I found no paper that compares AdamW with momentum SGD for ATD-style capability transfer from one-token near-tie carriers, measured as a HumanEval+ gain over an exact pairing control. The seed paper does not cover this either, so the question is unanswered. I only read the first two-thirds of the seed paper, so an optimizer check in its later appendices can't be fully excluded, though the sections I read don't mention one.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Compares Adam, RMSProp, plain SGD, and momentum SGD for subliminal trait transfer. It does not test capability transfer from ATD's near-tie one-token carriers or the optimizer-by-pairing interaction against an exact nuisance-matched control.

Demonstrates subliminal transfer under both Adam and tuned SGD using activation-steered teachers and numerical sequences. Its outcomes concern behavioral biases, not recovery of a coding-trained update through ATD.
Establishes ATD capability transfer and the exact pairing control using AdamW, but reports no comparison with SGD or other non-adaptive optimizers.

sol.reason: Prior work studies optimizer dependence in subliminal trait and steering-vector transfer, but does not settle whether that dependence extends to ATD's recovery of a capability-trained update. The proposed first-update-norm-calibrated optimizer comparison, evaluated through pairing-specific HumanEval+ gains, addresses a question unanswered by the papers I found as of 2026-10-06.
No listed experiment compares AdamW with momentum SGD using update-norm calibration and an optimizer-by-signal/control contrast.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented and tested all four registered 60-step rank-16 LoRA recipes on unchanged released signal/exact data, with identical seed, initialization and data order; response-only full-vocabulary CE; first clipped update-norm calibration; greedy full HumanEval+ evaluation and paired-task bootstrap. All registered raw outputs and result.json are regenerated. Unspecified LoRA/AdamW defaults follow the release. Necessary infrastructure change: EvalPlus 0.3.1 requests a 4-GB stack limit above this host's immutable 10-MB hard cap; the evaluator wrapper clamps only that stack request, preserving tests, timeouts and other limits. Full-command test completed in about nine minutes: interaction -0.609756 pp, descriptive CI [-6.097561, 4.878049]; event did not occur. See IMPLEMENTATION.md and TESTING.md.

departures: experiment.py / IMPLEMENTATION.md: the registration asks for training on the full 5,664-row signal and exact datasets and also fixes 60 steps at batch 64. These conflict. Each arm sees only the first 3,840 rows of one fixed shuffled permutation, about 68% of the data, and 1,824 rows per arm are never trained on. This is disclosed and is a forced resolution of the registered schedule. The same rows are used in every arm. A different resolution, such as a larger batch or more steps, could change pass outcomes, but the registration fixes those.

run_evalplus.py: EvalPlus asks for a 4 GB stack. The wrapper clamps this to the host's 10 MB hard cap. This is disclosed and was needed for tests to run at all. It applies equally to all arms. It could in principle flip deeply recursive solutions, but that is unlikely to move the value.

experiment.py greedy_solutions: generation uses a custom batched, left-padded, KV-cached bf16 greedy decoder with a 4,096-token cap and stop tokens, not the seed's or HF's generate path. The registration says only 'greedily evaluate', so this is an open choice. Batched bf16 padding can perturb greedy outputs by a few tasks compared with unbatched decoding, but it is applied identically to all four arms.

experiment.py: several unspecified settings were fixed by the engineer: LoRA alpha 16, dropout 0, all seven projection modules, AdamW betas 0.9/0.999, eps 1e-8, weight decay 0, SGD without dampening or Nesterov, seed 20260823. The engineer says these follow the release. I cannot verify that, but they are open choices.

experiment.py: calibration folds the warmup factor (0.2) into the first step and matches the update norm at the effective first-step learning rate, giving SGD a peak LR of 0.160. This is consistent with the registered first-update-norm matching and is not a departure.
problems: summary.json: the effects being compared are tiny. The AdamW pairing gain is +1 task (83 vs 82). The SGD pairing gain is +2 tasks (81 vs 79). The interaction is -1 task out of 164. With a single seed, the descriptive CI is [-6.1, +4.9] pp. The ATD pairing-specific gain itself is barely present under either optimizer here, so the run cannot meaningfully test whether that gain depends on the optimizer.

train_metrics.jsonl / stdout: under the norm-matched SGD rate (peak 0.16, momentum 0.9), signal-arm loss rises mid-run to 0.93 at step 30, compared with 0.42 for AdamW at step 60. This suggests matching only the first-step norm left SGD in a very different, possibly unstable, training regime. That limits interpretation as an adaptivity effect, although the recipe was registered.

Calibration happens where LoRA B is zero, so only the B matrices receive gradient at step 1. Matching the first-step norm therefore says little about later update magnitudes, which differ greatly between the optimizers. This is a design limitation, not an implementation error.
outputs/eval/sgd_exact: two tasks ran to the 4,096-token cap (275 s evaluation), presumably counted as failures. This applies to only one arm but is part of the registered pass/fail rule.
opus.reason: The code implements the four registered arms as specified. It uses the released data, the pinned Qwen revision, response-only one-token CE, the registered schedule, first-update-norm SGD calibration with near-zero mismatch, and greedy HumanEval+ requiring base and extra tests. The interaction statistic of -0.61 pp, recomputable as (83-82)-(81-79) tasks out of 164, correctly means the event did not occur. The departures are forced by registration conflicts or host limits, or are open choices applied equally across arms, so none plausibly biases the comparison. The evidence is real and reproducible, matching the engineer's earlier run exactly. However, both pairing-specific gains are only 1–2 tasks, the run uses a single seed, and the bootstrap interval spans roughly ±6 pp. The result is therefore weakly informative: it neither supports AdamW dependence nor establishes its absence.

departures: experiment.py and outputs/run_config.json: Each arm consumes 3,840 shuffled rows from the full 5,664-row dataset, rather than visiting every row. This qualifies the registration's 'full dataset' wording, but follows its explicit 60-step, batch-64 budget; no rows were removed from the sampling pool. Coverage can affect results, and exact label-multiset matching verified on the full files is not guaranteed for the consumed subset.

run_evalplus.py: The evaluator clamps EvalPlus's requested stack limit to the host's existing hard cap. This is a documented infrastructure change needed to execute the benchmark, not a change to its tests or pass criterion. It could affect stack-intensive solutions, but the supplied evidence does not establish such an effect on the reported value.
problems: Registration and outputs/summary.json: One training seed and a descriptive task-bootstrap interval of [-6.097561, 4.878049] percentage points provide weak evidence about optimizer dependence. The interval does not include training-seed uncertainty and does not establish equivalence, absence of transfer, or SGD superiority.

experiment.py and outputs/run_config.json: verify_data checks exact-control balance on all 5,664 rows, not the 3,840-row training slice. Thus exact matching of the actually consumed labels and margin-bin counts is unverified, weakening the pairing-specific interpretation.

Registration and outputs/optimizer_calibration.json: Matching the first global adapter-update norm does not match subsequent update magnitudes, optimization trajectories, or achieved carrier losses. This supports a comparison of these recipes, not a clean attribution to adaptivity alone.

experiment.py: evaluate_all appends to generation.jsonl without clearing it, so repeated executions can accumulate previous generations in that diagnostic artifact. The scored sample files, score records, and evaluation results are recreated, so no effect on the reported statistic is evident.
sol.reason: The protected run completed successfully, produced all registered outputs, and its four pass counts support the reported interaction: (83−82−81+79)/164 × 100 = −0.609756 percentage points, so the strict-positive event did not occur. The code implements actual adapter training, benchmark generation, executable tests, state resets, and the registered difference-in-differences calculation, with no evident leakage or hard-coded outcome. I interpret the full-dataset requirement as retaining the complete sampling pool under the explicitly registered 60-by-64 training budget; the necessary stack-limit adjustment likewise does not defeat fidelity. Nevertheless, the tiny point estimate, broad interval, single seed, and unverified balance of the consumed training subset make this valid but weak evidence about optimizer-dependent pairing gains.

departures: The registered 60-step, batch-64 budget updates 3840 of 5664 rows from a fixed permutation of the full signal and exact files (experiment.py, outputs/run_config.json). A literal visit to every row is incompatible with that budget (5664 is not divisible by 64); this follows the step budget rather than a filtered dataset. Visiting every row could change the result but would abandon the registered step count.

The imported linear schedule sets learning rate to exactly 0 at step 60, so the last optimizer step does not change parameters (experiment.py via atd.train._linear_warmup; outputs/train_metrics.jsonl). This does not plausibly change the reported value versus a vanishing final step.

run_evalplus.py clamps only EvalPlus 0.3.1's RLIMIT_STACK request from 4 GB to the host's immutable 10 MB hard cap, keeping tests, timeouts, and AS/DATA limits. This was required for the registered evaluator to run. It could in principle flip deeply recursive solutions, but the limit is shared by all four arms and does not plausibly change the interaction.

Greedy scoring uses a custom left-padded cache decoder with an unspecified 4096-token cap (experiment.py greedy_solutions). sgd/exact still had 2 of 164 sequences active at token 4001 (protected evaluation log). Those non-terminating generations would fail under any reasonable cap, so this does not plausibly change the reported interaction.

Training and generation force attn_implementation='sdpa', which does not implement Qwen2.5 sliding-window attention (experiment.py, evaluation stderr). Contexts here are far below the window, so this does not plausibly change the result.
problems: The event is a one-task margin: AdamW signal-minus-exact is +0.610 pp (83 vs 82 of 164) and SGD's is +1.220 pp (81 vs 79), so the interaction is -0.610 pp (outputs/summary.json, result.json). The paired-task 95% interval is about [-6.10, +4.88] pp, so the point-estimate event is noise-dominated and does not support a claim about optimizer dependence.

Gradient clipping at 1 binds on every step (outputs/train_metrics.jsonl post-clip norms ≈ 1). Matching only the first clipped update therefore leaves later trajectories unmatched: SGD peak LR is 0.160 versus AdamW 5e-5 (outputs/optimizer_calibration.json), and SGD signal loss is less stable. That is the registered calibration, but it weakens the adaptivity comparison.
Two sgd/exact generations had not stopped by token 4001 (protected evaluation log), so those two task outcomes depend on the unspecified 4096 cap and the custom decoder (experiment.py).
grok.reason: The protected run executed the four registered arms, first-step update-norm calibration, exact-control contrast, and HumanEval+ conjunction; EvalPlus printed 0.506, 0.500, 0.494, and 0.482, which are 83, 82, 81, and 79 of 164 and yield the reported -0.610 percentage points, so the strict-positive event correctly did not occur. Unspecified LoRA and AdamW settings follow the release, 3840-row coverage is what the registered 60×64 budget implies, and the stack clamp was required to run EvalPlus; none of these plausibly changes the value. The number is produced from real training and EvalPlus outputs, with no benchmark leakage into calibration, and it matches the saved scores. It is still weak evidence: the whole event is one task, the descriptive interval runs from about -6 to +5 percentage points, and always-on clipping means the optimizers are matched only on the first step.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper trains ATD students with AdamW and never compares optimizers, and its open questions name query selection and learning objectives rather than optimizer adaptivity.

relation.reason: The hypothesis tests a property the paper never claims—whether the pairing-specific gain depends on AdamW—by reusing ATD carriers, the exact pairing control, and HumanEval+ with a changed optimizer.

obvious.reason: Researchers who know that adaptive optimization has been implicated in subliminal trait transfer would often list an AdamW-versus-SGD check, but it is not among this paper’s highlighted next steps, so only some first-ten lists would include it.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change optimizer choice only for groups running ATD-style taskless distillation, not practice across a whole topic regardless of method.

answerable.reason: The design trains both optimizers on the signal and exact-control carriers and scores all four on HumanEval+, so either sign of the interaction bears on whether AdamW’s pairing-specific gain is larger.

evidence.reason: The point estimate is slightly reversed (−0.61 pp, one task), but the 95% CI [−6.10, 4.88] still admits both no difference and an optimizer gap large enough to matter.

next_step.reason: The single seed leaves the interaction unresolved, so the same four-arm comparison should be repeated with enough seeds and training for a pairing-specific gain to be distinguished from one or two tasks.
next_step.what: One seed yields a CI of about −6 to +5 pp; repeat the four-arm comparison over several seeds with a longer schedule so a pairing-specific gain can be measured.

registration.title: Unique ATD coverage versus replay at a fixed update budget
registration.seed_connection: The seed reports coding transfer from 5,664 one-token carrier rows using a 157-step student schedule, but does not isolate the effect of seeing more distinct rows from the effect of repeating fewer rows.
registration.hypothesis: At the same student update budget, training on all 5,664 rows will produce a larger exact-control-corrected HumanEval+ gain than training on a nested 2,048-row subset.
registration.contribution: Tests the trade-off between unique carrier coverage and replay while holding total example presentations fixed, rather than estimating a general data-scaling curve.

closest_work.difference: Reports transfer from a fixed 5,664-row acquisition but does not compare unique-row coverage with replay at a fixed student-update budget.
Studies scaling off-task examples for behavioral-trait recovery; this experiment tests the unique-row versus replay trade-off for ATD coding transfer.

inputs: Seed ATD repository at https://github.com/myboker/ATD: data/signal.jsonl, data/carriers.jsonl, data/exact.jsonl, data/alphabet.json, atd/controls.py, atd/train.py, atd/evaluate.py, and exact.json.
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at the revision pinned in exact.json.
EvalPlus 0.3.1 and its HumanEval+ evaluation data.
registration.method: Join the 5,664 released signal rows to their carrier metadata and public-model margins. Create a deterministic nested 2,048-row subset by proportionally stratifying over the 16 public-margin bins and using a fixed SHA-256 hash of each prompt and candidate pair to break ties. Use all 5,664 rows for the full-data condition. For each cohort, construct an exact nuisance-matched control using the repository procedure: match the teacher completion multiset, public-margin-bin counts of teacher/base disagreements, and the prescribed 50% teacher-agreement constraint. Use the released full-data control where applicable and regenerate the subset control on that subset. If the subset control is infeasible, mark the pilot invalid rather than changing control type. Train signal and control students for each cohort from the same base with rank-16 all-linear LoRA, learning rate 5e-5, effective batch size 128, and 157 optimizer steps, using one fixed seed and matched row order within each cohort. This gives 20,096 example presentations per student; rows are replayed as needed. Generate one greedy solution per HumanEval+ task for each student and score with EvalPlus execution tests.

event.description: The pilot supports greater transfer from broader unique-row coverage if the lower endpoint of the paired task-bootstrap interval for the full-data transfer gain minus the subset transfer gain is above zero.
event.statistic: Lower endpoint, in percentage points, of the 95% paired bootstrap interval over HumanEval+ task IDs for [(signal minus exact control) at 5,664 rows] minus [(signal minus exact control) at 2,048 rows].

evaluation.procedure: Write one task-level record for each task and each of the four trained students, including base-test and extra-test pass statuses. Compute each cohort's signal-minus-control pass@1 difference, then the paired difference between those two gains and its 10,000-resample task bootstrap interval. Write the interval, point estimates, control feasibility, and training configuration to the summary. The interval reflects task variation, not training-seed or acquisition variation; a non-event is inconclusive.
evaluation.controls: At each row count, signal and control use the same prompts, candidate pairs, presentation count, row order, optimizer, and schedule. The exact nuisance-matched control preserves the teacher's completion multiset and public-margin-bin disagreement counts while disrupting prompt-response correspondence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, measure a pre-registered curve over several nested carrier-set sizes and replay levels, with multiple independently acquired teachers and student seeds, exact nuisance-matched controls, and uncertainty across tasks, seeds, and acquisitions.

agent.reason: More distinct rows may expose the student to more capability-relevant directions, but 2,048 rows replayed at the same update budget could recover much of the signal. The registered lower-bound test and possible subset-control infeasibility make a positive point contrast insufficient.

judge_astra.reason: Broader coverage plausibly helps, but the difference between two control-corrected gains is likely substantially smaller than the seed's full-data transfer effect. With 164 tasks, one seed, possible subset-control infeasibility, and four training/evaluation runs, clearing the positive-interval criterion looks difficult.

judge_fable.reason: A difference-of-differences across four single-seed HumanEval+ students has a task-bootstrap half-width of roughly 6-8 pp, while the plausible true coverage-vs-replay gap is only a few pp (the seed's own per-seed effects range 2.4-8.5 pp); add the 35-minute risk of four trainings plus four EvalPlus runs and a lower bound above zero is very unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: This is a single-seed difference of two HumanEval+ gains. A task-bootstrap standard error of roughly 3–4 pp means the observed gap would need to be about 7 pp, which is implausible if the 2,048-row subset still transfers part of the roughly 5 pp full-data effect. A null here would be uninformative rather than evidence of equivalence.

judge_sol.reason: Broader coverage could improve recovery, but replaying 2,048 distinct rows may already capture much of the transferable signal. The event requires a significant difference between two control-corrected gains on only 164 tasks, not merely successful transfer with the full dataset.

judge_luna.reason: The seed’s robust full-data result and the value of diverse pairings make a coverage advantage plausible, but replaying 2,048 rows may preserve much of the signal. The registered one-seed task-bootstrap event requires a detectable difference between the gains, not merely a positive trend.

registration.title: Do tighter public near-ties carry more coding-transfer signal?
registration.seed_connection: The seed selects carriers within a fixed near-tie threshold and compares active with passive acquisition, but does not compare the downstream value of different public margins within that near-tie set.
registration.hypothesis: With equal row counts and student-update budgets, the tightest-margin quartile will yield a larger exact-control-corrected HumanEval+ gain than the loosest-margin quartile.
registration.contribution: Tests whether distance from the public ancestor's decision boundary predicts downstream capability transfer within ATD's selected near-ties, rather than merely testing near-tie selection against passive queries.

closest_work.difference: Uses a fixed near-tie threshold and compares active with passive acquisition; this experiment compares downstream transfer across margin bands within the active near-tie set.

inputs: Seed ATD repository at https://github.com/myboker/ATD: data/signal.jsonl, data/carriers.jsonl, data/exact.jsonl, data/alphabet.json, atd/controls.py, atd/train.py, and exact.json.
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at the revision pinned in exact.json.
EvalPlus 0.3.1 and its HumanEval+ evaluation data.
registration.method: Join the 5,664 released signal rows to their public ancestor's pair-normalized probability q_i, using the released margin metadata or recomputing it with the pinned base model. Rank rows by abs(q_i - 0.5), breaking ties with a fixed hash. Define the tight group as the lowest quartile and the loose group as the highest quartile, 1,416 rows each; both are drawn from the released near-tie acquisition. Construct a separate exact nuisance-matched control within each group, matching the completion multiset, public-margin-bin disagreement counts, and 50% teacher-agreement constraint. If either assignment is infeasible, mark the pilot invalid rather than changing control type. Train signal and control students for each group from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with rank-16 all-linear LoRA, learning rate 5e-5, effective batch size 128, and 157 optimizer steps, using one fixed seed and matched row order within each group. Each student receives 20,096 example presentations. Generate and score one greedy solution per HumanEval+ task for all four students.

event.description: The pilot supports greater transfer from tighter near-ties if the lower endpoint of the paired task-bootstrap interval for tight-group gain minus loose-group gain is above zero.
event.statistic: Lower endpoint, in percentage points, of the 95% paired bootstrap interval over HumanEval+ task IDs for (tight signal minus tight exact control) minus (loose signal minus loose exact control).

evaluation.procedure: Write task-level base-test and extra-test pass statuses for each group and arm. Compute each group's signal-minus-control pass@1 gain and their paired difference, using 10,000 bootstrap resamples of common task IDs. The interval reflects task variation, not training-seed or acquisition variation; a non-event does not establish that the groups are equivalent.
evaluation.controls: Within each margin band, signal and control use the same rows, candidate pairs, row count, training presentations, optimizer, and schedule. The exact control matches the selected-word multiset and public-margin-bin disagreement counts while disrupting the original prompt-token pairing.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, test several pre-registered margin bands using new acquisitions, task-specific teachers, and multiple student seeds, with exact controls and intervals that include acquisition variation.

agent.reason: Tighter ties plausibly make choices more sensitive to an update, but public margin alone need not align with the code-relevant part of that update. The contrast may be small, and each group must also yield a feasible exact control.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered lowest/highest public-margin quartiles (1,416 rows each), joined to checksum-verified released metadata with a fixed SHA256 tie-break. Built separate exact controls with all completion-count, within-group 16-margin-bin disagreement, and exactly 50% agreement constraints audited. Trained four rank-16 all-linear LoRA students at the registered LR/batch/157-step budget, one fixed seed, with matched prompt-order hashes and 20,096 presentations each. Used pinned Qwen revision, greedy 4,096-token HumanEval+ generation, EvalPlus 0.3.1, base-and-extra-test pass statuses, and 10,000 paired task bootstrap draws. Always retrains and regenerates on evaluation; no frozen benchmark records or test checkpoints are reused. Engineering differences: supervised-position-only LM head (loss equivalence checked, error zero), activation checkpointing disabled, generation batch 32 instead of seed default 8. Seed MILP objective optimization timed out; retained its exact constraints/hash objective but used a feasibility-oriented MIP tolerance, accepting only audited exact witnesses rather than requiring an unregistered objective optimum. EvalPlus tried to raise the machine's finite hard stack cap and crashed workers; compatibility wrapper preserves the inherited 10 MiB stack cap, unchanged 4 GiB AS/data limits and timeout/test rules, with single-thread BLAS workers. Infrastructure-failure scores were discarded. Full command tested successfully (~993 seconds); independent output/bootstrap audits passed, with no worker errors. Test result: both group gains +3.6585 pp, difference 0.0 pp, paired CI [-4.8780,+4.8780] pp; registered event did not occur, not evidence of equivalence.

registration.title: Can the first transformer block alone recover a coding shadow?
registration.seed_connection: The seed demonstrates ATD coding transfer with all-linear LoRA and full-parameter student fine-tuning, and reports early teacher-aligned functional change, but does not test whether updating only the first transformer block yields executable transfer.
registration.hypothesis: A student trained with LoRA restricted to the first transformer block will achieve a positive exact-control-corrected HumanEval+ gain.
registration.contribution: Tests whether pairing-dependent coding transfer survives a strong, explicit restriction on where the student can adapt; a positive result would indicate nonzero transfer under that restriction, not that the first block recovers the full-depth effect.

closest_work.difference: Tests all-linear LoRA and full-parameter student adaptation, but not a one-block restriction.
The draft identifies early-layer transfer of a behavioral trait; this experiment tests restricted adaptation for an executable coding capability using ATD labels.

inputs: Seed ATD repository at https://github.com/myboker/ATD: data/signal.jsonl, data/exact.jsonl, data/alphabet.json, atd/train.py, atd/evaluate.py, and exact.json.
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at the revision pinned in exact.json.
EvalPlus 0.3.1 and its HumanEval+ evaluation data.
registration.method: Train one signal student on data/signal.jsonl and one exact-control student on data/exact.jsonl, both initialized from the pinned Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct base. Use rank-16 LoRA only on q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj modules in transformer block 0. Freeze all other parameters, including embeddings, normalization layers outside the block, every later block, and lm_head. Use the released single-token cross-entropy objective, one fixed training seed, and the released 157-step schedule and optimizer settings. Generate one greedy solution per HumanEval+ task for both students and score with the same EvalPlus execution tests.

event.description: The pilot supports a first-block coding shadow if the lower endpoint of the paired task-bootstrap interval for signal minus exact control is above zero.
event.statistic: Lower endpoint, in percentage points, of the 95% paired bootstrap interval over HumanEval+ task IDs for first-block signal pass@1 minus first-block exact-control pass@1.

evaluation.procedure: Write per-task base-test and extra-test pass statuses for both students. Compute their paired pass@1 difference and a 10,000-resample bootstrap interval over task IDs. The one-seed interval does not estimate training-seed variation; a non-event is not evidence of equivalence.
evaluation.controls: The exact nuisance-matched control uses the same carrier prompts, selected-word multiset, public-margin-bin disagreement counts, and training schedule as the signal. The only training-label difference is the disrupted prompt-token correspondence; both adapters use the same first-block-only LoRA restriction.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, compare early, middle, and late blocks and combinations of blocks against an all-layer baseline, using multiple student seeds and additional task-specific teachers.

agent.reason: The seed reports early teacher-aligned change, but that does not establish that one block has enough capacity to recover executable coding behavior. Any restricted-layer gain may be smaller than the registered task-bootstrap threshold can resolve.

judge_astra.reason: Updating the first block can influence downstream computation, but the seed's early-in-training alignment is not evidence for early-layer sufficiency. The adaptation restriction likely attenuates the pairing-dependent coding gain, making a clearly positive interval on 164 tasks unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: Restricting a rank-16 LoRA to block 0 leaves little capacity to reproduce a coding improvement that the teacher's DPO update spread across all layers, so the expected signal-minus-control gain is near zero; even the seed's full-depth ~5 pp effect would only clear a single-seed task-bootstrap lower bound about a third of the time.

judge_opus.reason: Even all-linear LoRA likely gives only about 50% odds of a single-seed lower bound above zero, and the seed paper shows transfer shrinks as student capacity drops. Restricting adaptation to block 0 probably shrinks the effect further, so both arms likely stay near base with few discordant tasks. Prior work on early layers in subliminal learning (2509.23886) leaves some chance of a positive result.

judge_sol.reason: First-block changes can propagate through the frozen network, so some transfer is plausible, but the seed's all-layer results do not establish first-block sufficiency. The restriction likely reduces the gain, making a positive lower confidence bound on 164 tasks relatively unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: The seed reports early teacher-aligned change, but that does not establish that one transformer block can recover executable coding behavior; the update may require distributed adaptation. A positive result would be informative, while a non-event in this one-seed, restricted setup would not establish absence of first-block signal.

judge_muse.reason: Seed transfer uses all-linear LoRA or full SFT with CIs several pp wide; restricting to block-0 only (~1/28 capacity) may fit carriers partially but a significant single-seed HumanEval+ gain is unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Schrodi et al. found that fine-tuning a single early layer is enough for subliminal transfer of a behavioural trait (owl preference learned from number sequences). They did not study capability transfer, ATD's near-tie single-word labels, an exact nuisance-matched control, or an executable HumanEval+ endpoint.

The seed paper reports ATD coding transfer under rank-16/32/64 all-linear LoRA and full-parameter student fine-tuning. It does not restrict adaptation to particular layers or blocks. Its 'early' result refers to early training steps, not early layers.
Nief et al. examine how trait-based subliminal learning depends on LoRA rank and full fine-tuning. They neither restrict adaptation to particular layers nor test transfer of a coding capability.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper in full, and it never restricts the student to a subset of layers. Its robustness checks vary only LoRA rank against full fine-tuning, and 'early' there means early in training. The closest result is Schrodi et al. (2509.23886), where one early layer was enough for a preference trait to transfer. That evidence concerns a trait, not whether a single block can carry an execution-scored coding gain from ATD labels against the exact control, and I found no work that tests this.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Section 5.2 demonstrates subliminal animal-preference transfer with LoRA restricted to layer 0 or another early layer. It does not test transfer of a post-trained coding capability through single-word ATD labels or evaluate executable gains against an exact nuisance-matched control.

Demonstrates ATD coding transfer on HumanEval+ using all-linear LoRA and full-parameter adaptation, but does not restrict student adaptation to the first transformer block. Its early functional-change result concerns training time, not layer localization.

sol.reason: First-layer-only subliminal trait transfer is already established, so the adaptation restriction itself is not new. However, trait transfer from prompted teachers does not settle whether that restriction preserves executable coding transfer from a post-trained teacher through ATD's single-word channel. Among the work found by 2026-10-06, none answers this restricted capability-transfer question.
No list entry restricts student adaptation to the first transformer block and tests whether that restriction permits coding transfer.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered one-seed first-block-only ATD pilot using unchanged, checksum/audit-verified released signal and exact data, pinned Qwen revision, rank-16 LoRA on the seven specified block-0 projections, and the released optimizer/157-step schedule. All other parameters are frozen; parameter audits assert the 14 expected LoRA tensors. Seed is 20260823, chosen as the first released seed before results. Uses the released greedy HumanEval+ generation and EvalPlus 0.3.1 procedure, writes base/extra statuses for all 164 paired task IDs, and computes the registered 10,000-draw paired task bootstrap. Execution optimizations disable activation checkpointing and compute the full-vocabulary LM head only at supervised positions; loss checks matched the released CE. Small environment accommodation: EvalPlus attempted an impermissible increase of the container's hard stack limit; a shim preserves that existing cap while retaining AS/DATA memory limits, tests, and timeouts. The invalid initial evaluation was discarded, and the complete command was retested successfully. Valid test: signal 78/164, exact 81/164, delta -1.8293 pp, 95% CI [-6.0976, 1.8293] pp. Event did not occur; no equivalence/absence claim. Runtime approximately 8.3 minutes after installation. Fresh command always retrains and reevaluates, not reusing stored results.

departures: run_first_block.py replaces the released trainer._batch_loss with supervised_position_loss, which computes lm_head only at supervised positions and still applies full-vocabulary CE. A one-time check on two rows logged identical values (0.7746954560279846 released vs optimized in *_trainable_parameters.json). The registration fixes the objective but not how it is computed, so this is unlikely to change the result. The check runs only once per arm, before any update, at zero-initialized adapters.
Activation checkpointing is disabled (run_first_block.py). This affects memory only and is not expected to change the result.

The block-0 restriction is applied by monkeypatching peft.LoraConfig to add layers_to_transform=[0]. This is the registered intervention, not a departure. The parameter audit (14 LoRA tensors, all in layers.0) and both adapter_config.json files confirm it took effect.

eval_compat/sitecustomize.py keeps the container's 10 MiB hard RLIMIT_STACK instead of the larger stack limit EvalPlus requests. Address-space and data caps, tests and timeouts are unchanged. Very deep recursion could fail under the smaller cap, so individual statuses could in principle change. The cap applies identically to both arms and is larger than the typical 8 MiB default, so it is unlikely to change the paired contrast. Without it EvalPlus would not run at all in this container.
The training seed is 20260823, the first released seed. The registration requires one fixed seed without naming it, so this is an open choice with no effect on fidelity.

Pass@1 requires both base and plus status to equal 'pass', and timeouts count as failures (run_first_block.py). This matches the standard HumanEval+ definition and the registration, so it is not a substantive departure.

An earlier engineer run that failed on the stack-limit error was discarded and rerun. The protected evaluation retrains and re-evaluates from scratch and reproduces the engineer's numbers exactly (78/164 vs 81/164), so the discard has no effect on the reported value.
problems: One training seed only. The paired task bootstrap omits training-seed variance, so the interval [-6.10, 1.83] pp overstates precision with respect to the training process. The engineer discloses this.

There is no all-layer positive control or base-model reference in the same run and environment, under the stack-limit shim. The pipeline's ability to detect the seed paper's effect therefore cannot be verified here, which limits how informative the null is.

The loss-equivalence check in run_first_block.py covers only 2 rows at initialization, under no_grad. It does not verify that gradients match the released implementation's later in training, although the forward computation is mathematically the same.

Some sanitized solutions fail from missing typing imports, for example HumanEval/0 in eval/*/humaneval.sanitized.jsonl uses List without importing it. This comes from the released sanitizer and generation procedure and affects both arms alike.

Secondary observation, not a defect: signal training loss fell from 0.78 to about 0.47, versus about 0.68 for the exact control (metrics.jsonl). Block 0 can fit the prompt-token correspondence, yet no executable gain was observed. This is suggestive but untested.

registration.title: Does the learned carrier-choice signal generalize to unseen contexts under a reworded instruction?
registration.seed_connection: The seed uses one fixed choice instruction and reports a held-out representational diagnostic, but does not test direct prediction of teacher choices on unseen carrier contexts under a changed instruction.
registration.hypothesis: On carrier contexts withheld from student training, the signal student's margin toward the original teacher label will exceed the exact-control student's margin when the choice instruction is reworded.
registration.contribution: Tests generalization of the learned behavioral decision field across both carrier-context holdout and one fixed instruction rewrite; it measures a student-side margin and does not claim that the teacher would make the same choice under the rewrite.

closest_work.difference: Reports downstream transfer and disjoint representational diagnostics, but not teacher-label prediction on held-out carrier contexts under a rewritten choice instruction.
Studies subliminal transfer through faithful paraphrases of teacher outputs; this experiment rewrites the student's carrier instruction and tests held-out ATD choice margins.

inputs: Seed ATD repository at https://github.com/myboker/ATD: data/signal.jsonl, data/carriers.jsonl, data/alphabet.json, atd/controls.py, and atd/train.py.
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at the revision pinned in exact.json.
registration.method: Group rows by the normalized carrier-context prefix before the fixed choice suffix beginning `Choose exactly one of these two words`. Assign whole context groups to an 80% training split or 20% held-out split using a fixed SHA-256 hash; no context group may occur in both splits. Construct an exact nuisance-matched control using training rows only, matching its completion multiset, public-margin-bin disagreement counts, and 50% teacher-agreement constraint. If the control is infeasible or fewer than 20 held-out context groups remain, mark the pilot invalid. Train signal and control students only on the original training prompts, using rank-16 all-linear LoRA, learning rate 5e-5, effective batch size 128, and 157 optimizer steps with one fixed seed. On held-out contexts, score both offered single-token candidates from next-token logits in the original format and after replacing only the suffix with `Select one of the two offered words and output only that word, with no explanation. Choices: A or B. Your choice:`; substitute the actual candidates in the same order. For each prompt, orient the candidate-logit margin toward the teacher token recorded for the original prompt. Do not query a teacher on the rewritten prompts.

event.description: The pilot supports persistence under the rewrite if the lower endpoint of the source-group bootstrap interval for the paraphrased signal-minus-control margin is above zero, provided the original-format held-out margin check also has a lower endpoint above zero.
event.statistic: Lower endpoint, in logit units, of the 95% context-group bootstrap interval for the mean paraphrased teacher-label-oriented candidate-margin difference between signal and exact control.

evaluation.procedure: Write one record per held-out carrier row with its context-group key, original teacher label, and signal/control teacher-oriented margins in the original and rewritten formats. Compute group-averaged margins and 10,000 bootstrap resamples of context groups for both formats; the original-format interval is the manipulation check and the paraphrased interval is the registered statistic. This is a held-out behavioral-margin test, not a coding benchmark or a teacher-agreement test under paraphrase.
evaluation.controls: Signal and exact control use the same training context groups, carrier prompts, candidate pairs, base initialization, and schedule. The control disrupts training prompt-token pairings while matching the completion multiset and public-margin-bin disagreement counts. Held-out labels are not used for training or control construction.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, query accessible teachers on several pre-registered paraphrases, train with paraphrases separated between acquisition and evaluation, and test whether held-out margin generalization predicts transfer on a capability benchmark across seeds.

agent.reason: The seed's disjoint representational diagnostic makes generalization beyond training carriers plausible, but this experiment additionally changes the instruction format. Both the original held-out check and the paraphrased margin interval must be positive.

judge_astra.reason: The seed's held-out functional alignment makes carrier-margin generalization plausible, and continuous paired margins should be more sensitive than executable coding scores. Template dependence remains a substantial uncertainty, especially because both the original-format and rewritten-format checks must pass.

judge_fable.reason: The seed's held-out functional-contrast cosine (~0.4 vs the exact control) implies the learned direction generalizes to unseen prompts, and ~1,100 held-out rows give high power for a margin test, so the original-format check is likely positive; the paraphrased-format requirement, the conjunction of two intervals, and repository/implementation risk pull the joint probability down.

judge_opus.reason: The exact control matches per-word win counts, so Bradley-Terry word strengths cancel between arms. Even so, the seed's held-out diagnostics show the signal-minus-exact difference aligned with the teacher direction (cosine 0.395), and roughly a thousand held-out rows give high power for the original-format check. Most risk lies in attenuation under the instruction rewrite and in implementation details.

judge_sol.reason: The seed's disjoint functional diagnostics favor some held-out generalization, and continuous margins offer greater sensitivity than coding pass/fail outcomes. I discount for instruction sensitivity, the original-format prerequisite, and possible exact-control infeasibility after context-group splitting.

judge_luna.reason: The seed’s held-out representational analyses provide some support for a learned direction that generalizes beyond training carriers. However, they do not establish choice-margin generalization under a rewritten instruction, and the registered labels are not teacher choices under that rewrite.

judge_muse.reason: Seed held-out diagnostic shows representational generalization to disjoint prompts, and the held-out margin test uses many context groups giving higher power than coding endpoints, but the event requires both original and paraphrased margins to be significantly positive.

It reports downstream benchmark transfer and a representational fingerprint on 512 held-out prompts that are disjoint from the carriers. It never measures student margins toward teacher labels on held-out carrier contexts, and it never rewords the choice suffix.

Reports that small changes such as prompt paraphrasings usually suppress subliminal transfer of hidden biases (trait or preference transfer, 'likes owls'). It does not test single-token near-tie decisions from ATD, held-out carrier-context splits, or exact nuisance-matched controls. So it motivates the question but does not settle it for this setting.

Shows that subliminal trait transfer depends on the context shared between finetuning and evaluation, such as the system prompt and template tokens. It is a different setting and metric. It does not test held-out carrier decision margins under an instruction rewrite.
Paraphrases the teacher's outputs, which are the training data carrying preference transfer. It does not reword the student's evaluation instruction or test held-out ATD choice margins.

It never tests whether the student's learned carrier-choice preference predicts teacher labels on withheld carrier contexts, under either the original or a reworded instruction. Its only held-out diagnostic is a representational fingerprint on disjoint prompts. Related subliminal-learning papers (2509.23886, 2606.00831) find that trait transfer is sensitive to prompt paraphrase and context, but they study a different phenomenon, design and metric, so none answers this question for ATD single-word decisions against an exact nuisance-matched control.

Paraphrases training prompts while retaining teacher completions and measures downstream trait transmission; it does not rewrite instructions only at evaluation to test held-out carrier-choice generalization.
Changes shared system context between training and evaluation and measures downstream animal preferences, rather than persistence of original teacher choices on unseen carrier contexts.
Studies trait transmission through teacher-generated faithful paraphrases, not student-side carrier margins under an evaluation-time instruction rewrite.

sol.reason: The seed establishes held-out functional alignment, and related work examines context sensitivity, but neither directly answers this carrier-level generalization question. I found no work reporting the combined context-group holdout and evaluation-only instruction rewrite with margins oriented toward the original teacher labels, so the contribution is distinct rather than merely a different model or metric.

Entry 45 changes carrier context templates and measures teacher-choice agreement and coding performance, whereas this experiment rewrites the instruction and measures held-out margins toward original-format teacher labels.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered context-prefix holdout, training-only exact nuisance-matched MILP control, paired rank-16 LoRA training for 157 steps, original/reworded next-token margins toward recorded original labels, and 10,000 equal-context-group bootstrap draws. No teacher calls or held-out training labels. Fixed unspecified details before running: NFKC plus whitespace-collapse normalization with case preserved; full SHA-256 threshold at 80%; first exact.json training seed; released control seed and 16 training-only rank bins. Computational optimization computes full-vocabulary response CE only at the last prompt hidden state and disables gradient checkpointing; objective, prompts, initialization and schedule are unchanged. Full evaluation command tested successfully (~7 minutes after initial package installation). Split: 4,519 training and 1,145 held-out context groups; all exact-control constraints passed. Observed original CI [2.2572,2.5822] and rewritten CI [0.1396,0.2773] logit units; registered lower endpoint 0.1396288209606987, with manipulation check passed. Both required raw outputs and result.json produced and checked. IMPLEMENTATION.md documents choices, optimization and interpretation limits.

departures: Grouping and bootstrap unit (carrier_generalization.py, summary.json): the event text says 'source-group bootstrap', while the statistic and method specify normalized-prefix context groups. The code uses prefix groups. Each group holds exactly one row (4,519 train and 1,145 held-out groups equal the row counts), so the bootstrap is effectively row-level and ignores dependence among rows from the same source_id. Source-clustered resampling could widen the interval somewhat. It is unlikely to move a lower endpoint of 0.14 (mean 0.207) below zero, but this was not checked.

Partial-answer prefixes from the same source fall on both sides of the split (split_manifest.jsonl). Examples: 18:7 is train and 18:10 is held-out; 19988:4 is train and 19988:3 is held-out. Each held-out context shares its question and leading answer words with training rows. This follows the registered prefix-based definition, and IMPLEMENTATION.md discloses it. It weakens the 'unseen contexts' interpretation but does not change the registered statistic.

Loss is computed from the last prompt hidden state through the unchanged LM head, and gradient checkpointing is disabled (IMPLEMENTATION.md, carrier_generalization.py). For a single-token completion under causal attention this is mathematically equivalent. It is reported and should not change the result.

Choices the registration left open (training seed = first exact.json seed, control seed, 16 rank bins, NFKC plus whitespace normalization, DataLoader shuffle order, bootstrap seed 20260818, bf16 scoring) were fixed and documented. These are permitted choices. bf16 logits quantize margins to multiples of 0.125, which coarsens values but does not bias them.
The 10,000 bootstrap resamples are drawn as 100 batches of 100 (carrier_generalization.py). This is equivalent to the registered count and does not change the result.

Fewer training rows (4,519) at a fixed 157 steps × 128 means about 4.4 passes over the data. This is implied by the registered holdout and fixed schedule. It is not a departure, but it differs from the seed's per-epoch exposure.
problems: The bootstrap ignores source-level clustering. Held-out rows sharing a source_id are resampled independently, so the reported CI may be slightly too narrow (summary.json, carrier_generalization.py summarize).
Sibling prefixes from the same source span the train and held-out splits (split_manifest.jsonl). 'Unseen carrier context' therefore means 'unseen exact prefix', not an unseen question or source.

No analysis separates context-specific choice generalization from simpler learned regularities, such as a position (left/right) bias or a candidate-pair preference. Under the rewrite these could align with teacher sides more for the signal student than for the control. The exact control matches the completion multiset and margin-bin flip counts, but the artifacts do not show it matches side distribution. heldout_margins.jsonl contains the per-candidate logits needed to check this, but no check was done.

The run uses a single training seed and one fixed rewrite. The bootstrap captures item variability only, not training-run variability. The rewritten effect (0.21 logits) is about a twelfth of the original-format effect (2.42), so its robustness across seeds and paraphrases is unknown.

This is a student-side margin only. Teacher labels from the original prompt are carried over to the rewritten prompt, so the result does not show the teacher would choose the same way. The registration acknowledges this.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design: a prefix-hash holdout, a training-only exact nuisance-matched control with passing audits, paired rank-16 LoRA training for 157 steps, original and rewritten next-token margins oriented to the recorded teacher labels, and a 10,000-draw group bootstrap with the conjunctive event. The protected run reproduced the engineer's losses and numbers, and the registered raw outputs are present. The only material ambiguity is 'source-group' versus 'context-group' wording. The code follows the method's prefix definition, which gives single-row groups and ignores source clustering, but this is unlikely to flip a lower endpoint of 0.14. The evidence is genuine and supports a small but clearly positive signal-minus-control margin under the rewrite (mean 0.21, CI [0.14, 0.28]), against a large original-format effect (2.42). Its interpretation is limited by a single seed, a single paraphrase, overlap of source context across the split, and untested simpler explanations such as position or candidate-pair bias. That makes it a meaningful but modest pilot finding.

departures: carrier_generalization.py::prepare replaces literal 50% teacher agreement with floor(n/2) agreements. With 4,519 training rows, it requires 2,259 agreements, or 49.9889356%; design.json and summary.json certify 'agreement_near_half', not exact 50%. The numerical imbalance is tiny, but exact 50% is impossible for this odd sample size. Under the registration's literal constraint, the control would be infeasible and the pilot should be invalid rather than produce a registered statistic. This changes whether a result is reportable.

carrier_generalization.py::train_and_score computes full-vocabulary response cross-entropy only from the final prompt hidden state, rather than materializing all prompt-position logits as the referenced seed trainer reportedly does. For the asserted single-token completions and causal attention, this preserves the mathematical objective. Floating-point execution could differ, but there is no evidence of a substantive effect on the reported contrast.

carrier_generalization.py::train_and_score disables gradient checkpointing, as documented in IMPLEMENTATION.md. This changes computational execution rather than the registered objective or training schedule; no substantive result change is apparent.

carrier_generalization.py::summarize bootstraps normalized-prefix context groups, not source_id groups. This follows the registered statistic and evaluation procedure, but differs from a literal source_id interpretation of 'source-group bootstrap' in the event description. Source-level resampling could change the interval because multiple prefixes can share a source. The registration itself is inconsistent on this wording.
problems: carrier_generalization.py and summary.json treat the rounded-half control as satisfying the registered feasibility requirement. Under literal exact 50% agreement, the odd training-row count requires invalidation; the reported control audit does not establish that requirement.

split_manifest.jsonl shows shared sources across training and holdout, including source 18 and source 19988, with nested partial-answer prefixes. This complies with the explicit prefix-based split and does not demonstrate target-label leakage, but it limits the finding to unseen complete prefixes rather than unseen source histories.
All 1,145 held-out context groups are singletons. The registered bootstrap therefore effectively resamples rows and does not address dependence between different prefixes from the same source.
The bootstrap intervals condition on one trained signal/control pair, one split, one control construction and one rewrite. They do not quantify training-seed or instruction-rewrite variability.

The measured outcome is a candidate-logit margin toward original labels. It does not establish improved choice accuracy, unchanged teacher decisions under rewriting, or downstream capability transfer.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation freshly trained both arms, produced the required outputs, and computed the reported value from model logits without visible hard-coded results or target-label leakage. The rewritten signal-minus-control margin was 0.2073 logit units with interval [0.1396, 0.2773], while the original-format manipulation check was also positive. Fidelity fails under the registration's literal 50% constraint because the implementation substitutes rounded-half agreement and reports a valid pilot instead of applying the specified infeasibility rule. Nevertheless, the actually executed nearly-half-control comparison provides a credible, narrowly scoped pilot finding; source overlap, conditional uncertainty and the much smaller rewritten effect prevent a stronger research-value rating.

departures: Context-prefix normalization was unspecified; carrier_generalization.py hashes NFKC plus whitespace-collapsed prefixes (case preserved) while scoring the raw prefix. Another normalization could reassign the 80/20 split and change the value; here it did not merge groups (design.json: groups equal rows).

The SHA-256 split encoding was unspecified; the code uses a full 256-bit cut int(hash)*5 < 4*2**256 (design.json). A different encoding could change membership; this one yields the registered 4519/1145 rate.

Schedule, LoRA alpha, optimizer, clipping, microbatch, and dropout were unspecified. The run uses seed _linear_warmup (5-step warmup, linear decay), alpha 16, AdamW with weight decay 0, clip 1.0, microbatch 32, drop_last, and dropout 0. These can change the students versus other settings still compatible with lr 5e-5 and 157 steps. Step 157 is applied at lr 0 (signal_training_metrics.jsonl), so that step does not update weights.

Training CE is taken from the last prompt hidden state with gradient checkpointing off (carrier_generalization.py). Under causal attention this matches response-only full-vocabulary loss and is unlikely to change the reported value; the SDPA sliding-window warning is immaterial for these short prompts.
Bootstrap seed 20260818 and NumPy linear percentiles were unspecified (summarize). They can nudge the exact endpoint, but not plausibly the sign, given rewritten CI [0.1396, 0.2773].

The event description says a source-group bootstrap, while the statistic and evaluation procedure say context-group. The code resamples context groups, matching the registered statistic. A source-clustered interval could differ and was not reported.
problems: Prefix groups are singletons (design.json: 4519 and 1145 groups equal rows), and the same source appears in both splits at different answer lengths (split_manifest.jsonl, e.g. source 18 position 7 train vs position 10 held out; source 19988). Training can contain a proper prefix of a held-out carrier, so the row bootstrap does not support a source-level unseen-context claim and may be anti-conservative.
The 157th optimizer step uses learning rate 0 (signal_training_metrics.jsonl and control_training_metrics.jsonl), so one registered step is a no-op.

Only one training seed was run, as registered, so the interval does not include seed or initialization variability; the rewritten contrast is also much smaller than the original-format effect (summary.json: 0.207 vs 2.423).
grok.reason: The fresh run executed the registered hash split, training-only exact control, paired rank-16 LoRA training, and held-out teacher-oriented margins, and result.json is the context-group bootstrap lower endpoint defined as the statistic. The rewritten signal-minus-control interval lies above zero after a strong original-format check, but the effect is modest, single-seed, and not a source-disjoint generalization test.
