registration.title: Cue-matched final-answer recovery in an NSD checkpoint
registration.seed_connection: The seed's reflection claim relies mainly on reflection-expression frequency and a case study. Its advertised checkpoint release permits a functional test using exactly checkable injected arithmetic errors, matched correct prefixes, and the same reflection cue for both models.
registration.hypothesis: With an identical initial reflection cue, the released Qwen3-4B NSD checkpoint exceeds its base model by more than three percentage points in balanced final-answer accuracy following matched correct and incorrect arithmetic prefixes.
registration.contribution: A behavioral test that does not equate reflective vocabulary with successful correction. Neutral-cue and no-prefix controls help distinguish cue responsiveness and ordinary solving improvements from recovery-specific effects. Final-answer success is not treated as proof that the injected line was explicitly repaired or retained.

closest_work.difference: Self-Correction Bench studies injected errors and reflection cues. This experiment compares a checkpoint trained by NSD with its base under identical cues and includes matched correct-prefix and clean-solving controls.
First Try Matters distinguishes confirmation from repair in natural reflections. This experiment uses controlled, verifiable intermediate arithmetic errors and exact final-answer scoring.

The self-distillation degradation study connects epistemic-expression suppression with performance. This experiment tests functional behavior under a common continuation budget rather than expression counts.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-4B from Hugging Face.

The advertised NSD collection at https://huggingface.co/collections/PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation; the exact default Qwen3-4B online solution-aware supervised artifact must be resolved and pinned before evaluation.
openai/gsm8k from Hugging Face, configuration main, official test split.
Existing CUDA PyTorch plus Transformers 4.57.6, huggingface_hub, datasets, NumPy, and PEFT only if the NSD artifact is an adapter.
registration.method:
Before model inference, resolve the artifact using public Hugging Face collection and model-asset metadata, not web search or performance evaluation. If the supplied collection slug is incomplete, list collections owned by PassionPrc and match the advertised NSD collection title. Select its explicitly designated main Qwen3-4B online, solution-aware, supervised checkpoint, or its sole unqualified main Qwen3-4B NSD release if no competing main release exists and metadata does not identify it as another regime. Do not substitute PG, wiki-conditioned, or a different Qwen base. If identity, derivation, compatibility, or downloadability is ambiguous, write artifact_unavailable and no research statistic. Freeze exact repository IDs and revisions in the implementation for the fresh-machine rerun. Check that base and NSD use compatible vocabulary and chat-control token IDs.

Load base and NSD sequentially on the GPU in BF16 with SDPA, the same tokenizer, and enable_thinking=False. If the release is an adapter, apply it to its verified Qwen3-4B base revision. Use existing PyTorch rather than reinstalling it, and do not install distributed inference stacks.

Select 96 distinct GSM8K test problems using seed 42. Require an integer final answer, at least two calculator annotations, and a first annotation that can be exactly verified using a restricted rational-arithmetic AST evaluator supporting constants, unary signs, +, -, *, /, and parentheses. Its result v must be an integer from 2 through 9999, with v-1 and v+1 having the same decimal width. Require the rendered question and longest prefill to fit within 512 tokens. Use all eligible problems if fewer than 96 exist; fewer than 64 is insufficient. Do not inspect model outputs during selection.

Create a correct assistant prefill 'First, {expression} = {v}.' followed by a newline. Create its incorrect counterpart by changing only v by +1 or -1, alternating sign by selected item index. Include no remaining reference solution. Put the original question in the user turn with a common request to solve briefly and end with 'FINAL: <number>'. Inject prefills into the open assistant turn after the normal non-thinking chat prefix, not as user-authored feedback.

Run five conditions for each model: correct prefix plus 'Wait, let me check that calculation.'; incorrect prefix plus the same reflection cue; correct prefix plus 'Now I will continue the solution.'; incorrect prefix plus that neutral cue; and a no-prefix, no-added-cue clean-solving condition. End each cue with a newline. Use greedy generation, length-bucketed batches, KV caching, and at most 256 new tokens. There are at most 960 continuations. Apply no conditional forced-readout intervention. Save token boundaries so the same trajectories can also be scored at a 128-new-token budget.

Parse the final numeric answer from the last FINAL marker, with a predefined last-boxed-number fallback only when no FINAL marker exists. Support signed integers, decimals, valid thousands separators, and simple rational forms; compare exactly with the dataset integer. An unparseable final marker or missing answer counts as incorrect. A truncated response with a valid final answer remains scoreable. Count Appendix E reflection expressions only in newly generated text, excluding the injected prefix and cue.

event.description: NSD has a balanced final-answer advantage over the base after matching the initial reflection cue.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 5000 paired problem-bootstrap estimates of B_NSD-B_base, where B_model is one half the sum of its incorrect-prefix and correct-prefix accuracies in the reflection-cue condition at the 256-token budget.

evaluation.procedure: Bootstrap whole questions with seed 31415, preserving both prefix variants, both models, and all cue conditions. Report the registered bound and separate incorrect-prefix and correct-prefix accuracies. Also report clean-solving accuracy, neutral-cue results, the model-by-prefix-correctness interaction (R_NSD-C_NSD)-(R_base-C_base), and results at both 128 and 256 new tokens. Report answer-parsing failures, truncation, generation length, and reflection counts. A primary advantage accompanied only by a similar clean-solving advantage must not be characterized as evidence of a recovery-specific mechanism. Correct-prefix final-answer accuracy does not establish preservation of the exact intermediate work. outputs/items.jsonl contains source IDs, arithmetic verification, prefixes, and gold answers. outputs/generations.jsonl contains exact prompts, continuations and token IDs, parsed answers, condition identifiers, correctness, and termination flags. outputs/paired_scores.jsonl contains per-question scores and diagnostics. outputs/summary.json contains statistics or an explicit unavailable/insufficient status. outputs/manifest.json contains artifact-resolution evidence, pinned revisions, tokenizer checks, seeds, versions, and timings. A non-significant result does not establish equivalent correction ability.
evaluation.controls: Models receive identical questions, prefills, cues, answer instructions, and generation budgets. Correct-prefix trials reveal success or damage when the supplied calculation is valid. The full model-by-cue comparison controls initial reflection activation. No-prefix trials measure ordinary solving ability. Two budget readouts expose verbosity sensitivity without introducing model-dependent forced answers. Evaluation uses existing gold answers and deterministic arithmetic, with no model judge or new annotation.

models: Metadata-resolved and pinned default Qwen3-4B online solution-aware supervised NSD checkpoint from the PassionPrc collection

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, evaluate independently trained NSD checkpoints on natural model errors, conceptual errors, harder tasks, and several compute budgets. Add explicit step-repair measurements and clean-solving controls to separate general competence, activation of existing correction abilities, and genuinely learned recovery behavior.

agent.reason: A common reflection cue may already activate much of the base model's ability to recover from these simple errors, leaving limited incremental benefit. The small paired sample, fixed generation budget, and unresolved checkpoint availability make the registered lower-bound event demanding.

judge_astra.reason: Reported reasoning gains and increased reflection expressions provide some support, but neither establishes better recovery once both models receive the same cue. The small question set, short generation cap, and exact-checkpoint requirement make the registered lower bound substantially harder to achieve than a positive mean difference.

judge_fable.reason: The checkpoint must be unambiguously resolved from the HF collection (substantial risk of artifact_unavailable), and even then GSM8K with an identical reflection cue leaves limited headroom; a ~8-10pp balanced advantage needed for the paired 5th percentile to exceed 3pp with 96 problems is much larger than NSD's reported MATH-500 gains suggest.

judge_opus.reason: Qwen3-4B is near ceiling on GSM8K, and an explicit 'Wait, let me check' cue makes off-by-one arithmetic errors easy for both models to catch. With 96 paired problems, the 5th-percentile criterion needs roughly a 7pp mean advantage. NSD's longer, more reflective outputs risk truncation at 256 tokens, and artifact resolution may also fail.

judge_sol.reason: The reported mathematical gains make an advantage plausible, but reflection-expression counts do not establish successful recovery, and identical cues may narrow the gap. Checkpoint resolution, the small paired sample, and the short continuation budget make the registered lower-bound advantage demanding.

judge_luna.reason: The paper reports stronger math performance and more reflection, making improved responses to a shared checking cue plausible. However, the GSM8K sample is small, both models receive the cue, the balanced-accuracy bound is demanding, and the exact checkpoint must be resolvable.

judge_muse.reason: 4B MATH-500 gains are small (+1.9pp) suggesting limited easy-task headroom, reflection frequency need not imply functional recovery, and the lower-bound >3pp event also requires successful checkpoint resolution.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper backs its reflection claim only with counts of reflection tokens per response on AIME/HMMT (Table 2) and a case study (Appendix D.4). It does not test whether the NSD checkpoint recovers from controlled injected errors, and it reports no matched correct-prefix, neutral-cue or cue-matched comparison against the base model.

Self-Correction Bench injects errors and adds 'Wait'-style cues to study blind spots in self-correction across off-the-shelf models. It does not compare an NSD-trained checkpoint with its Qwen3-4B base, and it has no matched correct-prefix or clean-solving controls.

This work separates confirmatory from corrective reflections in naturally generated reasoning traces. It does not use controlled, verifiable arithmetic errors, and it does not evaluate any self-distillation checkpoint.

This work links the suppression of uncertainty expression under self-distillation to performance drops. Its evidence comes from expression frequency and benchmark accuracy, not from a functional test of recovery after injected errors.

Reflective Recovery trains models on prefixes of failed trajectories and analyzes the self-correction that emerges. It does not test NSD, and it does not compare recovery from matched correct and incorrect prefixes under the same cue.

opus.reason: My searches found no work that runs this test: the NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint against its base, with cue-matched correct and incorrect arithmetic prefixes, neutral-cue and clean-solving controls, and exact final-answer scoring. The seed paper's evidence for reflection is limited to reflection-token counts and a case study. Other papers use injected errors or study suppressed uncertainty expression, but none applies these methods to NSD, so the question of whether NSD improves functional error recovery is still open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Self-Correction Bench already evaluates final-answer recovery from assistant-injected errors and activation by a 'Wait' cue, including fine-tuned models. It does not test NSD against its base with matched reflection cues, paired correct/error prefixes, and clean-solving controls.
The seed compares NSD with its base on ordinary reasoning benchmarks and supports its reflection claim through expression frequency and a case study, not controlled error-prefix recovery.
Tests doubt-cue interventions on truncated, naturally failed trajectories. It does not evaluate NSD or use exactly verified arithmetic perturbations paired with correct prefixes.

Compares trained Qwen3-4B models on flawed assistant prefills and clean solving, but studies explicit flawed-prefix RL training rather than NSD and lacks the matched correct-prefix and reflection-versus-neutral cue design.

sol.reason: Error injection, reflection-cue activation, and final-answer recovery are established methods, so the experiment's novelty is not the evaluation technique alone. However, no work found by 2026-10-06 answers whether NSD's negative-distribution training yields a functional advantage after initial reflection activation is matched, with controls separating that advantage from ordinary solving improvements.

opus.reason: Both compare an NSD-trained model with its base on paired correct and arithmetic-error drafts, scoring final-answer recovery and damage to test functional self-correction rather than reflection vocabulary. They differ in model, since this experiment uses the released 4B checkpoint while entry 37 trains a 1.7B pilot.

sol.reason: Both compare an NSD model with its base on paired correct and arithmetically corrupted drafts, measuring final-answer recovery and damage rather than treating reflection vocabulary as evidence of correction.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: `nsd_recovery_eval.py`, launched by `run_eval.sh`. It installs transformers 4.57.6, huggingface_hub, datasets, numpy and accelerate. It uses the PyTorch already on the machine (2.6.0+cu124), not the 2.8.0 the seed code pins.

**Picking the checkpoint (metadata only).** The registered collection slug is missing its hash suffix, so I listed PassionPrc's collections and found "NSD: Negative Self-Distillation" (`PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation-6a77490ea5ac3e76b2c2310e`). Requesting it with the token returned 403; an anonymous request succeeded. It lists exactly three models: NSD-Qwen3-1.7B, NSD-Qwen3-4B and NSD-Qwen3-8B. PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B has no model card and nothing in its metadata names a training regime. It is full weights, not an adapter. I chose it under the registration's rule for a "sole unqualified main Qwen3-4B NSD release". Caveat: metadata does not say it is the online, solution-aware, supervised checkpoint; that identity is inferred.

**Pinned revisions:**
- base: Qwen/Qwen3-4B @ 1cfa9a7208912126459214e8b04321603b3df60c
- NSD: PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B @ 59aa00319e92d277a7a7a341cf35dfc678e949c8

At run time the script re-runs the metadata checks and the tokenizer/config checks: identical vocabulary, same chat-control token IDs, same vocab size and architecture. If any check fails it writes `artifact_unavailable` and no statistic.

**How it runs.** It follows the registration as written: 96 GSM8K test items chosen with seed 42 (1,077 met the arithmetic criteria). Each first calculator annotation is checked with a Fraction-based AST evaluator. Wrong prefixes are off by ±1, alternating in sign. Prefills go into the open assistant turn after the non-thinking chat prefix. There are five conditions per model, decoded greedily (SDPA, BF16, batches sorted by length, KV cache, up to 256 new tokens). Answers are scored again at 128 tokens from the saved token IDs. The bootstrap is 5,000 paired resamples of whole questions with seed 31415.

**Choices I made where the registration was open:**
- The user-turn instruction reads "Solve the problem briefly. End your response with 'FINAL: <number>'."
- I read the interaction term (R−C) as R = wrong-prefix accuracy and C = correct-prefix accuracy, both under the reflection cue. I also report the same term under the neutral cue, and a model-by-cue contrast on balanced accuracy.
- Reflection phrases from Appendix E are counted case-insensitively, with letter boundaries, in newly generated text only.

**Test run on this machine (one repetition, about 3 minutes plus downloads).**
- Registered statistic (5th percentile of the bootstrap B_NSD − B_base, reflection cue, 256 tokens): −0.0156. Point estimate +1.0 pp, 95% CI [−2.1, +4.2] pp.
- The event (value > 0.03) did not occur.
- At 256 tokens, reflection cue: base 93.8% (correct prefix) / 94.8% (wrong prefix); NSD 95.8% / 94.8%.
- Clean solving with no prefix: 90.6% base vs 91.7% NSD, so the clean gap (+1.0 pp) matches the primary one.
- Interaction term: −2.1 pp.
- Neutral cue: both models fall to roughly 32–33% after a wrong prefix, against 90.6% after a correct one.
- At 128 tokens many responses are cut off (about 30% under the reflection cue), and parse failures track the truncation.

**How to read this.** Both models are near the ceiling under the reflection cue, which leaves little room for a 3-point lower bound. This is one checkpoint on easy arithmetic errors. A null result here does not show that the two models correct errors equally well, and getting the final answer right does not show the injected line was explicitly repaired.

departures: run_eval.sh installs accelerate in addition to the registered packages (transformers 4.57.6, huggingface_hub, datasets, numpy). It does not reinstall torch: manifest.json records the existing 2.6.0+cu124. This cannot plausibly change the result.

Checkpoint identity (nsd_recovery_eval.py, manifest.json): PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B was chosen under the registered fallback for a 'sole unqualified main Qwen3-4B NSD release'. The collection lists exactly one 4B model, with no card and no regime metadata, so its online, solution-aware, supervised identity is inferred rather than confirmed. The registration permits this rule. It changes the interpretation, not the computed value.

Tokenizer use (nsd_recovery_eval.py): the base tokenizer and chat template are used for both models. This matches the registered 'same tokenizer', so it is not a departure in substance. Any differing chat_template.jinja in the NSD repo is ignored. Vocabulary and control-token IDs were checked and match.
User-turn instruction wording ('Solve the problem briefly. End your response with 'FINAL: <number>'.') was left open by the registration. It is applied identically to both models. Not a departure.

Interaction term (summary.json) is read as R = incorrect-prefix accuracy and C = correct-prefix accuracy under the reflection cue. This is a reasonable reading of an underspecified definition. Extra neutral-cue and model-by-cue contrasts are added. Secondary only; the registered value is unaffected.
Reflection-phrase list REFL in nsd_recovery_eval.py is the engineer's rendering of 'Appendix E'. Its fidelity to the seed appendix cannot be verified here. It affects a diagnostic only.

Generation uses batches of 160 with left padding, sorted by length, and greedy decoding. This is consistent with the registered length-bucketed batching. Padding could cause tiny numerical differences in greedy outputs, applied symmetrically to both models. Unlikely to change the result materially.

Answer parser (parse_answer/parse_num) uses predefined heuristics: it takes the first number in the 80 characters after the last FINAL marker, uses a boxed fallback, and cuts at the first blank line. Edge cases could misparse a few responses. The parser is applied identically to both models, as registered.
problems: Ceiling effect (summary.json, engineer notes): under the reflection cue both models reach about 94–96% on correct and incorrect prefixes, and clean solving is about 91% for both. This leaves little room to detect a lower bound above 3 pp.
The 95% CI for B_NSD − B_base is [−2.1, +4.2] pp and includes a 3 pp advantage. The null therefore does not exclude a modest NSD benefit, and it does not establish equivalent correction ability.
The NSD checkpoint's training regime is inferred from the sole 4B entry in the collection, not confirmed by metadata (manifest.json decision field).

At the 128-token budget, roughly 30% of reflection-cue and 37% of clean responses are truncated, with parse failures tracking truncation (summary.json). The 128-token readout therefore mainly measures verbosity.
The injected errors are trivial ±1 arithmetic slips on the first step. Generalisation to substantive errors is untested, as the registration itself acknowledges.

The 256-token per-condition table is partly cut from the displayed summary.json, so some per-condition figures in the engineer notes cannot be fully cross-checked here. The displayed differences are consistent with them.
opus.reason: The code follows the registration closely. The checkpoint was resolved through the registered metadata fallback and pinned, the 96 GSM8K items were selected with exact arithmetic verification, ±1 prefills were injected into the non-thinking assistant turn, all five conditions were run per model with greedy decoding to 256 tokens, and the paired whole-question bootstrap uses the registered seed. No departure plausibly changes the registered value. The value of −0.0156 comes from real generations that are saved with token IDs and per-item scores, and the paired bootstrap and balanced-accuracy computation are correct. The evidence is weak, though. Both models sit near ceiling under the reflection cue, so the 3 pp threshold had little power to be exceeded. The CI (−2.1 to +4.2 pp) cannot rule out a small NSD advantage, and the clean-solving gap matches the primary gap. The neutral-cue control adds one informative observation: both models propagate the injected error at similar rates. Even so, the result is a credible but imprecise null on easy, single-step errors, using a checkpoint whose identity is inferred.

departures: run_eval.sh installs accelerate in addition to the registered dependencies. It does not use distributed inference, and the manifest confirms that existing PyTorch was retained. This extra installation has no apparent effect on the reported value.

nsd_recovery_eval.py implements a weaker fail-closed policy than described: tokenizer_checks.compatible does not include the computed vocabulary-equality or architecture-equality checks, and tokenizer/model download failures are not caught and converted to artifact_unavailable. These differences could matter in another execution, but vocabulary and architecture matched and downloads succeeded in this evaluation.

nsd_recovery_eval.py adds answer-extraction rules not specified in the registration: an 80-character window after the last FINAL marker, stopping at a blank line, and permissive numeric searching. The parser can accept an integer prefix of malformed thousands separators or find a number after non-answer text. These rules could change affected scores; the supplied excerpts do not demonstrate an effect on the registered 256-token statistic.

nsd_recovery_eval.py loads GSM8K without a revision and records a repository SHA afterward rather than pinning the loaded dataset. The registered model revisions were frozen correctly. registration.title: Does the NSD negative-teacher gate localize human-labeled reasoning errors? A ProcessBench step-level test with position-matched controls
registration.seed_connection: NSD's central mechanistic claim is that the gate G_t = max(0, p_neg - p_ref) 'identifies and isolates reasoning-critical tokens' / 'genuine reasoning flaws', but the paper only validates that the gate down-weights style tokens relative to task tokens (Table 3). It never checks whether gated mass actually sits on erroneous reasoning. This MVE computes the paper's exact gate (frozen Qwen3-4B, paper's prompts and question-only persona meta-prompt) on solutions with human-annotated first-error steps and asks whether the gate rises at the error.
registration.hypothesis: In erroneous ProcessBench solutions, the mean NSD gate (careless-student persona) on the human-labeled first-error step exceeds the mean gate on the preceding correct steps more often than it does at the same step index in position-matched correct solutions, by at least 10 percentage points.
registration.contribution: First step-level, human-label test of a negative-condition likelihood gate. Prior diagnostics of self-distillation scores are trajectory-level (correct vs incorrect rollout AUC) and concern positive/two-sided privileged scores; this tests NSD's negative-only, probability-space gate against step-level error locations, with direction controls (opposite 'careful' persona, irrelevant context) and uncertainty baselines (NLL, entropy) that would reveal whether any localization is specific to the negative condition or just confidence.

closest_work.difference: They check whether OPSD/RLCSD privileged-likelihood scores separate correct from incorrect trajectories (AUC ~0.5 on AIME with gpt-oss-20b). We test NSD's negative-only gate at the step level against human first-error labels, with a position-matched control and opposite-persona/irrelevant-context controls.

ProcessBench benchmarks trained PRMs and prompted critics on error localization; we use its labels to test a training-free gate derived from the policy's own token probabilities under a self-generated negative persona.

They show OPSD's per-token loss is indistinguishable between correct and incorrect rollouts and concentrates on low-information tokens; we test the negative-teacher analog and ask whether the mass rises at the erroneous step rather than only characterizing token types.

inputs: Model: Qwen/Qwen3-4B from Hugging Face (bf16, transformers>=4.51, sdpa attention)
Data: Hugging Face dataset Qwen/ProcessBench, split 'math' (1000 items; fields problem, steps, label, final_answer_correct)
Irrelevant passages: Hugging Face dataset Salesforce/wikitext, config wikitext-2-raw-v1, test split
Python packages: torch, transformers, datasets, numpy, scikit-learn (roc_auc_score)
registration.method:
All prompts use the Qwen3 chat template in non-thinking mode: prefix = tokenizer.apply_chat_template([{'role':'user','content':USER}], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False). Student/reference USER prompt (paper, App. C.3): 'Problem: {problem}

Let's think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}.' Persona-teacher USER prompt: 'Problem: {problem}

{PERSONA}

Now solve the problem following this instruction:

Let's think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}.' Wiki-irr USER prompt: 'Problem: {problem}

Below is some context you may find useful to answering the question above:

{PASSAGE}

Let's think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}.' PASSAGE = a random wikitext-2 test paragraph of >=500 characters truncated to 150 words (numpy RNG seeded by item index).

Personas are generated once per unique problem by the same Qwen3-4B (non-thinking mode, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, max_new_tokens 200, batched left-padded generate, seed 0). NEGATIVE meta-prompt (verbatim from the paper/repo): 'You are an expert Math Educator and AI Prompt Engineer. Your task is to analyze the following math problem and generate a "Generalized Attack Prompt" that will force an LLM to make a highly plausible, human-like cognitive error.

Anatomy of a Universal Attack Prompt:
1. Persona: Must start exactly with "You are a student who...". Describe a specific bad habit relevant to THIS problem.
2. Trigger: Abstract the problem's mathematical class. NEVER use specific numbers/variables from the current problem.
3. Flawed Execution: Instruct a naive heuristic or impulsive shortcut that would give a wrong answer.
4. Fatal Omission: Explicitly forbid the critical verification step.

Now, perform this task for the following problem:
Problem: {problem}

Output ONLY the "Generalized Attack Prompt". Start your response with "You are a student who...". Keep it concise (2-3 sentences).' POSITIVE (mirror) meta-prompt: identical text except: 'Generalized Care Prompt' replaces 'Generalized Attack Prompt' everywhere; 'that will lead an LLM to solve it in a highly careful, rigorous, human-like way' replaces 'that will force an LLM to make a highly plausible, human-like cognitive error'; 'Anatomy of a Universal Care Prompt'; item 1 says 'Describe a specific good habit relevant to THIS problem.'; item 3 is '3. Careful Execution: Instruct a systematic, rigorous method that avoids naive shortcuts.'; item 4 is '4. Mandatory Verification: Explicitly require the critical verification step.' Clean each generated persona: strip, remove any <think>...</think> block, keep the last paragraph if several, require it to start with 'You are' and be >=30 characters; otherwise use the fallback negative persona 'You are a student who rushes through problems, grabs the first shortcut that comes to mind, and never checks your work.' or fallback positive persona 'You are a student who works through problems carefully and systematically, avoids shortcuts, and always verifies your final answer.' Record the fallback rate.

Data handling: load all 1000 'math' items. The assistant text is the ProcessBench solution: '

'.join(steps). label is the 0-based index of the first erroneous step or -1 if all steps are correct (sanity-check that max(label) < len(steps); if labels look 1-based, subtract 1). Erroneous set E = items with label >= 1 (so at least one preceding step exists). Control pool C = items with label == -1.

Scoring: for each item and each of the 4 conditions (ref, neg, pos, wiki), token ids = tokenizer(prefix, add_special_tokens=False) + tokenizer(solution, add_special_tokens=False); run one no-grad forward pass (length-sorted batches of ~8, bf16) and record, for every solution token y_t, p_c(y_t) = softmax probability of the actual next token under condition c; under ref also record the full-vocabulary entropy H_t. Map each solution token to its step via the offset_mapping of the solution tokenization against the character spans of the steps in the joined text (separator tokens are assigned to the following step). Per-token signals: G_neg = max(0, p_neg - p_ref), G_pos = max(0, p_pos - p_ref), G_wiki = max(0, p_wiki - p_ref), NLL = -log p_ref, H = entropy. Per-step signal s(j) = mean of the per-token signal over the tokens of step j.

Statistic: for each item e in E with first-error step k and n steps, hit_e = 1[s(k) > mean_{j<k} s(j)]; P_err = mean of hit_e over E. Position-matched control: for each e, draw (numpy RNG seed 0, with replacement) one control item c from C with len(steps_c) >= k+1 and compute hit_c = 1[s_c(k) > mean_{j<k} s_c(j)]; P_ctrl = mean of hit_c over the drawn controls (drop a pair if no eligible control exists and report the count). lift = P_err - P_ctrl, computed separately for each signal (G_neg, G_pos, G_wiki, NLL, H). The registered statistic is lift for G_neg. Also compute: pooled step-level AUROC (error steps = positives, their preceding steps = negatives) per signal; top-1 localization rate (argmax over all steps of s(j) == k) versus mean chance 1/n; trajectory-level AUROC of the mean G_neg over all tokens for erroneous (label != -1) versus correct items; mean fraction of tokens with G_neg > 0 and mean G_neg; and the same lift statistic restricted to the generator subsets if time permits. Save all per-token values so the analysis can be recomputed.

event.description: The careless-persona gate's error-localization lift (P_err minus the position-matched control rate P_ctrl) exceeds 0.10.
event.statistic: lift_neg = P_err - P_ctrl for the per-step mean of G_neg = max(0, p_neg - p_ref)

evaluation.procedure: outputs/processbench_tokens.jsonl holds one record per item with the step index of every solution token and its p_ref, p_neg, p_pos, p_wiki and ref entropy, plus the personas and passage used. outputs/processbench_steps.jsonl holds per-item per-step means of each signal, label, number of steps and generator. outputs/summary.json holds, for each signal, P_err, P_ctrl, lift, number of erroneous items and matched pairs, pooled step-level AUROC, top-1 localization rate with its chance level, the trajectory-level AUROC of mean G_neg, mean gate-active fraction, and the persona fallback rate. The registered statistic is summary.json['lift']['G_neg'].
evaluation.controls: Position-matched correct solutions (same step index k) control for the structural fact that error steps come later than their preceding steps; the opposite 'careful' persona and the irrelevant-Wikipedia context test whether localization is specific to the negative direction; NLL and entropy under the reference prompt test whether the gate adds anything beyond plain uncertainty.

registration.full_scale_study: If the gate localizes errors beyond position, confidence and direction controls, run a full study of negative-persona gates as a label-free process-supervision signal: all four ProcessBench subsets, 1.7B/4B/8B models, solution-aware personas, comparison with trained PRMs (F1 on ProcessBench), and an NSD training run whose loss is restricted to gate-localized steps. If localization is absent or fully explained by NLL/entropy or shared with the careful persona, pivot the research program to the alternative mechanism (context-sensitivity/uncertainty regularization) and to behavioral explanations of NSD's gains.

agent.reason: Erroneous steps are somewhat less predictable, so the gate may inherit a weak room-to-move signal from low p_ref, but prior diagnostics find privileged-likelihood scores near chance for correctness, and a 0.10 lift after subtracting a position-matched control is a fairly demanding bar on off-policy solutions.

judge_astra.reason: The paper validates token-type reweighting, not alignment with annotated errors; a positive probability shift can instead reflect style or uncertainty. Off-policy ProcessBench traces and averaging across whole steps make a greater-than-10-point localization lift a demanding outcome.

judge_fable.reason: The probability-space gate compresses low-probability flawed tokens, so the per-step mean G_neg at the labeled error step should rise only weakly, mostly via mid-probability 'uncertainty' tokens or when the self-generated persona happens to match the actual flaw; a small positive lift is likely but clearing 0.10 over the position-matched control is roughly a coin flip tilted against.

judge_opus.reason: The probability-space gate gives little weight to low-probability error tokens and is dominated by style tokens, so I expect a weak lift from uncertainty correlation. Exceeding 0.10 against position-matched controls, with roughly ±0.03 noise on about 450 pairs, looks unlikely but possible.

judge_sol.reason: The paper validates token-type weighting, not error localization, and prompt-induced probability changes need not identify incorrect reasoning. Off-policy ProcessBench traces, plausible errors, and dilution from averaging whole steps make a localization lift above 0.10 relatively unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: The paper tests whether the gate separates style from task tokens, not whether it marks human-labeled errors. A question-only attack persona may not match a solution’s particular first error, making a lift above 10 percentage points a demanding result.

judge_muse.reason: The paper only shows the gate down-weights style tokens yet remains style-dominated (Table 3 ratio 2.6-3.5x) and OPSD analogues show chance-level correct-vs-incorrect separation; question-only personas untailored to foreign ProcessBench errors make 10pp lift beyond position unlikely, though generic uncertainty correlation leaves some chance.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This paper checks at the trajectory level whether OPSD/RLCSD privileged-likelihood token scores separate correct from incorrect rollouts (AUC ~0.5 on AIME) and examines how score mass concentrates by entropy. It does not test a negative-persona gate against human step-level first-error labels with position-matched controls.

ProcessBench provides the human first-error labels and benchmarks trained PRMs and prompted critics. It does not evaluate a training-free gate built from the policy's token probabilities under a self-generated negative condition.

The seed paper claims its gate isolates reasoning-critical tokens. Going by the experiment's description and the abstract, its validation is only style-versus-task token weighting. I did not read the seed's full text to confirm that it has no step-level error-localization analysis.
STEPS uses an annotator to find error spans and applies reverse KL to them during training. It does not test whether a likelihood-difference gate localizes human-labelled errors.

HSD argues that credit from a teacher conditioned on a successful peer concentrates where a failed rollout diverges from it. It uses a positive privileged teacher and offers no human step-label validation of a negative gate.

opus.reason: I found no paper that tests whether NSD's negative-teacher gate (or any negative-persona likelihood gate) rises at human-annotated erroneous steps. Existing diagnostics of self-distillation token scores work at the trajectory level or by token type, and they study positive or privileged teachers. ProcessBench has only been used to evaluate PRMs and critics. The step-level test with position-matched, opposite-persona and uncertainty controls therefore seems unaddressed, but my search was limited to a few arXiv queries and I did not read the seed's full text.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Introduces the exact NSD gate and evaluates its style/task-token weighting and training effects, but does not test alignment with human-annotated first-error steps.
Tests privileged one-sided and two-sided likelihood scores against trajectory correctness, rather than testing a negative-persona probability gate against step-level error locations.

Localizes errors using feedback-induced token-probability decreases filtered against non-diagnostic feedback. Its feedback-conditioned search experiments do not establish whether question-only negative personas identify annotated reasoning errors.

Evaluates first-error identification on ProcessBench using an unsupervised PRM trained from probabilities of explicit correctness markers, not likelihood shifts on solution tokens under negative conditioning.

sol.reason: As of 2026-10-06, I found no paper answering whether NSD's negative-persona gate concentrates on human-labeled first reasoning errors beyond position, uncertainty, and conditioning-direction controls. Prior work establishes related likelihood diagnostics and error-localization methods, but uses materially different conditioning or scoring mechanisms and does not settle this gate-specific question.

opus.reason: Both compute the NSD gate with Qwen3-4B on ProcessBench solutions under negative, irrelevant-context and related conditions, and test whether per-step gate mass singles out the labeled first-error step relative to preceding steps, compared against NLL/entropy baselines.

sol.reason: Both test whether NSD gates localize ProcessBench’s first erroneous step by teacher-forcing annotated solutions and comparing gate scores with reference surprisal and entropy.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the full registered Qwen3-4B bf16/SDPA ProcessBench math experiment: exact question-only negative and mirrored positive prompts, non-thinking chat template, item-seeded WikiText control, four-condition teacher-forced token probabilities, reference full-vocabulary entropy, exact probability-space gates, step mapping/means, seed-0 position-matched correct controls, all requested AUROCs/localization/gate/fallback metrics, generator subsets, and all registered raw files plus result.json. No hypothesis, event threshold, dataset selection, persona validation/fallback, or scientific control changes. Memory optimization projects only solution prediction positions in chunks after one full transformer forward per item/condition; identical-batch HF logits checks passed. Unspecified implementation choices documented: generation batch 16, top_k=0 (temperature/top-p only), scoring batches up to 8 with 16k token cap, start-offset assignment for boundary-straddling tokens. Tested bash evaluate.sh successfully in about 15.5 minutes; 1000 items, 479 matched pairs, zero drops, zero persona fallbacks. Token-based recomputation reproduced lift_neg=0.09185803757828809 (P_err=0.40292275574112735, P_ctrl=0.31106471816283926), below the strict >0.10 event. Four unit tests, identical-batch probability/entropy integration test, and full data/output integrity checks passed. Preliminary differing-batch bf16 numerical check failed tight tolerance; validation documents it, and experiment code/results were unchanged. Evaluation regenerates personas and outputs rather than reusing cached results.

departures: experiment.py generate_personas sets top_k=0, so persona sampling uses only temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. This overrides Qwen3's shipped generation_config default of top_k=20. The registration does not specify top_k, so this is an open, disclosed choice. It changes which personas are sampled and so could shift G_neg slightly, but there is no reason to expect a systematic effect.

experiment.py score_condition runs model.model and then applies lm_head only at solution positions, in chunks, rather than computing full logits in one forward pass. test_forward.py and forward_test.log show agreement with ordinary HF logits within about 1.6e-6 in probability on identical batches. This is a memory optimization and does not plausibly change the result.

Batches are capped by a 16k-token budget and are right-padded. Batch composition affects bf16 numerics; VALIDATION.md reports differences of about 3e-3 against unpadded scoring. This choice is open in the registration, and differences of that size are unlikely to move a step-mean comparison materially.
experiment.py compute_summary computes P_err over matched pairs rather than over all of E. Zero pairs were dropped (479 of 479), so this has no effect.

experiment.py encode_solutions assigns a token that straddles a step boundary by its start offset. The registration only specifies how separator tokens are handled, so this is an open choice with negligible impact.
Persona generation uses batch size 16 and puts all negative jobs before all positive jobs. Both are open choices. They affect sampled personas only through the RNG stream.
problems: outputs/summary.json gives no uncertainty for lift_neg. With 479 pairs the binomial standard error of the lift is roughly 0.03, so 0.092 cannot be distinguished from the 0.10 threshold. The strict event's non-occurrence is a near miss, not a clear refutation of a roughly 10-point lift.
The position-matched control is a single random draw per erroneous item (seed 0). This adds sampling variance that is not quantified, and no repeated draws or bootstrap are reported.

The hit statistic compares step means of a sparse, non-negative gate. Position matching does not control for differences in step length or token composition between error steps and correct steps. This is a limitation of the registered design, not an implementation error.
This is one run with one model (Qwen3-4B) and question-only personas, all as registered. The findings may not generalize to the solution-aware or trained settings used in NSD.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered prompts, data, four conditions, probability-space gates, step mapping, position-matched controls and statistic. The only notable unspecified choice is top_k=0 for persona sampling, which is disclosed. The protected evaluation regenerated everything and reproduced the engineer's values exactly; recompute.py independently rebuilds the summary from token records, and the forward-pass check passed. Results: lift_neg = 0.092, so the event did not occur. That lift is comparable to the careful-persona gate (0.100), the irrelevant-context gate (0.109) and NLL (0.088), and far below reference entropy (0.255). G_neg's pooled step AUROC is 0.53 and its top-1 localization (0.12) is below chance (0.17). Together these give credible evidence that the negative gate's localization is not specific to the negative direction, although the threshold miss itself lies within sampling uncertainty and no confidence intervals are reported.

registration.title: Is the NSD gate direction-specific? Overlap between tokens boosted by a careless persona, a careful persona, a mismatched persona and irrelevant context on the model's own rollouts
registration.seed_connection: NSD penalizes tokens whose probability rises under a 'careless student' negative condition and interprets them as flawed-reasoning tokens. Yet the paper's own ablation shows a random irrelevant Wikipedia passage works about as well as the persona (wiki-irr 6.6 vs online 7.8 average gain, and best under the policy-gradient variant), hinting that the gate may detect context-sensitive tokens rather than flaws. This MVE computes the paper's gate on the base model's own MATH-500 rollouts under the negative persona and under an opposite 'careful' persona and measures how much of the penalized mass the two opposite conditions share.
registration.hypothesis: Tokens boosted by the careless persona are also boosted by the opposite careful persona far more often than tokens of equal reference confidence: the G_neg-mass-weighted rate at which gated tokens have p_pos - p_ref > 0.01 is at least 1.5x the p_ref-stratified base rate of that event.
registration.contribution: Directly quantifies, at token level and on on-policy rollouts, whether NSD's penalized mass depends on the semantic direction of the condition. The OPSD literature has shown context-induced teacher behavior can dominate target-specific privilege (mismatched solutions work), and AntiSD analyzed PMI of positive privileged contexts by token category, but no work has measured the overlap between opposite-direction negative conditions for a repulsive gate, nor broken NSD's gate mass down by reflection/commit/number token categories.

closest_work.difference: OP2SD shows that OPSD gains survive replacing the paired reference solution with one from another problem (training-level evidence of context-induced behavior). We measure the analogous question for NSD's negative condition training-free at token level, comparing matched, mismatched, opposite and irrelevant conditions.

AntiSD analyzes which token categories a solution-conditioned (positive) teacher inflates or deflates via PMI. We analyze a negative persona's probability-space gate and its overlap with an opposite persona, which AntiSD does not consider.

Instructive Decoding contrasts noisy or opposite instructions at inference and finds 'opposite' works best, but never measures token-level overlap between opposite instructions' boosted tokens; we quantify that overlap for NSD's gate.

inputs: Model: Qwen/Qwen3-4B from Hugging Face (bf16, transformers>=4.51)
Data: Hugging Face dataset HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 (split test; fields problem, answer)
Irrelevant passages: Hugging Face dataset Salesforce/wikitext, config wikitext-2-raw-v1, test split
Python packages: torch, transformers, datasets, numpy, scipy (spearmanr)

event.description: The p_ref-stratified overlap ratio between the negative gate's mass and tokens boosted by the opposite careful persona exceeds 1.5.
event.statistic: R_matched = [sum_t G_neg,t * 1(p_pos,t - p_ref,t > 0.01)] / [sum_t G_neg,t * b(bin(p_ref,t))]

evaluation.procedure: outputs/rollout_tokens.jsonl holds one record per problem with the rollout text, token strings, and per-token p_ref, p_neg, p_pos, p_mis, p_wiki, plus the personas and passage used. outputs/summary.json holds R_matched for pos, mis and wiki, the unstratified ratios, per-bin base rates b(bin) and per-bin Spearman correlations, gate-mass shares by token category, mean signed Delta_neg on reflection vs other tokens, mean G_neg, gate-active fraction, and the persona fallback rate. The registered statistic is summary.json['R_matched']['pos'].
evaluation.controls: Stratifying by p_ref removes the structural 'room to move' confound (low-confidence tokens can be boosted by any context). The mismatched persona (another problem's negative condition) tests problem-specificity; the irrelevant Wikipedia context tests whether a non-persona perturbation gates the same tokens; the opposite persona is the direction control.

registration.full_scale_study: If opposite personas largely gate the same tokens (ratio well above 1.5), run full NSD training with positive, mismatched, neutral-instruction and persona-free perturbation conditions at 1.7B/4B/8B to test whether gains are independent of the condition's semantics, and develop a cheaper perturbation-only variant. If the overlap is at or below the stratified base rate, the direction matters and the follow-up is to study which persona content maximizes flaw-specific gating and to design persona curricula.

agent.reason: Both personas share the 'You are a student who…' framing and the extra-instruction perturbation, which likely boosts a common set of context-sensitive tokens, but direction-specific effects on commit vs. verification tokens pull the other way; 1.5 sits near my median estimate of the stratified overlap ratio.

judge_astra.reason: Shared persona scaffolding and general context sensitivity make substantial co-boosting likely, consistent with the paper's competitive wiki-irr results. Reference-probability stratification leaves shared sensitivities to position and discourse uncontrolled, so the ratio could exceed 1.5 without identifying shared flaws.

judge_fable.reason: Both personas share the same prompt structure and 'student' framing, so tokens strongly boosted by the careless condition are plausibly boosted by the careful one more often than p_ref-matched tokens (shared context sensitivity), but direction-specific commit/verification tokens dilute the overlap, making the 1.5x threshold a near coin flip, slightly favoring the event.

judge_opus.reason: Both personas share template structure and problem-class content, token sensitivity to context is shared, and within-bin room-to-move survives the coarse stratification. A simple model puts the ratio near 1.5 at correlation 0.5 and above it once heterogeneity and the mean shift are added.

judge_sol.reason: Opposite personas share substantial prompt structure and mathematical context, so correlated probability shifts can persist after reference-confidence stratification. The paper's competitive wiki-irr results support, without establishing, a generic context-sensitivity account that makes substantial overlap plausible.

judge_luna.reason: The paper’s competitive irrelevant-context variant makes generic context sensitivity plausible, but opposite careful and careless instructions may boost different tokens. I see the confidence-stratified overlap threshold as uncertain rather than strongly favored.

judge_muse.reason: The paper's own wiki-irr matches persona gains (Fig.4) and is best under the policy-gradient variant (Table 8), implying generic context-sensitivity; shared added prompt structure makes correlated boosts likely even after p_ref stratification, so >1.5x overlap is likely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Shows that teachers conditioned on correct and on incorrect solutions share behavioral shifts that largely cancel in a contrastive objective. The evidence comes from training and solution contexts. The paper does not measure, at token level, how a careless persona and a careful persona overlap in which tokens they boost, and it does not stratify by p_ref or compute NSD's G_neg gate.

OP2SD shows at training level that OPSD gains survive swapping in a mismatched reference solution, which points to context-induced teacher behavior. It does not test negative personas, opposite-direction conditions or token-level gate overlap.

The seed paper reports that the wiki-irr condition performs about as well as the persona, and it gives style-to-task gate ratios for the wiki, solution-aware and question-only conditions. It never computes the gate under an opposite careful persona or a mismatched persona, and never measures overlap between conditions.
AntiSD breaks down by token category, using PMI, what a positive solution-conditioned teacher inflates or deflates. It does not cover negative personas or overlap between opposite conditions.
Instructive Decoding contrasts noisy or opposite instructions at inference time, but it does not quantify overlap between the tokens that opposite instructions boost.

opus.reason: No paper I found measures whether NSD's negative-persona gate picks out the same tokens as an opposite careful persona, a mismatched persona or irrelevant text, on on-policy rollouts with a p_ref-stratified overlap ratio. The closest work, 2609.21561, finds that opposite-direction teachers share behavioral shifts, but its evidence comes from training with correct- and incorrect-solution contexts, not from a token-level overlap measurement of persona conditions. The seed paper and OP2SD point toward the question without answering it.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper compares negative-persona and irrelevant-Wikipedia conditioning through training results and style/task gate weights, but does not measure overlap between careless- and careful-conditioned probability boosts on the same rollouts.

RLCSD contrasts correct and incorrect privileged solutions to cancel shared stylistic shifts and analyzes token categories. It does not test opposite persona instructions or quantify the confidence-stratified overlap of NSD's positive-gap gate mass.

This paper scores trajectories under excellent- versus poor-reasoning contexts and tests semantic contrasts against neutral contexts. Its decoding and reranking experiments do not measure which tokens both opposite conditions boost relative to an unconditioned reference.
AntiSD analyzes privileged-context probability shifts for deliberation and shortcut tokens, but not overlap across opposite persona conditions or NSD's repulsive gate.
OP2SD tests target-specific versus mismatched solution context through training interventions; it does not test semantic direction-specificity of negative conditioning at token level.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes that context can induce correctness-independent token shifts, and already uses opposite reasoning contexts for contrastive scoring. However, I found no work answering whether NSD's penalized probability-gap mass is shared by careful and careless conditions on identical on-policy rollouts, with reference-confidence stratification and mismatched/irrelevant controls; this is a distinct diagnostic question rather than merely a different model, dataset, or metric.

registration.title: Do released NSD checkpoints gain in non-thinking mode by generating longer, thinking-like responses? Length, think-tag emission and accuracy under truncation budgets
registration.seed_connection: NSD trains and evaluates Qwen3 hybrid models in non-thinking mode and reports large gains (+12 points on AIME 2024 for 4B) together with a doubling of reflection tokens, but never reports response length. Concurrent work finds that repulsive self-distillation on Qwen3-4B in non-thinking mode reactivates the model's dormant thinking mode and inflates response length. NSD is a gated, bounded, KL-anchored repulsion, so whether its checkpoints show the same behavioral shift is open. This MVE evaluates the paper's released checkpoint against its base model and measures length, think-tag emission and accuracy as a function of a post-hoc token budget.
registration.hypothesis: On AIME 2024 + AIME 2025 in non-thinking mode, the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint produces responses whose mean token length is at least 1.5 times that of the base Qwen3-4B.
registration.contribution: Provides the missing behavioral characterization of NSD-trained models (length, truncation, think-tag emission, reflection counts) and a budget-matched accuracy comparison, which disentangles 'better per-token reasoning' from 'more reasoning tokens'. Baumann et al. studied ungated repulsion during their own training runs, not the released NSD checkpoints or NSD's stabilized objective.

closest_work.difference: They show that plain repulsive self-distillation from a solution-conditioned teacher switches Qwen3-4B into its thinking mode and inflates length until collapse. We test whether NSD's stabilized persona-based repulsion (released checkpoints) exhibits the same shift and whether its accuracy advantage persists at matched token budgets.
They show attractive self-distillation shortens responses and suppresses uncertainty verbalization; we measure the opposite direction on NSD checkpoints and relate it to accuracy under truncation.
They analyze thinking vs non-thinking accuracy as a function of output budget for base Qwen3 models; we apply a budget-curve analysis to compare an NSD-trained model with its base.

inputs: Base model: Qwen/Qwen3-4B (Hugging Face)

NSD checkpoint: the Qwen3-4B NSD model from the paper's Hugging Face collection PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation (enumerate with huggingface_hub.HfApi().list_models(author='PassionPrc'); pick the 4B checkpoint, preferring names indicating the online/solution-aware supervised run; record the chosen repo id). Fallback if no 4B checkpoint exists: the 8B checkpoint with Qwen/Qwen3-8B, else the 1.7B checkpoint with Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B.
Data: AIME 2024 (HuggingFaceH4/aime_2024, 30 problems) and AIME 2025 (yentinglin/aime_2025 or math-ai/aime25, 30 problems); MATH-500 (HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500)
Python packages: vllm, transformers, datasets, math-verify (pip install math-verify), numpy
registration.method:
Generation with vLLM (bf16, max_model_len 10240, gpu_memory_utilization 0.9), one model at a time. Prompts follow the paper's evaluation script: USER = '{question}\n\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer within \\boxed{}.' wrapped with tokenizer.apply_chat_template([...], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False). Sampling as in the paper's eval script: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, repetition_penalty 1.05, seed 0. AIME 2024+2025: 60 problems x 4 samples, max_tokens 8192. MATH-500: 500 problems x 1 sample, max_tokens 4096. Run the identical pipeline for the base model and the NSD checkpoint.

Per response record: generated token ids and text, token length, finish reason (truncated at max_tokens or stopped), whether the text contains '<think>' or '</think>' (thinking-mode signature; in non-thinking mode the template already closed an empty think block in the prompt), count of reflection phrases (case-insensitive substrings: wait, actually, hmm, let me reconsider, let me rethink, i made an error, i made a mistake, that's wrong, that is wrong, incorrect, reconsider, rethink, re-examine, let me check, let me verify, double check, double-check, going back, revisit, on second thought), and correctness: extract the last brace-balanced \\boxed{...} and compare with the gold answer using math_verify (parse/verify), falling back to normalized string equality (strip, \\dfrac->\\frac, remove \\left/\\right and spacing commands, drop trailing '.0').

Budget curves: for each cap c in {512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192}, decode the first c generated tokens and re-extract the boxed answer from that prefix; the response is correct at cap c only if the prefix already contains a complete boxed answer that matches gold. Accuracy@c per model and dataset, and Delta@c = Acc_NSD@c - Acc_base@c.

Statistic: length_ratio = mean token length of NSD responses / mean token length of base responses over all 240 AIME responses. Also report median lengths, the length ratio on MATH-500, truncation rates, think-tag rates, mean reflection counts, full-budget accuracies, and the Delta@c curve.

event.description: NSD responses on AIME 2024+2025 (non-thinking mode) are at least 1.5x longer on average than base-model responses.
event.statistic: length_ratio = mean(NSD response token length) / mean(base response token length) over the 240 AIME responses

evaluation.procedure: outputs/generations.jsonl holds one record per (model, dataset, problem id, sample) with the response text, token length, finish reason, think-tag flag, reflection count, extracted answer, gold answer and correctness at the full budget and at each cap. outputs/summary.json holds, per model and dataset, mean and median length, truncation rate, think-tag rate, mean reflection count, accuracy at each cap and the Delta@c curve, plus the chosen NSD repo id; it also holds the registered length_ratio on AIME.
evaluation.controls: The base Qwen3-4B under the identical prompt, sampling parameters and budgets is the control; post-hoc truncation at identical caps compares the two models at matched budgets; MATH-500 checks whether the length shift is specific to hard problems.

models: PassionPrc NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint (from the nsd-negative-self-distillation collection)

registration.full_scale_study: If NSD responses are much longer (and especially if think tags appear or the accuracy advantage vanishes at small caps), run a full budget-controlled comparison: NSD vs base in thinking mode at matched budgets, NSD applied to Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (no dormant thinking mode), length-controlled baselines such as prompting the base model to verify, and re-evaluation of all seven benchmarks at several caps. If lengths are similar and the advantage persists at all caps, the follow-up targets per-token mechanisms (which tokens change) instead.

agent.reason: Doubling of reflection tokens and the known lengthening effect of repulsive self-distillation make a >1.5x length increase plausible, but NSD's KL anchor and bounded penalty may limit it, and there is a real chance the 4B checkpoint cannot be fetched.

judge_astra.reason: The reported increase in reflection phrases and gains on hard non-thinking tasks make substantial length inflation plausible, although neither directly measures length. The 8K ceiling and uncertainty about the available checkpoint keep the 1.5x event from being near-certain.

judge_fable.reason: The doubled reflection counts, the exploratory case study and the unreported lengths all point to longer NSD responses, but base Qwen3-4B non-thinking already produces long (sometimes looping) AIME outputs, so a 1.5x mean ratio is uncertain, and the event also depends on a downloadable 4B NSD checkpoint existing.

judge_opus.reason: Large AIME-only gains and doubled reflection counts suggest longer outputs, but unchanged AIME24 reflection counts, the KL anchor, the 8192-token cap compressing the ratio, and checkpoint-availability risk make a 1.5x mean ratio less likely than not.

judge_sol.reason: The reported increase in reflection phrases and much larger non-thinking-mode gains make substantial length growth plausible. Reflection density can increase without proportional length growth, however, and token-cap censoring, checkpoint identification, and generation runtime add uncertainty.

judge_luna.reason: NSD roughly doubles the reported reflection-token frequency, and the registered related work makes length inflation plausible. But that does not imply a 50% increase in mean length, especially with NSD’s bounded objective, KL anchor, and non-thinking setup.

judge_muse.reason: NSD doubles mean reflection counts but shows similar reflection on AIME 2024 where gains are largest (Table 2), and non-thinking NSD 35.8% remains far below thinking baseline 75.8% (Tables 1,7), evidence against full thinking reactivation; some length growth is plausible but 1.5x mean is a high bar.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Baumann et al. show that ungated repulsive self-distillation, starting from Qwen3-4B in non-thinking mode, lengthens responses, triggers think-tag emission and eventually collapses. They do this during their own training runs on DeepMath, with a 28k-token budget and no GRPO. They never evaluate NSD's persona-conditioned, gated, KL-anchored objective or its released checkpoints, and they do not compare the two models at matched truncation budgets.

The NSD paper itself reports accuracy and the number of reflection tokens per response (7.5 for NSD vs 3.6 for the base 4B model). It also notes that Intuitor overthinks in thinking mode. It never reports response length, truncation rate or think-tag emission for NSD in non-thinking mode, and it has no accuracy curve over token budgets.
This paper shows that attractive self-distillation shortens responses and suppresses expressions of uncertainty. It does not cover repulsive or NSD-style training.

This paper studies privileged self-distillation on thinking models, including how it interacts with rollout budget and reflection markers. It does not study NSD checkpoints or the non-thinking-to-thinking mode switch.

opus.reason: Baumann et al. (2609.21561) already show that plain repulsive self-distillation inflates response length and reactivates Qwen3-4B's thinking mode. That makes the hypothesis well motivated, but it does not answer the question for NSD's gated, KL-anchored objective or its released checkpoints. No paper I found measures length, truncation or think-tag emission for NSD models, or compares NSD with its base model at matched token budgets. The NSD paper reports reflection counts but no response lengths, so the question remains open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Measures response growth, think-tag emission, truncation and accuracy for repulsive self-distillation on Qwen3-4B, but uses solution-conditioned teachers without NSD's stabilization mechanisms; it does not evaluate released NSD checkpoints or their post-hoc accuracy-versus-budget curves.
Reports NSD accuracy gains, reflection frequencies and thinking-mode evaluations, but not NSD response-length statistics, generated think-tag rates or accuracy under multiple truncation caps.
Studies thinking versus non-thinking accuracy and truncation under matched output budgets for base models, not NSD-trained checkpoints versus their bases.

sol.reason: Baumann et al. already establish the proposed behavioral concern and much of the diagnostic approach for unstabilized, solution-conditioned repulsion. However, NSD changes both the teacher conditioning and the token-level objective through selective gating, bounded unlikelihood and reference anchoring, so those results do not settle whether NSD exhibits the same shift. Among the work found available by 2026-10-06, none reports the proposed NSD-specific length and budget-curve characterization.

opus.reason: No list entry evaluates released NSD checkpoints for response length, think-tag emission and accuracy under truncation budgets.

sol.reason: No listed experiment compares released NSD checkpoints with base models on response length, thinking-tag emission, and accuracy under matched truncation budgets.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented and tested the complete registered evaluation: Hub enumeration selects PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B (immutable revision pinned) against Qwen/Qwen3-4B; 60 AIME problems × 4 responses and 500 MATH-500 problems × 1 response per model; identical registered non-thinking prompts, sampling, bf16/context settings and output budgets. Preserves token IDs/text, computes complete-box math-verify correctness, reflection/think-tag/truncation metrics, and all registered post-hoc prefix curves. Writes result.json and both required raw outputs. No methodological deviations or fallbacks were needed; tensor parallelism is 1 on the provided single GPU. Full test produced 1,480 records and passed consistency checks; observed AIME length_ratio was 1.548921667023574. Generation and initialization totaled about 24 minutes, plus roughly 3 minutes for fresh dependency installation. Results are one-seed, budget-censored observations, not a causal determination. Details and tested revisions are in IMPLEMENTATION.md.

registration.title: Does NSD training transfer robustness to adversarial 'careless student' instructions and irrelevant context at inference? Base vs released NSD checkpoint under prompt perturbations
registration.seed_connection: NSD pushes the student away from a teacher conditioned on a negative persona, and the repository describes the method as 'training the model to resist adversarial reasoning errors'. But the student only ever sees plain prompts during training; whether resistance transfers to the case where the negative condition appears in the model's own input is untested. This MVE puts the paper's own negative conditions (and its wiki-irr distractor) into the inference prompt and compares the accuracy drop of the base model and of the released NSD checkpoint.
registration.hypothesis: On MATH-500, the NSD-trained Qwen3-4B loses at least 5 accuracy points less than the base Qwen3-4B when a self-generated careless-student persona is inserted into the prompt (drop = plain-prompt accuracy minus persona-prompt accuracy).
registration.contribution: Tests an implicit robustness claim of NSD that no experiment in the paper addresses, using distractor types from the prompt-perturbation literature. Prior perturbation work measures fragility of untrained models or trains directly on distractors; here the training signal only used the perturbation on the teacher side, so transfer is non-obvious.

closest_work.difference: They show irrelevant context and pathological instructions degrade reasoning in 13 untrained LLMs (the source of NSD's wiki-irr strategy); we test whether NSD training, which uses such perturbations only as teacher conditions, reduces the degradation when the perturbation is in the model's own prompt.
GSM-DC shows training on distractor-augmented inputs improves robustness; NSD never trains on perturbed inputs, so we test an indirect transfer.
They document that role-playing personas can hurt zero-shot reasoning; we use adversarial personas as a probe for a trained model's resistance rather than for persona selection.

inputs: Base model: Qwen/Qwen3-4B (Hugging Face)

NSD checkpoint: the Qwen3-4B NSD model from the paper's Hugging Face collection PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation (enumerate with huggingface_hub.HfApi().list_models(author='PassionPrc'); choose the 4B checkpoint, preferring names indicating the online/solution-aware supervised run; record the repo id; fallback to 8B with Qwen/Qwen3-8B or 1.7B with Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B if no 4B exists)
Data: HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 (split test)
Irrelevant passages: Salesforce/wikitext, config wikitext-2-raw-v1, test split
Python packages: vllm, transformers, datasets, math-verify, numpy

event.description: The NSD checkpoint's accuracy drop under the careless-persona prompt is at least 5 points smaller than the base model's drop.
event.statistic: drop_persona(base) - drop_persona(NSD), where drop_persona = Acc(PLAIN) - Acc(PERSONA) in percentage points on MATH-500

evaluation.procedure: outputs/generations.jsonl holds one record per (model, condition, problem) with the prompt condition, persona or passage used, response text, token length, extracted answer, gold answer and correctness. outputs/summary.json holds the six accuracies with confidence intervals, drop_persona and drop_wiki per model, the registered difference, the wiki difference, mean lengths per condition, and the chosen NSD repo id.
evaluation.controls: The plain-prompt accuracy of each model is its own baseline, so the statistic compares drops rather than absolute accuracies; the irrelevant-context condition separates resistance to adversarial instructions from resistance to generic distraction; identical personas and passages for both models remove prompt-sampling variance; response lengths are logged to flag a length-mediated explanation.

models: PassionPrc NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint (from the nsd-negative-self-distillation collection)

registration.full_scale_study: If NSD confers robustness, run a full robustness benchmark (GSM-DC, the four perturbation families of Chatziveroglou et al., held-out persona types, instruct-only models) across 1.7B/4B/8B NSD checkpoints and OPSD/Intuitor/TTRL baselines, with length-controlled analysis, and test whether training on wiki-irr versus persona conditions yields different robustness profiles. If no transfer is found, the 'resist adversarial reasoning errors' framing should be dropped in favor of the behavioral or regularization accounts.

agent.reason: The student never sees persona prompts during training, so transfer of robustness is uncertain; a 5-point smaller drop could arise through longer, more reflective generations, but noise and checkpoint availability also work against the event.

judge_astra.reason: NSD never directly trains the student on perturbed inputs, so resistance to explicit instructions to make mistakes need not transfer. A five-point reduction in the accuracy drop would require benefits beyond what the modest reported clean MATH-500 improvement alone suggests.

judge_fable.reason: Persona-induced drops are governed mainly by instruction following, which NSD training (plain prompts only, small KL-anchored updates) is unlikely to change much; a modest transfer is possible but a 5-point smaller drop against a noisy four-accuracy statistic, plus checkpoint dependence, makes the event unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: The student never saw the persona in its own input during training and its weight changes are small, so an explicit flawed instruction probably degrades both models similarly. A 5-point smaller drop exceeds the roughly 2.8-point noise and needs real transfer.

judge_sol.reason: The student trains on plain inputs, so avoiding negative-teacher behavior does not directly teach resistance to adversarial instructions in its own input. Increased checking could transfer, but a five-point reduction in the accuracy drop is a demanding threshold for this indirect effect.

judge_luna.reason: NSD trains against negative-teacher-favored tokens and reports more reflection, which could help resist these prompts. However, the student is trained on plain prompts rather than on the attacks as inputs, so a reduction in the accuracy drop of at least five points is uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: NSD trains the student only on plain prompts with KL anchoring and only +1.9pp on MATH-500, giving little basis for 5pp less drop under an explicit careless instruction that instruction-following will likely obey in both models.

Studies irrelevant-context robustness after clean or distractor-augmented fine-tuning, including gains without distractor supervision. It does not study NSD or indirect robustness transfer from teacher-only negative conditioning.
Compares persona and neutral reasoning prompts and mitigates persona-induced errors through inference-time ensembling, rather than evaluating robustness acquired through negative self-distillation.

GASP evaluates robustness learned through adversarial self-play, but directly trains the reasoner on corrupted conditioning. The proposed experiment instead tests transfer when perturbations appeared only in the teacher's training context.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the full registered MATH-500 comparison: base-generated question-only personas, seeded Wikitext passages shared across models, all 3000 inference prompts with registered vLLM/chat/sampling settings, boxed-answer math-verify scoring with normalized fallback, Wilson intervals, paired flip counts, response lengths and fallback rate. Selected and revision-pinned Qwen/Qwen3-4B and PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B; no model-size fallback. Collection access returned 403 and the sole released 4B repository has no card identifying its training variant; this uncertainty is recorded rather than asserting online/supervised provenance. Answer strings are boxed for LaTeX parsing; no prompts, generation limits, controls or event were changed. Finalized command tested end-to-end, 3000 records validated; runtime approximately 14 minutes after installation. Local registered statistic +0.4 points, below threshold. Earlier engineering test gave -0.8; fixed seed did not give bit-identical repeats, documented without treating threshold failure as equivalence. Fresh evaluation deletes all intermediates and regenerates results once.

This was disclosed. The same rule applies to all six cells, so it is unlikely to move a difference of drops by more than a fraction of a point.

Model and dataset revisions are pinned through model_lock.json and data_lock.json, which were created during the engineer's test runs. This adds reproducibility and does not change the registered inputs, so no effect on the result.

Wikitext paragraphs are raw dataset rows filtered to at least 500 characters, and tokenization artifacts such as ' @-@ ' are kept. The registration leaves this open, and both models see the same passages, so the effect on the persona statistic is negligible.

Persona generation inherits the solve-time top_p, top_k and repetition_penalty along with the registered temperature of 0.7 and 200 max tokens. Persona content rules are not enforced; for example, the persona for problem 498 names $a_3 = a_1$. With a base drop of about 1 point, that would require NSD accuracy to rise by roughly 4 points under the persona, which is nearly unattainable. The null therefore says little about whether NSD transfers robustness to adversarial instructions.

Checkpoint provenance is unknown (outputs/hub_collections.json shows the 403; the repo has no model card). The result applies to PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B, not necessarily to the online/supervised NSD variant the hypothesis concerns.

Sampling precision: from the per-problem contribution histogram (-2:6, -1:40, 0:415, 1:34, 2:5), my estimate of the standard error of the statistic is about 2.2 pp, giving a 95% interval of roughly [-5.9, 2.7]. This excludes the registered +5 effect but cannot rule out small positive or negative differences.
