registration.title: Did the gate matter? Attributing the released NSD-Qwen3-4B checkpoint's token-level log-probability shift to the negative-condition gate within matched base-probability and token-class cells
registration.seed_connection: NSD's objective penalizes only sampled tokens with G_t = max(0, pi_neg - pi_ref) > 0 and claims to leave other tokens anchored by the KL term, with the sigmoid bound concentrating gradients on mid-confidence tokens (Appendix A) and linguistic/style tokens preserved. Because G_t <= 1 - pi_ref, an alternative reading is that NSD simply suppresses low-to-mid-probability sampled tokens regardless of the negative condition. The paper reports that it released trained checkpoints; comparing the released 4B model with its base on fresh base rollouts tests directly whether the realized change is a suppression of gate-flagged tokens beyond what base probability alone predicts.
registration.hypothesis: On base Qwen3-4B rollouts over MATH-500, tokens flagged by the negative-condition gate (G_NEG >= 0.02, solution-aware condition) have a more negative log-probability change under the released NSD-4B checkpoint than unflagged tokens (G_NEG = 0) of the same base-probability bin and token class, by at least 0.05 nats on a gated-token-weighted average.
registration.contribution: First post-hoc attribution of what an NSD-trained model actually changed at the token level, distinguishing gate-targeted suppression from generic low-probability suppression by matching on base probability and token class, with positive-condition and irrelevant-context gates as comparison gates, and a check of the paper's style-token-preservation and mid-confidence-gradient claims in released weights. Related-work characterizations below are taken from the team's drafts and were not independently verified.

closest_work.difference: Ding & Zhang (as described in the drafts) show OPD learning concentrates on low-log-probability tokens and a teacher-free fixed negative advantage suffices; this experiment tests, in a released NSD model, whether the realized change is explained by base probability alone or additionally by the negative-condition gate.

Shrestha & Tessier (as described in the drafts) align OPSD student changes with reference-induced supervision for attractive self-distillation during their own training; this experiment analyzes the publicly released repulsive, gated NSD checkpoint with probability-and-class matching.

Baumann et al. (as described in the drafts) analyze behavioral shifts of repulsive self-distillation at the response level; this experiment analyzes the token-level shift of a gated, regularized repulsive method and attributes it to the gate.

inputs: Models: Qwen/Qwen3-4B (base) and the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint. The seed paper links a Hugging Face page without naming checkpoints; the team's drafts report a collection 'PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation' (unverified). Discovery procedure is in the method.
Data: HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 (500 problems; fields 'problem', 'answer'); Salesforce/wikitext wikitext-103-raw-v1 test paragraphs (150-400 words) for the irrelevant-context gate
Software: transformers, torch, datasets, huggingface_hub, math-verify, scipy, numpy, pandas, pyarrow (peft only if the checkpoint is a LoRA adapter)

event.description: Within cells matched on base probability and token class, the NSD checkpoint suppresses negative-gate-flagged tokens more than unflagged tokens, indicating gate-targeted rather than merely probability-driven learning.
event.statistic: D_NEG = gated-token-weighted mean over base-probability x token-class cells of [mean Delta on tokens with G_NEG >= 0.02 minus mean Delta on tokens with G_NEG = 0], where Delta = log p_NSD(y_t) - log p_base(y_t) on base rollouts under the plain prompt, in nats

evaluation.procedure: outputs/rollouts.jsonl holds one line per problem: rollout text, token ids, truncation flag, correctness, NEG/POS condition texts with fallback flags, WIKI passage. outputs/token_table.parquet holds per (rollout, position): token id, token string, class and flags, p_base under REF/NEG/POS/WIKI, p_nsd under REF, REF entropies of both models, Delta, G_NEG, G_POS, G_WIKI, p_ref bin. outputs/summary.json holds the chosen NSD repo id and candidate list (or the abort status), per-cell counts and d_cell for each gate, the registered statistic D_NEG with bootstrap 95% CI, D_POS, D_WIKI, D_NEG - D_POS and D_NEG - D_WIKI with CIs, the bin-only variants, within-cell correlations, the Delta-vs-probability profile, Delta by class and token type, the style-task ratio of |Delta|, suppression-mass shares, entropy changes, the number of condition fallbacks and the base rollout accuracy. The registered statistic is the point estimate of D_NEG.
evaluation.controls: Matching on base-probability bins removes the dependence of the gate on 1 - p_ref, and matching on token class removes class composition differences; D_POS (positive-condition gate) and D_WIKI (irrelevant-context gate) show whether any gated-versus-ungated difference is specific to the negative condition or arises for any context perturbation; the flicker band 0 < G < 0.02 is excluded so that near-ties on high-confidence tokens do not dilute the comparison; the same rollouts and token ids are scored under every context and both models, so all comparisons are paired at the token level. Gates recomputed on base rollouts with fresh conditions are a proxy for the online training signal, which is acknowledged in the analysis.

models: released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint (discovered on the Hugging Face Hub as described; abort if absent)

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, repeat the attribution across training checkpoints (gate alignment over time), across the 1.7B/4B/8B releases and with the exact online conditions logged during training, and train a teacher-free control with the gate replaced by 1 - pi_ref to confirm that gate-targeted suppression is what separates NSD from generic low-probability suppression. If it does not occur, the follow-up is a direct training comparison of NSD against a teacher-free negative-advantage objective at matched compute, since the gate would not be the operative mechanism.

agent.reason: Requires the released 4B checkpoint to exist in a loadable format (perhaps 70%), and then a consistent persona effect on confident connectives versus hedges could produce gate-aligned suppression, but idiosyncratic gate activations, dilution over many flagged tokens and the gentle training (lr 1e-6, KL anchor) make a 0.05-nat matched difference uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: The objective directly discourages gated tokens, making excess suppression plausible, but freshly reconstructed gates need not resemble the conditions encountered during training. Unverified checkpoint availability and the substantial scoring workload further reduce the probability of obtaining the registered contrast.

judge_fable.reason: Requires discovering and loading an unverified released 4B checkpoint (~55% likely) through a complex pipeline; conditional on that, gate-specific suppression beyond base probability is roughly a coin flip, since the wiki-irr results suggest much of NSD's effect is generic flattening of uncertain sampled tokens, although NSD's boosted reflection tokens (ungated under a careless persona) could push D_NEG negative.

judge_opus.reason: The experiment needs the released 4B checkpoint to exist and be discoverable; my estimate for that is about 0.6, and it is unverified. If the checkpoint is found, the model was trained to suppress exactly these frozen-teacher-gated tokens, NSD also raised reflection tokens (which the NEG gate leaves ungated), and generic volatility effects push the same way, so a matched gap of at least 0.05 nats is fairly likely (about 0.7).

judge_sol.reason: The stated objective makes gate-aligned suppression plausible, but fresh conditions may poorly reproduce the historical training gates, while coarse probability bins leave residual confounding. Finding and loading the unverified checkpoint is an additional prerequisite.

judge_luna.reason: If the intended checkpoint is available, its training objective directly penalizes sampled tokens boosted by the negative condition, making a negative matched shift plausible. Fresh gates on base-model rollouts may not align with the online training gates, and the checkpoint discovery path is unverified, so I discount the estimate.

judge_muse.reason: NSD explicitly suppresses gated tokens with KL anchoring others and improves accuracy markedly, favoring D_NEG<-0.05, but Fig.6 shows tiny KL drift with anchor and the 4B release may be absent, reducing unconditional probability.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's own analysis (Section 5.1 style-task ratio, Section 5.3 gate flicker, Appendix A gradients) looks at the gate weights and the loss during training. It never compares the trained checkpoint's token log-probabilities with the base model's, and it never controls for base probability or token class. So it does not test whether the change is gate-targeted or just generic suppression of low-probability tokens.

Ding & Zhang show that on-policy distillation (OPD) gains come mostly from suppressing low log-probability tokens, and that a fixed negative advantage matches teacher-provided ones. This supplies the alternative hypothesis. They do not study NSD or its negative-condition gate, and they do not match on base probability to separate the gate's effect from the effect of probability alone.

Baumann et al. study the behavioural shifts of repulsive and attractive self-distillation in their own training runs, mostly at the response level (length, switches into thinking mode). They do not analyse NSD's gated objective or a released NSD checkpoint at the token level.

Shao et al. do a token-level gradient analysis of reverse-KL OPD with a frozen teacher (low student-probability tokens dominate the gradient norm). The objective is different, and there is no post-hoc test of a gate in trained weights.

Meng et al. characterise token-level shifts between base and RLVR models in general. The method is RLVR, not gated repulsive self-distillation, and there is no attribution to a gate with positive-condition or irrelevant-context comparison gates.

opus.reason: I found no paper that tests, in a trained NSD model, whether its token-level log-probability shifts follow the negative-condition gate beyond what base probability and token class predict. The seed paper only looks at gate weights during training, and Ding & Zhang supply the low-probability-suppression explanation but never test it against NSD's gate. The closest works cover parts of the question (gate statistics during training, low-probability suppression in OPD, response-level effects of repulsion), but none answers it.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed analyzes gate weights by token class, probability-dependent gradients, and conditioning variants, but does not compare realized checkpoint shifts between gated and ungated tokens matched on base probability and token class.

Measures student log-probability changes on fixed initial-model responses and their alignment with reference-induced supervision, including unrelated-context controls. It studies attractive OPSD, not whether NSD's negative gate predicts suppression beyond base probability and token class.

Tests low-probability token selection and teacher-free fixed negative advantages in OPD training. It establishes the competing mechanism motivating this experiment, but does not test gate-specific changes in NSD.

Reports base-versus-trained token log-probability shifts and probability-dependent gradient concentration in sampled-token OPD, but does not connect endpoint suppression to a negative-condition gate using matched cells.

Studies attractive, repulsive, and contrastive self-distillation through behavioral dynamics and credit-pooling/permutation ablations, without testing NSD's gated, regularized checkpoint or the registered matched suppression statistic.

sol.reason: Prior work supplies closely related checkpoint diagnostics, context controls, and evidence for generic low-probability suppression, so the analysis approach is not wholly new. However, among work available by 2026-10-06, I found none answering whether realized NSD suppression is specifically associated with its negative-condition gate after matching on base probability and token class.

opus.reason: No list entry analyzes a released NSD checkpoint's token-level log-probability changes against gate flags within matched probability and token-class cells.

sol.reason: It measures probability-and-class-matched token suppression in a released checkpoint, whereas related entries such as #3 and #34 manipulate gate placement during new training.

registration.title: Repulsion signature of the released NSD-Qwen3-4B: response length, thinking-mode leakage, truncation and length-capped accuracy on AIME 2024/2025 in non-thinking mode
registration.seed_connection: NSD is a gated, bounded form of repulsive self-distillation applied to Qwen3 in non-thinking mode, trained with a 4096-token response cap but evaluated with a 32K output budget (Section 3). The paper reports that reflection tokens per response roughly double after training (Table 2) and that AIME accuracy rises by about 10 points for Qwen3-4B, but never reports response lengths, truncation rates or whether the trained model re-enters Qwen3's dormant thinking mode. Whether NSD's gate, KL anchor and sigmoid bound avoid the length-inflation signature associated with repulsive objectives, and how much of the AIME gain survives at the training-time cap, is untested.
registration.hypothesis: In non-thinking mode on AIME 2024 + AIME 2025 under identical prompts and sampling, the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint produces responses whose mean token length is more than 1.5 times that of base Qwen3-4B.
registration.contribution: First measurement of the behavioral profile (length, truncation, think-tag emission, reflection density) of a released NSD checkpoint and of how much of its AIME gain is retained when generation is capped at the 4096-token training length, without any training. Related-work characterizations below are taken from the team's drafts and were not independently verified.

closest_work.difference: Baumann et al. (as described in the drafts) observe that un-gated repulsive self-distillation wakes Qwen3-4B's latent thinking mode and inflates length during their own training; this experiment checks whether the released, regularized NSD checkpoint shows the same signature at inference and whether its gains persist at the training cap.

Kim et al. attribute self-distillation degradation to suppressed uncertainty verbalization; this experiment measures the opposite direction (increased verbalization and length under NSD) and asks whether it accompanies the accuracy gain.

OPSA (as described in the drafts) reports response length growing to ~12K tokens during teacher-free negative-advantage training of Qwen3-1.7B; this experiment tests whether NSD checkpoints show comparable growth at inference.

inputs: Models: Qwen/Qwen3-4B (base) and the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint. The seed paper links a Hugging Face page without naming checkpoints; the team's drafts report a collection 'PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation' (unverified). Discovery procedure is in the method.

Data: AIME 2024 (HuggingFaceH4/aime_2024; 30 problems; fields 'problem', 'answer') and AIME 2025 (math-ai/aime25; 30 problems; fields 'problem', 'answer'; fallbacks: opencompass/AIME2025 configs AIME2025-I and AIME2025-II with fields 'question'/'answer', or MathArena/aime_2025). Optional: HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 first 200 problems.
Software: vllm, datasets, huggingface_hub, math-verify, numpy, pandas (peft only if the checkpoint is a LoRA adapter)
registration.method:
Setup. Immediately `pip install vllm datasets huggingface_hub math-verify numpy pandas` and download both models in parallel. Checkpoint discovery: huggingface_hub.HfApi().list_models(author='PassionPrc'); if empty, also list_models(search='negative-self-distillation') and list_models(search='NSD-Qwen3'). Keep ids mentioning Qwen3-4B (or '4B') and NSD; prefer ids indicating the default online solution-aware supervised variant (containing 'online', 'sol' or 'solution'; avoid 'wiki', 'question', 'pg', 'policy', 'lora', '1.7B', '8B'); if several remain take the alphabetically first; log the chosen id and all candidates. If the repo is a LoRA adapter (adapter_config.json), pip install peft, merge onto Qwen/Qwen3-4B and save the merged model locally for vLLM. Use the base tokenizer and chat template if the checkpoint lacks tokenizer files; assert equal vocabulary size and identical hidden size and layer count to Qwen/Qwen3-4B. If no 4B NSD checkpoint can be found or loaded, do not substitute any other model: write outputs/summary.json with status 'aborted_no_checkpoint' and the candidate list, and stop.

Generation. Run each model in its own Python process with vLLM (dtype='bfloat16', max_model_len=13312, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9), base first. Prompts use the Qwen3 chat template with enable_thinking=False and add_generation_prompt=True; user message = the paper's student prompt "Problem: {problem}\n\nLet's think step by step and output the final answer within \\boxed{}." SamplingParams(temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, max_tokens=12288, n=4, seed=0); no repetition penalty (the paper's stated sampling). For each of the 60 problems x 4 samples (240 generations per model) record: text, generated token ids, token count, finish_reason (truncated = 'length'), whether the text contains '<think>' or '</think>', whether it starts (after stripping whitespace) with a thinking-style opener ('Okay', 'Alright', 'Let me', 'Hmm', 'So,'), the count of reflection phrases (case-insensitive substrings: wait, actually, hmm, let me reconsider, let me rethink, i made an error, i made a mistake, that's wrong, that is wrong, incorrect, reconsider, rethink, re-examine, let me check, let me verify, double check, double-check, going back, revisit, on second thought), the last complete \\boxed{...} answer and correctness (integer equality after stripping whitespace, commas and a trailing .0; math_verify as fallback). Report reflection phrases per response and per 1,000 generated tokens.

Post-hoc length caps. For cap in {1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 12288}: decode only the first cap generated tokens, extract the last complete \\boxed{} within that prefix, and grade (distributionally identical to generating with max_tokens=cap). Compute Avg@4 and Pass@4 per model per cap over the 60 problems, and the gain retention R = (Acc_NSD@4096 - Acc_base@4096) / (Acc_NSD@12288 - Acc_base@12288) with a bootstrap CI (reported as undefined if the denominator is below 2 points; R is a noisy quantity at this scale and is reported only with its CI).

Optional. If a model's AIME generation finished in under 6 minutes, additionally run 200 MATH-500 problems x 1 sample x max_tokens 4096 with the same prompt and sampling for that model, to obtain the length ratio and accuracy on easier problems.

Statistics. Primary: mean generated-token count over the 240 NSD generations divided by the mean over the 240 base generations, with a 1000-resample bootstrap over problems (resampling the 60 problems with all their samples for both models) for the 95% CI. Also report median and 90th-percentile lengths, truncation rate, think-tag rate, opener rate, reflection densities, Avg@4/Pass@4 at every cap with bootstrap CIs, and the MATH-500 statistics if run.

event.description: The NSD checkpoint's non-thinking AIME responses are substantially longer than the base model's under identical prompts and sampling (the repulsion length signature).
event.statistic: Mean generated-token count of NSD responses divided by the mean generated-token count of base responses over all AIME 2024 + AIME 2025 generations (60 problems x 4 samples per model, max_tokens 12288)

evaluation.procedure: outputs/generations_base.jsonl and outputs/generations_nsd.jsonl hold one line per generation (benchmark, problem id, sample index, text, token ids, token count, finish_reason, think-tag flag, opener flag, reflection count, boxed answer, correctness, and correctness at each post-hoc cap). outputs/summary.json holds the chosen NSD repo id and candidates (or the abort status) and, per model: mean/median/90th-percentile length, truncation rate, think-tag rate, opener rate, reflection phrases per response and per 1,000 tokens, Avg@4 and Pass@4 at each cap with bootstrap CIs, the gain-retention ratio R with CI, the optional MATH-500 statistics, and the registered statistic (mean-length ratio NSD/base) with its bootstrap 95% CI. The registered statistic is the point estimate of the mean-length ratio.
evaluation.controls: Base Qwen3-4B under identical prompt, chat template, sampling parameters, seed and token budget is the paired control; post-hoc caps give a length-matched comparison of accuracy; truncation, think-tag and opener rates separate 'longer but complete' responses from runaway or thinking-mode generation; the paper's own sampling settings are used without additional penalties so that length differences reflect the weights, not decoding.

models: released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint (discovered on the Hugging Face Hub as described; abort if absent)

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, a full study would (a) re-evaluate NSD, OPSD and the label-free baselines at matched token budgets across all seven benchmarks with 8 samples, (b) compare NSD in non-thinking mode against base Qwen3-4B in thinking mode at equal budgets to test whether NSD's gains are a partial activation of the latent thinking mode, and (c) retrain NSD with and without the KL anchor and sigmoid bound while tracking length and think-tag emission to identify which component controls the drift. If it does not occur, NSD's reflection increase is not length inflation, and the follow-up studies which token-level changes produce the extra reflection and accuracy.

agent.reason: Conditional on the checkpoint existing, a doubling of reflection tokens per response and large non-thinking AIME gains make substantially longer responses likely, with the 12288-token cap allowing runaway generations to inflate the mean; the checkpoint-availability risk pulls the overall probability down.

judge_astra.reason: The reported increase in reflection counts and training against shortcut-inducing conditions make substantial length growth plausible, though neither establishes a 1.5-fold increase. Checkpoint discovery, long-generation runtime, and censoring at 12,288 tokens temper this forecast.

judge_fable.reason: Same checkpoint dependence; conditional on it, a 4x increase in reflection phrases makes substantially longer AIME responses likely, but the KL anchor, 1e-6 learning rate and 4096-token training cap limit drift, and base-model truncation loops at the 12288 cap would compress the mean-length ratio, so exceeding 1.5x is about even odds.

judge_opus.reason: The run is checkpoint-dependent and carries timeout risk, which is higher precisely when NSD outputs are long. The repulsive objective should lengthen responses, but base non-thinking AIME outputs are already a few thousand tokens and NSD's reported reflection counts (about 7 per response) are far from thinking-mode levels, so a mean-length ratio above 1.5 under a 12K cap is less likely than not.

judge_sol.reason: The paper's increased reflection counts and exploratory case study make substantial length growth plausible, although increased reflection density could explain these without a length ratio above 1.5. Checkpoint availability and long-generation throughput reduce the unconditional probability.

judge_luna.reason: The paper reports roughly doubled reflection-phrase frequency, but that does not imply 1.5 times as many total tokens; the KL anchor, bounded penalty, and non-thinking setup argue against assuming large length inflation. The length result is also sensitive to long-tail generations, and this experiment depends on the unverified release.

judge_muse.reason: Reflection frequency is unchanged on AIME 2024 (6.9 vs 6.8, Table 2) and 2 epochs at LR 1e-6 with KL anchor constrain drift, so >1.5x mean length inflation is unlikely even if the checkpoint is found.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Baumann et al. show that un-gated repulsive self-distillation, with no extra stabilisation and with the teacher conditioned on a correct or an incorrect solution, makes Qwen3-4B in non-thinking mode produce longer responses, start emitting think tags and eventually collapse from truncation. They track this in their own training runs with a 28k-token budget. They do not evaluate NSD, which uses a gate, a KL anchor and a sigmoid bound and repels from a self-generated 'careless reasoner' condition. They also do not check whether gains survive when output is capped at the training length.

The seed paper reports that NSD's reflection tokens rise from 3.6 to 7.5 per response on Qwen3-4B (Table 2), plus accuracy and an ablation showing training collapses without the KL term. The sections I read report no response lengths, truncation rates, think-tag emission or accuracy under a length cap. The experiment measures exactly these for the released checkpoint.

Kim et al. find that attractive, solution-conditioned self-distillation shortens responses and suppresses expressed uncertainty. They do not study repulsive or negative-teacher objectives, or NSD checkpoints.

Kaur et al. study privileged self-distillation on thinking models and count verification and hedging markers after length normalisation. They do not cover NSD or a non-thinking-mode length or think-tag analysis of a repulsion-trained checkpoint.

The experiment's drafts cite OPSA as reporting response-length growth during teacher-free negative-advantage training of Qwen3-1.7B. I did not open this paper, so I cannot confirm that description. In any case it concerns a different method and model, not inference-time behaviour of the released NSD checkpoint.

opus.reason: I found no paper that measures response length, truncation, think-tag emission, or accuracy at the training-time cap for the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint, and the seed paper's analysis sections report only reflection-token counts and accuracy. The closest work (Baumann et al., 2609.21561) establishes the length and thinking-mode signature for un-gated repulsion during its own training. Because NSD's gate, KL anchor, sigmoid bound and self-generated negative condition were designed to change exactly that behaviour, Baumann's result does not answer whether this checkpoint shows the signature.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Reports response-length growth, thinking-tag emission and truncation collapse for repulsive self-distillation starting from non-thinking Qwen3-4B. It studies sign-reversed distillation from solution-conditioned teachers, not NSD's negative-condition teacher, adaptive gate, sigmoid-bounded penalty and KL anchor, and does not measure NSD's accuracy-gain retention at 4096 tokens.

The seed reports NSD accuracy and reflection counts per response, including on AIME 2024/2025, but does not report response-length distributions, non-thinking-mode leakage, truncation rates or accuracy across inference token caps.

Reports longer, more reflective reasoning under teacher-free negative-advantage training, including non-thinking Qwen3 models. Its OPSA objective differs substantively from NSD, and it does not evaluate the released NSD checkpoint or its budget-dependent gain retention.

Measures accuracy, response length and length-normalized deliberation markers across evaluation budgets, including the 4096-token training cap. It studies attractive privileged-context distillation in thinking models, rather than the behavioral consequences of regularized NSD in non-thinking mode.

sol.reason: The diagnostic approach is not new: prior work already measures repulsion-induced length growth, mode switching and truncation, while other work evaluates distillation across token budgets. However, those findings do not establish whether NSD's materially different gated, bounded and anchored objective exhibits the same signature or whether its AIME gains survive the training-length cap. I found no paper available by 2026-10-06 that answers those NSD-specific questions.

opus.reason: No list entry evaluates the released NSD checkpoint's response length, truncation, think-tag leakage or length-capped AIME accuracy against the base model; entry 16 is a prompt-only control on the base model.

sol.reason: No list entry compares a released NSD checkpoint with its base model for response-length inflation and accuracy retention across output caps.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered inference-only experiment, including exact checkpoint discovery (selected PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B), architecture/vocabulary checks, parallel downloads, separate base/NSD vLLM processes, 60 AIME problems x 4 samples, registered prompts/non-thinking template/sampling/budgets, diagnostic JSONL records, all post-hoc caps, integer/math-verify grading, and 1000 paired problem-level bootstrap resamples. Full evaluation command tested successfully; raw outputs validated and four unit tests passed. Test statistic was 1.8023761495686275, bootstrap 95% CI [1.5757974814752, 2.092359267118584]. No changes to hypothesis, event, models, controls, decoding parameters, sample counts or evaluation. Infrastructure-only compatibility fix: pin CUDA 13.0 compiler/CRT/NVVM matching the installed PyTorch runtime, select that compiler instead of the image's CUDA 12.4 compiler, and supply expected library links/path for FlashInfer JIT. Both timed AIME generation runs exceeded six minutes, so optional MATH-500 was not run. Gain-retention CI explicitly counts and excludes undefined zero-denominator bootstrap replicates; this convention is documented.

departures: experiment.py (worker) builds prompts for both models with the base Qwen/Qwen3-4B tokenizer and chat template, even though the NSD repo ships its own tokenizer files and chat_template.jinja (model_metadata.json). The registration requires identical prompts and the Qwen3 template, and only mentions the base template as a fallback when tokenizer files are missing. The vocabularies were asserted identical, so this keeps prompts matched rather than changing the question. Unlikely to change the length ratio unless the NSD template differs materially, which was not checked.

experiment.py (analyze): the gain-retention bootstrap CI drops and counts the 7 resamples with a zero denominator. The registration does not specify this rule. It affects only the secondary R statistic (point value 0.0, CI [-4.0, 0.70]), not the registered length ratio.

evaluate.sh / requirements.txt: pinned package versions and a pip-supplied CUDA 13.0 nvcc with symlinked libraries for FlashInfer JIT, needed for vLLM to run at all (see the setup_failure*.log files). This is infrastructure only, with no plausible effect on the result.

Optional MATH-500 was skipped because both AIME runs took longer than 6 minutes (timing_base.json 468 s, timing_nsd.json 1021 s). This follows the registered conditional rule and is not a departure in substance.

No departure in data (HuggingFaceH4/aime_2024 and math-ai/aime25, 60 problems), checkpoint choice (PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B, the only 4B candidate per discovery.json), user prompt, enable_thinking=False, sampling (T=0.6, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, n=4, seed=0, max_tokens=12288), max_model_len, post-hoc caps, grading, or the paired problem-level bootstrap.
problems: outputs/generations_nsd.jsonl: the visible tail record (aime_2025_29, sample 3) is a degenerate repetition loop that runs to the 12288 cap with no boxed answer. At least part of the length inflation is runaway looping rather than longer complete reasoning. The headline ratio should therefore be read together with the NSD truncation rate, which was cut from the visible summary.json, and the think-tag rate, not as evidence of re-entering thinking mode.

Ratio of means with lengths capped at 12288: base p90 already equals 12288 and the base truncation rate is 10.8%. Capping likely understates the true inflation and makes the ratio depend on the budget, which is shorter than the paper's 32K.

outputs/summary.json: the NSD accuracy gain at 12288 is only about 4.2 points (CI roughly [0.4, 8.3]), well below the roughly 10-point AIME gain the paper reports at 32K. The gain at 4096 is 0.0, giving R = 0 with a very wide CI. Whether this checkpoint is the paper's default NSD variant cannot be confirmed from the repo name.
Chat template for NSD taken from the base tokenizer rather than the checkpoint's own chat_template.jinja (experiment.py worker); template equality was not verified.
One checkpoint, 60 problems, 4 samples each, and a single seed. The CI [1.58, 2.09] clears the 1.5 threshold, but not by a wide margin.

The protected run reproduced the engineer's earlier value exactly (1.8023761495686275). This is consistent with seeded vLLM sampling, and main() deletes old outputs before running, so the outputs come from the fresh run.
opus.reason: The code runs the registered inference-only comparison as specified: the discovered PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B checkpoint against base Qwen3-4B, the registered AIME sources, prompt, non-thinking template, sampling and budget, with post-hoc caps and a paired problem-level bootstrap. The only departures are an infrastructure CUDA fix, a secondary-statistic CI convention, and use of the base chat template for both models, none of which plausibly changes the length ratio. The registered statistic, 1.80 with CI [1.58, 2.09], is computed from fresh generation records and supports the >1.5 event. The visible NSD output shows repetition loops hitting the cap, so the inflation partly reflects degenerate runaway generation. The NSD accuracy gain is small (+4 points at 12288 and 0 at 4096), which limits how far the result speaks to the seed paper's claims. This makes it a credible, meaningful but modest-precision finding about a single checkpoint.

departures: evaluate.sh and requirements.txt add package-version pins and CUDA 13 compiler/runtime-link configuration not specified in the registration. Version selection was left open, and the CUDA changes address demonstrated build failures. They could affect implementation-level numerical reproducibility, but there is no evidence of a changed sampling rule, control, or experimental question.

This can affect the secondary retention CI, but not the registered mean-length ratio or event.

registration.title: Collateral effects of NSD on non-math capability: non-math MMLU-Pro accuracy and chat-response NLL of the released NSD-Qwen3-4B versus base Qwen3-4B
registration.seed_connection: NSD motivates its gating and sigmoid bounding by the risk that unlikelihood training 'catastrophically degrades the model's foundational language capabilities' and claims that its design 'preserves the model's linguistic priors' and 'foundational language capabilities', yet every reported evaluation is a math benchmark. Whether two epochs of gated unlikelihood on MATH with a 0.01 KL anchor leaves general knowledge, non-math reasoning and ordinary chat behavior intact is untested and not obvious: the KL anchor and the low learning rate argue for preservation, while repulsive objectives are known to shift response style broadly.
registration.hypothesis: The released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint loses at least 3 percentage points of accuracy relative to base Qwen3-4B on non-math MMLU-Pro questions under identical greedy non-thinking decoding.
registration.contribution: First out-of-domain evaluation of an NSD-trained model, directly testing the paper's preservation claim with a knowledge/reasoning benchmark and a decoding-free distribution-shift measure (NLL of ordinary assistant responses), while accounting for the length and answer-extraction confounds. Related-work characterizations below are taken from the team's drafts and were not independently verified.

closest_work.difference: EDGE-OPD (as described in the drafts) studies side effects of privileged-context OPSD on general capabilities; this experiment measures side effects of the repulsive NSD objective on a standard knowledge benchmark and chat NLL.

Shenfeld et al. report that attractive self-distillation causes less forgetting than SFT/RL; this experiment asks whether the same holds for NSD's repulsive, gated unlikelihood objective in its released weights.

Baumann et al. (as described in the drafts) document instability and behavioral drift of repulsive self-distillation on math; this experiment quantifies drift on non-math tasks for the regularized NSD release.

inputs: Models: Qwen/Qwen3-4B and the released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint. The seed paper links a Hugging Face page without naming checkpoints; the team's drafts report a collection 'PassionPrc/nsd-negative-self-distillation' (unverified). Discovery procedure is in the method.
Data: TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro, split test (fields question, options, answer, category); HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k, split test_sft (field messages)
Software: vllm, transformers, datasets, huggingface_hub, numpy, pandas (peft only if the checkpoint is a LoRA adapter)
registration.method:
Setup. Immediately `pip install vllm transformers datasets huggingface_hub numpy pandas` and download both models in parallel. Checkpoint discovery: huggingface_hub.HfApi().list_models(author='PassionPrc'); if empty, also list_models(search='negative-self-distillation') and list_models(search='NSD-Qwen3'). Keep ids mentioning Qwen3-4B (or '4B') and NSD; prefer ids indicating the default online solution-aware supervised variant (containing 'online', 'sol' or 'solution'; avoid 'wiki', 'question', 'pg', 'policy', 'lora', '1.7B', '8B'); if several remain take the alphabetically first; log the chosen id and all candidates. If the repo is a LoRA adapter (adapter_config.json), pip install peft, merge onto Qwen/Qwen3-4B and save locally. Use the base tokenizer and chat template if the checkpoint lacks tokenizer files; assert equal vocabulary size and identical hidden size and layer count to Qwen/Qwen3-4B. If no 4B NSD checkpoint can be found or loaded, do not substitute any other model: write outputs/summary.json with status 'aborted_no_checkpoint' and the candidate list, and stop. Both models run with the Qwen3 chat template, enable_thinking=False and add_generation_prompt=True, each in its own vLLM process (dtype='bfloat16', max_model_len=6144, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9), base first. If vLLM cannot be imported 10 minutes after the first command, fall back to HF generate (batched, left padding acceptable for generate) with 40 questions per category and max_new_tokens 2048, and log it.

Part A (non-math MMLU-Pro). From the test split exclude category 'math'; for each remaining category draw 100 questions with a fixed seed (take all if fewer), yielding about 1,300 questions. User message: "The following is a multiple choice question about {category}. Think step by step and then finish your response with \"The answer is (X)\" where X is the letter of the correct option.\n\nQuestion: {question}\nOptions:\nA. {option_1}\nB. {option_2}\n..." listing all options with letters A-J. Greedy decoding (temperature 0), max_tokens 4096. Answer extraction: last match of the case-insensitive regex `answer is \\(?([A-J])\\)?`; fallback: the last standalone capital letter A-J (regex `\\b([A-J])\\b`) in the final non-empty line; no extraction => scored incorrect and flagged no_extraction. Record per question: category, response text, token count, finish_reason, extracted letter, gold letter, correctness.

Part B (chat-response NLL). Take the first 200 conversations of ultrachat_200k test_sft; use the first user turn and the first assistant turn; drop conversations whose assistant turn has fewer than 32 tokens; truncate assistant text to 768 tokens. Build prompt_token_ids = chat-template token ids for the user turn (add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False) + the tokenized assistant response, and obtain per-token log-probabilities of the assistant tokens from each model with vLLM SamplingParams(max_tokens=1, prompt_logprobs=0), reading the logprob of the actual token at each assistant position. If prompt_logprobs is unavailable in the installed vLLM, run a separate HF scoring process (right padding or one sequence at a time, float32 log_softmax). Report mean NLL per token for each model and the difference NSD - base with a 1000-resample bootstrap CI over conversations.

Statistics. Primary: Accuracy(NSD) - Accuracy(base) in percentage points over all sampled non-math questions, with a 1000-resample paired bootstrap over questions for the 95% CI. Also: per-category accuracies; accuracy for the quantitative group (physics, chemistry, engineering, computer science, economics, business) versus the remaining categories; accuracy restricted to responses with an extracted answer, together with each model's no-extraction rate and truncation rate; mean response token length per model; the chat NLL difference. A difference whose CI includes zero is reported as inconclusive, not as evidence of preservation.

event.description: The NSD checkpoint shows a material drop in non-math MMLU-Pro accuracy relative to the base model under identical greedy decoding.
event.statistic: Accuracy(NSD) minus Accuracy(base) in percentage points over the sampled non-math MMLU-Pro questions (about 1,300 questions, 100 per non-math category)

evaluation.procedure: outputs/mmlu_pro_base.jsonl and outputs/mmlu_pro_nsd.jsonl hold one line per question (question id, category, response text, token count, finish_reason, extracted letter, gold letter, correct flag, no_extraction flag). outputs/chat_nll.jsonl holds per conversation the assistant token count and the mean NLL under each model. outputs/summary.json holds the chosen NSD repo id and candidates (or the abort status), overall and per-category accuracies, quantitative versus non-quantitative group accuracies, the registered statistic with its paired bootstrap 95% CI, accuracy among extracted responses, no-extraction and truncation rates, mean response lengths, the chat NLL means and difference with CI, and the inference engine used. The registered statistic is the overall paired accuracy difference in points.
evaluation.controls: Base Qwen3-4B evaluated with the identical prompt, decoding and extraction is the paired control; greedy decoding removes sampling noise; the generous 4096-token cap and the separately reported no-extraction and truncation rates distinguish genuine capability loss from length- or format-driven failures without post-treatment selection; the quantitative/non-quantitative split shows whether any change is confined to math-adjacent categories; the chat NLL provides a decoding-free measure of distribution shift (descriptive, since any fine-tune can raise it).

models: released NSD Qwen3-4B checkpoint (discovered on the Hugging Face Hub as described; abort if absent)

If accuracy is preserved within a tight CI, the follow-up tests whether the preservation holds when NSD is trained longer or with weaker KL anchoring.

experiment/run.py broadens aborted_no_checkpoint handling to some preparation failures and any NSD worker failure, including failures after successful loading. This could misclassify a failed experiment, but none of these branches affected the completed evaluation or its reported value.
problems: outputs/summarize.log reports the fresh-run accuracy difference as -1.3846 percentage points with a 95% CI of [-3.5385, 0.7692]. This interval includes both zero and drops exceeding the registered three-point threshold, so the experiment establishes neither degradation nor preservation at that margin.

outputs/summary.json shows higher NSD no-extraction and truncation rates, especially in quantitative categories: no extraction increases from 4.83% to 10.50%, and truncation from 7.50% to 12.83%. These are meaningful end-to-end behavior differences, but the reported diagnostics do not identify whether the accuracy loss reflects underlying reasoning, verbosity, or answer completion. Accuracy among extracted responses conditions on different post-treatment subsets and cannot resolve that question.

The engineer's earlier run in evaluation.log and the notes reports -0.7692 percentage points, whereas the protected fresh run reports -1.3846 despite matching documented model revisions and sample fingerprints. The cause is not established; greedy decoding does not guarantee numerical reproducibility, and the bootstrap does not incorporate this execution variability.

experiment/run.py does not invoke experiment/validate.py, and the archive contains no fresh outputs/validation.json. The engineer's claimed independent integrity checks therefore should not be treated as checks demonstrated for the protected run.

outputs/nsd.log and outputs/prepare.log contain a tokenizer-regex warning. experiment/prepare.py checks vocabulary mappings and one template probe, not complete tokenizer equivalence. However, both models receive the same base-tokenized input IDs, so the warning alone does not establish an input mismatch or invalidate the measured comparison.

The chat NLL finding covers the first 200 UltraChat conversations, with 198 retained and responses capped at 768 tokens. Its lower NSD NLL measures likelihood on those reference responses, not generated chat quality, general capability preservation, or which NSD training component caused the change.
sol.reason: The completed evaluation follows the registered checkpoint discovery, fixed paired sample, prompts, greedy non-thinking decoding, extraction rules, statistic, and strict event threshold; no result-changing substantive departure is evident. The code computes the value from downloaded data and model-generated responses, and the protected result agrees with the fresh summary rather than the engineer's earlier test. Base accuracy was 60.85% versus 59.46% for NSD, but the uncertainty leaves both no difference and a material drop plausible. The descriptive quantitative-category completion changes and lower chat NLL provide meaningful, bounded evidence, warranting research value 2 without supporting a broad preservation claim.

Both models share that stack, so the paired comparison is unchanged; absolute generations could differ from another vLLM build, but the registration left versions open.

Extra vLLM engine settings in experiment/worker.py (max_num_seqs=128, max_num_batched_tokens=16384, seed=42, default prefix caching/cudagraphs) beyond the registered dtype, max_model_len=6144, and gpu_memory_utilization=0.9. These can perturb long greedy traces; they did not change temperature, max_tokens, prompts, or the event rule. A prior run of the same code differed by about 0.6 pp, so a small numeric change is plausible, not a change of question.
NLL SamplingParams in experiment/worker.py adds temperature=0 to the registered max_tokens=1, prompt_logprobs=0. Prompt-token logprobs are unaffected.

experiment/discover.py has an unused fallback that can re-include a LoRA id if no clean 4B candidate remains. It was not taken: the only eligible id was PassionPrc/NSD-Qwen3-4B. Could not change this result.

problems: Greedy outputs are not run-stable: the engineer's earlier evaluation.log run scored about -0.77 pp (CI about [-2.85, 1.38]) versus the fresh run's -1.38 pp (CI [-3.54, 0.77]) in outputs/summarize.log, with different quantitative truncation counts, while chat NLL matched exactly. NSD tokenizer regex warning in outputs/prepare.log and outputs/nsd.log (fix_mistral_regex not set). outputs/summary.json CI [-3.54, 0.77] includes both zero and the -3 threshold, so the pre-registered ≥3 pp drop is neither shown nor excluded. The write-up correctly calls this inconclusive rather than preservation.

The quantitative -3.33 pp gap is almost entirely no-extraction/truncation (NSD 10.5%/12.8% vs base 4.8%/7.5%) while accuracy among extracted answers is slightly higher for NSD (69.83% vs 69.18%). That confound is measured as registered, but the inclusive primary statistic mixes format failure with answer errors.
grok.reason: The fresh run executed the registered Hub discovery, identical non-thinking prompts, 100-per-category non-math sample, greedy 4096-token decoding, extraction-as-incorrect rule, paired bootstrap, and chat prompt-logprob NLL. The reported -1.3846 pp is the exact paired count from the 1300 generations (base 791 correct vs NSD 773), not a hard-coded result. Literal departures are version pins, unused discovery fallback, and vLLM batch settings; none change the question, and the event stays false. The finding is credible but not tight: the CI includes zero and -3, a second run moved the estimate by ~0.6 pp, and the quantitative deficit is truncation rather than extracted-answer loss, while chat NLL is slightly lower for NSD.

grok.what_it_asks: Compare released NSD-Qwen3-4B with base Qwen3-4B on non-math MMLU-Pro accuracy under identical greedy decoding to learn whether NSD training degrades non-math capability.

relation.reason: The hypothesis tests the paper’s stated claim that gated unlikelihood preserves foundational language ability, by asking whether the NSD model loses non-math accuracy relative to the base model.

next_step.reason: The CI is too wide to separate no effect from a 3 pp drop, and part of the quantitative gap traces to truncation and failed extraction rather than wrong answers.
