event.description: Averaged over completed tasks, the compiled 0.6B LoRA is more than 10 accuracy points better on real test sets than the same frozen 0.6B interpreter given the 8 TF-IDF-nearest synthesized pairs in context.
event.statistic: mean over completed tasks of [acc(LORA, Qwen3-0.6B) - acc(ICL-RET8, Qwen3-0.6B)] on TEST, strict correctness, 0-1 scale

evaluation.procedure: Accuracy on TEST for each (task, model, condition), macro-F1 (classification) or mean set F1 (ner), invalid rate, n, mean prompt tokens, seconds per 100 calls. Registered statistic = unweighted mean over completed tasks of acc(LORA-0.6B) - acc(ICL-RET8-0.6B). Secondaries: per-task table for all conditions; fraction of the (LORA - ZS) gap recovered by ICL-RET8 and by ICL-RAND8; LORA-0.6B minus ICL-RET8-1.7B (does the compiled small interpreter beat a 3x larger untrained one); acc(LORA-NOSPEC) - acc(LORA) (run-time dependence on the specification) and the prompt-token saving; acc(LORA+RET8) - acc(LORA); mean distinct labels among retrieved demos; paired bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples of test items, seed 0) per task and for the registered mean. outputs/scores.jsonl: one line per (task, model, condition) with accuracy, macro-F1 or set F1, invalid rate, n, mean prompt tokens, seconds per 100 calls. outputs/predictions.jsonl: one line per TEST item per condition with input, gold, raw generation, parsed prediction and retrieved demo indices where applicable. outputs/pool.jsonl: the synthesized pairs per task. outputs/summary.json: registered statistic, secondaries, CIs, per-task table, synthesis statistics, teacher used, skipped tasks, wall-clock per stage.
evaluation.controls: All conditions share the identical synthesized pool and test sets; ICL-RAND8 separates retrieval from mere example access; ZS controls for the specification alone; demonstrations use the same [INPUT]/[END_INPUT] blocks as the query to avoid format mixing; the 1.7B rows show whether a larger untrained interpreter matches the compiled 0.6B; the teacher ZS row bounds attainable accuracy; invalid rates are reported because chatty in-context outputs could be penalized by the parser; token counts expose the run-time cost side of the trade-off. Single training seed; per-task CIs reported.

registration.full_scale_study: If the margin is below 10 points: a cost/accuracy Pareto study of 'compile by retrieval' vs 'compile by training' across interpreter sizes (0.6B-8B), k in {2,4,8,16}, pool sizes and task families with longer outputs, including on-device latency, plus a hybrid in which the LoRA is trained with retrieved demonstrations in its prompt. If the margin is above 10 points: a study of why in-context use fails on small interpreters (demo-order sensitivity, label-space confusion) to justify the training cost in the seed's service, and, if LORA-NOSPEC holds up, a spec-free run-time scaffold to cut per-call tokens.

agent.reason: The LoRA should clearly beat 8-shot retrieved in-context use on a 0.6B interpreter, with large gaps on trec and name extraction, but on sentiment, topic and spam the kNN-like retrieved demonstrations may leave only a few points, making a mean margin above 10 points uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: I expect LoRA to help, but retrieved demonstrations should recover some of that benefit on these short-output tasks, making a greater-than-ten-point average advantage demanding. A smaller margin would still be informative without establishing equivalence or showing that training is unnecessary.

judge_fable.reason: Fine-tuning should beat retrieved in-context demonstrations on a 0.6B interpreter, but TF-IDF retrieval acts like a kNN label hint on topic/spam/question-type tasks and can recover a good share of the gain, so a mean margin above 10 points is less likely than a 4-8 point margin.

judge_opus.reason: The LoRA should clearly beat retrieval-ICL on subj, trec and NER. The margin is likely small on rt, sms and agnews, where 0.6B priors or TF-IDF nearest-neighbour label copying already work. The expected mean margin is around 6–10 points, just under the 10-point bar.

judge_sol.reason: LoRA may use the synthesized supervision more reliably than a small decoder processing long, potentially label-skewed demonstration prompts. Nevertheless, retrieved examples could recover enough performance on these relatively straightforward tasks to keep the average advantage below ten points.

judge_luna.reason: Training on 800 pairs should give the LoRA a useful advantage over eight retrieved demonstrations, particularly for a small interpreter. But retrieval may be strong on lexically local tasks, and the detailed specifications may already let the frozen model handle many classifications, so a mean margin above 10 points is uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Small decoders use 8 retrieved demos poorly and TF-IDF retrieval from a synthetic pool transfers weakly to real queries, but demos still teach format and label space so the LoRA advantage is likely positive yet below the demanding 10 point mean.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: T-Few compares PEFT (IA3) with in-context learning using human-labeled few-shot examples on T0 and GPT-3. It does not use a teacher-synthesized pool, per-query retrieved demonstrations, a spec-in-context 0.6B decoder interpreter, or the seed's fixed 100-step LoRA compile.

Mosbach et al. compare few-shot fine-tuning with ICL on OPT models using gold data and test out-of-domain generalization. They use no synthetic supervision, no retrieval from a generated pool, and no measurement of run-time spec or token cost.
SG-ICL uses model-generated demonstrations in context but never fine-tunes on the same generated pool. The training-vs-retrieval comparison is missing.
The seed compares compile by training only with PAW's amortized fast compiler. It reports no in-context or retrieval baseline that uses the same synthesized pairs and no spec-free run-time ablation.
PAW compares compiled adapters with direct prompting of larger models (e.g., Qwen3-32B). It does not test a 0.6B interpreter given demonstrations retrieved from a teacher-synthesized pool.

opus.reason: Many earlier papers compare fine-tuning with in-context learning, including T-Few and Mosbach et al. However, all of them use human-labeled examples. None of the papers I found trains a LoRA on a teacher-synthesized pool and compares it with in-context use of demonstrations retrieved from that same pool on a small spec-prompted interpreter. The seed itself omits this baseline, so the question of whether the gradient step does work beyond giving the model access to the examples remains open. My searches were fairly narrow and turned up no direct match, so a closer paper may exist that I did not find.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Inference-Time Distillation retrieves teacher-generated demonstrations for a frozen student and reports a fine-tuned GPT-4.1-mini comparator. It studies multi-step agents rather than specification-synthesized text functions on a sub-billion-parameter interpreter.

COSMOS directly compares QLoRA with retrieval-augmented ICL and measures performance-cost tradeoffs. Its demonstrations come from labeled benchmark training sets rather than a teacher-synthesized pool.

This DSL-generation study compares fine-tuning on synthetic input-output pairs with retrieving synthetic demonstrations. It compares fine-tuned Codex against prompted GPT-4, rather than controlling the interpreter model.
The seed compares specification-specific training with amortized compilation, but does not compare training with retrieval from the same synthesized pool.

sol.reason: Prior work already examines the central choice between parameter adaptation and retrieving teacher-generated examples into a frozen student's context, including fine-tuned comparators and runtime-cost accounting. The proposed same-interpreter control, specification-only synthesis, fixed short training budget, and no-specification ablation refine that established comparison rather than introduce an unanswered adaptation question. None of the papers found reports the exact registered experiment or its ten-point margin.

opus.reason: Both ask whether gradient training adds accuracy beyond giving the frozen 0.6B interpreter the specification plus synthesized demonstrations in context, measured on real classification test sets against zero-shot and teacher baselines; the registered version differs mainly in retrieving the demonstrations per query.

sol.reason: Both test gradient training against in-context use of the same synthesized supervision on the frozen 0.6B interpreter using real-test accuracy, with retrieval refining demonstration selection in the registered version.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: run.sh installs the packages, downloads Qwen3-8B, 1.7B and 0.6B in the background, then runs main.py, which carries out the registered pipeline. The steps are: test sets, teacher synthesis using the seed's prompts verbatim, TF-IDF retrieval, the 100-step rank-64 LoRA compile (no warm start), and all registered conditions (0.6B: ZS, ICL-RAND8, ICL-RET8, LORA, LORA-NOSPEC, LORA+RET8; 1.7B: ZS, ICL-RET8; teacher: ZS). It writes the registered raw outputs, a paired bootstrap, the secondaries and result.json.

Test run on this machine, one repetition, end to end through `bash run.sh`, about 11 minutes. The teacher was Qwen3-8B; the 4B fallback was not needed. Registered statistic = 0.166 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.139–0.190) over 6 completed tasks. Per task: rt +0.25, subj +0.11, agnews +0.31, irony −0.15, sms +0.11, ner +0.37. The value is above the 0.10 threshold, so the registered event occurred in this run. This is one run with one training seed, and a fresh machine may give a slightly different value.

Deviations and implementation choices:
1. trec was skipped by the registered rule. The 8B teacher produced only 158 unique valid pairs in 5 batches (2402 of 2560 items were case-insensitive duplicate inputs), below the 480 minimum. The statistic is therefore over 6 tasks, not 7.
2. In the classification pools, the teacher's output is stored as the canonical label word parsed from it. All synthesized outputs parsed cleanly (0 invalid).
3. Dataset loading falls back to the HF `refs/convert/parquet` revision for any dataset, not only conll2003, because datasets 5.x has no script support. In the test run every dataset loaded.
4. Within each condition, test prompts are sorted by length for batching; the original order is restored in the outputs. Timings were measured at the registered batch sizes.
5. Order of installs and downloads: transformers was not preinstalled, so `huggingface_hub` and `hf_transfer` are installed first, then the downloads start, and the other packages install while they run. With huggingface_hub 1.x, the hf_transfer setting is probably a no-op.
6. For ner, the "distinct labels among retrieved demos" figure counts distinct lower-cased output strings. ner "invalid" means an empty generation.
7. The time guard and the 8-minute teacher fallback are timed from when run.sh starts.

Observations from the test run (descriptive only):
- With demonstrations in context, the 0.6B model often collapses to one label. ICL-RAND8 predicted "negative" for all 300 rt items. As a result, ICL-RET8 (mean accuracy 0.599) and ICL-RAND8 (0.522) were below zero-shot (0.651). So the "fraction of the gap recovered" figures are negative or unstable, and should not be read as recovery.
- irony is the exception: there LoRA was worse than both zero-shot and ICL-RET8, so the compile hurt.
- LORA-NOSPEC fails almost completely (mean accuracy 0.012): the compiled LoRA still needs the specification in its prompt at run time.
- Adding retrieved demos to the LoRA prompt (LORA+RET8) lowered accuracy by 0.09.
- The compiled 0.6B LoRA roughly matched the untrained 1.7B with retrieved demos: +0.043 averaged over tasks, with the sign varying by task.
- Teacher (8B) zero-shot mean accuracy was 0.833.
- The registered ner parser reads only the first line, so it mis-parses ICL outputs that start with an "[OUTPUT]" line. This affected only 4 of 300 ICL-RET8 ner items.

departures: Task trec was dropped (main.py synthesize and the POOL_MIN check). The 8B teacher produced only 158 unique valid pairs (2402 duplicates), so the registered skip rule (fewer than 480 pairs) applied. The statistic is the mean over 6 tasks, not 7. This is the registered rule, so it is not a fidelity defect, but it does change which tasks are averaged.
In main.py load_any, the 'refs/convert/parquet' revision fallback is tried for every dataset, not only conll2003. Every dataset loaded, so this cannot have changed the result.

In main.py synthesize, classification pool outputs are replaced by the label word parsed from the teacher's output. The registration only requires that the output parse to a label word. The synthesis stats show 0 invalid items. This could alter demonstration and training targets only if the teacher wrote extra text around the label, so the effect is likely negligible.

In main.py generate, test prompts are sorted by length before batching and the original order is restored afterwards. The registration leaves batch composition open. Under greedy decoding this can only shift bf16 numerics slightly, so the effect is negligible.

In main.py generate, generation runs under torch.autocast(bf16). Models are already bf16, and the LoRA adapters are fp32 cast to bf16. The registration does not fix the evaluation precision. Effect is negligible.

In main.py compile_lora, the training order comes from one RandomState(0) whose successive permutations are concatenated. The registration's wording 'reshuffled each pass with seed 0' is ambiguous. This is a legitimate reading with at most minor effect.

In run.sh, huggingface_hub and hf_transfer are installed before the downloads start. With huggingface_hub 1.x the hf_transfer setting is a no-op (see the .dl logs). The 8B finished in about 12 s and no 4B fallback was needed. No effect on the result.

For ner, 'invalid' is defined as an empty generation, and 'distinct labels' counts distinct lowercased output strings. The registration leaves both undefined for ner. These affect only secondary reporting.
For sms, message text is .strip()-ed before the 1200-character filter and the first-300 selection. Effect is negligible.
The time guard and the teacher fallback are both timed from the start of run.sh, which is the registered 'first command'. No departure.
problems: The registered contrast is inflated by a weak baseline. In-context use hurts the 0.6B model relative to zero-shot: mean ICL-RET8 is 0.599 and ICL-RAND8 is 0.522, against 0.651 for ZS. Both ICL conditions often collapse to one label (ICL-RAND8 predicts 'negative' for all rt items).

From the per-task accuracies in outputs/scores.jsonl, LORA minus ZS averages about +0.11, while LORA minus ICL-RET8 is 0.166. About a third of the margin therefore comes from ICL degrading below zero-shot, not from the gradient step outperforming a working retrieval baseline. This affects the interpretation the seed connection proposes.

The effect is heterogeneous across tasks (summary.json per_task): +0.37 on ner, +0.31 on agnews, and -0.15 on irony, where the compiled LoRA (0.373) is worse than zero-shot and below the 60% literal base rate.

The bootstrap CI [0.139, 0.190] reflects only resampling of test items. It ignores the single training seed, the single synthesized pool, and the variation across only 6 tasks. A task-level interval would be much wider and would likely include 0.10.
There is one repetition and one LoRA seed. The fresh-machine run reproduced the engineer's run.log values exactly, which shows determinism, not robustness.
The 8B teacher 'ceiling' is below the 0.6B and 1.7B zero-shot scores on irony (0.66 vs 0.70 and 0.817), so it does not bound attainable accuracy on that task.

The registered ner parser reads only the first line, so ICL outputs that begin with an '[OUTPUT]' line are mis-scored. The engineer reports this affects 4 of 300 ICL-RET8 items, which is a small bias against ICL.

Zero-shot accuracy of 0.6B on agnews is 0.273, below the 0.25-plus-margin one would expect from a model using the spec. This inflates LORA-ZS on that task but does not enter the registered statistic directly.
opus.reason: main.py implements the registered pipeline closely: tasks, specs, the seed's synthesis prompts, TF-IDF retrieval, prompt formats, the 100-step rank-64 LoRA recipe, decoding settings, all conditions and the statistic. The only substantive change, dropping trec, follows the registered skip rule, and the other departures are implementation choices with negligible effect. The fresh-machine evaluation regenerated all registered outputs from real model generations and real test data, and reproduced the submitted run's numbers exactly. The registered value of 0.166 (event occurred) is therefore credible for this setup. It should be read with care: much of the margin comes from in-context demonstrations making the 0.6B model worse than zero-shot, the effect reverses on irony, and the CI ignores seed, pool and task-level variance. The secondaries are informative: LORA-NOSPEC collapses, LORA+RET8 hurts, and the compiled 0.6B roughly matches 1.7B with retrieved demonstrations. Overall this is a meaningful but single-seed, moderately supported finding.

departures: main.py, build_task('sms'): uses Hugging Face Dataset.shuffle(seed=0), rather than the registered NumPy RandomState-based randomization. These randomization procedures are not interchangeable, so the first 300 SMS rows can differ. This can change SMS accuracy and the registered mean.

main.py, build_task('sms'): strips SMS text before length filtering and evaluation, whereas the registration specifies the sms column without this normalization. This can alter inputs or eligibility near the length cutoff, although its actual effect is not established.

main.py, synthesize: replaces accepted classification outputs with their parsed canonical label words instead of retaining the teacher's output strings. This can change both training targets and demonstrations when accepted outputs contain additional text or different capitalization. Zero invalid outputs does not establish that normalization changed nothing; the original teacher generations were not retained.

main.py, synthesize: strips synthesized inputs before duplicate detection and storage, checks minimum input length after stripping, and strips NER outputs before checking their length. These are additional normalization and acceptance rules that could change pool membership or prompt/target text; their actual effect cannot be determined from the supplied excerpts.

main.py, parse_ner: deletes brackets, braces, parentheses, quotes and backticks throughout the first line, rather than merely stripping the registered brackets/quotes and item boundaries. In particular, deleting internal apostrophes can alter legitimate person names while gold names retain them. It also interprets 'letters' using only [a-z]. These differences can change NER correctness, though no conclusion-changing effect is demonstrated.

main.py, load_any: adds the refs/convert/parquet fallback to every dataset and retries separately for each revision and dataset identifier, expanding the registered loading/retry policy. This is a reasonable compatibility accommodation for unsupported dataset scripts; different revisions or additional successful retries could affect data or task inclusion, but no adverse effect is established here.

main.py, generate: sorts prompts by token length before batching and restores their original order afterward. Batching order was left open by the registration, so this is an acceptable implementation choice. It changes throughput and potentially numerical batching behavior, but there is no demonstrated accuracy effect.

main.py, generate and main: reported seconds per 100 calls exclude prompt construction, retrieval, the initial token-length calculation and sorting. They measure the subsequent batched generation/tokenization loop rather than complete application-call wall time. This changes the interpretation of the timing secondary, not the registered accuracy statistic.

run.sh: installs huggingface_hub and hf_transfer before starting downloads, omits the registered pip -U option, and loads datasets only after package installation. The transfer flag is also deprecated and ineffective in the installed Hub version. These differences can affect dependencies and elapsed time, but the fresh run completed well before the time guard, with no demonstrated effect on the statistic.

main.py, wait_for: checks the eight-minute teacher fallback only after unconditional waits for the smaller models, and accepts an already-present 8B completion marker even if that check occurs after the deadline. This differs from a strict deadline-triggered fallback rule, but all downloads completed promptly here, so it did not affect this run.
problems: main.py: the SMS sampling implementation is a material, unreported departure from the registered randomization procedure.
outputs/pool.jsonl: only normalized synthesized pairs are retained, preventing verification of whether canonicalization changed accepted teacher targets or demonstrations.

main.py, parse_ner: global character deletion can corrupt names relative to the gold representation. Separately, the engineer reports four ICL-RET8 NER outputs affected by the registered first-line parser; that limitation is not itself an implementation departure and cannot alone overturn the threshold result.

outputs/summary.json: bootstrap intervals condition on the completed tasks, synthesized pools and single training run. They do not quantify variation across task selection, synthesis seeds or training seeds.

outputs/scores.jsonl and outputs/summary.json: the mean advantage is heterogeneous and partly reflects a weak ICL configuration. RT LoRA accuracy is almost unchanged from zero-shot, while irony training substantially hurts accuracy; the result does not establish that gradient updates are generally necessary.

main.py and outputs/scores.jsonl: timing measurements omit retrieval and other application overhead and represent batched throughput, not individual deployment latency. Shorter prompts also do not guarantee faster generation: NER LoRA is slower than frozen ICL-RET8 in the reported measurements.

The no-spec ablation removes a component present throughout training, so its failure demonstrates sensitivity to this runtime prompt change, not an inherent inability to train a specification-free compiled function. Teacher zero-shot performance is likewise a reference, not a strict accuracy ceiling.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation produced real model outputs and a registered-form mean advantage of 0.16556, with a paired item-bootstrap interval of approximately 0.139–0.190 across six tasks; TREC's exclusion followed the registered minimum-pool rule. Fidelity is unfaithful because the SMS randomization can change the evaluated sample, with additional normalization and parsing departures affecting the implementation. The supplied code supports the reported computation without hard-coded outcomes, apparent evaluation-label leakage, or a demonstrated error that reverses the conclusion, so the evidence is valid for the implemented comparison. Shared pools, multiple controls and a clear conditional margin make this a meaningful finding, but one-run uncertainty, task heterogeneity and the specific weak ICL configuration limit its broader significance.

departures: main.py synthesize() replaces classification teacher outputs with the canonical parsed label word before they enter the shared pool, instead of keeping the raw string once it parses to a label (engineer reported). That can change ICL demonstration text and LoRA targets if raw strings were not already bare labels; raw teacher generations were not saved, so a small shift cannot be excluded, but the specs demand one label word and every kept output parsed, so it did not plausibly move the reported mean across 0.10.

main.py load_any() tries revision refs/convert/parquet for every dataset, not only conll2003 as registered (engineer reported). The default load is tried first and succeeded, so this did not change the test data or the result.

main.py build_task() for sms strips whitespace and drops texts longer than 1200 characters after the seed-0 shuffle and before taking 300 rows; the registration says shuffle the train split then take the first 300, with long rows dropped. No evidence any SMS exceeded 1200 characters, so this did not plausibly change the result.

run.sh installs huggingface_hub and hf_transfer before starting downloads, and HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER is a no-op on huggingface_hub 1.x (engineer reported). This was required for the run to start; the registered models downloaded and it did not change the statistic.
problems: The mean is not uniform: summary.json per_task is rt +0.25, subj +0.11, agnews +0.31, irony -0.15 (CI entirely below 0), sms +0.11, ner +0.37, so agnews and ner dominate and irony reverses the claim.

Much of the registered gap is ICL degradation rather than a compile gain over the specification: scores.jsonl / summary.json show 0.6B ICL-RET8 mean accuracy about 0.599 versus ZS about 0.651, and on rt LORA (0.817) barely exceeds ZS (0.813) while ICL collapses; gap-recovered ratios are negative or unstable (rt about -74).

trec was skipped under the registered <480-pair rule (summary.json: 158 unique pairs, 2402/2560 duplicate inputs), so the statistic is over the six tasks the teacher could diversify, not the full suite.
Only one training seed; the paired bootstrap in summary.json resamples test items only and does not capture training variability.

The registered first-line NER parser mis-reads ICL generations that start with an [OUTPUT] line (engineer notes: 4/300 ICL-RET8 ner items); effect on the mean is about 0.002 and does not change the event.
Synthetic pools are generic and label-imbalanced (summary.json: irony 480/320, sms 462/338), which limits how far the LoRA-versus-retrieval contrast generalizes.
grok.reason: The fresh run executes the registered method, data, controls, and statistic: shared 800-pair pools, TF-IDF k=8, the 100-step rank-64 LoRA recipe, and the unweighted mean of per-task accuracy gaps, computed as 0.166 with item-bootstrap 95% CI 0.139-0.190 over six tasks. Listed departures are either unused on the success path or too small to plausibly change that value or the question. Scores, predictions, and pools are real model outputs with no leakage or hard-coded results, and they reproduce the logged accuracies. The pre-registered event is supported, but the evidence is not uniformly strong: irony goes the wrong way, two tasks drive the mean, and retrieval ICL often falls below zero-shot, so the gap is not purely a gradient-step gain over example access.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether a rank-64 LoRA trained on teacher-synthesized examples is more accurate than the same frozen 0.6B interpreter shown the eight most similar of those examples as in-context demonstrations, on held-out real tasks.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares compile-by-training only with the amortized compiler and does not name a retrieval or in-context baseline on the same synthesized pairs as undone work.

relation.reason: The experiment uses the paper's synthesize-then-LoRA compile as a working part and tests it against retrieval in-context use, a comparison the paper never makes and on which its claims do not depend.

obvious.reason: Several readers would list training against in-context use of the same synthetic pool, but the paper's own open ends would fill most first-ten lists and fewer would specify nearest-example retrieval rather than a generic few-shot control.

who_would_care.reason: A clear margin either way would change whether people who compile 0.6B functions from specifications keep the training step or replace it with retrieval, not how the rest of adaptation research works.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements about the minute-scale gain over the amortized compiler, the example-bearing scaffold, the 100-step rank-64 recipe, and the absence of a retrieval baseline match the paper.

answerable.reason: The design measures accuracy of the compiled LoRA and of retrieval ICL on the same pool and the same test items, so either direction would bear on the comparison.

grok.what_came_out: On six tasks with 300 test items each and one training seed (Qwen3-8B teacher, Qwen3-0.6B interpreter; trec skipped), compiled LoRA beat TF-IDF retrieval ICL by 0.166 accuracy on average (paired bootstrap 95% CI 0.139–0.190), with per-task gaps +0.25, +0.11, +0.31, −0.15, +0.11, and +0.37.

prerequisite.reason: Training loss fell on every completed task and invalid rates on the two compared conditions were essentially zero, so the accuracy gap can be read directly.

evidence.reason: The mean gap of 0.166 has a paired bootstrap 95% CI of 0.139–0.190, entirely above the claimed 0.10 margin, so item-level noise does not explain the LoRA advantage.

next_step.reason: The 0.6B LoRA-versus-retrieval gap is large and its item-level interval sits above 10 points, which justifies a broader study of the same comparison rather than a repair.

opus.what_it_asks: Does a 100-step LoRA compiled on teacher-synthesized pairs for the frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter beat the same untrained interpreter given the most similar synthesized pairs as in-context demonstrations, on real test inputs, and so show that the gradient step adds value beyond access to the examples?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares compile by training only with the fast amortized compiler, has no in-context baseline that uses the synthesized pairs, and never names one as future work.

relation.reason: The paper's compile recipe and its synthesis prompts are working parts of the experiment, and they are set against an alternative use of the same synthesized pool that the paper makes no claim about, so the paper's fast-compiler result stands whichever way this comes out.

obvious.reason: Asking whether few-shot prompting with the same synthesized examples would do as well as fine-tuning is a standard reviewer question for any distill-then-finetune paper.

who_would_care.reason: The answer mainly decides whether the PAW service, and similar spec-to-adapter systems, need the training step or could offer a zero-GPU retrieval option.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements about the paper match its text: about a minute of training, a 2:1 teacher mix, a scaffold carrying instructions and examples, and a rank-64 LoRA recipe with warm start; small recipe differences such as batch size are choices of the plan, not claims about the paper.

answerable.reason: Both conditions share the pool, the test sets and the interpreter, so a clear gap or no gap in either direction bears on whether training adds value beyond in-context use of the examples.

opus.what_came_out: On Qwen3-0.6B with an 8B-teacher pool, averaged over 6 completed tasks (300 test items each, one seed, trec skipped), LoRA minus retrieved-8-shot ICL was +0.166 (paired bootstrap 95% CI 0.139–0.190); the gap was positive on five tasks (+0.11 to +0.37) and negative on irony (−0.15, CI −0.21 to −0.10), and ICL-RET8 averaged 0.599, below zero-shot at 0.651.

prerequisite.reason: Training clearly took (loss fell, LoRA beat zero-shot on five of six tasks), and the ICL condition responded to retrieval (+0.077 over random demos), so the comparison is readable, although the ICL baseline fell below zero-shot.

evidence.reason: The averaged gap of 0.166 has a CI well above zero and even above the 0.10 bar, and it is consistent across five of six tasks; irony is a single reversed task within a hypothesis stated as an average.

next_step.reason: The run answers its question, but the in-context baseline did worse than zero-shot and often collapsed to one label, which raises the worry that the demonstration format handicapped it.
next_step.what: Rerun ICL-RET8 with a stronger demonstration format (demos as multi-turn chat exchanges and label-balanced retrieval) to check that the LoRA margin survives a well-functioning in-context baseline.

sol.what_it_asks: It compares task-specific LoRA training of Qwen3-0.6B with retrieved in-context demonstrations from the same teacher-synthesized pool on real classification and person-name extraction inputs to learn whether training yields higher accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper neither measures this training-versus-retrieval comparison nor explicitly identifies it as an unanswered question.

relation.reason: The experiment puts the paper's synthesized supervision to a new retrieval-based use and tests a comparative advantage over that alternative that the paper does not claim.

obvious.reason: Fine-tuning versus in-context reuse of synthetic examples is a familiar follow-up, but retrieving demonstrations per query is more specific than merely adding a prompting baseline.

who_would_care.reason: Researchers across compact-model specialization could use the answer when choosing between synthetic-data fine-tuning and retrieval-based prompting.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's checkable descriptions of synthetic supervision, the frozen 0.6B interpreter, the example-bearing scaffold and 100-step LoRA compilation do not contradict the paper.

answerable.reason: Directly evaluating both specified systems on identical real test inputs makes either an advantage or its absence informative without requiring reproduction of the paper's original result.

sol.what_came_out: In one training-seed evaluation of Qwen3-0.6B on 300 inputs each from Rotten Tomatoes, SUBJ, AG News, TweetEval irony, SMS Spam and CoNLL-2003 person extraction, LoRA averaged 76.4% accuracy versus 59.9% for retrieved ICL using the same Qwen3-8B-synthesized pools, a 16.6-point advantage with an item-bootstrap 95% interval of 13.9–19.0 points.

prerequisite.reason: Training losses decreased and both main conditions produced scorable predictions, while poor ICL performance is an outcome of the tested baseline rather than a failed prerequisite.

evidence.reason: The hypothesis concerns the task-average advantage, whose confidence interval is clearly positive, although irony shows a confident task-specific reversal and the interval does not capture training-seed variation.

next_step.reason: The tested comparison is answered, but retrieved ICL averaging below zero-shot leaves prompt-format sensitivity as a concrete gap to close before a larger study.
next_step.what: Repeat the comparison with retrieved demonstrations rendered as separate user/assistant turns, keeping the synthesized pools, retrieval choices, test inputs and trained adapters fixed.

registration.title: The best use of a small unlabeled sample at compile time: seeding teacher synthesis with real inputs versus labeling them directly
registration.seed_connection: The seed's teacher prompt is 'Generate n diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification' with nothing but the specification, so the teacher must imagine what inputs look like, and evaluation is only on LLM-generated inputs. Real deployments of the seed's examples (email triage, website questions, log lines) have unlabeled inputs lying around. This MVE tests the two cheapest ways to use 128 of them inside the seed's pipeline: show them to the synthesizing teacher as unlabeled style exemplars, or have the teacher label them and mix them into the synthesized training set, and measures the effect on accuracy on real gold-labeled inputs.
registration.hypothesis: Seeding each synthesis call with 8 unlabeled real inputs drawn from a pool of 128 raises the compiled 0.6B function's gold-test accuracy by at least 3 points on average over spec-only synthesis at the same pair count, teacher and recipe.
registration.contribution: AttrPrompt and ZeroGen diversify generated data without real inputs, Ding et al. seed generation with labeled few-shot examples, and Prompt2Model mixes generated data with retrieved real labeled datasets. None tests label-free seeding with a small unlabeled pool inside a spec-to-LoRA compile pipeline, compares it with the alternative of teacher-labeling the same pool, or checks the copying and diversity side effects. The outcome is uncertain: the teacher may copy the exemplars (low diversity), ignore them, or transmit only the class prior.

closest_work.difference: AttrPrompt diversifies generated data via LLM-proposed attributes with no real inputs and encoder-classifier students; this MVE conditions on unlabeled real inputs inside a spec-only compile pipeline and compares with direct labeling of the same inputs.
Seeds GPT-3 generation with labeled 2/10-shot examples; this MVE uses label-free exemplars (8 per call from a pool of 128) and a generative 0.6B LoRA student.
Prompt2Model adds retrieved real labeled datasets; here only unlabeled real inputs are used, either as synthesis context or as teacher-labeled training pairs.
The seed pipeline synthesizes from the specification alone and is evaluated only on LLM-generated inputs.

inputs: Models (HF Hub): Qwen/Qwen3-8B (teacher; Qwen/Qwen3-4B as a time fallback), Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (interpreter)
Datasets (HF Hub): cornell-movie-review-data/rotten_tomatoes, SetFit/subj, fancyzhx/ag_news, CogComp/trec, cardiffnlp/tweet_eval (config irony), ucirvine/sms_spam
Python: torch, transformers>=4.51, peft, datasets, accelerate, scikit-learn, hf_transfer
Seed recipe (compile.py of github.com/programasweights/compile-by-training) restated verbatim in the method

event.description: Averaged over completed tasks, the function compiled from exemplar-seeded synthesis beats the function compiled from spec-only synthesis by at least 3 accuracy points on real gold-labeled test inputs.
event.statistic: mean over completed tasks of [acc(SEEDED) - acc(SYN)] on TEST, strict label match, 0-1 scale

evaluation.procedure: Accuracy per (task, arm) = fraction of TEST items whose parsed prediction equals the gold label word (invalid = wrong); macro-F1 (sklearn, labels = label words, invalid mapped outside the label set), n and invalid rate also recorded. Registered statistic = unweighted mean over completed tasks of acc(SEEDED) - acc(SYN). Secondaries: mean acc(MIX) - acc(SYN); mean acc(SEEDED) - acc(MIX); the same differences in macro-F1 (to see how much of any gain is class-prior matching); number of tasks with a positive SEEDED - SYN difference; change in shift AUC from SYN to SEEDED and its across-task relation to the accuracy gain (descriptive); copy rates and distinct-2 for both arms; TEACHER-ZS and STUDENT-ZS; paired bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples of test items, seed 0) per task and for the registered mean. outputs/scores.jsonl: one line per (task, arm or reference) with accuracy, macro-F1, n, invalid rate, pair count, label distribution. outputs/predictions.jsonl: one line per TEST item per arm/reference with input, gold, raw generation, parsed prediction. outputs/pools.jsonl: all SYN, SEEDED and MIX pairs with arm, origin (synthetic or teacher-labeled real) and, for SEEDED, the exemplar indices shown in the generating call. outputs/diagnostics.json: shift AUCs, copy rates, distinct-2, lengths, label distributions, synthesis statistics, wall-clock per stage. outputs/summary.json: registered statistic, secondaries, CIs, per-task table, teacher used, skipped tasks.
evaluation.controls: SYN and SEEDED differ only in the appended exemplar block (same teacher, sampling settings, pair count, dedup, recipe, prompt, seed and test set); MIX uses the same 128 inputs in the alternative role (labeled training pairs) at equal N, so the two uses of the same unlabeled sample are directly comparable; copy-rate and shift-AUC diagnostics separate genuine distribution matching from memorizing the 128 exemplars; macro-F1 and label distributions expose prior-matching effects; TEACHER-ZS bounds attainable accuracy. Single training seed; per-task signs and CIs reported.

registration.full_scale_study: If seeding gains at least 3 points: sweep exemplar pool size (8-1024) and exemplars per call, compare exemplar selection strategies (random vs clustering for coverage), seed the run-time scaffold's examples as well, combine seeding with direct labeling, test on 20+ specifications including generative functions graded by a local judge with multiple seeds, and add an 'upload unlabeled inputs' step to the compile service. If seeding does not help, examine whether the teacher ignores exemplars (prompt variants, larger teachers) or whether direct labeling of a small unlabeled sample is the better default.

agent.reason: Showing real unlabeled inputs should move synthesized inputs toward the real style and prior (large expected gains on subj, sms and trec), but the effect must survive a single-seed batch-16 compile and possibly noisier labels on more realistic inputs, so a 3-point mean gain is about even odds.

judge_astra.reason: Unlabeled exemplars plausibly improve vocabulary, style and class-prior matching, particularly for SMS and subjectivity. However, improved surface resemblance need not improve decision-boundary coverage, so exceeding three accuracy points on average remains uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: Showing the teacher real unlabeled inputs should reduce distribution shift and transmit the natural class prior, and the high-shift tasks (sms, irony, subj, trec) are scheduled first, so a mean gain of 3+ points is somewhat more likely than not conditional on a clean run; execution risk (two synthesis arms, three compiles per task) and training variance at 480 pairs keep the overall probability moderate.

judge_opus.reason: Seeding should help modestly, mostly through realistic style and real class priors on sms, subj and trec. Its gain is capped by the probably modest teacher-labeled-real-versus-synthetic input gap, so a mean of at least 3 points is uncertain.

judge_sol.reason: Unlabeled exemplars should help synthesis reproduce real SMS, tweet, and review styles, making an accuracy gain plausible. However, style matching does not necessarily supply difficult decision boundaries, and residual label errors or limited diversity could keep the gain below three points.

judge_luna.reason: Real exemplars could anchor generated inputs to the style of tweets or SMS messages, but the specifications already describe the input formats and the teacher may ignore or copy the exemplars. A three-point average gain across tasks therefore seems possible but not more likely than not.

judge_muse.reason: Eight real exemplars per call should steer Qwen3-8B synthesis toward real SMS and tweet style with task order front-loading high-shift tasks, but 8B style-following is uncertain and diversity and copying effects may dilute the 3 point mean gain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Veselovsky et al. ground ChatGPT generation in real tweets whose labels have been thrown away. They find grounding beats simple prompting (macro-F1 0.55 vs 0.48) on a single sarcasm task with an E5 encoder student. Each prompt shows one real text, which the model makes both sarcastic and not sarcastic. Their only comparisons are zero-shot ChatGPT annotation and training on gold labels. They never train on teacher-labeled versions of the same real inputs at equal N, which is the MIX arm here. They also run no copy-rate check and use no spec-to-LoRA generative student.

SynthesizRR seeds synthesis with passages retrieved from a large unlabeled corpus and shows gains in diversity and distillation. Its baseline is 32-shot labeled prompting, not specification-only synthesis. The corpus is a large retrieval source rather than a small sample of 128 deployment inputs, and the paper does not compare against teacher-labeling those inputs.
Ding et al. seed GPT-3 generation with labeled few-shot examples. This experiment uses unlabeled exemplars and also tests direct labeling as the alternative use of the same pool.
AttrPrompt gets diversity from attributes the LLM proposes itself, with no real inputs and no labeling-versus-seeding comparison.
Prompt2Model mixes synthetic data with retrieved real labeled datasets. It does not use a small unlabeled pool, either as synthesis context or as teacher-labeled pairs.
This is the seed paper. It synthesizes from the specification alone and evaluates on LLM-generated inputs. It does not use real unlabeled inputs and does not evaluate on gold-labeled real data.

opus.reason: Prior work already suggests that grounding synthesis in unlabeled real text helps. The clearest case is Veselovsky et al., which compares grounded and spec-only synthesis on one sarcasm task, so the first half of the question is partly anticipated. No paper I found sets up the main comparison here: seeding with the 128 inputs versus teacher-labeling the same 128 and mixing them in at equal N, across several tasks, inside a spec-to-LoRA compile pipeline with a small generative student, with checks for copying and distribution shift. My search tool returned noisy results and I ran out of searches, so I may have missed some 2025–2026 work, but nothing I found settles the question.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: BARRED trains task-specific LoRA guardrails from specifications and small unlabeled seed sets, but uses dimension decomposition and debate-based validation. It does not isolate the effect of adding unlabeled exemplars to otherwise identical synthesis or compare against directly teacher-labeling the same pool.

FreeAL prompts an LLM with randomly selected unlabeled texts to generate style-matched labeled examples. These examples serve as demonstrations for annotating real inputs, rather than as the student's synthetic training set in a controlled seeded-versus-unseeded comparison.

Synthetic Data Generation with Large Language Models for Text Classification: Potential and Limitations compares example-guided and zero-shot synthesis at matched training sizes on real gold tests, including SMS spam and tweet irony. Its exemplars include human-provided labels, so it does not answer whether unlabeled inputs alone help or whether labeling that same sample is preferable.

Is GPT-3 a Good Data Annotator? compares direct annotation of real inputs with synthetic training-data generation, but its few-shot generation uses labeled demonstrations and does not test unlabeled contextual seeding against spec-only synthesis.

The seed establishes specification-to-synthetic-supervision-to-LoRA compilation, but its synthesis prompt contains no real-input exemplars and it does not compare alternative uses of an unlabeled deployment sample.

sol.reason: Unlabeled-example-guided synthesis is already established in FreeAL and BARRED, so that ingredient alone is not novel. However, the work I found does not answer the controlled question of whether label-free contextual seeding improves over specification-only synthesis, compared with teacher-labeling the same limited pool at equal training-set size; the distinction is not merely the model or compilation interface.

opus.reason: No list entry tests seeding teacher synthesis with unlabeled real input exemplars or compares that with teacher-labeling the same small unlabeled pool.

sol.reason: No listed experiment compares unlabeled-real-input-seeded synthesis with spec-only synthesis and direct labeling of the same small real-input pool.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the registered MVE as written in exp.py and summarize.py. run.sh runs the whole thing: it installs packages, downloads the models in the background, runs the experiment, then writes result.json and the outputs. Teacher: Qwen3-8B bf16 (it downloaded within seconds, so the 4B fallback was never used). Student: Qwen3-0.6B, with LoRA r64/alpha16 on all projection layers, AdamW 2e-4 with cosine decay to 2e-5 over 100 steps, batch 16, loss on the target only. Synthesis uses the seed paper's prompts verbatim, with sampling at temperature 1.0 / top_p 0.95 / top_k 0. Task specs, parser, dedup, the 480-pair cap, the 320-pair minimum, the SEEDED exemplar block, MIX construction, diagnostics, bootstraps and the 26-minute guard all follow the registration.

Test run on this machine (one full run of the same command, about 17 min after setup; synthesis is sampled, so a rerun may differ slightly):
- Five tasks completed: sms, irony, subj, rt and agnews.
- **trec was skipped under the registered "at least 320 pairs" rule.** Spec-only SYN synthesis produced only 145 unique valid pairs in 4 batches, mostly because of duplicate questions. SEEDED produced 450. So this skip is itself a result about synthesis yield.
- **Registered statistic: mean acc(SEEDED) − acc(SYN) = 0.0205**, bootstrap 95% CI [0.009, 0.034].
- Per task: sms +0.035, irony +0.115, subj −0.060, rt +0.003, agnews +0.010.
- **The 0.0205 is below the 0.03 threshold, so the registered event did not occur.** SEEDED beat SYN on 4 of 5 tasks, and the CI excludes zero. That is evidence of a small positive effect; it is not evidence that the effect reaches 3 points.

Secondaries:
- MIX − SYN: −0.002, CI [−0.014, 0.010].
- SEEDED − MIX: +0.0225.
- Macro-F1, SEEDED − SYN: +0.036.
- Shift AUC fell from 0.996 (SYN) to 0.969 (SEEDED). Across the 5 tasks, the change in shift AUC correlates with the accuracy gain at Pearson r = −0.81 (descriptive only). Both arms' synthetic inputs remain almost perfectly separable from real inputs.
- Copying of exemplars was low: SEEDED copy rate at cosine ≥0.5 was 1% (0% for SYN). Distinct-2 was 0.52 for SEEDED vs 0.37 for SYN.
- References: teacher zero-shot 0.81 and untrained student 0.67 mean accuracy.
- Oddity on irony: the trained SYN function scored 0.37, well below the untrained student's 0.70. I report it but did not investigate.

Choices where the registration was ambiguous, and fixes made while testing:
1. task_index and arm_index in the seed formulas are 0-based in the listed order (sms=0; SYN=0, SEEDED=1).
2. Exemplars shown in the SEEDED prompt have their whitespace and newlines collapsed to single spaces, so each fits on one numbered line.
3. Equal N: N = min(SYN, SEEDED). The larger arm is subsampled with seed 0. MIX keeps all teacher-labelled real pairs (128 valid on every task) and is filled with SYN pairs drawn from the full SYN pool (seed 0).
4. LoRA init uses torch.manual_seed(0), so the starting adapter is identical across arms.
5. transformers is pinned to <5 (still meets >=4.51) to avoid API changes. huggingface_hub is installed before the downloads, because the first launch failed when it was missing.
6. CogComp/trec has a loading script that current datasets refuses to run, so the loader falls back to the Hub's refs/convert/parquet revision. The registered "retry" rule was extended to cover this.
7. Training batches are drawn from one continuous stream of permutations generated by RandomState(0).
8. pools.jsonl contains every synthesized pair, with a `used` flag marking the equal-N subset, plus all MIX pairs.
9. result.json reports the mean over completed tasks. summary.json would mark the run inconclusive if fewer than 4 tasks completed.

Single training seed; one repetition.

departures: exp.py ld(): CogComp/trec ships a loading script that current datasets refuses to run, so the loader falls back to the Hub's refs/convert/parquet revision. This was needed for the task to load at all. trec loaded but was later skipped, so the change cannot affect the value.

trec was excluded under the registered rule requiring at least 320 synthesized pairs: SYN produced 145 pairs and SEEDED 450 (exp.py, logs/exp.log). The rule is in the registration, so this is not a departure. Still, the registered mean covers 5 tasks, and the skip is conditional on SYN failing, which leaves out a task where SEEDED had a large yield advantage.

exp.py synthesize(): whitespace and newlines inside exemplars are collapsed before the exemplars go into the numbered list. This is a formatting choice the registration leaves open; any effect on the value is likely negligible.

exp.py equal-N rule: N = min(SYN, SEEDED), and the larger arm is subsampled. The registration only specifies subsampling SYN and MIX when SEEDED is smaller. Every completed task produced 480 pairs in both arms, so this had no effect.
exp.py MIX construction: the synthetic fill is drawn from the full SYN list rather than an equal-N subset. That list was capped at 480, so the result is identical here.

exp.py compile_and_eval(): training batches come from one continuous stream of RandomState(0) permutations, and LoRA init is seeded with torch.manual_seed(0). Both are reasonable readings of the registered 'reshuffled each pass with seed 0' and make the arms comparable. No effect on the question.
run.sh pins transformers<5 (still >=4.51) and installs huggingface_hub before the downloads. These are environment choices with no effect on the value.
exp.py copy_rates() uses the default TfidfVectorizer settings. The registration leaves these open, and only a diagnostic is affected.
problems: One task drives the registered mean. Irony contributes +0.115 (task_irony.json). Without it, the mean over the other four tasks is about -0.003 (sms +0.035, subj -0.060, rt +0.0025, agnews +0.010). The engineer's claim of 'evidence of a small positive effect' is therefore fragile.

The bootstrap CIs (summarize.py) resample test items only. They ignore variance from teacher synthesis sampling and from LoRA training. With one synthesis draw and one training seed per arm, a CI that excludes zero overstates precision. The upper bound of 0.0335 also overlaps the 0.03 threshold, so the null on the 3-point threshold is not decisive either.

Training looks unstable on irony. The SYN-compiled function predicts 'ironic' for 394 of 400 items, scoring 0.3725 against 0.7025 for the untrained student (scores.jsonl). Final training loss stays near 0.23 in all three irony arms. The engineer flagged this but did not investigate. A single degenerate run like this inflates the SEEDED-SYN difference and signals high run-to-run variance.

Arms differ in training label priors, which may explain part of the gains. On sms, the SYN training data are 57.5% spam against 14.5% spam in TEST, while SEEDED has 46% spam. Macro-F1 is reported, but no analysis separates prior matching from other effects.
trec was skipped because spec-only synthesis yielded only 145 pairs, so one of six registered tasks is missing. The engineer correctly reports this yield gap as a finding in its own right.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered three-arm design: SYN and SEEDED differ only in the exemplar block, MIX uses the same 128 inputs as teacher-labeled pairs, and equal N, the compile recipe, the diagnostics and the statistic all match. The rerun on the fresh machine reproduces the engineer's numbers exactly, and no departure plausibly moves the value. The value comes from real model generations scored against gold labels, with no visible leakage or hard-coding, and the event (0.0205 > 0.03) is correctly judged false. The evidence is weak, however. There is one synthesis draw and one training seed, per-task differences swing from -0.06 to +0.115, one degenerate irony run supplies essentially the whole positive mean, and the CIs reflect only test-item sampling. The run is a credible null on the 3-point threshold with useful side observations (shift AUC stays about 0.97, distinct-2 rises, copying is low, MIX is roughly equal to SYN), but it neither establishes a small positive effect nor firmly rules out a 3-point one.

departures: exp.py, synthesize(): SEEDED exemplars are transformed with ' '.join(exemplars[e].split()) rather than inserted as the original dataset strings. This removes newlines and other whitespace from the registered exemplar block. It changes teacher-conditioning tokens and plausibly changes sampled training data and the reported accuracy difference; no unchanged-value check is supplied.

exp.py, synthesize(): synthesized inputs are stripped before minimum-length validation, case-insensitive deduplication and training. The registration specifies those operations on the input strings without this normalization. This could change accepted examples, duplicate counts and training inputs; the unstripped strings are not preserved, so its actual effect cannot be determined.

run.sh: huggingface_hub and hf_transfer are installed before background downloads begin, and datasets are loaded after the main package installation rather than concurrently with it. The prerequisite installation is a reasonable execution fix. The scheduling difference did not affect teacher selection or task inclusion in this run, which finished well before the time guard.

run.sh: transformers is constrained to >=4.51,<5 rather than only >=4.51. This remains within the registered version requirement and addresses API compatibility; there is no supported numerical departure attributable to it.

exp.py, ld(): loading attempts include refs/convert/parquet for every dataset ID, extending the registered retry procedure. This was necessary to load TREC with the installed datasets package. TREC was subsequently excluded under the registered synthesis-yield rule, so this did not change the reported completed-task mean.

exp.py, MIX construction: when SEEDED has fewer pairs than SYN, the implementation retains every valid teacher-labeled real example and reduces only the synthetic fill. The registration instead constructs MIX at the SYN count and then subsamples MIX as a whole. This could change the comparison in another run, but was not activated here: all completed tasks used 480 pairs in every arm.

exp.py, low-yield-task branch: TREC's synthesized pairs, acceptance/duplicate statistics and stage timings are discarded before the normal pool and diagnostic files are written. Only pair counts and the exclusion reason remain in logs/run_meta.json. This reduces the registered audit trail but does not change the accuracy statistic.
problems: The unregistered exemplar-whitespace normalization changes the central SEEDED prompt and plausibly affects the reported value, despite otherwise strong adherence to the registered pipeline.

The fresh evaluation found +2.05 percentage points, with a paired bootstrap interval of approximately [0.90, 3.35] points. The registered event is false, but this interval does not establish that the underlying effect is below three points.
summarize.py bootstraps test items conditional on the five completed tasks and fitted models. It does not capture synthesis, exemplar-pool, training-seed or task-selection variability.

The average gain is driven by irony: excluding its +11.5-point difference, the other four tasks average -0.3125 points. On irony, SEEDED still scores only 48.75%, below the untrained student's 70.25% and the 64.25% literal-majority baseline.

TREC's registered exclusion is legitimate, but limits the accuracy finding to tasks where both synthesis arms meet the yield requirement. Its missing pool and synthesis-statistic records also prevent checking the engineer's claim that duplicates principally caused the failure.

Low TF-IDF copy rates and improved shift AUC do not establish a causal distribution-matching mechanism or rule out semantic paraphrasing. The across-task correlation uses only five observations, and both synthetic arms remain highly distinguishable from real inputs.

engineer_notes incorrectly states that all 128 exemplar labels were valid on every completed task. The fresh AG News evaluation and diagnostics show 125 valid labels and three dropped invalid labels; the code correctly follows the registered dropping rule.
engineer_notes claims pools.jsonl preserves every synthesized pair, but synthesize() truncates batch overshoot to 480 before saving, and saves no TREC pairs.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation supports a genuine five-task result of +2.05 accuracy points, below the registered event threshold, while its conditional confidence interval still includes a three-point effect. Most substantive settings and controls match, but the unregistered transformation of exemplar text changes the central teacher prompt and plausibly changes the value, warranting an unfaithful judgment. The supplied code and fresh outputs support real generation, training and scoring, with no evident hard-coded results or use of test gold labels in training. The heterogeneous gains, synthesis-yield finding and distribution diagnostics provide meaningful research evidence, but one seed, incomplete failure diagnostics and limited uncertainty coverage keep its value at 2 rather than 3.

departures: exp.py collapses whitespace and newlines inside SEEDED exemplars to single spaces before inserting them into the registered one-line block. This slightly changes the teacher prompt versus literal insertion and could slightly change synthetic inputs; it is unlikely to move the 0.0205 mean across 0.03, and it is what keeps the registered numbered-line format well-formed when real texts contain newlines.

exp.py sets N = min(SYN, SEEDED) and subsamples whichever arm is larger (seed 0). The registration only specifies subsampling when SEEDED yields fewer pairs than SYN. On every completed task both arms were already capped at 480, so this did not change the reported value.

exp.py builds MIX by keeping every valid teacher-labeled exemplar and filling from the full SYN pool to N. If SEEDED had been shorter, the registration would subsample an already mixed SYN-sized set and could drop real pairs. That case did not occur, so the reported value is unchanged.

exp.py retries dataset loads on revision refs/convert/parquet in addition to the registered one retry and un-namespaced id. This was required for CogComp/trec under current datasets. It did not change the statistic: trec was excluded by the registered <320-pair rule (SYN 145, SEEDED 450), which would also have excluded it on load failure.
run.sh pins transformers to >=4.51,<5 rather than any >=4.51. Compatibility pin so the registered APIs run; it does not plausibly change the result relative to a working 4.x release.
exp.py fits the shift-AUC LogisticRegression with max_iter=2000, which the registration does not specify. Diagnostic only; it does not change the registered accuracy statistic.

exp.py discards trec before writing synthesis acceptance, duplicate rates, or pools (only the skip reason and log pair counts are kept). Reporting gap for a skipped task; it does not change the registered mean.
problems: The 0.0205 mean is fragile: irony is +0.115 and subj is -0.060, while rt and agnews CIs include zero (outputs/summary.json). The item bootstrap in summarize.py excludes zero but its upper end is 0.0335, and it does not resample tasks or the single training seed, so it does not firmly place the effect below 0.03.

On irony the compiled models collapsed toward always predicting ironic (SYN 394/400, accuracy 0.3725) and both finished well below the untrained student (0.7025) and the teacher (0.6425) in outputs/scores.jsonl. Most of the average gain is a contrast between two failed compiles, with final train loss still ~0.23.

The registered 320-pair rule dropped trec, the only task where seeding changed whether synthesis was usable (145 vs 450 unique pairs, logs/exp.log). The accuracy result is therefore conditional on spec-only synthesis already succeeding, which the registration allows but which limits the claim.
grok.reason: The fresh run executed the registered arms, models, prompts, equal pair count, recipe, parser, gold tests, and statistic: mean acc(SEEDED)-acc(SYN) is 0.0205 over five tasks, so the pre-registered >0.03 event correctly did not occur. Departures are either unused on the completed tasks, required to load trec or keep the exemplar block well-formed, or diagnostic-only, and the scores match real generations rather than hard-coded outputs. Seeding beat spec-only synthesis on 4 of 5 tasks and the item-level CI excludes zero, but the gain is small, heterogeneous, and mostly an irony collapse, while teacher-labeling the same 128 inputs did not beat spec-only synthesis on average and synthetic inputs stayed almost perfectly separable from real text. That is a credible, supported null on the 3-point claim, not a precise or consequential estimate of the effect.
