registration.title: Do spec-generated test sets flatter compiled functions? Student-versus-teacher gaps on LLM-generated test items versus real items of matched difficulty, for the same specs
registration.seed_connection: The seed's headline result (0.836 vs 0.224 LEM) is measured on FuzzyBench-Hard. As the drafts describe it (not verified from the seed text), FuzzyBench's inputs and references were generated by an LLM from each spec. That is the same kind of distribution compile-by-training trains on. If generated test sets favor students distilled from generated data, both absolute accuracy and comparisons with prompted models are inflated. Holding the spec fixed and changing only the source of test items isolates this.
registration.hypothesis: For the same specs, the accuracy gap between a compile-by-training student and its teacher prompted at run time is at least 3 points more favorable to the student on LLM-generated test items than on real human-labeled test items that passed the same agreement filter.
registration.contribution: A same-spec measurement of evaluation bias on generated test sets in student-versus-teacher comparisons. It controls for difficulty: the real items are filtered by the same generator-agreement rule that FuzzyBench-style test sets use, so ceiling compression on easy filtered items cannot produce the effect. Absolute overestimation of student accuracy, and inflation of the student's gain over the untrained base model, are reported alongside. Prior work compares synthetic and real benchmarks across different tasks, or uses synthetic test sets to choose data generators.

closest_work.difference: PAW reports FuzzyBench (generated) and WRENCH (human-labeled) results on different tasks, so any reversal is confounded by task. Here the specs are fixed and only the source of test items varies.
RoSE uses other generators' synthetic data as a proxy test set for choosing a generator. It does not measure bias in student-teacher comparisons.
Prompt2Model reports that gains on generated evaluation sets carried over to three real benchmarks. Here the bias is measured on six tasks with a difficulty-matched real control.

inputs: Teacher Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507; independent generator microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct (fallback ibm-granite/granite-3.3-8b-instruct); student Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B; Hugging Face

Hugging Face datasets: fancyzhx/ag_news, fancyzhx/dbpedia_14, dair-ai/emotion, cardiffnlp/tweet_eval (config sentiment), ucirvine/sms_spam, mteb/mtop_domain (config en; fallback mteb/amazon_massive_scenario config en)
Seed paper Appendix D prompt; vllm, transformers, peft, datasets, torch
registration.method:
(1) Tasks and specs. Use verbatim; map integer labels to names in dataset order.
- T1 ag_news test, input = text: 'Classify the main topic of a news article (headline and summary). Return only one of these labels: World, Sports, Business, Sci/Tech.'
- T2 dbpedia_14 test, input = title + '. ' + content: 'Classify the type of entity described by an encyclopedia entry (title and opening sentences). Return only one of these labels: Company, EducationalInstitution, Artist, Athlete, OfficeHolder, MeanOfTransportation, Building, NaturalPlace, Village, Animal, Plant, Album, Film, WrittenWork.'
- T3 emotion test: 'Identify the main emotion expressed in a short first-person English sentence. Return only one of these labels: sadness, joy, love, anger, fear, surprise.'
- T4 tweet_eval sentiment test: 'Classify the sentiment of a tweet. Return only one of these labels: negative, neutral, positive.'
- T5 sms_spam (seeded 50/50 split; use the test half), input = sms: 'Decide whether an SMS text message is spam or ham (a normal, legitimate message). Return only one of these labels: spam, ham.'
- T6 mtop_domain test: 'Route a user's request to a virtual assistant to the domain that should handle it. Return only one of these labels: ' + label_text names joined by commas + '.'
View REAL: 600 test items per task, seed 0.

(2) Label parsing.
- First line; lowercase; delete whitespace, underscores, hyphens, slashes, quotes, backticks, asterisks and trailing punctuation. Normalize labels identically, so 'Sci/Tech' and 'SciTech' both become 'scitech'.
- An exact match returns that label. Otherwise return the longest normalized label occurring as a substring; if it is preceded by 'not' and 'not'+label is not a label, return INVALID. Otherwise INVALID, which is scored wrong.

(3) Run-time prompt: a user message '{spec}\n\n[INPUT]\n{x}\n[END_INPUT]' (input truncated to 256 tokens), each model's chat template (Qwen3: enable_thinking=False). Greedy decoding, max 16 new tokens.

(4) Teacher synthesis in vLLM.
- Appendix D system prompt: 'You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with a top-level key 'examples'. Each example must be an object with string keys 'input' and 'output'.' User prompt: 'Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification.\n\n[SPEC]\n{spec}\n[END_SPEC]'.
- Sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 2048, distinct seeds.
- Parse, keep valid labels, and drop duplicate inputs. Collect 1500 per task (cap 600 calls): the first 1200 train the student, the remaining 300 form view SYN-T.
- The teacher then predicts all views at run time.

(5) Independent generated view SYN-G, made with the generator in vLLM.
- System prompt: 'You are a meticulous data synthesizer. Given a function spec, you must generate diverse input/output pairs. Return STRICT JSON with the following schema: {"pairs": [{"input": string, "output": string}, ...]}. All outputs must satisfy the above constraint for every pair. Return ONLY JSON.'
- User prompt: 'Generate input/output examples for this function.\n\nSpec: {spec}\n\nNumber of pairs: 8\n\nRules:\n- Produce exactly the requested number of pairs when feasible.\n- Inputs should be varied and realistic.\n- Outputs must be consistent with the spec.\n- Return ONLY JSON, no commentary.'
- Sampling: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95.
- Keep valid labels. Drop duplicates and any input identical to a teacher-synthesized input.
- Agreement filter: the generator relabels each input with the run-time prompt (greedy), and the item is kept only if the two labels match. Keep 400 per task (cap 400 calls) and log any shortfall.

(6) Difficulty-matched real view REAL-F.
- The generator labels every REAL item with the run-time prompt. REAL-F = the REAL items whose generator label equals gold, which is the same agreement rule applied to real data.
- Log the size of REAL-F per task. If it has fewer than 150 items, flag the task.

(7) Students.
- S: Qwen3-0.6B bf16 with fresh PEFT LoRA: r=64, alpha=16, dropout 0, targets q,k,v,o,gate,up,down projections. Warm start unavailable. Target label + <|im_end|>, loss on label tokens only. AdamW, lr 2e-4 with cosine decay to 2e-5 over 100 steps, no warmup, batch 32, examples shuffled and cycled. Trained on the 1200 teacher examples with seeds 0 and 1 (12 builds), in one persistent process.
- B: base Qwen3-0.6B, no adapter.

(8) Scoring: S (both seeds), T and B predict every item of REAL, REAL-F, SYN-G and SYN-T.

(9) Execution order: teacher vLLM phase; free the GPU; generator vLLM phase; free the GPU; train; predict.

event.description: Averaged over the six tasks, the student's gap to the run-time teacher is at least 3 points more favorable on generated items (SYN-G) than on real items that passed the same agreement filter (REAL-F).
event.statistic: I_F = mean over tasks of [(acc_S - acc_T) on SYN-G - (acc_S - acc_T) on REAL-F], where acc_S is averaged over the two student seeds

evaluation.controls:
- REAL-F applies the generator agreement filter to real items, matching difficulty selection and preventing ceiling compression from producing the effect.
- The generator comes from a different family than the teacher, and the filter uses only the generator.
- Teacher inputs are deduplicated out of SYN-G.
- Two student seeds are used.
- The base-model contrast I_B checks for generic gap shrinkage.

registration.full_scale_study: Functions beyond classification (extraction, normalization) with real inputs and programmatic or human references. Several generator families and verification rules, the released PAW and compile-by-training programs, and larger prompted baselines. A recommended real-input audit protocol, or a correction factor, for benchmarks of compiled functions.

agent.reason: Distilled students usually match their teacher on synthetic-style items but fall behind on real tweets and emotion sentences, even after difficulty filtering. My rough per-task guesses put I_F around 4-5 points, but ceiling compression on easy tasks (spam, AG News) could pull it under 3.

judge_astra.reason: Generated test inputs are likely to resemble the student's synthetic training distribution more closely than real inputs do, favoring the student relative to its prompted teacher. Agreement filtering does not actually equalize difficulty or class composition, so a relative shift above three points remains quite plausible.

judge_fable.reason: Student-teacher agreement should be higher on prototypical generated items than on real items even after difficulty matching, giving a positive I_F, but my central estimate (~3-5 points) sits near the threshold and the three-model, two-vLLM-phase pipeline is fragile within 35 minutes.

judge_opus.reason: On generated items both models sit near ceiling, which compresses the student-teacher gap. On real items, even after the agreement filter, a 0.6B student trained on synthetic data should trail the teacher more, especially on emotion, tweets and dbpedia with its skewed labels. Rough per-task estimates put I_F around 3 to 5 points, so the outcome sits close to the threshold.

judge_sol.reason: Generated inputs are likely more canonical and closer to the student's synthetic training distribution, reducing its deficit to the teacher. Generator-agreement filtering does not ensure comparable difficulty or label distributions, so a three-point contrast remains fairly likely but would not uniquely establish evaluation bias.

judge_luna.reason: Canonical generated inputs may be easier for the student, which could make its gap to the teacher more favorable than on real inputs. But the agreement-filtered real view may also be easy, and the synthetic labels are not independently verified.

judge_muse.reason: Students distilled from generated data typically favor generated tests, but REAL-F selects easy real items via the same generator-agreement filter and SYN-G uses a different generator family. That matching may dilute the gap contrast near the 3pp threshold.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: PAW reports results on FuzzyBench (generated) and on WRENCH (human-labeled), but these are different tasks. It never holds a spec fixed while swapping generated test items for real ones, and it does not apply an agreement filter to real items to match difficulty.

The seed paper evaluates only on FuzzyBench-Hard plus 44 hand-written avatar instructions. It has no real-data control for the compiled student and no comparison with a prompted teacher on real versus generated items. Its only related remark is the Limitations note that synthetic supervision may inherit teacher errors.

RoSE uses one generator's synthetic data as a proxy test set for ranking other generators, and checks that ranking against human test sets. It does not measure whether generated test sets inflate a distilled student's gap to its teacher.

Prompt2Model reports that gains measured on generated evaluation sets carried over to a few real benchmarks. It does not estimate the bias as a same-spec, difficulty-matched difference in student-teacher gaps.

This work checks whether fully synthetic IR test collections are biased toward LLM-based systems. The domain is retrieval, not spec-compiled classifiers, and there is no distilled student or teacher comparison.

opus.reason: None of the papers I found answer the specific question: for a fixed spec, is a compile-by-training student's gap to its prompted teacher more favorable on LLM-generated test items than on real items that passed the same generator-agreement filter? Related work compares synthetic and real benchmarks across different tasks, uses synthetic test sets to select generators, or studies synthetic-test bias in retrieval. I recall a 2024 study of synthetic data as a benchmark (Maheshwari et al., possibly arXiv 2409.11968) that compared synthetic and real versions of the same NLP tasks, but my searches could not retrieve it, and as I remember it, it ranks LLMs rather than measuring student-teacher gaps against a difficulty-matched control.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Prompt2Model compares fine-tuned model rankings on generated evaluation sets and their real counterparts, and compares students with the teacher on real benchmarks. It does not measure how changing test-item source changes the student–teacher gap under a common agreement filter.

Efficacy of Synthetic Data as a Benchmark measures synthetic-versus-real performance discrepancies and generator self-bias across prompted LLMs, but does not study students trained on synthetic supervision versus their run-time teachers.

When LLMs Benchmark Themselves isolates test-generation self-bias from evaluator self-bias, primarily in translation. It does not test whether independently generated items favor distilled students relative to their teachers compared with agreement-filtered real items.

RoSE evaluates synthetically trained classifiers on other generators' synthetic data and human-labeled data to select training-data generators. It does not evaluate the prompted teacher alongside the student or estimate the proposed source-dependent student–teacher contrast.

Preference Leakage demonstrates that LLM judges favor students trained by related generators. It varies evaluator relatedness rather than test-input origin and does not report the proposed classification-accuracy contrast.

sol.reason: Prior work already studies synthetic-versus-real evaluation discrepancies, generator self-bias, and evaluation bias affecting distilled students, so these broad concerns are not new. However, I found no work answering the specific same-spec question through a student–teacher gap contrast between independently generated items and human-labeled real items subjected to the common generator-agreement criterion.

opus.reason: Entry 17 tests shifted generated test sets, but none compares student-versus-teacher gaps on LLM-generated items against agreement-filtered real human-labeled items for the same specs.

sol.reason: Entry 17 tests distribution-shift generalization, but not inflation of student–teacher accuracy gaps on generated versus real test items subjected to a common agreement filter.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented all six registered tasks/specs, teacher synthesis and independent Phi generation, exact-input deduplication, generator-only agreement filtering, 12 fresh rank-64 LoRA builds (two seeds, 100 steps), greedy S/T/B predictions on all four views, the registered label parser, paired 2000-item bootstrap, and all secondary statistics/flags/raw outputs. Final command tested successfully after deleting outputs/adapters; independent audit passed for 41,628 prediction rows. Final I_F=0.0790351, CI95=[0.0617340,0.0962280], seeds=[0.0803548,0.0777155]; no ceiling or size-shortfall flags. I_B=0.0786168, so the observed contrast is not clearly distillation-specific; gain-over-base inflation is only 0.0004184 at the point estimate. Plumbing adjustments: datasets 4.x rejects MTOP's legacy script, so loaded the original en/*.jsonl files it references (4386 test rows), not the differing Parquet split; reselected/re-filtered/re-evaluated REAL accordingly. Fixed overly strict JSON parsing before training to accept intact fenced JSON and pair arrays, reusing saved responses and retaining the first 400 eligible items; unchanged prompts/seeds/caps/filter, surplus logged/excluded. Independent synthesis max_tokens=2048 was unspecified in registration. Logged input datasets and generator filtering are frozen in data/ for fresh evaluation; every evaluation retrains all 12 students and recomputes all S/T/B predictions/statistics. No prediction cache or adapter is submitted. Full details are in README.md.

departures: T6 MTOP (experiment.py prepare, data/tasks.json): datasets 4.x rejects the legacy loader script, so the code reads the original en/{split}.jsonl files from the same repository, with 4386 test rows. The registered fallback dataset was not used. This is a plumbing change needed to run the registered dataset, and it is arguably closer to the registered data than the 2185-row Parquet split. It changes which 600 items form REAL for T6, so it could shift the T6 contribution slightly, but it does not change the question.

MTOP reselection (README.md, engineer notes): REAL for T6 was first drawn from the Parquet split, then discarded, reselected, re-filtered and re-evaluated. This is a forking path if preliminary I_F values were seen before the switch. It has a principled provenance justification, and it affects only one of six tasks.

Generator JSON parsing (experiment.py parse_pairs, repair_generator.py): the parser was loosened after collection to accept intact Markdown-fenced JSON and top-level pair arrays, and saved responses were re-parsed. All 400 generator calls had already been made under the strict parser. The registration only says 'Parse', so this is an open implementation choice. Prompts, seeds, the call cap and the filter are unchanged, and the first 400 eligible items in call order are kept, which matches what incremental collection would have produced. It is unlikely to bias the value.
Independent-generator max_tokens=2048 (experiment.py generator): the registration leaves this unspecified. It is an open choice, with negligible effect.

Frozen synthesis (evaluate.sh, experiment.py): real selections, teacher synthesis, generator synthesis, the agreement filter and REAL-F labels are reused from the engineer's earlier run in data/. The protected evaluation re-ran only training, the S/T/B predictions and the statistics. The registration does not forbid this, and raw responses plus all rejected candidates are logged. However, the synthetic views come from one stochastic draw that the evaluation did not reproduce. This does not change the computation, only its independent verification.
Label-only loss (experiment.py train): the loss is computed by projecting only supervised hidden positions through lm_head. This is mathematically the same objective, with no effect on the result.
Student inference in vLLM with LoRARequest; REAL-F predictions reused from REAL rows: this is implementation only, and audit.py checks that the raw outputs are identical. No effect.
Run-to-run nondeterminism: the protected run gives I_F=0.07867, the engineer's run 0.07904. The difference is negligible relative to the 0.03 threshold.
problems: The registered base-model control undercuts the hypothesis's mechanism. I_B (0.0786) is about equal to I_F (0.0787), and gain-over-base inflation is only about 0.0004. The favorable shift on SYN-G relative to REAL-F therefore applies equally to the untrained 0.6B base model, so it is a generic shrinkage of the gap to the teacher, not a distillation-specific effect. The registered event is met literally, but 'generated test sets flatter compiled functions' as a distillation effect is not supported. The engineer reports this correctly.

The likely driver is teacher-side. SYN-G references are Phi labels on Phi-generated items, while REAL-F references are gold labels that Phi agrees with. This plausibly lowers the teacher's (Qwen3-4B) accuracy on SYN-G through disagreement on ambiguous synthetic items. That cannot be confirmed here because outputs/summary.json per-task tables are not shown.

All synthetic and filtered data in data/ come from the engineer's earlier run and were not regenerated by the protected evaluation. There is one draw from a single teacher and a single generator family, and no repetition of synthesis.
T6 REAL was reselected after a preliminary Parquet-based evaluation (README.md). This is a minor garden-of-forking-paths risk.
The seed paper's description of FuzzyBench as LLM-generated is acknowledged in the registration as unverified, so the seed connection rests on an unverified premise.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: the six specs, Appendix D teacher synthesis, the independent Phi generator with exact-input deduplication against teacher inputs, generator-only agreement filtering applied to both SYN-G and REAL items, fresh rank-64 LoRA students over two seeds with the registered schedule, greedy run-time prompts, the registered parser, and a paired within-task bootstrap. The departures are either necessary plumbing (MTOP loading), open choices (JSON parsing, max_tokens), or computationally equivalent. The protected run retrained all adapters and recomputed every prediction from real model outputs. It reproduced I_F≈0.079 with a 95% CI of [0.062, 0.096], well above the 0.03 threshold, and audit.py independently recomputed the statistic. The finding is meaningful but narrower than the hypothesis: the nearly identical I_B shows that generated test sets shrink any small model's gap to the prompted teacher, not specifically a distilled student's. With a single synthesis draw and one generator family, this is a credible, moderately informative result rather than strong evidence of distillation-specific bias.

departures: experiment.py: prepare(), teacher(), and generator() reuse submitted, frozen real selections, synthetic datasets, and generator agreement labels. The fresh evaluation therefore reran training and S/T/B inference, not synthesis or filtering. This preserves the recorded experiment's inputs but does not independently reproduce their construction or test variation across newly generated datasets.

experiment.py and README.md: MTOP was loaded from the original repository's English JSONL files rather than through its unsupported legacy dataset loader. The earlier, differing Parquet selection was reportedly discarded. Dataset choice could change the result, but the final substitution is supported as a compatibility repair intended to recover the registered split.

experiment.py: parse_pairs() accepts intact fenced JSON and top-level pair arrays despite the synthesis prompts requesting keyed JSON objects. repair_generator.py applied this broader parser to saved independent-generator responses and retained the first 400 eligible items. This materially changes acceptance relative to the initial implementation, but the registration did not prescribe a JSON-wrapper rejection rule; it is a documented parsing repair rather than an outcome-based selection rule.
experiment.py: independent synthesis uses max_tokens=2048. This can affect generated examples and truncation failures, but the registration left that parameter unspecified.

experiment.py: candidate validation additionally rejects empty or whitespace-only inputs, and generator deduplication considers previously encountered candidates and all teacher candidate records, including rejected or surplus records. These details could affect selection if such cases occur; the registration leaves malformed-input handling and the precise deduplication pool underdefined, and the supplied excerpts do not establish a consequential discrepancy.

evaluate.sh and experiment.py: teacher inference occurs after student/base inference, with the teacher reloaded, rather than at the registration's stated earlier prediction point. This resolves the fact that independent generated items are unavailable during initial teacher synthesis. No plausible effect on the statistic is evident.
problems: Registration: applying the same binary agreement filter does not establish matched difficulty. Generated self-consistency and agreement with externally supplied real-data references select different populations; difficulty, class balance, ambiguity, and input style can still differ.

Registration and experiment.py: synthetic references are generator-produced labels, whereas real references come from the datasets. Generator agreement is not independent verification of synthetic label correctness, so reference-quality differences remain entangled with input-source differences.

Engineer notes: the earlier run's I_B nearly equals I_F, and its gain-over-base inflation is approximately zero. This undermines a distillation-specific interpretation, although it does not establish equivalence or absence of training-specific bias. Those secondary values are not shown for the protected run.

experiment.py: the bootstrap conditions on six fixed tasks, frozen synthesis/filtering, and two trained student seeds. It does not quantify uncertainty across tasks, synthesis realizations, filtering realizations, or a broader population of training builds; within-call and near-duplicate dependencies could also reduce effective sample size.

audit.py: the audit independently recomputes arithmetic but imports the experiment's parser and item construction. It checks stored agreement relationships without independently reproducing generator outputs or verifying dataset provenance.

Registration: the seed benchmark's generation procedure is explicitly unverified, and neither the seed text nor cited comparison papers are supplied. The experiment therefore cannot establish that the seed's headline result is inflated.
sol.reason: The protected run produced I_F=0.07867 with a 95% item-bootstrap interval of [0.06161, 0.09578], exceeding the registered 0.03 threshold for both student seeds, and its arithmetic was independently recomputed over 41,628 prediction rows. The visible code implements the registered systems, training, views, scoring, and primary statistic, with documented compatibility repairs and choices where the registration was underdefined. This is credible evidence of a source-dependent student–teacher comparison on these fixed datasets, but the agreement filter does not identify a difficulty-controlled causal effect. The earlier base-model control further limits the distillation-specific interpretation, making the finding meaningful without supporting the broader claim that the seed benchmark specifically flatters compiled functions.

departures: MTOP English was loaded from the repository JSONL files the legacy script references (4386 test rows), not datasets.load_dataset or the differing Parquet split (experiment.py prepare, data/tasks.json). Necessary to obtain the registered dataset; does not change the result relative to that test split.

Independent-generator max_tokens=2048 was filled in where the registration leaves it unspecified (experiment.py generator). Open choice; responses in data/generator_*.json are intact, so this cap did not truncate the kept items.

JSON parsing accepts Markdown fences and top-level pair arrays, not only the specified object schema (experiment.py parse_pairs, repair_generator.py). Fence-stripping was required to recover any Phi items; bare arrays could slightly change SYN-G membership if any were among the first 400 eligible items. Late shown bare arrays are surplus. Unlikely to move I_F materially.

Teacher run-time prediction is a later process, after SYN-G exists, rather than inside the teacher synthesis phase (evaluate.sh, experiment.py teacher_eval). Required by the registered views; does not change scores.
REAL-F reuses the REAL greedy decode instead of a second generation (experiment.py eval_systems). Same prompt and item; audit.py checks raw outputs match. Does not change the result.

Synthesis, REAL selections, and generator agreement labels were frozen in data/ and not regenerated on the evaluation machine (experiment.py teacher/generator early returns). This is the single registered draw; it does not change the value for that draw, though a new draw could differ.

Duplicate rejection includes rejected generator inputs and all teacher-record inputs, not only accepted items (experiment.py generator). Slightly stricter than a minimal reading of 'drop duplicates'; could swap a few SYN-G items, not the question.

Label normalization also strips Unicode quotes and some non-ASCII trailing punctuation (experiment.py normalize). Minor extension; could change rare parses, not the reported value in any material way.

AdamW defaults and a cosine schedule that hits 2e-5 at step 99 are unspecified details of the registered optimizer (experiment.py train). Open choices; could slightly change weights, not the question or the event definition.
problems: Generated inputs often ignore the spec's input format: T1 SYN-G items in data/generator_T1.json are short headlines, while the spec asks for headline plus summary and teacher items include both. SYN-G versus REAL-F therefore confounds source with style and difficulty beyond the agreement filter.

The registered base-model control, in the engineer's adjacent run, was I_B≈0.0786 with gain-over-base inflation≈0.0004, so the contrast is not distillation-specific. The fresh log confirms I_F and the CI but does not print I_B; summary.json was written and not shown.
Stochastic synthesis and agreement labels were not reproduced on the evaluation machine (data/, evaluate.sh). Fresh training and S/T/B predictions were recomputed and audited.
Accepting bare JSON arrays and deduping rejected inputs (experiment.py) are inclusion rules the registration does not spell out; any effect on the exact I_F is unquantified and likely small.
grok.reason: The fresh run retrained all 12 LoRA students and recomputed greedy S/T/B predictions; audit.py recomputed I_F=0.07867 from 41,628 rows, with CI [0.062, 0.096] and both seeds above 0.03, so the registered event is supported by real outputs rather than a hardcoded result. Prompts, models, view construction, agreement filters, training recipe, and the I_F definition match the registration; remaining differences are open parameters, load/parse fixes required to run, or equivalent scheduling. The result is a precise same-spec contrast on six classification proxies, not a direct audit of the seed's compiled functions or FuzzyBench. The pre-registered base-model control in the adjacent run is essentially as large as I_F, so the shift should not be read as specific to compile-by-training.

registration.title: Do local specification edits cause regressions beyond ordinary rebuild variation?
registration.seed_connection: The seed packages compiled functions as versionable software artifacts, but does not test whether changing one specification clause preserves behavior on inputs unaffected by that clause. This experiment audits that property using a frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter and independently trained task adapters.
registration.hypothesis: Recompiling after a one-clause semantic change causes more previously correct, unaffected inputs to become incorrect than recompiling an unchanged specification.
registration.contribution: A controlled semantic-regression test that separates intended behavior changes from unintended regressions and subtracts no-op rebuild variation. Exact reference functions and shared training inputs remove teacher-label and synthetic-input variation from this initial audit.

closest_work.difference: MUSCLE studies compatibility when the pretrained base model changes. Here the base remains frozen and the function specification changes; an executable reference identifies precisely which inputs should retain their behavior.
RIPPLE studies localized prompt-policy edits in frozen workflow agents. This experiment studies retrained, independently packaged task adapters and includes a paired no-op recompilation control.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
PyPI packages transformers>=4.51,<5, peft>=0.15,<1, accelerate and safetensors; use the machine's existing CUDA PyTorch.
Two locally generated, oracle-labeled policy datasets defined in the method; no external annotations or hosted compiler calls.
registration.method: Implement an API-free LoRA compiler, not the seed's hosted mapper initialization. Use two binary functions, with outputs 1 and 0. Email function: fields action_required in {false,true}, deadline_hours in {2,8,24,48,72}, sender in {manager,colleague,vendor}, cancelled and bulk. Original output is 1 iff not cancelled, not bulk, action_required, and either deadline_hours<=24 or sender=manager. Revised specification changes only 24 to 8. Log function: severity in {info,warning,error,critical}, environment in {production,staging}, resolved, maintenance and customer_impact. Original output is 1 iff environment=production, not resolved, (not maintenance or severity=critical), and (severity=critical or (severity=error and customer_impact)). Revised specification changes only the maintenance clause to not maintenance. Write complete natural-language specifications stating every condition, priority and output label. Render facts with three fixed training templates, including affirmative and explicit negative wording; use two different test templates and disjoint record identifiers. For each function generate 320 training inputs: include every latent state at least once, then fill to balance the original reference labels. Use exactly the same input pool for all compilations, relabeling only for the revised specification. Generate a fixed test set of 640 unaffected inputs, balanced between original labels, and 128 affected inputs, sampling states uniformly within each stratum. For each repetition s in {11,29}, train an original artifact with seed s, a no-op rebuild with seed s+1000, and a revised artifact also with seed s+1000. Couple the no-op and revised adapter initializations and minibatch index order. Every artifact uses a frozen BF16 base, LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0, q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projection targets, AdamW with zero weight decay, learning rate 2e-4 decaying cosinusoidally to 2e-5, 60 optimizer steps, effective batch 16 and microbatch 8. Mask prompt tokens in the loss; maximum sequence length 384. The scaffold contains the full specification followed by delimited input, using Qwen's chat template with thinking disabled. At evaluation use deterministic binary decision scores: compare the next-token logits for the single-token labels 0 and 1. Do not choose hyperparameters using test results. Keep all artifacts and record exact configurations.

event.description: The semantic edit produces more than three percentage points of excess regression on the unaffected region, relative to the matched no-op rebuild.
event.statistic: Mean over the two functions and two training seeds of NFR_revised minus NFR_noop, where NFR is the fraction of all unaffected test inputs that the original artifact classified correctly and the rebuilt artifact classified incorrectly.

evaluation.procedure: Evaluate original, no-op and revised artifacts on identical test inputs. Compute regressions only where the two reference functions agree. Affected-region accuracy is a diagnostic, not part of the registered statistic. Write the specification pairs and truth-function definitions to outputs/specifications.json; input pools, latent fields and references to outputs/training_examples.jsonl; per-input predictions, label logits, references and affected/unaffected flags to outputs/predictions.jsonl; one registered aggregate statistic to outputs/scores.jsonl; and seeds, package/model revisions, training settings and timings to outputs/run_manifest.json. Preserve per-function and per-seed observations in the prediction file. Weak original accuracy limits interpretation of a small regression statistic; a non-event does not establish compatibility.
evaluation.controls: The no-op and revised builds share initialization, optimization schedule and input order. All builds use the same training inputs and exact labels. The interpreter is unchanged. Test strata are defined by reference functions rather than model predictions.

registration.full_scale_study: Extend to many specification families, stronger initialization methods and repeated edit sequences. Compare cold recompilation, warm-start updates and edit-targeted replay, evaluating intended changes and invariant-region regressions separately.

agent.reason: Changed supervision can move decision boundaries outside the edited region, even with shared training inputs. However, subtracting matched no-op rebuild variation makes the three-percentage-point event substantially harder to reach than simply observing regressions.

judge_astra.reason: Shared oracle-labeled inputs and the paired no-op control remove major sources of rebuild variation, so exceeding three points of excess regression is possible but not especially likely. There is also an implementation ambiguity: covering all 240 email states requires 229 negative examples, making exact class balance impossible within 320 examples.

judge_fable.reason: The no-op and revised builds share initialization and batch order, so the excess regression comes mainly from the relabeled boundary states and the class-imbalance shift (especially for the log function, where 64 of 160 positives flip); I expect a real but modest excess of roughly 1-5pp, with ceiling effects possible if the 0.6B student reaches ~95% accuracy, making >3pp roughly a coin flip.

judge_opus.reason: Classifiers on fully covered 5-field states should be fairly accurate and the rebuilds are coupled, so most excess regression would be small. The main risk is the log edit, which relabels about 20% of training examples, pushes the class balance to about 30% positive, and makes every unaffected positive depend on reading the maintenance field under held-out templates; a lumpy template- or state-level failure there could push the mean above 3 points.

judge_sol.reason: Exact labels and complete latent-state coverage favor localized updates, while subtracting no-op rebuild variation makes the three-point excess harder to obtain. Changed label balance and held-out wording could nevertheless cause regressions outside the edited region.

judge_luna.reason: The matched rebuilds, exact labels, and coverage of every policy state make the comparison informative, but each edit changes labels in only a small part of its state space. A greater-than-3-point excess of regressions on unaffected cases would require spillover beyond those changed states, which is plausible but not my default expectation.

judge_muse.reason: No-op and revised share inputs, initialization and order and differ only on two flipped states and minor scaffold wording, so excess unaffected flips beyond seed variation are likely small; 3pp excess needs systematic spillover.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It presents compiled LoRA functions as stored, versioned software artifacts. From its abstract and my searches, it does not appear to test regressions on unaffected inputs after editing one clause of a specification, though I did not read its full text.

MUSCLE measures negative flips when the pretrained base model is updated. The experiment keeps the base frozen and changes the task specification, and it uses an exact reference function to define which inputs should keep their behaviour.

RIPPLE shows that local edits to a prompt policy in frozen workflow agents can spread to other behaviour. It does not involve retrained adapters, an executable reference that separates affected from unaffected inputs, or a paired no-op rebuild control.

This paper, like Churn Reduction via Distillation (2106.02654), studies prediction churn between retrainings of the same model, which corresponds to the experiment's no-op baseline. Neither measures excess regression caused by a semantic edit to the specification.

opus.reason: I found no prior work that recompiles an adapter after a one-clause specification edit and measures negative flips on inputs the edit should not affect, after subtracting a matched no-op rebuild. Related work covers changes to the base model (MUSCLE), churn between ordinary retrainings, and prompt-policy edits in agents (RIPPLE). None of these answers this question. My search covered titles and abstracts only, so a less visible match could still exist.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Studies negative flips after retraining text classifiers with additional data or classes. It does not test localized changes to existing decision rules using fixed training inputs and a matched unchanged-specification rebuild.

Measures NLP regressions from model updates, including random-seed-only retraining. It establishes ordinary rebuild variation but does not isolate excess regression caused by a local semantic specification change.

Evaluates locality when fine-tuning models to change factual knowledge, including LoRA-based editing. It updates existing models rather than independently recompiling original and revised functions, and lacks the paired no-op recompilation control.

Shows non-local effects and interactions from localized prompt-policy edits in frozen workflow agents. It does not retrain task adapters or measure oracle-defined invariant-region regressions relative to unchanged-specification rebuilds.

Introduces specification-specific adapter compilation and evaluates correctness, compilation cost, and applications, but does not evaluate behavioral compatibility across semantic specification edits.

sol.reason: Negative flips, rebuild instability, and edit-locality failures are established topics, so those broad ideas are not new. However, none of the work I found answers whether cold recompilation after a one-clause semantic change produces excess regressions on an exactly defined unaffected region beyond matched no-op rebuild variation. The fixed interpreter, shared oracle-labeled input pool, and coupled rebuild control distinguish this question from the existing update and editing experiments.

opus.reason: No list entry measures regressions on unaffected inputs after a one-clause specification edit relative to a matched no-op rebuild; #25 only rebuilds an unchanged specification and #35 compares warm versus cold starts after revisions.

sol.reason: Unlike entry 35’s warm-start comparison or entry 25’s rebuild-variance audit, this measures regressions on semantically unaffected inputs after an edit against a paired no-op rebuild.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the registered experiment as written. It is an API-free LoRA compiler: the Qwen3-0.6B base is frozen in BF16; LoRA r16/α32, dropout 0, on q/k/v/o and gate/up/down; AdamW with weight decay 0; cosine learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5 with no warmup; 60 steps; effective batch 16 (microbatch 8 × 2 accumulation); loss only on target tokens; max length 384; Qwen chat template with thinking disabled; decisions taken from the "0" vs "1" next-token logits.
- **Data.** Both functions and specifications follow the registration. Training uses 3 templates and testing uses 2 different templates, with disjoint record IDs. Each training pool has 320 inputs: every latent state at least once, then filled to 160/160 original labels. The same pool is used for every build; only the revised build is relabelled. Each test set has 640 unaffected inputs (320 per original label) and 128 affected inputs.
- **Seeds and coupling.** Repetitions use s ∈ {11, 29}. The original build uses seed s; the no-op and revised builds both use s+1000, so they share adapter initialisation and minibatch order.

Choices the registration left open:
- No gradient clipping.
- The training target is the label token plus `<|im_end|>`.
- Data-generation RNG seeds are fixed and recorded in the manifest.
- Adapters are saved to `artifacts/`. I deleted them before submitting to stay under the copy limit; the evaluation run recreates them.
- An extra file, `outputs/diagnostics.json`, holds per-cell NFRs and accuracies.

No hyperparameters were tuned.

**Result from my test run (about 7 minutes end to end):** the statistic was −0.0094, below the 0.03 threshold, so the registered event did not occur. Per cell (excess regression = NFR_revised − NFR_noop):

| Function, seed | Excess regression |
|---|---|
| email, 11 | +0.078 |
| email, 29 | −0.034 |
| log, 11 | −0.092 |
| log, 29 | +0.011 |

How to read this:
- **Rebuild noise is large.** No-op rebuilds alone caused regression rates (NFR) of 0 to 0.11, so the four cells disagree in sign and two repetitions give little power. The negative mean does not show that edits preserve unaffected behaviour.
- **Original accuracy on unaffected inputs was only 0.79–0.96**, which, as the registration warns, limits how far a small statistic can be interpreted.
- **Some log builds look under-trained.** One no-op build ended with training loss 0.24.
- **Affected-region accuracy (diagnostic only) was mixed.** Revised builds learned the edit well in 3 of 4 cells; in the email seed-29 cell they reached only 0.47 against the revised labels.

**Reproducibility:** GPU nondeterminism may shift the value slightly when the evaluation is re-run.

departures: exp.py: the training target is the label token followed by <|im_end|>. The registration does not specify this; the engineer disclosed it. Loss is the token mean over those two tokens, so the end token dilutes the label loss slightly. It could slightly change training dynamics but is a legitimate open choice.

exp.py: no gradient clipping and no warmup on the cosine schedule. Neither is specified by the registration, and both were disclosed. Per-step losses in run_manifest.json spike early (for example 1.41 at step 2), so this may add to rebuild variance. It is not a departure from the registration.
exp.py: the cosine schedule is evaluated at steps 0–59, so the final learning rate is just above 2e-5 rather than exactly 2e-5. This is negligible.
exp.py: each training and test input gets one template chosen at random, with fixed data seeds 1000+i and 5000+i. This is an open choice, recorded in run_manifest.json, and is unlikely to matter.

Engineer notes: the adapters were deleted before submission. run.sh runs rm -rf artifacts and the evaluation regenerated all 12 adapters, so the 'keep all artifacts' requirement is met in the evaluated run. No effect on the result.
outputs/diagnostics.json is an extra, unregistered file. No effect on the result.

No other departures found. Data construction (320 training inputs covering all states and balanced 160/160 on original labels; 640 unaffected test inputs at 320 per label; 128 affected), seed coupling (s versus s+1000 for both no-op and revised), the LoRA and optimizer settings, the chat template with thinking disabled, logit-comparison decoding and the NFR statistic computed over all 640 unaffected inputs all match the registration.
problems: Precision is very low. There are only 4 cells, with excess regressions of +0.078, −0.034, −0.092 and +0.011, a standard deviation of about 0.07. The standard error of the mean (−0.0094) is about 0.035, so a 3-point effect is not ruled out. The run neither supports nor refutes the hypothesis.

The test inputs are heavily clustered by latent state (outputs/specifications.json state_counts). Unaffected positives come from only 9 states for email and 3 for log, and affected inputs from 2 states each. The 640 'unaffected' inputs are therefore far from independent, and a cell's NFR can swing on a handful of latent states.

Original artifacts are weak (outputs/diagnostics.json). Accuracy on unaffected inputs is 0.79–0.80 for log and 0.81 for email seed 29. Original log artifacts reach only 0.41–0.44 on the affected inputs under their own specification. As the registration warns, this limits how far a small regression statistic can be interpreted.

Training is unstable or under-trained in some builds. log_original_seed1011 (the no-op build) ends with loss 0.24, and that cell's no-op NFR of 0.111 drives its −0.092 excess. The control is noisier than the treatment, so coupled rebuilds did not reduce variance.

In the email seed-29 cell the revised build reached only 0.47 on the affected inputs against the revised labels (outputs/diagnostics.json). The intended edit was not learned there, which confounds that cell's regression comparison.
The engineer's interpretation in the notes is appropriately cautious (a non-event does not establish compatibility); no overclaiming was found.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design faithfully: same input pools, oracle labels, coupled no-op and revised seeds, registered LoRA and optimizer settings, logit-based decisions, and the registered NFR-difference statistic. Remaining choices such as the end-token target and no clipping were left open by the registration and were disclosed. The reported −0.0094 is computed correctly from real per-input predictions saved in predictions.jsonl, and the four cell values reproduce the mean. However, rebuild noise dominates: cell values range from −0.09 to +0.08, original accuracy is weak, some builds are under-trained, and one revised build failed to learn the edit. The test set is also effectively a small number of latent states, so the result is a non-event with an uncertainty interval that comfortably includes the 3-point threshold. The evidence is valid but largely uninformative about the hypothesis, apart from showing that rebuild variance in this compiler setup is large.

departures: exp.py: the cosine schedule uses step/60 for updates numbered 0–59, so the last applied learning rate is approximately 2.0123e-5 rather than exactly 2e-5. This is a minor endpoint/discretization discrepancy, not a substantively different schedule; it is not plausibly material to the reported aggregate.

outputs/run_manifest.json: versions are recorded for torch, transformers and peft, but not for the explicitly requested accelerate and safetensors dependencies. This incomplete provenance cannot change the evaluated value itself, but could hinder exact reproduction.
problems: outputs/diagnostics.json: excess regression varies substantially across cells, from -0.0921875 to +0.078125. Two training seeds per function provide weak precision for a general claim about recompilation.

outputs/diagnostics.json: original unaffected-region accuracy ranges from 0.7921875 to 0.9609375, and no-op regression reaches 0.1109375. The registered statistic therefore measures retention relative to imperfect and variably stable original artifacts.

outputs/diagnostics.json: the revised email seed-29 artifact achieves only 0.46875 affected-region accuracy. Its low invariant-region regression cannot be interpreted as successful, behavior-preserving implementation of the edit.

exp.py and outputs/specifications.json: the test records repeatedly sample a small finite state space using two held-out templates. All latent states occur in training, and each edit affects only two states. This is legitimate under the registration, but limits semantic coverage and generalization; record counts are not independent task or training replications.

run.sh: pip and Python commands are piped without pipefail, so their failures could be masked by the shell exit status. The protected run's completed outputs establish delivery here, but the runner has a failure-reporting weakness.
sol.reason: The implementation preserves the registered truth functions, input pools, specification edits, frozen base, paired adapter initialization and minibatch order, evaluation rule, NFR denominator and aggregation. The fresh evaluation completed, retained all required outputs and adapters, and reported -0.009375, consistent with the four cell values; the code computes this statistic from model predictions rather than hard-coding it. The registered event did not occur, but this does not establish compatibility or absence of edit-induced regressions. Substantial cell heterogeneity, imperfect originals, incomplete edit success and only two training repetitions make this valid but weak pilot evidence.

departures: Cosine schedule in exp.py applies lr(step)=2e-5+(2e-4-2e-5)*0.5*(1+cos(pi*step/60)) on steps 0..59, so the last step is about 2.01e-5 rather than exactly 2e-5. This could not plausibly change the result.

exp.py evaluate() breaks logit ties toward 0 (pred=1 iff logit1>logit0). The registration says to compare the 0 and 1 logits but does not specify ties. Sampled margins are several logit units, so this is unlikely to change the result.

Training loss in exp.py is on the label token plus <|im_end|>, with no gradient clipping and default AdamW betas. The registration requires prompt masking but does not fix the target string, clipping, or betas. These are open choices; the extra target token could change learning relative to a label-only loss, but it does not contradict a registered setting.
problems: Cell excesses in outputs/diagnostics.json disagree in sign (+0.078, -0.034, -0.092, +0.011) and no-op NFR alone reaches 0.111, so the four-cell mean has less precision than the 0.03 threshold.

Several log artifacts are undertrained (stdout and outputs/run_manifest.json): log noop seed 1011 ends at loss 0.241, and original affected accuracy is only 0.41-0.44, so NFR mixes optimization failure with the edit.
Unaffected tests are with-replacement resamples of few latent states (exp.py; specifications.json: 9 and 3 unaffected-positive states), so the 640-input denominator overstates independent evidence.

Email seed 29 revised affected accuracy is 0.469 (outputs/diagnostics.json), so that cell did not learn the intended edit; the registration treats this as diagnostic only, but it weakens a semantic-regression reading.
A mean of -0.009 below 0.03 does not show that one-clause edits preserve unaffected behavior; outputs/scores.jsonl only records that the pre-registered event did not occur.
grok.reason: The fresh run implements the registered compiler, data, paired seeds, shared pools, oracle relabeling, and mean excess-NFR statistic; the printed value -0.009375 matches the four cells and scores.jsonl and is produced from real logits, not a hardcoded result. Open choices and the cosine endpoint do not change the registered question or plausibly move this value. The result is still weak: rebuild noise exceeds the 3pp threshold, cells disagree in sign, some runs never learn the function, and test items repeat a handful of states, so failing the event does not show that local spec edits are regression-free.

registration.title: Coverage repair versus perfect label repair in synthetic compilation data
registration.seed_connection: The seed varies teacher mixture and dataset size, and acknowledges inherited teacher errors. It does not isolate whether missing semantic cases or incorrect labels are the larger bottleneck at a fixed training budget.
registration.hypothesis: At fixed dataset size and optimization budget, repairing semantic-state coverage improves held-out contract accuracy more than perfectly correcting the labels of teacher-proposed inputs.
registration.contribution: An oracle-backed input-coverage-by-label-correction factorial that measures separable downstream bottlenecks. It is not proposed as a new general synthetic-data generator; its contribution is controlling class balance, surface realization, dataset size and student training while contrasting coverage and label repair.

closest_work.difference: BARRED already combines dimension-based coverage and debate-based label verification. This experiment measures their relative effects using exact labels, shared input rendering and fixed-size paired training pools rather than introducing another combined generation pipeline.

CircuitSynth enforces structured validity and coverage through a neuro-symbolic generator. Here small, enumerable policies enable a cheaper causal audit of coverage versus label correctness in the downstream adapter.

Adaptive Coverage selects representative synthetic examples. This experiment uses known semantic states rather than embedding coverage and compares the resulting gain directly with perfect relabeling.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-4B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B as the local teacher.
Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B as the frozen student.
PyPI transformers>=4.51,<5, peft>=0.15,<1, accelerate and safetensors.
Two locally generated six-Boolean-field policy datasets specified in the method.
registration.method: Use two binary policies with exact Python references. Escalation policy has fields resolved, production, security_incident, blocked, VIP and deadline_due; output 1 iff not resolved and ((production and security_incident) or (blocked and (VIP or deadline_due))). Access policy has fields active, signed, admin, trained, staff and restricted; output 1 iff active and signed and (admin or (trained and staff and not restricted)). Specifications explicitly state that fields are independent and all 64 combinations are admissible. For each policy ask the local 4B teacher, with thinking disabled and temperature 0.8, to propose 256 diverse input records in batches of eight, with all six fields present and Boolean-valued. Ask it to include both decision classes but do not require particular field combinations. Accept records based only on schema validity; do not deduplicate semantic states or reject incorrect-policy combinations. Cap generation at 40 batch requests per policy and fail transparently if 256 valid records cannot be obtained. Call this input pool S. Construct pool B with 256 programmatic records, matching S's exact oracle-positive and oracle-negative counts, while cycling as evenly as possible through the latent states within each class. Apply the same seeded renderer to both pools, using identical field wording and field-order distributions and disjoint opaque record IDs. Label both pools with the same local teacher protocol: full specification plus one rendered record, and forced-choice next-token scoring for 0 versus 1 with thinking disabled. Independently compute exact oracle labels. This yields four arms: S with teacher labels, S with oracle labels, B with teacher labels, and B with oracle labels. Freeze these pools across student repetitions. Train each arm independently for seeds 11 and 29, coupling initialization and example-index schedules across arms. Use frozen BF16 Qwen3-0.6B, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout 0 on q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projections; output-only cross-entropy, AdamW, zero weight decay, 60 steps, effective batch 16, microbatch 8, sequence length 384, and cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5. Use the same full-specification scaffold throughout. Evaluate using binary label logits. The blind test contains eight newly rendered records per latent state, with held-out record IDs and two held-out templates; reference labels come only from the Python policies. No hosted APIs or PAW initialization are used.

event.description: The gain from coverage repair under correct labels exceeds the gain from perfect relabeling of teacher-proposed inputs by more than five percentage points.
event.statistic: Mean over policies and student seeds of (accuracy_B_oracle minus accuracy_S_oracle) minus (accuracy_S_oracle minus accuracy_S_teacher), with accuracy macro-averaged equally over the 64 latent states.

evaluation.procedure: Compute the registered contrast on the fixed exhaustive-state test. The B_teacher arm supplies factorial diagnostics but is not included in the primary contrast. Write teacher requests, raw generations and schema rejections to outputs/teacher_generations.jsonl; all accepted records, pool assignments, state IDs, teacher labels, oracle labels and rendered inputs to outputs/data.jsonl; arm-by-seed test decisions and label logits to outputs/predictions.jsonl; the single registered contrast to outputs/scores.jsonl; and revisions, configurations and timings to outputs/run_manifest.json. Inspect label-error and state-frequency information through the raw data to interpret the contrast. The test distribution is an explicit contract-coverage distribution, not an estimate of real user traffic.
evaluation.controls: All arms have equal example counts, common renderers, matched oracle class counts between input pools, identical student configurations and coupled training randomness. Teacher labeling uses the same protocol on both pools. Semantic verification corrects labels without filtering inputs.

registration.full_scale_study: Repeat across more policies, teacher families and synthesis budgets, then replace exact state enumeration with practical coverage estimates. Test whether compile-time resources should preferentially purchase new semantic cases or additional label verification.

agent.reason: I expect teacher-proposed inputs to concentrate on familiar semantic states while the 4B teacher makes relatively few labeling errors on these explicit policies. outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: experiment.py, run by run.sh. It implements the registered 2x2 factorial: input pool (S = proposed by the teacher, B = programmatic coverage-repaired pool) × label source (labels from the Qwen3-4B teacher vs oracle labels from the Python policy). It covers the two policies (escalation and access) and student seeds 11 and 29. The student is frozen BF16 Qwen3-0.6B with LoRA r16/alpha32/dropout 0 on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down. Training is 60 steps, effective batch 16 (microbatch 8), max length 384, AdamW with weight decay 0, and a cosine learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5. The loss is cross-entropy on the single 0/1 output token. Teacher labels and student evaluation both compare the next-token logits for '0' and '1', with thinking disabled. No hosted APIs and no PAW initialisation are used. Within a seed, all arms share the LoRA initialisation (same torch seed before get_peft_model) and the same example-index schedule.

How the pools are built:
- **S:** the 4B teacher runs at temperature 0.8 with thinking off. It gets 32 batched requests first, then rounds of 8, capped at 40 requests in total. If it cannot supply 256 valid records, the run stops and says so. Records are accepted on schema validity only: exactly the six keys, all JSON Booleans. There is no deduplication and no semantic filtering.
- **B:** matches S's oracle positive and negative counts exactly. Within each class it cycles evenly through that class's latent states, in a seeded shuffled order.
- **Rendering:** both pools use the same seeded stream of templates and field orders. Training uses 4 templates and the test uses 2 held-out ones. Record IDs are opaque and disjoint across S, B and test.
- **Test set:** 8 records per latent state, giving 512 per policy. Labels come from the Python policies only.
- **Metric:** accuracy macro-averaged over the 64 states.

Small choices the registration left open (all recorded in run_manifest.json):
- Sampling uses top_p=1 and top_k=0, i.e. pure temperature sampling, since only the temperature was registered.
- A request that returned more than 8 valid records contributes only its first 8; the extras are logged as rejections. In the test run every request returned exactly 8.
- Each record is labelled with a single-turn chat prompt: the full specification, then the rendered record, then "Answer with a single digit: 0 or 1."

Test run on this machine: about 12.4 minutes end to end. Value = -0.0762, which does not exceed the 0.05 threshold, so the registered event did not occur in this run.

The policy × seed breakdown in scores.jsonl shows the two policies pointing in opposite directions:
- **Escalation:** coverage gain is +0.30 and +0.34; relabel gain is -0.17 and +0.05; contrast is +0.47 and +0.29.
- **Access:** coverage gain is +0.02 and +0.04; relabel gain is +0.55 and +0.58; contrast is -0.53 and -0.54.

From the raw data:
- S covers only 23 of 64 states for escalation and 14 of 64 for access.
- The teacher's label error rate on S is 17% for escalation and 71% for access. On access the teacher labelled 246 of 256 S records as positive, against an oracle count of 64.

So whether coverage or labels is the bigger bottleneck depends on the policy, through how badly the teacher's labels fail. The mean being below the threshold comes from averaging two large, opposite effects; it does not mean the two kinds of repair are equivalent.

Caveats:
- There are only 2 seeds per policy, and escalation varies a lot by seed (S_teacher scored 0.78 vs 0.51).
- Both the teacher generation and the training are not bit-deterministic on GPU, so a rerun on a fresh machine may give a slightly different value. On escalation the run-to-run variation could plausibly be several points.

departures: experiment.py: teacher proposals were issued as one round of 32 requests, then rounds of 8, capped at 40. The registration asks for batches of eight records with a 40-request cap, which this satisfies, and batching is an implementation detail. The run used exactly 32 requests per policy. Could not change the result.

experiment.py GEN_CFG: sampling used top_p=1.0 and top_k=0 (pure temperature 0.8), overriding Qwen3's default generation_config. The registration specifies only temperature, so this is an open choice, and it is disclosed in the notes and run_manifest.json. It could shift the diversity and state coverage of S, and therefore the size of the coverage gain, but it does not depart from the registration.

experiment.py parse_generation: valid records beyond 8 in one response are logged as rejections, and there is a fallback parser for a dict containing a records/examples/inputs list. These are open choices. Every request returned exactly 8 valid records, so neither rule affected the value.

experiment.py label_prompt: the labeling instruction 'Answer with a single digit: 0 or 1.' and the single-turn chat format are an open prompt choice. The same prompt is used for teacher labeling and the student scaffold, consistent with the registration.
experiment.py: the cosine schedule has no warmup and the LR is set per step from 2e-4 to 2e-5. This is an open detail, the same for all arms, and not change-inducing.

No departures found in the pool construction, matched class counts, shared seeded renderer stream, disjoint IDs, test design, student configuration, coupled seeds and schedules, or the statistic. I recomputed the mean of the four contrasts as -0.07617, matching scores.jsonl.
