registration.title: Training a compiled validator on real upstream mistakes rather than synthetic mutations
registration.seed_connection: The seed composes independently compiled functions and uses validators around generated answers and executable action programs. This experiment asks whether a validator's training distribution should depend on the actual upstream compiled function.
registration.hypothesis: A validator trained on an upstream adapter's actual semantic mistakes provides higher held-out pipeline utility than an otherwise matched validator trained on randomly mutated reference outputs.
registration.contribution: A controlled interface-training comparison for two adapters sharing a small frozen interpreter. Actual mistakes and artificial negatives are paired by command and approximately matched in action-sequence length and edit distance, and the endpoint is deployment utility rather than generator-validator agreement.

closest_work.difference: RankAlign improves consistency between generator and validator rankings. Here the goal is rejecting objectively incorrect programs, not aligning beliefs, using separate task adapters and an executable reference.

Update-Free On-Policy Steering trains verifiers on robot-policy rollouts. This experiment tests whether actual-rollout training beats hardness-matched artificial negatives for compact language-function composition under a held-out length shift.
SCAN supplies the compositional command domain and references. The experiment concerns downstream validation of a compiled generator, not simply command-to-action generalization.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
SCAN length split from https://github.com/brendenlake/SCAN: length_split/tasks_train_length.txt and length_split/tasks_test_length.txt.
PyPI transformers>=4.51,<5, peft>=0.15,<1, accelerate and safetensors.
registration.method: Parse SCAN commands and provided action sequences. Map I_WALK, I_LOOK, I_RUN, I_JUMP, I_TURN_LEFT and I_TURN_RIGHT to the six output tokens WALK, LOOK, RUN, JUMP, LEFT and RIGHT. The actor emits a whitespace-separated sequence using only these tokens. Its natural-language specification fully describes SCAN semantics: direction prepends a turn; opposite uses two turns; around uses four turn/action units; twice/thrice repeats the complete unit; and concatenates; after reverses clause order. For each seed in {11,29}, train an actor on 256 fixed training-split commands, stratified between reference lengths <=10 and 11–22. Keep a separate 512-command mining pool and 192-command calibration pool from the training split, excluding actor training examples. Use 512 fixed test commands from the length-test split. All pools are disjoint by command. Actor training uses frozen BF16 Qwen3-0.6B, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout 0 on all seven attention/MLP projection types; 80 output-only cross-entropy steps, effective batch 16, microbatch 8, maximum sequence length 384, AdamW with zero weight decay and cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5. Generate actor outputs greedily with thinking disabled and a 160-new-token cap. A parser rejects empty outputs or tokens outside the six-token vocabulary. Mine up to 192 schema-valid but semantically incorrect actor outputs, taking a seeded random subset if necessary. Let K be the available count; use all if fewer than 192. Train two validators on the same K commands and the same K reference-positive programs. The rollout-aware validator gets the K actual incorrect actor programs as negatives. The mutation validator gets incorrect programs made by randomly inserting, deleting and replacing actions in the corresponding references. Match each negative's length exactly and target its token-level Levenshtein distance to the actual actor error; allow 100 attempts, retaining the closest-distance non-reference candidate and logging residual mismatch. Both validators receive the full semantics, command and candidate, and output 1 for an exact correct action sequence or 0 otherwise. Couple validator initialization, index order and hyperparameters; use the actor training recipe with maximum sequence length 512. Score validators by logit(1)-logit(0). On the common calibration actor outputs, select each acceptance threshold maximizing utility U = fraction accepted-and-correct minus four times fraction accepted-and-incorrect. Include reject-all among threshold choices and break ties toward the higher threshold. Freeze thresholds before test evaluation. Parser-invalid outputs are automatically rejected. If K=0, record that the validator-training comparison was infeasible rather than fabricating negatives. No large teacher or hosted service is required.

event.description: Rollout-aware validator training improves held-out pipeline utility by more than 0.05 relative to matched mutation training.
event.statistic: Mean across the two actor seeds of U_rollout_validator minus U_mutation_validator on the fixed length-test commands, using calibration-selected thresholds and incorrect acceptance cost four.

evaluation.procedure: Use provided SCAN action sequences as exact references after the fixed token mapping. The actor predictions are identical for the two validators within a repetition. Evaluate utility over all test commands, including parser rejections with zero utility. Write mining, calibration and test actor outputs with references and parser decisions to outputs/actor_predictions.jsonl; paired validator examples, edit distances and matching residuals to outputs/validator_training.jsonl; calibration/test validator logits and accept/reject decisions to outputs/validator_scores.jsonl; thresholds selected without test access to outputs/thresholds.json; the registered utility difference to outputs/scores.jsonl; and configurations, pool membership, revisions, K and timings to outputs/run_manifest.json. Report feasibility failure if no semantic mining errors exist. Calibration is an empirical decision rule, not a safety guarantee under the length shift.
evaluation.controls: Common actor outputs, identical positive examples, command-paired negatives, matched negative counts and lengths, logged edit-distance matching, coupled validator training randomness, and identical calibration utility and threshold-selection procedures.

registration.full_scale_study: Study interface-aware compilation across larger program trees, more realistic commands and several upstream versions. Compare independent compilation with periodically refreshing downstream training on newly observed upstream errors.

agent.reason: Actual actor mistakes can expose systematic failure patterns that hardness-matched random mutations miss. The small validator, held-out length shift and reject-all calibration option could nevertheless eliminate a measurable utility advantage.

judge_astra.reason: Actual upstream mistakes could teach validators to reject costly errors that matched random mutations miss. However, weak actor generalization on the length split and calibration selecting near-reject-all thresholds could leave little separation between the pipelines.

judge_fable.reason: The 0.6B actor will be near 0% exact match on the SCAN length split, so utility differences are driven by which validator accepts more wrong long outputs under OOD; rollout negatives plausibly transfer better than random mutations, but both validators could reject nearly everything (tie near zero) or the calibrated rollout validator could accept more, and the implementation is complex.

judge_opus.reason: On the SCAN length split the actor will be almost always wrong, so test utility depends mainly on how calibration thresholds transfer under shift, not on validator quality. A more discriminative rollout validator may pick a more permissive threshold and be penalized, and both validators may reject everything. A mean gain above 0.05 needs the mutation validator to be specifically lenient on coherent-looking actor errors.

judge_sol.reason: Actual actor mistakes may remain more structurally plausible than mutations despite length and edit-distance matching, giving rollout-aware training an advantage. Conservative calibration and poor actor generalization under the length shift could instead leave both validators rejecting nearly everything.

judge_luna.reason: Training on the actor's actual mistakes could teach the validator its characteristic failure modes better than edit-matched mutations. However, mining and calibration use the training split while the test is a length split, so those error patterns may not transfer well enough to produce the required utility gain.

judge_muse.reason: On-policy negatives often help, but both validators train on short commands and face length-shift to long test with cost-4 utility favoring reject-all, so >0.05 gain is possible but uncertain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: UF-OPS trains verifiers on a robot policy's own rollouts and uses them to steer at execution time. It does not compare rollout-trained verifiers against matched synthetic negatives, it involves no language functions or compiled adapters, and it reports no cost-weighted acceptance utility under a length shift.

RankAlign aims to make generator and validator rankings consistent. It does not ask whether a validator trained on a specific upstream model's real errors rejects incorrect programs better than one trained on mutated references.

This paper builds both controlled-induced and naturally occurring clinical hallucinations. It reports that detectors developed on the controlled ones generalize to the natural ones. That is related to the synthetic-versus-natural-negatives question, but it covers detection in summarization, uses no trained validator in a pipeline, and has no matched comparison of negative sources.

The seed paper composes compiled functions and puts validators around their outputs, but as far as I found it does not study where a validator's training data should come from or how it depends on the upstream function.
SCAN is used only as the domain and source of references. It is about generalizing from commands to actions, not about validating a generator's outputs downstream.

opus.reason: My searches covered verifiers trained on on-policy versus synthetic negatives, hallucination detectors trained on natural versus injected errors, and the compiled-function setting. None turned up a controlled comparison of a validator trained on an upstream adapter's real errors versus one trained on reference mutations matched in length and edit distance, scored by calibrated, cost-weighted pipeline utility. The broader idea that training on a model's own errors can beat synthetic corruption appears in other areas, such as robot verifiers, grammatical error correction, and hallucination detection. Even so, I found no prior work that settles this specific question, though a missed paper remains possible.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: TrueTeacher compares factual-consistency evaluators trained on model-generated summaries versus perturbed references, controlling dataset size and studying domain shift. It does not hold positives fixed while pairing actual upstream errors with length- and edit-distance-matched mutation negatives.
UF-OPS trains verifiers on policy rollouts and compares on-policy with other-policy training data, but does not compare actual failures against matched mutations of correct programs.
The seed demonstrates independently compiled function composition and output validation, without comparing downstream validator training distributions.

sol.reason: The broad idea of learning verification from realistic model mistakes rather than artificial corruptions already appears in TrueTeacher, and policy-specific verifier training appears in UF-OPS. However, neither answers the controlled question of whether upstream-error provenance improves pipeline utility when positives, commands, negative counts, lengths and approximate edit distances are held constant; I found no prior work reporting that comparison.

opus.reason: No list entry compares a validator trained on an upstream adapter's actual errors with one trained on matched synthetic mutations; #38 tests a syntax validator with retry, not validator training data.

sol.reason: No listed experiment compares validators trained on actual upstream mistakes versus matched artificial mutations using calibrated held-out pipeline utility.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the registered SCAN experiment in run.py, and run_eval.sh runs it. One full test run on the A100 took about 9 minutes. That run produced value = 0.0: the difference was 0.0 for each actor seed (11 and 29). So the registered event (difference > 0.05) did not occur.

What the 0.0 means: for both seeds, threshold selection on the calibration pool chose reject-all for both validators, so both had a test utility of exactly 0. The diagnostics below are AUCs I computed from outputs/validator_scores.jsonl after the run. They suggest that under the registered recipe (80 LoRA steps on a 0.6B model) neither validator learned to tell correct programs from incorrect ones:
- **Rollout validator:** final training loss stayed near ln2 (≈0.67). AUC was 0.45–0.51 on calibration and 0.53–0.56 on test, i.e. chance level.
- **Mutation validator:** training loss fell to about 0.53. Its scores ranked actual actor outputs the wrong way round: AUC 0.19–0.25 on calibration and 0.34–0.38 on test.

This is a null result produced by the "reject-all" floor. It is not evidence that the two kinds of training are equivalent in general. With a validator that learns more, the comparison could come out differently.

Other numbers from the run:
- **Actor accuracy:** about 62% exact-correct on the in-distribution mining and calibration pools, but only about 3% on the length-test commands. Over 99.5% of outputs passed the parser.
- **Mined errors:** K = 192 for seed 11 and 191 for seed 29. Seed 11 had more than 192 errors, so a seeded subset was taken.
- **Mutation matching:** lengths match exactly. Edit distance matched exactly for 97% (seed 11) and 92% (seed 29) of pairs. The largest residual was 9, and every residual is logged.

Implementation choices where the registration was not specific:
1. **Fixed pools:** the actor-training (128 commands of length ≤10 plus 128 of length 11–22), mining (512), calibration (192) and test (512) pools are sampled once with seed 0 and shared by both actor seeds. They are deduplicated by command and checked to be disjoint. The actor seed controls LoRA initialisation, data order, the mining subset and the mutations.
2. **Validator setup:** each validator is a fresh rank-16 LoRA on the base model. The two validators in a repetition share the same initialisation seed and the same order seed. Positives and negatives are interleaved by command index, so the two data orders correspond exactly.
3. **Loss and learning-rate schedule:** the validator target is a single "1" or "0" token, and the score is logit("1") − logit("0") at the answer position. The actor target is the action sequence plus <|im_end|>. The cosine schedule runs from 2e-4 to 2e-5 with no warmup, and there is no gradient clipping.
4. **Thresholds:** candidate thresholds are every calibration score plus reject-all. A command is accepted if it parses and its score ≥ the threshold, and ties go to the higher threshold. thresholds.json is written before any test utility is computed.
5. **Unscored outputs:** outputs the parser rejects are not scored by the validators and count as rejected, contributing zero utility.

scores.jsonl also records, for context, the per-seed utility of accepting every valid output, of an oracle, and of rejecting everything. No hosted models were used.

departures: Validator training truncation (run.py train_lora with VAL_MAXLEN=512): when prompt plus candidate exceeds 512 tokens, ids and labels are cut from the end. The single '1'/'0' target token is lost, so these examples carry no supervision and are silently dropped. For seed 29 this hit 36 of 382 rollout examples and 31 of 382 mutation examples (run_manifest.json). The 512 limit was registered, but the effective number of training examples differs between the two conditions, which slightly weakens the matched-count control. It could change validator quality marginally, but is unlikely to change a reject-all outcome.

Scores are taken from bf16 logits under autocast (run.py score). The logit(1)-logit(0) values are therefore quantized to multiples of about 0.125, producing many ties (validator_scores.jsonl shows values like 0.125, 0.625, 1.0). The registration says only 'score by logit(1)-logit(0)' with a BF16 model, so this is arguably inherent. It coarsens threshold choice and could reduce achievable discrimination.

Fixed pools are sampled once with POOL_SEED=0 and shared across actor seeds (run.py, run_manifest.json). This is consistent with 'fixed' commands in the registration, and the engineer reported it. It does not change the result.

The SCAN data files were supplied with the submission (data/*.txt) and used instead of a fresh download. Their sizes and contents look like the genuine length split, but no file hash is recorded. Provenance is only a minor concern and is unlikely to change the result.

Choices left open by the registration: no warmup and no gradient clipping (a loss spike to about 5 at step 2 is visible in run_manifest.json), interleaved positive/negative ordering that is then permuted, and parser-invalid outputs left unscored and rejected. These are reported and allowed by the registration. The missing warmup may have contributed to the validators failing to learn, but it is not a departure.

No other departures found. Model, LoRA configuration, step count, batch sizes, greedy decoding with thinking disabled, 160-token cap, K mining rule, length-exact mutation with logged edit-distance residuals, coupled validator seeds, calibration-only threshold selection including reject-all with ties to the higher threshold, cost 4, and the registered statistic all match the registration.
problems: Both validators failed to learn. Rollout validator training loss ended at about 0.67–0.69, roughly ln2 (run_manifest.json, outputs_log.txt). All four calibration threshold selections chose reject-all (thresholds.json). The 0.0 difference is a floor artifact and says nothing about which training distribution is better.

The event was nearly unreachable by design. Actor test accuracy is about 3% (oracle utility is 0.033 and 0.031 in scores.jsonl). A difference above 0.05 would therefore require the mutation validator to have negative test utility, rather than the rollout validator being better.

The final '1'/'0' label is silently removed from over-length validator examples (run.py train_lora truncation), so some examples train on nothing. The number affected differs between the rollout and mutation conditions.
bf16 quantization of the score logits (run.py score) produces heavy ties in validator_scores.jsonl.
The engineer's AUC diagnostics, including the inverted ranking for the mutation validator, are post hoc and not written to any registered output. They are plausible but unverified here.
Two seeds with a single run each give no estimate of variance.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely. The only notable implementation issues are label-dropping truncation at the registered 512-token limit and coarse bf16 scores, neither of which plausibly changed a value produced by reject-all in every case. The reported 0.0 comes from real actor and validator outputs, with thresholds frozen on calibration before test evaluation, so the evidence is valid. It is uninformative, though: neither validator learned to discriminate, every threshold defaulted to reject-all, and with 3% actor accuracy on the length-test commands even an oracle could not exceed the 0.05 margin. This is a weak null that reflects an under-trained validator recipe and a near-unreachable event, not evidence about rollout-aware versus mutation training.

departures: Training-input truncation in run.py silently removes supervision rather than ensuring complete registered examples fit. train_lora truncates prompt-plus-target from the right. Since validator targets contain exactly one token, every truncated validator example loses its entire target and contributes no supervised loss. outputs/run_manifest.json reports 36/382 such examples for seed 29's rollout validator and 31/382 for its mutation validator. This changes the effective training examples, class balance and coupled minibatch supervision, and could change learning, thresholds and the reported utility difference. The same truncation logic applies to actor training, but the displayed manifest excerpt does not establish whether actor examples were truncated.

Threshold/test chronology in run.py differs from the registered instruction to freeze thresholds before test evaluation: test actor outputs and test validator logits are computed before threshold selection. thresholds.json is written before test utility is calculated, and select_threshold receives only calibration scores and labels. Thus the ordering departs from the registration, but the visible code provides no test-dependent threshold choice or plausible effect on the reported value.
problems: run.py does not preserve validator targets when enforcing the context limit. The known, unequal numbers of entirely unsupervised examples undermine the registered matched-data controls; validator_training.jsonl records nominal pairs rather than which examples actually supplied training loss.

outputs/thresholds.json and outputs/scores.jsonl show that all four validators reject everything. The zero difference therefore demonstrates identical deployed decisions here, not equivalent validator capabilities or equivalent training distributions.

outputs/scores.jsonl gives oracle utilities of 0.033203125 and 0.03125. Conditional on the mutation validators rejecting everything, even perfect rollout validators could achieve a mean improvement of only about 0.0322, below the registered 0.05 event threshold. This limits how informative the endpoint is for these actors.

The engineer_notes AUC diagnostics are not independently established for the protected run by the displayed evidence. Final minibatch losses near ln(2), or approximately chance AUCs without uncertainty estimates, do not establish absence of learning. The notes' statement that seed 11 required subsampling also does not describe the protected run, which found exactly 192 eligible errors.

run.py uses the submitted SCAN files without verifying their correspondence to upstream, then records the current repository-head revision after execution. That revision is not demonstrably tied to the consumed file contents. This is a provenance limitation, not evidence that the data were altered.
sol.reason: The protected execution and score files consistently establish a mean utility difference of 0.0, with reject-all selected for both validators in both seeds. Fidelity is unfaithful because known target-dropping truncation plausibly changes training and breaks the intended matched supervision, although its actual effect on the zero result is unknown. The reported value is nevertheless valid for the executed pipeline: it is calculated from real outputs using the registered utility, with no visible hard-coding, metric error or test-dependent threshold selection. Research value is limited because the comparison collapses to reject-all, actor accuracy leaves little positive-utility headroom, and the result does not establish equivalence between the training approaches.

departures: run.py end-truncates at the registered max length (384 actor / 512 validator), which can drop the only supervised target token; run_manifest.json shows 36/382 rollout and 31/382 mutation truncations for seed 29. Overflow handling was unspecified. It could affect learning, but it did not plausibly change this reported 0.0: rollout loss stayed near chance on the untruncated majority, and the mutation validator reduced loss yet still selected reject-all.

run.py appends <|im_end|> to actor targets and stops greedy generation on <|im_end|> or <|endoftext|>. The registration specifies greedy decoding, thinking disabled, and a 160-token cap, but not the stop token. This did not plausibly change the result: parser-valid rates were 0.996-1.000 and both utilities were the reject-all floor.

run.py forces attn_implementation='sdpa' and uses AdamW defaults with no warmup and no gradient clipping, none of which the registration specifies. These did not plausibly move either calibrated policy off reject-all, so they did not change the reported difference.
problems: Both validators selected reject-all, so test utility is exactly 0 on both seeds and the registered contrast is censored (outputs/thresholds.json, outputs/scores.jsonl, outputs_log.txt). A difference of 0.0 does not show the two training methods are equivalent.

Under the registered 80-step recipe the rollout loss stayed near ln(2) (0.686 and 0.670) and the mutation loss only fell to 0.579 and 0.536 (outputs_log.txt, outputs/run_manifest.json). Seed 11 rollout scores in outputs/validator_scores.jsonl are often a constant 0.125 on both correct and incorrect calibration items, so the validators did not learn a deployable check.

End-truncation in run.py can remove validator labels on long programs (seed 29: 36 rollout and 31 mutation examples in outputs/run_manifest.json), which weakens training but is not what sets the reported utilities.
grok.reason: The code runs the registered comparison: seeds 11 and 29, fixed disjoint SCAN pools, the specified LoRA recipe, greedy thinking-disabled decoding, command-paired length- and edit-distance-matched negatives, coupled validator training, and calibration utility with incorrect-acceptance cost 4. The fresh run's 0.0 is produced from real model outputs; both thresholds are reject-all, and the logged accept-all and oracle utilities match exact counts on 512 test commands, so the statistic is not hard-coded or leaked. Unspecified truncation and decoding details did not plausibly move this floor result. The pre-registered >0.05 event therefore did not occur, but the evidence is weak about the hypothesis because neither validator was deployable and the utility gap cannot show a difference.

registration.title: Does a stale adapter obstruct a correct updated run-time scaffold?
registration.seed_connection: A seed artifact contains both adapter weights and a specification-bearing prompt scaffold. This experiment tests whether updating only that discrete component can leave the hybrid artifact less faithful to the new specification than the untuned interpreter.
registration.hypothesis: On inputs whose required output changes, retaining the old task adapter while installing the new correct scaffold reduces semantic accuracy relative to the unadapted interpreter using that same new scaffold.
registration.contribution: An actionable hybrid-artifact compatibility audit using a full adapter-by-scaffold crossover. Counterbalanced edit directions and exact references distinguish stale-adapter interference from output-format failures and general difficulty with the revised task.

closest_work.difference: The verbal conflict study manipulates default response tendencies and in-context rules. Here separately versioned, task-specific LoRAs and scaffolds are crossed after local policy updates, with deployment-style semantic compatibility as the endpoint.

PAW establishes the hybrid pseudo-program-plus-adapter representation and tests raw versus rewritten specifications. This experiment tests inconsistent versions of those two components rather than denoising or removing a component.

Knowledge-conflict work studies discrepancies between stored facts and supplied context. This experiment induces known conflicts through compiled decision-function versions and includes newly recompiled compatible artifacts.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
PyPI transformers>=4.51,<5, peft>=0.15,<1, accelerate and safetensors.
Two exhaustive six-Boolean-field policy families and executable references defined in the method.
registration.method: Implement cold, API-free task-adapter training on a frozen BF16 interpreter. Policy A is escalation, with resolved, production, security_incident, blocked, VIP and deadline_due. Old output 1 iff not resolved and ((production and security_incident) or (blocked and (VIP or deadline_due))). New policy changes only (VIP or deadline_due) to deadline_due, so affected cases change 1 to 0. Policy B is access, with active, signed, admin, trained, staff and restricted. Old output 1 iff active and signed and ((admin and trained) or (staff and trained and not restricted)). New policy changes only (admin and trained) to admin, so affected cases change 0 to 1. Use full, explicit natural-language specifications with identical surrounding wording and output labels 0/1. Generate 320 training inputs per policy, including every latent state and then balancing old-policy labels. Reuse those inputs for old and new training with exact version-specific labels. Render with three fixed training templates and opaque record IDs. Test with two held-out templates and disjoint IDs: 256 affected records sampled uniformly over affected states, plus 640 unaffected records balanced by reference label. For each seed 11 and 29 train old and new adapters from coupled initializations and the same example-index schedule. Use LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0 on q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projections; AdamW, zero weight decay, 60 steps, effective batch 16, microbatch 8, maximum sequence length 384, output-only loss and cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5. The run-time scaffold is the full specification followed by delimited facts in the Qwen chat template with thinking disabled. Evaluate all four old/new adapter-by-old/new scaffold combinations, plus the base with no adapter under each scaffold. Also evaluate an explicitly semantics-equivalent old-spec paraphrase with the old adapter as a prompt-change control; fix this paraphrase before running models. Decisions use the next-token logits for 0 versus 1, avoiding confounding semantic errors with malformed label generation. The new specification is authoritative for the stale-adapter/new-scaffold condition. Do not modify weights during crossover evaluation.

event.description: The stale adapter causes more than five percentage points of harm on the changed region relative to disabling the adapter while retaining the new scaffold.
event.statistic: Mean over both policies and both seeds of accuracy_base_with_new_scaffold minus accuracy_old_adapter_with_new_scaffold on affected test inputs.

evaluation.procedure: Compute changed-region accuracy using exact new-policy references. Weight policies equally so tightening and loosening edits contribute equally. Compatible-pair accuracy, unaffected-region accuracy and the old paraphrase control remain diagnostics in raw records. Write specifications and truth functions to outputs/specifications.json; training inputs and both reference labels to outputs/training_examples.jsonl; per-case crossover conditions, label logits and decisions to outputs/crossover_predictions.jsonl; the one registered interference statistic to outputs/scores.jsonl; and configurations, model/package revisions and timings to outputs/run_manifest.json. A large gap without useful compatible-artifact accuracy would not establish a deployable function; retain those diagnostics. A small gap is not evidence of general compatibility.
evaluation.controls: Frozen shared base, exact labels, complete component crossover, newly trained compatible artifacts, no-adapter controls, a semantics-preserving prompt-change control, and opposite edit directions across the two policies.

registration.full_scale_study: Measure compatibility matrices across many artifact versions, adapter strengths and edit types. Test atomic component updates, prompt-only hot fixes, adapter disabling and rollback policies before adding such mechanisms to a neural-function deployment system.

agent.reason: Training each adapter on one fixed policy is likely to create an old-rule preference that a scaffold-only update does not fully override. Counterbalanced edit directions make the registered harm plausible, although adapters that improve general rule interpretation could instead help under the new scaffold.

judge_astra.reason: Training each adapter under one fixed specification is likely to preserve the old decision rule despite a small scaffold update, and evaluation specifically on changed cases should expose that interference. The main risks are insufficient learning of the old rule or a base interpreter that also fails on the affected cases.

judge_fable.reason: A LoRA adapter trained on a constant specification largely learns facts-to-label mapping and ignores prompt text, so the stale adapter with the new scaffold should mostly emit old labels (~20-30% correct on the changed region) while the unadapted base with counterbalanced edit directions should average near 50%; the main risks are a weakly trained old adapter or a base model that keys on the same surface features in the wrong direction.

judge_opus.reason: A LoRA trained under a constant scaffold will very likely keep producing old labels on affected inputs whatever a minimally edited spec says, giving near-zero changed-region accuracy. The counterbalanced edit directions keep a bias-dominated base model near 50%. The main failure mode is a base model whose heuristics happen to be wrong in both directions.

judge_sol.reason: Training against one fixed specification gives an adapter substantial opportunity to encode the old decision mapping rather than defer to an updated scaffold. A five-point interference effect therefore seems likely, although weak compatible-adapter learning or poor base-model accuracy could limit the gap.

judge_luna.reason: The old adapter is trained to produce the old labels precisely where the revised policy flips them, while the no-adapter baseline still sees the complete new rule. The main uncertainty is whether the adapter can follow the revised scaffold anyway, and whether the unadapted 0.6B model can execute these Boolean rules reliably.

judge_muse.reason: Adapters trained on exact full-state data will likely retain old decisions on 3-4 flipped states despite the new scaffold, while base with new scaffold should be near chance or better, and opposite edit directions average out label bias.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This paper finds that fine-tuning that strengthens an in-weight default response lowers accuracy when an explicit in-context rule conflicts with that default, which is the closest mechanism to this experiment. Its setting is a Stroop-like colour-word task on Gemma/Pythia. It does not cross separately trained task LoRAs with old and new specification scaffolds after a policy edit. It also has no no-adapter baseline under the new scaffold and does not measure accuracy on the region whose labels changed.

The seed paper introduces artifacts that bundle a LoRA adapter with a run-time scaffold and says they can be versioned. It never tests what happens when the two components come from different versions, and it reports no adapter-by-scaffold crossover.
PAW sets up the pseudo-program-plus-adapter representation and compares raw with rewritten specifications. It does not test mismatched component versions or stale-adapter interference.

Knowledge-conflict work looks at clashes between stored facts and retrieved context. It does not look at a decision-function adapter trained on an old policy and paired with a new specification prompt, and it has no matched recompiled or no-adapter controls.

opus.reason: I found no paper that crosses old and new task adapters with old and new specification scaffolds on the same frozen interpreter. None measures whether a stale adapter does worse than no adapter on inputs whose labels changed. The verbal-conflict study (2608.11510) shows a related effect, where a fine-tuned default competes with an in-context rule, but its task, models and deployment framing are different, so it does not answer this compatibility question. The seed paper and PAW never test mismatched component versions.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Meet Dynamic Individual Preferences: Resolving Conflicting Human Value with Paired Fine-Tuning trains separate single-preference LoRAs and evaluates each under both matching and opposing explicit preference prompts, alongside base-model controls. This already provides an adapter-by-instruction crossover showing interference; the proposed experiment substitutes local Boolean-policy amendments, exact references, and affected/unaffected-region diagnostics.

Uses LoRA training to strengthen a default response mapping and measures deterioration under conflicting explicit rules relative to the pre-fine-tuning model. It does not train separately versioned, specification-conditioned decision functions or perform the proposed complete version crossover.

Fine-tunes an LLM to memorize name–city associations, then supplies conflicting updated associations in context and compares with the base model. It establishes training-induced obstruction of contextual updates, but uses factual recall rather than policy execution and lacks the two-version adapter crossover.
The seed packages task adapters with specification-bearing scaffolds, but evaluates compatible compiled artifacts rather than deliberately crossing inconsistent component versions.

sol.reason: The closest prior work, arXiv 2604.12479, already crosses separately trained LoRAs with matching and opposing authoritative prompt instructions and includes unadapted controls, substantially addressing the registered interference question. Local policy edits, exact Boolean references, changed-region scoring, and the paraphrase control sharpen the diagnosis, but primarily change the task and evaluation details rather than the underlying experimental question and comparison.

opus.reason: No list entry crosses old and new adapters with old and new scaffolds to test whether a stale adapter interferes with an updated scaffold; #19 and #45 only ablate whether the scaffold is present.

sol.reason: Unlike the scaffold ablations in entries 19 and 55, this crosses conflicting adapter and specification versions to measure whether a stale adapter harms compliance relative to disabling it.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built (experiment.py, launched by run.sh): I set it up as registered. It trains task adapters cold, with no API calls, on a frozen BF16 Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (revision c1899de2…), using transformers 4.57.6, peft 0.21.2 and torch 2.6.
- Policies: A (escalation; the edit tightens, so affected cases go 1→0) and B (access; the edit loosens, so affected cases go 0→1). Each policy has old and new specifications with the same surrounding wording, executable truth functions, and an old-spec paraphrase that I fixed in code before any model ran.
- Training data: 320 inputs per policy, covering all 64 states plus extra samples so old labels are balanced 160/160. Each input is rendered with 3 training templates, giving 960 examples, which is exactly 60 steps × 16. The two seeds (11, 29) produce the same example order for the old and new adapters. Coupled initialization of each old/new pair was confirmed by a parameter hash.
- Training settings: LoRA r16/α32, dropout 0, on q/k/v/o and gate/up/down. AdamW with zero weight decay, microbatch 8 × 2, cosine learning rate from 2e-4 down to 2e-5 at the last step. Loss is on the output only (the label token plus <|im_end|>).
- Scaffold: the Qwen chat template with thinking disabled, as "{spec}\n\n[INPUT]\n{facts}\n[END_INPUT]", the same format as the seed's compile.py.
- Test set: 2 held-out templates and record IDs disjoint from training. 256 affected records sampled uniformly over affected states, plus 640 unaffected records balanced by label.
- Decisions: whichever of the "0" and "1" next-token logits is larger.
- Conditions: all 4 adapter × scaffold pairs, the base model with each scaffold, the old adapter with the paraphrase, and one extra diagnostic (base model with the paraphrase). LoRA weight hashes were identical before and after evaluation, so weights were not modified.

Small implementation choices, which don't change the question:
- The base-model conditions are evaluated inside each (policy, seed) run with peft's disable_adapter. They are deterministic, so their values are the same for both seeds.
- Only one fixed test set is drawn per policy, using a data seed separate from the training seeds.

Result from my test run of this exact command, which took about 6 minutes: the statistic is **−0.123**. That is below the 0.05 threshold, so the registered event did not occur.
- Policy A gap: −0.748. Old adapter with the new scaffold scores 0.754 and 0.742 on affected cases; the base model with the new scaffold scores 0.000.
- Policy B gap: +0.502. The base model scores 1.000. The old adapter with the new scaffold scores 0.000 with seed 11 but 0.996 with seed 29.

Caveats:
1. On the affected cases the untuned base model's decision does not change between the two scaffolds. It outputs "1" on policy A's affected states (accuracy 0) and on policy B's (accuracy 1). Its unaffected-region accuracy is close to chance (0.52–0.73). So the no-adapter control acts mostly as a constant-label predictor here, and the sign of each policy's gap mainly reflects that bias rather than adapter interference. Under this design, the opposite edit directions largely cancel.
2. The two seeds disagree sharply on policy B, so two repetitions say little about variance.
3. The old policy-A adapters learned their own function poorly (on their own scaffold: about 0.49 accuracy on affected cases and about 0.75 on unaffected ones, against old-policy references).
4. The new adapters with the new scaffold are 1.00 on affected cases for both policies, but only about 0.65–0.71 on policy A's unaffected cases.

So this is not evidence of general compatibility, and it is not evidence of a deployable stale-adapter hot fix. All diagnostics are in outputs/run_manifest.json and outputs/crossover_predictions.jsonl.

departures: experiment.py evaluates the no-adapter (base) conditions inside each (policy, seed) loop using PeftModel.disable_adapter(). Decoding is deterministic, so the values repeat across seeds. This is equivalent to the registered control and cannot change the result.
experiment.py draws a single fixed test set per policy using a separate DATA_SEED (20260903) shared by both training seeds. The registration leaves this open, so it does not change the result.
experiment.py adds an unregistered diagnostic condition, base|old_paraphrase. It is purely additive and does not enter the statistic.
experiment.py applies the output-only loss to the label token plus <|im_end|>, not to the label alone. This is a reasonable reading of 'output-only loss' and is unlikely to change the result.
experiment.py uses an AdamW cosine schedule with no warmup. The registration does not mention warmup, so this is an open choice that does not change the question.
The paraphrase control is fixed in source code before any model run, as the registration requires. This is not a departure.

No departure affects the statistic. The statistic in scores.jsonl and result.json follows the registered definition: it averages over seeds within each policy, then weights the policies equally, using affected-region accuracy against the new references.
problems: The no-adapter control is degenerate. In run_manifest.json and the eval log, the base model outputs a constant label on affected states under both old and new scaffolds: 0.000 on A and 1.000 on B. Its unaffected accuracy is near chance (0.52–0.73). The base therefore ignores the specification edit, and the sign of each per-policy gap mostly reflects the base's label bias rather than stale-adapter interference.

Because the edit directions are opposite and the base is label-biased, the per-policy gaps of −0.748 and +0.502 largely cancel in the equal-weighted mean (−0.123). The registered statistic is therefore close to uninformative about the hypothesis.

The old policy-A adapters did not learn their own function on the changed region. Against old references they score about 0.50 and 0.48 on affected cases under the old scaffold. A 'stale' A adapter therefore does not reliably encode the stale behaviour, which weakens the A arm as a test of interference.

The seeds disagree sharply on policy B. Old adapter with new scaffold scores 0.000 for seed 11 and 0.996 for seed 29. With two repetitions, variance and the existence of the effect cannot be assessed.

The changed region contains only 3 latent states for A and 4 for B (specifications.json). The 256 affected test records are repeated renderings of these few states across 2 templates, so their effective sample size is far below 256 and the accuracies are near-quantized.
Training shows instability with no warmup. For example, A old seed 11 loss jumps from 0.45 to 4.50 at step 2 (run_manifest.json). This may contribute to the poor old-A fit and the seed sensitivity.

The new A adapters with the new scaffold reach only about 0.65–0.71 on unaffected cases. Compatible-artifact quality for policy A is therefore weak, which the registration says must be retained as context.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: policies, data generation, LoRA and optimizer settings, coupled initialisation and schedule, the full crossover with base and paraphrase controls, logit-based decisions and the exact registered statistic. None of the minor choices affect the reported value. The value of −0.123 is computed from real model logits with no leakage or hard-coding, and the event (gap > 0.05) did not occur. The evidence is weak, however. The untuned base acts as a constant-label predictor that ignores the scaffold, the old-A adapters never learned the old changed-region behaviour, the two seeds give opposite outcomes on B, and the changed region spans only 3–4 latent states. Together these mean the null neither establishes nor rules out stale-adapter interference. The diagnostics, such as seed-11 policy B where the stale adapter fully overrides the new scaffold, are suggestive but too unstable to support a credible finding.

departures: experiment.py adds a base|old_paraphrase condition beyond the registered old-adapter paraphrase control. This is an additional diagnostic, excluded from the registered statistic; it does not plausibly change the reported value. No other substantive departure is identifiable: template expansion, output-end-token loss, a shared test set across training seeds, and using disable_adapter() resolve implementation details left open by the registration.
problems: outputs/scores.jsonl and the protected evaluation show a baseline floor/ceiling problem: on affected inputs, the base predicts 1 under both old and new scaffolds, producing 0% new-reference accuracy for A and 100% for B. The resulting gaps therefore cannot cleanly establish stale-adapter obstruction of an otherwise correctly functioning interpreter.

The protected evaluation shows weak compatible-artifact performance for policy A. Old-adapter/old-scaffold affected accuracy against the old reference is approximately 50.4% and 47.7%; new-adapter/new-scaffold unaffected accuracy is approximately 64.8% and 70.6%. A useful deployed policy function is not established for this family.

The paraphrase diagnostics reveal substantial sensitivity without a semantic edit. In the protected evaluation, the base's affected predictions flip from all 1 under the original old scaffold to all 0 under the equivalent paraphrase for both policies. Policy A's old adapters also change substantially, weakening attribution specifically to version conflict rather than general prompt sensitivity.

outputs/scores.jsonl shows extreme training-seed heterogeneity for B: stale-adapter/new-scaffold affected accuracy is 0% for seed 11 and 99.6% for seed 29. Two seeds provide little precision about the prevalence or magnitude of interference.

experiment.py samples the 256 affected records from only three latent states for A and four for B, using one shared test set across seeds. The numerous records do not provide broad policy coverage or independent training replications, and no uncertainty estimate accompanies the aggregate.

run.sh uses package version ranges, and experiment.py downloads the model without a pinned revision. outputs/run_manifest.json records the versions actually used, but future executions of the unchanged command can resolve to different software or model revisions.

This is valid descriptive evidence for the executed setting, but its interpretation is weakened by baseline label bias, poor policy-A learning, paraphrase sensitivity, and policy-B seed instability. It neither establishes general compatibility nor supports a dependable adapter-disabling or prompt-only update policy.

registration.title: Selecting compilation checkpoints with partial semantic contracts instead of reference labels
registration.seed_connection: The seed uses a fixed training schedule and an LLM judge for semantic evaluation. This experiment asks whether inexpensive specification-derived contracts can select a better saved adapter without a fully labeled validation set or a run-time teacher.
registration.hypothesis: Selecting a saved adapter by its violation rate on partial metamorphic contracts yields higher held-out semantic accuracy than always deploying the final fixed-step checkpoint.
registration.contribution: A small, reference-free checkpoint-selection test for compiled text functions. The selector checks both invariance and required output changes, so a consistently empty output cannot pass all contracts. Its success is evaluated using separate exact references, not inferred from consistency alone.

closest_work.difference: MetaCompress evaluates teacher-student behavioral fidelity. This experiment uses specification-derived input transformations to choose among student checkpoints and tests whether that choice improves independently measured correctness.
Mutation Validation selects models through retraining on mutated labels. Here selection needs no additional training and uses partial input-output relations on saved task adapters.

LLMORPH exposes inconsistent NLP behavior through metamorphic tests. This experiment evaluates whether such tests can serve as a useful deployment-selection criterion, rather than merely finding failures.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-4B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B for local training-label generation only.
Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B as the frozen interpreter.
PyPI transformers>=4.51,<5, peft>=0.15,<1, accelerate and safetensors.
Locally generated arXiv-link and ticket-extraction inputs, partial contracts and exact test references specified in the method.
registration.method: Use two text-to-JSON-array functions. Function A extracts modern arXiv identifiers only from https://arxiv.org/pdf/YYMM.NNNNN URLs, permitting optional vN and .pdf suffixes, stripping versions, ignoring /abs/ URLs, deduplicating and preserving first occurrence. Generate valid months and disjoint identifier banks for training, contract selection and test. Function B extracts # followed by one to five ASCII digits outside balanced double-quoted spans, removes leading zeros, returns identifiers as strings such as #23, deduplicates and preserves first occurrence. Generated text has no escaped or nested quotes. Training inputs contain zero to three candidate items, including distractors, with a small fixed fraction of duplicates and version/leading-zero cases. For each function obtain 256 labels from local BF16 Qwen3-4B with the full specification, thinking disabled, greedy decoding and a 96-new-token cap. Accept any syntactically valid JSON array of strings without semantic correction. Retry malformed responses once; if needed generate at most 64 replacement inputs. Save all raw responses and rejection reasons. Keep this teacher-labeled training set fixed for student seeds 11 and 29. Train one adapter per function and seed using frozen BF16 Qwen3-0.6B, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout 0 on q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projections; AdamW, zero weight decay, 80 steps, effective batch 16, microbatch 8, maximum sequence length 512, output-only cross-entropy and cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5. Save candidate checkpoints at steps 0, 20, 40 and 80. Use an identical full-specification scaffold throughout. For each function build 64 disjoint contract-source inputs, evenly assigning three transformations. A: append a fresh /abs/ link, duplicate an existing qualifying /pdf/ link, or append a fresh qualifying /pdf/ link. B: append a fresh ticket inside a balanced quoted span, duplicate an existing outside ticket, or append a fresh outside ticket. Invariant transformations require identical parsed arrays; fresh qualifying additions require the transformed output to equal the source output followed by the newly normalized identifier. Fresh identifiers must be absent from the entire source input. Generate eligible sources for duplicate relations. Invalid JSON counts as a violation. The selector receives only source text, transformed text and the relation operation, never full reference outputs. Select the checkpoint with the lowest violation fraction, breaking ties toward the earliest step, and persist that choice before test evaluation. The blind test has 256 inputs per function with zero to six items, held-out text templates and more combinations of distractors, duplicates, versions or quoted spans. Evaluate only the selected and final checkpoints, caching predictions when they coincide. Student generation is greedy, thinking-disabled, with a 128-new-token cap. Implement exact Python references solely for training-data diagnostics, contract sanity tests and final evaluation; never use their full outputs to choose checkpoints.

event.description: Contract-based selection improves blind semantic accuracy by more than three percentage points relative to deploying step 80.
event.statistic: Mean across both functions and both student seeds of exact parsed-array accuracy_selected_checkpoint minus exact parsed-array accuracy_step80.

evaluation.procedure: First freeze selections using contract violations alone, then load the blind reference outputs. JSON whitespace is immaterial, but values, normalization, deduplication and order must match exactly; malformed outputs are incorrect. Write raw teacher labels, accepted examples and syntax rejection reasons to outputs/teacher_labels.jsonl; source/transformed inputs, relation metadata and all checkpoint outputs and violations to outputs/contracts.jsonl; selected steps and pre-test selection timestamps to outputs/selection.json; selected/final predictions and exact references to outputs/test_predictions.jsonl; the single registered accuracy gain to outputs/scores.jsonl; and seeds, revisions, configurations and timings to outputs/run_manifest.json. Unit-test the contracts on the reference functions and verify that an always-empty predictor fails every fresh-item addition. Contract consistency itself is not treated as evidence of correctness.
evaluation.controls: Selected and final artifacts come from the same training trajectory and share teacher data, scaffold and decoding. Selection and test identifier banks are disjoint. Required-change contracts control for consistently wrong constant outputs. Full test references are unavailable to the fixed selection rule.

registration.full_scale_study: Test contract-guided checkpoint selection and early stopping across many functions, teacher-error regimes and contract families. Compare with teacher-labeled validation and LLM judging, including cases where models satisfy partial contracts while remaining systematically wrong.

agent.reason: The final checkpoint may already be strongest after this short training schedule, leaving limited selection headroom. Partial contracts can reward consistent but incomplete extraction, and the earliest-checkpoint tie-break can select an undertrained artifact.

judge_astra.reason: Contract selection could help if later checkpoints overfit teacher errors, but the final checkpoint may remain best after this short training schedule. Partial contracts and a small selection set can also misrank semantic accuracy, making a greater-than-three-point average improvement relatively unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: With a cosine schedule over 80 steps the final checkpoint is usually the most accurate and most self-consistent among steps 0/20/40/80, so contract selection will most often pick step 80 (difference 0) or pick an earlier, worse checkpoint by noise; a mean gain above 3pp requires earlier checkpoints to be systematically better, which is unlikely here.

judge_opus.reason: With a short cosine schedule, step 80 is usually the most accurate checkpoint, and teacher errors are systematic, so they are shared by all checkpoints. Ties go to earlier steps and the 64-relation selection signal is noisy, so the expected gain is about zero or negative.

judge_sol.reason: The contracts can detect some teacher-induced errors, but the event requires an earlier checkpoint to outperform a relatively short final training schedule. Partial relations and only 64 contract sources may select consistency without reliably delivering a three-point improvement in blind correctness.

judge_luna.reason: The contracts test useful invariances and required changes, so they could identify a checkpoint that generalizes better than the fixed final step. But the relations compare a model's outputs with its own transformed outputs rather than requiring complete, correct source outputs; 80-step training may also simply improve accuracy through the final checkpoint.

judge_muse.reason: With 80-step training on 256 labels the final checkpoint is typically best, and 64 noisy consistency checks with tie-to-earliest are more likely to misselect than to detect >3pp overfitting.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: MetaCompress uses behaviour-preserving metamorphic relations to measure how faithfully distilled code-model students follow their teachers. It does not choose among checkpoints of one training run, and it does not check whether such a choice improves correctness measured against exact references.

Mutation Validation picks models by retraining them on mutated labels. The proposed selector needs no retraining: it applies partial input-output contracts, both invariance and required-change, to saved LoRA checkpoints.

LLMORPH uses metamorphic tests to expose inconsistent NLP behaviour. The experiment asks a different question: can contract violation rates serve as a deployment-selection rule that raises held-out exact accuracy?

This paper compares checkpoint selection against keeping the final checkpoint in SFT, but its selectors rely on labelled validation data (generated accuracy, NLL, checkpoint agreement). It does not use reference-free, specification-derived metamorphic contracts.

This paper uses metamorphic relations without labels to help select models, but the relations test whether feature attributions are faithful, for tabular regressors. They are not used to select checkpoints of a text-to-JSON function by correctness.
The seed paper trains on a fixed schedule and judges semantics with an LLM. It does not study checkpoint selection or contract-based validation.

opus.reason: I searched for prior work on metamorphic or property-based checkpoint selection, label-free model selection, and checkpoint-versus-final comparisons. The existing work either uses metamorphic tests to find faults or measure fidelity, or selects checkpoints using labelled validation data. None of it uses specification-derived invariance and required-change contracts to pick a saved adapter, then measures the gain over the final checkpoint against independent exact references. The search was limited, so a closer paper may exist, but none of the work I found answers this question.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: 360-MLC selects saved checkpoints using reference-free multi-view geometric consistency. It does not test specification-derived invariance and required-change contracts as a selector for teacher-trained text functions, or isolate their accuracy gain over the terminal checkpoint.

The Augmentation Consistency Metric supports checkpoint and hyperparameter selection without target labels, but combines augmentation agreement with labeled source accuracy, an additionally trained classifier and prediction diversity. The proposed selector instead uses only explicit partial input-output contracts.

This paper combines invariance and computable required-answer changes to detect unreliable figure-reading outputs without labels. It evaluates error detection, not whether these relations select a more correct saved training checkpoint.
LLMORPH checks metamorphic relations in NLP outputs without reference labels, but reports fault detection rather than contract-guided checkpoint selection evaluated through independent correctness.
The seed trains specification-specific adapters with a fixed schedule and evaluates semantic correctness; it does not evaluate reference-free contract-based checkpoint selection.

sol.reason: Reference-free consistency-based model selection and required-change metamorphic testing both have substantial precedent, so neither ingredient alone is new. However, the closest selection studies use geometric consistency or source-supervised auxiliary scores, while the closest mixed-relation work evaluates output reliability rather than deployment selection. I found no prior work answering whether specification-derived invariance and required-change contracts alone select a more accurate compiled-function checkpoint than the terminal checkpoint, with correctness measured separately.

opus.reason: No list entry uses reference-free metamorphic contracts to select among saved checkpoints; #5 evaluates several checkpoints but does no selection.

sol.reason: No listed experiment selects saved checkpoints using reference-free metamorphic contracts and measures their accuracy gain over deploying the final checkpoint.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built (exp/run_all.py, launched by run.sh): the registered experiment, run end to end, in about 5 minutes on an A100.

Data and contracts
- Function A extracts arXiv IDs from /pdf/ URLs. Function B extracts tickets that appear outside quotes. Text generation is seeded.
- The identifier banks for training, selection and test are disjoint, and the code asserts this. Test inputs use held-out templates, 0–6 items, and more duplicates, versions, leading zeros and quoted spans.
- Each function has 64 contract sources: 22, 21 and 21 per transformation, as even as 64 allows.
- The selector only ever sees the model's own source and transformed outputs plus the relation metadata. Invalid JSON counts as a violation.
- Unit tests check that the reference functions break no contracts, on the selection set and on 1800 stress contracts, and that an always-empty predictor fails every fresh-addition contract. All of these pass, and the run aborts if any fails.

Teacher and student
- Teacher labels come from local BF16 Qwen3-4B, greedy, thinking off, 96-token cap, 256 per function. All 512 were accepted on the first try, so no retries or replacements were needed.
- Diagnostic only: teacher labels match the exact reference for 82.8% of A inputs and 66.0% of B inputs, so the students learn from noisy labels.
- Students are BF16 Qwen3-0.6B with LoRA (r=16, alpha=32, dropout 0, all attention and MLP projections). They train with AdamW (no weight decay) for 80 steps, effective batch 16 via 2×8, max length 512, loss on output tokens only, and cosine LR from 2e-4 to 2e-5. Checkpoints are kept in memory at steps 0, 20, 40 and 80.
- Seeds 11 and 29 share the same teacher data and scaffold.
- The selection rule is lowest violation fraction, with ties going to the earliest step. Each selection is written to selection.json with a timestamp before that run's test generation starts.
- Test references are computed only after all selections are frozen. Only the selected and step-80 checkpoints are scored, and predictions are reused when they are the same checkpoint.

Choices the registration didn't specify
- Gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, the usual HF default.
- No LR warmup.
- Teacher parsing removes a surrounding markdown code fence before checking JSON syntax. This is purely a syntax step and never applied in this run.
- Student outputs are parsed strictly: whitespace is ignored, otherwise the output must be a JSON array of strings.
- The teacher's one retry adds a "that was not a valid JSON array" follow-up message, because a greedy retry with the same prompt would just repeat itself.
- Checkpoints are not written to disk.
- The step-0 checkpoint is the LoRA at initialisation (B=0), which equals the base model.

Result of the test run
- Selected steps: A/seed11 → 80, A/seed29 → 20, B/seed11 → 80, B/seed29 → 40.
- Accuracy gains of the selected checkpoint over step 80: 0, +0.8, 0 and +8.6 points.
- Mean gain: 0.0234. That is below the 0.03 threshold, so the event did not occur in this run.
- The positive mean comes mostly from one run (B/seed29). With only 4 runs and 2 functions, this is weak evidence either way. It does not show that contract selection helps, and it does not show that it is equivalent to using step 80.
- A rerun on a fresh machine may differ slightly because of GPU nondeterminism.

departures: exp/run_all.py keeps candidate checkpoints in memory and does not write them to disk. The registration speaks of 'saved' adapters. The engineer reported this, and it cannot change the value because the same state dicts are restored for contract and test generation.

exp/run_all.py clips gradient norm at 1.0 and uses no learning-rate warmup. The registration does not specify either. The engineer reported both. They could affect the training trajectories, but they are open choices.

exp/run_all.py strips a markdown code fence from teacher output before checking JSON syntax. The engineer reported this. outputs/teacher_labels.jsonl and the teacher stats show 256/256 labels accepted on the first try for both functions, so it had no effect.
exp/run_all.py implements the teacher's single retry as a follow-up chat turn rather than a plain repeat. The engineer reported this. No retries happened, so it had no effect.

The function specification prompts in exp/run_all.py (SPEC) explicitly tell the model to ignore /html/ URLs and bare identifiers for A, and spell out the double-quote rule for B. The engineer did not report this wording. It is consistent with the registered semantics, and the same scaffold is used for teacher, students and contracts as registered, so it does not change the question.

Contract-source inputs in exp/run_all.py use the training text templates and style with the separate 'sel' identifier bank. The registration does not specify contract templates, and the engineer did not report this choice. It could influence how well the contracts transfer to the held-out test templates, but it is an open choice.
Contract counts are 22/21/21 per transformation (outputs/run_manifest.json), because 64 cannot be split evenly by three. This is necessary and immaterial.

exp/run_all.py generates teacher, contract and test outputs with left-padded batched greedy decoding. Batching can cause small numerical differences relative to unbatched greedy decoding. This is not specified by the registration and is unlikely to matter. The evaluation rerun reproduced the engineer's submitted run_nohup.log numbers exactly.

Student outputs are parsed strictly in exp/run_all.py: a fenced JSON array counts as invalid. As a result, the step-0 base model violates every contract (outputs/contracts.jsonl). This matches the registered rules that invalid JSON is a violation and malformed outputs are incorrect.
The loss is a token-sum normalized by the token count of the 16-example effective batch. This is a reasonable implementation of output-only cross-entropy and is not a departure.
problems: The gain is very noisy. The four runs give gains of 0, +0.8, 0 and +8.6 points, so the mean of 2.34 points is driven by a single run (B_seed29). No confidence interval or paired test is reported in outputs/scores.jsonl.

The selection signal is coarse. With 64 contracts, one contract is 1.56 points of violation rate. For example, A_seed29 chose step 20 over step 80 on a difference of one contract, and B_seed11 had steps 20 and 40 tied (outputs/selection.json). Selections therefore may not be stable under different contract samples.

Only two functions, two seeds and four candidate checkpoints were tested. Step 0 is always trivially rejected, so the real choice is among three checkpoints. This limits what the outcome can say about contract-based selection in general.
The result cannot be read as equivalence. The point estimate is positive but below the 0.03 threshold, and the engineer's notes correctly avoid claiming either a benefit or no difference.
opus.reason: The code in exp/run_all.py implements the registered pipeline closely: teacher labels from Qwen3-4B, LoRA students on Qwen3-0.6B with the registered hyperparameters, and checkpoints at steps 0, 20, 40 and 80. The contracts include required-change relations and pass the reference and always-empty unit tests. Selections are persisted before test generation, test references are computed only after all selections, and the statistic is the registered mean of per-run accuracy differences. The departures are open choices or had no effect, and the evaluation rerun reproduced the submitted log exactly, so the value 0.0234 (event not occurred) is genuinely produced from real model outputs without leakage. However, the evidence is weak: one of four runs drives the positive mean, the 64-contract selector separates checkpoints by one or two contracts, and no uncertainty estimate is given. The run therefore neither supports the hypothesis nor establishes a credible null.

departures: exp/run_all.py: Teacher parsing strips surrounding Markdown code fences before checking JSON, potentially accepting responses that are not themselves valid JSON arrays. All 512 responses passed on the first attempt without this unwrapping, so it did not change this result.

exp/run_all.py: A malformed teacher response is retried using an added assistant response and corrective user message rather than the unchanged scaffold. This could affect labels if exercised, but no retries occurred.

exp/run_all.py: If 64 replacement inputs were exhausted before obtaining 256 accepted labels, the code would continue with fewer examples rather than abort. This fallback could affect sample size and results, but both functions obtained exactly 256 labels here.

exp/run_all.py and outputs/run_manifest.json: Gradient clipping at 1.0, no learning-rate warmup, and FP32 LoRA parameters over the frozen BF16 base are implementation choices not explicitly specified in the registration. They can affect training outcomes, but the registration leaves these choices open.

exp/run_all.py: The cosine schedule applies updates indexed 0 through 79 with denominator 80, making the last applied learning rate approximately 2.00694e-5 rather than exactly 2e-5. This is a minor endpoint difference, not a plausible material explanation for the reported value.

exp/run_all.py: Candidate adapter states are saved only in memory and discarded after evaluation, rather than persisted as checkpoint files. This does not change selection or scoring, but prevents direct reuse or inspection of the trained adapters.

exp/run_all.py: Test predictions are generated after each individual selection is persisted, before every other run's selection has been frozen. All actual blind-test reference outputs are computed only after every selection is frozen, and predictions do not feed into subsequent selections, so this ordering does not change the result or establish leakage.

exp/run_all.py: The reference implementations do not enforce every specification boundary: RE_B uses Unicode-aware '\d' rather than an ASCII digit class, and RE_A does not validate months or enforce a complete URL boundary. The generators produce ASCII digits, valid months, and well-formed URLs, so these discrepancies do not affect the evaluated inputs.

exp/run_all.py: Unspecified sampling choices restrict coverage, including ticket values with two to five significant digits, no zero-valued or single-digit tickets, and arXiv versions v1 through v9. These choices can affect performance and generalizability, but do not replace a registered sampling distribution.
problems: outputs/scores.jsonl: The mean gain is 0.0234375, below the registered strict threshold of 0.03. The registered event did not occur; this is not a fidelity defect.

outputs/scores.jsonl and exp/run_all.py: There are only two functions and two training seeds, with teacher data, contracts, and function-specific test inputs shared across seeds. These are not four independent task-and-data replications, and the fresh-machine rerun does not add independent experimental conditions.

outputs/scores.jsonl: B/seed29 contributes 22 of the 24 net additional correct predictions; A/seed29 contributes two, and the other selections equal step 80. The aggregate improvement is therefore concentrated in one trajectory, with no reported uncertainty analysis.

outputs/run_manifest.json and outputs/selection.json: Partial-contract scores remain weak correctness indicators. An always-empty predictor violates 21/64 contracts, fewer than the 22/64 violations of the selected B/seed11 checkpoint. Required-change contracts prevent perfect constant-output consistency, but do not ensure that the selector favors semantically accurate behavior.

exp/run_all.py: Reference sanity tests establish consistency with the generated contracts, not independent correctness across the full function domains. Missing edge-case coverage and non-persisted adapters limit broader validation and artifact reuse.
sol.reason: The fresh-machine execution completed successfully, produced every registered raw-output file, and computed the statistic from real model generations without an evident path from blind references into checkpoint selection. No outcome-affecting departure from a specified requirement is established, so the implementation is faithful and the reported evidence is valid. The observed gain is 2.34375 percentage points, which does not meet the registered greater-than-three-point event. Its concentration in one trajectory, limited task coverage, and shared datasets make this a valid but weak pilot finding, not evidence of equivalence or absence of benefit.

departures: exp/run_all.py clips gradients at 1.0. The registration specifies AdamW and zero weight decay but not clipping. This is an open optimizer choice; it could change training and the reported gain relative to unclipped updates.

exp/run_all.py parse_teacher strips a surrounding markdown fence before accepting a teacher label. The registration accepts only syntactically valid JSON and does not include this repair. It did not change this run: all 512 labels were first-try acceptances, and the inspected raw responses are bare JSON.

exp/run_all.py retries a malformed teacher response with an added follow-up turn rather than the original prompt. Unused (zero retries), so it did not change the result; a same-prompt greedy retry could not have differed.

Checkpoints are held in memory rather than written to disk (exp/run_all.py). The selected step is still written to outputs/selection.json before that run's test generation. This does not change the reported value.
LoRA weights are fp32 on a frozen bf16 base (outputs/run_manifest.json). Adapter dtype was unspecified. It could slightly change numerics but does not change the question.
problems: outputs/scores.jsonl: the 0.0234375 mean is not a stable effect. A_seed11 and B_seed11 selected step 80 so their diffs are structural zeros, A_seed29 is +0.0078125, and B_seed29 is +0.0859375, so one cell sets both the sign and the distance to 0.03.

outputs/selection.json: function B violation fractions (about 0.31-0.41) barely differ from the always-empty rate 0.328125 in outputs/run_manifest.json, so the selector has little contract signal on B.

Contract sources use training templates and 0-3 items (exp/run_all.py make_contracts) while the blind test uses held-out templates and 0-6 items. That is allowed, but the selection distribution is not the evaluation distribution, which weakens what a miss on the 0.03 bar means.
grok.reason: The run matches the registered models, sizes, decoding, LoRA setup, contract relations, leakage controls, selection rule, and mean exact-match statistic; the extras are open choices or unused failure paths that did not change this value. The fresh evaluation recomputed 0.0234375 from real greedy outputs, with selections frozen before reference scoring, so the registered >0.03 event did not occur. That negative is real for these four cells but uninformative about the hypothesis: two diffs are zero by construction and almost all of the positive mean is B/seed 29, so the result shows neither a reliable gain nor equivalence to step 80.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper uses a fixed training schedule and an LLM semantic judge, but it neither runs contract-based checkpoint selection nor names that comparison as undone.

relation.reason: Compile-by-training—a specification, teacher labels, and a LoRA on a frozen small interpreter—is a working part of the run, extended with reference-free contract selection that the paper neither uses nor claims results about.

obvious.reason: A fixed schedule makes early stopping a common follow-up, but choosing the checkpoint by partial metamorphic contracts rather than labels is a specific comparison only one or two researchers would put on a first list of ten.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change how groups that compile and ship specification-specific adapters without labeled validation pick a checkpoint, not how people using other methods work.

prerequisite.reason: Contract unit tests passed, training cut violation rates far below the untrained checkpoint, and held-out accuracies were well above zero, so the selected-versus-final comparison can be read.

evidence.reason: The mean gain is positive but almost entirely from one of four runs, and with only four function–seed repetitions that spread still allows both no real gain and a gain large enough to matter.

next_step.reason: The comparison is readable but four highly variable runs cannot settle it, so the same question has to be asked again with more repetitions.

obvious.reason: Checkpoint selection or early stopping is a natural worry after reading the paper, but doing it with label-free metamorphic contracts against the final checkpoint is a specific step that only one or two researchers would likely list.

Each figure comes from 256 test inputs per run, over 2 functions × 2 seeds, with no interval.
