sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares choosing teacher-trained adapters by partial metamorphic-contract violations with deploying final fixed-step adapters on arXiv-link and ticket extraction to learn whether reference-free checkpoint selection improves held-out semantic accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports fixed-schedule training and semantic evaluation, but neither tests contract-guided checkpoint selection nor explicitly identifies that question as unfinished.

sol.what_came_out: On Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters, contract selection achieved mean exact parsed-array accuracy of 62.01% versus 59.67% for step 80, a 2.34-percentage-point gain with trajectory gains of 0, 0.78, 0 and 8.59 points across two student seeds for each of two synthetic extraction functions, evaluated on 256 held-out inputs per function with no uncertainty interval reported.

prerequisite.reason: Training losses fell sharply, trained checkpoints achieved non-floor test accuracies of 39.45–79.30%, and the reference-contract and empty-output sanity checks passed.

evidence.reason: With no uncertainty interval and only two functions and two seeds, the positive mean driven largely by one trajectory leaves both no systematic benefit and a useful benefit plausible.

next_step.reason: The comparison worked operationally, but too few independent repetitions leave its average benefit unresolved, making increased replication the identifiable repair.
next_step.what: Repeat the comparison with more independent training, teacher-data and contract-data seeds, and report paired test uncertainty together with variation across trajectories.

registration.title: Does balancing rare clause combinations make synthetic-label repair more valuable?
registration.seed_connection: The seed varies teacher mixture and data volume, but these changes can alter both input coverage and semantic label errors. Its structural response validation does not independently establish label correctness.
registration.hypothesis: On registered rare clause combinations, oracle correction of teacher labels has a larger accuracy benefit under balanced training coverage than under a skewed input mix, by more than three percentage points.
registration.contribution: A matched-pool factorial diagnosis of coverage and label correctness in short-budget function compilation. Both input mixes use the same renderer and candidate pool, with matched oracle-output distributions. The experiment estimates an interaction, not a new coverage principle or selection algorithm.

closest_work.difference: Rather than proposing training-aware target coverage, this experiment directly intervenes on exposure and label correctness in a small, executable-contract factorial.
The teacher is fixed, and both input mixes come from one controlled candidate pool rather than comparing stronger and cheaper generators.
Prompt-driven model construction is the starting point; the added question is whether coverage and semantic-label repair interact under a fixed compilation budget.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, downloaded from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, for local labeling only.
Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, downloaded from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, as the frozen interpreter.
Compatible released Transformers, PEFT, NumPy, and huggingface_hub packages from PyPI; retain the existing CUDA-enabled PyTorch installation.
Procedural ticket and interval generators, strict output parsers, and executable Python oracles implemented below.
registration.method: Implement a standalone local compiler without hosted services or an amortized warm start. Use two tasks. Tickets: input is exactly six updates with id matching [A-Z]{3}[0-9]{3}, status open/closed, priority integer 0..3, and blocked Boolean. Only the last update for each id counts. Return a JSON array of ids whose last update is open, priority at least 2, and not blocked, ordered by their last-update positions. Define D as any repeated id and B as any latest update that is open, priority at least 2, and blocked. When D is true, require at least one repeated id whose eligibility changes between an earlier update and its last update. The four cells have index 2D+B. Calendar: input has three busy intervals with integer start/end and cancelled Boolean, plus a query interval; all starts are less than ends. Return BUSY iff a non-cancelled interval overlaps the query under half-open semantics, otherwise FREE. Define T as any non-cancelled interval touching a query endpoint and C as any cancelled interval with positive-length overlap; cell index is 2T+C. Generate intervals around queries with start 20..180 and length 1..10, enforcing the requested flags and result by construction or rejection sampling. Unit-test both oracles on overrides, last-update ordering, endpoint touching, and cancelled overlap. With data seed 2027, make a candidate pool per task containing 192 inputs in cell 0 and 96 in each other cell. Tickets has oracle-output cardinality proportions 1/2 empty, 1/4 one id, and 1/4 two ids within every cell; Calendar is equally FREE/BUSY within every cell. Before teacher inference, select two 256-input datasets: balanced uses 64 per cell; skewed uses 160 from cell 0 and 32 from each other cell. Preserve the stated oracle-output proportions within each selected cell. Selection is random within these bins and never depends on teacher correctness. Obtain labels for the candidate pool with the local 4B teacher, literal task specifications, greedy decoding, batch 16, and at most 64 new tokens. Accept JSON arrays of strings for Tickets and exact FREE/BUSY for Calendar without checking semantic correctness. Permit one format-only retry for a malformed answer; if a selected input still lacks a valid label, mark the execution inconclusive rather than replacing it based on correctness. Canonicalize JSON whitespace only. Each input mix receives either teacher or oracle labels, yielding four arms per task. Train each arm with seeds 11 and 29, yielding sixteen adapters. Use frozen bf16 Qwen3-0.6B with SDPA, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout zero, q/k/v/o and gate/up/down projection targets, fresh default LoRA initialization paired across arms, AdamW, learning rate 2e-4 cosine-decayed to 2e-5, batch 16, and 48 updates. Use three precomputed shuffled passes through the 256 inputs; label interventions share identical schedules. Train answer-only cross-entropy including EOS, with maximum sequence length 512 and no silent truncation. The scaffold is the literal specification, no demonstrations, rendered using the thinking-disabled Qwen chat template. Generate 64 fresh tests per cell before training with seed 2028 and the same within-cell oracle-output proportions. Ticket test ids must be absent from the entire candidate pool; Calendar tests must exclude candidate inputs. Evaluate greedily in batches up to 64 with at most 64 new tokens. Save adapters, scaffolds, and metadata. Start timing before installation; use a 32-minute graceful cutoff and write an inconclusive result if all registered conditions cannot finish. Do not reduce conditions, steps, or test counts after seeing results.

event.description: Balancing rare clause exposures materially increases the benefit of semantic-label repair.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of a paired bootstrap distribution of (accuracy_balanced_oracle - accuracy_balanced_teacher) - (accuracy_skewed_oracle - accuracy_skewed_teacher) on the three nonzero cells, equally averaging cells, tasks, and training seeds.

evaluation.procedure: Tickets correctness requires a parsed JSON array identical to the oracle, including order; Calendar requires the exact uppercase label. Invalid outputs are incorrect. Calculate the interaction on cells 1, 2, and 3. Use 2000 bootstrap resamples of test inputs within task and cell, retaining all arm and seed predictions together. The interval is conditional on these tasks, pools, and builds, not uncertainty over teachers or independently generated pools. Require balanced-oracle accuracy on the full test set to reach 0.75 for each task and training seed; otherwise report statistic -1 and an explicit inconclusive status, while retaining all component results. outputs/data.jsonl stores candidate inputs, oracle and teacher labels, format retries, cells, output-cardinality bins, selections, and tests. outputs/teacher.jsonl stores full labeling requests and raw responses. outputs/training.jsonl stores losses, schedules, and input/output token counts. outputs/predictions.jsonl stores all raw student answers and oracle verdicts. outputs/config.json records specifications, seeds, package versions, resolved model revisions, artifact locations, and phase times. outputs/scores.json stores the registered statistic, interval, all factorial scores, achieved exposures, semantic error rates and error types by cell and selected mix, and eligibility checks. Also report both main effects. Different error prevalence or error severity may mediate an interaction; the design does not rule these explanations out. A threshold miss does not establish independence or equivalence.
evaluation.controls: Label repair changes only labels within an input mix. Both mixes share a candidate pool, renderer, example count, oracle-output distribution, model, scaffold, initialization policy, optimizer budget, and test cases. Semantic correctness never determines input selection. Actual token counts are recorded because equal steps and examples are not an exact FLOP match. No LLM judge or human annotation is used.

registration.full_scale_study: Repeat with independently generated pools, more executable specifications, and multiple open teacher families. Test whether coverage allocation should be coupled to verification, and whether the interaction is explained by error prevalence, error severity, or learning difficulty rather than data volume alone.

agent.reason: The interaction requires teacher errors in the reweighted cells and a substantial differential learning response to repairing them; better coverage alone is insufficient. Sixteen builds, per-seed capability gates, and the confidence-bound threshold further reduce the chance of the registered event.

judge_astra.reason: Correcting labels and balancing coverage can each help without producing the required positive interaction, especially if teacher mistakes are sparse. The three-point lower-bound threshold, per-build accuracy floors, and sixteen-adapter execution budget make this a low-probability event.

judge_fable.reason: The gate (balanced-oracle accuracy >= 0.75 on both tasks and both seeds after only 48 LoRA updates on Qwen3-0.6B, including the JSON-array Tickets task with supersession) is unlikely to be met, and even then the registered interaction is a noisy difference-of-differences whose 5th percentile must clear 0.03; the 4B-teacher plus 16-adapter pipeline also strains the 32-minute cutoff.

judge_opus.reason: Balanced-oracle accuracy must reach 0.75 for every task and seed, which is doubtful after only 48 LoRA updates on 0.6B for interval and supersession reasoning. Even if that gate passes, a difference-of-differences averaged over three cells must clear 0.03 at the 5th percentile, which needs a point estimate around 0.07 or more, and its direction is ambiguous because more noisy data can also average out teacher errors.

judge_sol.reason: Repairing labels and balancing exposure may each help without producing a positive interaction of the registered size. The balanced-oracle competence gates and sixteen-build workload further reduce the chance of clearing the bootstrap lower bound.

judge_luna.reason: The factorial is well controlled, but if the procedural teacher is already accurate, label repair will have little benefit; even with errors, the extra rare-cell exposure need not amplify that benefit. The lower-tail interaction across both tasks makes the three-point threshold demanding.

judge_muse.reason: A 5th-percentile interaction above 3pp needs a large mean effect and teacher errors concentrated in rare cells, but the short-budget student may learn comparably from noisy labels in both mixes.

It does not run a factorial that intervenes separately on exposure balance and oracle-versus-teacher labels, and it does not estimate their interaction on rare clause combinations.

The seed paper varies teacher mixture and data volume in compile by training, so coverage and label correctness change together. It never separates them with matched input pools and oracle label repair.
This paper compares correctness-gated and filtered distillation arms on fixed sources. It does not vary the coverage mix or test how coverage interacts with label correction.
This paper distills into Qwen3-0.6B and compares teachers per sub-task. It has no coverage-by-label-repair factorial and no executable oracles.

opus.reason: Prior work treats coverage and synthetic-label error as separate or jointly scored factors. The closest example is TATC's theory and selection method, but I found no paper that runs a matched-pool factorial crossing balanced versus skewed coverage with teacher versus oracle labels and estimates their interaction for compiling short specifications into adapters. The specific question of whether balanced coverage makes label repair more valuable appears unanswered.

closest_work.difference: TATC analyzes input information and synthetic-label error jointly, including controlled-label experiments, but does not test whether balancing rare clause combinations increases the benefit of oracle label repair in neural-function compilation.

BARRED combines dimension-based coverage with debate verification and separately studies both components. It does not cross balanced versus skewed exposure with label-only oracle correction; its verification can refine or discard inputs.

Studies coverage, diversity, and correctness under compute-matched teacher sampling, with coverage and verification ablations, but does not isolate the coverage-by-label-repair interaction using a fixed teacher and matched input pool.
The seed studies teacher mixtures and data volume, not independent interventions on clause-combination exposure and semantic label correctness.

The distinct contribution is the matched-pool factorial question: whether changing rare-combination exposure, while preserving oracle-output proportions, changes the benefit of label-only oracle repair under a fixed compilation budget. None of the work found answers that interaction question in the proposed way.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: everything in main.py, launched by run.sh. run.sh starts the clock before pip installs transformers==4.57.1 and peft==0.17.1 and keeps the existing torch 2.6. It is a standalone local compiler with no hosted services and no amortized warm start, built as registered:
- Two tasks, Tickets and Calendar. Each has a procedural generator, a strict output parser and an executable Python oracle. The oracle unit tests cover overrides, last-update ordering, endpoint touching and cancelled overlap.
- Candidate pools of 192/96/96/96 inputs per cell (data seed 2027), with the registered within-cell output proportions.
- Two selections made before any teacher labels exist: balanced (64 per cell) and skewed (160/32/32/32), chosen at random within each cell and output bin.
- Teacher labels from local Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507: literal specification, greedy decoding, batch 16, at most 64 new tokens, one format-only retry, format checking only.
- 16 rank-16 LoRA adapters on bf16 Qwen3-0.6B. LoRA initialisation is paired across arms within each seed (checked: all lora_B start at zero, and there is one fresh adapter per seed). Three precomputed shuffled passes give 48 updates of batch 16, shared between the teacher and oracle arms. Cosine schedule from 2e-4 to 2e-5, answer-only loss including EOS. The longest sequence was 371 tokens, so nothing was truncated.
- Fresh tests: 64 per cell, seed 2028. Ticket test ids are absent from the pool and Calendar test inputs exclude pool inputs.
- Scoring: a bootstrap over test inputs within task and cell (2000 resamples), the eligibility gate (balanced-oracle accuracy at least 0.75 for each task and seed), and the 32-minute graceful cutoff. All registered raw outputs are written, plus adapters, scaffolds and metadata under outputs/adapters.

Choices the registration leaves open:
- Inputs are rendered as one JSON object per line.
- "Touching a query endpoint" means interval end == query start or interval start == query end.
- Calendar busy intervals start within [max(20, qs−11), min(180, qe)] around the query.
- AdamW uses torch defaults (weight_decay 0.01).
- The cosine runs from step 0 to step 47, so the last update is at 2e-5.
- LoRA parameters are held in fp32 on the frozen bf16 base.
- The format retry is a follow-up chat turn stating the required format, because repeating the same prompt greedily would return the same answer.
- Inconclusive runs report value −1.

Observed in two full test runs on this machine (about 8.5 minutes each). Both runs gave identical numbers.
- The registered value is −1, status inconclusive_eligibility. Calendar seed 11 reached only 0.734 balanced-oracle accuracy, below the 0.75 gate. The other three task/seed pairs passed (0.789, 0.770, 0.809).
- Component results, kept in scores.json but not the registered statistic:
  - Interaction point estimate on cells 1–3: 0.059, bootstrap 5th percentile 0.018. By task: Tickets 0.003, Calendar 0.115.
  - Main effect of coverage (balanced minus skewed) on cells 1–3: 0.053.
  - Main effect of label repair (oracle minus teacher) on cells 1–3: 0.300.
- Teacher semantic error rates across the whole candidate pool:
  - Tickets 0.67, mostly extra ids.
  - Calendar 0.20, mostly false BUSY, and rising with cell (0.06 in cell 0 to 0.43 in cell 3).
- So error prevalence differs by cell and by task, and the design cannot separate it from coverage.

Caveat on the Calendar teacher labels: the 4B teacher started reasoning on all 480 Calendar inputs and was cut off at 64 tokens, so every Calendar label came from the format retry. That retry sees the partial reasoning in its context. This follows the registered protocol, but those labels are therefore not pure first-response outputs. No selected input was left without a valid label.

GPU nondeterminism on a fresh machine could move borderline accuracies slightly. The registered event is decided only from the value the evaluation run produces.

departures: main.py teacher_phase: the one format-only retry is a follow-up chat turn that contains the truncated first reply. The engineer reported this. Every one of the 480 Calendar pool inputs (calendar_teacher_malformed_first_attempt=480 in scores.json) began with prose reasoning, was cut off at 64 tokens and was labeled from the retry. The registration allows one format-only retry and leaves its form open, so this follows the protocol. It does mean the Calendar teacher labels depend on partial reasoning rather than a direct answer, which shapes the teacher error profile: mostly false BUSY, rising from 0.06 in cell 0 to 0.43 in cell 3. It does not change the registered value, which is decided by the eligibility gate.

main.py: AdamW uses torch defaults with weight_decay 0.01, the cosine schedule reaches 2e-5 at step 47, and LoRA parameters are held in fp32 on the frozen bf16 base. The engineer reported these. They are choices the registration leaves open, and are unlikely to change the result.

main.py: adapters are saved in bf16 after evaluation. Scores come from the fp32-LoRA in-memory models, so the saved artifacts differ slightly from what was evaluated. This does not affect the reported value.
main.py parse_cal strips surrounding whitespace before the exact FREE/BUSY match, which is slightly looser than 'exact uppercase label'. Negligible effect.

main.py make_cal: busy-interval starts are sampled from [max(20, qs−11), min(180, qe)]. This is an open detail within the registered 20..180 range, applied identically to pool and tests. No effect on comparability.

Data and test seeds are derived (for example default_rng([2027,0,ti]) and default_rng([2028,ti])) rather than used as raw integers. This is an open implementation choice with no effect on the validity of the comparison.
problems: The registered outcome is inconclusive. In outputs/scores.json, Calendar seed 11 balanced-oracle accuracy is 0.734, below the pre-registered 0.75 gate, so the value is -1 and the hypothesis is neither supported nor refuted.

The non-registered component results are fragile. The interaction point estimate of 0.059 comes almost entirely from Calendar (0.115); Tickets gives 0.003. In the run log, Calendar skewed-oracle accuracy (0.652 for both seeds) is no better than skewed-teacher accuracy (0.660 and 0.664). Calendar balanced-oracle accuracy varies by seed (0.734 vs 0.809), and the test-input bootstrap does not capture this training-seed variance. The component bootstrap 5th percentile of 0.018 therefore should not be read as evidence for or against the hypothesis.

Calendar teacher labels were all produced through the retry path after truncated reasoning (outputs/teacher.jsonl). The Calendar label-error profile is therefore an artifact of the 64-token cap combined with the retry protocol, not of direct teacher answers. This limits what 'semantic label repair' means for that task.

Teacher error prevalence differs strongly by task and cell: Tickets 0.55 in cell 0 to 0.84 in cell 3, mostly extra ids. As the registration acknowledges, the design cannot separate prevalence from coverage as the cause of any interaction.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered factorial as specified. Generators and oracles have unit tests. Pools, selections, test exclusion, teacher labeling with one format retry, paired LoRA initialization, schedules shared across label arms, answer-only loss with EOS, greedy evaluation, the within-task-and-cell paired bootstrap and the eligibility gate all match the registration, and every registered artifact was written. The protected run reproduced the engineer's numbers and correctly applied the pre-registered gate. Calendar seed 11 balanced-oracle accuracy of 0.734 fell below 0.75, so the value is -1 and the status is inconclusive; this is a legitimate registered outcome, not an implementation defect. The evidence is real and correctly computed, but it is uninformative about the hypothesis. The component interaction is carried by one task, two seeds and a student that barely learned Calendar, and the bootstrap does not reflect seed variability.

On a literal reading of the registered exact-label rule, this is more permissive and could change component accuracies for whitespace-padded answers. It cannot reverse this run's eligibility failure: stricter parsing could only lower the already-failing Calendar balanced-oracle accuracy.

main.py, canon: parsing and reserializing Ticket labels with json.dumps can normalize string escape representations as well as JSON whitespace. The registration permits whitespace canonicalization only. Such normalization could change training tokenization if escaped strings occurred; their occurrence is not established by the displayed excerpts. This does not affect the Calendar oracle arm responsible for the reported -1.

main.py and run.sh: the cutoff is enforced through periodic checks, not during installation, downloads, model loading, individual training updates, or finalization. Consequently, the implementation does not guarantee an inconclusive result for every possible over-budget execution. This did not affect the observed run, which finished in approximately 509 seconds.
problems: outputs/scores.json: Calendar seed 11 balanced-oracle accuracy is 0.734375, below the registered 0.75 eligibility requirement. The primary result is therefore inconclusive; -1 is a sentinel, not an estimated negative interaction.

Inspection supports implementation of the core factorial, pre-label selection, paired initialization and schedules, executable scoring, and paired bootstrap; the listed departures do not plausibly alter this run's reported sentinel. The value is derived from real generated outputs, with no visible hard-coded result, test leakage, or conclusion-changing scoring error. It supplied all 480 Calendar teacher labels (outputs/scores.json) and could change teacher-arm scores, but the reported value is the oracle-only eligibility sentinel, so it did not change the reported value.

These are unspecified operationalizations of the registered generator, reported by the engineer. They define the data and could move accuracies, including the borderline gate, but they do not contradict a more specific registered rule.

Bootstrap seed 20260 is unregistered (main.py). It does not affect the reported value, because ineligibility forces -1 before the percentile is used.

grok.reason: The code runs the registered factorial: matched pools and mixes, greedy 64-token teacher labels with one format retry, paired LoRA initializations, shared label-arm schedules, 48 updates, held-out tests, and the eligibility-gated statistic. The fresh evaluation reproduced balanced-oracle accuracies 0.789, 0.770, 0.734, and 0.809, so the code correctly wrote -1 with inconclusive_eligibility. Those open choices do not contradict the registration, and the reported sentinel is computed from real oracle-arm generations without leakage or hard-coding. The outcome is valid but weak for the hypothesis: it is a gate sentinel, Calendar teacher labels are entirely retry completions, and cell-varying error rates confound coverage with label quality.

registration.title: Does scaffold diversification improve wording robustness at the cost of specification editability?
registration.seed_connection: A seed artifact packages adapter weights together with a textual run-time scaffold. Equivalent restatements and genuine contract changes therefore both operate on text while leaving previously compiled weights intact.
registration.hypothesis: Equivalent-scaffold training reduces the accuracy penalty from unseen equivalent wording but also reduces compliance with a genuine scaffold-only rule edit, with both effects exceeding three percentage points.
registration.contribution: A lifecycle test of hybrid prompt-plus-weight artifacts. It measures robustness relative to canonical-scaffold accuracy and uses functioning fresh edited builds to distinguish prompt–weight conflict from inability to learn the revised contract.

closest_work.difference: Prompt variation is not proposed as new; this experiment tests whether its equivalent-wording benefit has a cost when the instruction meaning changes.
The conflicting knowledge is a deliberately installed executable rule in a task-specific adapter, with known affected regions and matched edited recompiles.
The hybrid artifact interface motivates the test, but the experiment evaluates maintenance and edit compatibility rather than amortized compilation accuracy.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Compatible Transformers, PEFT, NumPy, and huggingface_hub packages from PyPI; retain the existing CUDA PyTorch installation.
Two procedural tasks, original and edited Python predicates, and predeclared scaffold strings specified below.
registration.method: Implement oracle-supervised local compilation, not the seed warm start or hosted service. Tickets: six updates contain opaque id, status open/closed, priority 0..3, and blocked Boolean. Last update per id wins. Original output is YES iff any latest update is open, unblocked, and priority at least 2; otherwise NO. The edit raises the threshold to 3. Calendar: three busy intervals with cancelled flags and a query, all integer start/end with start < end. Original output is BUSY iff any non-cancelled interval satisfies start < query.end AND query.start < end; otherwise FREE. The edit uses inclusive endpoints, replacing both strict comparisons with <=. Use a shared schema/output-only header for each task. Before any model evaluation, save four equivalent training rules and four equivalent test rules. Ticket training rules are: prose stating last update then the conjunction; NO-by-default with a final-entry exception for open, unblocked priority 2 or 3; a numbered retain-last/filter/any algorithm; and an existential predicate over final entries. Ticket test rules are: NO unless a qualifying final entry exists; reverse-scan each id once and check the conjunction; discard overwritten, closed, blocked, and priority-0/1 entries then test nonemptiness; and NO iff every final entry is closed, blocked, or below priority 2. Calendar training rules are: the explicit strict-overlap predicate; FREE-by-default with positive-length non-cancelled intersection as the exception; discard-cancelled then compare max(starts) < min(ends); and FREE iff every interval is cancelled or ends at/before query.start or starts at/after query.end. Calendar test rules use, respectively, the negation of the universal FREE condition; checking the query against each surviving interval; rejecting cancelled and disjoint/touching intervals before testing nonemptiness; and pseudocode with the two strict comparisons. Every Calendar wording explicitly says endpoint touching alone is FREE. Write complete natural-language strings following these definitions and freeze them before training. The canonical edited scaffold is the first training style with only the registered rule change and no obsolete examples. Generate 256 original-rule training inputs per task with seed 2027, balanced by output. Ticket inputs use three distinct ids appearing twice each in varied order, with broadly sampled statuses, priorities, and blocked flags. Enforce uniqueness after renaming ids by first occurrence, so cosmetic id changes alone cannot create new training or test configurations. Calendar queries start 20..180 and have length 1..10; generate varied overlapping, disjoint, touching, and cancelled intervals, rejecting duplicates after subtracting query.start from all endpoints. Before training, generate 128 ordinary tests, 128 changed-region tests, and 128 unaffected tests per task, excluding training configurations under these uniqueness checks. Ticket changed cases must contain a qualifying priority-2 latest update but no qualifying priority-3 latest update. Calendar changed cases have non-cancelled endpoint touching but no positive-length non-cancelled overlap. Train fixed-scaffold and diversified-scaffold original adapters plus a fresh canonical edited adapter for each task and seed 11 or 29: twelve adapters total. All use identical training inputs; edited builds change only labels and contract. The diversified arm uses each of the four training scaffolds once per input across four shuffled epochs, while fixed uses the canonical scaffold throughout. Pair example schedules and initialization across arms. Use frozen bf16 Qwen3-0.6B, SDPA, thinking disabled, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout zero, all seven attention/MLP projection types, AdamW, batch 16, 64 updates, cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5, answer-only cross-entropy with EOS, and length limit 512 with no silent truncation. Evaluate original adapters on ordinary tests under canonical and all four unseen equivalent scaffolds; changed tests under both old canonical and edited canonical scaffolds; and unaffected tests under both canonical contracts. Evaluate fresh edited adapters under the edited canonical contract and the unadapted base under both canonical contracts. Decode greedily with at most eight new tokens. Save all artifacts. Include installation and download time, and stop gracefully at 32 minutes with inconclusive status if the complete design cannot finish; never tune on tests.

event.description: Scaffold diversification exhibits a joint robustness/editability trade-off.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of a paired bootstrap distribution of min(R,E), where R is the fixed-minus-diversified difference in canonical-to-equivalent accuracy drop, and E is fixed-minus-diversified edited-contract accuracy on changed cases; each component equally averages tasks and training seeds.

evaluation.procedure: Require exact YES/NO or FREE/BUSY after surrounding whitespace removal; extra prose is incorrect. For each arm compute the ordinary-test drop as canonical accuracy minus accuracy averaged over the four unseen equivalent scaffolds. R compares these drops, rather than absolute equivalent-prompt accuracy, to reduce confounding by better overall task learning. E compares compliance with the edited oracle on changed cases. Bootstrap 2000 times within task and test region, retaining all prompts, arms, and seeds for each input; recompute both components and their minimum. These intervals are conditional on the selected scaffolds, cases, and builds. For every task, seed, and original arm require old-canonical accuracy at least 0.80 on ordinary cases and 0.85 on changed cases under old labels. Require each fresh edited build to reach 0.80 on changed cases. Failure yields statistic -1 and explicit inconclusive status, not evidence for safe hotfixing. outputs/specifications.json stores all exact frozen scaffold strings, schemas, predicates, and edit definitions. outputs/cases.jsonl stores inputs, splits, uniqueness signatures, old/new labels, and region membership. outputs/training.jsonl stores curves, schedules, and token counts. outputs/predictions.jsonl stores all conditions, raw outputs, correctness, and obsolete-output indicators. outputs/config.json stores model/package revisions, artifact locations, seeds, and phase times. outputs/scores.json stores the statistic, interval, both components, per-task capability checks, base and recompile controls, total hotfix error, obsolete retention, and unaffected-region regression. A threshold miss does not establish scaffold editability.
evaluation.controls: Original arms share inputs, labels, initialization, ordering, updates, role placement, and output requirements; only equivalent scaffold exposure changes. Fresh edited builds use the same inputs and budget and establish that the revised rules are learnable. Unadapted evaluations diagnose existing instruction-following limitations. Unaffected cases measure collateral errors, and old-scaffold changed-case tests establish that the obsolete rule was actually installed.

registration.full_scale_study: Measure the robustness/editability frontier over more functions, scaffold styles, training strengths, and student sizes. Compare specification-parameterized training, incremental adapter patches, and full rebuilds, developing evidence-based invalidation rules for meaningful contract changes.

agent.reason: Diversification could improve instruction following without reducing editability, or both arms could largely ignore meaningful edits. Requiring both a reduced equivalent-wording penalty and worse edit compliance, each beyond three percentage points with functioning controls, is demanding.

judge_astra.reason: Diversification could improve wording robustness while also improving responsiveness to genuine rule changes; alternatively, both arms might resist edits similarly. Obtaining both registered effects beyond the joint lower-bound threshold while passing every competence check seems unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: Twelve adapters must all pass demanding accuracy gates (e.g., >=0.85 FREE on touching-only cases, >=0.80 on supersession YES/NO), and both components R and E are likely near zero since LoRA'd models tend to ignore scaffold wording and scaffold-only rule edits alike, making min(R,E) > 0.03 at the 5th percentile improbable.

judge_opus.reason: About 20 strict capability checks must all pass, including FREE on endpoint-touching cases and a working edited recompile. The gate also forces old-rule outputs on changed cases, so edited-contract compliance in both arms will likely sit near the floor, leaving E small. The event additionally needs R and E to be robustly above 3pp at the same time.

judge_sol.reason: Wording-robustness gains are plausible, but reduced edit compliance is not inevitable: diversification could instead preserve instruction following. Requiring both effects, alongside multiple capability checks, makes the joint event unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: Scaffold diversification may reduce the wording penalty, but whether it makes an old adapter less compliant with a changed rule is ambiguous and could go in the opposite direction. The joint threshold and capability gates make the registered event harder than either effect alone.

judge_muse.reason: Wording-robustness gain is plausible, but the joint event also requires following an unseen threshold/endpoint edit zero-shot, while fine-tuned 0.6B models will likely both default to the installed obsolete rule.

The experiment's own description treats it as covering the robustness benefit of varied prompts, not whether that variation makes a deliberately edited instruction harder to follow when it conflicts with an adapter-installed rule.

Cited by the experiment as work on conflicts between in-context and learned knowledge. I did not open it. The experiment differs in planting an executable rule in a task-specific LoRA, editing only the scaffold text, and comparing against fresh rebuilds with the edited rule.

Program-as-Weights compiles natural-language specs into adapters for a frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter and reports accuracy and memory use. Its abstract does not mention scaffold wording robustness or editing an existing artifact's specification.
The seed paper introduces compile by training and reports accuracy and compile cost. Its abstract does not mention testing prompt diversification, robustness to rewording, or scaffold-only edits.

Shows that the choice among paraphrased training prompts affects forgetting and generalization, and optimizes the prompt during training. It does not measure whether the model follows a changed rule at run time when that rule conflicts with the weights.

opus.reason: My searches found no paper that tests whether training on varied equivalent prompts trades robustness to rewording against compliance with a real scaffold-only rule edit, using fresh rebuilds as a control. That holds for hybrid prompt-plus-adapter artifacts and for small task adapters generally. The closest work I found covers only one side of the question: prompt variation for robustness, the effect of which training prompt is chosen, knowledge conflicts, or the compilation paradigm itself. None of it answers the joint trade-off. This conclusion rests on abstract-level search results, and I did not read 2502.12859 or 2407.13048 in full.

closest_work.difference: PAFT compares fixed-prompt and diversified-prompt fine-tuning and reports robustness to unseen equivalent wording, but does not test whether diversification reduces compliance with genuine runtime rule edits.

It does not manipulate equivalent-scaffold training exposure, install controlled rules in task-specific adapters, or evaluate matched fresh edited builds; its execution tests target the original contracts.

Establishing Knowledge Preference evaluates instruction–parametric knowledge conflicts and trains models to prioritize instructions, rather than testing whether equivalent-wording diversification makes a deliberately learned executable rule harder to override.

The seed packages adapters with runtime scaffolds and evaluates compilation accuracy, supervision choices, latency, and applications, but does not evaluate scaffold-only contract changes or their interaction with training-time scaffold diversification.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (main.py, specs.py, run.sh): the registered design as written. Qwen3-0.6B runs frozen in bf16 with SDPA attention and thinking disabled. Supervision comes from an oracle predicate. For each task (tickets, calendar) and each seed (11, 29) there are three arms: fixed-scaffold, diversified-scaffold (each of the 4 training rules used once per input across 4 shuffled epochs) and a fresh edited build. That makes 12 LoRA adapters: rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0, all 7 projection types, AdamW, batch 16, 64 updates, cosine learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5, loss on the answer plus <|im_end|> only, and a hard error if any sequence exceeds 512 tokens. Within each task and seed, all arms share the same input order and the same LoRA initialization (torch.manual_seed(seed)).

Cases and tests: 256 balanced training inputs per task with seed 2027, then 128 ordinary, 128 changed-region and 128 unaffected tests. Duplicates are removed using signatures that rename ids by first occurrence (tickets) or shift endpoints by query.start (calendar). Decoding is greedy with at most 8 new tokens, and only an exact label counts as correct. Scoring follows the registration: bootstrap within task and test region (B=2000), the 5th percentile of min(R,E), and the capability gates. If any gate fails the statistic is -1; a 32-minute time guard also sets it to -1.

Unspecified details I chose myself: weight decay 0, gradient clipping at 1.0, no warmup, and the prompt layout (header, then rule, then input, all in one user turn). The scaffold strings were written and frozen in specs.py before any training.

Smallest deviation: the registration says the edited calendar scaffold differs from the canonical one only by the rule change. Besides replacing < with <=, I also had to flip the canonical sentence "endpoint touching alone is FREE" to "...is BUSY", because otherwise the scaffold would contradict itself. I count this as part of the registered inclusive-endpoint edit.

Result of my one full test run (about 5.5 minutes including installs and download): the experiment is inconclusive and reports statistic = -1. All four calendar original-arm builds failed the capability gate. Their old-canonical accuracy on ordinary cases was 0.50–0.70 (gate 0.80), and on changed cases with old labels it was 0.00–0.875 (gate 0.85). Final training losses for these builds were about 0.22–0.27. All ticket builds passed, scoring 0.97–0.99. All fresh edited builds passed the 0.80 changed-case gate: tickets 1.0/1.0, calendar 0.875/1.0. However, the calendar edited builds were weak on unaffected cases (0.65 and 0.50).

The following numbers are diagnostic only, because a gate failed. Point estimates were R = -0.004 and E = +0.146. Most of E came from the calendar task, where the original builds did not work. For the bootstrap, the 5th–95th percentile range of R was [-0.030, 0.020] and the 5th percentile of min(R,E) was -0.030. On tickets, where every gate passed, diversification did not reduce the drop under unseen equivalent wording. That drop was 0.18/0.08 for fixed versus 0.13/0.13 for diversified, mostly from test scaffolds 3 and 4. Tickets E was -0.023.

Interpretation: none of this supports the hypothesis, and it is not evidence that scaffold edits are safe either. With 64 updates, the student did not learn the original strict-overlap calendar rule, so the calendar half of the design cannot answer the question. I did not change the generator, the hyperparameters or the scaffolds after seeing results, since that would be tuning on tests. The re-run should reproduce this up to GPU nondeterminism. I deleted the saved adapters (463 MB) from /workspace before submitting; the evaluation run saves them again under outputs/adapters.

registration.title: Do semantically correct JSON handoffs need normalization between independently compiled functions?
registration.seed_connection: The seed demonstrates composition and permits semantically equivalent outputs with different JSON whitespace or object-key order. Component semantic correctness does not itself establish that another neural component will consume every legal representation reliably.
registration.hypothesis: For a consumer trained on one legal encoding, canonicalizing actual semantically correct producer outputs improves downstream correctness by more than five percentage points.
registration.contribution: A conditional handoff audit using actual independently trained producers, not only synthetic encoding perturbations. A serialization-diverse consumer supplies an inexpensive prevention control. This is explicitly a narrow-training-interface stress test, not a claim that all composed neural functions fail.

closest_work.difference: The endpoint is a producer–consumer handoff on actual certified producer outputs, with a serialization-only intervention, rather than standalone encoding sensitivity.
No LLM retry or semantic repair occurs: the primary intermediates already satisfy their contracts, and normalization changes only their serialization.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Compatible Transformers, PEFT, NumPy, and huggingface_hub packages from PyPI; retain the existing CUDA PyTorch installation.
Procedural note templates, record generators, strict duplicate-key-rejecting JSON parsers, and extraction/filtering oracles specified below.
registration.method: Build an alert pipeline with separate producer and consumer LoRA artifacts. Records have exactly id matching [A-Z]{3}[0-9]{3}, severity INFO/WARN/ERROR, acknowledged Boolean, and maintenance Boolean. Producer A reads notes containing one to three records and emits the ordered JSON record array. Its specification permits arbitrary JSON whitespace and object-key order. Use four note templates: 'Record ID has severity SEV; acknowledgment is yes/no; maintenance is yes/no'; 'For ID, maintenance is yes/no and acknowledgment is yes/no; severity is SEV'; 'Severity SEV applies to ID. Acknowledged: yes/no. Maintenance: yes/no'; and 'ID: severity=SEV, acknowledged=yes/no, maintenance=yes/no'. Separate records with newlines and preserve their order. Consumer B accepts any valid serialization of this schema and returns ids of ERROR records that are unacknowledged and outside maintenance, in array order, as a JSON array without prose. Generate 512 producer-training examples and an independent 512-array consumer-training set using seed 2027. In each set use 128 examples with final alert-output cardinality 0, 1, 2, and 3; choose a feasible record count up to three and sample the remaining attributes. IDs are independent and opaque. Train two producers with identical notes, specifications, and semantic targets: compact canonical-key targets versus two-space-indented reverse-key targets. Canonical key order is id,severity,acknowledged,maintenance. Train two consumers on identical semantic arrays and labels: fixed-encoding uses compact canonical inputs only; diversified uses compact canonical, compact reverse-key, indented canonical, and indented reverse-key inputs evenly across exposures. For seeds 11 and 29 compile these four variants independently, yielding eight adapters. Use frozen bf16 Qwen3-0.6B, SDPA, thinking-disabled chat templates, literal specification-only scaffolds without demonstrations, fresh rank-32 LoRA with alpha 32, dropout zero, all seven projection types, AdamW, batch 16, 64 updates, cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5, answer-only cross-entropy including EOS, and sequence limit 512 with no silent truncation. Pair initialization and example schedules between corresponding variants; record the differing input/output token counts. Before training generate 256 tests with seed 2028, 64 per alert cardinality, with ids absent from both training sets. Decode producers greedily with at most 256 new tokens. Parse using an object_pairs_hook that rejects duplicate object keys. Require exact fields, valid string/enumeration values, and actual Boolean types, not integers. For every schema-valid producer answer, send each consumer both the untouched raw answer and a canonicalization of that predicted object: explicitly reconstruct keys in canonical order and serialize with compact separators. Never use oracle records for this transformation, and never alter values or array order. Decode consumers greedily with at most 48 new tokens. Also run both consumers on canonical oracle records and compact reverse-key oracle records. Save all adapters and scaffolds. event.description: Serialization-only normalization rescues a material number of downstream decisions despite an already correct producer.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of a paired bootstrap distribution of canonicalized-minus-raw accuracy for the fixed-encoding consumer among semantically certified producer outputs, equally averaging the two producer variants and two training seeds.

evaluation.procedure: Certify producer output only when the strict parser accepts it and its ordered record array equals the oracle in fields, values, and types, ignoring whitespace and object-key order. Consumer correctness requires a parsed JSON array identical to the final oracle id array, including order. Compute the primary paired difference only on certified producer outputs. Bootstrap 2000 times over logical test-note ids, keeping both producer variants, both consumer variants, seeds, and handoff conditions together; certification masks and denominators must be recomputed in each resample. The interval is conditional on these generated cases and builds. Require at least 64 certified outputs for every producer/seed and fixed-consumer canonical-oracle accuracy at least 0.85 for each seed. Otherwise write statistic -1 and inconclusive status. outputs/cases.jsonl stores notes, records, final references, training/test assignments, and template ids. outputs/pipeline.jsonl stores raw producer answers, parse/schema outcomes, certified objects, both actual consumer inputs, raw consumer answers, correctness, and oracle-control predictions. outputs/training.jsonl stores losses and token budgets. outputs/config.json records contracts, serializers, seeds, model/package revisions, artifact locations, and phase times. outputs/scores.json stores the scalar and interval, certified support counts, all conditional consumer scores, diversified-consumer prevention results, and unconditional pipeline accuracy counting invalid or incorrect producer outputs as failures. Report raw-format and normalization effects separately for compact and indented producers. A missed event alone does not establish serialization invariance.
evaluation.controls: Raw and normalized comparisons use exactly the same predicted content. Duplicate keys are rejected before normalization, preventing implicit semantic repair. Producer variants share semantic training data. Consumers share semantic arrays, labels, initialization, and update budgets; serialization diversity is their only training intervention. Canonical-oracle tests establish consumer competence, and reverse-key compact controls help distinguish key-order sensitivity from indentation length.

registration.full_scale_study: Evaluate larger independently compiled function trees and real artifact/version changes. Compare normalized boundaries, serialization-diverse training, and stricter interface contracts, testing whether component semantic metrics predict end-to-end correctness under legal representation shifts.

agent.reason: Compact-only consumer training provides a plausible mechanism for sensitivity to indented, reversed-key producer outputs, and the paired normalization intervention isolates it cleanly. However, existing JSON robustness, averaging across both producer formats, and the consumer-competence gate could prevent the lower bound from exceeding five percentage points.

judge_astra.reason: A small consumer specialized on one serialization could be sensitive to reversed keys and indentation, giving normalization a plausible benefit. However, averaging with the already-canonical producer dilutes that benefit, and the consumer-competence and producer-certification gates must all pass.

judge_fable.reason: The compact-canonical producer contributes ~0 by construction, so the statistic is about half the indented/reverse-key degradation, which for a pretrained JSON-literate model fine-tuned 64 steps is probably only a few points; gates on consumer competence (>=0.85) add further risk.

judge_opus.reason: The compact producer's outputs are already canonical, so its contribution is about zero and the averaged statistic halves the effect. The fixed consumer would need to lose roughly 14pp or more on indented, reverse-key inputs, a double format shift for a narrowly trained 0.6B adapter. This is plausible but uncertain, since pretrained JSON understanding may carry over; the gates look likely to pass.

judge_sol.reason: Fixed-format fine-tuning could make the consumer sensitive to indented, reverse-key producer outputs, giving normalization a meaningful benefit. However, existing model familiarity with JSON and averaging over compact-producer handoffs could keep the gain below the required lower bound.

judge_luna.reason: Normalization can help if the fixed consumer overfits to compact key order, but a pretrained model may already handle legal JSON order and whitespace changes. Averaging across a canonical producer and a reverse-key producer also dilutes any gain confined to the latter.

judge_muse.reason: Pretraining may give some encoding robustness and averaging includes a matched producer with near-zero effect, but an indented reverse-key shift plausibly causes a large rescue for the fixed consumer.

closest_work.difference: This paper measures how sensitive a single LLM graph reasoner is to node labeling, edge ordering and surface syntax, comparing fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned models. It finds that fine-tuning can increase sensitivity to format, which bears on the hypothesis. However, it has no producer–consumer handoff between independently trained adapters, no outputs from an actual neural producer, and no serialization-only canonicalization tested at the interface.

Based on the agent's own description (I did not read this paper): an LM-pipeline method that checks constraints and retries or repairs outputs. It does not keep the predicted content fixed and change only JSON key order and whitespace to measure the downstream effect.

The seed paper shows that compiled functions can be composed and that semantically equivalent JSON is accepted. It does not test whether a downstream compiled function reliably consumes every legal serialization, or whether normalizing outputs between functions helps.

opus.reason: Earlier work shows that LLMs, and fine-tuned ones in particular, can be sensitive to how equivalent structured inputs are serialized. 2511.10234 is the clearest example, and its finding partly anticipates the hypothesis. But my searches found no paper that tests a handoff between independently trained LoRA functions, using real producer outputs that are already semantically correct, with a canonicalization intervention and a control consumer trained on varied serializations. The specific question of whether normalizing serialization at the interface between compiled neural functions rescues downstream decisions appears to be unanswered, though my searches were not exhaustive.

However, among papers available by 2026-10-06, I found none answering the narrower question through serialization-only canonicalization of actual, strictly certified producer outputs consumed by independently trained neural functions. Conditioning on correct producer content and comparing raw versus normalized versions separates this contribution from malformed-output repair, schema redesign, and standalone format perturbation studies.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: one script, exp/run_exp.py, launched by run.sh. run.sh starts the clock before pip installs transformers 4.56.2 and peft 0.17.1 and before the model download, and the script stops gracefully at 32 minutes. Settings as registered:
- Base model: frozen bf16 Qwen3-0.6B with SDPA, Qwen3 chat template with thinking disabled.
- Prompts: the literal specification plus the input as a single user message, with no system message and no demonstrations.
- Adapters: fresh LoRA, rank 32, alpha 32, dropout 0, on all 7 projection types.
- Training: AdamW, batch 16, 64 updates (two passes over the 512 examples), cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5, loss only on the answer plus <|im_end|>, sequence limit 512 (the script raises an error rather than truncating).
- Data: seed 2027 for training data and seed 2028 for 256 tests (64 per alert count). Test IDs never appear in training. Each note uses one of the 4 templates.
- Producers: one trained on compact canonical-key targets, one on 2-space-indented reverse-key targets.
- Consumers: one trained only on compact canonical input; one trained on the 4 encodings evenly (256 exposures each, and each array gets two different encodings across its two passes).
- Pairing: within each seed, both producers share the same initialization (torch seed = run seed) and the same example schedule; so do both consumers. Seeds 11 and 29 give 8 adapters.
- Decoding is greedy. The parser rejects duplicate keys and non-standard constants, and requires real Boolean types.
- Canonicalization rebuilds the predicted objects with keys in canonical order and compact separators. It never uses the oracle records.
- Bootstrap: 2000 resamples over test-note IDs; certification masks and denominators are recomputed in every resample.
- Each seed's consumers take that seed's producer outputs.

Choices the registration left open:
- Template is picked per note, not per record.
- Consumer target is a compact JSON id array.
- Gradient clipping at 1.0 and the AdamW default weight decay of 0.01, neither specified in the registration.
- Adapters and scaffolds are saved under /workspace/artifacts, not outputs/.

Test run on this machine (about 5 minutes end to end):
- Both gates passed: 251–254 of 256 producer outputs were certified in every producer/seed cell, and the fixed consumer scored 1.0 on canonical oracle inputs for both seeds.
- Registered statistic (5th percentile): 0.032. Point estimate 0.045, 95th percentile 0.058. That is below 0.05, so the event did not occur in this run.
- Effect by producer, averaged over the two seeds:
  - Compact canonical producer: canonicalized-minus-raw is exactly 0. Its raw outputs already were the canonical serialization.
  - Indented reverse-key producer: fixed-consumer accuracy on certified outputs was 0.911 raw versus 1.0 after canonicalization (+0.089). Canonicalization rescued 29 cases (seed 11) and 16 (seed 29) and hurt none.
- Most failures (37 of 45) were cases with no alerts where the consumer wrongly returned an ERROR id; I didn't check whether these records were acknowledged or in maintenance.
- Fixed consumer on compact reverse-key oracle input: 0.871 and 0.938, so key order alone hurts it.
- The diversified consumer largely prevents the problem: canonicalized-minus-raw of +0.001 (95th percentile 0.003).

Caveats:
- The registered statistic weights the compact producer cell, whose effect is zero by construction, equally with the indented cell. This dilutes the measured effect. I kept the statistic as registered.
- All conclusions are conditional on these generated cases and these 8 builds.
- Missing the event does not show the consumer is insensitive to serialization; the indented-producer effect above is substantial.
- A fresh run on the evaluation machine should reproduce these numbers closely, but bitwise identity is not guaranteed.

departures: exp/run_exp.py clips gradients at norm 1.0, which the registration does not specify. The engineer disclosed this. It is applied identically to all eight adapters. With per-step losses mostly far below 0.1 after step 0, it is unlikely to have materially moved the reported value, but it could shift the trained adapters slightly.

exp/run_exp.py uses AdamW with torch's default weight decay of 0.01. The registration says only 'AdamW'. This is a default for a choice the registration left open, it was disclosed, and it is unlikely to change the result.

exp/run_exp.py picks the note template per note rather than per record, and the consumer target is a compact JSON id array. The registration left both open and both were disclosed. Neither changes the question.

Adapters and scaffolds are saved under /workspace/artifacts rather than outputs/. The registration requires saving them but gives no location, and config.json records the locations. This has no effect on the result.

run.sh pins transformers 4.56.2 and peft 0.17.1 but uses the preinstalled NumPy and huggingface_hub rather than installing them. The registration only asks for compatible packages, so this has no effect on the result.

The diversified consumer's schedule shows each array in two different encodings across its two passes, with 256 exposures per encoding (config.json). This is one valid reading of 'evenly across exposures' and does not affect the primary statistic, which uses only the fixed consumer.
Each seed's consumers consume only that seed's producer outputs. The registration does not address cross-seed pairing, so this is a reasonable reading with no apparent effect.
problems: Registered design weakness: the compact-canonical producer cells have a canonicalized-minus-raw difference of exactly 0 by construction. outputs/scores.json shows raw_identical_to_canonicalized_on_certified = 252 and 254. Equal averaging therefore halves the measured effect, and the >0.05 event was reachable only if the indented-producer effect exceeded about 0.1 with margin. The miss (p5 = 0.032, point estimate 0.045) is driven by this dilution, not by absence of an effect.

The indented-reverse producer changes both indentation and key order at once. The compact-reverse oracle control (fixed consumer accuracy 0.871 and 0.938) implicates key order. There is no indented-canonical oracle control, so the indentation contribution is not separately identified.

The bootstrap resamples test notes only. With two training seeds, build-to-build variability is not captured in the interval: per-seed rescue counts were 29 vs 16, and per-seed effects 0.115 vs 0.064. The interval is explicitly conditional on these builds, as the registration states.
The engineer's failure analysis (37 of 45 failures on zero-alert cases) is stated without checking the records, and it is not directly verifiable from the truncated outputs/pipeline.jsonl shown.

The task is a small synthetic schema with near-ceiling producers and consumers (canonical-oracle accuracy 1.0). This limits generality, though the registration acknowledges it as a narrow stress test.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: data, the eight paired adapters, the scaffolds, the hyperparameters, strict duplicate-rejecting parsing, oracle-free canonicalization, paired bootstrap with masks recomputed per resample, the gates and the statistic. The only unregistered additions are gradient clipping and default weight decay, applied uniformly to all adapters. The evaluation reproduced the engineer's numbers, and the reported p5 = 0.032 follows directly from real model outputs: rescue counts of 0, 29, 0 and 16 with no cases hurt, giving a point estimate of 0.0447. The registered event did not occur. This is largely because the compact-canonical cells contribute zero by construction, while the indented-reverse producer shows a substantial +8.9 pp normalization rescue. The oracle reverse-key control confirms key-order sensitivity in the fixed consumer, and the diversified consumer essentially eliminates the problem. This is a credible, well-controlled but narrow finding, conditional on two builds per variant.

departures: exp/run_exp.py adds gradient clipping at 1.0 and uses AdamW's default weight decay of 0.01. These can affect learned models and numerical results, but the registration leaves these optimizer details open.

exp/run_exp.py selects one note template per note rather than independently per record. This can affect task difficulty and numerical results, but the registration does not specify the template-selection unit.

This strengthens the required test-ID separation and could affect the particular generated dataset; uniqueness among training IDs is an otherwise unspecified sampling choice.

exp/run_exp.py checks the graceful cutoff only before whole training/evaluation phases, and run.sh does not time-limit installation or downloads. Thus completion or graceful termination within 32 minutes is not guaranteed. This implementation weakness did not affect the reported value: the fresh evaluation completed in 281 seconds.
problems: outputs/scores.json reports a pooled effect of 4.47 percentage points with bootstrap fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles of 3.20 and 5.79 points. The registered event failed, but this interval also does not establish that the effect is below five points or that serialization is irrelevant.

The bootstrap in exp/run_exp.py resamples test cases while holding the two training seeds and generated training sets fixed. As correctly acknowledged in outputs/scores.json, its precision does not describe uncertainty across new training datasets, additional builds, models, or deployment distributions.

The actual shifted producer changes both key order and indentation. The compact reverse-key oracle control demonstrates that key order alone can impair accuracy, but the controls do not separately estimate an indentation-only effect.

run.sh lacks pipefail, so installation or Python failures can be hidden by successful tail or tee processes. The result placeholder and exception handling mitigate this, and the completed artifacts and evaluation output independently support success in this run.
sol.reason: The displayed code implements the registered sizes, models, prompts, pairing, certification, serialization-only intervention, controls, bootstrap statistic, and event; the additional training and sampling choices were left open. The fresh evaluation and saved outputs support a value computed from real model generations, with no evident leakage, hard-coded result, or conclusion-changing scoring error. The registered fifth-percentile statistic is 0.0319976, below 0.05, but normalization rescued 45 certified indented-producer handoffs without hurting any, and diversified training largely prevented those failures. This is meaningful controlled evidence of a narrow interface sensitivity, warranting research value 2, not a demonstration of serialization invariance or a universal need for normalization.

exp/run_exp.py rejects non-standard JSON constants (NaN/Infinity) via parse_constant, beyond the registered duplicate-key object_pairs_hook. This could not change the result: such values would fail the registered type and enumeration checks and would not be certified or canonicalized.
Weight decay 0.01 is PyTorch AdamW's default and was left unspecified; using it does not differ from the registered optimizer and could not change the result relative to that default.
problems: The pre-registered average equally weights the compact-canonical producer, whose certified outputs were already identical to the canonical serialization (scores.json: raw_identical_to_canonicalized_on_certified equals the certified count for both seeds), so that cell contributes 0 and pulls the fifth percentile to 0.032 despite an indented-reverse effect of about 0.089 (45 rescues, 0 hurts). Separate by-producer scores are reported, so this is an estimand limitation, not a miscalculation.

The indented-reverse producer confounds indentation with reverse key order. The compact reverse-key oracle control shows key order alone drops fixed-consumer accuracy to 0.871 and 0.938, but the handoff rescue itself is not factorized; that matches the registered design.
grok.reason: The fresh evaluation ran the registered pipeline to completion and reproduced the registered statistic: the fifth percentile of the paired bootstrap is 0.032, so the greater-than-0.05 event did not occur. Data, prompts, LoRA recipe, greedy decoding, certification, canonicalization, gates, and the equally weighted four-cell bootstrap match the registration; gradient clipping is the only unregistered training knob and is unlikely to have moved this value. The point estimate 0.0447 equals the mean of the four cell differences, including 29/252 and 16/251 one-sided rescues, so the scalar is computed from generated case outcomes rather than hard-coded. The null is real for that average but does not show serialization invariance: canonicalization lifts the indented-reverse handoff to 1.0, key order alone hurts the fixed consumer, and serialization-diverse training removes the gap. That is a meaningful, controlled finding on a narrow synthetic interface, not particularly strong or consequential beyond it.

registration.title: Do near-miss-trained semantic guards transfer to unseen duration and ordering errors?
registration.seed_connection: The avatar application validates DSL syntax and bounds before execution, while the seed recommends output validation for important applications. A schema-valid program can nevertheless execute the wrong requested behavior.
registration.hypothesis: Compared with unrelated-mismatch training, near-miss training reduces wrong-program acceptance for both unseen duration errors and unseen ordering errors by more than ten percentage points at exactly 95% acceptance of correct programs.
registration.contribution: A cross-error-family generalization test for a separately compiled semantic guard. Length-preserving primary faults and a count baseline distinguish semantic transfer from omission/duplication cues, while an equal-acceptance operating point prevents indiscriminate rejection from counting as improvement.

closest_work.difference: The guard checks request-to-program behavioral equivalence rather than symbolic input preconditions.
The tested component is a separately reusable guard trained without reflected trajectories, evaluated on single-fault families absent from its negative training examples.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Compatible Transformers, PEFT, NumPy, and huggingface_hub packages from PyPI; retain the existing CUDA PyTorch installation.
Procedural command/program pairs, a strict schema validator, and a deterministic trace executor implemented below.
registration.method: Implement a command-to-program producer and two guards with separate adapters on frozen Qwen3-0.6B. A program is a JSON array with one to five objects, each having exactly act, repeat, and seconds. act is wave/jump/dance/turn/sit/clap, repeat is an integer 1..3, and seconds is an integer 1..4 giving duration per repetition. The executor expands each step into repeat ordered (act,seconds) events; equality means identical expanded traces. Reject duplicate JSON keys and Boolean values in integer fields. Generate source programs with two to four steps and no adjacent equal actions. Requests explicitly state per-repetition duration and execution order, with each action word appearing once per step. Training templates are: 'ACT R times, each repetition lasting S seconds'; 'ACT for S seconds per repetition, repeating R times'; and 'Perform R repetitions of ACT, taking S seconds on each repetition', joined with explicit sequential connectors. Test templates are disjoint: first/next/finally clauses with 'S seconds each, R repetitions'; numbered steps with duration stated before action and repetition count; and 'R times ACT; spend S seconds each time' followed by an explicit proceed-to connector. Save the exact renderers before training. Generate globally disjoint latent-program sets using seed 2027: 512 producer-training commands, 512 guard-training commands, 128 validation commands, and 256 test commands. Reject duplicate expanded traces across splits. Both guards receive the same 512 correct command/program pairs and 512 incorrect pairs. Easy-negative training substitutes an independently generated program with the same step count, requiring a different trace and differences in both an action and a repetition count; reject pure-duration and pure-swap mismatches. Near-miss training changes exactly one action for 256 commands or one repetition count for 256 commands. All negatives pass the schema validator. Use the same balanced compact-canonical and indented-reverse-key candidate serializations for both guards and every label/type. The guard contract asks whether the candidate fully implements the requested ordered actions, repetition counts, and per-repetition durations, outputting only OK or NO. For each test command create four single-fault negatives: change one duration, swap two steps, omit one step, and duplicate one step. Verify each changes the expanded trace and remains schema-valid; the primary endpoint uses duration and swap only. Omission and duplication are diagnostics. Compile the producer for 60 updates and each guard for 80 updates, with paired seeds 11 and 29: six adapters. Use frozen bf16 Qwen3-0.6B, SDPA, thinking disabled, rank-16 LoRA, alpha 32, dropout zero, all seven attention/MLP projections, fresh paired initialization, AdamW, effective batch 16, cosine learning rate 2e-4 to 2e-5, answer-only cross-entropy with EOS, and maximum length 512 without truncation. Score a guard by log-likelihood(OK plus EOS) minus log-likelihood(NO plus EOS), summing completion-token log probabilities in fresh contexts. Use batched teacher-forced scoring rather than free generation. For the primary ROC summary, derive each guard/seed threshold from test-positive scores: scores above threshold are accepted, and threshold ties receive a fractional acceptance weight chosen to make positive acceptance exactly 0.95. This is an empirical discrimination metric, not deployment calibration. Also greedily decode producer test outputs with at most 192 new tokens, check their schema and trace, canonicalize schema-valid predicted programs without repair, and score them with both guards using inclusive thresholds calibrated on validation positives. Add a count-only baseline that compares the number of action-word occurrences in the request with candidate step count; it does not use latent fields or the executor. Save artifacts and record phase times. Include installation/download time and terminate gracefully at 32 minutes with inconclusive status if the complete registered evaluation cannot finish.

event.description: Near-miss training transfers to both held-out, length-preserving semantic fault families.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of a paired bootstrap distribution of min(D_duration,D_swap), where each D is easy-negative minus near-miss wrong-program acceptance at 95% correct-program acceptance, averaged over the two training seeds.

evaluation.procedure: Use expanded-trace equality as behavioral truth and independently verify schema validity for every injected fault. Wrong acceptance is the mean threshold acceptance weight on that family's negatives. Compute duration and swap improvements separately, average each over seeds, and take their minimum. Bootstrap 2000 times over source test commands, retaining their positive and all negative scores for both guards and seeds. Recompute positive thresholds and tie weights inside every bootstrap resample. Intervals are conditional on the selected commands and trained guards. Fixture/schema failures or incomplete conditions yield statistic -1 with inconclusive status. outputs/pairs.jsonl stores source requests, latent programs, candidate programs, traces, splits, serializers, and corruption families. outputs/guard_scores.jsonl stores completion likelihoods, score differences, and oracle labels for validation and test cases. outputs/producer_predictions.jsonl stores actual producer answers, schema validity, trace correctness, normalized guard inputs, scores, and validation-threshold decisions. outputs/training.jsonl stores curves and budgets. outputs/config.json records exact templates/contracts, seeds, model/package revisions, artifact locations, and timings. outputs/scores.json stores the primary statistic and interval, both family effects, all four fault-family escape rates, ROC thresholds/tie weights, validation-calibrated coverage, count-baseline results, and natural producer-error diagnostics. Do not interpret the injected-fault distribution as naturally occurring compiler-error prevalence or a deployment safety guarantee. A threshold miss does not establish absence of transfer.
evaluation.controls: The guards share positive pairs, source commands, serialization distributions, negative counts and step counts, scaffold, initialization, training budget, and evaluation cases. Primary faults preserve step count, so count rejection cannot explain the primary result. Exactly matched positive acceptance handles threshold ties without giving one guard an advantage from rejecting more correct programs. Natural producer errors are secondary, so a highly accurate producer does not remove the primary diagnostic opportunity.

registration.full_scale_study: Evaluate validation-calibrated guards on naturally occurring errors from multiple producer versions and model families, including multi-fault programs. Measure risk/coverage stability, execution overhead, and guard reliability after producer upgrades.

agent.reason: Near-miss training could encourage more precise checking, but action and repetition negatives need not teach duration or ordering validation. The event requires substantial improvement for both unseen families at exactly 95% correct-program acceptance, not merely better average rejection.

judge_astra.reason: Near-miss supervision plausibly encourages finer comparisons than unrelated negatives, but neither duration faults nor order swaps are directly taught. Requiring the weaker transfer effect to clear a ten-point lower confidence bound at matched 95% correct-program acceptance is considerably harder than improving accuracy on familiar faults.

judge_fable.reason: With 80 updates, unseen test templates, and a 0.6B guard, discrimination will be weak for both guards; transfer to duration-only faults is the likely bottleneck, and the min over two families at the 5th percentile exceeding 0.10 requires both effects to be robustly large.

judge_opus.reason: Near-miss negatives never vary durations, and action changes can be caught by bag-of-actions matching, so transfer to both duration faults and order-only swaps is doubtful. The minimum of the two gains must exceed 0.10 at the 5th percentile, which likely requires both gains to be around 0.16 or more.

judge_sol.reason: Near-miss training may encourage finer request–program alignment, but neither primary fault family appears among its training negatives. A confident ten-point improvement for both duration and ordering faults at matched positive acceptance is a demanding transfer claim.

judge_luna.reason: Near-miss negatives plausibly teach the guard to detect a single semantic mismatch, but duration errors and especially order swaps are held-out fault families. The gain must exceed ten points for both at the registered acceptance rate, so transfer is plausible but uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Near-miss training never varies duration while easy negatives incidentally do, so both guards likely ignore the seconds field and a 10pp duration improvement favoring near-miss is very unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper compiles a natural-language specification into a LoRA adapter and checks avatar DSL outputs only for syntax and bounds. It does not train a separate semantic guard or test whether training on one kind of near-miss negative carries over to unseen kinds of errors.
