outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered local oracle/generator and fixed-budget random-versus-coverage comparison using Qwen3-0.6B, identical seeded rank-8/alpha-16 response-only LoRA training (240 pairs, batch 8, 80 AdamW updates at 2e-4), common balanced test set, and greedy strict-JSON exact-match scoring. Required result.json, outputs/scores.jsonl, and outputs/summary.json are rebuilt from fresh training. Smallest unavoidable change: 300 examples across seven nonzero strata is nonintegral, so six have 43 and stratum 111 has 42. Tested the evaluation command including installation/download; completes in about three minutes. Corrected floating-point threshold misclassification using exact rational counts, without changing data or model settings; technical rerun reproduced all predictions. Observed random=0.95, coverage=1.00, difference exactly 0.05, so the registered strict >0.05 event did not occur. Threshold miss is inconclusive, not equivalence. Model revision and dependency versions pinned; detailed notes in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

departures: Pool allocation (experiment.py make_data, config_before_training.json): six non-baseline strata have 43 pool examples and stratum 111 has 42, because 300/7 is not an integer. This was disclosed and is unavoidable. The 30-per-stratum coverage draw and the 25-per-stratum test set are exact, so it is very unlikely to have changed the result.

Event comparison was changed after the first run (experiment.py; run.log vs run_verified.log). The first run used float subtraction, got 0.050000000000000044 and set event=true. The code now uses exact rational counts and gives exactly 1/20, event=false. This flipped the event label but not the data, predictions or value. The registration specifies strictly greater than 0.05, so the exact comparison is the correct reading. It was disclosed, and predictions were reproduced in the protected run.

Unspecified choices fixed by the engineer (experiment.py): AdamW weight decay 0.01 (the PyTorch default), no LR schedule or clipping, LoRA on all seven attention/MLP projections with dropout 0, bf16 base, max_new_tokens 96, decode batch 16 with left padding, 1–3 valid IDs per input, train ID values 000–599 and test 600–999, and the chosen template texts. All are left open by the registration, identical across conditions and recorded in config, so they are unlikely to bias the comparison.
Pool and test generators both use Random(17) (experiment.py). This is not a departure: ID ranges and templates differ, and disjointness of inputs and of numeric values is asserted.
Seed repo compile.py was consulted only for prompt and module-name conventions (README.md). No hosted compiler or teacher was used, as the registration requires. No effect.
problems: Ceiling effect (outputs/summary.json): coverage scored 200/200 and random 0.95 balanced. The observed difference equals the largest difference possible given random's accuracy, so the strict >0.05 event was arithmetically unreachable unless random fell below 0.95. The task and budget were too easy to test the registered threshold well.

Single training seed and one selection draw (registered as 1 repetition). Selection effects cannot be separated from training or draw variance. The 10-versus-0 error gap, concentrated in strata 100, 110, 111 and 101, is suggestive but not established.

The evaluation code was modified after the first run, flipping the event from true to false (run.log, run_verified.log, IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md). The change is mathematically correct and disclosed, but it is a post-observation edit to the decision logic and reviewers should note it.

ID_PATTERN in experiment.py has no leading boundary, so a string such as XBUG-123 would match. The generator never produces such inputs, so the scored results are unaffected; it only matters for oracle generality.
Training loss reached about 1e-4 in both conditions (summary.json), which is consistent with memorisation of 240 examples. The differences show up only on held-out quoted-distractor strata.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered generator, oracle, sampling rules, LoRA settings, held-out balanced test set and strict-JSON exact-match statistic. The only change is the unavoidable 43/42 pool split. The protected fresh run reproduced the engineer's predictions and produced the reported value from real model outputs, with disjoint train and test IDs and templates and identical initial adapters. The difference is exactly 1/20, so the strict >0.05 event correctly did not occur; the earlier event=true came from a float-rounding bug that was disclosed and fixed. The evidence is weak as a test of the registered hypothesis. Coverage hit a perfect ceiling, so the threshold was unreachable given random's 0.95, and there is only one seed. The observed pattern (random errs only on quoted-distractor strata) is suggestive, but the result is inconclusive rather than a strong finding.

departures: experiment.py::make_data allocates the 300 nonzero-stratum pool examples as six strata of 43 and stratum 111 of 42, rather than equally across seven strata. This necessarily changes the pool relative to the impossible fractional allocation and could affect selections and predictions, but it is a minimal adjustment needed to instantiate the registered design; training and test quotas remain exactly registered.

experiment.py::SPAN_PATTERN excludes newlines inside quoted or backtick-delimited spans, whereas the specification does not impose that restriction. This could produce incorrect oracle labels for multiline quoted spans, but the generator never produces such spans, so it does not change this run's labels or reported result.
problems: outputs/summary.json documents only one selection/training seed and 25 test examples per stratum. This limits precision and does not measure variability across selected subsets, training seeds, or generated test sets; technical reruns are not independent experimental repetitions.

experiment.py::generate_example always includes 1–3 valid unquoted IDs and uses tightly constrained distractors and templates. The finding concerns this synthetic distribution, not correctness across the full specified function domain or performance on teacher-generated datasets.
experiment.py::SPAN_PATTERN does not implement multiline balanced spans, although this limitation does not affect the generated evaluation examples.

requirements.txt does not pin PyTorch or every transitive dependency. outputs/config_before_training.json records the tested PyTorch version, but the submission's dependency-pinning claims are broader than the installation script guarantees.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation successfully trained both conditions from fresh model loads, produced all registered outputs, and agreed with the supplied summary: random selection achieved 190/200 correct and coverage selection achieved 200/200. The code preserves the registered sampling comparison, training controls, common balanced test set, strict JSON scoring, and statistic, with a necessary integer allocation adjustment and no consequential scoring departure on generated inputs. Exact rational arithmetic correctly gives a difference of 0.05, so the strict greater-than-0.05 event did not occur; the earlier submitted floating-point event classification is not the evaluated result. This is a credible, narrowly meaningful five-percentage-point improvement, with all random-condition errors occurring in quoted-distractor strata, but it neither establishes the registered greater-than-threshold hypothesis nor equivalence and lacks multi-seed or multi-function support.

departures: Rare-stratum pool counts are six strata of 43 and stratum 111 of 42, not 300 divided equally across seven strata (experiment.py make_data; outputs/config_before_training.json). Integer counts make an equal split impossible. Coverage still draws 30 per stratum and the test set is balanced, so this only shifts random-sampling probabilities by a fraction of an example per stratum and does not plausibly change the reported difference of 0.05.
problems: Random balanced accuracy is already 0.95, so perfect coverage can reach a difference of only 0.05 and cannot pass the strict >0.05 event (outputs/summary.json). The threshold miss is therefore uninformative and is not evidence that coverage fails to help.

One seed and one stereotyped function: quoted distractors are always the phrase 'old mention <ID>' (experiment.py generate_example). All 10 random errors fall in quoted-distractor strata, but this single run cannot separate a stable coverage effect from seed noise or surface-template memorization.
grok.reason: The evaluation reran the registered comparison: same Qwen3-0.6B LoRA recipe, shared prompt, 240 oracle-labeled pairs, 80 updates, balanced 200-example test, and macro-averaged exact-match difference, with only the unavoidable 43/42 rare-pool split. Fresh training produced random accuracy 0.95 (190/200) and coverage accuracy 1.00, so the difference is exactly 1/20 and the strict >0.05 event correctly did not occur. Scores come from decoded model outputs with disjoint IDs, no leakage, and no hard-coded results; rational comparison also avoids the earlier float misclassification of 0.05. Because random performance already sits on the ceiling boundary, this single-seed miss is valid but weak evidence about the registered hypothesis.

registration.title: Does teacher self-consistency improve the compiled function?
registration.seed_connection: The seed uses teacher-generated supervision and notes that synthetic data may inherit teacher errors. It does not report a controlled comparison of consensus-filtered versus single-sample teacher labels on the resulting compiled function.
registration.hypothesis: For a fixed set of inputs, training on three-sample majority labels from a local open teacher improves held-out compiled-function accuracy over training on one sampled label per input by more than 0.05.
registration.contribution: A downstream test of teacher self-consistency in single-function compilation, not just agreement among generated labels. Rule-based test labels make the final student effect measurable without an API judge or human annotation.

closest_work.difference: Prompt2Model uses self-consistency to select pseudo-labels during a broader task-model generation pipeline; this MVE tests whether that choice improves a compiled adapter's accuracy on a single rule-verifiable function.
Self-consistency improves inference-time reasoning by aggregating sampled reasoning paths; this MVE aggregates teacher labels at compile time and evaluates the trained student's held-out behavior.
The seed uses mixed teacher supervision and flags teacher errors as a limitation, but does not isolate teacher self-consistency's effect on student accuracy.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 from Hugging Face as the local data-generating teacher, and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B as the student interpreter.
A Python generator and exact rule-based oracle implemented in the experiment script; no hosted APIs, human labels, or external dataset are used.
The supplied seed repository's compile.py is reference code only; do not invoke its API-backed synthesis or compiler path. Use PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT.
registration.method: Specify the function as: return a JSON array of distinct issue IDs matching BUG- or OPS- followed by exactly three digits; ignore IDs inside balanced double-quoted or backtick-delimited spans, ignore DOC IDs, and preserve first-appearance order. Generate 192 unique training inputs, balanced over the eight combinations of quoted distractor, repeated valid ID, and DOC distractor, plus 240 oracle-labeled test inputs using held-out surface templates and ID values. For each training input, sample three completions from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9, with thinking disabled and a maximum of 96 new tokens. The single-label dataset uses the first completion. The consensus dataset uses the modal parsed, canonicalized ordered ID list; break ties by shortest canonical JSON string, then lexicographically. Treat unparseable completions as one shared INVALID label and retain those examples; do not repair or replace labels using the oracle. Train separate Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters on the same 192 inputs and respective labels with identical task prompts, response-only loss, rank 8, alpha 16, AdamW at 2e-4, batch size 8, 80 optimizer steps, maximum sequence length 512, and fixed seed 17. Decode greedily and count malformed predictions as incorrect. Save raw teacher completions so consensus decisions can be audited.

event.description: The student trained on majority-vote teacher labels has more than 0.05 higher held-out exact-match accuracy than the student trained on the first teacher sample.
event.statistic: held-out exact-match accuracy (three-sample majority labels) minus held-out exact-match accuracy (first sample)

evaluation.procedure: Compare each student's parsed ordered ID list against the oracle list on the same 240 test inputs. Write each input, oracle answer, all three teacher completions, the selected labels, both student predictions, and correctness indicators to the raw files. Write the registered accuracy difference and configuration to summary.json. Do not use oracle labels to alter training examples.
evaluation.controls: Keep training inputs, teacher prompts, all sampled completions, student model, training updates, decoding, and test inputs fixed across conditions; only the target-label selection rule differs. A missed threshold is inconclusive, not evidence of equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, compare consensus and other low-cost filtering methods across multiple specifications and open teacher families, measuring downstream accuracy and compile-time cost.

agent.reason: Self-consistency can correct variable teacher mistakes, but errors from repeated samples of the same model may be correlated, and this structured extraction task may produce few errors to correct. Even a better label set need not improve the trained student's accuracy by five points.

judge_astra.reason: The 4B teacher may already label this short, rule-specified task accurately, leaving limited room for consensus to help. Correlated errors and the student's tolerance of occasional noisy labels further reduce the likelihood of a greater-than-five-point downstream gain.

judge_fable.reason: At temperature 0.7 a 4B instruct teacher's three samples will usually agree on this near-deterministic extraction, so majority labels fix only a few percent of inputs and the downstream student difference is likely within single-run noise.

judge_opus.reason: The labels change on only the roughly 10% of inputs where the first sample differs from the mode. Systematic teacher errors survive majority voting, and a greedily decoded student already averages out random label noise, so the downstream difference is likely under 3 points. Beyond noise, the main route to the event is an implementation asymmetry, such as raw versus canonicalized single-sample targets.

judge_sol.reason: Voting can remove stochastic labeling mistakes, but this deterministic extraction task may give the 4B teacher relatively little independent error to correct. Systematic mistakes survive voting, and modest improvements in label quality need not produce a five-point student gain.

judge_luna.reason: Majority voting can reduce noisy labels, but all three samples come from the same teacher and prompt, so errors may be correlated; the student may also learn the simple rule despite occasional bad labels. Those factors make a downstream gain above five points less likely than a smaller improvement.

judge_muse.reason: Three-sample voting can fix variance errors but not systematic 4B-teacher biases on quoted spans, so label gains and their transfer to the student will likely be modest and may fall short of 0.05.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Prompt2Model picks the labels for its generated training data by self-consistency, as one part of a larger pipeline that produces a task model. I found no evidence that it isolates how consensus labels versus single-sample labels affect the trained student's held-out exact-match accuracy on a function that can be checked by rules.

Self-consistency combines sampled reasoning paths at inference time to improve the answering model itself. The experiment instead combines teacher labels when the function is compiled, then measures a separately trained LoRA student.

The seed paper's supervision sweeps vary only the teacher mix (GPT-5.4-mini vs. a 2:1 mini/GPT-5.5 mixture) and the number of examples. Its limitations section notes that synthetic data may inherit teacher errors, but it runs no consensus-filtering ablation.

This paper also distills a teacher into a Qwen3-0.6B student for structured extraction, but it compares teacher types rather than label-aggregation rules, and scores outputs with LLM judges rather than an exact oracle.

opus.reason: Training on majority-vote or self-consistent LLM labels is a known idea, used in Prompt2Model and in self-improvement work. However, my searches found no paper that runs this controlled comparison: the same inputs and the same sampled teacher completions, trained once on three-sample majority labels and once on the first sample, with downstream student accuracy measured against an exact rule-based oracle in a single-specification compile setting. The seed paper itself only sweeps teacher mixture and data scale, so the question looks unanswered, though my search was limited and could have missed an ablation buried in a larger paper.

registration.title: Do static demonstrations in the scaffold still help after LoRA training?
registration.seed_connection: Compile by Training packages both a trained adapter and a run-time scaffold, and describes the scaffold as encoding instructions and examples. The seed does not isolate the value of keeping fixed demonstrations in that scaffold after adapter training.
registration.hypothesis: At a fixed training-pair budget, adding four fixed demonstrations to the specification scaffold improves held-out exact-match accuracy over the specification alone by more than 0.05.
registration.contribution: A focused ablation of the packaged run-time scaffold for gradient-trained functions. It tests the marginal value of demonstrations after training, distinct from whether the adapter itself can be compiled or whether demonstrations help a prompt-only model.

closest_work.difference: The seed describes the scaffold and training recipe but does not ablate static demonstrations from the run-time scaffold.
PAW compares compiler inputs and pseudo-program variants for an amortized hypernetwork-generated adapter; this MVE tests fixed run-time examples with an adapter trained directly on task examples.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
A Python generator and exact rule-based oracle implemented in the experiment script; no external dataset, human labels, or hosted API is required.
The supplied seed repository's compile.py is reference code only; do not use its hosted compiler or teacher API. Use PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT.
registration.method: Specify the function as: return a JSON array of distinct issue IDs matching BUG- or OPS- followed by exactly three digits; ignore IDs inside balanced double-quoted or backtick-delimited spans, ignore DOC IDs, and preserve first-appearance order. Generate 240 training pairs and 200 test pairs by code. Reserve disjoint ID values and four surface templates for the test set. Select four fixed demonstration pairs from the 240 training pairs, spanning different input patterns. Train two LoRA adapters on the identical 240 input–output pairs. In the spec-only condition, every training and test prompt contains the natural-language specification and current input. In the spec-plus-demonstrations condition, every training and test prompt additionally contains those same four fixed demonstrations. Use response-only loss, rank 8, alpha 16, AdamW at 2e-4, batch size 8, 80 optimizer steps, maximum sequence length 512, and fixed seed 17; use the same initialization and batch order across conditions. Decode greedily and treat invalid JSON predictions as incorrect.

event.description: The spec-plus-demonstrations scaffold has more than 0.05 higher held-out exact-match accuracy than the spec-only scaffold.
event.statistic: held-out exact-match accuracy (specification plus four demonstrations) minus held-out exact-match accuracy (specification only)

evaluation.procedure: Parse each prediction as a JSON array and compare its ordered values with the rule-based oracle on the same 200 test inputs. Write per-example predictions, correctness, golds, and condition to scores.jsonl; write the registered difference and configuration to summary.json. No LLM judge is used.
evaluation.controls: Both conditions use the same four demonstrations as training examples, training pairs, model, LoRA initialization, optimizer, update count, test set, and decoding. The prompt scaffold is the only intended difference. A missed threshold is inconclusive, not evidence of equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, compare scaffold content and length across more function families, test long inputs where context competition may matter, and measure accuracy alongside run-time cost.

registration.title: A compiled adapter versus in-context use of the same examples
registration.seed_connection: The seed motivates compiling a reusable local function instead of repeatedly supplying a large-model call. It does not compare compile-by-training with the same compact interpreter prompted with the full set of generated examples at run time.
registration.hypothesis: With the same 128 rule-verified pairs available to both methods, the trained adapter exceeds the no-update interpreter prompted with all 128 pairs by more than 0.05 held-out exact-match accuracy.
registration.contribution: A matched-data comparison of a trained, reusable function with a strong local in-context baseline on one specified text function, rather than comparing different model sizes or hosted APIs.

closest_work.difference: T-Few rigorously compares parameter-efficient tuning and in-context learning on standard benchmarks; this MVE evaluates the same comparison for one compiled fuzzy function using a compact shared interpreter and the same example set.

Prompt2Model builds deployable models from natural-language instructions and compares against a prompted API model; this MVE holds the local base model fixed and uses its generated support pairs for both methods.
PAW reports a no-compiler prompting baseline, but not a full-context, same-example comparison against the seed's compile-by-training procedure.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
A Python generator and exact rule-based oracle implemented in the experiment script; no external dataset, human labels, or hosted API is required.
The supplied seed repository's compile.py is reference code only; do not use its API-backed compiler or teacher path. Use PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT.
registration.method: Specify the function as: return a JSON array of distinct issue IDs matching BUG- or OPS- followed by exactly three digits; ignore IDs inside balanced double-quoted or backtick-delimited spans, ignore DOC IDs, and preserve first-appearance order. Generate 128 unique rule-labeled training pairs with compact inputs, plus 200 test pairs using unseen ID values and held-out surface templates. Train a rank-8, alpha-16 LoRA adapter on all 128 pairs using the specification and current input, response-only loss, AdamW at 2e-4, batch size 8, 80 optimizer steps, maximum sequence length 512, and fixed seed 17. The in-context baseline uses the same frozen base model without an adapter and places all 128 training pairs, compactly serialized, in the prompt with the same specification and test input. Verify before evaluation that each in-context prompt fits within 16,000 tokens; keep every generated support input short enough to fit and do not truncate demonstrations. Use greedy decoding and the same output-token limit for both conditions. Parse JSON arrays for scoring; malformed outputs are incorrect.

event.description: The trained adapter exceeds the all-128-example in-context baseline by more than 0.05 held-out exact-match accuracy.
event.statistic: held-out exact-match accuracy (trained adapter) minus held-out exact-match accuracy (all-example in-context baseline)

evaluation.procedure: Run both methods on the identical 200 test inputs. Compare each parsed ordered ID list to its oracle answer. Write per-example predictions, correctness, golds, and the token count of the in-context prompt to scores.jsonl; write the registered difference and configuration to summary.json. Accuracy is the registered statistic; prompt length is diagnostic only.
evaluation.controls: Use the same local base model, specification, 128 support pairs, test inputs, greedy decoding, and output limit. The ICL condition uses all support pairs, not a smaller hand-picked subset. A missed threshold is inconclusive, not evidence of equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, evaluate the accuracy–latency–artifact-size frontier across several function types, support-set sizes, and repeated calls per function.

agent.reason: Parameter-efficient tuning has beaten in-context learning in broader comparisons, and an adapter may generalize better to unseen templates. But the baseline uses all the same examples in context, so it may perform strongly on this explicit extraction task and leave less than a five-point gap.

judge_astra.reason: Task-specific updates plausibly outperform a compact model's use of 128 demonstrations in a long prompt, particularly for quotation handling and deduplication. Nevertheless, the full-example in-context baseline could be strong enough to keep the difference below five points.

judge_fable.reason: A frozen 0.6B model given 128 demonstrations in a ~10k-token prompt will mostly copy the format but fail the quoted-span, DOC and dedup rules, while five epochs of LoRA on the same pairs should clearly beat it; most implementation failure modes (thinking tokens, run-on generation) hurt the ICL side.

judge_opus.reason: A 0.6B model doing 128-shot in-context learning over about 10k tokens is unlikely to reliably infer the quote, DOC and deduplication exception rules. A LoRA trained for about 5 epochs on the same pairs should learn them substantially better. The main risks are a training bug, a test set with few distractors, or surprisingly strong many-shot copying.

judge_sol.reason: I expect task-specific updates to be more reliable than learning the rule from a long, 128-example prompt on a 0.6B interpreter. However, this simple extraction task could make full-context ICL competitive; the seed's comparison against an amortized compiler does not directly establish this advantage.

judge_luna.reason: Training can encode the behavior in adapter weights and avoid relying on a 128-example prompt, which may be difficult for a 0.6B model to use consistently. However, the full-example in-context baseline is strong for this explicitly specified extraction task, so the trained adapter's advantage is not assured.

judge_muse.reason: A frozen 0.6B model is likely to use 128 examples in a long prompt poorly compared with gradient specialization on the same clean pairs, making a >0.05 adapter advantage likely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper compares compile-by-training only with PAW's fast amortized compiler, using teacher data and LEM on FuzzyBench-Hard. It has no baseline in which the frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter is prompted at run time with the same generated examples.

PAW reports a short-prompt baseline using the raw specification (9.8%) and same-base fixed-LoRA and full fine-tuning baselines. It does not compare a trained adapter against the same 0.6B interpreter prompted in context with the full training set.

T-Few compares parameter-efficient tuning with few-shot ICL on standard classification benchmarks, mostly against larger ICL models. It does not test the same compact model on one rule-verified structured-extraction function with 128 examples in context.

Mosbach et al. compare fine-tuning and ICL on the same models with the same number of examples. Their results are mixed and depend on model size and example count, so they do not settle this particular case (0.6B model, 128 examples in context, held-out templates).

Many-shot ICL reports that ICL with hundreds of examples can perform comparably to fine-tuning, but with frontier long-context models rather than a 0.6B interpreter in the compile-by-training setting.
Prompt2Model compares its distilled small model with a prompted large API model, not with the same small base model prompted with the same generated examples.

opus.reason: Comparing fine-tuning with ICL on the same examples is well studied in general (T-Few, Mosbach et al., many-shot ICL). However, those studies find that the outcome depends on the task, model size and number of examples, so they don't settle this case. Neither the seed paper nor the PAW paper reports an all-128-example in-context baseline on the frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter against a LoRA trained on those same examples. This is a narrow instance of a known question, but I found no work that answers it.

sol.label: close variant

Controls the base model and support examples when comparing fine-tuning with ICL, includes compact models, and investigates LoRA adaptation. It uses few-shot classification and challenge datasets rather than the specified extraction function and 128-example context.

sol.reason: The central matched-data, same-model comparison between a reusable trained adapter and in-context demonstrations was already investigated, including an all-demonstration ICL baseline against rank-8 LoRA. outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registration in experiment.py using pinned Transformers/PEFT dependencies and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B at a recorded commit. registration.title: Separately compiled components versus one end-to-end function
registration.seed_connection: The seed demonstrates applications that compose independently compiled functions with ordinary code, while noting that systematic evaluation of composition remains future work. This MVE compares a modular compiled pipeline with a monolithic compiled function on held-out combinations.
registration.hypothesis: At a matched input-token training budget, two separately trained components combined by deterministic code outperform a single end-to-end adapter by more than 0.05 joint accuracy on held-out combinations of component patterns.
registration.contribution: A small controlled test of the seed's composition claim: separate local functions and deterministic output assembly are compared with one adapter on recombinations absent from monolithic training.

closest_work.difference: The seed presents composed applications but no controlled held-out-combination comparison between modular compiled functions and a monolithic function.
PAW describes program composition in applications; this MVE evaluates separate executable adapters against one end-to-end function using a fixed, oracle-labeled split.

Compositional fine-tuning decomposes tasks into components during training; this MVE tests separate run-time compiled functions joined by deterministic code, compared with a monolithic compiled function.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
A Python generator, exact oracle, and deterministic JSON assembler implemented in the experiment script; no external dataset, human labels, or hosted API is required.
The supplied seed repository's compile.py is reference code only; do not use its hosted compiler or teacher path. Use PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT.
registration.method: Generate short messages with a status clause and an issue-reference clause. Define the priority component as returning NOW when the current unquoted clause requests action by today's end or says a release is blocked pending action, and LATER otherwise; include quoted opposite-priority distractors. Define the ID component as returning a JSON array of distinct BUG- or OPS- plus three-digit IDs outside balanced double-quoted or backtick-delimited spans, ignoring DOC IDs and preserving first-appearance order. Define the composite function as a JSON object with priority and ids fields. Use four status-clause template families and four ID-layout template families. Make 160 training inputs from 12 of the 16 cross-family pairings, omitting the four diagonal pairings (family 1 with layout 1, and so on). Make a 160-input test set with 40 examples from each omitted pairing, using new values; every individual status family and ID layout must appear in training in other pairings. Labels come from the generator's latent priority and the exact ID oracle. Train the modular system as two independent Qwen3-0.6B LoRA adapters: one maps message to priority, the other maps message to IDs. Combine their parsed predictions with deterministic Python code. Train the monolithic system to map the same message to the composite JSON object. Use rank 8, alpha 16, response-only loss, AdamW at 2e-4, batch size 8, maximum sequence length 512, fixed seed 17, and greedy decoding. Match total training input-token presentations: 20 optimizer steps for each modular adapter and 40 steps for the monolithic adapter. Parse outputs strictly; a malformed component or composite prediction counts as an incorrect joint answer.

registration.title: Coverage versus repetition for a compiled text function
registration.seed_connection: The seed varies the number of unique training pairs, but does not isolate the effect of covering more input-feature combinations when the total number of training presentations is fixed.
registration.hypothesis: At the same number of training presentations and optimizer updates, broader feature-combination coverage improves accuracy on unseen combinations by more than 5 percentage points compared with repeating a smaller set.
registration.contribution: A controlled, single-function test of within-task combinational coverage, distinct from corpus-scale synthetic-data diversity and held-out-specification evaluation.

closest_work.difference: Studies diversity in synthetic corpora; this test varies combination coverage within one function at a matched presentation budget.
Evaluates PAW across specifications and data budgets, but does not compare broad versus repeated input-combination coverage for one function.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Python generator with a deterministic label oracle; CUDA PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT. No external dataset or hosted API.
registration.method: Implement a function that classifies the current, unquoted customer request as REFUND, REPLACE, TROUBLESHOOT, or OTHER, ignoring quoted history. Generate a full factorial bank with 4 intents, 8 cue phrasings per intent, 4 input layouts, 4 quoted-decoy conditions (none or one of the other intents), and 2 placements of the current and quoted sections. A seeded constrained splitter must create a balanced 64-cell narrow set, a balanced 320-cell broad set that contains those same 64 cells, and 256 held-out cells disjoint from the broad set. Assert that every factor value occurs in the narrow set, all single-factor marginals are balanced in each set, and aggregate input-token counts for the two training arms differ by no more than 2%; abort rather than silently use a split that fails these checks. The narrow arm sees its 64 examples five times; the broad arm sees all 320 once. For each of two seeds, train a fresh rank-8 LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B targeting q_proj and v_proj, with bf16, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-4, and 40 updates. Use the same natural-language specification in the prompt, mask prompt tokens from the loss, and greedily decode the label. Implement local Transformers/PEFT training directly; do not use hosted PAW services or a PAW warm start.

event.description: The event occurs if broad-coverage training has more than a 5 percentage-point mean accuracy gain over repeated-example training on the held-out feature combinations.
event.statistic: Mean across two seeds of broad-arm exact accuracy minus narrow-arm exact accuracy on the same held-out inputs.

evaluation.procedure: Score exact label accuracy on all 256 held-out inputs for both arms and both seeds. Save each input’s factor values, target, prediction, and correctness, and report per-factor accuracies and token counts as diagnostics alongside the registered paired accuracy difference.
evaluation.controls: Both arms use the same specification, base model, balanced factor marginals, optimizer, 320 example presentations, 40 updates, and held-out set. The 64 narrow examples are included once in the broad set; the intended treatment is additional unique feature combinations rather than extra presentations.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, repeat the comparison across independently specified functions, surface-form and compositional holdouts, and more training seeds; test whether coverage effects persist at several example and compute budgets.

This is the Program-as-Weights (PAW) paper. It evaluates PAW across specifications and data budgets, but it does not compare broad feature-combination coverage with repetition of a smaller set for one function.

registration.title: Does compile-time noise augmentation improve local-function robustness?
registration.seed_connection: The seed trains adapters from task-specific examples but does not test training-time input augmentation. PAW’s input-perturbation evaluations make robustness a relevant next question.
registration.hypothesis: Replacing clean training renderings with label-preserving surface perturbations improves exact accuracy on perturbed inputs by more than 5 percentage points.
registration.contribution: A paired, fixed-data-budget test of compile-time augmentation for one local function, separating training-time exposure from test-time perturbation.

closest_work.difference: Reports performance under test-time input perturbations; this experiment changes compile-time training inputs and measures the effect on perturbed test inputs.
Studies synthetic-data selection for OOD NLI; this test focuses on label-preserving textual variation for a structured extraction function.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Python generator and oracle, CUDA PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT. No external dataset, hosted model API, or human annotation.
registration.method: Specify a function that reads CURRENT MESSAGE, ignores QUOTED HISTORY and tracking lines marked CANCELLED, returns the active tracking identifier in uppercase, and returns NONE if no active identifier exists. Generate 320 training messages and 256 held-out messages with disjoint identifiers, balanced across identifier-present versus NONE cases and relevant quoted/cancelled distractors. For each message, create three deterministic, label-preserving variants: alter casing in prose and identifiers, vary whitespace and punctuation around fixed separators, or substitute semantically neutral filler phrases while leaving control markers unchanged. The clean arm trains on the canonical 320 messages. The augmentation arm trains on exactly one variant per underlying message, assigning the three perturbation types as evenly as possible; it does not receive additional examples. For each of two seeds, train a fresh rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B for 40 updates with batch size 8 and learning rate 2e-4, using loss only on the answer. Use the same specification and underlying records in both arms. Greedily decode in batches. Evaluate each model on the canonical held-out messages and all three variants. Count an answer as correct only if its trimmed text exactly equals the uppercase oracle identifier or NONE; extra explanation is incorrect. Use a local Transformers/PEFT loop, not hosted PAW or teacher endpoints.

event.description: The event occurs if the augmented arm improves mean exact accuracy on perturbed held-out inputs by more than 5 percentage points over the clean-only arm.
event.statistic: Mean paired accuracy difference, augmented minus clean, averaged over two training seeds and the three held-out perturbation types.

evaluation.procedure: Write the training and held-out records with oracle outputs and variant types, then predictions and correctness for each arm, seed, test record, and rendering. Compute the registered statistic using only the three perturbed renderings; report canonical accuracy and each perturbation type separately as diagnostics.
evaluation.controls: Both arms use the same 320 underlying training messages and labels, example presentations, model, optimizer, prompt, and held-out records. The augmentation arm replaces canonical renderings rather than receiving more labeled examples. The oracle is used for generation and scoring, not model input.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, compare individual augmentation types and their combinations across more functions, input shifts, and seeds, while pre-registering a clean-input accuracy guardrail.

agent.reason: Training on the specified variants could help with casing and formatting, but the base model may already handle these changes well. The bundled perturbations and possible accuracy ceiling make a mean gain above five points uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: Exposure to the tested perturbation families should help, particularly when identifier casing must be normalized. However, unchanged control markers and relatively mild whitespace and filler changes could keep the gain averaged across perturbations below five points.

judge_fable.reason: The casing perturbation (lowercase identifiers that must be output uppercase) is a shift the clean arm never sees, which likely gives the augmented arm a large edge on that one type, but the other two perturbation types should yield small differences and the extraction task may sit at low accuracy for both arms, making the three-type mean of >5pp roughly a coin flip.

judge_opus.reason: The result hinges on the casing variant. A clean-trained copier will probably output lowercase or mixed-case identifiers, which exact match rejects, while the augmented arm learns to uppercase. But only about half the cases contain an identifier, and the whitespace and filler variants likely show little difference, so the three-type average lands near the 5-point threshold.

judge_sol.reason: Casing augmentation targets a plausible uppercase-copying failure, while unchanged control markers and mild whitespace or filler edits may produce smaller benefits. Averaging across all three perturbation types, with half the targets being NONE, makes the five-point threshold relatively demanding.

judge_luna.reason: Training on label-preserving casing, separator, and filler variations directly exposes the model to the perturbed test inputs without adding examples. The specification and pretrained model may already confer robustness, so a gain above five points is plausible but uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Markers are unchanged so clean training may partly generalize, but learning to uppercase varied-case identifiers and parse altered separators likely gives augmentation a >5pp edge on perturbed tests.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper trains LoRA adapters for Qwen3-0.6B on synthetic examples written by teacher models. It evaluates semantic accuracy on FuzzyBench-Hard and runs teacher-mix and data-scaling sweeps. It never trains on perturbed inputs and never tests robustness to perturbed inputs.

PAW, the system the seed builds on, compiles fuzzy functions into adapters for a frozen 0.6B interpreter. According to the experiment's own description, PAW reports results under perturbed test inputs. From the abstract, it does not appear to compare compiling on clean versus perturbed training inputs. I did not read the full text to confirm this.

Noise-Aware Training is the main general precedent. It shows that training on a mix of clean and synthetically noised inputs makes NER sequence labeling more robust to OCR errors and misspellings. It differs in model (pre-LLM sequence labelers, not a LoRA-tuned 0.6B decoder), task, perturbation type, and design: it mixes clean and noisy data, while the experiment replaces clean renderings at a fixed budget and uses exact-match generation.

This paper studies how to select synthetic data for out-of-distribution NLI generalization. It does not test label-preserving surface perturbations at training time for an extraction function with control markers. Its relevance comes from the experiment's own description; I found no evidence of closer overlap.

opus.reason: The general idea that training on matched perturbations improves robustness to them is well established, for example by Noise-Aware Training (2005.07162). However, I found no work that tests this at a fixed data budget for a compiled LoRA function on Qwen3-0.6B with casing, whitespace and filler perturbations and exact-match scoring. That effect size (more than 5 percentage points) could plausibly be small, because the pretrained interpreter may already handle casing and whitespace changes, so the prior work does not settle the question. My search was limited to a few queries, so I cannot rule out an unfound closer paper.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Tests training-time augmentation with casing, punctuation, synonyms and paraphrases against clean-only training, evaluating clean and noisy inputs for intent classification and slot labeling. The proposed experiment instead uses synthetic tracking-identifier extraction, Qwen3 LoRA, exact match and replacement-only augmentation under a fixed example budget.

Reports clean-only versus perturbation-augmented fine-tuning of generative language models for structured intent and slot outputs, with aligned clean and perturbed evaluations. Its augmentation adds examples rather than replacing each canonical example, and its main method also introduces consistency regularization.
Provides the compile-by-training setting and compact adapter-based functions, but does not report a controlled training-time surface-augmentation experiment.

sol.reason: Prior work already tests the central question of whether training exposure to label-preserving textual variation improves robustness of structured language functions on perturbed held-out inputs. The local-function framing, synthetic extraction task and fixed-budget replacement control refine that established comparison rather than introduce a substantially different question or method. I found no paper reporting this exact protocol, and the prior results do not determine whether its registered five-percentage-point event will occur.

registration.title: Do separately compiled functions retain accuracy in a two-stage pipeline?
registration.seed_connection: The seed demonstrates applications composed from compiled functions, including a website helper, but does not give a controlled end-to-end comparison with a jointly trained function.
registration.hypothesis: At a matched total number of example presentations and optimizer updates, a two-stage pipeline is no more than 10 percentage points less accurate than a directly trained joint function.
registration.contribution: A small, exactly scored comparison of error propagation through independently trained local components versus one function trained for the combined behavior.

closest_work.difference: Demonstrates composed functions in deployed applications but does not compare pipeline and joint accuracy under a matched training budget.
Includes multi-function applications, whereas this experiment isolates a two-stage pipeline and evaluates its end-to-end exact accuracy.
Studies multiple LoRAs for composite tasks; this test passes a predicted intermediate label between separately trained functions.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Python support-message generator and exact oracle, CUDA PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT. No external dataset or hosted API.
registration.method: Generate support messages with CURRENT REQUEST, optional QUOTED HISTORY, and route-specific identifiers. The first function predicts REFUND, EXCHANGE, REPAIR, or OTHER from the current request while ignoring quoted history. The second receives the original message and a route, then returns the identifier belonging to that route, or NONE for OTHER. The joint function maps the original message to a JSON object containing both route and identifier. Generate 512 balanced training cases (128 per route) and 400 disjoint held-out cases (100 per route), including quoted distractors and held-out template combinations. Within each training route, assign 64 cases to the route component and the other 64 to the identifier component. Train the identifier component with the gold route; at test time pass it the route component’s prediction. Train the joint function on all 512 cases. For each of two seeds, use fresh rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRAs, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-4, and local masked-answer loss: 40 updates for each pipeline component and 80 for the joint model. Thus each strategy gets 640 example presentations per seed. Use the same frozen base model and greedily decode in batches. Count a case correct only if both final route and identifier match the oracle; invalid component outputs count as incorrect. Report route-stage accuracy, identifier accuracy conditional on gold and predicted routes, and end-to-end latency as diagnostics. This is a local LoRA probe, not a reproduction of the PAW warm start.

event.description: The screening event occurs if mean two-stage pipeline accuracy is more than 10 percentage points below joint-function accuracy; passing this margin is not evidence of equivalence.
event.statistic: Mean across two seeds of pipeline exact accuracy minus joint-function exact accuracy on the same 400 held-out cases.

evaluation.procedure: Save the component and joint outputs for every held-out case and seed, including the predicted intermediate route, final identifier, and exact-match correctness. Compute the paired end-to-end accuracy difference as registered and report component-level scores and inference latency as diagnostics.
evaluation.controls: The strategies share the training pool, held-out cases, frozen base model, LoRA rank, batch size, optimizer, and total presentations and updates. Pipeline components use stratified disjoint halves of the training pool; the joint function uses the full pool. The gold-route training versus predicted-route inference interface is part of the pipeline being tested.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, test longer pipelines and additional workflow families, vary component data budgets, and compare direct error propagation with deterministic interface validation while measuring latency.

agent.reason: The components solve simpler subtasks, and the ten-point margin is a permissive screening threshold. Still, each component gets only half the training pool, and route errors can propagate, so a larger pipeline deficit is plausible.

judge_astra.reason: I use the explicit numerical condition, pipeline minus joint accuracy > -0.10, since the event description states the opposite direction. The simple intermediate route and ten-point tolerance make this fairly likely, although propagated routing errors and smaller component training sets remain risks.

judge_fable.reason: The 10pp tolerance is lenient and the pipeline components have simpler outputs than the joint JSON, but the joint gets twice the per-subtask supervision and pipeline errors compound, so the result is genuinely uncertain with a slight lean toward the pipeline staying within the margin.

judge_opus.reason: The route and identifier subtasks are easy and both strategies get the same number of presentations, so pipeline error propagation should cost a few points at most. The main ways to miss the lenient −10 point margin are undertrained 40-step components or implementation failures.

judge_sol.reason: I interpret the explicit numerical event as pipeline minus joint accuracy > -0.10; the prose event description states the opposite inequality. That margin seems attainable on simple routing and extraction, although compounded errors and the gold-route-to-predicted-route mismatch could produce a larger deficit.

judge_luna.reason: The component tasks are structured, and the registered event allows the pipeline to trail the joint function by nearly ten points. Route errors can compound when the predicted route replaces the gold route, however, and passing the margin would not establish equivalence.

judge_muse.reason: Pipeline stages emit simpler outputs than joint JSON and route errors alone decide end-to-end failure, so half-data specialization will likely stay within 10pp despite gold-to-predicted route shift.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper shows compiled functions composed into deployed applications, such as the website helper. It does not report a controlled comparison between a two-stage pipeline and a single jointly trained function under a matched training budget.

Program-as-Weights introduces compiled fuzzy functions as reusable adapters for a frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter. Its abstract describes no end-to-end comparison where one function's predicted label feeds a second function and is scored against a joint function. This judgment rests on the abstract only.

Compositional fine-tuning trains one smaller LM on a curriculum of component tasks and compares it with end-to-end training at equal data. It does not chain independently trained modules, so it does not measure error passed through a predicted intermediate label, and it does not use LoRA adapters on a frozen base.

Studies combining multiple LoRAs for composite tasks inside one model, not a sequential pipeline of separately trained adapters compared with a joint adapter at a matched number of updates. This is based on the experiment's own description; I did not open this paper.

opus.reason: I found no paper that compares a pipeline of separately trained LoRA functions, with predicted routes passed between them, against one jointly trained adapter at a matched number of example presentations and updates. The closest work, compositional fine-tuning (2210.12607), compares decomposed with end-to-end training at equal data, but inside one model rather than as chained independent modules. The PAW and compile-by-training papers show composition without this controlled measurement. Pipeline-versus-joint comparisons are a long-standing general theme in NLP, and my searches were limited, so a close analogue could exist that I missed.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: OneNet compares a predicted-domain routing pipeline followed by intent and slot extraction against unified joint prediction, including an oracle-domain control. The registered experiment substitutes synthetic support messages, serial LoRA adapters, exact route-and-identifier scoring, and matched aggregate training budgets.

Section 5 compares separately trained planner and executor models with an end-to-end model initialized from the same checkpoint and supervised using the same underlying examples. It studies image editing rather than text classification and extraction, and does not use the registered split-data, matched-update LoRA protocol.
The seed demonstrates composed compiled functions but does not conduct the registered pipeline-versus-joint comparison.

sol.reason: Prior work already evaluates the central comparison: error propagation through separately trained components passing a predicted intermediate output versus unified prediction, with OneNet providing a particularly close routing-and-extraction precedent. The synthetic task, LoRA implementation, scoring rule, and aggregate-budget controls make this a controlled variant of that comparison, although no paper found reports the exact configuration or establishes its proposed 10-percentage-point margin.

opus.reason: Both compare a router-plus-sub-function pipeline of separately trained adapters, composed in code, against a single jointly trained adapter at a matched training budget. Both report end-to-end accuracy and stage-level accuracy.

sol.reason: Both compare a budget-matched two-node compiled pipeline with a single end-to-end adapter, measuring exact final-output correctness and component-level failures.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered fresh-LoRA Qwen3-0.6B composition probe with 512 balanced training and 400 disjoint held-out cases, quoted distractors, held-out opening/closing combinations, stratified disjoint component halves, two seeds, rank-8 q_proj/v_proj adapters, batch 8 and lr 2e-4. Each component receives 40 updates/320 presentations; joint receives 80/640. Strict exact scoring saves all requested raw outputs plus gold-route identifier diagnostics and CUDA-synchronized batched latency. No methodological changes; unspecified generator/optimizer/LoRA details are documented in README. Registration prose says screening difference < -0.1, whereas serialized relation says greater; statistic is unchanged and summary reports both comparisons. Full evaluation command tested successfully in 118 seconds including installation/download; independent audit passed. Observed pipeline 392/400 and 391/400, joint 400/400 both seeds, mean difference -0.02125; within the prose margin is not evidence of equivalence.

departures: composition_experiment.py fixes several choices the registration leaves open: LoRA alpha 16 and dropout 0; AdamW with no weight decay and a constant learning rate; training seeds 17 and 29; data seed 260904199; bfloat16 with TF32; inference batch 32; output caps of 8/16/64 tokens; the system prompts; thinking disabled in the chat template. These are allowed choices. With zero invalid outputs and loss near zero for every stage, the caps and prompts do not appear to have changed the value.

composition_experiment.py calls set_seed(seed) before each get_peft_model, so the route, identifier and joint adapters share the same LoRA initialization within a seed. This is an open choice and is neutral between the strategies.

composition_experiment.py samples training cases as seeded shuffled epochs cut off at exactly 40 or 80 updates. That is 1.25 passes over each pool, so some cases are seen twice and others once. The budget is matched exactly as registered (640 presentations and 80 updates per strategy per seed), so this has no effect beyond the registered design.

composition_experiment.py (generate_data) defines the grammar. There are 8 fixed intent sentences per route, shared by the training and held-out splits. Every current request contains all three route-specific identifiers. 75% of cases carry quoted history from a different route. Only opening/closing combinations are held out. The registration says 'held-out template combinations', so this is consistent with it, but held-out generalization is limited to new combinations of shared atoms. This affects how far the result can be interpreted, not its fidelity.

composition_experiment.py strips the route prediction and passes it to the identifier stage as is; invalid routes are not repaired. There were 0 invalid route, identifier or joint outputs in both seeds, so this did not affect the value.

composition_experiment.py reuses the base after PeftModel.unload(), which triggers a PEFT warning about an existing peft_config. In training_log.json the trainable parameter count is 1,146,880, which matches one fresh rank-8 q/v adapter on Qwen3-0.6B. Adapters were therefore not stacked, and the value is unchanged.

Registration-internal inconsistency: the prose defines the event as a difference below -0.1, but the serialized relation is 'greater' than -0.1. The engineer reports both booleans in composition_summary.json without changing the statistic. The harness marked the event as occurred under the serialized relation. This is not an implementation departure.

Extras beyond the registration: a gold-route identifier diagnostic, a paired-case bootstrap interval, and split breakdowns by route and by quoted versus unquoted cases. These are diagnostics only and do not affect the primary value.
problems: Registration (event): the prose ('pipeline more than 10pp below joint') and the serialized relation ('greater', -0.1) point in opposite directions. As a result, 'registered event occurred: True' in the protected evaluation actually means the pipeline stayed within the margin, and the prose-defined screening event did not occur.

outputs/composition_summary.json: the joint function is at ceiling (400/400 in both seeds). The comparison therefore cannot resolve how good the joint function is beyond this easy synthetic grammar, and a 10pp margin is a loose target.

Design confound inherent to the registration: under the matched budget, the route component sees only 256 cases (320 presentations), while the joint function learns routing from 640. All pipeline errors come from the route stage, on quoted-history cases: the identifier given a gold route is 100%, and unquoted cases are 100%. The gap may reflect halved per-component data rather than composition as such.

composition_experiment.py: only 8 intent sentences per route, shared across splits, with only opening/closing combinations held out. Two seeds, one workflow, and a bootstrap interval that covers case uncertainty only and does not quantify seed variability.

README.md and the engineer notes claim 'no methodological changes'. This is accurate, but the latency diagnostic is warm, batched and amortized, and does not reflect single-request end-to-end latency. The engineer acknowledges this.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design: the data sizes, balanced disjoint component halves, adapter settings, matched update and presentation budgets, the gold-route-train / predicted-route-test interface, greedy decoding and strict exact scoring all match. The only open issue is the registration's own contradiction in the event direction, which the engineer reported transparently. The protected run reproduces the engineer's earlier results exactly: pipeline 392/400 and 391/400 against joint 400/400, a mean difference of -0.02125, with saved per-case raw outputs and no leakage of identifiers across splits. The evidence is real and internally consistent: every pipeline error is a route-stage misclassification on a quoted-distractor case. However, the task is a small synthetic grammar where the joint function saturates, and the 10pp margin is easily met. Two seeds give weak precision over training randomness, and the gap may reflect each component receiving half the data rather than composition itself, so the finding is valid but of limited consequence.

departures: Event interpretation differs from the registration's prose: the protected evaluator uses the serialized relation, difference > -0.1, and reports True, whereas the prose screening event requires difference < -0.1 and is False. composition_experiment.py and outputs/composition_summary.json preserve the statistic and report both comparisons. This does not change the numerical result, but reverses the screening-event interpretation.

composition_experiment.py adds a paired-case bootstrap interval and quoted/unquoted and per-route breakdowns beyond the registered reporting requirements. These supplementary analyses do not alter training, scoring, exclusions, or the primary result.
problems: The registration contains contradictory event directions. The protected evaluation's 'registered event occurred: True' must not be interpreted as evidence that the pipeline lost more than 10 percentage points.

composition_experiment.py tests one finite synthetic grammar with shared intent sentences across training and test; held-out template combinations concern openings and closings. This provides limited evidence about generalization to new request language or other workflows.

The registered allocation gives the route component 256 distinct training cases and 40 updates, while the joint function receives 512 cases and 80 updates. Aggregate budgets are matched, but the comparison does not isolate composition effects from stage-specific training allocation or differences in supervised answer lengths.

The bootstrap interval in outputs/composition_summary.json quantifies case uncertainty conditional on the two training seeds, not uncertainty over training seeds. Neither the observed margin nor this interval establishes general equivalence.

The latency diagnostic in composition_experiment.py sums separately timed, resident-model stage calls and excludes model loading and adapter handoff or switching costs. It is batched amortized timing, not a measurement of deployed single-request pipeline latency.
The seed paper and cited related papers are not supplied, so the claimed literature gap and connection to their results cannot be independently verified here.
sol.reason: The supplied code and fresh evaluation support execution of the registered data split, fresh unmerged LoRA training, matched aggregate budgets, predicted-route interface, greedy decoding, and exact scoring; unspecified prompt and optimizer details are implementation choices rather than conflicting replacements. The reported mean difference is correctly computed as -0.02125, or -2.125 percentage points, from pipeline accuracies of 98% and 97.75% versus 100% joint accuracy, with no apparent hard-coded result or train/test leakage. The diagnostics locate every observed pipeline failure at the routing stage, while gold-route identifier accuracy is perfect, and the prose screening event therefore did not occur despite the automated True flag. This is a credible, meaningful finding for the narrow registered workflow, but the limited task diversity, two seeds, ceiling performance, and budget-allocation confound prevent stronger general conclusions.

departures: composition_experiment.py adds the EOS token to masked answer labels; the registration specifies local masked-answer loss but not EOS. Unlikely to change these near-ceiling accuracies.

parse_joint in composition_experiment.py rejects extra JSON fields, duplicate keys, and non-canonical identifier strings, stricter than a JSON object that contains route and identifier. Did not change the result: invalid_joint_outputs is 0 and joint accuracy is 1.0 on both seeds in outputs/composition_summary.json.

Registration-unspecified choices are fixed in composition_experiment.py and README.md: LoRA alpha 16, dropout 0, AdamW with zero weight decay and constant LR, bfloat16/sdpa, seeds 17 and 29, inference batch 32, max_new_tokens 8/16/64, enable_thinking=False, 75% quoted distractors, opening/closing holdout via (opening+closing)%4==0, exact prompts, and all three reference IDs in every current request. These are open choices. Token caps did not bind (0 invalid outputs). The others could change absolute difficulty but not the registered comparison structure.

Evaluation stderr warns that a peft_config attribute was already present (peft tuners_utils.py:196) after unload() in composition_experiment.py. If prior adapters remained in the forward pass, later stages would not be fresh LoRAs on the same frozen base and the value could change. High, similar initial losses across seeds make a material effect unlikely; later-stage trainable-parameter counts are not visible in the truncated training log.
problems: Registration prose screens on difference < -0.1, but the serialized relation is greater than -0.1. The harness therefore marked the event True for -0.02125, while the prose screening event did not occur. outputs/composition_summary.json reports both booleans and leaves the statistic unchanged.

Ceiling and a loose margin: mean pipeline accuracy 0.97875 versus joint 1.0, so the 10pp screen is weakly informative and is not evidence of equivalence. The case-bootstrap interval [-0.0325, -0.01125] excludes 0 but is conditional on only two training seeds (outputs/composition_summary.json).

Held-out data reuse all eight intent phrases per route; only opening/closing pairs are disjoint (generate_data in composition_experiment.py), so the probe mostly tests memorized template routing plus format following.
The PEFT re-injection warning leaves a residual, unproven doubt that adapters after the first were fully fresh.
grok.reason: The run matches the registered sizes, disjoint 64/64 component split, matched 640 presentations and 80 updates, fresh rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRAs, gold-route training with predicted-route inference, greedy exact-match scoring, and the pipeline-minus-joint statistic. Unspecified generator and optimizer details are open choices; the stricter JSON rule and token caps did not bind, and the PEFT unload warning is unlikely to have moved accuracies that replicated exactly across runs. The value -0.02125 comes from saved model outputs and is internally consistent (8 and 9 joint-only errors, all pipeline misses explained by route-stage errors).
