obvious.reason: Modular-versus-joint training is a familiar comparison, but fewer researchers would prioritize that specific baseline than would raise the broader concern about composition errors.

who_would_care.reason: A decisive answer would inform modular-versus-monolithic design across research on local neural-function workflows, rather than only users of this compiler.

misreads_paper.reason: The registration accurately describes the seed's composition demonstrations and lack of a controlled joint-function comparison, and its remaining claims about other work are not contradicted by the supplied paper.

answerable.reason: Meaningful accuracy retention requires the component and joint adapters to learn their assigned mappings, since similarly unsuccessful training could otherwise produce a misleadingly small gap.
answerable.needs: Successful learning of component and joint mappings

sol.what_came_out: On 400 held-out generated support messages with Qwen3-0.6B across two training seeds, pipeline accuracy was 97.875% (392/400 and 391/400) versus 100% for joint training in both seeds, a difference of −2.125 percentage points with a paired-case 95% bootstrap interval of [−3.25, −1.125] points conditional on those seeds.

prerequisite.reason: Route accuracy reached 97.75–98%, identifier accuracy with gold routes and joint accuracy both reached 100%, and no invalid outputs were reported, supporting successful learning and readable scoring.

evidence.reason: The case-conditional interval supports accuracy retention with a modest but detectable pipeline loss, rather than a large degradation, without establishing general equivalence across training seeds or workflows.

next_step.reason: The run answers the comparison on this workflow, but perfect gold-route identifier and joint scores leave one important gap about retention when downstream processing is also error-prone.
next_step.what: Repeat the matched-budget comparison on a harder support-message workflow with held-out intent patterns and non-ceiling identifier and joint accuracy.

registration.title: Local in-context examples versus a compiled LoRA
registration.seed_connection: The seed argues that compile-time training can improve a reusable function, but its main comparison is with PAW’s fast compiler rather than using the same task examples in the runtime prompt.
registration.hypothesis: For the same compact interpreter, specification, and task-specific examples, a compiled LoRA improves held-out accuracy by more than 5 percentage points over in-context use of those examples.
registration.contribution: A narrow per-function comparison of compilation with an example-in-context alternative, including the different runtime-token and compile-time costs.

closest_work.difference: Provides a broader PEFT-versus-ICL comparison; this pilot holds the Qwen3 model, specification, and synthetic example set fixed for one function.
Includes a zero-shot prompting baseline, but does not compare an adapter with the same function-specific examples placed in its inference context.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Python triage-data generator and exact oracle, CUDA PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT. No external dataset or hosted teacher API.
registration.method: Define a triage function that returns NOW for an action required today or an active blocker, QUEUE for a requested action without same-day urgency, and FYI for an announcement or message with no requested action. Generate 96 short training examples balanced across labels and 240 held-out examples balanced across labels using new wording templates and values. The label is determined by explicit generator rules, and generated examples must not be ambiguous. Train a rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B for 40 updates with batch size 8 and learning rate 2e-4, using the specification and the 96 pairs with prompt-token loss masked. Train two LoRA seeds. For the in-context condition, use the unadapted same base model and put the identical specification and all 96 training pairs in each test prompt; for the LoRA condition, use only the specification and test input. Use the same chat template, disable thinking, greedily decode at most 8 new tokens, and accept only an exact label. Assert with the tokenizer that the ICL prompt fits within 8192 tokens; do not silently truncate. Run ICL once because it is deterministic and score the same test set. This is a deployment trade-off, not a matched-FLOPs comparison: record training time, runtime prompt tokens, and inference latency as diagnostics.

event.description: The event occurs if compiled-LoRA accuracy exceeds in-context-example accuracy by more than 5 percentage points on the held-out cases.
event.statistic: Mean accuracy of the two LoRA seeds minus the ICL accuracy on the same 240 held-out inputs.

evaluation.procedure: Save the generated training and test pairs, predictions and correctness for each condition, token counts, and timings. Compute exact label accuracy and the registered difference; retain the same fixed demonstration order for all ICL test prompts.
evaluation.controls: Both conditions use the same base model, specification, 96 examples, test set, chat template, and greedy decoding. The LoRA receives examples during training; ICL receives those examples at every inference call. Their inference compute is intentionally different and must not be described as matched.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, vary functions, example counts, prompt budgets, and reuse counts, and measure the accuracy, compile-time, inference-latency, and total-token point at which compilation pays off.

agent.reason: The ICL model receives all 96 examples at every query, while the LoRA gets a limited training run and must generalize to unseen wording. Fine-tuning could avoid demonstration interference, but a gain above five points seems unlikely.

judge_astra.reason: Fine-tuning could improve label adherence and avoid difficulties with a long demonstration context, but 96 examples may already make ICL highly accurate on this simple triage task. The seed's improvement over PAW provides little direct evidence for a greater-than-five-point advantage over this different baseline.

judge_fable.reason: A 0.6B model with ~5k tokens of 96 demonstrations typically underperforms a LoRA trained for several epochs on the same pairs on a clear 3-label task, consistent with prior PEFT-vs-ICL findings, though ceiling effects or a surprisingly competent ICL baseline could keep the gap under 5pp.

judge_opus.reason: An unadapted 0.6B model with 96 demonstrations in a roughly 5k-token prompt is typically weak, with recency and label biases and poor transfer to new templates. A LoRA trained on the same pairs should beat it by well over 5 points unless 40 steps overfit to the training templates.

judge_sol.reason: Training could improve label adherence and avoid long-context interference, but the identical 96 demonstrations give ICL substantial task information. The seed's improvement over a fast compiler, using a warm start and much more training data, provides only weak evidence for this particular five-point advantage.

judge_luna.reason: Fine-tuning may help the small model internalize the task, but the in-context condition uses the same 96 examples on every query and could already perform well. A greater-than-five-point LoRA advantage is therefore possible, not assured.

judge_muse.reason: A 0.6B model typically underuses 96 demonstrations in a long context, while 3-epoch LoRA directly learns the exact 3-way label format, though new-template generalization adds uncertainty.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: T-Few compares parameter-efficient fine-tuning with few-shot in-context learning on standard benchmarks, mostly against ICL on other models such as GPT-3. It does not test a Qwen3-0.6B interpreter with one specification and the identical synthetic example set used both for LoRA training and in the runtime prompt.

Mosbach et al. compare few-shot fine-tuning and ICL under controlled conditions (same model, same number of examples) on NLI-style tasks, focusing on out-of-domain generalization. They find the two methods perform similarly but vary a lot depending on the setting, so their results do not settle this specific per-function comparison.

Program-as-Weights (PAW) compares compiler-generated LoRAs with zero-shot prompting, fixed LoRAs and full fine-tuning of the 0.6B interpreter. It reports no condition where the task examples are placed in the interpreter's prompt.
The seed paper compares compile-by-training only with PAW's fast amortized compiler. It has no in-context-example baseline built from the same synthesized data.

opus.reason: Neither the seed paper nor PAW compares a compiled LoRA with the same examples given in context to the same compact interpreter. They only report zero-shot prompting and other adaptation baselines. General studies comparing PEFT with ICL (T-Few, Mosbach et al.) run the same kind of comparison, but their results are mixed and depend on the setting, so they do not answer whether compilation beats in-context examples by more than 5 points for a function compiled for a small interpreter like this one.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Few-shot Fine-tuning vs. In-context Learning: A Fair Comparison and Evaluation compares adaptation using the same base models and few-shot examples, including compact OPT models and a LoRA fine-tuning condition. The proposed pilot changes the task to synthetic triage, uses Qwen3-0.6B and 96 examples, and scores greedy label generation.

Fine-Tuned In-Context Learners for Efficient Adaptation compares fine-tuning-only and ICL-only on fixed downstream datasets across example budgets, includes LoRA experiments on Gemma-2, and separately evaluates Qwen3 models including 0.6B. It does not report this exact triage function or the fixed 96-demonstration, rank-8 recipe.

Few-Shot Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning is Better and Cheaper than In-Context Learning already studies held-out classification accuracy and upfront-training versus repeated-inference costs. Its principal comparisons use different backbones and an IA3-based recipe rather than the proposed same-model LoRA comparison.

sol.reason: Prior work already investigates the central comparison—using limited task examples in model adaptation versus inference context—with same-model controls, LoRA conditions, and training/inference cost analysis. Although the seed omits this baseline, adding a synthetic triage task, a particular Qwen3 recipe, and a five-percentage-point threshold is a narrow variant of that established experimental question; the cited results do not determine whether this pilot's threshold will be exceeded.

opus.reason: Both compare the same frozen Qwen3-0.6B, prompted with the specification plus training pairs in context, against a LoRA trained on those pairs. Both measure the held-out accuracy gap alongside latency and cost.

sol.reason: Both compare a trained LoRA with in-context demonstrations on the same frozen interpreter, measuring held-out label accuracy and runtime cost.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registration without changes: fixed rule-labeled balanced 96/240 triage data with new held-out templates/values; full-96-example ICL with explicit 8192-token assertions; two rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRAs, 40 updates, batch 8, LR 2e-4, masked prompt loss; identical pinned Qwen3-0.6B, specification/chat template, disabled thinking, greedy max-8-token decoding, and exact-label scoring. Saves all registered raw outputs, training logs/adapters, token counts, synchronized batched timings, and result.json; independently validates raw scores. Unspecified choices (alpha 16, dropout 0, AdamW/no weight decay/constant LR, BF16, seeds 42/43) are documented. End-to-end evaluation command passed in ~72 seconds including installation/download. Observed ICL 91/240, LoRA 229/240 and 230/240; statistic 0.5770833333333334. All completions were valid labels; maximum ICL prompt 2560 tokens. No post-result tuning. Timings are batch-8 throughput diagnostics, not matched-compute or single-request latency. Scope and SDPA backward nondeterminism warning documented in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

These are documented. They could shift LoRA accuracy by a few points but cannot plausibly close a 57.7-point gap.

triage_experiment.py chooses the ICL prompt format: all 96 demonstrations as 'Message: ...\nLabel: ...' blocks under an 'Examples:' header in a single user turn after the system specification. The registration does not fix this format. ICL accuracy could be sensitive to it, for example compared with multi-turn demonstrations, but it is a legitimate open choice.

triage_experiment.py runs inference in left-padded batches of 8 rather than one request at a time. This could cause tiny BF16 numeric differences in greedy outputs. It is very unlikely to change the statistic materially.
triage_experiment.py records latency as synchronized batch-8 generate throughput, not single-request latency. This is disclosed and affects only the diagnostics, not the statistic.

triage_experiment.py sets torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=True), and the SDPA backward pass ran non-deterministically (warning shown in the log). LoRA training is therefore not bit-reproducible. The effect on the result is negligible.
problems: ICL failure mode (outputs/icl_summary.json): ICL per-label accuracy is NOW 1.0, QUEUE 0.0, FYI 0.1375, with almost every prediction being NOW. The gap is therefore driven by the unadapted 0.6B model collapsing onto one label under this single prompt format and demonstration order.

No zero-shot baseline and no alternative ICL formats or orderings were run. We cannot tell whether the 96 in-context examples helped at all, or how format-sensitive the ICL condition is. This limits interpretation beyond 'this ICL setup versus this LoRA'.

Narrow, easy test setting (outputs/icl_data.jsonl): the data come from synthetic templates, and the messages contain explicit cue phrases such as 'not urgent', 'no action needed' and 'cannot continue'. Test templates and values are disjoint from training, but the task is easy for a fine-tuned model. The result covers one function, one model and two seeds.

IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md quotes timings from the engineer's earlier run (ICL generate 14.69 s), which differ slightly from the protected evaluation (14.28 s). This is minor; the accuracies match the evaluation exactly.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design: the same pinned Qwen3-0.6B, a balanced rule-labelled 96/240 split with disjoint test templates and values, ICL with all 96 examples under per-prompt 8192-token asserts, two rank-8 q/v LoRAs trained for 40 updates at batch 8 and LR 2e-4 with masked prompt loss, the same chat template with thinking disabled, greedy decoding of at most 8 tokens, and exact-label scoring. The remaining departures are disclosed open choices that cannot plausibly erase a 57.7-point gap. The fresh evaluation regenerated all outputs from real model generations, and validate_outputs.py independently recomputed the statistic. I see no leakage or hard-coding. The finding is credible and the margin is robust across both LoRA seeds, but it is narrow. ICL collapsed to predicting NOW, under one prompt format with no zero-shot or format controls, on an easy synthetic function, so it says more about this 0.6B ICL setup than about compilation versus ICL in general.

departures: triage_experiment.py: The registration leaves the concrete templates, slot values, data seed, demonstration order, and training seeds unspecified. The implementation fixes these choices, including training seeds 42/43. They could affect the numerical result, but are permitted implementation choices rather than registration violations.

triage_experiment.py and model_lock.json: Additional unspecified choices include a pinned Qwen3-0.6B revision, LoRA alpha 16/dropout 0, standard initialization, AdamW without weight decay, constant learning rate, no gradient clipping, and BF16/SDPA execution. This operationalizes the registration's unspecified latency measurement as batched throughput rather than single-request or end-to-end latency. It affects cost interpretation but does not change the registered accuracy comparison.

triage_experiment.py: Each condition receives an additional unscored one-example generation warm-up. The scored ICL test set is still evaluated once; the warm-up does not train the model or plausibly change the reported statistic.
problems: outputs/icl_summary.json: The fixed ICL baseline has 0% QUEUE accuracy and 13.75% FYI accuracy, despite producing valid labels. Without alternative demonstration orders/formats or a specification-only baseline, the experiment cannot distinguish a broadly useful compilation advantage from failure of this particular full-example ICL configuration.

triage_experiment.py and outputs/training_seed_42.json/outputs/training_seed_43.json: Only one small model, one synthetic function, one generated split, and two training seeds are tested. No uncertainty interval or broader robustness evaluation is supplied.

triage_experiment.py: Timing diagnostics omit parts of deployment cost and use batched generation. They do not establish single-request latency or a general compilation reuse break-even point.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation completed successfully, retained the registered outputs, and passed validation that recomputed exact scores from predictions on the paired test set. It obtained ICL accuracy of 37.9167% and mean LoRA accuracy of 95.625%, yielding the registered difference of 0.5770833333333334 and exceeding the strict 0.05 threshold. The supplied code implements the registered sample sizes, example sharing, training schedule, prompt controls, decoding, and scoring without visible test-label leakage, hard-coded results, or affected exclusions. This is a credible and meaningful narrow finding, but the weak fixed ICL configuration, template-structured dataset, and limited replication prevent treating it as strong general evidence that compilation outperforms ICL.

departures: triage_experiment.py decodes greedily in left-padded batches of 8, which the registration does not specify. Batch/SDPA numerics could in principle flip a token versus single-example decoding, but all 720 completions were exact valid labels and the 57-point gap makes a change to the reported difference implausible.
Inference 'latency' in outputs/icl_summary.json is synchronized batch-8 generate throughput, not single-request latency. It is not part of the statistic and could not change the reported value.

evaluation.log shows the base generation_config still has temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, and top_k 20 while do_sample=False. Transformers ignores those flags for greedy decoding, so this did not change the result.

ICL formatting (one user turn, Message/Label blocks, one fixed shuffled order of all 96 pairs in prompt_ids) is not prescribed. That open choice could change ICL accuracy and therefore the difference; it does not replace a specified prompt.

No specification-only zero-shot arm (triage_experiment.py), so LoRA at 95.6% cannot be separated from what the written spec already gives the base model.

One synthetic function whose labels follow explicit lexical cues; held-out cases are new templates of the same cues (triage_experiment.py). Clearing a 5-point bar here is an easy target and does not support a general compile-versus-ICL claim.
Prompt format and demonstration order were not varied, and inference cost is batch throughput rather than single-request latency (outputs/icl_summary.json).
SDPA backward emitted a nondeterminism warning (evaluation.log). The two seeds agreed and this run's scores recompute, but training is not strictly deterministic.

Raw predictions, the evaluation log, and validate_outputs.py agree on 91/240 versus 229/240 and 230/240, difference 0.5770833333333334, with no leakage or hardcoded score. The result is real but weak: ICL never predicts QUEUE, there is no spec-only control, and the task is a single lexical template family, so beating a 5-point bar does not meaningfully test compilation against competent in-context use.

registration.title: Can a compiled function’s native confidence flag its errors?
registration.seed_connection: The seed recommends validation or deterministic control paths when correctness matters, but does not test whether a compiled function’s own generation scores can prioritize validation.
registration.hypothesis: Negative mean generated-token log probability ranks incorrect outputs above correct outputs with a macro-AUROC greater than 0.65 within both seen- and held-out-format test strata.
registration.contribution: A low-cost error-ranking test using scores already available from local generation, without training another confidence model or using a hosted judge.

closest_work.difference: Changes fine-tuning to improve uncertainty estimates; this experiment evaluates the unmodified generation scores of a compiled LoRA.
Estimates semantic answer distributions with a trained method; this pilot tests native token scores against exact labels from a deterministic function.
Notes the need for validation where correctness matters but does not measure whether generation confidence can prioritize it.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.
Python triage-message generator and exact oracle, CUDA PyTorch, Transformers, and PEFT. No external dataset, hosted model, or human annotation.
registration.method: Specify a function that reads CURRENT MESSAGE and QUOTED HISTORY and returns exactly one label: NOW for a current action needed today or an active blocker, QUEUE for a nonurgent current action request, and FYI for an announcement or message with no requested action. The deterministic generator inserts quoted cues that may contradict the current request. Generate 96 balanced training cases and 384 held-out cases, balanced across labels and divided evenly between a training-template family with new values and held-out layouts/quoted-distractor combinations. Train a fresh rank-8 q_proj/v_proj LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B for 40 updates, batch size 8, and learning rate 2e-4 for each of two seeds. Use masked prompt loss and the same specification. Greedily generate at most 8 tokens for each test input. From the generation-step logits, compute the mean log probability over generated non-special text tokens and use its negative as the error-risk score; invalid or non-label outputs are errors. Compute AUROC separately for each seed and each of the two input-format strata, then average the four AUROCs. If any seed-by-format stratum has fewer than 10 correct or 10 incorrect cases, set the registered statistic to -1 as an explicit non-estimability sentinel, mark it unestimable, and do not interpret it as chance-level confidence. Also report class-specific error counts and output lengths as diagnostics.

event.description: The event occurs only if all four seed-by-format strata have at least 10 correct and 10 incorrect cases and the mean within-stratum AUROC exceeds 0.65; otherwise the statistic is the stated -1 sentinel and the event does not occur.
event.statistic: Mean AUROC of negative mean generated-token log probability for exact-output error, computed within the two format strata for each of two training seeds; -1 if any stratum is not estimable.

evaluation.procedure: Write one row per test input and seed with its format stratum, oracle label, generated text, parsed label, per-token and mean log probability, risk score, and correctness. Compute each within-format AUROC and the registered statistic, and write the estimability flag and error counts to the summary.
evaluation.controls: Use the same adapter, specification, greedy decoder, and test cases for scoring each seed. Confidence is computed without oracle information; the deterministic oracle is used only to label held-out correctness. Report this as a one-function screening test, not a calibration guarantee.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, measure risk-coverage and validation savings across multiple compiled functions, output structures, and distribution shifts, and compare native scores with separately trained or semantic uncertainty estimates.

agent.reason: Token confidence may distinguish clear mistakes from ambiguous cases, but errors can also be made confidently. The seen-format strata may have too few errors to meet the estimability requirement, making the registered event less likely.

judge_astra.reason: The seen-format cases may produce too few errors to satisfy the estimability requirement for both seeds. Even when estimable, label-token effects and confident mistakes under format shifts could weaken native log-probability error ranking.

judge_fable.reason: Softmax-style confidence often gives AUROC above 0.65 for misclassification in-distribution, but the shifted stratum may have confidently wrong distractor errors, and there is a meaningful chance a seed exceeds ~95% accuracy on the seen-template stratum, triggering the -1 non-estimability sentinel.

judge_opus.reason: The LoRA is likely near 95%+ accurate on the seen-template stratum, which would leave fewer than 10 errors per seed and trigger the −1 sentinel. If the strata are estimable, label-token confidence would plausibly give an AUROC above 0.65, but estimability is roughly a coin flip or worse.

judge_sol.reason: Native likelihood may rank some mistakes, but confident quoted-history errors and label-token effects could weaken AUROC. Requiring at least ten errors and ten correct cases in every seed-by-format stratum is an additional hurdle, particularly if seen-format accuracy is high.

judge_luna.reason: Generated-token likelihood may rank uncertain outputs, but errors could be systematic and confident. Also, if the seen-format stratum is very accurate, it may not contain the ten errors required for estimation, making the registered event less likely.

judge_muse.reason: All four 192-case strata need >=10 errors to avoid the -1 sentinel, and quoted-contradiction mistakes may be confidently wrong, making mean AUROC >0.65 uncertain.

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It recommends validation when correctness matters, but it never measures whether the compiled function's own token log probabilities can rank its errors. Its evaluation uses an LLM grader, not confidence scores.

The earlier Program-as-Weights paper proposes compiling fuzzy functions into adapters for a Qwen3-0.6B interpreter. Its abstract reports accuracy, memory use and speed, with no analysis of uncertainty or error detection. I did not read the full text.

Studies misclassification detection with confidence scores for BERT classifiers fine-tuned on public text-classification datasets, and proposes a regularized fine-tuning method. The registered experiment instead tests unmodified mean generated-token log probabilities of a generative LoRA function, using a deterministic oracle and held-out input formats.
Estimates uncertainty for fine-tuned LLMs with LoRA ensembles on multiple-choice datasets. The registered experiment uses no ensemble and only native single-model generation scores.
Cited by the experiment as work that changes fine-tuning to improve uncertainty estimates. The experiment instead evaluates unmodified scores. I did not read this paper.

opus.reason: Neither the seed paper nor its Program-as-Weights predecessor tests whether a compiled function's native generation confidence ranks its own errors, and my searches found no paper doing this for compiled or specification-trained local functions. Using softmax or likelihood confidence to detect errors in fine-tuned models is a well-known general baseline. It does not settle the question for this specific setup: a small LoRA trained on a synthetic spec-defined task and evaluated within seen and held-out input-format strata. So the experiment is a distinct, if modest, screening question.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Evaluates unmodified average generated-token log probability after supervised fine-tuning, including AUROC for distinguishing correct from incorrect answers. The proposed experiment substitutes a small LoRA-trained triage function, deterministic correctness labels, and seen-versus-held-out-format strata.

Although its main contribution changes the training objective, its standard causal-language-modeling LoRA baselines already evaluate generation perplexity for error detection using AUROC. Perplexity is a monotone transform of negative mean token log probability; the proposed experiment changes the task, model, training scale, and stratification.

Tests output-probability confidence for classification-error detection with AUROC, including raw-probability baselines and supervised-fine-tuned models. Its principal score normalizes over valid labels rather than averaging generated-token log probabilities.

sol.reason: Prior work already investigates whether native generation probabilities can rank incorrect outputs after task-specific fine-tuning, without training a separate confidence estimator. registration.title: Finetuning versus few-shot prompting on identical weak-teacher supervision
registration.seed_connection: Seed reports compile-by-training improves LEM from 0.224 to 0.836 over one-shot weight prediction but never compares to training-free reuse of the same synthetic examples in context on the same small interpreter.
registration.hypothesis: LoRA finetuning on weak-teacher synthetic pairs beats few-shot prompting with the same pairs on the same frozen interpreter.
registration.contribution: Isolates the value of gradient descent in compile-by-training with a fully open stack and deterministic exact match on verifiable functions, holding teacher, spec, examples and base model constant.

closest_work.difference: Prompt2Model compares a finetuned small model to a prompted large model on the same description, not finetune versus few-shot on the same small interpreter with identical synthetic data.

That work compares in-context alignment versus instruction finetuning for general chat with human data and MT-Bench, not spec-specific compilation from weak-teacher synthetic pairs on verifiable functions.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B base model from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct teacher from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
Python packages torch, transformers, peft, accelerate from PyPI
No external dataset; training data synthesized by the teacher model and test data generated by Python rules in method
registration.method: Define 4 specs. S1: Extract arXiv IDs from /pdf/ links. Given text with URLs, output a JSON array of ID strings found in arxiv.org/pdf links. Ignore /abs/ links. If none output []. S2: Email triage. Return IMMEDIATE if message contains deadline, EOD, ASAP, urgent, signature needed, or action required case-insensitive, else WAIT. Output exactly one word. S3: Date normalization. Input is one date like Jan 5, 2026 or January 5, 2026. Output exactly YYYY-MM-DD. Day 1-28 year 2020-2029. S4: JSON field extraction. Input is single-line JSON object. Output value of key name exactly without quotes, or UNKNOWN if missing. Implement rule labelers: S1 regex for pdf IDs and json dumps, S2 keyword match, S3 month map to ISO, S4 json loads get. Generate 50 held-out tests per spec with Python random seed 123: S1 random 0-3 pdf plus 0-2 abs links with random IDs, S2 25 positive and 25 negative templates shuffled, S3 random month day year, S4 40 with name 10 without. Teacher: load Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in bfloat16. For each spec make 15 calls with n=8 using system You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with top-level key examples. Each example must be object with string keys input and output. and user Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC]. Use temperature 0.7 top_p 0.9 max_new_tokens 800. Parse JSON, keep input/output strings, dedupe by input, retry failures up to 2 times. Keep up to 120 per spec, require at least 80. Delete teacher and empty cache. Student scaffold is TASK: {spec} INPUT: {input} OUTPUT: with newlines. Conditions per spec on Qwen3-0.6B: A zero-shot base greedy, B few-shot base with first 8 teacher pairs prepended as INPUT OUTPUT demonstrations greedy, C LoRA finetune random init rank 16 alpha 32 targets q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj train on teacher pool 50 steps batch 16 AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5 warmup 0 max_len 1024 bfloat16 seed 0 masking prompt with -100. Inference greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 128. Normalized EM: S1 JSON list equality after loads else stripped string equality, S2 upper stripped equality, S3 stripped equality, S4 stripped equality.

event.description: Mean finetuned exact match exceeds mean few-shot exact match by more than 10 points averaged over specs
event.statistic: mean_EM_finetune_minus_fewshot

evaluation.procedure: For each spec compute EM for few-shot and finetuned on same 50 tests, average difference across 4 specs. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with one JSON per test holding spec, input, reference, zero few finetune predictions and correctness. Write outputs/summary.json with per-spec EMs and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same test sets, same teacher pools for few-shot and finetune, same base model tokenizer and scaffold, fixed seeds; zero-shot reported as sanity lower bound.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger study with more specs, weak versus frontier teachers, varied ranks steps and data sizes, and semantic evaluation to map when training beats prompting and at what compile cost.

agent.reason: Tiny base model should gain substantially from 120 finetuning pairs over only 8 in-context examples on format-sensitive extractions, though few-shot may already be strong on the simplest triage task.

judge_astra.reason: Fine-tuning can improve output formatting and stopping behavior, and it uses 80–120 examples while prompting sees only eight. These advantages favor a ten-point gain, although a positive result would not isolate gradient descent under equal example exposure.

judge_fable.reason: A LoRA-tuned 0.6B student learns the output format and stopping behavior that raw-text few-shot prompting of a chat-tuned 0.6B model typically lacks, so a >10-point gap is likely if the pipeline completes; main risk is the time budget (60 sequential teacher calls plus 400 non-terminating few/zero-shot generations) on a fresh 35-minute run.

judge_opus.reason: Finetuning sees about 100 or more teacher pairs while few-shot sees 8, so the 0.6B student plausibly gains well over 10 points on S1 (arXiv extraction) and S2 (email triage). Few-shot prompting is likely already strong on date and name extraction, and a weak 3B teacher's systematic errors (e.g., JSON escaping in S1) could shrink the gap. Whether few-shot completions get cut at the first newline is unspecified and could swing the result either way.

judge_sol.reason: Finetuning can stabilize formatting and task-specific behavior in a small interpreter, especially against only eight fixed demonstrations. A gain above 10 points remains uncertain because these simple tasks may already support strong few-shot performance, and the seed’s amortized-compiler comparison does not directly establish this advantage.

judge_luna.reason: Fine-tuning sees up to 120 synthetic pairs while few-shot sees only 8, so a gain above 10 points is plausible. But the specs are simple and explicit enough that Qwen3-0.6B may already do well in context, and the unequal example budget means the result would not isolate gradient descent alone.

judge_muse.reason: Finetuning should beat few-shot on the same weak-teacher pairs because Qwen3-0.6B base has weak in-context following and training improves format and rule learning, though teacher noise caps absolute EM.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: SELF-GUIDE (Sec. 4.2, Table 2) compares finetuning against in-context learning on the identical set of synthetic examples, on the same base model, for tasks defined by an instruction, and finds finetuning ~20 points better. The proposed experiment changes only details: weak external 3B teacher instead of self-generated data, Qwen3-0.6B with LoRA instead of Vicuna-7B, four verifiable spec functions with deterministic exact match instead of Super-NaturalInstructions tasks, and 8 in-context examples against a 120-example finetuning pool.
Seed compares compile-by-training only to one-shot Program-as-Weights weight prediction and to teacher/data-size sweeps; it has no in-context baseline using the same synthetic examples.
PAW compares compiler-generated LoRA against zero-shot prompting and fixed LoRA/full finetuning on the 0.6B interpreter, but never prompts with the synthetic examples in context.

Controlled finetuning vs in-context learning on the same model with the same number of examples, but on human-labelled classification data with an out-of-domain focus, not teacher-synthesized data for spec-defined functions.

opus.reason: The question of whether gradient finetuning beats in-context use of the same synthetic, spec-derived examples on the same model has already been tested directly in SELF-GUIDE, where finetuning won by about 20 points. The proposed experiment changes the model size, the teacher (weak external instead of self-generated), the tasks and the metric, but asks the same question in essentially the same way. That makes it a close variant rather than a new question, even though the seed paper itself lacks this baseline.

The proposed experiment instead uses weak-teacher, function-specific examples and rule-verified exact match.

The proposal changes the supervision source to specification-conditioned teacher generation and fixes a particular eight-shot/LoRA recipe.

Synthetic supervision, task-specific evaluation, and small-model/LoRA comparisons also appear in the closest literature, making this principally a variant in data generation, tasks, and adaptation recipe. None of these findings determines whether the registered experiment's particular greater-than-10-point event will occur.

opus.reason: Both put the same small Qwen3-0.6B interpreter in two conditions, prompted with the spec plus 8 teacher-synthesized pairs in context versus LoRA-trained on those pairs, to isolate the value of gradient training on arXiv/email-style functions.

sol.reason: Both compare LoRA finetuning against eight-example few-shot prompting on the same small interpreter using a shared teacher-generated pool, measuring held-out correctness.

What I implemented (exp/run.py, launched by run_eval.sh): the registered experiment as specified. There are 4 specs (S1–S4) and 50 held-out tests per spec, generated by Python rules with seed 123 and labelled by rule labelers. The teacher is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in bf16. It gets the registered system and user prompts, 15 calls per spec with n=8, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.9 and 800 new tokens. The 15 calls run as one batched sampling job. Replies are JSON-parsed and only string input/output pairs are kept, deduplicated by input; failed calls are retried up to 2 times and the pool is capped at 120 pairs. The teacher is then deleted. On Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (used as a raw causal LM with no chat template) there are three conditions:
- A: zero-shot.
- B: few-shot, with the first 8 pool pairs as INPUT/OUTPUT demonstrations.
- C: LoRA with r16/α32 on all 7 projection types, random (default peft) init, 50 steps, batch 16, AdamW, lr cosine from 2e-4 to 2e-5, no warmup, max_len 1024, bf16 autocast, seed 0, prompt tokens masked to -100, target " output"+EOS.
All conditions use greedy decoding with 128 new tokens and the registered normalized exact match. Outputs are outputs/scores.jsonl, outputs/summary.json and result.json.

Changes and choices:
1) Minimum pool size. In my first run S1 produced only 54 unique pairs, because many teacher replies could not be parsed, which breaks the "require at least 80" rule. The smallest fix I made: extra rounds of 15 identical teacher calls, up to 4 rounds, until there are at least 80 unique pairs. These pairs are added after the original ones, so the few-shot demos stay the first 8 pairs from the original calls. In the final run S1 needed 2 extra rounds; the other specs needed none. summary.json records this.
2) Post-processing. Prompts are not specified for a base model, which keeps generating extra INPUT/OUTPUT blocks. For every condition alike, the prediction is the first line of the continuation after stripping leading whitespace. All targets are single-line, and raw generations are saved too.
3) Batching. Generation is batched with left padding.
4) Diagnostics only, never used to filter. I record how often teacher labels agree with the rule labeler: S1 0.62, S2 0.64, S3 1.0 (on the 42 inputs the rule labeler could parse), S4 0.84. I also checked that no pool input overlaps the test inputs (0 for every spec).

Results from my final test run of the submit command, about 6.5 minutes end to end:

| Spec | Zero-shot EM | Few-shot EM | Finetuned EM |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | 0.24 | 0.34 | 0.42 |
| S2 | 0.00 | 0.54 | 0.88 |
| S3 | 0.98 | 0.96 | 1.00 |
| S4 | 0.04 | 0.78 | 0.18 |
| Mean | 0.315 | 0.655 | 0.62 |

The statistic mean_EM_finetune_minus_fewshot is -0.035, so the registered event (> 0.10) did not occur in this run.

Interpretation (inference, not established): the sign is mixed. Finetuning helped a lot on S2 and somewhat on S1, but hurt badly on S4. In the S4 pool, all 10 pairs I looked at had single-word names, and the teacher mapped "name": null to UNKNOWN. The finetuned model learned to output only first names (e.g. 'Bob' for 'Bob Muller'). This looks like finetuning absorbing weak-teacher biases more strongly than in-context demos do. The evidence is one repetition with 50 tests per spec and no confidence intervals, so it shows neither equivalence nor a general advantage for prompting.

Reproducibility: teacher sampling runs on the GPU, so a fresh machine may give somewhat different pools. My first run (before the S1 top-up fix) gave identical S2–S4 results.

departures: Teacher top-up rounds (exp/run.py synthesize): the registration has no rule for a spec that falls below 80 pairs. The code adds up to 4 extra rounds of 15 identical calls with new seeds. S1 used 2 rounds, which took its finetuning pool from about 54 to 120 pairs. Few-shot demos are unchanged because they are still the first 8 original pairs. The engineer reported this. It can change S1 finetune EM. However, S1 counts for only a quarter of the mean, so the event would flip only if S1 finetune EM reached 1.0, which is implausible. The alternative was not running at all.

Answer extraction (exp/run.py postprocess): every condition is scored on the first line of the continuation, not the full 128-token generation. The registration says only 'stripped equality'. Without this, the base model's few-shot and zero-shot runs, which keep emitting INPUT/OUTPUT blocks, would score near 0, and the event would be met almost automatically. The rule is applied equally to all conditions and all targets are single-line, so it is a reasonable reading of an under-specified registration. It does strongly determine the value. The engineer reported it.

Teacher sampling (exp/run.py teacher_generate): the 15 calls run as one batched left-padded job, with a fixed torch seed per attempt. 'n=8' is read as 8 pairs per call through the user prompt, not 8 sampled completions per call. The registration is ambiguous here. This could change pool contents and size, but neither direction of effect is clear.
Few-shot prompt format (exp/run.py fewshot_prompt): demos are inserted after TASK with blank-line separators. This is an open formatting choice and unlikely to matter.

Finetuning details left unspecified by the registration (exp/run.py finetune): lora_dropout 0.0, torch AdamW default weight decay 0.01, sampling by epoch reshuffle, right padding, and a target of ' '+output plus <|im_end|> EOS. These are open choices, and plausibly minor.

Student model: the registration calls Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B a 'base model', but the linked repo is the post-trained hybrid-thinking checkpoint. The code uses exactly the linked repo with the registered raw scaffold and no chat template, so this matches the registration as written.

Test generation (exp/run.py gen_tests): about 70% of S4 names are 'First Last' and S1 adds random '.pdf' suffixes. These are design details the registration leaves open. They create the distribution mismatch that drives the S4 result, but they are not a departure.
problems: There is a single repetition with 50 tests per spec and no confidence intervals or paired tests. Teacher sampling on the GPU is not guaranteed to be reproducible, so the pools, and with them S1/S4 finetune behaviour, could differ between runs (outputs/summary.json, the engineer's notes).

The aggregate statistic averages large effects of opposite sign: S2 +0.34 and S4 -0.60. S1 (+0.08) and S3 (+0.04) are small, and S3 is at ceiling with zero-shot at 0.98. The -0.035 null therefore depends heavily on which specs were chosen and does not show equivalence between finetuning and few-shot prompting.

The S4 finetune failure appears to come from teacher pool bias: names are almost all single words, and some null-valued keys were mislabelled UNKNOWN (outputs/teacher_pools.json). This is combined with a test set where about 70% of names are 'First Last'. It is a real finding, but it depends on how the test set was built.

Teacher label quality is low: agreement with the rule labeler is 0.62 for S1 and 0.64 for S2. S1 demos include an empty-output pair (teacher_pools.json item 8), which affects both conditions but may affect them differently.
Whether few-shot is viable at all depends entirely on first-line extraction (exp/run.py postprocess). This was reasonable but was not registered.
Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B is not a pure base model, which slightly muddies the 'base model' framing.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered specs, tests, teacher prompts, conditions, LoRA hyperparameters, decoding and statistic. Its two notable departures, the S1 top-up to meet the registered ≥80 minimum and first-line answer extraction applied to all conditions, are disclosed, defensible and either needed or under-specified by the registration. The S1 top-up could not plausibly flip the event. The value of -0.035 comes from real model generations saved in outputs/scores.jsonl, with zero pool/test overlap and no hard-coding, so the evidence is valid. However, the null is an average of strongly opposing per-spec effects (S2 +0.34, S4 -0.60) from one run with 50 tests per spec and nondeterministic teacher pools. It is therefore fragile, and it neither shows that finetuning and prompting are equivalent nor maps when one beats the other. The S4 mechanism, finetuning absorbing teacher bias such as first-name-only outputs, is an interesting hypothesis-generating observation, but the overall evidence is weak.

departures: exp/run.py::postprocess scores only the first nonblank line of each continuation, rather than applying the registered normalization to the complete decoded prediction. This affects every condition and demonstrably changes correctness: displayed zero-shot and few-shot generations have correct first lines followed by substantial additional text. It can change the reported difference and whether the registered event occurs.

exp/run.py::synthesize adds up to four extra rounds of 15 teacher calls when the original calls and retries yield fewer than 80 unique pairs. S1 used two extra rounds in the protected evaluation. This changes the registered call budget and finetuning data while preserving the first eight few-shot demonstrations, so it could change the result; however, some remedy was necessary to satisfy the registered minimum pool size.

The additional teacher calls in exp/run.py::synthesize are not individually retried up to twice, unlike the original calls. Failed additional calls are discarded, with another round attempted only if the accumulated pool remains below 80. This can affect which examples enter the training pool.

exp/run.py records meets_min_80 but does not enforce the registered minimum after exhausting the extra rounds. It would continue with an undersized pool rather than fail. This departure did not affect this evaluation because every final pool contained at least 80 pairs.
problems: exp/run.py::postprocess changes the registered exact-match endpoint. The supplied raw generations establish that the difference is consequential, but the registered full-continuation statistic cannot be reconstructed from the truncated scores shown here.

The registration's claim to isolate gradient descent using identical supervision is stronger than its actual design: few-shot prompting receives eight examples, whereas finetuning receives 80–120 examples. This is a registered design limitation, not an implementation departure.

outputs/summary.json shows strong task heterogeneity: finetuning gains 34 percentage points on S2 but loses 60 on S4. The aggregate negative difference therefore does not establish a general prompting advantage.

Only one repetition and four specifications were evaluated, with no uncertainty estimates. Fifty generated cases per specification do not measure variability across teacher pools, training seeds, or task selection.

Teacher supervision is noisy and imperfectly characterized. outputs/summary.json reports approximately 62%, 64%, and 84% rule agreement for S1, S2, and S4; S3's reported 100% agreement covers only 42 of 83 examples. The displayed S4 pool and prediction support a distribution-mismatch explanation, but do not establish that teacher-bias absorption caused the finetuning failure.
sol.reason: The protected run completed, produced the required artifacts, and reported a finetune-minus-few-shot difference of -0.035, so the implemented experiment did not meet the greater-than-0.10 event. The code supports this value as an aggregation of genuine model predictions, with no evident leakage or hard-coded scores. Fidelity nevertheless fails because first-line extraction materially changes the explicitly registered scoring rule. The results provide useful but limited evidence of task-dependent behavior under the modified protocol, not a clean isolation of gradient descent or evidence of equivalence or general prompting superiority.

departures: exp/run.py postprocess() scores only the first line of the continuation, while the registration defines normalized EM as stripped full-string equality (JSON-list equality for S1, uppercased for S2). This can change the result: scores.jsonl shows few-shot and zero-shot often continue with extra INPUT/OUTPUT text after a correct first line, whereas finetuned strings are often already a single line, so first-line scoring inflates prompting relative to finetuning.

exp/run.py synthesize() issues up to 4 extra rounds of 15 teacher calls when unique pairs are under 80. S1 used 2 extra rounds (summary.json: pool 120, 38 failed attempts). The registration allows only 15 calls plus 2 retries and does not define this top-up. Few-shot still uses the original first 8, but the S1 finetune pool changes, so the statistic can change.

exp/run.py user_msg() puts blank lines around [SPEC], whereas the registered user prompt is the single-line text ending 'specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC].' That prompt change can change the temperature-0.7 teacher pools and therefore both conditions' scores.

exp/run.py applies the cosine schedule with LambdaLR stepped after each of 50 optimizer updates, so the last update uses the 49/50 cosine value rather than exactly 2e-5. Losses are already near zero, so this is unlikely to change the reported value.
problems: First-line extraction in exp/run.py is not the registered EM and, on the visible scores.jsonl rows, systematically credits verbose few-shot answers that full-string equality would reject while leaving short finetuned answers unchanged.
S1 did not meet the registered call budget plus the >=80 constraint; the unregistered top-up in exp/run.py changed only the finetune side of that spec (summary.json teacher_stats).

The mean -0.035 in outputs/summary.json is a cancellation of S2 +0.34 and S4 -0.60, not a precise estimate; one teacher draw, 50 tests, and no interval cannot support equivalence or a general prompting advantage.
S3 is non-discriminative: zero-shot EM is already 0.98, and teacher-rule agreement is computed on only 42 of 83 pool inputs (summary.json).

Visible S4 teacher_pools.json outputs are mostly single given names, while exp/run.py builds many 'First Last' tests; the saved 'Ines' vs 'Ines Garcia' row matches finetune absorbing that mismatch, so the -0.60 gap is not a clean optimization comparison.
Teacher-rule agreement is only 0.62/0.64 on S1/S2 (summary.json), so rule-label EM mixes spec-following with weak-teacher error; that is the registered setup, but it limits what the mean identifies.
grok.reason: The fresh run of exp/run.py produced the reported -0.035 from real generations, with matching losses, pools, and scores and no test overlap or hardcoded EM, so the number itself is valid. It is unfaithful because first-line scoring is not the registered stripped exact match and the saved raw continuations show that choice can move few-shot EM relative to finetuning, and because S1 finetuning used extra teacher calls the registration does not allow. The near-zero mean is an uninformative cancellation across four toy specs, one already solved zero-shot, on a single stochastic teacher draw. That is real but weak evidence about the registered claim.

registration.title: Mixing two weak open teachers versus a single weak teacher
registration.seed_connection: Seed Table 1 shows 2:1 GPT-5.4-mini and GPT-5.5 mix raises LEM from 0.746 to 0.851 over mini-only; unknown if mixing helps when both teachers are small open models of similar capacity.
registration.hypothesis: Training on a 1:1 mix of two distinct small open teachers beats training on the same total count from a single teacher.
registration.contribution: Tests whether seed teacher-mix gains generalize to heterogeneous weak open teachers with controlled total quantity and deterministic scoring on verifiable specs.

closest_work.difference: Multi-teacher distillation aggregates ensemble logits for image classification, not mixing synthetic natural-language supervision from distinct open instruction models for spec-compiled LMs.
Self-Instruct uses single-teacher self-generation without mixing and does not test whether heterogeneous weak teachers complement each other.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B base model from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct
Python packages torch, transformers, peft, accelerate from PyPI
No external dataset; training data synthesized by the two teachers and test data generated by Python rules in method
registration.method: Define same 4 verifiable specs: S1 arxiv pdf extraction ignoring abs output JSON array, S2 email triage IMMEDIATE or WAIT by keywords deadline EOD ASAP urgent signature needed action required, S3 date phrase to YYYY-MM-DD, S4 JSON name extraction or UNKNOWN. Implement rule labelers and 50 tests per spec seed 123 as rule generation: S1 random pdf and abs links, S2 balanced templates, S3 random month day year, S4 mostly with name some without. Teachers: load Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in bfloat16, for each spec make 10 calls n=8 with system You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with top-level key examples. and user Generate 8 diverse pairs for [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC], temperature 0.7 max_new_tokens 800, parse and dedupe to 80 pairs. Offload and repeat with Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct for 80 pairs per spec. Conditions per spec with same total 80: Single uses 80 Qwen pairs only, Mixed uses first 40 Qwen plus first 40 Phi shuffled seed 0. Student Qwen3-0.6B scaffold TASK INPUT OUTPUT. Normalized EM: S1 JSON list equality, S2 upper equality, S3 and S4 stripped equality.

event.statistic: mean_EM_mixed_minus_single

evaluation.procedure: For each spec compute EM for single and mixed on same 50 tests, average difference across 4 specs. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with per-test predictions and correctness for both conditions. Write outputs/summary.json with per-spec EMs and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same total training count 80, same test sets, same student scaffold and training hyperparameters, fixed seeds; only teacher composition differs.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's Table 1 compares a 2:1 mix of a cheap teacher and a much stronger proprietary teacher (GPT-5.4-mini plus GPT-5.5) against the cheap teacher alone, scored by an LLM judge. That comparison mixes in extra capability, so it cannot separate the value of diversity from the value of a stronger teacher. The planned experiment mixes two weak open teachers of similar capacity at the same total count of 80 examples and scores them with deterministic exact match.

FuseGen uses several pretrained LMs to generate synthetic data for zero-shot small task models, with iterative selection, feedback and reweighting. It does not run a plain matched-count comparison of a 1:1 two-teacher mix against one teacher, and it does not compile natural-language specs into LoRA functions.

PerSyn sends each prompt to the best of several teachers when building instruction-tuning and math data. It studies how to route prompts to teachers, not whether a naive even mix of two weak open teachers beats a single one on small verifiable spec tasks.
This paper does multi-teacher distillation by combining ensemble outputs for image classification. It does not mix synthetic natural-language supervision.

This paper compares different teachers (reasoning, non-reasoning, managed pipeline) for distillation into Qwen3-0.6B and finds they pass on different capabilities. It trains one student per teacher and never trains on a mix of teachers' data.

opus.reason: The seed paper only tests mixing a weak teacher with a much stronger one, and the related work I found either uses selection or routing schemes (FuseGen, PerSyn), works on logits or vision (2302.07215), or compares teachers one at a time without mixing (2607.08268). None of it answers whether an unweighted 1:1 mix of two similar-sized open teachers, at the same total data, beats one teacher when compiling specs into small LoRA functions. My searches were broad but the search tool returned noisy results, so a closely matching paper could still exist that I did not find.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: The seed already compares mixed-teacher versus single-teacher synthetic supervision at fixed total example count for a Qwen3-0.6B function compiler. The proposed experiment changes teacher capacity and openness, mixture ratio, tasks, adapter initialization, and scoring.

TinyLLM uses heterogeneous open FLAN-T5-3B and Llama-2-chat-7B teachers and includes an ablation comparing diverse teachers against multiple rationales from the stronger teacher alone. It distills rationales alongside ground-truth answers using teacher-specific instruction prefixes, rather than synthesizing complete input-output pairs from function specifications.

sol.reason: The seed establishes the fixed-quantity mixing comparison in the same compilation pipeline, while TinyLLM already tests whether heterogeneous small open teachers contribute beyond additional samples from one teacher. Together these make the proposed contribution a close variant of existing teacher-diversity experiments, although neither reports this exact weak-teacher pair or its exact-match outcome.

opus.reason: Both train the 0.6B student at a fixed data count on labels from one local open teacher versus a 1:1 mix of two local open teachers and compare exact-match accuracy on rule-labeled tests; the match is imperfect because entry 42 frames its teachers as small versus large and has both label the same inputs.

sol.reason: Both compare single-teacher supervision with a fixed-size mixture of separately synthesized teacher examples under identical student training, measuring held-out correctness.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: run_experiment.py, launched by run_eval.sh. It installs transformers, peft and accelerate, then runs the whole pipeline in about 4 minutes on an A100. I ran it twice from a clean outputs directory and got identical numbers both times.

Result: mean_EM_mixed_minus_single = -0.025, so the registered event (> +0.05) did not occur. This is one run on 4 specs with 50 tests each, so it only rules out the predicted gain in this small setting. It does not show that mixing teachers has no effect.

Per spec, EM single → mixed:
- S1: 0.78 → 0.56
- S2: 1.00 → 1.00
- S3: 0.86 → 0.94
- S4: 0.96 → 1.00

The effect is mixed rather than uniformly negative: mixing hurt S1 by 22 points and helped S3 and S4 by 8 and 4 points. S2 hits the ceiling in both conditions, so it cannot separate them. I have not analysed why S1 drops.

Implemented as registered:
- **Tests:** rule-generated with seed 123, 50 per spec. S2 is balanced 25 IMMEDIATE / 25 WAIT. S4 has about 70% of inputs with a name.
- **Teachers:** Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, then Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, both in bf16. Each spec gets 10 sampled calls with n=8, temperature 0.7 and max_new_tokens 800. Outputs are parsed as JSON (with a regex fallback), deduplicated by input, and capped at 80 pairs.
- **Conditions:** Single uses 80 Qwen pairs. Mixed uses the first 40 Qwen pairs plus the first 40 Phi pairs, shuffled with seed 0.
- **Student:** Qwen3-0.6B in bf16 with the scaffold "TASK: …\nINPUT: …\nOUTPUT: ". LoRA is randomly initialised with r=16, alpha=32, on all attention and MLP projections. registration.title: Small open judge reproduction of LEM cosmetic versus substantive gap
registration.seed_connection: All seed correctness claims use GPT-5.5 LEM judge tolerating formatting differences but rejecting value order structure errors; paper never tests if an open 8B-or-smaller judge can reproduce this distinction.
registration.hypothesis: A small open judge prompted with the seed LEM grader still accepts cosmetic variants at a much higher rate than substantive errors.
registration.contribution: Tests LEM portability without human labels via controlled perturbations, measuring format tolerance versus error rejection for an open judge on compiled-function outputs.

closest_work.difference: That work measures judge-human correlation for extractive QA answer types, not spec-grounded tolerance for container and format versus value and order errors with controlled perturbations.
That work evaluates prompt-template effects on alignment-task judges, not whether a small judge reproduces the cosmetic versus substantive gap for compiled fuzzy functions.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct judge from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
Python packages torch, transformers, accelerate from PyPI
No external dataset; references and perturbed predictions generated by Python rules in method
registration.method: Define 3 specs: S1 arxiv pdf extraction output JSON array ignoring abs, S2 email triage IMMEDIATE or WAIT, S4 JSON name or UNKNOWN. Generate 25 rule tests per spec seed 456 total 75 with references from rules. For each create pred_exact equal reference, pred_cosmetic by Python: S1 if list length greater than 1 join IDs with newline else add surrounding spaces and newline and vary JSON spacing, S2 add leading spaces and trailing newline, S4 add surrounding spaces and newline. Create pred_substantive by Python: S1 drop one ID if more than 1 else replace with 0000.00000 or add extra fake ID, S2 flip label, S4 replace with WRONGNAME or UNKNOWN when reference not UNKNOWN. Judge: load Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct bfloat16. Use seed Appendix E LEM grader System prompt rules 1-6 and User template verbatim filling spec input reference model output. Use temperature 0 max_new_tokens 300. Parse verdict by json loads verdict field case-insensitive, fallback to substring CORRECT versus INCORRECT, default INCORRECT if unsure. Score all 75 exact, 75 cosmetic, 75 substantive independently.

event.description: Cosmetic acceptance rate exceeds substantive acceptance rate by more than 50 points
event.statistic: accept_cosmetic_minus_substantive

evaluation.procedure: Compute micro-averaged acceptance for cosmetic and substantive over 75 each, difference is statistic. Exact acceptance reported as sanity. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with one JSON per judgment holding spec input reference pred type verdict and parsed label. Write outputs/summary.json with rates and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same underlying cases for cosmetic versus substantive, same judge prompt and decoding; exact-match baseline shows cosmetic often fails string match while judge should pass.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger judge study with multiple open judges, more perturbation types, and human spot checks to qualify open LEM as a cheap proxy for frontier LEM.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: lem_judge.py, run by run.sh, which installs transformers and accelerate. It builds 3 specs × 25 rule-generated cases using random.Random(456): S1 extracts arXiv IDs from /pdf/ links into a JSON array and ignores /abs/ links, S2 triages email as IMMEDIATE/WAIT, S4 returns a JSON object's name or UNKNOWN. Each case gets three predictions made by Python rules: exact, cosmetic and substantive, as registered. The judge is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in bf16. It gets the seed Appendix E system prompt and user template verbatim; the one change is that the template's Python-escaped {{ }} is rendered as single braces. Decoding is greedy with max_new_tokens 300. Verdicts are parsed with json.loads on the verdict field (case-insensitive), then a substring fallback, then a default of INCORRECT. The script writes outputs/scores.jsonl (one record per judgment, including the raw judge output, parsed label, parse method and string-exact-match flag), outputs/summary.json and result.json.

Result, the same on two runs: exact accepted 1.00, cosmetic 1.00, substantive 0.587. The statistic is 0.413, so the registered event (>0.5) did not occur. String exact match was 1/0/0 for the three types, as the control expects. Acceptance of substantive errors broken down:
- S1: 0.96. Dropped IDs were accepted 11/11; the judge said things like "contains the correct identifiers in the same order".
- S2: flipped labels accepted 8/25 (0.32). Some of the judge's explanations argue for the right label but then say CORRECT.
- S4: name → UNKNOWN accepted 12/12; WRONGNAME accepted 0/13.

224/225 verdicts parsed as JSON. Reading the samples, this small judge looks mostly lenient rather than discriminating; its high cosmetic acceptance alone does not show format tolerance.

Choices and caveats:
1. As registered, the S1 spec pins a JSON array, while the registered cosmetic variant for multi-ID lists is newline-joined IDs. Strictly, the grader's rule 4 would make that variant INCORRECT. I kept it as registered; the judge accepted all 11 anyway, and summary.json breaks results down by perturbation.
2. For S4 when the reference is a real name, the substantive pred is WRONGNAME or UNKNOWN, picked by the seeded RNG; when the reference is UNKNOWN it is WRONGNAME.

registration.title: Student sensitivity to controlled semantic label noise
registration.seed_connection: Seed validates teacher outputs only for JSON format and notes synthetic supervision may inherit teacher errors, but provides no ablation of semantic label noise on final compiled accuracy.
registration.hypothesis: Replacing 30 percent of correct training outputs with mismatched outputs from the same task reduces student exact match by more than 10 points.
registration.contribution: Quantifies inheritance of semantic teacher errors with controlled output shuffling on verifiable tasks, separating format validity from semantic correctness for LoRA compilation.

closest_work.difference: That work analyzes teacher quality and regularization for image distillation with soft targets, not hard-label semantic noise in synthetic natural-language supervision for LoRA compilation.
Self-Instruct filters invalid synthetic instructions heuristically but does not quantify student degradation under controlled output corruption.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B base model from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
Python packages torch, transformers, peft, accelerate from PyPI
No external dataset and no teacher model; all training and test data generated by Python rules in method
registration.method: Define 4 specs: S1 arxiv pdf extraction, S2 email triage, S3 date to ISO, S4 JSON name. Implement rule generators. For each spec generate 150 rule-correct training pairs seed 789 and 50 held-out tests seed 123 with disjoint random draws: S1 random links, S2 balanced templates, S3 random dates, S4 random objects. Conditions: Clean trains on 150 correct, Noisy copies clean and replaces 45 outputs 30 percent with outputs randomly sampled from other training inputs in same spec seed 0 ensuring different string, preserving format. Student Qwen3-0.6B scaffold TASK INPUT OUTPUT. LoRA random init rank 16 alpha 32 attention and MLP targets, train 50 steps batch 16 AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5 max_len 1024 bfloat16 seed 0 separately for clean and noisy per spec total 8 runs. Inference greedy max_new_tokens 128. Normalized EM: S1 JSON list equality, S2 upper equality, S3 S4 stripped equality.

event.description: Mean clean exact match exceeds mean noisy exact match by more than 10 points
event.statistic: mean_EM_clean_minus_noisy

evaluation.procedure: For each spec compute EM for clean and noisy on same 50 tests, average difference across 4 specs. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with per-test predictions and correctness for both conditions. Write outputs/summary.json with per-spec EMs and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same inputs, same total count, same model scaffold and hyperparameters; only 30 percent outputs shuffled, fixed seeds isolate label-noise effect.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger noise study varying noise rates and types plus filtering by consistency or verifier models to design cheap semantic validation for compile-by-training.

agent.reason: 30% shuffled outputs is heavy corruption on small clean training sets, so a substantial drop is expected even allowing for chance-correct shuffles on binary triage.

judge_astra.reason: Random mismatched labels may soften probabilities without changing greedy predictions when the majority labels and pretrained priors support simple copying or normalization rules. A ten-point average decline remains plausible with these small datasets, but substantial robustness would not be surprising.

judge_fable.reason: Random format-preserving 30% label shuffling on copy-like or template tasks is often absorbed by greedy argmax decoding (majority signal wins), so degradation of a few points is as plausible as >10, though short 50-step training and the 0.6B model's limited capacity could amplify the damage; implementation is cheap and reliable.

judge_opus.reason: The noise replaces outputs with ones unrelated to the input, so the correct copy or mapping still holds the majority probability at each token, and greedy decoding should stay mostly correct. About 5 epochs of LoRA training limits memorization of the noisy examples. Only S2, a binary task with near-duplicate templates, plausibly loses much, so a mean drop above 10 points is unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Semantic corruption may impair accuracy, but 70% correct supervision and explicit instructions can preserve these simple rules despite random mismatches. A loss exceeding 10 points across all four tasks is less certain than some degradation, particularly for copying and date normalization under this short training schedule.

judge_luna.reason: Thirty percent mismatched targets in a 150-example pool can materially disrupt repeated LoRA training, making a clean-over-noisy gap above 10 points plausible. The explicit rules and the model’s prior task knowledge may let it resist some corruption, so I would not make the event near-certain.

judge_muse.reason: 30% mismatched outputs preserve format but corrupt the deterministic mapping, so clean training should learn the rules and noisy should drop substantially, though 50-step early stopping gives some noise robustness.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: RobustFT adds 30/50/70% noise to the responses used for LoRA SFT of 3B–9B LLMs. It uses QA and classification benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, PubMedQA, DROP, FPB) and compares noisy SFT against the base model without fine-tuning, not against clean SFT on the same data. It does not study a regime like compile-by-training: a 0.6B interpreter, about 150 synthetic examples, 50 LoRA steps, deterministic string-transformation specs and exact match on rule-generated answers.
The seed paper checks teacher outputs only for format validity (JSON). It reports no ablation that injects semantic label noise and measures the accuracy of the compiled function.

This paper studies distillation with soft targets for image classification and the role of teacher quality. It does not test hard, shuffled output labels in small synthetic text datasets used to train LoRA adapters.
Self-Instruct filters synthetic data with heuristics but never corrupts outputs on purpose to measure how much the student degrades.

opus.reason: Earlier work already shows that noisy responses hurt LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs in general. The clearest case is RobustFT, where performance drops with 30% noise. I found no work that matches clean and noisy training (same inputs, 30% of outputs shuffled within the task, format kept) under the compile-by-training regime of a tiny model, very little data and short training on verifiable string functions. So the size of the drop in this setting, and whether it exceeds 10 points, remains open. This rests on a small number of searches, so a closer match could exist.
