closest_work.difference: Analyzing the Effect of Noise in LLM Fine-tuning compares clean training with 20%, 30%, and 40% output-only corruption, including replacing QA answers with randomly sampled training-pool answers, using QLoRA on Qwen2-0.5B and Llama-2. The proposed experiment instead uses four rule-generated tasks, Qwen3-0.6B, a smaller training budget, and normalized exact match.

sol.reason: Prior work already tests the central question—how controlled semantic corruption of training outputs affects a compact, LoRA-adapted language model—using essentially the same clean-versus-corrupted comparison. The rule-generated tasks and compile-by-training framing change the application and measurement details rather than introduce a distinct experimental question; the specific greater-than-10-point event on these four tasks remains unmeasured.

opus.reason: Both inject a controlled fraction of format-valid but wrong training labels into rule-generated data, train the 0.6B LoRA, and measure the clean-test accuracy drop relative to clean training; entry 4 is also close but adds a filtering arm.

sol.reason: Both introduce controlled, structurally valid semantic errors into otherwise correct supervision and measure the resulting loss of clean-test correctness relative to clean training.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the experiment as registered, in exp/run.py (run with exp/run.sh). It uses 4 rule-generated specs (S1 arXiv pdf-ID extraction, S2 email triage into balanced IMMEDIATE/WAIT, S3 date to ISO, S4 JSON name field). Each spec has 150 training pairs (seed 789) and 50 test pairs (seed 123), with test inputs kept disjoint from training inputs. For the Noisy condition, rng seed 0 picks 45 of the 150 examples (30%). Each one gets the output of a different training example from the same spec, redrawn until the string differs. A check confirmed 45/45 outputs changed in every spec. The student is Qwen3-0.6B in bf16 with a "TASK:/INPUT:/OUTPUT:" scaffold. Training uses randomly initialised LoRA (r16, alpha 32) on all attention and MLP projections: 50 steps, batch 16, AdamW at lr 2e-4 with cosine decay to 2e-5, max_len 1024, seed 0, loss on output tokens + EOS only. Inference is greedy with max_new_tokens 128. Exact match is normalised as registered: S1 by JSON-list equality, S2 by upper-case equality, S3/S4 by stripped equality. Total is 8 runs.

Small implementation choices the registration left open: the spec wording and templates, the stop at EOS, and LoRA dropout 0. I made no changes to the registered design.

Test run on an A100, about 2 minutes:
- Clean EM was 1.0 on all four specs.
- Noisy EM was S1 1.0, S2 0.5, S3 1.0, S4 1.0.
- The statistic (mean clean EM minus mean noisy EM) is 0.125, above the 0.1 threshold, so the registered event occurred.

That result needs a strong caveat. The whole effect comes from one spec. On S2 the noisy-trained student answered "WAIT" for every test input, which scores 50% on the balanced test set. The S2 noisy training labels were still balanced (76 IMMEDIATE / 74 WAIT; 23 flips one way, 22 the other), so class imbalance does not explain this. The other three specs, which have many distinct outputs, showed no loss at all from 30% mismatched outputs. So the effect looks heavily dependent on the task: in these runs the failure appeared only on the 2-label classification task.

There was one repetition with a single seed, and n=50 tests per spec. Whether S2 always collapses this way, versus once in this seed and 50-step run, is untested. The value sits just above the threshold and is driven by one spec, so it should not be read as a robust general more-than-10-point effect.

departures: None of substance. exp/run.py follows the registered design: 4 rule-generated specs, 150 training pairs (seed 789), 50 string-disjoint tests (seed 123), 45/150 outputs replaced with a different output from the same spec (seed 0), Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B in bf16, the TASK/INPUT/OUTPUT scaffold, LoRA r16/alpha32 on all attention and MLP projections, 50 steps, batch 16, AdamW 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5, max_len 1024, seed 0, greedy decoding with 128 new tokens, the registered EM normalisations, and the mean per-spec difference against 0.1.

Choices the registration left open (exp/run.py): loss only on output tokens plus EOS, an EOS token appended to targets, LoRA dropout 0, and the spec wording and templates. These could affect absolute EM or training dynamics. They apply equally to both conditions and are allowed choices, not departures.

Consequence of the registered noise seed (exp/run.py make_noisy): the same 45 indices are corrupted in every spec (outputs/summary.json). This follows from the registered seed 0 and does not depart from the registration.

Registration ambiguity: it calls the model a 'base model' but links Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, which is the post-trained checkpoint, not Qwen3-0.6B-Base. The code loads the linked repo, which matches the registered identifier. This is unlikely to change the comparison between conditions.
exp/run.sh installs unpinned transformers>=4.51 and peft. This is a reproducibility detail and is unlikely to change the result.
problems: The whole statistic comes from one run on one spec. In outputs/summary.json S2 has diff 0.5 and S1, S3 and S4 have 0.0. The S2 noisy student predicts a constant 'WAIT', which scores exactly 0.5 on the balanced test set. With a single seed and one repetition there is no estimate of how often this collapse happens.

The S2 collapse is odd and unexplained. With 30% symmetric flips, each template still has a 70/30 correct majority, so a fitted model would be expected to keep the mapping. The collapse may reflect fragile 50-step training dynamics rather than a stable effect of semantic noise. The registered design cannot tell these apart.

Clean EM is at ceiling (1.0 on every spec), so the tasks are very easy. The S2 tests are string-disjoint from training, but they reuse the same 16 templates and 15 topics and differ mainly in the sender name. Held-out performance is therefore close to in-distribution recall.

Construct validity is limited. Outputs drawn at random from other inputs are unsystematic noise that the majority mapping can absorb, unlike consistent teacher errors. The null result on S1, S3 and S4 therefore says little about inheritance of real teacher errors.

The value 0.125 sits just above the 0.1 threshold, with n=50 tests per spec and no confidence interval. The binary 'event occurred' outcome is not robust evidence for a general drop of more than 10 points. The engineer's notes state this openly.
opus.reason: The code in exp/run.py implements the registered design closely, and the open choices (output-only loss, EOS, dropout 0) are left open by the registration and applied identically to both conditions, so it is faithful. The reported 0.125 is computed from real generations saved in outputs/scores.jsonl, with no leakage of test labels, hard-coding, or error that changes the conclusion, so the evidence is valid. The registered event technically occurred, but only because one binary-classification spec collapsed to a constant prediction in one seed. The three generative specs showed zero degradation at ceiling. The result is single-run, at ceiling and near the threshold, and uses noise unlike systematic teacher errors, so it is weak evidence about semantic error inheritance, though it hints at task dependence worth a multi-seed follow-up.

problems: outputs/summary.json: the entire aggregate difference comes from S2, whose EM falls from 1.0 to 0.5; S1, S3 and S4 each have zero observed difference. This does not support a broadly distributed degradation across tasks.

exp/run.py: only one training seed, corruption realization and train/test split are evaluated. The fresh-machine execution supports reproducibility of this configuration, not robustness across these sources of variation.

exp/run.py: each task has only 50 test examples from the same template-based generator used for training. The zero observed degradation on three tasks does not establish equivalence or immunity to semantic noise.

registration.title: Behavioral agreement of programs compiled from paraphrased specifications
registration.seed_connection: Seed promises one specification compiles to one reusable versioned function but never tests whether different wordings of the same intended behavior compile to behaviorally equivalent programs.
registration.hypothesis: Programs compiled separately from an original spec and two meaning-preserving paraphrases disagree on more than 15 percent of shared test inputs.
registration.contribution: Measures spec-wording brittleness of end-to-end compile-by-training by comparing behavior of independently synthesized and finetuned programs on shared rule-labeled tests.

closest_work.difference: That work measures embedding-model leaderboard instability over prompt phrasing, not functional divergence of separately compiled LoRA programs from paraphrased specs.
That work tests single-model robustness to injected instructions at inference time, not whether paraphrased specs compile to distinct persistent programs.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B base model from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct paraphraser and teacher from HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
Python packages torch, transformers, peft, accelerate from PyPI
No external dataset; paraphrases, training data and tests generated as in method
registration.method: Define 3 specs: S1 arxiv pdf extraction output JSON array, S2 email triage IMMEDIATE or WAIT, S3 date phrase to YYYY-MM-DD. Paraphrase: load Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct bfloat16, for each spec prompt Rewrite the following task specification in different words preserving exact meaning output format and rules. Return only the rewritten specification. Original: {spec} Rewrite: temperature 0.7 max_new_tokens 256 twice with different seeds to get P1 P2, retry if empty, save. Teacher synthesis with same model: for each of 9 variants 3 specs times original plus 2 paraphrases generate 80 pairs via 10 calls n=8 with system You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models and user Generate 8 diverse pairs for [SPEC] {variant} [END_SPEC] temperature 0.7 max_new_tokens 800 parse and dedupe. Offload teacher. Generate 50 rule tests per original spec seed 123. Train 9 LoRAs on Qwen3-0.6B scaffold TASK INPUT OUTPUT rank 16 alpha 32 30 steps batch 16 AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5 seed 0. Inference greedy max_new_tokens 128. Per test compute normalized equality across 3 variant outputs per spec: S1 JSON list equality, S2 upper equality, S3 stripped equality. Per-spec agreement is fraction where all 3 agree.

event.description: Mean three-way agreement across paraphrased programs is below 85 percent
event.statistic: mean_three_way_agreement

evaluation.procedure: Average three-way agreement across 3 specs on 50 tests each. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with per-test variant predictions and agreement flag. Write outputs/summary.json with per-spec agreement, per-variant EMs for context, and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same test sets, same teacher model and training hyperparameters across variants; only spec wording differs, fixed seeds.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger robustness study with more paraphrases, human-validated equivalence, and mitigation by multi-paraphrase synthesis or spec normalization.

agent.reason: Paraphrases of simple rule tasks should preserve intent, but independent synthesis plus short LoRA runs introduces variance that could push agreement just below 85%.

judge_astra.reason: Three-way agreement is sensitive to moderate non-shared errors, making agreement below 85% plausible across separately synthesized and briefly trained programs. Unverified paraphrase equivalence and synthesis variability also favor disagreement, but prevent attributing it specifically to wording sensitivity.

judge_fable.reason: Three independently synthesized (3B teacher, ~80 pairs, 30 steps) programs will almost surely disagree on >15% of inputs because per-program accuracy is far below the ~95% needed for 85% three-way agreement, so the event mainly hinges on finishing 90 teacher calls, 9 trainings and 450 inferences within the time budget.

judge_opus.reason: Three independently synthesized and trained 0.6B programs per spec will each make their own errors, especially on S1 JSON-array extraction and the binary triage task. Three-way agreement compounds these errors, so a mean below 0.85 is likely even before any paraphrase effect; there is no same-spec recompile control, so the drop cannot be attributed to wording alone.

judge_sol.reason: Three-way unanimity is demanding: modest, non-overlapping errors from separately synthesized small datasets can push agreement below 85%. Paraphrases may also alter rules, so an event would not establish sensitivity to genuinely equivalent wording rather than synthesis variability or semantic drift.

judge_luna.reason: Three-way agreement is a strict criterion, and independently synthesized datasets can produce variant-specific failures, so agreement below 85% is plausible. But the paraphrases should preserve simple rules, and the same teacher and student may produce correlated errors that count as agreement; dataset variation also confounds wording effects.

judge_muse.reason: Separate temperature-0.7 syntheses plus paraphrase drift and short LoRA training likely produce divergent programs, unless all variants learn the same accurate and correlated solution with high agreement.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Program-as-Weights (Section 8, Table 6) tests its one-pass amortized hypernetwork compiler on paraphrased, terse and noisy specs and reports only aggregate accuracy on FuzzyBench (0.6692 clean vs. 0.6614 paraphrase). It does not study compile by training, where the teacher synthesizes fresh data for each spec and a LoRA is finetuned on it. It also does not measure whether programs compiled from different wordings agree with each other on the same inputs, and similar aggregate accuracy does not establish agreement.

This is the seed paper. It evaluates the accuracy and latency of compile by training, plus teacher-mix and data-scaling sweeps. It never varies the spec wording or compares programs compiled from paraphrases of the same spec.

Prompt2Model also turns a task description into a model through synthetic data and finetuning. Its abstract describes evaluation from a single prompt per task and mentions no study of how paraphrasing the description changes the trained model's behavior; I only read the abstract.

Text-to-LoRA generates LoRAs from task descriptions with a hypernetwork, not with per-spec teacher synthesis and finetuning. Its abstract mentions no agreement test between adapters built from paraphrased descriptions; I only read the abstract.

opus.reason: The nearest prior work is Program-as-Weights. It already tests robustness to paraphrased specs, but for a different compiler (a one-pass hypernetwork), and it reports only aggregate accuracy, not whether separately compiled programs behave the same on each input. I found no paper that compiles a spec and its paraphrases separately through teacher synthesis plus LoRA finetuning and measures how often the resulting programs agree, so the question this experiment asks remains open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Program-as-Weights tests paraphrased specifications with unchanged inputs, but reports aggregate accuracy for an amortized adapter compiler, not cross-program agreement after independently synthesizing supervision and fine-tuning each variant.

Validating LLM-Generated Programs with Metamorphic Prompt Testing generates Python programs from paraphrased prompts and compares their outputs on shared inputs. It establishes the testing approach, but does not examine specification sensitivity propagated through synthetic-data generation and adapter training.

Text-to-LoRA evaluates adapters generated from alternative task descriptions, reporting benchmark performance and representation clustering rather than behavioral agreement between independently synthesized and fine-tuned programs.

sol.reason: Paraphrase-based behavioral testing is already established, and PAW directly studies robustness to specification paraphrasing. However, aggregate accuracy stability does not establish shared-input agreement, and neither these papers nor the seed reports that agreement for separately synthesized and trained adapters. The specific end-to-end compile-by-training question therefore remains unanswered by the prior work I found as of 2026-10-06.

opus.reason: Entry 26 compares accuracy and macro-F1 across terse, detailed and paraphrased specs on classification tasks, whereas this experiment measures per-item behavioral agreement among programs compiled from meaning-preserving paraphrases, so both the manipulation and the measurement differ.

sol.reason: Entry 26 measures accuracy sensitivity to specification wording and entry 25 measures output disagreement across recompilations, but neither tests behavioral agreement across programs compiled from meaning-preserving paraphrases.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: run_experiment.py, run by run_eval.sh, which pip-installs transformers, peft and accelerate. It runs the whole registered pipeline on one GPU in about 3 minutes:
1. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (bf16) paraphrases each of the 3 specs twice with the registered prompt, temperature 0.7, max 256 tokens, seeds 1 and 2, retrying if the output is empty. Paraphrases are saved to outputs/paraphrases.json.
2. The same model synthesizes training pairs: 10 calls with n=8 for each of the 9 variants, temperature 0.7, max 800 tokens, fixed seed. Outputs are parsed and deduplicated, keeping at most 80 pairs per variant. Raw text and pairs are saved.
3. The teacher is offloaded. 50 tests per spec are generated by rules with seed 123: S1 mixes arXiv /pdf/, /abs/ and non-arXiv links; S2 is templated deadline or FYI emails; S3 is absolute dates in various formats.
4. Nine LoRAs are trained on Qwen3-0.6B. Scaffold is "TASK: {variant spec}\nINPUT: {x}\nOUTPUT: " with an EOS target. Settings: r=16, alpha=32, all attention and MLP projections, 30 steps, batch 16, AdamW at lr 2e-4 cosine-decayed to 2e-5, seed 0, loss on output tokens only.
5. Greedy decoding with max 128 new tokens.
6. Normalization: S1 compares parsed JSON lists (falling back to the raw string if parsing fails), S2 compares upper-cased text, S3 compares stripped text.
Per-spec agreement is the fraction of tests where all 3 normalized outputs are identical; the statistic is the mean over the 3 specs. The script writes outputs/scores.jsonl, outputs/summary.json (per-spec agreement, per-variant exact match against the rule labels, training info) and result.json.

Small deviations, made to keep the question the same:
- The teacher system prompt and user template are the seed paper's full versions (Appendix D, including the instruction to return strict JSON). The registration paraphrases them; I used the full text so the output could be parsed.
- Non-string outputs from the teacher, such as JSON lists, are converted with json.dumps.
- The registration says "rule tests" without saying how to build them. I wrote the generators and the exact spec wordings myself.
- There is a fallback that makes up to 2 extra rounds of 10 calls if a variant has fewer than 16 pairs. It never triggered: S1 and S2 variants got 78–80 pairs, S3 variants 49–52, because the teacher produced many duplicates.

Results: I ran the pipeline twice on this machine and both runs gave the same numbers.
- Per-spec agreement: S1 0.32, S2 0.96, S3 1.00. Mean is 0.76, below the 0.85 threshold, so the registered event occurs.
- Per-variant exact match: S1 orig/P1/P2 = 0.84/0.52/0.36; S2 = 0.98/1.00/0.98; S3 = 1.00 for all three.
I have only confirmed the result reproduces on this one machine type. A fresh machine may differ slightly through GPU non-determinism.

Caveats:
- The result rests on one repetition and is driven almost entirely by S1. Two of the three specs agree at least 96% of the time, so the takeaway is that brittleness depends on the spec, not that it is uniform.
- The paraphrases are not checked for meaning preservation, and the registration does not require it. S1-P1 shifts meaning slightly: it says to exclude identifiers "found in /abs/ links", and its teacher data includes an example that outputs [] when the same ID appears in both a pdf and an abs link. So part of S1's disagreement may come from a real change in meaning, not just wording.
- The teacher labels are noisy; for example, S2-orig includes an FYI sales-report email labelled IMMEDIATE.
- Each variant's disagreement mixes three sources: different wording at synthesis, different scaffold text at run time, and different teacher samples. This one experiment cannot separate them.

departures: Teacher prompts (run_experiment.py TEACHER_SYSTEM/TEACHER_USER): the code uses the seed paper's full Appendix D system prompt and user template, which add 'Return strict JSON with key examples' and reword the user line. The registration gives a shorter wording. The engineer reported this. It applies equally to all 9 variants and makes the output parseable, so it is unlikely to change the question. It could shift the training data, and so the absolute agreement level.

Teacher and paraphraser decoding (chat_generate): top_p=1.0 and top_k=0 are set explicitly. This gives pure temperature-0.7 sampling and overrides the model's default nucleus and top-k settings. The registration specifies only temperature. Not reported. It is an open choice, but it plausibly makes the teacher data noisier and the variants more different from one another, so it could lower agreement.

Spec wordings for S1–S3 and the rule-based test generators (SPECS, gen_s1/gen_s2/gen_s3) were written by the engineer. The registration leaves these open. The engineer reported this. The test distribution, for example S1 mixing /pdf/, /abs/ and non-arXiv links, shapes how much disagreement can appear.

Pairs per variant: after dedupe and a cap of 80, S3 variants have 49–52 pairs instead of 80, and S1-P1 and S2-P1 have 78–79 (synthesis log, summary.json train_info). This follows from the registered parse-and-dedupe step. The engineer reported it. It is unlikely to matter, since S3 agreement is 1.0.
Fallback of up to 2 extra synthesis rounds when a variant has fewer than 16 pairs: not registered, but it never triggered (log, round 0 only). No effect.
Non-string teacher outputs (JSON lists) are converted with json.dumps (parse_pairs). This is needed for S1 to train at all. Reported. No effect on the question.

All 90 synthesis calls are batched under one seed (1000) with left padding, instead of 10 separately seeded calls per variant. This is an implementation choice. It makes the teacher samples depend on batch composition but does not change the design.

Training details the registration does not specify (train_and_predict): fp32 base with bf16 autocast, loss on output tokens only, EOS appended, truncation at 768 tokens, lora_dropout 0, all attention and MLP projections as targets. These are open choices applied identically to every variant.

Normalization (norm): output is stripped before every comparison. For S1, parse failures fall back to the raw string, and S1 list items are str-stripped. This is consistent with the registered equality rules and minor.
summary.json adds per-variant exact match against rule labels as context. Registered. No effect on the statistic.
problems: There is no same-wording baseline: no second independent compilation of the original spec with different teacher seeds. Teacher sampling noise alone could produce S1's 0.32 agreement, and S1 orig/P1/P2 exact match swings 0.84/0.52/0.36. The design cannot attribute the disagreement to paraphrase wording, which is the hypothesis.

The paraphrases are not meaning-preserving for S1 (outputs/paraphrases.json). P2 says 'Exclude any URLs ending with /abs/', which matches none of the /abs/{id} test links. P2's predictions do include /abs/ IDs (scores.jsonl tests 1 and 3). P1 changes the exclusion rule to apply to IDs. The engineer flagged only P1. Part of S1's disagreement therefore reflects changed meaning, not wording brittleness.
The statistic is driven entirely by one spec: S1 0.32 against S2 0.96 and S3 1.00. The run has one repetition with 50 tests per spec, so the event is effectively a single observation about S1.

Teacher labels are noisy even for the original spec (synth_data.json S1/orig: a books.google link plus an arXiv pdf link labelled []; version suffixes such as 'v2' are kept). Noisy data inflates program-to-program variance independently of wording.
Disabling top_p/top_k in chat_generate was not reported. It likely increases the variability of teacher samples and therefore of the compiled programs.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered pipeline: paraphrasing, synthesis, 9 LoRAs with the registered hyperparameters, greedy decoding, and the three-way agreement statistic. The main changes are the use of the seed paper's full teacher prompt and unregistered pure-sampling decoding, both applied uniformly and not changing the question, so I judge it faithful. The fresh-machine run reproduced 0.76 exactly from real model outputs, and the scores.jsonl records are consistent with the summary, so the evidence is valid. Its interpretive weight is low. The event rests on one spec (S1) in one repetition. Without a same-spec resampling baseline, wording effects cannot be separated from teacher sampling noise. One S1 paraphrase (P2) visibly changes the /abs/ rule, and P1 alters it slightly, so this is not purely a paraphrase effect.

departures: run_experiment.py, TEACHER_SYSTEM and TEACHER_USER: the registered synthesis prompts were replaced with expanded prompts requiring strict JSON, an 'examples' key, and a particular example schema. This changes the teacher's instructions and could materially change generated inputs, labels, parse success, and the reported agreement. The claim that these are the seed paper's full prompts does not make them the registered prompts.

outputs/paraphrases.json: the generated paraphrases do not reliably satisfy the registration's meaning-preserving premise. S1/P1 excludes identifiers found in /abs/ links rather than simply ignoring those links; S1/P2 substitutes 'URLs ending with /abs/' for the original exclusion; S2/P1 adds urgency and immediate-response requirements. These ambiguities or semantic changes could affect synthesis and predictions. They are failures of the intended premise, although the registered procedure did not require equivalence validation.

outputs/summary.json and run_experiment.py: the nominal 80 training pairs per variant became 80/78/80 for S1, 80/79/80 for S2, and 52/52/49 for S3. Different retained sample counts can affect training and agreement. Because the registration explicitly requires parsing and deduplication after ten requests for eight examples, a shortfall is not by itself an unauthorized sample-size change.

run_experiment.py, parse_pairs: non-string inputs and outputs are serialized with json.dumps, and malformed teacher responses can be salvaged by extracting individual objects. The registration does not specify these repair and acceptance rules. They can change which examples enter training; serializing JSON-list outputs is a reasonable representation conversion, while accepting partially malformed responses is an additional parsing choice.

run_experiment.py, teacher_phase: empty paraphrases are retried at most five times and then replaced by the original specification. The registration specifies retrying empty outputs but not a retry limit or substitution. This could inflate agreement if exercised, but the saved paraphrases and evaluation log show that it did not affect this run.

run_experiment.py, teacher_phase: variants with fewer than 16 retained pairs can receive up to two additional synthesis rounds, exceeding the registered ten requests per variant. This could change the data and result if triggered. The evaluation log shows only round 0, so this departure did not affect the reported value.

run_experiment.py, norm: S1 normalization coerces every list element to a stripped string rather than using literal parsed-JSON list equality, and S2 normalization strips surrounding whitespace before upper-casing. These operations can merge outputs that the registered equality rules would distinguish. No affected example is identifiable in the displayed excerpts, so their effect on this reported value is not established.

run_experiment.py, norm: an unparseable S1 output is retained as a 'RAW:' string and can count as agreement when all variants produce the same invalid output. The registration leaves JSON-parse failures unspecified. This rule could affect agreement, but it is an implementation choice for an unspecified case, and no consequential instance is demonstrated here.

run_experiment.py, chat_generate and teacher_phase: the ten requested completions per variant are generated together in one 90-prompt batch, with a single synthesis seed for that batch rather than separate generation calls. This preserves the requested number of completions but changes how random draws are assigned. It can change realized training samples; batching and the precise synthesis seed schedule were not fixed by the registration.

run_experiment.py: additional unspecified implementation choices include teacher top_p=1 and top_k=0, student stopping on either EOS or the padding token, a 768-token training-sequence cap, gradient clipping at 1.0, zero LoRA dropout, and attention-plus-MLP LoRA targets. These can affect results, especially if truncation or additional stopping occurs, but the registration leaves these details open. No consequential truncation is shown.

run_experiment.py, SPECS and test generators: the engineer supplied the exact original specifications and concrete test distributions. These choices determine the measured value, but the registration leaves their exact construction open, so they are not independently fidelity violations.
problems: run_experiment.py: the expanded teacher synthesis prompts are a substantive, potentially outcome-changing departure from the registered prompts.

outputs/paraphrases.json: semantic equivalence was not established, and several paraphrases introduce changed or ambiguous rules. Therefore disagreement cannot be interpreted solely as brittleness to meaning-preserving wording.

run_experiment.py: the specification changes both the synthesis prompt and the student scaffold at inference. Separately sampled training datasets also differ across variants, and there is no repeated same-spec compilation control. The experiment cannot separate wording effects from ordinary compilation variability or runtime prompt effects.

outputs/summary.json: the aggregate is dominated by S1, with 34 disagreements out of 50, versus two for S2 and none for S3. Three selected tasks and one registered repetition provide weak support for broader claims about the compilation method.

outputs/synth_data.json: visible teacher labels include an empty-array answer despite an explicit arXiv PDF link. Other visible examples collapse repeated PDF occurrences to one identifier, while the original specification does not explicitly prescribe deduplication. Unvalidated teacher labels add another source of behavioral differences.

run_experiment.py, gen_s2 and gen_s3: the email tests largely contrast urgent or deadline-bearing actions with obvious informational messages, and the date tests omit leap-day cases. This narrow coverage can conceal semantic drift and does not establish general behavioral equivalence.

outputs/summary.json: perfect agreement and exact match on S3's 50 generated tests establish success on those tests, not equivalence over the task's full input domain. There is also no untrained-base comparison to establish how much observed performance comes from compilation.

run_eval.sh and run_experiment.py: package versions and model revisions are not fully pinned. The fresh evaluation supports reproduction of this realized result, but not unrestricted reproducibility across future environments or independent compilation seeds.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed successfully and reported 0.76 agreement, below the registered 0.85 threshold; the per-spec counts imply 114 agreements out of 150 tests, and the statistic and event rule are implemented correctly. registration.title: Local synthetic finetuning versus prompting with a 7B teacher
registration.seed_connection: Seed reports 0.224 to 0.836 LEM with GPT-5 teachers and amortized warm-start; this tests if any gain remains fully offline with a local 7B teacher, random LoRA init, and programmatic scoring.
registration.hypothesis: Finetuning Qwen3-0.6B with LoRA on 7B-teacher synthetic pairs improves mean strict accuracy over frozen Qwen3-0.6B prompted with the same spec.
registration.contribution: Tests whether compile-by-training works fully offline with weak open teachers, random init, and exact-match, isolating training value from large-teacher quality and LLM-judge effects.

closest_work.difference: Prompt2Model uses GPT-3.5 teacher plus retrieval of real datasets and beats the teacher; this uses only a 7B open teacher with no retrieval, no human data, and compares finetuned vs prompted same 0.6B model on verifiable functions.
PAW compares amortized compiler vs prompting a 32B model; this compares local LoRA finetuning on synthetic data vs prompting the same 0.6B model, without any hosted compiler.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from HuggingFace hub (student)
Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingFace hub (teacher)
Seed teacher system and user templates reimplemented locally with no API calls
No external datasets; tests generated in code by reference Python oracles
registration.method: Do not call OpenAI or PAW APIs; run all models locally with transformers plus peft in bf16. Use 3 specs verbatim. S1 arxiv: Extract arXiv identifiers from /pdf/ links only. Input is free text with URLs. Output a JSON array of identifier strings in order, ignoring /abs/ links. If none output []. S2 triage: Classify email subject lines. Return IMMEDIATE if subject mentions deadline, urgent, EOD, signature needed, action required, due today, ASAP, or approval needed case-insensitive. Otherwise return WAIT. Return only one word IMMEDIATE or WAIT. S3 date: Rewrite dates to ISO. Input is one English sentence with one date like March 5, 2026 or 03/05/2026 or 5 Mar 2026. Output only YYYY-MM-DD with zero padding and no other text. Teacher synthesis uses system prompt You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with a top-level key examples. Each example must be an object with string keys input and output. User prompt is Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC]. For each spec generate 100 unique teacher pairs with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: chat with system plus user, temperature 1.0, max_new_tokens 1200, parse strict JSON top key examples with string input and output, drop empties and exact duplicates, repeat calls until 100 uniques or 20 calls max. Build held-out oracle tests with seed 0, 100 per spec. Arxiv: sample 0 to 3 pdf IDs plus 0 to 2 abs distractors, IDs as 4 digits dot 4 to 5 digits, embed links https://arxiv.org/pdf/{id}.pdf and https://arxiv.org/abs/{id} in templates Check these papers: {links}. and See {links} for details., expected by case-insensitive regex for arxiv.org/pdf/ IDs in order. Triage: sample 50-50 by keyword rule using the 8 phrases, IMMEDIATE templates embed phrase, WAIT templates use Weekly newsletter team updates and FYI lunch menu posted without keywords, expected IMMEDIATE if any phrase substring case-insensitive else WAIT. Date: sample random 2020 to 2030 date in 3 input formats Month D YYYY and MM/DD/YYYY and D Mon YYYY embedded in 5 sentence templates like Meeting notes for {date} are ready. and Reminder event on {date} at noon., expected ISO YYYY-MM-DD. Train one LoRA per spec on teacher pairs only. Prompt template is three lines: Specification: {spec} then Input: {input} then Output: then model output, with newlines between. Tokenize with Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer max_length 512, mask prompt tokens with -100, LoRA r16 alpha32 dropout 0 targeting q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj, AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine decay to 2e-5, 60 steps effective batch 16 via micro-batch 8 and 2 accum steps, bf16, seed 0, unload teacher before training and clear cache. Inference both conditions with same template greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 64 for triage and date and 128 for arxiv: frozen base versus base plus spec adapter. Score strictly: arxiv predicted stripped must parse via json.loads and equal expected list ordered, else incorrect; triage stripped upper must equal expected; date stripped must equal expected.

event.description: Finetuned 0.6B beats frozen prompted 0.6B by more than 10 points mean strict accuracy
event.statistic: mean accuracy gain finetuned minus prompted averaged over 3 specs

evaluation.procedure: Compute strict accuracy per spec per condition over 100 oracle tests. Write per-example records to outputs/scores.jsonl with fields spec, condition, input, expected, predicted, correct. Write aggregates to outputs/summary.json with fields acc_prompt_per_spec, acc_finetuned_per_spec, mean_prompt, mean_finetuned, delta, per_spec_95CI, teacher_oracle_agreement_per_spec. Statistic is mean_finetuned minus mean_prompt averaged over 3 specs.
evaluation.controls: Same 3 specs, same held-out oracle-labeled test sets 100 per spec, same prompt template and greedy decoding, same base Qwen3-0.6B weights; only adapter differs (finetuned vs none). Report per-spec accuracies with 95 percent normal CIs and teacher-label-vs-oracle diagnostic, but statistic uses held-out tests only. Random LoRA init, no amortized warm-start.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, scale to 10 plus specs, larger synthetic budgets, more steps and ranks, and compare open-teacher families and sizes to map the offline compile Pareto frontier.

agent.reason: Tiny 0.6B zero-shot struggles with strict JSON and exact format while the 7B teacher provides mostly usable supervision, so 60-step LoRA should lift mean accuracy well beyond 10 points.

judge_astra.reason: These narrow tasks offer substantial scope for LoRA to improve output-format compliance and task execution over a raw prompted 0.6B model. However, the seed’s large gain does not directly transfer to this smaller synthetic-data budget, weaker teacher, and different baseline.

judge_fable.reason: A raw-prompted Qwen3-0.6B will rarely produce strictly parseable, clean outputs, while ~10 epochs of LoRA on 100 teacher pairs reliably teaches format and the simple rules, so a >10-point gain is very likely if the pipeline completes; the main risk is implementation/time failure (sequential 7B generation for 3 specs, JSON-fence parsing, EOS handling).

judge_opus.reason: The frozen Qwen3-0.6B gets a raw, non-chat prompt and strict scoring, so it will often keep generating past the answer or format it wrongly. A LoRA trained on about 100 teacher pairs per spec learns the exact output format and when to stop, so a gain above 10 points is very likely. The main risks are omitting EOS in the training targets, which would make both conditions fail, and running out of time on teacher generation.

judge_sol.reason: Repeated supervised updates on these simple tasks should improve strict accuracy, especially output-format compliance, over the identically prompted small model. The seed used stronger teachers, more data, and a warm start, so its large gain does not directly establish a greater-than-ten-point gain here.

judge_luna.reason: The prompted 0.6B model may already handle these simple tasks well, limiting headroom, but 60 LoRA steps on 100 examples could improve exact formatting and rule reliability. The seed's larger gain used a harder benchmark, more data, and an amortized warm start, so I would not assume it transfers directly.

judge_muse.reason: Seed shows large gains with strong teachers and strict JSON/date tasks are likely near-floor for frozen 0.6B base, so even noisy 7B synthetic data should teach format for >10pt mean gain.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It uses hosted GPT-5.4-mini/GPT-5.5 teachers, warm-starts from the PAW amortized compiler, scores with an LLM judge, and compares against the PAW fast compiler. It reports no comparison with the frozen, prompted 0.6B model. The experiment swaps in a local 7B teacher, random LoRA init and exact-match scoring, and uses the prompted base model as the baseline.

ZeroGen already shows the same basic result. A small model is trained only on data a weak pretrained LM (GPT-2 family) generates from a task description, and it is compared against prompting that LM zero-shot. ZeroGen's students are LSTM/DistilBERT models on standard NLP benchmarks. The experiment instead uses an instruction-tuned 7B teacher, a 0.6B decoder LLM with LoRA, and three spec-defined string functions scored by an oracle.

Prompt2Model turns a task description into a finetuned small model. It uses a GPT-3.5 teacher plus retrieved real datasets, and its baseline is the teacher rather than the same small model prompted. The experiment has no retrieval, an open 7B teacher, and a baseline of the same model prompted.

PAW compares an amortized hypernetwork-style compiler that emits adapters for a 0.6B interpreter against direct prompting of large models. It does not test local LoRA finetuning on synthetic data from a weak open teacher against prompting the same 0.6B model.

Fabricator is an open-source toolkit for this generic pipeline: prompt a teacher LLM with a task description, then train a downstream student. It is tooling, not this specific comparison of a 0.6B LLM finetuned versus prompted.

opus.reason: Existing work already covers the core question, whether a small model finetuned on teacher-synthesized pairs from a task description beats zero-shot prompting. ZeroGen did this with a weak teacher and a prompting baseline, and Prompt2Model did it from a task description. The seed paper and PAW apply the same idea to 0.6B interpreters. What the experiment changes is the configuration: a local open 7B teacher, no warm start, exact-match oracle tests, and the same 0.6B model prompted as the baseline. That makes it a useful offline replication of the seed setup, but it differs from prior work in details such as teacher, student and metric, not in the question it asks.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: SELF-GUIDE compares task-specific synthetic finetuning against prompting the same unchanged model, with identical inference prompts and greedy decoding, including exact-match classification evaluation. It uses Vicuna-7B as both generator and student and up to three seed demonstrations, rather than a separate 7B teacher, a 0.6B LoRA student, and demonstration-free oracle-verifiable functions.

FuseGen reports synthetic-only training of small BERT classifiers using open teachers including Llama-2-7B and Vicuna-7B, with single-teacher generation baselines. Its main intervention is multi-teacher generation and sample reweighting, not a same-student finetuning-versus-prompting comparison on text functions.

Prompt2Model already converts natural-language instructions into synthetic supervision for small task-specific models, including temporal normalization without retrieved training data. It uses GPT-3.5, different student architectures, and a teacher-prompting baseline rather than the unchanged student.

The seed already synthesizes specification-specific pairs and trains Qwen3-0.6B LoRA functions, but uses proprietary teachers, amortized initialization, and semantic judging rather than local 7B synthesis, random adapter initialization, and oracle scoring.

sol.reason: SELF-GUIDE already investigates the central training-versus-prompting question using synthetic data from an open 7B model, while FuseGen supplies closely related evidence for synthetic-only adaptation of much smaller students from open teachers. The proposed teacher/student pairing, adapter initialization, three functions, and scoring protocol constitute a model- and benchmark-specific variant of these established experiments. I found no paper reporting this exact configuration, so the appropriate label is close variant rather than equivalent.

opus.reason: Both train a Qwen3-0.6B LoRA on open-teacher-synthesized pairs and compare it with the frozen 0.6B prompted with the same spec, using rule-based scoring on paper-style specs (triage, arXiv extraction).

sol.reason: Both compare a student finetuned on locally teacher-synthesized pairs against the same frozen student with the same specification prompt, measuring held-out functional correctness.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I ran: the registered pipeline in run_exp.py (run.sh installs transformers/peft/accelerate and then runs it). Everything runs locally in bf16 with transformers and peft. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generates the training pairs from the seed's synthesis prompt (8 pairs per call, temperature 1.0, at most 1200 new tokens, at most 20 calls per spec, stopping at 100 unique pairs). The teacher is unloaded before training. Each spec gets its own LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B, starting from random init: r16, alpha 32, all 7 projection modules, AdamW at 2e-4 with cosine decay to 2e-5, 60 steps, micro-batch 8 × 2 accumulation steps, prompt tokens masked. Both conditions use the same 3-line template, greedy decoding and the same oracle test sets (seed 0, 100 tests per spec), and are scored strictly as registered.

Result in my test runs: two full end-to-end runs both gave delta = 0.91. Strict accuracy, prompted vs finetuned: arxiv 0.00 vs 0.75, triage 0.00 vs 1.00, date 0.00 vs 0.98. The event threshold is >0.10, so the event occurs.

Caveat on what the 0.91 means: the frozen model's 0.00 scores come mostly from it not stopping. It keeps generating after the answer (for example "2022-08-18\nAnswer:\n2022-08-18..."), and strict matching counts that as wrong. As a separate diagnostic I also scored only the first line of each output; this is not the registered statistic. On first lines the prompted model scores arxiv 0.01, triage 0.39, date 0.83, against 0.75 / 1.00 / 0.98 finetuned. That is a mean gain of about 0.50, so part of the gain is real task competence. Still, much of the registered 0.91 is the adapter learning the output format and when to stop, not just the function itself.

Teacher labels checked against the oracles on the teacher's own inputs agree at: arxiv 0.46, triage 0.85, date 0.93 (date covers only the 74 of 100 inputs the oracle parser could read). The finetuned arxiv model (0.75) scores above the teacher's label agreement. The test inputs differ in distribution from the teacher's inputs, so I don't read much into that comparison.

The per-spec Wald (normal) CIs are as registered, but they are degenerate when accuracy is 0 or 1. I also report Wilson intervals and a paired CI on the delta as a supplement.

Deviations, kept as small as I could:
1. In the arxiv spec, Qwen2.5-7B wrote "output" as a JSON array, not a string. Under a literal string-only parse this gave 0 usable pairs (seen in my first run). I convert list-of-string outputs to their JSON string with json.dumps; this happened 104 times and is logged in summary.run_log.
2. Markdown ```json fences are stripped before json.loads.
3. All 20 allowed teacher calls are sampled in one batch, then used in order until 100 unique pairs are reached. This gives the same result as issuing the calls one at a time.
4. Sampling uses temperature 1.0 and leaves top_p 0.8 / top_k 20 at the teacher's generation_config defaults. The registration did not specify these.
5. An EOS token is appended to training targets.
6. Test generation details: arxiv links are joined with " and " and shuffled. Triage's IMMEDIATE templates are mine; WAIT uses only the two registered subjects. Date tests use 5 sentence templates, with "Month D, YYYY" written with a comma as in the spec.
7. The seed-paper repo was not used.

Other outputs: outputs/teacher_pairs.json, teacher_raw.json and tests.json. The whole evaluation takes about 3 minutes after downloads.

departures: run_exp.py train_adapter appends tok.eos_token to every training target. This is unregistered and was disclosed (deviation 5). It is a standard SFT choice the registration leaves open, but it probably drives much of the reported value. It teaches the adapter when to stop, while the frozen model never stops and fails strict matching.

run_exp.py parse_examples converts list-valued teacher outputs to JSON strings with json.dumps. This happened 104 times for arxiv and was disclosed. Without it, arxiv yields 0 usable pairs, so it is needed for the registered experiment to run. It makes the arxiv adapter possible at all.

run_exp.py parse_examples strips markdown ```json fences before json.loads, where the registration says strict JSON. This was disclosed. teacher_raw.json shows every teacher output is fenced, so it is effectively necessary to run.

run_exp.py synthesize samples all 20 teacher calls in one batch with num_return_sequences=20 and consumes them in order. This was disclosed. It is distributionally equivalent to sequential calls and is unlikely to change the result.

Teacher sampling inherits Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generation_config defaults: top_p 0.8, top_k 20 and possibly a repetition penalty. This was disclosed and the registration leaves it open. It could shift the teacher data somewhat.

The SYS prompt in run_exp.py quotes 'examples', 'input' and 'output', and USER inserts newlines around the [SPEC] block. These are small wording and format changes to the registered teacher prompts and are not disclosed. They are unlikely to matter.
The student template in fmt() ends with 'Output: ' including a trailing space. This was not disclosed. It is applied to both conditions and has minor possible effect on base-model behaviour.
train_adapter adds gradient clipping at 1.0 and refills the shuffle order across epoch boundaries, which can repeat examples within a batch. Neither is registered or disclosed, and both are minor.

Test construction in make_tests leaves several details open in the registration, all disclosed: IMMEDIATE triage templates are the engineer's, arxiv links are joined with ' and ' and shuffled, and date uses a comma format. The triage set is extremely easy, with 50 WAIT items drawn from only two fixed strings. This affects how informative the finetuned 1.0 is, not fidelity.
The date teacher-agreement diagnostic excludes 26 of 100 pairs that the regex oracle cannot parse. This was disclosed, is diagnostic only, and does not affect the statistic.
Extra unregistered first-line diagnostic and Wilson/paired CIs are added in summary.json. These are supplementary and do not affect the statistic.
problems: The registered 0.91 mainly measures output termination and format rather than task competence. In scores.jsonl the frozen model gets 0.00 on all specs because it runs on, for example a correct ISO date followed by 'Answer:...' or arxiv lists followed by rambling. The first-line diagnostic in summary.json gives a prompted baseline of 0.01/0.39/0.83, a gain of about 0.50 rather than 0.91.

The prompted baseline is weak by design: raw completion of Qwen3-0.6B with no chat template, no stop sequence and no examples. 'Beats prompting' is therefore a low bar and does not test a reasonable prompting setup.

The EOS-appended training targets (run_exp.py) give the finetuned model a stopping advantage the baseline cannot have. Here the registered design and an implementation choice combine to inflate the delta.

The test sets in tests.json are narrow and templated. Triage WAIT items are just two fixed strings and IMMEDIATE items come from five templates. Finetuned triage 1.0 and date 0.98 therefore say little about generalisation.

Arxiv teacher labels agree with the oracle on only 0.46 of pairs; some teacher pairs include /abs/ IDs or use bare /pdf/ paths. The finetuned arxiv model's 0.75 exceeds this, but only on an easy, uniform test distribution.
There is a single seed and only three specs. The Wald CIs registered in summary.json are degenerate at 0 and 1; Wilson intervals are provided as a supplement.

Even after coercion and fence stripping, 100 teacher pairs per spec are near-duplicate variations around the spec's example dates (many 2026-03-05). This limits diversity, though the result held anyway.

registration.title: Mixed open teachers versus single teachers at fixed budget
registration.seed_connection: Seed Table 1 shows 2 to 1 mini plus GPT-5.5 beats mini alone but confounds diversity with larger-teacher quality; this fixes budget and compares mixed versus best single with distinct open teachers.
registration.hypothesis: Mixing two distinct open teachers at fixed total examples yields higher student accuracy than either single teacher alone.
registration.contribution: Isolates diversity benefit from picking the best teacher at fixed total examples for per-function compilation, using two different open instruction models and verifiable eval with both singles as baselines.

closest_work.difference: That work mixes large closed models for domain QA without fixed-budget single-vs-mixed control; this fixes total pairs and compares single versus mixed open teachers for the same spec with identical training.
Self-Instruct generates from a single model and filters for validity; this tests whether mixing two model families improves student accuracy over single-family data at fixed budget.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from HuggingFace hub (student)
Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingFace hub (teacher A)
microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct from HuggingFace hub (teacher B)
Seed teacher templates reimplemented locally with no hosted APIs
registration.method: Run locally with transformers plus peft in bf16, no hosted APIs. Use 1 spec verbatim. Arxiv extractor: Extract arXiv identifiers from /pdf/ links only. Input is free text with URLs. Output a JSON array of identifier strings in order, ignoring /abs/ links. If none output []. Teacher synthesis uses system prompt You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with a top-level key examples. Each example must be an object with string keys input and output. User prompt is Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC]. Generate 80 unique pairs from teacher A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 80 unique pairs from teacher B Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, each with temperature 1.0 max_new_tokens 1000 strict JSON parse top key examples drop empties and exact duplicates repeat until 80 uniques or 15 calls max per teacher. Build 3 training sets with same total 80: singleA uses 80 from A, singleB uses 80 from B, mixed uses 40 random from A plus 40 random from B sampled with seed 0. Build 250 oracle tests with seed 1: sample 0 to 3 pdf IDs plus 0 to 2 abs distractors, IDs as 4 digits dot 4 to 5 digits, links https://arxiv.org/pdf/{id}.pdf and https://arxiv.org/abs/{id} embedded in templates Check these papers: {links}. and See {links} for details. and Papers: {links} discussed today., expected by case-insensitive regex for pdf IDs in order. Train one LoRA per condition with same config. Prompt template is three lines: Specification: {spec} then Input: {input} then Output: then model output, with newlines between. Tokenize with Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer max_length 512 mask prompt with -100, LoRA r16 alpha32 dropout 0 targeting q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj, AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5, 60 steps effective batch 16 via micro-batch 8 and 2 accum, bf16 seed 0, unload teachers before training. Inference greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 128 with same template. Score strictly: predicted stripped must parse via json.loads and equal expected list ordered else incorrect.

event.description: Mixed-teacher student beats best single-teacher student by more than 5 points at fixed budget
event.statistic: accuracy mixed minus max of singleA and singleB on 250 tests

evaluation.procedure: Compute strict accuracy per condition over 250 oracle tests. Write per-example records to outputs/scores.jsonl with fields condition, input, expected, predicted, correct. Write aggregates to outputs/summary.json with fields acc_singleA, acc_singleB, acc_mixed, best_single, delta, per_teacher_oracle_agreement, diversity_diagnostics. Statistic is acc_mixed minus best_single.
evaluation.controls: Same spec, same held-out oracle tests 250, same total pairs 80 per condition, same LoRA config, steps, batch, lr, seeds, prompt template and decoding; only teacher source mix differs. Report both singles, mixed, teacher-vs-oracle correctness and input diversity diagnostics.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's teacher-mix sweep compares GPT-5.4-mini alone with a 2:1 mix of mini and GPT-5.5 at a matched 3600 unique pairs. The mix brings in a stronger model, so diversity and teacher quality are confounded, and there is no single GPT-5.5 baseline. The experiment adds both single-teacher baselines and uses two open teachers.

FuseGen generates zero-shot training data from several pretrained language models and reports gains over single-model generation. Its gains come from a feedback, subset-selection and reweighting framework, though, not a plain fixed-budget mix compared against the best single teacher. It trains small task models for classification-style tasks, not per-spec LoRA functions with exact-match checks.

PerSyn sends each prompt to the teacher a router picks for it and compares against single-teacher and multi-teacher baselines on instruction tuning and math. It does not run a random 50/50 mix versus the best single teacher at a fixed total, and it does not compile one specification into a function.
This work generates maritime QA data from two closed models (GPT-4o and o3-mini) but, going by its abstract, does not compare single teachers with a mix at a fixed budget.

This study compares different teachers distilled into Qwen3-0.6B and finds that each transfers different capabilities. It reports separate students per teacher and a routing map. It does not test a mixed-teacher dataset at a fixed budget.

opus.reason: I found no prior work that holds the total number of synthetic examples fixed and asks whether a random mix of two teachers beats the better single teacher when compiling one natural-language spec into a small LoRA function. The seed paper's own sweep confounds diversity with teacher strength, and the multi-teacher papers I found (FuseGen, PerSyn) test selection or routing methods, not this plain controlled comparison. My searches were limited and the search tool returned many irrelevant results, so I may have missed related work on generator diversity, but nothing I found settles the question.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the fixed-budget singleA/singleB/40+40 mixed comparison with the registered models, prompts, seeds, 80 pairs per condition, LoRA settings, 60 updates, 250 oracle tests, greedy decoding, and strict ordered-JSON scoring. Tested evaluation successfully and audited all 750 records and aggregates. Local result: singleA 0.876, singleB 0.312, mixed 0.812; statistic -0.064, event did not occur. Disclosed ingestion accommodations, chosen before student scores: remove a complete enclosing JSON Markdown fence, accept a bare example-list container (Phi otherwise yielded only 48 pairs at its 15-call cap), and serialize native JSON labels to text without semantic edits. No oracle filtering, relabeling, extra teacher calls to fill the budget, or post-score tuning. Included checksummed raw locally generated teacher traces (A 10 source calls, B 15); evaluation reprocesses these and freshly trains all students, or performs local teacher generation if traces are absent. Detailed deviations, provenance, validation and limitations are in NOTES.md and README.md.

departures: Fence stripping (experiment.py teacher_json_body). One complete enclosing Markdown ```json fence is removed before the registered strict JSON parse. Under the literal parser every Qwen response failed to parse and yielded 0 pairs (feasibility/original_ingestion.log), so the experiment could not run without this. It changes which pairs are admitted but is a minimal wire-format fix. Disclosed.

Bare-list acceptance (experiment.py ingest_response). A bare JSON array of examples is accepted in place of the registered top-level 'examples' key. With the registered rule Phi reached only 48/80 pairs within 15 calls (feasibility/capped_container_shortfall.log, teacher_cache/original_shortfall.json), so this too was needed to run. It changes the singleB and mixed data: B calls 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10 were bare lists, and call 1 contributes scalar-string labels. This could affect singleB and mixed accuracy. Disclosed.

Label serialization (experiment.py). Native JSON output values such as arrays are serialized to text instead of being rejected for not being strings. The registration does not address this, and nearly all of Qwen's labels are native arrays. Without it the A pool would be empty, so it is a needed, label-preserving change. Disclosed.

Replayed teacher traces (teacher_cache/A.jsonl, teacher_cache/B.jsonl). The evaluation reprocesses checksummed traces generated locally earlier instead of regenerating teacher data. Generation is seeded once and does not depend on the ingestion rule, so the first-10-call B pool should match what fresh generation would give. Unlikely to change the result.

Teacher sampling settings (README). Both teachers use HF GenerationConfig defaults (top_k=50, top_p=1) and RNG seed 0. The registration leaves these open. They affect what data is generated but apply equally to both teachers. Disclosed.
Optimizer defaults. AdamW weight_decay=0.01 and default betas are used; the registration leaves these open. Equal across conditions; negligible.

Evaluation batching. Left-padded batches of 64 are used at evaluation, and the base model's generation_config sampling fields are ignored under do_sample=False. Greedy decoding holds as registered; batching effects are negligible.

registration.title: Finetuning widens teacher-like versus edge-case gap for a compiled extractor
registration.seed_connection: Seed teachers generate both inputs and outputs but evaluates on independent FuzzyBench; this measures whether finetuning overfits teacher input distribution versus harder same-logic edge inputs with a frozen baseline control.
registration.hypothesis: Finetuning on teacher-generated inputs widens the accuracy gap between held-out teacher-like inputs and programmatic edge-case inputs relative to the frozen base.
registration.contribution: Quantifies teacher-input narrowness induced by training by contrasting teacher-like vs edge inputs with oracle labels and a frozen gap baseline, which prior synthetic-tuning work does not isolate.

closest_work.difference: Self-Instruct evaluates on held-out instructions but not teacher-like vs harder inputs with same logic and frozen control; this fixes spec logic and varies input difficulty with oracle scoring.
PAW evaluates on FuzzyBench aggregates; this splits held-out teacher inputs from spec-relevant edge cases for one function with rule-computed ground truth.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from HuggingFace hub (student)
Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingFace hub (teacher)
Seed teacher templates reimplemented locally with no hosted APIs
registration.method: Run locally with transformers plus peft in bf16, no hosted APIs. Use 1 spec verbatim. Arxiv extractor: Extract arXiv identifiers from /pdf/ links only. Input is free text with URLs. Output a JSON array of identifier strings in order, ignoring /abs/ links. If none output []. Teacher synthesis uses system prompt You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with a top-level key examples. Each example must be an object with string keys input and output. User prompt is Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC]. Generate 200 unique pairs with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct temperature 1.0 max_new_tokens 1200 strict JSON parse drop empties and duplicates repeat until 200 or 30 calls max. Use first 120 for training, reserve last 80 as teacher-like test inputs relabelled by oracle. Train one LoRA on 120 training pairs. Prompt template is three lines: Specification: {spec} then Input: {input} then Output: then model output, with newlines between. Tokenize with Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer max_length 512 mask prompt with -100, LoRA r16 alpha32 dropout 0 targeting q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj, AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5, 60 steps effective batch 16 via micro-batch 8 and 2 accum, bf16 seed 0, unload teacher before training. Build teacher-like tests: 80 held-out teacher inputs with expected by case-insensitive regex for arxiv.org/pdf/ IDs in order, [] if none. Build edge tests 120 total with seed 2, 20 per category. Category abs-only: 1 to 3 abs links only expecting []. Category many-mixed: 3 to 4 links mixing pdf and abs. Category query: pdf links with suffix like ?download=1 or #page=2. Category markdown: links as bracket title close bracket open paren url close paren. Category uppercase: HTTPS://ARXIV.ORG/PDF/{id}.PDF with mixed case. Category clutter: 30 to 80 words filler plus 1 to 2 pdf links. All edge expected by same case-insensitive regex ordered. Inference both trained LoRA and frozen base with same template greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 128 on both splits. Score strictly: predicted stripped must parse via json.loads and equal expected list ordered else incorrect.

event.description: Finetuning widens teacher-like minus edge gap by more than 10 points versus frozen baseline
event.statistic: difference-in-gaps trained gap minus frozen gap where gap is teacher-like accuracy minus edge accuracy

evaluation.procedure: Compute strict accuracy for trained and frozen on teacher-like 80 and edge 120. Write per-example records to outputs/scores.jsonl with fields model, split, category, input, expected, predicted, correct. Write aggregates to outputs/summary.json with fields acc_trained_teacherlike, acc_trained_edge, acc_frozen_teacherlike, acc_frozen_edge, gap_trained, gap_frozen, statistic, per_category_edge_acc. Statistic is gap_trained minus gap_frozen.
evaluation.controls: Same student architecture and prompt template and decoding across splits; same oracle labels both splits; teacher-like inputs are held-out teacher generations relabelled by oracle to remove teacher label noise; frozen baseline shows intrinsic difficulty gap; report per-category breakdown.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, study mitigations: diversity prompting, programmatic augmentation, difficulty-aware synthesis, and mixed teacher plus template training to close the gap.

agent.reason: Teacher training matches teacher-like inputs but omits query, markdown, uppercase and many-link patterns, so the trained teacher-like minus edge gap should exceed the near-zero frozen gap by more than 10 points.

judge_astra.reason: Training could disproportionately improve teacher-like inputs while leaving uppercase links and unusual presentations behind. But several edge categories may already occur in teacher generations, and subtracting the frozen model’s difficulty gap makes a ten-point widening substantially less certain.

judge_fable.reason: The frozen baseline will likely be near floor on both splits, so the statistic reduces to the trained model's teacher-like-minus-edge gap; that gap is plausibly 10-30 points given uppercase/many-mixed/abs-only categories, but oracle relabeling of teacher inputs could depress teacher-like accuracy and shrink the gap.

judge_opus.reason: The frozen model is likely near zero under strict scoring on both splits, so the statistic reduces to the trained model's teacher-like minus edge gap. Edge categories such as uppercase links and 3–4 mixed links may cost some accuracy. Relabelling teacher-like inputs with the oracle (for example version suffixes the regex strips) also caps teacher-like accuracy, so a gap above 10 points is plausible but below even odds.

judge_sol.reason: The small synthetic training set could favor familiar URL patterns, particularly relative to uppercase and cluttered inputs. However, most edge cases retain the same straightforward extraction rule, and formatting improvements may transfer across both splits, making a greater-than-ten-point widening uncertain.

judge_luna.reason: Training examples and teacher-like tests share a source while edge tests deliberately shift URL form, so selective in-distribution gains are plausible. However, the extraction task is simple and the frozen model may generalize to those variations, making a greater-than-10-point widening uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Teacher generations likely use simple lowercase URLs while edge tests add uppercase, markdown, query and clutter variants, so training should lift held-out teacher-like accuracy more than edge versus a near-floor frozen gap.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper reports aggregate semantic accuracy (LLM-judged) on FuzzyBench-Hard, plus sweeps over teacher mixture and data scale. It uses the arXiv /pdf/ extractor only as an example and never compares held-out teacher-like inputs with programmatic edge cases. Its only related point is a one-line limitation that synthetic supervision may inherit teacher errors.

PAW proposes the fuzzy-function compiler and FuzzyBench and evaluates on aggregate benchmark scores. It does not split test inputs into teacher-distribution and edge-case sets for a single spec, and it does not compare a trained adapter against a frozen interpreter.

Prompt2Model trains small models on LLM-generated data from a task description and checks whether synthetic held-out data gives a reliable performance estimate compared with real test sets. That is related to the teacher-distribution versus real-distribution question, but it does not use rule-generated edge-case categories, oracle relabelling, or a difference-in-gaps measure against a frozen baseline.

Self-Instruct builds general instruction data and evaluates on held-out instruction sets. It does not fix one spec's logic while varying how hard the inputs are, and it has no frozen-baseline gap control.

opus.reason: No paper I found answers the question this experiment asks. The question is whether LoRA fine-tuning on teacher-generated inputs for one spec-defined function widens the accuracy gap between teacher-like inputs and rule-labelled edge cases, compared with the frozen base model's gap. The seed paper and PAW report only aggregate benchmark accuracy, and Prompt2Model and Self-Instruct look at nearby issues without this design. My searches were few and returned noisy results, so I may have missed broader work showing that synthetic data lacks diversity; I found nothing that tests this specific difference-in-gaps setup.

closest_work.difference: GOLD studies narrow teacher-generated input distributions and improves generalization through OOD-guided synthesis. It does not measure the change in a held-out teacher-like versus programmatic-edge accuracy gap relative to an untuned student with shared oracle labels.

RL Fine-Tuning Heals OOD Forgetting in SFT tracks divergent ID and OOD performance during training on controlled reasoning tasks. Its evaluations do not contrast teacher-generated inputs with independently constructed edge inputs under one unchanged extraction specification.

EDGEGEN compares generic and edge-aware synthetic training for tool-calling agents, including untuned baselines. It evaluates downstream agent performance rather than the training-induced change between teacher-like and edge-case test distributions.

The seed supplies the extractor example and synthesis pipeline, but evaluates aggregate FuzzyBench-Hard correctness and supervision choices without the proposed two-distribution, frozen-baseline comparison.

sol.reason: Prior work already establishes synthetic-input coverage limitations and documents SFT ID–OOD trade-offs, so those broad ideas are not new. However, I found no work answering the specific controlled question of whether specification-specific synthetic finetuning widens a teacher-like versus same-logic edge-case accuracy gap relative to the unchanged student, with both test splits scored by one deterministic oracle.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented local Qwen2.5-7B teacher synthesis, registered Qwen3-0.6B LoRA training, adapter-disabled frozen control, deterministic six-category edge generation, shared regex oracle, greedy decoding, and strict JSON-list scoring. Fresh evaluation regenerates data and trains; no saved adapter or test-run data are reused. Tested end-to-end in about 9 minutes: 200 unique pairs in 27 calls, 60 updates, and 400 score records. Observed statistic -0.22083333333333333; event did not occur. Narrow documented format adaptation: the local teacher emitted Markdown-fenced JSON with array-valued outputs, so remove only an exact outer JSON code fence before strict payload parsing and losslessly serialize array outputs as training text. No prompts, semantic labels, sample sizes, call cap, controls, event threshold, or scoring were changed. Details and limitations are in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

departures: experiment.py synthesize(): before json.loads, the code strips one exact outer Markdown code fence. The registration says 'strict JSON parse'. pilot_teacher_format.jsonl shows the strict parser accepted 0 pairs because every completion was fenced, so the registered experiment could not run without this change. It is reported and adds no salvage of malformed JSON. It changes which data exist, not the question.

experiment.py synthesize(): teacher outputs that are arrays of strings are serialized to JSON text instead of being rejected. The registration's 'string keys' wording does not clearly require string values, so this is a reasonable reading. It is needed to obtain any pairs and does not change label semantics.

experiment.py synthesize(): teacher sampling sets top_p=1.0 and top_k=0, overriding Qwen2.5's default generation config. The default repetition_penalty is left in place. The registration specifies only temperature 1.0, so this is an open choice. It shapes the teacher input distribution and therefore the exact value. It is unlikely to flip the event, because trained edge accuracy of 0.933 caps the statistic at about +0.067 even if teacher-like accuracy were 1.0.

experiment.py synthesize(): exact duplicates are judged on the (input, output) pair rather than on input alone. Two calls with malformed JSON (2 and 11) are rejected whole. Both follow the registered drop-duplicates and strict-parse rules. Effect is minor.

experiment.py train(): training order is a shuffle that repeats over the 120 pairs. The cosine schedule includes its endpoint. AdamW uses PyTorch defaults (weight_decay 0.01). PEFT may keep LoRA weights in FP32 under bf16 autocast. All are unspecified details and unlikely to matter.
