registration.title: Correctness filtering versus same-size random subset for synthetic training
registration.seed_connection: Seed notes synthetic supervision may inherit teacher errors but only validates JSON format; this tests whether training on oracle-correct subset beats same-size random subset at fixed compute.
registration.hypothesis: Training on the oracle-correct subset beats training on a same-size random subset of the same teacher pool at equal steps.
registration.contribution: Measures headroom for correctness filtering at fixed training compute and unique count, separating label precision from data quantity beyond format validation.

closest_work.difference: Self-Instruct filters invalid or similar generations, not correctness against an oracle; this filters to oracle-correct only versus same-size random and repeats to equalize examples.
Distilling step-by-step adds rationales as extra supervision; this keeps input-output format fixed and tests correct-only subset versus same-size random subset.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B from HuggingFace hub (student)
Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingFace hub (teacher)
Seed teacher templates reimplemented locally with no hosted APIs
registration.method: Run locally with transformers plus peft in bf16, no hosted APIs. Use 2 specs verbatim. S1 arxiv: Extract arXiv identifiers from /pdf/ links only. Input is free text with URLs. Output a JSON array of identifier strings in order, ignoring /abs/ links. If none output []. S2 triage: Classify email subject lines. Return IMMEDIATE if subject mentions deadline, urgent, EOD, signature needed, action required, due today, ASAP, or approval needed case-insensitive. Otherwise return WAIT. Return only one word IMMEDIATE or WAIT. Teacher synthesis uses system prompt You synthesize tiny supervised datasets for finetuning small language models from a natural-language task specification. Return strict JSON with a top-level key examples. Each example must be an object with string keys input and output. User prompt is Generate 8 diverse (input, output) example pairs that follow this specification. [SPEC] {spec} [END_SPEC]. Generate 120 unique pairs per spec with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct temperature 1.0 max_new_tokens 1200 strict JSON parse drop empties and duplicates repeat until 120 or 20 calls max. Verify each pair by oracle on teacher input. Arxiv expected by case-insensitive regex for arxiv.org/pdf/ IDs in order, compare to teacher output parsed via json.loads stripped for ordered equality, unparseable counts as incorrect. Triage expected by 8-phrase keyword rule case-insensitive substring, compare to teacher output stripped upper for equality, must be IMMEDIATE or WAIT. Let K be correct count per spec, if K fewer than 20 keep all and note count. Build filtered set of K correct and control set of K random sampled from full 120 with seed 0. Expand both to 960 training examples by repeating and shuffling with seed 0 to fill 60 steps times batch 16. Train one LoRA per spec per condition with same config. Prompt template is three lines: Specification: {spec} then Input: {input} then Output: then model output, with newlines between. Tokenize with Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer max_length 512 mask prompt with -100, LoRA r16 alpha32 dropout 0 targeting q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj, AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine to 2e-5, 60 steps effective batch 16 via micro-batch 8 and 2 accum, bf16 seed 0, unload teacher before training. Build 100 oracle tests per spec with seed 3. Arxiv tests sample 0 to 3 pdf plus 0 to 2 abs in templates Check these papers: {links}. and See {links} for details., expected by regex. Triage tests sample 50-50 by keyword rule with templates embedding phrases versus newsletter FYI templates, expected by rule. Inference greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 128 for arxiv and 64 for triage with same template. Score strictly as in verification.

event.description: Filtered correct-only training beats same-size random training by more than 5 points
event.statistic: mean accuracy filtered minus random averaged over 2 specs

evaluation.procedure: Compute strict accuracy per spec per condition over 100 oracle tests. Write per-example records to outputs/scores.jsonl with fields spec, condition, input, expected, predicted, correct. Write aggregates to outputs/summary.json with fields acc_filtered_per_spec, acc_random_per_spec, kept_K_per_spec, mean_filtered, mean_random, delta. Statistic is mean_filtered minus mean_random averaged over 2 specs.
evaluation.controls: Same specs, same initial teacher pools, same LoRA config, steps 60, batch 16, lr, seeds, prompt template, decoding, total examples 960 and unique count K matched via repetition; only subset composition differs. Same held-out oracle tests. Report kept counts and per-spec accuracies.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, develop learned verifiers without oracles: self-consistency, cross-teacher agreement, and small checker models, and test filtering plus augmentation at larger budgets.

agent.reason: Gain depends on 7B noise rate; with 15-25 percent noise, correct-only versus same-size random may help modestly, but easier-subset bias and noise tolerance make greater than 5 points uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: The teacher is likely to produce mostly correct labels on these straightforward functions, leaving considerable overlap between the filtered and random subsets. Moreover, errors on unusual teacher-generated inputs may not appreciably hurt performance on the simple test templates, limiting the filtering gain.

judge_fable.reason: Qwen2.5-7B is probably 80-90% correct on these simple specs, so the random K-subset overlaps heavily with the filtered set and triage noise barely affects the templated tests; a >5-point mean delta would mostly need to come from arxiv plus favorable noise.

judge_opus.reason: The triage tests are easy keyword-versus-newsletter cases, so both conditions should sit near ceiling and the arXiv spec alone would need a gain of about 10 points. Self-generated teacher labels are mostly correct, and greedy decoding mostly washes out non-systematic label noise, so the filtered-minus-random gain is likely small.

judge_sol.reason: I expect relatively high teacher-oracle agreement on these simple tasks, leaving heavily overlapping subsets and limited filtering headroom. Systematic errors could nevertheless produce a substantial gain, although filtering also changes input difficulty and coverage rather than isolating label correctness alone.

judge_luna.reason: Oracle filtering can remove genuine label noise, but a 7B model generating examples for these simple rules may have a high correct fraction, leaving little difference between filtered and random sets. Filtering may also discard useful harder examples.

judge_muse.reason: Self-consistent 7B generation on simple keyword/regex tasks is likely already high-accuracy, so 100% versus ~85-90% correct training at matched size may produce only borderline >5pt mean difference.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Haluptzok et al. fine-tune code LMs on synthetic puzzles that an interpreter has checked for correctness and compare this with unverified synthetic data. They find that verified data helps more. That is the same comparison: correctness-filtered teacher data versus unfiltered teacher data. The domain is programming puzzles rather than spec-derived text functions trained into a LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B. I did not re-read the paper to confirm that their unverified control matches the number of examples exactly.

Li et al. compare SFT on long chain-of-thought samples with incorrect answers against SFT on fully correct samples and find only about a 3.2-point drop. This is a controlled test of whether correct teacher outputs beat unchecked ones. It uses reasoning traces on a 32B model, not short input-output pairs for compact local functions.

The seed paper only checks teacher batches for valid JSON format. It ablates teacher mix and the number of unique pairs, but never filters for correctness. Its Limitations section notes that synthetic data may inherit teacher errors. The proposed experiment fills that gap within this pipeline.
Self-Instruct filters generations for validity and near-duplicates, not for oracle correctness. It has no same-size random control.

SELF-GUIDE builds task-specific synthetic data from a task description and fine-tunes on it with rule-based quality filters. It does not test oracle-correct versus random subsets at a matched number of unique examples.

opus.reason: Prior work already tests whether correctness-checked teacher data beats unchecked teacher data when a model is fine-tuned on synthetic examples: verified versus unverified code puzzles (2207.14502), correct versus incorrect chain-of-thought samples (2502.07374), and, more broadly, the noisy-label literature. The proposal differs mainly in setting: two hand-written specs, short input-output pairs, a 0.6B LoRA student and a repetition-matched random control. I couldn't confirm that any paper runs exactly this experiment, and prior results disagree across domains, so this is a close variant rather than an equivalent. My search coverage was limited because the search tool returned mostly irrelevant results for these queries.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Quality Matters: Evaluating Synthetic Data for Tool-Using LLMs compares correctness-screened synthetic subsets against equally sized random subsets, using LoRA on two tool-use datasets. The proposed experiment instead uses deterministic correctness oracles, two narrow text functions, and a fixed repetition-and-update schedule.

OpenThoughts compares answer-verification filtering with size-matched random filtering under a common training recipe. Its filters use LLM judgments and other proxies rather than exact oracles, and its supervision includes long reasoning traces.

sol.reason: Prior work already investigates the central controlled question: whether screening synthetic supervision for correctness improves downstream training relative to selecting the same number of examples randomly. Deterministic oracles and specification-specific neural functions make this a cleaner, narrower implementation, but the contribution is a close variant of existing matched-subset studies rather than a previously unexamined question.

opus.reason: Both check teacher-synthesized arXiv-extraction pairs against regex/oracle ground truth and train the student on correctness-filtered versus unfiltered teacher data. Experiment 4 also matches set size and repetition, which entry 57 does not.

sol.reason: Both test oracle-based filtering of erroneous teacher-synthesized supervision against unfiltered supervision using held-out rule-scored accuracy, with the registration refining the control to match subset size.

registration.title: Open-model semantic judge false-positive audit on controlled variants
registration.seed_connection: Seed reports LEM from a GPT-5.5 judge that tolerates formatting but rejects semantic errors; with no hosted APIs this tests whether an open 7B judge inflates scores on verifiable tasks.
registration.hypothesis: A Qwen2.5-7B LEM-style judge marks a non-trivial fraction of semantic errors correct on triage and extraction outputs.
registration.contribution: Audits an open-model LEM-style judge against deterministic scoring on identical controlled cosmetic versus semantic variants, testing judge inflation when the judge must also be small and open.

closest_work.difference: That study compares LLM-as-judge to EM and F1 on extractive QA; this compares an open LEM-style judge to verifiable exact match on compiled triage and extraction outputs including JSON containers.
PAW uses LLM evaluation for fuzzy functions; this audits whether a 7B open judge reproduces deterministic verdicts or inflates them on controlled variants.

inputs: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from HuggingFace hub (judge)
No external datasets; oracle tests and controlled variants generated in code
LEM-style judge prompts adapted from seed Appendix E for local use
registration.method: Run locally with transformers in bf16, no hosted APIs and no training. Use 2 specs verbatim. S1 triage: Classify email subject lines. Return IMMEDIATE if subject mentions deadline, urgent, EOD, signature needed, action required, due today, ASAP, or approval needed case-insensitive. Otherwise return WAIT. Return only one word IMMEDIATE or WAIT. S2 arxiv: Extract arXiv identifiers from /pdf/ links only. Input is free text with URLs. Output a JSON array of identifier strings in order, ignoring /abs/ links. If none output []. Generate 60 oracle tests per spec with seed 0, 120 total. Triage tests 30 IMMEDIATE with keyword phrases and 30 WAIT newsletter FYI, expected by keyword rule. Arxiv tests sample 0 to 3 pdf plus 0 to 2 abs in templates Check these papers: {links}. and See {links} for details., expected by case-insensitive regex ordered. For each test create 2 controlled predictions. Cosmetic should be CORRECT: triage add leading and trailing spaces and newlines around expected, arxiv keep same JSON values but add extra spaces and newlines and indentation. Semantic error should be INCORRECT: triage flip label IMMEDIATE to WAIT and WAIT to IMMEDIATE, arxiv if expected non-empty drop last ID else add fake ID 0000.00000, keep JSON array format. Total 120 cosmetic and 120 semantic variants. Judge each tuple with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using system prompt You judge semantic correctness given SPEC, INPUT, REFERENCE, PREDICTION. Ignore whitespace extra or missing spaces newlines tabs and JSON spacing indentation when spec does not pin exact spacing. Do not ignore different values missing or extra items wrong order or wrong label. If spec requires JSON array or single word, enforce correct values in valid format but ignore spacing. Output single JSON with key verdict CORRECT or INCORRECT. User lists SPEC plus INPUT plus REFERENCE plus PREDICTION. Decode greedy do_sample False max_new_tokens 128 batched size 4. Parse verdict by trying json.loads for verdict key, if fails search for substring INCORRECT first then CORRECT, since INCORRECT contains CORRECT, if neither found count as INCORRECT. Compute deterministic exact for reference: triage stripped upper equality, arxiv json.loads ordered equality.

event.description: Open judge marks more than 5 percent of semantic errors correct
event.statistic: false-positive rate fraction of 120 semantic errors judged CORRECT

evaluation.procedure: Read 240 judgments with expected verdict and judge verdict. Compute FPR as fraction of 120 semantic errors judged CORRECT and FNR as fraction of 120 cosmetics judged INCORRECT. Write per-variant rows to outputs/judgments.jsonl with fields spec, input, reference, prediction, variant_type, expected_verdict, exact_correct, judge_verdict, judge_correct. Write aggregates to outputs/scores.jsonl with fields FPR, FNR, mean_exact, mean_judge, confusion_counts, per_task_FPR. Statistic is FPR.
evaluation.controls: Identical controlled variants scored by both exact and judge; judge is blind to variant type; unparsable judge outputs count as INCORRECT; report confusion matrix exact vs judge and per-task FPR and FNR as diagnostics; no training, so no training confounds.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, validate open judges against human labels on broader specs, test prompt ablations including container-flexibility rules, and calibrate thresholds or hybrid exact-plus-judge metrics.

agent.reason: Flipped labels and dropped IDs are blatant for a 7B judge with explicit rules, so false positives should be rare, though prompt non-compliance and substring parsing could push FPR above 5 percent.

judge_astra.reason: With references supplied, flipped labels and missing or extra array elements should be relatively easy for the judge to reject. Lenient acceptance of incomplete arrays could still cross the threshold, but this audit is substantially easier than judging subtle semantic errors and does not directly test the seed’s judge.

judge_fable.reason: Label flips and empty-vs-nonempty mismatches are easy for a 7B judge, but no-CoT list comparison on 2-3 item arrays will miss some dropped items, placing the expected FPR right around the 5% threshold (needs >=7 of 120); highly feasible to run.

judge_opus.reason: Flipped triage labels, empty-versus-nonempty lists and fake IDs are obvious mismatches that a 7B judge prompted about missing or extra items should reject. Unparseable verdicts also default to INCORRECT. False positives would mostly come from about 30 cases where the prediction drops the last of 2–3 IDs, and at least 7 of 120 would require a systematic leniency toward omissions.

judge_sol.reason: The visible references and obvious label flips or missing/extra identifiers make these negatives easier than realistic semantic failures. At least seven false positives among 120 therefore seems unlikely, but passing this audit would not establish general judge reliability.

judge_luna.reason: The semantic variants are explicit flips, omissions, or additions, which a 7B judge should usually reject; more than 6 false positives out of 120 therefore seems unlikely. List comparisons and instruction-following can still fail.

judge_muse.reason: Flipped labels and dropped IDs are blatant but threshold needs only 7/120 errors, and a 7B judge with simple parsing is likely to be lenient that often.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed's Appendix B checks its LEM grader against 128 labeled items and reports FPR and FNR, but only for the hosted GPT-5.5 (FPR 0.025) and GPT-5.4-mini (FPR 0.05) judges on real outputs. It does not test a small open-weight judge, and it does not build matched cosmetic versus semantic variants of the same outputs scored against exact match.

Compares LLM-as-judge with EM and F1 on extractive QA and includes open-source judges, but measures correlation with human labels on natural QA answers. It does not plant label flips or dropped or added IDs in classification and JSON-array outputs graded against a specification.

Reports that answer matching against a reference, even with small models, comes close to human agreement on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. That supports small reference-guided judges in general, but it does not measure false positives on deliberately planted semantic errors in specification-defined functions.

Studies false positives of model-based verifiers compared with rule-based checkers, but for math answers and reward hacking during RL training. It does not cover spec-grounded triage or extraction outputs with controlled variants.

Uses targeted perturbations to measure how often evaluators miss planted errors, the same audit design, but for vision-language evaluators on image tasks rather than a 7B text judge with LEM-style prompts.

opus.reason: Auditing judges with planted errors (perturbations) is an established method, and the seed already reports grader FPR for its two hosted judges. Still, none of the papers I found measures whether a small open judge such as Qwen2.5-7B, given the seed's spec-grounded LEM prompt, accepts flipped labels or altered JSON ID lists, so prior results do not settle the question. The new elements are the model, the controlled variants and the task types. That makes the experiment a narrow extension rather than an equivalent study, though less than a fundamentally new question.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: FBI tests reference-guided evaluators, including open models, on targeted semantic corruptions and score-invariant variants, measuring how often corrupted answers receive perfect scores. This experiment substitutes deterministic triage/extraction oracles, whitespace-only controls, Qwen2.5-7B, and binary verdicts.

Audits code-correctness judges against executable tests and compares buggy mutations with semantically equivalent transformations of the same correct implementations. The registered experiment applies this diagnostic design to labels and JSON arrays rather than Java/Python implementations.

The seed already validates specification-grounded LEM judgments and reports FPR/FNR against author labels. The follow-up replaces hosted judges and author annotation with a small open judge and controlled, deterministically labeled variants.

sol.reason: Prior work already investigates false acceptance of deliberately corrupted outputs while using semantics-preserving variants as controls, including reference-guided evaluation and deterministic correctness checks. The proposed contribution is principally a task-, model-, and scoring-specific replication of that audit design, rather than a distinct research question. These precedents do not establish whether this particular Qwen judge will exceed the registered 5% threshold.

opus.reason: Both score controlled cosmetic-only versus substantive-error prediction variants with an open ~8B judge using Appendix E-style prompts. Both compare those verdicts with exact match, measuring how often semantic errors are accepted.

sol.reason: Both audit a local semantic judge using oracle-labeled cosmetic and substantive perturbations of extraction and triage outputs, measuring false-positive and false-negative rates.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: run.py does the registered audit end to end. It builds 120 oracle tests in code with seed 0: 60 triage tests (30 IMMEDIATE subjects containing keywords, 30 WAIT newsletter/FYI subjects; every expected label checked against the keyword rule) and 60 arXiv tests (0–3 /pdf/ links plus 0–2 /abs/ links, both registered templates, expected IDs from a case-insensitive ordered regex). Each test gets one cosmetic variant (whitespace/newlines around the label; JSON re-indented with extra spaces) and one semantic variant (label flipped; last ID dropped, or fake ID "0000.00000" added when the expected list is empty). Before judging, the script asserts that exact scoring marks all 120 cosmetic variants correct and all 120 semantic variants incorrect. The judge is Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in bf16 via transformers, greedy decoding, max_new_tokens 128, batch size 4 with left padding, and it never sees the variant type. Parsing: try json.loads for the "verdict" key, otherwise look for "INCORRECT" before "CORRECT", otherwise count as INCORRECT. Outputs are outputs/judgments.jsonl (registered fields plus task, judge_raw and judge_agrees_expected; judge_correct = the judge said CORRECT), outputs/scores.jsonl (FPR, FNR, mean_exact, mean_judge, exact-vs-judge confusion counts overall and per task, per_task_FPR, plus diagnostics per_task_FNR and the arXiv FPR split by drop-last vs fake-ID) and result.json. The whole run takes about 1 minute after the download.

Small departures, none of which change the question:
(1) I lightly punctuated the registered system prompt (commas, parentheses, quoting the JSON key) and ended the user message with a 'Return JSON: {"verdict": ...}' line, in the style of the seed's Appendix E.
(2) Before json.loads, the parser first pulls out the first {...} span, so a JSON object wrapped in other text still parses.
(3) I added an extra diagnostic field, judge_agrees_expected.
(4) The synthetic arXiv IDs are random YYMM.NNNNN strings; some are not real IDs (e.g. impossible month values), which doesn't matter for a format/value audit.

Result of my test run: FPR = 0.0 (0/120 semantic errors judged CORRECT; 0/60 for each task, including 0/45 drop-last and 0/15 fake-ID cases). So the registered event (FPR > 0.05) did not occur. FNR = 0.133 (16/120 cosmetic variants judged INCORRECT: 2/60 triage, 14/60 arXiv). In other words, in this setting the judge was too strict on whitespace and JSON re-indentation, not too lenient. All judge outputs parsed as JSON, so the fallback rule was never used.

Limits on what this shows: zero out of 120 bounds the true FPR to roughly ≤ 3% (95% upper limit) only for these two simple specs and these blatant, mechanically generated errors (flipped labels, a dropped or fake ID). It does not show that the judge avoids inflation on subtler errors, other tasks, or real model outputs. This is a single run with deterministic greedy decoding.

registration.title: Acceptance-level audit of the two-view verifier's sequential-conditional assumption
registration.seed_connection: Appendix C identifies Flash-Verify's mask-view distribution with an ordinary sequential conditional. The released generate.py constructs a two-view attention mask, but direct attention exclusions do not by themselves establish independence through multiple transformer layers. This experiment isolates that assumption without stale caches or fused kernels.
registration.hypothesis: A material fraction of tokens accepted by the paper's two-view verification rule are not modes of the corresponding fully recomputed sequential conditionals.
registration.contribution: Spiffy already acknowledges indirect context leakage in shared-context verification. This experiment does not claim to discover that general issue. It measures decision-level consequences for Flash-Verify's particular paired-token mask, with counterfactual draft changes and numerical controls, rather than inferring fidelity from downstream accuracy.

closest_work.difference: Spiffy discusses indirect leakage when entire draft blocks share bidirectional context. This experiment audits paired draft/mask tokens and measures unsupported acceptances against explicitly recomputed conditionals.

SimSD uses essentially the same temporal data/mask attention layout for speculative verification. This experiment tests the layout's conditional fidelity on a fully bidirectional model, rather than its throughput on block-diffusion models.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
openai/gsm8k, configuration main, train split, from Hugging Face Datasets
openai/openai_humaneval, test split, from Hugging Face Datasets; only prompts are used and no generated code is executed
https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM, especially llada/generate.py for the m11, m12, m21, m22 mask construction
registration.method: Load the frozen model on the A100 in FP32, disable TF32 and dropout, and use inference_mode. Install only the required model/data dependencies; no lm-eval harness or compiled attention extension is needed. Select the first 16 GSM8K questions and first 16 HumanEval prompts whose rendered prompts contain 32-192 tokens. Render math as 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' and use the original code-completion prompts. Append 64 MASK tokens. Produce short uncached traces: at each update consider the leftmost 16 remaining masks, commit all predictions with confidence at least 0.9, and commit the most confident one if none pass. Save states after one and four updates, omitting nonexistent states without replacement. For each saved state, obtain a fresh draft, commit the confident set D, and select up to eight remaining non-special-token proposals in descending draft-confidence order as S. Require at least two search positions for the audit. Implement a dense two-view forward using the checkpoint's existing weights, full bidirectional transformer blocks, and explicit original-position RoPE indices. Let C contain every original position outside S, with D committed; append draft copies d_i and MASK copies m_i for S. C rows may attend C and all m_i but no d_i. A d_i row may attend C, d_j for j<=i, and m_j for j>i. An m_i row may attend C, d_j for j<i, and m_j for j>=i. Apply this mask at every layer. Both copies use the original position index. Do not assume that passing attention_bias to an unmodified wrapper actually applies it. For each candidate i, separately recompute the ordinary, uncached, bidirectional model on the original-length sequence with D and the preceding drafts committed, while i and later search positions remain masked. Keep the candidate order fixed; these are forced-prefix conditional evaluations, not new rollouts. Apply the paper's rule to the two-view outputs: matching argmax, confidence at least 0.8, and stop at the first failure. This deliberately tests the paper's per-token rule, not the released code's cumulative-product rule. Record whether each accepted draft is the reference conditional's argmax. Count a disagreement only when the reference's winning-token probability exceeds the draft-token probability by more than 0.0001. On the first eight eligible states, also replace a candidate's own and later draft copies with their draft-pass runner-up tokens while keeping preceding drafts fixed; measure layerwise and final-output changes. Cap the study at the specified 64 saved states and eight reference conditionals per state.

event.description: The lower confidence bound on the unsupported-acceptance rate exceeds two percentage points.
event.statistic: The 2.5th percentile of 2000 prompt-cluster bootstrap estimates of total unsupported accepted candidates divided by total accepted candidates.

evaluation.procedure: Use bootstrap seed 101 and resample whole prompts, keeping their states and candidate records together. Require at least 50 accepted candidates; otherwise report the primary statistic as not estimable rather than evidence of fidelity. outputs/states.jsonl stores prompt IDs, input token IDs, committed sets, search orders, and masks. outputs/candidates.jsonl stores draft IDs, both distributions' top predictions and relevant probabilities, acceptance flags, and unsupported-acceptance flags. outputs/interventions.jsonl stores counterfactual changes by layer. outputs/summary.json stores the primary statistic, its underlying rate, counts, distribution-distance diagnostics, and validity checks. Record model, dataset, and code revisions in outputs/environment.json. These measurements concern model-conditional fidelity, not task correctness.
evaluation.controls: Validate the custom ordinary forward against the native model on two inputs before collecting results. Use the same FP32 backend and batch size for both audited computations. Verify original-position RoPE indexing with a permutation-equivalence test. The own/later-draft intervention must leave the target's first-block hidden state unchanged within numerical tolerance; otherwise the mask implementation is invalid. No KV reuse is permitted, separating attention-graph effects from cache staleness.

registration.full_scale_study: Audit conditional fidelity across multiple diffusion backbones, cache ages, search lengths, and numerical precisions; compare compact shared-state verification with independently recomputed verification branches, and determine whether conditional discrepancies produce meaningful task errors or only distributional differences.

agent.reason: The attention graph contains indirect paths through which excluded drafts can influence verification, giving a concrete mechanism for conditional mismatch. However, the registered event requires materially wrong argmax acceptances, not merely confidence changes, and the confidence filter may suppress many mismatches.

judge_astra.reason: The two-view graph permits multi-layer information paths and context representations that differ from ordinary sequential recomputation, making unsupported acceptances plausible. However, high-confidence prefix filtering, the minimum acceptance count, and clustered uncertainty make the registered event harder to establish than merely detecting distributional differences.

judge_fable.reason: The two-view mask provably allows two-hop leakage (m_i sees d_i via later mask copies) and gives C no direct view of prefix drafts, so some unsupported acceptances are expected; but most accepted candidates are first-in-order tokens whose true conditional rarely flips, so the rate may sit near 2-5% where the cluster-bootstrap lower bound would not clear 2%, and the custom dense two-view forward with position-controlled RoPE is hard to get right within the engineering budget.

judge_opus.reason: Under the registered mask, m_i attends later mask copies that themselves attend d_i, and C attends all mask copies, so own-draft leakage from layer 2 onward is real. An unsupported acceptance still needs mask-view confidence of at least 0.8 where the reference gives the draft roughly 0.5 or less. With about 80–150 prompt-clustered accepted candidates, the lower bound clears 2% only if the true rate is near 7% or more, and the custom dense forward adds failure risk.

judge_sol.reason: The specified attention graph permits indirect multilayer influence from own and later drafts, making self-confirming acceptances plausible. The main uncertainty is whether decision-level disagreements are frequent enough to clear the confidence-bound threshold and minimum acceptance count.

judge_luna.reason: The registered two-view graph permits information to travel through mask/context nodes over multiple layers, so disagreement with a fully recomputed conditional is plausible. The 32-prompt cluster bootstrap and minimum-acceptance requirement make the lower-bound event harder than merely detecting leakage.

judge_muse.reason: Indirect leakage through later mask copies and stale background guarantees the mask-view differs from the sequential conditional beyond the first layer, biasing agreement toward drafts. With low-confidence search tokens and a 0.0001 margin, a few percent unsupported acceptances exceeding the 2% lower bound is likely if ≥50 acceptances are obtained.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper (Flash-dLLM). Its appendix argues that the mask view equals a sequential conditional, and the paper judges fidelity by downstream accuracy and speed. I found no sign that it checks accepted tokens against fully recomputed, uncached conditionals.

Spiffy notes in general terms that context can leak indirectly when draft blocks share bidirectional context, and it keeps the model's output distribution with its own draft-graph verification. It does not audit Flash-Verify's paired draft/MASK mask or count unsupported acceptances against recomputed conditionals.

SimSD proposes a similar reference-token/current-token attention mask for speculative verification on SDAR block-diffusion models and reports throughput and quality. It does not test, token by token, whether that layout reproduces the true sequential conditionals.

This paper gives a theory of how information flows through stacked masked attention layers, using Hasse diagrams. It is relevant background on multi-layer leakage, but it runs no empirical audit of dLLM verification decisions.

opus.reason: My searches turned up no paper that measures how often tokens accepted by a two-view (draft/MASK) dLLM verifier disagree with the argmax of a recomputed, uncached sequential conditional. Related work (Spiffy, SimSD) either raises the leakage concern in passing or proposes similar masks and evaluates them only by throughput or task accuracy. The question of decision-level fidelity, with counterfactual draft swaps and layerwise checks, therefore looks unanswered, although I only searched arXiv and did not read the seed paper's appendix in full.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: SimSD uses the same paired data/mask temporal attention layout. Section 4.3 directly compares sequential denoising and parallel verification distributions, including self-drafting, and measures KL divergence, cross-entropy and top-1 agreement. The proposed experiment specializes this audit to uncached LLaDA and Flash-Verify's accepted prefix, adding confidence-gated disagreement rates and counterfactual draft interventions.

Spiffy Appendix A.2 explains indirect information leakage and layerwise hidden-state drift in shared-context verification. Its verification layout uses draft blocks rather than paired tokens, and its empirical validation relies on downstream accuracy rather than an acceptance-level conditional audit.

sol.reason: SimSD already investigates whether this paired-token verifier reproduces sequential conditionals, explicitly identifying higher-order hidden-state interactions as an approximation source and measuring distributional and top-1 discrepancies. Thus, its contribution is not limited to throughput evaluation, as the registration suggests. Acceptance-conditioned reporting, a fully bidirectional backbone and counterfactual controls refine that existing audit, but do not introduce a substantially unanswered core question; this does not establish the proposed experiment's outcome or its two-percent threshold.

opus.reason: Both audit, without cache reuse, whether the two-view verifier's mask-view outputs match separately recomputed full-sequence conditionals with exactly the confident tokens and preceding drafts committed, including perturbing current and later drafts to detect leakage; entry 21 is a close alternative.

sol.reason: Both audit uncached two-view verification against full sequential recomputation, including own/later-draft perturbations and numerical controls, to measure conditional discrepancies.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: audit.py, run by run.sh. It installs transformers 4.46.3, accelerate and datasets, then runs the whole audit. It loads GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 in FP32 with TF32 off, dropout off and inference_mode. A dense forward I wrote reuses the checkpoint's own weights. It applies full bidirectional attention with an explicit allow-mask at every layer and RoPE from explicit original-position indices. Every forward uses batch size 1 and no KV reuse, and both audited computations (two-view and reference) go through this same FP32 path. The prompts are the first 16 GSM8K-train questions and the first 16 HumanEval prompts whose rendered prompts have 32–192 tokens. Traces, draft pass, the two-view mask, the forced-prefix reference conditionals, the per-token acceptance rule, the 1e-4 disagreement tolerance, the runner-up interventions on the first 8 eligible states, and the bootstrap (seed 101, 2000 resamples of whole prompts) all follow the registration.

Choices where the registration was silent:
- The fresh draft for D and S looks at the same window as the traces: the leftmost 16 remaining masks.
- D is every window position with confidence ≥ 0.9 and may be empty. I did not force one commit here, because the registration says to commit "the confident set".
- Special tokens are the tokenizer's special and added tokens plus the known LLaDA control IDs.
- If fewer than 50 tokens were accepted, result.json would hold null. That did not happen.

Controls (all passed, recorded in summary.json under validity_checks):
- **Custom vs native forward**, two inputs: max |Δlogit| was 6.9e-5 and 7.0e-4, with full argmax agreement.
- **RoPE permutation test**: permuting tokens together with their positions changed logits by at most 1.3e-4. A negative control that permuted tokens but not positions changed them by 13.9.
- **Mask vs released code**: my mask block is identical to the m11/m12/m21/m22 construction in generate.py for K = 2–8.
- **Intervention invariance**: in every intervention, the target's hidden state after the first block was bitwise unchanged (max abs 0.0).

Primary result from my test run: 176 accepted candidates (63 of 64 states were eligible, 482 candidates in total), of which 5 were unsupported. The point rate is 2.84%. The 2.5th bootstrap percentile is **0.0064** and the 97.5th is 0.058. That is below the 0.02 threshold, so the registered event did not occur. This does not show the verifier is faithful: the interval is wide, includes 2%, and rests on only 5 unsupported tokens.

Secondary diagnostics (also in summary.json; descriptive only, no tests):
- The two-view output differs a lot from the recomputed conditional as a distribution, even when it rarely changes the accepted argmax. Mean TV is 0.23 over all candidates. It is 0.24 at k=0, where the reference has exactly the same visible tokens, so the gap there can only come from indirect leakage through later layers.
- 52 of the 176 accepted tokens would fail the γ=0.8 confidence test if it were applied to the reference conditional.
- Replacing a target's own and later drafts left its first-block state exactly unchanged. Even so, it changed the final top token in 18 of 60 cases and flipped the rule decision in 11 of 60. So own and later drafts do reach the mask view in deeper layers.
- For comparison only: the released code's cumulative-product rule accepted 162 tokens, 3 of them unsupported.

Limitations: a single repetition, short 64-token traces, one model in FP32, 32 prompts.

registration.title: Does attention-weighted cache drift identify more valuable refreshes than attention alone?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache motivates selective refresh through attention concentration. Elastic-Cache also reports that highly attended tokens can have unusually small representation drift. This creates a distinction between how much a cached token is consulted and how useful recomputing it would be.
registration.hypothesis: At the same token refresh budget, an oracle attention-times-drift ranking reduces masked-position output KL error by at least ten percent relative to normalized attention-only ranking.
registration.contribution: This is not a claim to introduce drift-aware caching. It measures causal refresh value at identical token states and cache ages, using output distributions rather than feature drift as the outcome. The oracle intervention estimates whether enough selection headroom remains to justify developing a practical low-cost predictor.

closest_work.difference: Elastic-Cache uses changes at highly attended tokens to trigger layer-aware refresh. This experiment directly compares the output-fidelity benefit of different equally sized refreshed token sets.

Polestar already performs drift-aware sparse refresh using clustered attention proxies. This experiment uses exact drift only as an offline oracle and isolates selection effects from differing decoding trajectories and refresh schedules.

EntropyCache motivates recency-based refresh and entropy-triggered recomputation. Recency is included as a control, but the primary question is whether combining influence and actual staleness improves causal refresh allocation.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
openai/gsm8k, main/train, and openai/openai_humaneval, test, from Hugging Face Datasets
https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM, especially Equation 2's implementation in llada/flash_cache_triton.py and the selective-query construction in llada/generate.py
registration.method: Use frozen FP32 GPU inference with TF32 disabled. Select the first 16 GSM8K questions and 16 HumanEval prompts with rendered lengths of 32-192 tokens; use 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' for math and the original code prompts. Append 64 MASK tokens. Run an uncached trace for 12 updates, committing exactly one most-confident token per update from the leftmost 16 masks. Save token states after updates 4, 8, and 12. For each prompt, evaluate the update-12 state against caches captured by full forwards at update 4 and update 8, giving 64 paired cache-age cases. Capture post-RoPE K and V at every layer for both old and current states. Implement a reference partial-query forward: Q consists of every position whose input changed since the old state plus the leftmost 16 current masks; all other positions initially use old K/V. Recompute Q from embeddings through every layer, overwriting its K/V before attention. Candidate refresh positions C are previously decoded positions, including prompt tokens, excluding Q. From this common no-extra-refresh forward compute a_i, the mean normalized attention received by i from the 16 masked queries across heads and layers. Compute oracle d_i as the mean across layers and heads of relative K drift plus relative V drift: norm(new-old)/(norm(new)+0.000001). Compare top-16 sets ranked by a_i and by a_i*d_i. For each intervention, restart from the identical old cache and replace only the selected C entries with current full-forward K/V at every layer; these selected entries are oracle cache patches, not claimed to be cheaply available online. Keep Q and all input tokens fixed. Measure mean KL(p_full||p_intervention) over the 16 masked positions using the full vocabulary and FP32 log-softmax. Include diagnostic controls using the released raw-logit ranking, the 16 most recently decoded positions, three seeded uniform-random sets, no additional refresh, and replacement of all non-Q entries. Refresh budgets and evaluation states must not be tuned using the resulting errors. Save scalar scores and selected indices, not all large cache tensors.

event.description: The lower confidence bound on the relative KL reduction from adding oracle drift exceeds ten percent.
event.statistic: The 2.5th percentile of 2000 prompt-cluster bootstrap estimates of (sum KL_attention - sum KL_attention_times_drift) / sum KL_attention.

evaluation.procedure: Bootstrap whole prompts with seed 202, retaining both cache ages and all paired interventions. outputs/states.jsonl records the three token states, cache ages, active query sets, and dataset IDs. outputs/refresh_sets.jsonl records attention scores, drift scores, and every selected refresh set. outputs/errors.jsonl records per-state and per-position KL, argmax disagreement, and numerical-control errors for each intervention. outputs/summary.json records the primary statistic and uncertainty alongside absolute KL values; if the attention-only error is indistinguishable from the all-fresh numerical floor, mark the relative statistic not estimable. outputs/environment.json records revisions and dependencies. A reduction in reference-model KL is not interpreted as an improvement in ground-truth accuracy.
evaluation.controls: All rankings act on identical states with exactly 16 eligible refresh positions. Newly changed tokens are always recomputed, preventing trivial benefits from refreshing stale MASK embeddings. All-non-Q replacement must recover the ordinary full forward within numerical tolerance. Raw-logit and normalized-attention rankings are reported separately because the released implementation accumulates unnormalized logits. Random and recency controls distinguish score utility from simply refreshing any additional context.

registration.full_scale_study: Develop inexpensive estimators of attention-weighted refresh value, compare them with Polestar, EntropyCache, and Flash-Cache under matched wall-clock budgets, and test whether the measured oracle headroom translates into better online accuracy-latency trade-offs on longer reasoning and code-generation trajectories.

agent.reason: Exact drift supplies information that attention alone lacks, and prior work reports that highly attended tokens can remain unusually stable. Nevertheless, representation drift need not translate into output KL improvement, and errors from unrefreshed masked positions could limit the measurable benefit.

judge_astra.reason: Oracle drift adds relevant staleness information that attention alone lacks, so substantial KL reductions are plausible. But averaged relative drift is not the same as downstream output sensitivity, and overlapping selections or error cancellation could prevent the lower bound from exceeding ten percent.

judge_fable.reason: An oracle attention-times-drift ranking should beat attention-only (which wastes slots on low-drift sink/global tokens), but the unrefreshable stale trailing masks and the few high-attention, high-drift decoded tokens that both rankings select create a common error floor, making a >10% lower-bound relative KL reduction uncertain; implementation of per-layer KV capture/patching adds risk.

judge_opus.reason: Attention times drift is a natural first-order estimate of impact and should beat attention-only ranking if attention concentrates on low-drift sinks. Several things make a lower bound above 10% uncertain: the two top-16 sets likely overlap heavily (stale response tokens score high under both), unrefreshable stale trailing masks dilute the relative reduction, and relative V-drift may inflate small-norm sink values.

judge_sol.reason: Attention weighted by actual representation drift is a plausible proxy for refresh value. However, short cache ages, averaging across layers, and stale masked positions excluded from candidate refreshes could limit the improvement below the registered lower-bound target.

judge_luna.reason: Attention multiplied by drift is a plausible proxy for how much a stale KV entry perturbs masked outputs, and the paired intervention is well targeted. But scalar drift and averaged attention may not predict KL contribution well, and the limited number of prompt clusters makes the required lower bound uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Elastic-Cache evidence that high-attention tokens can have small drift implies attention-only wastes some of its 16-token budget on stable tokens, which exact oracle drift can reallocate. A 10% relative KL improvement is modest for an oracle with two cache ages, though gains depend on drift variation across candidates.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Polestar picks KV positions to refresh online by drift alone, measured as KL between attention distributions at clustered centroid proxies. Its evidence is that high-drift tokens near the block carry most of the cache cosine error, plus end-to-end accuracy and throughput. It does not compare attention-only against attention-times-drift rankings at the same refresh budget and cache state, and it does not measure output-distribution KL.

Elastic-Cache reports that the most-attended token drifts least and uses that token as a trigger for when to refresh, with a layer-depth schedule for where. It does not rank individual tokens by attention combined with drift, and it runs no oracle comparison of refresh-set value.

The seed paper motivates selective refresh by how concentrated attention is (Flash-Cache) and focuses on IO-aware kernels and draft-and-verify decoding. It does not test whether adding drift to the attention score improves which tokens get refreshed.

EntropyCache uses decoded-token entropy to decide when to recompute and refreshes the k most recent tokens. It has no influence-times-staleness ranking and no controlled oracle comparison of rankings.
dLLM-Cache chooses response tokens to update by feature (value) similarity, which is a drift-only criterion. It does not compare that against attention weighting at a matched budget.

SPA-Cache finds tokens that need updating with a low-rank drift proxy and allocates budget across layers. It does not compare attention-only and attention-times-drift oracle rankings by their effect on output KL.

opus.reason: Several dLLM caching papers pick refresh tokens by drift (Polestar, dLLM-Cache, SPA-Cache), by attention (the seed's Flash-Cache, Elastic-Cache's trigger), or by recency (EntropyCache). In my searches, none of them runs a controlled oracle test of whether weighting attention by actual KV drift beats attention alone at the same budget, with identical states and cache ages and output KL as the measure. The pieces exist in prior work, but this headroom question appears unanswered; I can't rule out an ablation buried in a paper I did not read in full, though.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Polestar compares refresh selectors on the same cached trajectory at a matched budget, but measures identification of the most-stale KV positions. It does not compare attention-only against attention-times-exact-K/V-drift through oracle patches and masked-position output KL.
Flash-dLLM selects refresh positions using attention importance and evaluates decoding accuracy and throughput, without the proposed paired oracle-drift intervention.

Elastic-Cache uses attention-pattern changes at highly attended tokens to trigger depth-selective refresh, rather than comparing equally sized token-refresh sets for their causal output-fidelity benefit.

ACache compares attention-based and KV-deviation-based recomputation criteria at matched budgets for cross-request affix reuse, but does not combine attention with exact drift or isolate refresh value using identical-state oracle patches.

sol.reason: Attention-guided and drift-aware refresh are established, and Polestar already includes a matched-budget, common-trajectory selector analysis. However, none of the work found by the cutoff answers whether adding exact drift to attention improves the output-fidelity benefit of fresh-cache patches at fixed token states and cache ages; this distinction concerns the intervention and question, not merely the model, dataset, or metric.

opus.reason: No list entry tests an oracle attention-times-drift refresh ranking against attention-only ranking by causal output KL; entries 3, 24 and 35 compare attention variants, recency and random without drift, and entry 25 measures only a staleness proxy rather than output error after refresh.

sol.reason: No listed experiment causally compares equal-budget attention-only and attention-times-drift oracle refreshes using output KL; entry 25 measures drift associations and a staleness proxy instead.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: refresh_exp.py is my own FP32 reference forward pass for LLaDA-1.5 (TF32 off). It loads the safetensors weights directly and does RMSNorm → QKV → RoPE (theta 5e5, half-split rotate) → softmax attention → SwiGLU, then ln_f and ff_out. One code path handles both the full forward and the partial-query forward. In the partial forward, Q is recomputed from embeddings at every layer and its post-RoPE K/V are written into a copy of the old cache before attention.

Setup:
- Prompts: the first 16 GSM8K main/train questions and the first 16 HumanEval test prompts whose tokenized length (default add_special_tokens) is 32–192. Math prompts use 'Question: {q}\nAnswer:'. 64 MASK tokens are appended.
- Trace: 12 uncached updates, each committing the single most confident token from the leftmost 16 masks.
- Caches: K/V from full forwards on the update-4 and update-8 states, each evaluated against the update-12 state. That gives 64 cases, as registered.
- Scores: a_i is the mean softmax attention from the 16 masked queries, averaged over heads and over all 32 layers. d_i is relative K drift plus relative V drift, averaged over layers and heads.
- Refresh sets (16 positions from C each): attention, attention×drift, released-style raw-logit score (raw q·k, mean over masked queries and heads, summed over layers 2..31 as in flash_cache_triton.py), recency, three seeded random sets, no refresh, and all non-Q entries.
- Outcome: KL(p_full || p_intervention) over the full vocabulary, plus argmax disagreement.
- Bootstrap: 2000 prompt-cluster resamples with seed 202.

Interpretation choices and additions:
1) Recency ranks generated tokens by most recent update; leftover slots go to prompt tokens, rightmost first.
2) "All non-Q entries" means every position outside Q, including the still-masked positions to the right of the window, which also have stale K/V. An early version replaced only C and did not recover the full forward. With the fix the error is ~1e-8 KL per position, with max |logit diff| about 1e-4.
3) I added a diagnostic "all_candidates" (refresh all of C). It shows that stale right-side mask entries leave a floor in every 16-token intervention. These entries cannot be selected, because the registration restricts C to decoded positions.
4) Estimability rule, fixed before seeing the full results: the relative statistic is estimable if attention-only KL is more than 10× the all-fresh KL. It was estimable (ratio 1.3e-7).

Result from the test run (32 prompts, about 2 minutes plus model load): the registered statistic is −0.373 (point −0.094, 97.5th percentile 0.086). So oracle drift weighting did not reduce KL by ≥10%. The point estimate is a 9.4% increase in KL, but the interval includes zero, so this is not evidence that drift weighting is worse or equivalent. The pattern differed by task: worse on GSM8K (36.3 vs 30.9 summed KL), about equal on HumanEval (25.06 vs 25.13).

Diagnostics:
- Attention-only beats random (−43% to −51%) and recency (−25%).
- Released raw-logit ranking is close to attention (−2.5%, CI −10% to +4%).
- Attention cuts KL by 41% relative to no refresh.

These numbers are KL against the model's own full forward, not ground-truth accuracy. The submitted run regenerates every output from scratch.

departures: Model forward (refresh_exp.py): the engineer wrote a custom FP32 reimplementation of LLaDA-1.5 (RMSNorm, half-split RoPE with theta 5e5, bidirectional softmax attention, SwiGLU) instead of running the released modeling_llada.py. The registration does not require the released code. The logged decodes are coherent, which suggests the reimplementation is correct, but it was never checked numerically against the HF model. It could change the result only if the reimplementation is subtly wrong.

Prompt selection (refresh_exp.py select): the 32–192 length filter is applied to both tasks, and the first 16 items that pass are taken. The registration's wording ('first 16 GSM8K questions and 16 HumanEval prompts with rendered lengths of 32-192') leaves this open. Tokenization uses the default add_special_tokens, so a BOS token may be added, which the registration does not specify. Both are minor and could shift which prompts are used and their absolute KL values.

registration.title: Can refreshing only the verifier improve detection of incorrect cached drafts?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-dLLM deliberately shares a KV cache between drafting and verification. Shared stale context could make agreement less informative, even when the verifier is otherwise implemented correctly. This experiment examines that coupling independently of the two-view attention mask.
registration.hypothesis: A fully refreshed verifier discriminates correct from incorrect cached numerical drafts at least 0.05 AUROC better than a verifier sharing the drafter's stale background cache.
registration.contribution: The experiment crosses verifier cache freshness while holding candidate tokens, visible context, model weights, and correctness labels fixed. It tests whether shared approximation errors undermine verification, rather than assuming that higher self-agreement implies better correctness. The test is a controlled arithmetic-cloze assay, not a claim about full mathematical problem-solving accuracy.

closest_work.difference: Polestar jointly studies cache drift and token commitment. This experiment specifically measures the reliability of a second verification pass when its approximation errors are shared with the drafter.

COVER combines cached context with leave-one-out verification. This experiment avoids paired-view and diagonal-correction questions by evaluating only the first search candidate using ordinary serial conditional forwards, varying only background-cache freshness.

Reliable Parallel Decoding studies correctness under unresolved arithmetic context. This experiment supplies identical resolved context to both verifiers and instead varies whether its background representations have been refreshed.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
Locally generated arithmetic-cloze data with exact integer labels; no external annotation is needed
https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM for the shared-cache draft/verify design and LLaDA module structure
registration.method: Generate 256 unique problems with Python random seed 303: 64 in each combination of two-digit versus three-digit operands and final addition versus multiplication. Sample a,b,c,d uniformly from 10-99 or 100-999, calculate u=a+b and v=c+d, and set w=u+v or u*v. Prompt the model to compute these values and use the response format 'u = {u}\nv = {v}\nw = {w}'. This is a fixed-length cloze experiment: tokenize the complete response, identify tokens overlapping the three result-number spans, and disclose the nonnumeric formatting and target lengths. Never disclose masked result token identities through another input. Load the frozen model on the GPU in FP32 with TF32 disabled. Build an old state with all three result-number spans masked, and capture every layer's K/V with a full forward. Build a current state by revealing the correct u and v but leaving w masked. Produce the draft using a partial-query forward that recomputes all response-number positions at every layer while reusing the old K/V for all background positions, including prompt and formatting tokens. Record each w-position's argmax and confidence. Commit w proposals with confidence at least 0.9 into D. If search positions remain, select the highest-confidence one below 0.9, breaking ties by position. Keep all other search positions masked. Evaluate that same candidate with two verifiers on exactly the same D-committed input: one recomputes all response-number positions against the drafter's stale background cache, and one fully recomputes the entire sequence. Because this is the first search candidate, no speculative search prefix or duplicated draft view is needed. Score the fixed candidate by each verifier's full-vocabulary probability assigned to it; its correctness label is exact equality to the known target token. Do not replace the candidate when a verifier prefers another token. Cases with no search candidate are logged but do not enter the primary AUROC. Process all 256 problems without tuning operands, thresholds, or sample inclusion after inspecting labels.

event.description: The lower confidence bound on the refreshed-minus-shared verifier AUROC difference exceeds 0.05.
event.statistic: The 2.5th percentile of 2000 paired problem-bootstrap estimates of AUROC_refreshed - AUROC_shared_cache.

evaluation.procedure: Use bootstrap seed 304 and the same resampled candidate-label records for both AUROCs. Require at least 64 eligible cases and at least 10 correct and 10 incorrect drafts; otherwise mark the result not estimable. outputs/problems.jsonl contains operands, exact results, tokenized inputs, masked spans, and family IDs. outputs/verifier_scores.jsonl contains draft IDs, D, correctness labels, draft confidence, both verifier scores and argmaxes, and inclusion flags. outputs/controls.jsonl records all-fresh reference checks. outputs/summary.json contains the primary statistic, both AUROCs, confidence intervals, and descriptive risk-coverage and calibration summaries. outputs/environment.json records model and code revisions. AUROC measures discrimination, not an absolute error guarantee.
evaluation.controls: Both verifiers score identical proposals under identical visible tokens, including any incorrectly committed members of D. No two-view attention mask, external judge, or verifier training is used. On the first 16 eligible cases, rebuild every background cache entry from the exact verification input and confirm that the partial-query forward matches full recomputation. Fresh verification is allowed more computation: this is a diagnostic of reliability headroom, not a matched-cost speed claim.

registration.full_scale_study: Test verifier-only refresh on natural decoding trajectories with numerical and executable-code correctness labels, then determine whether selective or periodic verifier refresh can recover the reliability benefit within a practical latency budget without using a separate model.

agent.reason: Shared stale context could conceal draft errors, but this assay already recomputes every numerical response position, potentially leaving little useful difference between verifiers. Exceeding a 0.05 AUROC improvement at the lower confidence bound is demanding for the eligible subset of 256 problems.

judge_astra.reason: Shared stale representations could reinforce erroneous drafts, but refreshing may change calibration without substantially improving AUROC, especially when both verifiers already see the resolved intermediate numbers. Candidate eligibility, class balance, and the strict lower-bound requirement further reduce the chance of a positive event.

judge_fable.reason: The stale background holds only prompt/formatting tokens while the operand tokens u, v are recomputed fresh, and prior stale-cache results show mild degradation, so the refreshed-minus-shared AUROC gap is likely a few points at most; a lower confidence bound above 0.05 would need a ~0.1 gap with ~100-200 cases, which is unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: Both verifiers recompute the revealed u and v tokens, so stale background mainly affects prompt and formatting representations. Most draft errors, especially in multiplication, are intrinsic to the model rather than caused by staleness, so the AUROC gap is likely within a few hundredths, far from a 0.05 lower bound.

judge_sol.reason: Refreshing background representations could break some shared errors, but both verifiers already recompute every numerical position and use identical weights, suggesting strongly correlated scores. A lower-bound AUROC improvement above 0.05 requires a substantial discrimination gain, not merely changed confidence.

judge_luna.reason: Full refresh is the more faithful conditional and may improve draft-correctness discrimination, but the stale portion is mostly prompt and formatting context, and more faithful logits do not necessarily yield higher AUROC. I see a plausible effect, but not a likely gain exceeding 0.05 with the registered lower-bound criterion.

judge_muse.reason: Both verifiers share fresh u/v evidence and identical visible tokens, differing only in background prompt/formatting K/V contextualization, so predictions will likely be similar. A 0.05 AUROC lower-bound gain from background refresh alone is a high bar for this arithmetic-cloze assay.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper (Flash-dLLM) runs its draft and verify passes off the same KV cache. Its only freshness comparison is Flash-Verify with versus without the cache, scored by end-task accuracy and throughput on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP. It never holds the draft fixed while changing only the verifier's cache freshness, and it reports no AUROC for how well the verifier separates correct from incorrect drafts.

Polestar measures token drift to decide which stale cache positions to refresh and when tokens can be committed. It does not test whether a second verification pass that shares the drafter's stale cache is worse at spotting wrong drafts than a fully refreshed one.

COVER uses cache override and leave-one-out verification within a single forward pass, and it weighs cache drift when prioritising which tokens to check. It does not compare a stale-cache verifier against a fully recomputed verifier on identical candidates.

Reliable Parallel Decoding studies how reliable commitment is when upstream context is still unresolved, using layer-wise stability and entropy budgets. It does not vary the freshness of the background cache.

This paper finds that verification gets weaker as the solver and verifier become more similar, but it compares separate autoregressive LLMs at the model level. It does not study shared KV-cache approximation errors within one diffusion LLM.

opus.reason: Several papers touch on stale KV caches in diffusion LLMs, self-verification, and commitment reliability, but none I found isolates the verifier's cache freshness while keeping candidates, visible context and labels fixed, and then measures the change in AUROC. The seed paper's cache versus no-cache comparison only reports end-task accuracy, and it also changes how the drafts themselves are produced, so it does not answer this question. My search was limited, so a closer paper I missed cannot be ruled out.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Archer compares fresh and cached prompt states at matched rollback states, measuring subsequent program correctness and decoder-action disagreement. It does not test ground-truth discrimination of fixed cached drafts by refreshing only the verifier.
DualDiffusion verifies approximate cached drafts with full bidirectional computation, but does not compare refreshed and shared-stale-cache verifiers on identical proposals and visible context.
Flash-dLLM shares caches between drafting and verification and compares cached versus uncached end-to-end decoding. It does not isolate verifier freshness while fixing drafts and correctness labels.

COVER studies cache-override leave-one-out verification, self-leakage correction, and cache-stability-aware seed selection, rather than verifier-only background refresh for detecting incorrect fixed candidates.
Polestar links representation drift to cache refresh and token commitment, but does not evaluate whether sharing the drafter's approximation errors reduces a second pass's correctness discrimination.

sol.reason: The closest studies establish related cache-drift and verification mechanisms, and Archer already provides matched-state fresh-versus-cached interventions. However, none of the work I found answers whether refreshing only the verifier improves ground-truth discrimination of identical stale-cache drafts under fixed resolved context. That controlled reliability question is distinct, not merely a dataset or metric substitution.

opus.reason: Entries 2 and 36 measure acceptance flips under a refreshed cache, but none crosses verifier cache freshness and measures AUROC for discriminating correct from incorrect drafts against gold labels on an arithmetic cloze.

sol.reason: Entries 2 and 36 measure stale-versus-fresh verification sensitivity, not discrimination of correct and incorrect fixed drafts using arithmetic labels and AUROC.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: `run_experiment.py`, launched by `run_eval.sh`. It follows the registration as written. GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 (revision 84346fd9) is loaded in FP32 with TF32 disabled. I wrote my own layer-by-layer forward pass over the model's own modules so I could reuse K/V caches with partial queries. On problem 0 it matches the HF reference forward: max logit difference 1.3e-4, argmax agreement 100%. That check is recorded in `outputs/controls.jsonl`.

Data: 256 unique problems generated with `random.Random(303)`, 64 in each of {2-digit, 3-digit} × {add, mul}. The prompt uses the chat template and gives a–d plus the response format. The response is `u = {u}\nv = {v}\nw = {w}` followed by `<|eot_id|>`. Any token whose offsets overlap a result span is masked; this tokenizer splits numbers into single digits. Result values never appear anywhere else in the input.

Procedure for each problem:
- **Stale cache:** a full forward on the old state (u, v and w all masked) captures K/V for every layer.
- **Draft:** run on the current state (true u and v revealed, w masked). Every response-number position is recomputed at every layer; all background positions use the old K/V.
- **Selection:** w positions with confidence ≥ 0.9 are committed into D. The candidate is the highest-confidence search position below 0.9 (ties broken by position); other search positions stay masked.
- **Verifiers:** both score the same D-committed input. The shared-cache verifier repeats the partial-query forward against the stale cache. The refreshed verifier fully recomputes the sequence.
- **Score and label:** the score is the full-vocabulary probability each verifier assigns to the fixed candidate. The label is exact equality with the target token.

The bootstrap uses `numpy.default_rng(304)`, 2000 paired problem resamples, with midrank AUROC. Cache-rebuild control on the first 16 eligible cases: the partial-query forward with a cache rebuilt from the exact verification input matched full recomputation (max logit difference 8.8e-5, max probability difference 2.2e-5).

Choices I made where the registration was silent:
- `<|eot_id|>` is appended after the response.
- `result.json` would get `value: null` if the result were not estimable. That did not happen.
- I added summary extras: draft-confidence AUROC, ECE/Brier calibration, and risk at fixed coverage levels plus AURC.

Results from my full test run (the fresh-machine evaluation will produce its own; I expect the same numbers since the pipeline is deterministic, but I haven't confirmed bitwise equality):
- 111 of 256 problems were eligible: 68 correct and 43 incorrect drafts. All eligible cases came from the multiplication families (47 two-digit, 64 three-digit). The 145 excluded cases had no search candidate, i.e. every w position was drafted with confidence ≥ 0.9; this covers all 128 addition problems.
- AUROC was 0.891 for the refreshed verifier and 0.854 for the shared-cache verifier, a point difference of +0.037.
- The registered statistic (2.5th percentile of the bootstrap difference) is **-0.0020**, so the registered event (value > 0.05) **did not occur**.

The bootstrap 95% interval for the difference is [-0.002, 0.081]. So the data don't rule out either a zero gain or a gain above 0.05. This is not evidence that the two verifiers are equally reliable.

The test covers multiplication only and is a controlled arithmetic-cloze test, not full problem solving.

departures: run_experiment.py appends <|eot_id|> after the response and wraps the prompt in the chat template. The registration leaves both choices open. They slightly change the context all verifiers see but affect both arms equally, so they are unlikely to bias the paired difference.

run_experiment.py replaces the model's own forward with a hand-written layer-by-layer forward so that partial-query K/V reuse is possible. This was needed to run the registered design. It is validated against the HF forward (max logit difference 1.3e-4, argmax agreement 1.0 in outputs/controls.jsonl), so it is unlikely to change the value.

The Flash-dLLM repository is listed as an input but is never cloned or used. The shared-cache draft/verify scheme was rebuilt from the registration text. In outputs/environment.json, seed_code_revision is null, against the registration's request to record code revisions. This is a provenance gap with no effect on the value.
