registration.title: Does torch.compile or CUDA-graph capture of the plain PyTorch cache-update path already match Flash-Cache's fused Triton QKV+RoPE+cache-write kernel on an A100?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache's first contribution is a fused Triton kernel for QKV projection, RoPE and cache writes, motivated by the claim that the conventional multi-kernel PyTorch cache-update pipeline is memory-bound (Fig. 1a, a 1.37x per-layer speedup on an RTX 3090). The baseline is an eager pipeline; the paper does not compare against a compiled or CUDA-graphed version of the same pipeline, which is the standard remedy for launch- and intermediate-traffic-bound code, and does not report the result on the A100 used for its headline numbers.
registration.hypothesis: At the paper's per-batch-element query size (128 query rows, batch 1), the fused Triton kernel is less than 1.15x faster than the best generic PyTorch implementation of the same projection+RoPE+cache-write step (eager single-GEMM, torch.compile default, torch.compile reduce-overhead, or manual CUDA-graph replay) on an A100.
registration.contribution: Isolates how much of the fused-kernel gain comes from fusion that generic compilation or graph capture also delivers versus from the hand-written kernel, across batch sizes from the launch-bound to the GEMM-bound regime, with a bandwidth roofline and a numerical-equivalence check of the kernel.

closest_work.difference: Elastic-Cache (same authors) implements the cache update in eager PyTorch and is the conventional baseline of the seed; this benchmark adds compiled and CUDA-graph baselines that neither paper reports.

FlashAttention motivates IO-aware fusion for attention; the seed applies the idea to the cache-update path, and this microbenchmark tests whether that path is launch-bound (recoverable by compilation) rather than bandwidth-bound.

inputs: Seed repository https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM: the fused QKV+RoPE+cache-write Triton kernel in llada/flash_cache_triton.py together with the launch wrapper, rotary-table helper and block-table builder that llada/generate.py uses on the decoding path (read the code; no model weights are needed)
pip: torch (CUDA) with its bundled triton; fallback pip install torch==2.2.2 triton==2.2.0 if the kernel does not compile with the bundled Triton
registration.method:
SETUP. git clone the seed repository. Locate the fused kernel and the exact way llada/generate.py launches it during decoding (wrapper function, block table construction, rotary tables, weight layout, num_warps/num_stages); replicate that launch for the shapes below. Try the Triton bundled with the installed torch first; if the kernel fails to compile, pip install torch==2.2.2 triton==2.2.0 (closest to the Triton 2.0 the paper used) and retry; record torch/triton versions and the GPU name in the outputs.

SHAPES (LLaDA-8B): d_model = 4096, n_heads = 32, head_dim = 128, rope_theta = 500000. Cases B in {1, 4, 16, 32} batch elements, each with N = 1024 cache rows and Q = 128 query rows (M = 128*B): per element, 64 random distinct rows (tracked tokens) plus one contiguous run of 64 rows (masked window), all inside that element's cache range, sorted; pos = concatenation (int64). Inputs: x (M, 4096) bf16 ~ 0.5*N(0,1); the layer's QKV weight in the HF layout W_att (3*4096, 4096) bf16 ~ 0.02*N(0,1), whose three row blocks are Wq, Wk, Wv (convert to whatever layout the kernel wrapper expects, reading the wrapper); caches K, V (B*N, 4096) bf16 zeros; q_out (M, 4096) bf16; rotary sin/cos tables built with the repository's own helper for N positions and arranged per element as the wrapper does; the block table built with the repository's own builder for these query rows.

IMPLEMENTATIONS of one layer's cache-update step (returns q with RoPE applied; writes RoPE'd k and v into K[pos], V[pos]): (E3) eager, paper-style separate operations: q = F.linear(x, Wq); k = F.linear(x, Wk); v = F.linear(x, Wv); view (M, 32, 128); RoPE as in the HF LLaDA modeling file (cast q and k to float32 as rope_full_precision does, rotate_half via view/unbind/cat, multiply-add with the sin/cos rows at pos, cast back to bf16); K.index_copy_(0, pos, k_rot.view(M, 4096)); V.index_copy_(0, pos, v.view(M, 4096)). (E1) eager with the single fused GEMM qkv = F.linear(x, W_att) then split, which is what the HF LLaDA block does, followed by the same RoPE and index_copy_. (T1) torch.compile(E1) default mode; (T2) torch.compile(E1, mode='reduce-overhead') (same input tensors every call; note any 'skipping cudagraphs' warning); (G) E1 captured into a torch.cuda.CUDAGraph on static input tensors after warm-up on a side stream, then replayed. (F) the repository kernel through its wrapper with the block table and the num_warps/num_stages used in generate.py.

CORRECTNESS. Compute a float32 reference (E1 in float32). For each implementation and case, rel_err = max|out - ref| / max|ref| for q_out, K[pos] and V[pos]; pass iff all three < 0.02; record pass/fail. If F fails, report it and still time it; if E3 or E1 fail, the RoPE convention does not match the kernel's half-split convention and must be fixed before timing (the kernel's convention is authoritative; read it).

TIMING. For each case and implementation: 30 warm-up calls, then 200 timed calls each bracketed by a torch.cuda.Event pair with a final torch.cuda.synchronize(); record median and interquartile range in microseconds. Run the whole sweep 3 times in different implementation orders; keep per implementation and case the minimum of the three medians. Roofline reference per case: bytes_min = 3*4096*4096*2 (weights) + M*4096*2 (x) + 3*M*4096*2 (q, k, v outputs); time_min = bytes_min / 1.55e12 seconds (realistic A100-80GB HBM bandwidth), reported alongside each latency.

OUTPUTS. outputs/timings.json: every median and IQR per sweep, case and implementation; correctness flags; torch/triton versions; GPU name; whether T2 actually used CUDA graphs. outputs/summary.json: for each B, ratio_generic_over_fused = min(median E1, T1, T2, G) / median F, ratio_e3_over_fused = median E3 / median F, ratio_e1_over_fused = median E1 / median F, and latency / time_min for F and for the best generic implementation.

event.description: At B = 1 (128 query rows) the fused Triton kernel is less than 1.15x faster than the best generic PyTorch implementation (eager single-GEMM, torch.compile default, torch.compile reduce-overhead, or manual CUDA-graph replay)
event.statistic: ratio_generic_over_fused at B = 1 = min(median latency of E1, T1, T2, G) divided by the median latency of F, using per-implementation minima over three sweep orders

evaluation.procedure: Read outputs/summary.json; the statistic is ratio_generic_over_fused for the B = 1 case. Secondary: the same ratio at B = 4, 16 and 32 (the paper's headline batch), ratio_e3_over_fused at all B (to compare with the paper's 1.37x, noting that the paper's bars include attention and were measured on an RTX 3090), ratio_e1_over_fused, latency relative to the bandwidth roofline, correctness flags, and IQRs to judge timing stability. outputs/timings.json holds all raw medians, IQRs, flags and version information.
evaluation.controls: E3 reproduces the paper's description of the conventional multi-kernel pipeline; E1 reproduces the actual HF LLaDA single-GEMM path and separates GEMM merging from elementwise fusion; the float32 reference establishes that all variants compute the same function; three sweep orders control for thermal and clock drift; the roofline shows how far each implementation is from the bandwidth floor.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs: re-run the paper's end-to-end throughput comparison with a torch.compile'd or CUDA-graphed PyTorch cache path (and compiled scheduled attention) as an additional baseline across batch sizes 1 to 32, attributing the headline speedups to kernel engineering versus the algorithmic components (selective refresh, block scheduling, Flash-Verify). If it does not occur: profile the fused kernel against compiled code across query sizes and cache lengths to characterize where hand-written fusion wins and port the kernel to Dream-7B.

agent.reason: At 128 query rows the step is weight-bandwidth bound, so cuBLAS plus a compile-fused RoPE should land within ~15% of a 16-row-tile Triton GEMM and may beat it; the main risks are the repository kernel not compiling under the available Triton and wrapper/launch mismatches that invalidate the run.

judge_astra.reason: Optimized GEMM combined with compiler fusion or graph replay is a strong baseline, making a residual hand-fusion advantage below 15% at B=1 likely. Correctly reproducing the repository kernel is the main execution uncertainty; this microbenchmark would not establish equivalence of the complete inference systems.

judge_fable.reason: Fig. 1a's own breakdown shows the fused kernel (0.29 ms) far slower than the bandwidth floor while eager RoPE/gather dominate the baseline, so a CUDA-graphed or compiled single-GEMM path likely matches or beats it at 128 query rows; the main risk is obtaining and launching the repository kernel within budget.

judge_opus.reason: At 128 rows the cuBLAS QKV GEMM is close to the bandwidth floor, and compiled or graph-captured RoPE and index-copy add little. The seed's own Fig. 1a shows the fused kernel slower than the plain linear projection, so a 15% fused advantage is unlikely. The main risks are that the repository kernel fails to run or that the compiled baselines are poorly configured.

judge_sol.reason: At these shapes, an optimized single GEMM should account for most projection work, while compilation or graph replay can remove much of the ancillary eager overhead. I expect the best generic implementation often to fall within the 15% margin, although kernel compatibility and its actual implementation remain uncertain.

registration.title: Counterfactual test for draft leakage in Flash-Verify's single-pass verify mask (official code, LLaDA-1.5, GSM8K)
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Verify (Sec. 2.3, App. C) says the mask view of the k-th search token sees only the drafts that come earlier in causality order. If so, its output equals the model's sequential conditional, and each accepted block satisfies TV <= 1 - gamma. The official code (llada/generate.py, verify branch) does not enforce this. Its 32x32 verify mask lets mask view a attend to later mask views b > a. Each such view attends to draft views with index < b, which includes draft a. The mask also lets tracked tokens attend to every mask view. Across LLaDA's 32 layers, these two- and three-hop paths can carry a token's own draft, and later drafts, into its verifier. This MVE measures how much of Flash-Verify's acceptance depends on that leaked information.
registration.hypothesis: Official Flash-Verify uses gamma = 0.8 and the code's cumulative-product rule. More than 10% (net) of the tokens its verify pass accepts would no longer be accepted if, for each search index a, the draft tokens at indices >= a were replaced by [MASK]. The paper's semantics say the verifier at index a must not see those tokens.
registration.contribution: This is a causal, intervention-based measurement of draft-to-verifier leakage in the two-view (draft view / mask view) single-pass self-verification mask. Flash-Verify uses this mask, and SimSD uses the same structure. The MVE also checks App. C's equality claim against an exact, cache-consistent sequential reference computed with the same kernel, and counts how often the 1 - gamma block bound fails against that reference. Agreement-based evaluations cannot reveal this leak, because the leaked token usually coincides with the sequential argmax.

closest_work.difference: SimSD uses the same data/mask mask structure and only says it approximates sequential denoising through 'higher-order interactions'. It measures KL and top-1 agreement on the model's own correct tokens (SDAR), which cannot expose a self-leak. We intervene on the drafts and measure the resulting change in acceptance, using LLaDA-1.5 inside the official Flash-dLLM code.

This paper proves that multi-layer information flow follows the transitive closure of the mask, but gives no measurement on LLMs or on self-verification masks. We quantify the practical effect of exactly such closure paths.
SSD avoids cross-talk by verifying each tree node as a separate full sequence in a batch. We measure leakage in the cheaper single-pass shared-sequence mask.
XLNet's two-stream attention forbids query streams from attending to other query streams so targets cannot leak. Flash-Verify's mask violates this principle; XLNet does not study dLLM verification.

inputs: Official Flash-dLLM code: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM (llada/ directory: generate.py, flash_cache_triton.py, model/). Install transformers==4.49.0, accelerate and datasets; Triton ships with PyTorch.
Model: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from Hugging Face, bf16.
Data: openai/gsm8k, config 'main'. The train split supplies 5 fixed few-shot examples; the test split supplies the problems.
registration.method:
Setup. Work inside llada/ of the cloned repo; its imports assume this directory. Load the model as eval_llada.py does: config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained('GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5'); config.flash_attention = True; model = LLaDAModelLM.from_pretrained('GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5', torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, config=config).cuda().eval(); tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(same, trust_remote_code=True).

Prompts. Use lm-eval-style 5-shot GSM8K with no chat template, matching what the repo does for LLaDA-1.5. Take the first 5 train examples, format each as 'Question: <question>\nAnswer: <answer>', join them with '\n\n', then append '\n\nQuestion: <test question>\nAnswer:'. Use the first 160 test problems.

Decoding. Use a copy of generate_with_Flash_dLLM from generate.py. Pass prompts as a list of 1-D GPU token tensors, responses = ['']*160 and n_steps = [0]*160, with batch_size=32, gen_length=256, steps=256, block_length=16, threshold=0.9, gamma=0.8, track_num=4, mask_num=4, verify=True, temperature=0, mask_id=126336, eos_id=126081, tokenizer and stop_tokens=['Question:','</s>','<|im_end|>']. Change the copy in only two ways: (a) when a sample finishes, record its problem index, generated length (num_decoded[j] minus prompt length) and n_steps; (b) add the instrumentation below. Every accept/reject decision must remain the official one, so the trajectory is the official Flash-dLLM trajectory. A verify-mode forward (lengths[-1] = True) has no side effects: the verify branch of flash_fused_elastic_cache writes K/V to temporary buffers, never to the cache, and never updates attn_scores. It can therefore be re-run with modified inputs.

Instrumentation. Place it right after the official verify forward (output = model(x_query, use_cache=True, lengths=lengths, positions=positions)) and before the official acceptance loop. Layout of x_query:
- x_query concatenates one 32-token block per active sample, in active_batch order, skipping slots with i == -1. Block k starts at offset o = 32k.
- With T = seqlen_keep[j] and S = (32 - T)//2, slots [o, o+T) are tracked tokens, [o+T, o+T+S) are draft views holding drafts d_1..d_S in causality order (descending draft confidence), and [o+T+S, o+T+2S) are mask views.
- Official verify probability: p_a = softmax(float64 logits of mask slot a)[d_a]. Set it to 0 when the code's EOS-length rule applies (decoded_eos_pos[j] != -1 and the position is >= predicted_length[j]).
- m_off = number of leading indices with cumprod(p) >= 0.8; this equals the code's keep_num.

(1) Leak-removed counterfactual (LR). For a = 1..max S over active samples: clone x_query; for every sample with S >= a, overwrite its draft-view tokens at indices a..S with mask_id; re-run the verify forward with the same lengths and positions lists (official attn_mask). For those samples record q_a = softmax(mask slot a)[d_a], applying the same EOS rule. If the verifier truly sees only drafts with index < a, then q_a = p_a exactly. Set m_LR = number of leading indices with cumprod(q) >= 0.8.

(2) Exact cache-consistent sequential reference (EX). For a = 1..max S: keep x_query. For each sample with S >= a, replace its 32x32 block of the concatenated (32*n_active, 32) bool attn_mask (True = may attend) with allowed[r, c] = active[c] for every row r. Here active = tracked slots, plus draft slots with index < a, plus mask slots with index >= a. Every search position then appears once, with fully bidirectional attention as in an ordinary LLaDA forward. Run with positions[:5] + [new mask]. Record e_a = softmax(mask slot a)[d_a] and its argmax; compute m_EX the same way as m_LR.

(3) Controls, on the first 20 verify steps.
- Determinism: re-run the unmodified official verify forward and record max |delta logits| (expected 0).
- Leak-free sanity check: build an XLNet-style mask per sample (tracked rows see tracked only; draft row c sees tracked plus drafts with index <= c; mask row a sees tracked plus drafts with index < a plus itself). Run it on x_query, and again with all draft views set to mask_id. Record max |delta logits| at mask index 1 (expected exactly 0).

Logging.
- Per (problem, step, a): S, a, draft token, draft confidence, absolute position, whether another search position is adjacent, p_a, q_a, e_a, argmax under official/LR/EX, and full-vocabulary TV(official, LR) and TV(official, EX).
- Per (problem, step): S, m_off, m_LR, m_EX.
- GSM8K scoring: the prediction is the number after '####' if present, else the last number in the response (strip commas and '$'). It is correct if it equals the number after '####' in the gold answer.

event.description: Removing leaked draft information (drafts at the verified index and later) revokes, on net, more than 10% of the tokens that official Flash-Verify accepts in its verify pass.
event.statistic: R = 1 - (sum of m_LR) / (sum of m_off), summed over all verify steps of all 160 problems.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute R from outputs/steps.jsonl. Secondary statistics:
- R recomputed at gamma = 0.6 and 0.9 on the same logged probabilities.
- R_EX = 1 - sum(m_EX) / sum(m_off).
- Bound-violation rate: the fraction of official blocks with m_off >= 1 where 1 - prod_{a<=m_off} e_a exceeds 1 - gamma (App. C's bound against the exact reference).
- Mean (p_a - q_a); the rate at which the official argmax equals the draft but the LR argmax does not.
- Breakdown by whether another search position is adjacent.
- GSM8K accuracy and tokens per iteration of the run, as a sanity check against the paper (about 82% and about 5-6).

Output files:
- outputs/instances.jsonl: per-search-index records.
- outputs/steps.jsonl: per-step S, m_off, m_LR, m_EX.
- outputs/generations.jsonl: per-problem response, answer, correctness, iterations, length.
- outputs/controls.json: determinism and leak-free-mask diffs.
- outputs/summary.json: all statistics.
evaluation.controls:
- Determinism re-run: must show zero difference, so any LR change is not noise.
- XLNet-style leak-free mask invariance check: must show zero difference, confirming the substitution procedure changes nothing when no attention path exists.
- EX exact sequential reference: separates the leak from the other approximations in the mask.
- Decoding uses only official decisions, so all statistics refer to the real Flash-Verify trajectory.

registration.full_scale_study: Measure verify-mask leakage across GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP at 256 and 512 tokens, with gamma from 0.6 to 1.0. Attribute it to layers and attention paths. Compare leak-free single-pass verifiers (XLNet-style, three-view with draft-independent [MASK] context) and exact batched verification on the accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier with several seeds. Extend the test to SimSD-style masks on block-diffusion models.

agent.reason: The official mask does contain draft-to-verifier paths: later mask views attend to the draft being checked, and the tracked tokens attend to mask views. These paths let the verifier for the first search token see neighbours that already assume its draft, while the legitimate first-index conditional sees no drafts at all, so a material share of ~3 extra tokens/step plausibly depends on this echo. Leak strength and implementation risk keep this close to a coin flip, leaning yes.

judge_astra.reason: The described multi-hop attention paths permit self-conditioning, and cumulative-product acceptance can turn modest confidence inflation into substantial additional acceptance. A net revocation above 10% seems likely, although structural reachability alone does not establish the effect size.

judge_fable.reason: By the paper's own App. C description, mask views attend to later mask views (which attend to earlier drafts) and tracked tokens attend to mask views, so 2–3-hop leak paths to a token's own draft exist across 32 layers; with the code's cumprod>=0.8 prefix rule, even modest inflation of mask-view probabilities should revoke well over 10% of acceptances. Main risks are instrumentation bugs and the leak being weaker than expected.

judge_opus.reason: The mask structure does open multi-hop paths from a token's own draft and from later drafts into its verifier, and a self-consistency boost is plausible. But the effect is second-order, and legitimate sequential conditioning on committed and earlier draft tokens can already explain much of the acceptance. Whether more than 10% of verify-accepted tokens are revoked is close to a coin flip.

judge_sol.reason: The mask described in the registration permits multihop self-draft influence, and cumulative-product acceptance can magnify modest confidence changes. More than 10% net revocation seems likely, though the effect’s magnitude and the runtime of the instrumented reruns remain uncertain.

judge_luna.reason: If the registered mask description is accurate, multi-layer attention paths can carry a draft token into its own verifier, so removing those drafts is likely to change some decisions. Whether enough cumulative probabilities cross the acceptance threshold to revoke more than 10% net remains uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: App. C states mask view at i_k attends to mask views i_k..i_K, creating 2-hop paths for its own and later drafts across 32 layers; with gamma=0.8 cumulative-product acceptance, even modest confidence inflation likely revokes >10% net accepts.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It proposes the Flash-Verify draft/mask-view single-pass verification and claims, in App. C, that it equals the sequential conditional with a 1-gamma TV bound. In what I could find, it does not test for multi-hop draft leakage by intervening on the drafts, and it does not compare against an exact sequential reference.

SimSD uses a similar reference-token/mask structure and justifies its approximation by appeal to 'higher-order interactions'. Its abstract mentions no counterfactual test that removes drafts to measure self-leakage into the verifier, and I did not read the full paper. It is also evaluated on SDAR models, not on LLaDA within Flash-dLLM.

This is a theoretical framework: multi-layer information flow follows the transitive closure (Hasse diagram) of an attention mask. It gives no empirical measurement of leakage in dLLM self-verification masks or of its effect on acceptance.
SSD avoids cross-talk because it verifies tree nodes through hierarchical verification trees. It does not measure leakage in a shared-sequence two-view mask.
Self-speculative masked diffusions build a causal final-layer mask for draft and validate. The paper studies GPT-2-scale models and does not audit leakage in Flash-Verify-style two-view masks.

opus.reason: I found no paper that empirically measures, by intervention, how much draft information reaches the verifier through multi-hop attention paths in a single-pass draft/mask-view self-verification mask, or how much this changes acceptance compared with an exact sequential reference. Nearby work proposes these masks (Flash-dLLM, SimSD, SSD) or analyses mask information flow in theory (Hasse diagrams), but none answers this question. The seed paper was posted only about two weeks before the cutoff date, so a direct follow-up audit is unlikely to exist yet.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: SimSD uses the same paired data/mask attention structure and measures discrepancies from sequential denoising using KL, cross-entropy and top-1 agreement. It does not intervene on current/later draft tokens to isolate their influence on verifier acceptance.

Hasse Diagrams for Attention establishes multilayer information-flow reachability and provides principled mask constructions, but does not empirically measure draft leakage or its effect on speculative acceptance.

COVER addresses direct self-conditioning through cached KV states using diagonal correction. Its experiments concern revision effectiveness and decoding performance, rather than indirect leakage in a shared two-view verifier under fixed-trajectory draft interventions.

The seed paper asserts equality between mask-view outputs and sequential conditionals and derives deviation guarantees, but evaluates speed, accuracy and scalability without the proposed counterfactual leakage measurement or exact-reference audit.
XLNet separates query and content streams to prevent target-content leakage during pretraining; it does not measure leakage-dependent acceptance in diffusion self-verification.

sol.reason: The underlying information-flow concern is precedented, and SimSD already compares this type of parallel verifier with sequential denoising. However, I found no work available by 2026-10-07 that isolates current/later drafts through counterfactual substitutions on an unchanged decoding trajectory and measures their contribution to acceptance while auditing the sequential-reference guarantee; that contribution is more than a dataset, model or metric variant.

opus.reason: Both test whether the two-view verifier yields the sequential conditional by perturbing the current and later drafts, which the semantics exclude, and by comparing against an exact full-sequence reference.

sol.reason: Both test the verifier’s claimed sequential conditioning by perturbing current and later drafts and comparing its distributions with a sequential-recomputation reference.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented. fv_leak/run.py holds a copy of the official generate_with_Flash_dLLM from llada/generate.py and is run by run_eval.sh. It uses LLaDA-1.5 in bf16 with config.flash_attention=True, lm-eval-style 5-shot GSM8K prompts with no chat template, and the first 160 test problems. Settings are as registered: batch 32, gen_length 256, block 16, threshold 0.9, gamma 0.8, track_num 4, mask_num 4, verify=True. The copy differs from the official code in only two ways: (a) it records each problem's generated length and n_steps when the problem finishes; (b) it adds instrumentation right after the official verify forward. The instrumentation reruns the side-effect-free verify forward in two ways: with the LR draft substitution (drafts at indices >= a set to [MASK]), and with the EX per-block attention mask (every row may attend to the tracked slots, drafts with index < a, and mask views with index >= a). The two controls run on the first 20 verify steps: a determinism rerun, and the XLNet-style leak-free mask with all drafts set to [MASK]. Removing print statements and dead variables was the only other change.

Did the decisions stay official? Yes, checked: for every one of the 4331 step records, my m_off equals the code's keep_num (0 mismatches).

Small deviation. /workspace/seed is read-only, so instead of running inside llada/ I add /workspace/seed/llada to sys.path. The imports and behaviour are the same.

Results from my full test run of the submitted command (about 6.5 minutes of generation):
- **Registered statistic:** R = 1 − 5341/9465 = 0.436. This is above the 0.1 threshold, so the registered event occurred in this run.
- **Controls:**
  - The determinism rerun gave max |Δlogits| = 0.
  - The XLNet-style leak-free mask gave Δ = 0 at mask index 1. As an informational check, Δ at indices >= 2 is about 12–16, which shows the substitution does change outputs wherever an attention path exists.
- **Other gamma values:** R = 0.280 at gamma 0.6 and 0.5625 at gamma 0.9, recomputed from the same logged probabilities.
- **Exact sequential reference:** R_EX = 0.431, close to R.
- **App. C bound against the exact reference:** violated in 56.4% of the blocks with m_off >= 1 (1580 of 2803).
- **Per-token effects:**
  - Mean (p − q) = 0.045.
  - The official argmax equals the draft but the LR argmax does not in 3.5% of instances (4.4% for EX).
  - Mean TV is 0.094 between official and LR, and 0.126 between official and EX.
- **Adjacency breakdown:** LR revokes 47.9% of accepted tokens whose search position has an adjacent search position, versus 25.9% of the rest.
- **Sanity check against the paper:** GSM8K accuracy is 81.9% (131/160) at 5.54 tokens per iteration, consistent with the paper's roughly 82% and 5–6.

Caveats:
- Most of the revocation comes from the cumulative-product acceptance rule: a modest per-token probability drop pushes the running product below 0.8, which cuts off the rest of the block. The argmax change rate is much smaller (3.5%), so R measures lost acceptance, not that leaked tokens are wrong.
- This is one deterministic run (temperature 0) on 160 problems with one model and one task. I report no confidence intervals.
- R and R_EX are close in aggregate, but that alone does not show the two interventions act the same way on individual tokens.
- Before the full run I did a 32-problem smoke test with the same code (R about 0.437).

registration.title: Leak-free single-pass verify masks for Flash-Verify: is the tokens-per-step gain retained? (official code, LLaDA-1.5, GSM8K)
registration.seed_connection:
Flash-Verify gets its extra parallelism from one verify pass. That pass places a draft view and a [MASK] view of each search token in the query, under a causal mask. In the official mask (llada/generate.py), mask views attend to later mask views and tracked tokens attend to mask views. A token's own draft can therefore reach its verifier through multi-hop attention. Leak-free masks with the same one-pass cost exist:
- XLNet-style two-stream: mask views see only tracked tokens, earlier drafts and themselves.
- Three-view: adds draft-independent [MASK] context copies, so each verifier still sees later search positions as [MASK].
This MVE tests whether the paper's roughly 2x tokens-per-step gain over confidence-aware decoding survives leak-free verification.
registration.hypothesis: Keep epsilon = 0.9, gamma = 0.8 and the official cache settings. A leak-free three-view verify mask then retains more than 75% of official Flash-Verify's tokens-per-iteration gain over confidence-aware decoding on GSM8K.
registration.contribution: We propose a leak-free verify-mask design for dLLM self-verification that is training-free and costs no more than the official mask, and test it in the official Flash-dLLM pipeline. The test quantifies how much of Flash-Verify's parallelism gain relies on attention paths that violate its own causal semantics.

closest_work.difference: XLNet introduced two-stream attention without query-to-query attention for permutation LM training. We adapt the principle, plus a three-view variant that keeps [MASK] context, to training-free dLLM verification.
SimSD uses the same leaky data/mask mask for dLLM speculative verification and proposes no leak-free alternative.
SSD gets exact verification by putting each node in a separate full sequence (batch), at higher compute. Our masks keep a single shared pass.
Self-speculative masked diffusions obtain non-factorized predictions by training a causal final layer. Our variants need no training and run on LLaDA-1.5 as released.

inputs: Official Flash-dLLM code: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM (llada/). Install transformers==4.49.0, accelerate and datasets; Triton ships with PyTorch.
Model: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 (bf16).
Data: openai/gsm8k 'main' (train for 5 shots, test for problems).
registration.method:
Setup.
- Work in llada/ of the official repo. Load LLaDAModelLM as eval_llada.py does: AutoConfig with config.flash_attention = True, from_pretrained in bf16, cuda, eval.
- Prompts: lm-eval-style 5-shot GSM8K, no chat template. Take the first 5 train examples as 'Question: <q>\nAnswer: <a>', joined by '\n\n', then append '\n\nQuestion: <test q>\nAnswer:'.
- Problems: the first 256 test problems.
- Decoding: a copy of generate_with_Flash_dLLM with batch_size=32, gen_length=256, block_length=16, threshold=0.9, gamma=0.8, track_num=4, mask_num=4, temperature=0, mask_id=126336, eos_id=126081, stop_tokens=['Question:','</s>','<|im_end|>'].
- The copy records, per finished problem, the response, generated length (num_decoded minus prompt length), n_steps (iterations) and the number of verify-accepted tokens at every verify step.

Four conditions on the same problems and order:
(A) CONF: verify=False.
(B) PM: verify=True, official code unchanged.
(C) LFXL: verify=True with the official layout per sample ([T tracked | S drafts | S masks], T = 32 - 2S) but a different 32x32 bool mask (True = may attend): tracked rows see tracked only; draft row c sees tracked plus drafts with index <= c; mask row a sees tracked plus drafts with index < a plus itself, and no other mask views.
(D) LF3V: verify=True with a three-view layout per sample:
- T3 = 32 - 3S tracked slots, taken as full_pos[j, num_decoded - T3 : num_decoded]. This always includes the tokens committed by confidence in the current step, because T3 >= 16 - S >= keep_num whenever S <= 8.
- Then S draft views (x_draft at the S search positions), S mask views (mask_id) and S context views (mask_id).
- Query positions = [tracked, search, search, search].
- Set seqlen_keep[j] = T3, so verify_tracked_pos and key_pos_flat use the official formulas with T3. key_pos_flat therefore excludes the T3 tracked and S search positions.
- Mask: tracked rows see tracked plus all context views; context rows see tracked plus all context views; draft row c sees tracked, drafts with index <= c and context views with index > c; mask row a sees tracked, drafts with index < a, itself and context views with index > a.
- Store S per sample. The official code infers S as (32 - T)//2, which no longer holds. Read mask-view logits at offsets [T3+S, T3+2S) and drafts at [T3, T3+S) of the sample's 32-row block.

Acceptance in B-D is the official rule: the longest prefix whose cumulative product of mask-view probabilities of the drafts is >= gamma, with the code's EOS-length zeroing.

Sanity check before the main runs: at the first 5 verify steps, for each a, re-run the C and D verify passes with draft tokens at indices >= a set to mask_id. Confirm that the mask-view logits at index a are bitwise identical, and log max |delta| (must be 0).

Record the wall-clock time of each condition. GSM8K scoring: the prediction is the number after '####' if present, else the last number in the response (strip commas and '$'). It is correct if it equals the gold number after '####'.

event.description: The leak-free three-view verify mask keeps more than 75% of official Flash-Verify's tokens-per-iteration gain over confidence-aware decoding.
event.statistic: retention = (TPS_LF3V - TPS_CONF) / (TPS_PM - TPS_CONF), where TPS = (sum of generated lengths) / (sum of iterations) over the 256 problems.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute TPS per condition from the generation files, then the retention. Secondary statistics:
- Retention for LFXL.
- Verify-accepted tokens per verify pass for PM, LFXL and LF3V.
- GSM8K accuracy per condition, with paired McNemar tests against PM.
- Tokens per second.
- The sanity-check diffs.

Output files:
- outputs/generations_{CONF,PM,LFXL,LF3V}.jsonl: per-problem response, answer, correctness, iterations, generated length.
- outputs/verify_steps_{PM,LFXL,LF3V}.jsonl: per-verify-step S and accepted count.
- outputs/sanity.json: invariance diffs.
- outputs/summary.json: all statistics and timings.
evaluation.controls:
- CONF and PM are the paper's reference conditions.
- LFXL is a second leak-free design. It separates the cost of hiding later positions from the cost of giving them draft-independent [MASK] context.
- The bitwise invariance check confirms both new masks are actually leak-free.
- All conditions share problems, prompts, batch order and hyperparameters.

registration.full_scale_study: Compare the accuracy-throughput Pareto frontiers of the official, three-view and XLNet-style masks across gamma from 0.6 to 1.0 and several tracking budgets. Use full GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP with multiple seeds, and include fidelity to exact sequential verification. If retention is high, release the three-view mask as a drop-in fix for Flash-Verify and SimSD-style verifiers. If it is low, quantify how much throughput the paper's numbers owe to leakage.

agent.reason: Retention will be roughly one minus the leak share of verify-accepted tokens, and the three-view verifier is slightly more conservative than the exact conditional. If the leak echo is as consequential as I suspect, losing more than a quarter of the gain is somewhat more likely than not; the layout change also adds implementation risk.

judge_astra.reason: Legitimate conditioning on earlier drafts should preserve some benefit, but removing indirect information paths and reducing refreshed tracked slots can both lower acceptance. Retaining more than 75% of the incremental gain is consequently a demanding threshold.

judge_fable.reason: Retention is roughly 1 minus the leak-induced share of acceptances, which I expect to be ~20–35%, plus a further loss from fewer recomputed tracked tokens (T3 = 32-3S); the threshold of 0.75 sits near the center of my distribution, and the three-view layout is implementation-heavy and time-tight, so failures lean toward low retention.

judge_opus.reason: Retention above 75% needs the leak, plus the second-order legitimate information the three-view mask also removes, to account for less than about a quarter of verify acceptances. That is roughly even given my uncertainty about leak size. This run also has the highest implementation risk (new layout, inferring the search count S, key positions), and bugs here mostly push retention down.

judge_sol.reason: Legitimate conditioning on earlier drafts could preserve substantial parallelism, but the three-view design removes potentially confidence-inflating feedback and reduces refreshed tracking context. Retaining over 75% of the incremental gain is therefore a demanding threshold.

judge_luna.reason: The three-view design preserves direct high-confidence commits and supplies draft-independent masked context, so it could retain much of the verification gain. But the 75% cutoff is demanding: proper sequential conditionals and fewer tracked slots may reduce the number of extra accepted tokens.

judge_muse.reason: Three-view mask preserves earlier-draft conditioning plus draft-independent [MASK] context like speculative decoding, so most of the ~2x tokens/step gain should remain; main uncertainty is fewer tracked slots and S>8 fitting within 32 tokens.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It introduces Flash-Verify's single-pass verification with a draft view and a [MASK] view under its official mask. It reports the tokens-per-step gain over confidence-aware decoding, but I found no test of whether that gain depends on multi-hop attention paths through which a token's own draft can reach its verifier, and no leak-free mask variant.

SimSD designs a training-free single-pass attention mask over reference/draft and current tokens for dLLM speculative verification on SDAR models. Its abstract does not mention a leakage analysis, a leak-free two-stream or three-view mask, or a measure of how much throughput survives a leak-free mask.
XLNet's two-stream attention is the source of the leak-free principle, but it is used for permutation-LM pretraining, not training-free verification in a dLLM.

This work proposes a framework for designing information-flow masks (including Block Two-Stream Attention) for training consistency. It does not study inference-time dLLM verification or Flash-dLLM's gain in tokens per step.
Self-speculative masked diffusion gets valid non-factorized verification by training a causal final layer. It is not a training-free mask swap on LLaDA-1.5, and it does not measure leakage.

Trajectory-level speculative decoding for dLLMs uses blockwise verification with bidirectional masking and states conditions for exactness. It does not compare leaky and leak-free single-pass masks inside Flash-Verify.

opus.reason: My searches found no paper that checks whether Flash-Verify's (or SimSD's) single-pass verify mask lets a draft leak to its own verifier, or that measures how much of the tokens-per-step gain remains under leak-free two-stream or three-view masks at the same one-pass cost. The nearest work either proposes leaky single-pass masks (seed, SimSD), uses two-stream or causal masks at training time (XLNet, Hasse-diagram masks, self-speculative masked diffusions), or gets exactness by other means. This is based on searching abstracts only; I did not read the seed's or SimSD's full text, but nothing I found answers the question, so I judge it distinct.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM compares official Flash-Verify with confidence-aware decoding, but does not test whether its tokens-per-iteration gain survives blocking indirect draft-to-verifier attention paths.

SimSD uses paired data/mask views and acknowledges higher-order discrepancies from sequential denoising. It does not evaluate the proposed two-stream or draft-independent three-view masks, or measure gain retention after removing those paths.
XLNet establishes content/query-stream separation for permutation-language-model pretraining, not training-free diffusion self-verification or retention of Flash-Verify's parallelism gain.
SSD verifies separate candidate sequence states in a batched forward pass. Its lossless acceleration results do not answer the shared-query mask-ablation question posed here.
COVER addresses direct self-leakage through KV-cache override and diagonal correction for leave-one-out revision. It does not examine causal draft-prefix verification with two- or three-view masks.
Self-Speculative Masked Diffusions trains a hybrid non-causal/causal architecture, rather than changing verification masks in a released dLLM without training.

sol.reason: As of 2026-10-07, I found no work answering whether Flash-Verify retains its parallelism gain after the proposed removal of indirect draft-to-verifier paths. Although two-stream isolation and diffusion self-verification have substantial precedent, the three-view mask comparison and gain-retention experiment address an unsettled question rather than merely changing a dataset, model, or metric.

opus.reason: No list entry proposes leak-free XLNet-style or three-view verify masks and measures how much of the tokens-per-step gain they retain.

sol.reason: No listed experiment replaces the official verifier with leak-free two-stream and three-view masks and measures retention of its parallel-decoding gain.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: exp/run.py holds a copy of generate_with_Flash_dLLM from seed/llada/generate.py. It uses the official model code (flash_attention=True, bf16) and the official Triton kernels imported from /workspace/seed/llada. The copy changes only four things: the verify mask/layout chosen by mode; S stored per sample instead of inferred as (32-T)//2; logging; and the sanity check. Settings follow the registration: LLaDA-1.5, lm-eval-style 5-shot GSM8K prompts (first 5 train examples, no chat template), the first 256 test problems, batch 32, gen 256, block 16, eps 0.9, gamma 0.8, track_num 4, mask_num 4. The four conditions run in one process on the same problems in the same order:
- CONF: verify=False.
- PM: the official mask, unchanged.
- LFXL: two-stream mask on the official layout.
- LF3V: layout [T3 tracked | S drafts | S masks | S context-[MASK]], T3 = 32-3S, seqlen_keep = T3, with the registered mask.
Acceptance is the official cumulative-product rule, including the EOS zeroing.

Sanity check: at the first 5 verify steps of each verify run, I re-run the verify pass once for each index a, with drafts at indices >= a replaced by mask_id, and compare the mask-view logits at index a. LFXL and LF3V are bitwise identical (max |delta| = 0 over 1261 and 1273 rows). I also ran PM as an extra positive control that was not registered; it is not identical (max |delta| = 10.6), which shows the leak in the official mask is real. The sanity re-runs are included in each condition's wall clock; summary.json also reports their time separately.

Result from my test run of the exact evaluation command (one repetition, greedy decoding):
- Tokens per iteration: CONF 2.886, PM 5.656, LFXL 3.593, LF3V 4.211.
- Retention: LF3V 0.478 (below the 0.75 threshold, so the registered event did not occur); LFXL 0.255.
- Verify-accepted tokens per verify pass: PM 2.19, LFXL 0.57, LF3V 1.23.
- Accuracy: CONF 85.2%, PM 83.2%, LFXL 84.0%, LF3V 84.8%. Paired McNemar tests against PM are all non-significant (p = 0.38 to 0.83); with n=256 this does not show that accuracy is the same.
- Tokens per second: CONF 149.6, PM 227.1, LFXL 156.9, LF3V 177.9.

Changes from the registration: none in the design. The one interpretation I made is that S per sample uses the official formula, min(max(length_num - keep_num, 0), 8), in every condition. The 0.478 comes from a single run on one GPU; small numerical differences on another machine could shift it slightly. Full runtime is about 17 minutes plus the pip install and model download.

departures: exp/run.py runs the official mask (PM) through the bitwise leak check as an extra, unregistered positive control. It does not touch decoding or the retention statistic, so it cannot change the result.

exp/run.py sets S per sample with the official formula min(max(length_num - keep_num, 0), 8) in every condition. The registration leaves this open, the engineer disclosed it, and it matches the official code, so it should not change the result.

exp/run.py runs the sanity re-runs inside each verify condition's timed loop, which inflates wall clock by about 4.5 s per condition. This affects only the secondary tokens-per-second figure, and summary.json also reports tokens per second excluding the sanity time. It does not affect tokens per iteration or retention.

The engineer's notes quote tokens per second (CONF 149.6, PM 227.1) from the submitted full_run.log, not from the evaluation run (139.5 and 218.1 in outputs/summary.json). This is a reporting inconsistency in a secondary metric only. Tokens per iteration and retention are identical in both runs.

I found no departures in data, model, prompt format, sample size, decoding hyperparameters, either mask definition, the LF3V layout and read offsets, the acceptance rule, the scoring rule or the retention statistic. The masks built by build_mask match the registered specification row by row.
problems: No uncertainty estimate is given for retention: one deterministic run on 256 problems, with no bootstrap over problems. Still, 0.478 is far from the 0.75 threshold, and per-condition TPS differs by large margins.

The leak check covers only the first 5 verify steps of each run, as the registration specifies (about 1,260–1,270 rows). It supports, but does not exhaustively prove, leak-freeness over the whole run. Because the masks are fixed per S and the code is deterministic, this is a minor concern.

I could not verify from the files whether the verify forward pass writes the KV cache. If it does, the sanity re-runs could slightly perturb the first 5 steps of each verify run. Any effect would be confined to about 5 of more than 6,700 iterations and would apply to PM, LFXL and LF3V alike.
The notes mix tokens-per-second numbers from the engineer's earlier run (full_run.log) with evaluation results; the protected evaluation gives somewhat lower throughput.
The accuracy comparisons are non-significant McNemar tests at n=256 and cannot establish that the conditions are equally accurate. The engineer states this correctly.
opus.reason: The code in exp/run.py follows the registered design closely: the same official decoding loop, the registered 5-shot prompts and first 256 problems, the specified hyperparameters, two leak-free masks that match the registered definitions, the correct read offsets for the three-view layout, and the registered retention statistic. The protected run reproduced the engineer's numbers exactly. Retention was 0.478 for LF3V (below the 0.75 threshold, so the event did not occur) and 0.255 for LFXL, and the bitwise checks confirm both new masks are leak-free while the official mask is not (max delta 10.6). The result is a credible, controlled negative finding: about half of Flash-Verify's tokens-per-iteration gain over confidence decoding depends on attention paths that let a draft reach its own verifier. It is limited by one dataset, one gamma, one run with no confidence interval, and inconclusive accuracy comparisons, so it is meaningful but not strong enough for the top score.

departures: exp/run.py adds an unregistered invariance check for PM as a positive control. These discarded reruns add about 4.54 seconds to PM's measured wall time and affect its reported tokens per second, but do not enter the registered tokens-per-iteration statistic.

exp/run.py performs the sanity checks inside the measured generation runs, rather than as a separate check before the main runs. This affects wall-clock throughput; separate sanity timings are provided. There is no evidence that it changed generation counters or retention.

exp/run.py logs invariance failures without enforcing the registration's requirement that LFXL and LF3V differences must be zero. Both conditions actually passed every recorded comparison, so this procedural departure did not affect this run's conclusion.

exp/run.py's num_eq accepts numerical differences smaller than 1e-6 rather than requiring exact numerical equality. This could affect secondary accuracy scores for near-equal answers, although no affected case is established here; it cannot affect the registered retention statistic.
problems: The throughput loss cannot be interpreted as a clean numerical estimate of the gain caused solely by leakage. In exp/run.py, LF3V also changes tracked-token recomputation and cached-key composition, while LFXL removes later mask-view context. These are registered interventions, but they change more than an isolated information channel.

outputs/sanity.json establishes invariance under the specified replacement intervention at the first five verify steps. It does not independently establish correctness at every subsequent step or equivalence to exact sequential verification, which was not evaluated.

outputs/summary.json reports one configuration on the first 256 GSM8K test problems without uncertainty intervals for retention. The result supports the negative finding for this setting, not a universal failure of leak-free verification. The non-significant McNemar tests do not establish accuracy equivalence.

Wall-clock measurements include sanity reruns and use a fixed condition order without repeated timing trials. Although exp/run.py also reports throughput excluding sanity time, these measurements do not establish equal verification cost or a precise general speed comparison. The engineer's submitted full_run.log has different timings from the protected evaluation and should not be substituted for it.

run_eval.sh lacks pipefail, so set -e would not reliably detect a Python failure inside its logging pipeline; its final check also verifies only that result.json exists. Complete fresh-evaluation logs and artifacts provide evidence of successful execution here, so this robustness issue does not invalidate the observed result.
sol.reason: The visible implementation matches the registered data, prompts, model configuration, decoding settings, mask layouts, controls, and primary statistic, with no outcome-changing departure identified. The protected evaluation completed with all registered artifacts, and its aggregate lengths and iteration counts reproduce retention of 0.4781889969, below the registered 0.75 threshold. Both proposed masks passed the recorded invariance checks, while PM showed sensitivity to the prohibited draft replacements, providing a useful positive control. This is a credible and meaningful negative finding for the registered setting, but limited precision and the absence of an exact sequential reference prevent stronger causal or general claims.

departures: Sanity re-forwards are interleaved into the first 5 verify steps of the measured PM/LFXL/LF3V runs in exp/run.py, not run separately before the main runs, and PM is included though the registration required only LFXL and LF3V. outputs/summary.json wall-clock and tokens/second therefore include ~4.5s of sanity forwards per verify condition (also stored as sanity_check_s). This does not change tokens-per-iteration or retention if the verify pass does not write KV cache, as the engineer states; it can change only the secondary throughput numbers.

LF3V mask and context views are taken from x[search_pos] rather than the literal mask_id constant (exp/run.py). Those positions are still masked when verified, so content matches the registration and this should not change the result.

extract_pred in exp/run.py falls through to the last number in the whole response if '####' is present but the tail has no number. That can affect only accuracy, and only in that edge case; it does not change retention.
problems: The invariance check in outputs/sanity.json only shows that later drafts do not affect mask-view logits; it does not positively confirm that earlier drafts and context views are attended to. A more blocked mask would still pass. The acceptance ordering (PM 2.19 > LF3V 1.23 > LFXL 0.57) makes a fully blocked mask unlikely but is not a direct check.

Secondary tokens/second in outputs/summary.json includes sanity-check time for the verify conditions but not CONF. tokens_per_second_excl_sanity is also reported; the primary retention statistic is unaffected.
grok.reason: The fresh run implements the registered conditions, prompts, hyperparameters, masks, acceptance rule and retention statistic, and reproduces retention 0.478, so the event (retention > 0.75) did not occur. The listed departures do not plausibly change that value. Generations, iteration counts and verify-step logs are mutually consistent, the PM/CONF tokens-per-iteration ratio is about 1.96x as the paper claims, and the bitwise check shows LFXL/LF3V leak-free while PM leaks (max |delta| 10.6). Accepted tokens per pass support the reading that a large share of the gain depends on the leaky paths. Scope is one 256-problem GSM8K slice and one hyperparameter point, so the negative result is credible and meaningful but not a full characterization.

registration.title: Attention-ranked vs recency vs random selective refresh in Flash-Cache at equal budget: fidelity to full recomputation (GSM8K)
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache recomputes only a fixed budget of decoded tokens per step: 64 tokens (track_num 4 x block 16), ranked by attention logits that the masked window accumulates over layers. Fig. 1b motivates this, and the paper says it keeps cache-served states aligned with full recomputation. The paper reports no equal-budget comparison with trivial selectors such as the most recently decoded tokens or random tokens. The ranking also includes prompt positions, so attention-sink tokens may use up the budget.
registration.hypothesis: At an equal refresh budget of 64 tokens, attention-ranked selection reproduces the full-recomputation output exactly on at least 5 percentage points more GSM8K problems than recency-ranked selection does.
registration.contribution: This is the first equal-budget ablation of Flash-Cache's selection rule against a full-recomputation reference. It separates 'which tokens to refresh' from 'how many'. The same runs also isolate how much the selective-refresh approximation alone changes accuracy under an identical decoding order. That bears on Table 1, where Flash-Cache greedy beats no-cache greedy.

closest_work.difference: Elastic-Cache (same authors) decides when to refresh using attention drift of the most-attended token. It does not compare attention-based selection against recency or random selection at a fixed budget.
Sparse-dLLM evicts cache entries by attention saliency for memory savings. We test refresh selection, not eviction, inside Flash-Cache, against an exact reference.
Window-Diffusion reports locality and a brief post-decode transient in dLLM states, which suggests recency could suffice. It does not test Flash-Cache's attention ranking.
H2O compares heavy-hitter and recent-window KV retention for autoregressive LLMs. We run the analogous question for refresh in bidirectional dLLM decoding.

inputs: Official Flash-dLLM code: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM (llada/). Install transformers==4.49.0, accelerate and datasets.
Model: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 (bf16).
Data: openai/gsm8k 'main' (first train example as the single shot; test problems).
registration.method:
Setup.
- Work in llada/ of the official repo. Load LLaDAModelLM as eval_llada.py does: config.flash_attention = True, bf16, cuda, eval.
- Prompts: 1-shot GSM8K in lm-eval format, no chat template: 'Question: <train q1>\nAnswer: <train a1>\n\nQuestion: <test q>\nAnswer:'.
- Problems: the first 224 test problems.
- Decoding: a copy of generate_with_Flash_dLLM with batch_size=32, gen_length=256, block_length=16, threshold=0.9, gamma=0.8, verify=True, mask_num=4, temperature=0, mask_id=126336, eos_id=126081, stop_tokens=['Question:','</s>','<|im_end|>'].
- The copy records each finished problem's response string (as the function returns it, i.e. after stop-sequence truncation), generated length and n_steps.

Four conditions on the same problems and order:
- FULL: track_num=-1, the official option that recomputes every position at each step, i.e. an exact draft pass.
- ATT: track_num=4, official code.
- REC: track_num=4. In the 'Preparing for next iteration' block, skip the re-sort of full_pos[j, :num_decoded - keep_num] by attn_scores. full_pos then keeps the prompt positions followed by decoded positions in commit order, so the tracked slice holds the 64 most recently decoded tokens.
- RAND: track_num=4. Replace the attn_scores-based ranks with torch.randperm of the same length, from a generator seeded with 0 (a fresh permutation each step).

Everything else stays unchanged. As in the official design, the tracked tokens of the verify pass follow the same ordering. For ATT, also log at each step the fraction of the 64 tracked slots, excluding tokens committed in that step, that are prompt positions. Record wall-clock time per condition.

GSM8K scoring: the prediction is the number after '####' if present, else the last number in the response (strip commas and '$'). It is correct if it equals the gold number.

event.description: Attention-ranked refresh reproduces the full-recomputation response exactly on more than 5 percentage points more problems than recency-ranked refresh.
event.statistic: EM_ATT - EM_REC in percentage points, where EM_X = percentage of the 224 problems whose stripped response string is identical to the FULL response.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute EM against FULL for ATT, REC and RAND. Secondary statistics:
- Mean token-level common-prefix fraction with FULL.
- Final-answer agreement with FULL.
- Accuracy of each condition, with paired McNemar tests. FULL vs ATT shows whether selective refresh alone changes accuracy under an identical decoding order.
- Tokens per iteration and tokens per second.
- Mean prompt share of ATT's tracked slots.

Output files:
- outputs/generations_{FULL,ATT,REC,RAND}.jsonl: per-problem response, answer, correctness, iterations, length.
- outputs/att_prompt_share.jsonl: per-step prompt share for ATT.
- outputs/summary.json: all statistics.
evaluation.controls: FULL is the exact reference. RAND tests whether the choice of tokens matters at all at this budget. All conditions share prompts, batch order and decoding hyperparameters, so only the refresh selection differs.

registration.full_scale_study: Sweep refresh budget (16-256 tokens) against selector (attention, recency, recency plus attention sinks, random, attention excluding prompt) on GSM8K, MATH and HumanEval at 256 and 512 tokens. Measure per-step logit drift against full recomputation, accuracy and throughput. If recency matches attention, simplify Flash-Cache by dropping score accumulation. If attention wins, identify the heads and layers that make it work.

agent.reason: The attention-ranked and recency-ranked sets should overlap heavily: newly decoded and adjacent tokens dominate both, and attention may spend slots on sink or prompt tokens. The exact-match difference is therefore likely within a few points of noise, and recency could even win.

judge_astra.reason: High attention does not necessarily identify the stale representations most worth refreshing; recency could capture the largest post-commit changes. Whole-response exact matching may also suppress both agreement rates, making a greater-than-five-point attention advantage less likely.

judge_fable.reason: Staleness is concentrated in recently decoded tokens while high-attention prompt/sink tokens drift little, so recency should approximate full recomputation about as well as attention ranking; exact-string-match differences are noisy and a >5 pp systematic advantage for ATT seems unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: Both selectors share the dominant approximations: stale far-masked and prompt K/V. Attention ranking may waste slots on stable attention-sink and prompt tokens while recency refreshes the drifting left context. An exact-match gap above 5 points in attention's favour on 224 noisy paired problems is unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Attention concentration does not establish that high-attention states most need refreshing; recency directly targets recently changed positions. Whole-response exact match could also be low for both approximations, limiting the measurable attention advantage.

judge_luna.reason: Attention ranking is a plausible way to prioritize context relevant to current predictions, but recency may be a strong proxy for which cached states have changed, and the ranking may include prompt positions. Exact response matching is also a brittle measure, making a greater-than-five-point advantage uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Fig. 1b shows attention concentration but not that top-attended differ from recent, and ranking includes static prompt sinks that waste the 64-token budget; recency likely matches attention for fidelity to FULL, making >5pp exact-match lead unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Seed paper. It motivates attention-ranked tracking (Fig. 1b) and only varies the size of the track budget (Fig. 5), measuring accuracy and throughput. It never compares the attention selector against recency or random selection at the same budget, and never measures agreement with full recomputation.

EntropyCache refreshes the k most recently decoded tokens (k=64) on LLaDA/Dream with GSM8K, using a sliding window. Its argument for recency comes from tracking trajectories of individual tokens. It compares against d2Cache (attention rollout) and Elastic-Cache only as complete methods with different triggers and budgets. In the parts I read (main text through Appendix C.1), I found no selector swap at a fixed budget inside a single framework. I could not read the last part of its appendix (Appendix G and later), so an ablation there cannot be ruled out.

d2Cache selects which tokens to refresh using certainty and attention rollout. I only saw the abstract. Any ablations it has would be of its own selector, not Flash-Cache's top-k attention tracking measured for output fidelity against an exact reference.
Elastic-Cache (same authors) decides when and from which layer to refresh, based on attention drift of the most-attended token. It does not compare token selectors at a fixed budget.
Window-Diffusion reports locality and a short instability right after a token is decoded, which suggests recency could work. It does not test attention-ranked refresh against recency.
H2O compares heavy-hitter retention with a recent-window baseline for eviction in autoregressive LLMs. It does not study refresh selection in bidirectional dLLM decoding.

opus.reason: Prior work has both kinds of selector: attention-based ones (Flash-Cache, d2Cache) and a recency-based one (EntropyCache, also k=64 on GSM8K). However, I found no paper that swaps selectors inside one framework at an identical refresh budget and scores each against full recomputation. EntropyCache is the closest because it supports recency as a design choice, but its comparisons are between whole methods that differ in more than the selector. I could not read the end of its appendix, so this judgment is somewhat uncertain.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM introduces attention-ranked selective refresh and sweeps tracking budgets, but does not compare attention, recency and random selectors at equal budget or report exact-response agreement with full recomputation.
d2Cache already refreshes influential prompt and decoded tokens using attention rollout, but does not report the proposed equal-budget attention-versus-recency fidelity comparison.

Polestar compares drift-based, cosine-change, uncertainty and random refresh selection on the same trajectory and budget. It measures identification of stale KV positions, rather than comparing attention-importance ranking with commit recency through full-response fidelity.

ACache compares selective-recomputation criteria at matched budgets, including attention-based selection and random controls. Its selection is fixed per request over shared affix tokens for cross-request reuse, not dynamically reselected over decoded tokens within Flash-Cache.

Window-Diffusion analyzes recent versus earlier decoded tokens' representation stability and updates recently decoded tokens within inference phases, but does not directly compare recency and attention-ranked refresh at equal budget.

H2O compares attention-heavy-hitter and recent-token retention under constrained KV-cache budgets in autoregressive models. Cache eviction under causal attention does not answer which bidirectional dLLM states should be refreshed while retaining the full cache.

sol.reason: Attention-guided selective refresh and equal-budget selector ablations already exist, so those general ideas are not novel. However, none of the work I found answers whether attention-ranked refresh better preserves full-recomputation responses than commit-recency refresh at a fixed budget in Flash-Cache. That specific comparison remains distinct as of 2026-10-07.

opus.reason: Both compare Eq. 2 attention tracking against recency and random tracking at an equal budget under Flash-Verify, judging fidelity against full recomputation as well as accuracy.

sol.reason: Both compare attention, recency and random refresh selection at a fixed budget and measure decoding fidelity against a full-recomputation reference.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (exp/run.py, exp/run_eval.sh): the registered four-condition experiment, as registered. Setup: LLaDA-1.5 in bf16 with flash_attention=True. Prompts are 1-shot GSM8K in lm-eval format (first train example, no chat template), run on the first 224 test problems. I did not copy the decoding function by hand. The official generate_with_Flash_dLLM is read from /workspace/seed/llada/generate.py and changed by a few string replacements, each checked to match exactly once:
(1) a selector switch in the "Preparing for next iteration" re-sort:
- ATT/FULL: the official attn_scores sort.
- REC: no re-sort.
- RAND: torch.randperm from one CPU generator seeded with 0, a fresh permutation per slot per step.
(2) logging of the per-step prompt share.
(3) recording of per-problem iterations and length.
(4) print is silenced.
Everything else is the official code. Hyperparameters: verify=True, batch 32, gen_length 256, block 16, threshold 0.9, gamma 0.8, mask_num 4, the registered stop tokens. track_num is -1 for FULL and 4 for the other three conditions.

Small choices and changes:
- Before the timed conditions, an untimed ATT warm-up runs on the first 32 problems so that Triton compilation does not inflate ATT's wall-clock time.
- Prompt-share logging also runs for REC and RAND. This keeps the per-step overhead the same across the timed conditions. Their logs go to extra files (extra_*_prompt_share.jsonl).
- How I defined the secondary statistics:
  - Token prefix fraction = common token prefix / the longer token length.
  - Answer agreement compares the extracted numbers.
  - Prompt share = prompt positions among the 64 tracked decoded slots chosen for the next step, excluding positions committed in that step.
- Config comes from the repo's LLaDAConfig, not AutoConfig.
- Throughput = tokens returned by the function / wall time.
- result.json value = EM_ATT - EM_REC in percentage points.

Result from my full test run of the evaluation command on this machine. The evaluation regenerates it; FULL was deterministic across two runs, but I did not test reproducibility for the other conditions or on a fresh machine.
- Statistic: +4.46 pp. EM against FULL was 14.29% for ATT, 9.82% for REC and 3.57% for RAND. The threshold is > 5, so the registered event did not occur. ATT still beat REC in the paired comparison (15 vs 5 discordant problems, exact McNemar p=0.041, bootstrap 95% CI 0.45 to 8.48 pp). So the shortfall against the threshold is not evidence that ATT and REC are equivalent.
- Exact reproduction of FULL is rare for every selector. Mean token prefix fraction was 0.33 for ATT, 0.30 for REC and 0.16 for RAND.
- Accuracy:
  - FULL 81.25%, ATT 82.59%, REC 81.25%, RAND 74.55%.
  - FULL vs ATT: McNemar p=0.70. This does not show that selective refresh changes accuracy; it also does not establish that it leaves accuracy unchanged.
  - RAND is worse than FULL (p=0.024) and decodes fewer tokens per iteration (4.06, vs 5.72 for ATT and 5.45 for REC).
- On average 49% of ATT's tracked slots (excluding tokens committed that step) were prompt positions.
- Throughput was about 244 tok/s for ATT, 247 for REC, 198 for RAND and 98 for FULL.

Checks:
- A second FULL run gave 100% EM against the first, so run-to-run nondeterminism does not explain the gaps. It was run with the same batch configuration; it is kept in dev_full_repeat/.
- dev_smoke_n16_bs8/ is a 16-problem smoke test, used only to check the pipeline.

Caveat: continuous batching means the slot composition differs between conditions, which is inherent to the official code.

The evaluation took about 16 minutes here with the model already cached; on a fresh machine it also downloads the model (about 15 GB).

departures: exp/run.py adds an untimed ATT warm-up on the first 32 problems before the timed conditions. This is not in the registration. Only wall-clock time could be affected, not generations or the EM statistic.

RAND in exp/run.py uses one CPU torch.Generator seeded with 0 per condition and draws a fresh permutation per slot per step. This is consistent with the registration ('fresh permutation each step'). It is one realisation of a stochastic selector, so the RAND numbers carry seed variance.

exp/run.py passes steps=256, sliding_window=True, is_instruct=False and remasking='low_confidence' to the official function. The registration does not name these. They are presumably the official base-model settings, but this cannot be verified here. They are identical across conditions, so they are unlikely to change the ATT–REC difference.

Secondary-statistic definitions in exp/run.py are choices the registration leaves open: prefix fraction over the longer token length, and numeric answer agreement. A bootstrap CI and an exact McNemar test on EM are added beyond the registration. None of this changes the primary statistic.

With continuous batching in the official code, slot and batch composition differs between conditions even though problem order is shared. The registration's controls say all conditions 'share batch order'. Batch-dependent bf16 numerics could add divergence from FULL for every selector. This could lower absolute EM levels for ATT, REC and RAND, but it applies to all of them and is inherent to the registered code path.

The result sits close to the threshold. The bootstrap CI [0.45, 8.48] pp in outputs/summary.json includes 5, so the data neither confirm nor rule out a >5 pp advantage; only the direction (ATT > REC, p=0.041) is supported.
outputs/generations_RAND.jsonl comes from a single seed, so RAND results lack seed variance.

opus.reason: The code patches the official generate_with_Flash_dLLM with asserted, minimal string replacements. That indicates deterministic, genuine model outputs, and the EM statistic is computed transparently from the generation files. The registered event did not occur (4.46 pp vs >5). The paired data still show attention ranking modestly beating recency on exact reproduction (15 vs 5 discordant problems), with both far from reproducing full recomputation, ~49% of ATT's tracked slots spent on prompt positions, and random selection clearly worse in accuracy. exp/run.py logs prompt share for REC and RAND as well as ATT, producing extra_*_prompt_share.jsonl files. Its instrumentation also adds position cloning and CPU-synchronized logging operations. These can affect timing and throughput, especially when conditions take different numbers of steps, but do not evidently change token selection or the primary statistic.

outputs/summary.json reports a +4.46 percentage-point EM difference with bootstrap interval [0.45, 8.48]. The registered >5-point event did not occur, but the interval includes effects above 5 points. The nominal McNemar p=0.041 tests equal EM probabilities, not whether the advantage exceeds 5 points, and neither this result nor the threshold miss establishes equivalence.

dev_full_repeat/ is submitted development evidence, not a repeat performed by the protected evaluation. dev_full_repeat.log shows FULL generation completed before summarization failed because other conditions were absent. registration.title: Swap test: does Flash-Cache's fused Triton projection/RoPE/cache-write kernel speed up end-to-end decoding at batch 32 on an A100?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache's first contribution is an IO-aware Triton kernel that fuses QKV projection, RoPE and cache writes. Fig. 1a reports a 1.37x per-layer speedup, measured on an RTX 3090. The headline throughput uses batch 32 on an A100, where each draft pass projects about 4.6K query tokens. The kernel (_flash_qkv_proj_cache_fwd) processes 16 query rows per program per head and re-reads that head's weights for every 16-row tile. At this size that may be slower than one cuBLAS GEMM.
registration.hypothesis: Replacing the fused Triton projection kernels with unfused PyTorch operations (cuBLAS GEMMs, elementwise RoPE, indexed cache write), with everything else identical, raises end-to-end Flash-dLLM decoding throughput (tokens/s) at batch 32 on an A100 by more than 5%.
registration.contribution: Tests the IO-aware fusion claim at the paper's own operating point (A100, batch 32). This separates how much of Flash-dLLM's speed comes from kernel fusion versus its algorithmic components (fixed-size selective refresh, verification).

closest_work.difference: FlashAttention showed that IO-aware fusion speeds up attention. We test whether fusing the projection, RoPE and cache write pays off end to end at batch 32 against cuBLAS.
This work profiles diffusion LMs in general (arithmetic intensity, batching) but does not evaluate Flash-Cache's fused kernels or swap them out end to end.

inputs: Official Flash-dLLM code: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM (llada/). Install transformers==4.49.0, accelerate and datasets.
Model: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 (bf16).
Data: openai/gsm8k 'main' (5 train shots; test problems).
registration.method:
Setup.
- Work in llada/ of the official repo. Load LLaDAModelLM as eval_llada.py does (config.flash_attention = True, bf16, cuda, eval).
- Prompts: lm-eval-style 5-shot GSM8K, no chat template: the first 5 train examples as 'Question: <q>\nAnswer: <a>' joined by '\n\n', then '\n\nQuestion: <test q>\nAnswer:'.
- Decoding: generate_with_Flash_dLLM with gen_length=256, block_length=16, threshold=0.9, gamma=0.8, track_num=4, mask_num=4, verify=True, temperature=0, mask_id=126336, eos_id=126081, stop_tokens=['Question:','</s>','<|im_end|>'].

Variants. Add a global switch inside flash_cache_triton.flash_fused_elastic_cache.
- FUSED: the official code.
- UNFUSED, non-verify branch: replace the _flash_qkv_proj_cache_fwd launch with:
  q = F.linear(x_normed, self.q_proj.weight); k = F.linear(x_normed, self.k_proj.weight); v = F.linear(x_normed, self.v_proj.weight) (three separate GEMMs, as in conventional LLaDA code);
  sin = rotary_emb_pos[0][query_pos_flat]; cos = rotary_emb_pos[1][query_pos_flat] (shape M x 128);
  in float32, view q and k as M x 32 x 128 and compute t*cos + rotate_half(t)*sin, with rotate_half(t) = cat(-t[..., 64:], t[..., :64]); cast to bf16;
  self.k_cache[query_pos_flat] = k.view(M, 4096); self.v_cache[query_pos_flat] = v; pass this q on to the unchanged attention kernels.
- UNFUSED, verify branch: replace _flash_verify_qkv_proj_fwd in the same way. q, k and v get RoPE at query_pos_flat and go into the q/k/v buffers; there is no cache write.
- Attention kernels, MLP and the decoding loop are untouched.

Correctness check. On one batch, compare layer-0 outputs of both variants (q and the written K/V cache rows); relative error should be below 2e-2.

Timing at batch 32.
- For each variant, run one untimed warm-up generate call on 32 extra test problems.
- Then time runs on the first 160 test problems at batch_size=32 in the order FUSED rep1, UNFUSED rep1, FUSED rep2, UNFUSED rep2.
- Measure wall-clock seconds with torch.cuda.synchronize() around each call. tokens/s = num_tokens returned by the function / seconds. Also record the sum of n_steps (iterations).

Secondary measurements.
- One timed run per variant at batch_size=1 on the first 16 problems, after a 2-problem warm-up.
- A profiling pass of 20 decoding iterations at batch 32 that times only the projection stage per layer call with torch.cuda.Event, for each variant.
- Accuracy: the prediction is the number after '####', else the last number in the response; compare with the gold number.

- outputs/generations_{FUSED,UNFUSED}.jsonl: per-problem response, correctness, iterations.
