The main uncertainty is whether another implementation path refreshes or protects those entries.

judge_fable.reason: The outcome hinges on whether the agent's reading of keep_num/re-ranking in the released generate.py is correct and whether the verify pass really skips cache writes; if the premise holds the >5% rate is likely, but a misreading, block-based windowing, or a failed layer-0 ground-truth control would nullify it.

judge_opus.reason: The event depends on the designer's hedged reading that keep_num is overwritten before re-ranking being a real defect. It also depends on instrumenting the released Triton code and passing the 95% layer-0 ground-truth check within the limits. If the premise holds, the fraction is probably large; otherwise it is about 0.

judge_sol.reason: If the described keep_num overwrite and non-writing verify kernel are present, exceeding 5% seems likely because affected tokens lose their mandatory refresh. The main uncertainties are the actual selection semantics and successful instrumentation of the shipped kernels.

judge_luna.reason: The paper’s pseudocode explicitly includes newly decoded tokens in the next tracked set, which weighs against the suspected defect. The registered concern about keep_num suggests the released implementation could diverge from that rule; if it does, the proposed visibility failure is plausible.

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It says tokens decoded in an iteration are always refreshed at the next step (Alg. 2). It does not instrument its released verify-mode code to check this token by token, does not test the cached layer-0 keys, and does not report a fix or its effect.

Elastic-Cache, by the same authors, has a similar sliding-window cache design with refresh rules driven by attention. It does not audit whether accepted tokens keep [MASK] keys and values in the cache.

EntropyCache finds that decoded tokens stay volatile for several steps after unmasking and recomputes the most recently decoded tokens. This is a design motivation in a different method, not a check of the Flash-dLLM implementation.

opus.reason: Two searches turned up no work that audits the released Flash-dLLM code, so I judge this experiment distinct. Its question is whether tokens accepted by the confidence threshold under Flash-Verify are later served with stale [MASK] keys and values, checked against recomputed layer-0 keys. Related dLLM caching papers discuss stale caches or recomputing recently decoded tokens, but none tests this property of this implementation.

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM specifies automatic inclusion of newly decoded tokens in the next tracking set and reports decoding ablations, but does not audit whether its released verify-mode implementation preserves that invariant using per-token cached-key measurements.
Elastic-Cache studies sliding-window caching and adaptive refresh, not the interaction between draft acceptance, verification acceptance, and tracking-set re-ranking in Flash-dLLM.

dKV-Cache identifies the importance of recomputing tokens after their MASK-to-token transition and evaluates delayed caching, but does not test the suspected Flash-Verify bookkeeping failure or its targeted repair.

Diagnoses cache-induced content drift through instrumentation and refresh interventions in multimodal Fast-dLLM, rather than testing whether accepted tokens retain MASK-derived cache entries in Flash-dLLM.

sol.reason: The prior work establishes that cache states change upon unmasking and that refresh policies can affect generation, but it does not settle the registered implementation-specific question. Among papers found by 2026-10-07, none reports the proposed per-token visibility audit with layer-0 key validation and a targeted tracking-set repair; the seed's stated invariant is not an empirical audit of its implementation.

What I implemented: the experiment as registered, in one process (probe/run_audit.py). The model is loaded the way eval_llada.py does it: LLaDAModelLM, bf16, flash_attention=True. Prompts are raw-text 5-shot GSM8K, with stop tokens ["Question:","</s>","<|im_end|>"]. probe/generate_probe.py is generated from seed llada/generate.py by string replacement (probe/build_probe.py; the diff is in outputs/patches.diff). The hooks are: before/after each draft-pass model call, at each commit (how=1 or 2), and at sample completion. With probe=None, decoding is unchanged. I made no compatibility edits to the seed model or kernels.

Step 0 (outputs/repo_audit.json): from reading the code, premise_holds=true. In verify mode keep_num is reassigned to the verify-accepted count before the re-ranking (full_pos[:num_decoded-keep_num] sorted by attn_scores). Tokens accepted by the confidence threshold therefore compete with older tokens for tracking. The verify kernel writes only temporary K/V, not k_cache/v_cache.

Fix for run (c): in the two re-ranking lines, num_newly_decoded[j] replaces keep_num, only when verify=True. In verify mode num_newly_decoded[j] is reset every iteration and counts draft-accepted plus verify-accepted tokens. In non-verify mode it accumulates across iterations, so keep_num is kept there.

Choices where the registration was ambiguous:
- "First 3 batches" for the ground-truth check: slots are refilled continuously, so I checked every 10th draft pass while fewer than 3×32 samples had completed.
- "Within 2 positions of the next window": the token was within ±2 positions of a current masked-window position during at least one pass in which it was invisible.
- Throughput is wall time including the probe overhead. Run (a) also includes Triton compile and warm-up because it runs first, so the a-vs-c tokens/s comparison is biased in favour of (c). Tokens per iteration is not affected by this.

Results from my test run (one repetition):
- Registered statistic, run (a): 50 of 13,797 confidence-accepted tokens with a later draft pass were affected, a fraction of 0.0036 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.0025–0.0049). This is below 5%, so the registered event did not occur.
- Excluding EOS tokens: 0.0037.
- Affected tokens were served [MASK] K/V for a mean of 11 draft passes each. Only 2% of them were within 2 positions of the window.
- Invisible decoded tokens: 0.13 per sample per draft pass.

Controls all came out as expected:
- Verify-accepted tokens (how=2) in run (a): 0 of 9,291 affected.
- Run (b), verify=False: 0 of 9,554.
- Run (c), with the fix: 0 affected for both how=1 and how=2.
- Layer-0 key ground truth: agreed with the kv_tok flag at 576 of 576 checked positions (288 flagged [MASK]), so the ≥95% gate passed.

Speed and accuracy:
| Run | Tokens/iter | Tokens/s | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) verify, released code | 5.54 | 202 | 81.9% |
| (b) verify=False, 64 questions | 2.71 | 142 | 82.8% |
| (c) verify, with fix | 5.49 | 219 | 83.1% |

McNemar test, (a) vs (c): 0 vs 2 discordant questions, p=0.5. 160 questions cannot resolve 1–2-point differences, so this does not show the defect is harmless. Tokens per iteration barely moved (5.54 to 5.49).

Interpretation: the code path the registration describes exists, and it does leave some confidence-accepted tokens with [MASK] K/V for many passes. In this setting (GSM8K-256, track_num=4, mask_num=4, γ=0.8) it affected about 0.4% of eligible tokens, far below the 5% threshold. This result covers only this setting; I did not test other tasks or lengths.

The evaluation takes about 5–6 minutes including pip install and the model download.

registration.title: Accepted-prefix fidelity of two-view verification
registration.seed_connection: Appendix C identifies Flash-Verify's mask-view distributions with conditionals obtained by sequentially committing preceding drafts. This experiment tests that operational identification separately from approximate KV caching.
registration.hypothesis: Some tokens accepted by the paper-formulated two-view verifier disagree with a high-margin, fully recomputed sequential conditional in the same fixed verification order.
registration.contribution: A paired measurement of consequential conditional mismatches inside accepted prefixes, rather than a structural observation that attention contexts differ or an aggregate comparison of task accuracy. It distinguishes the verifier-induced distribution from the original bidirectional model's sequential conditionals.

closest_work.difference: Spiffy acknowledges indirect information leakage when sharing bidirectional context across speculative blocks. This experiment measures accepted-token consequences for within-window, duplicated draft/mask verification.

SimSD uses a closely related temporal attention mask and preserves the target distribution induced by that mask. This experiment compares such outputs with separately recomputed conditionals of the original bidirectional model.
FreeDave verifies separately represented candidate states to reproduce a decoding path. Here the object tested is the fidelity of a single shared-context, two-view verification pass.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5, an 8B checkpoint and tokenizer from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
GSM8K main test split from https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k
Flash-dLLM repository at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM, especially llada/generate.py and llada/flash_cache_triton.py, as references for the paired-view mask and RoPE indexing
registration.method: Load one LLaDA-1.5 checkpoint in BF16 on the A100, with eval mode and inference_mode. Use existing CUDA PyTorch and wheel dependencies; do not install the evaluation harness or compile flash-attn. Implement a transparent PyTorch forward using the checkpoint's embedding, normalization, projection, activation, residual, and output modules. Use float32 attention normalization and vocabulary log_softmax, and support explicitly supplied RoPE positions. Validate ordinary full-bidirectional execution against the unmodified Hugging Face model before collecting data: normalized logit RMS error must be below 0.01 and maximum confidence difference below 0.002. Select the first 48 GSM8K test questions for which the tokenized string 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' is at most 160 tokens. Append 96 mask tokens. Construct diagnostic traces by repeatedly performing full recomputation and committing the highest-confidence remaining position in the first 32 response slots; exclude the mask token from prediction, permit EOS, and do not terminate these diagnostic traces at EOS. Save states after 4, 12, and 20 commitments. At each state, draft over the first 16 remaining masked positions. Commit predictions with confidence at least 0.9 into a common context. Sort the remaining positions by decreasing draft confidence, breaking ties by original position, and take at most eight as search positions. Unsearched positions remain masked. Implement the paper's acceptance rule, not the repository's cumulative-product rule: accept an agreeing mask-view mode with confidence at least 0.8, stopping at the first failure. For search positions indexed in verification order, create draft views D_i and masked views M_i with identical original RoPE positions. Let C contain all other physical positions, including directly committed predictions. At every layer, C rows see C and all M but no D; D_i sees C, D_j for j<=i, and M_j for j>i; M_i sees C, D_j for j<i, and M_j for j>=i. Recompute every row; use no approximate cache. For every accepted search position i_k, separately run ordinary full-bidirectional inference on the original sequence with the directly committed set and preceding search drafts committed, but i_k and all later search positions still masked. These oracle evaluations may be batched as independent examples. Hold verification order fixed rather than reranking after each commitment. Use equal physical input lengths for verifier and oracle by adding ignored padding slots to oracle inputs. Record full-vocabulary total variation as a diagnostic, but define a consequential mismatch only when the accepted draft differs from the oracle mode and the oracle's top-one minus top-two probability margin is at least 0.05.

event.description: The accepted-prefix disagreement rate exceeds the registered tolerance after accounting for prompt-level uncertainty.
event.statistic: The lower endpoint of a 95% prompt-cluster bootstrap interval for the fraction of accepted search tokens that disagree with the sequential oracle and have oracle margin at least 0.05

evaluation.procedure: Pool accepted search tokens across the three states of each prompt. The denominator includes every accepted search token; the numerator includes only the defined high-margin oracle mismatches. Bootstrap the 48 prompt IDs with replacement 2,000 times using seed 2026 and recompute the pooled fraction; report its 2.5th percentile as the single registered statistic. Require at least 100 accepted search tokens from at least 20 prompts; otherwise write an insufficient-support status and a null statistic, not a zero. outputs/inputs.jsonl holds questions, token IDs, trace commitments, and snapshot states. outputs/token_scores.jsonl holds draft and verifier predictions, acceptance order, oracle modes and margins, distributional diagnostics, and numerical controls. outputs/summary.json holds counts, the point estimate, interval, registered statistic, and validity status. outputs/metadata.json holds model and repository revisions, software versions, validation errors, timing, and hardware information. A result below the threshold does not establish exact equivalence.
evaluation.controls: No approximate cache is used. Compare repeated identical oracle evaluations to quantify numerical noise. Independently batched copies of the same prefix-conditioned inputs must agree with individually evaluated copies within the forward-validation tolerances. Equal-length ignored padding controls shape-dependent arithmetic. The oracle margin requirement prevents near-ties from being counted as consequential mismatches.

registration.full_scale_study: Measure conditional fidelity across models, window sizes, verification orders, and cache policies; connect mismatches to complete-generation outcomes and evaluate masks or independently represented contexts that repair the identified discrepancy.

agent.reason: Multilayer attention paths and shared context representations can undermine the claimed identification with separately recomputed sequential conditionals. However, the accepted-prefix restriction, high-margin filter, and minimum-support requirement make this event substantially harder than detecting any logit discrepancy.

judge_astra.reason: Sharing context representations across different prefix conditions can change deeper-layer states, making consequential oracle disagreements plausible even without cache approximation. Exceeding the registered lower-bound threshold is less certain because high-confidence acceptance and the oracle-margin filter select relatively stable tokens.

judge_fable.reason: The two-view mask leaks draft identities through multi-layer paths (M_k reads M_{>k} rows that attended to D_k), so the mask-view conditional is not the sequential oracle and some high-margin mismatches are plausible; but accepted tokens carry >=0.8 verifier confidence, so flips to a different oracle mode with margin >=0.05 are probably only ~1-3% of accepted tokens, which with ~150-300 tokens leaves the bootstrap lower bound below 1% most of the time, and the custom LLaDA forward plus the >=100-accepted-token support requirement add failure risk.

judge_opus.reason: The registered mask lets drafts leak indirectly into mask views through later mask views and through context rows, so the verifier is not exactly the sequential conditional. But a counted mismatch requires at least 0.8 verifier confidence against at most about 0.475 oracle mass, which indirect leakage may rarely produce, and a lower bound above 1% needs a true rate of roughly 2.5–3%.

judge_sol.reason: The layerwise mask does not ensure that shared bidirectional hidden states match separately recomputed sequential contexts, making consequential mismatches plausible. The main uncertainties are whether enough mismatches survive prefix acceptance and the high-margin filter to clear the registered confidence bound.

judge_luna.reason: The two-view mask prevents context rows from attending to draft views, while the fully recomputed bidirectional oracle lets committed drafts affect those rows at later layers, making consequential disagreements plausible. The high-margin and minimum-support requirements keep this from being near-certain.

judge_muse.reason: Appendix C's identification ignores that context rows see masks instead of drafts and duplicated positions alter deeper-layer states, so divergence is expected, but confident-mode flips with >=0.05 oracle margin may still be rare for a >1% lower bound.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper proposes the two-view draft-and-verify scheme (Flash-Verify) and reports speed and task accuracy. Based on its abstract and the registration's account of Appendix C, it treats mask-view distributions as sequential conditionals rather than measuring that claim token by token against fully recomputed oracles. I did not read Appendix C myself.

SSD also uses the dLLM as its own drafter and verifier. Its abstract says it verifies drafts with hierarchical trees and produces output identical to stepwise decoding, but it reports that as an end-to-end property of its own method. From the abstract it does not appear to measure Flash-Verify's shared-context mask views against a recomputed bidirectional oracle at each accepted token.

SimSD designs a similar temporal or reference-token attention mask and evaluates throughput and benchmark quality on SDAR models. Going by its abstract, it does not test whether accepted tokens match separately recomputed bidirectional conditionals.

Spiffy is cited by the registration as noting indirect information leakage across speculative blocks. I did not retrieve this paper, so I am relying on that description; it does not appear to quantify high-margin mismatches inside accepted prefixes of a duplicated draft/mask verification window.

FreeDave is described in the registration as verifying separately represented candidate states. I did not retrieve it, but on that description it sidesteps the shared-context question rather than measuring the fidelity of a single two-view pass.

opus.reason: My searches found no paper that pairs tokens accepted by a shared-context draft/mask verifier for dLLMs with recomputed full-bidirectional sequential conditionals and counts high-margin mismatches. The nearest papers (SSD, SimSD, the seed paper) either claim losslessness or report speed and task accuracy for their own mask designs, without this oracle comparison inside accepted prefixes. Some of these judgments rest on abstracts only, so a paper reporting this comparison in its body could have been missed.

closest_work.difference: SimSD Section 4.3 already measures sequential-versus-parallel distribution discrepancies and top-one agreement for a closely related paired temporal mask. It does not measure high-margin sequential-oracle disagreements specifically among tokens accepted by Flash-Verify's agreement-and-confidence rule.

Spiffy Appendix A.2 identifies indirect information leakage through shared bidirectional context, but evaluates its effects primarily through downstream accuracy rather than paired oracle checks of accepted-token decisions.
FreeDave verifies independently represented candidate states to reproduce a sequential decoding path; it does not audit conditional fidelity or false acceptance in a shared-context two-view verifier.

Flash-dLLM Appendix C identifies mask-view outputs with sequential conditionals and provides bounds using that identification, but does not empirically compare accepted search tokens with separately recomputed sequential conditionals.

sol.reason: General non-equivalence between paired-mask verification and sequential denoising is not new: SimSD explicitly acknowledges and empirically measures it. The registered experiment asks the narrower operational question of whether those discrepancies survive verification as accepted, high-margin oracle-disagreeing tokens, while separating them from approximate caching and numerical noise. registration.title: Does refreshing the verifier's cache selectively reject wrong drafts?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Verify reuses the drafter's KV cache. Flash-Cache deliberately leaves many context representations approximate, so drafter-verifier agreement may share cache-induced errors.
registration.hypothesis: Refreshing context KV states before verification improves discrimination between correct and incorrect drafts compared with verification using the drafter's approximate cache.
registration.contribution: A same-input, same-draft intervention that changes only verifier cache freshness and uses uniquely specified, automatically computed token labels. It separates shared approximation errors from semantic error reinforcement and from changes in entire decoding trajectories.

closest_work.difference: DualDiffusion combines approximate drafting with more accurate verification, but compares generation pipelines. This experiment holds draft identities, order, input tokens, and the acceptance rule fixed while intervening only on verifier cache freshness.
ASRD studies errors reinforced by mixed-quality visible context and perturbs embeddings. Here visible token identities are identical between conditions and the intervention is a KV refresh.
Polestar uses representational drift for refresh and commitment decisions. This experiment measures whether refresh specifically improves the correctness discrimination of self-verification.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
A deterministic synthetic arithmetic-infilling dataset generated locally with integer arithmetic and seed 1729
Flash-dLLM code at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM, particularly its cache-update and verification routines
registration.method: Use one BF16 LLaDA-1.5 on the GPU in eval mode. Implement a PyTorch forward with explicit per-layer KV recording and overriding, using the checkpoint's modules and original RoPE positions. Computing all rows and overriding non-active KV entries is acceptable: this is a fidelity diagnostic, not a sparse-kernel timing claim. Validate the no-override path against the original Hugging Face model with normalized logit RMS error below 0.01 and confidence error below 0.002. Generate 192 distinct integer pairs with 100<=b<=a<=999 using NumPy default_rng(1729). The uniquely specified output is SUM=a+b as four zero-padded digits, DIFF=a-b as four digits, and PROD=a*b as six digits. Separate digits with spaces. The prompt explains this format and includes two fixed examples, computed by Python for pairs (317,184) and (426,215). Provide the output field names, separators, and spaces, but mask all 14 answer digits. Locate digit-token positions using tokenizer offsets and verify that each answer digit is one token; treat a failed mapping as an implementation error rather than silently changing the task. Initialize all layer caches with the fully masked answer. Reveal the first eight gold digits, left-to-right, in four updates of two digits each. After each update recompute the remaining masked digit positions plus the two newly revealed positions; preserve all other KV entries. This controlled teacher-reveal trace keeps visible context correct while inducing cache ages. Save snapshots after the first and fourth updates. At each snapshot run a cached draft on remaining digits, directly commit confidence>=0.9 predictions, and choose up to eight remaining search positions in descending cached draft-confidence order. Keep these draft identities and this order fixed in both verifier conditions. The shared-cache condition uses outside-query KV states from the cached draft. The refreshed-cache condition first fully recomputes the same current sequence, including the same directly committed predictions and with all search positions masked, and uses those recomputed outside-query KV states. Both verification passes recompute exactly the same live positions: the two most recently teacher-revealed digits, the directly committed positions, and duplicated draft/mask search views. Exclude cached entries for these live positions so that physical positions are not counted twice. In both passes apply the same paired-view mask: context rows cannot see search draft views; D_i sees preceding/current drafts and later masks; M_i sees preceding drafts and current/later masks. Both copies use the original position. Use the paper-formulated mode-agreement and mask-view confidence>=0.8 rule, stopping at the first rejection; do not substitute the repository's cumulative-product acceptance rule. Label each search draft correct or wrong by its exact expected digit token. A suffix rejected because an earlier position fails is counted as rejected, matching the actual prefix policy. Also record a full-recomputation draft as a diagnostic, without using it to redefine the primary candidate pool.

event.description: Verifier cache refresh improves balanced acceptance discrimination by more than the registered effect size.
event.statistic: The lower endpoint of a 95% prompt-cluster bootstrap interval for J_refreshed minus J_shared, where J is correct-draft acceptance rate minus wrong-draft acceptance rate

evaluation.procedure: For the fixed cached-draft search pool, compute J separately for the two verifier conditions. Correct-draft acceptance rate uses all correct search drafts as its denominator; wrong-draft acceptance rate uses all wrong search drafts. Pool the two cache-age snapshots and bootstrap entire arithmetic instances 2,000 times with seed 2026. Report the 2.5th percentile of the paired J difference. Require at least 50 candidates in each correctness class, each represented by at least ten distinct instances; otherwise return insufficient-support status and a null statistic. outputs/instances.jsonl contains operands, prompts, canonical answers, token mappings, and teacher-reveal states. outputs/verifier_scores.jsonl contains candidate identities, labels, both verifier distributions' summary scores, prefix acceptance decisions, and cache-age diagnostics. outputs/summary.json contains the registered statistic, class denominators, acceptance coverage, and interval. outputs/metadata.json records revisions, validation tests, runtime, and hardware. This measures controlled infilling, not free-running arithmetic accuracy.
evaluation.controls: Token identities, draft order, live recomputation positions, and acceptance thresholds are identical between verifier conditions. A fresh-cache control with every position active must reproduce ordinary full inference. Cached and refreshed verification must agree within numerical tolerance when both are supplied the same fresh cache. Teacher-revealed context contains no wrong tokens, separating cache approximation from erroneous visible context.

registration.full_scale_study: Repeat paired freshness interventions on on-policy mathematical and code-generation traces, identify when refresh rescues incorrect commitments, and test selective refresh triggers that preserve useful acceptance without paying for a full refresh at every step.

agent.reason: Short, correctly teacher-revealed answer contexts may produce only modest consequential cache drift. Refresh might change acceptance generally without improving balanced correctness discrimination enough to clear the five-point lower-bound threshold.

judge_astra.reason: Four small, gold-token reveal updates may not create enough harmful staleness for a large discrimination improvement. Refresh does not independently correct semantic mistakes, and rejecting an early wrong draft can also sacrifice correct suffixes, making a lower bound above 0.05 demanding.

judge_fable.reason: Cache ages of 1-4 teacher-reveal updates on a short, correct-context sequence should perturb KV states very little (Elastic-Cache/Flash-Cache show such staleness is benign), so shared and refreshed verifiers will make nearly identical accept/reject decisions and a J difference with lower bound >0.05 is unlikely; the per-layer KV override machinery is also the hardest to implement under the engineer's budget.

judge_opus.reason: Cache staleness in this teacher-reveal setup is mild (prompt, separators and older revealed digits), and prior caching results suggest it barely shifts predictions. A refresh-induced discrimination gain with a lower bound above 0.05 is implausible.

judge_sol.reason: Refreshing stale states should change some verification scores, but it need not preferentially reject incorrect arithmetic drafts. Shared semantic errors and prefix-induced rejection of correct suffixes make a lower confidence bound above a five-percentage-point discrimination gain demanding.

judge_luna.reason: Refreshing stale KV states could improve the verifier’s separation of correct from wrong drafts, but a changed decision need not improve that separation. The less-stale first snapshot may also dilute the contrast with the fourth.

judge_muse.reason: Refreshing only outside-query KV while holding drafts, order and live positions fixed is subtle, and the 0.05 J-improvement lower bound plus 50-per-class support on hard PROD digits makes the registered event unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DualDiffusion pairs a cheap, approximate drafter with a more accurate verifier, but it compares whole generation pipelines on accuracy versus number of steps. It does not hold draft identities, order and inputs fixed while changing only how fresh the verifier's KV cache is. It also does not measure how well the verifier separates correct drafts from wrong ones.

This is the seed paper. Its Flash-Verify step reuses the drafter's approximate Flash-Cache when verifying, and it reports speed and benchmark accuracy only. It does not test whether a refreshed verifier cache changes how often correct versus wrong drafts are accepted.

Elastic-Cache studies when and where to refresh the cache in diffusion LLMs, judged by end-task accuracy and speed. It has no draft-and-verify stage and no per-token analysis of verifier discrimination.

SSD uses the diffusion LLM itself as both drafter and verifier, with lossless verification trees. It does not examine how cache approximation affects the verifier's ability to discriminate correct from wrong drafts.

ASPIRE refreshes sparse context during drafting in autoregressive self-speculation, aiming at throughput. It is not about diffusion LLMs, and it does not run a controlled experiment on verifier cache freshness.

opus.reason: I found no prior work that runs a paired intervention changing only the verifier's KV-cache freshness, with the same drafts, the same inputs and the same acceptance rule, to measure whether diffusion-LLM self-verification gets better at telling correct drafts from wrong ones. The related papers cover cache-refresh policies, self-speculative decoding, and pairing an approximate drafter with an accurate verifier, but each is judged on end-to-end speed or accuracy, not on this question. I read only the opening section of the seed paper and the abstracts of the other papers; on that evidence the question looks open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM compares cached and uncached decoding pipelines and varies tracking budgets, but does not isolate verifier cache freshness while holding drafts, their order, and visible tokens fixed.

DualDiffusion verifies approximate drafts with a full-attention model, but evaluates generation pipelines rather than paired stale-versus-refreshed verification of identical candidates with correctness-stratified acceptance.

Archer studies bounded prompt-cache reuse during rollback and delayed feedback from tentative errors. The proposed experiment instead isolates cache freshness in paired-view prefix verification under a controlled teacher-reveal trace.

COVER uses KV overrides for context-preserving leave-one-out verification and studies cache-drift-aware seed selection, but does not test whether refreshing outside-query context selectively changes acceptance of correct versus wrong fixed drafts.
Polestar studies drift-guided cache refresh and token commitment, including cache-staleness diagnostics, rather than correctness discrimination by a verifier-only freshness intervention.
ASRD addresses error reinforcement through anchor-derived embedding perturbations in mixed-quality context, not a KV-refresh intervention with identical token identities and verification rules.

sol.reason: The prior work found establishes related mechanisms—accurate verification of approximate drafts, cache-drift management, and error reinforcement—but does not answer the registered verifier-only freshness question with the stated controls. Holding the candidate pool and verification policy fixed while measuring correctness-stratified acceptance separates this experiment from existing end-to-end pipeline and refresh-policy comparisons, beyond differences in dataset, model, or metric.

opus.reason: List entries 2 and 36 refresh the verifier cache too, but they measure acceptance reversals against the refreshed verifier as a model reference, while this experiment uses gold-labelled synthetic arithmetic to test whether refresh improves discrimination between correct and wrong drafts.

registration.title: Raw attention logits versus normalized attention mass for cache refresh
registration.seed_connection: Equation 2 ranks decoded positions using averaged unnormalized attention logits, whereas the motivating sparsity figure discusses normalized attention mass. These quantities need not select the same positions.
registration.hypothesis: At an identical refresh budget and decoding state, ranking by normalized attention mass yields lower output-distribution error than ranking by averaged raw attention logits.
registration.contribution: An equal-budget causal comparison of refresh utility on shared snapshots. Normalized attention is not proposed as a new attribution method; the contribution is testing whether the seed's scoring choice improves or harms the approximation it is intended to control.

closest_work.difference: The seed motivates refresh using attention concentration but implements raw-logit aggregation. This experiment isolates the scoring choice while holding refreshed-token count and decoding inputs fixed.
d2Cache uses attention rollout and also changes masked-token selection. This experiment compares simple raw and normalized scores without changing the decoding schedule or refresh budget.
EntropyCache prioritizes recently decoded tokens and schedules full refreshes. Recency is included here as a control, not combined with a different refresh schedule.

Polestar uses drift-based sparse updates and a different execution design. This experiment measures one-step output recovery from fixed-budget refresh interventions rather than comparing complete acceleration systems.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
GSM8K main test split from https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k
Flash-dLLM Equation 2 and llada/flash_cache_triton.py at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
registration.method: Load one BF16 LLaDA-1.5 and implement a transparent PyTorch forward capable of recording per-layer KV states, attention logits, normalized attention, and selective KV updates. A dense forward with non-active KV entries overridden by stored entries is acceptable because runtime acceleration is not an endpoint. Validate the fully active path against the native Hugging Face model using normalized logit RMS error below 0.01 and maximum confidence error below 0.002. Select the first 48 GSM8K test questions whose 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' prompt is at most 160 tokens. Append 96 mask positions. Generate a reference trace with full recomputation, committing one highest-confidence remaining token in the first 32 response positions per step, excluding the mask token and allowing EOS without early termination. Replay exactly these token commitments into a separate approximate-cache runner, so caching cannot change the input trajectory. Initialize its cache with a full pass at state zero. At each replay step update the first up-to-16 remaining masked positions in the first 32 response slots and the two most recently committed positions; leave other KV entries unchanged. At states after 8, 16, and 24 commitments, save the approximate-cache snapshot and obtain its attention scores from the mandatory masked queries. For every eligible prompt or decoded position outside the mandatory query, compute two scores across the same layers, heads, and masked queries: R_i=sum_l mean_h,j(Q_j dot K_i), and A_i=sum_l mean_h,j softmax_i(Q_j dot K_i/sqrt(head_dim)). Use all layers in both definitions and break ties by original position. From identical snapshot copies, run one additional pass updating the mandatory query plus eight extra positions selected by R, by A, by oldest cache-update age, or uniformly at random. Use five fixed random selections per snapshot with seeds 0 through 4. Also run a zero-extra-refresh pass. These intervention results do not feed back into the replay trajectory. Compare each policy's distributions at the mandatory masked positions with a fully recomputed distribution for the identical current token sequence. Compute KL(P_full || P_policy) from float32 log_softmax values over the entire vocabulary; do not use truncated top-k KL. Preserve the same number of extra positions and the same original RoPE indices in every equal-budget condition.

event.description: Normalized attention provides a reproducible, practically sized reduction in approximation error at the same refresh budget.
event.statistic: The lower endpoint of a 95% prompt-cluster bootstrap interval for 1 minus mean_KL_normalized divided by mean_KL_raw

evaluation.procedure: Average masked-position KL within each snapshot, then average the three snapshots within each prompt. Compute the fractional reduction from the equally weighted prompt means. Bootstrap prompt IDs 2,000 times using seed 2026, recomputing the ratio, and report the 2.5th percentile. If the raw-policy mean KL is below 0.0001 nats, return an insufficient-error-floor status and null statistic rather than celebrating a large relative change in negligible error. outputs/traces.jsonl contains prompts, token IDs, and fixed reference commitments. outputs/refresh_scores.jsonl contains raw and normalized rankings, selected positions, cache ages, all intervention KL values, mode disagreements, and the random controls. outputs/summary.json contains the registered statistic, interval, absolute error levels, and validity status. outputs/metadata.json holds revisions, native-forward validation, timing, and hardware. Random, age, and zero-extra conditions are diagnostic controls and do not alter the registered comparison.
evaluation.controls: All policies start from identical cache copies, receive identical input tokens, and refresh eight additional positions. Mandatory positions are excluded from selection. Full refresh supplies the distributional reference. Random and age selection test whether any gain is specific to the scoring rule; the zero-extra pass measures whether refreshing helps at all.

registration.full_scale_study: Compare refresh selectors across models, budgets, context lengths, and tasks using both paired output recovery and complete-generation quality, then determine whether normalized scores can be maintained efficiently in fused attention kernels.

agent.reason: Normalized attention mass more directly reflects attention-output weighting, but refresh utility also depends on representation drift and downstream propagation. These factors could favor raw-logit selection or prevent a reproducible improvement exceeding ten percent.

judge_astra.reason: Normalized attention prevents high-scale heads or layers from disproportionately dominating the refresh ranking, making reduced KL error plausible. However, attention mass does not measure representation drift, and overlapping selections or errors outside the eligible refresh set could limit improvement below the registered 10% threshold.

judge_fable.reason: Normalized attention mass is the theoretically better sensitivity proxy and raw summed logits can be distorted by large-norm sink tokens, but at a budget of 8 extra refreshes both selectors likely pick largely the same recently decoded/high-attention positions, so the relative KL gap is probably small and noisy across 48 prompts; a robust >=10% reduction plus a correct cache-override forward is a demanding combination.

judge_opus.reason: Normalized mass is plausibly a better selector than head-averaged raw logits, which high-norm or sink keys can dominate. But eight extra refreshes fix only part of the error (far masks and many prompt tokens stay stale), and the two rankings may overlap, so a lower bound above a 10% relative KL reduction is a high bar.

judge_sol.reason: Normalized mass better represents immediate attention influence than averaged logits, but refresh utility also depends on representational drift and cache age. Overlapping selections and errors arising from positions neither policy refreshes could keep the improvement below the registered 10% bound.

judge_luna.reason: Normalized attention mass is a more direct measure of how strongly keys contribute after softmax and avoids some cross-query and cross-layer logit-scale effects. But attention is only a proxy for cache error, so a greater-than-10% KL reduction with a positive bootstrap bound is uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Normalized mass weights layers and queries more evenly than summed raw logits and matches the sparsity motivation, but the two rankings may be correlated and the 10% fractional KL-reduction lower bound requires a consistent win.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM's Eq. 2 ranks decoded tokens by summed, unnormalized attention logits. Its Fig. 1(b) motivation is about normalized attention mass, i.e., how much of the softmax weight the top-32 tokens capture. The ablations I read vary the tracking budget, thresholds and window size, but none compares raw logits with normalized scores, and none measures one-step KL against full recomputation at an equal budget.

Elastic-Cache uses the most-attended token as a drift test to decide when and at which layers to refresh. It does not compare raw and normalized scores for choosing which tokens to refresh under a fixed budget.

MaskAhead ranks KV entries by their estimated contribution to the attention output, using mask queries in block-diffusion models. It applies this to selection and eviction (dropping entries), not to choosing which cache entries to refresh, and it does not test raw logits against softmax mass.

EntropyCache uses decoded-token entropy to decide when to recompute and refreshes the most recently decoded tokens. It does not compare attention scoring rules. The experiment includes recency only as a control.
d2Cache selects tokens with attention rollout and also changes the decoding schedule. It does not run a controlled raw-versus-normalized comparison at a fixed budget on shared snapshots.

VATP, in autoregressive KV pruning, shows that attention-score-only importance is incomplete and adds value norms. It works in a different setting and does not contrast raw logits with softmax-normalized scores for refreshing a dLLM cache.

opus.reason: I found no paper that compares unnormalized attention logits with normalized attention mass as the ranking for selective KV refresh in diffusion LLMs. The seed paper itself does not ablate this choice, and related dLLM caching work (Elastic-Cache, EntropyCache, d2Cache, MaskAhead) uses other signals or settings. The broader KV-pruning literature questions attention-based importance scores but does not answer this specific equal-budget question, so the experiment's question appears open.

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM ranks refresh positions using averaged unnormalized attention logits in Equation 2, but does not compare that selector against normalized attention mass on identical cache snapshots at a fixed refresh budget.

d2Cache selects refresh positions using normalized attention rollout and also changes masked-token selection. It does not isolate simple raw-logit versus normalized-mass ranking while holding the cache state and token trajectory fixed.

ACache uses aggregated normalized mask-to-affix attention to select tokens for recomputation and compares selection criteria at matched budgets. Its experiments concern cross-request affix reuse, without a raw-logit selector or shared-snapshot output-recovery comparison.

MaskKV aggregates normalized attention from masked queries to rank prompt tokens for eviction. It studies retention and budget allocation, not whether raw or normalized scores better select stale entries for refresh.

RCStat contrasts pre-softmax relevance statistics with post-softmax methods for autoregressive cache eviction and attribution. Its relative-contextualization scoring, adaptive head budgets, and eviction interventions do not answer the registered diffusion-cache refresh question.

sol.reason: Normalized attention-based selection and comparisons between pre- and post-softmax relevance signals already existed, so neither ingredient alone is new. However, among the work I found available by 2026-10-07, none answers whether normalization improves fixed-budget refresh utility through paired interventions on identical stale-cache snapshots with the decoding trajectory held fixed; that isolated comparison is distinct.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper uses raw logits in Eq. 2 and motivates the choice with normalized attention mass, but it never compares the two scores and does not name the comparison as future work or a limitation.

registration.title: Does self-verification add correctness information beyond draft confidence?
registration.seed_connection: Flash-dLLM motivates verification using confidence dynamics and agreement. Its theoretical guarantee concerns a model distribution, so the empirical information that verification supplies about actual correctness remains a separate question.
registration.hypothesis: Two-view verification scores improve held-out prediction of draft correctness after controlling for draft confidence, entropy, margin, position, and answer format.
registration.contribution: A supervised diagnostic with automatically exact labels that tests incremental information rather than comparing differently tuned decoding thresholds or treating self-consistency as ground-truth correctness.

closest_work.difference: FreeDave establishes agreement with a model decoding path. This experiment asks whether verification carries additional information about uniquely specified correct answers.
CadLLM uses confidence to adapt compute allocation. Here a confidence-based correctness probe is the matched baseline, and verification's incremental held-out value is measured directly.

ASRD identifies locally reinforced wrong predictions and perturbs candidates. This experiment evaluates unperturbed two-view verification after conditioning on the original prediction's uncertainty and token-position features.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
Locally generated arithmetic-infilling instances with exact Python integer labels and seed 366
Flash-dLLM paired-view mask from https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
scikit-learn for small CPU logistic-regression probes; no language-model weights are trained
registration.method: Use one BF16 LLaDA-1.5 in eval mode, with no approximate KV reuse. Implement the two-view forward in PyTorch using the checkpoint modules and explicit repeated original RoPE indices; validate an ordinary full-bidirectional pass against the native model with normalized logit RMS error below 0.01 and confidence error below 0.002. Generate 288 distinct integer pairs with 100<=b<=a<=999 using NumPy default_rng(366). Assign the first 96 instances to calibration and the remaining 192 to held-out evaluation before obtaining model outputs. For each pair, specify SUM=a+b as four zero-padded digits, DIFF=a-b as four digits, and PROD=a*b as six digits, separating digits with spaces. The prompt explains the format and gives fixed, Python-computed examples for (317,184) and (426,215). Field names, separators, and spaces are supplied; answer digits are masked. Use tokenizer offsets to identify digit positions and require one token per digit. For each instance evaluate three controlled states: no answer digits revealed, the four SUM digits revealed correctly, and the eight SUM and DIFF digits revealed correctly. At each state perform a full draft. Directly commit confidence>=0.9 predictions; from remaining digits select up to eight search positions in decreasing draft-confidence order. For verification create draft and masked copies with shared original positions. At every layer, context C sees C and all masked copies but no draft copies; D_i sees C, D_j for j<=i, and M_j for j>i; M_i sees C, D_j for j<i, and M_j for j>=i. Fully recompute all rows. Label each search draft by exact equality with its canonical digit token, regardless of whether it would be accepted. Collect baseline features: logit-transformed draft confidence, draft entropy, top-one/top-two margin, normalized search rank, search-set size, reveal stage, answer field, normalized digit position within its field, and draft-token category (digits 0 through 9 or other). The augmented probe adds verifier log probability assigned to the draft, verifier-mode agreement, verifier entropy, and verifier top-one/top-two margin. Fit both probes on calibration instances using standardized numeric features, one-hot categorical features, LogisticRegression with L2 penalty, C=1, max_iter=2000, and no hyperparameter search. Give every calibration instance equal total sample weight across its candidates. Freeze preprocessing and coefficients before evaluation. Evaluate every held-out instance with search candidates; never split candidates from one instance across calibration and test. Train an additional diagnostic control with four seeded random features instead of verifier features to expose improvements caused merely by extra probe capacity.

event.description: Verification features improve held-out correctness prediction by more than the registered Brier-score margin.
event.statistic: The lower endpoint of a 95% instance-cluster bootstrap interval for macro Brier_baseline minus macro Brier_augmented

evaluation.procedure: Within each held-out instance average squared correctness-prediction error across its search candidates and reveal states. Equally average these instance scores for each frozen probe. Bootstrap whole held-out instances 2,000 times with seed 2026 and report the 2.5th percentile of the paired Brier improvement. Require candidates from at least 100 held-out instances and at least 100 correct and 100 wrong held-out candidates; otherwise write insufficient-support status and a null statistic. outputs/instances.jsonl contains operands, exact answers, prompts, token mappings, split assignment, and reveal states. outputs/features.jsonl contains candidate labels, all model-derived features, top predictions, and frozen-probe predictions. outputs/probes.json contains preprocessing parameters and fitted coefficients. outputs/summary.json contains the registered statistic, interval, class counts, point scores, and random-feature diagnostic. outputs/metadata.json records revisions, validation tests, runtime, and hardware. The experiment establishes information in controlled infilling, not a causal improvement in generated answers.
evaluation.controls: The baseline includes uncertainty, draft identity category, output location, and reveal-stage features, preventing verification from winning simply by identifying easier positions. Both probes use identical calibration instances and regularization. Splitting and bootstrapping are by arithmetic instance. No approximate caching is used. The random-feature probe is a capacity control, not a selectable alternative primary baseline.

registration.full_scale_study: Evaluate verification's incremental reliability information on on-policy reasoning and code traces, study transfer of small correctness calibrators across tasks, and test acceptance policies at matched compute and accepted-token coverage.

agent.reason: Verification supplies changed-context predictions and agreement information that could improve correctness prediction beyond the registered draft features. Shared errors, limited calibration data, and already-informative baseline features could nevertheless keep the held-out Brier improvement below the required margin.

judge_astra.reason: Verifier agreement and draft log probability provide another context-conditioned view that could predict correctness beyond draft uncertainty. The rich baseline, correlated arithmetic errors, and limited calibration instances make a held-out Brier improvement clearing the 0.005 confidence-bound margin uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: Conditioning on earlier committed drafts genuinely resolves carry/borrow ambiguities for uncertain SUM/DIFF digits, and the paper's matched-throughput accuracy advantage over lowered epsilon suggests verification carries some correctness signal, so a modest held-out Brier gain is plausible; however self-leakage inflates verifier confidence toward the draft, PROD-dominated candidates are already explained by field/position features, and the lower bound must clear 0.005 with ~192 instances, all on top of implementation risk.

judge_opus.reason: Conditioning on other drafted digits likely adds some correctness signal, but the baseline already includes confidence, entropy, margin, field, position and stage. The Brier gain is probably about 0.005–0.01, so clearing a 0.005 lower bound with 192 instances is uncertain.

judge_sol.reason: Verification changes the conditioning information, so its features plausibly add correctness information beyond the draft-only probe. However, the rich baseline, correlated arithmetic mistakes, and limited calibration instances could leave the held-out Brier improvement below the required margin.

judge_luna.reason: Agreement and verifier confidence could add correctness information from a different conditioning context beyond draft uncertainty. However, the same model can reinforce confidently wrong arithmetic, and the held-out Brier threshold must be cleared across instance clusters.

judge_muse.reason: The verifier sees preceding drafts the draft did not, so agreement and verifier confidence should carry incremental correctness signal, and the 0.005 Brier lower bound is small, though the strong draft-uncertainty baseline may capture most of it.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper (Flash-dLLM) proposes KV-cache-driven draft-and-verify decoding and reports speed and accuracy. It does not test whether its verifier signals predict which draft tokens are actually correct once draft confidence, entropy, margin and position are controlled for.

FreeDave checks whether drafts agree with the model's own decoding path. It does not measure, on held-out data, whether verification predicts exact ground-truth correctness better than confidence alone.

RecGuide finds that draft logits can anticipate verification mismatches in diffusion-to-AR self-speculation and uses that to schedule drafting. The target there is verifier agreement, not ground-truth correctness, and it does not test what verification adds beyond confidence.

T2M compares error detectors for remasking, including current-token probability, by their effect on downstream task scores. It does not use exact token labels or a controlled probe to test whether verification adds information beyond confidence.

This paper tests whether same-model self-verification is a useful confidence signal beyond likelihood baselines, but for autoregressive LLMs on multiple-choice QA with prompt-based verification. It does not cover masked-diffusion two-view verification at the token level.

opus.reason: Searches turned up diffusion-LLM self-speculation, remasking and error-detection methods, and one autoregressive study of self-verification versus likelihood baselines. None asks whether same-model verification signals in a diffusion LLM predict exact token correctness on held-out data better than draft confidence, entropy, margin and position features alone. The closest papers (RecGuide, T2M, FreeDave) either predict agreement with the verifier rather than true correctness, or judge detectors only by their effect on downstream task scores, so the question still looks open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM supplies the two-view verifier and evaluates decoding speed–accuracy trade-offs, but does not test its incremental held-out correctness information after conditioning on draft uncertainty and position features.

Compares prompted same-model self-verification against likelihood-based confidence signals, including calibration metrics, but does not compare matched baseline and verifier-augmented correctness probes.

Studies arithmetic token correctness within confidence ranges using layerwise prediction stability. It does not evaluate an additional paired-view verification pass or its incremental predictive value under the registered controls.

Evaluates masking–reconstruction consistency as a solution-level correctness signal against confidence baselines, rather than testing two-view draft verification conditionally on a multifeature draft baseline.

Audits nonredundant reliability evidence from reasoning-prefix signals, including textual self-verification markers, but targets eventual trace success rather than exact candidate-token correctness from paired-view verification.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes self-verification and stability signals as correctness predictors, and some explicitly examine their value relative to confidence. However, I found no work answering the specific conditional question posed here: whether paired-view diffusion verification improves held-out exact draft-token correctness prediction over matched probes controlling for draft uncertainty, token identity, location, and reveal state. The distinction is the verification signal and conditional diagnostic design, not merely the arithmetic dataset or Brier-score metric.

opus.reason: No list entry fits a held-out logistic probe testing whether verifier features add correctness information beyond draft-confidence features; entry 39 only measures calibration of draft and mask-view confidences.

sol.reason: No listed experiment tests verification's incremental held-out correctness information using a fitted probe that controls for draft uncertainty, token identity, and position.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered 288-instance, three-state infilling diagnostic with frozen BF16 LLaDA-1.5, full recomputation, explicit shared-original-index RoPE, exact paired-view masks, baseline/verification/random-feature logistic probes, instance weighting, support checks, and the 2,000-replicate paired instance bootstrap. Tested the complete command successfully; all required outputs and result.json were regenerated. Registered native validation errors were zero. Local lower bootstrap endpoint was 0.0454867 (191 held-out instances; 680 correct, 1,492 wrong candidates). No registered method, event, or evaluation changes. opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: seed-366 pairs split 96/192 before inference, three reveal states, a 0.9 commit threshold with up to 8 search positions, the exact paired-view visibility rules (unit-tested), exact token labels, the registered baseline and verifier features, instance-weighted C=1 L2 logistic probes, a random-feature capacity control, and a 2,000-replicate instance-cluster bootstrap with seed 2026. The fresh-machine run reproduced the engineer's numbers exactly. The macro Brier score falls from 0.160 to 0.106, with a lower bootstrap endpoint of 0.045, far above the 0.005 threshold, while random features slightly hurt. I found no leakage, hard-coding or split contamination; labels are exact and the split and states were persisted before inference. The main caveats are an unvalidated paired-mask forward path, a BF16 order sensitivity of about 1%, and a narrow synthetic domain where the verifier also benefits from committed context. Together these make this a credible, meaningful but limited finding.

experiment.py::FullForward and collect restrict the final normalization and vocabulary projection to requested output rows, rather than materializing logits for every row. All hidden rows are still recomputed at every layer. This is a mathematically equivalent implementation optimization, not approximate caching; BF16 shape-dependent numerical differences are possible, but no conclusion-changing effect is demonstrated.

The evidence establishes predictive improvement for the specified regularized logistic baseline on selected controlled arithmetic-infilling candidates. A single random-feature control does not rule out baseline functional misspecification, and the experiment does not establish causal decoding improvement or transfer to other tasks and models.

grok.what_it_asks: It compares two-view verification scores with draft confidence and related draft-side features as predictors of whether a drafted digit is actually correct, on LLaDA-1.5 arithmetic infilling, to learn whether self-verification adds correctness information beyond draft confidence.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper measures decoding accuracy and a deviation bound against the model’s own sequential distribution, but neither reports this incremental correctness-probe comparison nor names it as undone.

relation.reason: Flash-dLLM’s two-view mask is a working part of the test, used to measure a correctness-information property the paper never claims, so the paper’s speed and accuracy claims stand either way.

obvious.reason: The paper’s own split between model-distribution agreement and data correctness would put this comparison on several first lists, but most readers would first write other-model, open-ended, or adaptive-threshold follow-ups.

grok.what_came_out: On LLaDA-1.5 arithmetic infilling, adding two-view verification features cut macro Brier from 0.160 to 0.106 (paired improvement 0.054, 95% instance-cluster interval [0.045, 0.062] over 191 held-out instances and 2,000 resamples; 680 correct and 1,492 wrong candidates), while four random features did not (improvement −0.0008, interval [−0.0014, −0.0001]).

opus.what_it_asks: Whether adding features from Flash-Verify's two-view (draft-view/mask-view) verification pass to a probe built on draft confidence, entropy, margin, position and format features improves held-out prediction of whether LLaDA-1.5's search-set draft tokens are actually correct in arithmetic infilling, i.e. whether self-verification carries correctness information beyond draft confidence.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares Flash-Verify with confidence-aware decoding only through end-task accuracy, throughput and tokens per step, and bounds deviation against the model's own distribution; it never measures the incremental correctness information of verifier signals, and its limitations do not name this question.

relation.reason: The paper's verify pass is a working part of the experiment, put to a use the paper does not make (correctness probing), and the paper's claims stand whichever way the result comes out.

obvious.reason: Many readers would wonder whether verification is better than just lowering the confidence threshold, but few would frame it as a held-out probe testing whether verifier signals add correctness information beyond confidence features.

who_would_care.reason: The answer mainly informs people designing self-verification or draft-and-verify acceptance rules for diffusion LLM decoding.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements, that the method is motivated by confidence dynamics and agreement and that the guarantee is stated against a model distribution, match the paper's Assumption 1 and Section 2.3.

opus.what_came_out: On LLaDA-1.5 (BF16) arithmetic infilling with 191 held-out instances (2,172 search candidates: 680 correct, 1,492 wrong), held-out macro Brier fell from 0.1596 (baseline probe) to 0.1056 (verification-augmented probe), a paired improvement of 0.054 with 95% instance bootstrap CI [0.0455, 0.0624]; the random-feature control changed Brier by −0.0008.

evidence.reason: The improvement interval lies well above zero, the improvement is large relative to baseline Brier, and the random-feature control shows it is not mere probe capacity, so the run shows what the hypothesis claims.

next_step.reason: The question is answered for this setting, but the verify pass also conditions on the directly committed confident tokens, so it is not yet known whether the paired-view structure or simply a second forward pass with those tokens committed supplies the information.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares draft-feature correctness probes with and without two-view verification features on LLaDA-1.5 arithmetic digit-infilling to learn whether verification improves held-out correctness prediction beyond draft uncertainty and output-position information.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper neither reports confidence-conditioned correctness probing nor explicitly leaves verification's incremental predictive information as an open question.

relation.reason: The experiment puts the paper's two-view verifier to a new diagnostic use, testing a conditional predictive property that the paper does not claim.

obvious.reason: Confidence-conditioned correctness diagnostics are familiar follow-ups to self-verification, but decoding ablations, cache policies, and transfer tests would dominate many researchers' first-ten lists.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would mainly change correctness scoring and acceptance design for groups using this two-view verifier, rather than researchers whose inference methods do not use it.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements about confidence-based motivation, agreement, and a theoretical guarantee relative to the model's own distribution agree with the paper.

sol.what_came_out: In one BF16 LLaDA-1.5 arithmetic-infilling run, verification features reduced held-out macro Brier error from 0.159614 to 0.105592, an improvement of 0.054022 with a 95% instance-bootstrap interval of [0.045487, 0.062401], across 2,172 candidates from 191 held-out instances.

prerequisite.reason: Both splits contained substantial numbers of correct and incorrect drafts, the support requirement passed, and the registered native-forward and mask checks passed.

evidence.reason: The verification-augmented probe showed a substantial improvement with an interval wholly above zero, while adding random features produced a small deterioration rather than a gain.

next_step.reason: The sizable and precisely estimated predictive gain justifies broader study of verification-feature utility, while the observed BF16 permutation discrepancy warrants precision-robustness checks within that study.

registration.title: Projection fusion versus dense GEMM with a fused cache-write epilogue
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache fuses QKV projection, RoPE, and cache writes and reports a per-layer RTX 3090 microbenchmark. Fusion reduces intermediate traffic but may trade away the efficiency of a large dense GEMM as batched query counts increase.
registration.hypothesis: On the A100, a packed cuBLAS QKV projection followed by one fused RoPE-and-scatter epilogue is faster than the seed's all-in-one projection kernel over the registered batched-query workload.
registration.contribution: An arithmetic- and layout-matched A100 performance envelope for the seed's specific fusion boundary, using real checkpoint weights and activations. It tests an inexpensive hybrid implementation rather than attributing whole-system speedups to fusion or proposing universal kernel superiority.

closest_work.difference: The seed compares its fused pipeline with a conventional implementation and gives a 3090 microbenchmark. This experiment uses an optimized packed-GEMM control, identical scattered cache destinations, and an A100 query-count sweep.

ClusterFusion++ expands fusion across complete decoder blocks on newer cluster-capable hardware. This experiment tests a narrower projection-versus-epilogue boundary on Ampere for diffusion-style scattered cache updates.

FlashInfer-Bench supplies correctness-aware workload benchmarking methodology. This experiment applies that discipline to a specific diffusion-cache fusion decision rather than constructing a general kernel benchmark.

inputs: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5
The first eight GSM8K main training questions from https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k
_flash_qkv_proj_cache_fwd in llada/flash_cache_triton.py from https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
Existing CUDA PyTorch/cuBLAS and Triton wheel installation
registration.method: Load LLaDA-1.5 once in BF16 on the A100. Run ordinary full-bidirectional inference on eight short GSM8K prompts with 64 appended mask positions, recording attention-normalized input rows at layers 0, 15, and 31. Use the real Q, K, and V projection weights from those layers. Tile recorded activation rows as needed to form 128 query rows per request; data preparation and normalization are outside the timed region for both methods. Benchmark batch sizes B=1,4,16,32, giving total query rows M=128,512,2048,4096. Allocate an identical flat BF16 cache with 512 physical slots per request. For each request choose 128 unique scattered destinations from a fixed permutation with seed 2026, and use original local positions for RoPE. Build the seed-format block table with 16 query rows per block and repeated per-request sine/cosine tables. Method F is the repository's unmodified _flash_qkv_proj_cache_fwd with BLOCK_M=16, BLOCK_D=64, num_warps=4, and num_stages=2. Method G packs the three projection weight matrices once outside timing, performs a single torch.mm into a preallocated M-by-3d buffer, and invokes one simple Triton epilogue that applies RoPE to Q and K and writes Q plus scattered K and V to the same destinations. Include the intermediate-buffer traffic and epilogue time in G. Do not autotune either method after seeing evaluation timings. Before timing, compare both methods with float32 PyTorch projection-and-RoPE references constructed from the same BF16 weights and inputs. Require finite outputs, normalized RMS error below 0.01 for Q/K/V, at least 99.9% of updated elements satisfying abs_error<=0.05+0.02*abs_reference, and bitwise preservation of every untouched cache slot. Reject a method with failed validation rather than relaxing tolerances. Record the extra packed-weight and intermediate-buffer memory used by G. Capture each validated method in its own CUDA graph with preallocated buffers, warm up 20 graph replays, then collect 20 interleaved timing trials per layer/batch case. Each trial times 50 graph replays with CUDA events and divides by 50; alternate method order between trials. Synchronize at trial boundaries and exclude downloads, JIT compilation, weight packing, and graph capture from kernel latency, while including them in total experiment runtime. This is a primitive-level study, not an end-to-end generation speed claim.

event.description: The validated hybrid projection pipeline provides at least 1.10x acceleration over the seed kernel on the registered workload.
event.statistic: The geometric mean across the 12 layer-by-batch cases of median_latency_F divided by median_latency_G

evaluation.procedure: For each of three layers and four batch sizes, take each method's median per-invocation latency across its 20 trials. Compute exp(mean(log(median_F/median_G))) with equal weight for all 12 cases. This geometric mean is the single registered statistic; do not select a favorable subset of shapes. If any registered case fails correctness or cannot run, write an invalid/incomplete status and null statistic rather than omitting it. outputs/timing_trials.jsonl contains method, layer, batch size, trial order, event timing, and per-invocation latency. outputs/validation.jsonl contains reference errors, untouched-slot checks, tensor layouts, and memory requirements for every case. outputs/summary.json contains all case medians and the registered geometric mean. outputs/metadata.json records model and repository revisions, software, GPU details, installation/download/JIT time, and total runtime.
evaluation.controls: Both methods use identical normalized activations, weights, RoPE positions, cache layouts, and scattered destinations. Correctness is checked against an independent float32 reference. Preallocation and CUDA graphs remove unequal allocation and Python-launch overhead from the primary comparison. Interleaved trial order controls thermal and clock drift. All registered layers and batch sizes enter the statistic.

registration.full_scale_study: Integrate shape-dependent selection of projection fusion boundaries into an inference engine, measure end-to-end latency and memory under heterogeneous query sizes, and repeat the hardware-specific crossover study on additional GPUs and model architectures.

agent.reason: The larger batched shapes should favor cuBLAS tiling and reuse over the seed's fixed small-row projection kernel, despite the intermediate-buffer traffic. Small-batch fusion advantages and the requirement to validate every registered case remain meaningful risks to the aggregate event.

judge_astra.reason: The larger query-count cases should favor an optimized packed cuBLAS GEMM over a fixed small-tile projection kernel, plausibly enough to exceed the 1.10 geometric-mean threshold. Successful execution and strict correctness validation of every case are substantial remaining risks.

judge_fable.reason: A Triton projection kernel with BLOCK_M=16 tiles re-streams the ~100 MB QKV weight per 16-row block and uses tensor cores poorly, so a packed cuBLAS GEMM plus a light RoPE/scatter epilogue should win by well over 1.1x at every registered M; the main risks are that the repository kernel does not exist or behave as registered, validation/layout mismatches, or the engineer failing to get the Triton+CUDA-graph pipeline running within budget.

judge_opus.reason: The seed kernel's 16-row tiles re-stream weights for every block and use small tensor-core tiles, so cuBLAS plus a light epilogue should be several times faster at large batches; the seed's own Figure 1a shows its fused kernel taking about 2.7x the plain linear time. The main risk is getting the unmodified repository kernel running and validated under the installed Triton.

judge_sol.reason: Packed cuBLAS GEMM is likely to outperform a fixed small-tile projection kernel at larger query counts, potentially outweighing the additional intermediate traffic across the registered workload. Unmodified-kernel integration and the requirement that every case pass correctness checks are important failure risks.

judge_luna.reason: Packed cuBLAS projection is plausibly faster at medium and large query counts, but the hybrid also pays for an intermediate buffer and a separate epilogue, while the fused kernel avoids that traffic. The 1.10× geometric-mean target across all shapes is therefore uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: The repository kernel's BLOCK_M=16 tiling is likely inefficient for M=2048-4096 compute-bound GEMMs where cuBLAS excels, favoring the hybrid, but the all-12-cases-valid requirement and small-M cases where fusion saves traffic create material downside risk.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper tests its fused kernel (projection, RoPE and cache write in one kernel) only against a conventional PyTorch pipeline with four separate kernels. It reports a single 1.37x per-layer speedup on an RTX 3090. It does not compare against an optimized packed cuBLAS GEMM followed by a fused RoPE-and-scatter epilogue, and it has no A100 sweep over query count with matched cache destinations.

CODA studies GEMM-plus-epilogue as a general abstraction for Transformer training operators. It does not benchmark that boundary against an all-in-one fused projection kernel for diffusion-LLM scattered KV-cache writes.

ClusterFusion++ is cited by the experiment and not opened here. As the experiment describes it, ClusterFusion++ fuses whole decoder blocks on cluster-capable hardware, a broader fusion scope that does not address this projection-versus-epilogue choice on Ampere.
FlashInfer-Bench is cited by the experiment and not opened here. As the experiment describes it, it offers general benchmarking methodology and does not evaluate this specific fusion decision.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper's method section. Its only kernel-level evidence compares the fused Flash-Cache kernel with an unfused PyTorch baseline on an RTX 3090, so the question of whether a packed dense GEMM plus a fused RoPE/scatter epilogue beats the all-in-one kernel on an A100 is left open. Searches on fused QKV/RoPE/cache-write kernels against GEMM epilogues found only general GEMM-epilogue work (CODA) and unrelated KV-cache papers, none of which answers this question. The searches were limited, so a closely matching kernel benchmark could still exist without having come up.

The contribution is therefore distinct, rather than merely a hardware or metric variant of an already reported experiment.
