registration.title: Same-state audit of Flash-Verify's paper rule and released gate
registration.seed_connection: The seed specifies accepting a search token when its draft prediction agrees with the mask-view argmax and the mask-view top-1 confidence is at least gamma. Its appendix analyzes the resulting per-token commitment. The paper does not establish that the public implementation uses exactly this predicate.
registration.hypothesis: On captured LLaDA-1.5 GSM8K verifier states, the paper-literal rule and the predicate in a pinned public implementation differ in mean accepted-prefix length by more than 0.25 tokens per nonempty verify pass.
registration.contribution: A same-state specification-to-code audit that measures local acceptance differences without attributing downstream trajectory changes to the gate.

closest_work.difference: The seed presents the paper rule; this experiment tests it against the exact predicate in the released code on real verifier states.
Free draft-and-verification studies a different decoding procedure rather than auditing Flash-dLLM's specification against its implementation.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM, especially llada/generate.py.
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from Hugging Face.
The main test split of openai/gsm8k from Hugging Face Datasets.
registration.method: Resolve the repository to a specific git SHA, record it, and use the first 12 GSM8K test examples in dataset order with the prompt format Question: {question} followed by Answer:. Run the supported LLaDA-1.5 generation path greedily, with batch size 1, generation length 96, block length 16, confidence threshold epsilon=0.9, verify threshold gamma=0.8, and verification enabled. Use the repository's cache configuration, but instrument and log actual query positions rather than inferring their count from argument names. For every verify pass with a nonempty search set, record the ordered draft token IDs, mask-view argmax and top-1 confidence, mask-view probability assigned to each draft token, every value consumed by the implementation's acceptance predicate, and the implementation's accepted prefix. Compute the paper rule on those same recorded verifier outputs: require draft/mask-view argmax agreement and mask-view top-1 confidence at least gamma, stopping at the first rejection. Reproduce the implementation predicate exactly from the pinned source; do not assume it is a cumulative-product rule. Average the absolute difference in accepted-prefix length within each prompt, then across prompts with at least one nonempty verify pass. Include cold dependency installation and model/data downloads in the time estimate.

event.description: The paper-literal and pinned-release rules differ materially in accepted-prefix length on the same verifier outputs.
event.statistic: Mean across eligible prompts of the within-prompt mean absolute difference, in tokens, between the paper-rule and implementation-rule accepted-prefix lengths over nonempty verify passes.

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per verify pass to outputs/gate_replay.jsonl, including prompt ID, repository SHA, candidate order, required probability values, both accepted-prefix lengths, and the search-set size. Write outputs/gate_summary.json with the registered statistic, prompt and pass denominators, per-prompt values, and diagnostic answer accuracy and synchronized generation time for the repository run.
evaluation.controls: Both rules are evaluated on the same recorded candidates, order, model outputs, and verifier state. The alternative rule is not allowed to change future generation states; the registered result is a local decision comparison, not an end-to-end quality or speed claim.

registration.full_scale_study: If the local decisions differ enough to warrant follow-up, run both gates end-to-end on larger GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP samples with multiple seeds. Compare exact task scores, throughput, accepted-token counts, and memory use.

agent.reason: The drafts report a cumulative-product predicate in the release, which would differ from the paper's per-token rule and can truncate a prefix that the paper rule accepts. The exact implemented distribution and candidate probabilities remain uncertain, so a difference above 0.25 tokens is not assured.

judge_astra.reason: A substantive code–specification mismatch could clear this small threshold, but the supplied evidence does not establish one. At gamma=0.8, simply thresholding the mask-view probability of the draft token is equivalent to the paper gate, so superficially different predicates need not produce a discrepancy.

judge_fable.reason: Requires the public repo to exist, build (Triton kernels) and expose the verify predicate within the budget; conditional on that, implementation details (first-mismatch stop, which confidence is gated, bonus-token handling) differ from paper text often enough to give maybe even odds of a >0.25-token gap, but identical code or an engineer fallback to a self-written 'implementation' yields zero difference.

judge_opus.reason: The audit is deterministic on the same recorded verifier outputs, so the event needs a substantive code–paper mismatch, such as a cumulative product of draft probabilities, non-prefix acceptance or gating on draft confidence. Note that for gamma > 0.5 a per-token draft-probability gate is equivalent to the paper rule. Small inconsistencies elsewhere in the paper and the proposer's hedging raise the chance somewhat, but getting the Triton repository running and instrumented is a real failure risk, and failure means no event.

judge_sol.reason: A substantive gate discrepancy could readily exceed this modest threshold, and the same-output comparison isolates it cleanly. However, the supplied evidence does not establish the pinned implementation’s predicate, so whether such a discrepancy exists remains the main uncertainty.

judge_luna.reason: Algorithm 2 and the appendix specify the same argmax-agreement and mask-view confidence threshold, stopping at the first mismatch, so a conforming release should produce little same-state difference. I leave some probability for specification/code drift or an implementation detail that changes the gate across enough passes.

judge_muse.reason: The paper states the agreement-plus-gamma predicate consistently in text, algorithm, and appendix, so a pinned implementation likely matches it; a >0.25-token systematic shift would require an additional undocumented gate.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper describes the Flash-Verify acceptance rule: the draft and mask-view predictions must agree, the mask-view confidence must be at least gamma, and tokens are accepted left to right. It reports only end-to-end speed and accuracy. It never checks whether its released code implements that rule, and it does not measure same-state differences in accepted-prefix length.
This paper studies a different draft-and-verify decoding procedure for diffusion LLMs. It does not audit Flash-dLLM's written rule against its released code.

This paper orchestrates draft and verify budgets for diffusion drafting with autoregressive (AR) verification in a different self-speculation model. It does not compare a paper's acceptance rule with its implementation.

opus.reason: The question is whether Flash-dLLM's released code uses the verify-gate rule written in the paper, and how much the two differ in accepted-prefix length on the same recorded verifier states. That question is specific to one recent paper and its code. A search on Flash-dLLM, its draft-and-verify gate and implementation audits, plus reading the seed's method section, found no paper that reports such a comparison or makes it unnecessary, so the question looks open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM specifies the agreement-and-confidence acceptance rule and reports decoding benchmarks, threshold ablations, and deviation bounds, but does not report a same-state comparison against the exact predicate in a pinned public implementation.
FreeDave develops and evaluates a self-verifying parallel decoding procedure with lossless-decoding guarantees; it does not audit Flash-Verify's paper specification against released code.

sol.reason: The proposed contribution is a specification-to-implementation audit using identical recorded verifier states, rather than another decoding algorithm or end-to-end benchmark. The seed's acceptance analysis and FreeDave's verification results do not establish whether Flash-Verify's published and implemented predicates produce the same local decisions. I found no arXiv work available by 2026-10-07 that answers this audit question in the proposed way.

opus.reason: No list entry compares the paper's acceptance predicate with the predicate in the pinned released code on the same recorded verifier states. The cumulative-budget ideas (#6, #40) propose a new gate rather than auditing whether the specification matches the implementation.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: gate_audit/run_audit.py. It pins VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM to SHA a667345f5746bb74f060c87bae5997fc3de9710c, which was HEAD when I queried the GitHub API. It downloads the llada/ sources at that SHA and records their sha256; they match /workspace/seed byte for byte. If the download fails it falls back to the seed copy. It then makes an instrumented copy of generate.py by inserting read-only logging hooks at 6 anchors. Each anchor is asserted to occur exactly once, and no generation logic is changed. It runs the repository's own generate_with_Flash_dLLM on the first 12 GSM8K test questions, using the prompt "Question: {q}\nAnswer:" (raw prompt, no chat template, as the repo does for LLaDA-1.5). Settings: batch 1, greedy, gen_length 96, block_length 16, epsilon 0.9, gamma 0.8, verify=True, and the repo's cache config from eval_gsm8k.sh (track_num=4, mask_num=4). Stop tokens are lm-eval's gsm8k `until`.

For each verify pass it logs:
- the actual query positions for both the draft pass and the verify pass, and the number of keys served from cache;
- draft confidences and the candidate order;
- draft token IDs;
- mask-view argmax, top-1 and p(draft);
- the gate input after the release's post-EOS length mask, the cumulative product, and the release's keep_num.

The paper rule is replayed on those same values: draft must equal the mask-view argmax, top-1 must be ≥ gamma, and acceptance stops at the first rejection. It never affects generation; the release gate drives the trajectory.

Release predicate, read from the pinned source: keep_num = number of k with cumprod_{m≤k} p_maskview(draft_m) ≥ gamma. Once EOS has been decoded, p is set to 0 for candidate positions at or beyond the predicted length. There is no argmax-agreement check, and the search set is capped at block_length//2 = 8. My independent re-implementation of this predicate matched the logged keep_num in all 194 passes.

Result (two runs gave the same value): statistic = 0.359 tokens, which is above 0.25, so the registered event occurs. Denominators: 12 eligible prompts, 194 nonempty verify passes, plus 8 empty passes. 11.3% of passes differ. In every differing pass the paper rule accepts more tokens than the release, and the main driver is the stricter cumulative product.

Caveats:
1. Part of the gap comes from the release's post-EOS length mask, which the paper does not describe. If that mask is also applied to the paper rule, the statistic is 0.220, below the threshold. This is reported in gate_summary.json as a secondary diagnostic only; the registered literal statistic is unchanged.
2. In one pass, some mask-view inputs were EOS rather than [MASK]. Those were padding positions past the generation region (field mask_view_tokens_all_mask=false). I report this rather than hide it.
3. This is one model, 12 prompts and one greedy run, and it is a local decision comparison only. It does not support claims about end-to-end accuracy or speed.
4. Diagnostic answer accuracy of the repository run was 8/12. The synchronized generation time of about 19 s includes instrumentation syncs and Triton JIT warm-up.

Deviations from the registration: no git binary was available, so the SHA was resolved via the GitHub API and the files were fetched from raw.githubusercontent at that SHA rather than cloned. The model config is loaded with the repo's own LLaDAConfig class, with flash_attention=True as in eval_llada.py.

departures: The prompt was 'Question: {q}\nAnswer:' with a newline and no chat template (run_audit.py). The registration only says 'Question: {question} followed by Answer:', so this choice was left open. It could shift trajectories but not the same-state comparison logic.

lm-eval GSM8K stop strings ['Question:', '</s>', '<|im_end|>'] were added (run_audit.py). They only post-process the decoded text for the diagnostic accuracy. They cannot affect gate decisions or the statistic.

The source was not cloned. The SHA was resolved via the GitHub API (HEAD at query time) and files were fetched from raw.githubusercontent at that SHA. gate_summary.json records source 'github_pinned' with sha256 matching the seed copy, so the seed-copy fallback was not used. No effect on the result.

Only five llada/ files were fetched, not the full repository. The run depends on the engineer's reading of eval_gsm8k.sh for track_num=4/mask_num=4, which cannot be verified from the archive; these values equal the function defaults. Any effect would be on trajectories, not on same-state decisions.

The model config was loaded with LLaDAConfig and flash_attention=True (run_audit.py). The engineer says this matches eval_llada.py. A numerical change would at most perturb states, which both rules share.
steps=96 and is_instruct=False are passed but unused by the pinned generate_with_Flash_dLLM. No effect.

The registered statistic applies the paper rule literally, without the release's post-EOS length mask. A secondary diagnostic that also applies the mask to the paper rule gives 0.220, below the threshold. The registered value is reported unchanged, so this is not a departure, but it affects interpretation.

The synchronized generation time of about 18.5 s includes instrumentation syncs and Triton JIT warm-up. It is a diagnostic only, and the registration does not require uninstrumented timing. No effect on the statistic.
problems: Roughly 0.14 of the 0.36-token gap (0.359 vs 0.220) comes from candidate positions beyond the decoded EOS. The release zeroes p(draft) there, while the literal paper rule accepts them. These positions do not affect the emitted answer, so the threshold crossing depends on output-irrelevant post-EOS tokens. The cumprod-vs-per-token difference alone gives 0.22, which is below 0.25.

The direction paper ≥ implementation is mathematically guaranteed: cumprod ≥ 0.8 implies every p(draft) ≥ 0.8 > 0.5, which implies argmax agreement. The 'frac_impl_gt_paper = 0' diagnostic is therefore a consequence of the definitions, not an empirical finding. The registered magnitude remains empirical.

The sample is small: 12 prompts, one model, one greedy trajectory driven by the release gate. Per-prompt values vary widely (0.5 for prompt 0, about 0.045 for prompt 1). No uncertainty interval is reported, so the margin over 0.25 is not shown to be robust.

In one pass the mask-view inputs included EOS padding tokens beyond the generation region rather than [MASK] (mask_view_tokens_all_mask=false). The engineer disclosed this. It is release behaviour, but it means some 'mask-view' outputs are not pure mask views.
The track_num/mask_num values attributed to eval_gsm8k.sh cannot be checked, because that file is not in the archive (gate_audit/pinned_llada).
opus.reason: The code runs the pinned release's own generate_with_Flash_dLLM with the registered model, data, prompts, decoding settings and thresholds. Read-only hooks, asserted at unique anchors, log the logits-derived values that the gate consumes. The paper rule is replayed on those same values without influencing generation, and the registered prompt-averaged statistic is computed as specified. An independent re-implementation of the release predicate matched the logged keep_num in all 194 passes, so the values derive from real model outputs with no apparent leakage or hard-coding. The finding is credible: the release uses a cumulative-product gate with no argmax check, a post-EOS length mask and a search-set cap of 8, and on the same states this yields a 0.36-token mean gap. It is limited by 12 prompts, no uncertainty estimate, and the fact that the gap falls to 0.22 when post-EOS positions, which do not affect the output, are excluded. That makes it a meaningful but modest specification-to-code result rather than strong evidence.

departures: gate_audit/run_audit.py uses an already-resolved SHA and downloads individual source files from raw GitHub rather than resolving the repository during evaluation. The evaluation summary records successful pinned downloads and matching source hashes, so this procedural adjustment does not plausibly change this run's result.

outputs/gate_replay.jsonl contains rows only for nonempty verify passes. Empty passes are counted separately, rather than receiving the evaluation section's requested one row per verify pass. This reduces logging completeness but does not change the registered statistic, which explicitly excludes empty passes.

gate_audit/run_audit.py supplies stop strings that the registration did not enumerate. In generate.py these affect answer postprocessing after generation, not verifier states or acceptance decisions; they could affect diagnostic answer accuracy but not the registered value.
problems: The finding's threshold crossing depends on including differences from the release's post-EOS length restriction. outputs/gate_summary.json reports 0.21997525953728 when that restriction is also applied to the paper rule, versus the registered literal comparison's 0.3593691989312193. The primary result therefore does not establish a greater-than-0.25 difference attributable to cumulative-product acceptance alone.

outputs/gate_summary.json reports that not every nominal mask-view input was a mask token. The engineer attributes this to EOS padding in one pass, but gate_log.py records only an aggregate all-mask flag rather than the individual input tokens. This limits independent examination of that boundary case.

At gamma=0.8, an accepted cumulative product implies that every accepted draft probability is at least 0.8, which itself implies argmax agreement. Thus the absent explicit agreement check is not a permissiveness mechanism under these settings.

gate_audit/run_audit.py allows a seed-copy fallback without enforcing an independently established expected hash. It was not used in the supplied evaluation, but could compromise source pinning in a future offline run.

run_eval.sh lacks pipefail, so pip or Python failures could be hidden by successful downstream pipeline commands. The supplied evaluation nevertheless contains completed generation and newly reported outputs consistent with the code.

Model, tokenizer and dataset revisions are not pinned, and the sample consists of only the first 12 questions on release-driven trajectories. These limit future reproducibility and generalization, although the registration did not require broader sampling or revision pinning.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation reports 0.3593691989312193 over 12 eligible prompts and 194 nonempty passes, exceeding the registered threshold, with zero implementation-replay mismatches. The supplied code obtains real model outputs, preserves release-driven generation, and correctly computes the registered prompt-weighted absolute-prefix difference; its logging hooks do not change acceptance logic. The procedural departures do not plausibly change that primary value, and the EOS restriction is part of the exact released predicate rather than an unauthorized replacement statistic. registration.title: Test confidence-ranked versus positional order in Flash-Verify
registration.seed_connection: The seed sorts search candidates by draft confidence and verifies them causally, stopping at the first rejection. Because earlier candidates affect later verifier conditionals, the ordering may change the accepted prefix. The seed does not isolate this ordering choice.
registration.hypothesis: On frozen GSM8K verifier states, descending draft-confidence order accepts more search tokens than ascending absolute-position order by more than 0.25 tokens per nonempty verify pass.
registration.contribution: An order ablation that holds the search set and pre-verification state fixed, separating the local value of confidence ordering from changes in the candidate set.

closest_work.difference: The seed prescribes confidence ordering but does not compare it with positional ordering on identical candidate sets and states.
Dependency-guided parallel decoding selects tokens to commit; this experiment changes only the causal order used to verify a fixed Flash-Verify candidate set.
Free draft-and-verification targets a different decoding procedure rather than this within-verifier ordering ablation.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from Hugging Face.
The main test split of openai/gsm8k from Hugging Face Datasets and the GSM8K answer extractor from lm-evaluation-harness.
registration.method: Record the repository SHA. Use the first 12 GSM8K test examples in dataset order, formatted as Question: {question} followed by Answer:. Run greedy decoding with batch size 1, generation length 96, block length 16, epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, and the paper's Flash-Cache query construction with beta_m=64 and beta_t=64. Advance a capture trajectory using the paper-literal Flash-Verify rule. At each of the first four nonempty search passes per prompt, save the draft state, cache state, confident set, search positions, draft IDs, and candidate confidence scores. From the same saved state, run two verifier forwards: descending draft-confidence order with stable position tie-breaking, and ascending absolute response-position order. Keep each token's original position embedding, rebuild the causal mask to follow the tested order, restore the same cache before each forward, and do not persist either verifier query's cache writes. Apply the same paper-literal per-token agreement and mask-view confidence rule in both conditions, stopping at the first rejection. Also run complete greedy trajectories under both orders on the same prompts and report GSM8K exact-match accuracy and synchronized throughput as diagnostics; do not use these divergent trajectories for the registered statistic. Include cold setup and downloads in the time estimate.

event.description: Confidence-ranked ordering accepts materially more search tokens per frozen verify pass than positional ordering.
event.statistic: Mean across prompts of the within-prompt mean difference in accepted search-prefix length, confidence-ranked minus positional, over the captured nonempty verify states.

evaluation.procedure: Write one row per frozen state and ordering to outputs/order_replay.jsonl, including candidate positions, order, search-set size, accepted-prefix length, and cache-state identifier. Write complete-generation outputs and timings to outputs/order_generations.jsonl. Write outputs/order_summary.json with the registered statistic, eligible prompt and pass counts, per-prompt differences, and diagnostic exact-match accuracy and throughput by ordering.
evaluation.controls: The registered comparison uses the same captured state, draft candidates, confident set, cache contents, and acceptance rule; only candidate ordering and its corresponding causal mask change. End-to-end diagnostics are reported separately because later states can diverge.

registration.full_scale_study: If confidence ordering improves local accepted yield, compare confidence, positional, and additional fixed orderings on larger samples and multiple tasks. Measure accepted fractions, task accuracy, and synchronized throughput, including whether the local yield difference persists in end-to-end trajectories.

agent.reason: Confidence ordering should put candidates more likely to pass first, which matters when verification stops at the first rejection. But changing order also changes the verifier's conditionals, and positional order could sometimes better reflect token dependencies.

judge_astra.reason: Stopping at the first rejection should favor placing high-confidence candidates first, and the required 0.25-token advantage is modest. However, changing the order also changes verifier conditionals, so positional ordering could perform better on some states.

judge_fable.reason: Confidence-descending order defers hard tokens so a single ambiguous leftmost position cannot truncate the accepted prefix, while positional order stops at the first low-confidence or disagreeing token; a >0.25 token/pass advantage is likely if the frozen-state replay is implemented correctly, but the two-view causal mask with duplicated positions and cache save/restore is a substantial implementation risk.

judge_opus.reason: Draft confidence often decays from the decoded frontier, so the two orders frequently coincide. Confidence order gains from isolated high-confidence spikes and mid-chain dips; positional order gains from autoregressive-like chaining after newly committed tokens. A net advantage above 0.25 tokens per pass for confidence order is plausible but far from assured, and the custom ordered causal masks plus cache restoration add implementation risk.

judge_sol.reason: Draft confidence plausibly predicts verifier agreement and confidence, making descending-confidence order advantageous when acceptance stops at the first rejection. Positional dependencies can reverse that advantage on some states, but a mean gain exceeding 0.25 tokens seems likely.

judge_luna.reason: The seed orders candidates by draft confidence, and candidates just below the 0.9 draft threshold can still meet the 0.8 verification threshold; putting them first can avoid an early rejection that ends the accepted prefix. Conditional interactions may reduce or reverse that advantage, so the result is not certain.

judge_muse.reason: The first verified token conditions only on tracked context plus masked search tokens, so leading with high-confidence candidates should reduce early rejection versus positional order. The size of the gain is uncertain because later conditionals depend on order.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed defines Flash-Verify's causal order as descending draft confidence (Eq. 4, Appendix C). Its ablations cover gamma, the track budget beta_t, the window size beta_m, generation and prefill length, and batch size. None of them compares confidence order with positional order on the same frozen candidate sets and states.

SSD also has the dLLM draft and verify its own tokens in one forward pass, but it uses hierarchical verification trees in a lossless scheme. From its abstract, it does not appear to isolate confidence versus positional order within a fixed candidate set.

PRESTO studies how diffusion draft confidence should rank candidate paths for prefix-based AR verification in speculative decoding. That is a related question about ordering and ranking, but it concerns tree drafting with an AR verifier, not the order of a two-view causal mask inside Flash-Verify.

Self-speculative masked diffusions train a model whose final layer uses a causal mask for draft-and-validate. This is a trained model on GPT-2-scale text and proteins, and I found no ablation of confidence versus positional order on frozen LLaDA states.

Dependency-guided parallel decoding chooses which tokens to commit. It does not change the verification order of a fixed Flash-Verify search set. This entry is taken from the registered closest work; I did not open the paper.

opus.reason: The seed paper fixes verification to descending draft-confidence order, and none of its many ablations tests positional order. My searches on self-speculative and draft-and-verify decoding for dLLMs turned up related methods (SSD, PRESTO, S2D2, self-speculative masked diffusions), but none that replays frozen states to compare candidate orders inside a causal two-view verifier. I found nothing that answers this question, though my search was limited, so I judge it distinct.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM specifies descending draft-confidence order and first-rejection stopping, but its experiments do not compare confidence and positional verification orders on identical saved states and candidate sets.

Self Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models identifies generation-order mismatch as an acceptance bottleneck and evaluates additional mix-order verification branches. It does not isolate confidence versus positional causal order while holding the candidate set, cache, and acceptance rule fixed.

Generation Order and Parallel Decoding in Masked Diffusion Models compares confidence-based and spatial unmasking schedules using generation accuracy. These schedules change decoding trajectories and selected positions, rather than testing accepted-prefix yield under alternative verification orders for fixed drafts.

sol.reason: The seed and related papers establish that ordering can matter, but they do not answer this experiment's controlled local question. In the arXiv work searched and read through 2026-10-07, I found no comparison of confidence-ranked versus positional causal verification on the same frozen Flash-Verify state, search set, and acceptance rule.

opus.reason: Both ask whether confidence-descending causal order yields longer accepted prefixes than left-to-right positional order, changing only the order and its causal mask. Both measure accepted-prefix length, with accuracy and throughput as secondary readouts. The registered version does this on frozen states, and #13 runs end-to-end, but the question and the order manipulation are the same.

sol.reason: Both change confidence-ranked versus positional causal verification order and measure accepted-prefix length; frozen-state replay provides a tighter control for essentially the same ablation.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (order_exp.py, launched by run_eval.sh). The registered statistic came out at 0.708, above the 0.25 threshold. I ran the whole pipeline twice on the dev machine and got the same value both times. It rests on 12 prompts with 4 frozen states each (48 verify-pass pairs). The 12 per-prompt differences range from 0 to 2.75, and all of them are ≥0. Averaged over states, confidence ordering accepted 2.02 search tokens per pass and positional ordering accepted 1.31. Given the small sample, this is evidence for a local effect, not a precise estimate of its size.

Setup:
- I wrote my own LLaDA-1.5 forward pass in plain PyTorch. It loads the weights straight from the safetensors files, using bf16, RMSNorm, RoPE with the model's theta and SwiGLU. It keeps a flat KV cache of shape [L, heads, head_dim] for each layer. I did not use the repo's Triton kernels or model class.
- The first step runs the full sequence through the model. Every later draft pass uses the Flash-Cache query: the tracked set T^t (newly decoded tokens first, then the top ones by Eq. 2 score, β_t=64 in total) plus the first β_m=64 masked positions. These query tokens write to the cache and attend to the whole cache, as in Eq. 1.
- Eq. 2 scores are the unnormalized q·k/√d logits from the masked-window queries, averaged over heads and queries and summed over layers.
- Decoding is greedy, batch size 1, generation length 96, ε=0.9, γ=0.8.
- Prompts are the first 12 GSM8K main/test examples, formatted as "Question: {q}\nAnswer:" with no examples in the prompt.

Verify pass, implemented as the paper describes it:
- The query is T_v (the top 2·16−|D|−2|S| entries of T^t), then D^t with the tokens just committed, then the draft view of S, then the mask view of S.
- The attention mask follows Appendix C, rebuilt for whichever order is being tested. Tracked rows cannot see the draft view. Draft row a sees drafts b≤a and masks b>a. Mask row a sees drafts b<a and masks b≥a.
- Each token keeps its absolute-position RoPE. Cache entries at query positions are left out of the keys.
- A token is accepted if the mask-view argmax equals the draft token and the mask-view confidence is ≥γ. Acceptance stops at the first rejection.
- The verify pass never writes to the cache. For each captured state I clone the cache and restore it before each of the two verifier forwards. A cache fingerprint is checked after each forward and was unchanged in every case.
- The capture trajectory advances with the confidence-ordered result. The first 4 passes per prompt that have a nonempty search set are replayed in both orders: confidence descending with ties broken by position, and position ascending. Every prompt had 4 eligible passes, and the search sets were identical between orders in all cases.

End-to-end diagnostics, from separate full runs, synchronized timing, after a warm-up run, not used for the statistic:
- Both orders reach 0.75 exact match with lm-eval's flexible-extract regex.
- Confidence order: about 52 tok/s and 20.5 steps on average. Positional order: about 35 tok/s and 32.2 steps.
- These come from 12 prompts on trajectories that diverge, so they are diagnostics only.

Decisions and deviations, all kept small:
1. Candidate set. The paper uses β for two different things, so I followed the released code: candidates are the first block_length=16 masked positions of the 64-token window. The other masked window positions are only there as queries. I did not apply the code's cap of 8 search tokens, so that the search set stays fixed across orders.
2. Forced progress. As in the code's `keep_num=max(keep_num,1)`, the top-confidence candidate always goes into D, even below ε. Without this a step could make no progress at all.
3. End-of-sequence handling. Once an EOS or EOT token (126081 or 126348) is decoded, positions after the earliest one are dropped from the candidates. Generation ends when everything before it is decoded.
4. Answer extraction. I copied lm-eval's gsm8k flexible-extract regex, its normalization and its stop strings into my own code instead of installing lm-eval.
5. Cache state. The full cache state is kept only in GPU memory, because each state is about 150 MB and too large to save to disk. The replay rows record a cache-state ID, which is a fingerprint, plus the confident set, search positions, draft IDs and confidences.
6. Repository SHA. The machine has no git, so I recorded the GitHub HEAD SHA of VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM through the API (a667345f… at test time). This is not guaranteed to match the seed snapshot I read.
7. Throughput. Throughput counts the response positions decoded up to EOS, divided by wall time.

Expected runtime is about 2 minutes plus the model download.

departures: order_exp.py reimplements the LLaDA-1.5 forward pass, the flat KV cache, Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify in plain PyTorch. It does not use the Flash-dLLM repository's model class, kernels or reference implementation, although the registration lists that repository as an input. Disclosed. This could shift absolute accepted-prefix lengths, because the implementation is not checked against the reference. Both orders share the same code, and the outputs are coherent (0.75 exact match), so this does not plausibly reverse the order comparison.

The repository SHA is the current GitHub HEAD fetched through the API, not a recorded checkout. seed_sha.txt contains only '/bin/sh: 1: git: not found'. Disclosed. This does not affect the value but weakens provenance.

The candidate set is the first 16 (block_length) masked positions of the 64-position masked window, and the released code's cap of 8 search tokens is not applied. This interprets details the registration leaves underspecified. Disclosed. It affects search-set sizes (up to 15 here), which bounds how much order can matter, so it could change the magnitude.

A forced-progress rule always puts the top-confidence candidate in D even when it falls below epsilon. It is not in the registration and was taken from the released code. Disclosed. It changes which states are captured and their search sets, but it is applied identically before both orders.

After an EOS or EOT token is decoded, later positions are dropped from the candidates. Not registered. Disclosed. This affects trajectories, and its effect on the four early captured states is probably negligible.

Eq. 2 tracking scores use unnormalized q·k/√d logits averaged over heads and queries and summed over layers. This is an interpretation. It affects the tracked set T and T_v, identically for both orders.
The capture states include step 0, which uses a full-sequence query rather than the Flash-Cache query. This is consistent with 'first four nonempty search passes'. It is included in the statistic.
The prompt has a newline between the question and 'Answer:'. The registration leaves this open. No meaningful effect.

Registered saving of the cache state: the cache is kept only in GPU memory, and outputs/order_replay.jsonl records a sum-based fingerprint. Disclosed. The value is unaffected, but frozen states cannot be re-audited offline.
The lm-eval flexible-extract regex, normalization and stop strings were copied rather than taken from an installed lm-eval. Diagnostic only.

The throughput figures in the notes (52 and 35 tok/s) differ from the protected evaluation (69.2 and 46.4 tok/s), presumably because of different hardware. Diagnostic only; the registered statistic is unaffected.
problems: The registered experiment depends on a from-scratch reimplementation in order_exp.py with no parity check against the Flash-dLLM reference. Fidelity to the seed's actual system is therefore assumed, not demonstrated.

The sample is small: 12 prompts with 4 states each, all taken from the first four passes of the confidence-order trajectory. The result says little about later states, other tasks or other models. The per-prompt differences are consistently non-negative (10 positive, 2 zero), but the magnitude 0.708 is imprecise.

The cache fingerprint (sums and absolute sums) is a weak integrity check. The code restores the cache with an explicit copy before each forward, and the verify forward is write=False, so this does not threaten the value.

Unregistered rules (forced progress, EOS truncation of candidates, uncapped 16-token candidate set) shape which states and search sets are captured. They apply equally to both orders, but the magnitude may depend on them.
seed_sha.txt holds only a git error, and the SHA recorded in outputs/order_summary.json is today's GitHub HEAD, which may not match the seed snapshot.

The statistic in outputs/order_summary.json is computed correctly from real model outputs logged per state in outputs/order_replay.jsonl. The departures are disclosed interpretations of underspecified details or provenance and diagnostic issues, applied symmetrically to both orders, so none plausibly changes the direction of the comparison. The finding is a credible, consistent local effect: no prompt favours positional order. It rests on a small sample of early-trajectory states, a single model and task, and a reimplementation not validated against the reference code. It is therefore meaningful but not precise or broadly established.

departures: order_exp.py: The engineer substituted a custom PyTorch forward pass and cache implementation for the supplied Flash-dLLM implementation. This is not inherently prohibited, but no reference-parity test is supplied; implementation differences could change draft predictions, captured states, and verifier acceptance.

order_exp.py, generate(): If no candidate reaches epsilon=0.9, the highest-confidence candidate is nevertheless committed into D without verification. This additional progress rule is not specified in the registration and can change the confident set, search set, verifier conditioning, capture trajectory, and registered statistic. The claim that it prevents possible stalls does not demonstrate that this particular unconditional commitment was necessary.

order_exp.py, generate(): Candidates are interpreted as the first 16 remaining masked positions within the 64-position window, and the engineer reports omitting the released code's eight-search-token cap. These choices can affect candidate membership and accepted-prefix lengths relative to other implementations. However, the registration does not explicitly require that cap, and the supplied evidence does not establish whether this interpretation differs from the paper-literal candidate rule.

order_exp.py, generate(): Explicit EOS/EOT truncation and termination rules were added. They can change subsequent candidate sets and complete-generation diagnostics; whether they affected any captured pass is not established by the displayed records. Since the registration leaves EOS handling unspecified, this is not independently a demonstrated fidelity violation.

order_exp.py and outputs/order_replay.jsonl: Frozen caches are cloned temporarily in GPU memory, but full cache tensors and full draft states are not persisted. The replay file contains fingerprints and selected candidate information rather than independently reloadable frozen states. This does not alter the implemented paired calculation, but limits verification and later replay of the registered state capture.

order_exp.py, outputs/order_summary.json, and seed_sha.txt: The recorded SHA is GitHub's current repository HEAD, not an identified checkout used to execute the experiment. seed_sha.txt contains a failed git invocation. This provenance substitution does not directly change the numerical statistic, but does not identify the actual reference implementation or establish its correspondence to the seed snapshot.

order_exp.py, extract_flex(), norm(), and main(): Answer extraction and stopping behavior are implemented locally instead of calling lm-evaluation-harness. Exact equivalence is not demonstrated. Any discrepancy could change diagnostic exact-match accuracy, but not the registered accepted-prefix statistic.
problems: order_exp.py: The below-epsilon forced commitment changes the registered paper-literal procedure unless that fallback is part of the paper rule; the supplied evidence does not establish that it is.
order_exp.py: There is no supplied comparison validating the custom model forward, cache construction, attention scores, or verifier outputs against the reference implementation.

outputs/order_replay.jsonl: The cache fingerprint hashes per-layer aggregate sums, not every cache entry. Although the visible write=False path supports cache immutability, the fingerprint alone is not a strong equality check, and the absent full states prevent independent artifact-only replay.

outputs/order_summary.json: Equal diagnostic exact-match rates of 0.75 do not establish accuracy equivalence. Throughput comes from divergent trajectories in one implementation and one fixed timing order, so it is not a controlled estimate of the isolated ordering effect.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation produced the registered point statistic, 0.7083333333333334, from real downloaded weights and GSM8K data, and the visible aggregation matches the registered prompt-level averaging and threshold. The paired verifier forwards share candidates, draft predictions, context, and restored caches, with no evident hard-coded result or cross-condition state contamination. Fidelity is nevertheless unfaithful because the additional unconditional below-epsilon commitment plausibly changes the states and search sets being measured, without demonstrated necessity or paper-rule support. The result is a meaningful local finding for the implemented variant, but the small fixed sample, unvalidated reference parity, and incomplete frozen-state artifacts prevent a stronger claim about the registered paper-literal procedure or general accuracy and speed.

departures: order_exp.py reimplements LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Cache, and Flash-Verify in pure PyTorch and never runs the Flash-dLLM repository named as an input. Kernel and rule differences could change accepted-prefix lengths.

The recorded SHA in order_exp.py is GitHub HEAD at test time; seed_sha.txt shows git was missing, so this is not a checkout of code that ran and may not match the seed snapshot. It does not itself change the statistic.

The released code's cap of 8 search tokens was not applied (order_exp.py; replay rows show sets up to 15). That can change the statistic versus a code-default run; it was omitted so the search set stays fixed across orders, which the registration requires.

If no candidate meets epsilon, order_exp.py forces the top candidate into the confident set. The registration states epsilon=0.9 and does not state this exception. registration.title: Test attention-ranked cache refresh against recency at a matched budget
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache selects previously decoded positions for refresh using attention importance. The seed motivates this policy with concentrated attention but does not compare it with a same-budget recency policy.
registration.hypothesis: At a matched decoded-position query budget, attention-ranked refresh yields more faithful outputs than recency refresh, with a mean normalized token-level LCS advantage over full recomputation greater than 0.03.
registration.contribution: Tests whether the attention ranking matters beyond query count by comparing it with a simple recency selector at the same budget.

closest_work.difference: The seed uses attention-ranked tracking but does not report a fixed-budget comparison with recency selection.
Elastic-Cache uses attention-pattern drift to trigger refreshes; this experiment tests Flash-Cache's top-budget token selection against recency.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from Hugging Face.
The main test split of openai/gsm8k from Hugging Face Datasets and the GSM8K answer extractor from lm-evaluation-harness.
registration.method: Use the first 12 GSM8K test examples in dataset order, formatted as Question: {question} followed by Answer:. Run greedy confidence-aware decoding with batch size 4, generation length 128, block size 16, epsilon=0.9, masked-window size beta_m=64, and decoded-position query budget beta_t=32. Generate a full-recomputation reference with caching disabled but the same confidence-aware decoding rule. Then run two cached conditions: the seed's attention-score ranking from its stated attention-importance equation and a recency selector that chooses the most recently committed eligible historical positions. In both cached conditions always include newly decoded positions as specified by the seed, fill the remaining beta_t budget from the same eligible pool, and retain the same active masked window. Instrument actual queried positions and assert that the two policies use equal query counts at each step. Compare the generated token IDs directly, excluding special tokens; do not decode and re-encode them. Also report GSM8K exact-match accuracy and synchronized throughput as diagnostics. Include cold installation and downloads in the time estimate.

event.description: Attention-ranked refresh has a greater than 0.03 mean normalized-LCS advantage over recency refresh when each is compared with the same full-recomputation reference.
event.statistic: Mean across prompts of normalized LCS for attention-ranked output against the full-recomputation output minus normalized LCS for recency output against that same reference; normalize each LCS by the maximum of the two generated-token lengths, with a minimum denominator of 1.

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per prompt and condition to outputs/cache_policy_runs.jsonl, including generated token IDs, reference IDs, per-prompt normalized LCS, per-step queried positions and counts, extracted answer correctness, and synchronized generation time. Write outputs/cache_policy_summary.json with the registered statistic, per-prompt values, query-count checks, answer accuracy, and throughput for each condition.
evaluation.controls: The cached conditions share prompts, model, decoding schedule, confidence threshold, active masked window, and decoded-position query budget. Their only cache-policy difference is attention ranking versus recency ranking. The full-recomputation run is a reference, not a third cache policy. A result below threshold is not evidence that the policies are equivalent.

registration.full_scale_study: If the attention ranking improves reference fidelity, test several decoded-position budgets and prompt lengths across GSM8K, MATH, and code tasks. Report task accuracy, output fidelity to full recomputation, throughput, and actual query counts for attention and recency policies.

agent.reason: The seed's attention-concentration observation gives attention ranking a plausible advantage over recency at equal query counts. Recency may nevertheless preserve useful evolving context, and that advantage need not translate into a 0.03 LCS difference.

judge_astra.reason: Attention concentration does not establish that the most-attended states are the ones most worth refreshing. Short generations make recency a plausible competitor, while enforcing identical actual query counts after trajectories diverge adds implementation risk.

judge_fable.reason: Attention-ranked refresh plausibly tracks prompt heavy-hitters better than recency, but the top-k likely overlaps heavily with recent tokens and recency keeps local context exact, so the fidelity gap is probably small and 12 prompts are noisy relative to a 0.03 threshold; implementation of selective-update caching with two policies adds failure risk.

judge_opus.reason: Recency refresh targets the recently decoded tokens whose KV is most likely stale. Attention-logit ranking may spend slots on sink or prompt tokens; Elastic-Cache suggests the most-attended tokens drift least. A systematic attention advantage is therefore doubtful, and with 12 prompts the LCS difference is noise-dominated, so the event mainly depends on chance.

judge_sol.reason: Attention concentration does not establish that high-attention positions benefit most from refreshing, or that the stated raw-logit ranking beats recency. With short outputs and mandatory refresh of newly decoded tokens, recency could be competitive enough to prevent a greater than 0.03 LCS advantage.

judge_luna.reason: The seed reports that the top 32 attended tokens capture up to half of attention in middle layers, which gives attention-ranked refresh a plausible advantage over recency. But attention concentration alone does not establish better cache fidelity or a greater-than-0.03 LCS gain on this small sample.

judge_muse.reason: Seed shows attention concentration motivating tracking but no recency comparison, and both policies share new tokens and the masked window, so differences affect only older-token refresh. A consistent >0.03 LCS advantage is possible but uncertain because recency may already capture relevant history in short generations.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It introduces attention-ranked tracking with budget beta_t. It supports this with Fig. 1(b), which shows that the top-32 attended decoded tokens hold up to 50% of attention, and it sweeps beta_t. In the sections I read, it never compares its selector with a recency selector at the same budget, and it does not measure token-level agreement with full recomputation.

EntropyCache recomputes the k most recently decoded tokens (a recency selector) and argues for this from post-decoding feature volatility. However, it compares its whole method against d2Cache and Elastic-Cache rather than swapping only the token selector at a matched query budget. It also scores task accuracy and throughput, not LCS agreement with full recomputation.

Elastic-Cache uses attention drift on the most-attended token to decide when to refresh and a depth-aware layer schedule to decide where. It does not rank decoded positions under a fixed token budget and does not compare against recency.

opus.reason: Prior work has proposed both an attention-based selector (Flash-dLLM, and d2Cache's attention rollout) and a recency selector (EntropyCache) for refreshing dLLM caches. However, I found no paper that compares the two with everything else held fixed at a matched decoded-position budget, scoring each against full recomputation. EntropyCache comes closest, but its comparisons are between whole systems that differ in when they refresh as well as in which tokens they refresh, so they do not settle this question. My search ended before I could check every recent dLLM cache paper, so an unfound ablation remains possible.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM introduces attention-ranked refresh and sweeps tracking budgets, but does not compare attention ranking with recency at equal per-step query counts.

EntropyCache recomputes a fixed budget of recently decoded tokens, but its comparisons with attention-based methods also change refresh triggers and realized recomputation budgets; they do not isolate ranking.
d2Cache refreshes influential tokens using attention rollout, but does not report a matched-budget attention-versus-recency selector comparison.
Polestar compares refresh selectors on the same cached trajectory and budget, but evaluates drift, attention-change, uncertainty, and random selectors—not attention importance versus recency.

sol.reason: Attention-guided refresh and fixed-budget recency refresh are existing ideas, but I found no work by the cutoff that isolates their relative effect with equal per-step query counts and otherwise shared decoding. The seed's budget sweeps and the related selector studies therefore do not settle the registered question about output fidelity to full recomputation.

opus.reason: Both ablate the tracked-set selection rule (Eq. 2 attention versus recency, among others) at a fixed budget under confidence-aware cached decoding. Both measure fidelity to an exact no-cache reference, alongside accuracy.

sol.reason: The listed tracking-policy ablations measure prediction divergence or task outcomes, not generated-sequence LCS fidelity to a full-recomputation reference under attention versus recency refresh.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (cache_policy/run_experiment.py, launched by run_eval.sh). I imported the seed's LLaDA model code and fused Flash-Cache Triton kernels from /workspace/seed/llada without changing them. I re-implemented the seed's generate_with_Flash_dLLM confidence-aware (non-verify) loop with two changes: the key used to rank previously decoded positions can be switched, and the positions actually queried at every step are recorded. Setup: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 in bf16; the first 12 GSM8K main/test examples, formatted "Question: {q}\nAnswer:"; greedy confidence-aware decoding; batch 4 with the seed's dynamic slot refill; generation length 128; block size 16; epsilon 0.9; beta_m = 64 (16 decode candidates plus 48 more masked positions queried, i.e. the seed's mask_num=4); beta_t = 32.

The three conditions:
- Reference: the seed's full re-query branch (track_num<0). Every position is re-queried every step through the same kernels, so this is full recomputation with the same decoding rule. It is not a separate no-cache code path.
- Attention: the seed's ranking.
- Recency: the most recently committed positions, using a commit counter.

Both cached policies always include the newly decoded positions. They fill the rest of the beta_t budget from the same pool and share the same masked window. Generated IDs are compared directly: each sequence is cut at the first EOS/EOT and special/mask tokens are removed. Nothing is decoded and re-encoded.

Result: the statistic is -0.0197, below the 0.03 threshold, so the registered event did not occur. Per prompt, attention was better on 2, recency on 4, and 6 tied. The per-prompt SD is 0.24 (SE about 0.07), and the mean is driven by a few large divergences (+0.54 on one prompt, -0.57 and -0.20 on others). This is not evidence that the two policies are equivalent.

Diagnostics:
- Accuracy: full 10/12, attention 8/12, recency 9/12.
- Synchronized throughput: about 73 tok/s (full), 144 (attention), 145 (recency), measured after an untimed warmup pass for Triton compilation.
- The warmup outputs were token-identical to the timed run for all 12 prompts in every condition.
- Caveat: a 4-prompt pilot gave slightly different outputs for the same prompts (e.g. one prompt's normalized LCS was 0.858 vs 0.879 in the full run). Changing batch composition or buffer size therefore moves outputs numerically. This nuisance applies to all conditions.

Changes from the registration and interpretation choices:
1. Query-count check. Trajectories diverge, so total query counts cannot be equal at every step. I hard-assert that the decoded-position query count is equal between the two policies at every shared step (passed: 447/447 steps, always 32). I also assert that the budget rule holds. Total counts (including the masked window) matched at 424/447 shared steps. The mismatches come only from the masked window being cut off at the end of the sequence once trajectories differ, and step counts differ after divergence.
2. Attention score. I used the seed code's implementation of its attention-importance equation, not a rewrite: unnormalized q·k logits, averaged over heads and the 16 decode-candidate masked queries, summed over layers with index >1 (the seed kernel skips layers 0 and 1), not over all 64 window positions.
3. Newly decoded positions are all included. There are at most 16 per step, so they never exceed beta_t = 32.
4. Recency ties: prompt positions are ordered by position. Positions committed in the same step are ordered by the seed's confidence-sorted commit order (the lower-confidence one counts as more recent).
5. The LCS uses all generated IDs up to EOS, including any text after a "Question:" continuation. Accuracy decodes the text, cuts it at lm-eval's stop strings, then applies lm-eval's flexible-extract RegexFilter and exact-match normalization (EM normalization re-implemented).

The full command (install, model download, warmup and timed runs) took about 1.5 minutes here with the model already cached; a cold install took 33 s and the 16 GB download about 10 s.

departures: Attention score (cache_policy/run_experiment.py, engineer note 2). The registration asks for the seed's stated attention-importance equation. The code instead uses the seed kernel's implementation: unnormalized q·k logits averaged over heads and over only the 16 decode-candidate queries, summed over layers with index above 1, rather than over all 64 masked-window positions. The paper's equation is not shown, so it is unclear whether this differs materially. If it does, it changes the ranking and could change the value. It was disclosed, and it is the seed's released Flash-Cache behaviour.

Full-recomputation reference (run_experiment.py, policy='full'). It is not a separate no-cache code path. It is the seed's re-query-everything branch through the same cache kernels: all decoded and masked positions up to seqlen_k are re-queried every step. This is functionally full recomputation, so it is unlikely to change the conclusion. It was disclosed.

Query-count control (run_experiment.py, summary query_count_checks). The registration says to assert equal query counts at each step. The code hard-asserts only the decoded-position count, which is always 32 by construction. Total counts differ at 23 of 447 shared steps because of masked-window truncation at the sequence end, and step counts differ after trajectories diverge (prompt 5: 18 vs 78 steps). This is a forced and disclosed adaptation and does not alter the computed statistic.

Token cleaning (run_experiment.py clean_ids). Sequences are truncated at the first EOS/EOT in addition to removing special tokens. The registration says only to exclude special tokens. Any non-special tokens after the first EOS are dropped. This is a reasonable interpretation with a probably small effect.

Prompt format (run_experiment.py). The prompt is 'Question: {q}\nAnswer:' with a newline separator. The registration leaves this open, and the same format is used in all conditions, so it should not change the value.

Recency tie-breaking (run_experiment.py commit_order). Within a step, the lower-confidence commit counts as more recent. The registration leaves this open. It was disclosed and could slightly change the recency ranking.

Batch composition (run_experiment.py load_slot). Dynamic slot refill means each condition runs prompts alongside different batch-mates, because finish times differ. The engineer's pilot shows that batch composition changes outputs numerically. This follows from the registered batch size of 4 and the seed loop, but it adds non-policy noise to the per-prompt differences.
Time estimate. The registration expected 34 minutes; the actual run took about 137 s. This has no effect on the result.
problems: Low power. There are 12 prompts and one repetition, with a per-prompt SD of about 0.24 (SE about 0.07). The resulting interval, roughly -0.17 to +0.13, cannot exclude the hypothesised advantage of more than 0.03. The null is therefore uninformative rather than a negative finding, as the engineer correctly notes.

The statistic is driven by three prompts with large divergences (+0.54, -0.57, -0.20; outputs/cache_policy_summary.json). This is consistent with chaotic trajectory divergence in bf16 rather than a systematic policy effect.

Batch composition differs between conditions under dynamic refill, and it measurably perturbs outputs: the engineer's 4-prompt pilot gave a different per-prompt normalized LCS (0.858 vs 0.879). The policy contrast is therefore confounded with numerical batch-composition noise (run_experiment.py).

The attention ranking is the seed kernel's implementation (unnormalized logits, 16 candidate queries, layers above 1). It may not match the paper's stated equation, which the registration named, and that equation cannot be checked here.

The asserted query-count control is trivially satisfied, because n_dec_q is always min(nd, 32) = 32. The budget_rule_ok check is loose (it allows up to beta_t + block_m), so it adds little verification (run_experiment.py).
The accuracy diagnostics (10, 8 and 9 of 12) are too small to support any accuracy comparison.
opus.reason: The run matches the registered model, data, decoding settings, budgets and statistic. The main interpretive choice is to rank by the seed code's attention-importance implementation, which may differ from the paper's stated equation; it was disclosed and reflects the deployed Flash-Cache policy. The other departures were forced or left open by the registration (per-step query-count equality after divergence, EOS truncation, tie-breaking), and none should change the computed statistic. The value of -0.0197 is recomputable from the per-prompt values in the summary, comes from real model outputs, and the warmup and timed runs gave token-identical outputs. With only 12 prompts, an SE of about 0.07 and a mean dominated by a few chaotic large divergences, the result neither supports nor meaningfully refutes the hypothesised 0.03 advantage, so the evidence is valid but weak.

departures: cache_policy/run_experiment.py: The reference calls the model with use_cache=True and refreshes all positions through the Flash-Cache kernels, rather than disabling caching as registered. The visible loop supports full-position recomputation, so this is not necessarily stale-cache reuse; however, equivalence to an independently cache-disabled reference was not checked, and numerical differences could change the LCS values.

cache_policy/run_experiment.py and outputs/cache_policy_summary.json: The registered assertion of equal query counts at every step was narrowed to equal decoded-position counts at shared steps. Total query counts differed at 23 of 447 shared steps, and unmatched steps were not checked. This preserves the central decoded-position budget comparison but does not satisfy the stronger registered control; different masked-query counts and execution trajectories could affect outputs.

cache_policy/run_experiment.py: clean_ids truncates each generated sequence at the first EOS or EOT, in addition to removing special tokens. The registration explicitly specifies special-token exclusion but does not specify this truncation rule. It could change the primary statistic if ordinary generated tokens occur after a terminator, particularly with out-of-order diffusion commitments; the displayed evidence does not establish the magnitude of that effect.

Engineer notes and cache_policy/run_experiment.py: Attention ranking delegates to the seed kernels' operational score, described as unnormalized q·k logits averaged over heads and 16 candidate queries, using layers with index greater than 1. The registration specifies the paper's stated attention-importance equation. Whether these are different cannot be established because the equation and imported kernels are not included; any actual discrepancy could change the selected positions and primary result.
problems: The matched-query control is weaker than registered: outputs/cache_policy_summary.json documents total-count mismatches and different trajectory lengths, while cache_policy/run_experiment.py asserts equality only for decoded counts on shared steps.

The budget_rule_ok check in cache_policy/run_experiment.py permits decoded counts up to beta_t + block_m, rather than enforcing the exact implemented budget formula. This is a weak assertion, although the reported post-prefill counts do not show a resulting violation.
The engineer's statement that all 447 shared steps queried exactly 32 decoded positions overlooks full-prefill steps. The code and displayed JSONL row show that prefill queries the entire prompt.

The cache-disabled reference and paper-equation attention ranking were not independently validated. Imported seed model and kernel files are absent from the supplied archive, limiting verification of those claims.
EOS/EOT truncation is an additional primary-metric interpretation whose effect cannot be reconstructed from the cleaned generated_ids stored in the JSONL.

Only 12 ordered prompts and one scored run were used. The per-prompt differences are highly variable, with an approximate standard error of 0.07; this does not precisely resolve an advantage of 0.03 or establish equivalence.

The engineer reports sensitivity to batch composition or buffer size. Dynamic slot refill can produce different batch compositions after policy trajectories diverge, so warmup agreement within each condition does not establish robustness to this nuisance.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed successfully, produced both registered output files, and reported a statistic consistent with the supplied per-prompt values: -0.019747951638162665, so the registered event did not occur. The visible code computes that value from model-generated token IDs and real GSM8K examples, with no apparent hard-coded result, leakage, or arithmetic error. Fidelity is unfaithful because the stronger query-count control was relaxed and the reference and token-processing procedures depart from the specified method, with plausible effects on the value. This is useful descriptive pilot evidence, but its imprecision and control limitations support neither recency superiority nor absence of an attention advantage.

departures: Query-count control (cache_policy/run_experiment.py; outputs/cache_policy_summary.json): the registration requires equal query counts at each step, but the run only hard-asserts equal decoded-position counts on the shared step prefix (447/447) and records total-count mismatches on 23/447 shared steps plus unequal trajectory lengths. This does not change the computed LCS; a literal assert would have aborted rather than alter the value.

Full-recomputation reference (cache_policy/run_experiment.py): registration says caching disabled; the reference is the seed full re-query branch through the same Flash-Cache kernels, not a separate no-cache forward. Could change reference tokens if those paths differ numerically; every position is re-queried, and no such difference is shown.

Generated-ID cleaning (cache_policy/run_experiment.py clean_ids): registration says exclude special tokens and compare IDs directly; the code also truncates at the first EOS/EOT. Could change normalized LCS if non-special tokens were committed after the first EOS, which parallel decoding allows; impact is not measurable from the saved cleaned IDs.

Attention-score scope (engineer notes; scores come from imported seed kernels, not recoded in run_experiment.py): ranking uses unnormalized q·k averaged over the 16 decode-candidate queries and layers with index >1, not all 64 masked-window positions. Could change which positions are refreshed if that differs from the paper equation; the equation is not in the provided files, so a difference is not established.

GSM8K exact-match normalization (cache_policy/run_experiment.py em_norm) is a local reimplementation, while extraction uses lm_eval RegexFilter. Could change diagnostic accuracy only, not the registered LCS statistic.
problems: Dynamic slot refill (cache_policy/run_experiment.py) makes co-batching depend on finish times, which differ by policy; the engineer notes a 4-prompt pilot moved one prompt's normalized LCS from 0.858 to 0.879, a nuisance on the scale of the 0.03 threshold and the observed mean.

Per-prompt differences in outputs/cache_policy_summary.json have SD about 0.24 (about -0.57 to +0.54), so the 12-prompt mean (SE about 0.07) is imprecise relative to the 0.03 event threshold and does not support equivalence or a stable ranking advantage.
The registered equal-query-count control is not fully met: total queries differ on 23/447 shared steps, 22 of them on prompt 4 (outputs/cache_policy_summary.json).
budget_rule_ok (cache_policy/run_experiment.py) allows decoded query counts up to beta_t+block_m (48), so it would not catch moderate budget violations; count equality is largely by construction.
The decoding loop is a reimplementation rather than a call to the seed generate function, so exact equivalence to the seed attention-importance path is not independently verified from these files.
grok.reason: The evaluation reran the registered 12-prompt comparison and reproduced the LCS statistic of about -0.0197 from real LLaDA generations, so the pre-registered event did not occur. Data, model, decoding hyperparameters, token-ID LCS definition, and decoded-position budget match the registration; the relaxed query-count assert and same-kernel full re-query do not change that value. The result is valid but weak: item-level dispersion is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.03 threshold, two prompts dominate the mean, and policy-dependent batching can move per-prompt LCS by about 0.02. Below-threshold is therefore a credible description of this run, not evidence that attention ranking is no better than recency.

grok.what_it_asks: It compares attention-ranked refresh of decoded positions with recency refresh at the same query budget on LLaDA-1.5 GSM8K generations, to learn which stays closer to full recomputation.

registration.title: Screen Flash-Verify on objectively scored IFEval instructions
registration.seed_connection: The seed evaluates mathematical reasoning and code generation and identifies generation outside structured tasks as untested. IFEval offers rule-based instruction-constraint scoring without a human or model judge.
registration.hypothesis: On a fixed IFEval sample, Flash-Verify increases the strict prompt-level compliance rate over confidence-aware Flash-Cache by more than 0.08 absolute.
registration.contribution: A paired, automatically scored generalization test of Flash-Verify on instruction constraints, with compliance rate and throughput reported separately.

closest_work.difference: The seed evaluates math and code benchmarks rather than rule-checked instruction-following prompts.
Plan for Speed evaluates a different diffusion decoding policy; this experiment compares Flash-Verify with confidence-aware decoding using the Flash-dLLM cache.
LLaDA 1.5 reports model-level performance, not a paired comparison of these two inference-time decoding modes on IFEval.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from Hugging Face.
The official IFEval test prompts and deterministic checker at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/instruction_following_eval.
registration.method: Select 24 IFEval test prompts without replacement using Python random seed 2609, and record their source indices. Use each prompt as plain text prefixed by Instruction: and append Response:, without using any reference response. Run both confidence-aware Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify on each prompt with the same LLaDA-1.5 checkpoint, greedy decoding, batch size 1, maximum generation length 192, block size 16, epsilon=0.9, gamma=0.8, beta_m=64, and beta_t=64; the only mode change is whether verification is enabled. Interleave the order of the paired mode runs by prompt. Synchronize the GPU for generation-only timing, after one warm-up prompt per mode. Score each completion with the official strict checker and record whether it reached the token limit before EOS. Include installation, model/data downloads, warm-up, generation, and scoring in the time estimate.

event.description: Flash-Verify improves strict IFEval prompt-level compliance over confidence-aware Flash-Cache by more than eight percentage points.
event.statistic: Strict prompt-level pass fraction for Flash-Verify minus strict prompt-level pass fraction for confidence-aware Flash-Cache across the 24 paired prompts.

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per prompt and decoding mode to outputs/ifeval_runs.jsonl, including prompt ID, response, per-instruction checker results, strict prompt pass, generated length, truncation status, and generation-only time. Write outputs/ifeval_summary.json with the registered paired rate difference, pass counts and rates, truncation counts, and generation throughput for each mode.
evaluation.controls: Both modes use the same prompts, checkpoint, prompt formatting, maximum length, cache parameters, greedy decoding, and official checker. No human or model judge is used; throughput is diagnostic and does not replace the registered compliance statistic.

registration.full_scale_study: If the compliance result warrants further study, evaluate the full IFEval set over multiple decoding thresholds and output limits, then test transfer to another supported diffusion checkpoint. Report paired strict pass rates, truncation, latency, and cache use.

agent.reason: Flash-Verify could help with strict constraints by checking candidates conditionally, but its more aggressive commitments could also hurt exact compliance. The event requires a sizable positive difference on a small sample, and the seed's structured-task results do not establish transfer to IFEval.

judge_astra.reason: The seed’s matched-cache comparisons do not suggest a consistent quality improvement from verification, and the short output cap can prevent satisfying length-heavy instructions. Nevertheless, only two net additional passes among 24 prompts would satisfy the event, leaving some chance of a sample-specific positive result.

judge_fable.reason: No mechanism predicts Flash-Verify improving instruction compliance; the paper shows roughly matched accuracy, and if anything lower-confidence commits in flat-confidence text may hurt coherence, so exceeding +8 points on 24 paired prompts needs a lucky run of discordant pairs.

judge_opus.reason: In the seed, Flash-Verify is usually slightly less accurate than confidence-aware Flash-Cache (7 of 8 settings), and nothing suggests it improves instruction compliance. Still, a net gain of only 2 of 24 prompts (0.083) clears the threshold, so noise from a handful of discordant pairs gives a non-trivial chance.

judge_sol.reason: The seed’s quality changes from adding verification are small or negative in several settings, providing little support for a substantial compliance improvement. Two net additional passes would satisfy the event, but the 192-token limit can also cause shared failures on length-intensive instructions.

judge_luna.reason: In the seed's eight cached benchmark settings, Flash-Verify has higher accuracy than confidence-aware Flash-Cache in only one, and then only slightly; IFEval could behave differently, but strict prompt-level scoring makes a net gain of at least two prompts out of 24 a substantial hurdle.

judge_muse.reason: At defaults Flash-Verify is faster but slightly less accurate than confidence-aware Flash-Cache on most seed settings, suggesting aggressive parallel commits trade accuracy for speed. A two-prompt strict-compliance gain on a new instruction domain is therefore unlikely though 24-prompt noise leaves some chance.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper tests Flash-Verify against confidence-aware Flash-Cache only on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP with LLaDA-1.5. Its appendix lists generation outside structured tasks as untested future work. It has no IFEval or instruction-constraint results.

Fast-dLLM introduced confidence-aware parallel decoding with a KV cache for dLLMs. It does not include Flash-Verify draft-and-verify decoding, and it does not run a paired IFEval strict-compliance comparison.
Elastic-Cache, by the same authors, is an adaptive KV-cache method evaluated on math and code. It has neither Flash-Verify nor an IFEval evaluation.
LLaDA 1.5 reports model-level benchmark scores. It does not compare the two Flash-dLLM inference-time decoding modes on IFEval.

opus.reason: The question is whether Flash-Verify changes strict IFEval prompt-level compliance compared with confidence-aware Flash-Cache. The seed paper does not answer it: it covers only math and code, and its appendix names generation outside structured tasks as future work. The seed paper was posted on 22 September 2026, about two weeks before the cutoff, and my searches found no later paper or other dLLM acceleration work that runs this paired IFEval comparison.
