registration.title: Flash-Verify speedup on the instruct checkpoint
registration.seed_connection: Paper main results use LLaDA-1.5; repo scripts reference GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct with chat template but report no main numbers. Prefill and distribution shift may change verification benefit.
registration.hypothesis: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct GSM8K, Flash-Verify achieves at least 20 percent higher throughput than confidence-aware decoding with the same cache settings.
registration.contribution: Tests checkpoint and template generalization of Flash-Verify not reported in paper, separating method gain from base-checkpoint tuning.

closest_work.difference: Main results are LLaDA-1.5; this tests LLaDA-8B-Instruct with chat template wrapping.
LLaDA-1.5 paper introduces aligned checkpoint gains; this tests inference acceleration transfer to instruct variant.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code from https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct checkpoint from HuggingFace
GSM8K via lm-eval-harness 0.4.8 tasks gsm8k
registration.method: Clone https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM and work from Flash-dLLM/llada. Install with pip install -r ../requirements.txt. Export HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=true. Run two GSM8K evals on the instruct checkpoint with single process: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 accelerate launch --num_processes 1 eval_llada.py --model llada_dist --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size 8 --limit 60 --model_args model_path=GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct,gen_length=256,block_length=16,threshold=0.9,gamma=0.8,track_num=4,mask_num=4,verify=False,show_speed=True --output_path evals_results/instruct-conf --log_samples. Log to outputs/run_A.log. Run Config B identical except verify=True and --output_path evals_results/instruct-verify, log to outputs/run_B.log. Wrapper applies chat template automatically for instruct path. Parse Tokens per second from each log show_speed line and gsm8k accuracy from results JSON. Compute ratio = tps_verify divided by tps_conf. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with both tps, accuracies and ratio.

event.description: Verify throughput is at least 1.2x confidence throughput on instruct model
event.statistic: throughput ratio verify True divided by verify False on GSM8K

evaluation.procedure: Read outputs/scores.jsonl which holds tps_conf, tps_verify, acc_conf, acc_verify, n=60, and ratio=tps_verify/tps_conf. Statistic is ratio. Event occurs if ratio greater than 1.2.
evaluation.controls: Same first 60 GSM8K prompts, same instruct model, gen_length, block_length, threshold, gamma, track_num, mask_num; only verify flag differs.

registration.full_scale_study: If speedup holds, run full GSM8K, MATH and HumanEval on both LLaDA-1.5 and instruct checkpoints with batch sweep 1-32 to compare throughput-memory-accuracy tradeoffs across templates.

agent.reason: Paper shows ~1.37x verify gain at B=8 on base; instruct chat prefill may shrink it per Table 5b but timing variance is low so >1.2x is likely.

judge_astra.reason: Table 6 reports approximately 1.37x verification speedup at batch size 8 on LLaDA-1.5, providing some cushion above the 1.2x target. The different checkpoint, chat template, and shorter generation length could nevertheless reduce that advantage.

judge_fable.reason: The paper reports 1.35–1.41× verify-over-confidence throughput at B=8–16 for LLaDA-1.5, leaving decent margin over 1.2, and throughput is a stable statistic; the Instruct checkpoint is closely related, so the main uncertainty is pipeline failure or an unexpectedly different confidence profile.

judge_opus.reason: On LLaDA-1.5 the paper measures verify-to-confidence throughput ratios of about 1.28–1.37 at batch 4–8 and 1.35 at length 256. The near-identical instruct base should behave similarly, but the margin over 1.2 is modest. It depends on the tokens-per-step gain transferring, given that each verify step costs about 1.5 times a plain step.

judge_sol.reason: The paper reports approximately 1.37x verification-versus-confidence throughput at batch size 8 on LLaDA-1.5, making the 1.2x threshold plausible on a closely related checkpoint. Different confidence profiles and shorter generation lengths could nevertheless erase that margin.

judge_luna.reason: On LLaDA-1.5, Flash-Verify's throughput ratio over confidence-aware decoding is about 1.23–1.45, making a ratio above 1.2 plausible. Instruction tuning could change confidence and acceptance patterns enough to shrink that margin.

judge_muse.reason: Tables 1/5/6 show verify/conf speedups 1.23-1.50x on LLaDA-1.5 with small variance and worst 1.35x with long prefill, leaving margin above 1.2x unless instruct calibration collapses acceptance.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's only model is LLaDA-1.5, which is LLaDA-8B-Instruct further tuned with VRPO preference optimization. On that checkpoint it compares Flash-Verify against confidence-aware Flash-Cache many times on GSM8K: across generation lengths (1.38–1.41x), prefill lengths/shot counts (1.35–1.50x), batch sizes (1.08x at B=1, about 1.37x at B=8, 1.43x at B=32) and window sizes (1.4–1.5x). The proposed experiment changes only the checkpoint to plain LLaDA-8B-Instruct with a chat template, and uses very different settings (track_num=4, mask_num=4 instead of tracking budget 80 and window 64). It also runs on only 60 problems.
This paper introduces LLaDA-1.5 by applying VRPO to LLaDA-8B-Instruct, which shows how closely the two checkpoints are related. It reports no acceleration or Flash-Verify results.

opus.reason: I found no paper that reports Flash-Verify throughput on LLaDA-8B-Instruct. A targeted search turned up no follow-up work, and the seed paper itself evaluates only LLaDA-1.5. The seed paper also measured the exact statistic (Flash-Verify vs. confidence-aware throughput on GSM8K) many times, finding about 1.35–1.5x at batch sizes of 8 or more, which largely answers the question. What remains open is a model-level detail: transfer to the untuned Instruct weights with a chat template, plus the different window and tracking settings.

Different source versions could change results, but the supplied evidence shows no decoder modification or substantive mismatch with the registered implementation.

run_experiment.sh adds installation constraints: datasets==3.6.0 and the already-installed Torch/Triton versions. Dependency versions can affect execution and throughput, but the registration did not specify these versions, and the datasets constraint is a documented compatibility measure. The conditional torchvision-removal step made no observed change: outputs/optional_dependency_check.log is empty.

run_experiment.sh additionally sets TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false and PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, and captures stderr alongside stdout. These can affect tokenization or logging overhead within the repository's timing interval, but there is no plausible material effect on the reported comparison demonstrated here.

parse_results.py resolves the registration's unspecified GSM8K accuracy filter by reporting flexible-extract exact match. This changes the accuracy numbers relative to strict-match: flexible accuracy is 47/60 in both arms, whereas strict accuracy is 23/60 and 31/60. It does not change the registered throughput statistic or event.

parse_results.py adds fail-fast checks for positive finite throughput, unique result files, exactly the first 60 documents, matching requests, and agreement between sample and aggregate accuracy. These introduce additional conditions under which reporting would fail, but all checks passed; no examples were excluded or substituted, so they did not affect this value.
problems: run_experiment.sh always runs confidence first and verification second without warmup or counterbalanced repetitions. eval_llada.py times initialization of generation and any compilation encountered inside that interval; shared Triton kernels compiled by the first arm can be reused by the second. The magnitude of this possible order/compilation contribution is not measured, so the ratio is not an isolated steady-state algorithmic speedup.

There is only one protected A/B comparison, on the first 60 GSM8K test examples and one A100 configuration. There is no registered estimate of timing variability or evidence establishing transfer across the complete benchmark, other batch sizes, or other hardware. Submitted development runs are not additional protected evaluation repetitions.

eval_llada.py and generate.py measure repository-internal generated-token counts over an interval that also includes prompt tokenization, allocation, decoding/postprocessing, and response printing, while excluding checkpoint loading and harness scoring. Tokens are counted before textual stop-sequence trimming. The result should therefore be described using this specific throughput definition, not as pure kernel throughput or complete application throughput.

The arms produced different token totals: outputs/run_A.log reports 11379 and outputs/run_B.log reports 11195. Consequently, the 1.53877 throughput ratio is not the same quantity as the fixed-prompt completion-time ratio, approximately 1.564.

Equal flexible-extract accuracy does not establish accuracy equivalence or identical per-example correctness. outputs/control_check.json also records different strict-match accuracies, showing that the equality claim depends on the extraction metric.

generate.py increments n_steps once per iteration although verification executes two model forwards per iteration. Thus the printed 'Total nfe' values are not comparable counts of model forward evaluations across arms; this does not corrupt the wall-clock throughput calculation.

generate.py accepts a prefix using cumulative draft-token probabilities against gamma, without an explicit draft/mask argmax-agreement check. This differs from the formulation described in README.md. It is not an implementation departure from the registration, which explicitly prescribed the repository decoder, but the finding should be attributed to that implementation rather than assumed to validate the prose formulation.
sol.reason: The protected run used the registered checkpoint, automatically applied chat wrapping, first 60 GSM8K examples, five-shot prompts, batch size, decoding/cache parameters, and verify-only A/B change. The operational differences and unspecified accuracy-filter choice do not constitute a substantive fidelity defect. This is a meaningful, narrowly scoped implementation-transfer finding, but fixed-order compilation exposure, absent timing precision, and limited accuracy evidence prevent a stronger general speedup or quality-preservation conclusion.

registration.title: Self-verification versus aggressive single-pass thresholding
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Verify adds a second forward pass to recover sub-threshold tokens; paper compares to confidence-aware at epsilon 0.9 but not to more aggressive epsilon that matches parallelism. This isolates verification value beyond threshold tuning.
registration.hypothesis: At similar or higher parallelism, Flash-Verify with epsilon 0.9 achieves higher GSM8K accuracy than aggressive single-pass decoding with epsilon 0.7.
registration.contribution: Matches parallelism via epsilon tuning to test whether two-pass self-verification adds accuracy over single-pass threshold lowering, which paper does not test.

closest_work.difference: Paper compares verify vs confidence at fixed epsilon 0.9; this compares verify at 0.9 to aggressive 0.7 single-pass.
Fast-dLLM proposes single-pass confidence-aware decoding; this tests if second verify pass beats aggressive single-pass.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code from https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 checkpoint from HuggingFace
GSM8K via lm-eval-harness 0.4.8 tasks gsm8k
registration.method: Clone https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM and work from Flash-dLLM/llada. Install with pip install -r ../requirements.txt. Export HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=true. Run Config V: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 accelerate launch --num_processes 1 eval_llada.py --model llada_dist --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size 8 --limit 100 --model_args model_path=GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5,gen_length=256,block_length=16,threshold=0.9,gamma=0.8,track_num=4,mask_num=4,verify=True,show_speed=True --output_path evals_results/aggr-verify --log_samples, log to outputs/run_V.log. Run Config C identical except threshold=0.7,verify=False and --output_path evals_results/aggr-conf07, log to outputs/run_C.log. Parse gsm8k accuracy and Tokens per iter from each run. Compute diff = acc_verify minus acc_conf07. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with both accuracies, tokens per iter, throughputs and diff.

event.description: Verify accuracy exceeds aggressive single-pass accuracy
event.statistic: accuracy verify epsilon0.9 minus accuracy conf epsilon0.7 on GSM8K as fraction

evaluation.procedure: Read outputs/scores.jsonl which holds acc_verify, acc_conf07, tok_per_iter each, n=100, and diff=acc_verify-acc_conf07. Statistic is diff. Event occurs if diff greater than 0.0.
evaluation.controls: Same first 100 GSM8K prompts, same model, gen_length, block_length, track_num, mask_num; only threshold plus verify differ to contrast two-pass vs aggressive one-pass.

registration.full_scale_study: If verify wins, sweep epsilon 0.5-0.9 and gamma 0.6-0.9 on full GSM8K and MATH to map accuracy vs tokens-per-step frontiers for one-pass vs two-pass decoding.

agent.reason: Verify should filter aggressive errors at similar tokens-per-step per Fig.6, but GSM8K is tolerant to epsilon 0.7 and n=100 noise leaves outcome uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: Figures 5(b) and 6 already compare verification against swept single-pass confidence thresholds and suggest an accuracy advantage in this regime. That advantage appears modest relative to uncertainty from 100 questions, and the registered event does not require the claimed parallelism match.

judge_fable.reason: Fig. 6 implies confidence-aware at ε=0.7 (~80.3%) trails Flash-Verify at γ=0.8 (~81.6–82%) by only ~1.3pp, so the direction is supported but a strict >0 result at n=100 (with ties counting as failure) is only ~60% likely even if the run succeeds.

judge_opus.reason: Figures 5b and 6 suggest Flash-Verify at gamma 0.8 beats confidence-aware decoding at epsilon 0.7 by about 1.5–2 pp (≈81.7 vs ≈80.0). That gap is smaller than the n=100 noise, and a tie counts as failure.

judge_sol.reason: Figures 5–6 already suggest a modest accuracy advantage for verification around gamma 0.8 over single-pass decoding at epsilon 0.7. A strict positive difference on only 100 paired questions remains vulnerable to ties and sample variation.

judge_luna.reason: The paper's results generally favor Flash-Verify's accuracy-throughput tradeoff, and a single-pass threshold of 0.7 should commit less reliable tokens than 0.9. However, same-threshold accuracy comparisons are mixed, and the 100-prompt evaluation leaves room for a noisy or small difference.

judge_muse.reason: Fig.6 shows Flash-Verify exceeds confidence-aware accuracy at matched thresholds with higher tokens/iter, and epsilon 0.7 single-pass should be worse than epsilon 0.9, though n=100 leaves sizable paired noise.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: The seed paper already makes this comparison on the same model (LLaDA-1.5) and benchmark (GSM8K). Figure 6 sweeps the confidence-aware threshold ε against the Flash-Verify verify threshold γ and reports accuracy, throughput and tokens per iteration. At matched throughput (Flash-Verify at 7.2 tokens/iter vs confidence-aware at 5.6), Flash-Verify is 3.5 points more accurate, and the gap narrows as parallelism rises. Figure 5(b) gives the matching accuracy–throughput frontiers. Remark 2 argues that lowering ε is not equivalent to verifying. The registered run tests one pair (ε=0.9 with verify vs ε=0.7 without) on 100 prompts at generation length 256 with small track/mask budgets. I could not confirm that ε=0.7 is one of the plotted points.
Fast-dLLM introduced single-pass confidence-threshold decoding and studied threshold choice, but it has no self-verification pass to compare against.

opus.reason: The experiment assumes the seed paper only compared verify and confidence-aware decoding at a fixed ε=0.9. In fact the seed paper's Figure 6 and Figure 5(b) sweep the confidence-aware threshold and compare accuracy against Flash-Verify at matched throughput and tokens per iteration, on the same model and task. That answers whether verification adds accuracy beyond simply lowering the threshold. The registered experiment differs only in details (one specific ε pair, 100 prompts, generation length 256, different budgets), so I rate it a close variant rather than distinct.

sol.label: equivalent

closest_work.difference: The seed paper already compares Flash-Verify against confidence-aware single-pass decoding across threshold settings, reporting accuracy, throughput, and tokens per iteration. The registration selects a particular 0.9-versus-0.7 comparison on 100 prompts with different cache budgets.

sol.reason: Flash-dLLM: IO-Aware KV Caching and Parallel Decoding for Fast, Memory-Efficient Diffusion LLMs already addresses this question in Section 3.3, Figures 5(b) and 6, by varying confidence-aware thresholds and comparing them with Flash-Verify at different parallelism and throughput levels. Thus, the registration's premise that the paper compares only at fixed epsilon 0.9 is contradicted by its ablations; the proposed operating points and smaller sample do not introduce a new experimental contribution.

opus.reason: #23 asks whether Flash-Verify (epsilon 0.9, gamma 0.8) is more accurate on GSM8K than lower-threshold single-pass confidence decoding (epsilon 0.7) at comparable parallelism; it adds extra arms but contains the same core comparison.

sol.reason: Both compare Flash-Verify at epsilon 0.9 against aggressive single-pass decoding at epsilon 0.7 to assess GSM8K accuracy relative to decoding efficiency.

registration.title: Future masked window size in Flash-Cache
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Cache includes mask_num blocks of future masked tokens in the query, default 4 blocks, with no ablation. Elastic-Cache claims distant masks act mainly as length bias and can be cached.
registration.hypothesis: Reducing future masked blocks from 4 to 1 retains GSM8K accuracy within 3 percentage points with verification disabled.
registration.contribution: First ablation of future mask window in Flash-Cache, testing length-bias hypothesis and potential to shrink per-step query.

closest_work.difference: Paper fixes mask_num 4 with no ablation; this compares 1 vs 4 future blocks.
Elastic-Cache proposes off-window MASK caching as length bias; this varies future window size in Flash-Cache.

inputs: Flash-dLLM code from https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM
GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 checkpoint from HuggingFace
GSM8K via lm-eval-harness 0.4.8 tasks gsm8k
registration.method: Clone https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM and work from Flash-dLLM/llada. Install with pip install -r ../requirements.txt. Export HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=true. Run two GSM8K evals with single process: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 accelerate launch --num_processes 1 eval_llada.py --model llada_dist --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size 8 --limit 100 --model_args model_path=GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5,gen_length=256,block_length=16,threshold=0.9,gamma=0.8,track_num=4,mask_num=4,verify=False,show_speed=True --output_path evals_results/mask4 --log_samples, log to outputs/run_A.log. Run Config B identical except mask_num=1 and --output_path evals_results/mask1, log to outputs/run_B.log. Parse gsm8k accuracy and Tokens per second. Compute diff = acc_mask1 minus acc_mask4. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with both accuracies, throughputs and diff.

event.description: Accuracy with 1 future mask block is within 3pp of 4 blocks
event.statistic: accuracy mask1 minus accuracy mask4 on GSM8K as fraction 0-1

evaluation.procedure: Read outputs/scores.jsonl which holds acc_A for mask4, acc_B for mask1, throughput_A/B, n=100, and diff=acc_B-acc_A. Statistic is diff. Event occurs if diff greater than -0.03.
evaluation.controls: Same first 100 GSM8K prompts, same model, gen_length, block_length, threshold, track_num, verify=False; only mask_num differs.

registration.full_scale_study: If retained, run full GSM8K and long-generation 512-1024 sweeps over mask_num 1-6 with memory profiling to define minimal future-context window for batched inference.

agent.reason: Distant masks act mainly as length bias per Elastic-Cache, so cutting 4 to 1 future blocks likely preserves accuracy within noise.

judge_astra.reason: Figure 7 already studies masked-window sizes down to 16 tokens and shows modest accuracy changes for confidence-aware decoding. Assuming mask_num corresponds to that window as registered, the retention event looks likely, but a positive result on 100 questions would not establish population-level non-inferiority.

judge_fable.reason: Fig. 7 already shows confidence-aware accuracy nearly flat across β_m=16–96 (~0.5pp gap), so a within-3pp result is likely (~75%) conditional on success; the remaining risk is mostly implementation/time-budget failure.

judge_opus.reason: Contrary to the registration's claim that no ablation exists, the paper's Fig. 7 already ablates the window: confidence-aware accuracy is nearly flat from window 16 to 64 (about 82.0 vs 82.7). The expected drop is therefore well inside 3 pp, and the main risks are noise and execution.

judge_sol.reason: Figure 7 already contains a closely related 16–96-token masked-window ablation with modest accuracy changes under confidence-aware decoding, supporting the 3-point margin. Passing this 100-item point-estimate test would not establish non-inferiority.

judge_luna.reason: The seed's Figure 7 already sweeps the masked window from 16 to 96 tokens for confidence-aware decoding, overlapping the registered 16-versus-64-token comparison. That makes the threshold event likely, though the first-100-prompt subset could differ from the paper's results.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: The experiment says the seed paper never ablates mask_num, but that is wrong. Section 3.3 ('Masked-window size β_m', Figure 7) sweeps the masked-window size β_m (default 64 tokens, which is 4 blocks of 16) for both confidence-aware decoding (verify off) and Flash-Verify, on GSM8K with LLaDA-1.5, reporting accuracy and throughput. It finds that accuracy improves up to an intermediate window size and throughput falls as the window grows. The registered run differs only in details: gen_length 256 instead of the paper's default 512, the first 100 prompts only, and two points (16 vs 64 tokens). The text does not say whether the 16-token point is one of the plotted values.
Elastic-Cache offers the idea that distant MASK tokens act mainly as a length bias and can be cached. It does not vary the future masked window inside Flash-Cache's fused-kernel, tracked-token setup.

The registered experiment changes only details (gen length 256, a 100-sample subset, two window sizes), and the seed paper largely settles how window size trades accuracy for throughput. Elastic-Cache studies distant MASK caching and ablates sliding-window size, but uses adaptive cache refresh rather than Flash-Cache's selective-update mechanism.

registration.title: Attention-guided versus random tracked-token selection at fixed cache budget
registration.seed_connection: Tests Flash-dLLM Fig 1b and Alg 2 claim that refreshing most-attended decoded tokens retains quality while bounding compute to beta_t plus beta_m.
registration.hypothesis: At fixed tracking budget track_num equals 4 blocks, attention-guided tracking achieves higher GSM8K accuracy than random tracking.
registration.contribution: Isolates selection policy from budget size with a budget-matched random control, which prior attention-guided diffusion caching work reports without.

closest_work.difference: Elastic-Cache uses attention drift to decide when and where to refresh but does not compare attention ranking to random selection at fixed budget.
Sparse-dLLM retains pivotal salient tokens and evicts others but does not ablate saliency versus random eviction at matched budget on reasoning tasks.
MaskKV uses mask-query attention scoring for eviction and compares to full cache, not to a random eviction control.

agent.reason: Top-32 capturing 50% middle-layer attention suggests attention helps, but Table 4 shows doubling budget gains only about 1pp and newly decoded tokens are always kept, so exceeding random by more than 3pp is uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: The paper demonstrates attention concentration, not that high-attention states benefit most from refreshing. Because both policies retain the full cache, a greater-than-3-point advantage is plausible but far from assured on 120 examples.

judge_fable.reason: Fast-dLLM-style stale caches cost only ~1 point, so a fair budget-matched random control likely trails attention tracking by well under 3 points on 120 noisy samples; however, if the randperm patch drops the automatic refresh of newly decoded tokens (which the sort may implement), random tracking collapses and the event occurs trivially, so the estimate blends a modest fair-case chance with a sizable confound-driven one.

judge_opus.reason: Seed Table 4 shows tracking budget affects accuracy by about 1–1.7 pts. Random selection is roughly a stochastic periodic refresh, so the expected gap if newly decoded tokens stay tracked is likely only about 1–3 pts, against a paired noise SD near 3 pts at n=120. If the randperm patch also drops the automatic inclusion of newly decoded tokens, random could degrade sharply, which raises the odds.

judge_sol.reason: Attention concentration does not establish which cached representations most need refreshing; random selection still preserves the full cache and refreshes newly decoded tokens. A modest attention advantage seems plausible, but exceeding 3 percentage points on 120 examples is less likely.

judge_luna.reason: The seed reports that a small set of top-attended tokens can account for substantial attention, making an advantage over random tracking plausible. But attention mass does not establish a final-answer accuracy gain, and a greater-than-3-point difference on 120 questions is a fairly demanding cutoff.

judge_muse.reason: Table 4 shows doubling track budget 48 to 96 gains only 0.8-1.7pp, implying fixed-budget selection effect likely below 3pp; with n=120 noise around 3.5pp, exceeding 3pp needs large true gap plus luck.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the seed paper. It motivates top-k attention tracking with Fig. 1b, which shows how concentrated attention is, and it sweeps the tracking budget β_t (48–96) over 5 seeds. In the sections I read, it never swaps the ranking rule for a random or recency rule at the same budget, so the selection policy is not separated from budget size.

d2Cache picks prompt and decoded tokens for KV update using attention rollout. Its ablations cover the update phase and sensitivity to p, k and σ. I found no comparison with random selection at a matched budget.

dLLM-Cache refreshes part of the response tokens, chosen by value-feature similarity, on LLaDA. I could not read its ablation section. I vaguely remember a random-vs-similarity selection ablation, but I did not confirm it. Even if it exists, it tests a similarity criterion inside a different caching scheme, not the per-step attention top-k tracking set used by Flash-dLLM.

Elastic-Cache uses the drift of the most-attended token to decide when and where to refresh. It does not rank a fixed set of tracked tokens, and I saw no random control (judged from the abstract only).
Sparse-dLLM evicts tokens by attention saliency. Judging from the abstract, it compares against other caching methods, not against random eviction at the same budget.

MaskKV scores prompt tokens for eviction using mask-query attention, aimed at long-context memory savings. Judging from the abstract, it has no random-eviction control and does not target refreshing decoded-token caches.

opus.reason: No paper I found tests Flash-dLLM's attention-ranked tracked-token set against a random set of the same size and compute shape. The seed paper only varies the budget, and the related dLLM caching papers (d2Cache, Elastic-Cache, Sparse-dLLM, MaskKV) report no random-selection control in what I read, mostly abstracts. The main uncertainty is dLLM-Cache: I could not check whether its ablations include a random-selection control. If they do, it would be a related but different test (value-similarity selection in a different scheme), so I judge the question still open.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Affix Cache for Diffusion Large Language Models, Appendix D.7/Table 21, compares attention-ranked, uniformly random, and bottom-ranked token recomputation at identical budgets, including GSM8K on LLaDA. It selects a fixed shared-affix subset once per request, whereas the proposed experiment reselects decoded tokens each iteration in Flash-dLLM.
Flash-dLLM introduces attention-guided decoded-token tracking and sweeps tracking budgets, but does not report a budget-matched random-selection control.

sol.reason: ACache already reports the central contribution claimed here: isolating attention-based token selection from recomputation budget using a matched random control in a diffusion LLM. Applying that comparison to Flash-dLLM's dynamic tracking changes the selection schedule and candidate tokens, making it a close variant rather than an exact replication.

opus.reason: Both change only the tracked-token rule inside confidence-aware Flash-Cache, swapping attention top-k for alternatives such as seeded random selection at the same budget with newly decoded tokens kept, and both measure GSM8K exact-match accuracy and speed; Experiment 1 simply drops the recency arm.

sol.reason: Both compare attention-guided and random tracking at a fixed refresh budget under confidence-aware Flash-Cache, measuring GSM8K accuracy and throughput.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered one-repetition GSM8K-256 5-shot, limit-120 experiment using the supplied seed snapshot copied to a writable directory. opus.reason: The code runs the registered comparison closely. Both arms use identical harness settings, prompts are verified by hash, the batch size is 16 with no OOM fallback, and the random arm differs from the attention arm only in the registered decoded_ranks line plus a fixed seed, so the tracked budget and compute shape are matched. The listed departures (copying the snapshot, pinning datasets, filtering records in the parser) do not plausibly affect the value, and an earlier engineer run reproduced the random arm exactly. The finding is a credible, well-controlled null against a large attention-ranking advantage in this configuration, but n=120 and one seed give limited precision, so it neither establishes equivalence nor shows that random selection is superior.

departures: experiment_driver.py copies /workspace/seed instead of cloning GitHub. run_experiment.sh explicitly pins datasets==3.6.0 in addition to the seed requirements. This is a compatibility accommodation for the registered harness and trust support; no task or prompt change is evident, and it does not plausibly change the primary statistic here.

The harness results cover only the first 120 GSM8K test documents, not the full 1,319-document benchmark or a separately randomized evaluation sample. Generalization beyond this pilot is limited.

The analysis in experiment_driver.py reports no paired uncertainty estimate or discordant-outcome analysis. The harness's individual accuracy standard errors are not uncertainty estimates for the paired difference.

The experiment therefore tests this specific implementation of attention-guided refresh, not every interpretation of the paper's saliency claim.

Equal refresh-budget settings do not imply identical total computation: the logs report 7,224 versus 7,247 sample-level decoding steps and different generated-token totals. Tokens per step measures decoding progress, not refreshed-cache positions.

Throughput has only one fixed-order measurement per policy, with attention first on the fresh machine. Kernel compilation/cache warming and differing generated lengths limit interpretation of the speed difference.
The registration's closest-work and novelty claims cannot be verified from the supplied evidence.

The fresh harness outputs show 95/120 correct for attention and 99/120 for random, correctly yielding -3.3333 percentage points; the registered greater-than-3-point event did not occur. The accommodations do not plausibly alter that primary statistic, and the value is calculated from real model outputs rather than hard-coded or submitted earlier results. This is a useful but weak pilot: its limited sample and single random seed do not establish equivalence, absence of an attention benefit, or a general advantage for random tracking.

The contrast is too noisy to be a strong finding: per-arm standard errors are about 3.5 points, and a reverse gap of four items does not establish equivalence or that attention ranking is useless.

grok.what_it_asks: Does attention-guided selection of tracked decoded tokens give higher GSM8K accuracy than random selection at the same tracking budget in Flash-dLLM on LLaDA-1.5?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper motivates attention-based tracking and sweeps the tracking budget, but it never compares that ranking with random selection and does not name this ablation as future work.

relation.reason: The experiment keeps Flash-dLLM’s fixed-budget tracker and only replaces attention ranking with a random permutation, a comparison the paper does not make and that leaves the paper’s reported accuracy claims standing either way.

obvious.reason: A paper that justifies selective refresh by attention mass and then never ablates the ranking rule leaves a matched-budget attention-versus-random comparison among the first controls most readers in this area would write down.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer at the stated scope, one budget on GSM8K for this tracker, would change practice only for groups that implement attention-guided selective refresh in diffusion-LLM caches.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan’s account matches the paper: Figure 1b motivates tracking the most-attended tokens, Algorithm 2 ranks by attention, and per-step compute is bounded by the tracking budget plus the masked window.

answerable.reason: Model, prompts, budget, and decoding settings are held fixed and only the ranking of tracked positions changes, so either accuracy ordering would answer the comparison.

grok.what_came_out: On LLaDA-1.5, GSM8K 5-shot, 120 samples and one run, attention-guided tracking scored 79.17% flexible-extract accuracy (stderr 3.72 points) versus 82.50% (stderr 3.48 points) for random tracking.

prerequisite.reason: Both policies finished on the same 120 prompts at the registered budget, and accuracies sit in the paper’s normal GSM8K range, so nothing required to read the gap failed.

evidence.reason: The point estimate favors random by 3.33 points, but one run of 120 items with per-arm standard errors near 3.5 points still leaves room for no difference and for an attention advantage large enough to matter.

next_step.reason: The comparison was actually applied, but 120 samples and a single seed cannot resolve a few-point accuracy gap, so the same question has to be rerun with that fault removed.
next_step.what: Too few cases: rerun both policies on the full GSM8K test set with multiple seeds so a few-point gap is distinguishable from noise.

opus.what_it_asks: Does choosing the tracked decoded tokens by attention score give higher GSM8K accuracy than choosing them at random at the same tracking budget, in Flash-dLLM's selective cache update on LLaDA-1.5, and so is attention-guided selection what preserves quality?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper motivates attention-guided tracking with Fig. 1(b) and varies the budget β_t, but it never compares against random selection at a matched budget and does not name such a comparison as future work.

relation.reason: The experiment tests the paper's design claim that the most-attended tokens are the right ones to refresh, using a budget-matched random control.

obvious.reason: A random-selection baseline at a matched budget is the canonical ablation for any importance-based token or cache selection scheme, and the paper visibly lacks it, so most researchers in the area would list it.

who_would_care.reason: The answer would mainly change how people using or extending Flash-dLLM's tracking mechanism design or justify the selection step.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan describes the paper's tracked-token mechanism and budget accurately, and track_num=4 blocks of 16 tokens matches the 64-token budget in Table 3.

answerable.reason: The comparison changes only the ranking line, holds the budget fixed, and runs both policies on the same prompts, so a clear accuracy difference either way would bear on the question.

opus.what_came_out: On LLaDA-1.5 with GSM8K 5-shot at generation length 256, attention-guided tracking scored 79.17% and random tracking 82.50% (difference −3.33 pp; harness stderr about 3.5–3.7 pp per arm), from one run on the same 120 problems with a single random seed.

prerequisite.reason: The patch diff shows randperm replacing the attention sort, the outputs differ between the two runs, and the prompt hashes match, so the manipulation was applied and the measurement worked.

evidence.reason: The point estimate goes in the opposite direction to the hypothesis, but with 120 items, one random seed and no interval, a paired standard error of roughly 3–4 pp leaves room for a real attention advantage of a few points, so the run does not rule out an effect that matters.

next_step.reason: The run did not settle the question because it used too few problems and a single random draw.
next_step.what: Too few cases and a single random seed: rerun on the full GSM8K test set with several random-selection seeds and report a paired confidence interval for the attention-minus-random difference.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares attention-guided with random tracked-token selection at a fixed cache-refresh budget in Flash-dLLM on LLaDA-1.5 and GSM8K to learn whether attention guidance improves answer accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports tracking-budget sweeps but neither compares attention-guided tracking with random tracking nor explicitly identifies that comparison as an open question.

relation.reason: The budget-matched random baseline checks whether the claimed usefulness of refreshing influential tokens depends on attention-based selection rather than simply refreshing some tokens.

obvious.reason: Comparing the central attention-based refresh heuristic with budget-matched random selection is a standard ablation likely to appear among most researchers' first ten follow-ups.

who_would_care.reason: At its stated scope, a decisive answer would primarily change refresh-policy choices for groups developing or using Flash-dLLM rather than establish a result across caching methods.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's description of attention-guided selective refresh matches the paper, and no statement about the seed paper is contradicted by its text.

answerable.reason: Directly replacing the ranking policy while retaining the tracking budget and evaluating answer accuracy could produce a clear result bearing on the proposed comparison.

sol.what_came_out: On LLaDA-1.5 with 5-shot GSM8K and 256-token generation, attention-guided tracking achieved 79.17% accuracy (95/120) versus random tracking's 82.50% (99/120), a −3.33-percentage-point difference in one repetition, with marginal standard errors of 3.72 and 3.48 points and no reported difference interval.

prerequisite.reason: The code applied different ranking policies while retaining the budget logic, and the completed evaluation verified matching prompts with accuracy measurements away from floor and ceiling.

evidence.reason: The four-answer reversal across 120 matched cases and one random-tracking seed, without paired uncertainty estimates, does not establish a reliable disadvantage or exclude a practically meaningful attention-guided advantage.

next_step.reason: The comparison executed successfully, but insufficient case coverage and a single random realization leave the accuracy difference unresolved.
next_step.what: Repeat the matched-policy evaluation on more GSM8K cases and several independent random-tracking seeds, reporting paired confidence intervals for the accuracy difference.

registration.title: Self-verification gain over parallelism-matched confidence-aware decoding
registration.seed_connection: Tests Flash-Verify claim that draft-and-verify with two views recovers correct low-confidence tokens that confidence-aware thresholding would waste.
registration.hypothesis: At matched tokens-per-step, Flash-Verify achieves higher GSM8K accuracy than confidence-aware decoding with lowered threshold.
registration.contribution: Controls for parallelism budget via threshold sweep plus interpolation, separating verification signal from extra parallelism, unlike fixed-threshold comparisons.

closest_work.difference: Fast-dLLM proposes confidence-aware parallel decoding but compares thresholds at fixed values without matching tokens-per-step to a verify pass.
FreeDave proposes draft-and-verify for lossless parallel decoding but does not isolate accuracy gain at interpolated matched parallelism versus threshold tuning alone.
Fast-dLLM++ selects commit sets from sorted confidence profiles without a second verification view, leaving open whether verification adds accuracy beyond profile tuning.

inputs: Seed repo https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.git, file llada/eval_llada.py
Model GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from HuggingFace
GSM8K 5-shot via lm-eval-harness auto-download, requires HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1
registration.method: Clone repo, install requirements, cd llada, set env HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1, mkdir outputs and evals_results. Run 4 configs with same gen_length 256 block_length 16 track_num 4 mask_num 4 batch_size 16 limit 80 num_fewshot 5 tasks gsm8k: A verify True threshold 0.9 gamma 0.8 output evals_results/gsm8k-verify log outputs/run_verify.log; B1 verify False threshold 0.9 output evals_results/gsm8k-c09 log outputs/run_conf_09.log; B2 verify False threshold 0.7 output evals_results/gsm8k-c07 log outputs/run_conf_07.log; B3 verify False threshold 0.5 output evals_results/gsm8k-c05 log outputs/run_conf_05.log; all with model_path GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 show_speed True log_samples confirm_run_unsafe_code via accelerate launch num_processes 1. Sort B1-B3 by tokens_per_step, let tv and av be verify tokens_per_step and accuracy. If tv lies within baseline min-max, linearly interpolate baseline accuracy at tv between bracketing neighbors; if outside, use nearest baseline accuracy and flag extrapolation. Statistic is av minus interpolated baseline in points. Write all configs plus interpolation details to outputs/scores.jsonl.

event.description: Verify beats interpolated confidence baseline by more than 1.5 accuracy points at matched tokens-per-step
event.statistic: acc_verify_minus_matched_pp

The four log files hold full stdout for verify and three confidence runs.
evaluation.controls: Same prompts, model, gen_length, block_length, tracking budget and batch size; only verify flag and threshold vary. Tokens-per-step matching is reported alongside accuracy so wall-clock overhead of extra forward pass does not confound algorithmic quality comparison.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run full GSM8K MATH HumanEval MBPP with dense epsilon-gamma grid and multiple seeds to map full accuracy versus steps and accuracy versus wall-clock Pareto for verify versus tuned confidence decoding.

agent.reason: Table 1 and Table 6 show verify doubles tokens per step yet slightly leads in accuracy, so lowering epsilon to match parallelism likely degrades the confidence baseline; interpolation noise and N=80 leave moderate uncertainty.

judge_astra.reason: The paper’s tokens-per-iteration curves suggest verification preserves more accuracy than aggressive confidence thresholding at similar parallelism. The 80-example sample and coarse interpolation weaken this prediction, particularly if the baseline rates fail to bracket verification’s rate.

judge_fable.reason: The paper's own Fig. 5b/6 data imply confidence-aware decoding at ~5.6 tokens/step scores ~77% versus ~81-82% for Flash-Verify, a ~4-5 point gap comfortably above 1.5; the main risks are 80-sample noise, tokens-per-iter accounting that halves the verify count, and environment/setup failure, with no code patching required.

judge_opus.reason: The seed's own Figure 6 implies about a 4-pt gap at matched tokens-per-step (verify 5.7 tok/step at ~81.7% vs confidence ε=0.6 at 5.6 tok/step and ~77%). registration.title: Confidence-ordered versus position-ordered verification queue
registration.seed_connection: Tests Flash-Verify design choice of causality order as draft-confidence descending with prefix acceptance until first mismatch.
registration.hypothesis: Confidence-descending verification order yields higher tokens accepted per step than position-ascending order at fixed gamma.
registration.contribution: Isolates ordering effect inside two-view self-verification, distinct from positional speculative decoding and sorted-set profile decoding which do not ablate order within a verify mask.

closest_work.difference: Speculative decoding verifies drafts in left-to-right positional order for losslessness, without testing confidence-descending order in diffusion self-verification.
Fast-dLLM++ selects parallel sets from sorted confidence profiles but does not test sequential verify order under a causal two-view mask.
FreeDave generates and verifies parallel candidates without ablating confidence versus positional verification order.

inputs: Seed repo https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.git, files llada/eval_llada.py and llada/generate.py
Model GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from HuggingFace
GSM8K 5-shot via lm-eval-harness auto-download, requires HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1
registration.method: Clone repo, install, cd llada, set env HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1, mkdir outputs evals_results. Run confidence-order baseline with original code: accelerate launch num_processes 1 eval_llada.py model llada_dist tasks gsm8k num_fewshot 5 batch_size 16 limit 120 model_args model_path GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 gen_length 256 block_length 16 threshold 0.9 gamma 0.8 track_num 4 mask_num 4 verify True show_speed True output_path evals_results/gsm8k-conforder log outputs/run_conforder.log. If OOM reduce batch_size to 8 then 4 then 1 for both configs. Backup generate.py and patch verify draft section to keep direct accepts identical as top keep_num by confidence but order remaining verify queue by ascending position id: after num_decoded is advanced by keep_num, take remaining positions from query_masked_pos suffix, sort ascending, assign to full_pos segment starting at num_decoded, so query_verify_pos takes first num_verify in positional order; rebuild causal verify mask from reordered queue order so each mask-view position attends to earlier drafts in new positional order preserving Eq 4 semantics, updating mask indices to follow reordered positions; leave gamma logic unchanged. Run same eval with output_path evals_results/gsm8k-posorder log outputs/run_posorder.log. Parse Tokens per iter and accuracy for both into outputs/scores.jsonl.

event.description: Confidence ordering yields more than 0.4 extra tokens per step versus positional ordering
event.statistic: tokstep_conf_minus_pos

evaluation.procedure: From outputs/scores.jsonl read tokens_per_step for conforder and posorder, compute difference conforder minus posorder. outputs/scores.jsonl holds one line per config with tokens_per_step, accuracy_pct, tokens_per_sec. Log files hold full stdout for each ordering.
evaluation.controls: Same prompts, model, thresholds, tracking budget and gamma; direct-accept set is identical, only order of remaining verify queue differs with mask rebuilt to follow new order, so difference is attributable to ordering under same acceptance rule.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, sweep gamma and block_length on full GSM8K and code tasks, trace acceptance curves by position in queue, and test hybrid orders combining confidence and position.

agent.reason: Descending order maximizes prefix length under the cumulative gamma rule, favoring confidence order, but direct accepts are fixed and draft confidence may imperfectly predict mask-view probabilities.

judge_astra.reason: Under the registered cumulative-prefix rule, placing higher-confidence candidates first should usually delay rejection enough to exceed the 0.4-token margin. Positional ordering could improve conditional predictions, but would need to offset this substantial selection advantage.

judge_fable.reason: Under the code's cumulative-product rule with prefix stopping, confidence ordering greedily front-loads high-probability tokens and should accept more, but positional order gains AR-like left-context conditioning that sharpens mask-view confidences, so the true gap may be below 0.4 tokens/step; the reorder-plus-mask patch also carries meaningful implementation risk (a broken mask would spuriously favor the event).

judge_opus.reason: The paper deliberately chose confidence order, which favors the event. However, the code appears to use a joint cumprod≥γ rule, under which left-to-right AR-like chains adjacent to newly committed tokens can rival confidence order, so the direction of the gap is uncertain. The 0.4 tok/step margin and a non-trivial queue/mask patch add risk.

judge_sol.reason: Confidence ordering should place candidates less likely to exhaust the cumulative probability budget or trigger rejection earlier, making a 0.4-token advantage plausible. Position ordering could recover some ground through stronger local conditioning, and correct mask reconstruction is essential.

judge_luna.reason: The seed sorts drafts by confidence, and stopping at the first failure makes putting likely-to-pass candidates first a plausible way to increase the accepted prefix. Draft confidence is only a proxy for verification success after causal conditioning, however, so the greater-than-0.4-token margin is uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Prefix stopping under cumprod makes descending confidence plausibly optimal for prefix length, but direct accepts are identical and positional left-to-right conditioning may compensate; 0.4 tokens per step is modest yet uncertain given narrow low-confidence queue and complex mask-rebuild patch risk.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper fixes the verification order as confidence-descending (Eq. 4 and Algorithm 2) and accepts drafts up to the first mismatch. The sections I read (method, main results, ablations and the appendix from about character 60,000 onward) contain no comparison with a position-ordered queue, and I did not read characters 48,000 to 60,000. The experiment would isolate that ordering choice.

SSD is also self-speculative decoding for dLLMs. Within a block it selects drafts by confidence and verifies them in priority order as a linear chain under lossless stepwise-decoding semantics. It does not use Flash-Verify's two-view mask or gamma gate. I read only the first part of the paper and could not check whether a later section compares confidence order with position order.

LoPA shows that token filling order strongly affects tokens per forward pass in dLLMs and searches over orders using parallel branches. It does not compare confidence-ordered and position-ordered verification queues within a draft-and-verify scheme.
Standard speculative decoding for autoregressive models verifies drafts strictly left to right. Ordering by confidence is not considered.

Spiffy uses auto-speculation with draft graphs calibrated offline to raise acceptance in dLLMs. It does not run a controlled ablation of confidence versus position ordering under a fixed acceptance rule.

opus.reason: None of the papers I found reports a controlled comparison of confidence-descending and position-ascending verification order in dLLM self-verification at fixed gamma, and the parts of Flash-dLLM I read do not ablate this choice. Related work shows that decoding order matters (LoPA) or uses confidence-priority verification chains (SSD), but none of it settles this question. One uncertainty remains: I could not read SSD's later analysis sections or a middle stretch of the Flash-dLLM paper, and either could contain a similar ordering ablation.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM defines confidence-descending causality order and first-rejection prefix acceptance, but does not compare it with position-ascending verification while preserving direct acceptance and rebuilding the verify mask.
SimSD supports arbitrary temporal orders through paired data-mask attention, but uses a separate diffusion drafter and does not report the proposed confidence-versus-position ordering ablation.

Self Speculative Decoding studies order-related rejection and adds mix-order verification branches; it changes the verification tree rather than comparing confidence and positional queues under the same two-view acceptance rule.
Compares confidence-based and spatial unmasking schedules for generation accuracy, not their effect on accepted-prefix length inside causal self-verification.

sol.reason: The seed establishes the verification mechanism and its confidence ordering, but its reported ablations do not isolate verification order. Related papers study generation schedules, arbitrary temporal masks, or alternative verification branches without settling this controlled queue-order comparison. I found no work available by 2026-10-07 that answers the proposed accepted-tokens-per-step question in the same way.

opus.reason: Both keep default Flash-Verify and change only the search-token order from confidence-descending to positional, measuring accepted tokens per step and accuracy; Entry 13 adds a random arm.

sol.reason: Both change verification causality order from confidence-descending to positional order while retaining prefix acceptance, measuring tokens per step, accuracy, and throughput.

registration.title: Prefix stopping versus independent acceptance in self-verification
registration.seed_connection: Flash-Verify stops at first rejection to keep an accepted prefix for the bounded-deviation guarantee; the throughput cost versus accuracy benefit of discarded suffix is unmeasured.
registration.hypothesis: Accepting all individually passing tokens without prefix stopping retains GSM8K accuracy within 2 points of prefix stopping.
registration.contribution: First causal test of prefix stopping cost versus benefit by actually running a relaxed rule, going beyond counterfactual suffix counts and theory that assumes prefix without measuring tradeoff.

closest_work.difference: Seed Appendix C justifies prefix stopping for the bound but does not measure how a relaxed independent rule trades accuracy for parallelism.
Self-speculative decoding for dLLMs also uses prefix verification without reporting relaxed acceptance tradeoff on accuracy and tokens per step.

inputs: Seed repo https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.git, files llada/eval_llada.py and llada/generate.py
Model GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from HuggingFace
GSM8K 5-shot via lm-eval-harness auto-download, requires HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1
registration.method: Clone repo, install requirements, cd llada, set HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1, mkdir outputs evals_results. Run prefix baseline with original cumulative cumprod gamma rule: accelerate launch num_processes 1 eval_llada.py model llada_dist tasks gsm8k num_fewshot 5 batch_size 8 limit 80 model_args model_path GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 gen_length 128 block_length 16 threshold 0.9 gamma 0.8 track_num 4 mask_num 4 verify True show_speed True output_path evals_results/gsm8k-prefix log outputs/run_prefix.log. If OOM reduce batch_size to 4 then 1 for both configs. Backup generate.py, patch verify section where x0_p_verify is computed by gathering mask-view probability of draft token then cumprod and gamma threshold to get keep_num: for independent rule compute per_token_p as same gathered probability, compute per_token_pass as per_token_p greater or equal gamma without cumprod, accept all passing positions with no stopping at first failure, decode those positions to draft tokens, leave rest masked; keep order, mask, tracking, threshold and gamma otherwise identical. At gamma 0.8 pass implies draft equals argmax. Run same eval with output_path evals_results/gsm8k-independent log outputs/run_independent.log. Parse accuracy and Tokens per iter into outputs/scores.jsonl.

event.description: Independent acceptance loses less than 2 accuracy points versus prefix stopping
event.statistic: acc_independent_minus_prefix_pp

evaluation.procedure: From outputs/scores.jsonl compute accuracy_pct independent minus prefix in points. outputs/scores.jsonl holds one line per rule with accuracy_pct, tokens_per_step, tokens_per_sec. Log files hold full stdout. Tokens per step gain is reported as diagnostic alongside accuracy difference.
evaluation.controls: Same prompts via same limit, same model, gen_length 128, block_length 16, threshold 0.9, gamma 0.8, tracking budget and batch size, verify True; only keep decision differs using identical logits per step, cumulative prefix versus independent per-token.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, test k-strikes tolerance, suffix requeueing and per-token prefix variants on full GSM8K MATH HumanEval to trade prefix guarantee for throughput; if large loss, retain prefix stopping.

agent.reason: Gamma 0.8 per-token is conservative and confidence 0.8 loses under 2pp in Fig 6, but independent accepts a much larger superset and conditions later tokens on rejected drafts, so retention within 2pp is plausible but not assured.

judge_astra.reason: Independent acceptance may recover useful suffix tokens, but the intervention also relaxes the cumulative-confidence budget and admits predictions conditioned on rejected drafts. Passing the observed accuracy cutoff remains quite plausible on 80 problems, without establishing non-inferiority.

judge_fable.reason: Independent per-token acceptance at 0.8 is far looser than the cumulative gamma=0.6 setting that already cost ~1.4 points in the paper, and it commits tokens conditioned on rejected drafts, so a 3-7 point GSM8K drop at gen_length 128 seems more likely than a <2 point loss; noise on 80 samples and possible patch bugs add uncertainty in both directions.

judge_opus.reason: Moving to per-token acceptance without prefix stopping probably admits extra tokens conditioned on rejected drafts, so a 1–4 pt accuracy loss is plausible. The event allows a net loss of at most 1 sample out of 80, and noise alone gives roughly 60% under no effect. Patch bugs in non-contiguous commits would mostly hurt accuracy.

judge_sol.reason: This relaxation removes cumulative-confidence gating as well as prefix stopping, and can commit suffix tokens conditioned on rejected drafts, creating a credible accuracy-loss mechanism. The small, short-generation evaluation still leaves considerable probability that the measured loss stays below 2 points; that outcome would not establish equivalence.

judge_luna.reason: Prefix stopping keeps later verification conditionals aligned with the context actually committed; accepting suffix tokens after a rejection can therefore harm quality. Some such errors may not change GSM8K exact-match, but the registered independent rule also replaces the code’s cumulative probability check with a per-token check, complicating the comparison.

judge_muse.reason: Independent accepts a superset of prefix passes so accuracy cost should resemble modest gamma lowering of about 1pp in Table 4, well within 2pp margin; lenient greater-than -2 threshold plus n=80 noise makes passing likely even with some conditioning mismatch.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper (Flash-Verify) stops acceptance at the first rejection along the decoding order. Appendix C argues that this keeps the accepted block a prefix, which the per-token and block deviation bounds need. Its ablations vary only γ, the track budget β_t, the window size β_m, generation length, prefill length and batch size. It never runs a non-prefix (independent per-token) acceptance rule, so it does not report how that rule changes accuracy or tokens per step.

SSD (self-speculative decoding for dLLMs) also uses the dLLM as both drafter and verifier, with hierarchical verification trees. It aims for output identical to step-by-step decoding, which rules out relaxed acceptance. The abstract describes no comparison against independent acceptance.

TAPS, like PRESTO (2607.22634) and D^2SD (2606.04446), works on diffusion-drafted speculative decoding with an autoregressive verifier. They change drafting and tree selection under prefix-conditioned verification. None of them compares stopping at the first rejection with accepting tokens independently inside a dLLM's own self-verification.

opus.reason: I found no paper that runs a dLLM self-verification scheme with acceptance stopped at the first rejection and again with independent per-token acceptance, then compares accuracy and tokens per step. The seed paper justifies prefix stopping only in theory, and related dLLM speculative-decoding work either keeps prefix verification or targets lossless output. So, based on the papers my searches returned, the question looks unanswered.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM uses prefix-stopped self-verification and explains its role in the bounded-deviation guarantee, but does not evaluate accepting independently passing tokens beyond a rejection.
SSD retains hierarchical prefix verification; its acceptance-limit and mix-order studies do not run the proposed independent acceptance rule or measure its accuracy tradeoff.

LSP directly compares prefix-first and scattered commitment on GSM8K, but selects tokens using marginal logit margins and spatial prefixes, rather than relaxing stopping within a confidence-ordered, causally conditioned self-verification pass.

Approximate Speculative Decoding measures relaxed verification versus strict stopping, but accepts budgeted mismatches to preserve a contiguous prefix; it explicitly does not skip rejected positions to commit later passing tokens.

sol.reason: Prior work already studies commitment topology and relaxed speculative verification, so the broad prefix-versus-parallelism motivation is not new. However, none of the work found tests the specific intervention of retaining all individually passing self-verified tokens while leaving rejected positions masked, using the same verification mechanism as the prefix baseline. That question remains distinct from marginal-confidence scheduling and mismatch-tolerant contiguous-prefix decoding.

opus.reason: Both rerun Flash-Verify with the first-mismatch prefix rule replaced by accepting every individually passing search token, and compare accuracy and tokens per step on GSM8K.

sol.reason: Unlike entry 12's prefix-only ablation, it replaces cumulative-product prefix acceptance with independent per-token thresholds, changing confidence aggregation as well as prefix stopping.

registration.title: Draft-agreement versus mask-confidence-only verification acceptance
registration.seed_connection: Tests Flash-Verify acceptance requiring draft-mask agreement plus mask confidence versus confidence-only, isolating agreement value and paper-versus-code gap.
registration.hypothesis: Requiring draft agreement via draft-token probability achieves higher accuracy than accepting on mask-view max probability alone at same gamma when each rule commits its own prediction.
registration.contribution: Ablates agreement conjunct with fair decoding source and same cumulative gamma rule, clarifying whether second-view agreement adds filtering value beyond confidence-only acceptance.

closest_work.difference: Speculative decoding uses target-draft agreement for lossless acceptance with separate draft and target models, not self-verification with two views from one diffusion model.
FreeDave verifies parallel candidates to match one-token-per-step output without comparing agreement-sensitive versus max-confidence acceptance at fixed gamma.
Fast-dLLM accepts on marginal confidence alone without a second view, leaving open whether second-view agreement adds filtering value.

inputs: Seed repo https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM.git, files llada/eval_llada.py and llada/generate.py
Model GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 from HuggingFace
GSM8K 5-shot via lm-eval-harness auto-download, requires HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1
registration.method: Clone repo, install, cd llada, set env HF_DATASETS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE true and HF_ALLOW_CODE_EVAL 1, mkdir outputs evals_results. Run agreement baseline with original code: accelerate launch num_processes 1 eval_llada.py model llada_dist tasks gsm8k num_fewshot 5 batch_size 16 limit 120 model_args model_path GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 gen_length 256 block_length 16 threshold 0.9 gamma 0.8 track_num 4 mask_num 4 verify True show_speed True output_path evals_results/gsm8k-agree log outputs/run_agree.log. If OOM reduce batch_size to 8 then 4 then 1 for both configs. Original code computes x0_p_verify by gathering mask-view probability of draft token then cumprod and gamma threshold. Backup generate.py, patch only that probability and decoding source to use mask-view max probability over vocab instead of gather on draft token for cumprod decision, keep cumprod, gamma comparison and queue order unchanged, and for accepted positions commit mask-view argmax tokens instead of drafts, so when draft equals argmax both commit same token and when they differ max-only commits argmax. Run same eval with output_path evals_results/gsm8k-maxonly log outputs/run_maxonly.log. Parse accuracy and tokens_per_step for both into outputs/scores.jsonl.

event.description: Agreement-sensitive acceptance beats max-confidence-only by more than 1.5 accuracy points at same gamma
event.statistic: acc_agree_minus_maxonly_pp

evaluation.procedure: From outputs/scores.jsonl compute accuracy_pct agree minus maxonly in points. outputs/scores.jsonl holds one line per config with accuracy_pct, tokens_per_step, tokens_per_sec. Log files hold full stdout for each acceptance rule with tokens-per-step reported to show acceptance-rate tradeoff.
evaluation.controls: Same prompts, model, draft threshold, gamma, tracking and batch size; only probability used for keep decision and decoding source differ, cumulative rule and queue order are identical.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, sweep gamma 0.6 to 0.95 on full GSM8K MATH HumanEval, compare per-token versus cumulative thresholds and agreement versus max rules on full accuracy versus tokens-per-step Pareto.

agent.reason: Max-only commits the better-informed mask argmax when draft differs and accepts a superset, so it may match or beat agreement; agreement beating it by more than 1.5pp requires frequent harmful over-acceptance unlikely at gamma 0.8.

judge_astra.reason: At gamma 0.8, a draft surviving the cumulative rule must already be the mask-view argmax, so the rules first diverge at confident revisions. Agreement could prevent downstream stale-draft conditioning errors, but its accuracy advantage is uncertain, and just two net additional correct answers would cross the registered threshold.

judge_fable.reason: With cumprod >= 0.8, any accepted token already has draft probability >0.5 and hence equals the argmax, so the two rules differ only when a chain continues past a confident disagreement, which is rare; outputs will be nearly identical and the expected accuracy difference is ~0, making a >1.5 point win for agreement mostly a noise or implementation-bug outcome.

judge_opus.reason: Max-only differs from agreement only where the mask-view argmax disagrees with the draft inside the cumprod budget, which is probably uncommon, so the true accuracy gap is likely small. A net gain of 2 samples out of 120 for agreement occurs about 30–38% of the time from trajectory noise alone.

judge_sol.reason: The cumulative 0.8 gate already implies mask-view mode agreement for accepted draft tokens, so the intervention initially matters at confident disagreements. Committing the mask-view argmax can correct drafts as well as make later conditioning inconsistent, leaving little direct evidence for an agreement advantage exceeding 1.5 points.

judge_luna.reason: Draft agreement could prevent commitments based on inconsistent views, but the max-only arm commits the mask-view argmax and may correct draft mistakes rather than merely remove a filter. I therefore do not expect the agreement arm’s greater-than-1.5-point accuracy advantage to be the likeliest outcome.

judge_muse.reason: Max-only uses larger probabilities than draft-gather so accepts longer prefixes, analogous to lowering gamma which Table 4 shows costs about 1pp, just below 1.5pp threshold; exceeding threshold thus needs favorable noise on n=120.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper defines Flash-Verify's rule as draft–mask agreement plus a mask-view confidence threshold gamma. It compares Flash-Verify against confidence-aware decoding, and sweeps gamma and the tracking budget. It never removes the agreement conjunct to test a rule that accepts on mask-view max probability alone and commits the mask-view argmax. It also does not examine the code's cumulative-product (cumprod) form of the gamma test.

In SSD the same dLLM drafts and verifies through hierarchical verification trees, with lossless exact-match acceptance against stepwise decoding. It does not ablate agreement against confidence-only acceptance under a lossy gamma threshold.

FreeDave drafts and then verifies in a second pass to match one-token-per-step output. It does not compare a rule that requires agreement with a rule that accepts on max confidence alone at a fixed gamma.
SimSD verifies drafts in dLLMs with reference tokens and an attention mask. Its abstract reports no ablation that separates the value of agreement from confidence-only acceptance.
Fast-dLLM accepts tokens on marginal confidence from a single view, with no second-view agreement check. The ablation asks whether adding that check helps.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper's method, ablations and appendix in full. They describe or sweep gamma, the tracking budget, the window size, and Flash-Verify versus confidence-aware decoding, but never remove the agreement conjunct. Searches on dLLM self-speculation and verification (SSD, FreeDave, SimSD, Spiffy, CORA-Diff) turned up no paper comparing agreement-plus-confidence acceptance with confidence-only acceptance from the same verify view at a fixed gamma. My searches were limited, so a closer ablation could still exist, but the question appears unanswered.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Flash-dLLM compares Flash-Verify against draft-pass confidence-aware decoding and sweeps verification thresholds, but does not ablate draft-sensitive versus mask-view maximum-probability acceptance within the same verification pass.

FreeDave verifies candidate sequences to reproduce one-token-per-step decoding; it does not compare agreement-sensitive and confidence-only verification with identical cumulative thresholds and each rule committing its own prediction.

Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking compares WINO with unmasking-only decoding and includes a consistency-based remasking ablation, but examines revision of already committed tokens rather than the proposed controlled verification-acceptance comparison.
Fast-dLLM studies marginal-confidence parallel unmasking without a second verification view, so it does not isolate the additional filtering supplied by draft agreement.

sol.reason: I found no work available by 2026-10-07 that reports this specific controlled acceptance-rule comparison. The seed paper's Flash-Verify versus confidence-aware results change the verification procedure itself, rather than holding the mask-view computation, cumulative gamma rule and queue order fixed while changing draft-sensitive scoring to maximum-probability scoring. Related verification and remasking studies therefore do not answer whether draft agreement adds accuracy beyond mask-view confidence under the registered comparison.

opus.reason: Both ablate the agreement requirement by committing the mask-view argmax whenever its confidence passes gamma with no draft-agreement check, and compare accuracy and tokens per step against the full agree-plus-gamma rule.

sol.reason: Both ablate draft–mask agreement against mask-confidence-only acceptance that commits mask-view predictions, measuring accuracy and decoding efficiency, with cumulative gating serving as a shared implementation variant.
