outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: run_eval.sh installs the dependencies, downloads fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder (100000.safetensors + config.yaml) and openai-community/gpt2 (tokenizer and embedding source), then runs local_edit.py. The script loads the repo's TextAutoencoder on CUDA and restores the encoder and decoder state dicts strictly. Restoring the decoder writes its trained lm_head.weight into the tied embedding table. I assert that the tie holds and that the table equals the checkpoint weights, not the original GPT-2 ones. It also restores encodings_mean/std. Dropout, NPU fused attention, FlexAttention and compilation are all off. The encoder's target_latent_len is set to 256 so tensors stay short, and decoder.chunk_size=1. Decoding uses argmax, logits are thrown away, and batches are 16 sequences.

Data: XSum test documents, shuffled with seed 42. A snippet is the first 256 GPT-2 tokens of a document; documents shorter than 256 tokens are skipped and not counted. This gave 1024 snippets. In each snippet I take the first valid pair of standalone 2–4 digit integers, with digit runs exactly aligned to token boundaries, both inside token positions 32–223, separated by at least 32 tokens. Decimal and comma-number fragments are excluded. Replacements have the same digit count and token length and are searched cyclically starting at original+37. Each pair passes a check that retokenizing the edited text gives exactly 256 tokens, differing only in the two edited intervals. That left 360 candidate pairs; 664 snippets were logged as having no valid pair.

Eligibility was fixed before any hybrid was built: both the original and the edited sequence had to decode back exactly. 134 of 360 pairs passed (37% coverage; 226 rejections, all logged). The registration says "at most 256", so the denominator is 134. Hybrids use raw decoder-facing latents. For k in {0,4,16}, z′ rows are copied only over each edit span plus the next k rows (overlaps merged). I also decoded a full-suffix replacement arm, the full z′ and an identity reconstruction of z.

Result: the k=0 arm reproduced the edited sequence exactly in 134/134 pairs. The one-sided 95% Wilson lower bound is 0.980 (two-sided interval [0.972, 1.0]), so the registered event (above 0.8) occurred. Every other arm also scored 134/134, with no collateral changes.

Checks:
- Encoder latents before the first edit are bit-identical between z and z′ (max abs diff 0), and decoded prefixes are preserved in every arm.
- The unchanged suffix rows really do differ between E(original) and E(edited): mean relative L2 difference is 0.034 per pair, maximum 1.14 at a single row. So the k=0 arm is decoding genuinely stale suffix rows, not identical ones.

Caveats on how far this result reaches:
- It covers only the 37% of pairs that reconstruct exactly. That filter may select texts on which the decoder is more robust, so the result says nothing about the other 63%.
- It covers only same-length numeric substitutions, a single run, and 256-token snippets.
- The average suffix perturbation is small, which may be why locality holds for this kind of edit.
- Because n=134 and success was 100%, the arms cannot be told apart; the k=4, k=16 and full-suffix results are diagnostics only.

Numerical setting and limitations:
- The registration did not fix precision. I used bf16 autocast, as the repo's encode and decode paths do. I did not test whether fp32 would raise the reconstruction coverage.
- Snippets carry no EOS prefix.
- The seed repo's git revision could not be read (manifest shows null); the Hugging Face model revisions are recorded.
- The whole run takes about 25 s after downloads.

It also requires digit runs to align exactly with token boundaries, with at most one leading space, and excludes comma-grouped numbers. registration.title: Late source guidance for counterfactual numerical fidelity at matched denoising cost
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM's summarization protocol applies CFG only at high noise, sigma in [0.9,1.0], and chooses inference settings using ROUGE. Exact numerical identity may require source conditioning later than the phase that establishes a summary's topic.
registration.hypothesis: Allocating two additional source-guidance evaluations to the final denoising steps improves paired numerical adaptation more than allocating the same evaluations immediately after the existing high-noise guidance window.
registration.contribution: Guidance scheduling and counterfactual summarization evaluation are not new. This experiment joins them in a fixed-NFE causal comparison targeting literal numerical responsiveness in continuous-latent generation, without training a verifier or using a general factuality judge.

closest_work.difference: Limited-interval guidance is studied primarily for image sample quality, where late guidance is often unnecessary. This test asks whether exact textual facts have a different useful guidance phase.

This work evaluates entity-level factual adaptiveness and uses model-based counterfactual selection and training augmentation. The proposed test uses mechanically constructed number substitutions and changes only inference-time guidance placement; it does not assume the substitutions establish a measured conflict with parametric knowledge.

The decoder-interface audit identifies difficult numeric and low-margin token tails. This experiment tests an intervention aimed at source fidelity rather than using those signals for early exit or readout simplification.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM, especially src/aurora/sampling/block_sampler.py and src/aurora/diffusion/scheduler.py.
Hugging Face models: fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum, 300000.safetensors and config.yaml; fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, 100000.safetensors and config.yaml.
GPT-2 tokenizer/configuration/embedding-source weights: openai-community/gpt2.
Dataset: EdinburghNLP/xsum, test split; small scoring dependencies: rouge-score and num2words.
registration.method: Load frozen EMA models through the official CUDA pipeline, retaining checkpoint normalization and disabling optional compilation/FlexAttention, NPU operators, and self-conditioning CFG. Ordinary conditional self-conditioning remains enabled. Download only required weights/configurations/tokenizer files and retain installed CUDA PyTorch. Seed-shuffle the XSum test split with seed 42. Select the first 64 eligible documents with at least 384 source tokens and a standalone two-digit integer appearing both within the first 384 source tokens and in the reference. Exclude decimal fragments. Replace every whole-number occurrence of that integer in the source prefix and reference with a different two-digit integer absent from both originals. Search replacements deterministically starting 37 above the original, wrapping within 10-99, and require the complete edited prefix to retain exactly the same token length and unchanged tokens outside replacement spans. Use the unmodified and edited 384-token prefixes directly, without added instructions or EOS. Do not select cases based on generated outputs. Generate 48 tokens in three 16-position blocks with 16 Euler steps and the checkpoint's shift-7 sigma grid. Let B be step indices whose sigma is at least 0.9. Both arms use CFG scale 2 on B. The early-extension control additionally guides the first two indices after B; the late-extension arm instead additionally guides indices 14 and 15, using zero-based indexing. Guidance is otherwise off. Both arms therefore have identical denoiser evaluation counts. To avoid an unmeasured stale-self-conditioning effect when guidance resumes after a gap, supply x_0_self_cond=None on every unconditional CFG pass in both arms; keep the conditional self-conditioning path unchanged. This controlled protocol is explicitly not a byte-for-byte reproduction of the released sampler. Reuse identical block-noise tensors across arms and across original/counterfactual inputs for seeds 101 and 202. Batch equal-length prompts, approximately 8-16 at a time, and truncate decoded summaries at first EOS. An anchor is present if the summary contains its standalone decimal form or its num2words cardinal form after lowercasing and normalizing hyphens/whitespace. A document-seed pair succeeds only if the original summary contains the original anchor but not its replacement, and the counterfactual summary contains the replacement but not the original. Omissions count as failures.

event.description: Late placement of the extra guidance evaluations improves paired numerical adaptation by more than five percentage points.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 2000 paired document-bootstrap estimates of mean(pair_success_late - pair_success_early), averaging the two sampling seeds within each document.

evaluation.procedure: Write outputs/counterfactual_pairs.jsonl with document IDs, original/edited prefix IDs, references, anchor replacements, and construction checks. Write outputs/generations.jsonl with arm, seed, source variant, decoded summary and tokens, anchor-presence indicators, paired success, ROUGE-L against the corresponding reference, output length, and measured denoiser evaluation count. Write outputs/guidance_checks.json with the actual sigma grid, active step indices, equal-NFE checks, and clean autoencoder recovery of the anchors. Write outputs/summary.json with the registered statistic, paired mean and two-sided bootstrap interval, and diagnostic omission/stale-anchor rates. Write outputs/manifest.json with revisions, settings, and runtimes. The anchor metric measures only literal numerical responsiveness; neither it nor ROUGE establishes general factual correctness.
evaluation.controls: The two guidance schedules have equal NFE, guidance scale, solver steps, output budget, and block-noise tensors. Fixed 384-token prefixes eliminate partial-block repaint differences. Token-length-preserving substitutions control positional changes. Disabling self-conditioning only on unconditional passes in both arms removes stale unconditional-track history as an alternative explanation. Paired success penalizes omission and memorized reuse of the original number.

models: openai-community/gpt2, used only as tokenizer and embedding source

registration.full_scale_study: Map source-guidance timing against exact entity, quantity, date, and negation fidelity across continuous-latent models, solver budgets, and source lengths. Validate any gains under the native self-conditioning protocol and compare fidelity-diversity-ROUGE frontiers at matched NFE and wall-clock cost.

agent.reason: Late guidance could help preserve numerical details, but those choices may already be committed, and terminal extrapolation could instead destabilize decoding. The paired adaptation criterion and the confidence-bound requirement on 64 documents make a clear positive event relatively demanding.

judge_astra.reason: Late guidance may improve marginal numeral choices, but omissions and earlier content decisions may dominate this strict paired-success metric. Against another guidance-extended arm, obtaining a lower-bound improvement above five percentage points on 64 documents seems ambitious.

judge_fable.reason: At the last two Euler steps the noisy state already fixes the content, so conditional and unconditional predictions differ little and late guidance is nearly inert, while base rates of exact-number copying are low; a late-minus-early gain exceeding 5pp at the bootstrap lower bound over 64 documents is very unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: With the shift-7 grid, indices 14–15 sit at σ≈0.3–0.6, where tokens, numbers included, are already fixed by the noisy state, so late guidance should barely matter. The early extension acts where fine details may still be open. Low pair-success base rates and only 64 documents also make a >5-point lower bound very unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Late guidance might improve numerical identity when the relevant fact is already being summarized, but may not repair omissions or earlier fact selection. With 64 documents, crossing the five-percentage-point lower-bound threshold likely requires a larger and more consistent benefit than two relocated guidance evaluations provide.

judge_luna.reason: Late guidance might help refine literal numbers, but the paper's protocol concentrates guidance at high noise, when broader content is likely established. The paired metric also requires exact numerical adaptation in both source variants, so a reliable advantage exceeding five points seems unlikely.

judge_muse.reason: With 64 documents, the lower bound needs roughly an 11-15pp mean paired-success gain from moving two guidance evaluations to the final steps. Late detail refinement may help slightly, but such a large paired numerical-adaptation effect is unlikely.

closest_work.difference: This paper restricts guidance to a limited noise interval and evaluates image sample quality (FID). It does not study text, compare late versus early placement of extra guidance at equal NFE, or measure literal source fidelity under counterfactual edits.

Step AG finds that guiding only the early steps is enough for text-to-image and text-to-video quality and alignment. It does not test late-step guidance for exact textual facts in a continuous-latent language model.

This paper evaluates entity-level factual adaptiveness in summarization with model-selected counterfactuals and training augmentation. It does not intervene on diffusion guidance timing, and it does not use mechanical number substitutions.
The seed paper uses CFG only for sigma in [0.9, 1.0] and tunes it on ROUGE. It does not test reallocating guidance to late steps, and it reports no counterfactual numeric-anchor evaluation.
This paper learns CFG schedules adversarially for text-to-image alignment. It does not address text generation or numerical fidelity.

opus.reason: My searches found prior work on CFG schedules and limited-interval guidance, almost all of it for images, where the usual finding is that early guidance is enough. Separately, there is counterfactual factual-adaptiveness work for autoregressive summarizers. I found no paper that compares early versus late placement of extra source guidance at equal compute in a continuous-latent text diffusion model, and none that measures paired numeric adaptation, so the question appears unanswered.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Studies when CFG can be switched off in masked diffusion language models using paired continuations and lexical, structural, and instruction constraints. It does not compare equal-cost early versus late guidance additions for source-number adaptation under paired counterfactual edits.

Adapts retrieval guidance at each denoising step and token to improve factual grounding in masked-diffusion QA. It does not isolate guidance placement with fixed guidance strength and equal evaluation counts, or test paired numerical substitutions.

Tests constant versus decreasing source-CFG schedules in continuous embedding-space text generation, measuring paraphrase quality and diversity. It does not test whether late guidance improves literal factual responsiveness relative to an equal-cost early extension.

Analyzes benefits of later guidance in low-dimensional masked diffusion and evaluates guidance schedules on image generation. Its text experiments test guidance normalization, not timing effects on counterfactual source fidelity.

Evaluates counterfactual entity adaptiveness in summarization and proposes training augmentation. It explicitly excludes numerical entity categories and does not intervene on diffusion guidance timing.

The seed uses high-noise-only source CFG and selects summarization settings through guidance-scale and solver-step sweeps scored by ROUGE. It does not report the registered matched-NFE timing comparison or numerical counterfactual evaluation.

sol.reason: Prior work available by 2026-10-07 establishes guidance scheduling, prompt-specific guidance necessity, and counterfactual summarization evaluation, but none of the work I found answers this experiment's specific causal question. Whether relocating an equal number of source-guidance evaluations to final denoising steps improves paired literal numerical adaptation remains distinct from the reported quality, constraint-satisfaction, and factual-grounding comparisons.

opus.reason: Entry #57 compares guidance windows for ROUGE, but none compares early versus late placement of extra guidance at matched NFE for counterfactual numerical fidelity.

sol.reason: Unlike entry 57’s guidance-window comparison using ROUGE, this experiment reallocates equal guidance evaluations between early and late steps and measures counterfactual numerical adaptation.

outcome.executor_notes:
What was run: exp/run.sh installs the small dependencies and then runs exp/run_experiment.py. The script loads the released AURORA-LM pipeline from /workspace/seed/src on CUDA: it uses DiffusionGenerator / EvalDiffusionTrainer, the EMA weights, and the checkpoint's latent normalization. It downloads only the required files: aurora-gpt2-xsum 300000.safetensors + config.yaml, aurora-text-autoencoder 100000.safetensors + config.yaml, and the openai-community/gpt2 tokenizer, config and weights (the AE uses these as its embedding source).

Optional operators were switched off by setting operator_optimization.profile="off" after the config is loaded. This disables FlexAttention, the torch.compile MLP and the NPU ops. A command-line dotlist override could not be used because YAML parses "off" as False. Self-conditioning CFG is not used. Ordinary conditional self-conditioning is kept, as in the released sampler: the self-conditioning signal is the CFG-combined prediction.

Sampler: I copied the inner loop of BlockSampler.run with three changes: (a) it takes noise tensors generated in advance, (b) CFG at scale 2 is applied on an explicit set of step indices, and (c) every unconditional CFG pass gets x_0_self_cond=None. Settings were 16 Euler steps on the checkpoint's tanh shift-7 grid. B = {0..6} (sigma ≥ 0.9). The early arm uses B plus {7, 8} (sigma 0.895 and 0.875). The late arm uses B plus {14, 15} (sigma 0.584 and 0.411).

As a fidelity check, I ran the copy with the released unconditional self-conditioning track and the same noise, and compared it with the released BlockSampler.run (window 0.9–1.0, prefix of 384). The latents were bit-identical (max abs diff 0) and decoded tokens agreed 100%; this is recorded in guidance_checks.json.

The two arms used the same number of denoiser evaluations: 75 per batch (48 conditional + 27 unconditional), 1200 total per arm. Cache writes and prefill were also identical across arms.

Block noise came from a CPU torch.Generator seeded with 101 or 202, shape [64 docs, 3 blocks, 16, 768]. The same tensor was reused for both arms and for both the original and counterfactual input. Batches held 16 documents. Generation ran from the 384-token prefixes with no added instruction and no EOS. Prefixes are encoded the same way as the generator's token-id path (padded, attention mask over the first 384). Decoding uses the released _decode_prefix_generation and truncates at the first stop token.

Data: XSum test split, shuffled with seed 42, scanned in order. Of 4,867 documents scanned, 2,454 had fewer than 384 tokens and 2,349 had no shared standalone two-digit integer; the first 64 remaining documents were used. "Standalone" is defined by the regex (?<![\w.,:/])([1-9]\d)(?!\w)(?![.,:/]\d). This excludes decimal fragments and also, by my choice, fragments joined by thousands-commas, colons or slashes (e.g. "10:30", "24/7"). If several integers qualified, I took the one that appears first in the reference.

Replacement search: r = 10 + ((n − 10 + 37 + k) mod 90), with r ≠ n. r had to be absent from the original prefix and reference in both its decimal and its num2words form. The edited prefix had to re-tokenize to exactly 384 tokens, with tokens outside the replacement spans unchanged. I also added a check that the prefix text round-trips through the tokenizer; no document failed it.

Anchor matching: decimal regex or num2words cardinal form, after lowercasing and turning hyphens/dashes into spaces. One addition: a multiple-of-ten word (e.g. "fifty") does not count if it is followed by a unit word ("fifty four"). Omissions count as failures. ROUGE-L uses rouge-score with stemming. The bootstrap draws 2000 document resamples (numpy rng seed 20260803) of the per-document mean over seeds of late minus early.

Result (identical on a clean re-run of the full command, about 90 s): the registered statistic, the 5th bootstrap percentile, is 0.0. The paired mean difference (late − early) is 0.0078, with a two-sided 95% bootstrap interval of [0, 0.023]. One document favoured late, none favoured early, and 63 were tied. The registered event (> 0.05) did not occur.

This does not show that the two placements are equivalent. Paired success was low in both arms (early 7.8%, late 8.6%), mainly because the anchor was omitted: 70–84% of summaries contained neither number. Stale use of the original number in counterfactual summaries was 7.8% (early) and 5.5% (late). With so few successes the test has little power to detect any placement effect.

Interpretation caveat: because the source is cut at 384 tokens, generations often first finish the interrupted source sentence and only then start a summary. This is a direct consequence of the registered fixed-prefix protocol, which I did not change. The clean autoencoder recovered the anchor 100% of the time (mean token accuracy 0.9985 on the prefixes).

Environment: the installed torch is 2.6.0+cu124, kept as the registration requires; the repo pins 2.8.0. transformers 4.57.1 is installed by run.sh. As registered, this controlled protocol is not a byte-for-byte reproduction of the released sampler, because the unconditional passes do not use self-conditioning.

This changes which documents are eligible and which occurrences get replaced or detected. It was disclosed, and it applies equally to both arms, so it is unlikely to change the arm comparison.

registration.title: Are denoiser residuals unusually harmful after matching decoder-space error geometry?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM assesses latent capacity using Gaussian-corruption reconstruction, although its frozen decoder ultimately receives model predictions. This experiment compares teacher-forced denoiser residuals with randomized residuals while preserving more of their geometry than independent token-wise noise would preserve.
registration.hypothesis: Actual two-pass denoiser residuals cause more token-recovery errors than randomized residuals with matched decoder-space magnitudes, clean-latent inner products, and within-block residual correlations.
registration.contribution: The closest decoder-interface work already establishes directional sensitivity. This experiment tests naturally produced residuals and preserves their complete within-block Gram matrix, rather than confounding perturbation direction with radial shrinkage or cross-position error correlations.

closest_work.difference: Studies decoder margins, directional perturbations, and PCA degradation. This experiment compares actual AURORA denoising residuals with joint rotations preserving decoder-space residual geometry.
Introduces decoder-input noise during joint training. This experiment diagnoses a frozen decoder without adaptation.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM
OWT denoiser: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, including 250000.safetensors and its configuration
Autoencoder: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, including 100000.safetensors and its configuration
GPT-2 tokenizer and, only if required by the loader, embedding weights: https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2
Text: Hugging Face Salesforce/wikitext, configuration wikitext-103-raw-v1, test split
registration.method:
Use the repository checkpoint loader, including its EMA selection and latent normalization statistics. Verify artifact contents on load and record revisions; do not substitute another model if required artifacts are unavailable. Retain a compatible installed CUDA PyTorch, disable compilation, FlexAttention compilation, distributed execution and logging services, and use dense attention with the original masks. Run frozen networks in evaluation mode with BF16 autocast, while constructing perturbations and calculating diagnostics in float32 or float64. Download no external scoring model.

Select the first 192 nonempty, non-heading WikiText test rows containing at least 127 GPT-2 tokens. Form each 128-token sequence as EOS followed by the first 127 text tokens. Set runtime sequence and latent lengths to 128 with c=1. Encode and standardize using the checkpoint statistics. Positions 0:112 are clean history and positions 112:128 are the target block. For sigma in {0.6,0.8} and corruption seeds {11,22,33}, corrupt only the target as x=(1-sigma)*z+sigma*epsilon. Obtain an EMA prediction without self-conditioning, followed by a prediction at the identical noisy state self-conditioned on the detached first prediction. Keep clean history fixed and use no guidance. Derive document-specific random streams from a stable hash of row ID and seed.

Perform the matching in the coordinates actually received by the decoder. Let Y be the 16-by-D clean target in original encoder coordinates and R be predicted_target-Y after inverse normalization. Let B have orthonormal columns spanning the rows of Y, obtained by float64 SVD with rank tolerance 1e-7 times the largest singular value. Set R_parallel=R*B*B^T and R_perp=R-R_parallel. Compute a thin SVD R_perp=U*diag(s)*V^T. Draw a D-by-16 Gaussian matrix, project its columns orthogonal to B, and obtain an orthonormal matrix H by QR with positive-diagonal sign correction. Define R_control=R_parallel+U*diag(s)*H^T. Repeat with four independent H draws. This preserves R*R^T and R*Y^T, hence each position's error norm, radial component and predicted-latent norm, while randomizing the remaining orientation jointly across the block.

Before autocast, verify these constraints after conversion to float32. For each compared matrix require normalized discrepancy ||A-B||_F/(1+||A||_F) below 1e-4. Decode native and control targets with the identical clean 112-position decoder history. Score only non-special target tokens reconstructed correctly by the uncorrupted autoencoder. Exclude a document only if it has no eligible target tokens; fewer than 128 eligible documents is insufficient support. Record how much residual energy lies in the randomized component. Also record standardized-coordinate MSE: it is not constrained by this decoder-space matching. These are teacher-forced denoising residuals, not free-running generation errors. Do not change noise levels or matching rules after inspecting outcomes.

event.description: Native residuals increase token error by more than five percentage points relative to geometry-matched randomized residuals.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of the document-bootstrap distribution of mean(native eligible-token error rate minus matched-control eligible-token error rate).

evaluation.procedure: For each document, average the paired error-rate difference across both noise levels, three corruption seeds and four rotations. Bootstrap whole documents 5000 times with seed 991. Report the point estimate, a two-sided 95% interval and the registered one-sided lower bound. outputs/manifest.json contains row IDs, tokenization settings, software and artifact revisions. outputs/token_scores.jsonl contains gold IDs, clean/native/control decoded IDs, eligibility masks and errors for every condition. outputs/residuals.pt contains clean target latents, native decoder-space residuals and randomization seeds. outputs/geometry_checks.json contains matching discrepancies, randomized energy fractions and standardized-coordinate MSE diagnostics. outputs/result.json contains the statistic, intervals, clean reconstruction accuracy, sample counts and timings. Failed matching checks invalidate the comparison. A wide interval is inconclusive; failure to cross the threshold does not establish equivalence.
evaluation.controls: Identical texts, clean decoder history, EMA weights and corruption inputs; matching in decoder coordinates; preservation of within-block residual correlations and clean-latent inner products; clean reconstruction control; document-level uncertainty. Conclusions remain conditional on this checkpoint and teacher-forced setting.

models: openai-community/gpt2 embedding table only if required

registration.full_scale_study: Measure whether the same geometry gap appears in actual sampling trajectories and across independently trained latent widths. Then compare decoder adaptation using model-produced residuals against random-corruption adaptation, evaluating token fidelity and generation quality separately.

agent.reason: Denoiser errors can concentrate on competing token directions that joint rotations disperse, making a harmfulness gap plausible. However, preserving clean-latent inner products and residual correlations may remove much of that gap, and the event requires a lower confidence bound above five percentage points.

judge_astra.reason: Native residuals plausibly concentrate in directions associated with competing tokens, whereas rotations disperse that structure. However, preserving clean-latent inner products removes an important source of apparent harm, and a lower bound exceeding five percentage points is substantially harder than detecting any directional effect.

judge_fable.reason: Model residuals point toward alternative token latents while the geometry-matched controls spread the same energy over random directions the dropout-trained decoder tolerates well, so a gap is expected; but the teacher-forced denoiser with full clean context is probably quite accurate at sigma 0.6 and 0.8 (the paper's own noise-calibration logic implies strong signal at these levels for D=768), making a >5-point mean gap borderline, and the native loader/mask integration under a 60-call budget adds real failure risk.

judge_opus.reason: With 112 clean history positions and strong noisy evidence at sigma 0.6/0.8 (Fig. 5a), native teacher-forced errors should be only a few percent, so a >5-point gap at the 5th percentile is unlikely even if the rotated control is nearly harmless.

judge_sol.reason: Native residuals plausibly align with competing token features more strongly than randomized residuals, producing greater decoder harm. However, preserving clean-latent projections and within-block geometry removes important confounds and could substantially reduce the gap below the five-point lower-bound threshold.

judge_luna.reason: The matched residual geometry makes this a strong directional test, but the sign is uncertain: native residuals may align with decoder-sensitive directions, while randomized off-manifold directions could be more damaging. A difference exceeding five percentage points is a substantial bar.

judge_muse.reason: Fig.5a shows wide-latent decoders tolerate large isotropic corruption, so a >5pp lower-bound harm from orientation alone after preserving error norms, radial components and within-block correlations would require strong adversarial alignment of natural residuals; seed gives no evidence for this.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Audits ELF and also checks LangFlow, BitstreamDiffusion and Cola-DLM. It uses a decoder-margin bound, corrupts final latents and compares sensitivity along random, sentiment, PCA and decoder-gradient directions, with covariance-matched controls on the representation side. In the part I read, it does not compare actual denoiser residuals against randomized residuals that keep the full within-block Gram matrix and the inner products with the clean latent. It also does not study AURORA's block-causal latents.

Adds decoder-input noise during joint training of an LDLM to make the decoder more robust. It does not test whether a frozen decoder is more sensitive to the residuals the model actually produces than to geometry-matched random ones.

Shows that latent geometry metrics can look good while token decoding still fails in a BERT-latent refinement model. Its perturbations are token dropout, and it has no residual-versus-matched-randomization control.

The seed paper measures latent capacity by reconstructing from Gaussian-corrupted latents. It does not compare decoder errors caused by teacher-forced denoiser residuals with errors caused by geometry-matched controls.

opus.reason: The nearest prior work, 2606.08810, already shows that ELF's decoder is more sensitive in some directions than others and that MSE does not predict token recovery. I found no paper that asks whether naturally produced denoiser residuals are unusually harmful once their decoder-space geometry is preserved. The proposed control rotates each residual block jointly while keeping its error norms, radial component and cross-position correlations, and I found no prior use of this, on AURORA or any other latent text diffusion model. My search was limited: I read only part of 2606.08810, so a closer test buried in its later sections cannot be fully ruled out.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Establishes decoder directional sensitivity through matched-norm random, sentiment, PCA and decoder-gradient perturbations. It does not compare naturally produced denoiser residuals with joint rotations preserving both their within-block Gram matrix and inner products with clean latents.
Tests token reconstruction under Gaussian latent corruption and studies latent capacity and denoiser design, but does not perform the registered native-versus-geometry-matched residual comparison.
Studies Gaussian decoder-input noise during joint training and its effects on reconstruction and generation, rather than diagnosing a frozen decoder with geometry-matched model-produced errors.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes decoder anisotropy, but does not settle whether naturally produced denoiser errors are unusually harmful after controlling clean-latent alignment and cross-position residual correlations. Among papers available by 2026-10-07, I found no study reporting the paired native-versus-randomized residual comparison preserving RR^T and RY^T; this is a distinct diagnostic question and control design, not merely a different checkpoint or dataset.

opus.reason: Both ask whether actual denoiser prediction residuals harm decoding more than randomized perturbations of matched magnitude, by decoding clean latents plus native versus norm-matched random residuals and comparing token accuracy. The registered version uses the released checkpoint and stricter geometry matching, but the manipulation and measurement are essentially the same.

sol.reason: Both compare actual teacher-forced denoiser residuals with randomized, error-matched perturbations using decoded token recovery, with the registered experiment adding stronger geometric controls.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (exp/run_experiment.py, run by run_eval.sh): I loaded the released checkpoints through the repository's own DiffusionGenerator/EvalDiffusionTrainer loader. That loader handles the EMA, which I copied into the denoiser, and the latent mean/std from the checkpoint. The checkpoints were fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (250000.safetensors), fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder (100000.safetensors) and the GPT-2 embedding/tokenizer, which the repo loader requires. The script records HF commit SHAs and file SHA-256 hashes in the manifest.

Runtime settings: sequence length and num_latents are 128 (c=1). Operator optimisation uses a custom profile with no flex attention, no torch.compile and dense masks. There is no DDP and no wandb, and the networks run in bf16 autocast.

Data: the first 192 WikiText-103 test rows that, after strip(), are nonempty, are not '= ... =' headings, and have at least 127 GPT-2 tokens. Each sequence is EOS plus the first 127 tokens.

Denoising: only the 112:128 target block is corrupted, using x=(1-σ)z+σε with σ∈{0.6,0.8} and seeds {11,22,33}. ε comes from a per-document generator seeded by sha256(row_id, seed); the same ε is reused for both σ values. The EMA denoiser runs twice at the identical noisy state: first without self-conditioning, then self-conditioned on the detached first x0. It uses the repo's clean_history concat path, which applies the blockwise-causal mask with t=0 for the history. There is no guidance.

Matching was done in float64 in decoder coordinates, exactly as registered. I recover the row space of Y by SVD with rank tolerance 1e-7, split R into R_par and R_perp, take the thin SVD of R_perp, and draw a Gaussian matrix projected off B. QR with sign correction gives H. Four rotations per document are seeded by a hash of (row, seed, σ, k), and all seeds are saved.

Checks after casting to float32: Gram RR^T, cross RY^T, predicted-latent Gram and row norms, against a tolerance of 1e-4. In the test run all checks passed, with the largest discrepancy about 1.6e-8.

Decoding uses the identical clean 112-position encoder history. Eligible tokens are non-special target tokens that the clean autoencoder reconstructs correctly. The statistic is the per-document error-rate difference averaged over 2 σ × 3 seeds × 4 rotations, with a 5000× document bootstrap (seed 991).

Test-run results, on this checkpoint and in this teacher-forced setting only:
- Clean target reconstruction was 100%; all 192 documents and 3072 tokens were eligible.
- Mean error rate: native 0.095, control 0.010.
- Point estimate of the difference: 0.085, with a 95% CI of [0.078, 0.092]. The registered 5th-percentile statistic is 0.0795, which is above the 0.05 threshold.
- The gap depends strongly on σ. At σ=0.6 the difference is only 0.012; at σ=0.8 it is 0.158.
- The randomized share of residual energy is about 0.79 at σ=0.6 and about 0.63 at σ=0.8.
- Standardized-coordinate MSE, which the matching does not constrain, is slightly higher for the controls (0.133 vs 0.129 at σ=0.6; 0.235 vs 0.230 at σ=0.8).

Deviations, all minor:
- The installed PyTorch is 2.6.0+cu124, not the repo's pinned 2.8; I kept it, as the registration asks.
- WikiText rows are strip()'d before tokenization.
- ε is shared across the two σ levels for a given (row, seed); the registration does not specify this.
- The bootstrap interval comes from a single fixed run. The three corruption seeds are averaged inside each document rather than reported as separate repetitions.

These are teacher-forced residuals, not free-running generation errors.

departures: exp/run_experiment.py strips WikiText rows with str.strip() before tokenization. This removes the leading space, so the first text token changes, and it could shift which rows reach 127 tokens. The engineer reported it. It falls within what the registration leaves open, and an effect on the value is implausible beyond a negligible amount.

exp/run_experiment.py reuses the same epsilon for both sigma levels for a given (row, seed). The engineer reported it and the registration leaves it unspecified. It correlates the two sigma conditions but does not bias either one.

The registered 'repetitions: 3' is implemented as the three corruption seeds, averaged within each document, rather than as three separate runs of the pipeline. The engineer reported it. The registered statistic is computed exactly as specified.

The installed PyTorch is 2.6.0+cu124, not the repo's pinned 2.8. The registration allows this. The custom operator profile (torch RMSNorm, no NPU kernels, no flex attention, no compile) is needed to run on CUDA. Neither is expected to change the value materially.

EMA weights are applied by hand with trainer.ema.copy_to(den.parameters()) after the repository loader runs. Raw and EMA weights differ (abs diff 3.0e5 in manifest.json), so the copy did something. I cannot verify from the evidence that trainer.ema holds the checkpoint's EMA weights rather than raw weights. If it held raw weights, the native residuals and possibly the value would change.

time_t is given the corruption level sigma directly, for a model configured with flow-matching time sampling (shift 7.0). The code assumes that the model's time input equals the interpolation coefficient. That is plausible, since native error at sigma=0.6 is a sensible 1.3%, but it is not verified in the artifacts. A wrong mapping would change the native residuals.
geometry_checks.json reports the mean randomized energy fraction from rotation k=0 only. The fraction is identical across k by construction, so this has no effect.
The check also verifies predicted-latent Gram and row norms, which go beyond the registration. This has no effect.
problems: The headline value comes almost entirely from sigma=0.8. The difference there is 0.158; at sigma=0.6 it is only 0.012, which is well below the 0.05 threshold (result.json per_sigma). The registered pooled event is met, but the conclusion is strongly noise-level dependent and should not be stated as a uniform effect.

The control randomizes R_perp uniformly over the roughly 752-dimensional complement of the clean-target span. This preserves the block Gram but not the residual's alignment with the anisotropic latent data covariance or the decoder-sensitive subspace. The near-zero control error (about 1%) shows that the decoder ignores isotropic orthogonal noise. It does not show that the harm is denoiser-specific rather than a property of any residual concentrated in data-manifold directions. Standardized MSE is nearly equal (0.230 vs 0.235), which only partly addresses this.
The correctness of the EMA source (the manual trainer.ema.copy_to call) and of the sigma-to-time_t convention cannot be confirmed from the provided files (exp/run_experiment.py).
The scope is narrow: one checkpoint, 192 WikiText documents, teacher-forced single-block residuals, and two noise levels. The notes and result.json correctly state the teacher-forced limitation.
opus.reason: The code follows the registered pipeline closely. It uses the same data selection, 128-token sequences with a 112/16 split, sigma {0.6, 0.8} with seeds {11, 22, 33}, two-pass self-conditioned EMA predictions, the float64 decoder-space matching that preserves RR^T and RY^T, four rotations, eligibility filtering, and the 5000x document bootstrap with seed 991. The reported departures are either choices the registration leaves open or necessary platform changes. All matching checks pass by wide margins (max discrepancy about 1.6e-8), clean reconstruction is 100%, and the token-level outputs are consistent with the summary statistics, so the value appears to be produced genuinely from model outputs. The registered event is met clearly (5th percentile 0.0795 > 0.05, CI [0.078, 0.092]), but the effect is driven by sigma=0.8. The isotropic-rotation control leaves open whether the native residuals are harmful because they come from the denoiser or because they lie in data-manifold directions. This is a credible, precisely estimated but narrowly scoped diagnostic finding, with small unverifiable risks around EMA selection and the time convention.

departures: exp/run_experiment.py strips each WikiText row before tokenization. The registration specifies the first 127 text tokens from the raw test rows, without this preprocessing. GPT-2 tokenization is whitespace-sensitive, so stripping can change row eligibility, token identities, and which tokens occupy the target block; this plausibly changes the reported value.

Only one complete evaluation is evidenced, whereas the registration lists evaluation.repetitions=3. exp/run_experiment.py does run all three registered corruption seeds and correctly averages them within documents, as the statistical procedure requires. Whether three additional complete runs were intended is ambiguous; their absence limits replication evidence but does not change the prescribed single-run statistic.

The encoder call ae.get_latent in exp/run_experiment.py is not explicitly enclosed in trainer.autocast_context(), unlike denoising and decoding. This is a potential departure from the BF16-autocast requirement, but the supplied files do not establish whether get_latent applies autocast internally. Different encoder precision could change clean latents, eligibility, and the result.

outputs/manifest.json records Hugging Face artifact revisions and several software versions, but not the AURORA repository code revision. This leaves the code provenance incompletely recorded; it does not itself change the evaluated value, but can affect exact reproduction.

exp/run_experiment.py downloads the complete GPT-2 model.safetensors rather than an embedding-only artifact. The engineer reports that the repository loader requires this file, and the experiment contains no GPT-2 scoring call. This broader download is not evidence of a changed scoring model and has no demonstrated effect on the result.
problems: The whitespace preprocessing in exp/run_experiment.py plausibly changes the registered raw-text sample and target tokens; its description as minor does not establish numerical harmlessness.

Encoder autocast and the repository loader's checkpoint-content verification cannot be fully audited because the relevant repository implementations are not supplied. The visible script checks file existence, records checkpoint hashes, and demonstrates an EMA parameter change, but does not itself validate all checkpoint contents.
outputs/manifest.json omits the repository code revision, and three separately repeated complete evaluations are not evidenced.

The bootstrap in exp/run_experiment.py treats WikiText rows as independent documents. Rows can belong to the same article, so the reported interval may understate uncertainty for generalization across independent articles. This follows the registered row-based procedure rather than being an implementation substitution.

outputs/result.json shows substantial noise-level heterogeneity: the gap is approximately 1.24 percentage points at sigma=0.6 and 15.80 points at sigma=0.8. The pooled threshold result should not be described as exceeding five points at both noise levels.

The evidence concerns one checkpoint, selected WikiText rows, and teacher-forced clean history. It does not establish effects during free-running generation, benefits from decoder adaptation, or novelty relative to the cited papers.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation and visible code support a genuine model-output comparison: the statistic is computed from decoded token errors, all 192 rows qualify, and the recorded geometry checks pass comfortably. Nevertheless, stripping raw text before GPT-2 tokenization plausibly changes the registered inputs, making the implementation unfaithful under the stated criterion without making its empirical result invalid. The observed pooled gap is 8.52 percentage points, with a registered lower bound of 7.95 points, providing meaningful evidence that native residual orientation is more harmful than the specified geometry-matched randomization. I assign research value 2 because the controls are informative, but the finding remains checkpoint- and setting-specific, is concentrated at the higher noise level, and has uncertainty limitations from treating rows as independent documents.

departures: WikiText rows are strip()'d before the nonempty, heading, and length filters and before tokenization (exp/run_experiment.py). The registration does not mention strip(). That can change the first token and, rarely, which rows clear 127 tokens; with targets at positions 112:128 and GPT-2 BPE usually absorbing a leading space into the first token, it is unlikely to have changed the reported value.

Corruption noise ε is drawn once per (row, seed) and reused for both σ values (exp/run_experiment.py). The registration names seeds {11,22,33} and a hash of row ID and seed but does not require a redraw per σ, so this is an open choice; an independent-ε reading could change the value.

The registration lists repetitions: 3, but run_eval.sh is a single run and the three corruption seeds are averaged inside each document (exp/run_experiment.py), which matches the procedure text rather than three separate statistics. Logged seed-level rates are nearly identical, so this does not plausibly change the registered statistic or the event.
problems: The registered average pools very different noise levels (outputs/result.json per_sigma): the paired gap is about 1.2 percentage points at σ=0.6 and about 15.8 at σ=0.8, so the >5pp event is driven by σ=0.8.

Many selected rows are consecutive WikiText lines (outputs/manifest.json row_ids), so the document bootstrap may slightly understate within-article dependence; the gap is large and stable across corruption seeds, so this is unlikely to flip the event.

The comparison is only this checkpoint and teacher-forced clean-history residuals, as disclosed in outputs/result.json; standardized-coordinate MSE is slightly higher for controls, so the token gap is not an MSE artifact, but it is not a free-running generation result.
grok.reason: The evaluation reran the registered pipeline: released EMA checkpoints, the specified 192 WikiText sequences, two-pass teacher-forced denoising, float64 decoder-space Gram matching, float32 checks at about 1e-8, and the document bootstrap with seed 991. Outputs are internally consistent with real decodes, not hard-coded scores, and the registered fifth percentile is 0.0795 against a 0.05 threshold. Departures are either left open by the registration or too small to move that value. The finding is credible for this setting, but the headline average hides a much smaller gap at σ=0.6, and the result remains conditional on one teacher-forced checkpoint.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether actual teacher-forced AURORA denoiser residuals cause more token-recovery errors than randomized residuals that keep the same decoder-space magnitudes, clean-latent inner products, and within-block residual correlations.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper probes decoder robustness with isotropic Gaussian corruption of encoder latents and never compares denoiser residuals with geometry-matched random residuals, nor leaves that comparison as future work.

relation.reason: The experiment uses the paper's frozen autoencoder and denoiser to test whether residual direction is unusually harmful, a side property the paper does not claim, so the paper's reported results stand either way.

obvious.reason: After this paper most readers would first list scaling, sampling, or likelihood follow-ups; only one or two would specifically compare native residuals with joint rotations that preserve decoder-space Gram geometry rather than the broader isotropic-noise worry.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change how groups building this latent-diffusion decoder interface probe robustness and adapt decoders, but not practice across language modeling at large.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements that the paper measures latent capacity by Gaussian-corruption reconstruction and that the frozen decoder receives model predictions match the paper's text.

answerable.reason: The design decodes native residuals and geometry-matched controls under the same clean history and reports the paired token-error gap plus matching checks, so either a large gap or a near-zero gap would bear on the question.

prerequisite.reason: Geometry-matching discrepancies stayed near 1e-8, well under 1e-4, and clean target reconstruction was 100% with all 192 documents eligible, so the control and scoring filter both held.

evidence.reason: The native-minus-control gap is about 8.5 points and the 95% interval lies entirely between 7.8 and 9.2 points, so sampling noise cannot explain the higher native error the hypothesis predicts.

next_step.reason: The teacher-forced gap is already large and precisely estimated, so the same directional-harm question now justifies a broader study across trajectories and checkpoints rather than another tiny replication.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statement that the paper assesses latent capacity through Gaussian-corruption reconstruction, while the decoder at generation time receives model predictions, matches Sec. 4.1.1 and Sec. 3.5.

registration.title: Does an identical-text latent restart change the prior's continuation distribution?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM carries sampled continuous latents forward as history, whereas a text-only restart obtains history from its encoder. Perfectly preserved prefix tokens do not establish that these two histories induce the same next-block distribution.
registration.hypothesis: For round-trip-stable generated prefixes, replacing sampled history with the encoding of exactly the same tokens materially changes the first continuation-token distribution even when decoder history is held fixed.
registration.contribution: Continuous versus discretized latent inference has been compared previously. This experiment holds visible text exactly fixed, isolates the denoiser-history intervention using a common decoder context, and measures a distributional difference rather than paired sample disagreement.

closest_work.difference: Compares continuous and discretized sentence-level reasoning regimes using task accuracy. This experiment tests identical-text state replacement in a block-causal latent language model.
Studies generated versus ground-truth token prefixes. Here the complete visible prefix is unchanged and only its continuous representation changes.
Uses generated latent history and encoded textual prompts but does not provide this fixed-decoder, identical-prefix distributional restart test.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM
OWT denoiser: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, including 250000.safetensors and its configuration
Autoencoder: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, including 100000.safetensors and its configuration
GPT-2 tokenizer and, only if required, embedding weights: https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2
Prefixes generated within the experiment; no external dataset
registration.method:
Load the released OWT EMA denoiser, frozen autoencoder and checkpoint normalization using the native loader. Verify c=1 and block size 16. Record revisions. Keep compatible CUDA PyTorch; disable compilation, distributed execution, early stopping, classifier-free guidance and self-conditioning CFG, while retaining ordinary self-conditioning. In particular, disable sc_cfg_enabled rather than requesting a scale-one dual pass. Use dense attention preserving the original masks, BF16 inference, 16-step Euler sampling and the checkpoint's sampling shift. No external scorer is needed.

Generate 64 candidate latent prefixes of exactly 128 positions, without a supplied prompt, using eight blocks. Index prefix-generation noise by candidate ID and block with base seed 2026. Save standardized latent histories before decoding. Decode by argmax without EOS truncation, re-encode those exact token IDs without a string-tokenization round trip, and standardize again. Retain the first 32 candidates whose re-encoded histories decode to exactly the original 128 token IDs. Retain EOS IDs as ordinary prefix IDs and report their incidence. If fewer than 16 candidates qualify, report insufficient support; otherwise use all qualifying candidates up to 32 without changing the screening budget.

For each eligible prefix, generate one additional 16-position block using either RAW sampled history or REENCODED history. Use 64 independent initial Gaussian draws per prefix, paired across the two histories. Reset current-block self-conditioning identically at the start and then use previous-prediction self-conditioning. Both arms must rebuild their denoiser prefix cache from their supplied history; neither may reuse the cache from prefix generation. Immutable prefix caches may then be expanded across batched draws. Batch at least the draws within a prefix where memory permits; do not serially execute thousands of complete generation calls.

For the primary comparison, decode both arms' generated target latents using the same REENCODED decoder prefix. Thus only the denoiser's history is manipulated. Record the first new token, including EOS, before truncation. Also decode each target block with RAW decoder history, giving the complete two-by-two crossing of denoiser history and decoder history without additional denoising.

Split draws 0:32 and 32:64 into independent halves. In each half construct the empirical first-token frequency difference between the two denoiser-history arms under the common REENCODED decoder context. Their inner product estimates squared L2 distance between the two conditional token distributions without plug-in positive bias. Retain negative finite-sample estimates. As a replay control, repeat four draws for each of the first eight eligible RAW histories with identical noise and a freshly rebuilt cache; all decoded target IDs must agree. Eligibility depends only on the registered exact round-trip test, never on continuation outcomes.

outcome.executor_notes:
## What run.sh does
`setup_env.sh` installs the seed's runtime dependencies and keeps the preinstalled CUDA torch 2.6. It downloads three repos into the paths the checkpoint config expects, pinned to their current revisions, which are recorded in the manifest:
- fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt → `checkpoints/owt`
- fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder → `checkpoints/autoencoder`
- openai-community/gpt2 (config, tokenizer and safetensors files only) → `models/gpt2-small`

`exp.py` then runs the experiment, end to end in about 30 s of GPU time plus downloads.

## Implementation, as registered
- **Model loading:** I use the native loader (`load_config_from_checkpoint` + `DiffusionGenerator` → `EvalDiffusionTrainer.load_eval_checkpoint`), with EMA weights and the checkpoint's latent mean/std.
- **Checks verified:**
  - c=1: num_latents = max_seq = 1024 and decoder chunk size = 1.
  - Block size Q=16 and tanh shift 7.0.
  - Self-conditioning on; `sc_cfg_enabled=False`, so there is no dual pass.
  - No CFG and no early stop.
  - Flex attention and torch.compile are off (operator-optimization profile set to custom), and TORCHDYNAMO is disabled. Attention is dense SDPA with the native masks.
  - BF16 autocast, 16-step Euler sampling.
- **Prefixes:**
  - 64 candidates, 8 unprompted blocks each. Noise comes from CPU generators seeded `2026e6 + cand*1000 + block`.
  - The standardized RAW latents are saved before decoding. Decoding is argmax with no EOS truncation.
  - Re-encoding uses the exact token IDs, padded to 1024 as in the native token-id path, and is then standardized.
  - Eligibility is exact 128-token round-trip equality; I keep the first 32 eligible candidates.
- **Continuations:**
  - 64 draws per prefix. Noise seed is `2026e6 + 500000 + cand*1000 + draw`, and each draw uses the same noise in both arms.
  - Self-conditioning is reset at the start of the block and then uses the previous prediction.
  - For both arms the cache is rebuilt by a native block-causal prefill from the history supplied to that arm.
  - Draws are batched: 8 prefixes × 64 draws × 2 arms per call.
  - Every target block is decoded under both RAW and RE decoder histories, giving the full 2×2 crossing. I record the complete 16 target IDs and the first new token, EOS included.
  - I also checked that each decoded prefix part reproduces the eligible tokens.
- **Statistics:**
  - Per prefix, the split-half inner product of first-token frequency differences (draws 0:32 vs 32:64); negative values are kept.
  - Prefix bootstrap: 5000 resamples, seed 992.
  - Monte Carlo resampling of draws within each half, keeping each paired record together: 1000 resamples, seed 993 (I chose this seed; the registration does not specify one).
  - The diagnostics use the same estimator.

## Small changes (same question)
1. **Own sampler loop.** I wrote a short loop that mirrors `BlockSampler.run` (same prefill and generate mask builders, Euler `step`, self-conditioning `resolve`, write of each finished block at t=0). It does not call `run()`, because `run()` draws noise from the global RNG and the registration requires noise indexed by candidate and block.
2. **Prefill at full batch.** Caches are prefilled at the full batch size rather than computed once and expanded across draws. This is still a rebuild from the supplied history.
3. **Replay control.** I re-executed the identical batched call: same noise, cache rebuilt fresh, same batch composition. I compared draws 0–3 for the first 8 eligible RAW histories. This covers the registered 4×8 check. It deliberately does not test batch-composition invariance; a separate unregistered diagnostic covers that (below).
4. **Two unregistered diagnostics added.** A rerun with the two arms' batch slots swapped, and a paired first-token disagreement rate.

## Results from my test run (reproduced exactly on a clean rerun)
- **Eligibility:** 63/64 candidates round-trip exactly; the first 32 were used. All 64 candidates contain EOS (38 EOS tokens across the 32 eligible prefixes).
- **Controls:** replay passed with target-latent max difference 0.0. The slot-swap control gave identical IDs and latents.
- **Primary contrast** (denoiser history RAW vs RE, decoder history fixed to RE):
  - Mean split-half squared-L2 estimate: 0.0179.
  - Prefix-bootstrap 95% interval: [0.0081, 0.0299].
  - **Registered statistic (5th percentile): 0.0093, which is above 0.005, so the event occurs.**
  - Monte Carlo 95% interval conditional on these prefixes: [0.0128, 0.0244].
  - Per-prefix estimates vary a lot: 3 are slightly negative, 9 are exactly 0, and a few prefixes (0.13, 0.09, 0.08, 0.08) carry much of the mean.
  - Paired first-token disagreement rate: 31%.
- **Decoder history matters very little here.** With the denoiser history held fixed, switching decoder history changed about 0.1% of paired first tokens. The split-half estimate for that switch was exactly 0, so the native RAW/RAW vs RE/RE estimate equals the primary one.

## Scope
These results apply only to round-trip-stable prefixes from this one checkpoint and sampling setup, and only to this squared-L2 distance on the first token. They say nothing about which history yields better continuations, nor about equivalence under other distances.

registration.title: Should source guidance retain already-generated target history?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM combines block-autoregressive history with classifier-free source guidance. Removing the source alone and removing the entire latent history define different negative branches. A possible difference between training-time source dropout and released sampling behavior motivates an audit followed by a controlled intervention.
registration.hypothesis: Retaining generated target history in the source-dropped guidance branch improves XSum ROUGE-L relative to dropping all latent history.
registration.contribution: This tests the contents of the negative guidance branch rather than proposing CFG or history conditioning as new principles. It also records guidance-update magnitudes so an observed quality difference is not automatically attributed to training-distribution matching.

closest_work.difference: Studies guidance over temporal history in video diffusion. This experiment separates source-document conditioning from generated target history in text.
Evaluates guidance strength and first-block conditioning in latent language generation, rather than which history remains in later negative-branch calls.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM, especially src/aurora/train/diffusion_trainer.py and src/aurora/sampling/block_sampler.py
XSum denoiser: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum, including 300000.safetensors and its configuration
Autoencoder: https://huggingface.co/fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, including 100000.safetensors and its configuration

registration.method:
First inspect and record the released training and sampling paths. Verify whether source dropout retains target-history columns and whether native CFG supplies an empty clean_history to its negative branch. Proceed with the registered native comparison only if the latter behavior is confirmed; otherwise report a premise mismatch rather than silently redefining the baseline. The training audit is evidence about motivation, not an assumption about the outcome.

Load the XSum EMA denoiser and frozen autoencoder with checkpoint normalization. Record revisions, keep compatible CUDA PyTorch, use dense attention without compilation, and disable distributed execution and self-conditioning CFG while retaining ordinary self-conditioning. Use BF16 inference and no external model scorer.

Select the first 128 XSum test examples in dataset order whose complete source contains 64-512 GPT-2 tokens, whose source length is divisible by 16, and whose reference has at least 16 tokens. Pass article token IDs directly without added instructions, delimiters or truncation. If fewer than 128 qualify, report insufficient support. Block-aligned sources avoid mixed prompt/target boundary blocks.

Compare native all-history-dropped CFG with a target-history-retaining branch. In the modified negative branch, supply only the previously generated target latents, excluding source latents. Target-history positions must retain their original absolute RoPE positions beginning at the source length, and current-block positions must agree between branches. Build a separate negative-branch cache from those latents; do not reuse a source-conditioned cache. Keep the conditional-branch implementation unchanged. Keep independent conditional and negative self-conditioning tracks, never passing the conditional draft into the negative track. Generated target latents may themselves contain source information, so this branch is only operationally source-dropped.

Use block size 16, 16-step Euler sampling, the checkpoint sampling shift, CFG scale 2 and guidance only at sigma in [0.9,1]. Generate exactly four blocks in both arms, even if an earlier EOS appears; decode all 64 new positions and then truncate scoring text at the first EOS. Pre-generate Gaussian noise indexed by document ID, seed and block for seeds 41 and 42, shared across arms. Bucket examples by exact source length and batch both repetitions where possible.

Verify identical first-block token IDs in both arms for every example and seed. On the first eight examples additionally run both arms at CFG scale one; their complete generated token IDs must agree. At every guided evaluation record the conditional-minus-negative prediction RMS and the RMS of the guidance-induced Euler update relative to ordinary conditional prediction. Record model-call counts, runtime, EOS position and where token differences first appear after block one. Call counts are matched, but attention work is not FLOP-matched.

event.description: Retaining generated target history improves ROUGE-L by more than 0.5 points.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of the document-bootstrap distribution of mean ROUGE-L F1 improvement on the 0-100 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Compute ROUGE-L F1 using rouge_score.RougeScorer with use_stemmer=True against the unchanged reference. Average each document's paired improvement across the two noise seeds, then bootstrap documents 5000 times with seed 993. outputs/manifest.json contains selected IDs, token lengths, revisions and generation settings. outputs/code_audit.json documents the relevant branch behavior and positional/cache implementation. outputs/summaries.jsonl contains source, reference, full generated IDs, truncated text, arm, seed, ROUGE-L and lengths. outputs/guidance.jsonl contains prediction/update magnitudes by block and solver step. outputs/controls.json contains equality checks, call counts and timings. outputs/result.json contains the point estimate, intervals and registered lower bound, plus descriptive post-first-block changes and repetition measurements. Failed equality or position/cache checks invalidate the comparison. ROUGE changes alone do not identify factuality gains or the mechanism behind the effect.
evaluation.controls: Same complete sources, references, weights, normalization, solver, initial noise, guidance scale/window and decoding rules; aligned source boundaries; identical first-block and CFG-one controls; independent branch caches and self-conditioning; measured guidance magnitudes and compute rather than assumed strength or FLOP matching.

models: openai-community/gpt2 embedding table only if required

Add factual-consistency measures and norm-controlled interventions to distinguish training-distribution matching from useful history amplification or a change in effective guidance strength.

judge_sol.reason: Retaining target history could correct a conditioning mismatch, but it also changes effective guidance strength and affects only later summary blocks. Both the required code-audit premise and the confidence-bound improvement above 0.5 ROUGE-L points make the registered event uncertain.

judge_luna.reason: Retaining generated target history in the negative branch could make the guidance contrast better formed and improve later blocks, but it also changes the effective guidance direction, so a ROUGE-L gain is not assured. closest_work.difference: The seed paper describes prompt-conditioned CFG as one prediction with the prompt prefix and one without it (scale 2 on XSum), but the paper text never compares different contents for the negative branch. Whether the native branch drops all latent history is only checked in the released code, which the planned audit inspects and I did not.

This paper applies CFG to autoregressive token LMs. The negative branch is described as the continuation without the prompt, so it keeps the generated text and drops the prompt, much like the proposed arm. As far as its abstract shows, it does not compare this against dropping all history, and it does not use continuous-latent block diffusion or XSum.

Varies which history frames condition guidance in video diffusion, and reports that CFG-style history dropout performs poorly. It does not separate source-document conditioning from generated target history in text latent diffusion, and has no ROUGE evaluation.

A continuous latent block-causal diffusion LM (Cola DLM). Per the registered experiment's own description, it looks at guidance strength and first-block conditioning, not which history stays in the negative branch at later blocks.

Changes the source of the unconditional prediction (it substitutes a base model) in image and video diffusion. It does not test whether generated sequence history should be kept when the condition is dropped.

opus.reason: I found no paper that compares, in a block-causal latent diffusion language model, a negative guidance branch that keeps the generated target history and drops the source against one that drops all latent history, scored by XSum ROUGE-L. The closest ideas are AR-LM CFG, whose negative branch already keeps the continuation without the prompt (2306.17806), and history guidance in video diffusion (2502.06764). Neither tests this specific contrast in this setting, so the question remains open.
