registration.title: Inference-time block-size transfer: can the Q=16-trained block-causal denoiser be sampled with smaller blocks without retraining?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM reports (Fig. 7b) that models trained with smaller blocks generate better text (MAUVE 0.909 at Q=4 vs 0.815 at Q=16) but chose Q=16 for parallelism, training a separate model per block size. The released sampler supports an inference-time block-size override (KV-cache block-causal masks are built from the runtime block size), so the question is whether the quality gain from more sequential conditioning can be obtained at inference alone, despite the train/inference mismatch (noisy positions seeing clean positions inside their own training block; clean K/V computed with a 4-block-causal rather than 16-block-causal clean stream).
registration.hypothesis: Sampling the released Q=16 AURORA-LM-S model with inference block size 4 raises MAUVE by more than 0.03 over sampling it with block size 16 (32-step Euler ODE, no guidance), i.e., part of the trained-small-block gain transfers at inference.
registration.contribution: Tests a free knob the seed paper never explores (block-size mismatch between training and sampling in continuous block-causal latent diffusion) and quantifies the train/inference block-pattern mismatch cost; discrete block-diffusion work retrains per block size or post-trains for new block patterns.

closest_work.difference: BD3-LM studies block size for discrete masked block diffusion by training separate models per block size; it does not sample a model with a block size different from training, nor continuous latents.

Addresses train/inference mismatch of block patterns by post-training (multi-block teacher forcing) for discrete BD-LMs; this experiment is training-free and concerns smaller-than-trained blocks in a continuous latent model.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; run from repo root)
Checkpoints via `python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder`
GPT-2 Large: `huggingface-cli download gpt2-large --local-dir models/gpt2-large`
OpenWebText reference text: HF dataset stas/openwebtext-10k
registration.method: Build `DiffusionGenerator` from `checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors` (override operator_optimization.profile=off). For each inference block size Q_inf in {4, 8, 16, 32} call `generator.generate(num_samples=600, num_steps=32, batch_size=150, seed=42, solver='euler', self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0, block_size=Q_inf, max_gen_tokens=512, eos_mode='eos_wrap')` — the `block_size` kwarg reaches `trainer.pred_latents(block_size=...)` which sets the runtime block size used by `BlockSampler.run` (number of blocks = 512/Q_inf; KV cache written after each block). Verify in logs that `effective_block_size` equals Q_inf and that `num_generate_blocks*Q_inf == 512`. Record wall time and denoiser passes per sample. Score each config: MAUVE with the `mauve` package using GPT-2 Large features (models/gpt2-large, max_text_length=512) against 600 reference sequences built from stas/openwebtext-10k (EOS-separated docs chunked into 512-token pieces beginning with EOS, decoded with special tokens kept); compute features once per config and run `mauve.compute_mauve(p_features=..., q_features=..., seed=s)` for s in {1,2,3}, reporting the mean; also Gen-PPL (`aurora.eval.metrics_impl.compute_ppl`, models/gpt2-large), unigram entropy, and REP-4 (whitespace 4-gram self-repetition after stripping '<|endoftext|>'). Time guard: Q_inf=4 is the slowest (128 blocks); if the first Q_inf=4 batch projects more than 8 minutes for that config, reduce num_samples for all configs uniformly (minimum 300).

event.description: Inference block size 4 improves MAUVE over the trained block size 16 by more than 0.03.
event.statistic: MAUVE(Q_inf=4) − MAUVE(Q_inf=16), each averaged over 3 MAUVE k-means seeds on the same features

evaluation.procedure: outputs/scores.jsonl: one line per Q_inf with num_samples, mauve_mean, mauve_seeds (list), gen_ppl, entropy_mean, rep4_mean, passes_per_sample, gen_seconds, plus a final line with the registered difference MAUVE(4) − MAUVE(16) and the differences for Q_inf=8 and 32. outputs/samples_Q{Q}.jsonl: per-sample text and token ids.
evaluation.controls: Q_inf=16 is the trained setting (control); Q_inf=32 is a larger-than-trained block as a negative-direction control; Q_inf=8 is an intermediate point. Same seed, step count, length, references and scorer for all.

registration.full_scale_study: If the gain transfers, evaluate the released OWT and XSum models across inference block sizes at the paper's full protocol (1024 tokens, 1000 samples, 5 seeds; ROUGE on XSum), map the quality–latency frontier of inference-time block size, and test light post-training with randomized block sizes (block-size-agnostic two-stream masks) so one model covers the whole frontier; if the gain does not transfer, characterize which mismatch (noisy-to-clean within-block attention vs. clean-stream K/V computation) is responsible by ablating each separately.

agent.reason: Smaller inference blocks add sequential conditioning, but the clean-prefix K/V are then computed with 4-block rather than 16-block bidirectionality and noisy positions see clean same-block positions never seen in training; a +0.03 MAUVE gain against ~0.02 sampling noise seems less likely than a neutral or negative result.

judge_astra.reason: The paper's smaller-block advantage comes from separately trained models, not an inference-only intervention. More clean-prefix conditioning could help, but changes to attention and cached-prefix representations could offset enough of that benefit to miss the 0.03 MAUVE threshold.

judge_fable.reason: Sampling a Q=16-trained two-stream model with 4-position blocks creates mismatches on both the noisy side (clean positions inside what was a jointly noisy block) and the clean-KV side; discrete block-diffusion work needs post-training for such changes, so a net MAUVE gain above 0.03 (beyond roughly 0.02 MAUVE noise) seems unlikely, and the block_size kwarg path is itself an implementation risk.

judge_opus.reason: With relative RoPE, the clean-stream mismatch is essentially in-distribution, and the noisy-block mismatch (4 rather than 16 noisy keys) looks mild. Smaller blocks also give 4x the NFEs and more sequential conditioning, so a gain is likely. Clearing 0.03, however, depends on how much of the trained-model gain transfers, on a baseline MAUVE already near 0.89 against a ceiling around 0.97, and on noise of about 0.02 in the MAUVE difference.

judge_sol.reason: More sequential conditioning could help, but the paper’s smaller-block gains came from separately trained models. Changes to noisy/clean attention patterns and cached representations could offset that benefit, making a greater-than-0.03 MAUVE improvement somewhat unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: Separately trained Q=4 models outperform Q=16 models by 0.094 MAUVE, suggesting more frequent clean prefixes can help. However, a Q=16-trained denoiser sees larger noisy blocks and different prefix boundaries during training, so the inference-time change may not transfer cleanly.

judge_muse.reason: Trained Q=4 beats trained Q=16 by 0.094 MAUVE so smaller blocks help when trained, and runtime override makes inference transfer architecturally possible; uncertainty is whether unseen prefix lengths and noisy-to-clean mismatch erase the 0.03 gain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Adaptive Block Diffusion's Table 1 evaluates fixed-block discrete BD3-LM models (trained at block size 4 or 16) at other inference block sizes. For the block-16 model on LM1B, smaller inference blocks change likelihood perplexity only slightly (30.56 at 16, 30.25 at 8, 30.33 at 4), well short of the block-4-trained specialist (28.15 at its trained block size). However, that work covers masked discrete diffusion, measures likelihood rather than sample quality (MAUVE), and does not test a continuous flow-matching latent denoiser with two-stream clean/noisy attention.

BD3-LM trains a separate model for each block size and does not, in its own work, sample a model with a block size different from the one it was trained with. It also uses discrete tokens rather than continuous latents.

Multi-Block Diffusion uses post-training to fix the mismatch between training and inference block patterns in discrete BD-LMs, with the goal of decoding several blocks in parallel. It does not test training-free sampling with smaller-than-trained blocks in a continuous latent model.
The seed paper trains a separate model for each block size (Fig. 7b). In the parts of the paper I read, it does not sample the Q=16 model with any other inference block size.

AdaBlock-dLLM changes block size at inference time without retraining, but it uses semantic-aware adaptive scheduling for discrete masked dLLMs on reasoning benchmarks. It does not measure fixed smaller blocks on a continuous latent model, and it does not use MAUVE.

opus.reason: The closest evidence is Adaptive Block Diffusion. There, a discrete BD3-LM trained at block size 16 and run with smaller inference blocks shows only small perplexity changes, nowhere near what a model trained at the small block size achieves. That suggests, but does not settle, whether the gain transfers. No work I found samples a continuous-latent, flow-matching block-causal denoiser (such as AURORA-LM) with a smaller-than-trained block size and measures sample quality with MAUVE, so the specific question remains open.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Adaptive Block Diffusion, Section 5.1 and Table 1, evaluates fixed-block BD3LM checkpoints across inference block sizes without retraining, including a size-16-trained model evaluated at sizes 4, 8, 16 and 32. The proposed experiment substitutes AURORA-LM's continuous autoencoded latents and generation-quality metrics for discrete masked diffusion and evaluation perplexity.

DreamReasoner-8B, Section 4.1 and Table 2, crosses training block sizes 4 and 32 with inference sizes 4 and 32, directly testing smaller-than-trained sampling and its mismatch effects. It evaluates discrete diffusion on mathematical reasoning rather than continuous-latent free generation.

SSD-LM explicitly permits training/inference block-size mismatch and samples its size-25-trained Gaussian simplex-diffusion model with blocks of 12 and 20 tokens. However, it does not provide the proposed controlled, fixed-output-length quality comparison or use a block-causal latent KV-cache architecture.

sol.reason: AURORA-LM's Figure 7b trains separate models, but inference-only block-size transfer is already directly investigated in Adaptive Block Diffusion and DreamReasoner-8B. The registered experiment applies essentially the same fixed-checkpoint, changed-inference-granularity ablation to a continuous autoencoded representation and MAUVE, making it a close variant rather than an equivalent replication. Those precedents do not establish the outcome of the AURORA-LM experiment.

opus.reason: #58 overrides the inference block size too, but it asks whether larger-than-trained blocks preserve quality for parallelism; this experiment asks whether smaller-than-trained blocks raise MAUVE.

sol.reason: Entry 58 tests larger-than-trained inference blocks for parallelism, whereas this tests whether smaller-than-trained blocks inherit the quality advantage of smaller-block training.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered inference-only Q={4,8,16,32} comparison using released EMA weights, 32-step Euler, seed 42, batch 150, SC-CFG scale 1.0, 512 positions, eos_wrap and operator profile off. Hooks verify runtime blocks/length and count actual denoiser passes, including KV writes. MAUVE uses package GPT-2 Large features computed once per config and clustering seeds 1,2,3; seed-code Gen-PPL/entropy and whitespace REP-4 are retained. The registered time guard triggered (first Q4 batch 139.43s; projected 600 >8min), so all configs use 300 samples. Q4 retained its first two batches without restart. Observed MAUVE Q4=0.07423347, Q16=0.92473801; registered difference=-0.85050454, so event did not occur. IMPLEMENTATION.md details reference packing, adaptations and limits of interpretation.

The registered question accepts the released sampler as-is, but the mechanism remains unattributed.

opus.reason: The evaluation ran the registered inference-only comparison: Q_inf in {4, 8, 16, 32}, the released Q=16 weights, 32-step Euler, seed 42, SC-CFG 1.0, 512 tokens, eos_wrap, and MAUVE on GPT-2 Large features averaged over k-means seeds 1–3. Q=8 is about equal to Q=16, and Q=32 degrades (0.56), so the trained-small-block gain does not transfer at inference. Value is limited by the single generation seed, the reduced 300-sample protocol, and the absence of any check separating a genuine mismatch failure from a sampler defect at small block sizes.

The time guard explicitly reduces generator num_samples, not the reference count. experiment.py implements the time guard by interrupting the original 600-sample Q4 call before the third sampler batch and retaining its first 300 outputs; subsequent configurations request 300 directly. Restart behavior was not prescribed, and there is no quality-based selection or demonstrated additional effect on the statistic from retaining this prefix.

experiment.log reports FAISS's warning that clustering 600 pooled feature vectors into 30 centroids falls below its recommended training-point count. This limits confidence in fine-grained MAUVE comparisons, although it does not establish an erroneous score.

They cannot establish Q8/Q16 equivalence, population-level precision, or generalization across checkpoints and sampling protocols.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed successfully, produced every required raw output, and reported a computed Q4−Q16 MAUVE difference of −0.8505045446431247, so the registered event did not occur. The generated-sample reduction was authorized, but the additional reduction from 600 to 300 references can change the reported value and makes fidelity unfaithful. The displayed code derives scores from generated model outputs and loaded OpenWebText data, without hard-coded outcome values or evident leakage, supporting validity for the executed protocol. The large Q4 degradation, corroborated by low entropy, increased repetition, and the displayed repetitive/EOS-heavy output, is a meaningful bounded negative finding, but the limited sampling and clustering uncertainty prevent a stronger research-value judgment.

registration.title: Positional quality drift in 1024-token block-causal latent generation: does AURORA-LM-S degrade along the sequence?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM trains the denoiser with clean encoder latents as prefix context (parallel two-stream teacher forcing) but at inference conditions each block on its own generated latents, an exposure-bias-like mismatch. The paper reports only sequence-level Gen-PPL/MAUVE; its qualitative 1024-token samples (Appendix A.4) visibly deteriorate toward the end ('Yemen, Yemen', 'a day a day'). Whether quality systematically drifts with block index is untested.
registration.hypothesis: Under the paper's headline sampler family (32-step SDE-DPM++, SC-CFG w=4), the GPT-2-Large per-token NLL of AURORA-LM-S samples increases from early positions (tokens 64–319) to late positions (768–1023) relative to the corresponding change for real packed OpenWebText sequences, by at least 0.10 nats per token.
registration.contribution: First position-resolved quality analysis of a continuous-latent block-causal diffusion LM, with a real-text control that removes the scorer's context effect and an AR control generated under the same conditions; establishes whether error accumulation across generated latent blocks is a measurable failure mode.

closest_work.difference: Analyzes exposure-bias error accumulation for autoregressive token models via imitation-learning arguments; here the accumulating object is a generated continuous latent prefix in a block-causal diffusion model and the measurement is position-resolved scorer NLL against real-text and AR controls.
Tracks repetition along the denoising trajectory within a sequence for bidirectional continuous DLMs; it does not study degradation along the sequence position across generated blocks.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; run from repo root)
Checkpoints via `python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder`
GPT-2 Large scorer: `huggingface-cli download gpt2-large --local-dir models/gpt2-large`
AR control model: HF `gpt2` (124M; already downloaded to models/gpt2-small by the download script)
Real text: HF dataset stas/openwebtext-10k
registration.method: (1) AURORA samples: build `DiffusionGenerator` from `checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors` (override operator_optimization.profile=off) and call `generator.generate(num_samples=400, num_steps=32, batch_size=100, seed=42, solver='sde_dpmpp', self_cond_cfg_scale=4.0, eos_mode='eos_wrap')` with the default full length (1024 latents → 1024 tokens); keep the returned argmax token-id lists (1024 ids each; prepend EOS id 50256 if the first id is not EOS, as eos_wrap does for text). (2) Real control: GPT-2-tokenize stas/openwebtext-10k docs, build a stream EOS doc EOS doc ..., cut 400 non-overlapping 1024-id chunks each starting with EOS (wrap-packing format). (3) AR control: with HF `gpt2` (models/gpt2-small) sample 400 sequences of 1024 ids from the EOS prompt with `generate(do_sample=True, top_k=0, top_p=1.0, temperature=1.0, max_new_tokens=1023)`. (4) Scoring: feed each 1024-id sequence directly to GPT-2 Large (models/gpt2-large, bf16) with teacher forcing; record per-position NLL for positions 1..1023 (predicting token at position p from the prefix); do not drop any positions, but also store a per-position EOS indicator. For each source compute the mean NLL curve over sequences, early = mean over positions 64–319, late = mean over positions 768–1023, drift = late − early. Also compute, per source, REP-4 within windows (tokens 0–511 vs 512–1023, whitespace 4-grams of the decoded text) and the fraction of EOS tokens per 128-token bin. Time guard: if the first AURORA batch projects more than 10 minutes for 400 samples, reduce to 300 samples for all three sources.

event.description: AURORA-LM's late-minus-early NLL change exceeds that of real text by at least 0.10 nats/token (quality drifts downward along the sequence beyond the scorer's context effect).
event.statistic: D = (late − early)_AURORA − (late − early)_real, in nats per token

evaluation.procedure: outputs/scores.jsonl: one line per source (aurora, real, gpt2_ar) with num_sequences, nll_early, nll_late, drift, per-128-token-bin mean NLL (list of 8), per-bin EOS fraction (list of 8), rep4_first_half, rep4_second_half, overall gen_ppl; plus a final line with D (aurora vs real) and D_ar (gpt2_ar vs real). outputs/position_nll.npz: per-sequence per-position NLL arrays for all three sources. outputs/samples_aurora.jsonl and outputs/samples_gpt2.jsonl: token ids and decoded text.
evaluation.controls: Real packed OWT sequences control for the scorer's natural NLL decrease with context length and for EOS/document-boundary effects (same packing format); GPT-2 small ancestral samples are an AR control generated and scored identically, showing whether any drift is specific to block-causal latent generation.

registration.full_scale_study: If drift is present, run a teacher-forced vs. free-running comparison (generate block b from real encoder prefixes vs. from self-generated prefixes at matched positions, 1000 docs, 5 seeds), measure drift versus block size, guidance scale and sampler, and test mitigations such as noisy/self-generated prefix training (scheduled sampling in latent space), prefix re-encoding through the autoencoder before conditioning, and SC-CFG schedules that vary with block index; extend to the 1B model and 512-token contexts.

agent.reason: Generated-latent prefixes are off the training (encoder-clean) distribution so some incoherence drift is plausible, but guidance-induced repetition later in the sequence lowers GPT-2-Large NLL and works against the registered statistic, making a +0.10 nat excess over the real-text context gain uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: The clean-prefix training versus generated-prefix inference mismatch makes error accumulation plausible, but deteriorating coherence need not increase scorer NLL because repetition can lower it. Real-text adjustment also cannot fully remove differences in document boundaries and context predictability, leaving the registered positive drift uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: Error accumulation across 64 generated-latent blocks and a smaller scorer context benefit for less coherent text both push D upward, but w=4 guidance-induced copying lowers late NLL, EOS-density differences between generated and packed real text are unadjusted, and the paper's strong 1024-token MAUVE suggests no collapse, so exceeding 0.10 nats is less likely than not.

judge_opus.reason: The paper reports MAUVE of 0.89–0.95 at 1024 tokens under this sampler family, which rules out strong late-sequence degradation. Mode-seeking SC-CFG text tends to repeat earlier content, which would lower late-position NLL under GPT-2 Large. A +0.10 nat excess drift beyond real text would therefore require substantial exposure-bias error accumulation.

judge_sol.reason: Generated rather than encoder-produced latent prefixes create a plausible error-accumulation mechanism that aggregate evaluations do not test. Nevertheless, repetition and increasingly predictable continuations can lower GPT-2 NLL, so semantic deterioration need not produce the registered positive excess drift.

judge_luna.reason: Training uses clean latent prefixes while generation conditions on model-generated prefixes, a plausible source of error accumulation over 64 blocks; the qualitative samples also contain some late repetition and incompleteness. Still, the paper reports no position-resolved trend, so it is uncertain whether the scorer-adjusted drift exceeds 0.1 nats.

judge_muse.reason: Training uses clean encoder prefixes while inference conditions on 64 generated blocks, and Appendix A.4 long samples show late degeneration, predicting positive drift; uncertainty is whether packed-document scorer effects and late repetition that lowers NLL mask the 0.10 nat gap versus real text.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Measures whether exposure-bias distortion builds up over generation in autoregressive token LMs (it finds the distortion is limited and does not grow) by comparing ground-truth prefixes with self-generated ones. It does not cover block-causal continuous-latent diffusion, and it does not plot scorer NLL by position against a real-text control.

Makes an imitation-learning argument about exposure-bias error accumulation in autoregressive token models. The experiment instead measures drift across generated continuous latent blocks in AURORA-LM.

Self Forcing targets the train-test gap between ground-truth and self-generated context in autoregressive video diffusion and proposes a training fix. It covers video, not text, and does not measure drift by position in a latent text diffusion model.

Studies a different train-inference mismatch in discrete block diffusion LMs: decoding with prefix/block configurations not seen in training. It does not look at quality drift along the sequence caused by conditioning on self-generated prefixes.
The seed paper reports only sequence-level Gen-PPL/MAUVE plus qualitative samples. It contains no NLL analysis broken down by position or block.

opus.reason: My searches found no paper that measures scorer NLL by position along 1024-token samples from a block-causal continuous-latent diffusion LM, using a packed real-text control and a matched autoregressive control. The closest work studies exposure bias in autoregressive token models, where He et al. found little growing distortion; studies autoregressive video diffusion; or studies other kinds of train-inference mismatch in block diffusion. None of these settles whether quality drifts across generated latent blocks in AURORA-LM-style models. This verdict rests only on search results, not a full reading of any paper. Also, the description of the seed paper comes from the experiment write-up; I did not open the seed paper to confirm it contains no position-level analysis.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Measures length-dependent exposure-bias error accumulation in autoregressive GPT-2 using oracle-relative regret, rather than position-resolved external-scorer NLL drift in block-causal latent generation with packed-real-text and AR controls.

Studies irreversible errors and global coherence in discrete block diffusion through draft-and-refine interventions and sequence-level generative perplexity; it does not measure early-to-late degradation relative to real text.
Diagnoses repetition developing across self-conditioning denoising steps in continuous diffusion models, not quality drift across successive generated latent blocks along sequence position.
The seed reports aggregate generation metrics, block-size and sampler ablations, and qualitative long samples, but no controlled position-resolved quality-drift experiment.

sol.reason: The underlying concern about exposure bias and accumulating generation errors is established, but the papers found do not answer whether block-causal continuous-latent generation systematically deteriorates along sequence position. As of 2026-10-07, I found no paper reporting the proposed early-versus-late scorer-NLL comparison against packed real text, with an AR control, or an analysis that otherwise settles that specific question.

opus.reason: The exposure-bias entries (#20, #44) train miniature models and compare teacher-forced with free-running generation, whereas this experiment measures position-resolved NLL drift of the released checkpoint against real-text and AR controls.

sol.reason: Entries 20 and 44 compare clean-prefix and generated-prefix conditioning, whereas this measures positional NLL drift in free-running samples relative to real-text and AR controls.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented and end-to-end tested the registered AURORA sampling, real OWT wrap control, fixed-length GPT-2 ancestral control, GPT-2 Large bf16 per-position NLL, EOS bins, REP-4, raw outputs, and unchanged D statistic. Test used 400 sequences/source; time guard did not trigger. Observed D=-0.21926566483500975 (event did not occur). Minimal clarifications: prepend EOS to AURORA IDs when absent then retain 1024 IDs, saving raw IDs; real control uses repository-documented 1022-payload + leading/trailing EOS wrap packing because arbitrary stream cuts cannot all start EOS; disable AR EOS stopping to obtain registered fixed lengths. Added a narrow adapter for the published dataset script's obsolete extraction num_proc argument and quoted OmegaConf 'off'. No seed-code changes or outcome-dependent tuning. Details and limitations in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

departures: Real control packing (experiment.py real_control, outputs/real_packing.json). The registration asks for 400 non-overlapping 1024-ID stream cuts, each starting with EOS. The code builds EOS + 1022 consecutive stream IDs + EOS, citing the repository's wrap packing. This was disclosed. It inserts an artificial EOS before every chunk, so chunks start mid-document as in AURORA's training format. It also forces an EOS at position 1023, which falls in the late window. That EOS likely raises real late NLL by a few hundredths of a nat (the last-bin real NLL rises from 2.558 to 2.629), pushing D slightly more negative. It cannot plausibly move D from -0.22 to above +0.10.

AURORA token handling (experiment.py generate_aurora). When the raw argmax IDs lack a leading EOS, EOS is prepended and the sequence is truncated to 1024, dropping the last raw token. This was disclosed and the raw IDs are saved. The effect is a negligible one-token shift.

AR control (experiment.py ar_control). EOS stopping is disabled (eos_token_id=None) so every sequence has 1024 IDs; generation runs in FP32. This was disclosed. It affects only D_ar, not the registered statistic D.

Model download (experiment.py download). The code uses huggingface_hub snapshot_download of the same HF repos with allow patterns, not scripts/download_models.py. These are the same registered checkpoints, so no expected effect.

Compatibility shims: the OmegaConf string 'off' is quoted, local paths are overridden, and the stas/openwebtext-10k loader has its obsolete num_proc extract argument dropped. All are disclosed and have no expected effect on data or sampling.

Instrumentation (experiment.py generate_aurora). Monkeypatched hooks on _pred_latents_with_params and _decode_tokens_with_ar_stop implement the registered time guard. Captured tokens are asserted equal to the generator's returned tokens, and the guard did not trigger (outputs/time_guard.json). No effect.
problems: No uncertainty quantification (bootstrap CI over sequences) for D, although the registration did not require one. With 400 sequences per source and D 0.32 nats below the threshold, the null is very likely robust.

The real-control wrap packing places a forced EOS at position 1023 of every real chunk (outputs/scores.jsonl, last-bin EOS fraction ≈1/128). This slightly inflates the real late-window NLL and biases D downward, though not enough to matter here.

Scorer NLL is not a monotone quality measure. AURORA's REP-4 rises from 0.030 (first half) to 0.040 (second half) while real text stays flat (0.0130→0.0131). Increased repetition lowers NLL, so the larger NLL decrease for AURORA could partly reflect late repetition rather than better late quality. The null on NLL drift therefore does not rule out the qualitative deterioration seen in Appendix A.4.

There is a single sampling seed and a single checkpoint/sampler configuration, as registered. The large first-bin AURORA NLL (4.26) suggests early-block effects that lie outside the registered early window.

The AURORA sample decode includes a trailing EOS, and the last-bin EOS fraction is ≈1/128. How eos_wrap truncation interacts with raw IDs cannot be fully verified from the truncated file listings, but the effect is at most one token.
opus.reason: The code runs the registered sampler (32-step sde_dpmpp, SC-CFG 4, eos_wrap, 400 samples, seed 42), real and GPT-2 AR controls, GPT-2 Large bf16 per-position scoring, and the registered windows and statistic. The window indexing checks out (array column 0 is position 1), and the protected run reproduces the engineer's numbers exactly. The departures (wrap-style real packing with a trailing EOS, EOS prepend/truncation, AR EOS stopping disabled) are disclosed and either do not touch D or shift it by only a few hundredths, far from the 0.32-nat gap to the threshold. The result is a clear null: AURORA's NLL falls by 0.35 nats from early to late, more than real text's 0.13 fall, so D = -0.22. Meanwhile the GPT-2 ancestral control shows a large positive drift (D_ar = +0.72), demonstrating the metric can detect accumulation-type degradation. The finding is credible and meaningful but limited: there is no CI, one seed and one configuration, and the modest late rise in AURORA REP-4 shows that NLL drift may miss repetition-type degradation.

departures: experiment.py, real_control(): Instead of cutting the registered EOS-separated stream into 1024-ID chunks, the implementation cuts 1022-ID payloads and adds leading and trailing EOS tokens to every chunk. This changes payload boundaries and inserts a scored terminal EOS into every late window, so it can change real-text drift and D. The registration's requirement that every consecutive chunk start with EOS is inconsistent, but adding a terminal EOS is not necessary merely to repair that inconsistency.

experiment.py, generate_aurora(): After the registered conditional EOS prepend, the implementation truncates the resulting IDs to 1024. For affected samples this discards the final raw token. It can change positional scores compared with retaining all 1025 IDs, but resolves the registered fixed-length requirement and the scorer's 1024-position limit; raw IDs are retained for auditing.

experiment.py, ar_control(): EOS stopping is explicitly disabled, unlike the literal registered HF generate call, whose model configuration enables EOS stopping. This can change AR lengths and scores relative to that literal call, but is necessary to obtain the registered 1024-ID ancestral sequences without padding or exclusions. It does not directly change D, which uses only AURORA and real text.

experiment.py, download(): snapshot_download replaces the registered repository download script and huggingface-cli commands, with file-pattern filtering. The named repositories, checkpoint steps, scorer and AR model are retained. No value-changing model substitution is evident.

evaluate.sh and experiment.py: Execution occurs in /workspace rather than the seed repository root, with explicit project, checkpoint and model-path settings. These are operational path repairs; no plausible change to the sampled distribution or statistic is evident.

evaluate.sh: Dependencies are installed explicitly, including pinned transformers and datasets versions, followed by an editable seed[eval] installation with --no-deps rather than ordinary dependency resolution. Package versions were not registered, so this is an environment choice rather than an identified scientific-method change; no conclusion-changing effect is shown.

experiment.py, real_control(): A temporary DownloadManager.extract adapter drops the obsolete num_proc argument, and dataset loading enables trust_remote_code. These compatibility changes allow the specified dataset script to run. No change to document contents or selection is evident.

experiment.py, generate_aurora(): The operator profile override quotes the string 'off' to avoid OmegaConf interpreting it as a boolean. This preserves the intended registered setting rather than changing it.

experiment.py, generate_aurora(): Private prediction/decode methods are wrapped to implement timing and the registered reduction guard. The guard did not trigger: 400 sequences per source were used. The wrappers forward the original calls, and the code checks captured tokens against returned tokens, so no value-changing sampling alteration is evident.
problems: experiment.py, real_control(): The particular packing repair changes the registered real-text control and therefore the primary statistic. Its effect was not quantified with an alternative packing sensitivity analysis.

outputs/scores.jsonl: No confidence interval or other sampling-uncertainty estimate is reported for D or the repetition changes. The experiment supplies one generation seed, and the real sequences are adjacent payloads from 373 documents rather than 400 independent documents.

outputs/scores.jsonl: AURORA REP-4 rises from 0.030316 to 0.040202 despite decreasing scorer NLL. Thus lower late-position NLL cannot by itself be interpreted as improved overall text quality; repetition can make continuations more predictable.

Registration and experiment.py: The AR control provides a useful comparison but does not isolate latent-prefix exposure bias. Different models and generation procedures remain confounded, and no teacher-forced versus free-running latent-prefix intervention was performed.

evaluate.sh: validate_outputs.py is supplied but is not invoked by the protected evaluation command. Its reported earlier execution should not be treated as an independently observed validation of the fresh-run NPZ.
sol.reason: The protected run completed successfully, produced every registered raw output, and reported D = -0.21926566483500975, below the registered 0.10 threshold. The visible code computes the correct position slices and difference of drifts from actual model inference and dataset text, with no hard-coded result or apparent conclusion-changing scoring error. Fidelity is nevertheless unfaithful because the chosen real-text packing adds scored terminal EOS tokens and changes payload boundaries beyond what is required to resolve the contradictory starting-EOS requirement. This is a meaningful negative result for the implemented benchmark, but it does not establish absence of quality degradation or exposure bias, and its single-seed, uncertainty-free analysis does not merit the strongest research-value rating.

departures: Real-control packing (experiment.py real_control; outputs/real_packing.json): registration asked for a stream EOS+doc+EOS and non-overlapping 1024-id cuts each starting at a stream EOS. Implementation wraps non-overlapping 1022-id stream payloads (doc tokens plus inter-doc EOS, no leading stream EOS) as EOS+payload+EOS, so chunks are not EOS-aligned and position 1023 is a forced EOS. Needed because the literal non-overlapping EOS-aligned cut is impossible; matches the named wrap-packing format. Could shift real drift and thus D by a small amount, not enough to move D=-0.219 across +0.10.

AURORA scoring IDs (experiment.py generate_aurora): if raw argmax IDs do not start with 50256, code prepends EOS and keeps only the first 1024, dropping the last raw token and shifting every position by one. registration.title: Early-exit block denoising: committing the x0 prediction at σ=0.9 instead of finishing the trajectory
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM argues that a high-capacity latent lets the frozen decoder tolerate strong corruption (Fig. 5a: near-perfect token recovery up to σ≈0.6), that supervision should concentrate on high-noise states (tan-d, d=7, ~80% of training mass at σ>0.7), and that self-trajectory consistency keeps x0 estimates stable along the trajectory. Together these suggest the low-noise tail of each block's denoising may be redundant: the x0 estimate at a high σ could be committed directly as the clean block and the frozen decoder would absorb the residual error. Under the d=7 inference grid, steps with σ ≥ 0.9 are only ~42% of the 32 steps, so an exit at σ=0.9 would save ~58% of denoiser evaluations.
registration.hypothesis: Exiting each block's denoising when σ first drops below 0.9 and committing the current x0 prediction as the clean block (32-step Euler, no guidance) keeps MAUVE within 0.05 of the full 32-step trajectory, despite the committed estimate becoming the prefix for all later blocks.
registration.contribution: Early-stop decoding exists for bidirectional continuous DLMs (ELF-style), but not for block-causal latent generation where early-exit errors propagate through the clean prefix, and not for a system with a separately trained, perturbation-robust decoder; this tests whether the paper's decoder-robustness story translates into free NFE savings.

closest_work.difference: Uses early-stop (decode an intermediate clean prediction) for ELF-REG on reasoning tasks with a shared denoiser/decoder and full-sequence bidirectional denoising; it does not involve block-causal commitment of early estimates into a prefix, a frozen autoencoder decoder, or unconditional MAUVE/entropy evaluation.

PiD trains a sigma-aware pixel decoder so image latent diffusion can terminate early; here the frozen text decoder is unchanged and the question is whether its existing corruption tolerance suffices in blockwise text generation.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; run from repo root)
Checkpoints via `python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder`
GPT-2 Large: `huggingface-cli download gpt2-large --local-dir models/gpt2-large`
OpenWebText reference text: HF dataset stas/openwebtext-10k
registration.method: Copy `BlockSampler.run` (src/aurora/sampling/block_sampler.py) into a patched version with a parameter sigma_stop: inside the per-block step loop, after computing `pred` (the x0 estimate) at step i with sigmas[i], if sigmas[i+1] < sigma_stop then set x_block = pred.float() and break out of the step loop (the remaining steps are skipped); the block is then written to the KV cache and finalized exactly as in the original code. Count executed denoiser passes per block. Monkeypatch it onto the trainer's `_kv_cache_sampler`. Build `DiffusionGenerator` from `checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors` (override operator_optimization.profile=off). Configs: sigma_stop in {0.0 (full trajectory), 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95}, each with `generator.generate(num_samples=800, num_steps=32, batch_size=200, seed=42, solver='euler', self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0, max_gen_tokens=512, eos_mode='eos_wrap')`. Scoring per config: MAUVE via the `mauve` package with GPT-2 Large features (models/gpt2-large, max_text_length=512) against 800 reference sequences from stas/openwebtext-10k (EOS-separated docs chunked to 512 tokens beginning with EOS, decoded with special tokens kept), computing features once and averaging `compute_mauve(p_features, q_features, seed=s)` over s in {1,2,3}; Gen-PPL (`aurora.eval.metrics_impl.compute_ppl`, models/gpt2-large); unigram entropy; REP-4 (whitespace 4-gram self-repetition after stripping '<|endoftext|>'); mean executed passes per block. Time guard: if the full-trajectory config projects more than 5 minutes for 800 samples, reduce num_samples uniformly (minimum 400).

event.description: Early exit at σ=0.9 (about 42% of the denoiser evaluations) loses no more than 0.05 MAUVE relative to the full trajectory.
event.statistic: MAUVE(sigma_stop=0.9) − MAUVE(sigma_stop=0.0), each averaged over 3 MAUVE k-means seeds on the same features

evaluation.procedure: outputs/scores.jsonl: one line per sigma_stop with num_samples, mauve_mean, mauve_seeds (list), gen_ppl, entropy_mean, rep4_mean, passes_per_block, nfe_fraction (passes relative to full), gen_seconds, plus a final line with the registered difference MAUVE(0.9) − MAUVE(0.0) and the same differences for 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95. outputs/samples_stop{sigma}.jsonl: per-sample text and token ids.
evaluation.controls: sigma_stop=0.0 is the unmodified full trajectory (control); 0.5 and 0.8 check that mild early exit is harmless (sanity), 0.95 probes the breaking point. Entropy and REP-4 are reported because committing a conditional-mean estimate could lower Gen-PPL via blander, lower-entropy text, which MAUVE penalizes.

registration.full_scale_study: If early exit at high σ is nearly lossless, run the full paper protocol (1024 tokens, 1000 samples, 5 seeds, SDE sampler with SC-CFG) across exit points to build an NFE–quality frontier, combine early exit with few-step schedules and self-trajectory consistency budgets, evaluate on XSum ROUGE and the 1B benchmark suite, and train a σ-aware decoder variant to push the exit point further; if it fails, trace the failure to decoder tolerance of x0-mean estimates versus prefix error propagation using teacher-forced prefixes.

agent.reason: The decoder RMS-normalizes latents and self-conditioning makes x0 estimates partly 'decided' early (as in ELF early-stop), but committing a conditional-mean estimate at 10% signal and feeding it forward as clean prefix for 31 more blocks likely costs more than 0.05 MAUVE given the paper's own 8-step results.

judge_astra.reason: Robust decoding of corrupted true latents does not establish robust decoding of high-noise conditional-mean predictions. At sigma approximately 0.9, predictions can still mix token alternatives, and committing those estimates as subsequent prefixes is likely to cost more than 0.05 MAUVE despite consistency regularization.

judge_fable.reason: The paper's extreme high-noise training emphasis and self-trajectory consistency make a high-sigma commit less absurd than it sounds, but at sigma=0.9 the x0 estimate is still a posterior mixture over plausible continuations; decoding mixtures and feeding them back as the clean prefix likely yields within-block inconsistencies that MAUVE punishes well beyond 0.05 (compare the Q=64 and 8-step results).

judge_opus.reason: Committing the x0 estimate at sigma ≈ 0.9 means decoding from a state with per-dimension SNR of about 0.012, where direct decoding recovers only a minority of tokens. The paper's own 8-step runs, which commit at sigma ≈ 0.5, already lose about 0.14 MAUVE even with consistency training. Prefix error propagation makes the loss worse, so a drop of 0.05 or less is very unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: An x0 prediction at sigma=0.9 can remain an ambiguous conditional mean, unlike a true encoded latent perturbed by Gaussian noise. Skipping subsequent refinement and committing that estimate as later blocks’ context makes a MAUVE loss below 0.05 unlikely despite decoder corruption robustness.

judge_luna.reason: The paper's decoder-corruption analysis shows a sharp loss of token recovery in the high-corruption tail, so an x0 estimate committed near σ=0.9 may be poor and can contaminate later block prefixes. The reported gap between 8- and 32-step full trajectories also suggests that skipping refinement could cost more than 0.05 MAUVE.

judge_muse.reason: Fig. 5a shows decoder tolerance only to sigma~0.6 with sharp drops by ~0.8, while x0 at sigma=0.9 sees ~1% signal variance and errors propagate via generated prefixes; uncertainty is how much better the learned x0 prediction is than the noisy latent.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: ELF-REG uses early-stop, decoding an intermediate clean prediction, as a way to save NFEs. Its model denoises the full sequence bidirectionally, uses a shared-weight denoiser/decoder and is evaluated on reasoning and code pass@k. Committed early estimates never become the prefix for later blocks, and there is no frozen autoencoder decoder and no unconditional MAUVE evaluation.

This paper audits ELF checkpoints and proposes a margin-based rule that exits denoising about 17–28% earlier under a diagnostic monitor. It runs only 'boundary checks' on Cola-DLM, which is block-causal with a VAE decoder, and does not test a fixed-σ commit inside a block-causal sampler with a separately trained frozen query decoder. It also does not measure how early-exit error spreads through the clean prefix to affect MAUVE.

PiD trains a σ-aware pixel decoder so that image latent diffusion can stop early. The proposed experiment covers text, keeps the decoder unchanged and frozen, and asks whether the decoder's existing corruption tolerance is enough.

The seed paper studies decoder robustness to corruption, noise-level calibration and self-trajectory consistency. From the sections I read, it runs every block's trajectory down to t=0 and does not report truncating per-block denoising or committing intermediate x0 estimates. I read only part of the paper, so an appendix ablation cannot be fully ruled out.

opus.reason: Early-stop decoding is established for bidirectional continuous diffusion language models (ELF-REG, and the margin-exit diagnostics on ELF). However, I found no work that tests committing a high-σ x0 estimate as a clean block in a block-causal latent diffusion language model, where errors carry into the prefix for all later blocks and decoding goes through a separately trained frozen decoder. Prior results come from a different architecture and evaluation, so they do not settle whether AURORA-LM can exit at σ=0.9 with only a small MAUVE loss. That makes the question distinct, though the general idea is clearly related to existing early-stop methods.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: ELF-REG decodes an intermediate clean prediction after truncating continuous denoising, including at noise-dominated exit times. It uses full-response bidirectional denoising with a shared denoiser/decoder, rather than repeatedly committing early latent estimates as prefixes for subsequent blocks.

Continuous Language Diffusion as a Decoder-Interface Problem studies decoder robustness and fixed or margin-guided early exits in ELF. Its Cola-DLM boundary diagnostics do not evaluate free generation with early-exited latent blocks recursively conditioning later blocks.

Truncated Jump Sampling already stops an ODE trajectory and returns its clean-endpoint prediction without retraining. Its experiments concern image generation, not block-causal text generation with accumulated continuous-prefix errors.

C4 accelerates blockwise language generation through early token commitments and block exits, but operates on masked discrete models using confidence and stability gates. It does not commit high-noise continuous endpoint estimates through a separately trained frozen decoder.

PiD enables early termination of image latent diffusion by training a sigma-aware generative decoder to consume partially denoised latents. The proposed experiment instead leaves the text decoder unchanged and commits predicted-clean blocks into future conditioning.

sol.reason: Returning an intermediate clean prediction instead of completing denoising was already established, so the generic early-exit mechanism is not novel. However, none of the work found answers whether high-noise endpoint estimates can repeatedly become the continuous prefix in block-causal text generation while an unchanged, separately trained decoder preserves distributional quality. AURORA-LM itself studies corruption tolerance and reduced-step full trajectories, not this truncation-and-prefix-commitment experiment.

opus.reason: No list entry commits the x0 prediction at a high-sigma early exit; #54 only lowers the overall step budget.

sol.reason: Entry 54 reduces the step count across a complete denoising trajectory, whereas this truncates the trajectory at high noise and commits the intermediate clean prediction as the next prefix block.

registration.title: Inference-time block-size transfer: sampling the Q=16-trained AURORA-LM-S denoiser with block sizes 4, 8 and 32 without retraining
registration.seed_connection: Sec. 4.1.3 / Fig. 7b / Table 16b of the seed show MAUVE rising monotonically as the trained block size shrinks (0.909 at Q=4, 0.857 at Q=8, 0.815 at Q=16, 0.631 at Q=64), attributed to each block seeing a more complete generated prefix. Every point is a separately trained model whose two-stream clean-prefix mask was fixed at that Q, so the paper cannot say whether the gain is a sampling-time conditioning-granularity effect or training-time specialization. The released sampler is reported to accept a runtime block size, so the released Q=16 OpenWebText checkpoint can be sampled under other block sizes at zero training cost.
registration.hypothesis: Sampling the released Q=16 AURORA-LM-S denoiser with inference block size 8 (32 Euler steps per block, i.e. the same denoising compute per latent position) lowers GPT-2-Large generative perplexity of 512-token OpenWebText samples by at least 5% relative to block size 16, without lowering unigram entropy.
registration.contribution: First test of train/inference block-size transfer for a continuous block-causal latent diffusion LM. If transfer works, block size becomes a free inference-time quality/latency knob (BD3-LM and the seed's Fig. 7b retrain per Q); if it fails, the Fig. 7b trend is a training-time effect and two-stream clean-prefix training specializes the denoiser to its block boundaries.

closest_work.difference: The seed trains a separate model per Q (Fig. 7b, OWT128) and never samples a model under a block size other than its training value; here one released Q=16 model is sampled under Q in {4, 8, 16, 32}.
BD3-LM fine-tunes a distinct discrete block-diffusion model per block size and never evaluates block-size transfer at inference.
Set Diffusion obtains flexible decoding granularity by training a new set-causal model; here flexibility is tested post hoc on a fixed block-trained continuous model.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: git clone https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; pip install -e '.[eval]' (PyTorch>=2.5 CUDA; if an optional dependency fails, install the core package and pip install mauve-text faiss-cpu transformers datasets evaluate separately)

Released checkpoints: python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder -> checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors (+config.yaml), checkpoints/autoencoder/100000.safetensors (+config.yaml), models/gpt2-small (HF repos fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, gpt2 if the script is missing)
GPT-2 Large scorer/featurizer: huggingface-cli download gpt2-large --local-dir models/gpt2-large

OpenWebText documents for MAUVE references: HF dataset stas/openwebtext-10k (trust_remote_code=True); fallbacks Elriggs/openwebtext-100k, streaming Skylion007/openwebtext, then wikitext-103-raw-v1 test (record any substitution)
registration.method:
Setup: clone, install, download as listed. Load the generator as the repo README does: from aurora.eval.core.config import load_config_from_checkpoint; from aurora.eval.generators.diffusion import DiffusionGenerator; cfg,_ = load_config_from_checkpoint(ckpt, overrides=['operator_optimization.profile=off'], project_root=REPO); gen = DiffusionGenerator(cfg, ckpt, device='cuda:0'); gen._eval_protocol = lambda: {} (this stops the released OWT protocol, 64-step SDE-DPM++ with SC-CFG 4, from being applied; the attribute names are reported by earlier readers of the code; if they differ, grep aurora/eval for the protocol loader and the SC-CFG flag and disable both). Register a forward hook on the denoiser nn.Module (gen.trainer.denoiser or whichever module holds the Transformer blocks) that counts calls: a pilot with num_samples=1, max_gen_tokens=16, num_steps=32 must make 32 or 33 denoiser calls (one per step plus at most one cache-write call); about 64 means a guidance dual pass is still active (set self_cond_cfg_scale=None or 1.0 and the trainer's sc_cfg flag off) and must be fixed before proceeding.

Sampling call for every run: texts, ids, stats = gen.generate(num_samples=240, num_steps=S, batch_size=120, seed=s, solver='euler', self_cond_cfg_scale=None, eos_mode='eos_wrap', max_gen_tokens=512, block_size=Q, verbose=False) — 512 tokens, self-conditioning on, no guidance; batch 60 on OOM. The block_size argument is reported to reach trainer.pred_latents(..., block_size=...) through a use_runtime_block_size path and to be echoed in stats (effective_block_size, block_size_overridden); if generate lacks it, pass it to pred_latents or set the attribute the KV-cache sampler reads (grep 'block_size' in aurora/sampling and the trainer module). Verify that transfer is real: (i) block_size=16 passed explicitly reproduces the default call's texts exactly at seed 1; (ii) the hook count for a run equals (512/Q) x S plus at most 512/Q cache writes; (iii) print three samples for Q=8 and Q=32. If a Q raises an error that two fix attempts cannot resolve, write the error to scores.jsonl and skip it (the statistic needs only Q in {8, 16}).

Arms (Q, S, seeds): (16, 32, {1,2,3}) control; (8, 32, {1,2,3}) headline — same compute per position, twice the sequential stages; (32, 32, {1,2}) opposite direction; (4, 32, {1}); (8, 16, {1}) latency-matched arm with the same number of sequential denoiser calls as the control (64 blocks x 16 steps = 32 x 32). Record wall time, number of blocks and denoiser calls per run. Sanity anchor: the control should give Gen-PPL roughly 35-80 (the seed's Table 7 reports 50.5 at 1024 tokens for 32-step Euler without guidance); below 30 means guidance is still active, above 120 means the sampler is broken — debug before continuing. Time guard: time the seed-1 control run; if it exceeds 1.5 min, drop (4,32) and run (32,32) with seed 1 only; if it exceeds 2.5 min, additionally use seeds {1,2} and 160 samples for all remaining runs.

Post-processing (mirrors the repo's run_metrics): tokenize each text with the GPT-2 tokenizer (add_special_tokens=False), truncate to 512 tokens, drop texts with fewer than 16 tokens, decode with skip_special_tokens=True. Reference set, built once: load the OWT documents, shuffle with seed 0, concatenate consecutive documents separated by a blank line until at least 512 GPT-2 tokens, truncate to 512 tokens, decode; 240 references.

Metrics per run: Gen-PPL under GPT-2 Large (bf16): prepend the GPT-2 EOS token as BOS, score all text tokens in one forward pass, keep the per-token NLL array per text; Gen-PPL = exp(sum of NLL / number of scored tokens) over the run (the repo's compute_ppl definition; use the repo function only if it exposes per-text sums). Unigram entropy: Shannon entropy in nats of each text's GPT-2 token counts, averaged over texts. MAUVE: seed-1 runs only, report-only, via the mauve package (featurize_model_name='models/gpt2-large', max_text_length=512) or the repo's compute_mauve, against the 240 references; skip if fewer than 5 minutes remain. Diagnostics: per-token NLL averaged within 32-token bins along the sequence (16 bins) per condition; 500-resample text bootstrap (pooled over seeds) of the Q8/Q16 Gen-PPL ratio with its 2.5/97.5 percentiles.

event.description: Averaged over seeds 1-3, inference block size 8 (32 steps per block) yields at least 5% lower GPT-2-Large generative perplexity than the trained block size 16 (32 steps per block), with the Q=8 samples' mean unigram entropy no more than 0.05 nats below that of Q=16 (otherwise the statistic is set to 0).
event.statistic: mean over seeds of (GenPPL[Q=16,S=32] - GenPPL[Q=8,S=32]) / GenPPL[Q=16,S=32]; set to 0 if seed-mean entropy[Q=8] < seed-mean entropy[Q=16] - 0.05

evaluation.procedure: outputs/blocksize/scores.jsonl holds one line per (Q, S, seed) with gen_ppl, entropy_mean, entropy_std, mauve (seed-1 runs, else null), n_texts, n_blocks, denoiser_calls, wall_time_sec and error (null if none). outputs/blocksize/samples/Q{Q}_N{S}_seed{s}.jsonl hold, per generated sample, the token ids, the post-processed text, its GPT-2-Large NLL sum and token count. outputs/blocksize/block_nll.json holds the mean NLL per 32-token bin for every condition. outputs/blocksize/bootstrap.json holds the 500 bootstrap values and the 95% interval of the Q8/Q16 Gen-PPL ratio plus point ratios Q4/Q16, Q32/Q16 and (Q8,S16)/Q16. The statistic is computed from scores.jsonl as the mean over seeds {1,2,3} of the relative Gen-PPL reduction of (Q=8,S=32) versus (Q=16,S=32), with the entropy guard applied.
evaluation.controls: The trained block size Q=16 under the same sampler, seeds and model is the control; the explicit-override identity check and denoiser call counts verify that the override actually changes the block partition; Q=32 tests the mirror prediction (coarser blocks should hurt); (Q=8, S=16) matches the control's number of sequential denoiser calls to separate conditioning granularity from latency; the entropy guard and report-only MAUVE detect gains obtained through loss of diversity; the per-bin NLL profile localizes any gain along the sequence; the bootstrap interval quantifies sampling noise at 240 samples.

registration.full_scale_study: A full inference-time sweep of block size x steps-per-block x solver x guidance on OpenWebText (1024 tokens) and XSum with 1000 samples and 5 seeds, compared against models trained at each Q to build the train/test block-size mismatch matrix; if transfer works, an adaptive block-size sampler (small blocks early in a document, larger later) and a mixed-Q training recipe so that one checkpoint serves all latency operating points.

agent.reason: The two-stream training only ever showed the denoiser 16-wide noisy blocks at multiples of 16, so Q=8 sampling may transfer (finer committed context, as Fig. 7b suggests) or mildly hurt; even if it transfers, a 5% Gen-PPL drop without retraining is a strong ask, and the runtime-override path plus the arm count carry real implementation/time risk.

judge_astra.reason: The seed's smaller-block results make a modest improvement plausible, but those models were separately trained and evaluated primarily with MAUVE. Runtime Q=8 changes attention and cached-prefix distributions for the Q=16 checkpoint, so transfer—and a 5% perplexity gain satisfying the entropy guard—is uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: The released sampler reportedly exposes a runtime block size, so the run is feasible, but a Q=16-trained two-stream denoiser has never seen a clean prefix ending mid-block; the direction of the Q=8 effect is close to a coin flip and a >=5% Gen-PPL gain plus the entropy guard is a further bar, and the authors' own choice to ship Q=16 inference weakly suggests no free lunch.

judge_opus.reason: Smaller inference blocks remove the hardest block offsets and retrained smaller-Q models are much better, but the Q=16 model never saw 8-position noisy blocks (and possibly different clean-stream block masks), so the transferred gain may be small or offset by distribution shift; some implementation risk from the runtime block-size override.

judge_sol.reason: The seed’s trained-block MAUVE trend makes a benefit from finer conditioning plausible, and 5% is a modest PPL threshold. However, inference-only Q=8 changes noisy/clean attention boundaries outside the training configuration, and any gain must also survive the entropy guard.

judge_luna.reason: The seed’s separately trained models favor smaller blocks (MAUVE 0.857 at Q=8 versus 0.815 at Q=16), supporting finer conditioning, but that does not establish transfer: positions newly treated as clean prefix at inference were denoised jointly during Q=16 training. A 5% PPL reduction without a meaningful entropy loss is plausible, but uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Seed Fig. 7b shows trained Q8 beats Q16 and Q8 inference doubles total NFE, favoring lower PPL, but inference prefixes ending mid-training-block are unseen during training so transfer may degrade rather than help.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Adaptive Block Diffusion does test inference-time block-size transfer. It takes fixed-block BD3-LM models trained at block sizes 4 and 16 and evaluates them at other block sizes, measuring likelihood perplexity on LM1B and OWT. Quality drops off the training block size, though BD3-LM(16) at block size 8 is roughly unchanged (30.25 vs 30.56). Those models are discrete masked-diffusion models scored by likelihood. The registered experiment instead uses a continuous flow-matching latent denoiser with self-conditioning and a frozen decoder, and scores generated samples by Gen-PPL, entropy and MAUVE.

The seed paper trains a separate model for each block size Q (Fig. 7b, OWT128, MAUVE). I found no case in the sections I read where it samples a model at a block size other than the one it was trained with.
BD3-LM trains a separate discrete block-diffusion model for each block size and evaluates each at its own size. It does not study transfer to other block sizes at inference.

This work (TDAR/TCCF) varies block sizes at inference for discrete reasoning models, but relies on progressive block-size training to keep this stable. It is neither a continuous latent model nor a post-hoc test of a single fixed-Q checkpoint.
SDAR reports that larger discrete AR-converted block-diffusion models are more robust to the choice of block size. It does not cover continuous latent flow-matching denoisers.

opus.reason: The closest prior work is Adaptive Block Diffusion (2606.29275). It already shows that discrete fixed-block diffusion models specialize to the block size they were trained with and degrade at other sizes, so the general question has some prior evidence. However, that evidence comes from discrete masked diffusion scored by likelihood. Nothing I found tests block-size transfer for a continuous block-causal latent flow-matching LM like AURORA-LM, or uses sample-quality metrics. Given that change of model class, I don't think the existing results settle the question, so I judge the experiment distinct.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Adaptive Block Diffusion, Section 5.1/Table 1, evaluates fixed-block BD3LM checkpoints, including a block-size-16 model, across inference block sizes 1–128 without retraining. The proposed experiment instead uses continuous autoencoded latents and measures generated-text perplexity with an entropy guard rather than held-out likelihood bounds.

Blockwise SFT, Section 4.3/Figure 6, reports a training/inference block-size mismatch matrix with sizes {8,16,32,64}, testing whether fixed-block training specializes models to their decoding granularity. It uses discrete diffusion and mathematical-reasoning accuracy rather than continuous-latent unconditional generation.
The seed's Section 4.1.3/Figure 7b compares separately trained block-size specialists, not inference-time block-size changes on one fixed checkpoint.

sol.reason: Prior work already directly tests the central question of whether changing inference block size on a fixed-block-trained denoiser transfers successfully or exposes training-granularity specialization. The AURORA-LM experiment adds a continuous-latent model, generated-text quality/diversity metrics, and sampling-budget controls, making it a close variant rather than a new experimental question; I found no report of the exact AURORA-LM checkpoint experiment.

opus.reason: Both take the released Q=16 AURORA-LM-S denoiser and, without retraining, sample it with other runtime block sizes, comparing Gen-PPL, entropy and MAUVE to test train-to-inference block-size transfer.

sol.reason: Both change inference block size without retraining a fixed Q=16 checkpoint and measure Gen-PPL, entropy and MAUVE to test block-size transfer.

outcome.executor_notes:
Implemented as registered. setup.sh copies the seed repo to /workspace/repo, runs pip install -e, and downloads the released OWT Q=16 checkpoint, the autoencoder, GPT-2 small and GPT-2 Large. blocksize_exp.py loads DiffusionGenerator, sets _eval_protocol to return {} and sets trainer.sc_cfg_enabled=False, then samples 240 × 512-token texts per run with 32-step Euler, self-conditioning on and no guidance. Block size is passed through generate(block_size=Q), which goes to trainer.use_runtime_block_size.

Verification checks (all passed in my test run):
- The pilot made 32 denoiser step calls plus 1 cache write.
- Passing block_size=16 explicitly gave exactly the same texts as the default call.
- Call counts matched (512/Q)·S per batch for every arm; Q=8 and Q=32 samples were printed.

All arms ran: Q16×3 seeds, Q8×3, Q32×2, Q4×1, and (Q8, S16)×1. The time guard did not trigger (control took 38 s).

Deviations and small changes:
1. The registered override "operator_optimization.profile=off" is parsed by YAML as boolean False and crashes, so I set cfg.operator_optimization.profile="off" as a string after loading.
2. stas/openwebtext-10k fails because dataset scripts are no longer supported. As the registered fallback, MAUVE references come from Elriggs/openwebtext-100k; this is recorded in summary.json.
3. The identity check uses 4 samples × 64 tokens at seed 1, not a full run.
4. MAUVE (report-only) uses GPT-2-Large final-layer features at the last text token. They come from the same bf16 forward pass used for Gen-PPL, which has EOS prepended as BOS, and are passed to mauve.compute_mauve as p_features/q_features. So they are not computed by mauve's own fp32 featurizer.
5. Unigram entropy is computed on the GPT-2 re-tokenization of the post-processed text.

Results from my test run (the same numbers reproduced exactly on a full rerun of run_eval.sh):

| Arm | Gen-PPL by seed | Seed-mean entropy (nats) |
|---|---|---|
| Q16, S32 (control) | 63.8 / 64.7 / 61.1 | 5.007 |
| Q8, S32 | 63.5 / 63.6 / 65.0 | 4.985 |

- Statistic = −0.0141. Per-seed relative reductions are +0.004, +0.017 and −0.064. The entropy guard was not triggered, so the event did not occur.
- Bootstrap 95% CI of the Q8/Q16 Gen-PPL ratio is [0.959, 1.080]. This only says that no ≥5% gain was detected at this sample size; it does not show that the two block sizes are equivalent.
- Other arms, relative to Q16:
  - Q32: Gen-PPL ≈ 3.07×, MAUVE 0.61 vs 0.97.
  - Q4: Gen-PPL 1.13×, but entropy collapses to 2.98 and MAUVE to 0.14, so the Q4 samples are degenerate.
  - (Q8, S16): Gen-PPL 1.28×.
- MAUVE at seed 1 is 0.97 for Q16 and 0.99 for Q8, but with only 240 samples per side.

Interpretation (inference, not tested): at inference the Q=16 model tolerates Q=8 but does not improve, coarser blocks hurt badly, and Q=4 degenerates. That pattern points to training-time specialization rather than a free inference-time knob. It comes from one model and 240 samples per seed.

departures: blocksize_exp.py loads the config without the registered override list and then sets cfg.operator_optimization.profile='off' as a string. The registered dotlist override would be parsed as boolean False and crash, so this change was needed for the run to happen. The profile still reaches DiffusionGenerator/trainer init, so it should not change the value.

blocksize_exp.py builds the MAUVE references from Elriggs/openwebtext-100k because stas/openwebtext-10k fails with 'Dataset scripts are no longer supported'. The registration lists this as a fallback, and the substitution is recorded in summary.json. It affects only the report-only MAUVE, not the statistic.

blocksize_exp.py computes MAUVE from its own GPT-2-Large features: bf16, final-layer hidden state at the last text token, EOS prepended as BOS. These are passed as p_features/q_features rather than produced by mauve's fp32 featurizer or the repo's compute_mauve. Absolute MAUVE values can shift slightly, but MAUVE is report-only and cannot change the statistic. The engineer disclosed this.

blocksize_exp.py runs the explicit-Q=16 identity check on 4 samples x 64 tokens at seed 1, not on a full 240 x 512 run. It is a weaker verification but does not change any reported value. The engineer disclosed this.

blocksize_exp.py checks call counts per generate call as nb x (512/Q) x S with nb=2 batches of 120. Step calls and write_cache calls are counted separately. This is equivalent to the registered per-batch check (pilot gave 32 steps + 1 write).

blocksize_exp.py computes Gen-PPL with its own batched scorer: bs=16, right padding with attention mask, EOS as BOS, per-text NLL kept. The repo's compute_ppl is not used. The registration permits this, and the definition (exp of total NLL over total tokens) matches.
blocksize_exp.py adds an extra skip rule: non-headline arms are skipped if time is short. The rule never triggered (time_guard null, all arms ran), so it had no effect.

Undisclosed, unverifiable: checkpoints/owt/config.yaml sets causal_decoder.kv_cache.decode_latents_per_call=${diffusion.causal.block_size}=16 regardless of the runtime block size. The autoencoder decoder may therefore chunk differently from the denoiser blocks for Q!=16. The decoder is causal, so any effect is probably negligible, but the code that would show this is not displayed.
problems: outputs/blocksize/bootstrap.json resamples texts pooled across seeds and ignores seed-level clustering. Per-seed relative reductions range from +1.7% to -6.4%, so the CI [0.959, 1.080] may understate between-seed variability. Even so, its lower bound sits above 0.95 only narrowly.
Each condition has only 240 samples per seed, and MAUVE uses 240 vs 240 (faiss warns about too few points for 24 centroids), so MAUVE differences such as 0.97 vs 0.99 are not interpretable.
Printed Q=8 samples in exp_eval.log include degenerate pseudo-base64 strings. The sample-quality level is visibly low for both arms, which limits what Gen-PPL alone can say.

The engineer's 'training-time specialization' interpretation goes beyond the data. The experiment uses one checkpoint and does not compare against models trained at each Q. The engineer flags it as inference.
exp.log (an earlier engineer run) crashed with a JSON bool serialization error. The evaluated run completed and reproduced identical numbers, so this is not a problem for the reported value.
opus.reason: The evaluated code runs the registered design: released Q=16 OWT checkpoint, 32-step Euler, no guidance (pilot confirms 32 denoiser calls per 16-token block), 240 x 512-token samples, and all registered arms and seeds. Runtime block-size transfer is checked through effective_block_size and call counts. The statistic in result.json (-0.0141) recomputes exactly from scores.jsonl. The entropy guard is applied correctly and not triggered, and the control Gen-PPL (61-65) falls inside the registered sanity range. The departures (string profile override, registered dataset fallback, custom MAUVE featurization, smaller identity check) are disclosed or immaterial, and none touches the Gen-PPL statistic. The result is a credible null for the hypothesized at-least-5% gain, backed by strong secondary evidence that coarser blocks (Q=32, about 3x Gen-PPL) and very fine blocks (Q=4, entropy collapse) hurt. Precision is limited by 240 samples per seed and a single checkpoint.

departures: setup.sh copies the supplied seed repository rather than cloning GitHub, installs the core package plus separate dependencies rather than the evaluation extra, and downloads GPT-2 models from their openai-community repositories. The unused evaluate dependency is omitted. These are setup differences; the evidence does not establish a changed model or an effect on the reported statistic.

blocksize_exp.py assigns operator_optimization.profile="off" after configuration loading instead of using the registered override string. This repairs the reported YAML parsing problem and preserves the intended setting; it should not change the result relative to the intended registration.

blocksize_exp.py uses Elriggs/openwebtext-100k after stas/openwebtext-10k fails. This is an explicitly authorized fallback, recorded in summary.json. It can change MAUVE, but references do not enter Gen-PPL, entropy, or the registered statistic.

blocksize_exp.py performs the default-versus-explicit-Q16 identity check on four 64-token samples rather than the full registered sampling call. This weakens the control's coverage of full-length generation, but the check passed and full-run call counts matched; no change to the reported statistic is established.

blocksize_exp.py uses a forward pre-hook and reports denoising calls separately from cache writes, aggregated across two sampling batches. This differs from the registration's literal single-batch call-count formula but correctly accounts for the executed batches. It changes bookkeeping, not generation or the statistic.

blocksize_exp.py computes MAUVE using supplied last-token, final-layer features from the bf16 scorer with EOS prepended, rather than the registered MAUVE/repository text-featurization route. This can change the reported MAUVE values and their comparability to the seed paper. It does not affect the headline statistic or entropy guard.

blocksize_exp.py logs identity and full-run call-count checks without enforcing them as stopping conditions, and does not implement the registered control-PPL sanity/debug gate. All these checks were satisfactory in the fresh evaluation, so these enforcement differences did not affect its value.

blocksize_exp.py generally records an exception and proceeds immediately, rather than making the registered two repair attempts before skipping an unsupported block size; OOM receives one batch-size retry. Its statistic also accepts any available matched seeds, returns zero if none exist, and does not reject otherwise scored records solely because error is non-null. These rules could change a failed or incomplete evaluation, but all three headline seed pairs completed without errors here.

run_eval.sh gives the experiment script a default 1500-second budget, and blocksize_exp.py adds an unregistered rule to skip non-headline runs when fewer than 120 seconds remain. These could reduce exploratory coverage in a slower run. Neither that rule nor the registered time guard triggered, and all ten arms completed.
problems: The MAUVE implementation in blocksize_exp.py is not the registered featurization protocol. Its 240-sample comparisons also produced clustering warnings, so small differences such as Q8 versus Q16 should not be treated as reliable quality gains or directly compared with paper scores.

bootstrap.json gives an interval for the pooled, token-weighted PPL ratio, not for the registered mean of per-seed relative reductions or the entropy-guarded event. The interval therefore cannot be directly substituted for uncertainty on the registered statistic, and it does not establish equivalence.

The training-specialization interpretation is not causally established. One checkpoint under one solver and sequence length, without separately trained comparison models, cannot determine that the seed paper's block-size trend is exclusively a training-time effect. The Q4 and latency-matched findings additionally have only one seed each.

run_eval.sh and setup.sh lack fail-fast shell handling, including pipefail, while blocksize_exp.py permits partial-seed scoring and does not enforce several verification gates. These are reliability problems for future failed runs, although the fresh evaluation's complete RUN records and DONE output support successful execution here.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed all ten arms, retained every registered raw-output file, and produced the headline value from model-generated texts using the registered PPL calculation and entropy guard. The value was -0.014144554, with an entropy decrease of approximately 0.0222 nats, so the guard did not trigger and the registered event did not occur. The departures did not plausibly change that headline value in this completed run, although the MAUVE departure limits the auxiliary evidence. This is a meaningful narrow negative finding: Q8 did not deliver the registered improvement despite roughly doubling generation time, while Q32 substantially worsened PPL and Q4 showed a large entropy collapse. It does not establish Q8/Q16 equivalence or prove the proposed training-specialization mechanism.

departures: blocksize_exp.py sets operator_optimization.profile to the string "off" after load_config_from_checkpoint instead of the registered Hydra override operator_optimization.profile=off, which OmegaConf parses as boolean False and crashes. problems: MAUVE in blocksize_exp.py / scores.jsonl is not the registered featurizer, and the evaluation log warns that clustering 480 points to 24 centroids needs at least 936 points, so the diversity diagnostic beyond unigram entropy is weak.

summary.json per-seed relative reductions disagree in sign (+0.004, +0.017, -0.064). The text-level bootstrap CI of the Q8/Q16 ratio [0.959, 1.080] excludes a 5% gain, but three seeds do not; exclusion of the threshold is only moderate.

Identity verification in blocksize_exp.py is partial, though call counts (2048/4096/1024/8192), wall-time scaling, and quality shifts for Q=32 and Q=4 independently show the block-size override was real.
grok.reason: The evaluated run follows the registered sampler, arms, seeds, 240 by 512 samples, Gen-PPL definition, entropy guard, and statistic; the recorded fallbacks and the profile-string fix do not change that question.
