next_step.what: Debug dropout-off reconstruction and adjust training until all corner cells achieve comparable high clean accuracy, then repeat the corruption factorial.

registration.title: How much of the frozen decoder's token recovery is a language-model prior? Fill-in accuracy of the released AURORA autoencoder at information-removed positions versus GPT-2 small
registration.seed_connection: The seed reads token recovery under latent corruption (Fig. 5a) as retained latent information and uses it to justify a wide latent. Its autoencoder, however, is trained with 30% token-embedding dropout at the encoder input (Appendix A.1.1), which makes the decoder reconstruct roughly a third of all positions purely from left context, i.e. trains it as a causal language model. The paper never separates how much of a recovery curve is information in the latent versus contextual guessing by the decoder, which also bears on how to read Gen-PPL of decoded samples.
registration.hypothesis: At positions whose token identity is removed from the encoder input (the autoencoder's own training corruption), the released frozen decoder predicts the token from left context with at least 70% of the top-1 accuracy that GPT-2 small reaches from the same left context, i.e. the decoder carries a substantial language-model prior.
registration.contribution: TEncDM and COSMOS report decoder robustness to latent noise as a single accuracy/BLEU curve; no work measures the fill-in accuracy of a latent text decoder when a position's information is removed, anchors it against a dedicated causal LM, or splits the robustness curve by contextual predictability and token frequency, which is what distinguishes capacity from prior.

closest_work.difference: The seed presents token recovery under latent corruption (Fig. 5a) as retained information; it never measures the decoder's fill-in accuracy when a position's information is removed, nor splits recovery by predictability.

TEncDM motivates a contextual decoder trained on corrupted encodings and reports aggregate robustness; here the released AURORA decoder's language-model prior is measured directly against GPT-2 small on the same positions.
COSMOS reports decoder robustness to latent noise as one accuracy curve without decomposing latent information versus decoder prior.
CoDAR adds a context-aware autoregressive decoder to fix token rounding in embedding diffusion; here the question is how much language-model prior an existing latent text decoder already carries.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: git clone https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; pip install -e '.[eval]'

Released checkpoints: python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder (the OWT diffusion checkpoint is loaded only because its loader builds the autoencoder with its latent standardization statistics; weights from fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder; GPT-2 small lands in models/gpt2-small)
GPT-2 Large: huggingface-cli download gpt2-large --local-dir models/gpt2-large

Held-out text: HF dataset HuggingFaceFW/fineweb, config sample-10BT, split train, streaming=True (web text post-dating both models' training data); fallback wikitext (config wikitext-103-raw-v1) test split
registration.method:
Setup: clone, install and download as listed. Build the generator as the README does (cfg from load_config_from_checkpoint(ckpt, overrides=['operator_optimization.profile=off'], project_root=REPO); gen = DiffusionGenerator(cfg, 'checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors', device='cuda:0')) and take ae = gen.trainer.autoencoder (released OWT autoencoder: latent width D=768, 6+6 layers) and the GPT-2 tokenizer. Reported autoencoder API: get_latent(batch) -> (raw_latent, ...), normalize_latent / denormalize_latent (per-channel standardization), decode_latent(raw_latent, target_token_len) -> logits; if names differ, use the functions the prompt-conditioned sampler and the generator use for encoding and decoding.

Data: 300 windows of 512 GPT-2 tokens, each the first 512 tokens of a distinct document with at least 512 tokens, from the FineWeb stream (fallback: WikiText-103 test concatenated and cut into 300 windows; record the source). Batches: {'input_ids', 'attention_mask' (all ones), 'target_ids'}. Verify clean reconstruction: argmax decoding of the encoded latents must reproduce at least 98% of tokens (report the exact value).

Predictability labels: run GPT-2 small (models/gpt2-small, bf16) on each window; position j (j >= 1) is 'predictable' if GPT-2's top-1 prediction from tokens < j equals token j; store the GPT-2 log-prob of the true token. Frequency strata: token ids among the 500 most frequent ids in the 300 windows versus the rest.

Main measurement (variant C = the autoencoder's own training corruption): for each of 3 mask seeds, select 15% of positions j >= 2 per window at random; zero the token-embedding vector at those positions at the encoder input and encode. Implement either by replicating get_latent with the embedding output zeroed at the masked positions (reported helpers: ae.frozen_embed_tokens, ae.normalize_encodings, ae.encoder(token_embeddings=..., attention_mask=...)) or generically with a forward hook on the nn.Embedding module inside the autoencoder (weight shape [50257, 768]) that multiplies its output by a [B, T, 1] keep-mask during the encode call only (confirm the hook fires exactly once per encode and is removed afterwards). Decode the resulting latents for the whole window (argmax). Record acc_dec_C = top-1 accuracy at the masked positions; accuracy at unmasked positions (must be >= 0.99, otherwise the masking is wrong); acc_gpt2 = GPT-2 small top-1 accuracy at the same masked positions; the unigram baseline (always predicting the most frequent token id of the windows); the split of acc_dec_C by predictability and by frequency stratum; and the mean GPT-2 log-prob of the decoder's guess versus of the true token at those positions.

Removal variants (same positions, report-only): A = the raw encoder latent at the masked positions set to the zero vector (the extreme form of the training-time coordinate dropout); B = the standardized latent at the masked positions replaced by N(0, I) noise. For each, decode and report the same accuracies.

Corruption sweep: for sigma in {0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95} and noise seeds {0, 1, 2}: x = (1-sigma)*z_std + sigma*eps in standardized space; decode ae.decode_latent(ae.denormalize_latent(x), target_token_len=512).argmax(-1); report acc_all, acc_predictable, acc_unpredictable, and the same split within the rare-token stratum; interpolate the sigma* at which acc_all = 0.70 and report acc_predictable - acc_unpredictable there, overall and within the rare stratum. Fluency: for sigma in {0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} (noise seed 0) compute the GPT-2-Large corpus perplexity of the decoded texts (bf16, EOS prepended as BOS, exp(sum NLL / tokens)) relative to the clean decode, together with a random-substitution control in which the same fraction of positions as were wrongly decoded is replaced by uniformly random vocabulary ids, and a prior-fill reference in which those positions are replaced by GPT-2 small's top-1 prediction from clean left context.

event.description: At positions whose token identity has been removed from the encoder input (15% of positions, the autoencoder's own training corruption), the frozen decoder's top-1 fill-in accuracy is at least 0.70 times GPT-2 small's top-1 next-token accuracy at the same positions from the same left context, averaged over three mask seeds.
event.statistic: mean over mask seeds of acc_dec_C / acc_gpt2 at the masked positions

evaluation.procedure: outputs/decoderprior/removal.json holds, per mask seed and variant (C, A, B): accuracy at masked positions overall and split by predictability and frequency stratum, GPT-2 small accuracy at the same positions, the unigram baseline, unmasked-position accuracy, number of positions, the mean GPT-2 log-prob of decoder guesses versus true tokens, and the per-seed ratio acc_dec_C/acc_gpt2 with its mean (the statistic). outputs/decoderprior/sweep.jsonl holds one line per (sigma, noise seed) with acc_all, acc_pred, acc_unpred, the rare-stratum split and n_positions, plus the interpolated sigma* and the gap at sigma*. outputs/decoderprior/fluency.json holds, per sigma, decoded-text PPL, clean-decode PPL, random-substitution PPL, prior-fill PPL and token accuracy. outputs/decoderprior/predictability.json holds the fraction of predictable positions, GPT-2 small's overall accuracy, the clean reconstruction accuracy and the data source used.
evaluation.controls: GPT-2 small anchors the accuracy a dedicated causal LM of similar size reaches from the same left context (note: the autoencoder's token embeddings were initialized from GPT-2 small); the unigram baseline gives the no-context floor; unmasked-position accuracy verifies that the corruption is local; variants A and B show how the decoder behaves when the latent, rather than the encoder input, is uninformative; frequency stratification separates contextual predictability from token frequency in the sweep split; the random-substitution and prior-fill PPL references calibrate how fluent the decoder's wrong tokens are.

registration.full_scale_study: Retrain the autoencoder with token-embedding dropout p_x in {0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5} as an explicit decoder-prior-strength knob, re-plot the seed's Fig. 5a as information-above-prior-floor curves per width, and decode the same generated latents with decoders of different prior strength (and with a context-free nearest-prototype decoder) to measure how much of AURORA-LM's Gen-PPL and MAUVE is attributable to the decoder's language-model prior versus the latent prior.

agent.reason: The released autoencoder spent ~100B tokens reconstructing 30% of positions purely from left context with GPT-2-small-sized compute, so a sizeable language-model prior is likely, but whether it reaches 70% of a dedicated LM's top-1 accuracy while also serving robust copying is genuinely uncertain, and the embedding-masking hook may need manual replication of the encoder path.

judge_astra.reason: The substantial token-embedding dropout explicitly trains contextual fill-in, making 70% of GPT-2 small's accuracy plausible after extensive autoencoder training. Nevertheless, masking also removes some preceding context, and success would establish a prior in the encoder–decoder system rather than isolate the decoder's contribution.

judge_fable.reason: Thirty percent token-embedding dropout over ~100B token exposures trains a 6+6-layer causal fill-in model with GPT-2-small-initialized embeddings, so reaching 70% of GPT-2 small's top-1 accuracy is somewhat more likely than not; the main risks are mis-implementing the encoder-input masking and the usual repo/API uncertainty.

judge_opus.reason: With c=1 the decoder for token j sees only latents <= j, so 30% token-embedding dropout trained it as a causal LM over tens of billions of positions; its fill-in accuracy should be comparable to GPT-2 small, with the main handicap being 15% holes in its left context (about 15% relative loss).

judge_sol.reason: Token-embedding dropout gives the autoencoder a genuine causal missing-token prediction objective, making substantial fill-in accuracy and the 0.70 ratio likely. GPT-2 nevertheless receives intact histories, and variant C measures the encoder–decoder’s combined predictive prior rather than isolating the decoder.

judge_luna.reason: The released encoder is causal and trained with 30% token-embedding dropout, so it is explicitly trained to reconstruct some masked tokens from left-context latents; testing at 15% masking makes the 70%-of-GPT-2-small threshold plausible. Still, the decoder and anchor differ in training and the autoencoder’s embeddings were initialized from GPT-2 small, so this is not a fully independent comparison.

judge_muse.reason: The decoder was trained with 30% input dropout to fill missing tokens and has similar total capacity to GPT-2 small, making 70% of its accuracy plausible, though its 6-layer decoder and 15%-masked prior context are disadvantages.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper describes the token-embedding dropout and reports token recovery under latent corruption, and it treats that recovery as information kept in the latent. It does not measure how well the decoder fills in positions whose input was removed, compare against a causal LM, or split recovery by how predictable or how frequent tokens are.

TEncDM argues for a contextual decoder trained on corrupted encodings and reports aggregate robustness. It does not separate the decoder's language-model prior from latent information, and it uses no causal-LM anchor.
COSMOS gives a single curve of decoder robustness to latent noise. It does not decompose that curve into latent information versus contextual guessing by the decoder.

This paper reports decoder recoverability of target tokens under token dropout with BERT latents and argues that decoder recoverability should be part of evaluation. It uses a different model and does not compare against GPT-2 or split recovery by predictability or frequency, so it does not test how much of the recovery comes from a language-model prior.
CoDAR adds a context-aware autoregressive decoder to fix token rounding. It does not measure how much prior an existing latent decoder already carries.

opus.reason: I found no paper that measures a latent text decoder's fill-in accuracy at positions with their information removed, sets it against GPT-2 on the same left context, and splits the corruption-robustness curve by contextual predictability and token frequency. Related work (TEncDM, COSMOS, the draft-refinement report and the seed paper itself) reports robustness or recoverability only as aggregate numbers, without separating latent information from the decoder's prior. The search tool returned many off-topic results, so some uncertainty remains, but none of the papers it did surface answers this question.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Audits decoder contributions, corruption robustness, perplexity artifacts, and rare-token residual errors in continuous language diffusion. It does not remove target-token embeddings before encoding and compare the frozen decoder's fill-in accuracy with a causal LM on matched positions and contexts.

CoDAR compares contextual autoregressive decoding with pointwise token recovery, establishing benefits from linguistic context. Its recovery study does not isolate a decoder's prior through token-identity removal or anchor that prior against standalone next-token accuracy.

The seed measures aggregate reconstruction under latent corruption across latent widths and trains with token-embedding dropout, but does not report masked-input fill-in accuracy or recovery stratified by an external LM's contextual predictability.
COSMOS uses masking and noise during autoencoder training and evaluates aggregate decoder robustness, without the proposed information-removal comparison against a causal LM.

sol.reason: Prior work already establishes that contextual decoders affect token recovery and that decoded-text perplexity can obscure fidelity or diversity failures. However, none of the papers I found answers the registered question through target-token embedding removal, matched-position causal-LM accuracy, and contextual-predictability stratification. The central diagnostic is therefore distinct, although its corruption sweeps and perplexity checks overlap with existing analyses.

opus.reason: No list entry measures the frozen decoder's fill-in accuracy at information-removed positions against GPT-2 small to separate a language-model prior from latent information.

sol.reason: No list entry removes token identity from encoder inputs and compares decoder fill-in accuracy with a causal language model to separate contextual guessing from retained latent information.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the complete registered experiment: 300 FineWeb document windows, GPT-2 small predictability/frequency labels, three mask seeds, removal variants C/A/B, full standardized-latent corruption sweep, crossing interpolation, and GPT-2 Large corpus PPL with random-substitution/prior-fill controls. Tested the full evaluation command successfully twice; observed statistic 0.8328711, clean reconstruction 99.926%, and C unmasked accuracy >99.91% for every seed. Minimal compatibility repairs: absolute checkpoint/model paths and restoring string 'off' after OmegaConf parses the bare override as False. Variant C uses the permitted replicated encode path, zeroing normalized embedding features immediately before the encoder, matching released training code. Supplied seed imported via PYTHONPATH with equivalent dependencies rather than an editable installation into the read-only seed. Retained a small input-window cache/manifest for exact subset reproducibility. No changes to hypothesis, threshold, controls, corpus selection, or registered sweep. Details and interpretive caveats in decoderprior/NOTES.md.

departures: decoderprior/evaluate.py (encode): variant C zeros the token features after ae.normalize_encodings, not the raw nn.Embedding output. The registration names this helper path as an allowed implementation, and the engineer says it matches the released training corruption, but the training code is not in the archive. If the normalization adds a bias, zeroing before it would give a different input, so the value could shift slightly. It is unlikely to cross the 0.70 threshold, because variant A also gives a ratio of about 0.80.
decoderprior/run.sh: the seed is imported via PYTHONPATH with pinned dependencies instead of `pip install -e '.[eval]'`. This is an environment repair and should not change the result.

decoderprior/evaluate.py (build_ae): absolute checkpoint and model paths are set, and operator_optimization.profile is reset to the string 'off' after OmegaConf parsed it as False. This was needed to run and has no effect on the value.

decoderprior/data_windows.npz and data_source.json: the evaluation reused the engineer's submitted token-window cache instead of streaming FineWeb afresh. The stdout 'Data ready' line comes from the cached metadata. Document SHA-256 hashes are recorded, so the subset is checkable. It could change the result only if the cache were not the first 300 eligible documents, which nothing suggests.

decoderprior/evaluate.py: mask positions are an exact count of 76 = round(0.15×510) per window, drawn from positions 2..511. This is a reasonable reading of '15% of positions j>=2' and has no material effect.

decoderprior/evaluate.py: GPT-2 small is scored on the raw windows without a prepended BOS, so position 0 is excluded from the predictability splits. In the sweep, acc_all includes j=0 while the splits exclude it. This is a choice left open by the registration; all 113 clean-reconstruction errors fall at j=0, and the effect on any statistic is negligible.

decoderprior/evaluate.py: the sweep reuses the same noise draw across all sigma values within each seed (common random numbers). This is left open by the registration and does not affect the main statistic.

decoderprior/evaluate.py (ppl): decoded texts are re-tokenized and texts longer than 1024 tokens are scored in 512-token target chunks. These are scorer details the registration does not fix, and they affect only the report-only fluency numbers.
problems: Registration premise: FineWeb sample-10BT is not guaranteed to post-date GPT-2 or OpenWebText. Overlap could inflate both acc_gpt2 and acc_dec_C. The engineer flags this in NOTES.md; its effect on the ratio is unclear.

outputs/decoderprior/removal.json: masking several positions at once also removes some of the autoencoder's left context, while GPT-2 sees clean context. This biases the ratio downward (conservatively), so the measured 0.83 is if anything an underestimate.

Interpretation: the measurement covers encoder plus decoder, not the decoder alone. If the encoder can attend to right context, variant C's latent at a masked position may carry right-context information. Variant A (latent zeroed at the masked position) still gives roughly 0.307/0.383 ≈ 0.80, which limits this concern.

outputs/decoderprior/sweep.jsonl: at sigma*≈0.766 the predictable-minus-unpredictable gap is -0.012 overall and -0.078 in the rare stratum. This contradicts a simple prior-driven reading of the recovery curve near 70% accuracy, and the registration's narrative does not address it.
Scope: one released checkpoint, one corpus, 300 windows. The three seeds vary only the mask, not the data or the model.
opus.reason: The code runs the registered experiment as specified: 300 FineWeb windows, GPT-2 small labels, three mask seeds, variants C/A/B, the full sweep with interpolation, and GPT-2 Large fluency with both controls. The only departures are permitted implementation choices or repairs needed to run. The statistic is computed from real decoder and GPT-2 outputs, and the validity gates pass: clean reconstruction is 0.9993 and C unmasked accuracy exceeds 0.999. The per-seed ratios (0.825–0.839, 22,800 positions each) clear the 0.70 threshold with margin. Variant A shows a similar ratio, and the decoder's guesses get a higher GPT-2 log-prob than the true tokens. C accuracy is 0.72 at predictable positions versus 0.07 at unpredictable ones, which supports a substantial language-model prior. The finding is credible and informative, but it is limited to one checkpoint and one corpus, it does not isolate the decoder from the encoder, and the near-zero predictability gap at sigma* complicates the broader claim about the seed's recovery curves.

departures: decoderprior/run.sh and evaluate.py: The implementation imports the supplied seed through PYTHONPATH and installs dependencies directly, rather than cloning and installing the repository editable. It also downloads the specified model repositories through snapshot_download rather than the registered download commands. These are setup substitutions; there is no evidence that they changed the models, method, or reported statistic.

decoderprior/evaluate.py, build_ae: Absolute paths replace relative configuration paths, and the parsed Boolean False is changed back to the intended string 'off'. These are necessary compatibility repairs and do not appear to change the experiment.

decoderprior/evaluate.py, get_data: The protected evaluation reuses the submitted data_windows.npz and data_source.json instead of obtaining the windows anew from the FineWeb stream. Predictions are recomputed, not cached. Reusing the same eligible subset should not change the result, but the fresh run verifies only the array shape, not its correspondence to the document manifest or claimed stream selection.

decoderprior/evaluate.py, encode: Variant C zeros normalized embedding features immediately before the encoder, rather than hooking the embedding lookup output. This uses the registration's permitted replicated-encode alternative and is documented as matching training corruption. A pre-normalization intervention could behave differently, but this is not a material departure from the permitted method.

decoderprior/evaluate.py, encode: Encoder outputs are explicitly sliced to the first 512 latent positions before decoding. The notes describe additional positions as padding queries. Under the stated causal architecture this should not affect the evaluated positions; that invariance is not separately demonstrated in the supplied evidence.

decoderprior/evaluate.py: The 15% masking instruction is implemented as exactly 76 randomly selected positions per window, approximately 14.90% of the 510 eligible positions. This is ordinary integer rounding within an otherwise open sampling choice, not a material change to the experiment.

decoderprior/evaluate.py, ppl and main: Retokenized texts exceeding the scorer's context limit receive chunked scoring, and the sigma=0 fluency entry reuses the clean-decode score instead of separately scoring the standardized-latent round-trip decode. Chunking is a compatibility extension that scores every target. Reusing the clean score could affect that auxiliary PPL entry if round-tripping changed predictions, although the observed reconstruction counts agree; neither change affects the registered removal statistic.
problems: The decoder-specific interpretation is not isolated by variant C: it measures the frozen encoder-plus-decoder pipeline after input masking. Contextual prediction could be implemented partly by the encoder. Variant A provides useful supporting evidence, but there is no direct attribution of the measured capability between components.

The registration's 'same left context' characterization is not literally satisfied. Earlier positions are simultaneously masked for the autoencoder, whereas GPT-2 small receives clean left context. This inherited design limitation is explicitly recorded in removal.json and NOTES.md; the ratio is not a matched-information comparison.

FineWeb membership does not establish that these documents postdate both models' training data or are free of training overlap. NOTES.md acknowledges that publication dates were not validated, and the protected run does not independently validate the cached subset's provenance.

The supplied implementation does not include a right-context intervention or target-invariance test establishing absence of future-token leakage. The causal configuration supports the intended interpretation, but high unmasked reconstruction alone would not establish causality.
Three mask seeds on the same 300 windows measure masking variability, not independent corpus replication. No document-level confidence interval or population-level uncertainty estimate is supplied.

sweep.jsonl reports a negative predictable-minus-unpredictable recovery gap at the 70% crossing: approximately -1.15 percentage points overall and -7.85 points within rare tokens. This does not support a simple predictable-token recovery advantage at that crossing, and it does not establish equivalence or absence of a contextual prior.

fluency.json shows substantially lower PPL than random substitution at strong corruption, but decoded PPL around 572–585 remains roughly 30 times the clean value. These controls support nonrandom errors, not preserved clean-text fluency or a quantitative attribution of generated-sample quality to the decoder prior.
sol.reason: The protected run recomputed the registered mean-of-ratios statistic as 0.8328711031, above 0.70, and passed the registered reconstruction and unmasked-position checks. The code derives that value from model predictions rather than submitted test logs or hard-coded results, and no material departure affecting the primary statistic is evident. The experiment provides meaningful evidence of substantial contextual fill-in capability after token identity is removed, supported by the language-model anchor, unigram baseline, and removal controls. It merits research value 2 rather than 3 because decoder-specific attribution, matched-context comparison, corpus provenance, and population-level precision remain unresolved.

departures: Variant C zeros normalized encoder features after normalize_encodings, not the raw nn.Embedding output before normalization that the registered hook alternative and 'embedding output zeroed' wording specify (decoderprior/evaluate.py encode). Registration also says zero the token-embedding vector at the encoder input and allows a replicated path using those helpers, and the engineer claims this matches ae_trainer training corruption, which is not verifiable here. This is a different null vector at masked positions and could change acc_dec_C and the reported ratio.

Evaluation reused the submitted FineWeb window cache instead of re-streaming HuggingFaceFW/fineweb (decoderprior/evaluate.py get_data, decoderprior/data_windows.npz). Could change the exact value versus a fresh stream draw; no evidence the cache breaks the registered selection rule. Document dates were not checked against the post-training requirement (decoderprior/NOTES.md), which could slightly change the ratio but is unlikely to flip the threshold.
Mask count is Python round(0.15*(512-2))=76 (14.90% of j>=2), not 76.5 or 77 (decoderprior/evaluate.py). Negligible; would not plausibly change the conclusion.

Encoder latents are sliced to the first 512 positions before decode, dropping any padding queries up to 1024 (decoderprior/evaluate.py encode). Needed for the registered 512-token window; unlikely to change results given the passed chunk_size==1 assert and causal decode, but could if tail latents were visible.

Sweep uses one noise draw per seed shared across all sigma values rather than an independent draw per sigma (decoderprior/evaluate.py). Open relative to the registered noise seeds; could change sweep.jsonl accuracies and the interpolated gap, not the event statistic.

Fluency scores detokenized/retokenized text with extra chunking, and position-0 prior-fill uses GPT-2 small after EOS when that position is wrong (decoderprior/evaluate.py ppl). Can change fluency PPL (fluency.json n_tokens already differs across conditions); does not affect the registered event statistic.

AE encode/decode uses bf16 autocast, which the registration does not specify (decoderprior/evaluate.py). Could flip a few argmax tokens; not enough to plausibly move 0.833 below 0.70 given 99.93% clean reconstruction.

Install/load path differs: PYTHONPATH import and snapshot_download instead of pip install -e and scripts/download_models.py, plus restoring OmegaConf profile from boolean False to the string 'off' (decoderprior/run.sh, decoderprior/evaluate.py). Needed to run; no plausible effect on the statistic.
problems: Core manipulation differs from both registered implementations: post-normalization zeroing versus zeroing the embedding-module output (decoderprior/evaluate.py). That can change masked-position recovery, so the reported 0.83287 is not clearly the registered acc_dec_C ratio.
FineWeb sample was not re-fetched on the evaluation machine, and post-dating of model training data was not verified (decoderprior/data_windows.npz, decoderprior/NOTES.md).

Simultaneous 15% masks remove some autoencoder left context while the GPT-2 anchor uses clean left context, so the ratio is not a same-context prior comparison (outputs/decoderprior/removal.json caution). This was registered, but it biases the magnitude.

Headline statistic does not isolate a decoder prior from encoder contextualization. Seed-0 variant A (raw latent zeroed) is close, 0.3066 vs GPT-2 0.3827, but the event uses only variant C (outputs/decoderprior/removal.json).

At the interpolated 0.70 latent-noise crossing, the predictability gap is about -0.012 overall and -0.078 in the rare stratum (outputs/decoderprior/sweep.jsonl), so that robustness curve is not explained by the same prior. Fluency PPL is also only roughly calibrated because retokenization changes token counts (outputs/decoderprior/fluency.json).
grok.reason: The run really executed the released autoencoder and GPT-2 models: clean reconstruction is 99.93%, variant-C unmasked accuracy stays above 99.91%, and the reported mean of per-seed ratios recomputes to 0.83287 from removal.json, so the number is not hardcoded. It is unfaithful because variant C zeros normalized encodings rather than the token-embedding output specified by both registered implementations, which can change fill-in accuracy at the masked positions that define the event. The other differences are minor or confined to report-only sweep and fluency outputs. The measurement is still a credible, large-sample finding that input-masked recovery is far above unigram and concentrated on GPT-2-predictable tokens, with seed-0 variant A near 0.80 of GPT-2, but the context mismatch and the flat noise-sweep split keep it from a clean decomposition of decoder prior versus latent information.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether the released AURORA autoencoder, when a token's identity is removed from the encoder input, fills that token in with top-1 accuracy close to GPT-2 small's next-token accuracy from left context, indicating a language-model prior in the decoder.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports token recovery under latent corruption and 30% token-embedding dropout, but it neither compares decoder fill-in at identity-removed positions to a causal LM nor names that comparison as undone.

relation.reason: The hypothesis tests a side property of the paper's frozen autoencoder that the paper never claims, so the paper's capacity and generation results stand whichever way the ratio comes out.

obvious.reason: Given embedding dropout plus recovery-as-capacity in Fig. 5a, several specialists would list probing the decoder's context-only fill-in against a causal LM, but most first lists would be scaling and generation follow-ups.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change how groups using this autoencoder read reconstruction and decoded fluency, not how people across continuous language modeling work regardless of method.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's claims about 30% token-embedding dropout, Fig. 5a as a capacity probe used to justify wide latents, the 6+6 D=768 autoencoder, and GPT-2 small embedding initialization match the paper.

answerable.reason: The design computes the masked-position accuracy ratio against GPT-2 small on the same positions and reports the reconstruction and unmasked-accuracy checks needed to read it, so either outcome would bear on the question.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports token recovery under latent corruption as a function of width, but it never measures, and never names as open, how much of that recovery is contextual guessing by the decoder.

relation.reason: The experiment uses the paper's released autoencoder to test a property (a language-model prior in the decoder) that the paper makes no claim about, so the paper's claims stand whichever way it comes out.

obvious.reason: Concern about decoders that fix up corrupted latents is familiar, but few researchers would put among their first ten follow-ups a test that measures masked-position fill-in against a dedicated causal LM.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would mainly change how people using this autoencoder, or close variants of it, read its corruption-robustness and Gen-PPL numbers.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan correctly states that the paper uses p_x=0.3 token-embedding dropout and reads Fig. 5a as retained information, and its other statements match the paper's text.

answerable.reason: The design gives masked-position accuracy for the decoder, a GPT-2 anchor, a unigram floor and a locality check, so a ratio either well above or well below the bar bears directly on whether the decoder carries a substantial language-model prior.

opus.what_came_out: On 300 FineWeb windows of 512 tokens with the released OWT autoencoder (D=768), the decoder's fill-in accuracy at the 22,800 masked positions per seed was about 0.32 against GPT-2 small's 0.38 (ratio 0.833; per-seed ratios 0.839, 0.835 and 0.825 over 3 mask seeds), against a unigram floor of 0.038; accuracy was 0.72 at GPT-2-predictable positions and 0.07 at unpredictable ones, and in the latent-noise sweep the predictable-minus-unpredictable gap at the 70%-accuracy noise level was about -0.01.

evidence.reason: The ratio is 0.83 and consistent across three seeds of 22,800 positions each, far above the unigram floor and concentrated at contextually predictable positions, which noise alone would not explain.

next_step.reason: The run clearly shows a strong contextual prior at removed positions, while the sweep suggests this prior does not drive recovery under latent noise; what remains open is whether the prior shapes decoded diffusion samples, which a small test can settle before investing in retraining with different p_x.

sol.what_it_asks: It compares AURORA’s frozen decoder’s recovery of tokens whose encoder-input embeddings are zeroed against GPT-2 small’s next-token predictions on held-out web text to assess the strength of its contextual language-model prior.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports reconstruction under latent corruption but neither measures information-removed fill-in against a causal language model nor explicitly leaves that comparison open.

relation.reason: The hypothesis tests an unreported property of the released autoencoder by using its encoder and decoder under information-removal interventions.

obvious.reason: Decoder-prior concerns are familiar, but specifically comparing input-masked decoder fill-in with a standalone causal language model would likely appear on only one or two first-ten lists.

misreads_paper.reason: The account of dropout, causal organization, embedding initialization and robustness testing agrees with the paper, while attributing contextual prediction to the decoder is an inference rather than a contradiction.

sol.what_came_out: On 300 FineWeb document windows, the released AURORA OWT autoencoder achieved a mean masked-token accuracy ratio of 0.83287 relative to GPT-2 small across three mask seeds with 22,800 targets each, with seed ratios spanning 0.82478–0.83899 and no confidence interval reported; seed-zero accuracies were 32.11% versus 38.27%.

prerequisite.reason: Clean reconstruction reached 99.926%, and the evaluation confirmed that unmasked-position accuracy exceeded the required 99% for every input-masking seed.

evidence.reason: The consistently substantial recovery across three masks on 300 documents, together with seed-zero target-latent-zeroing accuracy of 30.66% versus a 3.82% unigram floor, supports contextual prediction beyond noise, although the main condition alone cannot locate the prior uniquely in the decoder.

registration.title: Prefix re-anchoring: replace each generated latent block with the frozen encoder's re-encoding of its decoded tokens before it becomes context in AURORA-LM-S generation
registration.seed_connection: AURORA's block-causal denoiser is trained with two-stream teacher forcing. Every target block attends to clean prefix blocks produced by the frozen causal encoder (Sec. 3.4, Eq. 10). At inference, however, each block is conditioned on the model's own previously generated latents (Sec. 3.5, Eq. 16). The encoder is causal and prefix-aligned: latent i depends only on tokens 1..i (Sec. 3.2). So decoding a finished block and re-encoding the token prefix gives exactly the kind of clean prefix seen in training. The paper never measures how far generated latents drift from the encoder's latent manifold, or whether this train/test mismatch hurts later blocks.
registration.hypothesis: Replacing each finished latent block, before it is written to the KV cache as context, with the frozen encoder's re-encoding of its decoded tokens lowers the GPT-2-Large generative perplexity of 1024-token unconditional AURORA-LM-S samples by at least 5%. The comparison is against the standard continuous-prefix sampler: 32-step Euler ODE, self-conditioning on, no SC-CFG.
registration.contribution: This is the first measurement, in a block-causal continuous-latent LM trained only on encoder-produced clean prefixes, of two things. (i) How far generated latent blocks lie from the encoder's re-encoding of their own decoded tokens, as a function of block position and step budget. (ii) The effect of removing that gap at inference. A gain would motivate token-grounded samplers or training for continuous LMs. No gain, or a loss, would mean the uncommitted continuous prefix carries useful information beyond its tokens, which supports the paper's premise. CALM feeds back discrete tokens by architectural design. This experiment instead tests token re-grounding as an inference-time intervention in a model trained with continuous context.

closest_work.difference: CALM found that continuous latent vectors are worse inputs than discrete tokens, so it trains its next-vector model on the previous chunk's tokens. Here the model was trained only with continuous clean encoder latents as context, and token re-grounding is tested purely at inference against the model's native continuous-prefix sampler.
SSD-LM commits every block to tokens by design in simplex space. It never compares committed and continuous context, and has no learned causal encoder to re-project with.

Diffusion-LM's clamping rounds intermediate predictions to the nearest static word embedding inside the denoising of one sequence. Here completed blocks are re-projected with a contextual causal encoder, and the effect on later blocks is measured.
Studies discrete projection at commitment in a continuous next-token-embedding AR model trained from scratch, not a block-causal latent diffusion model with a frozen contextual autoencoder.
Cola-DLM conditions on generated continuous latent blocks, as AURORA does. It does not measure off-manifold drift or test re-encoding.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]')

AURORA-LM-S checkpoints from Hugging Face: fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (denoiser, step 250000) and fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, fetched with `python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder`. This also puts the GPT-2 small tokenizer and embedding source at models/gpt2-small.
openai-community/gpt2-large at models/gpt2-large (Gen-PPL scorer and MAUVE featurizer)

OpenWebText documents for MAUVE references and the autoencoder sanity check: stas/openwebtext-10k. Fallback: the first documents of Skylion007/openwebtext, streamed with revision='refs/convert/parquet'.
registration.method:
Setup and loading:
- Load with `cfg,_ = aurora.eval.core.config.load_config_from_checkpoint('checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors', project_root=REPO)` and `gen = aurora.eval.generators.diffusion.DiffusionGenerator(cfg, ckpt, device='cuda:0')`.
- Use `tr = gen.trainer`, which provides denoiser, autoencoder, ema, noise_scheduler and features.self_cond.
- If torch.compile or flex-attention recompiles per shape and is slow, set `cfg.operator_optimization.profile='off'` before constructing the generator.

Sampler: write `sample(reanchor, num_steps, seeds)` by copying the unconditional (no-prefix) path of `aurora/sampling/block_sampler.py::BlockSampler.run`, with these settings:
- Deterministic Euler (`tr.noise_scheduler.step(..., method=None)` on `tr.noise_scheduler.get_sigmas(N)`).
- EMA weights (`with tr.ema.average_parameters()`), block size 16, 64 blocks (1024 latents).
- Self-conditioning on via `tr.features.self_cond.resolve`, with x_0_self_cond=None at each block's first step.
- SC-CFG off: exactly one denoiser forward per step.

After a block's denoising loop yields `x_block` [B,16,768] (standardized latent space), and before the cache-write call (`tr.denoiser(x_t=..., time_t=zeros, kv_cache=..., block_start_idx=16*b, write_cache=True, block_size=16)`):
1. Set `ctx = cat(ctx_latents, x_block)`, where ctx_latents are the latents already written to the cache.
2. Compute `logits = tr.autoencoder.decode_latent(tr.autoencoder.denormalize_latent(ctx), target_token_len=16*(b+1))`. Take the argmax of the last 16 positions as the block's tokens and append them to the committed token tensor `tok`. Also record their mean max-softmax probability.
3. Re-encode: `raw,_ = tr.autoencoder.get_latent({'input_ids': tok, 'attention_mask': ones_like(tok)})` and `z_re = tr.autoencoder.normalize_latent(raw[:, 16*b:16*(b+1)])`.
4. Diagnostics per sample: relative squared distance ||x_block - z_re||^2 / ||z_re||^2, flattened cosine, and the decoder's max-probability when z_re replaces x_block in the same context.
5. Set `x_ctx = z_re` if reanchor else `x_block`. Write the KV cache with x_ctx and append it to ctx_latents.

Both arms execute steps 1-5. In the baseline arm the diagnostics do not alter generation. Both arms use identical seeds, so every block starts from the same Gaussian noise and block 0 is identical.

Final tokens:
- Baseline: argmax decode of the full generated latent sequence, as in DiffusionGenerator.generate.
- Re-anchored: the committed tokens.
- Format texts as the repo's eos_wrap mode (`aurora/eval/utils/eos_mode.py`): decode with skip_special_tokens=False and prepend one '<|endoftext|>' unless the first token is EOS.

Runs:
- Primary: 32 steps. Secondary: 16 steps.
- 512 samples per arm (4 batches of 128, batch seeds 1-4, the same in both arms).

Sanity control: encode and decode 64 OpenWebText sequences of 1024 GPT-2 tokens (prefixed with EOS). Token accuracy must be at least 0.99; otherwise stop and report.

Metrics:
- Corpus Gen-PPL: `aurora.eval.metrics_impl.compute_ppl(texts, model_id='models/gpt2-large')`.
- Per-sample NLL sums and token counts using the same first-EOS masking.
- Mean unigram entropy: `compute_token_entropy`.
- Repeated-4-gram fraction.
- MAUVE: `compute_mauve` against 512 OWT documents, with both sides truncated to 1024 GPT-2 tokens and decoded with skip_special_tokens=True.

event.description: In the primary configuration (32-step Euler, no SC-CFG, 512 samples of 1024 tokens), re-anchoring reduces corpus-level GPT-2-Large Gen-PPL by at least 5% relative to the standard sampler.
event.statistic: PPL_reanchor / PPL_baseline - 1 (corpus-level GPT-2-Large Gen-PPL, 32-step configuration)

evaluation.procedure:
Both arms' eos_wrap texts are scored with the repo's compute_ppl (GPT-2 Large; token NLL pooled over the corpus, first EOS kept, later EOS masked). The statistic is PPL_reanchor/PPL_baseline - 1 at 32 steps.

Also reported:
- The same ratio at 16 steps.
- The mean paired per-sample log-PPL difference, with a 2000-resample bootstrap 95% CI.
- Per-arm mean unigram entropy, repeated-4-gram fraction and MAUVE.
- Per-block drift curves: mean relative squared distance, cosine, and decoder max-probability on generated vs re-encoded latents.
- The autoencoder sanity accuracy.

Output files:
- outputs/samples.jsonl: one record per sample (arm, steps, seed, token ids, text).
- outputs/drift.jsonl: per-arm, per-step-budget, per-block diagnostics.
- outputs/per_sample_ppl.jsonl: per-sample NLL sum and token count for each arm and budget.
- outputs/metrics.json: all aggregate metrics, the sanity accuracy and the statistic.
evaluation.controls:
- Paired baseline arm with identical seeds and initial noises; drift diagnostics computed in both arms.
- Autoencoder round-trip check on real text to validate the encode/decode path.
- Entropy, repetition and MAUVE reported to detect perplexity changes caused by lost diversity.
- 16-step secondary budget to see whether the effect scales with sampling error.

registration.full_scale_study:
- Re-anchoring across solvers (Euler, SDE-DPM++), step budgets (8-64), SC-CFG scales and the released protocol, with 5 seeds x 1000 samples, plus prompt-conditioned XSum.
- Partial re-anchoring (interpolating generated and re-encoded latents) and noise-matched controls.
- Training-time variants: teacher forcing on re-encoded generated prefixes, prefix-noise augmentation.
- Analysis of how off-manifold drift accumulates with sequence length and relates to sample quality.

agent.reason: At the last Euler step the denoiser predicts from a fairly clean input (σ≈0.25), and the decoder is highly redundant, so re-encoded latents are probably close to the generated ones. A ≥5% Gen-PPL gain needs systematic off-manifold drift that accumulates over 64 blocks, which is possible but not the likeliest outcome; a bug in the custom loop would also count against the event.

judge_astra.reason: The clean-prefix training/inference mismatch makes re-encoding a plausible improvement for unguided Euler sampling, but projection can also discard useful continuous information. The 5% improvement is uncertain, and repeatedly encoding and decoding growing prefixes creates substantial implementation and runtime risk.

judge_fable.reason: Off-manifold prefix drift is plausible (the decoder tolerates huge latent corruption, so generated latents can be far from the encoder manifold without decoding errors) and committing tokens should improve coherence, but the rank-128 prefix input pathway may make the denoiser insensitive to drift, re-anchoring could raise diversity and hence PPL, and the 5% threshold plus a heavy, KV-cache-level implementation with ~35-min budget adds real failure risk.

judge_opus.reason: The last solver step predicts the clean latent at sigma≈0.25, and the decoder is robust at that noise level. Generated blocks therefore probably lie close to the encoder latents of their own decoded tokens, so replacing them with re-encodings should change little. A drop of 5% or more in Gen-PPL needs substantial prefix drift and compounding error, which is possible in the blurrier setting without guidance but unproven; the custom sampler also adds implementation risk.

judge_sol.reason: Clean-prefix teacher forcing makes re-anchoring a plausible improvement, but hard decoding and re-encoding could discard useful uncertainty rather than merely correct drift. Repeated full-prefix round trips also create substantial implementation and runtime risk.

judge_luna.reason: Re-encoding decoded blocks could bring inference prefixes closer to the encoder-produced prefixes used in training. But it may also discard useful information in generated latents or shift later-block conditioning, so a 5% perplexity gain is far from assured.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: denoiser trains on clean encoder prefixes (Sec 3.4 Eq.10) but infers on generated prefixes (Sec 3.5 Eq.16), and token-projection helped other diffusion LMs. Inference: re-anchoring should reduce mismatch but hard argmax errors may propagate and 32-step drift may be small, making a 5% corpus PPL gain uncertain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: CALM feeds the previous chunk's discrete tokens back as input by design and trains that way. It does not test token re-encoding at inference in a model trained only on clean continuous encoder-latent prefixes, and it does not measure how generated latents drift from re-encoded ones.

Cola-DLM is a block-causal DiT that, like AURORA, conditions on its own generated continuous latent blocks. As far as I found, it neither measures drift from the encoder manifold nor tries re-encoding decoded tokens.

HC-DLM reads tokens out of the continuous latent at every denoising step and feeds them back as a scaffold, but this is part of a trained joint model inside a single denoising chain. It is not a post-hoc inference intervention that re-encodes completed blocks with a frozen causal encoder.

Diffusion-LM's clamping snaps intermediate predictions to the nearest static word embedding inside one sequence's denoising. It does not re-project finished blocks with a contextual encoder before they are used as context for later blocks.

This paper treats error accumulation in continuous autoregressive models on music audio with noise augmentation at training time and low-level noise at inference. It does not re-ground context through tokens and a frozen encoder.

This report finds that generated latents can sit close to real encoder latents yet decode poorly, but it covers non-autoregressive draft refinement. It does not test re-encoding the prefix in block-causal generation.

opus.reason: I found no paper, the seed included, that measures how far a block-causal continuous-latent diffusion LM's generated blocks drift from the frozen encoder's re-encoding of their decoded tokens, or that tests swapping in those re-encodings as context at inference. The nearest work either feeds tokens back as an architectural or training choice (CALM, HC-DLM), clamps to static embeddings inside one sequence's denoising (Diffusion-LM), or fixes continuous-AR error accumulation by other means (noise augmentation). None of these settles the question for a model trained only on encoder-produced continuous prefixes. The search tool returned many off-topic results, so I can't rule out uncited or very recent work.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Latent Reasoning via Sentence Embedding Prediction trains with frozen-encoder, ground-truth latent context and explicitly compares decode-and-reencode feedback, M(h)=E(D(h)), against continuous pass-through, M(h)=h (Sections 3.2–3.5), including robustness to error accumulation (Section 4.3). The proposed experiment transfers this comparison to AURORA's block-causal diffusion sampler, measures unconditional Gen-PPL rather than reasoning accuracy, and adds block-position and solver-budget drift diagnostics.

Large Concept Models already investigates generated embeddings leaving the encoder-produced distribution using ordinary and decode/reencode round-trip distances to reference embeddings (Section 2.4.1). It does not report replacing completed generated context with re-encoded text and comparing subsequent generation against continuous feedback.

sol.reason: The central inference-only intervention and its continuous-feedback control already appear in Latent Reasoning via Sentence Embedding Prediction, under frozen-encoder teacher forcing. AURORA's contextual block latents, diffusion sampling, and detailed drift curves extend that established comparison, making this a close variant rather than an equivalent experiment. I found no prior report of the exact AURORA configuration or its specified Gen-PPL effect.

opus.reason: Both test whether generated latent prefixes drift from encoder-produced latents. Both replace each completed block with encode(argmax_decode(prefix)) before it becomes context, then measure round-trip drift by block and GPT-2 Large perplexity, entropy and MAUVE; #38 runs on a miniature trained model and Experiment 1 on the released checkpoint.

sol.reason: Both test generated-prefix drift by replacing completed latent prefixes with decode–reencode projections and measuring round-trip distance and downstream generation quality.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (reanchor/run_experiment.py, launched by run.sh):
- I copied the unconditional path of BlockSampler.run with the registered settings: deterministic Euler (method=None), EMA weights, block size 16, 64 blocks of 768-d latents, self-conditioning via tr.features.self_cond.resolve (None at each block's first step), and one denoiser forward per step (no SC-CFG).
- Steps 1-5 of the registration run for every block before the cache write: decode the context, take the argmax tokens of the last 16 positions and commit them, re-encode all committed tokens with the frozen encoder, normalize, compute the diagnostics, then write either x_block (baseline) or z_re (re-anchor) to the KV cache.
- Baseline final tokens are the argmax decode of the full generated latent sequence. Re-anchor final tokens are the committed tokens. Texts use eos_wrap.
- Settings: 512 samples per arm, batch seeds 1-4 with 128 samples each, 32-step primary and 16-step secondary.
- Scoring: Gen-PPL with the repo's compute_ppl (GPT-2 Large); per-sample NLL with the same first-EOS masking; compute_token_entropy; repeated-4-gram fraction; MAUVE against 512 docs from stas/openwebtext-10k; paired log-PPL difference with a 2000-resample bootstrap.
- AE sanity check: 64 EOS-prefixed 1024-token OWT sequences round-tripped at token accuracy 0.99902, which passes the 0.99 bar.

Changes from the registration, each made to keep the same question:
1. Each seed's two arms run in one batch of 256: rows 0-127 baseline, 128-255 re-anchor. Each block's noise is drawn once as randn(128,16,768), the same draw a single-arm batch makes with that seed, and both halves share it. This was needed to fit the 35-minute limit. Mathematically the arms are independent; bf16 kernels may differ by numerical noise.
2. While re-encoding during sampling, I set encoder.target_latent_len=0 so the encoder only computes as many queries as there are tokens. The encoder is causal and masks positions past the valid length, so the valid-position latents should be unchanged. This also saves time.
3. operator_optimization.profile is set to 'off'. On this A100 the FlexAttention path errored inside the AE encoder.
4. MAUVE: the GPT-2-Large featurization is done by my own batched code (final token, last layer, max 1024 tokens), then mauve.compute_mauve runs with its defaults. This is meant to match what aurora's compute_mauve does, but I did not compare the two outputs. The refs are the first 512 docs of stas/openwebtext-10k, as registered; those are probably OWT training docs rather than held-out text.
5. models/gpt2-small and gpt2-large are fetched with allow_patterns (safetensors and tokenizer files only) instead of the full download_models.py backbone download, to save time.
6. The AE sanity sequences are packed simply: EOS, then docs separated by EOS, cut to 1024 tokens. I did not reproduce the full Duo wrap packing.

Result of my full test run (21.5 min, from the full evaluation command; on a fresh machine add about 2 min for installs and downloads):
- **Primary statistic:** PPL_reanchor/PPL_baseline − 1 = **+0.179** at 32 steps (Gen-PPL 61.53 vs 52.17). The registered event (< −0.05) did not occur; re-anchoring made perplexity worse.
- Paired mean log-PPL difference (re-anchor − baseline) was +0.168, 95% CI [0.102, 0.236]. Only 34% of samples had lower PPL under re-anchoring.
- **16 steps:** ratio +0.239 (90.28 vs 72.89), paired difference +0.215, CI [0.157, 0.273].
- **Diversity:** entropy and repetition are about equal between arms (32 steps: entropy 5.345 vs 5.348, rep-4 0.065 vs 0.067), so lost diversity does not explain the PPL difference.
- **MAUVE:** low in both arms (32 steps: 0.221 baseline vs 0.244 re-anchor; 16 steps: 0.214 vs 0.212). This is far below the paper's MAUVE. Likely contributors are the 512/512 sample size, the different reference set, no SC-CFG and/or my featurization, but I did not isolate the cause, so MAUVE here supports only within-run comparison.
- **Drift:** generated blocks sit at relative squared distance ≈ 0.19 from their re-encodings (cosine ≈ 0.90), and this is roughly flat across block position. The decoder's max-probability is 0.995 on generated latents and ≈ 1.0 on re-encoded ones. Re-encoding changes almost no tokens (fraction ≈ 1e-5).
- The baseline's incrementally committed tokens match the full decode at 0.9999.
- The baseline 32-step PPL (52.2) is in line with the paper's Euler 32-step, no-SC-CFG value (50.5, Table 7).

Interpretation (inference, not tested): generated latents are measurably off the encoder's manifold even though they decode to the same tokens. Replacing them with token re-encodings hurts later blocks, which suggests the uncommitted continuous prefix carries information beyond its tokens that the denoiser uses. This is one run of 512 samples per arm with one autoencoder and checkpoint, so it does not establish the effect across solvers or guidance settings.

departures: Both arms run in one batch of 256 (rows 0-127 baseline, 128-255 re-anchor) sharing one randn(128,16,768) noise draw per block (reanchor/run_experiment.py::sample_batch). The registration asked for identical seeds and noises, and this gives exact pairing. Only bf16 numerical noise could differ. Reported. Unlikely to change the result.

ae.encoder.target_latent_len is set to 0 during in-loop re-encoding (run_experiment.py). The registration calls get_latent with default settings. The engineer argues that valid-position latents are unchanged because the encoder is causal, but this was never checked against a full-length encoding. The AE sanity check uses the default path, not this one. Reported but unverified. It could alter z_re, and therefore the re-anchor arm, if the variable_query encoder's outputs depend on query count. The near-1.0 decoder confidence on z_re makes a large distortion less likely.
operator_optimization.profile='off' (run_experiment.py load_generator). The registration explicitly allowed this. Unlikely to change the result.

MAUVE uses the engineer's own batched GPT-2-Large last-token featurization plus mauve.compute_mauve defaults, instead of aurora's compute_mauve, and was not cross-checked. There are only 512 refs, and clustering warnings appear in the log. Reported. Affects only a secondary metric, not the statistic.

MAUVE refs are the first 512 docs of stas/openwebtext-10k, loaded via the second (parquet) attempt after the first failed. These are likely training-distribution docs. This matches the registration's data source. Secondary metric only.
GPT-2 small and large are fetched with snapshot_download allow_patterns instead of download_models.py's full backbone download (run.sh, --skip-backbone). Unlikely to change the result.
AE sanity sequences use simple EOS-packing instead of the repo's Duo wrap packing (run_experiment.py::ae_sanity). The check passed at 0.999. Does not affect the statistic.

Per-sample NLL is computed by the engineer's own per_sample_nll, not the repo function. The corpus PPL from per-sample values (52.21 and 61.60) closely matches compute_ppl (52.17 and 61.52), so the reimplementation is consistent. Does not affect the statistic, which uses compute_ppl.
problems: The target_latent_len=0 shortcut for in-loop re-encoding (reanchor/run_experiment.py) was never compared to a full-length encode. The sanity check validated a different code path. The re-anchored arm therefore rests on an untested equivalence, though the decoder's ~1.0 max-prob on z_re and the near-zero token-change fraction (outputs/drift.jsonl) are reassuring.

Autoencoder eval mode is not set explicitly in the script (the encoder config has dropout 0.1). It presumably comes from DiffusionGenerator. The ~0.99999 re-encode confidence suggests no dropout noise, but this is not confirmed.

The registered drift-vs-step-budget analysis is reported, but the relative squared distance of ~0.19 between generated and re-encoded latents could partly reflect any encoder-path discrepancy, not purely generator drift.

MAUVE values (~0.21-0.24) are far below the paper's and use unverified custom featurization with only 512 refs (outputs/metrics.json, log clustering warnings). They support only rough within-run comparison.
There is a single run with one checkpoint, one solver, 512 samples per arm, and no SC-CFG. As the engineer notes, the result does not generalize to other samplers or guidance settings.

registration.title: Denoising-loss cloze scoring: ranking multiple-choice continuations with AURORA-LM-S's block-causal denoiser instead of likelihoods or generation
registration.seed_connection: The seed evaluates its scaled model only with a generative two-shot string-matching protocol (Sec. 4.3, App. A.2.9). Continuous-latent LMs have no tractable likelihood, and Cola-DLM argues that likelihood estimates are misaligned with generation. Yet AURORA's training objective, the clean-endpoint flow-matching loss with clean encoder prefixes and two-stream masking (Eqs. 10-11), gives a per-block conditional fit score. It can be computed for any candidate continuation of a context, without sampling.
registration.hypothesis: Ranking options by their mean clean-latent (x0) denoising error gives AURORA-LM-S (130M denoiser, OpenWebText) at least half of GPT-2 small's above-chance zero-shot accuracy, pooled over PIQA, ARC-Easy and HellaSwag. The error is conditioned on the encoder latents of the context and averaged over the training noise distribution.
registration.contribution: A training-free, sampling-free scoring rule that would let continuous-latent LMs take standard cloze-style zero-shot benchmarks. Its skill is quantified on identical items against an AR model of the same size. The result shows whether this model class can be benchmarked like AR models, or whether the noisy generative protocols used by the seed and Cola-DLM are unavoidable.

closest_work.difference: Diffusion Classifier ranks class prompts by image-diffusion denoising error. Here the candidates are text continuations, scored by a block-causal latent text denoiser under clean-prefix teacher forcing, on language benchmarks.
PLAID is likelihood-trained embedding diffusion with a tractable ELBO. AURORA has a deterministic frozen encoder and no likelihood, so a heuristic denoising-error ranking is tested instead.

Cola-DLM estimates likelihood via CNF change of variables with VAE posteriors, reports it misaligned with generation, and falls back to generative evaluation. We test a cheap denoising-error ranking on a related block-causal latent model.
CALM's BrierLM is a likelihood-free language-modeling metric estimated from model samples. We rank given candidates by denoising error, with no sampling.

inputs: AURORA-LM code (https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM) and checkpoints fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt and fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, via scripts/download_models.py --model owt autoencoder (provides models/gpt2-small)
PIQA validation: baber/piqa (fallback ybisk/piqa with revision='refs/convert/parquet')
ARC-Easy test: allenai/ai2_arc, config 'ARC-Easy'
HellaSwag validation: Rowan/hellaswag (fallback revision='refs/convert/parquet')
openai-community/gpt2 (GPT-2 small reference)
registration.method:
Load the model as in the repo's DiffusionGenerator: `cfg,_ = load_config_from_checkpoint('checkpoints/owt/250000.safetensors', project_root=REPO)`, `tr = DiffusionGenerator(cfg, ckpt, device='cuda:0').trainer`. Use EMA weights (`with tr.ema.average_parameters()`), bf16 autocast and no grad.

Items:
- PIQA: all 1838 validation items.
- ARC-Easy: first 1000 test items after shuffle(seed=42).
- HellaSwag: first 1000 validation items after shuffle(seed=42), with standard lm-eval preprocessing: ctx = activity_label + ': ' + ctx_a + ' ' + ctx_b.capitalize(), remove ' [title]' and bracketed tags, collapse spaces; same cleaning for endings.

Context and continuation strings:
- PIQA: 'Question: {goal}\nAnswer:' + ' {sol}'.
- ARC: 'Question: {question}\nAnswer:' + ' {choice text}'.
- HellaSwag: '{ctx}' + ' {ending}'.
- Tokenize context and continuation separately with the GPT-2 tokenizer.

AURORA score for each (item, option):
- Build `ids = [EOS] + F[-k:] + [EOS] + ctx_ids + opt_ids + [EOS]*p`. F is the GPT-2 tokenization of the fixed filler 'The following passage was taken from a large public collection of web documents about news, science, history, sports, cooking, travel and technology.' k in [0,15] is the smallest value that makes len([EOS]+F[-k:]+[EOS]+ctx_ids) a multiple of 16, so the option starts exactly at a block boundary. p pads the option's last block with EOS; extra all-EOS blocks may be appended to bucket lengths, since later blocks cannot affect earlier ones.
- Encode with `raw,_ = tr.autoencoder.get_latent({'input_ids': ids, 'attention_mask': ones})` and `z = tr.autoencoder.normalize_latent(raw[:, :S])`. Optional speed-up: temporarily set `tr.autoencoder.encoder.target_latent_len` to a small value after verifying on 5 sequences that the valid-position latents are unchanged.
- Noise levels: sigma_k = `tr.noise_scheduler._tanh_t_to_sigma(t_k)` with t_k = (k-0.5)/8, k=1..8. These are the quantiles of the training noise distribution (shift 7). Draw M=2 Gaussian noises per sigma, generated per item from a fixed seed and shared by all options of that item (common random numbers).
- For each of the 16 draws: x_t = (1-sigma)*z + sigma*eps, then `pred = tr.denoiser(x_t=x_t, time_t=sigma*ones(B), x_0_self_cond=None, clean_x=z, block_size=16)`. This is the training two-stream forward: each noisy block sees clean earlier blocks.
- Score = mean of (pred - z)^2 over the 16 draws, the option's positions and the 768 channels. Predict the option with the lowest score.

GPT-2 small: per-token mean log-probability of the continuation tokens given the context (no filler). Predict the argmax.

Controls:
- Context-free AURORA scoring on the first 500 items per task: ids = [EOS]+F[-k:]+[EOS]+opt_ids with block alignment.
- Single-sigma variants (sigma_1 only, sigma_8 only), computed from the stored per-draw errors.

event.description: Denoising-loss scoring recovers at least half of GPT-2 small's above-chance zero-shot accuracy, pooled over PIQA, ARC-Easy and HellaSwag on identical items.
event.statistic: Skill ratio = sum over tasks of (acc_AURORA - chance) / sum over tasks of (acc_GPT2small - chance), tasks = PIQA, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag

evaluation.procedure:
Accuracy per task for each scorer on the same items. chance_t is the mean over items of 1/(number of options). The skill ratio is computed as defined; if GPT-2's pooled margin is 0 or negative, the run is reported as invalid.

Also reported:
- Per-task accuracies with Wilson 95% CIs.
- Context-free accuracy.
- Single-sigma accuracies.
- Fraction of items where AURORA and GPT-2 agree.

Output files:
- outputs/item_scores.jsonl: per item and option, the AURORA score, the 16 per-draw errors, the context-free score when computed, the GPT-2 mean log-prob, and the gold label.
- outputs/metrics.json: per-task accuracies, chance levels, control results and the skill ratio.
evaluation.controls:
- Chance baseline.
- GPT-2 small (124M, trained on WebText) as a same-size AR reference on identical items and strings.
- Context-free scoring, to measure how much ranking comes from option priors (frequency, length) rather than context.
- Common random numbers across options.
- Single-noise-level variants as sensitivity checks.

models: AURORA-LM-S OWT denoiser + AURORA text autoencoder

registration.full_scale_study:
- Develop denoising-loss scoring into a likelihood-free evaluation suite for continuous-latent LMs.
- Compare noise weightings (training distribution, ELBO-style weights, high-noise only), more draws and PMI calibration.
- Extend to 10+ tasks and multiple model sizes and checkpoints.
- Measure rank agreement with AR log-likelihoods, with generative-protocol scores and with CNF likelihood estimates.
- If successful, re-benchmark published latent diffusion LMs with cloze-style scoring.

agent.reason: High-noise x0 errors should track how predictable an option's latents are from context, so above-chance accuracy on ARC-Easy and PIQA is likely. Reaching half of GPT-2 small's pooled skill is roughly a coin flip, given frequency and length biases and possible misalignment between the proxy and likelihood.

judge_astra.reason: Conditional denoising error plausibly contains useful contextual information, but recovering half the AR model's above-chance advantage is not assured. Clean-latent MSE can reflect latent geometry, reconstruction difficulty, and option priors rather than semantic correctness; averaging noise draws does not remove these biases.

judge_fable.reason: Denoising MSE under the training (high-noise-heavy) weighting is a loose likelihood proxy, 16 noise draws give noisy option rankings, and frequency/centrality biases of the latent geometry may dominate; GPT-2 small's pooled margin (~0.35) means AURORA needs roughly PIQA 57 / ARC-E 35 / HellaSwag 28.5, which is at the edge of what I expect.

judge_opus.reason: With nearly orthogonal, equal-norm token latents, high-noise x0 error behaves roughly like a linear-in-probability proxy for token likelihood. That should give above-chance accuracy, especially on PIQA and ARC-Easy, with paired noise across options reducing variance. Reaching half of GPT-2 small's pooled above-chance margin of about 0.34 is still demanding for a heuristic L2 score, and the internal API calls (time conditioning, self-conditioning input) could be misused.

judge_sol.reason: Conditional denoising error plausibly contains enough compatibility information to recover half of GPT-2-small's above-chance margin. However, squared latent error is not likelihood, and candidate rankings could be dominated by representation geometry, length, or option priors.

judge_luna.reason: Clean-latent denoising error may provide a context-sensitive signal, but it is not a conditional likelihood and could reward candidates that are easy to denoise rather than correct. Recovering half of GPT-2 small's above-chance margin therefore seems ambitious.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: seed uses only generative evaluation (Sec 4.3) and Cola-DLM reports likelihood misaligned with generation; scoring averages 16 draws over OOD cloze prompts. Inference: rankings are likely noisy and near chance, so reaching half of GPT-2 small's pooled above-chance margin is unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Diffusion Classifier ranks class prompts by how well an image diffusion model denoises under each one. The experiment applies the same idea to text: it ranks candidate continuations by clean-latent denoising error from a block-causal latent text denoiser that sees the clean prefix, and tests it on PIQA, ARC-Easy and HellaSwag against GPT-2 small. The core principle comes from this paper. Applying it to continuous-latent language models has not been reported.

This paper also treats denoising error as a stand-in for likelihood in zero-shot image classification with Stable Diffusion and Imagen. It does not cover text continuations, language benchmarks or latent text diffusion models.

The seed paper tests AURORA-LM-L only through generative two-shot prompting with answer extraction on nine benchmarks. AURORA-LM-S is evaluated only on generation (MAUVE, Gen-PPL, ROUGE). Its denoising loss is never used to rank answer options.

Cola-DLM argues that likelihood is not a good measure of capability for continuous latent diffusion language models and uses generation-based benchmarks instead. Its abstract does not mention cheap denoising-error ranking of candidate answers.

TextLDM is a continuous latent diffusion language model trained on OpenWebText2 and compared with GPT-2. Its abstract reports generation quality, not cloze-style multiple-choice scoring by denoising loss.
PLAID has a tractable likelihood bound (ELBO), so it can be scored by likelihood directly. The experiment needs a heuristic score because AURORA has a deterministic encoder and no likelihood.

opus.reason: I found no prior work that ranks multiple-choice text continuations by the denoising or flow-matching loss of a continuous-latent language model and compares the result with an autoregressive model of the same size. The scoring idea comes from Diffusion Classifier (2303.16203) and related image work. The continuous-latent text papers I found (the seed paper, Cola-DLM, TextLDM) evaluate through generation or likelihood, so the question is still open. I could not check LangFlow or ELF directly because I hit the tool-call limit, so a small risk remains that one of them already did something similar.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: STAR-LDM already ranks candidate text continuations using Monte Carlo estimates of conditional latent denoising error alone, reporting zero-shot PIQA, ARC-Easy and HellaSwag accuracy against autoregressive references (Section 5, Table 1). It uses Sentence-T5 sentence embeddings and ELBO-weighted noise-prediction error rather than AURORA's prefix-aligned block latents and training-distribution-averaged clean-endpoint error.

Diffusion Classifier establishes training-free classification through averaged denoising errors, including shared noise across candidates, but ranks conditioning prompts for a fixed image rather than text continuations for a fixed context.
The seed supplies the block-causal clean-latent objective but evaluates downstream benchmarks through generated-answer matching, not denoising-error candidate ranking.

sol.reason: STAR-LDM already tests the central contribution: using conditional continuous-latent denoising errors, without generating answers, to rank options on the same three language benchmarks. The proposed experiment changes the model, latent organization, error parameterization, weighting and comparison statistic, making it a close variant rather than an equivalent experiment.

opus.reason: No list entry proposes ranking multiple-choice options by the denoiser's clean-latent denoising error as a likelihood-free cloze scoring rule.

sol.reason: No list entry ranks candidate continuations using the latent denoiser’s clean-prediction error; the benchmark audits use generation or autoregressive likelihood scoring instead.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: `score_cloze.py`, launched by `run_eval.sh`. `run_eval.sh` installs the seed repo, runs `setup_models.py` to download the checkpoints, then scores the items. The scoring follows the registered method:
- **Model:** AURORA-LM-S OWT 250k checkpoint loaded through DiffusionGenerator, with EMA weights, bf16 autocast and no grad.
- **Items:** all 1838 PIQA validation items; ARC-Easy test and HellaSwag validation each shuffled with seed 42, first 1000 kept.
- **Input layout:** filler prefix with block alignment, so every option starts at a block boundary. Each option is EOS-padded to a 16-multiple.
- **Noise:** sigma_k = `_tanh_t_to_sigma((k-0.5)/8)` with shift 7. Two Gaussian draws per sigma give 16 draws. The noise comes from a per-item seeded generator and all options of an item share it (common random numbers).
- **Forward pass:** the training two-stream forward, `denoiser(x_t, time_t=sigma, x_0_self_cond=None, clean_x=z, block_size=16)`.
- **Score:** squared error averaged over the 16 draws, the option's latent positions and the 768 channels. The lowest score is the prediction.
- **GPT-2 small:** per-token mean log-prob of the option given the context, with no filler.
