evidence.reason: Judging from 256 samples per configuration in one repetition rather than a reported interval, the substantial 30.3% primary reversal and consistent direction across guidance settings provide evidence against the claimed GPT-2-Large advantage.

next_step.reason: The primary reversal warrants checking an actually sampled entropy-matched AR point before committing to a much larger comparison based on the interpolated frontier.
next_step.what: Directly tune and sample GPT-2-small near the matched temperature of 0.854, repeating across independent seeds and estimating uncertainty in the entropy-matched perplexity ratio.

registration.title: Training-free exposure-bias test for AURORA-LM-S: condition each new latent block on the re-encoded tokens of the generated prefix instead of on the denoiser's own generated latents
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM trains its block-causal denoiser with clean frozen-encoder latents of real text as the prefix of every block (two-stream teacher forcing, Sec. 3.4, Eq. 10). At inference, each block is instead conditioned on the denoiser's own previously generated blocks (Sec. 3.5, Eq. 16). At c=1 the frozen query encoder and decoder are prefix-causal (Eqs. 2-3): encoder latent i reads tokens 1..i, and decoder token j reads latents 1..j. A finished block can therefore be decoded to tokens and re-encoded into exactly the kind of latent the denoiser saw as context in training. Comparing the two conditioning modes isolates this train-test mismatch in the paper's blockwise generation with no retraining. The paper never measures it.
registration.hypothesis: Under unguided 32-step ODE sampling with self-conditioning, conditioning each new AURORA-LM-S block on the frozen encoder's re-encoding of the decoded prefix, instead of on the generated latents, lowers GPT-2-Large generative perplexity by more than 5% (relative) while lowering mean unigram entropy by no more than 0.05 nats.
registration.contribution: A paired, inference-only causal measurement of exposure bias in a continuous-latent block diffusion LM trained with continuous teacher forcing. The three outcomes are separable. (a) Re-encoding helps: the mismatch costs quality, and a free inference fix exists. (b) Re-encoding hurts: generated latents carry useful non-token context. (c) Nothing changes: read together with the measured drift, generated latents are near-canonical or the denoiser is insensitive to the difference. The experiment also reports per-block drift of generated latents from the encoder manifold, and how often the frozen decoder is uncertain on generated versus real latents.

closest_work.difference: CALM reports that feeding predicted continuous vectors back as input hurts, so it trains its next-vector AR model on discrete-token inputs from the start. Here the released model was trained on continuous encoder-latent context, and token grounding is imposed only at inference through the frozen prefix-causal encoder. This measures the mismatch rather than designing around it.
SSD-LM conditions each block on previously decoded discrete tokens by construction. It has no learned continuous latent context and no grounded-versus-ungrounded comparison.

Self Forcing removes exposure bias in autoregressive video diffusion by training on self-generated context. This experiment is inference-only and first asks whether the mismatch matters at all for block-causal text latents.
Cola-DLM's block-causal latent DiT also conditions on its own generated latent blocks, but it neither re-encodes them nor measures their drift.
The seed paper trains with clean encoder prefixes and samples with generated prefixes without quantifying the mismatch.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; keep a preinstalled torch>=2.5 if the pinned build conflicts)

Released checkpoints via 'python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder': HF fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (250000.safetensors), fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder (100000.safetensors), GPT-2 small backbone/tokenizer
GPT-2 Large (HF 'gpt2-large' / 'openai-community/gpt2-large'), used as Gen-PPL scorer and MAUVE featurizer
OpenWebText documents: HF 'stas/openwebtext-10k' (fallback 'Elriggs/openwebtext-100k')
pip packages: mauve-text, transformers, datasets
registration.method:
(0) Preflight and stop rule.
- Install the repo, then download the checkpoints and GPT-2 Large.
- Load the OWT model as the repo's generation script does. Expected names (verify in the code): cfg,_ = load_config_from_checkpoint(ckpt, project_root=REPO); gen = DiffusionGenerator(cfg, ckpt, device='cuda:0'); tr = gen.trainer; ae = tr.autoencoder; tok = tr.tokenizer.
- If torch.compile warm-up or recompilation is slow, pass the config override operator_optimization.profile=off.
- Generate 8 samples with the stock generator (solver 'euler', 32 steps, self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0, 512 tokens, eos_mode 'eos_wrap', seed 1) and time them.
- If the repository, the checkpoints or CUDA execution cannot be made to work within 10 minutes: write summary.json with status 'release_unavailable', the error text and event_occurred=null, then stop. Do not substitute other models.
(1) Patched sampler.
- Copy the unconditional path of the repo's KV-cache block sampler (expected: BlockSampler.run in src/aurora/sampling/block_sampler.py) into a new function with a boolean flag reencode.
- Keep EMA weights, self-conditioning, SC-CFG, solver updates and KV-cache handling unchanged.
- Insert steps (a)-(e) immediately after the denoising loop of block b ends and before the time-0 forward that writes the block into the KV cache. At that point x_block is final, in normalized latent space, with shape [B,16,768].
(a) P = 16(b+1). prefix = concatenation of the context blocks finalized so far and x_block, shape [B,P,768].
(b) Decode ae.decode_latent(ae.denormalize_latent(prefix), target_token_len=P) in sub-batches of at most 32 samples. For positions 16b..16b+15 keep only the argmax ids and the float32 maximum softmax probability. Never hold full-vocabulary logits for the whole batch. Append the ids to a token buffer T.
(c) Re-encode: raw = encoder latents of T[:, :P] with an all-ones attention mask (expected: ae.get_latent({'input_ids': ..., 'attention_mask': ...})[0]). z_re = ae.normalize_latent(raw)[:, 16b:P].
(d) Diagnostics, computed in both arms:
- drift_b = mean over samples, positions and channels of (x_block - z_re)^2 in standardized units, plus its ratio to the mean of z_re^2.
- confidence_b = mean maximum probability, and the fractions of block-b tokens with maximum probability below 0.5 and below 0.9, when decoding x_block.
- On the first 200 samples of each run: token agreement_b = fraction of block-b tokens whose argmax decode is the same when block b is x_block or z_re (same context).
(e) If reencode is true, set x_block = z_re. Everything downstream receives x_block: the cache write, block finalization, and the context for later blocks.
- The baseline arm is the same function with reencode=False.
- Decoding and encoding run in eval mode without dropout and consume no random numbers. With the same seed, both arms therefore receive identical initial noise (and identical SDE noise), and sample i is paired across arms.
- Final texts: the baseline arm uses the argmax decode of the full generated latent sequence, as the stock generator does; the re-encode arm uses buffer T. Both go through the stock generator's id-to-text post-processing and tok.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=False).
- When the SC-CFG scale is 1.0, the no-self-conditioning forward may be skipped (prediction = self-conditioned prediction). This is numerically identical.
(2) Checks (written to sanity.json).
(i) With reencode=False, the patched function reproduces the stock generator on the preflight setting for at least 99% of tokens.
(ii) On 16 real 512-token chunks, decoding the first 256 latents with target_token_len=256 gives the same tokens as the first 256 tokens of the full-length decode.
(iii) Autoencoder round trip on 200 real 512-token chunks: token accuracy (expected at least 99.5%), and the confidence statistics of step (1d) on real latents.
(iv) In the main runs, block-0 tokens are identical across arms for at least 99% of samples. In the re-encode arm, decoding the final stored latent sequence reproduces T for at least 99% of tokens.
(3) Runs.
- All runs generate 512 tokens (32 blocks) with eos_mode 'eos_wrap'. Generate only these blocks; do not generate 64 and truncate.
- Primary configuration: solver 'euler', 32 steps, self-conditioning on, self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0 passed explicitly (no guidance), 1000 samples per arm, batch at most 500, seed 1.
- Secondary configuration (the released guided protocol): solver 'sde_dpmpp', 64 steps, self_cond_cfg_scale=4.0, 500 samples per arm, seed 1.
- Pilot: time one primary re-encode batch first. If the four runs are projected to exceed 17 minutes, use 300 samples per arm in the secondary configuration. If still over, also use 600 per arm in the primary configuration. These fallbacks are pre-registered; record which applied.
(4) Real text.
- GPT-2-tokenize the OWT documents and concatenate them with EOS (50256) separators.
- Cut 512-token chunks that each start with EOS, decode with skip_special_tokens=False, and shuffle with seed 0.
- The first 1000 chunks are the MAUVE references. The next 1000 are the real-text ceiling set; its first 200 serve check (iii).
(5) Metrics per run.
- Gen-PPL: retokenize each text with the GPT-2 tokenizer and truncate to 1024 tokens. Corpus Gen-PPL = exp of the token-weighted mean GPT-2-Large NLL over positions >= 1. Keep each sample's mean NLL.
- Second-half Gen-PPL: the same, restricted to positions in the second half of each retokenized sequence, still conditioned on the first half.
- Unigram entropy: per-sample entropy in nats of the empirical distribution of its retokenized ids, averaged over samples.
- MAUVE: mauve-text with GPT-2-Large features, max_text_length=512, mauve seed 25, reference features computed once. If the package cannot load a local model path, compute features manually and pass p_features/q_features.
- Real-text ceiling: MAUVE of the ceiling set against the references.

event.description: In the primary (unguided) configuration, re-encoding lowers corpus Gen-PPL by more than 5% relative to the paired baseline arm, and the re-encode arm's mean unigram entropy is no more than 0.05 nats below the baseline arm's.
event.statistic: Guarded relative Gen-PPL reduction in the primary configuration: (GenPPL_baseline - GenPPL_reencode) / GenPPL_baseline if mean entropy_reencode >= mean entropy_baseline - 0.05, otherwise -1

evaluation.procedure:
Computation:
- Compute Gen-PPL, second-half Gen-PPL, entropy and MAUVE for the four runs against the same references.
- The statistic comes from the primary pair with the entropy guard applied. The unguarded reduction is also reported.
- Paired uncertainty: bootstrap over sample indices (10,000 resamples) of the mean per-sample difference in GPT-2-Large mean NLL and of the relative corpus Gen-PPL reduction, with 95% intervals.
- A Gen-PPL increase of more than 5% under re-encoding at matched entropy is reported as evidence that generated latents carry useful non-token context.
- Diagnostics: drift, drift ratio, token agreement and decoder confidence versus block index, in both arms of both configurations, compared with decoder confidence on real latents.
Interpretation: re-encoding both moves the context onto the encoder manifold and commits it to argmax tokens. A null result therefore does not by itself show that generated latents are canonical (the drift curves address that), and a positive result is read alongside the confidence diagnostics.
Files:
- samples.jsonl: one record per sample (configuration, arm, index, token ids, text, mean NLL, entropy).
- blocks.csv: one row per configuration, arm and block, with drift, drift ratio, token agreement and confidence statistics.
- metrics.json: all per-run metrics and wall-clock times.
- sanity.json: the check results.
- summary.json: the statistic, the unguarded reduction, the guard result, bootstrap intervals, the fallbacks applied and the event flag.
evaluation.controls:
- Paired baseline arm: same checkpoint, patched code path, seed and noise, with re-encoding off.
- Reproduction of the stock sampler.
- Prefix-decoding and autoencoder round-trip checks on real text, showing that re-encoding is near-lossless on real data.
- Block-0 identity across arms.
- Entropy guard, so that diversity loss cannot count as a quality gain.
- Real-text MAUVE ceiling.
- Guided secondary configuration (released protocol), to see whether the effect survives guidance. Under SC-CFG the cached block is a guidance-extrapolated estimate, so the unguided pair carries the primary interpretation.

registration.full_scale_study: Five seeds; lengths up to 1024 tokens; several solvers, step counts, SC-CFG scales and block sizes; and the released XSum checkpoint. If re-encoding helps, compare it at matched compute with training-time remedies at OWT128 scale: noise-augmented clean prefixes, training on re-encoded or self-generated prefixes (self-forcing style), and a denoiser with token-grounded context. Also add an arm that perturbs the re-encoded context with isotropic noise of the measured drift magnitude, to test whether the structure or only the size of the drift matters. If re-encoding hurts, probe which non-token information generated latents carry, for example with linear probes for upcoming tokens.

agent.reason: The generated latents are x0 predictions made from a fairly low-noise state, so they are probably close to canonical encoder latents, and a 130M denoiser should tolerate modest drift in its context; a Gen-PPL reduction above 5% with entropy held is plausible but below even odds. On top of that, there is release risk (code built for Ascend NPUs, untested on CUDA) and the custom sampler patch has to be implemented correctly.

judge_astra.reason: Training on encoder-produced prefixes makes latent drift a plausible quality bottleneck, so re-encoding could improve consistency with the decoded text. However, it also discards latent uncertainty, may reduce entropy, and requires substantial sampler modifications; the guarded improvement is not assured.

judge_fable.reason: The final x0-prediction step should leave generated latents close to the encoder manifold and the decoder/denoiser are robust to small perturbations, so a >5% Gen-PPL gain from re-encoding is possible (cross-block incoherence from ambiguous latents) but not the most likely outcome; the patched KV-cache sampler plus four runs, checks and MAUVE is also the most implementation-risky registration under the 35-minute budget.

judge_opus.reason: My expectation is that generated latents stay fairly close to the encoder manifold. The final step is a low-noise clean-latent prediction, and with D=768 the token content is near-certain at that noise level, so re-encoding probably moves corpus Gen-PPL by only a few percent. A >5% gain is plausible if the shift compounds over 32 blocks, but less likely than not. The heavily patched KV-cache sampler and the CUDA port of NPU-developed code add failure risk.

judge_sol.reason: Re-encoding plausibly reduces the mismatch between training prefixes and generated latent context, but it also removes continuous information that may help subsequent blocks. The tight entropy guard and substantial sampler modifications make the registered event harder to achieve than a generic quality improvement.

judge_luna.reason: The denoiser is trained with clean encoder-latent prefixes, so re-encoding decoded prefixes could reduce a real train–inference mismatch. But it also hardens each block to argmax text and may discard useful continuous information; the paper does not report generated-latent drift, so a greater-than-5% perplexity gain without the entropy penalty is uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Re-encoding grounds context on the training manifold, but argmax commitment discards uncertainty and early blocks are identical across arms, so a >5% full-sequence PPL gain is possible but unlikely if drift is small.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: CALM's ablation found that feeding predicted continuous vectors back as autoregressive input hurts, so it designs the model around discrete-token inputs during training. The experiment instead uses a model already trained on continuous encoder-latent context and compares, at inference only and with paired noise, conditioning on generated latents versus conditioning on the decoded and re-encoded prefix. It also measures how far generated latents drift from real encoder latents.

The seed paper trains with clean encoder prefixes and samples by conditioning on its own generated blocks (Eqs. 10 and 16). In the sections read, it never quantifies this mismatch and never tries re-encoding.
Cola-DLM uses a similar block-causal latent DiT that conditions on its own generated latent blocks. It does not re-encode them or measure their drift.
SSD-LM conditions each block on decoded discrete tokens by design. It has no learned continuous latent context, so there is no grounded-versus-ungrounded comparison.

This work also diagnoses the gap between generated latents and the encoder or decoder (decoder recoverability of latents that look close to real ones). But it studies draft refinement with BERT latents, not block-causal context conditioning, and does not test re-encoding the generated prefix.
Self Forcing addresses exposure bias in autoregressive video diffusion with a training-time fix. It is not an inference-only re-encoding test, and it is not about text latents.

opus.reason: I found no paper that runs this paired, inference-only test of decoding and re-encoding the generated prefix in a continuous-latent block-diffusion language model, or that measures how far generated text latents drift from the encoder's latents block by block. The closest work is CALM's training-time finding that feeding predicted vectors back as input hurts. That is a different setup and does not settle whether re-encoding helps a model trained on continuous latent context, like AURORA-LM. The seed paper and Cola-DLM both condition on generated latents without measuring the mismatch.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Latent Reasoning via Sentence Embedding Prediction trains a latent autoregressor on ground-truth embeddings from a fixed encoder, then compares direct propagation of predicted latents against decoding and re-encoding them at inference (Sections 3.2–3.5). It also tests whether this language grounding mitigates perturbation-induced error accumulation (Section 4.3). The proposed experiment applies this same conditioning intervention to block-causal diffusion text generation, adding paired sampling, entropy-guarded Gen-PPL and blockwise drift/confidence diagnostics.

Large Concept Models generates continuous sentence embeddings autoregressively, including with diffusion, and reports round-trip embedding diagnostics after decoding and re-encoding. These diagnostics compare predictions with ground-truth continuation embeddings; the paper does not report the proposed inference comparison between re-encoded and directly propagated generated prefixes.

CALM reports degraded performance with latent-vector inputs and instead trains its autoregressive backbone with compressed discrete-token inputs. This changes the trained input representation rather than testing decode–re-encode feedback solely at inference in a model trained on encoder-latent context.

AURORA-LM uses clean encoder prefixes during training and generated latent prefixes during sampling, but its reported ablations concern latent capacity, diffusion objectives, self-trajectory consistency and block granularity—not the proposed prefix re-encoding comparison.

sol.reason: The central inference-only comparison already appears in Latent Reasoning via Sentence Embedding Prediction: pass generated continuous states directly to subsequent steps, or decode and re-encode them using the fixed text interface. Applying that comparison to AURORA-LM changes the model, task and evaluation while adding useful diagnostics, making it a close variant rather than an unprecedented experiment. None of the work found establishes the proposed AURORA-specific effect or its preregistered threshold.

opus.reason: Both test exposure bias by replacing each completed generated latent prefix with the re-encoding of its argmax-decoded tokens. Both measure latent drift and compare generation quality (perplexity, entropy, MAUVE) against ordinary latent-prefix conditioning; entry 38 uses a miniature retrained pipeline instead of the released checkpoint.

sol.reason: Both replace generated latent prefixes with their decode–reencode projections and measure subsequent generation quality alongside latent round-trip drift.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I ran: `run_eval.sh` copies the seed repo to /tmp/aurora_repo, runs `pip install -e '.[eval]'` with transformers==4.57.1 and datasets==4.8.5 pinned, downloads the released OWT denoiser (250k), the autoencoder (100k), GPT-2 small and GPT-2 Large, then runs `reencode/run_reencode.py`. My full test of this command took about 21 minutes end to end.

Implementation: I copied the unconditional path of BlockSampler.run into a new function, keeping EMA weights, self-conditioning, SC-CFG, the solver step, the KV cache and `_finalize_generated_block` unchanged. Steps (a)-(e) are inserted after each block's denoising loop and before the time-0 cache write:
- decode the prefix in sub-batches of 32, keeping argmax ids and max-probability only for block b;
- re-encode the token buffer T with an all-ones attention mask, then normalise and slice the block-b latents;
- compute drift, decoder confidence, and token agreement on the first 200 samples;
- in the re-encode arm only, replace x_block with the re-encoded latents.

Both arms consume identical random numbers, so samples are paired. Metrics follow the registration: GPT-2-Large Gen-PPL, second-half Gen-PPL, unigram entropy, MAUVE with seed 25 against 1000 OWT reference chunks, a 1000-chunk real-text ceiling, and a 10k paired bootstrap.

Deviations, kept as small as possible:
1. **No skipped forward pass at self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0.** The registration allowed skipping the no-self-conditioning forward, assuming it was numerically identical. It isn't: in bf16, no_sc + (sc − no_sc) ≠ sc. With the skip, check (i) matched the stock generator on only 82% of tokens. So both forward passes run in both arms, exactly as the stock generator does, and check (i) now agrees on 100% of tokens.
2. **Dataset fallback.** stas/openwebtext-10k is script-based and won't load with current `datasets`, so the registered fallback Elriggs/openwebtext-100k is used (the first 6000 documents, non-overlapping 512-token chunks each starting with EOS, shuffled with seed 0).
3. **Pre-registered size fallback.** The pilot projected 17.5 minutes for the four runs, so the secondary (guided) configuration used 300 samples per arm. The primary configuration kept 1000 per arm.
4. **Manual MAUVE features.** These are GPT-2-Large final-layer hidden states at the last token (text truncated to 512 tokens), passed to mauve as p_features/q_features.
5. **Dependency pins.** transformers and datasets were pinned because the latest versions break the dataset and hub imports.

Results from my test run (repetitions=1, seed 1):
- **Primary, unguided 32-step Euler.** Gen-PPL is 62.25 for the baseline and 70.55 with re-encoding, a −13.3% change (95% bootstrap CI −17.5% to −9.3%). Entropy passes the guard (5.020 vs 5.017). The statistic is −0.133, so the registered event (a reduction greater than 0.05) did not occur. Re-encoding made Gen-PPL worse by more than 5% at matched entropy, which is the registration's outcome (b): evidence that generated latents carry useful non-token context. MAUVE also fell, from 0.949 to 0.887.
- **Secondary, guided (SDE-DPM++, 64 steps, SC-CFG 4).** Gen-PPL went from 30.12 to 28.84 (+4.2% reduction, CI −3.7% to +11.7%, so not distinguishable from zero), but entropy dropped by 0.055 nats, so the guard fails.
- **Diagnostics.** The drift ratio of generated latents from the re-encoded ones is about 0.17–0.19 unguided and about 0.22–0.26 guided. Token agreement is about 1.0. Decoder confidence is about 0.995 on generated latents versus 0.99998 on real latents.

All sanity checks pass:
- (i) stock reproduction: 1.0;
- (ii) prefix decoding: 1.0;
- (iii) autoencoder round trip: 0.99999;
- (iv) block 0 identical across arms in ≥99.6% of samples, and the re-encode arm's final latents decode back to T on ≥99.99% of tokens.

These numbers are from one seed. Under the re-encode-only, no-retraining setup tested here, the evidence is that re-encoding hurts unguided quality. They do not show what training-time fixes would do.

departures: Real-text source (run_reencode.py, metrics.json 'dataset'): stas/openwebtext-10k failed to load because dataset scripts are no longer supported, so the run used the registered fallback Elriggs/openwebtext-100k. This only affects the MAUVE references and the real-text ceiling, not the Gen-PPL statistic. Pre-registered, so not a fidelity defect.

Only the first 6000 documents of the fallback dataset are tokenized (run_reencode.py, n_docs = min(len(ds), 6000)). This yields 4408 chunks, enough for the 2000 needed. It is not mentioned in the registration and is only partly disclosed. It affects MAUVE references only and cannot change the statistic.

Secondary (guided) configuration ran 300 samples per arm instead of 500 (summary.json fallbacks_applied). The pilot projection of 17.5 min exceeded the registered 17 min trigger, so this is the pre-registered fallback, recorded as required. It does not affect the primary statistic.

The optional skip of the no-self-conditioning forward at SC-CFG scale 1.0 was not used. Both forwards run, as in the stock sampler (SKIP_NOSC=0). The registration permitted but did not require the skip, and its 'numerically identical' premise was wrong in bf16 (82% vs 100% stock agreement). Using the stock path is the more faithful choice.

MAUVE is computed from manually extracted GPT-2-Large final-layer last-token features passed as p_features/q_features (run_reencode.py mauve_score). The registration allows this fallback. It affects MAUVE only.
transformers==4.57.1 and datasets==4.8.5 are pinned in run_eval.sh. This was needed for the registered pipeline to import and run, and plausibly does not change the value.

TF32 matmuls are enabled globally, including for the float32 GPT-2-Large scorer (run_reencode.py). This is a small numerical effect applied symmetrically to both arms and cannot plausibly move a 13% gap.

The primary re-encode arm is split into a pilot batch via run_arm plus a direct sample_patched continuation. The baseline is a single run_arm. Decode and encode consume no RNG, so the noise streams should align; block-0 identity of 0.993 supports pairing. Not a departure in substance.
problems: Single seed and single checkpoint (registered repetitions=1). The bootstrap CI covers sample variability only, not seed or run-to-run variability.

The engineer's reading of outcome (b), 'generated latents carry useful non-token context', is stronger than the evidence strictly supports. Token agreement is 1.0, so re-encoding changes no committed tokens; it only replaces about 18% (drift ratio) of the latent signal. The result shows the denoiser does better conditioned on its own off-manifold latents than on canonical encoder latents of the same tokens. It does not identify what that extra content is; it could be self-consistency with its own sampling trajectory rather than useful semantics. The registration itself flags this conflation.

Secondary (guided) results conflict in direction with the engineer's earlier quick run (quick_out/summary.json: -33% at n=32 vs +4.2% at n=300 in the evaluation). The guided effect is therefore not established; at n=300 the CI includes zero and the entropy guard fails.
The quality metric is GPT-2-Large Gen-PPL plus MAUVE only. The MAUVE drop for the primary pair (0.949 to 0.887) is not accompanied by MAUVE uncertainty.
Real-text references come from only the first 6000 fallback documents, which is undisclosed in detail. This is minor and limited to MAUVE.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered patched block sampler, with re-encoding inserted after each block's denoising loop and before the cache write. Both arms are paired, all registered checks pass (stock reproduction 1.0, prefix decoding 1.0, round trip 0.99999, block-0 identity 0.993), and the guarded statistic is computed exactly as registered. Every departure is either a pre-registered fallback or a permitted choice, and none touches the primary statistic. The protected run reproduces the engineer's reported numbers: re-encoding raises unguided Gen-PPL from 62.2 to 70.5 (statistic -0.133, 95% CI -17.5% to -9.3%) at matched entropy, so the event did not occur and the registered 'hurts' outcome holds. This is a credible, well-controlled negative finding against the hypothesis that a free inference-time exposure-bias fix exists. Its value is limited by the single seed and checkpoint, by Gen-PPL/MAUVE as the only quality measures, and by the mechanistic interpretation being underdetermined.

departures: Data scope: reencode/run_reencode.py uses only the first 6000 documents of Elriggs/openwebtext-100k before constructing and shuffling 4408 chunks. The dataset fallback itself was registered, but this document cap was not specified. It can change MAUVE, the real-text ceiling and real-latent diagnostics; it does not affect the unconditional generations or the primary Gen-PPL statistic.

Sample size: outputs/reencode/summary.json records 300 samples per secondary arm rather than 500, following the registered runtime fallback after a 17.5-minute projection. This can change secondary estimates and their precision, but is an authorized adjustment and leaves the primary 1000-sample pair unchanged.

Runtime choices: run_eval.sh pins transformers and datasets; reencode/run_reencode.py disables operator optimization, enables TF32, and retains both self-conditioning forwards at scale 1. The dependency and precision choices were not fixed by registration, disabling optimization was permitted, and skipping the forward was optional. Numerical behavior can depend on these choices, but retaining both forwards preserves stock behavior, with observed stock reproduction of 100%.

MAUVE implementation: reencode/run_reencode.py supplies manually computed GPT-2-Large final-layer features rather than asking mauve-text to load the model. This was a registered alternative. Features are taken at the last position within the first 512 tokens; causal attention makes later scored tokens irrelevant to that feature. This does not affect the primary statistic.

Failure handling: run_eval.sh and reencode/run_reencode.py do not enforce the registered ten-minute release-availability deadline. Downloads occur outside the Python preflight exception handler, installation/download failures can be followed by continued execution, and the shell pipeline does not propagate Python failures reliably. These differences could change failure status on another run, but the protected run reached successful CUDA preflight well within the deadline and completed.

Sanity acceptance: reencode/run_reencode.py accepts 99% prefix-decoding agreement for check (ii), whereas the registration calls for identical prefix tokens. Actual agreement was 100%, so the weaker acceptance rule did not affect this result.

Diagnostic reporting: outputs/reencode/sanity.json reports real-latent confidence means and below-0.9 fractions by block, but only a global below-0.5 fraction. Thus the requested blockwise confidence comparison is not fully reported for that threshold. This limits auxiliary diagnostic completeness, not the primary statistic.

Timing accounting: the primary re-encode continuation in reencode/run_reencode.py does not add its final decoding time to the final_decode timer. registration.title: Compute-matched autoregressive reference under AURORA-LM-L's own 2-shot generative benchmark protocol: Pythia-1.4B (final and intermediate checkpoints) versus the reported AURORA-LM-L scores
registration.seed_connection: The scaling evaluation (Table 4) compares AURORA-LM-L (about 1B-parameter denoiser) only with Cola-DLM. Several AURORA-LM-L scores are at or below the level of a uniformly random valid option: HellaSwag 18.4 and MMLU 22.2 against 25, and SIQA 30.2 against 33.3. Table 6 reports about 1,406 EFLOPs (denoiser) plus about 157 EFLOPs (autoencoder), under 3ND accounting with one multiply-accumulate counted as one operation. Doubling to standard FLOPs gives about 3.1e21 (our conversion). The denoiser saw about 590k x 1024 x 512 = 3.1e11 tokens. Pythia-1.4B was trained on about 3.0e11 tokens with 6ND of about 2.5e21 FLOPs (about 0.8x). Running the paper's documented protocol (Appendix A.2.9, Tables 10 and 17) on this public AR model shows whether AURORA-LM-L's scores reflect competitive capability or a protocol floor.
registration.hypothesis: Under the seed's 2-shot generative answer-extraction protocol with strict option matching, Pythia-1.4B's macro-average over the benchmark tasks exceeds AURORA-LM-L's reported macro-average over the same tasks by more than 5 percentage points.
registration.contribution: The missing compute-matched autoregressive reference for the paper's scaling claim. It adds a decomposition of each score into parse rate and accuracy among parsed outputs, per-task random-valid-option baselines, protocol-independent log-likelihood accuracies, and a within-model compute curve from Pythia intermediate checkpoints. Together these show how much of each score under this protocol is format compliance rather than knowledge.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper compares AURORA-LM-L only with Cola-DLM under this protocol, with no AR reference, no parse-rate analysis and no random-option baselines.

Cola-DLM compares against AR and diffusion baselines trained on its own data, under its own evaluation. Here the AURORA protocol (Table 17 demonstrations, first-newline truncation, option matching, 512-token context filter) is re-run on a public compute-matched AR model.
Pythia releases the models and intermediate checkpoints and evaluates them by log-likelihood scoring. It does not evaluate them under a generative answer-extraction protocol.

inputs: HF EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b at revisions 'main' (step143000), 'step72000' and 'step36000'
HF Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer only (no weights), used for the paper's 512-token context-budget filter

Datasets (if a script-based loader fails, retry with revision='refs/convert/parquet', then any public mirror with identical content): Rowan/hellaswag (validation), cais/mmlu 'all' (test), allenai/ai2_arc 'ARC-Challenge' (test), allenai/openbookqa 'main' (test), allenai/winogrande 'winogrande_xl' (validation), allenai/social_i_qa (validation), juletxara/xstory_cloze 'en' (split 'eval'), ehovy/race 'all' (test), rajpurkar/squad (validation)
The seed paper's Table 17 two-shot demonstrations (Appendix A.6) and Table 4 per-task numbers
registration.method:
(1) Items. For each task:
- Load the listed split and apply Dataset.shuffle(seed=42).
- Take the first 1000 items (all if fewer) and build the 2-shot prompt of step 2.
- Keep items whose prompt has at most 480 tokens under the Qwen3 tokenizer, so that the prompt plus 32 generated tokens fits AURORA-LM-L's 512-token context.
- Use the first 500 surviving items (all if fewer).
- Record counts before and after filtering.
- Map numeric or letter labels to option positions (ARC items have 3-5 options labelled A-E by position).
- If a task cannot be loaded from any listed source within 3 minutes, drop it and record the drop.
(2) Prompts.
- Each prompt is the task's two demonstrations from the seed paper's Table 17, copied verbatim, followed by the test item, separated by blank lines. Demonstrations and test item share the same format.
- Formats, with ' | ' marking a newline:
  - HellaSwag: 'Context: {ctx} | (A) {e1} (B) {e2} (C) {e3} (D) {e4} | Answer: {answer}'.
  - MMLU, ARC-Challenge and OpenBookQA: 'Question: {question} | (A) .. (B) .. (C) .. (D) .. | Answer: {answer}'.
  - RACE: 'Article: {article} | Question: {question} Options: (A) .. (B) .. (C) .. (D) .. | Answer: {answer}'.
  - SIQA: 'Question: {context} {question} | (A) .. (B) .. (C) .. | Answer: {answer}'.
  - StoryCloze: 'Story: {four context sentences} | (A) {ending1} (B) {ending2} | End: {answer}'.
  - WinoGrande: 'Sentence: {sentence with _} | (A) {option1} (B) {option2} | Answer: {answer}'.
  - SQuAD: 'Context: {context} | Question: {question} | Answer: {answer}'.
- Answers are the full option text, as in Table 17.
- The test item ends with 'Answer:' ('End:' for StoryCloze), with no trailing space.
(3) Generation. Greedy decoding, at most 32 new tokens, bf16, left padding (pad = EOS), batch 32-64. Decode only the new tokens, truncate at the first newline and strip.
(4) Matching.
- normalize(s) = lowercase, remove punctuation, remove the whole words a, an and the, collapse whitespace.
- Strict matcher (primary; the literal reading of the paper's 'accepts either an explicit option letter or the corresponding option text'):
  (a) If the stripped raw output is a single valid option letter, optionally followed by '.' or ')', or starts with a parenthesized valid letter such as '(B)', choose that option. Detect letters before normalization, because normalization deletes the article 'a'.
  (b) Otherwise, if normalize(output) equals normalize(option text) for exactly one option, choose it.
  (c) Otherwise the item is unparsed and counted wrong.
- Lenient matcher (secondary): apply the strict matcher; if the item is still unparsed, choose the unique option whose normalized text is a prefix of the normalized output, or of which the non-empty normalized output is a prefix.
- SQuAD: exact match if normalize(output) equals the normalization of any gold answer.
(5) Models. Run Pythia-1.4B at revisions main, step72000 and step36000 on all loaded tasks. These are about 0.8x, 0.4x and 0.2x of AURORA-LM-L's compute. Intermediate checkpoints are not learning-rate annealed, so they are lower bounds at their compute.
(6) Log-likelihood reference, for the multiple-choice tasks and every model. Use the same 2-shot prompt and score the continuation ' ' + option text. acc = argmax of summed log-probability; acc_norm = argmax of mean per-token log-probability.
(7) Per task and model, record: strict and lenient accuracy, parse rate, accuracy among parsed items, random-valid-option baseline (mean of 1/number of options; not applicable to SQuAD), acc and acc_norm.
(8) Macro-averages.
- Average over the loaded tasks.
- AURORA-LM-L's comparison macro uses its Table 4 values for the same tasks: MMLU 22.2, ARC-C 21.2, OBQA 27.8, HellaSwag 18.4, WinoGrande 50.3, StoryCloze 54.8, SIQA 30.2, RACE 30.6, SQuAD EM 38.2.
- Also report how many AURORA-LM-L scores fall below the random-valid-option baseline computed on the filtered items.
- 95% interval for Pythia's macro: bootstrap over items within tasks (2000 resamples).

event.description: The final Pythia-1.4B checkpoint's strict-matcher macro-average exceeds AURORA-LM-L's reported macro-average over the same tasks by more than 5.0 points.
event.statistic: Pythia-1.4B (revision main) strict-matcher macro-average accuracy over loaded tasks minus AURORA-LM-L's Table 4 macro over the same tasks, in percentage points

evaluation.procedure:
Computation:
- Compute all per-task metrics for the three checkpoints, the macro-averages and the statistic.
- Report per-task differences from AURORA-LM-L, the bootstrap interval, and the lenient-matcher version of the statistic.
Files:
- generations.jsonl: one record per model and item (task, item id, raw output, truncated output, strict and lenient parsed option, correctness, Qwen3 prompt length).
- ll_scores.jsonl: summed and mean log-probabilities per model, item and option.
- task_metrics.json: all per-task numbers and filter counts.
- summary.json: the macro-averages, the statistic, the lenient statistic, the bootstrap interval, the dropped tasks and the event flag.
evaluation.controls:
Controls:
- Random-valid-option baseline per task.
- Parse rate and accuracy among parsed items, separating format failure from wrong answers.
- Log-likelihood accuracy as a protocol-independent knowledge reference.
- Intermediate checkpoints as lower-compute points.
- Strict and lenient matchers to bracket matcher uncertainty.
Caveats:
- The paper's exact subsets and matcher are not public, and its context filter also involved Cola-DLM. The comparison therefore carries protocol uncertainty, which the 5-point margin is meant to absorb.
- Training data differ: AURORA-LM-L's mixture is 28% academic, mathematical and knowledge text plus synthetic text. A Pythia advantage is informative, while a null result is weak given floor effects.

registration.full_scale_study: A single-harness study on full filtered splits with several seeds, covering AURORA-LM-L (if released), Cola-DLM, and compute-matched AR models trained on comparable data mixtures. All models would be scored both generatively and by likelihood- or denoising-based scoring, to establish whether continuous-latent diffusion LMs are compute-competitive on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks.

agent.reason: AURORA-LM-L's macro (32.6) is only about 4 points above the protocol's chance-level macro, and Pythia should parse reliably. However, a 1.4B model selecting answers generatively is close to chance on the knowledge tasks, strict matching with a 32-token cap hurts long HellaSwag endings, and SQuAD could go either way, so my central estimate of the gap is about 3 points, short of the 5-point bar.

judge_astra.reason: The reported near-chance multiple-choice scores leave room for an autoregressive advantage, but Pythia-1.4B need not be a strong generative option selector. Strict full-answer matching and the 32-token limit make a five-point macro advantage considerably harder than outperforming on individual tasks or through likelihood scoring.

judge_fable.reason: AURORA-LM-L's 32.6 macro is roughly the 'random option with perfect parsing' level, so Pythia-1.4B must be clearly above random under strict generative matching on StoryCloze, SIQA, HellaSwag and SQuAD to clear 37.6; my rough per-task estimates land around 35-38, making the 5-point margin close to a coin flip, slightly below.

judge_opus.reason: Under generative 2-shot answering with strict matching, Pythia-1.4B is likely near chance on the 4-option knowledge tasks and loses HellaSwag items whose long endings exceed 32 tokens. Its main edge would be on StoryCloze, SIQA and SQuAD, so my central estimate is a macro of about 34–36 against 32.6. Beating it by more than 5 points needs several upside surprises.

judge_sol.reason: AURORA-LM-L's reported scores leave room for an autoregressive advantage, but strict option matching and 32-token truncation can cause substantial formatting failures for a small base model. A five-point macro advantage is possible, but not my central expectation under this particular generative protocol.

judge_luna.reason: AURORA-LM-L’s reported 32.6 macro-average and low scores on several multiple-choice tasks make it plausible that Pythia will exceed it by five points, especially given Pythia’s roughly comparable compute. Strict generative matching, different pretraining data, and possible format failures leave that margin uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: AURORA-LM-L scores at or below chance on several tasks suggest a protocol floor a competent AR model should clear, but the strict exact-text matcher and AURORA's strong SQuAD score make the 5-point margin borderline.

opus.label: distinct

It has no autoregressive reference at matched compute, no breakdown into parse rate versus accuracy, no random-option baselines and no log-likelihood check. The experiment supplies all of these.

It also does not separate format compliance from accuracy, and it does not use a public model such as Pythia.
Pythia releases the models and intermediate checkpoints and evaluates them only by log-likelihood scoring, never under a generative answer-extraction protocol like AURORA's.
Studies generative answer matching versus multiple-choice scoring in general, not for diffusion language models at matched compute and not against AURORA's protocol.

opus.reason: I found no paper that runs a public autoregressive model at matched compute (Pythia-1.4B or similar) under AURORA-LM-L's 2-shot generative protocol, or that splits those scores into parse rate, accuracy and random-option floors. Cola-DLM's matched-compute AR baselines under a similar strict-matching few-shot protocol are the closest evidence. They cover a different diffusion model and do not test whether AURORA-LM-L's near-random scores reflect real capability or a floor set by the protocol, so the question remains open.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: ar_protocol/run.py, launched by run_eval.sh. It follows the registration: 9 tasks, shuffle(seed=42), first 1000 items, Table-17 two-shot prompts in the registered formats, a filter keeping prompts of at most 480 Qwen3 tokens, the first 500 survivors, greedy decoding of at most 32 tokens in bf16 with left padding, truncation at the first newline, strict and lenient matchers, SQuAD normalized exact match, log-likelihood acc and acc_norm on the same 2-shot prompt, Pythia-1.4B at revisions main, step72000 and step36000, and a 2000-resample within-task bootstrap. The test run took about 7.3 minutes end to end.

Result from the test run (registered statistic = strict macro of Pythia-1.4B@main minus AURORA-LM-L's Table 4 macro): 27.86 − 32.63 = −4.77 pp. The bootstrap 95% interval is [−6.1, −3.4]. With the lenient matcher the statistic is −3.97. The event (> +5) did not occur: under this protocol Pythia-1.4B does not beat the reported AURORA-LM-L numbers. Per-task differences (Pythia minus AURORA):
- StoryCloze −22.8: Pythia's strict parse rate is 72%, and it is 44% accurate among parsed items.
- HellaSwag −6.2: parse rate 48%.
- ARC-C +5.0.
- Every other task is within about ±5.5.

Other checkpoints:
- Strict macros are 26.8 at step72000 and 23.3 at step36000.
- Macros of 2-shot log-likelihood accuracy over the multiple-choice tasks are 32.2 at main, 32.2 at step72000 and 31.2 at step36000. Most tasks are near chance with this prompt format.

AURORA-LM-L's reported score falls below the random-valid-option baseline, computed on the filtered items, on 4 of 8 multiple-choice tasks: HellaSwag, MMLU, ARC-C and SIQA. Most of Pythia's unparsed outputs are free-text continuations rather than option text.

Changes and implementation choices:
1. allenai/social_i_qa is script-based, so it loaded through the registered fallback revision='refs/convert/parquet'. All 9 tasks loaded; none were dropped.
2. RACE: only 298 of 1000 candidates passed the 480-token filter, so n=298. All filter counts are in task_metrics.json.
3. Generation stops early once every sequence has produced a token containing a newline. This gives the same truncated output as decoding all 32 tokens and then cutting at the first newline.
4. The strict letter rule only accepts uppercase A–E, so the lowercase article "a" is not read as a letter. ARC options are lettered by position.
5. In WinoGrande demonstrations, the typographic apostrophe is written as ASCII "didn't".
6. ar_protocol/sanity_ll.py is an extra check, not part of the registered outputs and not run by the evaluation command. It confirms the log-likelihood scorer works: zero-shot StoryCloze without the option list, 300 items, gives 64.7%. registration.title: Is AURORA-LM-S's sample quality sensitive to the inference sigma-grid alone? Sweep only the sampling shift on the released checkpoint trained with tan-d shift 7
registration.seed_connection: The seed attributes large MAUVE differences to training-time noise allocation (Fig. 6b, Table 14: at OWT128, tan-d d=1 gives MAUVE 0.229 and d=7 gives 0.839) and frames this as calibrating the training noise distribution to latent width. According to the released code, a single shift parameter of the flow-matching scheduler sets three things: the training sigma density, the neighbour used by self-trajectory consistency (which the paper says uses 'the same schedule parameterization as sampling', Sec. 3.4), and the inference sigma grid. The ablation therefore probably changed the sampling step allocation together with the training allocation. With the released model, trained at shift 7, the inference grid can be varied while training is held fixed.
registration.hypothesis: Sampling the released AURORA-LM-S (trained with tan-d shift 7) on a shift-1 sigma grid instead of its native shift-7 grid, with the same 32-step deterministic ODE and no guidance, lowers MAUVE by more than 0.10.
registration.contribution: A direct measurement of how much quality depends on the inference grid for a fixed, width-calibrated model. A large sensitivity means the paper's attribution of the noise-allocation effect to training density is confounded, and that training density and sampling grid should be decoupled and tuned separately. A small sensitivity supports the training-density interpretation. A 128-step control tests whether any grid effect is a discretization effect that vanishes with finer steps, and a shift-15 grid tests whether an inference grid that differs from the training shift gives a free gain.

closest_work.difference: EDM decouples the training noise distribution from the sampling discretization for image diffusion and shows that each matters. Here the decoupling is a diagnostic applied to a released text-latent model whose published ablation varied both through one parameter.
Shows for images that the best noise schedule moves toward more noise as resolution grows, changing training and sampling together. Here training is held fixed and only the sampling grid varies.
InfoNoise adapts the training noise distribution online, including for language. Here only the inference grid of a frozen model is manipulated.
The seed paper varies the shared shift and attributes the effect to training-time allocation without separating out the inference grid.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; keep a preinstalled torch>=2.5 if the pinned build conflicts)
Released checkpoints via 'python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder' (HF fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, GPT-2 small backbone/tokenizer)
GPT-2 Large (HF 'gpt2-large'), used as MAUVE featurizer and Gen-PPL scorer
OpenWebText documents: HF 'stas/openwebtext-10k' (fallback 'Elriggs/openwebtext-100k')
pip package mauve-text
registration.method:
(0) Preflight and stop rule.
- Install, download, and load the OWT model as the repo's generation script does. Expected: cfg,_ = load_config_from_checkpoint(ckpt, project_root=REPO); gen = DiffusionGenerator(cfg, ckpt, device='cuda:0'); tr = gen.trainer. Names may differ.
- Use the override operator_optimization.profile=off if compilation is slow.
- If the release cannot be made to run within 10 minutes, write summary.json with status 'release_unavailable' and event_occurred=null, then stop.
(1) Code check (write grid_sanity.json).
- In the scheduler code (expected: a FlowMatchScheduler with sample_sigma, prev_sigma, get_sigmas and a shift attribute), record:
  - whether the training sigma sampler, the consistency neighbour and the inference grid all read the same shift;
  - which grid the code uses at inference when training uses logit-normal time sampling;
  - which variable the denoiser's timestep embedding receives: sigma itself, the uniform variable tau, or a step index.
- Save get_sigmas(32) for shifts 1, 3, 7 and 15 and confirm that they differ.
- Manipulation, depending on the conditioning variable:
  - If the denoiser receives sigma, set tr.noise_scheduler.shift = d_inf before sampling and restore 7 afterwards.
  - If it receives tau, build the grid for d_inf in sigma as sigma(tau; d) = d tan(pi tau/2) / (1 + d tan(pi tau/2)) at uniform tau. Convert each sigma to the model's conditioning value with the training shift 7, tau_model = (2/pi) arctan(sigma / (7 (1 - sigma))), so the model is always told the true noise level of its input.
  - If it receives a step index, record 'not testable', write summary.json with event_occurred=null, and stop.
- Reproduction: with shift 7, 8 samples from your sampling call must match the stock generator token-for-token.
(2) Sampling settings shared by all runs:
- released OWT checkpoint;
- solver 'euler' (deterministic ODE), self-conditioning on, self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0 passed explicitly (no guidance);
- 256 tokens (16 blocks). Generate only these blocks, e.g. via num_generate_blocks or a max_gen_tokens setting that stops block generation; do not generate 64 blocks and truncate;
- eos_mode 'eos_wrap', 1000 samples per run, batch 500-1000.
(3) Runs.
- 32 steps: d_inf=7 with seeds 1, 2 and 3; d_inf=1 with seeds 1, 2 and 3; d_inf=3 and d_inf=15 with seed 1.
- 128 steps: d_inf=1 with seed 1 and d_inf=7 with seed 1.
- For every run, save the sigma grid and the numbers of steps with sigma > 0.9 and with sigma < 0.5.
- Pilot: time the first 32-step run. If all runs are projected to exceed 16 minutes, drop runs in this order: the 128-step d_inf=7 run, then d_inf=15, then seed 3 of both arms. This order is pre-registered; record what was dropped.
(4) Real text.
- GPT-2-tokenize OWT documents and concatenate them with EOS (50256) separators.
- Cut 256-token chunks that each start with EOS, decode with skip_special_tokens=False, and shuffle with seed 0.
- 1000 chunks are the MAUVE references; 1000 others form the real-text ceiling.
(5) Metrics per run.
- MAUVE: mauve-text with GPT-2-Large features, max_text_length=256, mauve seed 25, reference features computed once.
- Gen-PPL: GPT-2 Large on retokenized texts, exp of the token-weighted mean NLL over positions >= 1.
- Mean per-sample unigram entropy (nats) of the retokenized ids.

event.description: Averaged over seeds 1-3, MAUVE on the native shift-7 grid exceeds MAUVE on the shift-1 grid by more than 0.10 at 32 steps.
event.statistic: Mean over seeds 1-3 of MAUVE(d_inf=7) - MAUVE(d_inf=1), 32-step deterministic ODE, no guidance, 1000 samples of 256 tokens each

evaluation.procedure:
Computation:
- Compute MAUVE, Gen-PPL and entropy for every run.
- The statistic is the seed-averaged paired difference: same seed and initial-noise stream, different grids.
Also report:
- per-seed values and their standard deviation, as the noise estimate;
- the d_inf=3 and d_inf=15 points;
- the 128-step results: whether the shift-1 grid at 128 steps comes within 0.03 of the native 32-step MAUVE, and how much the native grid itself changes at 128 steps;
- Gen-PPL and entropy shifts, the real-text ceiling, and the code-check findings.
Interpretation: the result is read as grid sensitivity of this model, not as a decomposition of the paper's Table 14, which used different models (OWT128, D=1024). Changing the grid also breaks the S=16 consistency pairing used in training.
Files:
- grid_sanity.json: the code-check findings, the saved grids and the reproduction result.
- samples.jsonl: one record per sample (d_inf, steps, seed, index, text).
- metrics.json: all per-run metrics and wall-clock times.
- summary.json: the statistic, the per-seed differences, any dropped runs and the event flag.
evaluation.controls:
- The native shift-7 grid is the reference.
- Three seeds for the key contrast.
- Checkpoint, solver, step count, sample count, length and references are identical across runs, so the grid is the only manipulated variable.
- A 128-step control for discretization.
- A real-text MAUVE ceiling.
- Gen-PPL and entropy, to check that MAUVE changes are not purely diversity effects.
- The conditioning-variable check, ensuring the model is always told the true noise level of its input.

registration.full_scale_study: A 2x2 factorial (training shift 1 or 7, crossed with inference shift 1 or 7), with self-trajectory consistency on and off, on OWT128 models at latent widths 256 and 1024 with three training seeds. This separates the contributions of training density, consistency pairing and inference grid to the width-dependent noise-allocation effect. It would be followed by a decoupled design that trains with the best density and picks the inference grid separately for each model.

agent.reason: The released model's MAUVE barely moves with step count or solver even when Gen-PPL changes a lot (Table 7: 0.885 at 16 steps versus 0.893 at 32; SDE at 16 steps with Gen-PPL 98 still gives 0.848). A shift-1 grid that is coarse only at the top will more likely raise Gen-PPL than cut MAUVE by more than 0.10, unless the time conditioning is mishandled.

judge_astra.reason: The shift-1 grid allocates substantially fewer steps to high noise and departs from the schedule used for consistency training, making a sizeable finite-step degradation plausible. Nevertheless, the paper's large training-sweep difference does not directly estimate this fixed-checkpoint inference effect.

judge_fable.reason: A shift-1 32-step grid spends only ~4-6 steps in the sigma>0.83 region where this shift-7-trained model makes its decisions (comparable to an ~8-step native grid, which cost ~0.1 MAUVE in the paper's OWT128 ablation), so a sizable drop is likely but the released model is more step-robust (16 vs 32 steps differ by 0.008), putting the >0.10 threshold near the median; implementation of the grid/conditioning manipulation adds some risk.

judge_opus.reason: On the shift-1 grid only 3–4 of 32 steps fall above sigma≈0.85, which is coarser there than the native 8-step grid. The paper's own few-step results (8 steps: 0.672 vs 32 steps: 0.815) show MAUVE drops of this size from coarse high-noise steps. Against that, the released model was robust from 16 to 32 steps, and the shift-1 grid's fine mid- and low-noise steps may compensate. A drop above 0.10 is close to a coin flip, discounted for release and implementation risk.

judge_sol.reason: If the scheduler coupling is as registered, the shift-1 grid removes many high-noise updates and departs from the discretization used for consistency training, making a sizeable degradation plausible. Nevertheless, consistency regularization could provide robustness, and the released checkpoint differs from the OWT128 models behind the paper's largest reported effects.

judge_luna.reason: The paper’s large noise-shift effect compares models trained with different noise allocations while using a shared shift for sampling; this experiment isolates the inference-grid contribution for one trained model. The shift-7 grid places many more 32-step nodes at high noise than shift 1, so a substantial drop is plausible, though the flow may be robust to discretization changes and its consistency training used a different step budget.

judge_muse.reason: Shift-1 versus shift-7 grids allocate high-noise steps very differently so some MAUVE drop is expected, but Table 7 shows MAUVE is robust to inference changes, making a >0.10 drop uncertain.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's noise-allocation sweeps (Fig. 5b, Fig. 6b) change the tan-d shift. Its inference sweep (Table 7) varies only the solver, step count and SC-CFG scale; the sigma grid stays fixed. It never varies the inference grid on a model trained at a fixed shift, so it does not separate grid effects from training-density effects.

EDM treats the training noise distribution and the sampling discretization as separate factors, but for image diffusion. It says nothing about block-causal text-latent flow models or the shared-shift confound in AURORA-LM.

Studies how the best noise schedule depends on resolution in image diffusion, changing training and sampling together. It does not hold a trained model fixed while sweeping only the inference grid, and it does not cover text.
Adapts the training noise distribution online, including for language, but does not test how sensitive a frozen model is to its inference grid.
Shifts the timestep at inference on pretrained image and motion diffusion models to correct variance under temperature sampling. Its question is different and it does not cover text latents.

Image-diffusion work such as EDM separates training noise from sampling discretization as a general idea, but my searches found no study that does this for AURORA-LM or similar continuous text-latent diffusion models. That prior work does not settle the question, so the experiment is distinct.

EDM separates training noise allocation from sampling discretization and sweeps the inference-grid exponent on pretrained models, including a discretization-error analysis. The proposed experiment applies this established diagnostic to continuous text latents with a different grid parameterization.

AURORA-LM reports noise-allocation ablations across trained configurations and fixed-checkpoint sweeps of solver, step count and guidance, but does not report the proposed fixed-checkpoint, inference-shift-only sweep.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: grid_sweep/run_sweep.py, launched by grid_sweep/run_all.sh. The script installs dependencies and puts seed/src on sys.path, so nothing is written into /workspace/seed. It downloads the released OWT denoiser, the autoencoder, GPT-2 small and GPT-2 Large into /workspace/work, then runs the registered sweep.

Code check (saved in grid_sweep/grid_sanity.json):
- One FlowMatchScheduler.shift controls all three things: the training sigma density (sample_sigma), the self-trajectory-consistency neighbour (prev_sigma, S=16) and the inference grid (get_sigmas).
- The released scheduler has no logit-normal branch. sample_sigma always uses the tanh map, and get_sigmas returns None unless time_sampling is 'tanh'. So the code can't tell us which inference grid the paper's logit-normal ablation used.
- The denoiser's timestep embedding receives sigma itself, both in training (t = sigma) and in the BlockSampler (time_t = sigma_cur). The manipulation is therefore to set tr.noise_scheduler.shift = d_inf before sampling and restore 7 afterwards.
- The saved 32-step grids for shifts 1, 3, 7 and 15 all differ.
- Reproduction check passed: 8 samples from my shift-7 call matched the stock generator token-for-token.

Sampling: stock DiffusionGenerator.generate with solver 'euler', self_cond_cfg_scale=1.0 passed explicitly, eos_mode 'eos_wrap', max_gen_tokens=256 (generates exactly 16 blocks, no truncation), 1000 samples per run, batch 1000.

Changes from the registration:
1. I set cfg.operator_optimization.profile='off', which the registration allows. With 'auto' on CUDA, FlexAttention crashes at runtime.
2. Reference text comes from the fallback dataset, Elriggs/openwebtext-100k (first 6000 docs). stas/openwebtext-10k fails because dataset scripts are no longer supported.
3. GPT-2 small and GPT-2 Large are fetched as openai-community/* with HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1. The bare 'gpt2' repo returned a 404 from the Xet download backend.
4. For MAUVE, I compute GPT-2 Large last-token final-layer features myself, batched with padding and truncated to 256 tokens, then call mauve.compute_mauve(p=references, q=generations, seed=25). The reference features are computed once. This should match mauve-text's own featurizer up to numerics, but I did not compare the two directly.

Dropped run: the pilot took 67.6 s per 32-step run, so the full set was projected at 13.5 min. Under the pre-registered drop order this is the first-listed drop, and only the 128-step d_inf=7 run was dropped. This is recorded in summary.json.

Result from my full test run (the evaluation reruns everything; the same seeds should give near-identical numbers):
- **Registered statistic: 0.148**, above the 0.10 threshold, so the event occurred.
- MAUVE on the native shift-7 grid at 32 steps: 0.919, 0.953, 0.915. On the shift-1 grid: 0.752, 0.767, 0.823.
- Per-seed differences: 0.166, 0.186, 0.092 (sd 0.050). One of the three seeds is below 0.10, so the margin over the threshold is modest relative to seed noise.
- Shift 3: 0.903. Shift 15: 0.958 (one seed, within the native grid's seed spread, so no evidence of a free gain).
- Shift-1 grid at 128 steps: 0.923, within 0.03 of the native 32-step mean (0.928). This suggests the grid effect is mostly a discretization effect that finer steps remove.
- Gen-PPL: about 78 on the native grid vs about 186 on the shift-1 grid. Mean entropy: 4.65 vs 4.74 (real text 4.72).
- Real-text MAUVE ceiling: 0.941. Several model runs score above it, which points to MAUVE noise at about ±0.02–0.04.

How to read this: it measures how sensitive this one model is to its inference grid, not a decomposition of the paper's Table 14 (different models, OWT128, D=1024). Changing the grid also breaks the S=16 consistency pairing used in training.

Runtime: about 24 min on the A100, of which about 10 min is MAUVE clustering, plus 2–4 min of install and download. That should fit within the 35-minute limit, but the margin is not large.

departures: grid_sweep/run_sweep.py sets cfg.operator_optimization.profile='off'. The registration explicitly allows this, and the reproduction check against the stock generator passed under it. It should not change the result.

Reference and ceiling text come from the registered fallback Elriggs/openwebtext-100k (first 6000 docs) because stas/openwebtext-10k no longer loads. This is a registered fallback. It applies equally to all arms, so it cannot bias the paired statistic.
GPT-2 small and GPT-2 Large are fetched as openai-community/* with HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1 (run_all.sh). The weights are the same, so the result is unaffected.

MAUVE features come from a custom featurizer in run_sweep.py, not mauve-text's own: GPT-2 Large final-layer hidden state of the last real token, right-padded with an attention mask, truncated to 256 tokens. These are then passed as p_features/q_features to mauve.compute_mauve(seed=25). This matches mauve-text's featurization in substance (last-token final hidden state; causal masking makes right padding harmless), but no direct comparison was run. Any numeric difference would apply to all arms alike.

Real-text chunks start only at document boundaries (non-overlapping 256-token windows beginning at each document's EOS), not as arbitrary EOS-led cuts of the concatenated stream. The registration's wording allows this. It is shared across arms and affects only absolute MAUVE levels and the ceiling, not the paired difference.

registration.title: Where should prompt guidance act for text latents? Middle-noise versus AURORA-LM-S's high-noise-only classifier-free guidance interval on XSum
registration.seed_connection: AURORA-LM-S's XSum protocol applies classifier-free guidance only for sigma in [0.9, 1.0] at w=2, with an unconditional pass that sees no prefix (Appendix A.2.4). The paper sweeps the scale and the step count (Table 8) but reports no alternative intervals. In image diffusion, guidance has been found harmful at high noise and most useful in a middle interval. AURORA's wide latents stay decodable under heavy corruption (Fig. 5a), which could instead mean that text content is fixed only at very high noise: the opposite prediction.
registration.hypothesis: On XSum, applying classifier-free guidance only for sigma in [0.7, 0.9], with its scale tuned on validation, gives higher test ROUGE-L for AURORA-LM-S than applying it only for sigma in [0.9, 1.0] with its scale tuned on validation by the same procedure.
registration.contribution: Tests, on a released conditional model, whether the guidance-interval finding from image diffusion transfers to continuous text latents, and locates where along the trajectory prefix conditioning acts for text. This bears on guidance and noise-schedule design for continuous text diffusion. Both intervals receive the same validation tuning, which avoids comparing a newly tuned interval against a scale that may have been chosen on test data.

closest_work.difference: Shows for image diffusion that guidance is harmful at high noise and best applied in a limited middle interval. This is untested for text-latent diffusion, where AURORA applies guidance only at the highest noise.
ELF uses prefix and self-conditioning guidance for continuous text flows and reports scale trade-offs, but not guidance intervals.
Introduces classifier-free guidance applied at every noise level. It does not study where along the trajectory guidance should act for text.
The seed paper fixes the interval at [0.9, 1.0] and sweeps only scale and step count.

inputs: AURORA-LM code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM (pip install -e '.[eval]'; keep a preinstalled torch>=2.5 if the pinned build conflicts)
Released checkpoints via 'python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model xsum autoencoder' (HF fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum, fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, GPT-2 small backbone/tokenizer)
XSum: HF 'EdinburghNLP/xsum' (fallbacks: the same with revision='refs/convert/parquet', or 'knkarthick/xsum')

registration.method:
(0) Setup and stop rule.
- Install the repo and download the checkpoints.
- Load XSum and save the validation and test splits with save_to_disk('data/xsum') (fields document, summary, id).
- Run the repo's preprocessing on validation and test only: python data/prepare_xsum_conditional.py --input_dir data/xsum --output_dir data/xsum-gpt2-1024-conditional --tokenizer_path models/gpt2-small --block_size 1024 --max_condition_len 960 --min_target_len 16.
- If the release or the preprocessing cannot be made to work within 10 minutes, write results.json with status 'release_unavailable' and event_occurred=null, then stop.
(1) Sampling.
- Use the released conditional protocol except for the guidance window and scale: 32-step Euler ODE, repaint=True, max_gen_tokens=64, eos_mode='first_eos', batch 64.
- Use seed 1 in every configuration, so initial noise is shared, and the same articles in the same order in every configuration.
- Load the model once in a single Python driver. Expected API (verify): DiffusionGenerator(...).generate_multi_prefix(prefixes, num_steps=32, batch_size=64, seed=1, repaint=True, max_gen_tokens=64, eos_mode='first_eos', cfg_scale=w, cfg_sigma_window='lo,hi').
- Alternative: python -m aurora.eval.run_eval on one GPU with --prefix_dataset data/xsum-gpt2-1024-conditional --prefix_split {validation|test} --metrics rouge --num_steps 32 --batch_size 64 --eos_mode first_eos --repaint --max_gen_tokens 64 --cfg_scale w --cfg_sigma_window 'lo,hi' --seed 1.
- Guidance is active when lo <= sigma <= hi, as in the code. Outside the window the conditional prediction is used.
- If torch.compile recompiles for variable prefix lengths, add the override operator_optimization.profile=off.

evaluation.procedure:
Computation:
- Compute per-article ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L for every configuration.
- Compute the primary statistic as defined, and also report the point estimate and the upper bound. An upper bound below zero means high-noise guidance is better.
- Report all paired differences against High@w_H and against High@2.0, with bootstrap intervals, and the chosen scales.
- Reproduction check: compare High@2.0 mean test ROUGE-L with the paper's 28.86 (the paper's evaluation subset may differ).
Files:
- val_predictions.jsonl: one record per configuration and validation article (configuration, window, w, article id, prediction, reference, ROUGE-1/2/L).
- test_predictions.jsonl: the same for the test articles.
- results.json: chosen scales, per-configuration means, the primary statistic with point estimate and interval, all paired differences, window-to-step coverage, pilot fallback, reproduction check and the event flag.
evaluation.controls:
- Both intervals are tuned with the same validation procedure.
- The comparison is paired: same articles, same seed and same initial noise.
- No-guidance and full-interval runs bound the effect.
- The low-noise interval tests whether guidance acts late.
- Reproduction check against the paper's reported High@2.0 ROUGE-L.
- The decision rests on a bootstrap interval rather than a point estimate, because the expected differences are of the order of the seed-to-seed spread (0.18 ROUGE-L in Table 8).

closest_work.difference: This paper establishes the guidance-interval idea (guidance hurts at high noise and works best in a middle interval), but only for image diffusion such as EDM2 and SD-XL. It does not test continuous text latents or ROUGE-scored summarization.
This is the seed paper. It applies classifier-free guidance at a fixed high-noise window and reports only the guidance scale and step count. In the portion I read, it has no ablation of the interval.

This paper studies guidance schedules for masked (discrete) diffusion, including text, and finds that early high guidance hurts while late guidance helps. That is a different noising process from flow matching on continuous text latents, and it does not compare a middle window with a high-noise window.
Step AG finds that restricting guidance to the first denoising steps is enough, but only for text-to-image and text-to-video models. It does not cover text generation.

ELF studies prefix and self-conditioning guidance scales for continuous text flows. It reports no guidance intervals. I did not find this paper through search; I am relying on the proposal's description of it.

opus.reason: I found no work that compares a middle-noise guidance window with a high-noise-only window for continuous-latent text diffusion, and none that does so on XSum or with AURORA-LM. The closest work covers image diffusion (interval guidance, Step AG) or masked discrete diffusion, and the two point in conflicting directions, so they do not settle the text-latent question. The seed paper fixes the window and tunes only the scale and step count.

The experiment therefore addresses an unresolved transfer question rather than merely reproducing an established interval result.
