registration.title: Does AURORA’s noisy-input bottleneck capture decoder-sensitive directions beyond latent covariance?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA predicts a full-width clean latent while restricting the noisy-latent input through a low-rank projection. Its bottleneck-width ablation measures generation quality, but not which input directions the learned projection retains.
registration.hypothesis: On held-out WikiText windows, the effective rank-r bottleneck subspace captures at least 0.05 more frozen-decoder token-loss gradient energy than the stronger of a rank-r latent-covariance PCA subspace and the mean of matched random subspaces.
registration.contribution: Adds a decoder-sensitivity diagnostic to the bottleneck-width results, with PCA as a covariance-based control. A positive result would motivate testing decoder-aware bottlenecks, but would not establish a generation-quality improvement.

closest_work.difference: JiT motivates a low-rank noisy-input pathway for image denoising; this tests whether AURORA’s learned text-latent pathway preserves directions important to its token decoder.
AURORA reports generation quality across bottleneck widths, but not decoder-gradient alignment of the effective input subspace.
This work studies whitening for sentence-level retrieval; here PCA is a rank-matched control for token-decoder gradient energy in AURORA latents.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; load the released OWT prior checkpoint fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt and shared autoencoder fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, with the checkpoint’s GPT-2 BPE tokenizer and latent statistics.
Hugging Face dataset Salesforce/wikitext, configuration wikitext-2-raw-v1; use train and validation splits.
registration.method: Run the released PyTorch model in eval mode on CUDA. From the OWT prior, extract the two linear maps of the noisy-input bottleneck and form their effective composition W_in = W_up W_down in float32. Compute its SVD and define numerical rank r using a cutoff of 1e-6 times the largest singular value. Tokenize nonempty WikiText lines with the checkpoint tokenizer, concatenate them with EOS separators, and take the first 32 nonoverlapping 64-token windows from train and 32 from validation. Encode both sets deterministically and standardize with the checkpoint’s per-channel statistics. Fit a centered channel covariance matrix on train latents and retain its top r eigenvectors as the PCA control. For each validation window, form x = (1−0.5)z + 0.5ε with a fixed seeded Gaussian draw, invert latent standardization, and compute the frozen decoder’s mean token cross-entropy against the window’s original tokens. Backpropagate this loss to x. For each window, calculate the fraction of total squared gradient energy captured by the row space of W_in, the top-r PCA subspace, and each of 32 seeded Gaussian-orthonormal rank-r subspaces; use the mean random-subspace fraction as the random control. The per-window effect is the learned fraction minus the larger of the PCA fraction and mean random fraction. Do not update any parameters. Bootstrap validation windows with replacement 10,000 times; the registered statistic is the 10th percentile of the bootstrap mean effect.

event.description: The 10th-percentile bootstrap lower endpoint for the mean learned-minus-best-control gradient-energy fraction is greater than 0.05.
event.statistic: 10th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap means of learned_fraction − max(top_PCA_fraction, mean_random_fraction)

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per validation window with the learned, PCA, and mean random gradient-energy fractions and their difference. Write the point estimate, registered bootstrap statistic, rank, and settings to the summary file.
evaluation.controls: Use identical per-window gradients for all subspaces, rank-match the PCA and random controls to the effective bottleneck rank, fit PCA only on train windows, and fix all noise and subspace seeds. This is a local sensitivity diagnostic, not a causal test of generation quality.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, train compute-matched denoisers with the standard bottleneck and a decoder-gradient-informed bottleneck initialization or constraint. Compare latent prediction and decoded OWT generation at a fixed inference budget.

agent.reason: The bottleneck is trained to retain information useful for latent prediction, but that need not align with decoder cross-entropy gradients. The five-point margin over the stronger of the PCA and random controls, with a bootstrap lower endpoint, makes the event demanding.

judge_astra.reason: The learned projection could retain decoder-relevant directions, but its latent-denoising objective may primarily select covariance-related structure. Beating the stronger rank-matched control by 0.05 at the bootstrap lower endpoint is therefore a demanding event.

judge_fable.reason: The denoiser's low-rank input projection is trained only on latent MSE with isotropic noise, so its row space should largely coincide with the high-variance (PCA) directions of the standardized latents; a robust ≥0.05 excess in decoder-gradient energy over the better of PCA and random (10th-percentile bootstrap) requires decoder-specific alignment that nothing in training induces.

judge_opus.reason: A bottleneck trained to denoise mostly high-noise inputs should keep high-variance directions, much like PCA. That makes beating both PCA and random subspaces by more than 0.05 unlikely, though the single-article WikiText PCA fit is a weak control that could let the subspace learned on OpenWebText win.

judge_sol.reason: The learned bottleneck may retain decoder-relevant linguistic directions, but it is optimized for latent reconstruction rather than decoder-gradient capture. Exceeding both PCA and random controls by a bootstrap-supported 0.05 is a demanding criterion.

judge_luna.reason: The released bottleneck was optimized for latent-MSE denoising, not decoder-gradient energy, and may mostly capture covariance directions. Beating the PCA control by more than 0.05 with a bootstrap lower bound is a high bar.

judge_muse.reason: W_in is trained only with latent MSE and never sees decoder loss, while autoencoder latent dropout pz=0.6 encourages distributed sensitivity, so a rank-128 learned subspace is unlikely to beat rank-matched PCA by 0.05 with 90% confidence.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper only reports MAUVE across noisy-input bottleneck widths (D_b = 32 to 1024), a corruption-robustness probe of the decoder and a target/loss-space ablation. Its main text and appendix contain no analysis of which input directions the learned low-rank projection keeps, and no comparison against PCA or random subspaces using decoder-gradient energy.

JiT is the source of the low-rank noisy-input bottleneck idea for pixel-space image denoising. This is based on how AURORA cites it, not on my own reading of JiT. It is not known to analyse how its bottleneck subspace aligns with a token decoder's loss gradients in a text latent space.
Whitening or PCA of sentence embeddings for retrieval. Here PCA is only a rank-matched control, and the quantity measured is the token-decoder gradient energy captured by AURORA's learned bottleneck.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper's experimental sections and appendix tables. It evaluates the bottleneck only through generation quality at different widths and never checks whether the learned input subspace aligns with frozen-decoder loss gradients beyond what covariance PCA or random subspaces capture. My arXiv searches for analyses of low-rank denoiser input projections against decoder-gradient or PCA baselines, in text or in JiT-style image models, found no matching work, though the searches returned mostly irrelevant results, so coverage is limited. On that evidence the question appears unanswered, but this is not proof that no such work exists.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: AURORA-LM ablates noisy-input bottleneck width using generation metrics, but does not measure decoder-loss gradient energy captured by the learned input subspace or compare it with rank-matched PCA and random subspaces.

Continuous Language Diffusion as a Decoder-Interface Problem studies PCA bottleneck degradation, decoder margins, and directional sensitivity in ELF. It does not test whether a trained denoiser's noisy-input bottleneck preferentially retains decoder-sensitive directions beyond latent covariance.
JiT introduces and ablates low-rank noisy-input embeddings for image denoising, but does not perform the proposed frozen-decoder gradient-alignment comparison.

MoRAE separates covariance conditioning from alignment between flow residuals and decoder-Jacobian sensitivity in motion latents. Its diagnostic concerns prediction errors, not gradient energy retained by a learned noisy-input projection relative to PCA and random controls.

sol.reason: The closest prior work establishes noisy-input bottlenecks and shows that covariance or latent error alone does not characterize decoder sensitivity. However, none of the work I found answers the specific question by comparing a learned denoiser-input row space with rank-matched PCA and random subspaces using held-out frozen-decoder token-loss gradient energy.

opus.reason: No list entry measures how much frozen-decoder gradient energy the learned bottleneck row space captures relative to PCA and random subspaces; entries 14, 45 and 53 instead manipulate projections and measure accuracy or generation quality.

sol.reason: No list entry measures decoder-gradient energy captured by the learned bottleneck subspace against rank-matched PCA and random-subspace controls.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (bottleneck_alignment.py, launched by run_eval.sh): it downloads fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (250k), fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder and gpt2. It builds the released pipeline through the seed code's DiffusionGenerator (PYTHONPATH=seed/src; the seed directory is not modified). It then extracts input_proj.0 (W_down, 128x768) and input_proj.1 (W_up, 768x128) and forms W_in = W_up W_down in float64, using the EMA weights, which are the inference weights. The SVD gives numerical rank r=128 under the 1e-6 relative cutoff; the next singular value is about 6e-15. The raw, non-EMA weights give the same rank and nearly the same fractions, and both are reported.

Data: WikiText-2 raw. Nonempty lines are tokenized with the checkpoint's GPT-2 tokenizer, each line including its trailing newline, and joined with EOS. The first 32 nonoverlapping 64-token windows are taken from train and the first 32 from validation. Encoding is deterministic, in fp32 with TF32 off, and I keep the first 64 latents. Latents are standardized with the latent_mean/std stored in the diffusion checkpoint. PCA uses the top-r eigenvectors of the centered channel covariance, fitted on train only. On each validation window: x = 0.5 z + 0.5 ε (seeded), de-standardize, run the frozen decoder, take the mean token cross-entropy, and backpropagate to x in the standardized space. The fraction for a subspace V is ||G V||²/||G||², where G is the window's 64x768 gradient. The random control is the mean over 32 seeded QR-orthonormal Gaussian rank-128 subspaces. The effect is learned − max(PCA, mean random). I took 10,000 bootstrap means (seed 0) and report their 10th percentile. No parameters are updated.

Result from the test run: registered statistic = −0.0133. The event (> 0.05) did not occur. Point estimate of the mean effect = +0.0020; bootstrap 2.5–97.5% range of the mean is [−0.023, +0.023]. Mean captured fractions: learned row space 0.420, PCA 0.418, random 0.166 (r/D = 0.167). PCA beat random on all 32 windows.

Interpretation: the learned bottleneck captures far more decoder-gradient energy than random subspaces. However, it captures about the same as covariance PCA, so this diagnostic shows no decoder-specific advantage beyond PCA. A gap of 0.05 or more is unlikely given the bootstrap range, but this does not prove the two are equivalent. The setting is narrow: one noise level, 32 windows, and WikiText rather than OWT. It is also a local sensitivity measure, not a measure of generation quality.

Deviations and observations:
1. The registration did not specify EMA vs raw weights; I used EMA. Raw-weight results are in summary.json.
2. Contrary to the paper's description, the code loads the token embedding from frozen GPT-2 small. I used the pipeline as released.
3. Sanity check: clean validation reconstruction accuracy is 0.998 (CE 0.174). Mean CE at σ=0.5 is 0.109, lower than the clean CE. I did not investigate why; one possible cause is that the decoder was trained with latent dropout without rescaling.

The evaluation run took about 1.5 minutes including installs and downloads.

registration.title: Is AURORA’s decoder sensitivity to localized corruption position-dependent?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA’s encoder organizes latents in prefix order, and its paper probes decoder recovery under global latent corruption. It does not test whether corruption at different latent blocks has different effects on a common downstream text span.
registration.hypothesis: At corruption level σ=0.5, the range across eight latent blocks in mean excess decoder cross-entropy on the same final 16 output tokens is greater than 0.10 nats per token.
registration.contribution: Measures position-dependent influence through AURORA’s causal latent-to-token decoder while holding the scored output tokens fixed. This is a decoder-sensitivity probe, not evidence that a position-specific prior schedule will improve generation.

closest_work.difference: SeqDiffuSeq studies learned position-specific noise schedules for embedding-space sequence-to-sequence diffusion; this probe measures localized decoder sensitivity in AURORA’s prefix-causal latent space.
COSMOS studies decoder robustness to corruption in compressed latents; this compares the downstream effects of corruption across blocks in AURORA’s full-width causal representation.
AURORA reports global corruption robustness across latent widths, but not a block-position sensitivity profile.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; use fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder and the latent standardization statistics from fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt. The denoiser need not be run.
Hugging Face dataset Salesforce/wikitext, configuration wikitext-2-raw-v1, validation split; use the checkpoint’s GPT-2 BPE tokenizer.
registration.method: Load the released OWT autoencoder and statistics in eval mode. Tokenize nonempty WikiText validation lines, concatenate with EOS separators, and take the first 32 nonoverlapping 128-token windows. Use the uncompressed c=1 latent sequence. For each window, encode and standardize its latents, then decode the clean latents and compute token cross-entropy on output positions 113–128. Divide the 128 latent positions into eight consecutive blocks of 16. Draw one seeded Gaussian tensor per window. For each block in turn, replace only that block with (1−0.5)z + 0.5ε, leave every other latent clean, invert standardization, and decode. Compute cross-entropy on the same output positions 113–128 for every block condition; these positions form a common downstream suffix for the eight blocks under the uncompressed causal mapping. Subtract the clean-latent cross-entropy. Average each block’s increase over windows, and calculate the maximum-minus-minimum across the eight block means. Bootstrap windows with replacement 10,000 times, preserving all paired block conditions, and use the 10th percentile of the bootstrap range as the registered statistic.

event.description: The 10th-percentile bootstrap lower endpoint for the range of blockwise mean excess cross-entropies exceeds 0.10 nats per token.
event.statistic: 10th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap estimates of max_block_mean_increase − min_block_mean_increase

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per window and block with clean and corrupted cross-entropy on positions 113–128 and their difference. Write the eight point estimates, observed range, and registered bootstrap statistic to the summary file.
evaluation.controls: For each window, use the same clean latent, scored output span, and seeded Gaussian tensor for all block conditions. A result below threshold is only evidence against a large effect in this probe, not proof of positional equivalence.

models: AURORA-LM-S OWT checkpoint for latent statistics

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, train a prior with position-conditioned noise allocation while holding the sequence-level noise marginal fixed, then compare it with the global-schedule prior on decoded generation quality and efficiency.

agent.reason: AURORA’s prefix-causal decoder makes position-dependent effects plausible, especially when the final block is directly corrupted. However, the wide latents may be robust at this noise level, limiting the range across blocks.

judge_astra.reason: Corrupting the block containing the scored tokens should matter more than corrupting distant context. However, the paper’s strong wide-latent reconstruction robustness around σ=0.5 makes exceeding the specific 0.10-nat threshold uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: Under the c=1 causal decoder, only corruption of the final block should matter, so the range is essentially block-8 excess CE at σ=0.5; Fig. 5(a) suggests wide latents (D≈768) still decode ~98–99% correctly at σ=0.5, putting the excess near the 0.10-nat threshold, and the 10th-percentile bootstrap plus extra clean context tilt it slightly below.

judge_opus.reason: The range is set almost entirely by corrupting block 8, the latents of the scored tokens themselves. Fig. 5(a) shows decoders with D≥512 near 100% token recovery at σ=0.5, so the excess cross-entropy for the D=768 autoencoder is probably below 0.1 nats per token. Rare or space-variant WikiText punctuation tokens leave some chance of exceeding it.

judge_sol.reason: Corrupting the final block directly damages latents associated with the scored tokens, whereas earlier-block corruption leaves those latents intact. Position dependence is therefore likely, although the paper’s moderate-noise robustness results make the 0.10-nat magnitude threshold less certain.

judge_luna.reason: Because the latents are prefix-ordered, corrupting the last block may be harder for the fixed suffix to compensate for than corrupting an earlier block. Still, the paper reports robustness to latent corruption, so the range may not exceed 0.10 nats per token.

judge_muse.reason: With c=1, token 113-128 information first appears in latents >=113, so corrupting block 8 must raise suffix CE far more than corrupting early blocks that never saw those tokens, easily exceeding 0.10 nats.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper corrupts the whole latent sequence (x_σ=(1−σ)z+σε) and reports token-recovery accuracy for different latent widths (Fig. 5a). It does not corrupt individual blocks, does not fix a scored downstream token span, and reports no block-position sensitivity profile.

COSMOS, as the seed paper describes it, studies a compressed Perceiver-resampler latent. From its abstract-level description, it is about smoothness and robustness to corruption in general, not position-specific downstream influence in a prefix-causal full-width latent. I did not read the full text.
SeqDiffuSeq learns position-specific noise schedules for embedding-space seq2seq diffusion. It does not measure how a frozen decoder responds to corruption localized at different latent positions.

This paper measures how well tokens can be recovered from frozen BERT latents under token dropout in a different architecture. It looks at overall recoverability, not at whether corrupting different latent blocks changes cross-entropy on a fixed token suffix differently.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper's main text and the relevant appendix. Its only corruption probe applies noise to all latent positions at once and compares latent widths. It never corrupts single blocks while scoring a fixed downstream span. My searches turned up no other work that measures position-dependent decoder sensitivity in AURORA's prefix-causal latent space, or in a similar text-latent autoencoder, so as far as I found, the question has not been answered. The searches were limited and mostly returned irrelevant results, so I can't rule out unindexed or very recent work.

closest_work.difference: AURORA-LM Section 4.1.1 corrupts whole latent sequences and compares token-recovery accuracy across latent widths; it does not isolate corruption location while scoring a fixed downstream suffix.

Studies decoder sensitivity through noise sweeps, directional perturbations, margins, and token-level diagnostics in ELF and Cola-DLM, but does not compare localized latent-block corruption effects on a common output suffix.
COSMOS evaluates decoder robustness using Gaussian latent corruption and whole-text BLEU, rather than varying the corrupted block and holding scored output positions fixed.

SeqDiffuSeq measures denoising difficulty at different target-token positions and learns position-specific schedules; it does not measure how different corruption-source positions influence the same downstream tokens through a frozen latent-to-text decoder.

sol.reason: The closest prior work establishes global decoder-corruption robustness and position-dependent denoising difficulty, but neither answers the registered source-position influence question. The distinguishing intervention is to move localized corruption across latent blocks while keeping the scored suffix fixed, rather than merely changing the dataset, model, or metric. I found no work available by 2026-10-07 reporting that comparison or largely settling it.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (position_sensitivity.py, launched by run_eval.sh): the probe as registered.
- Models: I loaded the released shared autoencoder (fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, 100000.safetensors) through the seed repo's `Aurora` wrapper in eval mode, using the OWT checkpoint's config. I then replaced the latent mean/std with the standardization statistics stored in fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (250000.safetensors), which is what the repo's eval code does. The denoiser is never run. The GPT-2 BPE tokenizer comes from `gpt2`.
- Data: nonempty lines of WikiText-2-raw validation, tokenized one line at a time and joined with an EOS token after each line. I took the first 32 nonoverlapping 128-token windows.
- Procedure: the uncompressed c=1 mapping is used; I checked that the decoder chunk_size is 1. For each window I encode, take the first 128 latents (D=768) and standardize them. Each window gets one Gaussian tensor with seed 1234+window, and the same tensor is reused for all eight block conditions. For each block of 16 latents in turn, only that block is replaced by 0.5·z + 0.5·ε; I then invert the standardization, decode, and compute cross-entropy on output positions 113–128. The clean-latent cross-entropy on the same positions is subtracted. The bootstrap resamples windows 10,000 times (seed 0), keeping each window's eight block conditions together, and the registered statistic is the 10th percentile of the resulting max-minus-min range.
- Outputs: points.jsonl has 256 rows (one per window and block). summary.json holds the eight block means, the observed range, the bootstrap percentiles and the registered value; result.json is written as required.

Deviations:
1. Encoder and decoder run in fp32 with autocast off. The released config uses bf16 autocast; I switched to fp32 so that bf16 rounding would not add noise to the small cross-entropy differences. The model weights and computation are otherwise unchanged.
2. Flex attention is turned off, so the repo's own dense-mask fallback is used. This does not change the result.

Result from my test runs: the clean reconstruction is essentially perfect, with token accuracy 0.9985 and mean CE on positions 113–128 of about 6e-6. The block-mean increases in CE are about 1e-6 or smaller for blocks 1–7 and 3.2e-4 for block 8. The observed range is 3.2e-4 nats, and the registered statistic is 3.9e-5, far below the 0.10 threshold, so the event did not occur.

Two extra checks, not registered and not written to the outputs:
- I re-ran at σ=0.8 and σ=0.95 to confirm that corruption actually reaches the decoder. Corrupting block 8 raised CE on positions 113–128 to 2.58 and 12.4 nats respectively, while blocks 1–7 still had essentially zero effect.
- So the corruption is applied correctly. At σ=0.5 the decoder is simply very robust, which matches the paper's Fig. 5a. Even at higher noise, the suffix tokens depend almost entirely on their aligned latent block.

As the registration says, this is evidence against a large position-dependent effect at σ=0.5 in this probe, not proof that block positions are equivalent. The near-zero values reflect a floor effect: the decoder's robustness at this noise level means no block produces much effect at all.

A full re-run takes about 1–2 minutes, including pip installs and roughly 2 GB of checkpoint downloads. Results were identical across my two runs.

departures: position_sensitivity.py runs the encoder and decoder in fp32 with autocast off. The released config (checkpoints/*/config.yaml) uses bf16. The engineer reported this. It could shift values by rounding-level amounts (about 1e-6), which is negligible against the 0.10 threshold.
position_sensitivity.py sets flex_attention=False. Both released configs already set flex_attention: false, so this is not a real change and cannot affect the result.

The tokenizer is downloaded from the 'gpt2' hub repo into models/gpt2-small rather than taken from the checkpoint. The checkpoint config points text_encoder at the same 'models/gpt2-small' GPT-2 BPE vocabulary. This was not reported. It has no plausible effect, since the vocabulary is identical (vocab_size 50257).

position_sensitivity.py encodes each 128-token window on its own and keeps lat[:, :128]. The autoencoder was trained on 1024-token wrapped sequences. This is an implementation choice the registration leaves open, and the clean reconstruction accuracy of 0.9985 shows the encode–decode path works.

The Gaussian tensor is drawn per window (seed 1234+w), and each block condition uses its own 16-position slice of it. This is consistent with the registration's 'one seeded Gaussian tensor per window'. It does not change the result.
The σ=0.8 and σ=0.95 runs described in the engineer notes were not registered and appear in no output file. They are not part of the evaluated value and cannot be verified.

registration.title: Does AURORA’s latent MSE rank denoising predictions by decoded text error?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA trains its prior with clean-latent x0 regression and decodes predicted latents into tokens. Its objective ablation compares aggregate generation quality, but not whether per-example latent error tracks the decoder’s token-level error.
registration.hypothesis: Across two fixed noise levels, the average within-level Spearman correlation between sequence-level latent MSE and excess decoder token cross-entropy is below 0.30.
registration.contribution: Measures per-example alignment between AURORA’s latent training loss and a decoder-facing error, after subtracting the autoencoder’s own reconstruction loss. A weak association would motivate, but would not establish the value of, a decoder-aware training objective.

closest_work.difference: AURORA compares aggregate generation quality across prediction targets and loss spaces; this tests whether latent MSE ranks held-out examples by their decoded token error.
TextLDM studies latent representation alignment; this experiment measures the association between AURORA prior error and excess token loss from its frozen decoder.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; load fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt and fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, including the checkpoint tokenizer and latent statistics.
Hugging Face dataset Salesforce/wikitext, configuration wikitext-2-raw-v1, validation split.
registration.method: Load the OWT prior using its released inference/EMA weights and load the frozen autoencoder. Tokenize validation text with the checkpoint’s GPT-2 BPE tokenizer, concatenate nonempty lines with EOS separators, and take 64 nonoverlapping 128-token windows. For each window, encode and standardize the latents. At each σ in {0.7, 0.9}, draw two fixed Gaussian noise tensors and form xσ = (1−σ)z + σε. For each noisy sequence, evaluate the prior with the block-causal two-stream teacher-forcing mask: each target block can use its own noisy positions and only the true clean prefix before that block; it must not see clean current-block targets or future clean blocks. Omit self-conditioning. Compute sequence-level x0 MSE over valid latent positions. Denormalize the x0 prediction, decode it, and compute token cross-entropy against the original tokens. Also decode the uncorrupted encoded latents and compute the same cross-entropy; define excess cross-entropy as predicted-latent CE minus this clean reconstruction baseline. Average each sequence’s MSE and excess CE over the two noise draws at each σ. Compute Spearman correlation across the 64 sequences separately at each σ. Bootstrap sequences with replacement 10,000 times, recompute both correlations and their arithmetic mean, and use the 90th percentile of those mean correlations as the registered statistic.

event.description: The 90th-percentile bootstrap upper endpoint for the mean within-noise-level rank correlation is below 0.30.
event.statistic: 90th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap replicates of mean(Spearman_rho_at_0.7, Spearman_rho_at_0.9)

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per window and noise level with the two draw-level latent MSEs, predicted decoder CE, clean decoder CE, and excess CE. Write both point correlations, their mean, and the registered bootstrap statistic to the summary file.
evaluation.controls: Use the same held-out windows at both noise levels, average two noise draws per sequence, compare against each sequence’s clean autoencoder reconstruction baseline, and enforce the two-stream mask to prevent target leakage. This is an association screen, not a causal test of a different training loss.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, train compute-matched priors with latent MSE and with a decoder-aware auxiliary loss or sensitivity weighting, then compare held-out decoded token fidelity and generation quality.

agent.reason: Latent MSE and decoder error may both reflect sequence difficulty, but token loss depends on which latent directions are wrong, not just their total squared error. The association could therefore be weak, though the bootstrap upper-endpoint criterion is conservative.

judge_astra.reason: Holding noise fixed removes an important confound, but content difficulty can still increase both latent MSE and decoded cross-entropy; subtracting clean reconstruction loss does not remove this shared difficulty. I expect an association that is often too positive for its bootstrap upper endpoint to fall below 0.30.

judge_fable.reason: Both per-sequence latent MSE and excess decoder CE are driven by how predictable/rare a WikiText window's content is, so a moderate-to-strong positive rank correlation (>0.3) seems more likely than the registered weak one; some probability mass comes from saturation/floor effects at σ=0.9/0.7 and from mask-leakage implementation errors that would spuriously flatten the correlation.

judge_opus.reason: Across sequences, latent MSE and decoded cross-entropy both track how predictable the content is, so a clearly positive Spearman correlation (likely above 0.4, especially at σ=0.9) is expected. The event mainly arises from implementation errors such as mask leakage or garbage predictions.

judge_sol.reason: Decoder-insensitive latent directions could weaken the association, but token predictability should contribute to both MSE and excess cross-entropy. Averaging across tokens and noise draws may strengthen that shared signal, making an upper bootstrap endpoint below 0.30 relatively difficult.

judge_luna.reason: Latent MSE and decoded token cross-entropy may both worsen on harder-to-recover examples, but direction-sensitive decoding can break that ranking. The bootstrap upper-endpoint requirement makes a weak association only moderately likely.

judge_muse.reason: Latent MSE and excess token CE share underlying sequence predictability, so moderate positive rank correlation is expected; a 90th percentile below 0.30 with n=64 requires near-zero true correlation.

However, those findings do not determine whether denoising MSE ranks held-out sequences by excess decoder loss at fixed noise levels. outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (mse_decoder/run.py, launched by mse_decoder/run_eval.sh): The script loads the released OWT denoiser (fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, 250k checkpoint) through the repo's own EvalDiffusionTrainer path, together with the frozen autoencoder (fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder) and the GPT-2 tokenizer. The latent statistics come from the checkpoint. The denoiser is evaluated with EMA weights (trainer.ema.average_parameters(), as the released sampler does).

Data: wikitext-2-raw-v1 validation. Nonempty lines are stripped, tokenized with the checkpoint tokenizer and joined with EOS separators. The first 64 nonoverlapping 128-token windows are used. Each window is encoded and only the first 128 latents are kept. Because the encoder is prefix-causal, these latents depend only on that window's tokens. The latents are then standardized with the checkpoint statistics.

Noise: σ ∈ {0.7, 0.9}, with two fixed CPU-seeded Gaussian draws per σ, and x_σ = (1−σ)z + σε. The denoiser is called with clean_x=z and block_size=16, which uses the repo's two_stream_teacher mask: a noisy block sees its own noisy block plus clean blocks strictly before it, and never the clean current or future blocks. Self-conditioning is omitted (x_0_self_cond=None) and time_t=σ.

Measurements:
- Per-sequence x0 MSE over all 128×768 positions and channels.
- The x0 prediction is denormalized and decoded by the frozen decoder, and mean token CE is taken against the original tokens.
- Clean-reconstruction CE comes from decoding the uncorrupted latents. Excess CE = predicted CE − clean CE.
- MSE and excess CE are averaged over the two draws, then Spearman ρ is computed per σ across the 64 windows.
- Bootstrap: 10,000 resamples of windows, the same indices for both σ, numpy seed 20260803. The registered statistic is the 90th percentile of mean(ρ_0.7, ρ_0.9).

Outputs: points.jsonl (one row per window × σ, with draw-level MSEs, predicted CE, clean CE and excess CE), summary.json, and result.json.

Changes from the registration:
1. I set operator_optimization.profile="off" so the model uses plain SDPA attention. The checkpoint's auto profile picks FlexAttention on CUDA, and that failed at runtime on this torch build. This changes only the attention kernel, not the math or the masks.
2. The registration does not say how to treat line whitespace; I chose to strip lines before tokenizing.
3. The model was trained on 1024-token sequences, but the windows are 128 tokens. I ran the denoiser and decoder at length 128 (8 blocks). The block-causal and causal masks mean the first 128 positions do not depend on later ones.

Sanity checks: clean reconstruction gives token accuracy 99.8% and mean CE 0.106. Token accuracy of the decoded prediction is about 0.88 at σ=0.7 and about 0.25 at σ=0.9.

Result from my test run (two full runs from scratch gave identical values): ρ(σ=0.7)=0.550, ρ(σ=0.9)=0.555, mean 0.552. Bootstrap 90th percentile = 0.629 (5th–95th percentiles: 0.429–0.651). This is above 0.30, so the registered event did not occur. On these 64 held-out windows, sequence-level latent MSE is moderately associated with excess decoder CE.

Caveats: this is an association screen on one dataset, 64 windows and two noise draws. It is not a causal test of a decoder-aware loss.

departures: mse_decoder/run.py sets cfg.operator_optimization.profile='off', so attention runs on plain SDPA instead of the FlexAttention path that 'auto' selects. The engineer disclosed this as a runtime necessity. It should not change the math, but nothing in the archive shows the SDPA path applies the two_stream_teacher mask identically. The observed latent MSEs (0.40 at σ=0.7, 0.85 at σ=0.9) are too high to fit visible clean current-block targets, which argues against leakage. Unlikely to change the result.

mse_decoder/run.py strips each line before tokenizing. The registration leaves whitespace handling open and the engineer disclosed it. This changes the token stream and window contents slightly. It could shift ρ marginally but is unlikely to move it from about 0.55 to below 0.30.

mse_decoder/run.py runs the encoder, denoiser and decoder at length 128 rather than the 1024-token training length, and keeps latents[:, :128] from get_latent. This is disclosed and needed to evaluate 128-token windows. Clean reconstruction accuracy of 99.8% suggests the truncation is consistent. Unlikely to change the result.

mse_decoder/run.py computes MSE over all 128×768 positions and channels. The registration says 'valid latent positions'; with no padding in these windows all positions are valid, so this is equivalent. No effect.

mse_decoder/run.py builds x_σ through tr.noise_scheduler.add_noise(z, eps, sigma) and conditions with time_t=σ. The archive does not show the repo function, so I cannot confirm it implements exactly (1−σ)z+σε with no time shift. This is undisclosed only in that it is unverified. If a shift were applied, the effective noise levels would differ; the per-level MSE magnitudes look plausible for the registered σ.
The denoiser forward runs under the trainer's bf16 autocast context. This is not specified by the registration and is the standard inference precision. Negligible effect.
problems: The repo's add_noise and predict_x0 conventions and the SDPA mask path are not visible in the archive, so the exact noise parameterization and the absence of leakage are inferred, not verified. The observed MSE levels and the drop in accuracy from σ=0.7 to σ=0.9 are consistent with correct behaviour.

Excess CE at σ=0.9 averages about 22 nats, well above log|V|≈10.8. This means the decoder is confidently wrong on noisy latents, so CE at that level mostly measures decoder overconfidence rather than graded fidelity. The correlation there is about a heavily saturated quantity.

The design is limited: 64 windows from one dataset, two noise draws and two noise levels. Sequence-level correlation can be driven by window difficulty, for example numbers or headings that inflate both quantities. As the registration says, this is an association screen, not a test of the value of a decoder-aware loss.
opus.reason: The code in mse_decoder/run.py follows the registered method closely: EMA weights, the block-causal two-stream mask with self-conditioning omitted, σ∈{0.7,0.9} with two fixed draws, excess CE over a clean-reconstruction baseline, per-σ Spearman correlations, and the 90th percentile of 10,000 paired bootstrap means. The departures (SDPA kernel, stripped lines, length-128 evaluation) are disclosed, needed to run, or left open by the registration, and none plausibly moves a point estimate of about 0.55 below 0.30. The outputs are produced by the code from real model passes, and the protected rerun reproduces the engineer's numbers exactly. The MSE magnitudes argue against target leakage. The registered hypothesis (association below 0.30) is clearly refuted, with a bootstrap 5–95% range of 0.43–0.65. This is a credible, meaningful negative result for the motivating claim, though narrow in scope and partly driven by saturated CE at σ=0.9.

Different kernels can introduce numerical differences, but this is a runtime-enabling change, with no demonstrated change to the intended attention semantics or conclusion.

mse_decoder/run.py strips leading and trailing whitespace before tokenization. This can change GPT-2 tokens, window boundaries, and the numerical result. Whitespace handling was unspecified in the registration, so this is an allowed implementation choice.

mse_decoder/run.py selects the first 64 windows rather than specifying another selection scheme. Different windows could change the correlations, but the registration did not prescribe random sampling or window indices; the registered sample size and nonoverlap are preserved.

mse_decoder/run.py retains only the first 128 encoder latents and evaluates the denoiser and decoder at length 128 rather than the checkpoint's 1024-token training length. This implements the registered 128-token windows, rather than changing their length. Equivalence to a padded longer evaluation relies on the stated causal-prefix behavior; no comparison is supplied.

mse_decoder/run.py uses np.nanpercentile, which would exclude undefined bootstrap correlations, although the registration specifies no exclusion rule. The protected evaluation reports zero NaN replicates, so this additional rule did not affect the reported statistic.
problems: mse_decoder/run.py bootstraps individual windows from a contiguous initial portion of WikiText. Adjacent windows may share articles and content, so independence and corpus-level coverage are not established; the bootstrap percentiles should not be interpreted as assured corpus-level confidence bounds.

The essential mask, scheduler, checkpoint-loading, and causal-prefix behavior are delegated to seed/src implementations not displayed here. The supplied configuration and calls support the intended setup, but there is no included mask-perturbation test or short-versus-padded equivalence check.

mse_decoder/run_eval.sh downloads repositories without immutable revisions, leaves several dependencies unpinned, and suppresses installation failure with "|| true". These weaken future reproducibility and failure reporting, although the protected evaluation completed successfully.

The experiment measures sequence-level association for one checkpoint, 64 windows, two noise levels, and two draws per level. It does not establish token-level alignment, generation-quality alignment, or whether a decoder-aware objective would improve training.
sol.reason: The visible code preserves the registered measurements, clean-reconstruction subtraction, within-level correlations, paired sequence bootstrap, and strict event threshold; the identified choices and changes do not establish a fidelity defect. The fresh protected evaluation completed successfully, produced both registered output files, and reported a computed statistic of 0.6290717924271586, so the event below 0.30 did not occur. The observed correlations of approximately 0.550 and 0.555 provide meaningful evidence of moderate positive association in this evaluated sample, rather than merely an inconclusive failure to detect an effect. This is a credible negative finding for the proposed weak-alignment hypothesis, but its sampling limitations and noncausal design prevent broader claims about latent MSE adequacy or alternative training objectives.

departures: mse_decoder/run.py strips each WikiText line before the nonempty filter and GPT-2 tokenization; the registration only says to concatenate nonempty lines with EOS separators. registration.title: Does preserving a partial prompt block improve AURORA’s XSum continuation?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA generates latent blocks left to right and uses clean repainting to retain known prompt positions when a source ends inside a block. The paper specifies this inference rule but does not report a paired ablation of retaining versus replacing those positions.
registration.hypothesis: On paired partial-block XSum prompts, clamping the known source tail to its encoded latents produces a positive mean ROUGE-L gain over redrawing and denoising that tail.
registration.contribution: Tests the practical value of AURORA’s partial-block prompt-handling rule against an explicitly defined alternative. It is an inference-policy test, not a comparison of diffusion architectures.

closest_work.difference: AURORA specifies clean repainting for partial prompt blocks but does not report this paired retain-versus-replace comparison.
Cola-DLM is a related latent-diffusion model; this experiment isolates AURORA’s specific handling of a partial source block.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; load the XSum checkpoint fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum and shared autoencoder fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder.
Hugging Face dataset EdinburghNLP/xsum, test split, using document and summary fields; use the model’s GPT-2 BPE tokenizer and a ROUGE-L F1 implementation with stemming.
registration.method: Run the released XSum model in eval mode on CUDA. Shuffle the test split with seed 42 and select the first 24 documents with at least 136 GPT-2 tokens. For each document, let n be the largest token count no greater than min(source length, 448) such that n mod 16 = 8; use the first n source tokens and require n ≥ 128. Compare two arms on the same document. In the preserve arm, encode all n source tokens; keep complete blocks through position n−8 as clean context and clamp the eight known latents at positions n−7 through n to their encoder values throughout denoising of the partial boundary block. In the replace arm, use the same complete prefix through n−8, but initialize all 16 positions n−7 through n+8 in the boundary block from Gaussian noise and denoise them, so the known source tail is replaced rather than clamped. In both arms, sample through absolute position n+72, using five block calls of size 16 and a 16-step deterministic Euler sampler with ordinary self-conditioning and no extra classifier-free guidance (conditional scale 1). Reuse the same initial Gaussian noise at every shared generated absolute position n+1 through n+72; use a fixed per-document seed for the replacement positions n−7 through n. Decode the continuation at positions n+1 through n+64, strip EOS markers, and score against the reference summary with stemmed ROUGE-L F1 on the 0–1 scale. Bootstrap the 24 paired document differences with replacement 10,000 times; the 10th percentile of the mean preserve-minus-replace difference is the registered statistic.

event.description: The 10th-percentile bootstrap lower endpoint for the paired mean ROUGE-L gain from preserving the partial source tail is greater than zero.
event.statistic: 10th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap means of ROUGE-L_preserve − ROUGE-L_replace

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per document with the source length, selected n, reference, both decoded continuations, and both ROUGE-L scores. Write the paired mean difference and registered bootstrap statistic to the summary file.
evaluation.controls: Both arms use the same source documents, complete clean-prefix blocks, block size, solver steps, number of block calls, and initial noise at shared generated positions. Only treatment of the eight known positions in the partial block changes. A missed threshold does not establish equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, evaluate all partial-block offsets with multiple generation seeds and matched sampling budgets; measure ROUGE alongside source-content preservation on a larger XSum sample.

agent.reason: Keeping true source-tail latents is consistent with the model’s clean-prefix training and could help compared with redrawing them. But only eight tokens differ, so a robust ROUGE-L gain across 24 examples is uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: Retaining genuine source latents plausibly helps, but eight tail tokens provide relatively little additional information within these long prompts. With only 24 documents and one paired generation per document, a modest benefit may not clear the positive-lower-endpoint criterion.

judge_fable.reason: Truncating the source at n tokens with no separator means both arms mostly continue the article rather than summarize, and preserving 8 real source tokens versus regenerating them adds negligible information, so the paired ROUGE-L difference is likely noise around zero with only ~10–20% chance of a positive 10th-percentile bound; implementation complexity adds failure risk.

judge_opus.reason: The prompt has no summary separator, so both arms probably write document-like continuations. Only 8 boundary tokens differ, which makes the paired ROUGE-L difference small and noisy across 24 documents. Clamping clean latents at noisy timesteps could also mildly hurt the preserve arm, and custom-sampler implementation risk lowers the odds further.

judge_sol.reason: Preserving known source latents should generally help conditioning, but eight tail tokens may add little summary-relevant information beyond the complete prefix. With only 24 pairs and a truncated-source, unguided sampling protocol, a reliably positive ROUGE-L gain is uncertain.

judge_luna.reason: Clamping retains eight known source latents, whereas replacement regenerates part of the prompt before the scored continuation. That makes a positive paired ROUGE-L gain plausible, though the 24-document sample leaves uncertainty.

judge_muse.reason: Retaining the true 8-token tail should help on average, but it is a small fraction of a >=128-token prefix and paired ROUGE-L on 24 docs is noisy, making 90% confidence above zero uncertain.

closest_work.difference: The seed paper describes clean repainting only as an implementation detail (Appendix 6.2.4): when a prompt ends inside a block, the known positions are fixed to their encoder latents. Its ablations cover latent width, compression, bottleneck width, noise allocation, prediction target, self-trajectory consistency, block size, guidance scale and step count. None of them compares fixing those known positions against regenerating them from noise.

Cola-DLM is the source AURORA cites for using complete prompt blocks as causal context. Its abstract and its description in the seed paper do not mention a paired test of how to handle a partial prompt block. I did not read its full text, so this is not fully confirmed.

opus.reason: I read the seed paper's method, experiments and inference-protocol appendix. Clean repainting is stated as the rule used, but no paired comparison against regenerating the partial block's known tail is reported. My arXiv searches for this kind of prompt-boundary ablation in block diffusion or latent-diffusion language models found nothing relevant, though the searches returned mostly unrelated results and may have missed something. This retain-versus-replace inference test on XSum therefore looks unanswered in the work I found.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Cola-DLM already ablates first-generation-block conditioning in Section 5.2, Table 5, and Appendix 17.1: clean clamping of known prompt latents versus noisy/partial repaint and left/right padding. The proposed experiment instead uses AURORA on XSum, a fully unguided redraw baseline, and paired noise with bootstrap ROUGE-L inference.

AURORA-LM specifies clean repainting for partial prompt blocks in Appendix 6.2.4 but does not report the proposed retain-versus-replace ablation; its XSum inference sweeps vary guidance and solver steps.

sol.reason: Cola-DLM already experimentally studies whether known prompt latents in a mixed boundary block should remain clean and fixed, reporting better continuation performance with persistent clean conditioning than with weaker repainting or padding alternatives. The registered experiment is not an exact replication because its full-redraw control differs, but it closely revisits that established boundary-preservation question on another model and task.

opus.reason: Entry 59 uses the released AURORA-LM-S checkpoint on XSum prompts that end inside a block and compares clean repainting with generating the whole boundary block from noise, scored by ROUGE at fixed seeds, which is essentially this paired preserve-versus-replace test.

sol.reason: Both compare clean repainting of known positions in a partial XSum prompt block against regenerating the entire boundary block from noise, measuring paired summary ROUGE.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: run_eval.sh installs the dependencies (the preinstalled torch is kept), downloads fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum (300k checkpoint), fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder, the GPT-2 tokenizer and the EdinburghNLP/xsum test split, then runs repaint_boundary.py. It imports the seed code from seed/src and uses the released DiffusionGenerator to load the model: EMA weights, eval mode, CUDA.

The two arms use a custom block loop that mirrors the released BlockSampler.run repaint path:
- Prefill: the complete clean blocks through position n−8 go into the KV cache with the released block-causal prefill mask.
- Block calls: five calls of size 16 cover absolute positions n−7 to n+72. Position ids run on continuously, as in the released repaint mode.
- Sampler: 16-step deterministic Euler with the released tanh sigma grid. Ordinary self-conditioning goes through features.self_cond.resolve. There is no SC-CFG and no CFG (conditional scale 1).
- Preserve arm: the 8 encoder latents at n−7..n are clamped at initialisation, after every step and at the end. The denoiser gets repaint_tail_len=8, so those positions get a t=0 time embedding, exactly as in the released code.
- Replace arm: all 16 boundary positions start from noise and are denoised, with repaint_tail_len=0 and no clamping.
- Noise: each document gets an 80×768 Gaussian tensor from a CPU generator seeded 1000 + document index. Both arms use the same values at n+1..n+72; the replace arm also uses the values at n−7..n.
- Decoding: each arm's full latent sequence (length n+72) goes through the frozen decoder. I take the argmax tokens at n+1..n+64, remove EOS tokens, and score against the reference with rouge_score ROUGE-L F1 (stemming on).
- Bootstrap: 10,000 resamples of the 24 paired differences (numpy seed 12345); the registered statistic is their 10th percentile.

Document selection follows the registration: shuffle the test split with seed 42, take the first 24 documents with at least 136 GPT-2 tokens, and set n = the largest value ≤ min(length, 448) with n mod 16 = 8. Every selected document has n ≥ 136.

Deviations and interpretation choices:
1. FlexAttention would not run with the installed torch (2.6; the repo pins 2.8). I set operator_optimization.profile=off, which switches to plain SDPA. This changes only which kernels run, not the method.
2. "Strip EOS markers" is applied literally: EOS tokens are removed from the 64 decoded tokens. As a secondary, unregistered view, summary.json also reports scores with truncation at the first EOS, which is the released eval convention.
3. The decoder is fed each arm's own latents at n−7..n: encoder latents in the preserve arm, generated latents in the replace arm.

Result from my full test of the evaluation command (it reran end to end with the same value):
- Mean ROUGE-L: 0.187 (preserve) vs 0.202 (replace).
- Paired mean difference: −0.0144; preserve scored higher on 10 documents and lower on 14.
- Registered statistic (10th bootstrap percentile): −0.0295, so the event (> 0) did not occur.
- Secondary first-EOS view: mean difference +0.025, 10th percentile −0.004. The sign of the mean difference depends on the EOS convention, so this sample gives no conclusion in either direction.

Missing the threshold does not show the two arms are equivalent: the sample is 24 documents with one generation seed.

departures: repaint_boundary.py sets operator_optimization.profile=off, which uses plain SDPA instead of FlexAttention, and the run uses the preinstalled torch 2.6 rather than the pinned 2.8. This was needed to run at all. It changes kernels and bf16 numerics only, so it is unlikely to change the sign or size of the result materially.

repaint_boundary.py uses a custom block loop instead of calling the released BlockSampler.run. The engineer says the loop mirrors the released repaint path: block-causal prefill, continuous position ids, t=0 time embedding through repaint_tail_len=8 for clamped positions, clamping after every step, and a t=0 KV-cache write of each finished block. The seed source is not in the archive, so I cannot verify this. If repaint_tail_len or the self-conditioning handling of clamped positions differs from the released rule, the preserve arm would not be exactly AURORA's clean repainting, and the value could change.

Self-conditioning in the preserve arm feeds the model's prediction, not the clean tail, at the clamped positions (repaint_boundary.py). The registration is silent on this, and it could slightly affect the preserve arm.

Decoding: each arm's full latent sequence goes through the decoder, with the arm's own latents at n−7..n (encoder latents in preserve, generated latents in replace). The registration leaves this open. It was disclosed. It plausibly affects token boundaries at n+1.

EOS handling: EOS tokens are removed from the 64 decoded tokens, not truncated at the first EOS. This follows the literal registered wording ('strip EOS markers') and was disclosed. summary.json shows the sign of the mean difference flips under first-EOS truncation (+0.025), so this registered choice drives the sign.
rouge_score 'rougeL' is used rather than 'rougeLsum', with stemming. This is consistent with the registered 'ROUGE-L F1 with stemming'.
EMA weights, bf16 autocast, tf32 disabled, CPU-generated noise seeded 1000+doc index, and bootstrap seed 12345 are all choices the registration leaves open. None plausibly changes the question.

No separator token is inserted between source and continuation. The registration specifies only the first n source tokens, so this is not a departure, though I cannot check whether it matches the training format.

Document selection, the n rule, n+72 generation, the n+1..n+64 decode window, 24 documents, 10,000 bootstrap resamples and the 10th percentile all match the registration (checked against the printed len/n pairs, e.g. 209→200, 344→344).
problems: The design confounds position and scoring window. In pairs.jsonl and stdout, replace-arm continuations usually begin mid-sentence ('her life in a hen party crash…', 'killed by an alligator…', 'indecent image of himself…'), while preserve-arm continuations begin a summary. This suggests that when the source tail is redrawn, the model starts the summary about 8 positions earlier, so the fixed n+1..n+64 window cuts its opening and includes more post-summary text. The registered statistic therefore partly measures a window and alignment artifact rather than the quality of the conditioning.

With EOS stripped, text generated after the summary's end is scored. The result reverses sign under the released first-EOS convention (mean +0.025, p10 −0.004 vs registered mean −0.014, p10 −0.030). So the conclusion is fragile to post-processing, which the engineer correctly reports.

There are only 24 documents and one generation seed. The bootstrap 10th–90th percentile range is [−0.030, +0.0005]. A missed threshold does not establish that the arms are equivalent or that preserve is worse.

Fidelity of the custom loop in repaint_boundary.py to the released repaint path (repaint_tail_len semantics, self-conditioning at clamped positions) cannot be verified from the archive, because the seed source is absent.
eval_test.log is an engineer-submitted earlier run. It matches the protected rerun exactly, which supports determinism but is not independent evidence.

The registered event did not occur: the 10th percentile is −0.030 with a paired mean of −0.014, and preserve won on 10 of 24 documents.
