relation.reason: The experiment uses the paper's released model and its inference rule and tests a property of that rule, about which the paper makes no performance claim, against a newly defined alternative.

obvious.reason: Ablating a small boundary-handling detail of prompt-conditioned inference is a niche question that only a researcher reading the appendix implementation note closely would list.

who_would_care.reason: The answer would only affect people implementing prompt handling for block-causal latent diffusion models like AURORA.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan says AURORA uses clean repainting for partial prompt blocks and does not report this ablation; both statements match Appendix 6.2.4.

answerable.reason: The plan scores a fixed 64-token window with EOS tokens stripped, while XSum summaries are much shorter, so the paired difference speaks to summary quality only if text after the first EOS does not drive the score.
answerable.needs: scored 64-token EOS-stripped window reflects summary quality

opus.what_came_out: On 24 XSum test documents with one generation seed, using the AURORA-LM-S XSum checkpoint, mean ROUGE-L was 0.187 with the tail preserved and 0.202 with it replaced (paired difference −0.014, bootstrap 10th–90th percentile −0.030 to +0.0005, preserve better on 10 of 24); truncating at the first EOS instead gave a difference of +0.025 (10th percentile −0.004).

prerequisite.reason: The sign of the paired difference reverses between the registered EOS-stripped scoring and first-EOS truncation, so the run cannot show whether the registered metric measures summary quality rather than post-summary text.
prerequisite.which: scored 64-token EOS-stripped window reflects summary quality

evidence.reason: The registered difference is small and negative, but its 80% interval nearly reaches zero, it rests on 24 documents and one seed, and it flips sign under the alternative EOS convention, so the run supports neither a gain nor a meaningful loss.

next_step.reason: The run did not settle the question, and it shows two faults: an EOS convention that changes the sign of the result, and a small single-seed sample.
next_step.what: Score summaries truncated at the first EOS (the released convention), and use more documents and several generation seeds.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares clamping known source-tail latents with replacing and denoising them in AURORA’s partial prompt blocks on XSum, to learn whether preserving the tail improves continuation ROUGE-L.

in_the_paper.reason: The appendix specifies clean repainting but neither reports a preserve-versus-replace comparison nor explicitly identifies its benefit as an open question.

relation.reason: The experiment changes AURORA’s prompt-boundary policy to test a benefit that the paper does not claim or measure.

obvious.reason: This implementation-specific ablation would plausibly appear on one or two first-ten lists, behind the paper’s more central representation, scaling, and efficiency questions.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would primarily change boundary handling for groups using AURORA or closely related latent-block generators.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan accurately describes blockwise generation and clean repainting, and the paper contains no reported paired ablation contradicting its account.

answerable.reason: The two policies directly manipulate the proposed treatment and measure their paired effect on the stated ROUGE-L outcome without requiring a separate paper result to reappear.

sol.what_came_out: On 24 paired XSum test documents with one generation draw per document, the released 130M AURORA-LM-S XSum model yielded mean ROUGE-L of 0.18739 when preserving versus 0.20179 when replacing, a paired difference of −0.01440 with a 10th–90th-percentile bootstrap interval of [−0.02950, 0.000514].

prerequisite.reason: The code applies distinct boundary policies, verifies preservation of the known latents, and produces varying non-floor scores, with no demonstrated prerequisite failure.

evidence.reason: The 24-pair, single-draw comparison does not establish a reversal with its reported interval reaching zero, while first-EOS scoring gives an uncertain positive difference of 0.02454 with a lower endpoint of −0.00394.

next_step.reason: Limited precision and sensitivity to output termination leave the direction unresolved but identify a concrete way to repeat the comparison.
next_step.what: Address limited document and generation-seed coverage by repeating the paired comparison on more documents and independent shared-noise seeds, keeping EOS removal as the fixed primary metric and reporting first-EOS truncation separately.

registration.title: Is repetition associated with lower GPT-2-small NLL in AURORA’s short OWT samples?
registration.seed_connection: AURORA reports external-model generation perplexity and a separate lexical-diversity measure. The paper does not analyze whether per-sample repetition covaries with the external scorer’s NLL.
registration.hypothesis: Across fixed-length AURORA samples, higher whitespace-token REP-4 is associated with lower GPT-2-small per-token NLL, with Spearman rho below −0.20.
registration.contribution: Checks whether a repetition–scorer association observed in a related continuous-DLM discussion also appears in AURORA. This is a sample-level association screen; it cannot establish that repetition causes a scorer preference and uses GPT-2-small rather than AURORA’s reported GPT-2-Large scorer.

closest_work.difference: ACE is the closest repetition-focused continuous-DLM work; this experiment measures a sample-level repetition–NLL association in AURORA rather than intervening on self-conditioning.
AURORA reports corpus-level generation perplexity and lexical entropy, but not their per-sample association with REP-4.

inputs: Code: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM; load fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt and fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder.
Hugging Face open model gpt2 for the GPT-2-small causal-LM scorer; no text corpus is required.
registration.method: Generate 64 unconditional samples from the released OWT model, each with exactly 96 latent positions, block size 16, a 16-step deterministic Euler sampler, ordinary self-conditioning, and no extra self-conditioning guidance (scale 1). Use a distinct fixed seed per sample and decode exactly 96 token IDs without EOS-based early stopping. For scoring, feed those same GPT-2 BPE token IDs to GPT-2-small and compute mean next-token NLL over positions 2–96. For REP-4, decode each sample, remove literal EOS markers, lowercase, and split on whitespace; compute the fraction of 4-gram occurrences that repeat an earlier identical 4-gram. Bootstrap samples with replacement 10,000 times and compute Spearman rho between REP-4 and NLL in each replicate. Use the 90th percentile of bootstrap rho as the registered statistic. If fewer than 48 samples have defined REP-4 or REP-4 has no variation, mark the statistic not estimable and do not trigger the event.

event.description: The 90th-percentile bootstrap upper endpoint for the sample-level Spearman correlation is below −0.20.
event.statistic: 90th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap Spearman correlations between REP-4 and GPT-2-small NLL

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per generated sample with its token IDs or text, REP-4, NLL, and valid-token counts. Write the point Spearman correlation, bootstrap statistic, and validity status to the summary file.
evaluation.controls: Use one checkpoint and fixed sampler settings, compute both metrics on the same fixed-length generated sequence, and bootstrap samples rather than treating token positions as independent. The result is observational and may reflect content or fluency as well as repetition.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, test the association across multiple checkpoints and seeds using AURORA’s longer selected OWT sampling protocol and GPT-2-Large scoring, then use controlled matched text perturbations to distinguish repetition effects from sample-content confounds.

agent.reason: A negative repetition–NLL association is plausible, but transfer to AURORA is uncertain and sample content can affect both measures. The short samples, possible limited REP-4 variation, and bootstrap threshold make the registered event fairly demanding.

judge_astra.reason: Repeated phrases can make subsequent tokens easier for an autoregressive scorer, so a negative association is plausible. Nevertheless, short samples may produce many tied zero REP-4 values, and the bootstrap criterion requires a substantially negative observed correlation.

judge_fable.reason: Needs a point Spearman of roughly ≤−0.35 with n=64, but in 96-token samples most REP-4 values will be exactly zero (heavy ties), capping the attainable magnitude unless many samples are degenerate loops, which the 16-step Euler MAUVE of ~0.89 makes unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: In 96-token samples with no extra guidance, most samples will have REP-4 of exactly zero. Heavy ties cap the attainable Spearman magnitude, and the event needs a point estimate of about −0.35 or lower. The direction is likely negative, but the magnitude is probably too small.

judge_sol.reason: Repeated passages can be easier for a causal scorer to predict, so a negative association is plausible. However, 96-token samples may have sparse, heavily tied REP-4 values, and content or fluency variation could prevent the bootstrap upper endpoint from falling below −0.20.

judge_luna.reason: At 96 tokens, repeated four-grams may be sparse or tied, and any repetition–NLL association is confounded by content and fluency. The use of GPT-2-small also differs from the paper’s GPT-2-Large scorer.

judge_muse.reason: Repetition generally lowers NLL, but 96-token fluent samples will yield many zero or near-zero REP-4 values with little variation, making a confidently strong rho below -0.20 unlikely.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: ACE already reports, at the sample level, that Gen-PPL from a GPT-2-Large scorer falls across REP-4 bins for unconditional continuous-DLM samples (ELF), using the same whitespace REP-4 definition. It explicitly excludes AURORA-LM from its transfer tests. The registered experiment changes only the model (AURORA's block-causal latent DLM), the scorer (GPT-2-small instead of Large), the sample length (96 tokens) and the statistic (bootstrap Spearman rho rather than binned perplexity).

Shows that generative perplexity under a frozen GPT-2-Large scorer rewards predictable but low-quality text, regardless of which model generated it. It does not compute a per-sample repetition–NLL correlation for AURORA.
The seed paper reports corpus-level generation perplexity and entropy only. It has no per-sample analysis of repetition against scorer NLL.

opus.reason: Prior work largely settles the underlying question. ACE shows at the sample level that a GPT-2 scorer gives lower perplexity to more repetitive continuous-DLM samples, and it uses the same REP-4 metric. Generative-perplexity-hacking work shows the same scorer preference holds whatever the generator. No paper I found measures this association on AURORA, which ACE deliberately excludes, but the remaining differences are the model, the scorer size and the correlation statistic. So the experiment is a close variant rather than a new question.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Section 3.1 and Figure 1(b) already examine the association between whitespace-token REP-4 and external-model Gen-PPL in unconditional ELF samples, reporting decreasing Gen-PPL across repetition bins. The proposed experiment substitutes AURORA, shorter samples and GPT-2-small, and uses bootstrapped Spearman correlation rather than binned perplexity.
AURORA-LM reports corpus-level GPT-2-Large generation perplexity, lexical entropy and MAUVE, but does not report the proposed per-sample REP-4–NLL association.

sol.reason: The ACE paper already investigates the central question using repetition and external language-model scoring on unconditional continuous-DLM generations. Testing it on AURORA with a different scorer, sequence length and correlation statistic is a close variant of that association analysis, although neither the exact AURORA result nor the registered numerical threshold is established by the prior work.

opus.reason: No list entry tests the per-sample association between REP-4 repetition and external-scorer NLL; entry 60 addresses metric stability under resampling and parser choice.

sol.reason: No list entry measures the sample-level association between generated-text REP-4 and external-model NLL at fixed sampling settings.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (ppl_rep/run_experiment.py, run from ppl_rep/run_all.sh; setup.sh installs packages and downloads fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt (250k), fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder and gpt2):
- Generation: 64 unconditional samples from the released AURORA-LM-S OWT checkpoint. I used the repo's own BlockSampler through trainer.pred_latents with these settings: 6 blocks × 16 = 96 latent positions, 16-step deterministic Euler, EMA weights, ordinary self-conditioning and no SC-CFG (sc_cfg disabled, which is the same as scale 1 but uses a single forward pass). Block-AR EOS early stopping was disabled. Each sample is generated alone with its own seed (1000+i, i=0..63). The latents are de-standardised and decoded by the frozen decoder into exactly 96 argmax token IDs, with no EOS truncation.
- NLL: the same 96 GPT-2 BPE IDs are fed to GPT-2-small (HF "gpt2", fp32), and NLL is the mean next-token NLL over positions 2–96 (95 tokens).
- REP-4: the IDs are decoded to text, literal <|endoftext|> markers are removed, the text is lowercased and split on whitespace, and REP-4 is the fraction of 4-gram occurrences that repeat an earlier 4-gram.
- Statistics: point Spearman correlation, then 10,000 bootstrap resamples of samples (rng seed 12345). The registered statistic is the 90th percentile of the bootstrap rho. The validity rule (≥48 samples with defined REP-4 and REP-4 not constant) is implemented; if the statistic were not estimable, result.json would get NaN and the summary would be marked not_estimable.

Small implementation changes, which do not change the question:
1. The decoder's FlexAttention path failed on this GPU (a q/k/v dtype mismatch). I set operator_optimization.profile="off", which uses the eager/SDPA kernels; this changes kernels, not the model. I also cast the de-standardised latents to fp32 before decoding.
2. In some bootstrap resamples every REP-4 value is identical, so Spearman rho is undefined. This happened in 437 of the 10,000 resamples, which were excluded; the 90th percentile is taken over the other 9,563. The registration does not say how to handle this case.

Result from two full test runs of the submission command (identical, about 2.5 minutes each): all 64 samples have defined REP-4, point Spearman = −0.150, bootstrap 10th/50th/90th percentiles = −0.279 / −0.153 / −0.017. The statistic is −0.017, which is not below −0.20, so the event did not occur.

Caveats:
- REP-4 is almost always zero in these short samples: only 3 of 64 samples are non-zero, with 4 distinct values. The "correlation" is therefore mostly a comparison of 3 samples against 61 ties.
- Because REP-4 barely varies, this run is a weak test. It does not show that there is no association; it only fails to support one under this protocol.
- GPT-2-small is used rather than the paper's GPT-2-Large, and the sampling protocol (96 tokens, 16-step Euler, no guidance) differs from the paper's 1024-token, 64-step SDE-DPM++, SC-CFG 4 setting.
- Every sample's first token is EOS; it is kept as GPT-2's context token and is not scored.

departures: Undefined bootstrap replicates. ppl_rep/run_experiment.py drops resamples in which every REP-4 value is identical. This happened in 437 of 10,000 resamples, so the 90th percentile is taken over 9,563 rhos. The registration does not cover this case. The choice shifts the reported value slightly. Treating those resamples as rho=0 would only move the 90th percentile closer to zero, so the event outcome would not change.
Validity rule. run_experiment.py adds an extra estimability check: NLL must not be constant. It was not triggered (status ok), so it had no effect.

Attention kernels. In run_experiment.py, operator_optimization.profile is set to 'off' (eager/SDPA instead of FlexAttention), and the de-standardised latents are cast to fp32 before decoding. These are numerical and kernel changes needed for the code to run. They do not plausibly change the conclusion.

Self-conditioning guidance. SC-CFG is disabled (sc_cfg_scale=None, tr.sc_cfg_enabled=False) rather than run at scale 1. With ordinary self-conditioning this should be equivalent, as the registration intends.

Sampler details. The 'deterministic Euler' sampler comes from pred_latents(solver='euler'). The checkpoint config (checkpoints/owt/config.yaml) has dynamic.ode_sampling: false, and the _SamplingParams object built in run_experiment.py is never used. Nothing in the visible evidence confirms that the Euler path is noise-free. If it were stochastic, the samples would come from a different decoding setting.
Unspecified choices. EMA weights and argmax decoding of latents to token IDs are not specified in the registration. They are reasonable open choices.

Leading EOS token. Every sample's first token is EOS (50256). It is kept and serves as GPT-2's unscored context, so each sample has 95 scored tokens of content. REP-4 removes the literal EOS. This matches the registered position 2–96 scoring and does not change the result.
Disclosed deviations from the paper. GPT-2-small scorer, 96-token length, 16 steps and no guidance differ from the paper's protocol, but they are part of the registration, not departures from it.
problems: REP-4 is nearly degenerate. outputs/ppl_repetition/summary.json shows rep4_n_nonzero=3 and rep4_n_unique=4 out of 64 samples. The Spearman rho effectively compares 3 samples against 61 ties, so the statistic has very little power to detect the hypothesised association. The 96-token whitespace REP-4 design almost guaranteed this.

Bootstrap distribution. Excluding the 437 all-tied resamples (run_experiment.py) is an unregistered handling rule that conditions the bootstrap distribution on at least one nonzero REP-4 being drawn. It does not affect the event outcome.

Unverified sampler. Whether the Euler sampler is deterministic is asserted in the notes and code comments but cannot be checked from the files shown (ode_sampling: false in checkpoints/owt/config.yaml).

Weak point estimate. The point Spearman of -0.15 rests on 3 samples with nonzero REP-4. It should not be read as evidence for or against an association, and the non-event should not be read as evidence that no association exists.
opus.reason: The code runs the registered pipeline: 64 seeded samples of 96 tokens from the released OWT checkpoint, GPT-2-small NLL over positions 2–96, whitespace REP-4, and the 90th percentile of 10,000 bootstrap Spearman rhos. The departures are either needed to make the code run or are choices the registration leaves open, and none plausibly changes the event outcome. The reported value is computed from real generations and scores, and the evaluation reproduced the engineer's earlier run exactly, so the evidence is valid. However, REP-4 is nonzero for only 3 of 64 samples, so the correlation is close to degenerate. The non-event (90th percentile -0.017, not below -0.20) is therefore weak and largely uninformative about whether repetition covaries with scorer NLL. Its main lesson is that this short-sample protocol cannot answer the question.

departures: ppl_rep/run_experiment.py sets operator_optimization.profile="off" instead of retaining the checkpoint's default optimization profile. This hardware workaround could cause numerical differences in generation or decoding, but was reportedly necessary to run; there is no evidence of a material effect on the result.

ppl_rep/run_experiment.py casts de-standardised latents to fp32 before decoding, an unregistered precision adjustment. It could alter logits and potentially argmax token IDs through numerical differences, but accompanies the reported decoder compatibility workaround.

ppl_rep/run_experiment.py excludes 437 undefined bootstrap correlations and computes percentiles over 9,563 defined correlations, rather than obtaining the registered percentile over 10,000 correlations. The registration supplies no exclusion rule for these resamples. This changes the bootstrap distribution used for the reported endpoint and could change its value, although the implemented endpoint does not trigger the event.

ppl_rep/run_experiment.py additionally requires finite NLL for sample inclusion and nonconstant NLL for estimability. These criteria were not registered, but did not affect this run: all 64 samples were retained and NLL varied.
problems: outputs/ppl_repetition/summary.json labels the statistic as a percentile of 10,000 bootstrap correlations, although only 9,563 defined correlations entered the percentile calculation. The undefined-resample policy was not preregistered.

outputs/ppl_repetition/summary.json reports only three samples with nonzero REP-4 and 61 zero-valued ties. Consequently, the association estimate is supported by very little repetition variation, despite satisfying the registered estimability rule.

The reported bootstrap 10th and 90th percentiles span approximately -0.279 to -0.017. Failure to meet the event threshold therefore does not establish absence of an association or exclude correlations below -0.20.

ppl_rep/setup.sh does not pin model repository revisions or several dependency versions, and the implementation relies on /workspace/seed/src outside the supplied archive. This limits exact future reproducibility, without invalidating the observed fresh-machine run.
sol.reason: The fresh-machine evaluation completed successfully, found both registered output files, and reported an endpoint of -0.01706325 from code that generates samples and computes their metrics rather than hard-coding a result. Fidelity is unfaithful because the unregistered exclusion of undefined bootstrap correlations affected which replicates entered the reported statistic; the hardware accommodations and additional inactive validity checks are not the decisive defects. The evidence remains valid for the implemented conditional-on-defined bootstrap calculation, and the registered event was not supported. Research value is limited because repetition occurred in only three samples, making this a weak association screen rather than a well-supported null finding or a causal test.

departures: ppl_rep/run_experiment.py sets operator_optimization.profile='off' and casts denormalized latents to fp32 before argmax because FlexAttention failed. Required to run; could change a few tokens via numerics, but does not change the question and there is no evidence it moved the reported percentile.

ppl_rep/run_experiment.py drops bootstrap replicates with undefined Spearman rho (437/10000; summary.json n_boot_undefined) and takes the 90th percentile over the other 9563. The registration does not specify this exclusion. It changes the exact number versus NaN propagation or imputation, but not the event: the defined 90th percentile is about -0.017, and standard imputations stay far above -0.20.
ppl_rep/run_experiment.py also treats the statistic as not estimable if NLL is constant, which the registration does not require. This did not bind and could not change this result.

Self-conditioning CFG was disabled (sc_cfg_enabled=False, sc_cfg_scale=None) rather than run as an explicit scale-1 pass. Registration asks for ordinary self-conditioning and scale 1; the checkpoint default is sc_cfg off with w=1.0 (owt/config.yaml). Unlikely to change the result if scale 1 is the CFG identity.
problems: outputs/ppl_repetition/summary.json: REP-4 is nonzero in only 3 of 64 samples (4 unique values), so Spearman is essentially three samples versus 61 ties. The event not occurring does not show that repetition is unassociated with NLL.

ppl_rep/run_experiment.py never sets diffusion.dynamic.ode_sampling, whose shipped default in owt/config.yaml is false, while the registration requires a deterministic Euler sampler. pred_latents is not in the archive, so it is unclear whether sampling was deterministic ODE Euler or stochastic Euler; that could change the samples and the statistic.
The reported -0.017 is the 90th percentile of 9563 defined bootstrap draws, not of all 10000 replicates (ppl_rep/run_experiment.py); disclosed and not event-changing here.
grok.reason: Checkable settings match the registration: 64 unconditional 96-token samples, block size 16, 16 Euler steps, ordinary self-conditioning without extra guidance, no EOS early stop, GPT-2-small mean NLL on positions 2–96, whitespace REP-4, and a 10,000-draw bootstrap 90th percentile compared with -0.20. The fresh run executed that code on real checkpoints and wrote -0.017, so the event did not occur, and the kernel, dtype, and undefined-rho choices do not plausibly flip the event. Fidelity is still unknown because the code never forces ode_sampling on despite a false checkpoint default, so deterministic Euler is not verified. The measurement is genuine but weak: with REP-4 almost always zero, failing the preregistered threshold is uninformative about the repetition–NLL hypothesis.

registration.title: Early versus late token recovery under fixed latent corruption in the frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder

Prefix order implies early and late positions have different context redundancy, which the paper never splits out.
registration.hypothesis: At fixed moderate latent corruption sigma=0.6, late token positions recover more accurately than early positions in the frozen prefix-aligned autoencoder.
registration.contribution: Beyond the width-averaged recovery curves, this isolates whether the causal prefix order creates positional redundancy. A positional gap would motivate uneven noise allocation or step budgets across positions in block-causal priors.

Studies token rounding as bottleneck with a contextual autoregressive decoder; does not test prefix-ordered latent position asymmetry under Gaussian corruption.

registration.contribution: Goes beyond Gen-PPL entropy and MAUVE to test n-gram repetition collapse from self-conditioning guidance. Directly informs whether the released SC-CFG 4.0 setting should be reduced when diversity matters.

registration.title: Block-boundary alignment of the conditioning prefix improves XSum summarization under clean repainting
registration.seed_connection: Seed Appendix A.2.4 encodes the prompt as clean latents and uses clean repainting when the prefix ends inside a block. The quality cost of mid-block termination versus boundary-aligned termination is never measured.
registration.hypothesis: Conditioning prefixes that end at latent block boundaries yield higher ROUGE-L than prefixes that end mid-block and require clean repainting.
registration.contribution: Isolates a boundary-handling penalty not ablated in prior prefix-conditional diffusion work. A positive result motivates boundary-aware truncation or padding instead of naive truncation plus repainting.

closest_work.difference: Uses block-causal diffusion with prompt prefix conditioning but does not ablate intra-block termination versus boundary-aligned prefixes with repainting.
Introduces block diffusion with KV caching and flexible length and studies likelihood, not repainting alignment penalty on summarization ROUGE.
Infers block boundaries from dependency geometry during decoding, not prefix truncation alignment for conditioning.

inputs: AURORA-LM code repo DiffusionGenerator generate_multi_prefix with repaint True
HuggingFace fyv587/aurora-gpt2-xsum 300000.safetensors via scripts/download_models.py --model xsum
HuggingFace fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder and gpt2 backbone via same script
HuggingFace EdinburghNLP/xsum test split and rouge-score package
registration.method: Install with pip install -e . and rouge-score datasets. Download with python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model xsum autoencoder. Load xsum checkpoint with DiffusionGenerator on cuda. Load XSum test, GPT-2 tokenize articles, keep those with at least 300 tokens, take first 120 with seed 42. For each article make aligned prefix from first 256 tokens and misaligned prefix from first 264 tokens, detokenize to text. With block size Q 16 and c 1, 256 is exactly 16 blocks and 264 is 16 blocks plus 8. Generate one summary per prefix with repaint True, solver euler, num_steps 16, cfg_scale 2.0, cfg_sigma_window 0.9 comma 1.0, batch_size 8, max_gen_tokens 64, eos_mode first_eos, seed 123.

event.description: Mean ROUGE-L with boundary-aligned prefixes exceeds that with mid-block prefixes by more than 0.5 points on 0-100 scale
event.statistic: mean ROUGE-L F1 times 100 for 256-token aligned prefixes minus mean for 264-token mid-block prefixes

evaluation.procedure: For each of 120 articles generate one summary from the 256-token prefix and one from the 264-token prefix with identical sampler settings. Score each against the XSum reference with rouge-score ROUGE-L F1 times 100. Write one JSON line per article with article id, both summary texts and both ROUGE-L scores to outputs/xsum_alignment.jsonl. Compute mean ROUGE-L per condition and their difference. Write outputs/scores.json with means, difference and N.
evaluation.controls: Paired articles: same 120 articles under both truncations, same sampler, CFG, steps, seed and model; only truncation length differs. Misaligned sees 8 more source tokens, so any aligned win is conservative and cannot be due to seeing more context. Report mean summary lengths per condition.

registration.full_scale_study: If aligned wins, sweep intra-block offset 0 to 15, multiple prefix lengths and datasets, and compare repaint versus pad versus re-encode boundary strategies with full ROUGE and factuality eval.

registration.title: High-noise training benefit grows with latent dimensionality in tiny flow-matching denoisers
registration.seed_connection: Seed Sec 4.1.2 Fig 6b Tables 11 and 14 shows wider latents prefer larger tan-d shift d and higher m0.7 mass. Whether this is a general dimensionality effect versus an artifact of the large text pipeline is untested.
registration.hypothesis: The relative benefit of high-noise-heavy over low-noise-heavy flow-matching training is larger for high-dimensional latents than for low-dimensional latents.
registration.contribution: Tests the width dependent schedule claim in a minimal controlled setting with tiny MLPs and known ground truth, separating dimensionality from tokenizer, autoencoder and Transformer confounds present in large sweeps.

closest_work.difference: Adjusts noise schedule for high-resolution pixel diffusion with U-Nets; does not test width-controlled latent denoising with tan-d high-noise mass interaction.
Proposes information-uniform and Gumbel schedulers for embedding diffusion; does not isolate D-dependent gain of high-noise training in a synthetic control.
Derives variance-minimizing linear information-loss schedules for likelihood training; does not test high-noise benefit interaction with latent width.

inputs: No external models or datasets; synthetic PyTorch only with torch and numpy
registration.method: Implement tan-d sampling sigma tau d equals d tan pi tau over 2 divided by 1 plus d tan pi tau over 2 with tau uniform 0 1 for d 1 low and d 7 high. For each D in 32 256 fix 8 means sampled standard normal with seed 0, sample z as random mean plus 0.5 standard normal, then per-dimension standardize with 10000 samples to mean 0 var 1. Model is MLP input D plus 1 sigma scalar to 512 to 512 to D with LayerNorm and SiLU. Train each of 4 configs 6000 steps batch 512 AdamW lr 1e-3 MSE x0 loss mean over dims, sampling sigma from its schedule each batch and forming x sigma equals 1 minus sigma times z plus sigma times eps. Use torch manual_seed 0. Evaluate as in evaluation.

event.description: Relative high-noise gain is more than 5 percentage points larger at D 256 than at D 32
event.statistic: relative high-noise improvement at D256 minus relative improvement at D32 where improvement is MSE_low minus MSE_high over MSE_low on high-noise test

evaluation.procedure: Train four MLPs for D in 32 256 crossed with low tan-d d1 and high tan-d d7. Evaluate each on 2000 held-out latents with sigma uniform 0.7 to 1.0, compute per-dimension x0 MSE. Compute relative improvement per D as MSE_low minus MSE_high divided by MSE_low. Write outputs/synthetic.json with all four MSEs and both relative improvements. Statistic is relative improvement at D256 minus that at D32.
evaluation.controls: Same mixture count K 8, same MLP architecture and hidden size, same optimizer steps batch size and seeds per D; only D and training noise distribution vary. Per-dimension MSE makes D 32 and D 256 comparable. High-noise test distribution is fixed uniform 0.7 to 1.0 for all four models. Report absolute MSEs to check floor or ceiling effects.

models: none - tiny MLP trained from scratch

registration.full_scale_study: If the interaction occurs, sweep D 32 to 1024, bottleneck widths, mixture complexity and real text VAE latents to fit a scaling rule for high-noise mass m0.7 versus width.

agent.reason: High-noise training should help high-noise tests for both D, but whether the relative gain is 5pp larger at D=256 depends on arbitrary capacity and data choices with per-dim SNR identical.

judge_astra.reason: High-noise training better matches the evaluation region, but both schedules have the same ideal conditional-mean denoiser, so the interaction depends on finite-capacity and optimization effects. Increasing dimensionality also increases mixture separability, making the seed’s generation-quality results only indirect evidence for the specified relative-MSE interaction.

judge_fable.reason: Direction is mechanistically sensible (component identification remains possible at higher sigma only when D is large), but with x0-space loss and ~3M training samples both schedules should get close to the optimal denoiser, so the differential relative gain likely lands below 5pp; no infrastructure risk.

judge_opus.reason: With about 3M training samples and even the d=1 schedule placing about 26% of them above sigma=0.7, both MLPs should come close to Bayes-optimal high-noise MSE. The high-noise schedule's relative gain is likely a few percent at both widths. D=256 should benefit somewhat more, because its component-identification transition sits at higher sigma, but probably by less than 5 points.

judge_sol.reason: High-noise training matches the test region better, but both schedules share the same optimal conditional-mean denoiser, and this small mixture may be learned well under either schedule. Larger D also changes component separability, so the seed’s MAUVE interaction need not translate into the registered relative-MSE interaction.

The result is still uncertain because it uses one synthetic mixture and seed, and need not transfer to text latents.

closest_work.difference: RAE argues on theoretical grounds for a timestep shift that depends on latent dimension, and tests it in a real ImageNet pipeline with a DiT and pretrained representation encoders. It does not run a minimal synthetic control with tiny MLPs and a known Gaussian-mixture ground truth. It also does not measure whether the gain from high-noise training on high-noise x0 MSE grows from D=32 to D=256.

simple diffusion shifts the noise schedule as resolution grows in pixel-space U-Net diffusion, so the dimension it varies is image resolution. It does not vary latent width with the architecture and data generator held fixed, and it does not compare tan-d training-noise distributions.

Derives variance-minimizing information-loss schedules for likelihood training. It does not test whether the benefit of high-noise training interacts with latent width.

opus.reason: Prior work already supports the general idea that larger signals or latents need more high-noise training mass: the resolution-dependent shifts in simple diffusion and SD3, and the dimension-dependent shift in RAE. All of that evidence comes from full image pipelines, where dimension is tangled up with architecture and data, and none of it measures this experiment's statistic. I found no paper that runs the controlled synthetic test proposed here (tiny MLP denoisers on Gaussian mixtures at D=32 vs 256, crossed with tan-d d=1 vs d=7, scored on high-noise x0 MSE). The searches were keyword-based and not exhaustive, so a matching toy study could have been missed.

closest_work.difference: AURORA-LM crosses learned text-latent width with tan-d training schedules and reports MAUVE. It does not isolate the dimensionality-by-training-noise interaction using a controlled Gaussian-mixture distribution and small denoisers.

Studies dimension-dependent schedules for Gaussian-mixture targets using exact velocity fields, addressing sampling discretization rather than the effect of training-noise allocation on learned denoising accuracy.

Analyzes optimal training-noise allocation and tests small MLPs on controlled distributions, but does not cross ambient dimension with high- versus low-noise-heavy training to test the proposed interaction.

sol.reason: The general idea that higher-dimensional representations require greater high-noise emphasis was already established before the cutoff, including in the seed paper. However, I found no work that settles whether the relative denoising benefit grows with dimensionality when the distribution family is controlled and the tokenizer, autoencoder, and Transformer pipeline is removed. The proposed contribution is therefore a distinct controlled test of that interaction, rather than a new noise-scheduling principle.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper's width-by-schedule matrix (Table 11) measures MAUVE of generated text from a full text pipeline, which is not the same kind of measurement as denoising MSE in a synthetic setting, and the paper does not name a synthetic or isolated test of the dimensionality effect as future work.

relation.reason: The hypothesis asks whether the paper's width-dependent noise-allocation finding holds as a general dimensionality effect once tokenizer, autoencoder and Transformer confounds are removed, which tests a stated result under a control for confounds.

obvious.reason: Resolution- and dimension-dependent schedule shifts are well known from image diffusion, so a controlled toy test of the width-schedule interaction would occur to some readers, but few would place it among their first ten follow-ups to a text-generation paper.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer about whether high-noise allocation should scale with latent width would mainly change practice for groups building continuous-latent text diffusion models and tuning their schedules.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statement that wider latents prefer larger shift and higher high-noise mass repeats the paper's own summary of Sec 4.1.2, even though Table 11 is not strictly monotone.

answerable.reason: The comparison can show a width interaction only if the high-noise test MSE separates the two schedules at all, which fails if both models are already near the Bayes-optimal error at high noise; the design includes no optimal reference to check this.
answerable.needs: high-noise MSE not saturated at Bayes optimum for both schedules

opus.what_came_out: The relative high-noise MSE gain of d=7 over d=1 was 0.21% at D=32 (0.8555 to 0.8537) and 1.54% at D=256 (0.5729 to 0.5641), a difference of 0.0133, from one seed per configuration with 2000 paired held-out synthetic latents, tiny MLPs and no interval.

prerequisite.reason: The run computes no Bayes-optimal or seed-variance reference, so it cannot show whether the tiny gaps reflect saturation near the optimum or a real schedule effect.
prerequisite.which: whether high-noise MSE is saturated near the Bayes optimum for both schedules

evidence.reason: The difference points in the claimed direction but is tiny, and with one training seed and no interval the run cannot separate it from seed noise or rule out either no interaction or a meaningful one.

next_step.reason: The run did not settle its question, and its main faults are visible: one seed with no variance estimate and no optimal reference, both cheap to fix in this synthetic setup.
next_step.what: Rerun with several training seeds to obtain intervals, add the analytically computable Bayes-optimal posterior-mean MSE for the Gaussian mixture as a reference, and consider a sample-quality metric beyond high-noise MSE.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares high-noise-heavy with low-noise-heavy flow-matching training in MLP denoisers on synthetic Gaussian mixtures to test whether the relative high-noise denoising benefit grows with latent dimensionality.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper measures width-dependent schedule benefits through text-generation quality, but neither reports this synthetic denoising-error comparison nor explicitly identifies it as an unanswered question.

relation.reason: The synthetic comparison checks whether the paper's width-dependent noise-allocation claim holds when the text autoencoder and Transformer pipeline are removed.

obvious.reason: A direct dimensionality-by-noise-allocation comparison is a natural follow-up to the calibration finding, although not every researcher would prioritize that particular comparison.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer about dimensionality-dependent training-noise benefits could affect schedule choices across continuous diffusion and flow-matching research.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's account of width-dependent noise calibration is consistent with the paper, and the paper does not report the proposed synthetic isolation experiment.

answerable.reason: The comparison can bear on the question only if the trained MLPs learn usable denoising functions rather than simply failing to learn the synthetic distributions.
answerable.needs: MLPs learn nontrivial denoising

sol.what_came_out: On standardized eight-component Gaussian mixtures, two-hidden-layer MLPs produced low/high-noise-training test MSEs of 0.855503/0.853685 at D=32 and 0.572928/0.564081 at D=256, giving relative improvements of 0.2125% and 1.5442% and an interaction of 1.3317 percentage points, with 2,000 paired test latents per dimension, one training repetition, and no uncertainty interval.

prerequisite.reason: The held-out errors below the approximately unit-variance standardized-target baseline indicate nontrivial denoising at both widths, and the run shows no prerequisite failure.

evidence.reason: The small positive interaction points in the hypothesized direction, but 2,000 test cases per width with one training repetition and no interval do not establish that sampling or training variability cannot explain it.

next_step.reason: The run leaves a small directional effect unresolved because it lacks independent repetitions and uncertainty estimates, a gap that can be repaired directly.
next_step.what: Repeat across independent training and mixture seeds, retain paired per-latent losses, and estimate an uncertainty interval for the dimensionality-by-schedule interaction.

registration.title: Few-step block-causal sampling concentrates fluency loss at block boundaries
registration.seed_connection: Seed Sec 3.3 generates blocks left to right with parallel denoising inside each block and Sec 4.1.3 shows overall MAUVE falls when steps shrink. Where in the block the loss concentrates is not measured.
registration.hypothesis: The fluency penalty at latent block boundaries relative to block interiors is larger with 8-step sampling than with 32-step sampling.
registration.contribution: Localizes few-step degradation to block starts rather than reporting corpus averages. A positive result motivates boundary-aware step allocation or overlap, distinct from global self-conditioning fixes.

closest_work.difference: Studies block diffusion likelihood and efficiency with KV caching but not positional NLL gap versus denoising steps in continuous latents.
Adapts block boundaries from dependency geometry to improve accuracy, not measuring fixed-Q boundary penalty as step budget shrinks.
Traces few-step loss to train-inference mismatch in self-conditioning coupling, not to block-boundary localization.

inputs: AURORA-LM code repo DiffusionGenerator unconditional generate
HuggingFace fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt 250000.safetensors via scripts/download_models.py --model owt
HuggingFace fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder and gpt2 backbone via same script plus gpt2 small weights for scoring
HuggingFace wikitext wikitext-103-raw-v1 test for 50 human control passages
registration.method: Install with pip install -e . . Download with python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model owt autoencoder. Load owt checkpoint with DiffusionGenerator on cuda. Generate 70 unconditional samples at 8 steps and 70 at 32 steps with solver euler, self_cond_cfg_scale 1.0, no prefix CFG, batch_size 7, max_gen_tokens 128, eos_mode eos_wrap, seed 200 so initial noise matches across step budgets. Score offline with gpt2 small in float32 batch 8 as in evaluation. Take 50 Wikitext test passages truncated to 128 tokens as human baseline scored identically.

event.description: Boundary-minus-interior NLL gap is more than 0.1 nats larger at 8 steps than at 32 steps
event.statistic: mean boundary minus interior token NLL gap at 8 steps minus that gap at 32 steps

evaluation.procedure: Retokenize each generation to up to 128 GPT-2 tokens, run GPT-2 small teacher forcing to get per-token negative log likelihood. Map token index t to block t integer-divided by 16; boundary is t mod 16 less than 2 with block id greater than 0, interior is the rest. Per sample compute mean boundary NLL minus mean interior NLL. Average gaps to gap8 and gap32 over 70 samples each and over 50 human passages. Write per-sample gaps to outputs/boundary_nll.jsonl. Write outputs/scores.json with gap8 gap32 human gap and statistic. Statistic is gap8 minus gap32.
evaluation.controls: Same checkpoint solver guidance batching max tokens and seeds for 8 and 32 steps; only step count varies. Fixed GPT-2 small scorer for all texts. Human Wikitext baseline with same block mapping controls for tokenizer or language-inherent boundary effects. Length-matched 128-token generations.

registration.full_scale_study: If the gap widens at few steps, sweep steps crossed with block sizes Q 4 to 64 and test boundary-aware samplers that spend extra solver steps or overlap on block starts with fluency and coherence eval.

agent.reason: Block joints may be less coherent especially with few steps, but within-block parallel positions could instead be worse than sequential boundaries, making the registered positive direction uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: The seed supports worse aggregate quality with fewer steps, but not its concentration at block starts, which also have reliable immediate context from the completed prefix. Cross-block inconsistency could produce the registered interaction, although retokenization may blur the correspondence between scored positions and latent block boundaries.

judge_fable.reason: Block-start tokens are the most strongly conditioned on the clean prefix, so few-step degradation is more likely to concentrate mid/late block (shrinking the gap), the measurement is noisy (SE of the difference ~0.12 nats vs 0.1 threshold), and retokenization may misalign token and latent positions.

judge_opus.reason: Few-step error should concentrate in block interiors far from the clean prefix rather than at block starts, which would push the statistic negative. However, the statistic's standard error (about 0.14 nats from 14 boundary tokens per sample and 70 samples) is comparable to the 0.1 threshold. Retokenization misalignment would further blur any positional effect.

judge_sol.reason: The seed establishes overall few-step degradation, not its concentration at block starts; starts can benefit from fully completed preceding context. Re-tokenization can also shift the presumed latent-block boundaries and attenuate a genuinely localized effect.

judge_luna.reason: The paper finds substantially worse overall MAUVE at eight than at 32 denoising steps, and block starts plausibly have less preceding context. But it does not show that few-step degradation is concentrated at boundaries; joint denoising within each block could yield a mostly uniform penalty instead.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: Sec 3.3 denoises all positions in a block in parallel conditional on the prefix, and Sec 4.1.3 shows only global MAUVE loss at few steps. Inference gives no strong reason boundaries suffer differentially versus block ends, leaving a >0.1-nat gap increase uncertain given noisy 14-token boundary means.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Names a 'block boundary problem' in discrete block-diffusion LLMs (LLaDA2.1) and measures it with a self-containedness divergence across positions in a block. It does not test how a boundary-minus-interior fluency gap changes with the number of denoising steps, and it does not study continuous-latent flow-matching models.
The seed paper reports only corpus-level drops in MAUVE and perplexity as sampling steps decrease. It gives no breakdown by position within a block.

Attributes few-step degradation in continuous language flows to a train-inference mismatch in self-conditioning, measured with corpus-level generative perplexity. It does not look at where in the sequence the loss occurs or at block structure.
Introduces block diffusion and reports its likelihood and efficiency. It does not measure a positional NLL gap at block boundaries against step budget in continuous latents.
Adapts block boundaries to improve accuracy. It does not measure how the boundary penalty under fixed-size blocks changes as the step budget shrinks.

opus.reason: I searched arXiv for block-boundary effects, step-count dependence, and per-position fluency in block diffusion. No paper I found compares the boundary-versus-interior token NLL gap at different step budgets, in continuous-latent or discrete block diffusion. The closest is Multi-Block Editing (2607.22663), which documents boundary sensitivity in discrete dLLMs with a different metric and without varying step count, so the question remains open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Localizes future-context sensitivity and predictive uncertainty to block ends in discrete diffusion models, but does not test whether reducing denoising steps increases an external-scored block-start-versus-interior NLL gap.
Reports aggregate MAUVE across sampling-step budgets and block sizes, without measuring positional fluency degradation or a boundary-by-step-budget interaction.
Studies fluency degradation from fewer steps per block and distance from available context, but does not compare boundary-minus-interior NLL gaps across step budgets.
Diagnoses few-step degradation through solver/self-conditioning coupling in continuous language flows, without examining localization at block boundaries.

sol.reason: Boundary-related degradation and few-step quality loss were already studied before 2026-10-07, so neither broad idea is new. However, the closest work does not answer the registered question: whether fewer denoising steps disproportionately worsen externally scored fluency at block starts relative to interiors in a fixed block-causal model.

opus.reason: Entries 20, 26 and 54 track degradation across blocks or along sampling trajectories, but none measures the NLL gap at block boundaries versus block interiors as the step count changes.

sol.reason: No list entry tests whether reducing sampling steps increases the block-boundary-versus-interior token NLL gap at fixed model weights.

The registration is silent on EOS handling. Mid-text EOS tokens and their high-NLL successors land in boundary or interior bins depending on position, so this could shift the per-sample gaps in either arm.

run_experiment.py: boundaries are defined on retokenized GPT-2 indices, as registered. Retokenized lengths are 120–128 while every decoder output had exactly 128 tokens (scores.json scored_lengths), so retokenized positions drift away from true latent-block positions. Mid-sequence EOS tokens from eos_wrap are scored without any rule, adding noise whose placement relative to boundaries is arbitrary.
opus.reason: The code runs the registered experiment: same checkpoint, 8 vs 32 Euler steps, Q=16, seed 200 with verified paired initial noise, batch 7, 128 tokens, eos_wrap, GPT-2 small float32 teacher forcing, and the registered boundary rule and statistic. The only change is a backend attention fix needed to run, applied identically to both arms. The reported value -0.100 is computed correctly from real generations and is reproduced by the protected run, so the registered event (>0.1) did not occur. The evidence is weak as a test of boundary localization. Both generated arms show boundary NLL below interior NLL, which suggests the measure is dominated by high-NLL first-block 'interior' tokens and by retokenization/EOS misalignment rather than true block starts. With one seed and no uncertainty estimate, the null speaks mainly to this specific operationalization, not to whether few-step degradation concentrates at block boundaries.

departures: run_experiment.py changes the generation backend to profile='custom', disables FlexAttention, and disables MLP compilation. run_experiment.py selects the first 50 non-heading Wikitext test rows containing at least 128 GPT-2 tokens. Passage selection was unspecified, so this is an allowed implementation choice. Selection can change the human gap, but the human gap does not enter the registered statistic.

run_experiment.py adds initial-noise hashing, assertions, runtime configuration output, and token-level audit records. Assertions introduce abort conditions rather than sample exclusions; the protected run passed them. These additions provide no evidence of changing the reported value.
problems: The registered metric implemented in run_experiment.py assigns boundaries using retokenized positions rather than verified original decoder or latent positions. IMPLEMENTATION.md also describes conditional leading-EOS insertion without an alignment correction, creating an additional possible boundary offset.

run_experiment.py includes the entire scored first block in the interior reference. Its shorter teacher-forcing contexts can introduce a position-dependent NLL difference unrelated to block transitions. The near-zero human gap does not establish that generated texts have the same context-length effects.

outputs/scores.json reports only point estimates, without paired uncertainty estimates or an interval relative to the registered 0.1-nat threshold. The fresh evaluation reproduces the fixed-seed result but does not supply additional independent sampling evidence.

GPT-2 token NLL is a fluency proxy, not a direct measurement of fluency or coherence. No aggregate quality comparison is reported to establish a few-step penalty whose location could then be identified.
The Wikitext control does not reproduce generation-specific EOS handling or retokenization drift, so it cannot validate alignment to actual latent block starts.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation completed successfully, produced both required raw outputs, and reported a statistic of -0.1002800269 nats, so the registered greater-than-0.1 event did not occur. The visible code computes that value from generated texts and Wikitext using the registered aggregation, with no apparent hard-coded result or outcome-dependent exclusion. The implementation is faithful despite necessary backend repairs and explicitly permitted scoring choices. Research value is limited because the operational boundary labels are not verified latent boundaries and the point estimate lacks uncertainty; it supports failure of the registered event in this run, not equivalence, absence of boundary effects, or a reliable opposite-direction mechanism.

departures: Backend repair in run_experiment.py (also outputs/runtime_config.json): operator_optimization profile set to custom, FlexAttention disabled, and MLP torch.compile disabled because released FlexAttention failed on this CUDA/torch stack. Position t=0 is omitted from teacher-forced NLL (run_experiment.py). Required by teacher forcing with no added BOS; it is never a boundary token under the registered rule (block id>0 and t%16<2), so it does not change the boundary set and only slightly changes the interior mean.

Interior means include sequence-start tokens, and eos_wrap generations begin with <|endoftext|> so the first content token's high NLL falls in the interior (run_experiment.py). That can make boundary-minus-interior gaps negative without a boundary fluency penalty. Humans lack that prefix, so human_gap near 0 does not fully control the artifact.

One fixed seed and no uncertainty (registration repetitions=1; outputs/scores.json). The point estimate rejects the pre-registered >0.1 event but does not establish absence or equivalence of a boundary effect.

registration.title: Early versus late token recovery under fixed latent corruption
registration.seed_connection: Seed Fig5a reports aggregate token-recovery accuracy versus latent corruption sigma for varying D; its query-based autoencoder induces a prefix-aligned causal order to support blockwise generation but never tests whether robustness varies along the prefix.
registration.hypothesis: At moderate corruption sigma=0.5, tokens in the second half of a 128-token sequence are recovered more accurately than tokens in the first half, beyond any clean-accuracy gap.
registration.contribution: First position-stratified test of a prefix-aligned decodable text latent with difference-in-differences control for intrinsic difficulty; reveals whether causal accumulation helps or hurts robustness and informs block ordering beyond aggregate curves.

registration.method: 1. Clone via git clone https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM and cd into repo, then pip install -e . plus datasets transformers safetensors omegaconf torch and mkdir -p outputs. 2. Fetch: run python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model autoencoder and verify checkpoints/autoencoder/config.yaml plus 100000.safetensors and models/gpt2-small exist, inspecting script --help if names differ and downloading gpt2 from HuggingFace as fallback. 3. Load on cuda:0 with DEVICE_TYPE=cuda torch.no_grad eval mode seed 42: load GPT2 tokenizer from models/gpt2-small with pad set to eos, load AE config from checkpoints/autoencoder/config.yaml with OmegaConf and if config requires fixed length override dataset.max_sequence_len and causal_encoder.target_sequence_len and latent num_latents to 128 so N equals L equals 128, otherwise use variable-length mode with N equals round(cL), instantiate TextAutoencoder with encoder_cfg causal_encoder decoder_cfg causal_decoder embed path models/gpt2-small, load weights from 100000.safetensors using aurora.utils.checkpoint_io following src/aurora/train/ae_trainer.py key mapping, move to cuda, inspect src/aurora/models/autoencoder.py encoder.py decoder.py for exact class and method names and adapt but document. 4. Data: load wikitext-103-raw-v1 test text field, drop empty rows, tokenize each without special tokens truncation false, concatenate all ids, split into non-overlapping 128-token chunks, take first 200 chunks as true ids. 5. In batches of 8: get token features via autoencoder.get_token_features or equivalent, encode via autoencoder.encoder to clean z [B,128,768] sliced to first 128 latents, sample eps from N(0,I) same shape with torch Generator seed 1000 plus batch index, compute x05 equals 0.5*z plus 0.5*eps and x00 equals z, decode each via autoencoder.decoder with target_token_len 128 to logits [B,128,50257], pred equals argmax, compute per-token correctness versus true ids, early equals mean over positions 0-63 late equals mean over 64-127. Save per-chunk early and late for sigma 0 and 0.5.

event.description: Late-prefix tokens recover more accurately than early-prefix tokens at sigma 0.5 beyond clean gap by more than 5 percentage points
event.statistic: difference-in-differences (mean late05 minus mean early05) minus (mean late00 minus mean early00) over 200 sequences

evaluation.procedure: Load outputs/scores.jsonl where each line holds chunk id plus early05 late05 early00 late00 accuracies; compute means over 200 chunks; statistic equals (mean late05 minus mean early05) minus (mean late00 minus mean early00); write outputs/summary.json with means statistic N paired standard error and clean accuracies. Sanity requires mean clean accuracy above 0.90 else flag loading error but still report statistic. outputs/scores.jsonl holds per-chunk accuracies, outputs/summary.json holds means and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Paired within-chunk comparison with same chunks and same noise sample for early versus late; difference-in-differences versus sigma 0 clean run controls intrinsic difficulty and paragraph-start effects; fixed noise seeds.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run full sweep sigma 0 to 1 with 9 values by position quartiles and frequency strata on 1000 chunks with 5 noise seeds, plus train small causal versus non-causal AEs at D 128 and 1024 to test causality and guide block-size choice.

agent.reason: Later positions have more redundant prefix copies, but D768 accuracies are near ceiling at sigma 0.5 so a 5pp DiD gap is large, plus autoencoder length-override loading risk.

judge_astra.reason: The seed’s wide-latent corruption curves suggest recovery is near ceiling at sigma=0.5, leaving little room for a five-percentage-point adjusted gap. Longer prefixes provide more context but do not necessarily make each newly introduced token more redundantly encoded.

judge_fable.reason: Fig. 5a suggests a 768-D latent is still near-perfect at sigma=0.5, so there is little error mass for a position effect to show up in; even inside the transition region the context-benefit mechanism mostly affects the first ~10-20 positions, making a >5pp half-vs-half difference-in-differences unlikely (some chance from implementation noise or an unexpectedly fragile model).

judge_opus.reason: Fig. 5a suggests a 768-wide latent is near ceiling at σ=0.5, which would make the difference-in-differences about zero. The decoder recovers token j only from latent j plus context, so late positions gain mainly a context prior worth well under 5 points. A positive effect from the first sequence position no longer being the training-time EOS token is possible, but only if σ=0.5 falls in the steep part of the curve.

judge_sol.reason: The seed’s wider-latent recovery curves suggest accuracy may remain near ceiling at sigma=0.5, leaving little room for a five-percentage-point positional difference. Longer prefixes could help recovery, but that directional effect is not established by the aggregate results.

judge_luna.reason: Later positions have a longer causal latent prefix available, which could help recover tokens when the latents are corrupted. However, the released 768-wide representation may already recover nearly all tokens at σ=0.5, making the registered five-point difference-in-differences a demanding threshold.

judge_muse.reason: Later positions have more prefix context but also depend on more corrupted latents and pack longer prefixes into the same width; with accuracy still high at sigma 0.5 a >5pp late-favoring DiD is unlikely.

Measures decoder robustness to Gaussian latent noise using aggregate BLEU in a globally attending compressed text autoencoder, without testing robustness along a causal prefix.

However, the work found does not answer whether later positions in a prefix-aligned causal text latent suffer less corruption-induced recovery loss than earlier positions, beyond their clean-accuracy gap. The registered experiment therefore asks a distinct positional-robustness question rather than merely changing the dataset or metric of an already answered experiment.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered paired recovery experiment on the first 200 WikiText-103 raw test chunks (128 tokens), released 100000-step AE, raw-latent sigma 0/0.5 corruption, batch size 8 and fixed CUDA noise seeds 1000+batch index. Strict encoder/decoder loading restores trained tied embeddings and token-feature normalization; no denoiser or latent standardization. Outputs scores.jsonl, summary.json, result.json plus provenance. Minimal adaptations: writable copy of supplied seed repository instead of git clone (git unavailable); repository-supported CUDA SDPA backend with unchanged causal masks; permitted N=L=128 config overrides. Float32 inference. End-to-end command tested, then retested after deleting model folders/work copy/outputs with a fresh HF cache; identical statistic 0.00031250000000004885, paired SE 0.0009525591, clean accuracy 0.998046875. experiment.py and outputs/runtime_config.yaml set npu_fused_attention=false (it was true in checkpoints/autoencoder/config.yaml) and use CUDA SDPA with the causal masks unchanged. This is a backend change needed to run on CUDA and could cause at most tiny numerical differences.

experiment.py runs inference in float32 with TF32 disabled, while the checkpoint config lists bf16 training precision. The registration does not fix inference precision, so this is a permitted choice and is unlikely to move a 0.03 pp statistic meaningfully.

experiment.py overrides dataset.max_sequence_len, target_sequence_len and all num_latents from 1024 to 128. The registration explicitly permits this, but the model is then run off its training length of 1024. This could affect absolute accuracies; it is permitted.

The value of the null is low, however. Clean and corrupted accuracies are both at about 99-100%, so the DiD statistic is mechanically capped near 1 pp and the 5 pp event could hardly have occurred; the run shows that sigma=0.5 in raw latent space is too mild to reveal positional robustness differences, rather than that none exist.

The first 200 chunks in experiment.py are consecutive segments of one corpus prefix. The paired standard error in summarize() treats chunks as independent units, although neighboring chunks can share document and topical dependence; it is not a demonstrated corpus-representative uncertainty estimate.

Only one fixed noise realization and one released checkpoint are evaluated. As outputs/summary.json correctly states, its standard error does not measure variation over noise seeds, and repeated execution of the same realization is not an independent experimental repetition.

The clean difference-in-differences control removes the observed baseline accuracy gap, but it does not isolate causal accumulation from token composition, latent scale or other position-dependent properties. There is no causal-versus-non-causal architectural control.

sol.reason: The visible code preserves the registered checkpoint, data recipe, 200 paired chunks, corruption formula, decoding rule, statistic and strict event threshold; the adaptations are permitted choices or necessary engineering changes. The noisy late-minus-early gap is 0.421875 percentage points, but the clean gap is already 0.390625 points, leaving only 0.03125 points of adjusted advantage, far below the registered five-point event. This is a credible, narrowly meaningful negative finding for the specified condition, not evidence of equivalence, absence of all position effects, or a causal explanation.

registration.title: Midpoint latent interpolation fluency
registration.seed_connection: Seed motivates high-capacity continuous latents as a generative interface bridging diffusion and discrete decoding but evaluates only denoising generation, not interpolation smoothness which is a core promise of continuous spaces.
registration.hypothesis: Linear midpoint of two encoded texts decodes to text whose GPT-2 perplexity is less than 2 times the mean endpoint perplexity with median ratio below 2.
registration.contribution: First interpolation test of AURORA query-based decodable latent with reconstruction-controlled endpoints and splice diagnostic; separates decodable from smooth representation beyond smoothness claims that lack interpolation evaluation.

closest_work.difference: Shows naive autoencoder interpolation often yields artifacts without manifold regularization on images; we test whether text AE with dropout alone is smooth.
Claims compressed smooth latent for text diffusion via joint reconstruction plus alignment but evaluates only denoising generation, not latent interpolation.

inputs: AURORA-LM repo https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM for autoencoder encode decode
HuggingFace fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder via python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model autoencoder
HuggingFace gpt2 backbone into models/gpt2-small via same script for tokenizer and for GPT-2 LM scoring with AutoModelForCausalLM
wikitext-103-raw-v1 test split via datasets.load_dataset wikitext wikitext-103-raw-v1 split test for 200 chunks of 64 tokens
registration.method: 1. Clone via git clone https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM and cd into repo, then pip install -e . plus datasets transformers safetensors omegaconf torch and mkdir -p outputs. Run python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model autoencoder and verify checkpoints/autoencoder and models/gpt2-small, inspecting --help and using gpt2 fallback if needed. 2. Load tokenizer from models/gpt2-small with pad equals eos and AE with max length overridden to 64 so N equals L equals 64 if fixed length required else variable-length mode, eval on cuda:0 DEVICE_TYPE=cuda seed 42, following src/aurora/models and train/ae_trainer.py for exact load calls. 3. Prepare 200 distinct 64-token chunks from wikitext-103-raw-v1 test by concatenating tokenized non-empty rows without special tokens and splitting into 64-token blocks, filtering to blocks with 20 or more unique tokens, taking first 200; form 100 pairs from consecutive chunks. 4. For each pair encode to zA and zB [64,768] via get_token_features plus encoder; compute zMid equals 0.5 times zA plus zB; decode zA zB zMid via decoder with target_token_len 64 and argmax to ids and to text via tokenizer batch_decode skip_special_tokens True; also build token-splice baseline text from first 32 ids of A plus last 32 ids of B decoded same way as diagnostic. 5. Score PPL with GPT-2 LM from models/gpt2-small using AutoModelForCausalLM eval bf16 on cuda batch 8: tokenize each decoded text truncated to 128 tokens, compute mean NLL over shifted non-pad positions, PPL equals exp NLL; record PPL_A PPL_B PPL_Mid PPL_Splice per pair; ratio equals PPL_Mid divided by mean of PPL_A and PPL_B.

event.description: Median midpoint-to-endpoint perplexity ratio is below 2
event.statistic: median over 100 pairs of PPL_mid divided by mean endpoint PPL

evaluation.procedure: Load outputs/pairs.jsonl where each line holds pair id plus PPL_A PPL_B PPL_Mid PPL_Splice and ratio plus decoded texts; compute median ratio as statistic and mean endpoint PPL and splice PPL for reference; write outputs/summary.json with median mean N and histograms. Endpoints are AE reconstructions not originals to control for AE error; token-splice baseline reported only as diagnostic. outputs/pairs.jsonl holds per-pair PPLs and texts, outputs/summary.json holds median and summaries.
evaluation.controls: Endpoints are AE reconstructions not originals to control for reconstruction error; same decoder and scorer for all three; fixed pairs and seeds; splice diagnostic controls for naive mixing.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run 11-point interpolation grid with attribute pairs plus human fluency and embedding-side smoothness metrics and compare explicit smoothness regularizers; if not, study dropout and alignment fixes for smoothness.

agent.reason: Dropout-trained decoder may stay fluent under mixing, but position-wise averaging of distinct 64-token prefixes is likely off-manifold without explicit smoothness regularization, making median ratio below 2 uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: Reconstruction and coordinate dropout do not ensure that linear midpoints decode coherently; mixing position-aligned representations could produce substantially less fluent hybrids. Adjacent, topically related chunks and possible endpoint copying nevertheless give the perplexity threshold a reasonable chance of being met without genuine semantic interpolation.

judge_fable.reason: Each latent position must carry its own token, so a convex midpoint of two unrelated chunks most plausibly decodes to a position-wise interleaving or garbage with GPT-2 perplexity several times the endpoints; the main routes to a ratio below 2 are degenerate repetitive outputs or a broken autoencoder load that makes all three decodes equally bad.

judge_opus.reason: Latents are aligned to token positions, so the midpoint superimposes two different tokens at every position. The decoder will most likely pick A's or B's token roughly at random, or a third token, giving jumbled text. GPT-2 perplexity on jumbled text is typically several times that of the endpoints, so a median ratio below 2 would need about 93% consistency with one endpoint.

judge_sol.reason: Coordinate dropout encourages robustness to missing features, not necessarily to averaging two different text representations, so midpoint decoding could produce incoherent token mixtures. However, short WikiText endpoints can themselves have high perplexity, making the twofold threshold relatively permissive.

judge_luna.reason: The autoencoder is trained for reconstruction, not explicitly for smooth interpolation, so midpoint decodes may be poor. Consecutive text chunks and the relatively permissive two-times perplexity threshold make a median pass plausible, but GPT-2 perplexity is only an indirect fluency measure.

judge_muse.reason: High-capacity AE trained only with dropout lacks explicit smoothness regularization so midpoint of distinct encodings likely decodes to disfluent blends; consecutive-chunk pairs and lenient 2x threshold give some chance.

registration.title: Width-dependent benefit of high-noise training in toy flow matching
registration.seed_connection: Seed Table11 Fig5b shows wider text latents prefer larger tan-d shift d equals 7 while narrow prefer smaller d, attributing it to signal strength versus dimensionality but confounded by AE text data and Transformer capacity.
registration.hypothesis: With fixed intrinsic rank and MLP denoiser, the test-loss gain from shifting training noise from d equals 1 to d equals 7 is larger for ambient width D equals 256 than for D equals 32.
registration.contribution: Isolates dimensionality mechanism in controlled synthetic flow matching with no text or Transformer confounds and multiple seeds, testing whether Simple-Diffusion SNR reasoning extends from image resolution to latent channel width.

closest_work.difference: Derives SNR shift for higher image resolution via average pooling with spatial redundancy; we test channel-width shift for fixed intrinsic rank without spatial structure.
Observes width-dependent optimal d on OpenWebText with joint AE plus Transformer; we reproduce with known ground-truth manifold and tiny MLP.

inputs: No downloads: synthetic Gaussian subspace data generated on the fly in PyTorch; requires torch only
registration.method: Implement single python script with torch on cuda and mkdir -p outputs. Data: for each D in 32 and 256 fix intrinsic rank k equals 8; sample random orthonormal A [D,k] once per D with seed 0 via randn plus QR; clean raw equals A times s where s from N(0,I_k); estimate per-channel mean and std from 50000 pilot samples per D with seed 10 then standardize subsequent z equals (raw-mean)/std with std clamped min 1e-5. Noise: eps from N(0,I_D), x_sigma equals (1-sigma)z plus sigma eps. Model: MLP input D plus 16 sigma embedding to hidden 256 ReLU to hidden 256 ReLU to output D; sigma embedding 16 dims sinusoidal with freqs exp(-log10000 times arange8 divided by 8) concat sin and cos of sigma times freqs. Training: AdamW lr 1e-3 batch 1024 steps 5000 online samples per config; sigma sampling via tan-d sigma equals d tan(pi tau over 2) divided by 1 plus d tan with tau uniform 1e-3 to 1-1e-3, d in 1 and 7, clamp 1e-5 to 1-1e-5; loss per-dim MSE; run 12 trainings for D cross d cross seeds 42 43 44 with torch manual_seed. Eval: shared eval sets per D with seed 999: 5000 fresh z per D, sigma grid 10 values linspace 0.05 to 0.95, one noise per z per sigma with seed 1000, mean per-dim MSE averaged over grid as uniform test loss Loss_D_d_seed; also save per-sigma curves. Gain per seed: gain32 equals Loss32_1 minus Loss32_7, gain256 equals Loss256_1 minus Loss256_7; statistic equals mean over 3 seeds of gain256 minus gain32.

event.description: Wide gain minus narrow gain is positive averaged over 3 seeds
event.statistic: mean over seeds of gain256 minus gain32 where gainD equals testMSE with d1 minus testMSE with d7 per-dim MSE uniform sigma eval

evaluation.procedure: Load outputs/losses.json with 12 test losses plus per-sigma curves pilot stats and training config; compute per-seed gains and mean difference as statistic with standard error across seeds and test sampling; write outputs/summary.json with losses gains statistic and curves. Controls are same k same MLP hidden same steps same eval grid, only D and training d vary; per-dim MSE makes scales comparable; fixed hidden favors narrow so wide advantage is conservative. outputs/losses.json holds all losses and curves, outputs/summary.json holds gains and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same intrinsic rank k equals 8 same hidden size same steps same eval grid; only ambient D and training shift d vary; per-dim MSE makes scales comparable; 3 training seeds.

models: none - 2-layer MLP 256 hidden trained from scratch

registration.title: Periodic-80 versus human text under a modern scorer with native vocabularies
registration.seed_connection: Seed unconditional claim rests on Gen-PPL with GPT-2 Large where AURORA-S 23.56 beats ELF-B 24.11; hacking work shows naive periodic samplers can beat trained models and references with that scorer.
registration.hypothesis: With length 128 and k equals 80 built in Qwen tokenizer vocab, periodic sampler achieves lower mean log-perplexity than human text when scored by Qwen2.5-0.5B.
registration.contribution: Tests whether Gen-PPL hack threshold is scorer-dependent at a borderline k where outcome is uncertain, using scorer-native construction to avoid tokenizer-transfer confound; goes beyond hacking work which uses only gpt2-large without testing modern-scorer fix.

closest_work.difference: Demonstrates periodic mirror phrase hacks with gpt2-large on LM1B and OWT and proposes distributional suite; does not test Qwen modern scorer or borderline k80 transition with native vocab.
Proposes MAUVE distributional metric; we test scorer-swap fix rather than distributional replacement.
