registration.title: Post-hoc channel ablation tests whether width robustness requires training
registration.seed_connection: Seed Fig.5a claims wider D preserves token recovery under x_sigma equals (1-sigma)z plus sigma eps over broader sigma. This tests whether that benefit survives post-hoc channel removal on the released 768-D autoencoder.
registration.hypothesis: Full 768-D released latents retain robustness to sigma 0.6 corruption substantially better than the same latents with only 256 channels kept, beyond any clean accuracy gap.
registration.contribution: The seed paper compares separately trained autoencoders with different D, confounding training dynamics, decoder size and dropout. This isolates inference-time capacity by ablating channels of one released checkpoint with multiple subsets and absolute-accuracy reporting, which no prior work does for prefix query autoencoders.

closest_work.difference: COSMOS trains compressed smooth latents with dropout but never tests post-hoc channel ablation to separate trained width from redundancy.
Simple Diffusion studies schedule shifts for image resolution, not text latent channel ablation under Gaussian corruption.

inputs: AURORA-LM code https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM
checkpoints fyv587/aurora-text-autoencoder via python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model autoencoder, backbone gpt2 to models/gpt2-small
WikiText-103-raw-v1 test via HuggingFace datasets wikitext
registration.method: Clone via git clone https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM and cd into repo. Install with pip install -e . plus datasets transformers safetensors omegaconf torch CUDA and mkdir -p outputs. Run python scripts/download_models.py --dest checkpoints --model autoencoder to fetch checkpoints/autoencoder/100000.safetensors plus config.yaml and models/gpt2-small, inspecting --help and using gpt2 fallback if needed. Load TextAutoencoder from src/aurora/models/autoencoder.py with checkpoint config keeping N equals L equals 1024 c equals 1, eval mode, cuda, bf16 with fp32 fallback, DEVICE_TYPE=cuda, following src/aurora/train/ae_trainer.py for checkpoint key mapping and src/aurora/models/decoder.py for decode call. Load WikiText-103-raw-v1 test text field, GPT2 tokenize from models/gpt2-small without special tokens, concatenate ids, chunk into 1024-token blocks, keep first 32 blocks. Batch 4 encode with attention_mask all ones to z_enc [B,1024,768] via get_token_features plus encoder. Generate eps_full N(0,I) same shape per block with torch Generator seed 123. For 3 fixed random subsets S of 256 indices from 0-767 via randperm seeds 0 1 2, compute clean sigma 0 and noisy sigma 0.6 latents: x_full equals (1-sigma)z plus sigma eps_full, x_abl by restricting z and eps to S then embedding back with zeros elsewhere with no rescaling to match training dropout without rescaling. Decode each with decoder.forward encoder_latents equals x target_token_len 1024 or equivalent decode_latent, argmax, compare to input_ids for token accuracy per block per condition.

event.description: Ablated latents degrade more from clean to sigma 0.6 than full latents by over 10pp
event.statistic: extra degradation (acc_clean_abl minus acc_noisy_abl) minus (acc_clean_full minus acc_noisy_full) at sigma 0.6 averaged over chunks and subsets

evaluation.procedure: Tokenize WikiText-103-raw-v1 test with models/gpt2-small tokenizer, concatenate and split into non-overlapping 1024-token chunks, take first 32. Encode each chunk batch 4 with released autoencoder to get z_enc [1024,768]. For 3 fixed 256-index subsets seeds 0 1 2 and sigma 0 and 0.6 compute x_full and x_abl with nested Gaussian draws seed 123. Decode all with LatentDecoder, argmax logits, compute token accuracy vs input_ids per chunk per subset. Aggregate means over chunks and subsets, compute extra degradation statistic equals mean (acc_clean_abl minus acc_noisy_abl) minus (acc_clean_full minus acc_noisy_full) at sigma 0.6. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with one JSON per chunk per subset holding acc_clean_full acc_noisy_full acc_clean_abl acc_noisy_abl, and outputs/metrics.json with means per condition and statistic and floor flag if mean acc_clean_abl below 0.5. outputs/scores.jsonl holds per-chunk accuracies, outputs/metrics.json holds means and statistic.
evaluation.controls: Same 32 texts, same 3 fixed channel subsets, same Gaussian draws with nested eps for ablated condition, same decoder and no rescaling to match training dropout pz 0.6; clean vs noisy compared within each width to control clean gap.

registration.full_scale_study: If extra degradation is large, it supports training wide decodable latents rather than post-hoc compression. If small, it motivates compressing or pruning the released latent and retraining the prior at lower D.

agent.reason: Keeping 256 of 768 channels matches training dropout sparsity so clean should not floor, while losing two-thirds of noisy observations at sigma 0.6 should substantially increase degradation versus full latents.

judge_astra.reason: Keeping only one-third of the channels plausibly reduces noise averaging and token separation enough to exceed the ten-point degradation threshold. Training with 60% latent dropout makes catastrophic clean-accuracy collapse less likely, although post-hoc masking is still not equivalent to training a narrower representation.

judge_fable.reason: Keeping 256 of 768 channels removes two-thirds of the evidence the dropout-trained decoder can average over, so at sigma=0.6 the ablated latents should degrade far more than the full latents (which Fig. 5a suggests remain near-perfect), comfortably exceeding 10pp unless the released checkpoint fails to load or behaves as expected at neither width.

judge_opus.reason: Keeping 256 of 768 channels is already below the trained dropout regime (about 307±14 channels kept). With noise at σ=0.6 on those channels, accuracy should fall sharply while the full latent stays near its clean level, giving extra degradation well above 10 points. It fails only if the raw latent scale makes σ=0.6 either negligible or destructive for both conditions, or if loading the model fails.

judge_sol.reason: Retaining only one-third of the channels should reduce recovery evidence under Gaussian corruption, while dropout training makes reasonably strong clean recovery plausible. This favors substantial additional noisy degradation, although learned redundancy could keep the difference below ten percentage points.

judge_luna.reason: The autoencoder’s 60% latent-feature dropout means the decoder was trained to tolerate missing coordinates, so retaining 256 of 768 channels may still decode clean latents reasonably well. Gaussian corruption of the retained channels should expose a robustness cost, but dropout-induced redundancy and a low ablated clean accuracy could keep the extra degradation below ten points.

judge_muse.reason: Keeping 256/768 channels removes two-thirds of redundant evidence for averaging Gaussian noise at sigma 0.6 while clean gap stays small due to 60% dropout training; >10pp extra degradation is plausible unless dropout already made subsets sufficient.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed paper's Fig. 5a trains separate autoencoders at D in {128,256,512,1024}. It then corrupts their latents with x_sigma=(1-sigma)z+sigma*eps and decodes them directly. It never removes channels after training from a single checkpoint, so it cannot separate the effect of trained width from channel redundancy.

This paper finds that full 768-D BERT latents recover tokens much better than compressed 256-D latents. But the 256-D latents are a separately compressed representation, the corruption is token dropout rather than Gaussian latent noise, and no channel subsets of one checkpoint are tested.

COSMOS trains compressed, smooth text latents with dropout regularization. The experiment's own description says it does not test post-hoc channel ablation under Gaussian corruption; I did not open this paper to confirm that.
Studies how to shift noise schedules for image resolution. It does not ablate text-latent channels or measure token recovery.

opus.reason: The closest evidence is the seed paper's own width sweep and the BERT-latent result in 2605.15557. Both compare representations trained or compressed separately; neither zeroes random 256-channel subsets of one trained autoencoder and measures extra degradation under Gaussian corruption. My searches for post-hoc channel ablation, latent-dropout robustness and channel truncation (Matryoshka-style) found no study that answers this question, so it appears open, though my search was limited.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: AURORA-LM Fig. 5a directly decodes Gaussian-corrupted latents from separately trained autoencoders of different widths; it does not compare full and post-hoc channel-masked latents from one frozen checkpoint.

COSMOS tests decoder robustness to Gaussian latent noise and ablates training-time latent dropout, but does not test how inference-time channel removal changes noise-induced degradation within one checkpoint.

Compares trained 256-D and 768-D BERT-latent systems on recovery from token-corrupted drafts using a learned DraftPrior, rather than directly decoding Gaussian-corrupted, channel-ablated representations with an unchanged decoder.

sol.reason: The closest papers establish relationships between trained latent capacity, robustness-oriented training, and token recovery, but do not answer the proposed same-checkpoint channel-removal question. Holding the representation and decoder fixed while measuring the additional noise-induced accuracy loss after channel removal is a substantive experimental distinction, not merely a dataset or metric change. I found no prior work reporting that comparison by 2026-10-07.

opus.reason: #14 projects a newly trained autoencoder's latents onto PCA subspaces, and #2 replicates latents, whereas this experiment zeroes random channel subsets of the released checkpoint and compares the extra degradation under corruption.

sol.reason: The list includes trained-width and PCA-projection tests, but none measures corruption-induced accuracy degradation after random channel removal from a single released autoencoder.

Strict checkpoint loading, CUDA bf16 autocast, direct decoder argmax accuracies. Produces result.json, 96-record outputs/scores.jsonl, and outputs/metrics.json including absolute means and floor flag. Full evaluation command tested successfully (69s); audit independently recomputed statistic 0.7274983723958334, floor flag false. Infrastructure-only differences: used supplied seed snapshot in writable copy rather than network git clone; editable --no-deps avoids replacing CUDA PyTorch; official AE downloader with --skip-backbone plus selective downloading of same GPT-2 PyTorch/tokenizer files skips unused framework duplicates; CUDA SDPA replaces NPU-specific backend. problems: Interpretation (registration and NOTES.md): ablating channels of one checkpoint does not test whether width robustness 'requires training'. There is no separately trained 256-D model, so the result shows only that this decoder pools noise robustness across all 768 channels.

Much of the effect may follow from simple SNR aggregation. With nested noise and the same per-channel SNR, keeping a third of the channels reduces the evidence available per token, so a large gap is fairly expected. The registered threshold of 0.1 is a low bar relative to the observed 0.73.

Possible out-of-distribution confound (evaluate_ablation.py): zero-filling two thirds of the channels while adding noise to the rest may be an input the decoder never saw. The registration assumes training latent_masking p=0.6 is channel dropout, but nothing shown verifies this; it may be per-token masking.

Noise is added to raw encoder latents rather than to the per-dim normalized latents the diffusion model may use (latent_norm_type per_dim). The sigma-0.6 condition may therefore not correspond to the corruption level in seed Fig. 5a. This follows the registration but limits comparability.

Only one noise realisation is used (repetitions 1) on 32 WikiText chunks, and no confidence interval is reported. Spread across the three subsets is modest (noisy ablated accuracy 0.11 to 0.19), so the conclusion is not threatened.
opus.reason: The code follows the registered procedure closely: released 100k checkpoint loaded strictly, first 32 WikiText test chunks of 1024 tokens, three randperm subsets of 256 channels, nested Gaussian noise, zero-fill without rescaling, direct decoder argmax, and the registered extra-degradation statistic. All departures are infrastructure or numerics and could not plausibly move a 73 pp gap. The value of 0.7275 comes from real model outputs, was reproduced exactly between the engineer's run and the protected run, and has a negligible clean-accuracy gap (floor flag false). The evidence credibly shows that the released decoder's noise robustness depends on all channels even though 256 channels suffice to decode clean latents. However, the experiment cannot separate trained width from post-hoc channel count. The effect is also partly expected from SNR pooling and may be confounded by zero-filled out-of-distribution inputs, so it is a meaningful but not decisive finding.

opus.what_it_asks: On the released 768-channel AURORA-LM autoencoder, it compares how much token-recovery accuracy falls under σ=0.6 Gaussian latent corruption for the full latents versus the same latents with only 256 random channels kept and the rest zeroed, to learn whether the width-robustness benefit appears from the number of channels at inference alone, without training at that width.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper's width study (Fig. 5a) compares separately trained autoencoders and never removes channels from one trained model after training, and it does not name this as open work.

relation.reason: The experiment uses the paper's released autoencoder and its corruption probe to test a channel-redundancy property the paper makes no claim about; the paper's trained-width claim stands whichever way it comes out.

obvious.reason: Researchers would more naturally retrain at different widths or probe noise levels, so post-hoc channel ablation of the released checkpoint under noise is an uncommon first follow-up.

who_would_care.reason: Only people working with this autoencoder, or with similar prefix query latent autoencoders, would act on whether its channels can be pruned after training.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements about Fig. 5a, the 768-D released latent width and dropout without rescaling all match the paper's text.

answerable.reason: The comparison can be read only if the decoder still reconstructs clean ablated latents nearly perfectly; otherwise the degradation measure would be confounded by a floor, and the design can check this but not ensure it.
answerable.needs: ablated clean accuracy stays high

opus.what_came_out: On 32 WikiText-103 1024-token chunks with the released 768-D AURORA autoencoder and 3 random channel subsets (one run, no interval), full latents went from 0.9996 clean to 0.891 noisy accuracy, while 256-channel latents went from 0.999 clean to 0.163 noisy (subset means 0.186, 0.109 and 0.194), an extra degradation of 0.727 that is consistent across every chunk.

prerequisite.reason: Clean accuracy for the ablated latents was 0.999, so the decoder handled zeroed channels and the floor check passed.

evidence.reason: The ablated condition lost about 73 more points than the full condition, with every one of the 96 chunk-by-subset records lying far apart, so noise cannot explain the gap even without a formal interval.

next_step.reason: The effect is very large and uniform across chunks and subsets, so a bigger study of this same post-hoc ablation question would add nothing; the more interesting comparison against a separately trained 256-D autoencoder is a different question.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares corruption-induced token-recovery loss for full 768-channel AURORA-LM latents versus the same latents restricted post hoc to 256 channels on WikiText-103, to determine whether retaining all channels provides robustness beyond any clean reconstruction gap.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares separately trained latent widths but neither reports this same-checkpoint channel-removal comparison nor explicitly identifies it as an open question.

relation.reason: The experiment modifies the paper's frozen latent representation to test post-hoc pruning robustness, a property the paper does not claim and whose outcome would not invalidate its trained-width comparison.

obvious.reason: Same-checkpoint channel ablation is a standard follow-up to the prominent width–robustness result, but this specific comparison would compete with several other natural follow-ups.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer at the stated scope would primarily affect groups using or pruning this particular autoencoder's latent interface.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan correctly describes the paper's separately trained width comparison and corruption-robustness finding, and its remaining statements about the paper are not demonstrably contradicted by the text.

answerable.reason: The robustness comparison is interpretable only if channel removal preserves sufficient clean decoding accuracy to avoid a floor-limited degradation measurement.
answerable.needs: Ablated latents remain cleanly decodable

sol.what_came_out: On the released 100k-step 768-channel AURORA-LM autoencoder and WikiText-103-raw-v1 test data, full-width accuracy fell from 99.96% clean to 89.12% at sigma 0.6, versus 99.90% to 16.31% with 256 channels retained, giving 72.75 percentage points of extra degradation across 32 chunks and three channel subsets in one Gaussian-noise repetition, with no interval reported.

prerequisite.reason: Clean reconstruction remained approximately 99.9% after ablation, passing the registered floor check and leaving the corruption comparison interpretable.

evidence.reason: Although no interval is reported, extra degradation ranges from 69.65 to 78.13 percentage points across the three subset means over 32 chunks, providing strong directional evidence with essentially matched clean accuracy.

next_step.reason: The large robustness loss despite preserved clean decoding justifies a systematic study of retained width, channel selection, and corruption strength within the same frozen-autoencoder comparison.

registration.title: Does query-specific routing add value beyond task-level model allocation?
registration.seed_connection: LLMRouter reports gains from learned routing but also includes a competitive query-independent EloRouter. Its released query-model outcome matrix permits a controlled test of whether matching individual questions to models adds value beyond recognizing benchmark sources.
registration.hypothesis: A lightweight query-conditioned router achieves more than one percentage point of held-out quality improvement over both a training-selected task-only policy and a control preserving its model-selection frequencies within task and query-length groups.
registration.contribution: Provides a held-out, allocation-controlled test of fine-grained routing value. It distinguishes useful question-model matching from task recognition and model-frequency effects, rather than attributing every improvement over a single global model to instance-level specialization.

closest_work.difference: Decomposes routing headroom by task and language, but explicitly fits and evaluates its static lookup tables on the same questions. This experiment learns policies without test outcomes and evaluates question-level matching on the published held-out split.
Reports proximity to a hindsight dataset oracle. This experiment uses a training-selected task baseline and an allocation-preserving permutation control rather than relying on a hindsight oracle.
Establishes strong lightweight routing baselines and embedding-space locality. This experiment asks whether their realized benefit survives removal of coarse task and allocation effects.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates, including published train/test splits and recorded performance/token counts.
Embedding model https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.

Reference loading and embedding code: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py and benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py. Implement a standalone replay script; do not install or run the full routing stack.
registration.method: Use the seven generic source tasks MBPP, MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge and MMLU, resolving spelling aliases from the source-task metadata. Construct one outcome vector per question over the declared candidate pool. Drop incomplete question vectors uniformly across policies; reject conflicting duplicate records. Remove whitespace-normalized train/test question duplicates from training. Select at most 800 training questions per source by a seed-1729 hash of question text; reserve a source-stratified 20% for validation and retain the published test questions. Never embed answers, scores or model identities. Encode queries on the GPU with the frozen Qwen embedding model, last-nonpadding-token pooling, L2 normalization, bfloat16 and a 512-token limit. Compare six inexpensive utility predictors: cosine-neighbor averages with k in {8,32,128}, and multi-output ridge regression with alpha in {1,10,100}. Each predicts the full vector of recorded model quality; choose the model with the largest predicted value. Select one predictor using validation macro-average quality, with ties resolved in the listed order, then refit on all selected training questions. Separately choose one fixed model per source using training mean quality. Define four query-length bins per source using training word-count quartiles. On test questions, calculate the router's model frequencies within each source-length bin. The allocation-matched control independently reallocates those selected models among questions in the same bin. Compute its expected quality analytically: for each question sum its recorded model scores weighted by that bin's model frequencies. Use lexicographic model-name tie breaking throughout. No answer-model inference or hosted API is performed; this is explicitly a replay of published outcomes.

event.description: The held-out router has a practically meaningful quality advantage beyond both task-only selection and its allocation-matched control.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 2,000 paired, source-stratified bootstrap estimates of delta = router macro-quality minus max(task-only macro-quality, allocation-matched macro-quality). Quality is on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Give each of the seven sources equal weight. Bootstrap original questions within source, keeping all model outcomes together; recompute allocation frequencies and the expected permutation-control score inside each resample. Do not refit routers during bootstrapping, so uncertainty is conditional on the fitted policies. Write dataset/model revisions, split IDs and exclusions to outputs/manifest.json; the retained quality/cost matrix to outputs/outcomes.parquet; test choices and predictor scores to outputs/predictions.jsonl; and the registered statistic, point contrast, interval and descriptive baselines to outputs/summary.json. Also report the training-selected global fixed model, each individual model and the hindsight per-question maximum as diagnostics, labeling the latter non-deployable. Failure to cross the event threshold does not establish absence of within-task signal.
evaluation.controls: Training-selected global and task-only baselines; source-and-length-conditioned allocation preservation; question-disjoint splits; identical outcome records for every policy. This is a quality-only test. Matching selection frequencies does not exactly match monetary cost, so costs are descriptive rather than evidence of savings.

registration.full_scale_study: Test whether the identified within-task signal survives independent candidate generations, new model pools and source-disjoint evaluation, then investigate representations that capture it at matched deployment costs.

agent.reason: Query-specific specialization is plausible, but the literature suggests that coarse task structure explains much routing benefit. Beating both controls by more than one percentage point at the bootstrap lower bound is substantially harder than beating the largest-model baseline.

judge_astra.reason: The task-only and allocation-matched controls remove substantial sources of apparent routing gains, so improvements over size-based fixed models are weak evidence for this event. Useful within-task signal is plausible, but clearing the one-percentage-point lower-bound threshold requires that these lightweight predictors capture it reliably.

judge_fable.reason: Embedding-based kNN/ridge routers usually realize only a small slice of the oracle gap, and most of that is task recognition; the task-only baseline plus a ~1pp bootstrap margin means the router needs roughly 2pp of genuine within-task matching value over the best per-source model, which is plausible but more often not achieved, and validation may even pick a large-k predictor that collapses to the task-only policy.

judge_opus.reason: The event needs roughly a 2-point point-estimate gain over the training-selected best model per source, to clear a 5th-percentile bar of 1 point. Gains from embedding-based kNN or ridge routing within a source among strong candidates are usually well under 1 point, and validation will likely choose smooth settings close to task-level allocation.

judge_sol.reason: Much of the seed’s reported gain could come from coarse task recognition or from beating a weak fixed-model reference. Fine-grained signal is plausible, but exceeding both stronger controls by a one-point lower confidence bound is substantially harder than the seed’s comparison.

judge_luna.reason: The paper’s gains over a global fixed-model baseline and its task-varying winners support query-level signal. But the task-only policy and allocation-matched control remove much of that headroom, making a greater-than-one-point lower-bound gain uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: Seed Table 2 shows large learned-router gains over single models, indicating headroom, but a training-selected task-only policy likely captures much of it; whether frozen-embedding kNN/ridge achieves >1pp within-task, within-length matching beyond model frequencies is uncertain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Splits the oracle-minus-best-single-model gap by task type and language, but fits and scores its fixed lookup tables on the same 294 questions with no held-out split and no learned query-level router. The experiment uses held-out evaluation on xRouteBench against a task-only policy chosen on training data, plus an allocation-preserving control.

Uses a similar control (a content-blind allocation that keeps the router's model shares) to test four off-the-shelf routers on RouterBench, BFCL, tau2-bench and WebArena. Most of those routers pick near-constant tiers. It does not train lightweight utility predictors, lacks a task-only baseline chosen on training data and query-length bins, and does not use xRouteBench.

Reportedly (per 2608.23023's description; not read directly) compares routers to a hindsight per-dataset oracle and suggests the gain may be mostly domain-level. The experiment uses a deployable task baseline chosen on training data and a permutation control rather than a hindsight oracle.
The seed paper reports learned routers beating the best fixed model but does not separate task recognition or model-frequency effects from question-level matching.

opus.reason: Recent work suggests task identity explains most of the routing gain (2608.23023, in-sample only) and uses share-matched content-blind controls for off-the-shelf routers (2608.14641). None of the papers found runs a held-out test that compares a learned lightweight query-level router against both a task-only policy chosen on training data and a control preserving model frequencies within task and length groups. The differences go beyond the dataset or the metric, since they cover holdout design, control structure and router type, so the question remains open.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Most of the LLM Routing Gap Is Task Type decomposes headroom using task-and-language lookup tables fitted and evaluated on the same questions. It does not test a held-out learned router against an allocation-preserving control.

Agent-as-a-Router compares held-out coding routers with a probing-set-selected DimensionBest policy. However, its successful router incorporates online execution feedback, and the comparisons do not preserve model-selection frequencies within task and length groups.

LLMRouterBench attributes routing gains partly to coarse domain structure through proximity to a hindsight Dataset Oracle. It does not report the proposed training-selected task baseline plus allocation-controlled matching test.

The Routing Plateau studies coarse capability learning, selection frequencies, within-domain performance and correctness prediction. These analyses do not isolate realized question-model matching using source-and-length-conditioned allocation preservation.

Oracle Gaps in Reliability Coverage uses outcome redistributions, including preservation of policy success totals, to test specialization versus sampling noise. It randomizes correctness outcomes rather than router assignments and does not control for task-level allocation.

sol.reason: The broad question of coarse versus instance-specific routing is already established, and prior work even includes held-out comparisons with task-only selectors. Nevertheless, I found no paper reporting the combined frozen-policy, held-out comparison against both a training-selected task policy and a source-and-length-stratified allocation-preserving control; that attribution test is a distinct contribution rather than merely a dataset or metric substitution.

opus.reason: Both use the released xRouteBench Generic matrix to test whether query-level routers add value beyond a training-selected per-subtask (task-identity) model choice.

sol.reason: Both compare held-out query-level routing against a training-selected source-task-only policy on the released Generic-track matrix to test value beyond task recognition, with the registration adding an allocation-preserving control.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented standalone published-outcome replay with pinned dataset/model revisions, frozen GPU BF16 Qwen embeddings, all six registered utility predictors, validation-only selection and refit, training-selected task/global baselines, source-length allocation expectation, and 2,000 paired source-stratified bootstrap resamples with frequency recomputation. Writes result.json and all four registered artifacts. No substantive registration changes; deterministic conventions for hash formatting, validation rounding, ridge intercept, quartile boundaries, and bootstrap RNG are documented. Rejected one conflicting ARC-Challenge training question uniformly. Tested the complete command twice and seven synthetic correctness tests. Retained 2,648 training and 3,500 test questions; k=128 selected; statistic=-0.018571428571428572, so the registered event did not occur. This does not establish absence of within-task signal; costs remain descriptive.

departures: replay.py: the kNN neighbours are pooled across all seven sources rather than drawn within each source. The registration leaves this open, but for MMLU-Pro, with only 63 training questions, k=128 neighbours must come mostly from other sources. This could change router quality, though it is a legitimate reading of 'cosine-neighbor averages'.

Data, recorded in manifest.json counts and README: the 800-per-source cap is never reached. Training sizes are 337 for MBPP, 63 for MMLU-Pro and about 450 for each other source, which weakens the router and the task-only selection for small sources. This is a dataset limitation, not an implementation departure, and it is disclosed.

replay.py: the train/test overlap filter compares against all published test texts, including non-registered sources, which is slightly broader than registered. The README reports zero overlaps, so there is no effect.

replay.py: unspecified details were fixed deterministically. These are the SHA-256 hash format, ceil(20%) validation size, ridge intercept with Cholesky solver, numpy linear quartiles with equal values placed in the higher bin, no instruction prefix for the Qwen3 embedding, left padding, and PCG64 seed 1729 for the bootstrap. All are open choices, documented in the manifest, and unlikely to move the result materially.
replay.py: the global fixed model is chosen by the micro (question-weighted) training mean rather than a source macro mean. It is a diagnostic only and does not affect the registered statistic.

replay.py: conflicting-duplicate detection compares whole records apart from embedding_id. One ARC-Challenge training question (36 records) was rejected for every policy, as the registration's rejection rule requires. The effect is negligible.
problems: Uncertainty is conditional on the fitted policies, a single embedding model and a single predictor family. The negative result therefore applies to this lightweight router, not to query-conditioned routing generally, as the summary.json cautions acknowledge.
MMLU-Pro has only 63 training questions and MBPP 337. Task-only selection and router fitting for these sources rest on small samples, so per-source contrasts there are noisy.
query_text in replay.py parses JSON when a query string begins with '[' or '{'. This could alter the text of some questions, though it is unlikely to matter for these sources.
outcomes.parquet and most of predictions.jsonl and manifest.json were not inspectable here. Claims of complete vectors and zero overlaps rest on the code paths and the README.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered pipeline as specified: alias-resolved sources, complete-vector filtering, the hash cap with validation split, frozen GPU BF16 Qwen3 last-token embeddings, the six predictors selected on validation macro quality and then refit, training-selected task-only and global policies, the analytic source-by-length allocation control, and a paired source-stratified bootstrap that recomputes frequencies. The remaining departures are open implementation choices or dataset limitations and do not plausibly change the conclusion. The fresh evaluation reproduced the engineer's value (-0.01857) exactly, and the result comes from published outcome records with no test leakage into model fitting or selection. The finding is a clear, precisely estimated null on this replay. The router beats its allocation-matched control by about 1.3 points (point estimate) but trails the training-selected task-only policy by about 1.2 points, with a bootstrap 90% interval entirely below zero. That is a meaningful answer to whether this lightweight query-conditioned router adds value beyond task allocation, limited by small training sets for some sources and by uncertainty that is conditional on the fitted policies.

problems: outputs/manifest.json: MMLU-Pro has only 63 selected training questions, including 13 validation questions. This limits source-specific learning and makes validation-based selection less precise; it is not a registration violation.

outputs/summary.json: Bootstrap uncertainty is conditional on the fitted policies and published outcome matrix. It does not include training/model-selection variability or variation from independently generated candidate answers.

outputs/summary.json: The positive router-minus-allocation-control contrast has no separately reported uncertainty interval, so it should remain a descriptive finding rather than an independently established advantage.
sol.reason: replay.py implements the registered preparation, predictors, validation selection, baselines, allocation control and paired bootstrap; its deterministic conventions resolve choices the registration left open. The fresh evaluation regenerated every required artifact, and the code computes the statistic from revision-pinned published outcomes without apparent test-outcome leakage or hard-coded results. The registered statistic was -0.01857 against a threshold of 0.01, with a point contrast of -0.01229 and a central 90% bootstrap interval entirely below zero, providing meaningful negative evidence about this fitted routing procedure. The router's positive allocation-control point contrast does not rescue the combined event, and the findings do not establish absence of within-task signal or generalize beyond this conditional replay.

departures: replay.py fills unspecified conventions rather than contradicting the registration: SHA-256('1729:purpose:query') and ceil(20%) for the validation holdout, ridge intercept with a cholesky solver, numpy linear quartiles with searchsorted(side='right'), and SDPA/left padding. Ridge was not selected, quartile edges do not bind because task-only beats the allocation control by ~2.6 points, and the fresh re-encode matched the reported statistic exactly, so these did not change the value; the ceil/hash choice could in principle flip k=128 vs ridge-10 (validation gap 0.0016) but is an open choice the registration left unspecified.

replay.py pools cosine neighbors across all seven sources (documented in the manifest). The registration requires cosine-neighbor averages and does not restrict the pool to the same source, so this does not change the registered question; a within-source pool would be a different router and could change the value.
replay.py selects the diagnostic global model by an unweighted training mean rather than a source macro-mean. That model is not in the registered delta and did not change the reported statistic.

replay.py unwraps JSON chat-looking query strings and joins message contents before embedding and word counts. The registration does not specify this parsing; word counts look like bare questions and there is no evidence answers, scores, or model identities were embedded.
problems: MMLU-Pro has only 63 training questions (outputs/manifest.json counts), so one equally weighted source has a noisy task-only model and cannot support a large within-task neighbor set.

outputs/summary.json: selected k=128 validation macro-quality is 0.849 but held-out router quality is 0.809, a four-point drop. The test labels are not used in fitting, so this is shift or neighbor overfitting, not leakage, but it limits how representative the training pool is.

Some source-length bins are tiny (outputs/summary.json allocation_groups includes n=6), so the analytical allocation control partly tracks the router there. This does not move the registered statistic, which is bound by task-only.

The router beats the allocation control by about 1.3 points (outputs/summary.json) while losing to task-only by 1.2 points. Only the combined contrast was pre-registered; the allocation gap should not be read as a confirmed within-task effect.
grok.reason: The run implements the registered sources, frozen Qwen embeddings, six predictors, validation selection and refit, task-only and frequency-matched controls, and the 2,000-resample paired bootstrap; open conventions are documented and do not change the question or the reported value. A fresh GPU re-encode reproduced statistic -0.01857 with no test leakage or hard-coded result, and the quality totals match the per-source rates. The selected k=128 router scores 0.809 macro-quality against 0.821 for task-only and 0.796 for the allocation control, so the pre-registered >1pp event did not occur and the bootstrap interval lies entirely below zero. That is a credible scoped null for these lightweight predictors on the published replay, not evidence that no within-task signal exists and not a test of a stronger learned router.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether a lightweight query-conditioned router improves held-out answer quality over a training-chosen model per source task and over a control that keeps that router's model frequencies within task and length groups.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares learned routers with global fixed models and a query-blind Elo ranking, but it neither runs a task-level allocation plus frequency-matched control nor leaves that comparison as unfinished work.

relation.reason: The test uses the paper's xRouteBench outcomes and a kNN-style scorer to ask whether question-level matching beats task allocation, a comparison the paper does not claim, so the paper's results stand either way.

obvious.reason: Given task-varying winners and a near-best query-blind Elo router, several researchers would list query routing against per-task allocation with a frequency-matched control, but not most first-ten lists.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares a query-conditioned utility router with training-selected task-only routing and source-and-length allocation-matched routing on held-out generic xRouteBench tasks to learn whether individual question–model matching adds quality beyond coarse allocation.

registration.title: Repeated labels versus broader coverage at a fixed supervision budget
registration.seed_connection: The seed constructs routing supervision by executing candidate models over queries. Its framework makes supervision construction separable from router architecture, allowing a direct experiment on how to spend a limited response-collection budget.
registration.hypothesis: At 768 training generations per candidate model, four measurements of 192 questions produce more than one percentage point better held-out routing accuracy than one measurement of 768 questions, under identical per-task model-selection quotas.
registration.contribution: Tests the opportunity cost of repeated supervision: reducing measurement noise versus covering more distinct questions. It does not claim that stochastic routing-label instability is new.

closest_work.difference: DARS already studies repeated decoding, label instability and observation-budget saturation. This experiment instead holds total training candidate calls fixed while trading distinct-question coverage against replication, and holds deployment model shares fixed.

Uses ten generations per question to construct more reliable routing labels, but does not establish whether those calls would be better spent labeling additional questions under this matched-budget protocol.

inputs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc, configuration ARC-Challenge, train and test splits.
https://huggingface.co/datasets/tau/commonsense_qa, train and validation splits; use the labeled validation split only as the final evaluation pool.
