https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; PyTorch, Transformers, a compatible prebuilt vLLM installation, datasets and scikit-learn.
registration.method: Canonicalize each question with its complete option list and remap source option labels to consecutive letters while preserving the correct option. Remove normalized-text duplicates across splits. Use seed-17 hash ordering, before generation, to select 384 training and 64 validation questions per task from the official training pools, plus 256 final-test questions per task from ARC test and CommonsenseQA validation. Only admit questions whose complete chat prompts fit within 768 tokens for both answer-model tokenizers. The breadth arm receives the first response from each model on all 768 training questions. The replication arm receives four independent responses per model on the first 96 training questions per task, hence 192 distinct questions and the same 768 training generations per model. Share the first draw where the arms overlap, but never expose an arm to labels outside its allocation. Generate two draws per validation question-model pair and three independent draws per test pair. This requires 6,272 candidate responses in total. Use temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, a 96-token output cap, per-request seeds derived from question/model/draw IDs, and the instruction: 'Give a one-sentence justification, then finish with FINAL: X, where X is one of the listed option letters.' Parse the last valid FINAL marker, falling back only to an explicit Answer marker or a response consisting solely of one option letter; otherwise score zero and flag the parse failure. Freeze and unit-test this parser before inference. Run each answer model in a separate batched bfloat16 vLLM process with max_model_len 2048 and at most 64 concurrent sequences. Encode question-plus-options with the frozen 0.6B embedding model. For each arm fit ridge regression to the target mean(correct_Phi) minus mean(correct_Qwen), choosing alpha from {0.1,1,10,100} using the common validation set. At deployment, within each task assign the half of questions with highest predicted differences to Phi and the remainder to Qwen; break score ties by question ID. This fixes both arms' model shares without consulting test labels.

event.description: Repeated measurement beats broader single-shot coverage by a meaningful margin at the registered acquisition budget and deployment model shares.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 2,000 paired, task-stratified bootstrap estimates of replication-arm accuracy minus breadth-arm accuracy, measured on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Score a selected model on a test question by its mean correctness over the three independent test draws; average equally across the two tasks. Bootstrap questions, keeping both models and all draws together, and reapply the half-per-task quota using frozen prediction scores in each resample. Do not refit the regressions. outputs/manifest.json records dataset/model revisions, sampling IDs, seeds and arm memberships. outputs/generations.jsonl contains raw responses, parsed answers, correctness, token counts, termination reasons and timings. outputs/routing.jsonl contains validation choices, fitted regularization values, test prediction differences and selected models. outputs/summary.json contains the registered statistic, contrast interval, individual-model scores, a random half-share control, parse/cap rates and acquisition/deployment token totals. The comparison is matched in candidate calls and model shares, not asserted to be matched in actual GPU seconds or output tokens.
evaluation.controls: Identical candidate models, decoding protocol, embedding representation, regression family, validation budget and test draws; nested question allocation; independent evaluation generations; fixed per-task model shares; parser and truncation diagnostics. Uncertainty is conditional on this training allocation, not evidence of equivalence across all allocations.

registration.full_scale_study: Map the coverage-versus-replication trade-off across acquisition budgets, decoding temperatures, model complementarity and router families, including independent allocation replicates and token-budget-matched adaptive collection.

agent.reason: Repeated measurements reduce label noise, but sacrificing three quarters of the distinct training questions is a substantial coverage penalty for the ridge predictor. DARS supports repeated supervision without establishing that it wins this equal-call comparison, especially with model-selection shares fixed.

judge_astra.reason: Replication reduces measurement noise but sacrifices three quarters of the distinct training questions, which is a substantial disadvantage for learning query-conditioned performance differences. Fixed model shares remove gains from simply favoring the stronger model, and the confidence-bound requirement makes a modest replication advantage insufficient.

judge_fable.reason: With two similarly accurate small models, a weak embedding-predictable difference signal, and 192 vs 768 training questions, both arms route nearly at random under the fixed 50/50 share; information-wise the arms are roughly matched with a slight edge to coverage, so replication winning by >1pp at the 5th percentile is unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: With a fixed number of calls, coverage should beat replication, because between-question variance that embeddings cannot explain does not shrink with repeated draws. Routing signal between two similar 3–4B models on multiple-choice tasks is also weak, so both arms will be near the random half-split, and a gain above about 3 points for replication is very unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Repeated draws reduce label noise, but with a fixed call budget and ridge regression I expect broader coverage usually to be more useful. The fourfold reduction in distinct questions and the confidence-bound requirement make the registered replication advantage unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: Repeated generations could reduce noisy correctness labels, but the replication arm has only one quarter as many distinct training questions per task, and question-level heterogeneity is likely important. That trade-off, plus the greater-than-one-point lower-bound requirement, makes the registered event unlikely.

judge_muse.reason: The breadth arm sees 4x distinct questions including the replication subset's shared first draws, while replication only adds extra draws on that subset; with ridge smoothing, extra coverage likely outweighs noise reduction, making a >1pp lower-bound win for replication unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DARS shows that single-shot routing labels are unstable. It finds that repeated observations, built from query rewrites and repeated decoding, improve routers compared with single-shot labels on the same 200 training queries. It also finds that gains level off at about a 3x3 observation grid, and it tests adaptive sampling. However, the single-shot baseline uses the same queries and fewer total calls. DARS never holds total candidate calls fixed while trading replication against covering more distinct queries, so it does not answer the coverage-versus-replication question.

Not read in this session; I am relying on the registered description. It uses about ten generations per question to build more reliable routing labels. As described, it does not compare that choice with spending the same calls on more distinct questions.

The seed paper provides the separable pipeline for building supervision and evaluating routers. As far as its abstract shows, it does not run a budget-allocation ablation on how routing labels are collected. I did not read its full text.

opus.reason: The closest work I read, DARS, establishes that repeated decoding makes routing labels more reliable and that the benefit saturates at a moderate number of samples. But in DARS, repetition always adds calls on a fixed query set; it never fixes the budget and trades replication against more distinct questions. My searches turned no LLM-routing paper that tests this matched-budget allocation, so the question looks open. One caveat: the general 'get another label' tradeoff is older work in crowdsourcing, so the new part here is applying it to routing supervision, not the idea itself.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DARS compares repeated-observation and single-shot supervision on the same 200 training queries and studies observation-budget saturation and adaptive replication. It does not trade replication against additional distinct training queries at a fixed total candidate-call budget or fix deployment model shares across arms.

Expected Reward Prediction trains ridge regressors on frozen prompt embeddings using mean rewards from 32 responses per prompt, including a correctness-based routing evaluation. It does not compare broader single-shot coverage with repeated measurements under matched acquisition budgets.
Constructs routing labels using majority voting over ten generations per question, but does not test whether those generations would be better spent on additional training questions.

Compares more distinct questions against more responses per question at matched SFT-example budgets, including one-versus-four response allocations. However, it trains generative students on verified reasoning traces rather than reducing measurement noise in routing targets, and does not evaluate routing under controlled model-selection shares.

sol.reason: Repeated supervision for LLM routing is established, but the closest routing studies do not measure its opportunity cost against broader question coverage at an equal candidate-call budget. Matched-budget question-versus-response allocation has been studied for synthetic-data fine-tuning, which does not settle the routing-supervision question. Among the work found by the cutoff date, none answers the registered allocation question with both acquisition calls and deployment model shares controlled.

opus.reason: No list entry trades replicated labels against broader question coverage at a fixed generation budget; entry 50 only measures how stable labels are across sampled completions.

sol.reason: The registration compares repeated labeling against broader question coverage at a fixed acquisition budget using held-out routing accuracy, whereas entry 50 measures label stability without that budget trade-off.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented and successfully tested the full registered experiment: 6,272 responses, nested 768-vs-192-question allocations with 768 training generations/model/arm, separate bf16 vLLM processes, frozen tested parser, frozen embeddings, ridge fitting, exact half-per-task quotas, and 2,000 paired stratified bootstraps with quotas reapplied. All required outputs and result.json are regenerated. No protocol changes; unspecified conventions fixed before inference include validation-target MSE for alpha selection, domain-separated seed-17 SHA256 ordering/seeds, and documented duplicate normalization. The provisioned test GPU reported H200 rather than the stated A100. Test statistic was -0.020833333333333336, so the event did not occur. Phi had 42.25% parse failures and 17.44% cap hits; failures remained zero-scored without relaxing the parser or cap. Details and conditional-uncertainty limitations are in registered/IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

departures: The answer instruction is sent as a system message, with the canonical question and options as the user turn (registered/experiment.py messages()). The registration does not say where the instruction goes. This could shift parse rates somewhat, but it is applied identically to both arms and is a reasonable reading of the registration.

Ridge alpha is chosen by validation target MSE with ties going to the smaller alpha, rather than by validation routed accuracy (experiment.py evaluate()). The registration leaves the criterion open. It changes the selected alphas (breadth 10, replication 1) and so could move the contrast a little. It is a legitimate filled-in choice and was fixed before inference.

Duplicate handling: every copy in a normalized-text group spanning splits is excluded, and within a split only the smallest ID is kept (prepare()). This fills an open detail. Only one within-split duplicate was removed and there were no cross-split groups (manifest.json), so it is negligible.

The parser accepts Markdown, brackets or parentheses around the letter after FINAL:/Answer:, and its Answer regex also matches 'Final answer: B' (registered/parser.py). It was frozen and unit-tested before inference and stays within the registered fallbacks. Its effect is small and the same for both arms.

Requests are submitted to vLLM in chunks of 256 with enforce_eager and gpu_memory_utilization 0.88, and run on an H200 instead of an A100. These are execution details only and do not affect the registered quantities apart from nondeterminism.

GPU and batching nondeterminism means the fresh run (value -0.01953, point contrast 0.0039) does not reproduce the engineer's earlier run (-0.02083, contrast 0.0117) quoted in the engineer notes and IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md. Both runs reach the same conclusion. Even with per-request seeds the result is not bit-reproducible.
problems: Phi parse failures are severe: about 42% of Phi responses in the engineer's run fail to parse and about 17% hit the 96-token cap (IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md, summary diagnostics). Many failures are responses that begin with the answer letter but have no FINAL marker, or are truncated (e.g. outputs/generations.jsonl, first record). This is exactly what the registration specifies. However, it means the routing target mostly measures whether Phi complies with the format, not its answer quality. Phi scores 0.444 against Qwen's 0.768 (summary.json), so routing still under-predicts Phi badly.

Because of the fixed half-Phi quota, both routers (about 0.627 and 0.631) score far below Qwen alone (0.768) and only about 2 points above the random half-share expectation (0.606). The comparison is between two weak routers, which limits how informative the result is about supervision allocation.

Precision is too low to settle the hypothesis. The 90% bootstrap interval for replication minus breadth is [-0.0195, 0.026] (summary.json). It contains both zero and the 1-point threshold, so the null result is inconclusive rather than a negative finding.

The bootstrap resamples test questions only. It does not capture variance from the training allocation, the training draws, or vLLM nondeterminism, and that last source alone moved the point contrast from 0.0117 to 0.0039 between runs (experiment.log vs the fresh evaluation). The registration acknowledges this limitation.
The engineer notes report the earlier run's statistic (-0.0208) rather than the fresh evaluation's value (-0.0195). The difference is minor and does not change the conclusion.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely. It uses nested 768-vs-192-question allocations with 768 training generations per model per arm, 6,272 responses in total, the registered decoding settings, a parser frozen before inference with zero scoring of failures, frozen embeddings, ridge regression on the Phi-minus-Qwen difference, exact half-per-task quotas, and 2,000 task-stratified bootstraps that reapply the quota without refitting. All departures I found are choices the registration leaves open or execution details, and none plausibly changes the conclusion. The reported value of -0.0195 is computed from real generations, with no test-label leakage and with the paired accuracy difference computed correctly. The evidence is weak, though. The interval spans both zero and the 1-point threshold, and the run is dominated by Phi's roughly 42% format-failure rate, which makes the routing target largely about format compliance. The result is therefore an inconclusive null for this single allocation, not a meaningful finding about coverage versus replication.

departures: registered/experiment.py::prepare additionally removes within-split normalized-text duplicates, whereas the registration specifies removing duplicates across splits. outputs/manifest.json records one such removal, arc:train:MEA_2012_5_8, and no cross-split duplicate groups. This could change the hash-ordered training or validation allocation if the duplicate would otherwise enter the selected prefix; the truncated allocation excerpts do not establish whether it actually changed the selected questions.
problems: The possible allocation effect of the additional within-split exclusion in registered/experiment.py cannot be resolved from the displayed portions of outputs/manifest.json and work/prepared.json.

outputs/summary.json reports a replication-minus-breadth contrast of 0.00390625 with a 95% percentile interval of [-0.02345377604166667, 0.030598958333333336]. This leaves both meaningful benefit and harm unresolved; failure of the registered event is not evidence of equivalence.
The uncertainty covers one training allocation and the observed evaluation draws, not variation across independently collected training allocations.

outputs/generations.jsonl shows Phi responses with a recognizable correct answer nevertheless receiving zero because the required marker is absent before truncation. This follows the registered scoring rule, but means the comparison measures formatting reliability as well as answer correctness; the engineer's aggregate failure rates describe the earlier run, not necessarily the protected evaluation.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation regenerated the required artifacts from real dataset loading and model inference, and the inspected scoring code contains no apparent hard-coded result or test-label leakage. The core budgets, models, prompts, decoding settings, quotas and bootstrap statistic match the registration, while validation-MSE alpha selection and embedding pooling fill unspecified choices. Fidelity remains uncertain because the additional within-split exclusion could alter the registered allocation, but its actual effect is not established by the displayed evidence. The fresh registered statistic is -0.01953125, so the event did not occur, but the wide contrast interval, single allocation and formatting-sensitive outcomes make this valid yet weak evidence about the broader coverage-versus-replication trade-off.

departures: Alpha is chosen by minimum common-validation target MSE, smallest alpha on ties (registered/experiment.py, outputs/routing.jsonl). The registration only says to choose alpha from {0.1,1,10,100} using the common validation set. This open choice could change the result: validation routed accuracy would pick breadth alpha 100 instead of 10 and replication alpha 0.1 instead of 1.0.

The registered instruction is delivered as the system message and the question as the user message (registered/experiment.py). Role placement was unspecified and could change generations and the result.

The frozen parser accepts parentheses and ordinary Markdown around FINAL/Answer markers and treats phrases such as 'Final answer:' as an Answer marker (registered/parser.py). Slightly broader than a minimal reading of the registered fallbacks; could change some labels, though observed Phi failures are mostly missing markers or 96-token cap hits.

Within-split dedup drops arc:train:MEA_2012_5_8 in addition to cross-split duplicates (registered/experiment.py, outputs/manifest.json). Registration says remove normalized-text duplicates across splits. Could swap one selected question and slightly change the value; unlikely to flip the event.

Embeddings use last-token pooling, left padding, L2 normalization, and bfloat16 on question-plus-options only (registered/experiment.py). Pooling was unspecified. Standard for this model, but another pooling would change the router and could change the result.
Ridge uses fit_intercept=True and solver cholesky (registered/experiment.py), unspecified. Could slightly change fitted scores.

vLLM extras not in the registration: enforce_eager, prefix caching off, gpu_memory_utilization 0.88, an LLM-level seed, and 256-request submissions with max_num_seqs 64 (registered/experiment.py, evaluate.sh). These can change sampled tokens; the engineer's earlier run and this evaluation disagree on arm accuracies.

Bootstrap breaks duplicate-ID ties by resample position and uses linear percentile interpolation (registered/experiment.py). Needed to define the registered bootstrap; negligible effect on the fifth percentile.
problems: Sampling is not bit-stable despite per-request seeds: experiment.log (engineer run) has contrast 0.01171875 and fifth percentile -0.020833, while the fresh evaluation (result.json, outputs/summary.json) has contrast 0.00390625 and fifth percentile -0.01953125. The event conclusion matches; the reported value does not.

Phi often fails the frozen FINAL format or hits the 96-token cap and is zero-scored (outputs/generations.jsonl; about 42% parse failures in the engineer run notes). Labels mix ability with format compliance, so the contrast is about this decoding/parser protocol, not clean model quality.

Precision is limited: outputs/summary.json 95% interval is about [-0.023, 0.031], so effects above +1pp remain compatible with the data. Uncertainty is also conditional on one seed-17 allocation and does not refit the routers, as registered.
grok.reason: The fresh run implements the registered design: pinned ARC-Challenge and CommonsenseQA items, both answer models, 6,272 generations, nested 768-versus-192 allocations at 768 calls per model, failures scored zero, ridge routing, exact half-per-task quotas, and the fifth percentile of 2,000 paired stratified bootstraps. Filled-in choices such as validation-MSE alpha selection, system-role instruction, and last-token embeddings were fixed before inference and do not change the question, though MSE versus routed-accuracy alpha selection could move the estimate. The value -0.01953125 matches the evaluation stdout and summary and is computed from real generations without test-label leakage, so the event failure is a genuine result of this run. Phi format failures and run-to-run sampling differences limit interpretation, and the interval still reaches about +3pp, but the pre-registered claim that replication beats breadth by more than one point at the lower percentile is a credible, controlled negative finding.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether four labels on fewer questions give higher held-out routing accuracy than one label on more questions when both use the same number of candidate generations and the same per-task model shares.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper builds routing supervision by running each candidate once per query and never reports, nor marks as open, a fixed-budget comparison of repeated labels against broader question coverage.

relation.reason: The experiment takes the paper’s candidate-response supervision and held-out routed-accuracy setup and uses it for a replication-versus-coverage split the paper does not measure.

obvious.reason: After this paper, first follow-up lists would mostly target router rankings, multi-turn failure, or personalization transfer, and only one or two would specifically trade repeated labels against more questions at a fixed call budget.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer at this one budget, ridge router, and forced half-share would change call allocation only for groups building similar small-model routing supervision, not routing practice at large.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan’s claims that the paper constructs routing supervision by executing candidates and separates that construction from router code match the paper and are not contradicted by it.

answerable.reason: The arms are matched on generations, models, embeddings, regression, validation, and deployment shares, so the reported contrast and interval would show either way whether replication beats breadth.

grok.what_came_out: On 512 ARC-Challenge and CommonsenseQA test questions, the replication arm scored 0.631 versus 0.627 for the breadth arm (difference 0.0039; 2000 task-stratified bootstraps, 95% interval [-0.023, 0.031]) with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct.

prerequisite.reason: Quotas, zero-scored parse failures, and both arm accuracies were produced as specified, and no required control failed in a way that blocks reading the contrast.

evidence.reason: The replication-minus-breadth estimate is only 0.39 points and the 95% bootstrap interval on 512 questions runs from -2.3 to +3.1 points, so both no gain and a gain above one point remain possible.

next_step.reason: The interval is too wide to settle a one-point gap, so the same comparison should be rerun with more test questions and repeated allocations rather than scaled up as is.
next_step.what: Too few test questions and a single allocation leave a one-point gap unresolved; rerun with a larger test set and several allocations.

opus.what_it_asks: At a fixed number of training generations per candidate model, does a router trained on four repeated samples of fewer questions route better between Qwen2.5-3B and Phi-3.5-mini on ARC-Challenge and CommonsenseQA than one trained on single samples of four times as many questions, to learn whether a supervision-collection budget is better spent on replication or on coverage?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper builds a dense query–model matrix with one response per pair and never discusses how to split a response-collection budget between repeated sampling and question coverage.

relation.reason: The experiment takes the paper's idea of building routing supervision by running every candidate on benchmark queries and varies how that supervision is collected, which the paper makes no claim about.

obvious.reason: Label noise from stochastic decoding is a known worry, but trading replication against coverage at a matched call budget is not among the first follow-ups most router researchers would list after this infrastructure paper.

who_would_care.reason: At the stated scope (two small models, a ridge router, one budget), a clear answer would mainly inform people who build routing supervision datasets in similar small settings.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's claims about the paper are accurate: supervision is built by executing candidates over queries, and the framework separates supervision construction from router design.

answerable.reason: The comparison can be read only if the ridge routers pick up real query-level signal; otherwise both arms collapse to random half-share routing and the label allocation cannot matter.
answerable.needs: routers learn above-random ranking signal

opus.what_came_out: On 512 test questions (256 ARC-Challenge, 256 CommonsenseQA, three draws each, one training allocation), routing between Qwen2.5-3B (0.768 accuracy alone) and Phi-3.5-mini (0.444 alone, with 42% parse failures) gave 0.627 for the breadth arm and 0.631 for the replication arm, a contrast of +0.004 with 95% bootstrap interval [-0.023, +0.031].

prerequisite.reason: Both routers beat the random half-share expectation of 0.606, the breadth arm by about 2 points and the replication arm by about 2.5 points, so some routing signal was learned, though only modestly; Phi's high format-failure rate means its labels partly measure format compliance, but this is part of the registered protocol.

evidence.reason: The point estimate is near zero, but the 95% interval runs from about -2.3 to +3.1 points, so it allows both no effect and a gain larger than the hypothesized 1 point.

next_step.reason: The run was too noisy to separate the arms, and Phi's frequent format failures blurred the supervision signal, so the question needs to be asked again with these faults removed.
next_step.what: Fix the noise and the label quality: use many more test questions and several independent training-allocation replicates, and reduce Phi's parse failures (for example with constrained answer formatting or a larger output cap), so the interval can rule an effect of 1 point or more in or out.

sol.what_it_asks: On ARC-Challenge and CommonsenseQA, this compares ridge routers trained using repeated candidate responses on fewer questions with routers trained using single responses on more questions, to learn whether repetition improves held-out routing accuracy at a fixed supervision budget.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper neither measures the replication-versus-coverage trade-off at a fixed supervision budget nor explicitly identifies that comparison as an open question.

relation.reason: The experiment changes the acquisition of candidate-response supervision used in the paper's supervised routing pipeline without testing a claim the paper makes about that allocation.

obvious.reason: The standard trade-off between reducing stochastic label noise and covering more examples would plausibly appear on several lists, but competes with many more immediate router and benchmark follow-ups.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would inform supervision-acquisition decisions across learned LLM routing methods rather than only users of this particular ridge router.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's descriptions of candidate-response supervision and the separation of data construction from router architecture agree with the paper's text.

answerable.reason: The specified acquisition allocations produce two routers whose independently measured held-out accuracies directly bear on the proposed budget trade-off.

sol.what_came_out: Using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct on 512 ARC-Challenge and CommonsenseQA test questions, replication achieved 63.09% accuracy versus breadth's 62.70%, a +0.39-percentage-point difference with a paired-bootstrap 95% interval of −2.35 to +3.06 points, conditional on one training allocation and three test draws per model and question.

prerequisite.reason: The acquisition counts, routing quotas and parser tests passed, and unparseable responses were included as errors in the explicitly defined outcome rather than requiring successful parsing as a separate prerequisite.

evidence.reason: The contrast interval includes both no improvement and improvements large enough to matter, so the small positive estimate does not establish either superiority or its absence.

next_step.reason: The run leaves the question unresolved because the contrast is insufficiently precise, which identifies a concrete problem to address before drawing a substantive conclusion.
next_step.what: Address insufficient precision by increasing held-out evaluation coverage and repeating the comparison over independent training allocations while preserving each arm's acquisition budget.

registration.title: Operational routing loss from benign request serialization
registration.seed_connection: The seed deploys routers across command-line, server and multi-agent interfaces, while its embedding pipeline operates on serialized query text. Those interfaces can change the router-visible envelope without changing the request executed by the selected model.
registration.hypothesis: Routine, unoptimized serialization wrappers cause more than 1.5 percentage points of avoidable routing-quality loss even when candidate inputs remain unchanged and encoder truncation is excluded.
registration.contribution: Measures task-quality consequences of benign interface changes, not merely route flips or adversarial steering. Holding the execution input fixed isolates the routing component from changes in candidate-model behavior.

closest_work.difference: Establishes adversarial rerouting with optimized confounder gadgets, primarily targeting expensive-model use. This experiment uses five fixed non-adversarial serialization forms and measures realized task-quality loss.
Studies adversarial and backdoor routing vulnerabilities. This experiment neither optimizes a trigger nor poisons training data, and explicitly removes truncation as an explanation.
Studies uncertainty from rewritten queries and decoding. Here candidate responses are frozen and only the router's representation of an otherwise identical execution request changes.

inputs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates.
https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
Reference code at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, especially benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py and llmrouter/models/knnrouter/router.py.
registration.method: Use MBPP, MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge and MMLU from the published generic matrix. Build complete candidate-quality vectors, reject conflicting duplicates, and remove normalized-text train/test duplicates from training. For an original query q define exactly five router views: prefix 'User request:' followed by a newline and q; q enclosed in user_request XML tags with newlines; JSON serialization of the object with role='user' and content=q using ensure_ascii=False; prefix '### Message' and suffix '### End message', separated from q by blank lines; and q enclosed by [USER] and [/USER] on separate lines. Candidate-model execution always remains the original q and uses its published recorded outcome. Before looking at outcomes, retain only questions for which the original and all five views tokenize to at most 512 tokens; never truncate an eligible view. Retain up to 800 training questions per source by seed-1729 hash order, reserve 20% for validation and use all eligible published test questions. Encode canonical training queries on the GPU with frozen Qwen embeddings, last-nonpadding-token pooling and L2 normalization. Fit a cosine-neighbor quality-vector router, selecting k from {8,32,128} solely on canonical validation macro-quality, then refit on all selected canonical training questions. Route each test question using its canonical view and all five wrapped views. Do not tune wrappers, select a worst wrapper, add wrapper training examples, or call answer models. The primary contrast averages uniformly over all five wrappers. Implement and test an inverse for each wrapper that recovers the original string exactly; routing the recovered string is a software sanity control, not a proposed novel defense.

event.description: Benign serialization alone causes a material loss in the quality of the model selected by the router.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 2,000 paired, source-stratified bootstrap estimates of canonical macro-quality minus the uniformly averaged macro-quality of the five wrapped views.

evaluation.procedure: Use the same recorded candidate-quality matrix for canonical and wrapped routes. Average equally over the seven sources and uniformly over wrappers. Bootstrap base questions within source, retaining all six views together rather than treating wrappers as independent observations. outputs/manifest.json records revisions, splits, eligibility exclusions and exact wrapper definitions. outputs/outcomes.parquet stores retained candidate outcomes. outputs/views.jsonl stores router inputs, token lengths, predicted quality vectors and selections. outputs/summary.json stores the registered statistic, paired interval, per-wrapper diagnostics, flip rates, beneficial versus harmful flips and recorded cost changes. Verify that inverse-wrapped queries reproduce canonical selections and that a fixed-model policy is unchanged. Report an inconclusive result as such; small average loss would not establish robustness to other wrappers or adversarial inputs.
evaluation.controls: Frozen execution requests and outcomes; no encoder truncation; fixed unoptimized wrapper set; canonical-only validation; fixed-model invariance and exact inverse-wrapper checks. This isolates a router-interface effect and does not claim to measure end-to-end response robustness when wrappers are also sent to answer models.

registration.full_scale_study: Study interface-invariant routing across real chat serializers and agent-role envelopes, then cross router-side and backend-side transformations factorially and evaluate structured-input encoders or augmentation against held-out interface families.

agent.reason: Benign wrappers may change routing decisions without producing substantial net quality loss, particularly when competing models perform similarly. Excluding truncation and averaging across five unoptimized wrappers makes the registered lower-bound loss threshold relatively demanding.

judge_astra.reason: These wrappers could change nearest neighbors and model selections without causing systematic quality loss. Excluding truncation, preserving execution inputs, and averaging all five unoptimized wrappers make a lower confidence bound above 1.5 percentage points relatively unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: Qwen3-Embedding representations are dominated by question content, and k-averaged quality vectors smooth residual neighbor changes; flips should be infrequent and roughly symmetric in benefit, so a systematic loss exceeding ~2.3pp (needed to clear 1.5pp at the 5th percentile) is improbable.

judge_opus.reason: Wrappers mostly reshuffle neighbors within the same source, especially if k=32 or 128 is selected. Flips among near-equivalent top models largely cancel, so an average loss over five wrappers of more than about 2 points needs drift across sources toward clearly worse models.

judge_sol.reason: Benign envelopes can shift last-token embeddings, but short unoptimized wrappers, no truncation, and uniform averaging should limit systematic damage. Route flips seem more likely than a net quality loss large enough to clear the 1.5-point lower-bound threshold.

judge_luna.reason: The wrappers preserve query meaning, and a modern embedding model may represent them similarly; moreover, route changes need not reduce quality. Still, wrappers could shift nearest-neighbor matches, so a systematic loss is plausible, though a greater-than-1.5-point average loss seems a high bar.

closest_work.difference: This paper optimizes adversarial confounder gadgets that push queries toward the expensive model, and it measures reroute rates. The experiment instead uses five fixed, benign serialization wrappers and measures the realized loss in task quality on a frozen outcome matrix.

This paper studies adversarial and backdoor vulnerabilities across the router life cycle. It does not test benign interface envelopes or quantify their quality loss while the execution input is held fixed.
R2A optimizes adversarial suffixes against black-box routers to force expensive-model selection. Its perturbations are adversarial, not benign serialization.

This is the closest in spirit: meaning-equivalent query variants (non-standard English registers) shift routing decisions, and the paper measures the quality cost of the routing decision itself. But the perturbation is linguistic register, the router is a length/complexity-based tier router, and the answer models see the variant too. The experiment uses structural wrappers, a kNN embedding router, and frozen execution inputs.
DARS uses semantics-preserving rewrites to build more robust supervision labels. It does not measure how router-only serialization changes affect test-time selection quality.
The DSC benchmark examines category-driven routing fragility, privacy and safety. It does not apply content-invariant wrappers or use paired bootstrap estimates of quality loss.
This paper applies the same content-invariant wrapper idea to LLM safety judges, not to model routers.

Content-invariant wrappers have been studied for safety judges and for answer-model benchmarking, but not for routing, so the question looks open as of 2026-10-07, though my searches cannot rule out unindexed work.

registration.title: Copy or regenerate after the same coordinator selects a specialist answer?
registration.seed_connection: LLMRouter's multi-turn pipelines terminate by generating an aggregated answer with a relatively small coordinator. Its poor multi-turn results motivate isolating whether a final generation call destroys useful specialist output after selection has already succeeded.
registration.hypothesis: In a weak-coordinator pipeline, copying the coordinator-selected specialist response yields more than two percentage points higher net answer accuracy than allowing that same coordinator to regenerate the final answer from the selected response.
registration.contribution: Holds the actual selection decision fixed before branching into terminal actions. This separates the consequences of final regeneration from differences in candidate generation or selector quality, with objective grading rather than an LLM preference judge.

closest_work.difference: Generative Self-Aggregation compares synthesis and selection over self-generated candidates. This experiment uses heterogeneous specialist outputs and branches only after an identical, weaker coordinator has selected one.

Compares judge-panel selection against synthesis using largely open-ended preference evaluation. This experiment fixes the selection result, uses one small coordinator and evaluates against public answer keys.
Studies intrinsic correction of a model's own reasoning. This experiment tests regeneration of an already selected external specialist answer within a routing pipeline.

inputs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc, ARC-Challenge test split.
https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k, main test split.
Specialists: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct.
Coordinator: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

PyTorch, Transformers and a compatible prebuilt vLLM installation. The seed's aggregation implementation is in https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/blob/main/llmrouter/models/knnmultiroundrouter/router.py.
registration.method: Select 256 ARC-Challenge and 256 GSM8K questions by seed-17 hash ordering, before any model execution. Canonicalize ARC options and retain full question content; admit questions only if their initial chat prompts fit within 768 tokens for all three models. Generate one greedy specialist response per question from each specialist with a 256-token cap, asking for concise reasoning followed by FINAL: <option letter or number>. Freeze these responses. For each question show both anonymized proposals to the coordinator in both possible orders. Ask it to choose the proposal most likely to be correct; constrain its one-token greedy output to the tokenizer's tokens for 1 and 2, verifying those tokens in advance. For each resulting selection create two branches. COPY returns the selected specialist response unchanged. REGENERATE gives the coordinator the original question and that same selected response, with the instruction 'Use the selected proposal as a starting point. Check it, correct any errors you find, and produce your final answer ending with FINAL: <answer>.' It receives no gold answer, correctness flag, model name or unselected proposal. Generate greedily with a 256-token cap. Cache regeneration by question and selected-specialist identity when the two presentation orders produce the same selection. Also obtain one direct greedy coordinator answer per question as a descriptive baseline. Use the same answer parser for specialist, regenerated and direct responses: prefer the last FINAL marker; allow only explicit Answer markers or an otherwise answer-only response as fallbacks. For GSM8K compare normalized decimal numbers to the value after the dataset's #### delimiter; do not execute model-produced expressions. Invalid answers score zero and are retained. Run models sequentially in batched bfloat16 processes with max_model_len 2048; do not fine-tune or use external judges.

event.description: Lossless termination after selection is both cheaper by construction and materially more accurate than the extra final-generation call.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of 2,000 paired, task-stratified bootstrap estimates of COPY accuracy minus REGENERATE accuracy, averaging the two presentation orders within each question and giving the two tasks equal weight.

evaluation.procedure: Score all branches using public answer keys only after inference. Bootstrap original questions while retaining both orders and their shared specialist outputs together. outputs/manifest.json records revisions, sampled IDs, exact prompts and parser rules. outputs/specialists.jsonl holds specialist and direct-coordinator responses, parsed answers, correctness, token counts and timings. outputs/terminal_branches.jsonl holds candidate order, selector result, selected response ID, regenerated text and paired scores. outputs/summary.json contains the registered statistic, interval, individual-model accuracies and the decomposition into correct-to-wrong destruction, wrong-to-correct rescue and unchanged outcomes. Report parse failures and cap hits separately, including a descriptive both-parseable analysis; do not automatically interpret formatting loss as a reasoning failure. Charge both specialist calls and selection to both deployment branches and additionally charge regeneration to REGENERATE; presentation-order replication is experimental overhead, not a deployed two-order policy.
evaluation.controls: Exactly shared candidate outputs and selector decisions; anonymized sources; both candidate orders; objective answer keys; common parsing; direct coordinator and individual specialists as descriptive baselines. COPY and REGENERATE intentionally differ in one extra call, so the experiment does not claim equal inference cost.

registration.full_scale_study: Vary coordinator-to-specialist capability ratios and task types, and learn a terminal policy choosing between copying and regeneration using only observable confidence or disagreement signals. Test whether this explains part of multi-turn routing degradation without assuming that all aggregation is harmful.

agent.reason: The specialist-to-coordinator capability gap makes destructive rewriting plausible. However, preserving one selected solution is easier than synthesizing conflicting proposals, and repairs or faithful copying could keep the net loss below the required two-point lower-bound margin.

judge_astra.reason: The smaller coordinator plausibly destroys some correct specialist answers during regeneration, giving copying a credible advantage. However, an explicit selected answer encourages preservation, while regeneration can rescue incorrect or truncated proposals; the net advantage may therefore fall short of the two-percentage-point lower-bound threshold.

judge_fable.reason: A 1.5B coordinator rewriting a stronger specialist's GSM8K solution plausibly loses answers through arithmetic drift, format slips and 256-token cap hits, favoring COPY, but it can also rescue truncated or wrong proposals and will mostly copy ARC letters; with ~512 questions the point gap needs to be roughly 4-5pp, making the registered threshold a near coin flip.

judge_opus.reason: A weaker 1.5B coordinator regenerating from a mostly correct proposal plausibly loses accuracy through over-correction, arithmetic slips and truncation at 256 tokens without the FINAL marker. Rescue of truncated specialist outputs and strong anchoring may keep the net loss near 2–4 points, short of the roughly 4.5 points needed.

judge_sol.reason: The smaller coordinator may corrupt already correct specialist outputs, making COPY a plausible winner. However, the selected response supplies useful reasoning and opportunities for rescue, so an advantage whose lower confidence bound exceeds two points is not assured.

judge_luna.reason: A weaker coordinator may damage a selected specialist answer, but it also sees the question and answer and could preserve or correct it. The net difference may be small, and the fifth-percentile threshold is demanding for 512 questions.

judge_muse.reason: The 1.5B coordinator is weaker than the 3B-class specialists, so regenerating likely corrupts more correct selections than it rescues, and formatting failures scored as zero count against regeneration, making a >2pp COPY advantage plausible.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This paper finds that judge-based selection beats MoA-style synthesis, but the two pipelines differ in more than the final step, and the comparison relies mostly on open-ended preference judging. It does not hold one selection decision fixed and then branch into copying the selected answer versus having a weak coordinator regenerate it, scored against objective answer keys.

Generative Self-Aggregation synthesizes an answer from many samples of the same model and contrasts this with selection and self-correction. It does not use heterogeneous specialists, does not fix the selection result, and does not isolate the effect of regenerating an answer that was already selected.

Self-MoA compares aggregating outputs from one model against mixing different models, and studies the trade-off between quality and diversity. Copying a selected answer versus regenerating it after the same selection is not one of its conditions.

This work shows that intrinsic self-correction often hurts reasoning, which is a related phenomenon. However, a model there revises its own answer, not an external specialist's answer selected inside a routing pipeline by a weaker coordinator.
Router-R1 trains multi-round routing plus aggregation with RL. It reports end-to-end results and has no controlled comparison between copying and regenerating at the terminal step.

opus.reason: Prior work compares selection with synthesis or aggregation, and separately documents that unaided self-correction tends to hurt. None of the papers I found keeps the candidate outputs and the selector's decision identical and then varies only the final action (copy the selected answer verbatim, or let the same weak coordinator regenerate it), with answer-key grading on ARC and GSM8K. The literature suggests which way the result might go, but it does not settle this specific question. One caveat: arXiv search returned many irrelevant hits, so I may have missed a closely matching paper.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Revision or Re-Solving? compares cached stronger-model answers against weaker-model revisions of those identical answers, using objective grading and direct-answer controls. The proposed experiment adds coordinator selection between two specialists before this paired comparison, rather than taking drafts from one fixed generator.

Studies cross-model revision with matched first-pass responses and measures beneficial versus harmful changes, including capability-asymmetric cases. It does not first have the reviser select among specialist proposals.
Compares judge-panel selection with synthesis over multiple heterogeneous candidates, rather than regeneration from only the already-selected response; evaluation primarily uses model preferences.

sol.reason: The role-reversed experiments in Revision or Re-Solving? already isolate the central contrast: retaining a fixed stronger-model answer versus allowing a weaker model to regenerate from that same answer, with objective evaluation. Coordinator-conditioned selection is an additional restriction on the incoming drafts, but the underlying paired test of whether the extra generation call preserves or destroys useful external output is closely established prior work.

opus.reason: No list entry branches after a fixed coordinator selection into copying versus regenerating the selected specialist answer; the multi-round entries instead vary decomposer or aggregator size or answer format.

sol.reason: The registration fixes a coordinator's specialist-selection decision before comparing copying with regeneration, whereas the listed aggregation experiments vary decomposition, controller capacity or output format without this matched terminal-action comparison.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the full registered 256 ARC + 256 GSM8K experiment with frozen heterogeneous proposals, verified masked one-token selector in both orders, identical selections before COPY/REGENERATE, regeneration caching, direct baseline, common fixed parser, objective grading, paired task-stratified bootstrap, and all required artifacts. Tested the complete installation/evaluation command and verified prompt/output alignment and branch invariants. No method or event changes; the supplied runtime reported H200 rather than advertised A100, recorded in manifest. Latest test statistic: 0.4892578125. Important caveat: all correct-to-wrong losses in that test involved regeneration parse failures; the descriptive both-parseable gap was zero, not evidence of equivalence or a comparably large reasoning loss.

departures: Hardware: the evaluation ran on an NVIDIA H200, not the advertised A100 (outputs/manifest.json; disclosed in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md). Greedy bf16 batching gives slight run-to-run variation: fifth percentile 0.493 and 0.489 in the engineer's runs versus 0.496 in the protected run. This cannot plausibly change the conclusion.

registration.title: Do policy-specific reward scales reverse meaningful quality-cost comparisons?
registration.seed_connection: The inspected benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py evaluate function min-max normalizes performance and monetary cost separately within each policy's selected evaluation rows. The seed interprets cost-weighted rankings as comparisons between routers. The mathematical possibility of incomparable scales is clear, but the frequency of materially misleading comparisons on its recorded workloads has not been measured here.
registration.hypothesis: More than ten percent of materially Pareto-dominated policy comparisons in the registered replay panel are reversed by policy-specific reward normalization.
registration.contribution: Quantifies the empirical consequence of an evaluation implementation choice using policies fixed from training data and real recorded costs. It is a finite-benchmark metric audit, not a new routing algorithm or a claim that the paper's published figures have already been shown incorrect.

closest_work.difference: Defines routing evaluation in a shared cost-quality plane and compares convex frontiers. This experiment measures how often policy-specific normalization contradicts materially separated comparisons in that physical plane.
Uses raw accuracy/cost Pareto analysis and common comparison metrics. This experiment isolates normalization scope while holding policies and outcome records fixed.

inputs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic, memory_locomo, memory_longmemeval, timeseries, multimodal_geometry3k, multimodal_mathvista, video and llm_candidates.
Reference implementation: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/blob/main/benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py, functions row_costs, preprocess_training_data and evaluate.
CPU packages datasets, pandas, NumPy and pyarrow. No model weights, GPU inference or hosted API calls are required.
registration.method: Load the seven non-personalized train/test outcome matrices and candidate prices. Pin and record dataset and repository revisions. Work on complete query-model vectors with finite performance and token counts; exclude an incomplete question for every policy rather than silently evaluating different denominators. Require quality values on the documented 0-to-1 scale and complete pricing coverage. Compute recorded dollar cost as (input_tokens*input_price_per_1m + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m)/1e6. Remove normalized-text train/test duplicates from training. For each configuration and beta in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}, set alpha=1-beta. Construct a fixed policy panel containing every single-model policy, one source-task profile policy and one source-task-by-length-quartile profile policy. Fit the profile policies using training data only: normalize quality and cost with min/max over all training query-model rows, and choose the model with highest mean alpha*normalized_quality-beta*normalized_cost in each group. Define word-count quartiles from training queries; use the task profile, then the global profile, for empty groups. If source metadata is absent use the dataset configuration as the task. Break ties lexicographically. Freeze policies before reading test outcomes and collapse policies with identical test selection vectors. Evaluate the exact registered local-normalization formula: for each policy separately, subtract the minimum and divide by range+1e-12 across that policy's selected test rows, then average alpha*normalized_quality-beta*normalized_cost. Also evaluate a shared-scale control using the fixed all-training-row extrema without clipping. Within each configuration and beta, call policy P materially dominant over Q when its raw mean quality is at least 0.01 higher and its mean cost is at most 0.90 times Q's positive mean cost. Count a reversal when the locally normalized reward of P is smaller than Q's by more than 1e-12. The primary statistic pools these directed, materially dominant comparisons across all configurations and weights. Reimplement the formula explicitly; do not silently substitute a changed upstream function or claim exact reproduction of unpublished routing traces.

event.description: Policy-specific normalization reverses a substantial fraction of comparisons that favor one policy in both raw quality and recorded dollar cost.
event.statistic: Number of reversed materially dominant comparisons divided by the total number of materially dominant comparisons across the registered panel. If the denominator is zero, report 0 with an explicit no-comparable-pairs status, not evidence of consistency.

evaluation.procedure: Use micro-average quality and dollar cost within each dataset configuration, matching the inspected evaluator's averaging unit. Freeze policy definitions from training data; no policy is selected using test quality. outputs/manifest.json records revisions, fields, prices, exclusions and policy definitions. outputs/replay_rows.parquet contains the retained quality/token/cost records. outputs/policies.jsonl contains test selections and raw and normalized policy metrics for each weight. outputs/dominance_pairs.jsonl records every eligible directed pair, its raw margins and reversal indicator. outputs/summary.json contains the registered fraction and its numerator/denominator, with per-configuration diagnostics. As secondary uncertainty analysis, bootstrap questions within configuration 1,000 times, keeping all policy outcomes paired and recomputing dominance and normalization. Interpret the primary event as an audit of this frozen matrix; sampled mean dominance alone is not proof of population-level dominance.
evaluation.controls: The shared-scale linear reward must never reverse a materially dominant comparison, providing an implementation check. Verify hand-constructed unit tests, retain identical question denominators, deduplicate identical policies and require nontrivial quality/cost margins. Only metric normalization changes during scoring; prices and outcomes remain fixed.

registration.full_scale_study: Audit trained-router selection and reported cost-sensitive conclusions under shared monetary units, calibration-fixed scales and matched-budget frontiers across multiple routing benchmarks, including whether evaluation-scale changes alter deployment choices on independently collected outcomes.

agent.reason: Policy-specific normalization removes absolute cost scale and introduces dependence on each policy's cost distribution, making economically inconsistent comparisons plausible across this heterogeneous panel. The uncertainty is whether reversals exceed ten percent after the material-dominance filters, rather than whether the normalization can produce reversals.

judge_astra.reason: Policy-specific normalization removes common monetary units and makes rewards sensitive to each policy's cost distribution and extrema. The heterogeneous policy panel and cost-heavy weights make a reversal rate above 10% likely, although mathematical possibility alone does not establish its empirical frequency.

judge_fable.reason: Per-policy min-max normalization leaves binary quality unchanged but replaces absolute dollar cost with each model's within-distribution relative position, so cheaper-and-better policies lose their cost advantage and small accuracy margins are routinely overturned at beta>=0.4; the main residual risks are input-dominated memory configs with similar cost shapes and dataset/field availability during implementation.

judge_opus.reason: Per-policy min-max normalization makes the cost term a scale-free shape statistic, so reversals are likely at beta=0.6–0.8 when quality gaps are small. However, cheap dominant models often have output-heavy, heavy-tailed costs (lower normalized cost), which offsets this and leaves the pooled fraction near 10%.

judge_sol.reason: Under the registered formula, per-policy scaling removes absolute cost levels and allows cost-distribution shape to drive rankings, especially at large cost weights. I expect the heterogeneous panel to produce enough reversals to exceed ten percent, but this would not by itself reproduce or invalidate the paper’s published rankings.

judge_luna.reason: Policy-specific min-max scaling discards cross-policy differences in quality and cost levels, so it can reverse comparisons that favor one policy on both raw measures. Whether reversals exceed ten percent depends on the number of materially dominant pairs and how much the policies’ score ranges differ.

judge_muse.reason: Per-policy min-max erases absolute dollar differences that define material dominance given the ~25x pricing range, leaving small quality margins versus normalized-cost shape noise, so >10% reversals across betas is likely if materially dominant pairs exist.

registration.title: Equal-budget routing supervision: broader queries versus repeated responses
registration.seed_connection: LLMRouter constructs routing supervision by collecting candidate responses for each query. This makes supervision collection itself a resource-allocation problem: repeated responses may improve label reliability, but displace observations on new questions.
registration.hypothesis: At a fixed supervision budget and deployment model-call quota, breadth and four-repeat supervision differ in held-out routing accuracy by more than one percentage point.
registration.contribution: The experiment charges repetition for its opportunity cost in query coverage. It uses one common experimental setup rather than comparing opposing allocation hypotheses under different models, routers, or quotas. Regularization is defined relative to mean loss, avoiding a sample-size-dependent change in penalty strength.

closest_work.difference: DARS studies repeated observations and adaptive replication. This experiment compares repetition against additional distinct questions under an exactly matched candidate-response budget.
Expected Reward Prediction uses repeated samples to estimate rewards. Here the research question is which observations to purchase, not whether an expected-reward predictor can be constructed.

inputs: Hugging Face openai/gsm8k, configuration main, official train and test splits.
Hugging Face allenai/ai2_arc, configuration ARC-Challenge, official train and test splits.
Hugging Face Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
Hugging Face sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
Python, PyTorch, prebuilt vLLM wheels, transformers, datasets, sentence-transformers, NumPy, and scikit-learn. Do not install the full seed repository.
registration.method: Remove exact question duplicates, normalizing line endings and outer whitespace, and remove training questions appearing in test. Retain four-option ARC questions and map their choices and gold answers consistently to A-D. Before sampling, require the rendered prompt plus its generation allowance to fit a 2,048-token context for both candidates. Select 192 training and 256 test questions per task by seeded hash order with seed 1729: 384 training and 512 test questions total. Generate four independent completions for every training query-model pair and two independent completions for every test pair, totaling 5,120 completions. Use native chat templates, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, no additional top-k restriction, and per-request seeds derived by a stable hash of query ID, model, split, and replicate. Request concise reasoning followed by a final 'Answer: LETTER' line for ARC or 'Answer: NUMBER' for GSM8K. Cap ARC at 96 output tokens and GSM8K at 256. Run candidates sequentially with batched GPU inference and release each model before loading another. Parse the last explicit Answer line. For GSM8K, compare unambiguous numeric values exactly using decimal or rational arithmetic after removing thousands separators; extract the reference after the gold #### delimiter. Missing or ambiguous answers score zero. A cap-hit response remains eligible and is scored normally if its final answer is present. Save test responses without using their correctness during fitting. Encode questions, including ARC choices, once using normalized MiniLM embeddings with a 256-token limit; append a two-dimensional task indicator and record embedding truncation. For allocation seeds 1001 through 1020, breadth receives one randomly chosen training completion per candidate on all 384 questions. Repetition receives all four completions per candidate on a stratified subset of 96 questions, 48 per task. Each learner therefore sees exactly 768 response samples. Predict the 3B-minus-1.5B correctness difference using ridge regression with an unpenalized intercept and objective mean squared error plus lambda times squared coefficient norm, with primary lambda=0.01. In scikit-learn this means alpha=n_training_queries*lambda. Use the same fixed feature transformation in both arms. For each fitted router and test task, send exactly the 128 highest predicted-gain questions to 3B and the remaining 128 to 1.5B, breaking ties by query hash. Freeze these assignments before scoring test responses. Repeat the analysis at lambda=0.001 and 0.1 only as registered sensitivity diagnostics; they cannot replace the primary result.

event.description: One supervision allocation has an accuracy advantage exceeding one percentage point, with a two-sided confidence interval establishing both its direction and practical magnitude.
event.statistic: Let [L,U] be the 95% paired-bootstrap interval for breadth-minus-repetition macro-accuracy. Report S=max(L,-U), a conservative lower bound on the magnitude of the allocation effect.

evaluation.procedure: For each test question, average the selected model's correctness over its two independent test responses, then average paired breadth-minus-repetition differences over the 20 allocation seeds. Weight ARC and GSM8K equally. Bootstrap question IDs within task 2,000 times with seed 2027, retaining all allocation conditions and response repeats together, and use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for [L,U]. The interval is conditional on the collected training bank and frozen routing assignments; allocation replays are not independent training-bank replications. Report the point estimate, interval, S, and which allocation is favored. Also report training-label variability, test-repeat disagreement, parsing and cap-hit rates, allocation variability, and sensitivity to regularization. Include a clearly labeled hindsight quota-constrained test oracle as an optimistic headroom diagnostic, not as a deployable baseline. manifest.json records revisions, IDs, prompts, software, seeds, exclusions, and cold-start timing. generations.jsonl records raw responses, parsed answers, correctness, token counts, and finish reasons. allocations.jsonl records the exact observations exposed to each learner. routes.jsonl records predictions and assignments. scores.json contains the primary statistic and diagnostics. Report actual collection tokens separately: 768 exposed samples per arm does not mean equal token cost, and collecting the reusable experimental bank costs more than either arm's budget. Mark an unfinished run incomplete rather than reducing the cohort after observing results.
evaluation.controls: Identical candidates, prompts, encoder, normalized regression objective, and deployment quotas. Include always-1.5B, always-3B, and hash-random half-escalation policies. Independent test responses prevent training-label reuse. Cap-hit and parsing diagnostics distinguish reasoning variability from the chosen output-budget interface. No test-label hyperparameter selection is allowed.

registration.full_scale_study: If a practically meaningful allocation effect is established, map its direction across supervision budgets, candidate families, deployment quotas, and output limits. Compare adaptive replication with acquisition of new questions using measured token and wall-clock budgets, and repeat with independently collected training banks.

agent.reason: At equal response-sample budgets, broader coverage and reduced label noise may yield similar estimation accuracy for this lightweight router. Either allocation could win, but establishing an advantage beyond one percentage point with the entire confidence interval is demanding.

judge_astra.reason: Breadth plausibly helps, but equal response budgets and the common estimator could leave only a small allocation effect. Establishing an advantage exceeding one percentage point, while completing the generation bank within the cold-start limit, is a substantial hurdle.

judge_fable.reason: Both arms train weak ridge routers on 384-dim MiniLM embeddings for a half-escalation quota, so routing accuracy differences between breadth and four-repeat supervision are likely under 1-2 pp, while the 95% question-bootstrap interval (512 questions) will be roughly ±2 pp wide; the event needs a point estimate of ~3+ pp with the interval clear of the ±1 pp band, which is improbable.

judge_opus.reason: Ridge regression on MiniLM embeddings, trained on 96–384 noisy queries, will barely predict the per-question 3B-minus-1.5B gain, so both arms should land near random half-escalation. With a test-question bootstrap 95% half-width of roughly 1.3 pp, the point difference would need to exceed about 2.3 pp, which a weak router is unlikely to produce.

judge_sol.reason: Repetition's reduction in label noise is partly offset by lost query coverage under the matched response budget. I expect the resulting ridge-router contrast often to be too small to place a two-sided interval wholly beyond the one-percentage-point margin.

judge_luna.reason: Breadth plausibly helps a query-specific router more than repeated labels do, but the difference may be modest and the confidence interval must clear a one-percentage-point magnitude threshold. The 5,120-completion cold-start run also leaves limited slack under the final runtime cap.

judge_muse.reason: Breadth likely helps a 386-feature linear router more than denoising 4x fewer queries, but S>0.01 needs a 2-3pp paired mean to clear sampling noise on 512 test questions; inference is uncertain because overall 1.5B vs 3B routing headroom may be small.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DARS shows that single-shot routing labels are unstable. It compares repeated-observation supervision (5×5 rewrites × decodes, plus 3×3 and adaptive 2×2/3×3 grids) against single-shot supervision on the same 200 training queries. It also measures the router variance that comes from single-shot resampling. The number of training queries is never traded against repeats under a matched candidate-response budget, so DARS shows that repetition helps, not whether it beats spending the same budget on new questions.

ERP predicts a model's expected reward under repeated sampling and uses those predictions to route. It does not study how a fixed supervision-collection budget should be split between more queries and more responses per query.

This paper finds that scaling breadth (batch size / number of instances) helps more than scaling rollout count, but in RLVR policy training rather than router supervision. Its comparison is also not an equal-budget repeats-versus-queries test for a learned routing predictor.

Pilot-Commit spends a fixed rollout budget across prompts in online GRPO training. The question is related (where to spend samples), but the setting is RL post-training, not supervised data collection for LLM routers or held-out routing accuracy under a call quota.

opus.reason: The closest work, DARS (2606.06924), shows that repeated observations improve routing supervision compared with single-shot labels on the same queries. It does not charge repetition for the questions it displaces, so it never runs an equal-budget breadth-versus-repetition comparison. In my searches I found no paper that runs this matched-budget comparison for router training. The nearest breadth-versus-depth results come from RL rollout allocation, which is a different learning problem.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DARS compares single-shot and repeated-observation routing supervision and studies adaptive replication, but retains the same training-query coverage. It does not compare repetition against additional distinct questions under an equal candidate-response budget.

ERP trains ridge predictors on prompt embeddings using rewards averaged over repeated responses. It establishes expected-reward prediction for routing, but does not compare alternative allocations between query coverage and response repetition.

This paper directly compares more distinct seed questions against more responses per question at matched sample counts. However, it fine-tunes answer-generating models on rejection-sampled reasoning traces, rather than estimating stochastic candidate-model rewards to train a quota-constrained router.

Clean or Annotate compares broad single annotation with redundant annotation under a fixed budget. Its repetitions recover categorical ground-truth labels from noisy annotators, rather than estimate candidate models' expected correctness for routing decisions.

sol.reason: The general breadth-versus-repetition allocation idea is established in annotation and synthetic-data training. The closest routing work studies repeated supervision without charging its opportunity cost in distinct-query coverage, while the matched-budget studies use materially different learning targets and downstream decisions. I found no prior paper answering the registered routing-supervision question under equal candidate-response counts and a fixed deployment quota.

opus.reason: No list entry compares supervision spent on many distinct questions with supervision spent on repeated responses at a matched sample budget; #50 only measures how stable labels are under sampling.

sol.reason: Entry 50 studies repeated-completion label stability, but does not compare repetition against broader query coverage under an equal supervision budget and deployment quota.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered experiment end to end using the specified datasets, Qwen candidates, MiniLM features, 5,120 independently seeded completions, 20 allocation seeds, exactly 768 exposed samples per arm, mean-loss ridge penalty (alpha=n_queries*lambda), task-specific half-escalation quotas, frozen routes before test scoring, controls, sensitivity diagnostics, paired bootstrap, and hindsight quota oracle. All five required raw outputs and result.json are generated from scratch. Tested the evaluation command successfully in 281.3 seconds including installation/downloads; independent artifact, quota, ridge-objective, and bootstrap audits passed. No registered design changes or cohort reductions. Fixed launch-time syntax and answer-line whitespace issues before collection. In the engineering test, S=-0.002392578125 and the registered event was not established. Parsing success was very low and ARC cap-hit rates high; these limitations are explicitly reported, without tuning prompts, budgets, or scoring after observing results. The conditional interval is not treated as evidence of general equivalence.

departures: experiment.py parse_answer counts a line as an answer only if it begins with 'Answer:' (regex ^[ \t]*Answer[ \t]*:). Lines such as 'Final Answer: 360' (seen in bank_1.jsonl) and 'the final Answer is 5.' score zero. The registration says only 'parse the last explicit Answer line', so this is a defensible but strict reading. It strongly shapes the near-zero labels and could change the value.

experiment.py numeric_value rejects GSM8K answer fields that contain units or explanatory text, and ARC answers must be a bare letter. The registration scores zero only for missing or ambiguous answers, so a unit-bearing single number such as '360 hours' is arguably unambiguous. This is an unregistered tightening. Its effect is unquantified but could change labels and the value.
experiment.py breaks routing ties by the normalized question-text hash rather than the query-ID hash. This is minor and very unlikely to change the result.

Duplicate handling in experiment.py keeps the first occurrence within each split and checks overlap against all official test questions before eligibility filtering. These are open choices and unlikely to matter.

No changes were found to datasets, models, prompts as specified, decoding settings (temp 0.7, top_p 0.95, top_k -1, caps 96/256, 2048 context), cohort sizes (192/256 per task), repeat counts (4 train, 2 test), the 768-sample budget, ridge alpha=n*lambda, the 128/128 quotas, the bootstrap (2000 draws, seed 2027, within task), the statistic S=max(L,-U), or the controls.
