registration.title: A usage-preserving test of a router's within-task matching value
registration.seed_connection: The seed attributes routing gains partly to matching individual questions with complementary models, while its generic track mixes distinct source benchmarks. Conditional reassignment can separate this fitted instance matching from task-level preferences without changing model usage.
registration.hypothesis: For a validation-selected lightweight router with nontrivial within-stratum model diversity, its macro-average matching contribution is practically equivalent to zero within a two-percentage-point margin.
registration.contribution: The intervention preserves a fitted router's exact task-by-length model counts and changes only question-to-model assignments. Per-task effects and a count-constrained hindsight oracle distinguish aggregate cancellation, limited available headroom, and failure to exploit available headroom.

closest_work.difference: LLMRouterBench compares routing with dataset-level references. This experiment uses a held-out negative control that preserves the fitted router's own conditional model usage rather than substituting a separately selected dataset oracle.

Expected Reward Prediction reports benefits beyond category-level baselines on reward-scored prompts. This experiment tests instance matching on automatically scored benchmark mixtures using conditional assignment permutation.

inputs: Hugging Face ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates, using released train and test records.
Hugging Face Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
Seed repository https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py and benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py, as schema references only.
Python, PyTorch, transformers, datasets, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and scikit-learn. No candidate LLM is executed.
registration.method: Use MBPP, MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU. Define task-name aliases explicitly without merging MMLU with MMLU-Pro. Establish the candidate pool from released metadata and model IDs present in both official splits before examining performance values; log any wholly absent candidates. Pivot records into query-by-model quality vectors. Deduplicate identical records, reject query blocks with conflicting duplicate scores, remove exact train-test question overlap, and retain complete finite vectors with documented scores in [0,1]. Normalize only line endings and outer whitespace for duplicate detection, preserving code indentation. Do not impute missing outcomes. Require at least 200 eligible training and 100 eligible test questions for every listed task, otherwise report an incomplete data-feasibility result. Within each task, use seed 17 to select up to 512 fitting and 128 validation questions; if fewer than 640 training questions are available, use an 80/20 fitting-validation split. Retain all eligible test questions. Encode unchanged query text using normalized last-nonpadding-token Qwen3 embeddings with a 512-token input limit, logging truncation. Fit pooled cosine kNN outcome regressors with k in {5,15,50,150} and inverse-distance weights, plus one multi-output ridge regressor with alpha=1 and an intercept. For zero-distance neighbors, average those neighbors only. Each model predicts every candidate's quality, avoiding arbitrary winner labels when outcomes tie. Select exactly one router by validation macro-quality, with fixed lexicographic tie-breaking between configurations and candidate IDs. Freeze its test assignments before reading test outcomes. Compute prompt-length quartile cutoffs separately within task from untruncated fitting-set tokenizer lengths. The primary negative control permutes the frozen assignments only within task-by-length strata. For each stratum, compute expected permuted quality exactly as the sum over models of assignment frequency times that model's mean recorded quality. Run 1,000 explicit seeded permutations to verify this expectation empirically and assert exact model-count preservation. Compute the expected fraction of assignments changed by permutation as the task-weighted average of 1-sum_m(p_m^2). A value below 0.10 is a predeclared degeneracy condition: retain all results, but do not count a trivial equivalence finding as the registered event. As a diagnostic only, compute the maximum possible quality under the same within-stratum model counts using a linear assignment solver with one slot for each allocated model call.

event.description: A noncollapsed fitted router's within-stratum matching contribution is contained within the practical-equivalence interval [-0.02,0.02].
event.statistic: S is the larger absolute endpoint of the 90% paired-bootstrap interval for routed minus expected conditionally permuted macro-quality. If the expected assignment-change fraction is below 0.10, set S=1.0 and flag the result as degenerate; retain the ordinary interval separately.

evaluation.procedure: Average quality within each task, weighting its length strata by their test-query counts, then weight the seven tasks equally. Bootstrap test-query IDs within task-by-length strata 2,000 times with seed 2027, recomputing assignment frequencies and the exact permutation expectation in each resample while keeping the fitted router fixed. Use the 5th and 95th percentiles for the equivalence interval. Report per-task contrasts prominently, including their signs and mean absolute magnitude, because macro-equivalence can conceal cancellation. Report routing entropy, expected assignment-change fraction, and the count-constrained oracle gap. Compare the router with validation-selected global-fixed and task-fixed selectors; do not describe absent overall gains as task-level gains. manifest.json records revisions, exclusions, split IDs, cutoffs, selected configuration, and timing. matrix.parquet stores eligible quality vectors. routes.jsonl stores frozen assignments and strata. permutations.jsonl stores seeds, count checks, and permutation scores. scores.json stores S, the ordinary interval, degeneracy status, per-task results, fixed-selector comparisons, and oracle diagnostics. This interval is conditional on the fitted training sample and cached outcomes; it does not establish that better routers lack instance-level opportunity or that one cached generation equals expected model capability.
evaluation.controls: Include global assignment permutation and validation-selected global-fixed and per-task-fixed selectors. The primary control preserves task, length stratum, and model counts exactly, but not realized dollar cost. The hindsight assignment oracle is explicitly nondeployable. All model and hyperparameter selection uses validation data only.

registration.full_scale_study: If nondegenerate practical equivalence holds, repeat the decomposition across stronger router families, independently regenerated candidate outcomes, and shifted workloads. Use the oracle and per-task diagnostics to distinguish unused within-task opportunity from genuinely limited opportunity under the observed model usage.

agent.reason: Task and length associations may explain much of the fitted router's performance, and the relatively large test set could establish practical equivalence. Genuine within-task effects, the noncollapse gate, or insufficient complete outcome blocks could prevent the event.

judge_astra.reason: Task and length preferences could account for much of this lightweight router's performance, and the paired design offers reasonable precision for testing the two-point equivalence margin. Genuine within-task matching or near-collapsed model usage could nevertheless prevent the event.

judge_fable.reason: Validation will likely select a smooth kNN/ridge router that switches among near-tied strong models, giving a small within-stratum matching contribution and a fairly tight 90% interval, so S<0.02 is plausible; but difficulty-matching effects could push the upper bound past 2 pp, routing could partly collapse, and the xRouteBench schema/availability and implementation carry real risk.

judge_opus.reason: Embedding kNN or ridge routers usually gain little within a task beyond their model mix; RouterBench-style evidence puts them near random mixtures. The paired 90% CI over about 3,500 test queries should be tight (about ±0.6 pp), so the event mainly needs a macro matching contribution under about 1.3 pp. Plausible category-level gains on MMLU-Pro and MMLU, plus data-completeness and degeneracy risks, make this close to a coin flip.

judge_sol.reason: A lightweight router may exploit task identity more reliably than within-task model complementarity, making practical equivalence plausible. The complete-vector requirements, noncollapsed-assignment gate, and possibility of genuine instance-matching gains reduce the unconditional probability.

judge_luna.reason: The seed’s aggregate routing gains do not establish instance-level matching after task and length effects are controlled, so practical equivalence is plausible; the test set also appears large enough to make the interval informative. The event still requires a noncollapsed router, and predictable within-stratum complementarity could exceed the two-point margin.

judge_muse.reason: Within-task instance gains beyond task and length usage are likely modest for kNN/ridge on cached 0-1 scores, so a 90% macro interval will plausibly sit inside +/-2pp with non-collapsed assignments, though headroom and diversity remain uncertain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The Routing Plateau paper compares 21 routers on five benchmarks (not xRouteBench). It finds that they cluster far below the oracle and argues that they mainly learn global-average model capability rather than query-specific signals. Its evidence comes from selection frequencies on hard versus easy queries, router-pair error exchange, concordance and within-domain plateaus. It does not use a negative control that shuffles a router's own assignments while keeping model counts fixed within each task and length stratum, it runs no equivalence test, and it has no count-constrained hindsight oracle.

LLMRouterBench re-evaluates routers against simple baselines and the oracle, and attributes the oracle gap to failures to pick a model that would have answered correctly. It does not separate a fitted router's within-task matching from its task-level model usage with a conditional permutation.

Expected Reward Prediction shows that its router beats a baseline that sends each prompt to the best model for its category, using reward-model scores on open-perfectblend. That is a gain over a separately chosen category baseline, not a usage-preserving permutation of the router's own assignments on automatically scored benchmark mixtures.
The seed paper reports that learned routers beat fixed-model baselines on xRouteBench. It does not break the gain into task-level preference and within-task instance matching.

opus.reason: The closest work I found, the Routing Plateau paper, supports the same idea: routers mostly learn coarse, global model-capability patterns. But it reaches that view through descriptive diagnostics, not a test of the fitted router's within-stratum matching value. None of the papers I found uses a negative control that shuffles the router's assignments while keeping model counts fixed within each task and length stratum, tests equivalence within a fixed margin, or adds a count-constrained oracle on xRouteBench. So the specific question is not settled, though the broader hypothesis is already plausible from existing evidence. I ran out of search budget before one final query for this kind of permutation analysis, so a closer paper could exist.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Section 6.6 already tests a nonconstant router against per-benchmark, model-share-preserving assignment permutations, computes the exact content-blind expectation, and uses paired bootstrap intervals and practical-equivalence tests. The proposed experiment changes the router and benchmarks, conditions additionally on prompt-length strata, uses a two-point margin, and adds a count-constrained oracle diagnostic.

Includes a random-permutation baseline preserving the fitted router's model-selection distribution, alongside per-category fixed selectors and verifiable-reward experiments. Its permutation is global rather than task-by-length conditional, and it does not conduct the proposed equivalence test.

Investigates whether routing gains mainly reflect coarse domain structure through dataset-oracle comparisons, but does not preserve each fitted router's conditional model counts when removing instance matching.

sol.reason: The central attribution experiment—separating question-to-model matching from the router's model-usage mixture through count-preserving reassignment and equivalence testing—was already reported in arXiv:2608.14641. Task-by-length conditioning and the constrained oracle refine that design, but the contribution is primarily a variant of an existing experiment rather than a new question or intervention. This prior work does not establish the registered two-percentage-point outcome on xRouteBench.

opus.reason: Entries #12, #42 and #21 compare routers against task-ID or per-task fixed baselines, whereas this experiment tests equivalence by permuting a fitted router's frozen assignments within task-by-length strata while preserving model counts.

sol.reason: Entries 12, 21 and 42 compare task-level and query-level routers, rather than isolating within-task matching through reassignment that preserves the fitted router’s task-by-length model counts.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the registered pipeline in run_experiment.py, which run_eval.sh runs. No candidate LLM is executed, and one full run takes about 1 minute.

**What it does**
- Loads xRouteBench `llmrouter_generic` and `llm_candidates` (dataset revision ea4b6e1b recorded in the manifest). All 18 candidates appear in both splits.
- Keeps the 7 registered tasks, mapped by explicit aliases; MMLU and MMLU-Pro stay separate.
- Normalizes only line endings and outer whitespace to detect duplicates. It deduplicates identical records (18 removed, one ARC block) and rejects query blocks with conflicting duplicate scores (none found). It removes exact train-test overlap (none found) and keeps complete, finite quality vectors in [0,1]. Nothing is imputed.
- Splits fitting and validation sets with seed 17. Every task had fewer than 640 training questions, so all used the 80/20 split.
- Embeds the unchanged query text with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B: last non-padding token, normalized, 512-token limit. Inputs truncated: 86 fitting, 13 validation, 27 test.
- Fits pooled cosine kNN regressors (k = 5, 15, 50, 150; inverse-distance weights; zero-distance neighbours averaged on their own) and one ridge regressor (alpha=1, with intercept). The router is chosen by validation macro-quality, and ties go to the lexicographically first configuration or candidate.
- Freezes the test routes and writes them to routes.jsonl, recording a hash, before any test outcomes are read.
- Length strata use quartile cutoffs computed within each task from untruncated fitting-set token lengths.
- Gives the exact conditional-permutation expectation, plus 1,000 seeded permutations. The empirical mean differs from the exact value by 3e-5, and model counts were asserted preserved in every permutation.
- Also reports: the expected assignment-change fraction, routing entropy, a global-permutation control, the count-constrained linear-assignment oracle, validation-selected global-fixed and task-fixed selectors, and a stratified paired bootstrap (2,000 resamples, seed 2027). The bootstrap recomputes model frequencies and the exact expectation in each resample.

**Outcome: the registered data-feasibility gate fails, so the result is incomplete**
- MMLU-Pro has only 63 eligible training questions; the gate requires at least 200. Every other task passes, and all tasks have 500 test questions.
- The registration says this should be reported as an incomplete data-feasibility result, so the statistic can't be counted. I set S = 1.0, the same convention the registration uses for degenerate cases, and flagged it in scores.json (`data_feasibility_complete` = false). result.json therefore holds value 1.0.
- The analysis still ran on all seven tasks, with MMLU-Pro on a 50-question fitting set and 13-question validation set. Its unflagged results are kept separately.

**Results without the gate flag (not the registered event)**
- Selected router: kNN with k=50. Expected assignment-change fraction is 0.694, so the router is not collapsed.
- Routed macro-quality is 0.7986 against 0.7830 for the expected conditional permutation, a contrast of +0.0156.
- The 90% interval is [0.0095, 0.0216], so S would be 0.0216. That exceeds 0.02, so practical equivalence would not hold even without the gate. The interval also excludes zero, which points to a small positive matching contribution.
- All 7 per-task contrasts are positive; the mean absolute contrast is 0.0156.
- The oracle's headroom over the permutation is 0.1276, but the router captures only about 0.016 of it.
- The router scores about 0.02 below both fixed selectors, which is a deficit, not a gain:
  - routed minus task-fixed: −0.0209, 90% interval [−0.0286, −0.0129];
  - routed minus global-fixed (cogito): −0.0200, 90% interval [−0.0291, −0.0114].

**Supplementary analysis (not registered, for information only)**
On the six tasks that pass the gate, the 90% interval is [0.0078, 0.0197], which does fall inside the ±0.02 margin. This was not the registered criterion, so I did not count it as the event.

**Caveats**
- I interpreted "task-weighted average" in the assignment-change fraction as equal weights across tasks, with strata weighted by their counts within a task.
- A question text appearing under two different tasks would have been dropped as a conflict; none occurred.
- All results are conditional on this one fitted sample and on cached single-generation outcomes.

registration.title: Do biographical personas improve held-out synthetic preference decisions?
registration.seed_connection: The seed conditions a preference judge on biographical personas while keeping candidate responses unpersonalized. Before training a personalized router, this experiment tests whether those profiles support repeatable decision value when the question and answers are held fixed.
registration.hypothesis: Under the registered local judge protocol, persona-specific selection achieves more than three percentage points higher cross-wording held-out preference reward than a pooled persona-agnostic selector.
registration.contribution: The test evaluates transferable decision value across independent judgment blocks, not merely whether personas produce different scores. It balances answer position and explicitly measures the unequal-variance baseline created by comparing a two-verdict personal selector with a twenty-verdict pooled selector.

closest_work.difference: Can LLM be a Personalized Judge? considers personalized judging and agreement with human preferences. This experiment isolates repeatable synthetic decision value on fixed answer pairs without claiming human validity.

APM addresses generic-quality and stereotype shortcuts through controlled preference mappings. This experiment audits seed-style biographical conditioning rather than replacing it with explicit randomized preferences.
This work studies persona-conditioned and averaged targets. Here, persona-specific choices are evaluated on independent, differently worded judgment blocks against a pooled per-question reference.

inputs: Hugging Face lmsys/mt_bench_human_judgments, using public turn-one questions and response texts only; original human preference labels must not be used.
The ten fixed persona descriptions from Figure 10 of the seed, reproduced in the method below.
Hugging Face Qwen/Qwen3-8B, with thinking disabled.
Python, PyTorch, transformers, datasets, huggingface_hub, and NumPy. Batched local next-token scoring is sufficient; no candidate generation or hosted inference is needed.
registration.method: Extract the first user message and first assistant answer from conversation_a and conversation_b in turn-one records. Require matching questions and distinct nonempty answers, and ignore winner fields completely. Omit model-identity metadata from judge prompts without editing answer content. Canonicalize pair order deterministically by answer hash. Before judging, require each answer to contain 32-512 judge-tokenizer tokens and every full prompt, across both templates and all experimental personas, to fit within 1,800 tokens without truncation. Select one eligible pair per unique question by seeded hash order, then up to 48 unique questions with seed 17. Require at least 24; otherwise report data infeasibility. Use these ten fixed profiles verbatim: (1) A 71-year-old retired nurse from Italy, volunteering in hospice care and advocating for compassionate end-of-life support. (2) A 54-year-old divorced mother from Spain, running a successful winery and promoting sustainable viticulture practices. (3) A 63-year-old retired teacher from China, teaching calligraphy and preserving the art form for future generations. (4) A 68-year-old retired engineer from Japan, practicing ikebana and teaching the art to younger generations. (5) A 21-year-old photographer from Paris who spends weekends volunteering. (6) A 34-year-old scientist from London who is a social media influencer. (7) A 41-year-old scientist from London who loves hiking. (8) An 87-year-old World War II veteran from Poland, sharing stories of his experiences and advocating for peace. (9) A 31-year-old social worker from Colombia, supporting victims of domestic violence and fighting for gender equality. (10) A 23-year-old aspiring musician from Brazil, fusing traditional and modern sounds and promoting cultural exchange through music. Cross every pair with every profile. Collect two independent judgment blocks, each containing both answer orders. Block one asks: 'You are simulating the following user persona: {persona}. As this persona, evaluate which assistant response you would personally prefer.' Block two asks: 'Taking the perspective of this person, which reply would you prefer for this question? Profile: {persona}.' Both then show the same question and two delimited answers and request exactly 1, 2, or T, with T meaning tie. Use the native chat template with thinking disabled. Verify that the three labels are distinct single tokens. Obtain unrestricted final-position logits in GPU batches, preferably using final-token-only projection to avoid materializing logits for every input position. Record the unrestricted probability mass on the allowed labels at temperature 0.7, then sample from their restricted logits at that temperature using independent recorded seeds. Map verdicts to preference for canonical answer A: 1 for A, 0 for B, 0.5 for tie, and average presentation orders within block. From one block, the personal selector chooses A when its own persona score exceeds 0.5; the pooled selector chooses A when the mean over all ten personas exceeds 0.5. Resolve all ties using the same question hash. Evaluate choices on the other block and reverse block roles. Add ten identical neutral-profile copies on twelve hash-selected questions as a noise control, with copy IDs never shown to the model. Add opposed explicit shorter-response and longer-response profiles on up to sixteen eligible pairs whose character and token lengths agree on which answer is longer and differ by at least a factor of 1.5. These controls are selected before any judgments and are excluded from the primary statistic.

event.description: Persona-specific selection has a cross-replicated reward advantage over pooled selection whose lower confidence bound exceeds three percentage points.
event.statistic: The one-sided 95% question-cluster bootstrap lower bound on the symmetrized held-out-block reward difference, personal minus pooled, for the ten biographical profiles.

evaluation.procedure: For held-out canonical-A preference y, choosing A earns y and choosing B earns 1-y. Compute the personal-minus-pooled difference for both cross-fitting directions, then average directions, personas, and questions. Bootstrap whole question IDs 2,000 times with seed 2027, retaining all profiles, blocks, and presentation orders together; report the fifth percentile as the primary statistic. Also run 1,000 within-question permutations of persona correspondence between blocks, preserving each block's marginal judgments. Report this null distribution and the identical-profile control alongside the raw effect: the pooled selector has more observations, so the null raw difference is not assumed to be zero. Report explicit length-preference adherence, position sensitivity, and unrestricted allowed-label probability mass. Forced syntax alone is not evidence that the model naturally followed the judging instruction. manifest.json records revisions, filters, timing, and decoding details. pairs.jsonl stores frozen questions and complete answers. personas.json stores exact profiles and templates. judgments.jsonl stores logits for the three labels, unrestricted allowed-label mass, sampled verdicts, seeds, orders, and canonical scores. selections.jsonl stores cross-fitted choices and rewards. scores.json contains the primary bound and controls. A non-event does not establish absent latent persona effects: individual decisions may be too noisy. A positive event establishes synthetic repeatability only, potentially including stereotypes, not agreement with human preferences.
evaluation.controls: Fixed question-answer pairs, balanced presentation order, independent sampling blocks, a fixed wording change, pooled selection, within-question persona-ID permutation, identical-profile copies, and explicit opposing length preferences. No original human or synthetic winner labels influence selection, prompts, or scoring.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, test whether the signal transfers across independent judge families and can be predicted on new questions from sparse user histories. Compare with shuffled-user and global-preference baselines, then assess transfer to public real-user preference datasets before making claims about human personalization.

agent.reason: I expect general answer quality and the pooled selector's lower sampling noise to outweigh many weak biographical effects. Repeatable persona differences remain plausible, but a cross-wording advantage whose lower bound exceeds three percentage points seems difficult.

judge_astra.reason: Biographical profiles do not prescribe explicit preferences, so I expect relatively weak cross-wording decision value beyond generic answer quality. The personal selector's noisier evidence and the limit of 48 question clusters make a lower confidence bound above three percentage points unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: A two-verdict persona-specific selector must beat a twenty-verdict pooled selector by a bootstrap lower bound of 3 pp on ~48 questions, which requires strong, wording-stable persona-divergent preferences from Qwen3-8B on MT-Bench pairs; LLM judges are dominated by shared quality/position effects, so the null expectation is near zero or negative.

judge_opus.reason: A personal selector built on 2 sampled verdicts is much noisier than a pooled selector built on 20. Biographical personas probably shift Qwen3-8B's verdicts on MT-Bench answer pairs only slightly and idiosyncratically. The raw personal-minus-pooled difference is more likely negative than a 3-point-plus advantage.

judge_sol.reason: Biographical cues may produce few stable preference reversals across these fixed answer pairs. Cross-wording variability and the personal selector's much smaller judgment budget make a lower confidence bound above three percentage points particularly demanding.

judge_luna.reason: Biographical profiles could induce repeatable preferences, but many may be weakly relevant to the answer pairs, and the one-sided bound must exceed three points with at most 48 question clusters. Any positive result would establish repeatability for this synthetic judge protocol, not agreement with human preferences.

judge_muse.reason: Personal uses 2 verdicts versus pooled 20 on the same block, so pooled has lower variance and shares global quality; a stable >3pp personal advantage from biographical text alone across a wording change is unlikely.

closest_work.difference: This paper tests whether persona-prompted LLM judges agree with human ground-truth preferences, finds the agreement weak and inconsistent, and adds verbal uncertainty. It does not compare a persona-specific selector with a pooled persona-agnostic selector on held-out synthetic judgment blocks with fixed answer pairs and a different prompt wording.

This paper uses persona-prompted LLMs to make synthetic preference labels for training a multi-judge aggregator. It contrasts individual-persona, mixed-persona and persona-mean ground truth only through how well the aggregator fits each target (R²). It does not test whether persona-specific choices beat pooled choices on independent judgment blocks with a different wording.

This paper probes internal preference representations behind persona-dependent pairwise task choices. It does not measure cross-block, cross-wording decision value of biographical personas against a pooled baseline for judging responses.

This paper finds that persona prompting gives uneven and often worse alignment for synthetic survey respondents. It is a different task (survey items, not pairwise response preferences) and has no held-out pooled-versus-personal selection test.

The seed paper uses persona-conditioned judging to build supervision for personalized routing and reports gains from user-conditioned routing. As far as its abstract shows, it does not check whether the persona-conditioned judgments carry repeatable, cross-wording decision value beyond a pooled per-question reference.

opus.reason: Prior work looks at whether persona-conditioned judges match human preferences, uses persona labels as aggregation targets, or studies persona-dependent preferences inside the model. None of the papers I found asks whether biographical personas give a persona-specific selector a held-out advantage over a pooled selector across independent, differently worded judgment blocks with fixed answers. I did not read 2605.21063 (APM), which the experiment itself lists as related, so I cannot rule it out. With that caveat, the specific question and its cross-fitted pooled-versus-personal design look unanswered, so the experiment appears distinct.

closest_work.difference: The seed uses biographical persona-conditioned judgments to supervise and evaluate routers, but does not test same-pair decision value across independent, differently worded judgment blocks against a pooled selector.

PersonalizedRouter evaluates routing with synthetic persona preferences under multiple judge configurations, treating configurations as distinct user perspectives rather than testing preference transfer between them on fixed answer pairs.
Compares individual, mixed, and averaged persona scoring targets for learned judge aggregation, but does not measure cross-replicated personal-versus-pooled selection reward.

PERSONA measures persona-conditioned preference agreement across models and humans, largely using persona-refined responses; it does not isolate held-out decision gains on unchanged, unpersonalized answer pairs.

Reports repeated-run stability of persona-conditioned situational choices and latent behavioral traits, not whether personal selections outperform pooled selections under an independent wording change.
Tests persona-conditioned judges against human preferences and studies uncertainty, rather than synthetic preference repeatability and its decision value relative to pooled judging.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes persona-dependent judgments, personalized routing gains, and some repeated-run behavioral stability, but these do not answer the registered decision-value question. Among work available by 2026-10-07, I found no experiment cross-fitting selections between independently sampled, differently worded judgment blocks on fixed unpersonalized answer pairs against a pooled per-question selector with unequal-observation noise controls. This is a distinct audit of transferable synthetic decision value, rather than merely a dataset, model, or metric substitution.

opus.reason: Persona-judge entries (#10, #18, #23, #38, #48, #56) measure flip rates, variance components or router generalization to new questions, not cross-wording held-out reward of persona-specific versus pooled selection on fixed answer pairs.

registration.title: An empirical audit of policy-dependent normalization and dominated winners
registration.seed_connection: The seed compares routers using weighted quality-cost rewards and reports cost-dependent ranking changes. This experiment checks whether the released evaluation code uses policy-dependent normalization and, if so, measures the empirical consequences without assuming that the inspected version generated the published figures.
registration.hypothesis: Under verified policy-dependent normalization, materially Pareto-dominated winners occur in more than 10% of a fixed set of source-task-by-weight settings, with this incidence persisting under paired query resampling.
registration.contribution: The mathematical possibility of Pareto-inconsistent rankings is not the contribution. The experiment measures their incidence and magnitude on held-out recorded outcomes for a predeclared policy catalogue, with source-code parity checks and a policy-invariant control.

closest_work.difference: RouterBench evaluates quality-cost frontiers. This experiment asks how often a particular scalar evaluation rule selects a policy dominated on its underlying quality and cost coordinates.
LLMRouterBench includes fixed-model references in Pareto analysis. Here the policy catalogue and outcomes remain unchanged while only the ranking rule changes.
ReCal concerns reward calibration in routing training. This experiment isolates evaluation-time comparability without altering supervision or optimizing a new router.

inputs: Hugging Face ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates, with released train and test records.
Seed repository https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py and benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py, downloaded at a resolved commit.
The historical input/output price table in Appendix C, Table 9, of the supplied seed paper.
Python, datasets, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn. No language model is downloaded or executed.
registration.method: Before examining evaluation results, pin the repository commit and inspect the scalar reward path in evaluate. Proceed only if quality and cost are each min-max normalized using the selected outcomes of the individual policy being scored. Preserve the exact source treatment of epsilon and constant vectors. Extract the unmodified arithmetic block and required pure helpers into a small callable; do not install or run the full pipeline. Verify numerical parity with a standalone implementation on synthetic fixtures containing ordinary, constant-quality, constant-cost, and outlier-cost vectors, and on a small recorded-policy fixture. If the source does not implement the hypothesized policy-dependent rule, report source mismatch rather than adapting the hypothesis. Use the seven generic subtasks MBPP, MATH, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU, giving 28 task-by-evaluation-weight cells. Define aliases explicitly. Establish the released candidate pool before examining quality values. Construct complete query-model blocks with finite quality in [0,1], recorded nonnegative input/output token counts, and an unambiguous mapping to the historical prices in Table 9. Log price discrepancies with downloaded metadata, but use the fixed Table 9 tariff throughout. Do not estimate missing counts from text length or replace missing counts or prices with zero. Remove identical duplicates, reject conflicting duplicate blocks, and remove exact train-test overlap. Require at least 200 fitting-eligible and 100 test questions in every task; otherwise report the run incomplete without changing the 28-cell denominator. Hash-select at most 1,000 fitting queries per task and retain all eligible official test queries. Compute historical-price dollar cost as (input_tokens*input_price + output_tokens*output_price)/1e6. For each task, build a fixed catalogue containing every always-select-model policy plus five query-aware policies. Fit a training-only TF-IDF vectorizer with unigram/bigram features, max_features=10000, and min_df=2. Fit multi-output ridge regressors with alpha=10 and LSQR to predict model quality and cost. Scale cost targets by the positive global fitting-set cost range, using positive fitting-set mean cost only if that range is zero. Clip quality predictions to [0,1] and predicted costs below at zero. The five query-aware policies maximize (1-beta)*predicted_quality-beta*predicted_scaled_cost for beta in {0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}. Freeze all test assignments before scoring. For each evaluation beta in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}, rank the entire catalogue using the verified source normalization rule, with lexicographic policy-ID tie-breaking. Mark the winner materially dominated when another catalogue policy has at least 0.01 higher raw mean quality and at most 90% of the winner's positive mean dollar cost. Let F be the fraction of the 28 cells with a materially dominated winner.

event.description: Materially dominated winners are sufficiently common that the fifth percentile of their bootstrap frequency exceeds 10%.
event.statistic: The fifth percentile of F across 1,000 paired within-task query bootstraps, with normalization and winner selection recomputed in every resample.

evaluation.procedure: Use the same resampled query indices for all policies and weights within a task, with bootstrap seed 2027. Keep policies fixed but recompute their normalization, scalar rewards, winners, and domination witnesses on each resample. The registered percentile is a bootstrap-stability screening quantity, not a guaranteed population confidence bound. Report nominal F, its bootstrap distribution, every nominal domination witness, quality losses, cost ratios, and constant-vector cases. Re-rank exactly the same policies using (1-beta)*raw_mean_quality-beta*raw_mean_cost/c_scale, with c_scale fixed from fitting data. Assert, up to documented floating-point tolerance, that this positive common-unit score never selects a Pareto-dominated policy. manifest.json records source and dataset revisions, candidate mappings, prices, exclusions, fitting IDs, hyperparameters, and timing. source_parity.json stores the extracted source hash and parity fixtures and results. matrix.parquet stores quality, token counts, prices, and computed costs. routes.jsonl stores frozen assignments. cell_scores.jsonl stores nominal raw coordinates, scalar rewards, winners, and witnesses. scores.json stores F, the bootstrap distribution, registered statistic, and common-unit results. Data or source-verification failures produce an explicit incomplete or not-applicable status, not an empirical negative finding. Conclusions concern this catalogue, tariff, and benchmark subset, not routing evaluations generally or the provenance of published figures.
evaluation.controls: Numerical parity against the source reward arithmetic, including constant-vector cases; all fixed-model policies rather than only smallest and largest models; identical outcomes and policy catalogue under both evaluation rules; a common-unit Pareto-consistency invariant in every bootstrap. Test outcomes never influence policy fitting or catalogue construction.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, audit original routing logs and additional public benchmarks using common units, explicit budgets, and raw Pareto frontiers. Determine which architectural conclusions survive policy-invariant evaluation, separating normalization effects from training, candidate-pool, pricing, and sampling effects.

agent.reason: Policy-specific scaling can erase between-policy cost differences, making materially dominated winners in several settings plausible. This forecast includes substantial uncertainty about passing source-parity checks and obtaining sufficiently complete token-count and pricing records.

judge_astra.reason: If the source uses the hypothesized per-policy normalization, the broad catalogue and cost-weight sweep make a stable dominated-winner incidence above 10% plausible. The exact source rule and sufficient complete token-count records remain substantial unverified prerequisites.

judge_fable.reason: The event is gated on the released evaluate path actually using per-policy min-max normalization of both quality and cost and on the dataset exposing token counts mappable to Table 9; if those hold, dominated winners under cost-weighted settings would likely be common (>10% of cells stably), but the conjunction of source-match, data-feasibility and implementation conditions keeps the overall probability modest.

judge_opus.reason: The proposer's specific details (epsilon handling, file paths) and the seed's Figure 5 hint that the scalar reward is not absolute-cost based. Examples: Largest-LLM ranks 5th on Memory at beta=0.8, and Smallest-LLM's rank worsens with beta on Memory and TimeSeries. If the source verification passes, per-policy min-max cost becomes a shape statistic, and dominated winners should be common. Even so, risks from source mismatch, missing token counts, price mapping and bootstrap instability compound.

judge_sol.reason: If verified, policy-dependent normalization provides a credible mechanism for materially dominated winners, especially at high cost weights. The supplied paper does not establish the source-code gate or completeness of released token counts, so these feasibility conditions substantially discount the probability.

judge_luna.reason: The event depends on finding the specific policy-dependent normalization path; the paper’s description of a weighted reward does not establish that the code uses it. If the path is present, dominated winners are plausible, but the source gate and the requirement for a material, bootstrap-stable incidence make the overall event uncertain.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Argues that the standard cost-accuracy Pareto objective rewards bad router behaviours (difficulty blindness, length reversal, semantic matching) and proposes another evaluation method. It does not look at per-policy min-max normalization in a scalar reward, and it does not count how often such a rule picks a Pareto-dominated winner while the policy catalogue stays fixed.
RouterBench evaluates routers by their raw quality-cost frontiers. It does not audit a scalarized ranking rule for Pareto-inconsistent winners.
LLMRouterBench includes fixed-model references in its Pareto analysis but does not separate out the effect of changing the normalization or ranking rule on the same outcomes.
ReCal calibrates and normalizes rewards during RL training of routers. It does not address whether evaluation-time scores are comparable across policies.
This is the seed paper whose evaluation rule would be audited. It reports rankings that depend on the cost weight but does not check whether its scalar reward can choose dominated policies.

opus.reason: I searched arXiv for work on how router rankings depend on normalization, router benchmarks that are not Pareto-consistent, and critiques of LLMRouter or xRouteBench evaluation, and found nothing that measures how often policy-dependent min-max normalization picks Pareto-dominated winners. The closest papers criticise the Pareto-efficiency objective itself (2610.02762) or calibrate training rewards (ReCal), so neither answers this question. The audit therefore looks distinct, though prior work could have been missed under terms I did not try.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The seed reports weighted quality-cost rankings and raw trade-offs, but does not audit whether policy-dependent normalization selects materially dominated winners or measure their incidence under paired resampling.

LLMRouterBench analyzes Pareto dominance across routers and fixed models. It does not isolate evaluation-rule effects by holding outcomes and policies fixed and comparing policy-dependent normalization with a common-unit score.
RouterBench develops quality-cost frontiers and frontier-based evaluation, rather than measuring how often a scalar ranking rule selects a policy dominated in raw mean quality and cost.

Economic Evaluation of LLMs supplies common-dollar utility scores and connections to Pareto optimality, but does not empirically audit policy-specific normalization or the frequency of dominated winners.

This empirical MCDA audit measures ranking instability under alternative degradation and problem decomposition. Those tests address different consistency properties from selecting raw-coordinate dominated winners under normalization fitted separately to each policy.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes Pareto-based routing evaluation, common-unit scalarization, and empirical ranking-consistency audits, so those ingredients are not individually novel. However, I found no paper answering the registered question: conditional on source verification, how frequently policy-dependent normalization selects materially dominated policies on a frozen held-out catalogue, with paired-bootstrap stability and an unchanged-catalogue common-unit control.

opus.reason: Cost-weight entries #13, #25 and #53 study retraining versus decision rules or ranking reversals, but none audits whether policy-dependent min-max normalization selects Pareto-dominated winners.

sol.reason: Entries 13 and 25 examine cost-weighted routing and normalization choices, not source-verified policy-dependent normalization and its incidence of materially Pareto-dominated winners.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: audit/run_audit.py, launched by run_eval.sh. Installation plus the run takes about 30 s. No language model is used.

Source check:
- I resolved LLMRouter main to commit 338335d2 and downloaded benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py at that commit. Its SHA-256 matches the /workspace/seed copy.
- I parsed `evaluate` with ast. Static checks confirm that quality and cost are each min-max normalised over the outcomes the policy being scored selected, with eps 1e-12 (so a constant vector normalises to 0).
- I extracted the norm_p and norm_c lines and the avg_reward expression unchanged and ran them as a callable.
- Parity with a standalone implementation was exact (max difference 0) on these synthetic fixtures: ordinary, constant-quality, constant-cost, outlier-cost, constant-both and fractional.
- The full unmodified `evaluate()` was also run on a recorded GSM8K fixture (30 queries, 2 policies, 4 betas) and matched on all 8 checks.
- A behavioural check confirms the normalisation is policy-dependent. So the rule was verified and the analysis went ahead.

Data and setup:
- Dataset: HF ulab-ai/xRouteBench at revision ea4b6e1b, configs llm_candidates and llmrouter_generic. The 18 pool names map one-to-one onto Table 9 with no price discrepancies. All costs use the Table 9 prices.
- Catalogue: 18 always-select-one-model policies plus 5 query-aware policies (training-only TF-IDF features → Ridge with alpha=10 and LSQR, predicting quality and scaled cost). Test routes were frozen before scoring.
- Scoring: 4 evaluation betas × 7 tasks = 28 cells. Bootstrap: 1,000 paired resamples, seed 2027.
- Excluded: in arc_challenge train, one identical duplicate row was removed and one query block with conflicting duplicates was rejected.

Deviation, run is formally INCOMPLETE: MMLU-Pro has only 63 fitting-eligible training questions in the released data, below the registered minimum of 200; every task has 500 test questions. As registered, the denominator stays at 28 cells. In the registered statistic, the 4 MMLU-Pro cells count as having no materially dominated winner, so the value is a lower bound. I also computed MMLU-Pro on its 63 fitting questions as a separately labelled exploratory check. None of its cells has a dominated winner, and the exploratory bootstrap 5th percentile equals the registered value. So the outcome does not depend on how this gap is handled.

Results:
- Nominal F = 2/28 = 0.071. In OpenBookQA and ARC-Challenge at beta=0.8, the source rule picks always-DeepSeek-V3.1. Other policies beat it by up to +0.098 and +0.064 quality at about 6% of its cost.
- Across the bootstrap, F has mean 0.106, median 0.071 and 95th percentile 0.214.
- Registered statistic (5th percentile) = 0.0357, which does not exceed the 0.10 threshold, so the registered event did not occur. This is a bootstrap-stability screen and does not show that dominated winners are rare in general.
- Dominated winners do occur and are fairly frequent in some cells: OpenBookQA at beta=0.8 in 98.7% of resamples, ARC-Challenge at 0.8 in 66.6%, MBPP at 0.6–0.8 in about 23%.
- Common-unit control: re-ranking the same policies by (1-beta)·quality − beta·cost/c_scale never selected a Pareto-dominated or materially dominated winner, nominally or in any resample.
- No policy had a constant quality or cost vector, nominally or in any resample.

Choices to be aware of:
- Ranking uses the unrounded source reward. The source reports avg_reward rounded to 4 decimals; ranking on the rounded value as a sensitivity check gives the same nominal F.
- alpha = 1 − beta, following the paper's sweep.
- Ties in the query-aware argmax go to the first model in sorted name order.

Conclusions apply only to this catalogue, the Table 9 prices and these 7 generic subtasks. They say nothing about how the published figures were produced.

opus.what_it_asks: Using LLMRouter's released evaluation reward, which min-max normalizes quality and cost over each scored policy's own selected outcomes, and a catalogue of fixed-model and query-aware routing policies on xRouteBench generic subtasks, how often does the reward's winner have another policy beating it on raw mean quality at clearly lower raw cost, compared with a common-unit reward?

registration.title: Natural specialist agreement as a stopping rule before synthesis
registration.seed_connection: The seed's multi-turn routers use a 3B coordinator, but decomposition, specialist selection, and aggregation change together. An agreement-only bypass isolates the net value of the final synthesis stage on identical cached specialist evidence.
registration.hypothesis: Bypassing a 3B synthesis coordinator when three candidate models unanimously name the same answer improves overall multiple-choice accuracy by more than two percentage points.
registration.contribution: The experiment measures correct-consensus damage minus wrong-consensus rescue on natural model outputs, rather than constructing deliberately wrong evidence or studying only initially correct answers. It computes the overall policy contrast without spending inference on disagreement cases where the policies are identical.

closest_work.difference: This work compares selection and synthesis across teams using judged outputs. Here the endpoint uses objective answer keys, identical cached evidence, and an agreement-only intervention.
MAgICoRe avoids excessive refinement using reward and confidence signals. This experiment is not a new learned stopping algorithm; it measures the accuracy balance of a fixed unanimity bypass.
Conformal Social Choice emphasizes that consensus can be wrong. This experiment directly measures whether synthesis repairs enough shared wrong answers to offset its damage and inference cost.

inputs: Hugging Face ulab-ai/xRouteBench, llmrouter_generic configuration, ARC-Challenge and MMLU test records with original questions, four choices, answer keys, and response texts.
Cached responses from qwen2.5-7b-instruct, mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3, and llama-3-8b-instruct-lite. These three proposer models are not executed.
Hugging Face Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as local coordinators.
Python, PyTorch, transformers, datasets, NumPy, and preferably prebuilt vLLM wheels for batched inference.
registration.method: Preflight cached response-text, choice, and answer-key availability before downloading coordinator weights. Do not infer gold answers from cached correctness scores. Require the three specified response texts and four unambiguous choices. Normalize option labels and gold mappings consistently to A-D. Construct prompts containing the complete question, choices, and all three complete responses under anonymous headers; omit model-identity metadata without editing response content. Require the native-chat rendering to contain at most 1,600 input tokens under both coordinator tokenizers, leaving room for analysis and the final-choice cue within a 2,048-token context. Do not truncate evidence. Select 256 eligible questions from each task by hash order with seed 17, without using correctness; report data infeasibility if either task has too few. Parse each specialist answer with a fixed parser accepting a terminal bare or parenthesized option letter, an explicit final-answer declaration, a boxed letter, or an answer-tagged letter. Use the last explicit answer declaration where applicable; never infer an option from arbitrary letters in a rationale. Unit-test the parser on mechanical fixtures. An unparseable or ambiguous response disables bypass but does not exclude the question. Freeze the cohort, parsed answers, agreement flags, and evidence orders before scoring against keys. Define two policies: always synthesize, and return the unanimous letter when all three parsed letters agree, otherwise reuse the always-synthesize answer. For a non-unanimous question their accuracy difference is identically zero, so do not run the shared synthesis branch on those questions. On unanimous questions, run each coordinator in two evidence orders: a seeded random permutation and its reverse. Use the instruction 'Answer the original multiple-choice question. The three anonymous responses below are fallible supporting evidence. Use them only if helpful; determine the best answer.' Generate at most 96 tokens of brief analysis with greedy decoding. Continue the same assistant response with a fixed 'Final answer:' cue and choose one token by argmax restricted to verified single-token A-D IDs. This guarantees a common answer interface even if analysis reaches its cap. Enable prefix caching when using a two-stage inference engine. Run a no-evidence direct-answer control once per unanimous question and coordinator with the same analysis and final-choice budgets. Load coordinators sequentially. The 3B contrast is primary; 7B is a predeclared capacity control. The cached models' outputs are not assumed statistically independent merely because they come from different models.

event.description: Agreement bypass has an overall accuracy advantage over 3B synthesis whose one-sided lower confidence bound exceeds two percentage points.
event.statistic: The one-sided 95% task-stratified question-cluster bootstrap lower bound on overall bypass-minus-always-synthesize accuracy for Qwen2.5-3B, averaging the two evidence orders.

evaluation.procedure: For a unanimous question, compute consensus correctness minus synthesis correctness, averaged over evidence orders. Assign difference zero to every non-unanimous question, including parser failures. Average within task and weight ARC and MMLU equally. This identifies the overall policy difference exactly without executing their common disagreement branch; do not report absolute overall accuracy for either full policy, since that branch was not measured. Bootstrap complete question IDs within task 2,000 times with seed 2027 and use the fifth percentile as the primary bound. Decompose the effect into correct-consensus damage and wrong-consensus rescue. Report their counts, rates, and uncertainty, along with agreement coverage, parser coverage, order sensitivity, direct-answer accuracy conditional on agreement, and 7B results. If wrong unanimous answers are rare, explicitly limit conclusions about repair ability. Estimate deployment inference avoided by bypass from the measured two-stage token usage on agreement cases, averaging orders rather than charging both as one deployment call. Distinguish logical input tokens from cached-prefill compute when available; do not attribute diagnostic-control overhead to deployment. manifest.json stores revisions, filtering, prompts, token limits, parser rules, and timing. evidence.jsonl stores complete cached evidence, parsed letters, agreement flags, and orders. generations.jsonl stores coordinator prompts, analyses, forced final letters, finish reasons, and token counts. per_query.jsonl stores keys, policy differences, and transition categories. scores.json stores the primary statistic and diagnostics. This is a final-stage intervention, not a reproduction or complete explanation of the seed's multi-turn results.
evaluation.controls: Identical cached evidence across policies; no ground truth in prompts or bypass decisions; correct and incorrect consensuses both retained; disagreement cases included with their exact zero contrast; reversed evidence orders; forced common final-answer format; direct-answer and stronger-coordinator controls. Length filtering is performed before correctness is inspected.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, test agreement-conditioned stopping across more candidate families, coordinator sizes, and tasks. Insert the intervention into actual decomposition-and-routing pipelines and estimate when the expected benefit of revising a shared answer exceeds its accuracy risk and inference cost.

agent.reason: Correct unanimous answers may usually survive synthesis, while wrong-consensus rescues subtract from the bypass benefit. Clearing the two-percentage-point lower-bound threshold, with the required cached evidence available, is considerably harder than observing occasional synthesis damage.

judge_astra.reason: The seed's weak multi-turn results do not establish that final synthesis alone causes substantial damage. Unanimous evidence should often anchor the coordinator, while forced valid final letters remove some formatting failures, making the required overall improvement difficult to establish.

judge_fable.reason: Unanimous 7-8B consensus is mostly correct and a 3B coordinator will usually follow it, so the net bypass gain is probably ~1-3 pp; exceeding a 2 pp one-sided lower bound needs a damage rate near 10%, which is possible given the 96-token truncation and forced-letter interface but not the most likely outcome, and data/parse feasibility adds risk.

judge_opus.reason: A 3B coordinator shown three agreeing answers will mostly follow them, so correct-consensus damage is probably a few percent of unanimous cases, partly offset by rescues. Unanimity and parser coverage dilute this further. The expected overall gain is about 1–2 pp, with a lower bound well below 2 pp.

judge_sol.reason: The reported multi-turn deficits do not isolate harm from synthesizing unanimous evidence, and complete rationales plus a common answer interface may make synthesis relatively reliable. Clearing the overall two-point lower-bound threshold requires appreciable damage after subtracting rescues, while cached-evidence eligibility adds failure risk.

judge_luna.reason: Unanimous answers may be reliable enough that a weaker coordinator sometimes damages correct consensus, but it may also repair shared errors or simply reproduce the consensus. Disagreement cases contribute exactly zero, making a greater-than-two-point overall advantage with a one-sided bound a substantial hurdle.

judge_muse.reason: A weaker 3B synthesizer may flip some correct unanimous evidence, consistent with poor seed multi-turn results, but it will often copy unanimous letters; achieving >2pp net overall advantage including zeros for disagreements is possible but demanding.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: MOSAIC already compares the same two policies on multiple-choice tasks: it returns the expert answer when three roughly 7-9B experts vote 3:0 and otherwise calls the aggregator. On MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA and GPQA the bypass matched the always-aggregate baseline, with differences of -0.04 to +1.00 pp. The registered experiment changes the details: a small Qwen2.5-3B coordinator with a 7B control, ARC and MMLU from xRouteBench, cached responses with fixed evidence, two evidence orders, a bootstrap lower bound above 2 pp, and an explicit split into damaged correct consensus versus rescued wrong consensus.

Beyond Consensus asks the same question, whether to skip synthesis when agents agree or always synthesize, and splits the net effect into harmful and beneficial flips on unanimous cases. Its proposers are perturbed copies of a single strong model (gpt-oss-120b), and it finds that synthesis wins. It also reports that the advantage fails with weak aggregators, and that swapping in an 8B aggregator costs about 2.5 pp. It does not test a 3B coordinator reading cached outputs from three different small models.
This paper compares selection and synthesis using judged outputs. It does not test an agreement-only bypass against answer keys.
MAgICoRe decides when to stop refining using reward-model and confidence signals. It does not measure the net accuracy of a fixed unanimity bypass in front of a separate synthesizer.

opus.reason: The core contrast, returning the unanimous answer versus always running the aggregator on multiple-choice questions, has already been measured. MOSAIC did it with three small heterogeneous experts and found a near-zero difference. Beyond Consensus ran the same contrast with a damage/rescue split and found synthesis helps with a strong aggregator but loses that advantage with weak ones. The new experiment mainly changes the coordinator (3B), the datasets and the statistics. That puts it close to existing work, though neither paper directly measures how large the damage is when a 3B coordinator synthesizes outputs from three different small models.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Agreement Before Diversity compares a frozen three-answer unanimity gate against unconditional synthesis using objective scoring and paired preservation-wins versus preservation-losses counts, with an exact zero contrast outside agreement cases. Its gate uses three samples from one trusted model, and synthesis reads an anchor plus additional heterogeneous proposals; this experiment instead gates on three heterogeneous specialists and synthesizes their cached evidence.

Beyond Consensus compares unanimity-gated and always-on synthesis on existing model-generated outputs and measures beneficial versus harmful answer changes. It primarily uses same-model, perturbation-generated traces and a refinement pipeline, rather than three cached heterogeneous specialists with a 3B coordinator and a 7B capacity control.

sol.reason: Prior work already studies the central question—whether accepting agreement instead of synthesizing improves accuracy—and provides the same paired accounting of synthesis damage versus rescue. The proposed heterogeneous proposer pool, small-coordinator controls, evidence-order reversal, and bootstrap threshold extend that comparison, but do not make its core contribution a distinct experimental question.

opus.reason: Multi-round entries #19, #22, #33 and #45 vary decomposition, aggregator size or format, but none tests a unanimity bypass of the synthesis coordinator on cached specialist evidence.

sol.reason: The listed aggregation and continuation experiments do not compare synthesis with a natural three-model-unanimity bypass on identical cached evidence, measuring consensus damage against wrong-consensus rescue.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented and tested the registered cohort, fixed fixture-tested parser, anonymous complete evidence, reversed orders, greedy 96-token analysis plus verified restricted A-D final token, direct controls, sequential 3B/7B coordinators, per-call KV prefix reuse, and task-stratified 2,000-question-cluster bootstrap. All required artifacts and result.json are generated afresh. Used transformers SDPA instead of optional vLLM; no substantive method/event/control change. Pinned dataset/model revisions and bundled a checksummed small source-data extract, not generations or model weights. Test primary bound was 0.000 (event false). The unchanged conservative parser accepts the registered terminal/explicit forms, not leading option-plus-text outputs: only four of 512 questions had parsed unanimity, all correct. No wrong-consensus repair inference is possible, and the zero empirical contrast does not establish population equivalence. Separate audit confirmed all 24 cached-continuation final choices against full unpadded prefill.

departures: experiment.py parse_answer: a terminal parenthesized letter is accepted only when it stands on its own line. The registration says only 'terminal bare or parenthesized option letter'. Cached llama responses of the form '(A) The climate ... changed over time. (A)' end in a terminal parenthesized letter but are left unparsed, which disables bypass for them. This is stricter than the registered rule. It could add a few unanimous questions and slightly change the primary value (e.g. negative if any damage occurred), but is very unlikely to make the bound exceed 0.02, because mistral coverage (~4.9%) caps unanimity at about 25 questions regardless.

experiment.py messages(): the 'question' field is the full xRouteBench query. That query includes the proposers' wrapper instruction ('You MUST put your final answer letter in a parenthesis') and an inline option list, and the Choices list is appended again. The registration asks for the complete question and choices but not the proposer's system instruction. This could slightly alter coordinator behaviour; impact on the 4 scored questions is likely negligible.

Inference uses transformers SDPA with a manual per-call KV cache instead of vLLM. The registration allows this ('preferably' vLLM). audit_report.json shows cached final letters matching full prefill on 24 of 24 calls. Not result-changing.

The final-answer cue ends with a space ('\nFinal answer: ') and is followed by a space-less letter token. This is a tokenization choice within the registered interface; the restricted argmax still guarantees an A-D answer. Unlikely to change the result.

Source data comes from a bundled checksummed extract (assets/source.jsonl) pinned to a dataset revision rather than a live download. Within the registration; not result-changing if the extract is faithful (not independently verifiable here).
problems: outputs/scores.json: only 4 of 512 questions (0 ARC, 4 MMLU) are unanimous, so the primary contrast and its bootstrap interval are degenerate at 0.0.
There are no wrong consensuses, so the registered damage-versus-rescue decomposition cannot be estimated.

outputs/scores.json parser coverage: mistral 4.9% and llama 44%, against 98% for qwen. Agreement is driven mostly by response format (leading '(X) text' outputs) rather than by actual agreement. Bypass is therefore almost never triggered, and the measured stopping rule is a format filter more than a consensus rule.

experiment.py parse_answer: requiring a terminal parenthesized letter to stand on its own line rejects '... text. (A)' llama responses that plausibly satisfy the registered 'terminal parenthesized option letter' rule. This further depresses agreement coverage.

Coordinator prompts embed the proposers' original system instruction and duplicate the option list (outputs/generations.jsonl). This is minor prompt contamination relative to the registered 'complete question' plus choices.
The README and notes correctly avoid claiming equivalence, but the evidence cannot speak to the hypothesis at the registered scale.
opus.reason: The pipeline runs as registered: frozen hash-selected cohort, anonymous complete evidence, two orders, a 96-token greedy analysis plus a restricted A-D final token, direct and 7B controls, and the task-stratified bootstrap. The fresh evaluation regenerated all outputs from real coordinator calls, and a separate audit confirmed the cached-continuation final letters. The main departure is a parser stricter than the wording of the registration for terminal parenthesized letters. Because mistral responses rarely use any accepted form, unanimity would stay tiny even with that fixed, so the event outcome is robust. The evidence is valid, but with 4 unanimous questions, all correct and all preserved, and no wrong consensuses, the result is nearly uninformative about synthesis damage or repair. It mainly documents that the registered parser and the cached response formats make the bypass rarely applicable.

departures: experiment.py::parse_answer() requires terminal bare or parenthesized letters to occupy their own line. The registration required acceptance of terminal option letters without that restriction. Thus a response such as '(A) explanation text (A)' is rejected despite its terminal parenthesized answer. This can disable otherwise eligible bypasses and could change the cohort's agreement flags, policy contrast, and bootstrap bound.

experiment.py::messages() retains the entire serialized dataset query, including its embedded '[System Instruction]' demanding a parenthesized answer and its existing choices, then appends another choices block. outputs/generations.jsonl confirms this extra prompt content. Compared with rendering the original question and choices alone, these retained instructions and duplicated choices could affect coordinator outputs; their effect was not measured.

experiment.py::messages() adds 'Give brief analysis. A separate final-answer cue will follow.' to the registered synthesis instruction. This could influence generations, but it reasonably operationalizes the registered brief-analysis and continuation procedure, whose exact additional wording was not specified.

experiment.py uses transformers SDPA with intra-call KV-cache reuse rather than vLLM, and load_source() reads a submitted checksummed dataset extract rather than downloading the dataset during evaluation. These are permitted implementation choices, not demonstrated substantive changes to the registered data or inference procedure; no resulting change to the reported value is established.
problems: experiment.py::parse_answer() adds an own-line restriction to terminal answers that the registration does not contain. The README's claim of no parser-method change overlooks this narrower acceptance rule.

outputs/scores.json shows severe parser coverage limitations: only 4.88% of Mistral responses parse, only 3.125% of questions have all three responses parseable, and only four questions trigger bypass. These are parser-conditioned agreement measurements, not comprehensive measurements of natural specialist agreement.

The four bypass cases are all MMLU questions with correct consensus. There are no ARC agreement cases and no wrong-consensus cases, leaving wrong-consensus rescue untested and damage estimates extremely sparse.

With only four bypasses among 512 equally weighted questions, the maximum possible positive empirical policy contrast is 0.78125 percentage points, below the registered two-percentage-point target even if synthesis damaged every bypass case.

outputs/scores.json reports degenerate bootstrap intervals for zero observed damage and contrast. These follow the prescribed bootstrap but cannot establish population equivalence or absence of damage; the submitted README appropriately acknowledges this limitation.

audit_report.json documents the engineer's earlier continuation checks, not checks rerun by the protected evaluation. It is supporting implementation evidence rather than independent verification of the fresh evaluation's continuations.
sol.reason: The protected evaluation ran both coordinators successfully, generated the required artifacts, and computed the reported zero from model outputs rather than a hard-coded result. However, the parser's additional own-line requirement narrows the registered stopping policy and could change its agreement decisions and statistic, making fidelity unfaithful. The zero contrast is credible for the implemented policy: both coordinators preserved all four observed correct consensuses under both orders. With such low activation coverage and no wrong consensuses, the experiment provides weak evidence and does not establish equivalence, absence of synthesis damage, or repair ability.

departures: Inference used a custom transformers SDPA bf16 greedy loop instead of preferred vLLM (experiment.py, run_evaluation.sh). Allowed by 'preferably'; evaluation stderr warns sliding-window attention is unimplemented for SDPA. Unlikely to change answers: inputs are ≤1600 tokens and Qwen2.5's window is far larger.

Stricter than an end-of-string reading of 'terminal' and could change agreement counts; visible misses in outputs/evidence.jsonl are leading '(A) text' without a terminal letter, which the registration also does not accept, so this likely did not produce the 0.0.

Parser also strips ** and __, accepts uppercase only, and returns None on immediate or/and alternatives or a conflicting terminal (experiment.py). Extra rules not spelled out in the registration; unlikely to have changed this result given the observed response formats.

Coordinator user text is the full cached query, including the proposers' system instruction and an embedded choice list, then choices are appended again (experiment.py messages, outputs/evidence.jsonl). Registration asked for the original question plus choices. Could change synthesis letters versus a stripped stem; with only four unanimous items it cannot push the lower bound above 0.02, and those four margins were large.

Evaluation used checksum-locked assets/source.jsonl instead of re-downloading ulab-ai/xRouteBench (experiment.py load_source). Would change the result only if the extract is not the registered records; not re-verified against Hugging Face in the fresh run.

Maximum overall bypass advantage on this cohort is 0.78125 percentage points, so the >2pp event is impossible regardless of synthesis, and wrong-consensus repair is unmeasured.

grok.reason: The code runs the registered cohort, conservative parser, agreement-only bypass, two reversed evidence orders, greedy 96-token analysis plus restricted A–D final token, direct and 7B controls, and the seed-2027 task-stratified bootstrap. The fresh evaluation actually downloaded both coordinators and ran the 12 agreement-case jobs per model; 0.0 is the arithmetic result of 508 exact zeros plus four correct consensuses that synthesis also preserved, with no gold used in prompts or bypass decisions. The extra analysis sentence, cue spacing, own-line parser, and SDPA backend are real differences but do not plausibly move this reported value. The result is valid yet uninformative about synthesis damage versus rescue: under the registered parser unanimity is too rare for a two-point overall gain, and no wrong consensus was observed.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether returning the shared answer when three candidate models agree, instead of always synthesizing their responses with a 3B coordinator, improves multiple-choice accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper never compares an agreement bypass with synthesis and only calls in general for better early stopping, which does not name this question as left undone.

relation.reason: The test uses xRouteBench cached answers and the paper’s 3B coordinator role, but applies an agreement-only synthesis bypass the paper neither claims nor runs.

obvious.reason: After the paper’s finding that aggregation adds redundant information and its call for early stopping, several routing researchers would list skipping synthesis when answers already agree, but most would first list stronger coordinators or learned sufficiency.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change practice only for groups that synthesize multiple model answers with a small coordinator, not for routing researchers using other methods.

next_step.what: Re-parse cached replies accepting leading parenthesized option-plus-text, then repeat the 3B bypass-versus-synthesis contrast.

opus.what_it_asks: On ARC-Challenge and MMLU questions from xRouteBench, does returning the shared answer when three cached small-model responses agree, instead of always passing them to a Qwen2.5-3B synthesis coordinator, raise overall accuracy, and so show whether the synthesis stage harms correct consensus more than it rescues wrong consensus?

in_the_paper.reason: After its multi-turn results the paper names early stopping and sufficiency estimation for multi-round routing and aggregation as needed future work, and an agreement-based stop before synthesis is a direct case of that.
in_the_paper.quote: These results highlight the need for better sufficiency estimation, early stopping, and more effective decomposition and aggregation.

relation.reason: The experiment uses xRouteBench's cached candidate responses and the paper's 3B-coordinator aggregation setting as working parts, and tests a stopping rule the paper does not evaluate.

obvious.reason: The paper flags early stopping, and agreement or self-consistency gating is a standard idea, so some researchers would list skipping aggregation when candidates agree, though not most.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer on whether synthesis after unanimous agreement helps or hurts would inform people building multi-LLM aggregation and multi-round routing pipelines generally, not only users of this benchmark.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's statements about the paper are accurate: its multi-turn routers do use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as base model, and they do bundle decomposition, selection and aggregation.

answerable.reason: The contrast can only be read if the fixed parser extracts enough specialist answers to yield a meaningful number of unanimous cases, including some wrong ones; the design cannot guarantee this.
