registration.title: Does an explicit task-identity router match learned routers on xRouteBench Generic?
registration.seed_connection: The seed reports large gains of learned routers over fixed-model baselines on the Generic track (e.g., RouterDC 80.56 and kNN 71.37 vs Largest-LLM 70.29), a track that deliberately mixes 13 subtasks (MMLU, GSM8K, MBPP, ...) with very different formats. Its kNN/SVM/MLP routers are best-model classifiers over query embeddings. Nothing in the paper separates recognising which subtask a query belongs to from predicting which model solves this particular query, and the only fixed baselines are Smallest/Largest-LLM rather than the best single model per subtask.
registration.hypothesis: On the xRouteBench Generic test split, a two-stage router that predicts the subtask from the query embedding and routes to that subtask's best model on training data comes within 1 percentage point of the best learned router trained on the same embeddings and supervision.
registration.contribution: Plateau-style analyses show routers cluster near a ceiling and learn coarse capability trends, but none quantifies on a mixed-task benchmark how much of the learned-router gain over the best single model is reproduced by an explicit task-recognition baseline, nor reports within-subtask gains against the per-subtask best model. This MVE provides that decomposition on the seed's own benchmark, supervision and embedding model, giving a concrete reinterpretation of its headline Generic-track numbers.

closest_work.difference: The Routing Plateau paper shows routers learn global-average capability trends and groups queries by domain, but never trains a task-classifier-then-best-model baseline, never measures within-subtask gain against the per-subtask best model, and does not use xRouteBench.
Shows kNN matches learned routers; does not decompose routing gains into between-task and within-task components or compare against a task-identity router.
Observes qualitatively that preference routers make category-driven decisions; does not quantify the fraction of routing gain explained by category identity against a per-category best-model policy.

inputs: HF dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configs 'llmrouter_generic' (train/test splits) and 'llm_candidates' (per-model prices); load with datasets.load_dataset, no token needed
Embedding model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from HF (fallback sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 if unavailable)
Python packages: datasets, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, torch, transformers
registration.method: Data: load config 'llmrouter_generic' train and test. Each row is one (query, model) record with fields task_name, query, model_name, performance (0-1; treat NaN as 0), input_tokens, output_tokens, embedding_id; decode JSON-encoded string fields the way the seed repo's benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py does. Group rows by (split, embedding_id) into unique queries and build a query x 18-model performance matrix per split (missing cells NaN; report how many). Hold out 10% of train queries (stratified by task_name, seed 0) as a validation set; the remaining 90% is the training set for every policy. Embed all train/val/test query texts with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (last-token pooling, L2-normalised, max_length 512, fp16, batch 64). Policies, each choosing one model per test query whose realised performance is read from the matrix: (P1) best-single = model with the highest mean training performance; (P2) task-oracle = for each test query take its gold task_name and route to the model with the highest mean training performance within that task (fallback P1 if the task has no training rows); (P3) task-classifier router = multinomial logistic regression (sklearn, C=1, max_iter=1000) on embeddings predicting task_name, then the P2 rule applied to the predicted task; (P4) seed-style kNN classifier: training label per query = model_name of the first row attaining the maximum performance in stored row order (pandas groupby('query')['performance'].idxmax(), exactly as llmrouter/models/knnrouter), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', metric='minkowski', p=2); (P5) seed-style MLP classifier on the same labels (hidden [256,128], ReLU, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, 50 epochs, batch 256, seed 0); (P6) kNN per-model predictor: for each test query average each model's performance over its k nearest training queries by cosine similarity and take the argmax (ties -> lower blended price), k in {5,10,20,50} selected on validation accuracy; (P7) MLP multi-output predictor: 18 sigmoid outputs trained with BCE against each model's performance (same architecture/training as P5), argmax; (P8) per-query oracle = max over models. The 'best learned router' is whichever of P4-P7 (including P6's k) has the highest validation accuracy. Compute test accuracy (mean realised performance x 100) of every policy, per-subtask accuracy of every policy, the within-subtask gain of the best learned router over P2 for each subtask, the task classifier's own test accuracy, and D = acc(best learned router) - acc(P3) with a 95% paired bootstrap CI over test queries (1000 resamples).

event.description: The validation-selected best learned router beats the task-classifier router (predicted subtask -> that subtask's best training model) by less than 1 percentage point of test accuracy on the Generic track.
event.statistic: D = test accuracy of the best learned router minus test accuracy of the task-classifier router, in percentage points

evaluation.procedure: outputs/mve1_per_query.jsonl holds one record per test query with task_name, the model chosen by every policy P1-P8 and the realised performance of each choice; outputs/mve1_summary.json holds overall and per-subtask accuracies of all policies, the validation accuracies used for selection, the task-classifier accuracy, the within-subtask gains, and D with its bootstrap CI. D is computed from the per-query file as 100*(mean performance of best learned router's choices - mean performance of P3's choices).
evaluation.controls: All policies use the same training rows, embeddings and test queries, so differences reflect only the routing rule. P1 (best single) and P8 (oracle) bound the achievable range; P2 (gold-label task oracle) separates task-classification error from the routing rule; P4 replicates the seed's own kNN so the reproduction can be checked against the seed's reported 71.37.

registration.full_scale_study: A cross-benchmark re-analysis (xRouteBench, RouterBench, LLMRouterBench) of how much reported routing gain is task recognition versus instance-level competence prediction, establishing the per-task best model as the mandatory baseline, reporting within-task headroom per benchmark, and adding a hierarchical task-first router to the LLMRouter library as a reference baseline.

agent.reason: Plateau-style evidence (kNN ≈ global-best Elo on five benchmarks, routers favouring globally strong models) suggests within-subtask gains over the per-subtask best model are near zero, and D has only ~0.6 pp of paired noise on 3,729 queries; the main risk is genuine subject-level complementarity among the 18 heterogeneous open models that a validation-selected per-model predictor can exploit.

judge_astra.reason: Strong subtask and prompt-format cues should make the task-classifier baseline competitive, while per-task averages avoid noisy per-query winner labels. The main uncertainty is whether P6/P7 capture enough genuine within-task specialization to exceed the one-point margin.

judge_fable.reason: Task identity is almost perfectly recoverable from the subtask-specific prompt templates, and routing literature (kNN-parity, plateau analyses) plus the near-identical RouterDC/GraphRouter scores suggest learned routers mostly converge to the per-task best model; within-task query-level gains on binary-correctness tasks are typically well under 1 pp, though subject-level variation in MMLU/MMLU-Pro and selection noise leave real uncertainty.

judge_opus.reason: Embeddings should identify the subtask almost perfectly. Per-model kNN and MLP predictors usually gain only fractions of a point beyond the per-task best model, so D < 1 is likely. Subject-level heterogeneity inside MMLU and MMLU-Pro (reasoning vs knowledge-heavy models) could push D near 1.

judge_sol.reason: Task-specific formats should make task recognition relatively easy and let the baseline capture substantial between-task specialization. The tight one-point threshold remains uncertain because the validation-selected predictors can exploit subject or difficulty differences within tasks.

judge_luna.reason: The fixed prompt formats likely make many task identities recoverable from embeddings, so a per-subtask best-model policy could explain much of the mixed-task gain. Query-level model strengths and confusion among similar QA subtasks could still leave the learned router more than one point ahead.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: Generic mixes 13 format-distinct subtasks and seed kNN/SVM use same embeddings that cluster by task. Inference: task classifier should near task-oracle and match P4-P7 best; uncertainty is confusion within shared MC templates and within-subtask gains.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: LLMRouterBench already compares learned routers (EmbedLLM, GraphRouter, MODEL-SAT, Avengers, RouterDC) against a 'Dataset Oracle' that sends each dataset to its single best model. It finds the top routers sit close to that oracle and concludes that much of the routing gain comes from capturing coarse domain structure. The registered experiment differs in four ways: it uses xRouteBench Generic and LLMRouter-style routers; it adds a deployable predicted-task classifier (P3) next to the gold-label task oracle; it picks the per-task best model on training data, whereas the Dataset Oracle peaks on the test set; and it reports per-subtask gains with a bootstrap confidence interval.

The Routing Plateau shows that about 21 routers cluster on one accuracy plateau and mostly learn global capability trends. Its by-domain grouping only checks that the plateau holds within each domain. It never trains a classify-the-task-then-pick-the-best-model baseline, never measures within-task gain over the per-task best model, and does not use xRouteBench.
Shows that a frozen-embedding kNN router matches learned routers, but does not split routing gains into a between-task part and a within-task part.
Observes qualitatively that preference-trained routers make category-driven decisions, but does not measure that against a policy that picks the best model per category.
On coding tasks it compares a heuristic router built on task-dimension performance statistics with LLM routers. It is not a decomposition of learned-router gains on a mixed-task benchmark.

opus.reason: LLMRouterBench (2601.07206) already asks the central question, how much routing gain is just per-dataset model selection. It answers it by setting learned routers beside a per-dataset best-model oracle and concluding that their gains largely reflect coarse domain structure. The registered experiment carries the same comparison over to xRouteBench Generic and makes it stricter: a predicted-task classifier instead of an oracle, best models chosen on training data, per-subtask gains and bootstrap CIs. That makes it a close variant rather than a new question. The finding may still not carry over, because the seed's Generic track shows wide gaps between routers (RouterDC 80.56 vs kNN 71.37), unlike the tight plateaus reported elsewhere.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: FineRouter's Section 4.4 and Table 2 compare task-classifier-then-top-model policies (Coarse CLS and Fine CLS), using training-data model rankings, against instance-level learned routing, with per-benchmark accuracies. The proposed experiment instead uses benchmark subtask identities, frozen embeddings and mean correctness, and adds a gold-task control and paired bootstrap analysis.

Expected Reward Prediction compares learned ERP and Zooter routers against a per-category policy selecting the model with the highest average training reward, and examines within-category predictive signal. It does not train the proposed task classifier or evaluate xRouteBench.

LLMRouterBench compares learned routers with a Dataset Oracle selecting one model per dataset and explicitly interprets their proximity as evidence of coarse domain recognition. It does not evaluate a predicted-task-then-best-training-model policy.

sol.reason: Scalable Prompt Routing via Fine-Grained Latent Task Discovery already performs the central comparison: explicit task recognition followed by task-level model selection versus instance-sensitive learned routing on a mixed QA, mathematics and coding workload. Applying that comparison to xRouteBench with different task labels, supervision and uncertainty reporting is a close variant; the gold-task control adds diagnostic detail rather than a substantially new research question.

opus.reason: Both test, on the xRouteBench Generic matrix, whether a router that predicts the subtask from query embeddings and sends it to that subtask's best training model recovers the gains of query-level kNN/SVM/MLP routers, with oracle references.

sol.reason: Both compare predicted-task-to-best-model routing against query-level routers on the Generic track, measuring how much routing gain is explained by task recognition.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I ran: mve1.py implements the registered MVE as written. It loads ulab-ai/xRouteBench 'llmrouter_generic' and 'llm_candidates', decoding JSON fields the way seed download_data.py does. It builds query×18-model performance matrices keyed by embedding_id. The train split has 4,489 queries and the test split 3,729; there are 0 NaN or missing cells. Train queries are split 90/10 into fit and validation sets, stratified by task_name with seed 0. Queries are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (fp16, last-token pooling, L2-normalised, max_len 512, batch 64). The script then runs policies P1–P8 as registered, picks the best learned router (P4–P7) by validation accuracy, and computes D with a paired bootstrap CI (1,000 resamples). It writes outputs/mve1_per_query.jsonl, outputs/mve1_summary.json and result.json, and recomputes D from the per-query file. Two full runs gave identical results.

Result: D = +0.31 pp, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.65, +1.32]. The validation-selected best learned router is P6, the per-model kNN predictor; k = 50 was chosen on validation. So the registered event (D < 1) occurs. However, the CI includes 1 pp, so this does not establish that the two routers are equivalent within 1 pp.

Test accuracies:
- P1 best single model (cogito-v2-1-671b): 80.54
- P2 task oracle: 81.02
- P3 task classifier: 77.21
- P4 seed-style kNN classifier: 60.42
- P5 MLP classifier: 61.37
- P6 per-model kNN predictor: 77.52
- P7 multi-output MLP: 77.89
- P8 per-query oracle: 92.93

**Important caveat: every learned policy and P3 score below the best single model on test.** So in this setup there is no learned-router gain over the best single model for task identity to "explain". Part of the reason is that train and test have very different task mixes. For example, mmlu_pro has 63 training queries but 500 test queries, and mmlu has 450 training queries. The task classifier is right on 90% of validation queries but only 70% of test queries (3% on mmlu_pro, 21% on mmlu), so most of P3's loss against P2 comes from misclassified tasks. Within-subtask gains of P6 over P2 are mostly negative; math is the exception at +2.4.

**Reproduction check failed:** P4, the seed's kNN, gets 60.42 when trained on the 90% fit set and 60.61 when trained on the full train split (a diagnostic only), against the seed's reported 71.37. I did not resolve this gap. Possible causes I did not test include the embedding precision (fp16 here versus the seed script's fp32) and differences in the released data or pipeline.

Small additions not specified in the registration:
- Ties in P1, P2 and P8 are broken by lower blended price, matching the rule registered for P6.
- The seed-style labels group by the flattened query text (two train texts are duplicates).
- The full-train P4 diagnostic is reported in the summary and the per-query file but is not a candidate for best learned router.
- P5 uses the registered 50 epochs and batch size 256, not the seed's hparams.yaml values (100 epochs, batch 32).

No hosted model APIs were used.

departures: mve1.py breaks ties in P1, P2 and P8 by lower blended price. The registration specifies this only for P6. The engineer reported it. P8's realised performance cannot change, and an exact tie in mean training performance for P1 or P2 is unlikely, so it should not change D.

mve1.py builds the seed-style labels (P4, P5) by grouping on the flattened query text instead of the raw 'query' field. The engineer reported it. Only two duplicate train texts are affected, so the effect is negligible, and P4 and P5 were not selected as the best learned router.
mve1.py adds a P4 trained on the full train split as a diagnostic only. It is not a selection candidate and has no effect on D.
mve1.py batches embeddings sorted by length, with left padding. The engineer did not report this. It has no effect on last-token embeddings beyond fp16 numerical noise.

The registered control is that P4 should reproduce the seed's kNN at 71.37. P4 scores 60.42 (60.61 on full train). This is not a code departure, but the setup does not reproduce the seed. The cause is untested; fp16 versus fp32 embeddings and a different data release are possibilities.
run_eval.sh does not pip-install torch and relies on it being preinstalled. The run succeeded, so there is no effect on the result.
problems: The registered reproduction control failed (outputs/mve1_summary.json). Seed-style kNN scores 60.42–60.61 against the seed's reported 71.37, so these numbers cannot be read as a reinterpretation of the seed's headline Generic results.

The hypothesis assumes learned routers gain over the best single model, and that premise fails here. P1 (cogito-v2-1-671b) scores 80.54 on test and beats every learned router (best 77.89) and P3 (77.21). There is therefore no learned-router gain for task identity to explain, and the D < 1 event says little about the intended decomposition.
D = 0.31 pp, but its 95% bootstrap CI of [-0.65, 1.32] includes 1. The event holds only on the point estimate; equivalence within 1 pp is not established. The engineer acknowledged this.

Train and test task mixes differ sharply. mmlu_pro has 63 train queries and 500 test queries, and the task classifier is 90% accurate on validation but 70% on test (3% on mmlu_pro, 21% on mmlu). P3's deficit therefore mostly reflects distribution shift, not the routing rule. The validation-based choice of best learned router (P6 at 78.23 vs P7 at 75.70) also did not carry over to test, where P7 scored higher.
P6 selected k=50, the edge of the registered grid, so P6 may be under-tuned. This is a minor point.
opus.reason: The code in mve1.py implements policies P1–P8, the validation split, the selection rule, D and the paired bootstrap essentially as registered. The few additions (price tie-breaks, grouping by query text, a diagnostic P4) do not plausibly move D, and the value is computed from real benchmark data and recomputed from the per-query file. The evidence is nonetheless weak for the registered question. The seed reproduction control fails by about 11 pp. The best single model beats every learned router, so there is no learned-router gain to decompose. The CI on D spans the 1 pp threshold. What remains useful is a credible but setup-dependent observation: on this release of the benchmark, neither learned routers nor the task classifier beat the best single or per-task-best model, and task-mix shift between train and test drives much of the routers' error.

departures: mve1.py adds lower-blended-price tie-breaking for P1, P2 and P8, with model index as a secondary tie-break. The registration leaves these ties unspecified, so this is a permissible implementation choice. Training-score ties could affect P1/P2 test choices and thus P3 and D; P8's realised performance is unchanged by its tie-break.

mve1.py constructs P4/P5 labels by grouping flattened query text ('qtext'), rather than literally grouping the registered 'query' field. Flattening could merge structurally distinct prompts and affect their labels; the data contain two duplicate training texts. Any effect would concern P4/P5, which finish well below P6 on validation, rather than directly changing the selected P6-versus-P3 comparison.

mve1.py adds a full-training-set P4 diagnostic and corresponding output fields. This diagnostic uses validation queries for training, unlike the registered candidate policies, but is excluded from router selection and D. It therefore does not change the registered result.

mve1.py length-sorts queries before embedding them in batches. Batch ordering was not specified in the registration. This can introduce small floating-point differences in embeddings, but there is no evidence of a material effect on the reported result.

mve1.py replaces all missing matrix cells with zero, whereas the registration distinguishes missing cells, retained as NaN, from observed NaN performance values, treated as zero. The evaluation reports no missing or NaN cells, so this departure has no effect here.

mve1.py implements P7 using BCEWithLogitsLoss and takes the argmax of logits instead of explicitly computing sigmoid outputs. This is mathematically equivalent to the registered sigmoid/BCE policy for model selection and does not change the statistic.
problems: outputs/mve1_summary.json reports D = 0.310 pp with a 95% paired-bootstrap interval of [-0.652, 1.324] pp. The point-estimate event occurs, but the interval does not establish that the learned router's advantage is below 1 pp.

The selected P6 scores 77.52%, versus 80.54% for P1; P3 scores 77.21%. Every learned candidate underperforms the best-single baseline on test, so this run supplies no positive learned-router gain over that baseline for task recognition to explain.

The seed-style P4 reproduction is unresolved: 60.42% with the registered fit set and 60.61% in the full-training diagnostic, versus the seed's quoted 71.37%. The evidence does not identify the cause, limiting reinterpretation of the seed's headline results.

Task-classifier accuracy falls from 90.20% on validation to 70.18% on test, including 3.2% on mmlu_pro and 21.2% on mmlu. Together with the reported task-mix shift, this limits how well validation selection characterises test behaviour.

The bootstrap interval in mve1.py conditions on one fitted set of policies and one validation-selected router. It does not quantify variability from training seeds, train/validation splits, or router selection.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation regenerated the required outputs using the registered dataset and embedding model, and the code correctly selects P6 on validation and recomputes D from per-query realised performance. The implementation differences are permissible choices, equivalent computations, or additions without a plausible material effect on the selected comparison. The observed event is supported, but equivalence within 1 percentage point is not established. The controlled finding that the best-single baseline outperforms every learned candidate is meaningful evidence for this setup, while the unresolved seed reproduction and distribution shift prevent a strong claim about what explains the seed paper's gains.

departures: P1, P2 and P8 break exact score ties by lower blended price then lower index (mve1.py argmax_price_tiebreak); the registration specified that rule only for P6. This is an unspecified tie rule. It could change P2's per-task model, hence P3 and D, only if a within-task training mean tied; no tie counts were recorded.

P4/P5 labels are grouped by flattened query text rather than pandas groupby('query') on the stored query field (mve1.py seed_labels). Train has 4489 embedding_ids but 4487 unique texts, so two queries are merged. Could nudge P4/P5 only; their validation accuracy is ~13 pp below P6, so this did not plausibly change the selected router or D.

Blended price is the unweighted mean of input and output per-1M prices, not token-weighted cost (mve1.py). The registration did not define the formula. Could change a P6 tie; unknown whether any tie at atol 1e-12 fired. k=50 was strictly best on validation, so the smaller-k tie-break did not matter.
Bootstrap resamples use numpy seed 0, which the registration did not set (mve1.py). This can move the CI endpoints but not D.

A full-train P4 diagnostic is scored and written into outputs/mve1_per_query.jsonl and outputs/mve1_summary.json but is excluded from best-router selection. Does not change D. Query text in the jsonl is truncated to 300 characters; scoring uses the full text.
problems: Seed kNN control failed: P4 test accuracy 60.42 and full-train diagnostic 60.61 versus the seed's 71.37 (outputs/mve1_summary.json). The pipeline is not anchored to the headline Generic-track number the study meant to reinterpret.

There is no learned-router gain to decompose: validation-selected P6 is 77.52 and P7 is 77.89, both below P1 best-single 80.54; gold task oracle P2 is only +0.48 pp over P1 (outputs/mve1_summary.json). D<1 compares two policies that both lose to a trivial baseline.
D=0.31 has 95% paired bootstrap CI [-0.65, 1.32], which includes 0 and the 1 pp threshold, so the point event does not establish that the routers match within 1 pp (outputs/mve1_summary.json).

Train/test task mix shift: task classifier is 90.2% on validation but 70.2% on test, and 3.2% on mmlu_pro and 21.2% on mmlu (outputs/mve1_summary.json). Most of P3's loss to P2 is misclassification under shift, not a clean task-identity comparison.

Fit-set idxmax labels are dominated by qwen2.5-7b-instruct (2359/4040, outputs/mve1_summary.json seed_label_distribution_fit), so the registered first-row label rule makes P4/P5 weak classifiers and is a plausible cause of the reproduction gap.
grok.reason: The evaluation re-ran mve1.py from scratch, recomputed embeddings with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, and reproduced D=0.310 from the per-query file, with the registered split, policies, validation selection of P6 (k=50), and paired bootstrap. Departures are tie rules and a two-query label grouping that do not plausibly move the reported D, so the run is faithful and the statistic is valid. The result is a supported negative: under this protocol learned routers and even gold task routing do not beat the best single model, and the seed kNN number is not recovered, so D<1 does not reinterpret the seed's Generic-track gains. The CI crossing 1 pp and the unresolved reproduction gap keep the evidence short of a precise confirmation.

grok.what_it_asks: An explicit router that predicts the subtask from the query embedding and routes to that subtask's best training model is compared with learned routers trained on the same embeddings and supervision, on xRouteBench Generic, to see whether learned routing is essentially task recognition.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares learned routers only with smallest and largest models on the mixed Generic track and never runs or names a task-identity router as unfinished work.

relation.reason: The test uses the paper's Generic data and classifier-style routers as working parts and adds a task-identity policy the paper does not evaluate, without testing a claim the paper states.

obvious.reason: A 13-subtask mix whose only fixed baselines are smallest and largest models makes a predict-the-subtask then per-subtask-best-model comparison one of the first follow-ups most routing researchers would write down.

who_would_care.reason: At the stated scope, a clear answer would change how groups using xRouteBench Generic read learned-router scores, not how researchers evaluate routing on other benchmarks.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's Table 2 figures for RouterDC, kNN, and Largest-LLM and its description of the 13-subtask mix and embedding classifiers match the paper, and no depended-on statement is shown false.

answerable.reason: The design scores the task-classifier router and the validation-selected learned router on the same test queries and reports their difference, so either a small or a large gap would answer the comparison.

grok.what_came_out: On 3,729 xRouteBench Generic test queries embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, one run of the validation-chosen per-model kNN (k=50) scored 77.52 against the task-classifier router's 77.21 (D=0.31 points, 95% paired bootstrap CI [-0.65, 1.32] over 1,000 resamples), while the best single model scored 80.54.

prerequisite.reason: The registered policies were trained and scored on a complete query–model matrix, and the failed seed-kNN reproduction check did not change the P6-versus-P3 comparison being read.

evidence.reason: The point gap is 0.31 points in the claimed direction, but the 95% interval [-0.65, 1.32] on 3,729 queries still includes both a near-zero gap and a gap above 1 point.

next_step.reason: The run does not resolve whether the gap is under 1 point because the bootstrap interval is wider than that margin, so the same comparison needs more queries before any larger decision.
next_step.what: The 95% interval [-0.65, 1.32] on 3,729 queries crosses 1 point; rerun the same task-classifier versus learned-router comparison on more queries so the interval can fall entirely below or above 1 point.

opus.what_it_asks: On the xRouteBench Generic track, it compares a two-stage router that predicts a query's subtask and sends it to that subtask's best training model against the best learned per-query router built on the same embeddings and supervision, to learn how much of the learned-router gain is just task recognition.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper's only fixed baselines are Smallest-LLM and Largest-LLM, it never builds a per-subtask best-model or task-classifier router, and it does not name this decomposition as open work.

relation.reason: The experiment tests the paper's claim that learned routers beat fixed baselines against a stricter baseline, a task-identity router, to see whether the claimed per-query routing gain holds up.

obvious.reason: A per-task best-model baseline is a familiar worry on mixed-task routing benchmarks, but setting a task classifier against learned routers would come to mind for only a minority of researchers.

who_would_care.reason: A clear finding that learned routers on mixed-task benchmarks mostly reproduce task recognition would change which baselines people across LLM routing report and how they read router gains.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's numbers match Table 2 (RouterDC 80.56, kNN 71.37, Largest-LLM 70.29), as do its statements that the only fixed baselines are Smallest and Largest LLM and that kNN, SVM and MLP are classifiers over embeddings.

answerable.reason: D itself can always be computed, but reading it as a decomposition of the learned-router gain needs the learned routers to actually show a gain over the best single model in this setup.
answerable.needs: learned routers beat the best single model (reproduce the seed's gain)

opus.what_came_out: With Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B embeddings on 3,729 Generic test queries in a single run, the validation-selected learned router (per-model kNN, k=50) scored 77.52 against 77.21 for the task-classifier router, giving D = +0.31 pp with a 95% bootstrap CI of [−0.65, +1.32]; in the same run the best single model (cogito) scored 80.54, the task oracle 81.02, and the seed-style kNN 60.42 against the paper's reported 71.37.

prerequisite.reason: Every learned router and the task-classifier router scored below the best single model, and the seed's kNN did not reproduce (60.4 vs 71.4), so there was no learned-router gain for task identity to explain.
prerequisite.which: learned routers beat the best single model / reproduce the seed's reported gain

evidence.reason: The prerequisite failed, and the CI for D also spans both zero and the 1 pp margin.

next_step.reason: The run shows why it could not answer its question: the learned routers fell below the best single model, the seed kNN number did not reproduce, and the train and test task mixes differ sharply (for example mmlu_pro, 63 train vs 500 test queries).
next_step.what: Resolve the reproduction gap with the seed pipeline (e.g., fp32 embeddings, seed hyperparameters, full train split) and account for the train/test task-mix shift, so that the learned routers show their reported gain over the best single model; then recompute D and the within-subtask gains.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares a subtask-classifier-then-task-best-model router with validation-selected instance-level learned routers on xRouteBench Generic to learn whether explicit task recognition matches their routing accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper neither measures this task-identity comparison nor explicitly identifies it as an unanswered question.

relation.reason: The experiment introduces a new routing policy using the paper's benchmark and supervision, without testing a stated claim that learned routers outperform task-identity routing.

obvious.reason: A task-specific model-selection baseline is a natural follow-up to a mixed-task routing benchmark, but this explicit task-classifier comparison would probably appear on only several researchers' first-ten lists.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer could change baseline selection and interpretation of routing gains across LLM-routing research.

misreads_paper.reason: The cited scores and classifier descriptions match the text, and the paper designates Smallest/Largest as its rule-based baselines without reporting a per-subtask-best baseline.

answerable.reason: The direct policy comparison and gold-task diagnostic can establish whether the specified task-classifier router matches the specified learned alternatives without requiring reproduction of the paper's headline gain.

sol.what_came_out: Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and precomputed responses from 18 candidates on 3,729 xRouteBench Generic test queries, one evaluated fit scored 77.21% for the task-classifier router versus 77.52% for validation-selected per-model kNN with k=50, giving a learned-minus-task gap of 0.31 percentage points with a 95% paired-bootstrap interval of −0.65 to 1.32.

prerequisite.reason: The task classifier learned to distinguish tasks and the performance matrix was complete, while the failed seed-kNN reproduction and absence of a fixed-model gain do not invalidate this direct policy comparison.

evidence.reason: The paired interval permits both essentially matching performance and a practically relevant learned-router advantage, so the point estimate does not establish near-equivalence.

next_step.reason: The comparison remains unresolved because its interval is insufficiently precise, identifying a concrete limitation to address before scaling up.
next_step.what: Add independent held-out queries with the Generic track's task proportions and repeat training and validation selection across seeds to obtain a more precise, robustness-checked accuracy-gap estimate.

registration.title: Relabel-then-classify (seed) versus predict-then-optimize for cost-aware routing under a fixed reward normalisation
registration.seed_connection: The seed's cost-aware protocol (benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py) replaces each training row's performance with alpha*norm(perf) - beta*norm(cost), takes the per-query argmax as a single 'best model' label, and trains best-model classifiers (kNN/SVM/MLP) on it; its Figure 5 then reports that router rankings reverse as beta grows. Its evaluation also min-max normalises reward over each router's own routed rows, so rewards are not comparable across routers. An alternative that uses the same kNN neighbourhoods is to estimate every model's quality and cost per query and apply the alpha/beta trade-off at decision time.
registration.hypothesis: With identical kNN neighbourhoods and a fixed (training-constant) reward normalisation, a predict-then-optimize router achieves a higher mean test reward than the seed's relabel-then-classify kNN router on xRouteBench Generic, by at least 0.01 averaged over beta in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}.
registration.contribution: RouterBench-style predictive routers and decision-aware routers exist, but no study compares, on the same features and benchmark, the specific relabel-then-classify supervision used by the LLMRouter library against predict-then-optimize across the cost sweep, nor measures how much of the seed's reported cost-aware behaviour is an artefact of single-label supervision and per-router reward normalisation.

closest_work.difference: Argues that scalar-quality prediction suffers an objective-decision mismatch and proposes ranking-based EquiRouter; it does not test the single-label relabelling scheme used by the seed, nor isolate the decision rule with fixed kNN features.
RouterBench introduces predictive kNN/MLP routers with a willingness-to-pay decision rule but does not compare them with relabel-then-classify supervision or evaluate on xRouteBench.

Studies instability of single-sample correctness labels for routing supervision; our MVE studies the loss from collapsing a full per-model reward vector into one argmax label and from per-router reward normalisation.

inputs: HF dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configs 'llmrouter_generic' (train/test) and 'llm_candidates' (input_price_per_1m, output_price_per_1m per model)
Embedding model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from HF
Python packages: datasets, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, torch, transformers
registration.method: Data and embeddings exactly as in the seed pipeline: load 'llmrouter_generic' train/test, decode JSON-encoded fields, group rows by (split, embedding_id) into unique queries, embed query texts with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (last-token pooling, L2-normalised, max_length 512). Cost per row = (input_tokens*input_price_per_1m + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m)/1e6 using llm_candidates prices. Normalisation constants: min and max of performance and of cost over ALL training rows (train split); norm_p and norm_c use these constants everywhere (train labels and test rewards). Hold out 10% of training queries (stratified by task_name, seed 0) as validation. For each beta in {0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8} with alpha = 1 - beta: (A) seed relabel-then-classify: r_row = alpha*norm_p - beta*norm_c; training label per query = model_name of the first row attaining the maximum r in stored row order (pandas idxmax, as in run_pipeline.preprocess_training_data followed by the kNN router's groupby idxmax); fit KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', metric='minkowski', p=2) on the 90% training embeddings; predict a model per test query. (B) predict-then-optimize: for each test query find its k nearest training queries by cosine similarity; p_hat_m = mean performance of model m over those neighbours, c_hat_m = mean cost of model m over those neighbours (NaN-skipping); choose argmax_m alpha*norm(p_hat_m) - beta*norm(c_hat_m); k in {5,10,20,50} selected once on the validation split by mean validation reward averaged over the four beta>0 values. Realised test reward of a chosen model = alpha*norm_p - beta*norm_c of that model's recorded test row (fixed constants). Report for each beta: mean realised performance, mean realised cost in USD, mean reward of A and B, the seed's own per-router min-max normalised reward (as in run_pipeline.evaluate) for reference, routing distributions, and the paired bootstrap 95% CI (1000 resamples over test queries) of reward(B) - reward(A). Also report, at beta = 0 only, three alternative tie-break rules for the classifier labels (random tie-break averaged over 5 seeds; cheapest tied-best model by row cost; tied-best model with the highest overall training mean performance) to show how much the stored row order alone moves accuracy and cost. The registered statistic is the mean over beta in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} of reward(B) - reward(A) under the fixed normalisation.

event.description: Predict-then-optimize with per-model kNN quality and cost estimates yields a higher mean reward than the seed's relabel-then-classify kNN by at least 0.01, averaged over the four cost weights, under a fixed training-constant normalisation.
event.statistic: mean over beta in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} of [mean test reward of predict-then-optimize kNN minus mean test reward of relabel-then-classify kNN], reward = alpha*norm_p - beta*norm_c with training min-max constants

evaluation.procedure: outputs/mve2_per_query.jsonl holds one record per (beta, test query) with the model chosen by A and by B, the realised performance, USD cost and fixed-normalised reward of each choice, and the selected k; outputs/mve2_summary.json holds per-beta means for A and B under both normalisations, the tie-break-rule results at beta=0, routing distributions, and the registered mean difference with its bootstrap CI. The statistic is the average over the four beta>0 values of the per-query mean of reward(B) - reward(A).
evaluation.controls: Both routers use the same embeddings, the same training queries and the same recorded test outcomes; only the supervision/decision rule differs. k for B is chosen on validation, never on test. Reporting the seed's per-router normalisation alongside the fixed one isolates the effect of the normalisation choice. The beta=0 tie-break arms separate the effect of label construction from the effect of cost weighting.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-run the seed's full cost sweep (all tracks, all embedding-based routers) with predict-then-optimize decision rules and a fixed normalisation protocol, compare performance-cost frontiers by hypervolume, and propose per-model reward-vector supervision as the default learning signal in the LLMRouter library.

agent.reason: Because performance is binary, the seed's relabelling turns every beta>0 label into 'cheapest correct model', so its kNN classifier sacrifices accuracy at low beta where the reward is dominated by alpha*perf, while predict-then-optimize trades off explicitly; the margin may still fall under 0.01 if cost normalisation makes cost terms negligible and the accuracy loss of the classifier is small.

judge_astra.reason: Retaining full quality/cost vectors should usually improve on voting over single-winner labels by this modest reward margin. B also receives validation-selected k while A fixes k=5, increasing its chances but weakening attribution of any gain solely to the supervision scheme.

judge_fable.reason: Under a training-constant min-max normalisation the seed's relabelling makes the label the cheapest correct model for every beta>0, so the classifier routes to cheap models even at beta=0.2 where the fixed reward still strongly favours quality; predict-then-optimize should win clearly at low beta and roughly tie at high beta, giving an average margin well above 0.01 unless cost normalisation behaves unexpectedly.

judge_opus.reason: With continuous costs and a max-normalised cost term, relabel-then-classify labels collapse to 'cheapest correct model', so classifier A routes mostly to cheap 8-9B models. Predict-then-optimize picks near-best-accuracy models, which should give roughly 0.5×10-15 pp of reward on average, well above 0.01. The main risks are a cheap-and-strong model dominating the labels, or implementation failure.

judge_sol.reason: Predicting the full outcome vector retains reward information that single-winner labels discard, making an advantage under a common reward normalization likely. Validation-selected neighbourhood size also favors the predictor, although weak local generalization could keep the improvement below 0.01.

judge_luna.reason: Predicting the per-model reward vector and choosing the highest estimated utility is more decision-aligned than voting over hard per-query winners. Noisy kNN estimates could make the advantage too small to clear the 0.01 threshold.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: seed collapses per-model rewards to one idxmax label with row-order tie-breaks. Inference: same-neighborhood predict-then-optimize with tuned k retains reward vectors and should gain >0.01; uncertainty is small typical reward gaps under fixed normalization.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: EquiRouter argues that routers trained to predict scalar scores suffer an objective-decision mismatch, and proposes learning rankings instead. It is evaluated on RouterBench. It does not compare argmax-relabelled single-label classifiers with predict-then-optimize on the same kNN features, and it does not examine per-router reward normalisation or tie-break artefacts on xRouteBench.

RouterBench introduces predictive kNN/MLP routers that use a willingness-to-pay decision rule, which is essentially predict-then-optimize. It does not compare them with relabel-then-classify supervision and does not use xRouteBench.

Shows that a well-tuned kNN router matches or beats complex learned routers, but does not isolate supervision style (argmax label vs per-model estimates) across a cost-weight sweep, and does not address normalisation artefacts.

SCOPE predicts per-model cost and accuracy so the trade-off can be set at decision time. It argues for this design but does not run a controlled comparison against single-label classifiers built from the same neighbourhoods.

Compares 21 routers (kNN and classifiers among them), finds an accuracy plateau, and attributes it to a correctness-prediction bottleneck. Its focus is accuracy limits, not cost-weighted label collapse or reward-normalisation artefacts.

opus.reason: Several papers propose or advocate decision-time quality/cost prediction (RouterBench, SCOPE, EquiRouter), but I found none that runs this controlled ablation. That ablation is relabel-then-classify versus predict-then-optimize, using identical kNN neighbourhoods across the alpha/beta sweep on xRouteBench, with fixed versus per-router reward normalisation and tie-break analysis. The question of how much of LLMRouter's reported cost-aware behaviour comes from its single-label supervision and evaluation protocol is still open.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Rethinking Predictive Modeling for LLM Routing already evaluates both kNN formulations with consistent embeddings: majority voting over neighbours' utility-maximizing model labels, and averaging each model's quality and cost before cost-aware selection (Section 5 and Appendix C.2). It uses different benchmarks and neighbourhood sizes, reporting selection utility at three preferences and predictive-routing Pareto AUC rather than the proposed paired, fixed-training-normalized reward statistic; it does not audit LLMRouter's normalization or stored-order tie breaking.

RouterBench already implements neighbour-averaged per-model quality prediction followed by willingness-to-pay optimization. It does not include the matched relabel-then-classify comparison and approximates decision-time cost using per-token pricing rather than neighbour-estimated query-dependent costs.

Breaking the Tie studies ambiguity in hard routing labels when several models answer correctly and compares hard and cluster-aware soft supervision. Its remedy is a trained soft-label classifier, not per-model kNN prediction followed by cost optimization, and it does not study reward normalization.

sol.reason: By the cutoff, arXiv:2505.12601 had already instantiated and evaluated the experiment's central contrast—utility-argmax-label kNN voting versus per-model kNN quality/cost estimation with decision-time optimization—using matched representations. The xRouteBench application, common fixed-normalized reward statistic, and seed-specific normalization and tie-breaking diagnostics add new details, but the main contribution is a close extension of that existing comparison rather than a distinct routing-supervision question.

opus.reason: Both compare, on xRouteBench, routing by a single per-model quality (and cost) predictor plus an alpha/beta decision rule at test time against the seed's approach of relabelling and retraining a classifier for each cost weight, across the beta sweep.

sol.reason: Both compare per-weight relabel-and-retrain routing with per-candidate quality prediction followed by cost-adjusted optimization, measuring reward and quality–cost trade-offs across the weight sweep.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: mve2/run_mve2.py, launched by run_eval.sh. It installs the dependencies, recomputes the embeddings, writes result.json and outputs/mve2_per_query.jsonl and outputs/mve2_summary.json, and takes about 70 s end to end on the A100. I tested it the same way it will be run.

Setup, as registered:
- Data: HF ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configs llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates, with the JSON-encoded fields decoded. The train split has 4,489 queries and the test split 3,729; each query has a row for all 18 models and no performance values are missing.
- Embeddings: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B in fp32, left padding, last-token pooling, L2-normalised, max_length 512. I used batch size 32 sorted by length instead of the seed's 8. Under masked left padding this should only cause tiny numerical differences.
- Cost per row: (input_tokens × input price + output_tokens × output price) / 1e6.
- Normalisation: fixed min-max constants taken from all training rows (performance from 0 to 1; cost from 1.9e-6 to 1.63e-3 USD).
- Validation split: 10% of training queries, stratified by task, seed 0.
- Router A (the seed's relabel-then-classify): per query, the label is the first row in stored order with the maximum reward, using pandas idxmax. The classifier is KNeighborsClassifier(5, uniform, minkowski p=2), fitted on the other 90%.
- Router B (predict-then-optimize): cosine k nearest neighbours in the same 90% set. It averages each model's performance and cost over the neighbours (skipping NaNs) and picks the argmax of the fixed-normalised trade-off. Candidate k values were {5, 10, 20, 50}; k=10 was chosen on validation only.
- The bootstrap is paired over test queries, with 1,000 resamples.

Small deviation: I grouped rows by embedding_id, as the registration says, rather than by query text as the seed kNN does (groupby('query')). This only matters for 2 query texts in train, which each map to 2 embedding_ids.

Results:
- **Registered statistic: 0.0045, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0011, 0.0103].** This is below the 0.01 threshold, so the registered event did not occur. The CI does not rule out a gain of about 0.01, so this is not evidence that the two routers are equivalent.
- Reward difference B − A by cost weight:

| β | B − A | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | +0.0173 | [0.007, 0.028] |
| 0.4 | +0.0031 | |
| 0.6 | −0.0009 | |
| 0.8 | −0.0015 | |

- At β=0 (not part of the statistic) the gap is +0.170.
- Under the seed's per-router min-max normalisation, the difference changes from +0.015 at β=0.2 to −0.067 at β=0.8. So the choice of normalisation changes the sign of the comparison at high cost weights.

Supplementary findings:
- **Ties drive the seed's labels.** At β=0, 93.5% of training queries have tied best models (11.9 tied on average), and the stored row order puts cheap models first.
- Test performance at β=0 depends heavily on the tie-break rule: stored row order 0.604, cheapest tied model 0.705, random 0.713 (mean of 5 seeds), tied model with the best overall training mean 0.807. Predict-then-optimize B reaches 0.775 at β=0.
- **The seed classifier ignores the cost weight.** For every β>0, its labels collapse to "cheapest correct model" (gpt-oss-20b on about 78% of test queries), and the routing barely changes as β grows. This is because the reward is constant across correct models apart from a very small normalised-cost term.

The summary file also includes per-task breakdowns, oracle and fixed-model reference rewards, and routing distributions.

departures: mve2/run_mve2.py embeds queries with batch size 32 after sorting by length. The seed uses batch size 8. The engineer reported this. With masked left padding and last-token pooling it should cause only tiny numerical differences, and both routers share the embeddings, so it is unlikely to move the statistic.

Query text for embedding is built by query_to_text, which joins the 'content' fields when the decoded query is a list of messages. The registration and the notes do not say whether this matches the seed's text construction exactly. It could perturb the embeddings slightly, but it affects A and B equally, so a material change to the B−A difference is unlikely.

Queries are grouped by embedding_id rather than by query text as in the seed kNN. This is not a departure from the registration, which specifies embedding_id. The engineer disclosed it, and it affects 2 training texts, so the impact is negligible.
Router B breaks argmax ties by model index (alphabetical order of model names). The registration leaves this open, and it does not change the question.
The per-beta bootstrap CIs use a separate RNG seed (1234) from the registered-statistic bootstrap (seed 0). This is a choice the registration leaves open and does not affect the point estimate.
problems: The registered result is inconclusive with respect to the threshold. The point estimate is 0.0045 with 95% CI [-0.0011, 0.0103], so the data neither exclude 0.01 nor exclude 0. The engineer correctly says this is not evidence of equivalence.

The construction of the registered statistic compresses differences at high beta. Performance differences are scaled by alpha = 1-beta. The fixed cost normalisation divides by a max of about 1.63e-3 USD, while typical routed costs are about 1e-5, so the cost term is tiny. The averaged statistic is therefore dominated by beta = 0.2, and the 0.01 threshold is relatively demanding. This is a registration design issue, not an implementation defect.
There is a single train/validation/test split and one run (as registered). There is no variance over validation splits or k selection.

Several claims in the engineer notes cannot be checked from the visible output because outputs/mve2_summary.json is truncated: about 78% of test queries routed to gpt-oss-20b at beta > 0, 93.5% tied training queries with 11.9 tied on average, and the seed-normalisation difference going from +0.015 to −0.067. The parts that are visible in stdout are consistent with them; for example, A's constant 0.7050 performance at beta > 0 equals the cheapest-tied-best arm.
run_eval.sh installs unpinned package versions, which is a minor reproducibility risk.
opus.reason: The code in mve2/run_mve2.py follows the registered method closely: fixed training min-max constants, a stratified 10% validation hold-out, seed-style idxmax relabelling with kNN(5), cosine-kNN predict-then-optimize with k selected on validation only, a paired bootstrap, the beta = 0 tie-break arms, and the seed per-router normalisation for reference. The only departures are minor embedding-batch details and choices the registration leaves open. The fresh evaluation reproduced the value 0.0045 from real data and recomputed embeddings, and the per-beta rewards in stdout are internally consistent with the reward formula; I found no leakage or hard-coding. The registered event did not occur, but the CI straddles both 0 and the 0.01 threshold, so this is an inconclusive null rather than a demonstrated absence of effect. The supplementary diagnostics are credible and informative: the seed labels collapse to the cheapest correct model for every beta > 0, and at beta = 0 stored-row-order tie-breaking costs about 0.2 in accuracy relative to an informed tie-break.

departures: mve2/run_mve2.py, embed_split: embeddings are computed in length-sorted batches of 32 rather than the seed's batches of 8 described in the engineer's notes. This departs from literal seed-identical embedding computation, although batch size was not explicitly fixed in the registration. It could introduce small floating-point differences; no evidence shows a consequential change to neighbours or the reported statistic.

mve2/run_mve2.py: min-max denominators include an additional 1e-12, and test-loop alpha values are rounded to ten decimal places. These are numerical implementation differences from the written formula. Their direct effects are negligible relative to the observed difference, confidence interval and event threshold.

mve2/run_mve2.py: additional missing-data rules include zero-price defaults for unmatched model names, dropping NaN training rewards, ignoring NaN realised rewards, and retaining jointly non-NaN pairs for differences. The registration explicitly permits NaN-skipping neighbour estimates but does not specify these other fallbacks. They could change results if activated; the supplied complete-data account and evaluation provide no evidence that they affected this run.

mve2/run_mve2.py: the supplementary highest-overall-training-mean tie-break computes model means from the 90% fitting subset. The registration's phrase 'overall training mean' does not clearly specify whether it includes validation queries. This is an implementation interpretation rather than a clear violation; using all training queries could change supplementary labels if model rankings changed, but would not affect the registered statistic.
problems: The registration describes identical neighbourhoods and says only supervision/decision rule differs, but its detailed method fixes A at k=5 while tuning B, which selected k=10. mve2/run_mve2.py follows that method, so this is a design limitation rather than an implementation violation: the comparison does not isolate the decision rule alone.

The engineer's notes claim that normalisation changes the comparison's sign at high cost weights. Their quoted beta=0.8 differences are negative under both normalisations: approximately -0.0015 fixed versus -0.067 per-router. Those numbers demonstrate a magnitude change, not a sign reversal at that weight.

The engineer's categorical statement that the classifier 'ignores the cost weight' overstates the evidence. The protected evaluation supports near-invariance over the tested positive weights, but A's realised performance and cost change at beta=0.8. Nor does the reward formula universally guarantee a cheapest-correct-model label.

The bootstrap in mve2/run_mve2.py measures test-query sampling uncertainty conditional on one fitting/validation split and the selected k. It does not capture training-split or hyperparameter-selection variability, and its interval includes both zero and the registered 0.01 threshold.

Grouping by embedding_id is explicitly registered and therefore is not a fidelity departure, despite being called a deviation from the seed in the engineer's notes. It does limit claims of exact seed reproduction for the reported duplicated query texts.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation recomputed embeddings, completed successfully, produced both registered raw outputs, and wrote a statistic consistent with the supplied computation and summary. The implementation follows the registered detailed comparison, with only negligible numerical differences and unspecified implementation choices, and there is no supported evidence of leakage, fabricated outcomes or conclusion-changing calculation errors. The registered gain was 0.004497 with a paired-bootstrap 95% interval of approximately [-0.00110, 0.01030], so the event did not occur, but neither equivalence nor exclusion of a 0.01 gain is established. The cost-sweep results and substantial supplementary tie-break sensitivity constitute meaningful evidence, while the unequal tuned neighbourhood sizes, conditional uncertainty and single-benchmark scope prevent a particularly strong causal or general conclusion.

departures: Embedding uses batch size 32 with length-sorted batches (mve2/run_mve2.py embed_split) instead of the seed pipeline batch size 8 implied by 'embeddings exactly as in the seed pipeline'. Masked left-padding and last-token pooling make this unlikely to change embeddings beyond tiny numeric noise, so it is unlikely to change the reported statistic.
Alpha is round(1-beta, 10) rather than 1-beta (mve2/run_mve2.py). The difference is ~1e-16 and does not change the result.

The beta=0 'highest overall training mean' tie-break computes model means on the 90% fit split only, not all training rows (mve2/run_mve2.py). It does not enter the registered statistic and is unlikely to change that supplementary arm.

B's test-time neighbours come from the 90% fit split, not necessarily every training query (mve2/run_mve2.py). The method's 'training queries' is ambiguous; this reading matches the control that both routers share the same training queries. Relative to using the held-out 10% as well, it could slightly change B's reward.

B breaks score ties by alphabetical model order via numpy argmax on a sorted model list (mve2/run_mve2.py). The registration does not specify a tie-break; exact ties in neighbour means are rare, so this is unlikely to change the mean reward.
problems: The 95% CI [-0.0011, 0.0103] in outputs/mve2_summary.json includes both 0 and the 0.01 threshold, so the negative event result does not rule out a gain of 0.01 and does not establish equivalence.

On this binary performance data the normalised cost term is too small to change argmax labels across beta in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}: evaluation log shows router A's test performance and cost essentially constant (perf 0.705, cost ~1.6e-5). The pre-registered average therefore mixes a real gap at beta=0.2 (+0.017) with near-zero gaps at higher beta. Per-beta results are reported, so this is a limitation of the registered summary, not a hidden error.
Batch-size deviation from the seed embedding pipeline (mve2/run_mve2.py) is unquantified, though implausible as a driver of the 0.0045 statistic.
grok.reason: The code runs the registered comparison: same xRouteBench Generic rows, fixed training min-max constants, a 10% task-stratified hold-out, seed-style pandas idxmax labels with a k=5 minkowski kNN, and predict-then-optimize with k chosen only on validation. Departures are either negligible or choices the registration leaves open, and none plausibly moves the reported value or changes the question. The fresh run recomputed embeddings and wrote 0.00450 with CI [-0.0011, 0.0103], which matches the logged per-beta gaps and is internally consistent with the performance and cost means, so the event correctly did not occur. That is a credible, mechanism-backed negative on the 0.01 claim, but the CI still reaches the threshold, so the evidence is meaningful rather than decisive.

sol.what_came_out: Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and recorded outcomes from the 18-model pool on 3,729 xRouteBench Generic test queries in one run, predict-then-optimize exceeded relabel-then-classify by 0.004497 in average fixed-normalized reward across the four positive cost weights (paired-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.001100, 0.010299]), with respective per-weight differences of +0.0173, +0.0031, -0.0009, and -0.0015.
