registration.title: How much of the xRouteBench Generic routing gain is benchmark identity? A train-fitted task lookup versus learned routers under argmax-label and full-matrix supervision
registration.seed_connection: The seed reports that learned routers improve 14.6% over the strongest fixed model and describes its Generic track (13 pooled source benchmarks) as testing whether a router 'can recognize these distinctions within an apparently uniform text setting'. It reports no best-single-model, task-level or oracle reference, so the shares of the gain due to (a) choosing one better global model, (b) identifying the source benchmark and (c) query-level selection inside a benchmark are unknown. The released library also appears to train its kNN/SVM/MLP routers on one argmax label per query (first row attaining the maximum, so ties among the many correct models are broken by file order) instead of the recorded 18-model outcome vector, which may explain part of their ~9-point deficit to RouterDC/GraphRouter in Table 2. Both questions can be answered offline from the released query-model matrix.
registration.hypothesis: On held-out Generic test queries, the best learned embedding router - including routers trained on the full query-model performance matrix - adds less than 2 points of mean recorded performance over a 13-entry lookup table that assigns each source benchmark the single model that is best on that benchmark's training split.
registration.contribution: Lee (2026) shows in-sample on 294 items that task type explains most of the oracle gap, and LLMRouterBench reports a dataset-level oracle; neither evaluates a train-fitted lookup on held-out queries against learned routers at xRouteBench scale (3,729 test queries, 18 models) with confidence intervals, and neither separates the lookup effect from the supervision effect of argmax-label training. The experiment delivers the Largest -> Best-single -> Task-ID -> learned -> within-task -> Oracle decomposition missing from the seed and, as a by-product with everything else held fixed, the paired effect of replacing argmax labels with full-matrix supervision for the same kNN and MLP.

closest_work.difference: Lee fits and scores a per-task-type table on the same 294 questions with no holdout and no learned router; here the lookup is fitted on the train split, scored on ~3,729 held-out queries and compared with learned routers under paired bootstrap CIs.

LLMRouterBench reports a dataset-level oracle as an analysis of the oracle gap on text datasets; here the dataset-level policy is a deployable train-fitted baseline compared head-to-head with learned routers on the seed's benchmark, together with within-task routing.

EquiRouter attributes router failures to an objective-decision mismatch and proposes ranking losses; here the specific argmax-label construction of the seed's library is contrasted with pointwise full-matrix supervision as a secondary, fully paired comparison.

Li argues frozen-embedding kNN matches learned routers in general; this experiment measures how much any embedding router adds beyond benchmark identity on xRouteBench and which supervision the kNN needs to get there.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench: config 'llmrouter_generic' (train and test splits; one row per (query, model) with task_name, query, model_name, performance, and if present input_tokens/output_tokens, ground_truth, choices) and config 'llm_candidates' (model_name, size, input_price_per_1m, output_price_per_1m). Load with datasets.load_dataset; if a config name is not found, use get_dataset_config_names and match by substring, logging the mapping.
Embedding model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Hugging Face, ungated).
Python: torch, transformers>=4.51, datasets, scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, scipy.

Optional reference only: benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py and llmrouter/models/knnrouter/router.py in https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter (may be cloned to check the label construction; not required).
registration.method: 0) Schema check: load both configs; print columns and sizes into the summary under 'schema'. Required: query, model_name, performance, task_name (if task_name is absent, derive it from a 'dataset'/'source'/'task' column; if none exists, write the summary with status 'aborted_no_task_identifier' and stop). Decode JSON-encoded string fields (values starting with '[' or '{'); if a query is a list of chat messages, join the 'content' fields with newlines. Preserve the downloaded row order. If no train split exists, build 5 stratified folds (by task_name) over unique queries with seed 0, treat each fold as test with the others as train, and flag this. 1) Matrices: unique queries keyed by query text; P[q,m] = recorded performance (NaN if missing); C[q,m] = input_tokens*input_price_per_1m/1e6 + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m/1e6 if token columns exist (else skip cost reporting). Retain models with recorded outcomes for at least 95% of train and of test queries; report the retained list and missing-cell counts. The decision set of a test query = retained models with a recorded outcome on that query; every policy selects within it. If the train split has more than 40,000 unique queries, subsample 40,000 stratified by task_name for all training (flag). 2) Embeddings: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B through transformers AutoModel; tokenizer padding_side='left', truncation at 512 tokens, last-token hidden state, L2-normalised, bf16 or fp32 on GPU, batch 64; one 1024-d vector per unique train/test query. 3) Seed-style labels on train: label_first(q) = model_name of the FIRST row in downloaded order among q's rows attaining the maximum performance; label_rand(q) = a uniformly random tied maximiser (seeded). Record the fraction of train queries with >=2 tied maximisers, the class histogram and entropy of label_first, and the most frequent label with its share. 4) Policies: (a) Largest-LLM = largest parsed 'size' (if two models tie, evaluate both: Largest-A = first in llm_candidates order, Largest-B = the other); (b) Best-single = highest mean train performance; (c) Task-ID lookup = for each task_name the model with the highest mean train performance on that task (ties -> lower mean train cost), unseen task -> Best-single; (d) kNN-cls = sklearn KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', p=2) on the embeddings with label_first (the seed protocol); kNN-cls-rand = same with label_rand, seeds 0-4; (e) kNN-reg = for each test query take the k nearest train queries by cosine similarity, score every model by the mean recorded performance over those neighbours (NaN ignored), pick the argmax (ties -> lower blended price); k chosen from {5,10,20,50} by 5-fold CV on train maximising replayed mean performance; (f) MLP-CE = 1024->256->128->K (K = classes present in label_first), ReLU, Adam lr 1e-3, weight_decay 1e-4, batch 256, 60 epochs, cross-entropy on label_first; route by the highest-probability class inside the decision set; (g) MLP-pointwise = same trunk with one output per retained model, BCE-with-logits against P[q,.] clipped to [0,1] with NaN cells masked out of the loss; route by argmax predicted score; (h) MLP-pointwise+task = (g) with a one-hot of task_name concatenated to the embedding; (i) Oracle = max over the decision set. Run (f)-(h) with seeds 0-4 and average per-query outcomes over seeds. 5) Within-task analysis: for each of the 7 task_names with the most test queries (expected 500 each), fit kNN-reg using only that task's train rows (k by CV inside the task) and compare its test performance with the within-task train-fitted best single model and the within-task oracle; report per-task gains and their mean. 6) Scoring: accuracy of a policy = 100 * mean over all test queries of the recorded performance of its selected model (micro); also the macro mean over task_name and the mean dollar cost. L* = the learned policy among {kNN-cls, kNN-cls-rand, kNN-reg, MLP-CE, MLP-pointwise, MLP-pointwise+task} with the highest seed-averaged micro accuracy on the test split. Delta_q = perf_L*(q) - perf_TaskID(q) (seed-averaged); paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples of test queries; the statistic is the 97.5th percentile of the bootstrap distribution of 100*mean(Delta_q). Also report: the full decomposition table (Largest-A/B, Best-single, Task-ID, every learned policy, Oracle) with the fraction of the Oracle-minus-Best-single gap closed by each; the paired supervision contrasts kNN-reg minus kNN-cls, MLP-pointwise minus MLP-CE and kNN-cls-rand minus kNN-cls with 95% bootstrap CIs; per-task tables; the label-tie statistics of step 3.

event.description: The upper bound of the 95% paired-bootstrap CI of [accuracy of the best learned embedding router minus accuracy of the train-fitted task-ID lookup] on held-out Generic test queries is below 2 percentage points, i.e. learned routers demonstrably add less than 2 points beyond benchmark identity.
event.statistic: 97.5th percentile of the paired bootstrap distribution of 100*(mean test performance of the best learned router L*, seed-averaged, minus mean test performance of the task-ID lookup) over Generic test queries

evaluation.procedure: outputs/e1_per_query.jsonl holds one line per test query with task_name, decision-set size, oracle performance, and for every policy (and every seed for seeded policies) the selected model, its recorded performance and cost. outputs/e1_summary.json holds the schema report, retained models and missing-cell counts, label-tie statistics, chosen k values, micro/macro accuracy and mean cost of every policy, the decomposition table with gap-closure fractions, the per-task tables, the within-task results, the supervision-contrast CIs, the identity of L*, the point estimate of Delta and its 95% CI, and the registered statistic under key 'ci_upper_learned_minus_taskid'.
evaluation.controls: Largest-LLM and Best-single bound the global-model component and Oracle bounds the query-level component; kNN-cls reproduces the seed's own label protocol with the same embeddings; taking the best of six learned routers on the test split is conservative for the registered 'adds little' event; the CI-upper-bound criterion prevents reading a non-significant difference as equivalence; the within-task analysis measures query-level signal with task identity removed; the paired supervision contrasts hold features, architecture, optimiser and seeds fixed so only the label construction differs.

registration.full_scale_study: A benchmark-identity and supervision audit of LLM routing evaluations: add train-fitted task lookups and full-matrix-supervised simple routers as mandatory baselines on xRouteBench, RouterBench and LLMRouterBench, evaluate all LLMRouter single-turn routers under task-stratified protocols (within-task routing, held-out benchmarks) and the full cost-weight sweep, and quantify the true query-level routing headroom per task family and per budget.

agent.reason: A train-fitted task lookup already captures the dominant task-level component, and prior work finds frozen-embedding routers add only modest within-task gains; but with ~3,700 paired queries the CI half-width is only about 1 point and the best-of-six selection on test adds bias, so the registered upper bound below 2 points requires a point gain under roughly 1 point, which is close to a coin flip leaning negative.

judge_astra.reason: Task identity and better global model selection should explain much of the gain in this pooled benchmark mixture. However, full-matrix supervision could uncover useful within-task variation, and the upper-confidence-bound criterion is more demanding than merely observing a small difference.

judge_fable.reason: A train-fitted per-task lookup is a strong baseline and frozen-embedding routers usually extract little within-task signal, but the registered criterion is tight: with ~3,700 paired queries the CI half-width is only ~1.1 points, so the event fails if the best of six full-matrix routers (kNN-reg, MLP-pointwise+task, selected on the test split) gains even ~1 point from sub-task structure or model-specific format/truncation failures that embeddings can predict.

judge_opus.reason: The event needs the 95% bootstrap upper bound of (best of six learned routers minus a train-fitted per-task lookup) to fall below 2 points. That requires a point estimate under about 1 point. Within-task routing gains are usually small, but truncation-driven and subject-level differences between the strong models, plus choosing the best router on the test set, could push the estimate past that, so this is close to a coin flip.

judge_sol.reason: A task lookup should capture substantial gains from pooling benchmarks with different capability requirements, while predicting model failures within a task is harder. Full-matrix supervision and selecting the strongest learned policy make the upper-confidence-bound criterion meaningfully harder to satisfy.

judge_luna.reason: A train-fitted task lookup should capture much of the between-benchmark capability variation, making a residual below 2 points plausible. But the seed’s strong query-aware results and selecting the best of six learned routers on the test split leave room for a larger within-task gain.

judge_muse.reason: Task identity likely captures most of the Generic gain and simple embedding routers may struggle to beat a train-fitted lookup, but picking the best of six on test and requiring the 95% CI upper bound below 2 points makes the event demanding.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Lee concludes that task type explains most of the routing gap, but on a 14-model × 294-item matrix where the per-task table is fitted and scored on the same items. There is no holdout, no learned router and nothing on xRouteBench. The proposed experiment fits the task lookup on the train split, scores it on about 3.7k held-out queries, compares it head-to-head with learned routers using paired bootstrap CIs, and adds a contrast between argmax-label and full-matrix supervision.

LLMRouterBench reports a dataset-level oracle and takes a small gap to it as a sign that coarse domain structure accounts for much of the gain. That oracle is a hindsight analysis on its own benchmark. It is not a train-fitted, deployable lookup compared with learned routers on xRouteBench, and it does not vary the supervision type.

The Routing Plateau paper finds that 21 routers on five other benchmarks converge and mostly learn global model-capability trends. From what I read (its main text up to Section 5.1), it includes no train-fitted benchmark-identity lookup baseline, does not test xRouteBench, and does not isolate argmax-label from full-matrix supervision. Its conclusion points the same way but does not settle the specific comparison.

EquiRouter traces router failures to a mismatch between training objective and routing decision, and proposes ranking losses on RouterBench. It does not test the specific tie-breaking argmax-label construction in LLMRouter's kNN/MLP routers, and it has no task-ID baseline.
Shows that a tuned frozen-embedding kNN matches complex routers on its own benchmark suite. It does not measure how much any router adds beyond benchmark identity, and it does not use xRouteBench.

This is the seed paper, and I only saw its abstract here. The experiment's own description says it reports no best-single-model, task-level or oracle decomposition for its 14.6% gain; I did not check that against the full text.

opus.reason: Prior work strongly suggests that much of the measured routing gain is coarse task or dataset structure: Lee does so in-sample, LLMRouterBench through a hindsight dataset-level oracle, and the Routing Plateau paper by showing routers mostly learn global trends. None of these papers compares a train-fitted task-ID lookup with learned routers on held-out queries from xRouteBench's Generic track. None tests whether the best learned router beats such a lookup by at least 2 points under a CI upper-bound criterion, and none isolates the effect of the seed library's argmax-label supervision. The direction of the answer is anticipated, but no paper I found answers this specific question.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: FineRouter's ablations compare a held-out, training-derived task-to-model policy (Coarse CLS, with rank-fused model recommendations) against prompt-specific quality prediction and their combination. It also explicitly diagnoses first-appearing-candidate bias from tied argmax labels. The proposed experiment instead uses exact source-benchmark IDs, mean recorded performance, and paired supervision contrasts with confidence intervals.
Lee decomposes the best-single-to-oracle gap using task and task-by-language lookup tables, but fits and evaluates them on the same 294 queries without comparing trained routers on held-out data.

LLMRouterBench compares learned routers with a hindsight Dataset Oracle and interprets their proximity as evidence of coarse domain routing. The proposed lookup is fitted only on training outcomes and evaluated on held-out queries.

Li evaluates both argmax-selection and full-utility-prediction formulations for kNN and MLP routers. The proposed experiment adds a controlled audit of the seed library's tie construction and relates supervision effects to a task-ID baseline.

sol.reason: The central comparison is closely anticipated by FineRouter: it already tests how much prompt-specific, full-score routing adds beyond a training-derived task-to-model policy on held-out queries, while identifying the same argmax-tie bias. Exact benchmark identity, the xRouteBench decomposition, and paired confidence-bound testing make this a more targeted audit, but the core experimental contribution is a close variant rather than a previously unanswered question.

opus.reason: Both use the released xRouteBench Generic matrix to compare a train-fitted per-subtask lookup router against query-level embedding routers and the oracle, asking how much of the routing gain is task identification.

sol.reason: Both compare a train-fitted source-task lookup with query-level learned routers on held-out Generic-track outcomes to measure routing gains beyond task identity.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented E1 as registered in e1/run_e1.py, launched by e1/run.sh. It runs in about 1 minute plus install time. Outputs go to result.json, outputs/e1_per_query.jsonl and outputs/e1_summary.json.

Data: I used ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config 'llmrouter_generic' (train: 80,802 rows, 4,487 unique queries after merging 2 duplicate query texts; test: 67,122 rows, 3,729 queries) and config 'llm_candidates'. No config renaming was needed. Every cell is filled for all 18 models, so no model was dropped and every decision set has all 18 models. Cost comes from input_tokens/output_tokens times the per-1M prices. Embeddings are Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B: left padding, truncation at 512 tokens, last-token hidden state, L2-normalised, bf16, batch 64.

Sanity check: our Largest-A (deepseek-v3.1, which ties cogito at 671B) scores 70.29 micro, the same as the seed's Largest-LLM figure.

Result on the test split (micro / macro accuracy):
- Largest-A: 70.29 / 58.39
- Best-single (cogito; same as Largest-B): 80.54 / 65.36
- Task-ID lookup: 81.02 / 72.87
- kNN-cls (seed-style first-argmax labels): 60.61
- kNN-cls-rand: 71.17
- kNN-reg: 77.83 (k = 50)
- MLP-CE: 61.14
- MLP-pointwise: 78.36
- MLP-pointwise+task: 78.44
- Oracle: 92.93

The best learned router (L*) is MLP-pointwise+task. L* minus Task-ID is -2.58 points, 95% CI [-3.52, -1.63]. The registered statistic, the CI upper bound, is -1.63. That is below 2, so the registered event occurs. More strongly, every one of the six learned routers is significantly below the Task-ID lookup in this setup.

Supervision effects:
- 93.6% of train queries have at least 2 tied maximisers (mean 11.9 ties).
- With first-row tie-breaking, label_first assigns qwen2.5-7b-instruct to 58.6% of queries.
- Switching to full-matrix supervision adds +17.2 points for kNN (CI [15.7, 18.7]) and +17.2 for the MLP (CI [15.9, 18.6]).
- Random tie-breaking alone adds +10.6 points (CI [9.3, 11.8]).

Task-ID minus Best-single is +0.48 points, CI [-0.51, 1.45], so the lookup's gain over Best-single is not established. Within-task kNN-reg minus the within-task best model has a mean of -0.74 over the 7 largest test tasks. It is positive only for MBPP, where the gain is significant (+4.2), and for MATH, where it is not significant.

Caveats:
- The chosen k (50) is at the upper edge of the registered grid {5, 10, 20, 50}. I did not extend the grid.
- MMLU-Pro has only 63 training queries.
- The results cover one embedding model and the registered hyperparameters, with no tuning.
- The 5-fold fallback for a missing train split is not implemented; it was not needed because a train split exists.

There were no deviations from the registration.

departures: e1/run_e1.py: the 5-fold stratified fallback for a missing train split is not implemented. The script aborts instead. A train split exists, so the branch never ran and this cannot change the result. The engineer disclosed it.

e1/run_e1.py: two duplicate train query texts were merged, and their 36 duplicate (query, model) cells were averaged for performance and cost. This follows the registered rule of keying queries by text. The averaging is an implementation choice the registration leaves open, and it affects 36 cells out of about 80,000, so it cannot plausibly change the result.
e1/run_e1.py embed(): texts are batched in length-sorted order instead of downloaded order. With left padding and attention masks this only changes bf16 numerics, so it is negligible.

e1/run_e1.py route_from_proba(): for kNN-cls, models with zero predicted probability fall back to the best-single ranking. The registration does not specify this. Every decision set contains all 18 models and the argmax is always a model with positive probability, so selections and the result are unaffected.

registration.title: Are xRouteBench's cost-weighted router rankings an artefact of per-router reward normalisation? Rescoring identical routing decisions under per-router, global and dollar-cost protocols
registration.seed_connection: Findings (i) and (iii) of the seed and Figure 5 state that router rankings reverse under tighter cost weights (RouterDC falls from first to tenth on Generic; MLPRouter becomes best on Vision for beta >= 0.4). In the released benchmark pipeline (benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py, evaluate()), the reported reward alpha*norm(perf) - beta*norm(cost) appears to min-max-normalise performance and cost over each router's OWN routed rows, so a router that always picks the cheapest model and one that always picks the most expensive both span their own [0,1] cost range and absolute cost differences between routers are largely erased; the cost term then rewards the shape of a router's cost distribution rather than its cost. Whether the published cost-weighted rankings survive a shared normalisation is untested.
registration.hypothesis: For cost weights beta > 0, router rankings computed from identical routing decisions with the released per-router normalisation and with a single global normalisation (min and max over all recorded test query-model cells of the track) disagree substantially: their mean Spearman correlation over tracks and beta values is below 0.7.
registration.contribution: RouterBench, LLMRouterBench and EquiRouter evaluate cost-quality trade-offs with absolute dollar or globally scaled costs; none has checked how the seed's per-router scaling affects conclusions, and the seed's headline 'rankings reverse under cost constraints' rests on it. Rescoring the same decisions under three protocols isolates the scoring effect from any routing effect and tells whether the reported reversals are properties of routers or of the protocol.

closest_work.difference: EquiRouter analyses routing collapse under cost budgets with dollar costs; it does not study how the evaluation reward's normalisation changes router rankings.
RouterBench defines a cost-quality evaluation with absolute costs; this experiment contrasts that style of global scaling with the seed pipeline's per-router scaling on identical decisions.
LLMRouterBench proposes Pareto-based cost metrics; here the question is the sensitivity of a specific published cost-weighted ranking to the normalisation choice, holding routers fixed.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configs 'llmrouter_generic', 'memory_locomo', 'memory_longmemeval', 'timeseries', 'video', 'multimodal_geometry3k', 'multimodal_mathvista' (train/test) and 'llm_candidates' (model_name, size, input_price_per_1m, output_price_per_1m); if a config name is not found, match by substring over get_dataset_config_names and log the mapping.
Embedding model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
Reference code: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, file benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py, functions preprocess_training_data and evaluate (clone the repository and copy them verbatim).
Python: torch, transformers>=4.51, datasets, scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, scipy.
registration.method: 0) Code check: clone the repository and locate the functions that build the composite training reward and compute the reported reward. Store verbatim in the results file the lines that normalise performance and cost, and a field released_eval_normalisation in {'per_router','global','other','not_found'} stating over which rows evaluate() takes min and max. If the repository or functions cannot be found, implement P1 exactly as described in step 5 and set p1_source='registration_description'. 1) Data: for each of the seven track configs load train and test; decode JSON-encoded fields; join chat-message lists by newline; build per split the unique-query list, P[q,m] = recorded performance (NaN if missing) and cost[q,m] = input_tokens*input_price_per_1m/1e6 + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m/1e6. Retain per track the models with recorded outcomes on >= 95% of that track's queries; decision set per query = retained models with recorded outcomes. If a track has no train split, use 5-fold CV by query (flag). If the Generic train split exceeds 40,000 unique queries, subsample 40,000 stratified by task_name (flag). 2) Embeddings: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, tokenizer padding_side='left', truncation at 512 tokens (right truncation, as in the seed script), last-token pooling, L2-normalised, batch 64. Report the fraction of memory-track queries longer than 512 tokens; as a secondary, re-embed the two memory tracks with truncation_side='left' (keeping the question) and recompute everything for them. 3) Weight settings (alpha,beta) in {(1.0,0.0),(0.8,0.2),(0.6,0.4),(0.4,0.6),(0.2,0.8)}. For each track and setting build the composite train reward as in the released preprocess: r[q,m] = alpha*normP[q,m] - beta*normC[q,m] with min-max taken over all train cells of the track for performance and cost separately. 4) Routers (9), trained per (track, setting), each selecting one model per test query inside the decision set (classifiers fall back to their highest-probability class inside the set): smallest (smallest parsed size), largest (largest size; first in llm_candidates order on ties, reported), cheapest (lowest mean train cost), best-single (highest mean composite train reward), kNN-cls (train label = model of the FIRST row in downloaded order attaining the maximum composite reward of that query; cosine 5-nearest-neighbour majority vote), LR-cls (torch linear softmax classifier on the embeddings with the same labels, Adam 1e-2, 30 epochs, batch 256, weight_decay 1e-4), MLP-cls (torch 1024->256->128->K, ReLU, Adam 1e-3, weight_decay 1e-4, batch 256, 40 epochs, seed 0, cross-entropy on the same labels), kNN-reg (score each model by the mean composite reward over the 20 cosine-nearest train queries, argmax), cascade (torch logistic regression on the embeddings predicting 1[r(q,smallest) >= r(q,largest)]; route to smallest if p >= 0.5 else largest). Nearest-neighbour searches use GPU matrix products. 5) Scoring the SAME decisions under three protocols; a router's routed test rows have performance p_i and dollar cost c_i. P1 (released): norm_p_i and norm_c_i are min-max scaled over that router's own routed rows; reward = mean_i(alpha*norm_p_i - beta*norm_c_i) (use the verbatim released evaluate(); if implemented from this description, a zero range gives 0 and is flagged). P2 (global): the same formula but min and max of performance and of cost taken over all recorded test cells of the track (all queries x retained models), shared by every router. P3 (dollar): reward = alpha*mean_i(p_i) - beta*mean_i(c_i)/c_ref with c_ref = mean per-query test cost of the model with the highest mean test cost on the track. 6) For each of the 28 cells (7 tracks x beta in {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}) rank the 9 routers under P1, P2 and P3 (average ranks for ties), compute Spearman rho(P1,P2), rho(P1,P3), rho(P2,P3) and the indicator that the top router differs between P1 and P2. Statistic = mean over the 28 cells of rho(P1,P2). Diagnostics: the five beta=0 cells (P1 and P2 must coincide on binary-metric tracks; they may legitimately differ on the F1-scored memory tracks because a router's own max F1 can be below 1 - report, do not treat as a bug); each router's mean norm_c under P1 versus under P2 per track, which shows directly what per-router scaling does to a constant-model router; the Generic track reported separately; the memory tracks with left truncation. If time allows, repeat LR-cls and MLP-cls with seeds 1 and 2 and report the range of the statistic.

event.description: Cost-weighted router rankings computed from identical routing decisions with the released per-router normalisation and with a global normalisation have a mean Spearman correlation below 0.7 across the 28 (track, beta>0) cells.
event.statistic: Mean over 7 tracks x 4 beta values of the Spearman rank correlation between the P1 (per-router normalisation) and P2 (global normalisation) rankings of the 9 routers

evaluation.procedure: outputs/e2_decisions.jsonl holds one line per (track, alpha, beta, router, test query) with the routed model, its recorded performance and dollar cost. outputs/e2_rankings.json holds the code-check result (released_eval_normalisation, verbatim lines, p1_source), per cell the P1/P2/P3 rewards and ranks of all routers, the three Spearman correlations and the top-router-change indicator, the beta=0 diagnostics, per-router mean norm_c under P1 and P2, the memory-track left-truncation variant, and the registered statistic under key 'mean_spearman_p1_p2' together with the fraction of cells whose top router changes.
evaluation.controls: Routing decisions are computed once and scored under all protocols, so ranking differences are attributable only to the scoring; P1 reuses the released code verbatim when available and the code-check records what the released code actually does, so a correlation of 1.0 would be the correct negative result if the released protocol is already global; beta=0 cells on binary tracks verify the implementation; constant-model routers (smallest, largest, cheapest) expose the mechanism because their absolute cost differences are the largest; P3 anchors both normalised protocols to dollar cost.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-run all local routers of LLMRouter on every xRouteBench track and all five weight settings and rescore under per-router, global and dollar-cost protocols to test whether the specific reported reversals (RouterDC dropping to tenth on Generic, MLPRouter leading Vision for beta >= 0.4) persist, then propose and validate a standardised absolute-cost reward and frontier metric for the benchmark.

Correlation should collapse on the memory tracks, where F1 spreads are tiny, and at high beta. The shared accuracy term and a possibly global released evaluate() are the main ways the event could fail.

judge_sol.reason: If the released normalization behaves as described, it can erase substantial absolute-cost differences between routers, making ranking changes likely. outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (e2/exp.py, run by e2/run_eval.sh; a full test run took about 7 min including pip install and downloads):

Step 0, code check. The released repository is already in /workspace/seed, so I did not clone it again. I pulled preprocess_training_data, row_costs and evaluate out of /workspace/seed/benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py with ast and exec'd them verbatim. The normalisation lines are stored word for word in e2_rankings.json. I also ran a small synthetic test: two routers with identical performance, one always on a cheap model and one always on a model with 100x the cost. The released evaluate() gave both the same reward, so I recorded released_eval_normalisation='per_router' and p1_source='verbatim_released_evaluate'.

Steps 1–6 follow the registration:
- **Tracks and splits:** 7 tracks loaded from HF ulab-ai/xRouteBench. All configs were found under their exact names, all had a train split, and the generic train set has 4,487 unique queries, so no subsampling was needed. All 18 models passed the 95% coverage filter on every track.
- **Costs:** dollar cost uses the llm_candidates prices.
- **Embeddings:** Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B in fp32, left padding, 512-token right truncation, last-token pooling, L2-normalised, batch 64.
- **Training:** composite train reward is min-max scaled over all recorded train cells. The 9 routers use the hyperparameters as registered.
- **Scoring:**
  - P1 is the verbatim released evaluate(), called on a temporary file that holds exactly each router's routed rows. This gives the same result as the full test file and is much faster.
  - P2 uses global min-max over all recorded test cells (queries × retained models).
  - P3 is dollar cost divided by c_ref.
- **Statistic:** Spearman rank correlations over the 28 cells (7 tracks × β>0); no cell had an undefined correlation.

Small implementation choices not fully pinned down by the registration:
- (a) Ranking uses the released avg_reward, which is rounded to 4 decimals. An unrounded P1 is also reported: mean ρ 0.611 vs 0.610.
- (b) Fallbacks when a router's chosen model has no recorded outcome for a query:
  - constant routers take the next model in their own ordering;
  - the cascade switches to the other model of its pair;
  - kNN-cls with no allowed vote takes the first allowed class.

registration.title: How much of xRouteBench's Generic routing headroom is answer-extraction and truncation artefact? A lenient re-grading audit of the recorded query-model matrix
registration.seed_connection: The seed argues that always calling the largest model is 'mediocre' (70.29 on Generic) and that 'many queries that the largest model fails are solved by smaller and cheaper ones', calling this the headroom routing exploits. According to the released data engine, responses were generated with a fixed output budget (max_tokens 512) and graded by strict patterns: multiple choice by the last parenthesised letter '(X)', GSM8K by the last number and MATH by the last \boxed{}. Verbose or format-non-compliant models can be scored wrong despite answering correctly, and truncated responses cannot be scored right, both of which inflate per-query complementarity between models and therefore the oracle-minus-best-single headroom and what routers learn.
registration.hypothesis: Re-grading the recorded Generic test responses with a lenient answer extractor removes at least 25% of the headroom between the per-query oracle and the best single model measured under the recorded strict grading.
registration.contribution: Molfese et al. and the Format Sensitivity Index document extraction and format effects on single-model leaderboards, and LLMRouterBench attributes the routing oracle gap to model-recall failures under one grader. No work has asked what share of a routing benchmark's complementarity headroom is grader-induced, which directly conditions the 'no single model covers all queries' claim and the supervision every router is trained on.

closest_work.difference: Studies answer-extraction inconsistencies in multiple-choice evaluation of single models; here the quantity of interest is the routing headroom (oracle minus best single) of a released routing matrix, with truncation accounted for.
Measures format/parseability sensitivity across prompt wrappers by regenerating outputs; this audit re-grades fixed recorded responses and asks whether routing complementarity survives.
Reports model-recall failures as the driver of the oracle gap under one grader; this experiment tests whether part of that gap is grader-induced.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config 'llmrouter_generic' test split (one row per (query, model) with task_name, query, ground_truth, choices if present, metric if present, model_name, response, output_tokens, performance) and config 'llm_candidates' (model sizes and prices). Match config names by substring if needed and log.

Grading reference (optional): llmrouter/utils/evaluation.py in https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter (multiple-choice exact match, GSM8K last-number rule, last_boxed_only_string/remove_boxed/is_equiv for MATH); copy if reachable.
Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Hugging Face, ungated) run with transformers for the checker validation.
Python: transformers, datasets, numpy, pandas, torch, regex.

event.description: Lenient re-grading removes at least a quarter of the strict-grading headroom between the per-query oracle and the best single model on the Generic test split.
event.statistic: 1 - H_lenient/H_strict, where H_g = (mean over test queries of the per-query maximum score over models) - (highest mean test score of any single model) under grading g

evaluation.procedure: outputs/e3_regraded.jsonl holds one line per (query, model) row with task_name, metric, strict score, lenient score, extracted answer strings, output_tokens and the truncation flags. outputs/e3_summary.json holds the schema report, the strict-vs-recorded replication agreement per metric, per-model strict/lenient accuracies and truncation shares, the O/B/H values under both gradings overall, per metric, per task, for the 17-model pool and on non-truncated rows, the checker Yes rates for the three validation groups, and the registered statistic under key 'headroom_removed_share'.
evaluation.controls: The strict label is the recorded performance itself, and the grader replication is a diagnostic rather than a dependency; the checker is calibrated on strict-correct and strict-wrong groups so its Yes rate on rescued rows can be read relative to its own false-positive floor; code, cem and F1 rows are left untouched so changes are attributable only to answer extraction on MC/GSM8K/MATH rows; truncated rows are reported separately because extraction cannot rescue them; the 17-model pool variant addresses the ambiguity about which pool Table 2 used.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-grade all xRouteBench tracks with reference-based LLM answer matching, regenerate the strongest models' responses with a larger output budget, and re-estimate the routing headroom, the Largest-LLM baseline and router rankings; if a large share is artefact, propose grading-robust supervision and format-compliance-aware cost accounting for routing benchmarks.

judge_astra.reason: Even substantial rescue rates need not shrink headroom: the best-single score must improve appreciably more than the oracle score. These extraction rules cannot repair most truncated answers and may primarily help models that still do not become the best single model.

judge_fable.reason: Removing a quarter of the oracle-minus-best-single headroom requires the best single model (which by construction is format-compliant under strict grading) to gain several points from lenient extraction while the 18-model oracle gains little; MC rescue only applies to responses with no parenthesised letter and strong models mostly box MATH answers, so the typical outcome is a 5-15% share, and the experiment aborts entirely if the HF split lacks response text.

judge_opus.reason: The run aborts if the release has no response text. Otherwise, the lenient MC rule still takes the last '(X)', so the most likely false negatives (verbose models discussing other options after answering) are not rescued. Truncated rows cannot be rescued, and strong models mostly comply with the format. The gain in best-single accuracy is therefore likely only 1-3 points against roughly 15 points of oracle headroom, well short of a 25% reduction.

judge_sol.reason: The proposed extractors can rescue some formatting failures but cannot recover final answers missing because of truncation. Removing a quarter of the headroom also requires the rescues to improve best-single performance substantially more than oracle performance, rather than merely improving scores broadly.

judge_luna.reason: The prompts explicitly request the forms used by the strict graders, so many failures may be genuine errors or truncations that lenient extraction cannot fix; rescuing non-best models could also raise the oracle rather than shrink headroom. Model-specific formatting misses could still improve the best-single score relative to the oracle, but I expect that effect to be limited.

judge_muse.reason: Prompts explicitly require '(X)' and \boxed{}, so no-format rescues should be rare and truncated rows cannot be rescued, and rescues may help small non-compliant models as much as the best single, leaving headroom largely intact.

They study their own Gemma 4/Llama generations on MMLU, MedQA and other benchmarks, compare an LLM judge with exact match, and target the ceiling of queries no model solves and E2B-to-31B gains. They do not re-grade a released routing matrix with a lenient extractor, and they do not measure what share of the oracle-minus-best-single complementarity headroom is grader-induced.

Chen shows that routing-oracle premiums are sensitive to scorer, pool and coupling choices, using archived stochastic tensors on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA. The main question is about coupling and decision classes under stochastic decoding. It does not treat strict-versus-lenient answer extraction or truncation as a source of headroom, and it does not use xRouteBench.

Its own results point in different directions depending on the benchmark, so it does not settle the registered statistic for xRouteBench, and I found no paper that does.

outcome.executor_notes:
Implemented as registered in e3_audit.py, run by run_eval.sh. The script installs its dependencies, downloads ulab-ai/xRouteBench (llmrouter_generic/test.parquet: 67,122 rows = 3,729 queries × 18 models; llm_candidates), then does the schema check, strict labels, replication of the seed's grader, lenient extraction for MC/GSM8K/MATH, truncation flags, per-model statistics, all headroom variants and the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct checker. It writes outputs/e3_regraded.jsonl, outputs/e3_summary.json and result.json. The full run takes under a minute after the model download.

Result from the test run: headroom_removed_share = 0.0606, below the 0.25 threshold, so the registered event did not occur.
- Strict: O=0.9293, B=0.8054 (cogito-v2-1-671b), H=0.1239.
- Lenient: O=0.9349, B=0.8185, H=0.1164.
- 17-model pool (no cogito): share 0.024.
- Truncated cells treated as missing: H falls from 0.076 to 0.061, share 0.195. This is still below 0.25, and it is only a secondary variant.
- Queries where the strict best model is wrong but some model is right: 465. 39 of these disappear under lenient grading.
- Lenient grading rescued 1,974 of 12,207 strict-wrong MC rows, 395 GSM8K rows and 37 MATH rows. Per-model accuracy rises considerably for some models (e.g. rnj-1 from 0.513 to 0.642, qwen2.5-7b from 0.576 to 0.643, mixtral-8x7b from 0.406 to 0.500). So the format artefact is real at the level of single models, but it moves little of the oracle-minus-best headroom.
- Checker Yes rates: rescued 0.88, strict-correct 0.94, strict-wrong-not-rescued 0.14. Rescued minus the false-positive floor is 0.74. A spot check found some false positives from the 'line', 'keyword' and 'paren' patterns (e.g. "ampere (A)", options listed mid-reasoning). These rows were kept as the registered extractor defines them.
- Replication of the seed's grader: MC agreement 0.99995, MATH 1.0, GSM8K 0.967. My replication compares numbers numerically. The recorded grader strips every '.', so "324.00" is scored wrong; that accounts for the 307 GSM8K rows marked wrong in the recorded labels but right in my replication.
- deepseek-v3.1's recorded strict accuracy is 0.7029, which matches the seed's Largest-LLM figure of 70.29.

Deviations and interpretation choices:
1. In the released data, aime_2020_2024 has metric 'GSM8K' and boolq has 'em_mc'. I let the metric column take precedence over the task_name mapping, so AIME is graded with the GSM8K rules.
2. In the checker prompt, {ground_truth} is the extracted reference answer (the MC label, the number after '####', or the last \boxed{} of the solution), because the GSM8K and MATH ground_truth fields are full worked solutions. The prompt is wrapped in Qwen's chat template.
3. output_tokens exceeds 512 on about 5.8% of rows (empirical max 1095, and only 1 row at the max). So 512 is not a confirmed hard budget. The registered ≥512 flag is used as written, and no second flag was triggered because the share at the max is below 1%.
4. Each query is identified by (task_name, query text).

departures: e3_audit.py grades aime_2020_2024 with the GSM8K rules because the released 'metric' column says GSM8K. The registration maps AIME to MATH only when 'metric' is absent, so this follows the registered precedence. The engineer disclosed it. It touches about 50 queries at most and has a negligible effect on the overall statistic.

In the checker prompt (e3_audit.py), {ground_truth} is the extracted reference answer (the MC label, the number after '####', or the last \boxed of the solution) rather than the raw ground_truth field, and the prompt is wrapped in Qwen's chat template. The engineer disclosed this. It affects only the validation Yes rates, not headroom_removed_share.

strip_string in e3_audit.py is the Hendrycks/LLMRouter version: '0.5' becomes \frac{1}{2} and a leading '.' becomes '0.'. The registration's paraphrase says '0.5 -> .5'. This is a minor normalisation difference on MATH rows only. MATH replication agreement is 1.0 and only 37 MATH rows were rescued, so it is negligible for the result.

GSM8K lenient extraction takes the latest-positioned candidate among '####', \boxed{} and 'answer is', and falls back to the last number. The registration lists these sources without saying how to order them, so this is a choice it leaves open. Most rescues (263 of 395) come from the numeric last-number fallback. They correct the recorded grader's decimal-stripping bug ('324.00'), which the registration's 'compare numerically' allows.
MATH lenient grading also applies numeric comparison to answers that are already boxed (34 rescues). The registration's 'also compare numerically' covers this. Effect: small.

The checker's 200 rescued rows are stratified with equal shares per metric, and the leftover quota is redistributed because only 37 MATH rows were rescued (GSM8K 82, MATH 37, MC 81). This is permitted by the registration and does not affect the statistic.

In the non-truncated headroom variant (e3_audit.py headroom with mask_col), B is each model's mean over its own non-truncated rows, so denominators differ across models. The registration leaves this open. It affects only a secondary variant (share 0.195).

The 512-token truncation flag is used as registered, even though output_tokens exceeds 512 on about 5.8% of rows (max 1095, per the engineer's notes). The second flag was not triggered under the registered 1% rule. This affects only the truncation diagnostics, not the main statistic.
Queries are keyed by (task_name, query text). The registration leaves this open. The 67,122 rows = 3,729 × 18 pivot shows no collapsing, so there is no effect.
problems: The lenient MC 'line' and 'keyword' patterns produce some false positives, for example a lettered option list mid-reasoning or 'ampere (A)'. The engineer's spot check acknowledged this. The checker's MC Yes rate on rescued rows is 0.90, against 0.91 on strict-correct rows, so the contamination looks modest. False positives raise both O and B, so they do not clearly bias the statistic in either direction.

No bootstrap or confidence interval is reported for headroom_removed_share. Given the large margin (0.061 against a 0.25 threshold) and the consistent variants (17-model pool 0.024, non-truncated 0.195), the conclusion is unlikely to flip, but its precision is not quantified.

The checker samples are small (for example 11 GSM8K rows in the strict-wrong group, with a Yes rate of 0.36). This hints that the regex extractor may miss some genuine artefacts. A model-based re-grader could remove more headroom, and this audit does not rule that out.

Truncation cannot be treated as a confirmed budget artefact, because 512 is not the empirical cap. The non-truncated variant therefore measures something only loosely tied to the registered truncation mechanism.

The 671B row 'deepseek-v3.1' reproduces the seed's 70.29, but the hindsight-best model is cogito-v2-1-671b at 0.8054. The headroom here is therefore relative to a stronger baseline than the seed's Largest-LLM, which is correct as registered but worth noting when comparing to the seed's claim.
opus.reason: The code in e3_audit.py implements the registered pipeline closely: recorded strict labels, a grader replication diagnostic, the prioritised lenient extractors, the truncation flag, headroom variants and the Qwen2.5-7B checker. The disclosed choices (metric-column precedence, extracted reference in the checker prompt, ordering of GSM8K candidates) are either left open by the registration or do not touch the statistic. The value 0.0606 is computed from the released 67,122-row matrix of real responses, and the grader replication (MC 0.99995, MATH 1.0, deepseek-v3.1 = 70.29) shows the data and labels are the seed's. Lenient grading substantially raises some small models' accuracies but barely moves the oracle-minus-best headroom. This conclusion holds in the 17-model pool and the non-truncated variant, and the checker supports that most rescues are genuine. This is a credible, well-controlled null for the registered regex-based re-grader. It is limited by the lack of uncertainty estimates and by leaving open whether a stronger model-based grader would remove more headroom.

departures: e3_audit.py only JSON-decodes choices, and only accepts dictionary-shaped choices. It does not generally decode JSON-encoded query, response or ground_truth fields as registered. Whether this affected any actual rows is not established by the supplied excerpts; if such fields were encoded, extraction and scores could change.

e3_audit.py introduces unregistered missing-value defaults: absent responses and ground truths become empty strings, and missing output_tokens becomes zero. These could affect rescues and truncation exclusions if missing values occurred; their incidence is not reported.

The MC diagnostic in e3_audit.py accepts whitespace, lowercase letters and digits inside parentheses. Its text fallback tests whether the reference occurs anywhere in the response rather than comparing extracted answer text. The diagnostic changes do not change the primary strict scores, which remain recorded performance; the substring fallback could also change lenient scores if used.

The MC lenient extractor in e3_audit.py is broader than the registered patterns: boxed answers may contain text wrappers or parentheses, keyword and line patterns accept additional Markdown decoration, and the single-letter rule removes punctuation, brackets and asterisks throughout the response rather than merely stripping surrounding whitespace. These extensions could change rescues and the primary statistic.

For GSM8K, e3_audit.py extracts the first numeric token immediately following each '####' or 'answer is' marker, then selects the latest candidate by marker position. This is not literally the registered last-number-after-marker rule when the following text contains multiple numbers. It could change lenient scores and headroom.

The GSM8K diagnostic in e3_audit.py uses floating-point comparison within 1e-9 rather than literal normalized-answer equality. This can change diagnostic agreement, but not the primary strict labels. The reported 307 recorded-wrong/replicated-right cases are observations; the engineer's attribution of all of them to decimal stripping is not independently demonstrated in the supplied material.

MATH normalization in e3_audit.py differs from the registration's explicit recipe: it maps 0.5 to a fraction rather than .5, removes percentage markers and some short left-hand equations, repairs square-root syntax, removes units only for a particular text-marker form, and does not generally remove trailing periods. These differences can change diagnostic agreement and lenient rescues.

The shared MATH boxed-answer parser in e3_audit.py additionally accepts fbox and unbraced 'boxed 5' forms. Lenient fallback depends on whether that parser returns an answer, rather than strictly on whether a registered boxed expression exists. This could change both diagnostic and lenient results.

The checker prompt in e3_audit.py substitutes extracted reference answers for the registered ground_truth field on GSM8K and MATH. This is disclosed in the engineer's notes but changes the prompt content. It could change checker Yes rates, although checker outputs do not feed the primary headroom statistic.

The checker calibration samples in e3_audit.py are restricted to MC, GSM8K and MATH. The registration explicitly restricts rescues to those metrics but does not impose that restriction on the two calibration groups. The sample totals remain 200/100/100; changing the calibration populations could change their Yes rates and the reported 0.74 contrast, but not primary headroom.
problems: The extraction-rule departures in e3_audit.py could affect the primary value. No exact-registration rerun or sensitivity analysis establishes their numerical impact, so 0.06060551427430394 should be identified as the implemented extractor's result.

The MC rules can mistake option listings, incidental parenthesized letters or decorated text for final answers. The engineer reports examples from an earlier spot check, but those examples are not independently inspectable in the supplied row excerpts.

The checker is not an independently established gold standard. Its 88% rescued-group Yes rate and 14% strict-wrong-group Yes rate do not establish rescue precision: the latter group can contain genuinely correct answers missed by both graders.

The checker groups have substantially different metric mixtures, and the rescued group is not sampled proportionally to rescue counts. Consequently, the unweighted 0.74 difference is not a calibrated population precision estimate.
The output_tokens >= 512 flag is not verified truncation. Recorded lengths exceed 512, reaching 1095, so exclusion under this flag cannot identify the causal effect of a confirmed generation limit.

The non-truncated variant in e3_audit.py averages each model over its own retained query subset while averaging the oracle over all queries with any retained cell. These different denominators introduce selection effects, limiting interpretation of its 19.5% headroom reduction.

Fixed recorded responses cannot reveal what genuinely truncated responses would have answered with a larger budget. This audit therefore does not quantify the total contribution of truncation or all possible answer-extraction artefacts.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed, produced both registered artifacts, and computed strict headroom 0.1238949222 versus lenient headroom 0.1163862067, yielding 6.06% removal rather than the registered quarter-headroom event. The data source, recorded-label control and primary formula were followed, but substantive extraction and checker departures make fidelity unfaithful. The value nevertheless comes from real downloaded responses and scores, with no visible hard-coded outcome, leakage or primary-statistic calculation error, so it is valid evidence for the implemented audit. This is a meaningful negative finding about that extractor on the recorded matrix, warranting research value 2, but it does not establish absence of broader grading or truncation effects.

departures: Checker prompt in e3_audit.py substitutes an extracted reference (GSM8K number after ####, MATH last boxed span, raw MC ground_truth) for the registered {ground_truth} and wraps that text in Qwen's chat template. Engineer reported both. This can change the checker Yes rates; it cannot change headroom_removed_share, which is computed before the checker and does not use its outputs.

Calibration samples in e3_audit.py are drawn only from MC/GSM8K/MATH rows, not from all strict-correct or strict-wrong rows, and the 200 rescued rows are equal-allocation stratified (37 MATH, 82 GSM8K, 81 MC) rather than proportional. Registration says stratified but does not fix the weights; the metric restriction is a narrower frame than written. Either choice can change checker rates only, not the registered statistic.

lenient_mc in e3_audit.py matches only uppercase A-J (or digits) with no case-insensitive flag, so lowercase keyword/line/boxed/single answers are missed even though the subsequent equality check is case-insensitive. This could slightly lower the statistic; with 2406 rescues moving H by only 0.0075, a material move toward 0.25 is implausible.

The single-letter rule in e3_audit.py deletes asterisks, periods, parentheses, brackets and colons, not only whitespace, and the line pattern allows markdown asterisks. Both are broader than the registration and could slightly raise the statistic (single=398 and line=728 of the MC rescues).

For MC rows whose ground truth is neither a letter nor a choice label, e3_audit.py scores lenient correctness by case-insensitive substring containment rather than the registered letter patterns. Rescue-source counts contain no text_fallback hits, so this did not change the statistic.

strip_string in e3_audit.py omits the trailing-'.' removal listed in the registration's MATH normalisation, and numerical comparison is also applied to boxed MATH answers, not only the no-boxed fallback. At most the 37 MATH rescues are affected; strict MATH replication agreement is 1.0, so this does not plausibly change the reported statistic.

Diagnostic GSM8K replication in e3_audit.py compares numbers numerically (1e-9) rather than by the registration's comma/dollar/trailing-dot string rule. Engineer reported the 307-row disagreement. The analysis uses recorded performance regardless, so this does not change the statistic.
problems: Lenient MC patterns in e3_audit.py are case-sensitive and, separately, slightly broader than specified on the single-letter and line patterns; both effects are small beside the 0.06 versus 0.25 gap.

The headline share is not adjusted for extractor false positives. Engineer notes spot-checked false hits from the line, keyword and paren patterns; e3_summary.json checker Yes rates are 0.88 on rescued rows versus 0.14 on strict-wrong non-rescued rows and only 0.68 on the 37 MATH rescues, so 0.061 is an unadjusted extractor effect.

output_tokens is not a confirmed 512-token budget: empirical max 1095 with one row at the max, and the engineer reports about 5.8% of rows above 512. The registered >=512 flag is still reported, but truncation-as-artefact is not identified, and it is not an input to the primary statistic.
The secondary non-truncated share is 0.195 and switches the best model to qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct (e3_summary.json). Still below 0.25, but the share is estimand-sensitive.
grok.reason: The fresh run of e3_audit.py recomputed the registered statistic from the released Generic matrix: headroom_removed_share 0.0606, with O/B/H arithmetic checking out and deepseek-v3.1 at 0.7029 matching the seed. Checker-prompt changes and small regex differences do not enter that statistic or plausibly move it from 0.06 to the 0.25 threshold, so the run is faithful and the evidence is valid. Lenient grading rescued 2406 strict-wrong MC/GSM8K/MATH rows and lifted some single-model scores by several points, yet oracle-minus-best headroom fell only from 0.124 to 0.116 and only 39 of 465 complementarity queries disappeared. That is a credible, well-anchored null on the registered question; it is not a 3 because false rescues are unadjusted, the 512-token truncation premise is not confirmed, and a missing-cell truncation variant moves the share to 0.195.

grok.what_it_asks: Compare strict recorded grading with lenient answer re-extraction on the same Generic query–model responses to learn what share of oracle-minus-best-single routing headroom is an answer-extraction artefact.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper states the complementarity headroom as a real finding and never reports a lenient re-grade of that gap or names extraction or truncation artefacts as undone work.

relation.reason: The hypothesis treats the paper’s claimed oracle-versus-best complementarity as possibly grader-induced and tests whether that stated headroom survives a more lenient measurement.

obvious.reason: After this paper, first follow-ups are cost-dependent rankings, multi-turn failure, and personalization transfer; a lenient-versus-strict re-grade of the oracle gap is a specific artefact check only one or two researchers would list.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change how groups that train or cite routers on this xRouteBench matrix read its complementarity and supervision, not routing practice on other benchmarks.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan’s citations of the 70.29 Generic largest-model score and of smaller models solving queries the largest misses match the paper, and the token-budget detail is attributed to the data engine rather than the text.

answerable.reason: The design recomputes oracle and best-single scores under both graders on the recorded matrix and reports checker rates, so either a large or a small removed share would bear on the question.

grok.what_came_out: On the full Generic test matrix (3,729 queries × 18 models, one deterministic pass), lenient re-grading moved headroom from 0.1239 (O=0.9293, B=0.8054, cogito-v2-1-671b) to 0.1164 (O=0.9349, B=0.8185), a removed share of 0.061; a Qwen2.5-7B checker said Yes on 0.88 of 200 rescued rows versus 0.14 of 100 strict-wrong and 0.94 of 100 strict-correct controls.

prerequisite.reason: The recorded matrix was present, strict-grader replication agreed closely, and the checker rated rescued rows far above its false-positive floor, so the lenient labels can be read.

evidence.reason: The full-matrix share removed is 0.061, and even the non-truncated variant is 0.195, so a removal of at least a quarter of headroom is ruled out rather than merely undershooting the bar.

next_step.reason: The complete recorded matrix already shows lenient extraction removes only a small slice of headroom, so the artefact explanation of that gap does not justify more spend.

opus.what_it_asks: On the recorded xRouteBench Generic query–model matrix, does re-grading responses with a lenient answer extractor instead of the recorded strict grader shrink the per-query-oracle-minus-best-single-model headroom, revealing how much of the routing headroom the paper relies on is a grading artefact?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper never re-grades responses or questions whether its strict extraction inflates oracle headroom, and it names no such limitation.

relation.reason: It tests whether the paper's stated headroom claim (many queries the largest model fails are solved by smaller ones) partly arises from a grading confound, using the paper's own released matrix.

obvious.reason: Grader and format artefacts are a known worry in benchmarking, but asking specifically what share of a routing benchmark's oracle headroom they cause is something only one or two of ten researchers would list.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan quotes the Largest-LLM 70.29 Generic figure and the 'many queries that the largest model fails' sentence accurately, and its other details (512 budget, grading rules) come from the code, which the paper's text does not contradict.

opus.what_came_out: On the full Generic test split (3,729 queries × 18 models, one deterministic pass, no interval), lenient re-grading cut headroom from 0.124 (oracle 0.929, best single cogito 0.805) to 0.116, a removed share of 0.061, with 0.024 for the 17-model pool and 0.195 on non-truncated cells; a Qwen2.5-7B checker said Yes on 88% of 200 rescued rows, against 14% of 100 strict-wrong rows and 94% of 100 strict-correct rows.

prerequisite.reason: The checker's Yes rate on rescued rows (0.88) sits near the strict-correct rate and far above the false-positive floor (0.14), so the extractor behaved roughly as intended; the remaining false positives would only overstate the removed share.

next_step.reason: A fairly generous extractor, validated by the checker, left almost all of the headroom intact, so the idea that extraction artefacts drive the routing headroom was credibly shown not to hold.
