closest_work.difference: The seed reports cost-weight-dependent router rankings, but does not compare per-router evaluation normalization with fixed training-set normalization or measure their rank agreement.
RouterBench evaluates absolute dollar-cost–quality curves and AIQ; it does not audit policy-dependent reward normalization or re-rank LLMRouter's policies.

The Routing Plateau compares routers using cost-aware utility with costs normalized by each query's maximum candidate cost. It does not experimentally contrast per-policy normalization against fixed training-set constants.

ROUTEAUDIT examines confounding from changes in verifier access, accounting, and scoring through matched evaluation contracts. Its experiments do not test per-router min-max normalization or its effect on router rankings.

sol.reason: Among arXiv work available by 2026-10-07, I found related cost-aware benchmarks and evaluation audits, but none answering whether LLMRouter's released per-router normalization changes rankings relative to training-consistent fixed normalization. The proposed contribution is a specific normalization intervention and ranking-agreement test, rather than merely another router comparison using an established cost metric.

opus.reason: Entries 13 and 25 examine cost-weighted rank reversals through decision rules or label construction, but none tests whether the evaluation code's per-router min-max normalization of the reward changes rankings compared with a fixed train-consistent normalization.

sol.reason: The registered experiment re-ranks unchanged policies under policy-specific versus fixed reward normalization, whereas the listed cost experiments change training labels, cost predictors, or routing rules.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered seven configs, five weights, kNN/MLP/Elo/Smallest/Largest routers, and 18 fixed-model policies. Retained delivered training order, registered targets/hyperparameters, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B float32 embeddings, and first-record replay. Both reward reductions preserve released four-decimal rounding; unrounded sensitivity is also reported. No scientific method, hypothesis, threshold, or evaluation-cell changes. Execution optimizations only: batch-32 frozen embedding generation/input caching and indexed first-row replay, with the released reduction copied verbatim and parity-tested against unmodified evaluate() on every track. Price-scaling keeps train constants fixed and separately checks rebasing. Full uncached command finished in about seven minutes; deleted-output rerun finished in about 3.5 minutes and reproduced CSVs/result byte-for-byte. All required outputs produced. Observed mean tau-b=0.5785714285714285 over 28 retained cells, so the registered <0.5 event did not occur. Beta-zero tau-b=1.0, 20/28 top co-winner sets differed, and all controls passed. Runtime tool reported H200 rather than the advertised A100; no scientific settings were changed.

departures: The protected evaluation reused cached inputs: compact parquet replays and float32 Qwen3-Embedding shards (artifacts/embeddings/*.npy, manifest marked as submitted). It did not re-download data or re-embed queries; stdout has no EMBED lines and the run took 228 s. The shards were produced by the same embed_inputs code in the engineer's earlier run (evaluation.log). Shape, norm and text-hash checks pass. Unlikely to change the result.

Embedding batch size 32 and float32 precision were chosen by the engineer (experiment.py, embed_inputs). The registration leaves these open. Any effect on routing is marginal and unlikely to move the rank statistic.

R_tc is rounded to 4 decimals, mirroring the released R_rel rounding, before ranking (score_policy). The registration does not specify this. The reported unrounded sensitivity statistic is identical, so it did not change the value.

The secondary 'top router differs' share compares sets of co-winners rather than a single top router (compute_summary). This is a choice within an open specification and affects a secondary statistic only.

Evaluation row matching uses an indexed first-match lookup instead of calling evaluate() directly. The reduction is copied from the seed source by AST and parity-tested against the unmodified evaluate() on every config. No effect on the value.

Elo battles iterate query groups in sorted order (train_elo), following the released trainer that the registration cites. kNN uses n_jobs=-1 and threadpool limits are applied. Neither has a scientific effect.
The run used an H200 GPU rather than the stated A100. Deterministic algorithms were enabled. No effect expected.
problems: Single training seed and repetition, with no uncertainty estimate. The registered mean tau-b of 0.579 sits close to the 0.5 threshold. Per-cell tau values move in steps of 0.2 with only five routers, so MLP or kNN training variation could plausibly shift the mean across the threshold (summary.json limitations).

The protected run did not regenerate embeddings or data caches. It relied on engineer-supplied artifacts (artifacts/embeddings/*.npy, artifacts/*.parquet), so the fresh-machine run is not a fully independent recomputation, although integrity checks and hashes are present.

Three of the five ranked 'routers' (Elo, Smallest-LLM, Largest-LLM) always pick a single model, and Elo here sends every query to one model. Five-item rankings are coarse, which limits how much the mean tau can say about learned routers.

The seed's run_pipeline.py is read from seed/benchmark_pipeline/, which is not in the archive listing. Verbatim copying is supported by the recorded source hashes and parity tests, but the source cannot be inspected here.
opus.reason: The code follows the registered data, targets, router replicas, the two reward definitions, the 28 cost-weighted cells, the Kendall tau-b statistic and the controls. registration.title: Probe-augmented routing: does the cheapest model's recorded answer predict which of 18 models will be correct?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's formulation lets the routing state include interaction history h_t, i.e. responses gathered so far. Its single-turn routers, however, see only the query. Its multi-turn routers, which add decomposition and aggregation by a 3B base model, underperform badly. The README describes the routing data format as storing each candidate's response; the engineer verifies this in xRouteBench. If so, the value of one cheap 'probe' response as extra routing state can be measured offline, with no new LLM calls.
registration.hypothesis: Adding the cheapest candidate's recorded response (embedding plus length) to a per-model success predictor raises Generic test routing performance by more than 1.5 points over the same predictor given only the query, averaged over 3 seeds.
registration.contribution: An offline test, needing no extra inference, of whether one cheap model's actual answer tells us which of 18 models will be correct, beyond what the query reveals. A shuffled-response control separates response content from added input capacity, and the probe's cost is charged. It directly checks the 'inputs beyond the query' remedy proposed for the routing plateau.

closest_work.difference: Proposes that inputs beyond the query, such as partial outputs, may be needed to break the routing plateau, but does not test this.
Cascade routing uses post-hoc quality estimators to decide whether to continue. Here we ask whether one cheap response predicts the correctness of all other candidates in 18-way selection.
Lookahead predicts latent representations of candidate outputs. Here an actual cheap model's answer is used as router input.
FrugalGPT scores (query, answer) pairs to accept or escalate in a fixed cascade. Here the answer informs a full multi-model selection.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench: config llmrouter_generic (train and test, including recorded responses) and llm_candidates (prices)
Embedding model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
Reference embedding procedure: benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter
Python packages: datasets, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, torch, transformers
registration.method:
Step 1, data. Load llmrouter_generic train and test with datasets.load_dataset('ulab-ai/xRouteBench', 'llmrouter_generic'). JSON-decode query, ground_truth and choices when they are strings starting with '[' or '{'. Load llm_candidates. If the response field is missing, stop and report. Row USD cost = (input_tokens*input_price_per_1m + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m)/1e6. Evaluate on unique test queries that have a performance row for every candidate, and report exclusions. A response is unusable if it is missing, empty after stripping, or begins (case-insensitive) with 'api error' or 'error:'.

Step 2, probe. The probe is the candidate with the lowest mean per-query USD cost on train, among candidates whose response is usable on at least 95% of train queries; report which model it is. For each train and test query, take the probe's recorded response (empty string if unusable) and its output_tokens.

Step 3, features. Use Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B with left padding, 512-token truncation, last-token pooling and L2 normalisation.
- e_q: embedding of the query.
- e_r: embedding of the probe response.
- z = log(1 + probe output_tokens) / log(1 + maximum probe output_tokens on train).
- Shuffled control: give each query the e_r and z of another query with the same task_name, via a fixed random derangement within each task_name (seed 0), done separately in train and test.

Step 4, predictors. Hold out 10% of train queries (seed 0) for validation. Each predictor outputs one score per candidate and is trained with masked BCE-with-logits against recorded per-model performance.
- Q-MLP: input e_q.
- R-MLP: input [e_q, e_r, z].
- S-MLP: input [e_q, shuffled e_r, shuffled z].
- Shared architecture: Linear(in, 512)-ReLU-Dropout(0.1)-Linear(512, 256)-ReLU-Linear(256, n_models). AdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 256, at most 60 epochs, early stopping with patience 6 on validation routing score, keeping the best epoch. Seeds 0, 1, 2.
- kNN-mean pair: Q-kNN uses cosine neighbours on e_q; R-kNN uses neighbours on the L2-normalised concatenation of separately normalised e_q and e_r. Average the per-model performance of the k nearest train queries and route to the argmax, breaking ties by mean train performance. Choose k on validation from {5, 10, 20, 50}.

Step 5, routing and cost. Route each test query to the argmax-predicted model and record that model's recorded performance.
- Q variants pay the chosen model's cost.
- R and S variants pay the probe's cost plus the chosen model's cost, unless the chosen model is the probe itself.

References:
- always-probe;
- best single model on train;
- oracle;
- a probe-correctness oracle that routes to the probe when its recorded performance is at least 0.5 and otherwise to the Q-MLP choice.

event.description: Giving the router the cheapest model's recorded answer improves Generic test routing performance by more than 1.5 points over the query-only router of identical design.
event.statistic: Mean over seeds 0-2 of (R-MLP test score minus Q-MLP test score) on llmrouter_generic, where a score is 100 x the mean recorded performance of the chosen models.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute the registered statistic, with a 95% CI from 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples of test queries applied to seed-averaged per-query outcomes.

Secondary analyses:
- S-MLP minus Q-MLP, to check whether any gain comes from response content.
- R-kNN minus Q-kNN.
- Gains on the hard subset (test queries where at most 3 candidates score at least 0.5) and per task_name.
- Mean USD cost per query of every variant.
- Validation AUROC of Q-MLP vs. R-MLP for predicting the probe's own correctness from its output.

Output files:
- outputs/variant_scores.csv: one line per (variant, seed) with test score, hard-subset score and mean cost.
- outputs/test_choices.jsonl: one line per (test query, variant, seed) with the chosen model, its recorded performance and the charged cost.
- outputs/summary.json: the registered statistic with CI, the secondary statistics, the selected probe model, and whether the statistic exceeds 1.5.
evaluation.controls: S-MLP has the same input size as R-MLP but breaks the query-response link, isolating response content. Q-MLP and R-MLP share architecture, data, validation split and seeds. The kNN pair checks that conclusions do not depend on the learner. Always-probe, best-single and oracle bracket the attainable range. The probe-correctness oracle bounds what perfect detection of probe errors could add.

registration.full_scale_study: Extend to all xRouteBench tracks and cost weightings, using cost-aware decision rules that charge the probe. Compare one to three cheap probes and partial-output probes (first N tokens regenerated with open models of 8B or fewer) against cascade-routing and Lookahead baselines. Test whether probe evidence narrows the oracle gap on hard queries where routers currently miss the lone correct model.

agent.reason: A query-only router already picks the strongest model per task. A cheap model's answer mostly reveals difficulty or whether that cheap model itself is right, rarely which other model will succeed where the default fails. So performance-first gains above 1.5 points are unlikely; the probe should mainly save cost.

judge_astra.reason: A realized probe response can reveal useful information about failures and problem structure, but the query-only comparator already benefits from full per-model supervision. Frozen response embeddings may mostly reveal shared difficulty rather than which alternative model succeeds, making a gain above 1.5 points uncertain.

judge_fable.reason: The cheap probe's response mainly reveals its own correctness and query difficulty, which helps cost-aware decisions but adds little to pure-accuracy 18-way selection beyond what the query embedding already captures; gains of 0.5-1.5 points seem more likely than >1.5, with the extra 1025 input dimensions possibly adding noise.

judge_opus.reason: When routing is performance-only, the router mostly picks the strongest model for each task. A cheap model's response mainly signals difficulty or length, which changes few argmax choices. Gains are likely confined to a few points on MATH or MBPP, which is well under 1.5 points across the whole Generic mix.

judge_sol.reason: A probe response can expose formatting failures, truncation and difficulty, but its frozen embedding may reveal little about which other candidate will be correct beyond the query-only predictor. A seed-averaged improvement above 1.5 points is possible, but the additional information could instead produce small gains or overfitting.

judge_luna.reason: A recorded probe answer can reveal query difficulty or correctness beyond the query embedding, so a gain above 1.5 points is plausible. Its signal may be redundant or difficult for the predictor to learn, and the registered event measures quality gain rather than net benefit after the added probe cost.

judge_muse.reason: Query templates already reveal task and difficulty, and inferring other models' correctness from one cheap answer requires verification that query plus response embeddings are unlikely to provide beyond about one point.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The Routing Plateau paper suggests that inputs beyond the query, such as partial output trajectories, may be needed to get past the plateau. Its abstract reports no test of this. The proposed experiment is that test, done offline with a cheap model's recorded full response.

Cascade routing uses post-hoc quality estimators on responses already generated to decide whether to continue through a cascade. It does not measure, against a query-only twin and a shuffled-response control, whether one cheap response improves 18-way per-model correctness prediction.
FrugalGPT scores (query, answer) pairs to accept or escalate within a fixed model order. The answer is used to decide whether to stop, not as a feature for choosing among all candidates.
Pro-Router reads the small model's token-level confidence to decide whether to escalate to one cloud model. That is a binary edge/cloud choice, not multi-model selection conditioned on the response.

Router-R1 is an RL-trained LLM router that adds model responses to its context over several rounds. It does not isolate whether a cheap probe response adds predictive value beyond the query, and it has no shuffled control.

ACAR uses the self-consistency variance of 3 probe samples to pick a 1-, 2- or 3-model execution mode among 3 models. It does not use a learned predictor of each model's correctness from a cheap response's content.
Lookahead predicts latent representations of candidate outputs rather than using a real cheap model's answer as router input.

opus.reason: I found no paper that runs a matched comparison between a query-only router and a router given the query plus a cheap model's actual response for multi-model (18-way) selection, with a shuffled-response control and the probe's cost charged. Earlier work uses cheap responses only to decide whether to escalate or to choose an execution mode (cascades, FrugalGPT, Pro-Router, ACAR), or folds responses into an LLM router without isolating their value (Router-R1). The Routing Plateau paper proposes this remedy, but its abstract reports no test. My search was limited by tool-call caps and turned up many off-topic results, so I may have missed relevant work.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: JiSi combines query embeddings, actual response embeddings, and response lengths to refine multi-model routing, including a router-only evaluation. However, it obtains responses from three query-selected candidates rather than testing whether one fixed cheapest model's answer predicts the correctness of the remaining candidates.

Cascade routing updates per-model quality estimates after model calls and permits arbitrary subsequent model selection. Its experiments use simulated quality signals or features such as log probabilities, response length, and agreement, rather than isolating the semantic information in one cheap answer against a matched query-only predictor.

Lookahead predicts candidate-response representations without generating answers at routing time. Its preliminary actual-response experiment scores each candidate's own query-response pair, not the correctness of other models from one cheap model's response.

Encoder-target decoupling uses an encoder model's prefill activations to jointly predict correctness across other models. It does not observe or test the additional information supplied by an actual generated probe answer.
The seed provides response-bearing routing states and evaluates multi-turn workflows, but does not report the controlled single-cheap-response augmentation experiment.

sol.reason: Response-aware routing and cross-model correctness prediction were already established, so the general motivation is not new. Nevertheless, the closest work does not settle whether the semantic content of one cheapest model's actual answer supplies useful routing information about otherwise unobserved candidates beyond the query; that single-probe cross-model question remains distinct in the work I found.

opus.reason: Entries 7 and 34 use a draft answer to decide whether to escalate or continue between two models, but none feeds the cheapest model's recorded response into an 18-way per-model success predictor with a shuffled-response control.

sol.reason: The registered experiment tests whether a cheap response improves full multi-model selection over query-only prediction, whereas the listed draft-aware experiments test verification or selective continuation.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered offline experiment: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B features; training-cost-selected probe; Q/R/S MLPs for seeds 0–2; within-task deranged-response control; validation-selected kNN pair; all reference policies; probe-inclusive USD costs; hard/task subsets; validation AUROC; and 2,000 paired query-bootstrap resamples. Required outputs and result.json are regenerated by the command. Pinned dataset/model revisions and dependencies. Tested the command with deleted required outputs and no feature artifacts; it reproduced the statistic exactly in about 3.4 minutes. Selected probe: llama-3-8b-instruct-lite. Statistic: 2.1744309253973064 points; 95% CI [1.6321802531310656, 2.707307666080151]. Small data-resolution clarification: two training query texts had distinct recorded executions under duplicate instance IDs. Retained each query's complete lowest-embedding_id execution vector, removing two repeated instances (36 rows), to preserve unique-query fitting/validation; documented in summary and README. All 3,729 unique test queries retained; no test exclusions. No hypothesis, controls, hyperparameters, threshold, or evaluation changes. Interpretation caveats: shuffled control gains 1.3672 points; kNN gain is small with CI spanning zero; substantial seed variability; R-MLP remains slightly below the best-single reference.

departures: experiment.py load_data: two training query texts appear under two embedding_ids with different recorded executions. Only the lowest-embedding_id execution vector is kept, dropping 2 instances (36 rows) out of 80,802. The registration does not address this case. The engineer reported it in the notes, README and summary.json adjustments. It affects 2 of 4,489 training instances and no test rows, so it cannot plausibly change the statistic.

experiment.py kNN pair: neighbours are drawn from the 90% fit split rather than all train queries ('k nearest train queries'). Ties are broken by fit-set mean performance rather than full-train mean. This was disclosed in the README. It affects only the secondary R-kNN minus Q-kNN comparison, not the registered statistic.

Protected run reused the engineer's submitted embedding artifacts ('Reusing verified feature artifacts') instead of recomputing them. The check covers only text-digest, model-revision and row count, not the embedding values themselves. The engineer's uncached experiment.log reproduces the same statistic (2.1744308 vs 2.1744309) and identical best epochs, so this probably did not change the result, but the protected run itself did not regenerate the features.
experiment.py: the probe-correctness oracle is charged the probe's cost plus the Q-MLP choice's cost. The registration leaves its costing open. Cost reporting only; no effect on the statistic.
experiment.py bootstrap: 2,000 resamples are drawn as 20 batches of 100 and use percentile limits. This is equivalent to the registered procedure, with no effect.

Query text for list-form queries is built by joining message contents (text()), which the code claims matches the reference generate_embeddings.py. This cannot be verified from the material shown. It applies equally to the Q, R and S variants.
problems: outputs/summary.json seed_differences_points are -0.07, +4.80 and +1.80. The mean gain of 2.17 depends heavily on one poorly trained Q-MLP run (seed 1, best epoch 5, test 75.66). With only 3 seeds, the registered event is fragile to training noise.

The bootstrap CI [1.63, 2.71] resamples test queries with the trained models held fixed. It omits seed or training variance, the dominant source of uncertainty here, so it overstates precision. The README acknowledges this.

The shuffled-response control S-MLP also gains 1.37 points over Q-MLP (CI 0.83–1.88). The content-specific R−S difference is only about 0.81 points, and no interval is reported for it, so most of the gain is not attributable to aligned response content.
The learner-robustness check fails to corroborate the gain: R-kNN minus Q-kNN is 0.25 points with a CI spanning zero.

outputs/variant_scores.csv: mean Q-MLP (78.04) and mean R-MLP (80.21) both score below the constant best-single-on-train reference (80.54). The predictors therefore do not yet route usefully, which limits what the R-vs-Q delta says about routing.

registration.title: Does the 14.6% headline gain on xRouteBench Generic survive a best-single-model baseline chosen on training data? Splitting the gain into fixed-model choice, task identification and query-level routing
registration.seed_connection: The abstract reports a '14.6% relative improvement over the strongest fixed-model baseline'. This equals RouterDC 80.56 over Largest-LLM 70.29 on Generic LLM Tasks in Table 2 (80.56/70.29 = 1.146). Largest-LLM is chosen by declared parameter count, not by measured quality, and the paper reports no fixed model selected on training data. Every xRouteBench test query was pre-run on all candidates, so any fixed model or lookup policy can be scored exactly by replay.
registration.hypothesis: The candidate with the highest mean training performance on llmrouter_generic scores on the test split within 5% (relative) of RouterDC's reported 80.56, i.e. at least about 76.7.
registration.contribution: A direct test of the seed's headline number against the standard best-single baseline on the seed's own benchmark and pool. It also decomposes the remaining gap into three parts: the between-task gain of a 13-entry per-subtask lookup chosen on training data, the within-task headroom (oracle minus lookup), and the reported router scores relative to both.

closest_work.difference: LLMRouterBench uses Best Single and Dataset Oracle references on its own 33-model benchmark. It does not test xRouteBench, the seed's 18-model pool, or the seed's headline claim.
Finds that routers mostly learn global capability trends and plateau. It does not re-score the seed's claim against a train-selected fixed model or a train-selected task lookup.
Defines oracle and cost-quality references for routing. It predates xRouteBench and its candidate pool.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench (public): config llmrouter_generic (train and test) for the primary test; configs memory_locomo, memory_longmemeval, timeseries, video, multimodal_geometry3k and multimodal_mathvista for secondary analyses; config llm_candidates for model_name, size, input_price_per_1m, output_price_per_1m and service.

Reported numbers from the seed paper (arXiv 2608.06867, Table 2): RouterDC 80.56, GraphRouter 80.54, SVMRouter 74.21, Largest-LLM 70.29 and Smallest-LLM 57.55 on Generic; GraphRouter's 7-set average 45.46; EloRouter's 44.68.
pandas, numpy, datasets.
registration.method:
0) Schema check. Load each config with datasets.load_dataset('ulab-ai/xRouteBench', cfg). Print column names, dtypes, row counts, the number of unique queries and the number of models per split, and write them to the summary. Rows are expected in long format, one row per query x candidate, with query, model_name, performance, input_tokens, output_tokens and ideally task_name. Decode string fields that start with '[' or '{' with json.loads, falling back to ast.literal_eval and then to the raw string. Identify a query by its query string (or embedding_id, if present). For each query and model, use the first matching row.
1) Dollar cost per row = input_tokens*input_price_per_1m/1e6 + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m/1e6.
2) Sanity check and aggregation choice. Parse each candidate's size string (e.g. '671B' gives 671; '46.7B' gives 46.7). Every model tied at the maximum declared size is a Largest-LLM candidate; there are expected to be two at 671B. Every model tied at the minimum is a Smallest-LLM candidate. Score each candidate on the Generic test split under two aggregations: (a) the mean over all unique test queries, and (b) the unweighted mean over task_name of per-task means. Multiply by 100. Choose the aggregation, and the Largest and Smallest candidates, whose scores are jointly closest to 70.29 and 57.55. Use that aggregation for every Generic number below and report all scores. If no combination comes within 1.0 point of both, still compute everything with aggregation (a) and set summary flag replication_failed=true.
3) BSM (best single model). Among models with non-NaN training rows, take the one with the highest mean training performance on llmrouter_generic. Break ties by lower mean training dollar cost. S_BSM = its test score (x100) under the chosen aggregation. NaN test rows are dropped, as the seed's replay evaluator does; report the count.
4) Primary statistic: G = 100*(80.56/S_BSM - 1).
5) Secondary analyses:
- Per-subtask lookup: for each task_name, take the model with the highest mean training performance within that task (ties to lower cost) and apply it to that task's test queries. If task_name is absent, report this and skip.
- Per-query oracle: the maximum recorded performance over all models.
- Hindsight best: the model with the highest test score (upper reference only).
- Headroom decomposition: (lookup - BSM) is the between-task gain; (oracle - lookup) is the within-task headroom. Report the gaps between reported RouterDC/GraphRouter/SVMRouter and both lookup and BSM.
- Top 5 models by training score and by test score, with their mean dollar costs.
- BSM on each of the other six datasets (train-selected), and the unweighted 7-set average, compared with 45.46 and 44.68.
- Cost-aware BSM: for each (alpha, beta) in {(1,0),(0.8,0.2),(0.6,0.4),(0.4,0.6),(0.2,0.8)}, take the fixed model maximizing training mean of alpha*perf - beta*cost/C_ref, where C_ref is the maximum over models of mean training cost. Report its test performance and mean USD cost.

event.description: The seed's headline gain falls below 5% relative once the comparator is the best single model chosen on training data instead of Largest-LLM.
event.statistic: G = 100*(80.56/S_BSM - 1), where S_BSM is the train-selected best single model's llmrouter_generic test score (x100) under the aggregation that best reproduces Table 2's fixed baselines.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute S_BSM and G. A bootstrap over unique test queries (2,000 resamples, seed 0; stratified by task_name if aggregation (b) is used) gives a 95% interval for S_BSM and the implied interval for G, holding 80.56 fixed. The summary notes that RouterDC's own standard error is about 0.65 points at n = 3,729, which matters if G lands near 5. Also report bootstrap intervals for the lookup and oracle scores.
- outputs/schema.json: printed columns, row counts and models per config/split.
- outputs/fixed_models.csv: one line per (dataset, model) with mean training performance, test performance under both aggregations, and mean dollar cost.
- outputs/lookup_table.json: the model chosen for each task_name.
- outputs/summary.json: the Largest/Smallest candidates and their scores against 70.29/57.55, the aggregation chosen, replication_failed, BSM identity, S_BSM, G and their intervals, lookup/oracle/hindsight scores, the headroom decomposition, 7-set averages, and the cost-aware BSM table.
evaluation.controls: Reproducing Largest-LLM and Smallest-LLM checks that the released data and aggregation match the paper. Selection uses training data only; the hindsight test-best model is an upper reference, not the baseline. The oracle is the ceiling, and the lookup separates task identification from query-level routing.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-run all of the seed's routers alongside best-single, per-subtask lookup and oracle baselines on every xRouteBench track and cost weight. Report router gains relative to the best single model and the lookup with paired confidence intervals, and add within-task evaluation splits to test whether any learned router captures within-task headroom.

registration.title: Is xRouteBench's cost-weighted reward blind to price? Testing the released evaluator on constant 'always model m' policies and on two-model mixtures
registration.seed_connection: The seed ranks routers by the weighted reward alpha*perf - beta*cost at five weights (Fig. 5) and concludes that rankings reverse under tighter cost constraints. In the released code, benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py evaluate() min-max normalizes performance and cost over the rows the evaluated router itself selected. If so, the cost term measures the spread within a router's own choices rather than its price level. The paper does not state its normalization, so linking the code to Fig. 5 is an inference; the repository says the pipeline mirrors the published settings.
registration.hypothesis: At (alpha, beta) = (0.2, 0.8), the released reward ranks the constant single-model policies in an order nearly unrelated to their actual mean dollar cost per query: the Kendall tau-b between reward and negative mean cost, averaged over the 7 non-personalized test sets, is below 0.3.
registration.contribution: A validity check of the metric behind the seed's cost-aware rankings. Constant policies have a known cost order, which makes the test clean. A two-model mixture sweep tests whether reward falls monotonically with spend for routers that mix models. The experiment also provides a router-independent alternative normalization.

closest_work.difference: RouterBench compares routers on cost-quality curves in absolute dollar cost. It neither uses nor audits within-policy normalization.
LLMRouterBench normalizes over all configurations jointly for its Pareto-distance metric. It does not examine per-router normalization.
Studies routers drifting toward expensive models, which is router behaviour, not the normalization of the evaluation metric.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench: test splits of llmrouter_generic, memory_locomo, memory_longmemeval, timeseries, video, multimodal_geometry3k and multimodal_mathvista; config llm_candidates (input and output price per 1M tokens).
Seed repository github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter (git clone), file benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py, function evaluate(), used as the reward implementation.
pandas, numpy, scipy, datasets.
registration.method:
0) Load each test split; print and save the schema (columns, models, unique queries). For each dataset and model, take the first row per unique query. Cost per row = input_tokens*input_price_per_1m/1e6 + output_tokens*output_price_per_1m/1e6.
1) Reward implementation. Clone the repository and read evaluate() in benchmark_pipeline/run_pipeline.py. Call it directly on a DataFrame holding the policy's selected rows, constructed in the format evaluate() expects (inspect its signature and the columns it reads), with alpha and beta set per weighting. If the call cannot be made without the full pipeline, reimplement it line by line. Save the copied source text of evaluate() to outputs/evaluate_source.txt and set summary flag used_repo_function true/false. If evaluate() does not min-max normalize within the evaluated rows, record exactly what it does; the statistic is still computed with the function as released. The expected reference behaviour: drop NaN performance; norm_p = (p - p.min())/(p.max() - p.min() + 1e-12); norm_c likewise for cost over the same rows; R_seed = mean(alpha*norm_p - beta*norm_c).
2) Fixed-reference reward: C_ref = the maximum over models of mean test cost on that dataset; R_fix = mean(alpha*p - beta*c/C_ref).
3) Weights: (1.0,0.0), (0.8,0.2), (0.6,0.4), (0.4,0.6), (0.2,0.8).
4) Constant policies. For each dataset, every model m with test rows defines the policy that always routes to m. Compute R_seed and R_fix at every weight.
5) Primary: for each dataset, scipy.stats.kendalltau (tau-b) between R_seed(m; 0.2, 0.8) and -mean_cost(m) across the constant policies, then average the 7 values.
6) Secondary analyses:
- tau between R_seed at (0.2,0.8) and R_seed at (1,0).
- tau between R_fix at (0.2,0.8) and -mean_cost (positive control; expected high).
- tau between R_seed and R_fix at every weight.
- Spearman correlation between R_seed at (0.2,0.8) and each policy's mean norm_c.
- Top policy under each metric and weight.
- Number of degenerate policies with p.max() == p.min(), e.g. a policy that answers all queries correctly getting norm_p = 0.
- Mixture sweep on llmrouter_generic and timeseries: take the cheapest model by mean cost (A) and the most expensive (B). For fraction f in {0, 0.1, ..., 1.0}, route a fixed random fraction f of queries to B (seed 0; the routed sets are nested as f grows) and the rest to A. Compute mean performance, mean USD cost, R_seed and R_fix at (0.2,0.8). Report the Spearman correlation of each reward with mean USD cost across f, and of mean performance with f.

event.description: The released reward at the heaviest cost weight fails to order constant policies by their actual dollar cost.
event.statistic: Mean over the 7 datasets of Kendall tau-b between R_seed(m; 0.2, 0.8) and -mean_cost(m) across the constant single-model policies.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute the per-dataset tau values and their mean. A bootstrap over test queries (1,000 resamples within each dataset, recomputing every policy's rewards on the resampled queries) gives a 95% interval for the mean tau.
- outputs/schema.json: the printed schema per dataset.
- outputs/evaluate_source.txt: the source of evaluate() as cloned.
- outputs/policy_rewards.csv: one line per (dataset, model, weight) with R_seed, R_fix, mean performance, mean cost and mean norm_c.
- outputs/mixture_sweep.csv: one line per (dataset, f) with performance, cost, R_seed and R_fix.
- outputs/taus.json: all per-dataset and averaged correlations with intervals, the mixture correlations, and used_repo_function.
- outputs/top_policies.json: the top policy per dataset, weight and metric, plus degenerate-policy counts.
evaluation.controls: Positive control: R_fix at the heavy weight should track cost closely; if it does not, the analysis is faulty. Negative control: at (1,0), R_seed and R_fix should rank policies by performance and agree, except on F1-scored datasets where normalization rescales performance. The mixture sweep tests monotonicity in spend directly.

registration.full_scale_study: Recompute Fig. 5 for all of the seed's routers with router-independent normalization and absolute-USD cost-quality curves (area under the curve, bootstrap Pareto frontiers). Test whether the reported reversals survive, e.g. RouterDC falling to tenth on Generic and MLPRouter leading Vision for beta >= 0.4, and contribute a corrected evaluator.

The accuracy term also pushes expensive models up, so tau should sit near zero or below. The residual risk is that the released function differs from those descriptions.

registration.title: A same-weights negative control inside xRouteBench: how often do two provider endpoints of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct disagree, relative to genuinely different models?
registration.seed_connection: xRouteBench's 18-model pool contains Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct twice (Table 9): qwen2.5-7b-instruct via NVIDIA and qwen2.5-7b-instruct-turbo via Together. Both receive identical prompts at near-greedy decoding. Their per-query disagreement cannot reflect a difference in base weights, though it can reflect serving precision, quantization or system-role handling. It therefore bounds the non-capability part of the query-model matrix that the seed uses as both router supervision and test bed, and that the seed calls 'exactly the headroom that routing exploits'.
registration.hypothesis: Per-query correctness disagreement between the two Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct endpoints is more than one third of the mean disagreement between the NVIDIA endpoint and the three non-twin pool models whose overall accuracy is closest to it, on the llmrouter_generic test split.
registration.contribution: Uses a near-zero-capability-difference pair already present in a published routing benchmark to bound how much apparent query-level complementarity is serving or decoding noise. It also estimates how much such noise inflates the per-query oracle over 18 models.

closest_work.difference: Compares single-sample with 10-sample majority labels and finds a small oracle drop. This experiment measures provider/serving noise at near-greedy decoding and scales it against genuine cross-model disagreement.
Formalizes oracle premiums under stochastic decoding from repeated samples. This experiment needs no resampling: it uses a same-weights twin already in the benchmark.
RouteGuard shows advisor pools are often redundant. This experiment calibrates disagreement against a pair whose true capability difference is about zero.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench: config llmrouter_generic (test, and train for a replication), the six other non-personalized configs (test) for per-track estimates, and llm_candidates (names, services, prices).
registration.method:
0) Load the splits; print and save the schema. Pivot each split to a query x model matrix of performance and output_tokens. Identify unique queries by query string (or embedding_id); for each query and model, take the first row.
1) Twins. Identify by llm_candidates name and service: the name containing 'qwen2.5-7b-instruct' without 'turbo' (expected service NVIDIA) is N; the name containing 'qwen2.5-7b-instruct-turbo' (expected Together) is T. Record exact names. Abort with a clear message in the summary if either is missing.
2) Binary restriction. D(a,b) = mean of 1[perf_a != perf_b] over queries where both a and b have performance exactly 0 or 1.
3) D_twin = D(N,T).
4) Comparators. Among models other than N and T, rank by |acc_m - acc_N|, with accuracies computed on the queries where m and N are jointly binary. Take the 3 closest models m1, m2, m3. D_match = the mean of D(N, m_k) over k = 1..3.
5) Primary: R = D_twin / D_match on the llmrouter_generic test split.
6) Secondary analyses:
- R against each m_k separately.
- D(N,m) for every model, alongside the independence expectation p(1-q)+q(1-p).
- Twin accuracy difference with an exact McNemar test.
- R per task_name, and per non-Generic dataset; flag sets with fewer than 50 jointly binary queries as low-n.
- R on the Generic train split.
- Share of twin disagreements in which either endpoint had output_tokens == 0 or output_tokens >= 507.
- Number of queries where T is the unique best model, i.e. where a router would be supervised to pay more for the same weights.
- Oracle inflation simulation: on Generic test, start from the observed binary matrix. In each of 200 simulations (seed 0), independently flip each model's binary outcome on each query with probability q_flip = D_twin/2, so that two independent copies disagree at about D_twin. Recompute the per-query oracle over all models. Report the mean oracle increase compared with the observed oracle, and its ratio to (observed oracle - best single model on test). This is a heuristic, because the observed matrix already contains noise.

event.description: Same-weights twin endpoints disagree on per-query correctness more than one third as often as accuracy-matched different models do.
event.statistic: R = D_twin / D_match on the llmrouter_generic test split, where D_match averages over the 3 accuracy-closest non-twin models.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute R with a 95% bootstrap interval over queries (2,000 resamples, seed 0, recomputing D_twin and D_match each time with fixed m1..m3).
- outputs/schema.json: the schema per config.
- outputs/twin_matrix.csv: per Generic test query, task_name and the performance and output_tokens of N, T and m1..m3.
- outputs/pairwise_disagreement.csv: per model, accuracy, observed disagreement with N, and the independence expectation.
- outputs/twin_summary.json: twin names, m1..m3, D_twin, D_match, R and its interval, per-comparator R, McNemar result, per-task and per-dataset R, train-split R, the collection-issue share, the count of unique-best-T queries, and oracle-inflation results.
evaluation.controls: The accuracy-matched different models are the reference for genuine capability differences. The independence expectation is an upper reference. The twin accuracy difference checks rough equivalence. D_twin is interpreted as an upper bound on pure serving noise, since the endpoints may differ in quantization or role handling.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-collect the Generic track with several open models served locally in bf16 and fp8 and with multiple samples per cell. Build expected-correctness labels, and measure how router rankings, oracle headroom and routing gains change once labels are denoised.

agent.reason: FP8-versus-bf16 serving and provider nondeterminism should flip only a few percent of short multiple-choice answers, though more on long MATH and MBPP outputs. That gives an estimated D_twin of about 0.05–0.07 against roughly 0.2–0.25 disagreement between accuracy-matched different models, so R is about 0.2–0.3. Collection errors on one endpoint could push it past 0.33.

judge_astra.reason: Near-greedy nominal twins should agree more than distinct models, but provider-specific prompting, precision, and truncation could plausibly push disagreement above this threshold. Endpoint names alone would not establish that the measured disagreement represents stochastic noise rather than stable serving differences.

judge_fable.reason: Same-weights endpoints served under different precision (FP8 turbo vs NIM) with long math/code generations and a ~512-token cap plausibly disagree on correctness for roughly 8-15% of queries, while accuracy-matched different models disagree on ~25-32%, putting R near or modestly above 0.33; any non-zero sampling temperature or endpoint-specific formatting issues would push it clearly over.

judge_opus.reason: At greedy or near-greedy decoding, FP8-versus-BF16 serving differences probably flip correctness on roughly 3–7% of Generic queries. Accuracy-matched models from other families typically disagree on about 20–25%, which puts R near or below 0.33. Exceeding the threshold likely requires non-trivial sampling temperature, truncation flips or collection failures, none of which the paper states.

judge_sol.reason: Potential precision, prompt-handling, and truncation differences could produce enough correctness disagreement to cross the threshold, especially on multi-step tasks. But nominally shared weights could instead yield much tighter agreement, and endpoint disagreement would not by itself identify stochastic noise.

judge_luna.reason: Near-greedy inference of the same nominal Qwen2.5-7B weights should usually disagree less than distinct, accuracy-matched models, favoring R at or below one third. But the turbo endpoint may differ in precision, templates, sampling, or model revision, so its disagreement could be substantial.

judge_muse.reason: Same-weights near-greedy resampling typically disagrees only a few percent while accuracy-matched different models disagree much more, so R above 0.33 needs large provider/quantization or prompt-handling differences; small test sets add noise.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: DARS shows that routing labels built from one sampled response are unstable under repeated decoding and query rewrites, and that this instability carries over into learned routers. It measures the instability by resampling the same endpoint. It does not use two provider endpoints of the same weights already in a benchmark pool, and it does not scale that disagreement against accuracy-matched different models in xRouteBench.

Formalizes how much routing oracles are inflated under stochastic decoding, using 30 archived samples per cell on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA. It does not use a cross-provider same-weights twin as a negative control, and it does not study xRouteBench.

A measurement study of how hosted open-weight model endpoints differ as services: price, latency, context length, protocol support. It does not measure per-query correctness disagreement between same-weights endpoints, and it does not treat that disagreement as noise in routing supervision.

Cited by the agent but not opened or verified here. As the agent describes it, it compares single-sample labels with 10-sample majority labels and reports a small drop in the oracle. That is resampling-based, not a provider-twin control scaled against cross-model disagreement.

The seed paper builds the query-model matrix and treats its complementarity as routing headroom. As far as I could tell from the abstract and my searches, it does not use its duplicated Qwen2.5-7B endpoints to calibrate how much of that complementarity is noise. I did not read its full text to confirm this.

opus.reason: Earlier work (DARS, the stochastic-oracle paper) already shows that single-sample routing labels are noisy and can inflate the oracle, so the general concern is not new. I found no paper that uses a pair of same-weights endpoints from two providers inside a published routing benchmark as a negative control, measuring their disagreement relative to accuracy-matched different models in xRouteBench. This conclusion rests on abstract-level searches, and I did not read the seed paper's full text, so related work missed by those searches cannot be ruled out; still, the specific question and design appear unanswered.

closest_work.difference: Uses same-condition reruns to compare web-agent outcome variability with gains from different observation representations. It does not compare same-checkpoint provider endpoints with accuracy-matched, different-weight models.

Measures quality and output-distribution variation across endpoints serving the same nominal model, but does not use endpoint twins to calibrate query-level complementarity or oracle headroom in a routing benchmark.

Audits stochastic hindsight-oracle premiums using repeated responses and coupling-aware success probabilities, rather than a provider-twin negative control scaled against cross-model correctness disagreement.
Tests single-sample label noise through ten-sample majority labels and oracle recomputation; it does not isolate cross-provider variation using duplicated nominal weights.

sol.reason: Prior work already examines noise-driven oracle headroom, same-condition rerun controls, and same-model endpoint variation, so those general ideas are not new. However, among work available by 2026-10-07, I found none answering the specific provider-versus-capability question through an internal endpoint-twin control compared with accuracy-matched, different-weight candidates in the same routing matrix. The seed lists the two Qwen endpoints but does not report this analysis.

opus.reason: No list entry uses the two same-weights Qwen2.5-7B provider endpoints as a negative control to scale per-query disagreement against genuinely different models; #50 resamples completions locally instead.

sol.reason: No listed experiment uses same-weights provider endpoints as a negative control and measures their disagreement relative to accuracy-matched different models.

registration.title: Do arbitrary tie-breaks in 'best-model' training labels drive the kNN/SVM/MLP router scores on xRouteBench Generic?
registration.seed_connection: In the seed's code, the kNN, SVM and MLP routers (llmrouter/models/knnrouter, svmrouter, mlprouter) take their training target from train_df.loc[train_df.groupby('query')['performance'].idxmax()]. This picks the first row in file order among models tied at the maximum, including on queries every model fails. With mostly 0/1 metrics and 18 candidates, ties are common. In Table 2 these routers score 68-74 on Generic, while RouterDC and GraphRouter, which train on the full per-model score vector, score about 80.5. The paper reads such gaps as differences in router design.
registration.hypothesis: On llmrouter_generic, replacing first-occurrence tie-breaking with a quality-prior tie-break (among tied models, the one with the highest training-set mean performance) raises replayed test performance by more than 3 points, averaged over the kNN, SVM and MLP routers.
registration.contribution: Separates label construction (how ties and all-fail queries are resolved) from router architecture in a widely used routing library. Random tie-breaking isolates row-order bias. Soft-label variants show what full-vector supervision gives with the same encoder. Comparison with the best single model shows whether any gain only amounts to 'becoming the best single model'.

closest_work.difference: Shows routers converge to a narrow accuracy plateau. It does not examine how ties in hard best-model labels are broken.
Shows a tuned kNN matching complex routers. It does not compare tie-breaking rules for argmax labels or measure their effect on a published ranking.
Re-evaluates routers against Best Single and Oracle baselines. It does not study label tie handling.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench: config llmrouter_generic (train/test) for the primary run; configs memory_locomo, memory_longmemeval, timeseries, video, multimodal_geometry3k and multimodal_mathvista for secondary runs; config llm_candidates (prices, sizes).
Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from Hugging Face (the seed's query encoder).

Seed repository github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, used as reference only: benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py (field decoding), benchmark_pipeline/generate_embeddings.py (embedding protocol), benchmark_pipeline/configs/hparams.yaml (router hyperparameters).
pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, PyTorch, transformers, datasets.
registration.method:
1) Load each config with datasets.load_dataset('ulab-ai/xRouteBench', cfg). Convert each split to pandas without sorting or re-indexing, so the RangeIndex equals the released row order. Print and save the schema. Decode string fields starting with '[' or '{' with json.loads, falling back to ast.literal_eval and then the raw string.
2) Embed each unique query string with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on GPU: padding_side='left', truncation at max_length 512, last-token pooling, L2 normalization, float32, batch size 64. Flatten chat-message lists by joining message contents with newlines. Key embeddings by query string.
3) Labels for each unique training query, grouped by the 'query' string:
- L0 (seed rule): model_name at groupby('query')['performance'].idxmax().
- L1: uniform random choice among models whose performance, rounded to 6 decimals, equals the group maximum; seeds 0, 1, 2.
- L2: among tied-maximum models, the one with the highest mean training performance on that dataset; remaining ties go to lower mean training dollar cost (input_tokens*input_price/1e6 + output_tokens*output_price/1e6).
- SOFT: the vector of all models' performances on the query (missing values = 0).
4) Routers, using the seed's hyperparameters (check hparams.yaml and use its values if they differ from these):
- kNN: KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', metric='minkowski', p=2).
- SVM: SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0, gamma='scale'). To bound runtime, fit SVM on one fixed random subset of at most 8,000 unique training queries (seed 0), the same subset for every label rule, and record this.
- MLP: PyTorch 1024-256-128-C with ReLU, cross-entropy, Adam lr 1e-3, weight_decay 1e-4, 100 epochs, batch 32, on GPU, torch seeds 0, 1, 2; the MLP score is the mean over seeds. Reduce epochs to 30 on any dataset where training would push total runtime past budget, and record this.
- kNN-soft: average the SOFT vectors of the 5 nearest training queries, route to the argmax, and break ties by the L2 prior order.
- MLP-soft: the same MLP with one output per model, trained with BCE-with-logits on SOFT (MSE if any target lies outside [0,1]), routed by argmax, seeds 0-2.
5) Replay evaluation, as in the seed's run_pipeline.evaluate: for each unique test query, take the recorded performance of the routed model from the first matching (query, model_name) row; drop and count NaN rows; average; multiply by 100. Also record the mean dollar cost of routed choices.
6) Primary run on llmrouter_generic: kNN, SVM and MLP with L0 and L2. kNN and MLP also run with L1 (3 seeds) and SOFT. Secondary: all variants on the six smaller datasets (SVM subset rule applies).
7) Context per dataset: the train-selected best single model (BSM) and its test score; the per-query oracle; for each router and rule, the share of test queries routed to BSM.

event.description: On llmrouter_generic, quality-prior tie-breaking raises replayed test performance by more than 3 points over first-occurrence tie-breaking, averaged over kNN, SVM and MLP.
event.statistic: Delta = mean over {kNN, SVM, MLP} of [test performance (x100) with L2 labels minus with L0 labels] on llmrouter_generic, with MLP scores averaged over 3 seeds.

evaluation.procedure:
Delta is the unweighted mean of the three L2-minus-L0 differences. A paired bootstrap over unique test queries (2,000 resamples, seed 0) gives 95% intervals for each router's difference and for Delta.
Label diagnostics per dataset:
- share of training queries with two or more models tied at the maximum;
- share whose maximum is 0;
- per-model label counts under L0 and L2;
- each model's mean position within its query group in the released order, and the Spearman correlation between that position and model price, to check whether L0 effectively means 'cheapest among tied'.
Report each L2 router's score minus BSM, and L0-versus-L2 differences in mean dollar cost.
- outputs/schema.json: the schema per config.
- outputs/results.csv: one row per (dataset, router, label rule, seed) with test performance, mean routed dollar cost, number scored and share routed to BSM.
- outputs/label_stats.json: the label diagnostics.
- outputs/routing_decisions.jsonl: the routed model and recorded performance for every test query under every variant.
- outputs/bootstrap.json: Delta, the per-router differences and their intervals, BSM and oracle scores.
evaluation.controls: L1 (random tie-break, 3 seeds) removes row-order bias without a quality prior: L1 minus L0 measures order bias, and L2 minus L1 measures the prior. SOFT variants show the effect of full-vector supervision. Replication check: compare L0 scores with Table 2 (kNN 71.37, SVM 74.21, MLP 68.12); a gap above 3 points is reported as evidence that the released row order or setup differs from the paper's. BSM and the oracle give scale, and the share routed to BSM shows whether L2 routers collapse to BSM.

registration.full_scale_study: Re-run all local routers of the seed's pipeline (including MF, Elo, Hybrid LLM, GraphRouter and RouterDC) under tie-aware labels on all xRouteBench datasets, all cost weights and several random re-splits. Test whether the published rankings survive, and propose a tie-aware labelling standard for routing libraries.

The event fails if the released row order differs or that model is weaker than expected.

First-occurrence labels favour whichever model comes first in row order, consistent with the 68–74 range in Table 2. The event therefore largely tracks whether the best single model clears about 74–75, and fails if the released row order happens to put a top model first.

judge_sol.reason: With many candidates and mostly binary outcomes, tied winners should be common, and a quality-prior tie-break could substantially improve the hard-label routers' default choices. The principal uncertainties are whether the released row order already favors strong models, baseline reproducibility, and runtime-driven training reductions.

It does not change how ties or all-fail queries are resolved in argmax 'best-model' labels, so it does not test whether label construction drives the published scores.

Re-evaluates routers against Best Single Model and Oracle baselines. It does not study label tie handling or hard-versus-soft supervision with the same encoder.
The seed paper. It uses first-occurrence argmax labels for kNN, SVM and MLP and treats score gaps as differences in router design. It has no ablation of label construction.

opus.reason: Several arXiv searches (tie-breaking in router labels, ambiguous or multi-correct routing labels, soft versus hard routing supervision, router evaluation pitfalls, reproductions of LLMRouter/xRouteBench) found no paper that varies the tie-breaking rule for argmax router labels, such as first-occurrence, random or quality-prior, and measures the effect on router scores. The closest work (the routing plateau study, the tuned kNN result, and re-evaluations against single-model and oracle baselines) looks at router convergence and baselines, not how the labels are built. My searches could have missed something, so this is a judgment that no prior answer was found, not proof that none exists.

closest_work.difference: Breaking the Tie identifies ambiguity when multiple LLMs answer correctly and constructs quality-informed labels. Its controlled ablation compares cluster-prior hard labels with cluster-weighted soft labels, not first-occurrence hard labels with training-set-mean-quality hard tie-breaking or randomized tie controls.

Expanding LLM Reasoning directly demonstrates earliest-index training-label bias using deterministic versus randomized ties and a tie-invariant listwise loss. It selects reasoning restart positions rather than candidate LLMs and does not test quality-prior tie-breaking.
Compares hard model-selection and full-score utility-prediction formulations, including kNN and MLP routers. It does not isolate alternative tie-breaking rules within hard best-model supervision.
The seed reports the relevant xRouteBench router scores and supplies the shared infrastructure, but does not experimentally intervene on hard-label tie resolution.

sol.reason: Prior work already recognizes ambiguous routing labels, studies quality-informed supervision, and demonstrates that deterministic label ties can bias learned selectors. However, I found no study isolating first-occurrence versus global training-quality-prior hard tie-breaking with fixed router architectures and randomized controls; the closest routing paper instead tests cluster-weighted soft supervision against quality-informed hard labels. The registered comparison therefore asks an unanswered question, rather than merely repeating an existing experiment on a different benchmark.

sol.reason: Both vary arbitrary tie-breaking and tie-aware supervision while holding cached candidate responses and router features fixed, then measure changes in held-out routing accuracy.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented all seven registered datasets, row-order-preserving L0/L1/L2 labels, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B float32 embeddings, seed-YAML hyperparameters, hard/soft routers, replay costs, BSM/oracle, diagnostics, and paired 2,000-resample bootstrap. Final command tested successfully; all MLPs used 100 epochs. Independent batched MLPs accelerate training without weight sharing; unit tests verified standalone logits/Adam updates. L1 uses three paired label/torch seeds. Minor unspecified-case resolutions: lexical order after exact quality-and-cost prior ties; first released query/model row for duplicate SOFT entries (36 duplicate Generic training rows). No hypothesis/event changes. Observed Delta=20.161792343901702, 95% CI [18.66558404399849,21.716008175408078]. All three L0 replication gaps exceed 3 points. L2 predominantly selects BSM and remains within 0.18 points of its score, with increased dollar costs; do not interpret the registered effect as a substantial advantage over BSM. Details in README_experiment.md.

experiment.py, SOFT duplicates: the first released row is used for the 36 duplicate (query, model) training rows. This is an unspecified case and does not touch the primary statistic.
experiment.py, tie rounding: L0 uses raw scores (literal seed idxmax) while L1/L2 use 6-decimal rounding. Both match the registration.

problems: bootstrap.json, replication: L0 scores on Generic (kNN 60.55, SVM 59.45, MLP 61.35) fall 6.8-14.8 points below Table 2 (71.37/74.21/68.12). opus.reason: The code implements the registered label rules, routers, seed hyperparameters, replay evaluation, statistic and paired bootstrap. registration.title: Do persona-conditioned LLM judges express persona-specific pairwise preferences beyond prompt-wording sensitivity? A deterministic, order-balanced test with the seed's judge prompt
registration.seed_connection: xRouteBench's personalized track, which trains and scores GMTRouter and PersonalizedRouter, is labelled by a persona-conditioned pairwise judge (DeepSeek-V3.1, the 'Persona preference judge' prompt in Appendix F) with PersonaHub personas; the candidate models never see the persona. The claim that 'personalization pays off' rests on GMTRouter 68.78 versus the user-agnostic EloRouter 66.40, a gap of about 2.4 points. It presumes that the judge's verdict for a fixed response pair depends systematically on the persona.
registration.hypothesis: With the seed's persona-judge prompt and an open 7B judge, swapping one persona for another changes the order-averaged probability of preferring response A by more than 0.03 beyond the change caused by rewording the judge instruction while keeping the same persona.
registration.contribution: Measures the persona-specific signal in pairwise judge labels on response pairs from the seed's own personalized split, with no human labels. Deterministic logprob-based preferences remove sampling noise, order averaging removes position bias, and a same-persona instruction-paraphrase condition calibrates generic prompt sensitivity. A positive control with style-contrasting personas shows whether the judge can express persona effects at all.

closest_work.difference: Measures agreement of persona-conditioned judges with human persona-labelled preferences. This experiment measures the size of persona-induced verdict shifts against a prompt-sensitivity baseline, on routing benchmark pairs.

PersonalLLM argues persona prompting yields homogeneous preferences and uses reward-model mixtures instead. This experiment quantifies persona specificity under the seed's own pairwise judge protocol.
GMTRouter trains a personalized router on judge-derived preferences. This experiment tests whether such labels carry persona-specific signal.
Characterizes judge biases such as position bias. It does not study persona conditioning.

inputs: Response pairs: Hugging Face ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config personalized (train and test). Use it if it holds recorded candidate response text for at least two models per query. Otherwise fall back to lmsys/mt_bench_human_judgments, split 'human', first-turn conversation_a/conversation_b pairs (deduplicated by question and model pair).
Personas: proj-persona/PersonaHub, config 'persona'.
Judge: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct served with vLLM (bf16).
Prompt template: the seed's 'Persona preference judge' box (Appendix F of arXiv 2608.06867).
registration.method:
0) Load the personalized config; print and save its schema. Record which response source is used.
1) Pairs. Pool train and test, keep queries with at least two non-empty responses from distinct models, and sample 300 queries (seed 0). For each query, pick two distinct models at random; their responses are A and B. Render chat-list queries as text by joining 'role: content' lines. Truncate each response to 1,200 judge tokens and record per-response truncation flags.
2) Personas. Sample 50 PersonaHub personas of at most 60 words (seed 0). For each pair, draw two distinct personas P and Q from these.
3) Conditions per pair:
- P1: the seed template verbatim with persona P: 'You are simulating the following user persona: {persona}. As this persona, evaluate which assistant response you would personally prefer. [User Question] {question} [Assistant 1] {answer_1} [Assistant 2] {answer_2} Output ONLY one of the following tokens exactly: 1 2 Tie Do not output anything else.'
- P2: the same persona P with a fixed paraphrased instruction: 'Imagine you are this person: {persona}. Judge, from this person's own perspective, which of the two assistant responses they would like better.' The rest is unchanged.
- Q1: the seed template with persona Q.
- NONE: the seed template with its first two sentences replaced by 'Evaluate which assistant response is better.'
4) Positive control. On the first 100 pairs, also run two style personas with the seed template: TERSE = 'A busy engineer who wants the shortest possible answer and dislikes any extra explanation.' and THOROUGH = 'A careful student who wants long, detailed, step-by-step explanations with examples.'
5) Judging. Send each prompt as the user message under the judge's chat template, in both orders: AB (A as Assistant 1) and BA. Use vLLM SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=1, logprobs=20). From the top-20 first-token logprobs, take the probabilities of tokens '1', '2' and 'Tie' (also ' Tie', 'tie'; sum variants) and renormalize over these three. Mark the prompt invalid if their total mass is below 0.5. Preference for A in one order: s = P(A-slot) + 0.5*P(Tie), where the A-slot is '1' in AB and '2' in BA. Then p_X = the mean of s over the two orders for condition X. Drop a pair if any of P1, P2 or Q1 is invalid.
6) Statistics:
- D_PQ = mean over pairs of |p_P1 - p_Q1|.
- D_para = mean over pairs of |p_P1 - p_P2|.
- Primary PE = D_PQ - D_para.
- Positive control D_style = mean |p_TERSE - p_THOROUGH| over the control pairs.
7) Secondary analyses:
- mean |p_P1 - p_NONE|, and the Pearson correlation of p_P1 with p_NONE across pairs;
- share of pairs where P1 and Q1 give opposite sides of 0.5 (with a 0.1 margin);
- position bias: mean |s_AB - s_BA| per condition;
- the same statistics restricted to pairs with no truncation;
- correlation of (p_TERSE - p_THOROUGH) with the length difference between A and B.

event.description: Swapping personas shifts the judge's order-averaged preference by more than 0.03 beyond rewording the instruction for the same persona.
event.statistic: PE = mean over pairs of |p_P - p_Q| minus mean over pairs of |p_P(seed wording) - p_P(paraphrased wording)|, in probability units.

evaluation.procedure:
Compute PE with a 95% bootstrap interval over pairs (2,000 resamples, seed 0). Also report D_PQ, D_para, D_style, the invalid rate and the secondary statistics. Total judge calls are about 300 pairs x 4 conditions x 2 orders + 100 x 2 x 2 = 2,800 single-token calls. Use enable_prefix_caching=True and max_model_len 4096.
- outputs/schema.json: the schema of the personalized config and the response source used.
- outputs/pairs.jsonl: per pair, the query id, the two models, the personas P and Q, and truncation flags.
- outputs/judgments.jsonl: per (pair, condition, order), the renormalized probabilities of '1'/'2'/'Tie', the total mass, the validity flag and s.
- outputs/summary.json: PE and its interval, D_PQ, D_para, D_style, the secondary statistics and the persona texts.
evaluation.controls: Same-persona instruction paraphrase (D_para) calibrates generic prompt sensitivity. Order averaging cancels position bias. Deterministic logprobs remove sampling noise. The TERSE versus THOROUGH positive control should show a large shift if the judge can express persona effects; if D_style is small, a null PE is uninformative. The NONE condition shows how far persona verdicts depart from generic quality judgments. Limitation: a 7B judge may respond to personas differently from DeepSeek-V3.1.

registration.full_scale_study: Repeat with the seed's judge and judges of several sizes on the full personalized split and all 200 personas. Relate each judge's measured persona specificity to how much persona-aware routers trained on its labels beat persona-agnostic ones, and validate against routing data with genuine per-user labels.

A 7B judge likely relies mostly on generic quality and position cues, and a perspective-changing instruction paraphrase may perturb verdicts about as much as swapping random PersonaHub personas. An excess above 0.03 is therefore less likely than not.

Order-averaged logprob shifts from persona swaps and from instruction paraphrases are likely of similar small magnitude, so the margin of 0.03 is hard to clear with a 7B judge.

Exceeding 0.03 after subtracting instruction-paraphrase sensitivity therefore seems less likely, with additional uncertainty from the smaller judge and validity filtering.

But many sampled persona traits may be irrelevant to a given response pair, and Qwen2.5-7B may not reproduce the seed's DeepSeek judge behavior.

That points to the same concern, but it does not test the seed's pairwise judge prompt with order-balanced logprobs, a same-persona paraphrase baseline, or a style-persona positive control.

The task is different (graded relevance, not pairwise response preference), the personas are role-based assessors rather than user personas, and there is no instruction-paraphrase calibration.

This paper quantifies how much annotation variance persona variables explain in subjective NLP datasets that have human labels. It does not study persona-conditioned pairwise judges or separate persona effects from general prompt sensitivity.

The seed paper describes its persona-conditioned DeepSeek judge and its 200 PersonaHub personas. In the appendix text I read, it reports no analysis of whether the judge's verdicts actually depend on the persona.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered experiment with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct bf16/vLLM: all four primary conditions, both orders, TERSE/THOROUGH controls, exact top-20 first-token probability extraction, validity filtering, paired bootstrap and secondary analyses. xRouteBench contains recorded response texts, so no fallback was used. Bare 'Tie' is two Qwen tokens; the prescribed single-token variants and invalid-mass rule were followed literally and this limitation is documented. Full evaluation command successfully tested (~4 minutes including installation/downloads); independent artifact audit passed. Test PE=0.0244652, 95% CI [0.0051973, 0.0454690], D_style=0.385929, 291 valid pairs. The registered event did not occur; the interval does not rule out PE above 0.03.

It is applied identically to every condition, so it is unlikely to change PE materially.

experiment.py prompt_ids applies Qwen's chat template, which silently adds the default system message 'You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud…'. The registration says only 'under the judge's chat template', so this follows the registration. It is the same in all conditions.

experiment.py extract_judgment counts only the single-token variants '1', '2', 'Tie' (which never occurs, because in Qwen 'Tie' is two tokens, 'T' and 'ie'), ' Tie' and 'tie'. The first token 'T' is not counted as a tie. This literally follows the registered rule and the engineer documented it. In effect, tie probability is about zero, and s is the renormalized 1-versus-2 split. Invalid outputs are only 0.8%, so the effect on PE is likely small.

experiment.py calculate_stats computes the primary D_style only on control pairs that also passed the primary drop rule (97 pairs). The registration says 'over the control pairs'. The all-valid-control value (0.388 on 99 pairs) is also reported and almost identical. No impact.
experiment.py drops a pair if either order of P1, P2 or Q1 is invalid. This is a reasonable reading of 'if any of P1, P2 or Q1 is invalid'. It removed 9 pairs, a negligible effect.
