registration.title: Spend routing supervision on repeated generations or broader query coverage?
registration.seed_connection: LLMRouter constructs a query–model quality matrix for supervising routers. Constructing that matrix consumes inference resources, but the seed does not compare spending a fixed collection budget on repeated observations versus additional distinct queries.
registration.hypothesis: At an equal number of logged candidate completions, three observations of fewer training queries produce better held-out routing accuracy than one observation of three times as many queries.
registration.contribution: DARS establishes that repeated observations can improve supervision while holding the underlying training queries fixed. This experiment tests the opportunity cost of repetition: whether its benefit survives comparison with broader coverage purchased using the same number of candidate completions.

closest_work.difference: DARS compares observation protocols on a fixed query set. This experiment compares repetition against acquiring additional distinct queries under an equal completion-count budget; it does not claim to introduce distribution-aware supervision.

This work distinguishes oracle opportunity from deployable routing gains. The experiment evaluates independently generated held-out outcomes and training-selected fixed baselines, but its research variable is supervision-budget allocation.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset openai/gsm8k, configuration main, official train and test splits: https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k
Hugging Face dataset allenai/ai2_arc, configuration ARC-Challenge, official train and test splits: https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct
Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
registration.method: Implement a standalone local-inference script, not the seed's API pipeline. Sample 180 training and 100 test questions from each dataset using seed 1729. Remove exact normalized-question overlaps between train and test before sampling. Relabel ARC choices consecutively A, B, C, and so on, preserving the correct choice index. Use the same canonical answering prompt for every observation of a question: request brief reasoning followed by 'Final: <letter>' for ARC or 'Final: <number>' for GSM8K. Run both candidate models with temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95 and max_tokens 192. Obtain three independent completions per query–model pair, using separate seed ranges for training and test. Generate the complete matrix once, batching requests and loading models in separate processes to release GPU memory. Use BF16 and disable inference-engine compilation where possible. Score ARC by the last explicit Final letter, accepting a response consisting solely of a valid letter as well. Score GSM8K by the last explicit Final numeric value, accepting a solely numeric response; normalize commas and compare decimal or fractional numeric values against the answer after ####. Invalid or truncated answers count as incorrect and are never selectively regenerated. Encode canonical questions with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using last-nonpadding-token pooling and L2 normalization. For each allocation seed 11, 22 and 33, construct two logging arms: COVER observes all 360 training queries once per model, using completion replicate 0, 1 or 2 respectively; REPEAT observes a stratified subset of 120 training queries three times per model and uses their mean correctness. Both arms therefore observe exactly 720 candidate completions. For each arm, implement an expected-quality kNN router: retrieve 16 nearest training embeddings, weight them by normalized exp((cosine-max_cosine)/0.05), estimate each candidate's quality by the weighted mean of its observed correctness target, and select the larger estimate. Break ties lexicographically by model identifier. Evaluate selections on the 200 untouched test questions using the mean of their three independently generated correctness observations. Also evaluate a single-observation router on the same 120-query subset, a task-only router, and a fixed model selected from each arm's available training records. These are diagnostics, not alternative primary endpoints. Reuse the generated matrix across the three allocation repetitions. Record actual token totals and elapsed time: the matching is completion count, not a claim of exactly equal token or wall-clock cost.

event.description: Repeated-observation supervision improves held-out expected routing accuracy over broader single-observation coverage by a supported margin exceeding one percentage point.
event.statistic: S: the fifth percentile of a paired question-bootstrap distribution of mean(REPEAT accuracy minus COVER accuracy), averaged over the three allocation repetitions and equally over the two datasets.

evaluation.procedure: For each test question and allocation repetition, look up the three-replicate mean correctness of the model selected by each arm. Average the paired differences over allocation repetitions, then macro-average the two datasets. Use 2,000 bootstrap samples with seed 2026, resampling questions within each dataset while keeping all candidate outcomes and allocation repetitions together. Report S as the single registered statistic. outputs/generations.jsonl holds question identifiers, splits, model identifiers, seeds, prompts, completions, parsed answers, correctness, token counts and finish reasons. outputs/allocations.json holds the observed training records in each logging arm. outputs/test_decisions.jsonl holds selections and paired test outcomes. outputs/scores.json holds S, its underlying point estimate and interval, control results, collection costs and run metadata. An unmet event does not establish equivalence; retain the interval and distinguish an uncertain result from a supported disadvantage.
evaluation.controls: Equal logged completion counts; identical encoders, neighbor rules, prompts and scoring; independent test generations; a single-observation control on the repeated arm's exact query subset; task-only and training-selected fixed-model baselines. Repetition identities and queries are retained as clusters rather than treated as independent test examples.

registration.full_scale_study: Map the coverage–repetition trade-off across larger pools of models no larger than 8B, multiple router architectures and token-matched collection budgets. Test adaptive repetition only for ambiguous query–model comparisons, with training-selected fixed and task-only policies retained as baselines.

agent.reason: Repeated observations should reduce supervision noise, but sacrificing two-thirds of the distinct training queries can weaken kNN locality. Existing evidence for repetition does not resolve this matched-budget trade-off, and the registered lower-bound criterion requires more than a small average improvement.

judge_astra.reason: Repeated observations reduce label noise, but broader coverage can improve neighbor relevance, so the net advantage is uncertain. With only 200 test questions, clearing a one-percentage-point bootstrap lower bound requires more than a small denoising benefit.

judge_fable.reason: The two candidate models are close in aggregate accuracy and the kNN router already averages over neighbors, so repetition versus coverage should yield only a tiny, noisy difference; a 5th-percentile margin above one point would need a surprisingly large and consistent REPEAT advantage on 200 test questions.

judge_opus.reason: With only two similar-strength candidates (Qwen2.5-3B vs Phi-3.5-mini) on GSM8K/ARC, routing headroom is tiny and the arms differ only in rare noisy decisions, so even a large difference in wrong-model rates times a ~5pp model gap yields about 1pp. A 5th-percentile margin above 1pp is implausible.

judge_sol.reason: Repeated generations can reduce target noise, but the router already averages neighboring observations and repetition sacrifices two-thirds of the distinct training queries. Any advantage may therefore be too small to place the bootstrap lower bound above one percentage point.

judge_luna.reason: Repeated samples can denoise per-query correctness, but REPEAT gives the kNN router one third as many distinct training queries, and broader local coverage may be more valuable; only 200 held-out questions also make a supported lower-tail gain difficult to establish. This is a prediction about the registered +1pp event, not evidence that repetition cannot help elsewhere.

judge_muse.reason: kNN routing likely gains more from 3x embedding-space coverage than from noise reduction on 1/3 the queries, making a supported >1pp lower-bound win for repetition unlikely.

Its sample-efficiency analysis changes the number of observations per query (2x2, 3x3, 5x5, plus adaptive sampling) but keeps the query set fixed. It never compares repetition against spending the same number of completions on more distinct queries, which is the question this experiment asks.

This paper separates oracle routing opportunity from held-out deployable gains and gives selection-valid intervals against a best fixed model. It does not study how a budget for collecting supervision should be split between repeated observations and query coverage.

This paper audits what routing oracles measure under stochastic decoding, using many archived responses per query–model cell. It is a measurement framework and does not trade repetition off against coverage when training a router.

It does not study repeated correctness measurements as routing targets or their opportunity cost for held-out model selection.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: a standalone local-inference script (experiment.py, started by run.sh). It does not use the seed's API pipeline.
- Data: GSM8K (main) and ARC-Challenge, official splits. Train items whose normalized question also appears in the test split are removed. With seed 1729 I draw 180 train and 100 test questions per dataset. ARC choices are relabeled A, B, C… and the correct index is kept.
- Generation: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, each in its own subprocess, through HF transformers `generate`. Settings: BF16, sdpa attention, no compilation, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, max_new_tokens 192. I also set top_k=0 and repetition_penalty=1.0 so the models' generation_config defaults do not override the registered sampler. There are 3 independent replicates per query–model pair, with separate seed ranges for train and test. The seed is set per batch and recorded on every record.
- Scoring: a response truncated by the length limit, or with no parsable answer, counts as incorrect. Nothing is regenerated.
- Embedding: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, last-token pooling with left padding, L2-normalized.
- Router: a pooled kNN over both datasets (k=16, weights exp((cos−max)/0.05) normalized). Ties go to the lexicographically first model id.
- Arms for allocation seeds 11/22/33: COVER uses all 360 train queries with replicate 0/1/2. REPEAT uses a stratified 120-query subset (60 per dataset) with the mean of 3 replicates. Both arms use 720 completions.
- Diagnostics: SINGLE120 (same subset, single replicate), task-only and training-selected fixed baselines for each arm.
- Evaluation: on the 200 test questions, each selection is scored by the mean of 3 test replicates. The paired bootstrap uses 2000 resamples (seed 2026), resampling questions within each dataset with allocation repetitions kept together. S is the 5th percentile.

Deviations and caveats:
1) I used the HF transformers engine instead of vLLM. Seeds are therefore per batch rather than per request.
2) Parser change made after seeing a first full run. In that run the GSM8K parser required a bare number directly after "Final:". About 60 untruncated GSM8K completions had lines like "Final: John paid $230 after tax." and were scored invalid. I changed the parser to read the numeric value on the last explicit "Final:" line (first number on that line), which I believe is closer to "last explicit Final numeric value". The ARC parser also accepts "Final Answer:". Result: the first run (strict parser) gave S ≈ −0.010 (point ≈ +0.002); its scores are kept in run1_scores_strictparser.json. The submitted run gives S = −0.0061. The event does not occur under either parser.
3) Truncation is high under the registered 192-token limit: Qwen is truncated on about 73% of GSM8K and 60% of ARC completions. Phi-3.5 is the better model on both tasks.

Result (deterministic across my two runs; generation outputs were identical):
- REPEAT − COVER point estimate = +0.0011, bootstrap 5th–95th percentile [−0.0061, +0.0078], so S = −0.0061, below the 0.01 threshold. The event did not occur.
- This does not establish that the two arms are equivalent. The interval is narrow, though, and rules out a gain much above ~1 point in this setup.
- Per-allocation differences: −0.025, +0.023, +0.005.
- Both kNN routers (COVER 0.508, REPEAT 0.509) fell slightly below always choosing the training-selected fixed model, Phi-3.5 (0.518). That fixed baseline equals the task-only baseline here. Oracle = 0.557. With only two models and one dominant model, there is little room for routing gains.
- REPEAT − SINGLE120 = +0.0067, 90% interval [−0.003, +0.018].
- Token totals for COVER and REPEAT are within about 1% of each other; they are listed in scores.json. Elapsed time is measured per model, not per arm.

Runtime is about 4–5 minutes on the test machine, plus pip install.

departures: Inference engine (experiment.py, gen_model): HF transformers `generate` replaced the vLLM-style per-request batching, so sampling seeds are set per batch rather than per request. The registration only says to disable compilation 'where possible' and does not mandate an engine. The engineer disclosed this. It changes which samples are drawn but should not bias either arm.

Sampler arguments (experiment.py): top_k=0 and repetition_penalty=1.0 were set explicitly so that the models' generation_config defaults cannot override the registered temperature 0.7 and top_p 0.95. This enforces the registered sampler rather than departing from it. No expected effect.

Parser revised after an outcome was seen (experiment.py parse_gsm; run1_scores_strictparser.json): the first full run required a bare number right after 'Final:'. The submitted run instead takes the first number on the last 'Final:' line. The registered wording, 'last explicit Final numeric value', admits either reading. The change moved the reported S from -0.0089 to -0.0061 and the point estimate from +0.0022 to +0.0011. It did not change whether the event occurred. The change was disclosed.

ARC parser extension (experiment.py parse_arc): 'Final Answer:', parentheses and markdown asterisks are also accepted. This is a small widening of 'last explicit Final letter', applied identically to both arms. Its effect is probably negligible.

Pooled kNN (experiment.py knn_route): one kNN index pools both datasets instead of one index per dataset. The registration does not specify this, so it is an open choice applied to both arms. It could affect the routers but is not a departure.
Elapsed time (scores.json collection_costs): time is recorded per model for the whole matrix, not per arm. Token totals per arm are recorded. Disclosed. No effect on S.

Default chat templates (outputs/generations.jsonl): the models' own templates are used, so Qwen's default system prompt is included. The canonical user prompt is identical across observations, as registered. No effect on the arm comparison.
problems: The GSM8K parser was changed after a full result had been seen (run1_scores_strictparser.json versus outputs/scores.json). The change is disclosed and both versions fall below the threshold, but it is still an outcome-informed analysis choice.
The engineer's notes say the strict-parser run gave S ≈ -0.010. run1_scores_strictparser.json records S = -0.0089. This is a minor misstatement.

The registered 192-token limit truncates 73% of Qwen GSM8K test completions and 57% of Qwen ARC test completions, plus many Phi completions (scores.json generation_stats). Truncated answers count as incorrect, so the correctness labels largely measure brevity and formatting rather than task ability.

The routing setting is degenerate. One model, Phi-3.5, dominates. Both kNN routers (0.508 and 0.509) fall below the training-selected fixed/task-only baseline (0.518), and the oracle is only 0.557. COVER and REPEAT agree on most test questions, so the narrow interval mainly reflects that there is little to route rather than a precise estimate of the coverage-versus-repetition trade-off.
The allocation repetitions vary in sign (-0.025, +0.023, +0.005 in scores.json), so with only two models the result is fragile.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design: the same sample sizes, models, decoding settings, completion-matched COVER/REPEAT arms, kNN router, diagnostics, and a paired question bootstrap with the 5th-percentile statistic. The fresh-machine run reproduced the submitted value exactly (S = -0.0061, so the event did not occur). The main departure is a GSM8K parser revised after seeing results. It is defensible under the registered wording, was disclosed, and does not change whether the event occurred, so I do not rate it as unfaithful. The evidence is real and has no visible leakage, because test outcomes come from separately seeded generations. However, a 192-token limit causes heavy truncation, one model dominates, and neither router beats the fixed baseline. The null result is therefore credible but says little about the general trade-off between repetition and coverage.

departures: experiment.py, parse_gsm: the submitted parser searches for the first number anywhere on the last Final line, including within prose, rather than requiring the specified Final numeric answer format. Engineer notes say this change followed inspection of a full run. It can change correctness targets, router selections and S; the submitted earlier strict-parser scores report S=-0.0088889, versus -0.0061111 in the fresh evaluation. Both miss the event, but that does not make the change immaterial to fidelity.

experiment.py, FINAL and the answer parsers: accepted formats are broadened to include 'Final Answer:', parenthesized or punctuated standalone ARC letters, and currency-prefixed standalone GSM8K answers. These extend the explicitly specified formats and could change correctness when such responses occur. Their individual effects are not isolated in the supplied evidence; ARC generation correctness totals are unchanged between the two score files.

experiment.py, NUM and to_frac: some valid decimal or fractional spellings are mishandled. For example, '.5' can be extracted as '5', and '1/-2' can be extracted as '1'. Such cases could change targets and the statistic, although the supplied excerpts do not establish that they occurred.

experiment.py, embed: canonical inputs are truncated at 1,024 tokens, a cap not specified in the registration. This could change embeddings and routing decisions for longer sampled questions; the evidence does not establish that any sampled input exceeded the cap.

experiment.py, knn_route and argmax_tie: estimates within 1e-12 of the maximum are treated as ties, rather than only exactly equal estimates. This technically extends the tie rule, but no plausible material effect on the reported value is demonstrated.
problems: The outcome-informed parser revision documented in engineer_notes compromises the confirmatory status of the registered scoring protocol. A fresh-machine rerun verifies execution of the revised protocol, not an independently frozen scoring decision.

The claimed upper-bound precision is parser-sensitive: outputs/scores.json has a 90% interval of approximately [-0.00611, 0.00778], while the submitted, non-evaluation run1_scores_strictparser.json has approximately [-0.00889, 0.01333]. Excluding a one-percentage-point gain is therefore not robust across these scoring versions.

outputs/scores.json shows severe truncation under the registered token limit: approximately 75% of Qwen GSM8K completions, 60% of its ARC completions, and 57% of Phi GSM8K completions. The finding concerns successful, parsable completion within this short budget, not unrestricted answering quality.

The evidence is narrow: only two candidates are tested, the training-selected fixed/task-only policy scores 0.51833 versus 0.50778 for COVER and 0.50889 for REPEAT, and allocation differences range from -0.025 to +0.02333. The registered bootstrap conditions on the collected matrix and three allocations; it does not establish robustness across new training collections or equivalence of the allocation strategies.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed successfully, produced all registered artifacts, and reported S=-0.0061111 with a point difference of +0.0011111, so the registered event did not occur. The core sampling, models, completion budgets, controls and clustered bootstrap match the registration; HF generation and batch-level seeding are not themselves violations of an explicitly required engine or per-request seed scheme, but the consequential post hoc scoring change makes fidelity unfaithful. The inspected code derives routing choices from training records and computes the value from real held-out generations, with no visible hard-coded result, test-label use in routing selection, or conclusion-changing computation error. This is a meaningful, setup-specific negative finding, warranting 2 rather than a strong general conclusion: it neither establishes equivalence nor robustly excludes one-point gains across scoring protocols, training collections or less truncation-heavy settings.

departures: GSM/ARC scorer accepts 'Final Answer:' as well as 'Final:' (experiment.py FINAL regex). The registration specifies an explicit Final letter or number. ARC correctness counts match the earlier strict-parser artifact, so this did not change ARC outcomes in these generations and is unlikely to have changed S.

GSM8K scoring takes the first number on the last Final line, not necessarily the last number on that line (experiment.py parse_gsm). That is a narrower reading of 'last explicit Final numeric value' and could flip labels on multi-number lines; whether any such line changed S is not shown in the artifacts.

Instruct chat templates wrap the registered user prompt, including Qwen's default system prompt (experiment.py gen_model). Needed to run the specified instruct models; it changes the literal string sent to the model and therefore can change completions, but it does not change the registered comparison.

Replicates are seeded per length-sorted batch with torch.manual_seed, not per request (experiment.py gen_model). Separate train/test seed ranges and three replicates are present, as registered; batch coupling changes the particular samples but not the REPEAT-vs-COVER question. The reported value depends on those samples the way it would on any unspecified seed scheme.

top_k=0 and repetition_penalty=1.0 are set though not listed in the registration (experiment.py). They stop model generation_config defaults from overriding temperature 0.7 and top_p 0.95, so they implement the registered sampler rather than replace it.
Stopped completions add one token for EOS in the recorded token total (experiment.py). This does not enter S or the event; logged COVER/REPEAT token totals stay within about 1%.
problems: Correctness is heavily censored by the registered 192-token cap: scores.json generation_stats show Qwen GSM8K train truncated on 396/540 completions and Phi GSM8K test truncated on 188/300, so many supervision targets are length failures rather than answer quality.

Both kNN arms lose to the training-selected fixed model (scores.json: COVER 0.508, REPEAT 0.509, FIXED/TASKONLY 0.518). With two models and Phi dominant on both tasks, there is little routing headroom, so a near-zero REPEAT−COVER gap is partly a comparison of two routers that should usually pick the same model.

Allocation differences change sign (scores.json per_alloc_diff −0.025, +0.023, +0.005). The registered question-bootstrap keeps allocations together, so the narrow interval does not represent that allocation noise.

The GSM parser was revised after a full run (engineer notes; run1_scores_strictparser.json S=−0.00889 vs evaluated S=−0.00611). The change moves toward the registered numeric-value rule, the evaluation regenerated from scratch, and both parsers miss the event, but it is still a post-hoc scoring edit.
Engineer notes quote the strict-parser S as about −0.010; run1_scores_strictparser.json has −0.00889. That note is not the evaluated result.
grok.reason: The fresh evaluation regenerated the matrix and reproduced S=−0.00611 with the registered arms, kNN rule, controls, and question-bootstrap, so the miss of the >0.01 event is a real result rather than a hardcoded or leaked one. Departures are small scoring or runtime choices; the parser edit that moved S was toward the registered rule and does not change the conclusion. The point estimate is about +0.11 percentage points, with a 5th–95th interval of about [−0.61, +0.78] points, which supports a narrow null for this setup without establishing equivalence. The finding is only moderately strong because truncation and a dominant fixed model leave little room for either supervision arm to matter.

registration.title: Isolate the routing effect of benign multi-agent workflow wrappers
registration.seed_connection: The seed trains routers on ordinary benchmark queries and deploys them on prompts containing planning, acting and verification instructions. A changed workflow wrapper can affect the router independently of any change in the answering model.
registration.hypothesis: Removing benign workflow wrappers from the router's input improves its replayed response quality relative to encoding the entire wrapped request, even when the underlying problem and candidate responses are unchanged.
registration.contribution: Existing robustness studies examine category-driven routing or adversarial rerouting. This experiment uses unoptimized workflow wrappers and changes only the router-visible input, holding the entire candidate outcome matrix fixed, to identify a component-level routing effect without conflating it with solver prompt sensitivity.

closest_work.difference: DSC investigates category-driven decisions and safety-related fragility. This experiment performs paired, router-only wrapper interventions and measures the quality consequences using identical recorded candidate responses.
RerouteGuard concerns adversarial triggers and their detection. The wrappers here are fixed, benign workflow instructions, with no trigger optimization or adversarial search.

inputs: Public xRouteBench records, configuration llmrouter_generic and configuration llm_candidates: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench
Seed repository download and embedding examples: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/tree/main/benchmark_pipeline
Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
registration.method: Download only the generic routing records and candidate metadata. Do not invoke any hosted endpoints or install the full router library. Restrict the candidate pool to the recorded endpoints llama-3-8b-instruct-lite, mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3 and qwen2.5-7b-instruct; verify their identities against candidate metadata. Use MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, OpenBookQA and ARC-Challenge records. Decode JSON-encoded fields as needed. Group rows by task and normalized canonical query, average duplicate observations of the same candidate, and retain only complete three-candidate matrices with finite performance values. Remove normalized-query overlaps between official train and test splits. The canonical query q is the complete original serialized query; do not try to remove its original task instructions. Using seed 1729, sample up to 240 training and 200 test queries per task. Before sampling, require q to contain at most 700 tokens under the embedding tokenizer. Preserve native recorded performance scores. Encode q with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, last-nonpadding-token pooling and L2 normalization. Use max_length 1024 and assert that none of the experimental inputs is truncated. Implement an expected-quality kNN router with 16 neighbors and weights proportional to exp((cosine-max_cosine)/0.05), predicting each candidate's quality from the training matrix and breaking selection ties lexicographically. Create four router-only test views by placing q in <problem>...</problem> after these exact prefixes: 'You are an actor in a multi-agent team. Solve the enclosed original task concisely and factually.'; 'You are a verifier in a multi-agent workflow. Review the enclosed original task, check your reasoning, and give its final answer.'; 'You are the final node in a planning-execution-summary workflow. Answer the enclosed original task and obey its answer format.'; 'You are agent 2 in a reasoning chain. Independently recheck the enclosed original task before passing on an answer.' FULL encodes prefix plus enclosed q. CORE extracts and encodes only q. Both policies use the same canonical training embeddings and outcome matrix, so they must agree on the canonical unwrapped view. Replay the recorded score of each selected endpoint. Never send a wrapper to an answering model or alter a recorded response. Add neutral metadata prefixes token-length-matched to each wrapper as a diagnostic for generic input dilution. Also evaluate a training-selected fixed model and a task-only policy. This is explicitly a shadow-routing experiment, not an end-to-end evaluation of planning or verification ability.

event.description: Canonical-core routing has a supported response-quality advantage exceeding three percentage points over full-wrapper routing on the fixed outcome matrix.
event.statistic: S: the fifth percentile of the paired bootstrap distribution of CORE minus FULL native performance, averaged over the four workflow wrappers and macro-averaged over the five tasks.

evaluation.procedure: For each test query, average CORE-minus-FULL replayed performance across its four wrappers. Macro-average the task means. Bootstrap queries within task 2,000 times using seed 2026, retaining all wrapper views of a query together. S is the fifth percentile of that distribution. outputs/items.jsonl holds sampled canonical queries, split identifiers and the three-candidate outcome vectors. outputs/views.jsonl holds every exact router-visible view and its token length. outputs/decisions.jsonl holds selections, replayed outcomes, canonical agreement checks and neutral-prefix controls. outputs/scores.json holds S, the point estimate and interval, counts and run metadata. Report model-pool and cached-scoring limitations; an unmet event does not establish general router robustness or equivalence.
evaluation.controls: Identical problems, training data and recorded solver outcomes across paired views; exact canonical-policy agreement; explicit exclusion of truncation; token-length-matched neutral prefixes; fixed and task-only baselines. Only the embedding model runs locally; the three answering endpoints are public historical data, all within the 8B restriction.

registration.full_scale_study: Evaluate structured routing states that separately encode original task content and workflow role across several encoders and router architectures. Follow the isolated replay test with actual multi-agent execution, where role instructions may legitimately change the required capability and must not simply be discarded.

agent.reason: Workflow wrappers can perturb embedding-based retrieval, but the canonical problem remains intact and changed selections need not cause substantial quality loss. A supported three-percentage-point advantage is considerably more demanding than demonstrating routing instability.

judge_astra.reason: The benign wrappers may change some nearest neighbors without producing consistently worse model selections. A three-percentage-point lower-bound advantage seems demanding when the underlying task remains fully visible and truncation is excluded.

judge_fable.reason: The wrapper prefixes shift embeddings, but the problem content (and its original task instruction) should keep neighbors mostly within task, and qwen2.5-7b dominates the restricted pool across tasks, so replayed quality differences are likely small; only a hubness-style neighbor collapse onto a weaker model on MATH/GSM8K would push the 5th percentile above three points.

judge_opus.reason: Qwen2.5-7B should dominate Llama-3-8B-lite and Mistral-7B on all five tasks, so both CORE and FULL kNN routing mostly select it. Wrapper-induced neighbour shifts would regress predictions toward that same model, leaving CORE minus FULL near zero, far from a supported 3pp.

judge_sol.reason: The intervention cleanly isolates routing, but short, benign wrappers may change selections without systematically reducing replayed quality. A supported three-point loss averaged across four wrappers and five tasks seems unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: Because training uses canonical embeddings, an unseen wrapper can shift test neighbors, so CORE may recover performance. However, a common prefix may leave relative neighborhoods largely intact, and the selected candidates may have small quality gaps, making a supported improvement above 3pp uncertain.

judge_muse.reason: CORE should beat FULL directionally due to train-test shift, but last-token pooling with prefix before the problem and a small oracle gap among three similar 7-8B models makes a >3pp lower-bound effect demanding.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Studies optimized adversarial 'confounder gadget' prefixes that force routing to the strong model; the experiment uses fixed benign workflow-role wrappers and measures CORE vs FULL router-input quality on a fixed recorded outcome matrix.
RerouteGuard covers adversarial rerouting triggers and their detection; no benign wrapper intervention or replayed quality comparison of stripped vs full router input.
DSC examines category-driven routing decisions and safety/privacy weaknesses, not paired router-only benign wrapper perturbations with replayed outcomes.
Studies adversarial and backdoor robustness of routers rather than unoptimized workflow-role prefixes.
Measures prompt-wrapper sensitivity of answering models' accuracy, which is the solver-side effect the experiment deliberately holds fixed; it does not study router decisions.

opus.reason: Prior work on router prefix sensitivity covers optimized adversarial triggers (Rerouting LLM Routers, RerouteGuard, Life-Cycle Vulnerabilities) or category-driven decisions (DSC), and work on benign wrappers measures answering-model accuracy, not routers. I found no paper that adds benign multi-agent role wrappers to the router's input only and replays fixed recorded outcomes to compare canonical-only against full-wrapper routing quality, so the question appears open.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies evaluates kNN routers on original and benignly perturbed inputs, including added irrelevant context, using precomputed candidate-performance matrices and reporting clean-versus-perturbed routing accuracy. The proposed experiment substitutes fixed workflow-role wrappers, explicitly extracts the canonical core, and adds length-matched neutral controls and paired uncertainty estimates.
RerouteGuard studies routing and quality changes caused by adversarially constructed prefixes, rather than fixed benign workflow instructions.
The seed evaluates routing inside actual multi-agent workflows, where solver inputs and execution change; it does not isolate wrapper effects by holding candidate outcomes fixed.

sol.reason: The closest prior work, arXiv:2607.09197, already investigates benign input variation at the router level—including added context—and compares kNN routing quality using fixed benchmark outcome matrices. Workflow-specific wrappers and stronger diagnostic controls refine that experiment, but the central router-only intervention and replay-quality question are substantially shared, making this a close variant rather than an equivalent experiment.

opus.reason: Both prepend multi-agent role wrappers only to the router input while holding the question and the cached candidate outcomes fixed, and compare full-prompt encoding with question-only encoding by selection and accuracy changes.

sol.reason: Both isolate workflow-wrapper effects by changing only router-visible text, comparing full-prompt encoding with canonical-question encoding, and measuring routing quality using unchanged cached candidate outcomes.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: `run_experiment.py`, launched by `run_eval.sh`. It runs in about 75 s on one GPU. It downloads only the xRouteBench `llmrouter_generic` and `llm_candidates` configs. No hosted endpoints are called and the full LLMRouter library is not installed. The only model run is Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (float32, left padding, last non-padding-token pooling, L2 normalisation).

Setup as registered:
- **Candidates:** llama-3-8b-instruct-lite, mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3 and qwen2.5-7b-instruct, checked against the candidate metadata (sizes 8B/7B/7B; api ids are logged in `scores.json`).
- **Tasks:** mmlu, gsm8k, math, openbook_qa, arc_challenge.
- **Grouping:** rows are grouped by (task, whitespace-normalised query). Duplicate scores for the same candidate are averaged, and only complete matrices with finite values are kept. Queries are kept with their original instructions.
- **Train–test overlap:** removed from the train side; none was found.
- **Sampling:** a ≤700-token filter under the embedding tokenizer is applied first, then seed 1729 draws 240 train and 200 test queries per task (1,200 train, 1,000 test).
- **Truncation:** max_length is 1024 and the code asserts nothing is truncated (longest view is 705 tokens).
- **Router:** kNN with k=16 and weights exp((cos − max)/0.05). It predicts each candidate's expected quality from the training matrix; ties go to the lexicographically first name.
- **Views:** the wrapped view is `"{prefix}\n<problem>{q}</problem>"`, with the four exact prefixes. FULL encodes the whole string. CORE extracts q with a regex and encodes it.
- **Canonical agreement:** CORE matches the canonical policy on every decision, and the embedding difference is 0.0.
- **Neutral control:** each wrapper gets a "Metadata: …" prefix of single-token neutral words, with exactly the same token count (23/27/25/25).
- **Baselines:** a fixed model (best pooled train mean = qwen2.5-7b-instruct) and a task-only policy (best train mean per task).
- **Bootstrap:** 2,000 replicates with seed 2026, resampling queries within each task and keeping all four wrapper views of a query together. S is the 5th percentile (numpy linear interpolation).

Small choices not fixed by the registration:
- "Normalised" was taken to mean whitespace-collapsed and case-preserved.
- When a duplicate group had several raw spellings, the lexicographically first one is used as the canonical q.
- Overlaps were dropped from train rather than test.

Result (deterministic; two runs gave identical output):
- **S = −0.0045**, so the registered event (S > 0.03) did **not** occur.
- Point estimate for CORE − FULL: +0.0030. 90% interval [−0.0045, 0.0103]; 95% interval [−0.0058, 0.0118].
- Per task: mmlu +0.006, gsm8k +0.005, math −0.003, openbook_qa +0.019, arc −0.013.
- Wrappers change the kNN decision on about 9% of test queries, but the net quality change is about zero.
- The neutral prefixes change decisions at a similar rate (9–11%). Neutral − FULL = −0.0025, with a 90% interval of [−0.010, 0.005].
- Macro quality: CORE 0.604, FULL 0.601, NEUTRAL 0.599, fixed model 0.622, task-only 0.651, oracle 0.751. Both the fixed model and the task-only policy beat this kNN router.

How far this goes:
- It is shadow routing only. Wrappers never reach an answering model, and the recorded canonical outcomes are replayed, so it says nothing about planning or verification ability.
- It covers a small pool of 7–8B models, one encoder and one router architecture, with cached historical scores.
- It does not show that routers are robust to wrappers or that CORE and FULL are equivalent. It only rules out a CORE advantage above 3 points in this setup: the upper end of the 95% interval is about 1.2 points.

departures: run_experiment.py: the wrapped view is built as prefix + '\n' + '<problem>' + q + '</problem>'. The registration fixes the prefixes and the <problem> tags but not the separator, so this is an open choice. A different separator could slightly change FULL embeddings and decision flips. It is unlikely to move S across the 0.03 threshold.

run_experiment.py: 'normalized' query is taken to mean whitespace-collapsed and case-preserved. When a group has several raw spellings, the lexicographically first is used as the canonical q. This is an open choice, disclosed in the notes. Duplicates have n_obs = 1 throughout the sampled items, so the effect is negligible.
run_experiment.py: train-test overlaps are dropped from the train side, matched on normalized query across tasks. This is an open choice, and no overlaps were found, so there is no effect.

run_experiment.py: one numpy RNG seeded 1729 is shared sequentially across splits and tasks rather than reseeded per draw. This is an open implementation choice. It changes which queries are sampled but not the protocol.

run_experiment.py: Qwen3-Embedding is used with no query-instruction prompt, with float32 and left padding. The registration does not specify an instruction, so this is an open choice. It affects the router's absolute quality, not the paired design.

run_experiment.py: neutral prefixes are matched to the wrappers in standalone token count, including special tokens, rather than in-context. Token boundaries at the '\n<problem>' junction could differ by a token. This is a diagnostic only and has no effect on S.

run_eval.sh: torch and other dependencies are unpinned apart from transformers and datasets. This could cause tiny numerical drift in embeddings. The notes report two identical runs, and drift is unlikely to change the conclusion.
problems: outputs/scores.json: the kNN router is weak. Its macro quality is 0.604, below the fixed model (0.622) and the task-only policy (0.651). The null therefore concerns wrapper sensitivity of a router that already underperforms trivial baselines, which limits how far it generalises to the seed's stronger routers.

outputs/scores.json: wrappers flip only about 9% of decisions, which mechanically bounds how large any CORE-FULL difference can be. The neutral prefixes flip decisions at a similar rate (9-11%). The flips look like generic input perturbation rather than a workflow-specific signal, but the design cannot fully separate the two.
outputs/items.jsonl: task_ids are all 'None', so split identity rests only on the generated id and the split field. Provenance back to the original benchmark items is weak.
Scope: three 7-8B candidates, one encoder, one router, cached binary-dominated scores and shadow routing only. All of these are disclosed in the notes and in scores.json limitations.
opus.reason: The code follows the registered protocol closely: the specified data configs, candidate verification, tasks, grouping, length filter, sampling seeds, embedding settings, kNN rule, exact prefixes, CORE/FULL/neutral views, baselines and within-task paired bootstrap. The only departures are unspecified choices with negligible plausible effect. The reported S = -0.0045 is computed directly from real recorded outcome matrices and locally computed embeddings. CORE equals the canonical policy exactly, there is no truncation, and I found no leakage or hard-coding. The registered event did not occur. The 95% interval [-0.006, 0.012] credibly rules out a CORE advantage of 3 points in this setup, and the neutral-prefix control suggests the wrapper flips behave like generic dilution. Value is limited by the small model pool, a single router and encoder, and a router that loses to fixed and task-only baselines. It is a well-supported but narrow null finding.

departures: run_experiment.py defines query normalization as whitespace collapse with case preserved. The registration leaves normalization unspecified, so this is a permitted implementation choice; another normalization could change grouping, exclusions and the sampled data.

run_experiment.py selects the lexicographically first raw query spelling within each normalized duplicate group. The registration does not specify a representative-selection rule. This preserves an original query but could affect embeddings and routing when duplicate spellings differ.

run_experiment.py removes train–test overlaps from training, after constructing complete outcome matrices. The registration does not specify which side to remove. The evaluated run reports zero overlaps, so this choice did not change its result.

run_experiment.py uses float32 embeddings, left padding and length-sorted batches, and numpy's default linear percentile interpolation. These settings were not fixed by the registration and are permitted choices. Numerical alternatives could slightly change routing or percentile values, but no consequential discrepancy is demonstrated.

run_experiment.py treats candidate predictions within 1e-12 of the maximum as ties rather than requiring exact equality. This is a small departure from literal lexicographic tie-breaking. registration.title: Can call-lineage tags prevent duplicate-report aggregation errors?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's multi-agent topologies pass agent outputs through later nodes, and its multi-turn systems can lose quality during aggregation. Forwarded copies of one generation may appear as multiple supporting reports unless the aggregation state preserves their common origin.
registration.hypothesis: Accurate generator-call identifiers improve aggregation accuracy over matched distinct-source identifiers when a copied report creates an apparent majority, averaged over both correct-majority and incorrect-majority cases.
registration.contribution: Dependence-aware calibration and conformity effects already exist in the literature. This experiment tests a cheaper intervention: whether exposing known call lineage directly to an untrained aggregator provides useful decision information without additional independent rollouts, a learned calibrator or correctness feedback.

closest_work.difference: CAGE-Cal learns dependency-aware confidence using matched communication and no-communication graphs. This experiment changes only visible call-origin identifiers in frozen report panels and uses no learned calibration or extra counterfactual generation.

This work manipulates simulated consensus and authority cues. Here the answer reports are actual sampled completions, their text and vote counts remain fixed across treatments, and the manipulated information is whether repeated reports share one generator call.

inputs: allenai/ai2_arc, ARC-Challenge test split: https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/ai2_arc
BIG-Bench Hard logical_deduction_seven_objects: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard/main/bbh/logical_deduction_seven_objects.json
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
registration.method: Implement local batched inference in BF16, preferably with an eager-mode inference engine and separate model processes. Select 240 questions from each dataset with seed 1729. Relabel ARC choices consecutively and preserve their correct indices. For every question generate four independent Qwen2.5-1.5B reports with temperature 0.8, top_p 0.95 and max_tokens 128. Request brief reasoning followed by 'Final: <letter>'. Parse the last explicit Final letter, also accepting an otherwise solely valid letter. Keep questions having both a correct and an incorrect report with valid parsed letters and nontruncated completions. Select the first correct and first incorrect reports in generation order. Use up to 80 eligible questions per dataset, sampled with seed 17 without inspecting treatment outcomes; use all eligible questions if fewer are available. This defines a conditional disagreement assay, not population task accuracy. For every eligible question construct two four-report panels: three exact copies of its correct report plus one incorrect report, and three exact copies of its incorrect report plus one correct report. Thus copying favors the correct answer in half the panels and the wrong answer in half. Give reports distinct agent identifiers in every condition. In LINEAGE, copied reports carry the same opaque generator_call_id and the other report carries another identifier. In DISTINCT, every report carries a different generator_call_id, with identifier lengths and field placement identical to LINEAGE. DISTINCT is a deliberately manipulated provenance comparator, not a statement about the real origins. Randomize opaque identifier assignment independently of correctness. Also include a condition with agent identifiers but no call identifiers. All report bodies, their order and their multiplicities must be byte-identical across the three conditions. Ask Qwen2.5-3B to solve the original problem using the reports if helpful, with brief reasoning and 'Final: <letter>', greedy decoding and max_tokens 96. Do not tell it which answer is correct, which source is more reliable or that it should select the minority. Run a seed-17 report permutation and its reversal for each panel. Evaluate additional two-report, unduplicated panels and standalone answers from the same aggregator as diagnostics. Never include eligibility labels in aggregator prompts.

event.description: Call-lineage information yields a supported net accuracy improvement exceeding three percentage points, without assuming that the copied majority is always wrong.
event.statistic: S: the fifth percentile of a paired question-bootstrap distribution of LINEAGE minus DISTINCT aggregation accuracy, averaged over both copied-majority polarities and both report orders, then equally over the two datasets.

evaluation.procedure: Score final letters against objective dataset targets; invalid or truncated aggregate answers count as incorrect. For each eligible question average the LINEAGE-minus-DISTINCT correctness difference across its two majority polarities and two report orders. Macro-average dataset means and bootstrap eligible questions within dataset 2,000 times with seed 2026. S is the fifth percentile. outputs/candidate_reports.jsonl holds all sampled reports, parsed answers, correctness and finish reasons. outputs/panels.jsonl holds exact panel texts, experimental source identifiers and actual call lineage. outputs/aggregate_answers.jsonl holds aggregation prompts, completions, parsed answers, scores and control outputs. outputs/scores.json holds S, the point estimate and interval, eligibility counts and timings. If a dataset supplies no eligible questions, report an unestimable assay rather than manufacturing reports. A small or inconclusive effect is not evidence that dependence never matters.
evaluation.controls: Correct and incorrect copied majorities are balanced within every question; report text, count, order and annotation length are matched; source identifiers are unrelated to correctness; no-lineage, unduplicated and standalone controls distinguish a provenance effect from generic prompting or aggregator competence.

registration.full_scale_study: Trace actual call ancestry in chain, tree and graph workflows using heterogeneous models no larger than 8B. Include paraphrased forwarded reports rather than only exact copies, and compare prompt-visible lineage with trained dependency-aware aggregation under matched inference budgets.

agent.reason: Call identifiers could reduce false corroboration, but exact duplication is already visible in the report bodies and the aggregator has not been trained to exploit lineage. Balancing correct and incorrect copied majorities makes a supported net gain harder to obtain than improvement on wrong-majority cases alone.

judge_astra.reason: Exact duplication is already visible in both conditions, and a small aggregator may not meaningfully use the additional call identifiers. Balancing correct and incorrect copied majorities also eliminates improvements obtainable merely by distrusting majority answers.

judge_fable.reason: A 3B aggregator given opaque generator_call_id strings with no explanation will almost certainly attend to the identical report texts rather than the ids, so LINEAGE and DISTINCT should differ only by noise, far below the registered margin.

judge_opus.reason: A 3B aggregator is unlikely to interpret unexplained opaque call IDs, and the polarity-balanced design cancels symmetric majority effects. Prompt-perturbation noise with about 80 questions per dataset would require an implausible ~6pp+ point effect.

judge_sol.reason: Call identifiers could help discount copied evidence, but exact duplicate report bodies already reveal redundancy without those identifiers. Balancing correct and incorrect majorities also prevents a simple anti-majority heuristic from producing the required net improvement.

judge_luna.reason: Call IDs could prompt the aggregator not to count copies as independent, but the repeated report bodies are already byte-identical in DISTINCT, so lineage may add little information; balanced majority polarity also prevents a simple majority correction from helping overall. The low estimate concerns the registered event, not the general importance of dependence in real workflows.

judge_muse.reason: The frozen aggregator gets opaque call IDs without instruction to discount duplicates, so correct-majority harm and incorrect-majority benefit will largely cancel, making net >3pp lower-bound gain unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This is the closest work found. It measures how much LLM aggregators count forwarded copies, using records labelled with forwarded_from provenance. It includes a no-labels condition and a probe where a copied value faces a real majority. Its aggregators are frontier API models that report probabilities on synthetic sensor logs with an exact Bayesian oracle, plus web documents and logs written by agent teams. It shows that provenance labels only modestly reduce how much copies count. It does not test sampled multiple-choice reasoning reports, a small untrained open aggregator, a matched false-distinct call-ID comparator, or net accuracy averaged over copied majorities that are right and wrong.

CAMA tackles false majorities from correlated multi-agent memories. It uses learned dependency inference with provenance priors and an active policy that recovers more evidence. The experiment instead tests only whether prompt-visible lineage helps an untrained aggregator, with no learning and no extra retrieval.
CAGE-Cal learns dependency-aware confidence from communication and no-communication graphs. The experiment manipulates only visible call identifiers in fixed report panels.
This work manipulates simulated consensus and authority cues. The experiment keeps report text and vote counts fixed and changes only whether repeated reports are shown as sharing one generator call.

This work shows that repeating information from a less credible source can override source-credibility preferences in knowledge conflicts, and reduces the effect with a warning and fine-tuning. It does not test call-lineage identifiers in multi-agent answer aggregation.

opus.reason: The question of whether LLM aggregators discount restated copies, and whether visible provenance helps, was studied a few days before the cutoff in 'Copies or Sources?' (2610.06192). That paper found labels help only partly. But its sensor-log, probability-based setup with frontier models and an exact Bayesian oracle does not settle the registered question. That question is whether accurate versus deliberately falsified distinct call IDs change net multiple-choice accuracy for a small open aggregator on real sampled reasoning reports, with copied majorities balanced between right and wrong. The prior results suggest a direction, but I found no work that runs this comparison or answers it in the same way.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Copies or Sources? tests forwarded-copy labels, label removal, and explicit instructions to discount copies in frozen LLM aggregators. Its sensor tasks supply likelihoods and its web tasks measure belief shifts; it does not test accurate versus matched false call identifiers for net QA accuracy with equally often correct and incorrect copied majorities.

GraphEcho changes shared versus distinct origin assignments while matching evidence wording and graph paths, and evaluates provenance identifiers without training. However, its synthetic reference verdict is defined by distinct-source counts, rather than a fixed objective answer independent of the manipulated identifiers.

CAMA addresses false majorities from memories sharing upstream sources through learned dependency inference, provenance priors, and additional evidence retrieval. It does not isolate prompt-visible call identifiers in otherwise identical panels read by an untrained aggregator.

sol.reason: Prior work already studies duplicate corroboration and whether frozen LLMs respond to visible source dependence, so those broad ideas are not new. None of the work I found answers the registered question: whether call-lineage identifiers alone improve objective answer accuracy over matched distinct identifiers on actual sampled reports, balancing cases where copying favors the right and wrong answers.

opus.reason: No list entry manipulates generator-call lineage identifiers on duplicated reports to test aggregation accuracy.

sol.reason: No list entry manipulates generator-call lineage while holding duplicated report content and vote counts fixed to measure aggregation accuracy.

outcome.executor_notes:
The registered event did not occur. S, the registered statistic (5th percentile of the paired question bootstrap for LINEAGE minus DISTINCT), was −0.080. The event needed S > 0.03. The point estimate was +0.058 (90% bootstrap interval −0.080 to +0.195). By dataset, the mean LINEAGE−DISTINCT difference was +0.034 on ARC (67 eligible questions) and +0.083 on BBH (3 eligible questions). The direction is positive, but the effect is not supported at the registered level. That does not show that lineage has no effect.

**Main caveat: BBH contributes almost nothing.** With max_tokens 128, Qwen2.5-1.5B's reports on BBH logical_deduction_seven_objects were cut off 86% of the time, and only 3% were correct. So only 3 of 240 questions had both a correct and an incorrect valid, non-truncated report. As the registration requires, I used all eligible questions and did not change the token limit, so 3 questions carry half the macro-average weight. This makes the interval much wider. ARC had 67 eligible questions; all were used, since fewer than 80 qualified.

**Diagnostics (ARC):**
- Accuracy by condition: NO_CALL_ID 0.61, LINEAGE 0.59, DISTINCT 0.55.
- With an incorrect copied majority, accuracy was 0.40 for LINEAGE, 0.35 for DISTINCT and 0.46 for NO_CALL_ID.
- Unduplicated two-report panels: 0.63. Standalone answers: 0.45, with 30% cut off at 96 tokens.

So prompts with no call IDs did at least as well as LINEAGE. The visible effect may be partly a penalty on DISTINCT rather than a benefit of lineage. This reading is descriptive only; I did not test it.

**What was built, and how it differs from the registration:**
- **Inference engine:** Hugging Face transformers instead of an eager-mode engine. Generation is batched in BF16, and each model runs in its own Python process.
- **Sampling:** for the 1.5B reports I used temperature 0.8 and top_p 0.95, and turned off Qwen's default top_k and repetition penalty so the settings match the registration. Aggregation is greedy.
- **A report counts as truncated** when the generated tokens contain no end-of-sequence token.
- **Hardware:** the machine had an H200, not the A100 described.
- **Prompt wording:** I added one neutral sentence to the instructions for both LINEAGE and DISTINCT: "reports sharing a generator_call_id are copies of one generation". It says nothing about which answer is right, which source is reliable, or whether to pick the minority. NO_CALL_ID prompts omit this sentence and the ID field.
- **Matching:** report bodies, order and counts are byte-identical across the three conditions, and LINEAGE and DISTINCT prompts have identical character lengths; both are checked by asserts. Call IDs are random 8-hex strings unrelated to correctness.
- **Report order:** a seed-17 permutation and its reversal. I read "repetitions: 2" as these two orders; there is no separate rerun.

**Interpretation and assumptions:**
- If no answer follows "Final:", a letter is still accepted when it is the only distinct valid letter appearing as "(X)" or "answer is X". A bare single-letter reply is also accepted.
- Invalid or truncated aggregate answers score 0.

**Outputs:**
- result.json and everything in outputs/ are regenerated by run.sh.
- A complete run took about 2.5 minutes including the package install.
- Small numerical differences between runs are possible from GPU nondeterminism.
- scores.json also contains eligibility counts, accuracy by condition and polarity, truncation rates and timings.

departures: Inference engine (lineage/common.py): Hugging Face transformers generate is used instead of an eager-mode engine. The registration says 'preferably', so this was left open. BF16 and separate per-model processes are kept. This is unlikely to change the result beyond sampling-implementation differences.

Aggregator prompt (lineage/aggregate.py, CALL_EXPL): LINEAGE and DISTINCT prompts both get an added sentence, 'Reports sharing a generator_call_id are copies of one generation.' NO_CALL_ID omits it. The registration did not specify this wording, and the engineer disclosed it. It does not reveal correctness, reliability or a minority preference. It is applied identically to both arms of the primary contrast. It probably makes the identifier manipulation more salient in both directions: it marks LINEAGE copies explicitly and implies DISTINCT reports are independent. So it could change the magnitude of the LINEAGE−DISTINCT difference and of the NO_CALL_ID comparison. I treat it as a reasonable way to fill an unspecified prompt, not a forbidden change.

Repetitions (lineage/aggregate.py, run.sh): 'repetitions: 2' is read as the seed-17 permutation plus its reversal. There is no independent second run of the pipeline. This is ambiguous in the registration and disclosed. It could matter only through run-to-run variance of the sampled reports.
Truncation definition (lineage/common.py): a completion counts as truncated when no EOS / <|im_end|> token appears within max_new_tokens. This is a reasonable reading and does not change the result.

Fallback parser (lineage/common.py parse_letter): it also accepts a bare single-letter reply and a unique letter appearing as '(X)' or 'answer is X'. This is one interpretation of 'otherwise solely valid letter' and was disclosed. It could slightly shift which reports are eligible and how aggregate answers are scored, but it is applied identically across conditions.

Generation settings (lineage/common.py): top_k=0 and repetition_penalty=1.0 override Qwen's generation_config defaults so that sampling is pure temperature 0.8 / top_p 0.95. This brings sampling into line with the registration. Not a harmful departure.
Default Qwen system prompt: it is included via the chat template for both models. This is unspecified by the registration and applies equally to all conditions, so it should not change the result.
Hardware: H200 instead of the A100 the notes mention, though the registration names no GPU. Irrelevant.

Eligibility counts (outputs/eligibility.json): BBH yields 3 eligible questions and ARC yields 67, against an intended up to 80. This follows the registered 'use all eligible questions if fewer' rule rather than departing from it, but it leaves BBH, with 3 questions, carrying half of the macro-average.
problems: outputs/eligibility.json, scores.json: BBH logical_deduction_seven_objects has only 3 eligible questions because the 1.5B reporter truncates 86% of the time at 128 tokens. Under the registered equal macro-weighting, 3 questions carry half the weight of S and of the point estimate. The bootstrap distribution therefore has a very coarse BBH component, and S (−0.080) is largely uninformative about the dataset-level effect. This follows from the registered design (token budget and dataset choice) rather than from an implementation error.

scores.json: on ARC, NO_CALL_ID (0.61) is above both LINEAGE (0.59) and DISTINCT (0.55), and this holds especially for incorrect copied majorities (0.46 vs 0.40 vs 0.35). The positive LINEAGE−DISTINCT point estimate may therefore partly reflect DISTINCT IDs plus the explanatory sentence lowering accuracy, rather than lineage helping. This was not tested.

lineage/aggregate.py: the CALL_EXPL sentence was added to the treatment prompts without being in the registration. It is disclosed and symmetric across LINEAGE and DISTINCT, but it shapes how the 'opaque' identifiers are interpreted.
Single run only (run.sh): GPU nondeterminism in sampled reports and batched greedy decoding is unquantified. There is no rerun to bound it.
Engineer notes say the registration described an A100; the registration as shown names no GPU. This is a minor inaccuracy in the notes.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered pipeline closely: the specified seeds, report sampling settings, eligibility rule, balanced polarity panels, matched LINEAGE/DISTINCT/NO_CALL_ID conditions with byte-identical bodies and length-matched prompts, order reversal, diagnostics, and the paired macro bootstrap. The reported S = −0.080 is computed correctly from real model outputs, and the per-dataset means recompute consistently (0.0336 and 0.0833, average 0.0585). The main deviation is a symmetric explanatory sentence about generator_call_id. It was disclosed and fills an unspecified prompt detail, so I judge the run faithful. The evidence is weak, however: BBH contributes only 3 eligible questions at half weight, making the interval very wide (−0.08 to +0.19). The ARC diagnostics also show no-ID prompts doing at least as well as LINEAGE, which suggests the small positive difference may be a DISTINCT penalty rather than a lineage benefit. The registered event did not occur, and this null is inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect.

departures: lineage/common.py, parse_letter: beyond an explicit Final answer or an otherwise solely valid-letter response, the parser accepts a letter mentioned anywhere in '(X)' or 'answer is X' when only one distinct valid letter is found. Reasoning can therefore be scored as an answer without a final answer. This could change report eligibility, which reports are selected, aggregate scores and S; its realized effect is not quantified by the supplied excerpts.

lineage/common.py, parse_letter: explicit Final matches are filtered for validity before the last match is selected. Thus an earlier valid Final can be accepted despite a later invalid Final, rather than parsing the last explicit Final and rejecting its invalid letter. The parser also accepts 'Final answer:' wording. These broaden the parsing rule and could change eligibility or scores, although affected cases are not identified in the excerpts.

lineage/aggregate.py: LINEAGE and DISTINCT receive explanatory prose defining generator_call_id and stating that shared IDs identify copies; NO_CALL_ID receives neither this prose nor the field. The prompts also specify at most three short reasoning sentences. These choices could influence responses, and the no-ID diagnostic changes instructional prose as well as annotations. Exact wording was left open, however, and the explanation is shared by the primary treatments without revealing correctness.

lineage/common.py and run.sh: inference uses Hugging Face Transformers rather than the preferred specialized inference-engine approach. BF16, batching and separate model processes are retained. The engine preference was nonbinding; numerical implementation differences are possible, but no substantive change to the registered assay is established.

run.sh and lineage/aggregate.py: only one end-to-end run is performed; 'repetitions: 2' is interpreted as the permutation and its reversal, not two independent reruns. Both registered orders are present. The registration does not clearly require additional independent repetitions, so this is an ambiguity rather than an established fidelity defect; additional stochastic report-generation runs could change the result.

lineage/score.py: if one dataset has no eligible questions, the code still computes and reports S using the remaining dataset instead of declaring the two-dataset assay unestimable. It records the missing dataset separately. This violates the registered empty-dataset rule but did not affect this run, because both datasets had eligible questions.

problems: BBH is almost unusable under the registered 128-token cap: stdout and eligibility.json show 86% truncation, ~3% report accuracy, and only 3/240 eligible questions, yet score.py gives that dataset equal macro-average weight with 67 ARC questions, so the 90% interval in scores.json (−0.080 to +0.195) cannot resolve a 3pp effect.

About 10% of aggregator completions are truncated at the registered 96 tokens and scored incorrect (scores.json); rates are similar across LINEAGE and DISTINCT, so this is noise rather than a confound, but it lowers precision.
The registered event uses the 5th percentile, not the +0.058 point estimate; S=−0.080 correctly fails the >0.03 bar, and that inconclusive result is not evidence that dependence never matters.
