registration.title: Does persona-conditioned routing supervision transfer between local judges?
registration.seed_connection: The seed creates personalized supervision using a persona-conditioned judge and observes different router rankings under simulated and real-user feedback. Before investing in personalized router architecture, synthetic labels should be tested for portability across the judging channel.
registration.hypothesis: Demographic and biographical persona conditioning produces a held-out personalization advantage that transfers between two different local judges after answer-order balancing.
registration.contribution: Prior work questions agreement between personalized judges and humans, and personalized routing benchmarks learn from persona-conditioned labels. This experiment isolates judge-channel portability using a fully crossed panel: every persona evaluates exactly the same questions and answer pairs, preventing persona identity from being confounded with query mix.

closest_work.difference: This work validates personalized judgments against human preferences and studies persona sparsity. The experiment tests reproducibility of routing-relevant persona effects across judge identities, not human alignment.

PersonalizedRouter learns graph-based routing from simulated preferences. This experiment tests the supervision channel before using a complex architecture, with fully crossed questions, personas, answer orders and local judges.

inputs: The 80 MT-Bench questions and category labels: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lm-sys/FastChat/main/fastchat/llm_judge/data/mt_bench/question.jsonl
Eight public persona descriptions from seed Appendix A.6, specified explicitly in the method
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct
registration.method: Use only the first user turn of all 80 MT-Bench questions. Generate two candidate responses per question using Qwen2.5-3B with greedy decoding and max_tokens 256: SHORT uses the system instruction 'Answer helpfully in one concise paragraph of at most 60 words'; DETAIL uses 'Answer helpfully with a structured explanation and a concrete example where appropriate, using at most 170 words'. These are two inference configurations of the same checkpoint, not two different generator models. Neither receives a persona. Use the following eight synthetic profiles: a 71-year-old retired nurse from Italy volunteering in hospice care; a 54-year-old divorced mother from Spain running a winery and promoting sustainable viticulture; a 63-year-old retired teacher from China teaching calligraphy; a 68-year-old retired engineer from Japan practicing and teaching ikebana; a 21-year-old photographer from Paris who volunteers on weekends; a 34-year-old scientist from London who is a social-media influencer; a 41-year-old scientist from London who loves hiking; and a 23-year-old aspiring musician from Brazil combining traditional and modern sounds. Cross every question and fixed response pair with every profile. Judge each comparison using both Qwen2.5-3B and Phi-3.5-mini, greedy decoding and max_tokens 16, under both response orders. Use one common judging instruction: 'You are simulating this user: {profile}. Which response would this user personally prefer for the question? Judge the responses, not their position. Output only 1, 2, or Tie.' Present the original question and anonymized responses. Never reveal configuration or generator names. Map each verdict back to SHORT credit: 1 for SHORT preference, 0 for DETAIL preference and 0.5 for Tie. An invalid verdict is uninformative credit 0.5 for both actions, recorded separately; do not selectively retry it. Average the two orders separately for each judge. Create five question-level folds stratified by MT-Bench category with seed 1729. For each fold and each transfer direction, train on one judge's labels outside the fold and evaluate on the other judge's labels inside the fold. Fit Ridge regression with alpha 10 and an intercept: GLOBAL receives category one-hot features; PERSONAL receives category, persona and category-by-persona one-hot features. Both predict SHORT credit and select SHORT at predictions at least 0.5, otherwise DETAIL. Train no graph network and use no test labels during fitting. Add two explicit-preference positive-control profiles, one preferring brief direct answers and one preferring detailed explanations with examples, but exclude them from primary fitting and scoring. Add a placebo fit that independently permutes persona identifiers within each training question. Also calculate within-judge held-out effects as diagnostics. Batch inference locally in BF16; the Qwen checkpoint serves as both generator and one judge, keeping the model-download set small.

event.description: A simple persona-conditioned policy retains a supported preference-credit advantage exceeding two percentage points when evaluated by a different judge.
event.statistic: S: the fifth percentile of the paired question-bootstrap distribution of cross-judge PERSONAL minus GLOBAL preference credit, averaged over the eight biographical personas and both judge-transfer directions.

evaluation.procedure: For a selected SHORT response use its order-balanced credit from the evaluation judge; for DETAIL use one minus that credit. Compute out-of-fold PERSONAL-minus-GLOBAL differences for each question, averaging personas and both transfer directions. Bootstrap questions within category 2,000 times with seed 2026, retaining their full crossed panels. S is the fifth percentile. outputs/responses.jsonl holds both fixed candidate responses and generation metadata. outputs/judgments.jsonl holds exact judge prompts, profiles, response order, raw verdicts, mapped credits and invalid-verdict flags. outputs/folds.json holds fold membership and feature definitions. outputs/policy_decisions.jsonl holds cross-judge, within-judge, positive-control and placebo decisions and credits. outputs/scores.json holds S, its point estimate and interval, assay checks and timings. Even a positive event establishes only portability of synthetic supervision across these judges; it does not validate demographic predictions about real people. An unmet event does not establish absence of genuine human personalization.
evaluation.controls: Every persona sees identical questions and response pairs; both answer orders are scored; both judge-transfer directions are evaluated; generators never see personas; candidate configurations share one checkpoint; explicit-preference profiles check conditioning ability; within-question persona permutations destroy individual structure while preserving query-level preference distributions.

registration.full_scale_study: Extend the crossed design to heterogeneous candidate models and additional independent judges, then calibrate portable synthetic effects against existing public human-preference records such as PRISM or PersonalRewardBench. Evaluate whether interaction-derived profiles transfer better than biographical descriptions without collecting new human annotations.

agent.reason: The biographical profiles provide no explicit preferences about brevity or detail, leaving the judges to supply potentially different interpretations. Category controls, regularization and cross-judge evaluation make a portable two-percentage-point lower-bound advantage a demanding event.

judge_astra.reason: Biographical profiles provide weak grounds for stable SHORT-versus-DETAIL preferences, particularly preferences that transfer between judges. The crossed design and order balancing remove several shortcuts that could otherwise create apparent personalization gains.

judge_fable.reason: Small LLM judges mostly prefer the longer response regardless of persona, and any persona-by-category effects are unlikely to be consistent between Qwen2.5-3B and Phi-3.5-mini; the cross-judge PERSONAL policy adds variance and may underperform GLOBAL, so a supported two-point gain is improbable.

judge_opus.reason: Small local judges are likely dominated by verbosity and position bias, so biographical personas rarely flip SHORT/DETAIL choices consistently across both judges. PERSONAL and GLOBAL decisions would mostly coincide, giving a near-zero difference.

judge_sol.reason: The biographies do not explicitly specify preferences for concise versus detailed answers, so generic answer-quality and verbosity preferences are likely to dominate. Cross-judge transfer and only 80 independent question clusters make a supported two-point personalization advantage particularly demanding.

judge_luna.reason: The fully crossed panel and order balancing make this a clean test of whether persona effects survive judge transfer. Yet the profiles do not state response-style preferences, and both the demographic signal and its consistency between Qwen and Phi may be weak; with 80 question clusters, the +2pp lower-tail bar seems difficult.

judge_muse.reason: Biographical profiles give only indirect cues for SHORT versus DETAIL style and judges likely share a global length bias, so a transferable cross-judge persona advantage exceeding a 2pp lower bound is unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: This paper checks persona-conditioned LLM judges against human ground truth and finds low agreement. It does not test whether a persona-specific routing advantage learned from one judge's labels holds up when a different judge scores it, and it does not use a fully crossed question × persona × answer-order × judge panel.

PersonalizedRouter trains a graph router on simulated persona preferences, including labels from an LLM judge, and reports gains under that same simulation. It does not test whether the persona-conditioned supervision carries over between judges, and it has no ridge baseline, placebo permutation or cross-judge held-out evaluation.

FSPO builds synthetic personalized preferences and tests transfer from synthetic users to real users. It does not test whether persona-conditioned labels transfer from one LLM judge to another for a routing decision.
This paper studies verdict instability within one judge and between judges on MT-Bench and other benchmarks, but without persona conditioning or routing policies.

opus.reason: Across several searches I found work on whether persona judges agree with humans, on routers trained from simulated persona preferences, and on general judge disagreement. I did not find any paper that trains a persona-aware routing policy on one judge's persona-conditioned labels and measures its held-out advantage under a different judge. The closest papers ask related questions (agreement with humans, or gains within one simulator) but do not settle whether the advantage survives a change of judge.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: PersonalizedRouter learns from persona-conditioned preferences and uses six judge configurations in PersonaRoute-Bench, treating them as distinct user perspectives. It does not train on one judge's labels and test the same personas' incremental routing benefit under another judge.

Can LLM be a Personalized Judge? compares multiple persona-conditioned judges against human preferences and studies persona sparsity and uncertainty. It does not test cross-judge transfer of a learned personalized selection policy.

SynthesizeMe transfers persona prompts inferred from real users' preference histories between models, evaluating against human labels. The registered experiment instead transfers supervision generated from fixed biographical personas between judging channels.

This crossed, multi-model study compares personality-conditioned color choices and chart-preference rankings. It measures cross-model consistency directly, rather than held-out transfer of a learned personalization advantage over a matched global policy.

The seed uses DeepSeek-V3.1 persona-conditioned routing labels and separately trains and evaluates routers on real-user feedback. Its ranking comparison does not test supervision transfer between judges on an identical persona-question-response panel.

sol.reason: Prior work available by 2026-10-07 already examines personalized-judge reliability, multiple judging configurations, and cross-model consistency or transfer of persona prompts. However, I found no paper testing whether biographical-persona supervision from one judge yields a held-out routing advantage over a matched persona-agnostic policy when evaluated by another judge on the same fully crossed, order-balanced response pairs.

opus.reason: Both train query-only and query-plus-persona preference predictors on one local judge's order-balanced persona labels, use a within-question persona-shuffle control, and test whether the personalization gain holds under a different judge.

sol.reason: Both test whether persona-conditioned routing gains generalize across judges using fixed response pairs, both answer orders, persona-agnostic and shuffled-persona controls, and held-out preference evaluation.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (main.py, run via run.sh): the registered fully crossed design. 80 MT-Bench first turns. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, greedy decoding, 256 max new tokens, BF16, produced the SHORT and DETAIL responses with the registered system instructions. Responses averaged 34 and 124 words, and 2.5% of pairs were identical. That gives 8 biographical profiles plus 2 explicit positive-control profiles, × 2 answer orders × 2 judges (Qwen2.5-3B, Phi-3.5-mini), with greedy decoding and 16 max new tokens: 3,200 judgments. Each verdict is mapped to a SHORT credit (1, 0, or 0.5 for Tie). An invalid verdict counts as 0.5, is flagged and is never retried. Credits are averaged over the two orders separately for each judge. Folds: 5-fold StratifiedKFold by category, seed 1729. Models: Ridge(alpha=10, intercept); GLOBAL uses category one-hot, PERSONAL uses category + persona + category×persona one-hot. Decision: SHORT if the prediction is ≥0.5. Training and evaluation are cross-judge in both directions, with no test labels used in fitting. Bootstrap: questions resampled within category, B=2000, seed 2026. Policies stay fixed during the bootstrap because they are out-of-fold. S is the 5th percentile. Diagnostics: a placebo that permutes persona labels within each training question, within-judge effects, a separate 10-profile fit to check the positive controls, invalid/order/position statistics, and cross-judge correlations.

Small deviations and implementation choices:
(1) The judge instruction text is used verbatim but placed after the question and the two responses, so the output-format request comes last. Responses are labelled [Response 1]/[Response 2]. Each judge's own chat template is applied, and for Qwen that adds its default system message.
(2) The verdict parser was fixed before I looked at the data. It strips leading punctuation and an optional leading "Response"/"Answer" word, then reads a leading 1, 2 or Tie. Phi often adds an explanation after the verdict, and that text is ignored.
(3) The positive-control wordings are my own: "a user who prefers brief, direct answers without extra detail" and "a user who prefers detailed explanations with concrete examples".
(4) The machine had an H200, not an A100.
(5) The question file is downloaded from the registered URL, with a local copy in data/ as a fallback.
(6) The two full runs on the machine took about 80–95 s each (packages were already installed on the second) and gave identical results.

Observed (one run, reproduced exactly): S = −0.0109; point estimate −0.0004; 90% interval [−0.011, 0.011]. So the registered event (S > 0.02) did not occur. Placebo minus GLOBAL is −0.006. Within-judge PERSONAL minus GLOBAL is −0.005 (Qwen) and +0.005 (Phi). Invalid verdicts: Qwen 0%, Phi 0.75%. The two orders agreed in 79% of Qwen's comparisons but only 37% of Phi's. Phi is strongly position-biased, preferring Response 2 in 51% of comparisons versus 30% for Response 1.

Positive controls: both judges shift in the expected direction. SHORT credit for the brief-preferring profile minus the detail-preferring profile is +0.175 (Qwen) and +0.197 (Phi), so explicit preferences do move the judges' verdicts. Cross-judge correlation of within-question persona residuals is ≈0.00, and the persona-level spread is small, especially for Phi (SD of persona means 0.021).

Interpretation: under these two small local judges, biographical persona conditioning gave no held-out advantage that transfers to the other judge, and the estimate is close to zero. This does not establish that genuine human personalization is absent. It does not test other judges or candidate pools. Nor does the null alone show the effect is zero, though the 90% interval excludes effects larger than about ±1.1 points.

departures: main.py judge_content puts the registered instruction after the question and the two responses, which are labelled [Response 1]/[Response 2]. The registration does not fix the prompt layout, and the instruction text is verbatim. This is reported and could shift verdicts slightly, but it does not change the question.

main.py applies each judge's chat template without a system message. For the Qwen judge this injects the default system prompt 'You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.' (visible in outputs/judgments.jsonl). The notes report it. It is a minor prompt difference that could slightly affect Qwen's verdicts.
The positive-control profile wordings are the engineer's own. The registration describes them only loosely. They are excluded from S, so they cannot change the primary value.

The verdict parser in main.py strips punctuation and a leading 'Response'/'Answer' word and ignores trailing explanation. The registration leaves parsing open. Only 0.75% of Phi verdicts were invalid, so the effect on S is negligible.

main.py adds unregistered diagnostics: a separate 10-profile cross-judge fit for the positive controls, a PERSONAL-minus-PLACEBO bootstrap, and per-direction and per-persona breakdowns. These are diagnostic only and do not affect S.
The placebo uses a single generator, rng_pl seeded 1729, shared across all folds and settings. The registration does not specify this. It affects only placebo diagnostics.

Generation and judging run in left-padded, length-sorted BF16 batches on an H200. The registration asked for batched BF16 and names no GPU. Numerics might slightly alter greedy outputs versus unbatched runs, but the result is deterministic across the three runs.
The engineer notes misstate the 90% interval as [-0.011, 0.011]. outputs/scores.json gives [-0.0109, 0.0094]. This is a reporting slip with no effect on the result.
problems: The judge assay is weak. Phi's two answer orders agree on only 37% of comparisons, and it picks Response 2 in 51% of comparisons versus 30% for Response 1. Its persona-mean SD is only 0.021. Qwen returns Tie 48% of the time. Much of the label variation is position noise or ties rather than persona signal (scores.json judge_verdict_stats).

Within-judge PERSONAL minus GLOBAL is also near zero: -0.005 for Qwen and +0.005 for Phi. Biographical persona effects are not learnable across questions even within a single judge. The cross-judge null therefore says more about the absence of a learnable persona signal than about non-portability as such.

Cross-judge transfer of the explicit positive controls is inconsistent. In the Phi→Qwen direction the brief profile scores PERSONAL minus GLOBAL = -0.0625, while the detail profile scores +0.106. In Qwen→Phi the gains are +0.0125 and 0. So the pipeline's sensitivity to genuinely portable preferences is only partly demonstrated, even though the judges do respond to explicit preferences (brief minus detail is about +0.18 to +0.20).

The 256-token cap often truncates DETAIL responses mid-sentence. In outputs/responses.jsonl the Hawaii post (195 words) and the documentary list both stop mid-sentence, despite the 170-word instruction. The SHORT-versus-DETAIL contrast is therefore partly confounded with completeness. This follows the registered settings and is not a departure.
2.5% of response pairs are identical, so they contribute only noise.
Qwen is both the generator and one of the judges, so self-preference is possible. This was registered.

There is a single repetition with one candidate pool and two small judges, which limits generality. The engineer's statement that the interval 'excludes effects larger than about ±1.1 points' is a bootstrap-based near-equivalence claim restricted to this setup.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: generation, judging, fold and Ridge settings, the crossed panel, invalid handling, placebo, within-category bootstrap and the S statistic all match. The only departures are open choices or reported layout details that should not plausibly move S. The evaluation run regenerated every output from real model calls, and it matches the engineer's two earlier runs exactly. S = -0.011 is far below the 0.02 threshold, and the 95% interval is roughly ±0.012, so the null is reasonably precise. Its interpretation is limited, though: Phi is heavily position-biased, persona effects are null even within each judge, and cross-judge transfer of the explicit positive controls is mixed. The finding is therefore a credible but narrow negative about these two small local judges rather than a strong test of whether synthetic supervision is portable.

departures: main.py places the common judging instruction after the question and responses, labels the candidates [Response 1]/[Response 2], and applies each model's chat template. Qwen's template adds its default identity/system message. These choices could affect judgments relative to another prompt layout, but the registration did not specify placement, message roles, or template handling; candidate provenance remains undisclosed.

main.py::parse accepts a leading verdict followed by explanations and strips punctuation and optional Response, Answer, or Assistant prefixes. This is more permissive than exact-string validation of the requested output format, and the displayed Phi outputs demonstrate that this permissiveness affects which replies receive informative credit. registration.title: Reopen the image or upgrade the text solver?
registration.seed_connection: The seed converts visual inputs to one shared caption before model selection. That protocol measures reasoning over a frozen textual representation, but cannot show whether failures are better addressed by choosing another text model or reopening the original image.
registration.hypothesis: Revising a caption with fresh image access and retaining the small text solver rescues more answers than either upgrading the text solver on the frozen caption or revising the caption without image access.
registration.contribution: Question-aware captioning is established prior work. This experiment adds a paired intervention diagnostic for routing: compare access to the original asset with increased downstream model capacity and an image-blind revision control. It tests the value of an upstream recovery action, not the novelty of caption conditioning.

closest_work.difference: PromptCap establishes question-aware captioning. This experiment uses that principle as a treatment and compares its recovery value against text-model upgrading and matched image-blind revision on the same instances.

This work trains an agent to choose captioning, retrieval and answering actions for knowledge-based VQA. The experiment instead freezes the initial caption and performs controlled recovery comparisons without agent training or external retrieval.
MMR-Bench studies multimodal candidate routing. This experiment diagnoses the shared caption bottleneck and separates changing downstream model capacity from restoring access to the original image.

inputs: MathVista testmini, using only multiple-choice items with an unambiguous gold choice: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AI4Math/MathVista
Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct
Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
registration.method: Download or stream MathVista testmini and select 192 multiple-choice items using seed 1729, before running models. Require that the official answer maps uniquely to one listed choice. Relabel choices consecutively A, B, C, and so on. Record original identifiers and image hashes. Use no human annotation and never give gold answers to any model. Run local batched BF16 inference, loading model workers separately and disabling inference compilation where supported. Bound Qwen2.5-VL image processing at max_pixels 401408, preserving aspect ratio, with the same preprocessing in every image-access condition. First produce one frozen caption c0 per image using Qwen2.5-VL-3B, greedy decoding and max_tokens 192, without the question: 'Describe the image factually. Include visible text, numbers, symbols, angles, lengths, relationships, axes and legends. Do not solve any problem or invent missing details.' Obtain a baseline answer using Qwen2.5-1.5B from the question, choices and c0. Then run three fixed recovery branches on every selected item, not only baseline failures. UPGRADE answers from the same question, choices and c0 using Qwen2.5-3B. VISUAL_REPAIR asks Qwen2.5-VL-3B to revise c0 with the image and question visible: 'Correct errors and omissions in this draft description. Describe the visible facts relevant to this question. Do not calculate the answer, select an option or state a solution. Draft: {c0}. Question: {question}.' BLIND_REPAIR uses exactly that instruction, draft and question with the same VL checkpoint, but in a fresh text-only conversation containing no image or image tokens. Both revisions have max_tokens 192. Feed each revised caption separately to the unchanged Qwen2.5-1.5B solver. All text-answering calls use greedy decoding, max_tokens 128 and the same instruction: 'Use the supplied image description to answer the multiple-choice question. Give brief reasoning, then Final: <option letter>.' Revisions never receive the baseline answer or choices. As a diagnostic baseline, have Qwen2.5-VL-3B answer directly from the original image, question and choices. Parse the last explicit Final letter, accepting an otherwise solely valid letter. Invalid or truncated answers count as incorrect and are not regenerated. Record generated tokens, image tokens and wall-clock times for all calls. This is an accuracy-only recovery-mechanism test: VISUAL_REPAIR entails an additional image pass and another solver call, so a positive result is not an equal-cost dominance claim. Fresh image access may aid both perception and reasoning; do not label all gains as purely perceptual without further evidence.

event.description: Fresh-image caption revision has a supported accuracy advantage exceeding three percentage points over both the larger text solver and image-blind revision.
event.statistic: S: the fifth percentile of the paired question-bootstrap distribution of min(accuracy_VISUAL_REPAIR minus accuracy_UPGRADE, accuracy_VISUAL_REPAIR minus accuracy_BLIND_REPAIR).

evaluation.procedure: Score all branches against the objective gold choice on the identical 192 items. In each of 2,000 bootstrap samples with seed 2026, resample items with all their branch outcomes together, calculate both accuracy differences and take their minimum. S is the fifth percentile of this minimum-gap distribution. outputs/items.jsonl holds item identifiers, questions, choices, gold-choice mappings, image hashes and preprocessing settings. outputs/captions.jsonl holds frozen, visually revised and image-blind revised captions with prompts, finish reasons and token counts. outputs/answers.jsonl holds baseline, recovery and direct-image answers, parsed choices, correctness and timing. outputs/scores.json holds S, both point differences and intervals, control performance and full resource accounting. An unmet event does not establish that captions preserve all relevant visual information.
evaluation.controls: The frozen caption is identical for baseline and text-model upgrade; visual and blind revision use the same checkpoint and instruction in fresh conversations; the small downstream solver and answer format remain fixed across revision branches; every branch is run on every selected item; direct native-image answering checks whether the caption cascade is unnecessarily elaborate.

registration.full_scale_study: Train and evaluate a stage-aware policy choosing among stopping, upgrading the text solver, reopening the image and direct native-image answering. Compare these actions under measured GPU-time and visual-token budgets across larger visual-math and chart datasets, using only models no larger than 8B.

agent.reason: Fresh image access can restore decisive evidence unavailable to a larger text solver, although the initial caption already requests detailed numerical and symbolic facts. The event requires a supported advantage over both controls, so improving the small solver's baseline alone will not suffice.

judge_astra.reason: Question-aware access to the original image can recover relevant facts that neither a frozen-caption solver upgrade nor blind revision can recover reliably. However, visual repair must beat both controls with a lower bound above three percentage points on just 192 items, making a positive point estimate insufficient.

judge_fable.reason: Question-aware caption revision with image access plausibly adds 8-15 points over a generic caption for perception-heavy MathVista MC items, while upgrading the text solver on a frozen caption is capped by caption content; the gap must exceed roughly ten points against the 3B upgrade to clear the 5th-percentile threshold with 192 items, making this a near coin flip with some multimodal implementation risk.

judge_opus.reason: Fresh-image revision likely beats image-blind revision clearly, but geometry-heavy MC items may favour upgrading the solver from 1.5B to 3B. With 192 items, the minimum gap needs about 11pp to clear 3pp at the 5th percentile, which is possible but not the central expectation.

judge_sol.reason: Question-aware image access can recover omitted visual facts that neither text-model upgrading nor image-blind revision can directly recover. However, the unchanged small solver and the requirement to clear both bootstrap comparisons on 192 items substantially limit the probability of success.

judge_luna.reason: Question-aware access to the image could recover details missing from a generic caption, making this the most plausible positive event. Still, c0 is explicitly asked to capture visual facts, BLIND_REPAIR also sees the question, and the visual arm uses an extra image-and-solver pass; supported gains over both alternatives on 192 items are far from assured.

judge_muse.reason: Question-aware visual revision should restore figure details missing from a question-blind frozen caption, while upgrade reuses the deficient caption and blind revision lacks the image, though small captioner and solver capacity temper confidence.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: SeeingEye has a small VLM translator that looks at the image again over several feedback rounds and passes structured text to a text-only reasoner. It is a trained agentic method tested on MMMU and MIA-Bench. It does not compare caption revision with fresh image access against upgrading the text solver on a frozen caption, and it has no image-blind revision control.

RAPID separates perception from reasoning. It trains the captioner with an RL objective (VPO) so it works with any external text reasoner, and it shows that swapping in stronger reasoners helps. It does not run a paired, training-free comparison of reopening the image versus upgrading the solver versus revising the caption without the image.
PromptCap establishes question-aware captioning, which the experiment uses as its treatment. PromptCap does not compare that treatment against model upgrading or an image-blind revision control.

MMA2A compares routing inputs in their native modality against a text-bottleneck baseline in agent networks, and reports a related accuracy gap. It does not cover visual-math caption revision, solver upgrading, or an image-blind revision control.

MM-OPD finds that symbolic or caption views can outperform raw images when the model is held fixed, which bears on the caption-bottleneck question. Its method is self-distillation training, and it does not compare recovery actions in a caption-based routing cascade.

opus.reason: Earlier work covers question-aware captioning (PromptCap), separating perception from reasoning with swappable reasoners (RAPID), and agentic re-perception loops (SeeingEye). None of the papers I found runs the experiment's specific paired test. That test checks whether caption revision with the image visible beats both a larger text solver on the same frozen caption and a matched revision made without the image, on the same MathVista items. The question looks unsettled, though related work makes the general idea of re-perceiving the image familiar.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Lost in Perception compares generic, question-aware and human-authored captions and measures failure recovery, but does not compare fresh-image revision against upgrading a solver on the identical frozen caption and matched image-blind revision.
RAPID evaluates caption-generation strategies and stronger external text reasoners, but optimizes the captioner through training rather than testing the proposed controlled recovery interventions.

M3-ACE studies visual-evidence correction and image-grounded reflection, including multi-agent refinement, but lacks the fixed-caption text-solver upgrade and same-checkpoint image-blind revision comparison.
PromptCap establishes question-aware captioning and separately evaluates language-model capacity; it does not isolate the recovery value of renewed image access using the proposed paired controls.
Aha Moment Revisited compares self-verification with and without images, but verifies candidate answers rather than repairing an upstream caption for an unchanged downstream solver.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes question-aware captioning, corrected-caption recovery, independently stronger text reasoners, and image-access ablations, so those ingredients are not novel. However, I found no paper answering the specific paired recovery question from an identical frozen caption: whether fresh-image revision with the small solver outperforms both frozen-caption solver upgrading and matched image-blind revision.

opus.reason: List entries compare native images with captions or vary the captioner, but none compares image-access caption revision against a text-solver upgrade and an image-blind revision control.

sol.reason: The vision entries compare input representations or caption sources, but none compares fresh-image caption repair against both a text-solver upgrade and matched image-blind repair.

outcome.executor_notes:
Implementation: exp/run_exp.py, launched by run.sh. run.sh pip-installs transformers 4.51.3, accelerate and datasets. Everything runs locally with HF transformers in BF16, SDPA attention, greedy decoding with repetition_penalty set to 1.0, and no torch.compile. The registered order is kept:
- From MathVista testmini, keep multi-choice items whose answer string equals exactly one listed choice, then draw 192 of them with numpy default_rng(1729). Choices are relabelled A, B, …; items.jsonl records the pid and an image hash.
- Qwen2.5-VL-3B (max_pixels 401408) writes a question-free frozen caption c0 (192 tokens).
- VISUAL_REPAIR rewrites c0 with the image and the question visible. BLIND_REPAIR uses the same checkpoint, instruction, draft and question in a fresh conversation with no image tokens. Both get 192 tokens.
- Qwen2.5-1.5B answers from c0 (BASELINE) and from each revised caption. UPGRADE is Qwen2.5-3B answering from c0. All answer calls use the registered instruction and 128 tokens.
- Diagnostic: Qwen2.5-VL-3B answers directly from the image, using the same instruction with "image" in place of "image description".
- S is the 5th percentile of min(VISUAL−UPGRADE, VISUAL−BLIND) over a paired item bootstrap (2,000 samples, seed 2026).

Deviations and interpretation choices:
1. One selected image has a side under 28 px (18×187), which the Qwen2.5-VL processor rejects. Images with a side under 28 px are upscaled with aspect ratio preserved so the short side is 28. This is applied identically in every image condition and flagged per item.
2. Parsing: take the last "Final: X". If there is none, accept a response that is only a letter, or one that refers to exactly one distinct valid option letter (e.g. "C. o'clock", "answer is (B)"). Otherwise the answer is invalid. I widened this fallback after a first test run, when I saw many un-tagged answers such as "C. o'clock …". The same parser applies to every branch. scores.json also reports a stricter Final-tag-only parse for comparison.
3. Following the registration, truncated answers (hit 128 tokens) count as incorrect even if a letter can be parsed.

Result of the test run on this machine: S = 0.068, above the 0.03 threshold, so the registered event occurred.

| Branch | Accuracy | Truncated (of 192) |
|---|---|---|
| BASELINE | 0.115 | 146 |
| VISUAL_REPAIR | 0.271 | 117 |
| BLIND_REPAIR | 0.146 | 127 |
| UPGRADE | 0.036 | 177 |
| DIRECT_IMAGE | 0.469 | 34 |

- VISUAL_REPAIR − UPGRADE: +0.234, 95% CI [0.17, 0.30].
- VISUAL_REPAIR − BLIND_REPAIR: +0.125, 95% CI [0.05, 0.20].
- Sensitivity checks, which are not the registered statistic: S is 0.057 with Final-tag-only parsing and 0.057 when truncation is not penalised.

Caveats:
- The 128-token answer cap dominates the results. UPGRADE's very low accuracy mainly reflects the 3B solver's verbosity being cut off, not a measured lack of reasoning ability. The VISUAL_REPAIR versus UPGRADE gap therefore should not be read as "reopening the image beats more downstream capacity" in general.
- Caption truncation at 192 tokens also differs: 78 for c0, 29 for the visual repair and 81 for the blind repair. Part of the visual-repair gain may come from shorter, more focused captions and the downstream truncation that follows, not only from new visual information.
- Fresh image access may help both perception and reasoning, so I do not claim the gain is purely perceptual.
- This is accuracy only, not equal cost: the visual-repair pipeline uses about twice the image tokens and more wall time (see resources_by_pipeline).
- Direct native-image answering beats every caption cascade by a wide margin.
- Two consecutive runs gave identical core-branch outcomes, but batched BF16 greedy decoding may vary slightly on other hardware. The test machine had an H200 GPU, not the stated A100. One full run takes about 4 minutes plus installation.

departures: exp/run_exp.py parse_letter: when no Final tag is present, the parser accepts a response that refers to exactly one distinct valid option letter, using several regex patterns. This reading of 'an otherwise solely valid letter' was widened after the engineer looked at outputs from a test run. The engineer reported it. It could raise accuracy in every branch, but the Final-tag-only sensitivity check still gives S=0.057 > 0.03, so it does not change the event.

exp/run_exp.py select_items: images with a side under 28 px are upscaled so the short side is 28, applied in every image condition. One item is affected. The engineer reported it. The change was needed for the processor to accept the image and is negligible for the result.
exp/run_exp.py DIRECT_INSTR: the direct-image diagnostic uses the solver instruction with 'image' in place of 'image description'. The engineer reported it. It affects only the diagnostic, not S.

exp/run_exp.py with outputs/items.jsonl: the MathVista question field is passed verbatim, and some items have answer choices embedded in it (e.g. pid 287 'A. R1 B. R2'). The repair prompts therefore sometimes see choices, although the registration says revisions never receive choices. The engineer did not report this. It applies equally to visual and blind repair, so its effect on S is probably small.
Hardware was an NVIDIA H200 rather than the A100 mentioned in the notes, and inference used the slow Qwen2.5-VL image processor. The engineer reported the GPU. Neither plausibly changes the result.
Solver prompt layout (description, question, choices block) and chat-template wrapping are choices the registration leaves open; no effect expected.
problems: outputs/scores.json: most answers hit the registered 128-token cap and are scored wrong. Truncation counts are 146/192 for BASELINE, 117 for VISUAL_REPAIR, 127 for BLIND_REPAIR and 177 for UPGRADE.

UPGRADE accuracy of 3.6% is far below chance for 2–5 option items. The VISUAL−UPGRADE gap therefore measures the 3B solver's verbosity under the cap, not the value of downstream capacity versus reopening the image.

outputs/scores.json caption_truncated (c0 78, visual 29, blind 81): visual repairs are shorter and more often complete. Frozen captions cut mid-sentence lead the solver to continue restating the description (see BASELINE item 0 in answers.jsonl). Part of the VISUAL−BLIND gap may therefore come from caption length and format, not new visual information.

registration.title: Breadth versus repeated decoding at an equal supervision-call budget
registration.seed_connection: LLMRouter acquires routing supervision by collecting candidate responses on benchmark questions. This experiment tests whether acquisition calls are better spent on additional questions or on more observations of existing questions.
registration.hypothesis: At a budget of 600 candidate-model calls per acquisition arm, broader question coverage improves held-out routing accuracy by more than two percentage points relative to three-response averaging.
registration.contribution: The contribution is the opportunity cost of repeated observations, not the idea of repeated-response supervision. Three predefined acquisition allocations reduce dependence on one nested subset, while independent test generations separate supervision acquisition from evaluation.

closest_work.difference: DARS studies repeated observations, rewrites, risk-aware targets, and adaptive sampling. This experiment exchanges repetition for additional distinct questions under an equal acquisition-call budget and does not reproduce the complete DARS method.
This work compares routing architectures and sample complexity. Here the predictor family is fixed and the intervention is the allocation of supervision-collection calls.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset allenai/ai2_arc, configuration ARC-Challenge, official train and test splits.
Hugging Face dataset allenai/openbookqa, configuration main, official train and test splits.
Hugging Face models Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct.
Hugging Face encoder sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
Standalone implementation using prebuilt vLLM/torch wheels, transformers, datasets, sentence-transformers, numpy, and scikit-learn; no hosted inference or LLMRouter installation.
registration.method: Use seed 241. Deduplicate complete question-plus-option text and remove exact train/test overlaps from training. Preserve every option, mapping source labels in their original order to A, B, and subsequent letters and remapping the gold label. Before sampling, require each complete specialist chat prompt to fit within 512 tokens under both candidate tokenizers and the question-plus-options embedding input to fit within 512 MiniLM tokens, including special tokens. Explicitly set SentenceTransformer.max_seq_length=512; do not truncate. From each training split select an outcome-blind reservoir of 200 questions and 40 disjoint development questions; select 160 questions from each test split. Before generation, create three paired allocations using seeds 24100, 24101, and 24102: each breadth allocation samples 150 questions per task from the reservoir, and its replication allocation samples a nested 50 per task. Each breadth arm therefore uses 300 questions times two candidates times one response, and each replication arm uses 100 questions times two candidates times three responses: 600 calls each. Collect one response per candidate on the union of breadth questions and two additional responses on the union of nested questions. Shared observations are reused across allocations; these are not independent acquisition replicates. Generate one independent response per candidate on development questions and three independent responses per candidate on test questions. Use temperature 0.7, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 128, and request brief working followed by <answer>LETTER</answer>. Derive and record request seeds from split, question key, candidate, and repetition. Parse the last complete answer tag containing exactly one valid option letter, optionally parenthesized. If no tag is present, accept only an explicit final-answer line or a final standalone valid letter. Ambiguous or malformed final fields score zero and remain in the analysis. Embed question-plus-options with frozen, normalized MiniLM on GPU and append a task one-hot feature. For each allocation and arm, fit a multi-output Ridge predictor to candidate correctness: single-response binary targets for breadth and three-response means for replication. Implement mean squared error per training question plus lambda times the squared coefficient norm by setting sklearn Ridge alpha=n_training_questions*lambda, with an unpenalized intercept. Select lambda from 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1 using development routing accuracy, choosing the larger lambda on exact ties. Select the candidate with the highest un-clipped prediction, breaking exact ties lexicographically. Run candidate models sequentially in subprocesses using BF16, batched inference, max_model_len=1024, and bounded batch sizes. Cache all responses. If the registered samples cannot be assembled, report insufficient data rather than changing datasets or sample sizes after observing outcomes.

event.description: Broader acquisition produces a practically relevant routing advantage averaged over the three predefined allocations.
event.statistic: One-sided 95% bootstrap lower bound on breadth macro-accuracy minus replication macro-accuracy, averaged over the three acquisition allocations, on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: For every test question and allocation, average correctness over the three independent generations of the selected candidate. These generations estimate a one-call candidate's correctness; they are not an ensemble policy. Average the paired breadth-minus-replication differences over allocations, then within task, then equally across the two tasks. Bootstrap questions 5000 times within task using seed 9241, retaining all candidate generations and allocation results together. The fifth percentile is the registered scalar; also report the point estimate, a two-sided 95% percentile interval, and each allocation's result. This uncertainty is conditional on the realized acquisition allocations and fitted policies. acquisition.jsonl stores eligibility decisions, sampled questions, source labels, allocation membership, and split hashes. responses.jsonl stores every raw generation, sampling seed, parsed answer, score, token count, and finish reason. predictions.jsonl stores fitted settings, candidate predictions, selections, and question-level differences. summary.json stores the primary scalar, controls, candidate complementarity, parse/truncation rates, conceptual call budgets, realized token totals, model revisions, package versions, and end-to-end runtime.
evaluation.controls: Both arms share models, prompts, development questions, independent test outcomes, embedding features, and predictor family. For each arm and allocation, evaluate training-selected global and task-only fixed candidates. Report direct candidate accuracies and the recorded test-cache oracle headroom, without treating that oracle as achievable expected accuracy. Equal acquisition calls do not imply equal tokens, FLOPs, or latency. Failure to trigger the event does not establish equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: Map the coverage-versus-label-precision frontier across acquisition budgets, independent acquisition draws, model families, and predictor architectures. Compare uniform repetition, ambiguity-targeted repetition, and new-question acquisition using realized collection costs.

agent.reason: Broader coverage should help when repeated decodes provide highly correlated supervision, but useful query-level differences between these candidates may be limited. A lower confidence bound exceeding two points is substantially harder to achieve than a positive average advantage.

judge_astra.reason: Broader coverage should help estimation, but two candidates may offer limited predictable routing headroom, and repetition improves target precision. A bootstrap lower bound above two points is substantially harder to achieve than a modest positive average effect.

judge_fable.reason: With two similar-strength 3B-class candidates, 384-dim MiniLM features and only 100–300 noisy training questions, both Ridge routers will mostly collapse to picking the per-task better candidate, so the arms should differ by roughly ±1–2 points; a one-sided lower bound above 2 points would require a ~4+ point point estimate, which is implausible.

judge_opus.reason: With two broadly similar candidates and a Ridge router on frozen MiniLM features, both arms will mostly converge on the task-level better model, so paired differences will be small and noisy. A one-sided lower bound above 2 points would need a large, consistent advantage across all three allocations, which seems unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Broader coverage can help, but repetition improves target precision and the fixed Ridge predictor may exploit little candidate complementarity on these tasks. The two-point lower-bound requirement is substantially harder to meet than merely obtaining a positive average breadth advantage.

judge_luna.reason: The threefold increase in distinct training queries plausibly improves coverage, but repeated sampling reduces noisy correctness targets, and both arms use only two related multiple-choice benchmarks. Because the event requires a lower bound above 2 points on 320 test questions, I expect a positive but often smaller or uncertain advantage.

judge_muse.reason: With 300 noisy versus 100 averaged labels the noise-per-sample trade-off is roughly balanced, so broader coverage likely yields only a small true gain and rarely enough for a one-sided lower bound to clear 0.02.

It also studies smaller sampling grids (2x2, 3x3) and adaptive sampling, but always on the same fixed 200 training queries per dataset, so it never measures what repetition costs. It does not compare spending the same number of candidate-model calls on more distinct questions with single responses against fewer questions with averaged responses.

According to the registration, this work compares router architectures and their sample complexity. It does not hold the predictor fixed while changing how a fixed budget of supervision-collection calls is split between breadth and repetition.

The seed paper (LLMRouter/xRouteBench) builds routing supervision from candidate responses and evaluates many routers. I did not find, and the registration does not cite, any experiment in it that trades question coverage against repeated decoding.

The closest work, DARS, varies the number of repeated samples on a fixed query set and never gives the saved calls to new questions, so it does not answer this question. A related general question, whether to relabel existing items or label new ones, is older work on labeling outside routing. My searches did not turn up a routing-specific version of it, though the search was not exhaustive.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: a standalone implementation in exp/main.py and exp/gen.py. It uses vLLM 0.8.5.post1 with the V0 engine, pinned to the preinstalled torch 2.6.0, plus transformers 4.51.3, sentence-transformers 4.1.0 and scikit-learn. It follows the registration: seed 241; deduplication within each split and removal of train/test overlaps; options remapped to A, B, ...; prompts must fit in 512 tokens under both candidate tokenizers and MiniLM, with no truncation. It draws a 200-question reservoir and 40 dev questions per training split and 160 questions per test split. It builds the three allocations with seeds 24100, 24101 and 24102: 150 breadth questions per task, plus a nested 50 per task for replication. Observations are shared across allocations, and each arm is budgeted at 600 calls. Sampling uses temperature 0.7, top_p 0.9 and max_tokens 128, with a per-request seed derived from a hash of role, question key, candidate and repetition. Parsing follows the registered rules, and malformed or unparsed answers score zero. Features are MiniLM embeddings (max_seq_length 512, normalized, on GPU) plus a task one-hot. The predictor is multi-output Ridge with alpha = n·lambda. Lambda is chosen by dev routing accuracy, taking the larger value on ties; ties between candidates go to the lexicographically first. The two models run sequentially in subprocesses with BF16, max_model_len 1024 and max_num_seqs 128. Each test score is the mean over 3 generations. The bootstrap resamples questions within task, 5000 times with seed 9241, and the registered value is its 5th percentile. All registered raw outputs and controls go to outputs/, and the scalar goes to result.json.

One deviation, disclosed. The registration says only to "request brief working followed by <answer>LETTER</answer>" and does not give the exact prompt wording. My first full run used the literal placeholder `<answer>LETTER</answer>` in the instruction. The models often copied it verbatim and ignored the brevity request: about 65% of responses hit the 128-token limit, and only about 25% had a valid tag, so accuracy was at or below chance. I therefore rewrote only the instruction text. The new prompt allows at most two short sentences of working, gives a concrete example (`<answer>B</answer>`), and says to write nothing after the closing tag. Sampling settings, the parser, scoring, data, samples and analysis are all unchanged. The new prompt applies identically to both arms and was chosen for format compliance: valid tags are now at least 99%, and truncation is 0.05% for Qwen and 1.7% for Phi. Note that the first run's breadth-minus-replication numbers had already been seen when I made this change, though those numbers came from near-random routing targets.

Result of the test run, which the fresh evaluation should reproduce up to vLLM nondeterminism:
- Registered statistic (one-sided 95% lower bound): -0.0080, against a threshold of 0.02, so the event did not occur.
- Point estimate: -0.0014; two-sided 95% interval [-0.0094, 0.0066].
- Breadth-minus-replication difference by allocation: -0.0052, +0.0010 and 0.0000.

Context for interpreting it:
- Phi-3.5-mini is the stronger model overall: 0.825 macro accuracy, against 0.796 for Qwen2.5-3B.
- The training-selected global and per-task fixed baselines both pick Phi in every arm, giving 0.825.
- Both arms' routers mostly or always select Phi, scoring 0.81–0.83 and not beating the fixed choice.
- The test-cache oracle reaches 0.908; it is not an achievable target.
- The result is conditional on the realized allocations and fitted policies. Failing to trigger the event does not show that breadth and replication are equivalent.
- Equal call counts did not mean equal tokens; realized token totals per arm are in summary.json.

departures: Prompt wording (exp/main.py messages()) was rewritten after a first full run whose breadth-minus-replication numbers the engineer had already seen. The new prompt allows at most two short sentences, gives the example <answer>B</answer> and forbids text after the tag. The registration leaves the exact wording open, and the change was made for format compliance and applied identically to both arms. Prompt wording plausibly changes the reported value, because the first prompt produced near-chance routing targets. The decision itself was driven by parse rates, not by the arm difference.

Parser (exp/main.py parse): when a tag is present, only the last tag is checked. If it is malformed, the response scores zero; the code neither searches earlier tags for a valid letter nor falls back to a final line or standalone letter. This is one reading of 'last complete answer tag containing exactly one valid option letter'. It affects about 0.7% of Phi responses and no Qwen responses, so it is unlikely to change the conclusion.

registration.title: Residual query-level routing benefit after supplying task identity
registration.seed_connection: The seed's generic track combines subtasks with different capabilities and answer contracts. Comparing against an explicit task-only selector distinguishes task recognition from matching individual questions to candidates.
registration.hypothesis: On the eligible generic-track subset, a validation-selected task-conditioned utility-kNN router adds less than two quality points over a training-selected task-only selector.
registration.contribution: This supplies an effect-size upper bound for a query-aware router that receives the same task information as its comparator. Whole candidate-score-vector permutations preserve task-specific candidate marginals and cross-candidate outcome dependence.

closest_work.difference: DSC diagnoses category-driven routing. This experiment compares a task-conditioned query-aware policy directly with an explicit task-only selector and bounds its incremental benefit.
The kNN study emphasizes architecture comparisons and performance locality. Here locality is evaluated within known tasks, beyond task-level candidate preferences.
This work describes random-feature and shuffled-label diagnostics. Here complete candidate-score vectors are permuted within task rather than shuffling winner classes.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates; download only generic records and candidate metadata.
Schema reference: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/blob/main/benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py, fetched at a recorded source revision.
Hugging Face model Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
Standalone transformers, datasets, numpy, pandas, and scikit-learn implementation. Recorded candidate outcomes are replayed data; no candidate weights or hosted endpoints are used.
registration.method: Decode JSON-encoded query fields using the public loader as a schema reference, recording the actual field mapping. Extract only the complete prompt text presented to candidates for embedding; never embed responses, gold answers, or the entire metadata object. Identify task labels from source metadata, not observed scores. Define the candidate pool as metadata-listed candidates appearing in both released generic splits. Canonicalize whitespace for keys while preserving original prompt text for embedding. Collapse equal-score duplicate query-candidate records; exclude conflicting duplicates, incomplete candidate vectors, non-finite scores, and scores outside the documented 0-to-1 quality scale. Remove training prompts appearing anywhere in the released test split. Require complete embedding inputs, including special tokens, to fit within 512 tokens; exclude rather than truncate and report exclusions by task. Retain tasks with at least 100 complete eligible queries in each released split and require at least two eligible tasks. Using seed 317, split training questions 80/20 within task, then cap fitting at 700 and development at 150 per task by outcome-independent hash order. Use up to 500 test queries per task. Embed raw prompt text with frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on GPU, using normalized last-nonpadding-token pooling, correctly handling the tokenizer's padding side, and batch size 32. Precompute cosine neighbors. The primary utility-kNN uses only fitting neighbors from the query's own task, averages their complete score vectors without converting them to winner labels, and chooses the highest estimated score. Select k from 5, 15, 31, and 63 by development macro-quality, choosing larger k on ties. The task-only selector chooses the candidate with highest fitting-set mean score within each task. Break candidate and neighbor ties deterministically using candidate IDs and query hashes. Keep fitting data fixed after model selection; do not refit on development data. As a diagnostic, create 100 null supervision datasets by jointly permuting whole score vectors among queries within task, separately in fitting and development data, using seeds 31700 through 31799. Reselect k for each null dataset and evaluate on unchanged real test outcomes. Also run an otherwise identical unrestricted-neighbor kNN as a diagnostic. If data contracts or minimum coverage fail, write an insufficient-data status and do not silently redefine the pool.

event.description: The positive incremental benefit of this task-conditioned query-aware router is bounded below the two-point minimum worthwhile effect.
event.statistic: One-sided 95% bootstrap upper bound on task-conditioned utility-kNN macro-quality minus task-only macro-quality, on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Look up unchanged recorded test scores for each policy's selected candidate. Calculate paired query differences, average within task, and weight eligible tasks equally. Bootstrap test questions 5000 times within task using seed 9317; the 95th percentile is the registered scalar. Report the point estimate and a two-sided 95% percentile interval. The bound is conditional on fitted policies, retained tasks, and the released response cache, not independent future generations. matrix.jsonl stores original prompt text, canonical keys, task labels, complete score vectors, exclusions, and split assignments. predictions.jsonl stores real and null selections and replayed scores. null_trials.jsonl stores each permutation's selected k, macro-quality, and gain over the invariant task-only baseline. summary.json stores the bound, control results, per-task effects, recorded oracle headroom, coverage and length exclusions, source/model/dataset revisions, and runtime.
evaluation.controls: Include a fitting-selected global fixed candidate, task-only selection, unrestricted-neighbor kNN, within-task whole-vector permutation nulls, and the recorded per-query oracle as a headroom diagnostic. Both primary policies receive task identity. A small upper bound limits this router's positive benefit; it does not establish two-sided equivalence or absence of useful instance-level information for other architectures. Task labels are a diagnostic resource, not assumed available in every deployment.

registration.full_scale_study: Compare additional query-aware architectures against mandatory task-only baselines under independent response regeneration, template changes, different candidate pools, and task-held-out evaluation. Investigate when benchmark granularity accounts for apparent routing gains and when genuine within-task headroom remains.

agent.reason: Supplying task identity makes the task-only baseline strong, and utility-kNN may largely reproduce its candidate preferences. Within-task specialization could nevertheless produce a meaningful residual gain, while incomplete cache coverage could prevent the registered evaluation.

judge_astra.reason: Task identity plausibly captures much of the useful candidate specialization, leaving this utility-kNN router little incremental benefit. The relatively large replay sample should support a tight upper bound, although genuine within-task specialization or insufficient eligible cache coverage could prevent the event.

judge_fable.reason: Within the generic subtasks the top candidates are near ceiling and local kNN estimates over 18 candidates are noisy, so the residual gain over a task-only selector is plausibly ≤1 point (possibly negative), which would put the bootstrap upper bound under 0.02; the main risks are the xRouteBench schema/config assumptions failing (insufficient-data status) or genuine within-task heterogeneity (e.g., MMLU-Pro, MBPP, format-truncation effects) pushing the gain to 1–2 points.

judge_opus.reason: Averaging local score vectors over 18 candidates within a task probably adds little beyond the task-best selector, and selection noise may even hurt. However, subject-level complementarity among strong models (for example on MMLU or MMLU-Pro) could give about one point, which would push the upper bound past 0.02. There is also roughly 10-15% risk of data-contract failure.

judge_sol.reason: Task identity likely captures much of the candidate specialization in this heterogeneous benchmark, while finite-neighborhood estimates can introduce selection noise. A sub-two-point upper bound seems plausible for this particular router, provided the released cache satisfies the completeness and eligibility requirements.

judge_luna.reason: Task identity may explain much of the generic-track performance because the tasks encode different capability demands, making a small residual gain plausible; within-task model complementarity could still produce a gain above 2 points. Even a passing bound would be conditional on this cache, eligible tasks, and kNN—not evidence of general equivalence.

judge_muse.reason: Task formats in the generic mix are easily separable by embeddings, so an explicit task mean likely captures most routable signal and leaves near-zero residual for within-task kNN, though some predictable within-task heterogeneity could still push the upper bound above 0.02.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: The Routing Plateau compares 21 routers on five other benchmarks and argues they learn coarse, global model-capability trends rather than query-specific signals. It does not give the router and a task-only selector the same task identity, does not bound the gain over that selector, and does not use xRouteBench or within-task permutation of score vectors.

This paper audits commercial routers. It finds they route by a query's source rather than its difficulty, and that they do not beat random routing between two well-chosen models. Its comparison is against random routing at matched cost, not against an explicit per-task best-model selector paired with a task-conditioned kNN. I read only the abstract, so I could not confirm that it lacks a per-source baseline.
DSC shows that preference-trained routers make category-driven decisions. It does not measure how much a query-aware router adds once task identity is supplied.

This paper shows a tuned kNN router matches complex learned routers and attributes this to locality of model performance in embedding space. It does not restrict neighbours to the query's own task or compare against a task-only baseline.

This paper uses random-feature and shuffled-label controls to show routers collapse to predicting the majority class. Shuffling winner labels differs from permuting whole score vectors within task, and it does not compare against a task-only selector.

This paper compares open-source routers against fixed-tier, content-blind controls on RouterBench and agentic benchmarks. It does not use a per-task best-model selector or a task-conditioned kNN, and does not use xRouteBench.

opus.reason: Several papers suggest that router gains come from coarse, task-level or global patterns rather than per-query matching: the routing plateau, routing by source over difficulty, and category-driven decisions. None of the work I found gives a query-aware router and a task-only selector the same task labels and then bounds the router's extra gain with a one-sided bootstrap and within-task permutation nulls, on xRouteBench or elsewhere. The findings point the same way, but the specific question is not settled. One caveat: I could not read the full text of 2610.02762, which may include a per-source baseline.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Opportunity Is Not Realizability compares prompt routers, including multi-output kNN, against a training-selected task-wise best model using held-out outcomes, paired inference, and confidence bounds on routing gains. The proposed experiment adds xRouteBench, explicitly task-restricted neighbors, a two-point macro-quality upper-bound criterion, and within-task whole-score-vector permutation controls.

LLMRouterBench compares learned routers with a dataset oracle and interprets their proximity as evidence that coarse domain recognition explains much routing performance. Its dataset oracle uses test hindsight, unlike the proposed training-selected task-only comparator.

The Routing Plateau studies coarse versus instance-specific routing signals and finds kNN competitive across routers and task domains, but does not perform the proposed task-only comparison with whole-vector permutation nulls.

sol.reason: The central comparison—query-aware routing benefit beyond a training-selected task-wise model choice—was already experimentally studied in Opportunity Is Not Realizability, including kNN with per-candidate correctness supervision and held-out statistical inference. The proposed macro-quality bound and conditional permutation diagnostics extend that established comparison, rather than introduce a distinct research question; the prior results do not establish the proposed two-point event.

opus.reason: Both use the released xRouteBench Generic matrix to compare a router that only knows the subtask (best training candidate per subtask) with query-level kNN routing, asking how much query-level modeling adds beyond task identification.

sol.reason: Both compare query-level routing with an explicit subtask-only selector on the released Generic-track matrix to measure routing benefit beyond task identity.

outcome.executor_notes:
Standalone implementation in run_experiment.py (run_eval.sh installs deps and runs it; ~80 s on A100). Replays recorded xRouteBench llmrouter_generic outcomes (dataset sha ea4b6e1b…); no candidate models or APIs are called. Embeddings come from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (sha 97b0c614…), fp32, batch 32, with normalized pooling on the last non-padding token, located from the attention mask so padding side doesn't matter. Prompts are not truncated: anything over 512 tokens (special tokens included) is excluded.

Data contract: the `query` field holds the full candidate prompt ([System Instruction] + [User Query]); it is decoded with download_data.py's maybe-JSON rule. Tasks come from `task_name` and the candidate pool is all 18 metadata-listed models. One train prompt carried conflicting task labels (aime/math) and was excluded. There were no conflicting-score duplicates and no out-of-range scores. Six tasks met the ≥100 eligible queries per split requirement: arc_challenge, gsm8k, math, mbpp, mmlu, openbook_qa. mmlu_pro was dropped (only 61 eligible train queries); the small tasks were dropped for having too few test queries. Length exclusions by task are in summary.json (for example 93 mmlu train prompts).

Result:
- Utility-kNN (k=63, chosen on dev) minus task-only macro-quality: point estimate 0.0094, one-sided 95% upper bound 0.0168, two-sided 95% CI [0.0007, 0.0181].
- So the registered event (upper bound < 0.02) occurred. The interval also lies slightly above zero, so this is a small, bounded positive gain, not evidence of no effect.
- Gains were concentrated in math (+4.6) and mbpp (+4.4); mmlu was −3.6.
- In the null, the real gain beat 99 of 100 within-task permutations (null mean −0.0039).

Controls:
- Unrestricted kNN minus task-only: +0.0023 (upper bound 0.0104).
- Global fixed candidate (cogito-v2-1-671b) is slightly ahead of task-only (−0.0038 for task-only minus global; the interval includes 0).
- Oracle headroom is 0.114 over task-only.

Implementation choices where the registration was silent:
- Global fixed candidate is the argmax of the task-macro fitting mean.
- Tasks are processed in sorted order. Within a task, the 80/20 split applies the seed-317 permutation to hash-sorted queries; caps are applied by SHA-256 hash order.
- Null seeds permute fitting rows and then dev rows for each task.
- Ties go to the lowest sorted candidate ID; neighbor ties go to the lowest query hash.
- The source revision is recorded as the latest GitHub commit touching download_data.py, because git was unavailable.

The bound is conditional on the fitted policies, the retained tasks and the released response cache.

departures: run_experiment.py adds an exclusion rule the registration does not contain: prompts whose records carry more than one task_name are excluded as 'conflicting_task_label'. It affected one aime_2020_2024/math training prompt. Neither task's retention or the fitting data changes in any material way, so it cannot plausibly move the value.

The registration asks for the schema reference to be fetched at a recorded source revision. The code instead records the latest GitHub commit touching download_data.py, plus a SHA-256 of a local seed copy, and reimplements the maybe-JSON rule rather than running the loader. The engineer reported this. It affects provenance only, not the value.

The registration leaves numerical precision open. The engineer chose fp32 embeddings and set the tokenizer to left padding, with side-agnostic last-token pooling located from the attention mask. This is consistent with the registration and does not change the question.

Several choices the registration leaves open were filled in: the global fixed candidate is the argmax of the task-macro fitting mean; tasks are processed in sorted order; the seed-317 permutation is applied to hash-sorted queries; each null seed permutes fitting rows and then development rows; ties go to the lowest sorted candidate ID and neighbor ties to the lowest query hash. All are deterministic and outcome-independent and are not expected to bias the value.

run_eval.sh installs unpinned dependency versions (transformers 5.19.0, datasets 5.1.0, recorded in summary.json). This is a reproducibility caveat only. The fresh-machine run reproduced the engineer's reported value.
