registration.title: Held-out sensitivity to serialization-equivalent winner-label priorities
registration.seed_connection: The seed trains lightweight routers from observed candidate performance. First-maximum winner labeling is a possible ordering dependency when several candidates tie. The association with the released implementation will be checked rather than assumed.
registration.hypothesis: Changing only the priority used to resolve tied training scores produces more than a three-point spread in held-out winner-label kNN quality.
registration.contribution: This is an order-only reproducibility audit, not another tie-aware labeling algorithm. Responses, score vectors, embeddings, neighbors, and query assignments remain fixed; the uncertain quantity is the deployment-quality sensitivity, not the mathematical existence of ambiguous labels.

closest_work.difference: CASLR studies capability-overlap noise and soft-label supervision. This experiment measures held-out sensitivity to serialization-equivalent priority changes in a stipulated first-maximum labeler.
EquiRouter studies sensitivity to prediction errors and budgets. Here observed scores are not perturbed; only tied-label priority changes.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset ulab-ai/xRouteBench, configurations llmrouter_generic and llm_candidates.
Source evidence to verify: https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/blob/main/llmrouter/models/knnrouter/router.py and benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py, fetched at a recorded commit or file hash.
Hugging Face encoder Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.
Standalone pandas, datasets, transformers, numpy, and scikit-learn implementation; replay recorded outcomes only.
registration.method: Before examining policy test quality, inspect the pinned kNN label-construction expression and compare its isolated behavior with first-maximum labeling on unique-maximum, tied-positive, and all-zero fixtures. Save source line ranges, hashes, and fixture results. The primary experimental rule is specified below regardless of current source behavior; do not claim a seed-code dependency unless the source check confirms it, and do not equate current code with the paper's historical version. Decode actual candidate prompt text and task metadata, excluding responses and gold answers from embeddings. Define the candidate pool as metadata-listed IDs present in both generic splits. Use whitespace-normalized keys but preserve original prompts. Collapse equal-score duplicates, exclude conflicting duplicates or incomplete/non-finite score vectors, validate the documented 0-to-1 scale, and remove training prompts present in test. Exclude complete inputs exceeding 512 embedding tokens rather than truncating. Retain tasks with at least 100 eligible queries in each split, requiring at least two tasks. Select up to 700 training and 500 test queries per task by outcome-independent hash order using seed 619. Keep all retained training questions, including all-zero vectors. Embed prompt text with frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B on GPU, normalized last-nonpadding-token pooling, and batch size 32. Precompute each test query's 15 closest training queries across the pooled training set, fixing neighbor ties by query hash and weights to 1/(0.01+cosine_distance). Generate 32 global candidate-priority permutations with seeds 1000 through 1031. For each priority, label each training query with the first priority-listed candidate attaining its exact maximum recorded score. This emulates reordering rows before a first-maximum labeler. Use a fixed lexicographic class index, fixed prediction tie-break, and unchanged neighbors for all policies. Route by weighted winner-label votes and replay the selected test score. Implement a utility-kNN control using the same neighbors and weights but averaging complete score vectors. Reconstruct its canonical vectors under every row order and assert invariant predictions and quality. Secondary diagnostics use released-record-order labels, 32 outcome-independent per-query priority permutations, and removal of all-zero training queries with neighbors recomputed. None replaces the primary global-priority analysis.

event.description: Serialization-equivalent priorities produce a material spread in held-out routing quality.
event.statistic: One-sided 95% bootstrap lower bound on percentile_90 minus percentile_10 of macro-quality across the 32 fixed global-priority policies, on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: For each priority policy, average recorded test quality within task and then equally across tasks. Compute the 90th-minus-10th percentile spread using linear quantile interpolation. Bootstrap test questions 5000 times within task using seed 9619, preserving every policy's outcome for each sampled question; recompute all policy means and their spread. The fifth percentile is the registered scalar. Priority orders are fixed interventions, not independent response generations or a model of actual latency-dependent completion. matrix.jsonl stores retained prompts, score vectors, source ordinals, keys, exclusions, and split hashes. priorities.jsonl stores priority lists, seeds, training-label frequencies, and source-fixture checks. predictions.jsonl stores per-query selections and replayed quality for the primary policies and controls. summary.json stores the spread and interval, per-task effects, routing-disagreement rates, unique-max and tie-category counts, invariant-control checks, secondary diagnostics, revisions, and runtime. Distinguish all-zero, all-equal-positive, and partially tied training vectors explicitly.
evaluation.controls: Freeze score evidence, embeddings, neighbor sets, weights, class indexing, and prediction tie-breaks. Utility-kNN must remain invariant. Released-order labels connect the intervention to the public serialization without claiming it preserves collection order. Per-query random priorities and all-zero removal assess boundaries of the global-priority stress test. Routing disagreement without a quality spread is not itself evidence of deployment harm.

registration.full_scale_study: Audit ordering sensitivity across classifier architectures, asynchronous collection pipelines, and independently regenerated outcome caches. Test whether router comparisons survive explicit tie policies and established score-vector or soft-label supervision.

A material quality spread therefore seems plausible, although routing changes need not translate into score changes and complete-matrix availability remains unverified.

The main risk is dataset access or parsing failure.

A substantial spread is therefore plausible under the stipulated labeler, without assuming the paper's historical implementation used that rule.

The uncertain step is whether this yields a held-out quality spread above 3 points: tied candidates may be similarly useful, and the stipulated priority rule need not match the historical implementation.

closest_work.difference: DARS shows that routing labels and learned policies change because generation is stochastic: repeated decoding and query rewrites can produce different scores. The proposed experiment keeps every recorded score fixed and changes only the priority used to break exact ties among top-scoring candidates in a first-maximum winner labeler. It then measures how much held-out kNN quality spreads across those priorities.
This paper establishes kNN as a strong LLM router and builds routing benchmarks. It does not examine how tie-breaking in winner-label construction affects held-out quality.
This paper studies the accuracy plateau shared by 21 routers, which it attributes to weak query-specific signals. It does not test sensitivity to the order or priority used to resolve tied labels.

This is the CASLR paper the proposal itself cites, but my searches did not find it, so I could not check it. Going by the proposal's own description, it targets noise from overlapping model capabilities and soft-label fixes, not an order-only audit with scores held fixed.

opus.reason: I found no paper that measures how held-out router quality changes when only the priority for breaking tied winner labels is altered, with scores, embeddings and neighbors all held fixed. The closest work (DARS, which studies label instability from stochastic decoding, plus kNN routing and plateau studies) addresses other sources of variation in routing labels and does not answer this question. One caveat: I could not retrieve the CASLR paper (2610.05982) that the proposal cites, so I am relying on the proposal's own description of how it differs.

closest_work.difference: CASLR identifies ambiguity from equally successful candidates and compares cluster-informed hard labels with soft-label supervision. It does not isolate held-out quality sensitivity to global candidate-priority permutations with recorded scores and retrieval geometry fixed.

DARS measures label and learned-policy instability across prompt rewrites and independently sampled responses. The proposed experiment instead freezes all response evidence and varies only how exact training-score ties are resolved.
EquiRouter diagnoses routing sensitivity by perturbing performance scores and varying budgets. It does not test serialization-equivalent winner-label priorities without score perturbations.
The seed introduces xRouteBench and evaluates winner-voting kNN alongside other routers, but does not report an order-only tie-label reproducibility audit.

sol.reason: Prior work already recognizes tied-candidate ambiguity and propagation of supervision instability into routing quality. However, none of the work found by 2026-10-07 answers the narrower question through an order-only intervention on first-maximum training labels, with fixed scores, neighbors, and prediction rules and an invariant utility-kNN control. This is a distinct empirical question, not merely a dataset or metric substitution.

opus.reason: Both ask whether first-best winner labels make held-out router quality depend on an arbitrary candidate priority, and both measure variability across tie-breaking priority orders against an order-invariant soft or score-vector control.

sol.reason: Both vary only the priority used to resolve tied training outcomes and measure the resulting held-out routing-quality sensitivity while keeping candidate identities and outcome evidence fixed.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented: run_experiment.py, which replays recorded outcomes only and generates nothing. The registered statistic came out at 0.196. That is the one-sided 95% bootstrap lower bound on the 90th-minus-10th percentile spread of macro-quality across the 32 global-priority policies. It is well above the 0.03 threshold, so the registered event occurred. The point spread is 0.210, and policy macro-quality ranges from 0.553 to 0.787. Spreads within single tasks run from 0.19 to 0.30. The fixed replay data produced these numbers on my test run. Exact values may move slightly on re-run because GPU embeddings are not bit-reproducible.

Source check:
- The local copy of llmrouter/models/knnrouter/router.py matches GitHub main at commit 338335d2 by sha256. So does benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py.
- The label expression is at lines 59–61: `routing_data_train.loc[groupby("query")["performance"].idxmax()]`. I ran that exact source text on fixtures. It matches first-maximum labelling for unique-maximum, tied-positive and all-zero cases. For tied rows the label changes when the row order changes.
- This confirms the current public code uses first-maximum labelling. It says nothing about the code version behind the paper's tables. The seed's own kNN uses sklearn KNeighborsClassifier with k=5 and uniform weights. My experiment uses the registered k=15 inverse-distance vote, not the seed classifier.

Data:
- Six tasks qualified: arc_challenge, gsm8k, math, mbpp, mmlu and openbook_qa. mmlu_pro had only 61 eligible training queries. That gives 2,483 training and 2,990 test queries over 18 candidates.
- 137 prompts were excluded for exceeding 512 embedding tokens. There were no conflicting duplicates and no prompts shared between train and test.
- Training score vectors are dominated by ties: 1,934 partially tied, 415 all-equal-positive, 88 all-zero, and only 46 with a unique maximum. That is why the labels depend so heavily on priority.

Controls and diagnostics:
- Utility-kNN (weighted average of score vectors over the same neighbours) is invariant under all 32 row orders, as asserted. It scores 0.819 macro. The best single model, cogito-v2, scores 0.833, and the oracle 0.943.
- Labels from the released record order give 0.639, at the 19th percentile of the global-priority policies.
- Per-query random priorities give a much smaller spread: 0.022, with bootstrap lower bound 0.019. Most of the effect therefore comes from a single global priority applied consistently, i.e. a systematic bias towards one model.
- Removing the all-zero training queries and recomputing neighbours leaves the spread essentially unchanged at 0.206 (lower bound 0.193).
- On average two policies route the same test query differently 93% of the time.

Smallest changes and choices not fixed by the registration:
1. The embedding text is "Task: {task_name}\n" plus the original prompt, which is my reading of "prompt text and task metadata". Responses and gold answers are not included.
2. A query unit is (task, whitespace-normalised prompt). Score-vector ties and vote ties are broken by exact comparison after rounding the vote sums to 10 decimals, taking the lowest lexicographic class index.
3. Released-order labels use, for each model, the ordinal of its first row.
4. Neighbour ties are broken by a hash of the query key.
5. Per-query priorities are seeded with `default_rng([seed, hash])`.
6. The registration expected 18 minutes; the run takes about 2 minutes plus installation.

Interpretation: this is an order-only stress test against stipulated fixed priorities. It does not model how outcomes were actually collected, and it does not claim the paper's reported kNN numbers suffer from this. The quality is replayed from recorded scores, not from new generations.

It affects the neighbours, but every policy shares those neighbours, so it is unlikely to drive the spread.

Vote sums are rounded to 10 decimals and ties go to the lowest lexicographic class index (vote_predict). This fills in the registration's 'fixed prediction tie-break'. It is the same for all policies and should have negligible effect.

Released-order labels use each model's first-row ordinal. Per-query priorities use seeds 2000–2031 via default_rng([seed, hash]). The registration leaves both unspecified. They affect secondary diagnostics only, not the registered statistic.
Scores outside 0 to 1 are excluded rather than failing validation. No such cases occurred (the only exclusion reason is exceeds_512_embedding_tokens), so there is no effect.

Token counts include special tokens and the 'Task:' prefix when applying the 512-token exclusion. This is a reasonable reading of 'complete inputs', and it changes which prompts are retained only marginally.
Runtime was about 2 minutes against 18 expected. This does not affect the result.

Each global priority therefore effectively makes its top-ranked model the label for most training queries. The large spread mostly reflects the heterogeneity of single-model accuracy across 18 candidates, so the 0.03 threshold was an easy target. The evidence is credible but predictable.

The source check (priorities.jsonl source_fixture_check) confirms first-maximum labelling in current main at commit 338335d only. sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares alternative global priorities for resolving tied training winners in kNN routing on xRouteBench generic tasks to learn whether priority alone changes held-out routing quality.

registration.title: Agreement forwarding versus unconditional synthesis with a small coordinator
registration.seed_connection: The seed reports weak multi-turn results with a small coordinating model. This experiment isolates the final synthesis decision while holding specialist proposals fixed.
registration.hypothesis: Forwarding agreed specialist answers and synthesizing only disagreements improves a 1.5B coordinator pipeline's accuracy by more than one percentage point over unconditional synthesis.
registration.contribution: Consensus gating is not new. The experiment tests its boundary with two heterogeneous small specialists and a 1.5B coordinator, measuring both avoided corruptions and sacrificed repairs under identical cached proposals.

closest_work.difference: SC-MoA studies unconditional aggregation recommendations and weaker aggregators. This test isolates agreement forwarding in a two-specialist, unrefined pipeline without a verifier or score-based override.
The selection-bottleneck study contrasts selection and synthesis on open-ended, judge-evaluated tasks. Here the gate observes only answer agreement and correctness uses public multiple-choice labels.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset allenai/ai2_arc, configuration ARC-Challenge, official test split.
Hugging Face dataset tau/commonsense_qa, validation split with public answer labels.
Specialists: Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct.
Primary coordinator: Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Stronger-coordinator diagnostic: Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
Standalone batched local inference using prebuilt vLLM/torch wheels and datasets; no hosted APIs or LLM judge.
registration.method: Use seed 827 to select 160 distinct questions per dataset before generation. Preserve all options, map source labels in order to letters, and remap gold labels. Require complete specialist chat prompts to fit within 512 tokens under all three tokenizers; never truncate questions or options. Each specialist independently answers with greedy decoding, max_tokens 160, brief explanation, and a final <answer>LETTER</answer>. Cache complete proposals. Apply one gold-blind parser to all outputs: accept a final complete answer tag containing a single valid option letter, optionally parenthesized; otherwise accept an explicit final-answer line, final standalone letter, or trailing parenthesized letter. Reject ambiguous or malformed final fields and record failures. Agreement requires two successfully parsed identical valid letters; two failures are not agreement. For every question, ask the 1.5B coordinator to answer the original question and options using the two anonymous drafts if helpful, with brief explanation and the same final-answer contract. Use greedy decoding, max_tokens 192, and both specialist presentation orders. The unconditional policy returns the coordinator answer. The gated policy forwards the common specialist letter on agreement and otherwise returns exactly the same cached coordinator answer. Ground truth never enters the gate. Generate a coordinator-only 1.5B answer without drafts as a diagnostic. Repeat both aggregation orders with the 3B coordinator; this is a capacity diagnostic using one of the specialists, not an independent coordinator-family comparison. Run Phi proposals first, then Qwen-3B proposals and stronger-coordinator aggregation in one subprocess, then Qwen-1.5B aggregation and direct answering. Use BF16, bounded batches, and max_model_len=2048. Check complete aggregation prompts fit without truncation. Cache all counterfactual calls, but count only calls the corresponding deployment policy would make in its token accounting. If the fixed sample cannot be assembled, report insufficiency rather than changing it after generation.

event.description: Agreement forwarding yields a positive, practically relevant net accuracy advantage for the small coordinator.
event.statistic: One-sided 95% bootstrap lower bound on gated macro-accuracy minus unconditional-aggregation macro-accuracy, on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Average each policy's correctness over the two presentation orders within question, then average equally across datasets. Bootstrap paired question-level differences 5000 times within dataset using seed 9827; the fifth percentile is the registered scalar. Also report the point estimate and a two-sided 95% percentile interval. responses.jsonl stores selected questions, raw specialist, direct-coordinator, and aggregation outputs, prompt/order identifiers, token counts, finish reasons, and parse results. policy_scores.jsonl stores agreement flags, frozen policy answers, correctness, and per-question differences. summary.json stores the statistic, controls, agreement rates, and separate counts for agreed-correct proposals changed to valid wrong answers, agreed-correct proposals changed to invalid outputs, and agreed-wrong proposals repaired by aggregation. Report these mechanisms separately so an accuracy benefit dominated by parser failures is not described as semantic protection. Include model revisions, package versions, and runtime. Deployment accounting charges specialist calls once per question and averages coordinator usage over orders; the gated policy omits coordinator calls only on agreement.
evaluation.controls: Identical cached proposals and disagreement-case aggregation outputs across policies; both presentation orders; coordinator-only answering; direct specialist accuracies; stronger-coordinator aggregation; common answer parser with gold-blind unit tests. Token savings on agreement are mechanical, whereas the net accuracy effect depends on corruption versus repair. A failed event does not establish equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: Map the recovery-versus-corruption boundary across specialist diversity, coordinator capacity and family, task difficulty, and proposal count. Compare established inexpensive gates with unconditional synthesis at matched total inference budgets.

agent.reason: The small coordinator may corrupt some correct agreements, but it may usually preserve an explicitly shared answer and occasionally repair wrong agreements. Those competing effects make a net gain with a lower confidence bound above one point uncertain.

judge_astra.reason: A weaker coordinator seems more likely to damage correct specialist consensus than to repair jointly wrong answers. However, it may already preserve most agreements, making the registered lower bound above one point considerably less certain than a positive point estimate.

judge_fable.reason: Agreed specialist answers are correct ~85–95% of the time while a 1.5B coordinator will occasionally deviate or fail the answer-tag format (plausibly 6–12% of agreed cases), giving a net gated advantage around 2.5–5 points; whether the one-sided lower bound clears 0.01 (needing roughly a 3-point point estimate with 320 questions) is close to a coin flip.

judge_opus.reason: Gating helps only when the 1.5B coordinator corrupts agreed-correct answers, whether semantically or through format failures, more often than it repairs agreed-wrong ones. With about 68% agreed-correct questions and roughly 1-point standard error, the lower bound clears 1 point only if corruption is about 5% or more, which is plausible but uncertain.

judge_sol.reason: A weaker coordinator plausibly corrupts more agreed-correct answers than it repairs agreed-wrong answers. However, agreement already provides a strong copying cue, so an advantage whose lower confidence bound exceeds one point is far from guaranteed.

judge_luna.reason: Specialist agreement may protect answers from a weaker 1.5B synthesizer, but the policies differ only when an agreed answer would have been changed, while disagreements use the same coordinator output. With 320 questions, a lower bound above 1 point requires a fairly large and consistent net gain.

judge_muse.reason: Forwarding valid agreements mechanically avoids 1.5B invalid outputs and corruptions while sacrificing few repairs of agreed-wrong, but a 1.5B coordinator often copies two agreeing drafts so the net gain may not clear a 1-point lower bound.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: SC-MoA (Beyond Consensus) runs a consensus-gating ablation. It reports that always synthesizing beats gating, and it decomposes the net effect into recoveries versus corruptions. Its main setting, though, is five perturbed proposals from gpt-oss-120b with a strong aggregator, anchored refinement and a score-based override. It only notes that the dominance condition fails at weak aggregators (8B). It does not test plain agreement forwarding with two heterogeneous small specialists and a 1.5B coordinator on multiple-choice QA.

MOSAIC skips the final aggregator when its experts agree, and reports accuracy within 0.1pp of always aggregating. It is a scheduling and throughput paper with larger models. It does not study whether a weak coordinator corrupts agreed answers or measure the corruption-versus-repair trade-off.

This paper compares judge-based selection with MoA synthesis on open-ended tasks scored by LLM judges. It does not test answer-agreement gating, small coordinators, or labeled multiple-choice accuracy.

This paper finds that upstream messages can make a downstream agent overwrite a correct answer, and that removing unreliable messages recovers some accuracy. This is related to the corruption mechanism, but it does not compare consensus-gated forwarding with unconditional coordinator synthesis.

opus.reason: Consensus gating is an established idea, and work available by this date covers nearby ground. SC-MoA shows strong aggregators beat gating, MOSAIC shows a bypass on agreement costs no accuracy at scale, and conformity studies show agents overwrite correct answers. None of the papers I found measures the net accuracy of agreement forwarding against unconditional synthesis with a weak (~1.5B) coordinator over two heterogeneous small specialists, with corruptions and repairs counted separately. SC-MoA's remark that weak aggregators fail its dominance condition hints at the answer, but it was not tested in this configuration, so the question remains open.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: MOSAIC already compares forwarding unanimous heterogeneous expert answers and aggregating only disagreements against unconditional aggregation on publicly labeled multiple-choice benchmarks. The proposal uses two fixed specialists, a 1.5B coordinator, different datasets, and additional paired order and parser controls.

Beyond Consensus compares consensus-gated and unconditional synthesis, isolates synthesis on identical pre-refinement proposals, and decomposes beneficial repairs versus harmful corruptions. Its principal experiments use more, mostly homogeneous proposers and larger models; its weaker-aggregator diagnostics do not reproduce the proposed two-specialist 1.5B setting.

sol.reason: MOSAIC already tests the central policy comparison in an unrefined heterogeneous-expert pipeline using multiple-choice accuracy, making it closer than the proposal's listed selection-bottleneck work. Beyond Consensus also establishes the repair-versus-corruption analysis and evaluates consensus-gating thresholds. The proposed coordinator size, specialist count, datasets, and tighter controls constitute a boundary-setting variant of these experiments, not an equivalent reproduction; the exact registered accuracy advantage remains unestablished.

opus.reason: No list entry tests a gate that forwards agreeing specialist answers versus always running coordinator synthesis; the multi-round entries instead vary decomposer or aggregator capacity or answer format.

sol.reason: No listed experiment compares forwarding agreed specialist answers with unconditional synthesis while holding specialist proposals and disagreement-case aggregation outputs fixed.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I implemented (exp/run.py, driven by run_eval.sh): the registered design. Seed 827 picks 160 questions each from ARC-Challenge test and CommonsenseQA validation, before any generation. Source labels are mapped in order to letters. Complete specialist chat prompts must fit within 512 tokens under all 3 tokenizers, with no truncation; nothing was skipped in either dataset. The specialists are Phi-3.5-mini and Qwen2.5-3B: greedy decoding, max_tokens 160, outputs cached. One gold-blind parser is used for everything (tag → explicit answer line → standalone letter → trailing parenthesised letter), with 15 unit tests. Agreement requires two parsed, identical letters. The Qwen2.5-1.5B coordinator runs in both presentation orders (greedy, 192 tokens). The gated policy forwards the agreed letter; otherwise it returns the same cached coordinator output that the unconditional policy uses. Diagnostics: a direct 1.5B answer without drafts, and aggregation by the 3B model in both orders. Stages run as separate subprocesses in the registered order (vLLM, BF16, max_model_len 2048). Statistics: average over orders within each question, macro-average over datasets, then 5000 paired within-dataset bootstraps with seed 9827. Token accounting charges coordinator calls only when the deployed policy would make them.

Result from my own run: the one-sided 95% lower bound is 0.206 (point estimate 0.242, two-sided CI 0.198–0.286). Macro accuracy is 0.766 gated vs 0.523 unconditional. Over the 472 agreed (question, order) pairs, the 1.5B coordinator:
- changed an agreed correct answer to a valid wrong answer 89 times,
- turned one into an unparseable output 76 times,
- repaired an agreed wrong answer 10 times.

So roughly 46% of the corruptions are format/parse failures, not semantic errors. In aggregation, 14% of the 1.5B coordinator's outputs had no parseable answer. Even so, the semantic corruptions alone (89 vs 10 repairs) exceed the 1-point threshold.

Controls:
- Direct accuracy: Phi 0.772, Qwen-3B 0.734, direct 1.5B coordinator 0.45 (37% parse failures).
- Agreement rate: 0.81 on ARC, 0.67 on CommonsenseQA.
- 3B coordinator diagnostic: gated minus unconditional is +0.005, with a lower bound of −0.002. In other words, almost no corruption with the stronger coordinator. This does not establish equivalence.

Deviation to disclose (a pilot changed one thing): my first full run used a defective prompt that showed the literal placeholder "<answer>LETTER</answer>" and an open-ended "brief explanation". Qwen-3B copied it as "LETTER C" and hit the 160-token cap 47% of the time. That left specialist parse failure at 44% for Phi and 83% for Qwen, and 6% agreement — a degenerate test. That pilot gave a lower bound of 0.0047 (event not met); its summary is kept in pilot_v1/summary.json. I then changed only the prompt wording: a concrete example "<answer>B</answer>", "at most three short sentences", and "do not discuss every option". The parser, max_tokens, sample, models and analysis are unchanged. Because I changed the prompt after seeing outputs, the reported value comes from the second prompt version (task_v2/aggregate_v2).

Other notes: the hardware was an H200, not an A100. The full run took about 94 s after a 114 s vLLM install. Caches are rebuilt from scratch on every run.

departures: Prompt wording (exp/run.py task_msgs and agg_msgs, prompt ids task_v2 and aggregate_v2). The engineer disclosed this change. A full run with the first prompt (pilot_v1/summary.json) gave a lower bound of 0.0047, so the event did not occur. After seeing those outputs, the engineer rewrote the prompts: a concrete example '<answer>B</answer>' replaced the placeholder, the explanation was capped at 'at most three short sentences', and 'do not discuss every option' was added. The reported value comes from the rewritten prompts. This plainly changed the result: it moved the statistic from 0.0047 to about 0.21 and flipped the event. It also changed coordinator behaviour, for example direct 1.5B parse failures rose from 11% to 33%.

The prompt-selection forking path was not part of the registration. The registration fixes a single run (repetitions 1) and forbids post-generation changes to the sample. A prompt-retry rule is not provided for. The pilot was degenerate (6% agreement), which partly justifies a fix, but the fix went beyond correcting the placeholder. This could change the result.

Concrete example letter 'B' in the prompts (exp/run.py). The example may bias small models toward B. In cache/agg_15.jsonl, Mercury_SC_416177 PQ, the 1.5B coordinator output only '<answer>B</answer>' in 7 tokens, although both drafts said C. That pattern is consistent with copying the example. Some 'agreed_correct_to_valid_wrong' corruptions may be prompt artifacts rather than semantic synthesis errors. This could inflate the result.

Nondeterminism between runs. The protected evaluation gives a statistic of 0.214, 476 agreed question-orders, Phi macro accuracy 0.759, and a 3B lower bound of +0.0016. The engineer's own run (eval_log.txt, quoted in the notes) gives 0.206, 472, 0.772 and -0.0016. Greedy vLLM outputs differ between runs. This does not change the primary event, but the 3B diagnostic's lower bound changes sign.

The engineer notes report figures from the engineer's own run, not from the evaluation. These include the 89/76/10 mechanism counts and the 14% parse failure figure; the evaluation gives 91/84/14 and 15.6%. This is a reporting mismatch only.
Hardware was an H200 and BF16 vLLM ran with enforce_eager=True and seed 0. The registration leaves these open, so they are unlikely to matter beyond nondeterminism.

Model and dataset revisions in outputs/summary.json are queried from the Hub at analysis time rather than recorded from the loaded weights. This is a minor provenance weakness and does not affect the value.
problems: The reported value depends on a prompt revised after the registered-prompt run returned a non-event (pilot_v1/summary.json: 0.0047). The effect is therefore prompt-contingent and selected after seeing results, although the change was disclosed.

In the evaluation, about half of the corruptions of agreed-correct answers by the 1.5B coordinator are unparseable outputs (84 of 175 in outputs/summary.json). Many are clear answers that the strict registered parser rejects, for example 'The correct answer is:

C. ...' and 'The best hypothesis ... is:

C. ...' in cache/agg_15.jsonl. Much of the gain is format failure, not semantic protection.

Some 'valid wrong' corruptions may come from the coordinator copying the prompt's example letter B (cache/agg_15.jsonl, Mercury_SC_416177). The semantic count of 91 corruptions versus 14 repairs is therefore not cleanly semantic.
The 1.5B coordinator is much weaker than both specialists (direct macro accuracy 0.48 versus 0.76 and 0.74, with 33% parse failures). A large gating advantage is close to expected by construction.
Run-to-run nondeterminism (eval_log.txt versus the protected output) flips the sign of the 3B diagnostic's lower bound. The engineer notes report the engineer's run, not the evaluated one.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered design closely: the sample, models, decoding settings, gold-blind parser, agreement rule, shared cached coordinator outputs, both presentation orders, the within-dataset paired bootstrap and mechanism reporting. The value of 0.214 is computed from real model outputs, with no leakage. However, the reported value comes from a prompt rewritten after the registered-prompt run failed the event at 0.0047. The rewrite added a concrete letter example that the 1.5B coordinator appears sometimes to copy, so the value is prompt-contingent and selected post hoc. Even taken at face value, roughly half the gating benefit is coordinator format failure under a strict parser, and the coordinator is far weaker than the specialists, so the finding that agreement forwarding beats synthesis by a sub-specialist 1.5B model is largely expected. The 3B diagnostic shows a near-zero effect, which gives useful context, but overall this is weak evidence about semantic protection.

departures: Post-pilot prompt revision (engineer_notes; exp/run.py, task_msgs and agg_msgs): after a full run on the same selected sample, the engineer replaced the literal LETTER example with <answer>B</answer> and added an at-most-three-sentences limit and an instruction not to discuss every option. Although exact prompt wording was not registered, this was outcome-informed revision rather than an initial implementation choice. It could materially change proposals, agreement, coordinator behavior and the reported value; the submitted pilot summary documents a substantially different operating regime.

Expanded accepted answer syntax (exp/run.py, parse_answer): tagged answers may contain a period, and independently optional opening and closing parentheses allow malformed fields such as <answer>(B</answer>. The registration specifies a single letter, optionally parenthesized, and rejection of malformed fields. These extensions could change parsing, agreement and accuracy; their frequency in actual generations is not established by the supplied excerpts.

Incomplete validation of the final tagged field (exp/run.py, parse_answer): the parser selects the last complete tag without checking for a later malformed tag or contradictory final-answer field. Such outputs can therefore be accepted despite the registered requirement to reject ambiguous or malformed final fields. This could change the reported value, although no affected-case count is supplied.

Different fallback final-field handling (exp/run.py, parse_answer): answer phrases are searched anywhere within the last three nonempty lines before considering the final standalone letter. An earlier 'Answer: A' can therefore override a later standalone B, and the parser does not fully validate the remaining field. This differs from rejecting ambiguous final fields and could affect policy scores; the actual magnitude is unknown.
problems: The prompt was revised after inspecting a completed run on the evaluation sample (engineer_notes; pilot_v1/summary.json). The bootstrap describes question-sampling uncertainty conditional on the revised protocol, not uncertainty introduced by this adaptive choice. No untouched-sample confirmation is supplied.

The parser's malformed-field and conflicting-final-field behavior does not fully match the registration (exp/run.py). Its 15 unit tests do not cover the problematic cases identified above, and no sensitivity analysis quantifies their effect.

registration.title: Does context sufficiency predict the benefit of generator escalation?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's memory track holds retrieved evidence fixed while selecting a generator. Its cascade formulation motivates escalation, but low confidence may reflect either missing evidence or limited generator capability.
registration.hypothesis: Adding a 3B model's context-sufficiency judgment improves held-out answer F1 by more than three points over a confidence-based escalation predictor at the same 50% quota of 7B calls.
registration.contribution: The test asks whether sufficiency predicts the marginal benefit of changing generators, rather than correctness or whether to abstain. Paired supporting-document interventions expose this distinction without assuming that document removal makes the question unanswerable.

closest_work.difference: Sufficient Context combines confidence and sufficiency for answering versus abstention. Here the target is the observed improvement from using another generator on the same context.
RAGRouter models document-aware generator suitability. This experiment isolates the incremental value of a low-dimensional sufficiency judgment under paired document substitutions.
This work benchmarks uncertainty-based escalation and calibration. Here controlled supporting-document removal tests an additional evidence-specific feature for escalation benefit.

inputs: Hugging Face dataset hotpotqa/hotpot_qa, configuration distractor, validation split; the official hotpot_dev_distractor_v1.json linked from https://hotpotqa.github.io is an equivalent source fallback.
Existing HotpotQA answers and supporting-fact document titles; no new annotation.
Hugging Face models Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
Standalone implementation using prebuilt vLLM/torch wheels, transformers, datasets, numpy, and scikit-learn.
registration.method: Use seed 2026 and select 480 bridge questions with exactly two distinct annotated supporting-document titles. Construct contexts before candidate inference. Each complete context contains both supporting paragraphs and two outcome-blind, hash-selected distractors. Its paired support-removed context replaces one seeded-random supporting paragraph with an unused distractor whose character length is closest to the removed paragraph, breaking ties by title. Keep four paragraphs and their positions fixed across versions and insert no missing-evidence marker. Preserve whole paragraphs. Retain only questions for which complete answer prompts under both tokenizers and the 3B probe prompt fit within 1152 tokens; apply eligibility before selecting the final sample. Split original question IDs into 288 fitting and 192 test IDs, keeping both versions together. There is no tuning split because model settings are fixed. Run both generators on both versions with greedy BF16 decoding and max_tokens 32, requesting only a short answer or UNKNOWN while allowing use of passages and existing knowledge. Score the entire stripped answer with standard HotpotQA normalization and token F1; UNKNOWN and empty outputs score zero. Save each 3B answer's mean generated-token log probability excluding EOS. Separately ask the 3B model whether the passages alone contain enough information to answer without additional factual knowledge, requiring exactly SUFFICIENT or INSUFFICIENT with max_tokens 8. The probe sees question and context, not gold answers, supporting annotations, or intervention labels. Parse the complete output into sufficient, insufficient, or invalid. Fit two Ridge regressors with alpha=10 and training-only standardization to predict F1_7B minus F1_3B. Both use negative mean answer log probability, log1p question-token length, log1p context-token length, and an UNKNOWN indicator. For missing/non-finite confidence, use the fitting-set median and add the same missing-confidence indicator to both regressors. The augmented regressor additionally receives one-hot probe categories. On the 384 test question-context instances, each policy assigns exactly the 192 highest predicted benefits to 7B and retains the 3B answer elsewhere, breaking ties by instance-ID hash. This is quota-constrained batch allocation; no test outcomes enter ranking. Generate with two sequential GPU subprocesses, placing 3B answers and probes in the same phase, then 7B answers, using bounded batches and max_model_len=2048. Do not truncate or change the sample after observing generations.

event.description: The sufficiency probe provides a practically useful additional signal for selecting generator escalations.
event.statistic: One-sided 95% bootstrap lower bound on augmented-policy F1 minus baseline-policy F1, on the 0-to-1 scale.

evaluation.procedure: Replay the frozen candidate answers under both quota-constrained policies. Average paired policy F1 differences across context versions within original question and then across the 192 test questions. Bootstrap original question IDs 5000 times using seed 92026, retaining both versions and fixed assignments together; the fifth percentile is the registered scalar. Report the point estimate and a two-sided 95% percentile interval conditional on the fitted predictors. contexts.jsonl stores paragraph constructions, hidden intervention labels, questions, gold answers, splits, and length metadata. generations.jsonl stores raw candidate answers, selected-token log probabilities, probe outputs/categories, F1 scores, token counts, and finish reasons. routes.jsonl stores features, predicted benefits, fixed assignments, and replayed outcomes for primary and diagnostic policies. summary.json stores the scalar, controls, probe-category and intervention-stratified escalation benefits, UNKNOWN/invalid rates, observed quota-constrained oracle headroom, revisions, and runtime. Account for deployment calls separately from counterfactual evaluation: both policies pay for all initial 3B answers and selected 7B calls; the augmented policy additionally pays for every probe.
evaluation.controls: Hold candidate responses, regression class, regularization, base features, and escalation quota fixed. Include confidence-only ranking, 20 predefined random quota-matched allocations, and 20 augmented predictors with probe categories independently permuted within fitting and test sets. Report all diagnostics rather than choosing the best on test. Supporting-document removal is not a gold sufficiency label: remaining passages or parametric knowledge may answer the question. Equal escalation quotas do not establish equal total compute or deployment efficiency.

registration.full_scale_study: Study evidence-aware escalation across model families, natural retrieval failures, and retrieval-repair alternatives. Compare policies at matched total FLOPs or latency including probe overhead, and test whether sufficiency features can be recovered from existing generator states without an additional model call.

agent.reason: Sufficiency predicts answerability more directly than the marginal benefit of switching generators, and missing evidence may impair both models similarly. The probe could add information beyond confidence, but the three-point lower-bound requirement is demanding with 192 independent test questions.

judge_astra.reason: Context sufficiency need not predict the marginal benefit of switching generators, and confidence plus UNKNOWN indicators may already capture much of its useful signal. With 192 held-out question pairs, exceeding a three-point bootstrap lower bound requires a substantial incremental effect.

judge_fable.reason: The 7B-minus-3B benefit is unlikely to differ much between complete and support-removed contexts (both models degrade together or fall back to parametric knowledge), the baseline already has confidence and UNKNOWN features capturing missing-evidence cases, and under a 50% quota even perfect version detection yields only ~0.25×(ΔB) gain, so exceeding a 3-point lower bound is very unlikely.

judge_opus.reason: A noisy 3B sufficiency judgment largely overlaps with the UNKNOWN indicator and confidence features. Escalation benefit may not even fall when supporting documents are removed, because the 7B model can draw on parametric knowledge. A lower bound above 3 F1 points would require large mean-benefit differences among the swapped escalations.

judge_sol.reason: Missing evidence may hurt both generators together, so sufficiency need not predict the marginal benefit of escalation. Beyond confidence and UNKNOWN indicators, the small-model probe must supply a fairly large residual effect to clear the three-point lower-bound threshold.

judge_luna.reason: A sufficiency judgment could predict when a larger generator benefits from the evidence, but it may be redundant with answer confidence and context length, and sufficiency need not predict the 7B-minus-3B F1 difference. The 192-question clustered test and the required lower bound above 3 points make the event unlikely, though the paired intervention is informative.

judge_muse.reason: The sufficiency probe comes from the same 3B model as the confidence features and length-matched interventions limit separable signal, so improving quota-constrained ranking enough for a 3-point lower bound would require implausibly large version differences in 7B-minus-3B benefit.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Sufficient Context combines an autorater's sufficiency label with model confidence to decide whether to answer or abstain. It does not use sufficiency to predict how much F1 improves when a quota-limited policy switches from a 3B to a 7B generator on the same passages.

RAGRouter learns which generator suits a given set of retrieved documents using learned representations. It does not measure what one explicit sufficiency judgment adds on top of a confidence baseline, and it does not use paired removals of supporting documents.
This work benchmarks escalation and calibration based on uncertainty. It does not include a feature about whether the evidence is sufficient, and it does not intervene on the retrieved context.

SkewRoute routes knowledge-graph RAG queries between smaller and larger LLMs using the skew of retrieval scores as a difficulty signal. It does not use an LLM's sufficiency judgment or predict escalation benefit, and it does not remove supporting documents.
S2G-RAG judges evidence sufficiency to decide whether to retrieve again in an iterative loop. It does not use sufficiency to choose between generators.

opus.reason: My searches found no paper that tests whether a small model's context-sufficiency judgment improves the choice of which questions to escalate to a larger generator, beyond confidence and at a fixed escalation quota, using paired removals of supporting documents. Existing work uses sufficiency for abstention or retrieval control, and other work routes RAG queries with document-aware or retrieval-score signals. The question of predicting the benefit of escalation from sufficiency therefore appears open, though searches can miss relevant papers.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Sufficient Context combines sufficiency and confidence for answering versus abstention. It does not test their incremental value for predicting the benefit of switching generators on unchanged context.

AutoMix escalates between generators using context-grounded verification of the smaller model's answer. Its signal concerns answer correctness or entailment, not answer-independent context sufficiency added to a matched confidence-based predictor.

RAGRouter learns document-aware generator suitability through embeddings and contrastive supervision. It does not isolate the incremental value of a sufficiency judgment under paired supporting-document substitutions.

RINSE uses paired evidence substitutions, including on HotpotQA, to evaluate answer-free sufficiency detection. Its target is evidence sufficiency itself, not the observed quality gain from generator escalation.

This work uses an evidence-gap verifier and predicted marginal benefit for selective visual-evidence escalation. Escalation changes the available evidence rather than replacing the generator while holding context fixed.

sol.reason: Prior work establishes sufficiency-assisted abstention, context-grounded model cascades, document-aware generator routing, and paired evidence interventions, so those ingredients are not new. Among the papers searched and read, including the seed, none answers whether an answer-independent sufficiency judgment adds value beyond answer confidence for predicting the measured benefit of changing generators on fixed context. The registered experiment therefore asks a distinct question rather than merely changing the dataset, model, or metric.

opus.reason: No list entry tests whether a context-sufficiency probe improves quota-matched 3B-to-7B escalation on HotpotQA under supporting-document removal; #7 compares a self-verifier with a query predictor, and #8, #29 and #37 study how retrieval coverage limits memory-track headroom.

sol.reason: No listed experiment tests whether a context-sufficiency judgment adds predictive value beyond confidence for generator escalation at a fixed larger-model quota under paired supporting-document interventions.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: a standalone script, exp/run.py, launched by run.sh. run.sh installs vllm, datasets and scikit-learn if they are missing, then runs four phases: build, gen3, gen7 and analyze. gen3 and gen7 run as two sequential GPU subprocesses. gen3 loads Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and produces both the 3B answers and the sufficiency probes; gen7 loads Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and produces the 7B answers.

How it follows the registration:
- **Data.** HotpotQA distractor validation from the HF dataset (it loaded, so the fallback was not needed). Of 5,918 bridge questions, 5,905 have exactly two supporting titles and enough distractors; 5,864 pass the 1152-token eligibility check. The check covers both tokenizers and the probe prompt for both context versions, and it runs before sampling. From those I sampled 480 questions with seed 2026 and split them by question ID into 288 for fitting and 192 for testing.
- **Contexts.** Each context has 4 paragraphs: both supporting paragraphs plus 2 distractors chosen by hash. The order is a seeded shuffle and stays the same in both versions. In the support-removed version, one supporting paragraph (chosen with a seeded RNG) is replaced in the same slot by the unused distractor closest in character length, ties broken by title. No missing-evidence marker is inserted.
- **Generation.** Greedy decoding in BF16 with max_tokens 32 for answers and 8 for probes, max_model_len 2048, batches of 128.
- **Scoring and confidence.** Official HotpotQA normalisation and token F1; UNKNOWN and empty answers score 0. Confidence is the mean log-probability of the selected tokens, excluding EOS tokens.
- **Predictors and policies.** Two Ridge models (alpha=10, standardised on the fitting set only) predict F1_7B minus F1_3B. The augmented model adds one-hot probe categories to the shared base features. Each policy sends the top 192 of the 384 test instances to 7B, with ties broken by instance-ID hash. The policy difference is averaged within each question, then across the 192 test questions, and bootstrapped 5000 times over question IDs (seed 92026). The 5th percentile is written to result.json.
- **Controls.** All registered controls are in summary.json: confidence-only ranking, 20 random quota-matched allocations, 20 runs with probe labels permuted, oracle headroom, and breakdowns by probe category and by intervention. Deployment calls are accounted separately from the counterfactual evaluation.

Small choices I made where the registration was silent (also listed under summary.json "revisions"):
- When parsing the probe, I strip whitespace, upper-case the output and drop one trailing period before the exact match; anything else counts as invalid.
- UNKNOWN means the normalised answer equals "unknown".
- The missing-confidence indicator is always included in both models. No confidence values were actually missing, so it is a constant column and its standardisation uses sd=1.
- vLLM runs with enforce_eager=True.

Results from my run, which I repeated from a clean outputs directory and got identical numbers:
- **Registered statistic:** −0.0026, well below the 0.03 threshold, so the event did not occur.
- **Point estimate:** −0.0009, with a two-sided 95% interval of [−0.0026, 0.0].
- **Policy F1:** baseline 0.509, augmented 0.508, confidence-only 0.519, random 0.481 on average, oracle 0.577, all-3B 0.447, all-7B 0.512.

Main caveat: the 3B probe barely varied. It answered INSUFFICIENT on 956 of 960 instances (477 of 480 complete contexts and 479 of 480 support-removed ones). So the feature carried almost no information, and the two policies routed 191 of their 192 test instances identically. This null therefore mainly shows that this particular probe prompt with a 3B model gave no usable signal. It does not show that context sufficiency in general is useless for deciding when to escalate. I wrote the probe wording before seeing any outputs and did not change it afterwards, because the registration forbids changes after observing generations.

Other observations: removing a supporting document sharply lowered both models' F1 (3B from 0.62 to 0.29) and shrank the average gain from escalating (0.082 on complete contexts vs 0.027 after removal). Equal 7B quotas do not mean equal compute: the augmented policy also pays for 384 probe calls.

departures: exp/run.py build(): a question is constructible only if it has at least 3 non-supporting paragraphs (2 hash-chosen distractors plus 1 replacement). The registration implies this but does not state it. It excluded 13 of 5,918 bridge questions before sampling and is outcome-blind, so it cannot plausibly change the result.

exp/run.py: vLLM runs with enforce_eager=True, max_num_seqs=128 and gpu_memory_utilization=0.85, all disclosed in summary.json revisions. These are execution settings; decoding stays greedy BF16 with max_tokens 32/8 and max_model_len 2048. Not expected to change the result beyond floating-point nondeterminism.

exp/run.py parse_probe: whitespace is stripped, output is upper-cased and one trailing period dropped before exact matching. This fills a gap the registration leaves open, and all 960 probe outputs parsed as valid, so it did not affect the value.
exp/run.py: UNKNOWN is detected as a normalised answer equal to 'unknown'. This is a reasonable choice where the registration is silent; at most it affects edge cases.

exp/run.py probe_msgs: the probe adds 'Do not answer the question.' and a system line. The registration fixes the probe's intent, not its wording, and the wording follows the registered description. It was written before any outputs were seen, so this is not a departure, though it may contribute to the degenerate probe behaviour.
Missing-confidence indicator is a constant column (sd forced to 1) because no confidence values were missing. This matches the registration and has no effect on predictions.
problems: outputs/summary.json: the 3B sufficiency probe is almost constant. It answered INSUFFICIENT on 956 of 960 instances, including 477 of 480 complete contexts that contain both supporting paragraphs. The probe category therefore carries essentially no information, and the augmented and baseline policies share 191 of 192 7B assignments.

Because the two policies are nearly identical, the narrow interval [-0.0026, 0.0] reflects identical routing, not a precisely estimated absence of benefit from sufficiency signals. The null speaks only to this prompt-model probe.

run2.log vs the protected evaluation: the confidence_only diagnostic (0.5163 vs 0.5189) and one permuted-probe result differ between runs. This indicates nondeterminism in 3B logprobs or tie ordering. The engineer's statement that a clean rerun gave identical numbers holds only for the primary statistic, not for all diagnostics.

outputs/summary.json: confidence-only ranking (0.519) beats both Ridge policies (about 0.509). The registered Ridge baseline is therefore not the strongest available comparator. This is a side observation, not a defect in the registered test.
opus.reason: The code in exp/run.py follows the registered design closely: the data source and filters, paired support-removed contexts with fixed paragraph positions, eligibility applied before sampling, the 288/192 question split, greedy BF16 generation, EOS-excluded mean log probability, Ridge with alpha=10 and fitting-only standardisation, the 192-of-384 quota with hash tie-breaks, and a question-level bootstrap with 5000 resamples and seed 92026. All registered controls are reported. The protected run reproduced the primary value of -0.0026 from real model outputs, with no sign of leakage or hard-coding. However, the probe returned INSUFFICIENT for 99.6% of instances, even on complete contexts, so the augmented predictor is effectively the baseline. The null therefore shows that this particular 3B probe prompt gives no usable signal; it does not inform the broader hypothesis that context sufficiency predicts escalation benefit. The supporting-document-removal effects and the oracle headroom are useful side findings, but overall the evidence is valid yet weak.

departures: exp/run.py, build(): adds construction guards for present, nonempty supporting paragraphs and at least three nonempty distractors, and deduplicates paragraphs by title. These checks are not separately specified in the registration. They could affect eligibility if triggered, but are reasonable prerequisites for constructing the registered contexts; the supplied evidence does not establish an additional, value-changing exclusion.

exp/run.py, build() and analyze(): uses derived seeds for splitting (2027), random controls (202600+k), and permutation controls (2026000+k). These choices can affect numerical results, but the registration specifies no exact split algorithm or control seeds; they are deterministic implementation choices based on the registered seed, not established violations.

exp/run.py, parse_probe(): uppercases the complete output and removes trailing periods before matching, rather than requiring a literal canonical output. Moreover, rstrip('.') removes any number of periods, whereas the engineer's notes and summary.json describe removing one. This could change categories and routing for noncanonical responses; no affected response is demonstrated in the displayed evidence.

exp/run.py, is_unknown(): recognizes UNKNOWN after HotpotQA normalization, potentially accepting capitalization, punctuation, or article variants. This could affect the UNKNOWN feature and routing if such variants occur. The registration leaves sentinel parsing unspecified, and no value-changing case is shown.

exp/run.py: always includes the missing-confidence indicator and also requests and saves 7B answer log probabilities. The indicator is constant because no confidence is missing, and 7B confidence is not used by either primary predictor. These additions do not plausibly change the registered statistic. enforce_eager=True and batches of 128 are also implementation choices within the registered decoding and bounded-batch requirements.

registration.title: Does a query-only router transfer to held-out code subtasks?
registration.seed_connection: The seed evaluates learned routers on a mixed generic-task track, but its main split does not test whether a router trained without a source benchmark transfers to that entire benchmark. This tests that gap using the seed's pre-recorded query-model outcomes.
registration.hypothesis: A TF-IDF router trained on non-code subtasks selects models that deliver higher cost-adjusted utility on held-out MBPP and HumanEval queries than a single model chosen by average training utility.
registration.contribution: This is a controlled, no-synthesis task-family transfer check on xRouteBench. Unlike TRouter's taxonomy-guided synthetic cold-start data or ICL-Router's learned capability representations, it tests whether a simple query-only router transfers when the code benchmarks are absent from training.

closest_work.difference: TRouter addresses cold-start routing with task profiles and synthesized QA; this pilot holds out actual xRouteBench source benchmarks and uses no synthetic examples.
ICL-Router evaluates OOD tasks with learned in-context model profiles; this pilot tests a conventional query-only classifier with the code tasks completely absent from its training data.

inputs: Public dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config llmrouter_generic, official train/test splits, and config llm_candidates for model prices.

Public code https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter, especially benchmark_pipeline/download_data.py for the dataset layout. Install only datasets, pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn; do not install the full router stack.
Use pre-recorded response, performance, and token-count rows only. Do not call APIs or load candidate model checkpoints.
registration.method: Group generic rows by task_name and query identity (embedding_id, falling back to a stable hash of task_name and query). Confirm that MBPP and HumanEval are present; use them only for the test evaluation. From the official training split, exclude those code tasks and form one target label per remaining query: the model maximizing U(q,m)=performance(q,m)-0.2*c_norm(q,m), where cost is computed from input/output token counts and the candidate price file, and c_norm is min-max normalized across the full 18-model pool for that query (set it to zero if the range is zero). Fit a word-unigram/bigram TF-IDF vectorizer and multinomial logistic regression on query text to predict that label. At test time route each MBPP/HumanEval query with this classifier. The baseline always selects the model with the highest mean U on the same non-code training rows. Use fixed seed 17 and no test-derived tuning.

event.description: Pass if the query-only router improves held-out MBPP and HumanEval mean utility by more than 0.02 over the fixed global-model baseline.
event.statistic: Mean over held-out code queries of U(selected by TF-IDF router)-U(selected by global training-mean baseline).

evaluation.procedure: Write one prediction record per held-out query to outputs/code_transfer_predictions.jsonl, including task, selected model, baseline model, and both observed utilities. Write the registered difference to outputs/code_transfer_summary.json. The threshold is an MVE effect-size screen, not a significance test; missing it would not establish that transfer is absent.
evaluation.controls: Use the same code test queries, full candidate pool, price-based cost calculation, and fixed cost weight for both policies. Neither policy may use code-task training rows or test outcomes during fitting; fix the split and seed.

registration.full_scale_study: Run leave-one-source-benchmark-out tests across all 13 generic subtasks and additional xRouteBench tracks; compare query-only, task-aware, and profile-based routers under the same held-out-task protocol, with uncertainty estimates across held-out benchmarks.

agent.reason: The held-out code split is severe, and the TF-IDF router never sees code outcomes; it may not learn to select a code specialist that only wins on those tasks. Shared capabilities and vocabulary could still produce some transfer, so the chance is not zero.

judge_astra.reason: With both code benchmarks excluded, lexical features and hard best-model labels provide little direct evidence about code-specific model strengths. Beating a training-mean fixed-model baseline by 0.02 would require useful cross-task capability correlations that this simple router may not capture.

judge_fable.reason: A TF-IDF classifier trained only on knowledge/math/commonsense queries will mostly emit its majority (cheap, frequently-correct) label on unfamiliar code prompts, while the best-mean-U fixed model (likely a strong, cheap model such as a gpt-oss variant) should also be competent at MBPP/HumanEval; beating it by >0.02 utility without any code supervision seems unlikely, though label-distribution quirks leave some room.

judge_opus.reason: With no code examples in training, the logistic-regression router will mostly predict the majority label for MBPP/HumanEval queries. Under argmax-U labels that is usually a cheap 8–9B model, which is likely weaker at code than the train-selected global model. It wins only if the default label happens to be a cheap but strong coder (e.g., qwen2.5-7b or mistral-small) and the baseline pays a large cost penalty on code.

judge_sol.reason: The seed’s in-distribution routing gains do not establish transfer to an excluded code family, and lexical features may not identify coding-specific model strengths. The baseline is selected by training utility rather than parameter count, making a gain above 0.02 harder.

judge_luna.reason: The router sees no code-task outcomes, so code-specific query language offers little learned signal; broad difficulty cues could transfer, but beating the non-code mean-utility baseline by more than 0.02 seems unlikely.

judge_muse.reason: With MBPP/HumanEval absent from training, code-specific TF-IDF terms are unseen so the classifier will likely collapse toward the majority class near the fixed baseline, making systematic >0.02 transfer unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: TRouter studies cold-start routing where in-domain training data is missing, using taxonomy-guided synthetic QA and a latent task-type router. It does not test a plain query-only classifier that never saw a real code task, on xRouteBench's MBPP/HumanEval and 18-model pool, against a best-fixed-model baseline under the same cost-adjusted utility.

ICL-Router tests out-of-distribution tasks with learned in-context capability profiles. It does not run a TF-IDF/logistic-regression router with both code benchmarks removed from training, evaluated on xRouteBench's pre-recorded outcomes.
RouterXBench measures cross-domain robustness, but for local-versus-cloud routers built on hidden states. It does not hold out one task family from a multi-model, price-based utility benchmark.
This is the seed paper. Its generic track uses mixed train/test splits that include every source benchmark, so it never measures transfer to a task family left out of training.

The Routing Plateau paper reports that routers mostly learn global-average model trends, which bears on the hypothesis. It is an in-distribution study, though, and does not test held-out task families or code transfer on xRouteBench.

opus.reason: Several papers study how routers generalize out of distribution (cold-start synthesis, in-context profiles, cross-domain robustness), but I found none that trains a router with an entire task family removed and then tests it on that family, as this experiment does with code on xRouteBench. None compares such a router with the best fixed model under the seed's price-based utility. Results from other model pools and datasets point in the same direction but don't answer this specific question, so I judge the experiment distinct, while noting that out-of-distribution router generalization as a general topic is already well studied.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: DecoR's CodaSet evaluation trains baseline routers, including kNN, RouterDC and EmbedLLM, exclusively on non-code tasks and evaluates them on held-out MBPP, reporting both quality and inference cost alongside individual-model results. This experiment substitutes TF-IDF logistic regression, adds HumanEval, uses xRouteBench, and specifies a training-selected fixed-model utility baseline.

Evaluates simple query-based routers, including linear methods, under cross-dataset transfer on RouterBench using recorded performance and price-based costs. It uses pretrained query embeddings and cost-quality frontier metrics rather than TF-IDF features and the registered fixed-weight utility difference.

sol.reason: The central transfer protocol—learning query-based routing without code-task training data and evaluating quality and cost on an unseen code benchmark—has already been studied in DecoR's baseline experiments. Together with prior cross-dataset evaluations of simple linear routers, this makes the proposed study primarily a change of representation, benchmark, and comparison metric, rather than a distinct transfer question. I found no exact report of the registered TF-IDF experiment.

opus.reason: Entry 57 also studies cross-subtask transfer, but it trains on knowledge QA, compares against in-domain cross-validation on a locally built matrix, and does not hold out MBPP/HumanEval from xRouteBench to measure utility against a train-selected global model.

sol.reason: Both withhold target task families from router training and measure whether query-based routing transfers to unseen math or code tasks.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered experiment without methodological changes: official splits, exclusion of all MBPP/HumanEval training rows, full 18-model price/token-based per-query utility, word unigram/bigram TF-IDF and multinomial logistic regression (seed 17), training-mean fixed baseline, and paired query-mean evaluation. Produces result.json and both registered raw outputs; complete-pool and artifact checks passed. Pinned the dataset revision and repaired a download dependency incompatibility by constraining the transitive huggingface-hub client to 0.30.2. No candidate checkpoints, APIs, synthesis, or test tuning. Exact evaluation command tested in a clean dependency environment and empty HF cache (~53 seconds), reproducing value 0.14956890949102 > 0.02. MBPP difference 0.15404; HumanEval 0.00977. Classifier selected GPT-OSS-20B on all 516 queries; baseline was Mistral-Small-3-24B. HumanEval's gain was cost-only (both policies' recorded performance zero), so passing the aggregate effect-size screen does not establish within-code query discrimination or significance. See IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

code_transfer.py pins dataset revision ea4b6e1b… instead of loading whatever is current. This is an open choice that only fixes the inputs and does not change the method.

code_transfer.py breaks ties by the lexicographically first model name, both for training labels and for the baseline. The registration does not specify tie-breaking. Exact ties in utility are rare because cost is min-max normalized per query and no query had a zero cost range, so the effect is likely negligible.
code_transfer.py query_text() decodes JSON-encoded chat queries before TF-IDF. This is an implementation choice the registration leaves open and is unlikely to matter here.

No other departures from the registered data, splits, candidate pool, cost formula, cost weight, baseline rule, seed or event were found.
problems: outputs/code_transfer_summary.json: the fitted 'router' predicts gpt-oss-20b for all 516 held-out queries. It is effectively the training majority-label policy (2689 of 4020 labels), not a query-dependent router. The 0.1496 gain is therefore a comparison between two fixed models (gpt-oss-20b vs mistral-small-3-24b). It does not show that query-level routing transfers to held-out tasks, which is what the hypothesis frames.

The gain comes from a mismatch between baseline rules. Mean utility on training picks mistral-small (0.7258). The argmax-per-query labels, which reward the cheapest correct model, are dominated by the low-priced gpt-oss-20b. A constant majority-label baseline would likely match the router exactly, and the registration did not include that control.

outputs/code_transfer_predictions.jsonl and summary: on HumanEval (n=16) the recorded performance is zero for both selected models, so the +0.0098 there is a cost-only difference. With n=16 and possibly uninformative pre-recorded scores, HumanEval contributes essentially no transfer evidence. The engineer disclosed this.
There is a single split, a single run and no uncertainty estimate (by design of this minimum viable experiment). The MBPP difference over 500 queries is large, but no confidence interval is reported.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered pipeline as specified. It uses the official splits with code rows excluded, the full 18-model price-based per-query normalized utility, unigram/bigram TF-IDF with multinomial logistic regression at seed 17, and the training-mean baseline. The measured gain is the difference between two fixed models, driven almost entirely by MBPP, rather than evidence that a query-only router discriminates between queries on held-out tasks. The HumanEval contribution is cost-only on 16 queries, so the result is valid but only weakly informative about the stated hypothesis.

grok.reason: The fresh run executes the registered protocol: official splits, all MBPP and HumanEval training rows excluded, full 18-model price-based utility, word unigram/bigram TF-IDF, multinomial logistic regression with seed 17, and the training-mean baseline, reproducing 0.14956890949102. The hub pin, revision pin, and unspecified tie-break do not change that comparison; the baseline was not a tie and the optimizer converged. The finding is credible but narrower than the title: the router emitted one model on every code query, the 0.15 gain is almost entirely MBPP, and HumanEval shows no performance transfer.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether a query-only TF-IDF router trained only on non-code tasks selects higher cost-adjusted utility models on held-out MBPP and HumanEval than a single model chosen by average training utility.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper scores routers on a mixed generic track that includes code, but it neither holds MBPP and HumanEval out of training nor names that transfer test as undone.

relation.reason: The experiment uses xRouteBench’s pre-recorded query–model outcomes as its working test bed, but asks a source-benchmark hold-out question the paper does not claim or measure.

obvious.reason: After a mixed 13-task routing benchmark, several researchers would list holding a task family out and comparing a simple query classifier to the best average model, but most first lists would follow the paper’s multi-turn, cost, and personalization findings instead.
