registration.title: Can 18 calibration examples integrate a previously unseen candidate model?
registration.seed_connection: The seed frames changing a candidate pool as a configuration change and evaluates query-model performance matrices. This pilot simulates adding a candidate after training and measures whether a small behavioral profile helps routing.
registration.hypothesis: A nearest-neighbor router given 18 calibration outcomes for a withheld candidate improves test utility over the same router restricted to the other 17 candidates.
registration.contribution: RouteProfile studies public metadata profiles, while ICL-Router learns compact profiles from model behavior. This pilot is a minimal nonparametric behavioral-profile control: it isolates the value of a fixed, small calibration budget on the seed's recorded outcome matrix without new model inference or profile engineering.

closest_work.difference: RouteProfile builds profiles from public model metadata and benchmark signals; this pilot uses only 18 observed query outcomes for one held-out candidate and tests the resulting routing utility.
ICL-Router learns in-context capability representations for new-model integration; this pilot tests a fixed TF-IDF nearest-neighbor profile without an LLM router or learned profile encoder.

inputs: Public dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config llmrouter_generic and config llm_candidates, including recorded responses, scores, token counts, and prices.
Public code https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/tree/main/benchmark_pipeline for the supported dataset names and download layout. Install datasets, pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn only.
Use the recorded deepseek-v3.1 rows as the simulated new candidate. No candidate checkpoint is run or downloaded.
registration.method: Collapse each official generic train/test split to unique queries keyed by embedding_id and task_name. Compute U(q,m)=performance(q,m)-0.2*c_norm(q,m), with c_norm min-max normalized over the full 18-model pool per query and the same scale used in both conditions. Hide every training outcome for deepseek-v3.1, then reveal its outcomes for exactly 18 unique training queries, selected deterministically with seed 17 and stratified as six each from knowledge, math, and code families. For each candidate and query, predict U by a similarity-weighted mean over its five most similar labeled training queries using word/bigram TF-IDF cosine similarity; the withheld candidate has only its 18 revealed labels, while other candidates have their full training labels. Route each official test query to the candidate with the highest predicted U. Repeat the same routing with deepseek-v3.1 removed, leaving every other setting and cost normalization unchanged. Use test outcomes only to score the two policies.

event.description: Pass if adding the 18-example profile raises mean test utility by more than 0.01 compared with the same router without the withheld candidate.
event.statistic: Mean test U with the profiled deepseek-v3.1 candidate available minus mean test U with that candidate excluded.

evaluation.procedure: Write per-query chosen models and observed test utilities for both pool conditions to outputs/new_model_predictions.jsonl. Write only the registered utility difference as the primary number in outputs/new_model_summary.json. The new candidate's non-calibration training outcomes and all its test outcomes are unavailable to the router; the latter are used only for scoring.
evaluation.controls: Use identical training queries, test queries, TF-IDF features, neighbor count, candidate prices, and full-pool cost normalization in both conditions. Select calibration queries without looking at their scores. This deterministic pilot is a screening test, not evidence of equivalence if it misses the threshold.

registration.full_scale_study: Measure a calibration-budget curve across several withheld candidates and task distributions; compare nearest-neighbor profiles with metadata-only and learned profiles, then test on genuinely newly released models with independently collected calibration outcomes.

agent.reason: DeepSeek-V3.1 may add useful capability, but 18 examples provide a noisy nearest-neighbor profile, and the cost penalty may discourage selecting it. It could still improve utility on queries where its strengths are represented by the calibration examples.

judge_astra.reason: Eighteen stratified examples provide some task-family information, but leave noisy five-neighbor estimates for a candidate competing with 17 extensively profiled alternatives. Complementary capabilities could produce a gain, but estimation error can also make adding the candidate harmful.

judge_fable.reason: DeepSeek-V3.1 has the highest output price in the pool, so under the 0.2 cost weight with per-query min-max normalization it is rarely the utility-optimal choice; a smoothed 18-example profile will route it mainly in hard, uncertain regions where it roughly breaks even against gpt-oss-120b/cogito, so the expected gain is near zero with a fair chance of a small positive from winner's-curse correction on the noisy 5-NN alternatives.

judge_opus.reason: With 18 labels, deepseek's kNN estimate is roughly its average utility within each task family, lowered by its high price. The other 17 candidates' maximum estimate usually exceeds it, so deepseek should be chosen mainly on hard queries. Those selections can help or hurt, and the pool already contains several strong models, so the expected gain is near zero.

judge_sol.reason: Eighteen outcomes provide a noisy five-neighbor profile across several distinct task families. The added candidate must improve on 17 fully profiled alternatives after accounting for cost, so a gain above 0.01 is plausible but not the most likely result.

judge_luna.reason: DeepSeek may add value on queries where its quality offsets its higher cost, and the stratified examples could provide a coarse profile. Still, 18 observations may be too sparse for reliable nearest-neighbor estimates, especially against a strong 17-model pool.

judge_muse.reason: Under 0.2 cost weight the expensive 671B candidate is rarely the utility maximizer over 17 alternatives, and 18-example 5-NN estimates are noisy, leaving little headroom for >0.01 mean gain.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: UniRoute (Jitkrittum et al.) already routes among more than 30 LLMs that were unseen during training. It represents each one by its observed correctness on a small set of representative prompts and plugs that into a nonparametric cluster-based router. The registered pilot uses a different benchmark (xRouteBench), a utility that charges for cost, TF-IDF kNN in place of clusters, a fixed budget of 18 examples, and a comparison of the pool with and without the new candidate. These are differences of detail, not of question.
ICL-Router profiles a new candidate on a query set and adds it without retraining. It uses a learned in-context representation inside an LLM router; the pilot uses a fixed kNN profile.

RouteProfile tackles new-LLM integration through profiles built from public metadata (model family, model cards, reported benchmark scores), not from observed query outcomes. It is a complementary approach rather than the same test.
Router-R1 generalises to unseen models by conditioning on simple descriptors, including example performance. It is an RL-trained LLM router, not a nonparametric calibration-profile test.

opus.reason: The central question, whether a small behavioural profile (outcomes on a handful of queries) lets a router take in a new LLM without retraining, has already been tested directly. UniRoute does it with a nonparametric, prompt-outcome-based router, and ICL-Router does it with learned profiles; both report that integration works. The pilot differs in benchmark, similarity features, budget size, the specific held-out model (deepseek-v3.1) and the with/without-candidate comparison. These are detail-level changes, and I found no paper that runs exactly this xRouteBench test.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Universal Model Routing for Efficient LLM Inference explicitly evaluates a kNN baseline that routes to previously unseen LLMs using their recorded outcomes on a small validation set, including calibration-size experiments. This pilot instead uses 18 stratified examples for one withheld candidate, TF-IDF similarity-weighted neighbors, full labels for existing candidates, and an included-versus-excluded utility comparison.

ICL-Router evaluates whether behavioral profiles enable new models to improve an existing routing pool without retraining. It uses learned in-context representations and an LLM-based predictor, with substantially larger profiles, rather than the pilot's fixed 18-example nonparametric predictor.

sol.reason: Prior work already tests behavioral calibration for previously unseen models, and UniRoute specifically evaluates nearest-neighbor outcome prediction under varying calibration budgets. The proposed experiment's dataset, lexical features, fixed budget, asymmetric label availability, and inclusion/exclusion contrast make it a narrow variant of that established approach. I found no report of this exact 18-example controlled comparison, so close variant is better supported than equivalent.

opus.reason: No list entry adds a withheld candidate using a small calibration profile; entry 15 changes the candidate pool but does not test few-shot integration of a new model.

sol.reason: No listed experiment tests integrating an unseen candidate using a small revealed calibration profile; candidate-pool ablations instead remove models and retrain routers.

registration.title: Do two persona-specific comparisons improve held-out preference matching?
registration.seed_connection: The seed reports gains from personalized routing and constructs persona-conditioned preference labels. This pilot asks whether a very small amount of repeated-user feedback contains useful signal before investing in a graph-based personalization method.
registration.hypothesis: For known persona IDs, a two-comparison, shrinkage-based preference profile predicts held-out pairwise choices better than a population-only model preference baseline.
registration.contribution: GMTRouter and PersonalizedRouter use graph-based personalization and study few-shot or new-user behavior. This pilot instead isolates the signal available from two prior comparisons on xRouteBench's persona-judge data with a transparent, low-cost baseline; it does not claim generalization to unseen personas or real human preferences.

closest_work.difference: GMTRouter models multi-turn user interactions with an inductive graph and few-shot histories; this pilot tests a two-comparison shrinkage baseline on the seed's persona-judged comparisons.

PersonalizedRouter evaluates graph-based preference modeling, including new-user and new-model settings; this pilot tests only repeated, known persona IDs and measures whether minimal user-specific history helps at all.

inputs: Public dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config personalized and its pre-recorded persona-judge outcomes.
Public code https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/tree/main/benchmark_pipeline for loading the xRouteBench configs. Install datasets, pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn only.
Use the existing user_id, embedding_id, model_name, and performance fields; do not collect new human judgments or run a judge model.
registration.method: Use only the official personalized training split. Group candidate rows into interactions by (user_id, embedding_id), falling back to a stable query hash, and retain groups with exactly two distinct candidate models. For each user with at least three interactions, select two support interactions by stable hash and reserve the remaining interactions as held-out targets. Compute global mean performance per model using only the pooled support interactions. For each user and model, compute a shrunk score (sum of that user's support performance plus five times the global model mean) divided by (number of that user's support rows plus five). On each held-out pair, choose the candidate with the higher shrunk score. The population baseline chooses the candidate with the higher pooled global mean. Score a selected response using its recorded persona-judge performance (win=1, tie=0.5, loss=0); average the difference first within each persona and then equally across eligible personas. Do not use test or held-out target labels to build either profile.

event.description: Pass if the two-comparison persona profile improves macro-average held-out preference score by more than 0.02 over the pooled baseline.
event.statistic: Equal-persona mean of held-out selected-response score under shrinkage personalization minus the score under the population-only baseline.

evaluation.procedure: Write one row per held-out pair to outputs/persona_low_shot_predictions.jsonl, including user ID, candidate pair, both selections, and observed preference scores. Write the registered macro-average difference to outputs/persona_low_shot_summary.json. Also record the eligible-pair records for audit; the threshold is a screening effect size, not a significance or equivalence claim.
evaluation.controls: Both policies use exactly the same two support comparisons per eligible persona and the same held-out pairs; the population baseline pools only those support comparisons. User IDs are treated as persistent persona identifiers, not as evidence about real-world identities. This experiment tests known-persona feedback only.

registration.full_scale_study: Vary the number and recency of support comparisons, compare shrinkage with GMTRouter and PersonalizedRouter on larger multi-turn preference datasets, and validate separately on held-out real-user sessions rather than only persona-judge labels.

agent.reason: Persona preferences may be consistent, but two comparisons cover few of the 18 models and the shrinkage prior pulls estimates toward the population baseline. The profile could help when a test pair includes a model represented in that user's support examples.

judge_astra.reason: Two comparisons expose each persona to few candidates and conflate persistent preferences with query and opponent effects. Strong shrinkage and limited support–target candidate overlap make a macro-average improvement above 0.02 unlikely.

judge_fable.reason: Two support comparisons cover at most 4 of 18 models and shift a shrunk score by only ~0.08, so decisions change on perhaps 5-10% of held-out pairs; even if that single-observation persona signal is mildly valid, the macro-average gain should be well under 0.02 given the seed's own ~2-point full-history personalization gains.

judge_opus.reason: Two support comparisons touch at most 4 of 18 models, and a prior weight of 5 shifts scores by at most about 0.08. Decisions should therefore change on only a few percent of held-out pairs. Persona-specific signal from the LLM judge also looks weak (rich graph routers gained about 2 points over Elo), so a macro difference above 0.02 would mostly need luck.

judge_sol.reason: Two comparisons cover very few models, and their outcomes mix persona-specific preferences with query difficulty and opponent strength. Shrinkage reduces noise but may leave too little personal signal to produce a macro-average gain above 0.02.

judge_luna.reason: Persona-specific preferences could make prior comparisons useful, but two interactions expose only a few of the 18 models and shrinkage limits their influence. That makes a gain above 0.02 uncertain, particularly with persona-judge rather than human preference labels.

judge_muse.reason: Seed Table 3 shows full graph personalization gains only ~2.4 points over the best agnostic router, so a two-comparison heavily shrunk profile exceeding 0.02 macro gain is possible but unlikely.

registration.title: Do neutral query wrappers cause harmful routing changes?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's routers consume query text, and the paper evaluates learned routing from pre-recorded query-model outcomes. This pilot checks whether benign changes to query serialization alter the decisions of a lightweight router.
registration.hypothesis: A query-only router incurs more than 0.02 mean utility loss when test queries receive neutral delimiters or framing text, relative to routing the canonical form.
registration.contribution: DARS estimates supervision uncertainty by re-running candidate models on semantic rewrites and repeated decodes; router-robustness work studies broader fragility and safety. This pilot is an inference-free router-only diagnostic: it holds the original outcome matrix fixed to isolate decision sensitivity, and does not claim that candidate answers are invariant to the wrappers.

closest_work.difference: DARS uses rewritten prompts and repeated candidate decoding to estimate distribution-aware training supervision; this pilot does no candidate re-generation and isolates whether the routing policy itself changes under fixed recorded outcomes.
How Robust Are Router-LLMs? audits category, safety, privacy, and adversarial behavior; this pilot measures a narrow benign-serialization effect on matched query-model utility.

inputs: Public dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config llmrouter_generic with official train/test outcomes and config llm_candidates for prices.
Public code https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/tree/main/benchmark_pipeline for the data layout. Install datasets, pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn only.
Use pre-recorded outputs only. Do not run candidate models on rewritten queries; the original-score lookup is explicitly a router-only proxy.
registration.method: Train a word/bigram TF-IDF multinomial logistic-regression router on canonical official training queries. The label for each training query is the model maximizing U=performance-0.2*c_norm, with cost computed from recorded tokens and prices and normalized across the full 18-model pool per query. For every official test query, obtain predictions on the canonical text and four fixed wrappers: prefix User request:, prefix Question to answer:, wrap in <query> tags, and prefix Please respond to the following:. Do not retrain or tune on wrapped test queries. Score every chosen model using that query's original recorded performance and cost, then compute canonical utility minus the average utility across the four wrapped forms. This statistic measures router-only sensitivity under a fixed outcome matrix; it is not an estimate of end-to-end answer quality under rewritten prompts.

event.description: Pass if neutral serialization wrappers reduce matched mean routing utility by more than 0.02 relative to the canonical query.
event.statistic: Mean across test queries of canonical-route U minus the average original-matrix U of the four wrapper-route selections.

evaluation.procedure: Write per-query canonical and wrapped predictions, selected models, and original-matrix utilities to outputs/serialization_stability.jsonl. Write the registered mean utility loss to outputs/serialization_summary.json. A positive result motivates an end-to-end rewrite study; a negative result does not establish response-level robustness because rewritten candidate responses were not generated.
evaluation.controls: Use one fixed training split, model, and cost definition for canonical and wrapped inputs; apply wrappers only to test router input. No rewritten candidate output or test label may enter router fitting or wrapper selection.

registration.full_scale_study: Generate candidate responses for semantically checked rewrites, then factorially separate router-choice changes from model-response changes across multiple router families and task tracks; report end-to-end quality and cost as well as route stability.

agent.reason: The wrappers add relatively little text to long prompts, so many TF-IDF decisions may remain unchanged, though borderline decisions can flip and affect the registered utility proxy. That proxy uses canonical outcomes, so it does not establish end-to-end harm on rewritten prompts.

judge_astra.reason: Short prefixes and tags should usually perturb word/bigram TF-IDF features only mildly, particularly for longer task-formatted queries. Crossing 0.02 requires not merely changed selections but systematically harmful changes under the fixed outcome matrix, averaged across four wrappers.

judge_fable.reason: Neutral wrappers add mostly common, low-IDF tokens (or OOV tokens that TF-IDF drops entirely), so predictions flip only for low-margin queries and typically to the runner-up class, where the utility gap is small; a mean loss above 0.02 would require an unusual systematic push toward a bad model.

judge_opus.reason: The wrappers add a handful of tokens, many of them common or out of vocabulary, so decisions flip on a minority of queries. Flips mostly move between models of similar quality for a weak TF-IDF router. The expected utility loss is probably well under 0.01, and the <query> wrapper may change almost nothing.

judge_sol.reason: These short wrappers should usually contribute few influential TF-IDF features, and routing changes can have offsetting effects on recorded utility. A loss above 0.02 averaged across four wrappers is substantially less likely than merely observing some changed predictions.

judge_luna.reason: Canonical inputs are in-distribution, but the wrappers add only a few tokens, many likely common or unseen in the TF-IDF vocabulary. Some routes may change, yet a mean utility loss above 0.02 seems unlikely; in any case, the fixed-outcome setup is only a router-sensitivity proxy.

judge_muse.reason: Short neutral prefixes add only a small perturbation to L2-normalized TF-IDF vectors and any flips lack systematic bias toward worse models, so mean router-only loss should be near zero.

closest_work.difference: Rerouting LLM Routers shows that adding a prefix can change routing decisions, but its prefixes are adversarially optimized 'confounder gadgets' that push queries toward the strong model. It does not test fixed, benign framing wrappers on a TF-IDF/logistic-regression router trained on xRouteBench with a utility loss computed from the recorded outcomes.

DARS uses meaning-preserving rewrites and repeated decoding to build better training labels, which requires re-running the candidate models. It does not measure whether a trained router's choices change when test queries get neutral wrappers and the recorded outcomes stay fixed.

The DSC benchmark checks router behaviour by query category, plus safety and privacy risks (e.g., where jailbreak attempts get routed). It does not apply benign serialization wrappers or measure utility loss on a fixed outcome matrix.
Life-Cycle Routing Vulnerabilities studies white-box and black-box adversarial attacks and backdoor attacks on routers, not sensitivity to neutral formatting.
RerouteGuard maps out rerouting attacks and builds a detector for them. Its benign queries serve only to check false positives; it does not measure how neutral wrappers change routing utility.

closest_work.difference: When is Routing Meaningful? Diversity and Robustness in Language Model Societies tests router decisions under meaning-preserving surface-form perturbations, including irrelevant prefixes, and reports original-versus-perturbed routing accuracy using recorded benchmark performance. The proposed pilot substitutes four fixed serialization wrappers, a TF-IDF logistic-regression router, xRouteBench, and cost-weighted utility.

registration.title: Can a cheap response-aware gate make a two-model cascade worthwhile?
registration.seed_connection: The seed finds that multi-turn routing does not consistently beat single-turn routing and identifies early stopping and sufficiency estimation as open needs. This pilot tests a small response-aware gate without making additional LLM calls.
registration.hypothesis: A TF-IDF/Ridge gate that inspects a cheap model's draft before deciding to accept or escalate improves cost-adjusted utility over the best fixed member of the same two-model pool.
registration.contribution: AutoMix uses a self-verification mechanism and POMDP-based routing, while Hybrid LLM predicts query difficulty to choose between small and large models. This pilot uses a CPU-only gate conditioned on the actual small-model draft, with no verifier LLM call, to test whether that inexpensive signal adds value on the seed's recorded outcomes.

closest_work.difference: AutoMix uses few-shot self-verification and a POMDP router; this pilot replaces the verifier with a fitted sparse text regressor and tests the sufficiency signal without additional model calls.

Hybrid LLM routes from predicted query difficulty and a desired quality level; this pilot conditions its gate on the cheap model's generated draft and charges the full small-then-large trajectory cost when escalating.

inputs: Public dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulab-ai/xRouteBench, config llmrouter_generic, plus config llm_candidates for token prices.
Public code https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/LLMRouter/tree/main/benchmark_pipeline for loading the recorded outcomes. Install datasets, pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn only.
Use recorded responses for qwen2.5-7b-instruct as the cheap draft and deepseek-v3.1 as the escalation candidate. Do not download or run either checkpoint and do not call an API.
registration.method: For each unique generic training query, pair the recorded qwen2.5-7b-instruct response and performance with the query text. Fit a word/bigram TF-IDF vectorizer and Ridge regression to predict the cheap response's performance from query plus draft. Produce out-of-fold training predictions with five folds grouped by query identity. Choose one global threshold from those predictions that maximizes training U for the rule accept cheap if predicted performance is at least the threshold, otherwise call the large candidate. For an accepted draft, trajectory cost is the small-model cost; for escalation, trajectory cost is small plus large cost. Define U=selected performance-0.2*(trajectory cost/(small cost+large cost)) per query. Select the best fixed single model between the same two candidates by mean training U. Fit the regressor on all training queries, apply the fixed threshold to official test drafts, and score the accepted small response or, on escalation, the large response. The large response is never an input to the gate.

event.description: Pass if the response-aware cascade exceeds the train-selected best fixed candidate by more than 0.01 mean test utility after charging the small draft on every escalated query.
event.statistic: Mean test U of the gated small-then-large policy minus mean test U of the best fixed single candidate selected on training data.

evaluation.procedure: Write each test query's predicted small-response performance, threshold decision, selected response, trajectory cost, and utility to outputs/cascade_gate_predictions.jsonl. Write the registered utility difference to outputs/cascade_gate_summary.json. The small regressor is local CPU code; its compute overhead is not included in token cost and should be measured in the follow-up study.
evaluation.controls: Use identical train/test queries and the same two candidates for the gate and fixed-model baseline. Use grouped out-of-fold predictions to set the threshold; do not tune it on test outcomes. Include the cheap-call cost on every escalation. The event threshold is a pilot effect-size screen, not a claim that smaller gains are absent.

registration.full_scale_study: Evaluate the gate across more model pairs and all xRouteBench task tracks, then validate with actual local-model generations and full trajectory accounting for gate latency, token cost, and end-to-end response quality.

agent.reason: A cheap draft may expose useful signals about difficulty or answer format, allowing the gate to avoid some expensive calls. However, sparse lexical features may not predict correctness well, and escalations pay for both calls.

judge_astra.reason: Task cues and conspicuous draft failures could let the gate concentrate escalation where it pays while retaining inexpensive successful answers, making a gain above 0.01 moderately likely despite the escalation overhead. A pass would establish improvement over a fixed model, but would not isolate the incremental contribution of draft features without a query-only gate control.

judge_fable.reason: The threshold is optimized on grouped out-of-fold training predictions, the training set is large, and task identity alone (MMLU-Pro vs GSM8K-style queries) gives the gate real signal about qwen2.5-7b failures where DeepSeek's gain exceeds the 0.17 escalation penalty; the main risk is that the small model is nearly as good as the large one on recorded outcomes, leaving the gain under 0.01.

judge_opus.reason: With a cost weight of 0.2, fixed qwen2.5-7b and fixed deepseek-v3.1 are probably close in utility, which is the regime where an informative gate helps most. Task identity and draft cues (e.g., MMLU-Pro, hard MATH, format failures) give the regressor real signal. The gain shrinks toward zero if deepseek's measured advantage over qwen in this pipeline is small, because escalation has to recover about 0.17 of performance per call.

judge_sol.reason: The mixed task distribution offers plausible opportunities to retain successful cheap drafts while escalating weaker ones, with out-of-fold predictions providing reasonable threshold calibration. However, predicting cheap-model performance is not equivalent to predicting escalation’s benefit, and paying for every discarded draft limits the gain.

judge_luna.reason: The query and cheap-model draft may help identify cases worth escalating, and selective routing could beat either fixed choice. However, a linear text regressor may not reliably predict response quality or the large model's relative advantage, so the gain is far from assured.

judge_muse.reason: The threshold can default to the fixed-small policy on training and only escalate when predicted cheap performance is low; a modest >0.01 gain is plausible if the draft carries sufficiency signal despite full escalation cost.

closest_work.difference: FrugalGPT already runs this kind of cascade. A cheap model answers first, and a lightweight learned scorer reads the query and the generated answer, with no extra LLM call. If the score is below a threshold tuned on training data, the query goes to a pricier model, and the cascade is charged for every model it calls. FrugalGPT's scorer is a DistilBERT regressor and its pools, datasets and cost-quality metrics are different. This pilot only changes those details: a TF-IDF/Ridge scorer, one Qwen-7B to DeepSeek-V3.1 pair, xRouteBench's recorded outcomes and a fixed linear utility.

AutoMix gets its sufficiency signal by having the model verify its own answer, which costs extra LLM calls, and routes with a POMDP. The pilot instead uses a fitted text regressor at no extra LLM cost. The question it asks, whether checking the draft makes escalation pay off, is the same.

Hybrid LLM routes on predicted query difficulty before any model runs, so its routing decision never sees the draft answer. The pilot's gate is conditioned on the draft and pays for both calls when it escalates.

This paper tests deferral scores in cascades of two or more models, optimises thresholds on training data and compares against the best single model selected the same way. It finds that two-model cascades beat that single model by 2.1–8.2 accuracy points on five benchmarks. The question is largely the same, but it uses confidence-style deferral scores rather than a TF-IDF regressor and does not use xRouteBench.

The seed paper benchmarks single-turn and multi-turn routers on xRouteBench, but I found no sign that it tests a gate that reads a small model's draft before deciding to escalate. The pilot adds that test on the seed's recorded data.

opus.reason: The core idea, a cheap learned scorer that reads the cheap model's answer and decides whether to escalate, with no verifier LLM call and the full cascade cost charged, was already introduced and tested in FrugalGPT. Recent cascade work (2605.06350) also finds that two-model cascades with thresholds set on training data beat the best fixed single model. What is new is only the specific scorer (TF-IDF/Ridge), the specific model pair, the cost-normalised utility and the xRouteBench data. That makes this a close variant rather than a new question, although I found no prior result for this exact pair and dataset.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered CPU-only word/bigram TF-IDF + Ridge response-aware cascade on recorded qwen2.5-7b-instruct and deepseek-v3.1 outcomes. Escalations pay small+large cost, fixed-large pays only large cost, and test responses never set the threshold. Required raw outputs and result.json are regenerated by the command, with independent recorded-response, cost, baseline-selection, exhaustive threshold and statistic checks. Tested command successfully after deleting all generated outputs: statistic 0.017567495658484034 (cascade U 0.5553014380306786 vs fixed DeepSeek U 0.5377339423721945), exceeding the strict 0.01 pilot screen. Minimal adaptations: compressed Hugging Face HTTP transport failed, so identical pinned public config parquets were fetched via stdlib HTTP and loaded with datasets' parquet builder; source hashes are saved. Four repeated training query/model rows were resolved by first source-order record, matching seed replay and the registration's unique-query unit; two large-model duplicate groups differ in responses/tokens but not performance. All 4487 unique training and 3729 official test queries retained, no split overlap. No checkpoints, LLM calls, API calls or annotation. Hparameters were fixed before the first machine run, not tuned after test inspection. Details in IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md.

These were checked only against the submitted manifest digest, so it was self-consistent replay, not independent re-extraction. The pinned source parquets and their hashes were also shipped. Four repeated train query/model rows were resolved by keeping the first record in source order. Two DeepSeek groups differ in tokens and cost but not in performance. The registration states no rule for this. It affects only training costs and the threshold fit, a negligible effect.

registration.title: Does a shared caption preserve the winning VLM on paired MathVista items?
registration.seed_connection: The seed converts visual inputs to a fixed caption before routing so all candidates receive the same text. This pilot tests whether that transformation changes which candidate is correct on the same items.
registration.hypothesis: For two local VLMs, the strict correctness winner changes between original-image and released-caption input on more than 20% of eligible MathVista multiple-choice items.
registration.contribution: VL-RouterBench evaluates routing on raw visual inputs. This pilot instead isolates candidate-winner reversals caused by the seed's shared-caption path, using paired inputs and fixed candidate models; it is not a new router or a broad VLM benchmark.

closest_work.difference: The draft describes MMR-Bench as studying modality-aware routing and cost-accuracy trade-offs; this pilot holds items and candidate models fixed and tests whether captioning changes their correctness winner.
The draft describes VL-RouterBench as evaluating routing on raw multimodal inputs; this pilot compares raw-image and shared-caption paths on paired items.
The seed uses a common caption to hold perception constant; this pilot measures whether that choice changes candidate selection.

inputs: The public ulab-ai/xRouteBench multimodal_mathvista test split, including source IDs, fixed captions, questions, choices, and labels.
The public MathVista testmini release and original images from https://mathvista.github.io/, joined to xRouteBench records by source ID; download only images for selected records.
Open weights Qwen/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, run locally with PyTorch and Transformers. No hosted API.
registration.method: Join the xRouteBench records to the original MathVista images and retain eligible multiple-choice items with both a stored caption and an image. If there are more than 64, choose 64 by sorting a deterministic hash of source ID; otherwise use all eligible items and report N. Do not sample or filter using correctness. For every item and each model, run two greedy generations with max_new_tokens=8 and the same prompt containing the question, choices, and request for one option letter: once with the raw image and no caption, and once with the stored caption and no image. Parse and score the letter against the source label. For each mode, a strict winner exists only when exactly one model is correct. Count a reversal only when both modes have a strict winner and the winners differ; ties in either mode count as no reversal. Use each model's supplied processor and run both models on the A100.

event.description: The fraction of eligible items with a strict candidate-winner reversal between raw-image and caption-only input exceeds 20%.
event.statistic: strict_winner_reversals_divided_by_all_eligible_items

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per item, model, and input mode with source ID, response, parsed option, correctness, token counts, elapsed time, and caption length. Write a summary with N, reversal count and fraction, per-model accuracies, and a paired item-bootstrap interval for the accuracy difference.
evaluation.controls: Use the same questions, choices, models, output instruction, greedy decoding, and parser in both modes; only the visual evidence path changes. Do not include the caption in the raw-image prompt. Use the released caption rather than running another captioner, so caption-generation cost is excluded: this pilot tests ranking preservation, not end-to-end cost. Not crossing the gate on this sample does not establish that captioning has no effect.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, compare raw-image and caption-based routing across more VLM families and visual benchmarks, measure how often the selected model changes, and include caption-generation cost in the quality-cost frontier.

agent.reason: The fixed caption could omit or rephrase useful visual evidence, but the two related Qwen models may retain the same correctness ordering; strict-winner ties also suppress reversals. The small paired sample adds uncertainty.

judge_astra.reason: The event requires both models to change correctness in opposite directions, with reversals exceeding 20% of all eligible items rather than just decisive items. That is a demanding threshold for two closely related Qwen VLMs, even if captioning substantially changes their absolute accuracies.

judge_fable.reason: With two weak VLMs on ~50-64 multiple-choice items, strict-winner reversals require both modes to have a unique correct model and the winners to differ; under plausible accuracies (~45-65%) and chance-level guessing this yields an expected reversal rate near 7-12%, well below the 20% gate, and only a systematic parsing/format failure of one model in one mode could push it over.

judge_opus.reason: Even if all four correctness outcomes (two models, two input modes) were independent coin flips, strict-winner reversals would occur on only about 12.5% of items, and the shared item difficulty and shared model family make reversals rarer. With roughly 50–64 eligible MathVista multiple-choice items, exceeding 20% would need systematic anti-correlation, which is implausible.

judge_sol.reason: The event requires opposite strict winners on over 20% of all eligible items, not merely an accuracy change between input modes. I expect correlated successes and errors from these related Qwen VLMs, with ties further limiting the reversal rate.

judge_luna.reason: A shared caption could omit or alter visual evidence, changing per-item correctness. But the event requires opposite strict winners in both modes on more than one fifth of all eligible items, and the stronger Qwen2.5-VL may often retain the lead.

judge_muse.reason: Reversal requires both modes to have opposite strict winners; with two correlated Qwen VLMs this needs systematic flipping beyond independent disagreement, whose maximum is below 20%, so crossing the gate is unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: In the seed paper, the vision track (Geometry3K, MathVista) routes text-only LLM candidates using fixed captions. It never compares candidates given raw images with candidates given captions, so it does not test whether the caption path changes which candidate wins.

VL-RouterBench builds quality and cost matrices from VLM logs on raw multimodal inputs across 14 datasets. Its abstract describes no paired raw-image versus caption-only condition and no measure of per-item winner reversal.

MMR-Bench shows that adding multimodal signals to the router improves routing quality and the cost-accuracy frontier. That concerns what the router sees. It does not test whether the candidates' own correctness rankings stay the same when they receive a shared caption instead of the image.

This paper compares a caption-then-answer pipeline with direct VLM answering on math and geometry tasks. Its results are aggregate accuracy and prompting effects, not per-item changes in which of two candidates is strictly correct.

This paper compares modality-native routing with a text-bottleneck path in agent networks and reports aggregate accuracy gains. It does not look at whether the best candidate model changes on paired items.

opus.reason: I found no prior work that measures how often the strictly correct candidate VLM changes between raw-image and shared-caption input on the same items, which is the question raised by the seed's caption-based vision routing. Related work either evaluates routing on raw images (VL-RouterBench, MMR-Bench) or compares captioning with direct VLM input only on aggregate accuracy (2410.05928, 2604.12213). None of these answers the winner-reversal question, although my search was limited to arXiv abstracts plus part of the seed paper.

sol.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: ReLope compares original-image and caption-only inputs on paired questions, recomputing correctness, but studies a model's accuracy and correctness-probe performance rather than reversals between two candidates' strict correctness winners.

IsoBench evaluates fixed models on paired isomorphic visual and textual inputs and reports an aggregate best-model change. It does not measure itemwise strict-winner reversals caused by replacing images with a shared generated caption.
CaptionQA measures downstream utility of model-specific captions and image–caption QA gaps, rather than winner preservation among fixed VLM candidates receiving the same caption.
VL-RouterBench evaluates routing using raw multimodal candidate outcomes; its modality ablations change router features, not candidate inputs through paired image-to-caption replacement.
MMR-Bench compares routing policies with different modality observables over fixed candidate outcomes, without recomputing candidate winners under shared-caption inputs.
The seed uses a frozen captioner to provide identical textual visual evidence to all candidates, but does not compare those candidate outcomes with their original-image outcomes.

sol.reason: Paired modality comparisons, caption-induced accuracy changes, and even aggregate best-model changes are established in prior work. None of the work I found available by 2026-10-07 answers whether one shared caption reverses the uniquely correct candidate on the same items; aggregate accuracy and within-model agreement do not settle that cross-candidate winner-preservation question.

opus.reason: Both run two Qwen VLMs on MathVista multiple-choice items with native images versus a shared question-blind caption and measure whether the winning model changes, differing only in caption source and in which summary statistic is emphasized.

sol.reason: Both hold items and two VLM candidates fixed, compare native-image against shared-caption inputs, and measure changes in correctness winners.

Even if both were reversals, the fraction would be 3/55 ≈ 0.055, still far below 0.2, so it cannot change the conclusion.

Batched generation (evaluate.py): generation used batches of 8 with left padding. The registration leaves batching open. Padding can occasionally perturb greedy outputs, but the effect would be tiny and the same in both modes.

Model generation configs (evaluate.py): sampling flags are overridden by do_sample=False. However, any non-sampling logits processor in the checkpoints' default configs (for example a repetition_penalty, if present) is not explicitly disabled. That would make decoding not purely greedy and could act slightly differently when captions contain option-letter tokens. This is not reported. Its effect is likely small and very unlikely to move 1/53 past 0.2.

Prompt detail (evaluate.py): in caption mode the caption is prefixed as 'Image description: ...'. The released caption is otherwise used verbatim, and question, choices and instruction are identical across modes, as registered. No departure of consequence.

Parser (evaluate.py): accepts a bare lowercase letter or a single uppercase letter inside prose; anything else is scored incorrect. The registration leaves parsing open, and the same parser is used in both modes. No departure.

Bootstrap reporting (outputs/summary.json): caption-minus-raw differences per model are reported along with between-model differences per mode. This is a superset of the registered 'accuracy difference' interval. No effect on the gate statistic.
problems: Narrow scope (outputs/summary.json): N=53 with two small models from the same family whose errors are likely correlated. Strict-winner reversals are rare almost by construction, so the null says little about routing across diverse VLMs.

Generation-config processors not checked (evaluate.py): non-sampling defaults in the model checkpoints were not explicitly neutralised or recorded, so 'greedy' decoding may include a logits modifier. The impact is likely negligible.

Strict-winner coverage not summarised (outputs/summary.json): the per-item paired_winners list is reported, but there is no summary count of items with a strict winner in both modes. That count is the real effective denominator for detecting reversals.

Missing caveat (README.md): the README appropriately says the null does not establish equivalence. It does not note that both models lose about 8–9 points of accuracy in caption-only mode, with bootstrap intervals that just include 0. Captioning may therefore still change quality even when the winner is preserved.

registration.title: Does a generic-task router lose its gain on an unseen source task?
registration.seed_connection: The seed's Generic LLM Tasks track combines multiple source benchmarks under one routing interface but evaluates within its benchmark split. This pilot measures transfer when training queries come from other source subtasks.
registration.hypothesis: With equal 100-query supervision, a text-only router's held-out gain over its training-selected fixed model is more than five percentage points larger with same-source than with leave-one-source-out training, averaged across eligible subtasks.
registration.contribution: ICL-Router and TRouter, as summarized in the drafts, address out-of-domain or cold-start routing with specialized profile methods. This pilot instead measures an equal-budget transfer gap for a fixed TF-IDF nearest-neighbor router on xRouteBench's generic source subtasks.

closest_work.difference: The draft describes ICL-Router as using capability profiles for out-of-domain routing; this pilot holds the router fixed and measures its transfer gap without adding a profile method.
The draft describes TRouter as synthesizing task profiles for cold-start routing; this pilot tests transfer from existing scored examples without profile synthesis.
This pilot isolates same-source versus held-out-source training on the seed benchmark rather than evaluating a broad router suite.

inputs: The public ulab-ai/xRouteBench llmrouter_generic train and test splits, including task_name, query, and per-candidate performance.
The xRouteBench candidate price metadata for deterministic tie-breaking.
Python, datasets, NumPy, and scikit-learn; use cached responses only, with no model weights, APIs, or inference.
registration.method: Deduplicate by task_name and query. Include every generic source task with at least 100 unique training and 100 test queries; the large tasks listed in the seed's benchmark table are expected to qualify. For each eligible target task and each of three fixed sampling seeds, draw 100 training queries from that task for the same-source condition. For the transfer condition, draw exactly 100 queries, balanced as evenly as possible across the other eligible tasks, and exclude all target-task training queries. Use the stored query text as the sole feature; do not pass task_name as a feature. Label each training query with the candidate having the highest native performance, breaking ties by lower price. Fit the same word TF-IDF unigram/bigram vectorizer and cosine 5-nearest-neighbor classifier in both conditions. In each condition, select a fixed-model baseline by highest mean training performance, with lower price breaking ties. On the identical full test set for the target task, compute each condition's routing gain as routed mean performance minus its own training-selected baseline's mean performance. Convert percentage-valued metrics to fractions before averaging. The experiment measures transfer of the serialized query distribution, including any prompt-template cues, rather than isolating abstract task capability.

event.description: The macro-average same-source routing gain minus leave-one-source-out routing gain exceeds 0.05.
event.statistic: mean_same_source_gain_minus_leave_one_source_out_gain

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per target task, seed, condition, and test query with selected model, selected-model performance, and the condition's fixed baseline and performance. Write a summary with per-task and per-seed gains, the macro-average event statistic, and a paired bootstrap interval over test queries stratified by target task.
evaluation.controls: Both conditions use the same target test items, candidate pool, router, and training-query count; only the training source changes. Fit vectorizers, labels, and fixed baselines using training data only. Report per-task results because prompt format and task content shift together in this design. Failure to cross the gate is not evidence of equivalence.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, run leave-one-source-out tests across all generic and other xRouteBench tracks, separate prompt-template shift from task-content shift, and compare multiple router families and training budgets.

agent.reason: Source tasks differ in both content and prompt format, so same-source examples may help the query-level router. However, TF-IDF can exploit template cues, and the condition-specific fixed baselines may shrink or alter the measured gain.

judge_astra.reason: Source exclusion should weaken nearest-neighbor matching, but the separately selected fixed-model baselines can absorb part of the source effect. A 100-example TF-IDF router may also have little within-source advantage, making a five-point macro-average difference in routing gains less likely than a raw accuracy drop.

judge_fable.reason: Labeling by 'highest performance, ties to cheapest' makes both routers mostly route to the same cheap model, so the same-source vs leave-one-source-out gap is driven mainly by MATH/MMLU-Pro-like tasks and is partly offset by the baseline term (the LOSO-selected fixed model is weaker on the target), giving an expected macro gap around 0.02-0.04 rather than above 0.05.

judge_opus.reason: Labels go to the best model with ties broken by lower price, so the kNN router routes mostly to the cheapest 8–9B models in both conditions, and both routing gains are likely negative. Only MATH should show a large same-source advantage. Elsewhere the same-source condition's task-specific baseline is stronger, which offsets that advantage, so a macro gap above 0.05 is unlikely.

judge_sol.reason: Source-task shift could substantially hurt lexical nearest-neighbor routing, but 100 same-source examples may themselves provide little gain over a well-selected fixed model. The condition-specific fixed baselines can also absorb part of the source-adaptation advantage.

judge_luna.reason: In the seed’s related results, kNN is only about one point above Largest-LLM on the generic-task average, tempering expectations that 100 same-source examples yield large gains. Still, training on other sources—especially across code and QA—could be substantially less useful than matched supervision.

judge_muse.reason: Same-source 5-NN with 100 queries likely beats transfer, but 5pp macro-average gain difference is large because kNN gains over the training-selected best model are small in the seed Table 2 and the transfer baseline is also weaker on target, partially offsetting routed differences.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: RouterDC reports in-distribution and out-of-distribution results, but on different task sets with a learned contrastive router. It does not run a matched comparison where the same target test set is routed after training on 100 same-source queries versus 100 queries from the other sources, and it does not use xRouteBench.

ICL-Router proposes a capability-profile method and reports out-of-distribution results for that method. The pilot instead holds a simple TF-IDF kNN router fixed and measures, per task, the paired drop in gain caused by leaving out the source task.

From the abstract, TRouter targets cold-start routing by synthesizing task profiles. The pilot adds no new method; it only measures how much transfer is lost when no target-source supervision is available.
LLMRouterBench re-evaluates many routers within a unified benchmark, but from the abstract it does not isolate same-source versus leave-one-source-out training at equal budget on xRouteBench.
This paper shows kNN routers are strong and sample-efficient within benchmarks. It does not compare matched same-source and held-out-source training.
The seed paper evaluates within its benchmark splits. The experiment's own description says the seed has no leave-one-source-out test; I did not read the seed's full text to confirm this.

opus.reason: Out-of-distribution evaluation of routers is common: RouterDC, ICL-Router and Agent-as-a-Router all report results on unseen tasks. However, I found no paper that runs this paired, equal-budget comparison (same-source versus leave-one-source-out training, same target test set, fixed kNN router, xRouteBench generic subtasks) or measures the resulting drop in routing gain. The general idea that routers degrade on unseen tasks is familiar, but the specific question does not appear to be settled; my search was limited to arXiv abstracts and I did not read full texts.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Section 6 and Table 4 already compare in-distribution and cross-dataset routing performance for fixed kNN routers on RouterBench. The proposal changes BERT embeddings to TF-IDF, uses balanced leave-one-source-out rather than one-source-to-another transfer, fixes supervision at 100 queries, and measures baseline-relative quality gain instead of cost–quality AUC.

Tables 3–4 report RouterDC and MetricRouter trained on three source datasets and evaluated on the remaining dataset, alongside in-domain results. The proposal applies this transfer comparison to a fixed nearest-neighbor router with equal supervision budgets and condition-specific training-selected fixed-model baselines.

Reports leave-one-task-out routing using 5-nearest-neighbor correctness predictors and measures improvements from adding target-task examples. Its main HELM evaluation selects one model for an entire task, rather than performing the proposal's per-query, equal-budget comparison.

sol.reason: Prior work already directly investigates routing degradation under source-task shift, including fixed kNN in-distribution versus cross-dataset comparisons and leave-one-dataset-out evaluations of standard routers. The matched 100-query budgets, xRouteBench data, lexical representation, and baseline-relative statistic refine that established experimental question rather than constitute a distinct contribution. I found no paper reporting the exact registered protocol or determining its five-percentage-point event.

opus.reason: Entry 57 also tests cross-subtask router transfer, but it uses one knowledge-to-math/code split with accuracy and default-to-one-model rates, whereas this is an equal-budget leave-one-source-out comparison of routing gain over a training-selected fixed model on xRouteBench.

sol.reason: Both compare in-domain with cross-subtask training of text routers and measure held-out routing performance to test generalization to unseen source tasks.

outcome.executor_notes: Implemented the registered cached-score TF-IDF unigram/bigram cosine 5-NN experiment with exactly 100 training queries per condition and seeds 17, 42, 2026. Six tasks qualify; MMLU-Pro has only 63 unique training queries and is excluded by the registered rule. Transfer samples use 20 queries from each of five other eligible tasks. All 18 candidates and full 500-query target test sets are preserved. Lower-price ties use the mean input/output price; uniform voting and residual lexical ties are explicit. Dataset revision and dependency versions are pinned. No substantive registration changes, inference, weights, or API calls. Produces 18,000 JSONL rows, per-task/per-seed summary, and a 10,000-resample paired test-query bootstrap interval conditional on fitted training samples. Evaluation command tested twice, including deletion and deterministic regeneration of required outputs; independently reconstructed the statistic from JSONL. Observed statistic -0.024, interval [-0.03356,-0.01444]; registered +0.05 event did not occur. This does not establish equivalence.

departures: Sampling seeds 17, 42 and 2026 were chosen by the engineer in experiment/task_transfer.py. The registration says only 'three fixed seeds', so this is an open choice. Different draws could shift per-seed values, especially for MBPP, but the choice is legitimate.

The price tie-breaker is the mean of input and output price per million tokens, with lexicographic model name breaking any remaining ties (task_transfer.py load_inputs). The registration says only 'lower price', so this is an open choice. It could change which cheap model gets a label, but it is legitimate.

Vote ties in the uniform 5-NN are resolved by price order: scikit-learn's mode takes the lowest class index, and indices are sorted by price. The registration does not specify this. Its effect is minor.
Train/test key overlaps are removed from training. The registration does not specify this, but the README reports there were none, so it had no effect.
When a candidate's score is repeated for the same query, the first stored score is kept. Inspection found one duplicated training query with identical scores, so this had no effect.
The dataset is pinned to revision ea4b6e1b (experiment/dataset_revision.txt). This is not a substantive change.

The bootstrap first averages seeds, then resamples only test queries within each task. The registration asked for 'a paired bootstrap interval over test queries stratified by target task', so this matches. The interval leaves out training-sample and between-task uncertainty, which is disclosed. It does not change the point estimate.
MMLU-Pro (63 unique training queries) and the small tasks (fewer than 100 test queries) are excluded. This follows the registered eligibility rule and is not a departure.
problems: Every same-source routing gain is negative: the macro same-source gain is -0.163, against -0.139 for transfer. Under the registered labelling rule, with mostly binary scores, the label is usually the cheapest correct model. The kNN router therefore routes toward cheap models such as gemma-2-9b-it and loses to the training-selected fixed model even in-domain. A comparison of 'lost gain' between conditions in which the router never gains is only weakly informative about transfer.

Because each condition's gain is measured against its own training-selected baseline, the statistic is driven heavily by baseline choice rather than routing quality. For example, MBPP seed 2026 transfer selected llama-4-maverick as its baseline and obtained a gain of +0.354. GSM8K's same-source baseline was llama-4-maverick while the transfer baseline was cogito. This is inherent to the registered design but limits interpretation (outputs/summary.json).

The reported 95% interval [-0.034, -0.014] conditions on the fitted training samples and task set. It greatly understates the seed-to-seed variability, which is shown by MBPP's per-seed differences of +0.024, -0.008 and -0.568. The interval should not be read as precision of the transfer gap. The bootstrap scope is disclosed in summary.json, but the README and engineer notes quote the interval without that caveat.

The conclusion that the event did not occur is robust: removing the MBPP seed-2026 outlier gives roughly +0.008, still well below 0.05. The negative sign of the statistic, however, depends on that one outlier.

The protected run reproduces -0.024, and I recomputed that value from the per-task means in summary.json. There is no leakage or hard-coding, and the departures are open choices that do not plausibly change the result. The evidence is nonetheless weak. Under the registered cheapest-correct labelling rule the router underperforms its fixed baseline in both conditions, so the contrast mostly reflects baseline selection and a single MBPP outlier rather than a genuine transfer gap in routing gain. The null is credible for this exact setup, but the narrow conditional interval overstates its precision.

registration.title: Does parameter-times-token count preserve local A100 latency rankings?
registration.seed_connection: The seed evaluates quality against token-priced inference cost. This pilot tests whether a simple parameter-and-token proxy agrees with actual local batch-one latency on one A100.
registration.hypothesis: More than 15% of non-tied within-query model-pair orderings from the parameter-times-token proxy disagree with measured latency for three small open models on ARC-Challenge.
registration.contribution: BEST-Route and LLMRouterBench, as summarized in the drafts, include latency analysis. This pilot isolates rank agreement between a simple compute proxy and warmed local A100 latency for small models, rather than comparing hosted endpoints or proposing a latency-aware router.

closest_work.difference: The draft describes BEST-Route as reporting latency and token-price costs; this pilot measures paired local A100 latency and proxy-order disagreement.
The draft describes LLMRouterBench as enabling latency-aware analysis at benchmark scale; this pilot isolates batch-one execution on one machine and a small model set.

inputs: The public allenai/ai2_arc ARC-Challenge test split; select 40 questions deterministically by a hash of question ID.
Open weights Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
Python, datasets, PyTorch, and Transformers. No hosted API.
registration.method: Use one fixed prompt containing each question and its choices, requesting only an answer letter. Load all three models on the A100 in float16, use greedy decoding with max_new_tokens=8 and batch size one, and run two warm-up calls per model. Randomize the order of timed query-model trials and repeat each pair five times. Synchronize CUDA immediately before and after each timed call; measure from tokenization through completed generation, excluding model loading. For each query-model pair, record the median latency and median input-plus-output token count, and count the model's exact parameter total from its loaded weights. Define the proxy as parameter_count times input_tokens_plus_output_tokens. For each question's three unordered model pairs, compare proxy and latency orderings. Treat a pair as tied for a measure if its relative difference is at most 5% of the larger value; exclude pairs tied for either measure. The primary statistic is the fraction of remaining pairs whose strict orderings disagree.

event.description: More than 15% of non-tied within-query model-pair orderings disagree between the parameter-token proxy and measured A100 latency.
event.statistic: disagreeing_non_tied_pairs_divided_by_all_non_tied_pairs

evaluation.procedure: Write one JSONL row per question, model, and timed repeat with token counts, parameter count, latency, and parsed answer correctness. Write a summary with the number of eligible pairs, inversion count, inversion fraction, and model software versions.
evaluation.controls: Use identical question content and answer instructions, batch size one, greedy decoding, warm-up calls, randomized trial order, and CUDA synchronization. Model loading is excluded from individual latency measurements but included in the experiment's total runtime. The result is limited to this model set and hardware; not crossing the gate does not validate the proxy generally.

registration.full_scale_study: If the event occurs, vary model families, prompt lengths, output lengths, batch sizes, quantization, and hardware, then test whether latency-aware routing improves measured quality-latency frontiers.

agent.reason: For these models, large parameter-count differences are likely to dominate tokenizer and kernel variation, leaving most pair orderings aligned. The 1.7B/3B comparison and prompt-token differences could still produce enough inversions to cross the threshold.

judge_astra.reason: The proxy treats input and output tokens alike, whereas batch-one latency depends differently on prefill, decoding length, and architecture overhead, so inversions are plausible. However, the model-size separations and short answer cap could preserve enough orderings to keep disagreement below 15%.

judge_fable.reason: At batch one in HF eager mode, per-token overhead (~15-30 ms) dwarfs the 0.5B-vs-1.7B latency gap, so any systematic one-token difference in answer length (e.g., 'B.' vs 'B') flips that pair's ordering while the parameter-dominated proxy never changes; whether >15% of pairs disagree hinges on output-length heterogeneity, which is plausible but not certain.

judge_opus.reason: With Hugging Face generation at batch size one, latency is probably limited by per-step CPU overhead, so it scales with layer count and output length rather than parameter count. The 0.5B and 1.7B models (24 layers each) then nearly tie, and the 3B model (36 layers) is only about 1.5x slower per step. Inversions above 15% therefore depend on one of the small models answering more verbosely than the terse 3B model, which is plausible but uncertain.

judge_sol.reason: Batch-one latency depends on serial depth, kernel overhead, and generated output length, which parameter count times total tokens does not adequately distinguish. However, the broad parameter-size differences could preserve enough orderings to keep inversions below 15%.

judge_luna.reason: Parameter-times-token count should mostly preserve these models’ size ordering, and batch-one A100 latency is likely to do likewise; repeated medians and tie exclusion also reduce noise. Architecture or implementation differences could still invert a model pair, but I consider enough inversions to cross the gate unlikely.

judge_muse.reason: Proxy order is fixed by 0.5B vs 1.7B vs 3B param gaps that token-count differences cannot overcome, and batch-one A100 latency is expected to preserve size order for these models, so >15% inversions among non-tied pairs is unlikely.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: LLMRouterBench says it supports latency-aware routing analysis on a large benchmark. As far as the abstract shows, it does not test whether a parameter-times-token compute proxy keeps the same within-query model-pair ordering as measured batch-one latency for local small models.
BEST-Route is described as reporting cost and latency for a routing method. It does not measure how often a simple compute proxy and measured A100 latency rank model pairs in opposite orders.

This paper builds a latency estimator for serving under load, focused on time-to-first-token with batching and queueing, and uses it inside a router. It does not test a static parameter-times-token proxy against isolated batch-one latency.

RouterWise shows that fixed per-model latency is a poor assumption in shared GPU clusters and uses profiled latency models. That differs from measuring how often a compute proxy and measured latency disagree for a small set of models on one machine.
This paper measures latency and throughput for 0.5–3B models across tasks, but as a combined efficiency metric. It does not compare proxy and measured latency orderings.
The seed paper evaluates routers on quality against token-priced cost and does not check its cost measure against measured latency.

opus.reason: I found no paper that measures how often a parameter-times-token compute proxy and measured warmed batch-one latency put model pairs in opposite orders, in a routing setting or elsewhere. Routing benchmarks and latency-aware routers either report latency or model it under load, but none answers this specific agreement question. The broader FLOPs-versus-latency mismatch is known in the efficiency literature, but I did not find a paper that settles it for this setup.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Measures open-model generation latency using Hugging Face on one A100 at batch size one and explicitly reports smaller models being slower than larger models at fixed input/output token lengths. The proposed pilot changes the model pool and workload to short ARC-Challenge answers and quantifies tie-filtered within-query inversions of parameter-times-token rankings.

Directly compares parameter-count and FLOP proxies with token-normalized local inference time for lightweight models. It uses quantized CPU inference and aggregate correlations rather than FP16 A100 inference and per-query pairwise inversion fractions.

sol.reason: Scaling Inference-Efficient Language Models already demonstrates latency-order reversals relative to parameter count on a single A100 with fixed token lengths, where multiplying by token count leaves the parameter ranking unchanged. The proposed experiment therefore revisits an established proxy-versus-measured-latency question with different models, prompts, and a more explicit disagreement metric. Neither paper establishes whether this particular pilot would cross its 15% threshold.

opus.reason: No list entry tests whether a parameter-times-token cost proxy preserves the ordering of measured local latency across model pairs.

sol.reason: No listed experiment directly compares within-query model rankings from a parameter-times-token proxy with measured local latency rankings.
