registration.title: Gated multi-round routing: decompose only when predicted complex
registration.seed_connection: Seed Table 2 shows always-decompose multi-round routers score about 22 avg vs 39-45 single-turn using fixed Qwen2.5-3B decomposer, attributing failure to redundant info and overhead, with no conditional decomposition test.
registration.hypothesis: LLM-gated decomposition that routes only predicted-complex queries to multi-round beats single-turn direct answering by more than 3 points on a 50-50 atomic-compositional mix.
registration.contribution: Tests training-free complexity gating with single 1.5B model for decompose, specialist and aggregate, isolating gating value from RL training and model selection; differs from sequential escalation cascades by gating on decomposability not confidence.

closest_work.difference: Router-R1 trains RL agent to interleave think and route actions with cost reward on QA benchmarks; we test zero-training Yes-No complexity gate with cached subanswers on BoolQ plus GSM8K.
FrugalGPT learns cascade escalation to larger models; we gate between single-call and decompose-answer-aggregate using same model.

inputs: HuggingFace dataset google/boolq split validation
HuggingFace dataset openai/gsm8k config main split test
HuggingFace model Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
Python libraries datasets, transformers, torch, accelerate, scikit-learn, numpy
registration.method: Do not use APIs. Implement locally with transformers. 1) Load BoolQ validation and GSM8K test. Sample 100 BoolQ plus 100 GSM8K with seed 2 total 200. 2) Single-turn direct with Qwen 1.5B-Instruct float16 greedy trust_remote_code True batch 8. BoolQ prompt is Passage plus Question plus Answer with ONLY Yes or No, max 8 tokens. GSM8K prompt is Answer the following math question step by step plus Question, max 256 tokens. Cache direct answers. Parse BoolQ by first Yes or No case-insensitive, GSM8K by extracting ground truth number after hash marks and checking equality with last number in prediction after removing commas. 3) Decompose once per query with prompt Given the query plus decompose into at most 2 meaningful sub-queries minimum 1 maximum 2 plus Output only sub-queries one per line, temp 0 max 128. Query is Passage plus Question for BoolQ and original question for GSM8K. Truncate to max 2 non-empty lines. 4) Specialist per subquery with prompt You are a helpful assistant plus Here is the sub-question for you to assist with plus subquery, max 128. 5) Aggregator with cached pairs. For BoolQ aggregator asks to use info if relevant and Answer ONLY Yes or No with final in answer tags, max 64, parse Yes No from inside tags. For GSM8K aggregator asks to reason step by step with final in answer tags, max 256, parse last number from inside tags. Cache aggregates. 6) Gate once per query with prompt Does this question require breaking into multiple sub-questions to answer correctly plus Answer ONLY Yes or No plus Question, max 8. Parse Yes No. Gated path reuses cached direct if No else cached decompose plus subanswers plus aggregate if Yes. Always-multi baseline uses decompose path for all. Record accuracy and call counts where single is 1, multi is 1 plus num sub plus 1, gated is 1 gate plus 1 if No else 1 plus num sub plus 1 plus gate.

event.description: Gated decomposition beats single-turn direct answering
event.statistic: gated_minus_single_accuracy

evaluation.procedure: Score single always-multi and gated from cached outputs with same parsers. Compute overall and per-dataset accuracies gate Yes rate overall and per dataset gate precision recall for queries where multi correctness exceeds single correctness mean calls per path and parse fail rates. Statistic is gated minus single overall accuracy. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with per-query source gate decision single multi and gated correctness and calls. Write outputs/metrics.json with accuracies difference bootstrap interval from 2000 resamples gate stats calls and fail rates.
evaluation.controls: Always-multi accuracy and gate rates reported. Caching ensures single multi and gated share identical subcalls so only gating differs. Same parsers for all paths.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger adaptive-decomposition study with learned gates, varied decomposer sizes, early stopping and cost-aware utility across more compositional benchmarks.

agent.reason: With a 1.5B model the decompose-specialist-aggregate path is likely worse than direct step-by-step on GSM8K while the gate preserves BoolQ singles, so gated overall seldom exceeds single by 6 queries.

judge_astra.reason: Predicted complexity is not the same as predicted benefit from decomposition, particularly when the same small model performs every stage. Direct GSM8K answering already includes step-by-step reasoning, while decomposition can lose necessary context and aggregation can introduce errors.

judge_fable.reason: A 1.5B model decomposing, answering sub-queries without full context and aggregating is very unlikely to beat direct answering on GSM8K/BoolQ (mirroring the seed's multi-turn collapse), and a training-free Yes/No decomposability gate has no mechanism to pick out the rare queries where the multi path helps, so gated accuracy should sit at or below single-turn.

judge_opus.reason: One 1.5B model does decomposition, answers sub-questions without the passage context, and aggregates under answer-tag and 256-token limits. That makes the multi path unlikely to beat direct answering by the 7 or more net queries needed on the gated subset, consistent with the seed's multi-round results.

judge_sol.reason: Avoiding harmful decompositions is insufficient: beating direct answering requires genuine multi-round improvements, probably concentrated on GSM8K. Using the same 1.5B model throughout, possible context loss in subquestions, and different answer-format requirements make a greater-than-three-point overall gain unlikely.

judge_luna.reason: The gate may distinguish BoolQ from GSM8K and avoid decomposing easier questions, making a modest lift plausible. Whether the 1.5B model’s decomposition, specialist answers, and aggregation improve enough over direct step-by-step answers is uncertain, particularly given the seed’s negative multi-turn results.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: seed Table 2 shows always-decompose ~22 avg vs 39-45 single-turn; inference: weak 1.5B decompose-aggregate is unlikely to beat direct enough on BoolQ/GSM8K for gating to gain >3pt.

opus.label: distinct

closest_work.difference: Router-R1 trains an RL policy that interleaves thinking and routing across several LLMs on QA benchmarks. It does not test a training-free Yes/No gate that switches one 1.5B model between answering directly and a decompose–answer–aggregate path on BoolQ and GSM8K.

This paper studies selective question decomposition, but for multimodal LLMs on VQA, and it gets there by fine-tuning on DecoVQA+ with a selective-decomposition objective. The proposed experiment is zero-shot, text-only, and measures accuracy against single-turn answering on a mix of atomic and compositional questions.

ACQO trains a module with curriculum RL to decide when to split a query into sub-queries, but only for retrieval query optimisation in RAG. It does not gate a multi-round routing pipeline against direct answering.
FrugalGPT escalates queries to larger models based on predicted answer quality. It does not gate on whether a query can be broken down, and it does not use one model for both paths.
The seed paper reports that multi-round routers that always decompose do much worse than single-turn routers. It does not test conditional, gated decomposition.

opus.reason: Deciding adaptively whether to decompose a query has been studied before: fine-tuned selective decomposition for VQA, an RL-trained query-reformulation module in RAG (ACQO), and RL-trained multi-round routing (Router-R1). However, I found no paper that tests a training-free self-gate deciding between direct answering and decompose–answer–aggregate with one small model, measured against single-turn answering on a mixed BoolQ/GSM8K set. The specific question raised by the seed paper's failing always-decompose result therefore appears to be unanswered.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: DecoSearch uses a zero-shot binary LLM judger to choose direct generation versus decomposition, uses the same backbone across components, and compares against direct-only and always-decompose ablations. It addresses text-to-SQL with DAG decomposition, schema pruning and execution-driven repair, rather than bounded two-subquery answering on BoolQ/GSM8K.

Select-Then-Decompose uses training-free, upfront LLM selection among single-call and explicit multi-call reasoning approaches, including an ablation without subsequent verification. The registered experiment restricts this selection to two paths and uses a smaller backbone, cached outputs and a different benchmark mixture.

CARD gates direct answering versus decomposition using predicted complexity and evaluates small reasoning models on GSM8K, including prompt-only complexity-estimation ablations. Its main estimator is trained, and its decomposition includes recursive thought-budget allocation rather than a fixed binary gate and at most two subqueries.

sol.reason: Prior work already experimentally examines upfront complexity-based selection between direct answering and decomposition, including training-free LLM decisions and comparisons with direct-only and always-decompose policies. The registered experiment is a narrower variant through its binary prompt, bounded decomposition, model choice and BoolQ/GSM8K mixture, rather than an unanswered methodological question. None of these papers reports the exact registered setup or establishes its specified greater-than-three-point outcome.

opus.reason: Exp 3 tests a zero-shot Yes/No complexity gate deciding whether a single 1.5B model should decompose, scored against direct answering. #34 trains a kNN sufficiency gate on query plus draft to decide whether to continue a 3B/7B pipeline, so the gate and the comparison differ.

sol.reason: Unlike entry 34's learned query-and-draft sufficiency gate, this uses a training-free, pre-answer complexity judgment to choose between direct answering and same-model decomposition.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I built: exp.py runs everything locally with transformers: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in float16, greedy decoding, batch size 8, chat template, no APIs. It samples 100 BoolQ validation and 100 GSM8K test items with random.Random(2), drawing BoolQ first and then GSM8K from the same RNG. It then runs five cached stages:
- direct answer (8 new tokens for BoolQ, 256 for GSM8K);
- decomposition into at most 2 sub-queries (128 tokens), keeping at most 2 non-empty lines;
- one specialist call per sub-query (128 tokens);
- aggregation with the answer required inside answer tags (64 tokens for BoolQ, 256 for GSM8K);
- a Yes/No gate (8 tokens).
The gated path reuses the cached direct answer when the gate says No and the cached multi-round path when it says Yes, so the three paths share identical sub-calls. Call counts follow the registration: single = 1, multi = 1 + number of sub-queries + 1, gated = 1 + (1 if No, else multi). Gate precision and recall are measured against the queries where multi was correct and single was not. Outputs are outputs/scores.jsonl, outputs/metrics.json (including a 2000-resample bootstrap) and result.json. A full run takes about 5 minutes on an A100, and two test runs gave identical results.

Result: the registered event did not occur. gated_minus_single_accuracy = -0.25 (bootstrap 95% CI [-0.32, -0.18]).

| Path | Overall | BoolQ | GSM8K |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single | 0.595 | 0.75 | 0.44 |
| Always-multi | 0.25 | 0.34 | 0.16 |
| Gated | 0.345 | 0.43 | 0.26 |

- The gate said Yes on 60% of queries.
- Only 6 of 200 queries had multi correct where single was wrong. The gate caught 5 of these (recall 0.83) but its precision was 0.04.
- Mean calls per query: single 1, multi 3.97, gated 3.78.

Main caveat: the always-multi aggregator failed to parse on 48.5% of queries (79% of GSM8K, 18% of BoolQ). For GSM8K, the few outputs I inspected were cut off at the registered 256-token limit before writing the answer tags. As registered, strict parsing inside the tags is kept and a failure counts as wrong, so part of the negative result is a format/budget effect, not purely a failure of decomposition. To size this I added a diagnostic metric that is clearly labelled and is not the registered statistic: it parses the whole aggregator text when the tags are missing. Under it, multi scores 0.42, gated 0.435, and gated minus single -0.16, so the conclusion stays negative.

Interpretations and small choices the registration left open:
1. The gate sees the same query text as the decomposer (Passage + Question for BoolQ). The registration only says "Question".
2. If the gate output had no Yes/No it would have defaulted to No; this never happened (gate parse-fail rate 0).
3. If the decomposer returned nothing, the original query would be used as the single sub-query.
4. Prompt wording paraphrases the registered templates and the seed paper's multi-round templates, cut down to the 2-sub-query limit.
5. GSM8K answers are compared as numbers (floats).

No other deviations.

departures: exp.py specialist prompt: the registration specifies only 'You are a helpful assistant' + 'Here is the sub-question for you to assist with' + subquery. The code inserts seed-paper-style text about a multi-agent process and asks for answers that are direct, brief or contextual. The engineer disclosed this as paraphrase. It could shift specialist outputs and multi accuracy somewhat, but it cannot change the gated-vs-single outcome (see the bound below).

exp.py gate prompt: the gate receives Passage + Question for BoolQ, while the registration says 'Question'. This was disclosed as an interpretation. It changes BoolQ gate decisions (Yes rate 0.64). It cannot make the event occur, because gated - single <= (#queries where multi beats single)/200 = 6/200 = 0.03, which is not > 0.03.

exp.py GSM8K aggregator prompt adds 'make your own reasoning', 'MUST be clearly marked' and 'Let's think step by step' to the registered 'reason step by step with final in answer tags'. This is a paraphrase within an open choice and has minor effect.
exp.py BoolQ questions are capitalised and given a '?' before prompting. This is not in the registration and its effect is negligible.

exp.py applies the chat template and sorts prompts by length for batching. The registration leaves this open. Batching in float16 with left padding may cause tiny numeric differences and has negligible effect.
exp.py uses the original query as the sub-query when the decomposition is empty. The registration leaves this case open and it probably rarely or never fired. No effect.
exp.py defaults to No when the gate cannot be parsed. The registration leaves this open and it never fired (gate parse-fail rate 0). No effect.

exp.py counts aggregator outputs without answer tags as wrong. This is consistent with the registered rule of parsing inside the tags, but the registration does not state it explicitly. It lowers multi and gated accuracy (multi parse failures 48.5%). Even under the lenient diagnostic, gated - single = -0.16, so the conclusion is unchanged.
exp.py GSM8K answers are compared numerically as floats rather than by string equality. This is equivalent for integer answers and has no effect.
exp.py adds a lenient diagnostic metric to metrics.json. It is clearly labelled and is not used as the statistic. No effect on the registered value.
problems: The registered 256-token budget for the GSM8K aggregator truncates most outputs before the answer tags: 79% parse failures on GSM8K (metrics.json). Multi and gated accuracy therefore partly reflect a format and budget artifact rather than the quality of the decomposition itself. This is a design weakness of the registration, not of the implementation.

The design structurally caps gated - single at the fraction of queries where multi beats single. Here that fraction is 6/200 = 0.03, so the event (> 0.03) was unattainable for any gate. The result mostly measures how weak the multi path is, not the quality of the gating.
The run uses a single repetition, n=200, one 1.5B model and one prompt set, so generality is limited. The bootstrap CI [-0.32, -0.18] is nonetheless far from the threshold.
exp.py loads scikit-learn but never uses it. This is cosmetic.
The gate sees the BoolQ passage, contrary to the literal 'Question' in the registration. The engineer disclosed this, and it cannot change the outcome.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered pipeline closely: same data and sampling seed, model, greedy decoding, token budgets, parsers, caching scheme, call counts, statistic and bootstrap. The remaining departures are disclosed paraphrases or open choices that cannot change the outcome. The evidence comes from real cached model outputs; per-query scores and aggregates are internally consistent, and nothing is hard-coded or leaked. Because only 6 of 200 queries had multi correct where single was wrong, no gate could have reached the > 0.03 threshold. The negative result is therefore robust: it holds under the lenient diagnostic (-0.16) and has a CI far below zero. However, the multi path is heavily handicapped by tag truncation under the registered budget, and the setup is small (one 1.5B model, one run). This makes it a credible but limited null about training-free gating at this scale rather than strong evidence about decomposition in general.

departures: exp.py normalizes BoolQ question text by capitalizing its first character and appending a question mark when absent. This preprocessing is not specified in the registration. It preserves the apparent question meaning but could change generated answers or gate decisions.

exp.py expands the decomposition prompt with requirements that subqueries be clear, self-contained and semantically coherent, and explicit prohibitions on headers and explanations. These additions could change the generated subqueries and therefore the reported accuracy; some wording discretion remains because the registration does not provide a verbatim template.

exp.py substantially expands the specialist prompt beyond the registered helpful-assistant and subquestion instructions. It introduces a multi-agent/specialized-model role, requests a brief explanation, and permits offering relevant context instead of answering when necessary. These behavioral additions could change subanswers and downstream correctness.

exp.py adds the example <answer>Yes</answer> to the BoolQ aggregation prompt. The registration requires answer tags but does not specify a Yes exemplar. This could affect formatting compliance or bias the generated answer.

exp.py expands the GSM8K aggregation prompt with an instruction to make its own reasoning, emphatic mandatory tagging, placement of the answer at the response's end, and a trailing 'Let's think step by step.' These largely implement the registered reasoning-and-tags request, but their wording and placement could affect output length, truncation and accuracy.

exp.py supplies the complete Passage-plus-Question text to the BoolQ gate, whereas the registered gate description says 'Question.' The intended scope is ambiguous, so this may be an open implementation choice rather than a definite violation. Nevertheless, including the passage could materially change routing and the reported value.

exp.py compares GSM8K answers using floating-point conversion and an absolute tolerance below 1e-6 rather than literal numeric equality. This could change labels for near-equal predictions, although the supplied evidence does not establish that it changed any evaluated case.

exp.py substitutes the original query as one subquery when decomposition returns no non-empty lines. This is an unspecified failure-handling choice compatible with enforcing the registered minimum of one subquery. It could affect results if triggered; its occurrence is not reported.
exp.py defaults an unparseable gate response to No. This fallback is not specified in the registration, but the evaluated gate parse-failure rate is zero, so it did not change this run's value.

exp.py adds a clearly labelled lenient-parsing diagnostic and an additional result.json output. These are supplementary outputs, not replacements for the registered statistic; they do not change the reported -0.25 value or event decision.
problems: exp.py's substantive specialist-prompt additions introduce behavior not contained in the registered prompt description and plausibly affect the auxiliary answers. This is the clearest fidelity defect; ambiguous gate-input scope and ordinary template wording choices should not independently be treated as established violations.

outputs/metrics.json reports aggregation parse failures on 97 of 200 queries, including 79% of GSM8K and 18% of BoolQ. The registered pipeline therefore measures substantial formatting and output-budget failure alongside answer correctness. The notes and visible cache excerpt support truncation as one cause, but do not establish the cause of every failure.

exp.py applies whole-output parsing to direct answers and tag-restricted parsing to aggregation, as registered. Consequently, the comparison does not isolate decomposition quality from answer-format compliance. The lenient diagnostic remains negative, but extracting the last number from an unfinished response is not a controlled repair of the aggregation procedure.

outputs/metrics.json shows only six queries where multi-round succeeds and direct answering fails. Derived from those reported counts, even an oracle selector over these cached paths could improve direct accuracy by only 6/200 = 0.03, not the registered strictly greater-than-0.03 threshold. Thus failure to reach the event cannot be attributed solely to the gate.

The registered 50-50 dataset mixture is not an independently validated 50-50 mixture of atomic and compositional questions. No supplied complexity annotations establish that the gate measures decomposability rather than other question or passage characteristics.

The evidence covers one sample, one model and one prompt/budget configuration. It supports a negative finding for this implementation, not a general claim that conditional decomposition cannot help. The reported bootstrap interval captures query-resampling uncertainty, not uncertainty across implementations or model configurations.
sol.reason: The fresh-machine evaluation completed, produced both registered raw outputs, and reported gated-minus-single accuracy of -0.25 with a paired bootstrap interval of [-0.32, -0.18], so the registered event clearly failed. The code generates and scores real model outputs without evident leakage, hard-coded results or a conclusion-changing scoring error, making the evidence valid. Fidelity is unfaithful because the specialist prompt adds substantive answer-or-context behavior beyond the registered instructions, although several other differences are ambiguous or harmless implementation choices. The large deficit, shared cached comparisons and still-negative lenient diagnostic support a meaningful configuration-specific negative finding, warranting research value 2, while severe parsing failures limit conclusions about decomposition or gating generally.

departures: Specialist prompt in exp.py adds multi-agent roleplay plus 'answer directly / brief explanation / concise' instructions that the registration does not contain (only 'You are a helpful assistant' plus the sub-question). Could change sub-answers and thus multi and gated accuracy.

Decompose prompt in exp.py adds 'clear, self-contained, and semantically coherent' and extra bans on headers/explanations beyond the registered skeleton. Could change sub-queries and the reported difference.
Gate input in exp.py is Passage+Question for BoolQ; the registration's gate prompt ends with 'Question' (engineer reported). Could change Yes/No decisions and gated_minus_single_accuracy.
BoolQ questions in exp.py are capitalized and given a trailing '?' if missing, which the registration does not specify. Could slightly change direct, decompose, and gate outputs.
exp.py wraps every prompt in the Qwen chat template; the registration does not mention a chat template. Open formatting choice, but it could change all generations versus raw completion.
GSM8K scoring in exp.py uses float absolute tolerance 1e-6 rather than exact equality of the comma-stripped number (engineer reported). Could flip a few items if string forms differ.

Aggregator prompts in exp.py are longer than the registration's functional description (auxiliary preamble, tag example, 'Let's think step by step'). Mostly an instantiation of an underspecified prompt; could slightly change aggregates.
If the gate text had no Yes/No, exp.py would treat it as No. Registration does not specify a default. Gate parse-fail rate was 0, so this did not change this result.
Empty decompositions fall back to the original query as one sub-query (exp.py). Implements the registered minimum of 1; unknown if used; unlikely to change the result.

exp.py also writes a lenient untagged diagnostic into metrics.json and scores.jsonl. It is labeled as not the registered statistic and is not written to result.json, so it does not change the reported value.
scikit-learn is listed in the registration and installed by run.sh but unused in exp.py. No effect on the result.
problems: Specialist and decomposer prompts in exp.py are richer than the registered skeletons, so -0.25 is not exactly the registered prompt's gap.
Gate sees full BoolQ passages (exp.py), which can inflate the Yes rate (0.64 on BoolQ in metrics.json) relative to a question-only gate.

Aggregator parse-fail rate is 0.485 overall and 0.79 on GSM8K (metrics.json) because the registered 256-token cap often cuts off before <answer> tags; the registered statistic therefore mixes format/budget failure with routing quality.

Only 6 of 200 items have multi correct and single wrong (metrics.json), so even a perfect gate yields gated_minus_single of exactly 0.03, which does not meet greater-than 0.03. Gating had almost no headroom given this multi-round system.
Single 200-item sample and one seed; precision is helped by the bootstrap CI but there is no repeated split.
grok.reason: The fresh run uses the registered data, model, n=200 seed-2 sample, greedy decoding, token limits, tag parsers, shared-cache control, and statistic, and result.json's -0.25 matches real generations whose slice accuracies and gate counts reconcile. It is unfaithful because the specialist and decomposer prompts add unregistered instructions and the gate sees BoolQ passages rather than the question alone, any of which could change the reported difference. The evidence is valid: no leakage or hard-coded scores, and the evaluation re-executed the model. The negative result is still meaningful—the CI [-0.32, -0.18] excludes +0.03, always-multi is far worse, and the labeled lenient parse remains -0.16—but token cutoffs and prompt deviations keep it from being a clean test of gating alone.

grok.what_it_asks: Whether a Yes/No complexity gate that sends only predicted-complex queries through decompose-then-aggregate beats always answering in one shot, on a mix of atomic yes/no and compositional math questions.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper reports that always-on multi-turn routing underperforms single-turn and calls for better sufficiency estimation, but it neither runs this gated-decomposition comparison nor names that test as future work, a limitation, or an open question.

relation.reason: The experiment reuses the paper's decompose-specialist-aggregate procedure and adds a training-free complexity gate the paper does not test, so the paper's claims about always-on multi-turn stand either way.

obvious.reason: After the headline result that extra decomposition rounds hurt and the explicit call for sufficiency estimation, most routing researchers would list a gate that decomposes only when predicted necessary against single-turn answering among their first follow-ups.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would change whether people across LLM routing condition decomposition on predicted complexity, but it would not change practice outside that topic.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's account of Table 2's multi-turn scores near 22, the Qwen2.5-3B multi-turn base model, and the attribution to redundant rounds matches the paper's reported numbers and text.

answerable.reason: The design scores the gated path and the single-turn path with the same parsers on the same queries, so a higher or lower gated accuracy would directly answer whether the gate beats direct answering.

grok.what_came_out: On 200 queries (100 BoolQ validation and 100 GSM8K test) with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, gated accuracy was 0.345 versus 0.595 for single-turn, a difference of -0.25 with a 2000-resample bootstrap 95% CI of [-0.32, -0.18].

prerequisite.reason: Aggregator tag failures were common, but BoolQ still showed a large gated deficit with only 18% parse failures and a lenient whole-text parse still left gated 0.16 below single-turn, so the comparison remains readable.

evidence.reason: The gate fired on 60% of queries and the accuracy gap is reversed and tightly estimated, with the CI upper bound of -0.18 ruling out a gain of more than 3 points.

next_step.reason: The gated path is largely worse on both datasets and under lenient parsing, so this complexity-gated decomposition was credibly shown not to beat single-turn and a larger repeat would not change that.
next_step.what: a

opus.what_it_asks: Does sending only the queries that a zero-shot Yes/No complexity gate flags through the paper-style decompose–answer–aggregate multi-round pipeline, and answering the rest directly, beat always answering directly with the same small model on a BoolQ plus GSM8K mix, and so show whether conditional decomposition rescues multi-round routing?

in_the_paper.reason: The paper does not test conditional decomposition, but after its multi-turn results it explicitly names sufficiency estimation, meaning when a single route is enough, as the open need that this gate addresses.
in_the_paper.quote: These results highlight the need for better sufficiency estimation, early stopping, and more effective decomposition and aggregation.

relation.reason: The experiment takes the paper's multi-round decomposition, specialist and aggregation templates as a working part and adds a gate the paper never tests; the paper's own claims stand whichever way it comes out.

obvious.reason: The paper itself points to sufficiency estimation, so adaptive or conditional decomposition would occur to several readers, but not to most as a first-ten item in this exact gated-versus-direct form.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would mainly change what people building multi-round or decomposition routers do; it would not change practice across routing generally.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's claims about the paper are accurate: multi-turn routers average about 22 against roughly 36–45 for single-turn routers, they use a Qwen2.5-3B base model, and the paper attributes the gap to redundant information and overhead without testing conditional decomposition.

answerable.reason: Gated accuracy can exceed direct answering only if the decompose–aggregate path actually works and yields parseable, sometimes better answers with the 1.5B model, which the design cannot guarantee.
answerable.needs: multi-round path produces parseable, sometimes-better answers

opus.what_came_out: With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 200 queries (100 BoolQ, 100 GSM8K) in one run, gated accuracy was 0.345 against 0.595 for direct answering, a difference of -0.25 (bootstrap 95% CI [-0.32, -0.18]); always-multi scored 0.25 with a 48.5% aggregator parse-failure rate, and a lenient untagged-parse diagnostic still gave gated minus direct = -0.16.

prerequisite.reason: The multi-round aggregator often failed to parse (79% on GSM8K, at least partly from truncation at 256 tokens), but the lenient diagnostic shows the comparison stays clearly negative (-0.16), so the fault did not change the direction of the main comparison.

evidence.reason: The gate was really applied and measured accuracy was far from its floor or ceiling, and gated routing was 25 points worse than direct answering with an interval excluding any gain; only 6 of 200 queries benefited from decomposition, and the gate's precision on those was 0.04.

next_step.reason: Decomposition with this model almost never helped, and the gate fires on 60% of queries with near-zero precision; the result stays clearly negative under lenient parsing, so this training-free gated approach was credibly shown not to work here.

sol.what_it_asks: The experiment compares complexity-gated decomposition–answer–aggregation with direct answering on a balanced BoolQ/GSM8K mix to test whether selectively decomposing predicted-complex questions improves accuracy.

in_the_paper.reason: The paper compares existing single-turn and multi-round routers but does not report or explicitly name this complexity-gated versus direct-answering comparison.

relation.reason: The experiment extends the paper's decomposition–specialist–aggregation procedure with an upfront complexity gate rather than testing a claim about an existing router.

obvious.reason: Complexity-gated decomposition is a familiar adaptive-computation follow-up to redundant multi-round calls, although not everyone considering sufficiency estimation would choose this particular comparison.

who_would_care.reason: A clear answer would inform researchers across adaptive LLM inference about when extra decomposition calls are preferable to direct answering.

misreads_paper.reason: The plan's account of weak multi-round performance, the fixed Qwen2.5-3B base model, and the absence of this conditional-decomposition experiment is consistent with the paper.

answerable.reason: The cached outputs and paired scoring can establish whether the specified gated pipeline improves end-to-end accuracy over direct answering without requiring the gate or decomposition to succeed beforehand.

sol.what_came_out: In one evaluated greedy run of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 100 BoolQ validation and 100 GSM8K test questions, gated accuracy was 34.5% versus 59.5% for direct answering, a difference of −25 percentage points with a bootstrap 95% interval of −32 to −18 points, while always-multi accuracy was 25%.

prerequisite.reason: The gate actually selected decomposition on 60% of queries, and relaxing strict-tag extraction still left gated accuracy 16 points below direct answering, so the extraction problem does not explain away the negative comparison.

evidence.reason: The registered comparison's interval is wholly negative, and the lenient extraction diagnostic also shows a substantial loss rather than the hypothesized gain.

next_step.reason: The loss is clear for this pipeline, but frequent aggregation parse failures leave its dependence on the aggregation output budget unresolved.
next_step.what: Repeat the paired comparison with a longer aggregation budget that permits completed answers and matched answer extraction on the direct and multi-round paths.

registration.title: Cross-domain transfer of kNN versus MLP from science to commonsense QA
registration.seed_connection: Seed reports no single router dominates but trains and tests mostly in-distribution per track. This tests the consistency claim under explicit domain shift, stressing whether router rankings generalize.
registration.hypothesis: kNN retains more routing gain out-of-distribution than MLP, beating MLP by more than 2 points on unseen CommonsenseQA after training only on ARC.
registration.contribution: Controlled train-one-domain test-another comparison of non-parametric versus parametric routers with identical small pool, embeddings and labels, format-matched 4-option and CV-tuned MLP. Prior OOD claims use different benchmarks or LLM-based routers, not frozen-embedding kNN versus tuned MLP under the same protocol.

closest_work.difference: Claims kNN is more robust under distribution shift than parametric routers but evaluates on different leaderboard splits, not a controlled ARC-train to CommonsenseQA-test transfer with fixed small pool.
Proposes in-context vectors for routing with claimed out-of-distribution gains and new-model generalization using an LLM router, not a comparison of frozen-embedding kNN versus MLP.
Shows methods cluster in-distribution across encoders and benchmarks but does not compare OOD retention of kNN versus MLP.

inputs: HuggingFace dataset allenai/ai2_arc config ARC-Challenge as source splits train plus validation
HuggingFace dataset tau/commonsense_qa as target splits train plus validation, fallback allenai/commonsense_qa, filtered to 4-option
HuggingFace models Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
HuggingFace embedding sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
Python libraries datasets, transformers, torch, accelerate, sentence-transformers, scikit-learn, numpy
registration.method: Do not use APIs. Implement locally with transformers. 1) Load ARC pool and CSQA pool. Shuffle ARC pool seed 0, take 400 for router-train and next 150 disjoint for ID test. For CSQA keep only items where answerKey in A B C D, drop E option text to make 4-option, shuffle seed 0, take 300 disjoint for OOD test. Use fixed 4-option prompt requiring final letter in parenthesis plus Question and Options A to D for all splits. 2) Run all three Qwen models locally float16 greedy max_new_tokens 16 batch 8 one at a time, parse by open-paren letter close-paren else standalone A to D, score vs gold with ARC key normalized from 1-4 to A-D. Define discriminative ARC train where three models do not all agree, label cheapest among correct order 0.5B then 1.5B then 3B, if kept less than 200 use full train with note. 3) Embed query-plus-options with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 normalized. For kNN do 5-fold StratifiedKFold shuffle True seed 0 on discriminative train to select k among 5 15 30 maximizing out-of-fold routed accuracy, tie smallest. Train final kNN with best k cosine uniform. For MLP use MLPClassifier activation relu solver adam max_iter 500 early_stopping True validation_fraction 0.2 n_iter_no_change 20 random_state 0, grid hidden 50 100 and alpha 0.001 0.01 0.1 via same 5-fold out-of-fold routed accuracy, tie smallest hidden then smallest alpha. Train final MLP with best hyperparams on same discriminative train. 4) Predict OOD 300 and ID 150 with both, score routed accuracy from step 2 correctness.

event.description: kNN OOD test accuracy exceeds MLP OOD test accuracy by more than 2 points when trained on ARC and tested on CommonsenseQA
event.statistic: ood_acc_knn_minus_mlp

evaluation.procedure: Compute OOD accuracy for kNN and MLP on CommonsenseQA filtered test. Statistic is kNN OOD minus MLP OOD. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with one JSON per OOD query holding id gold per-model correctness kNN and MLP predictions and both routed correctness. Write outputs/metrics.json holding train ID and OOD sizes filtered counts best hyperparams per-model accuracies ID accuracies for both routers OOD accuracies difference bootstrap interval from 2000 resamples and routing distributions.
evaluation.controls: Both share train embeddings labels and test queries. ID ARC test reported to verify MLP competitive in distribution. Best-single on OOD chosen from train to avoid leakage. Fixed seed 0.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run full cross-task matrix across knowledge, math, code and long-context in both directions for all single-turn families to establish when non-parametric routing is more transferable.

agent.reason: CV-tuned MLP with early stopping should match kNN in-distribution, and OOD both rely on noisy ARC neighbors for CSQA, so a 2-point kNN edge is plausible but far from assured.

judge_astra.reason: Limited training data and domain shift give kNN a plausible advantage over the MLP, but its neighborhoods need not remain useful on CommonsenseQA. Similar or nearly constant model selections could leave little separation, although the two-point threshold and sampling variability make the event reasonably plausible.

judge_fable.reason: Under ARC→CSQA shift both routers will mostly emit near-majority labels (1.5B) with arbitrary deviations, so the kNN–MLP OOD gap is largely noise around zero with a few points of spread; a >2-point kNN edge is possible but not favored.

judge_opus.reason: Out of distribution, both routers probably output label-prior mixes dominated by 1.5B, so the gap is set by artifacts (ties going to the cheapest class, MLP early stopping collapsing to the majority) and is near zero in expectation. A plausible fallback to full-train labels with 0.5B as the majority would favour a varied kNN over a collapsed MLP, which adds some chance of the event.

judge_sol.reason: The small, potentially imbalanced ARC training set could leave the early-stopped MLP weaker than kNN, making a two-point OOD gap plausible. Nevertheless, nearest-neighbor transfer is uncertain, and winning this comparison would not itself establish retained routing gain over a fixed model.

judge_luna.reason: The format-matched ARC-to-CommonsenseQA split tests a real domain shift, and kNN could have an edge over an MLP trained on limited ARC labels. But local neighbors may transfer poorly from science to commonsense, so a greater-than-two-point advantage is far from assured.

judge_muse.reason: Evidence: kNN is claimed more robust OOD than parametric routers; inference: both share small ARC discriminative train and likely stay near best-single, so >2pt kNN edge on 300 CSQA is possible but uncertain.

opus.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Runs a controlled cross-dataset OOD test: routers are trained on one RouterBench dataset and tested on the others (36 train-test pairs). RouterBench includes ARC-Challenge and commonsense tasks such as HellaSwag and Winogrande. kNN and MLP share the same BERT embeddings. The paper reports ID-to-OOD degradation (kNN k=100: 2.63 AUC points; MLP: 4.22) and average OOD AUC (73.91 vs 72.23). The new experiment differs in details: one ARC-to-CommonsenseQA pair, a locally run Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B pool, MiniLM embeddings, cheapest-correct classification labels with cross-validated hyperparameters, and routed accuracy instead of Pareto AUC.

Compares 21 routers, kNN included, across encoders and benchmarks and finds that they plateau at similar accuracy. In the parts checked, it does not focus on train-one-domain, test-another retention of kNN versus MLP.
Reports ID and OOD gains for an LLM-based in-context-vector router. It does not compare frozen-embedding kNN with an MLP.

opus.reason: Li (2505.12601) already asks the same question in largely the same way: whether a non-parametric kNN router holds up under cross-dataset shift better than parametric routers such as an MLP, using shared embeddings and a train-on-one, test-on-others protocol that includes ARC-Challenge as a source. It reports that kNN degrades less and transfers slightly better on average. The new experiment changes only the details: one ARC-to-CommonsenseQA pair, a small local Qwen pool, different embeddings, routed accuracy as the metric, and a 2-point threshold. The single-pair result could still differ from Li's averaged findings, but the general question is largely settled.

sol.label: close variant

closest_work.difference: Section 6 and Appendix H already compare kNN versus MLP under explicit train-one-dataset/test-another transfer across six RouterBench datasets, including ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag and Winogrande, using shared query embeddings and a fixed candidate pool. The registered experiment substitutes CommonsenseQA, a three-model Qwen pool and MiniLM embeddings, uses discriminative cheapest-correct classification labels, tunes hyperparameters by cross-validation, and measures routed accuracy rather than cost–performance AUC.

sol.reason: Yang Li's Rethinking Predictive Modeling for LLM Routing: When Simple kNN Beats Complex Learned Routers already tests the central question through controlled cross-dataset evaluations, reporting smaller average OOD degradation for kNN than MLP. Contrary to the registration's characterization, this prior work explicitly trains on one dataset and tests on others, rather than merely comparing leaderboard splits. The proposed datasets, pool, supervision and metric make this a close variant; the exact CommonsenseQA accuracy difference is not established by that prior result.

opus.reason: No list entry compares out-of-distribution retention of kNN versus MLP routers under train-on-ARC, test-on-CommonsenseQA shift. #57 and #17 study cross-domain transfer but not this non-parametric versus parametric contrast.

sol.reason: The transfer entries examine supervision regimes or kNN/SVM generalization, rather than the same controlled test of whether kNN outperforms MLP under domain shift.

outcome.executor_notes:
What I ran: run.sh installs the dependencies and runs run_exp.py, which takes about 3.5 minutes on an A100. Everything ran locally with transformers; no APIs were used. The method follows the registration: ARC-Challenge train+validation, shuffled with seed 0, gives 400 router-train items and the next 150 as the in-distribution (ID) test. CommonsenseQA (CSQA) comes from tau/commonsense_qa train+validation, keeping only items whose answerKey is A–D and dropping option E, shuffled with seed 0, and its first 300 items form the out-of-distribution (OOD) test. Every split uses the same 4-option prompt, which is the seed paper's standard multiple-choice template. The three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B) are run in fp16 with greedy decoding, max_new_tokens 16 and batch size 8. Answers are parsed as "(X)" first, falling back to a standalone A–D letter. Training uses the discriminative ARC subset: 255 items, so the 200-item fallback was not needed. The label is the cheapest correct model. Query-plus-options text is embedded with MiniLM and normalised. kNN chooses k from {5, 15, 30} and the MLP is tuned over the registered grid, both by 5-fold stratified out-of-fold routed accuracy. Outputs are outputs/scores.jsonl, outputs/metrics.json and result.json, plus an extra file, outputs/generations.jsonl, holding the raw generations.

One small change: ARC items without exactly 4 options (6 of 1,418) are dropped before shuffling, to match the fixed A–D prompt.

Result from the test run: kNN OOD accuracy is 0.700 and MLP OOD accuracy is 0.693, so ood_acc_knn_minus_mlp = +0.0067. The 2,000-resample bootstrap 95% interval is [-0.010, +0.023]. The registered threshold of 0.02 is not exceeded, so the event did not occur. The interval includes zero, so this does not show the two routers are equivalent either. On the ID test, kNN scores 0.647 and the MLP 0.667. The best single model, chosen on train, is 1.5B; it scores 0.667 ID and 0.700 OOD. Best hyperparameters: kNN k=30 (the largest value in the grid); MLP hidden=100, alpha=0.001 (the three alpha values gave identical CV accuracy).

Main caveat: the registered max_new_tokens=16 setting badly hurts the 3B model. It often starts with "To determine..." and is cut off before giving a letter. Parse failures for 3B were 224 of 400 train, 79 of 150 ID and 96 of 300 OOD. As a result, 3B scores below 0.5B (0.24 vs 0.31 on train) and is the label for only 13 of the 255 training items. Both routers therefore send almost everything to 1.5B: on OOD, kNN routes 292 of 300 there and the MLP 297 of 300. So this test mostly says that under this protocol the routers collapse to the best single model. It is weak evidence about whether kNN transfers better than an MLP in general. I kept 16 tokens because the registration fixes that value; a longer generation budget would be a different experiment.

departures: run_exp.py drops the 6 of 1,418 ARC-Challenge items that lack exactly 4 options, before the seed-0 shuffle. The permutation is therefore over 1,412 items, and the 400 train / 150 ID items differ from a shuffle of the raw pool. The engineer reported this. It follows from the registered fixed A-D prompt, which cannot hold 3- or 5-option items. It could shift the exact numbers slightly but should not systematically favour either router.

run_exp.py wraps the registered prompt in each Qwen model's chat template (apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt). The registration does not specify prompt formatting beyond its content, so this is an open choice. It affects all models and both routers equally.

run_exp.py reads 'three models do not all agree' as 'not all correct and not all wrong', using C.sum(1) % 3 != 0. This is a reasonable reading of an ambiguous rule. It produced 255 items, so the 200-item fallback was not triggered.

run_exp.py counts parse failures (no letter extracted) as incorrect. The registration has no explicit rule for this, but it is the natural implementation of 'score vs gold' and applies to both routers identically.
run.sh / run_exp.py add an extra artifact, outputs/generations.jsonl. It cannot change the result.

I found no departure in decoding (fp16, greedy, max_new_tokens 16, batch 8), the parse rule, the CSQA filtering, the embeddings, the CV grids and tie rules, the statistic, the bootstrap, or best-single-from-train.
problems: The registered max_new_tokens=16 truncates the 3B model's chain-of-thought-style answers. It had 224/400 train, 79/150 ID and 96/300 OOD parse failures (metrics.json), which puts 3B below 0.5B on train. The pool is effectively degenerate: 3B labels only 13 of 255 training items, and neither router ever routes to 3B.

Both routers collapse onto the best single model, 1.5B: kNN routes 292/300 OOD items there and the MLP 297/300. The +0.0067 difference comes from roughly 2 net items. The test therefore says almost nothing about whether non-parametric routing transfers better than parametric routing.

The bootstrap 95% CI [-0.010, +0.023] includes both 0 and the 0.02 threshold. The data cannot rule out the hypothesised >2-point advantage any more than they can confirm it. 'Event did not occur' is a point-estimate statement, not evidence of no effect.

The fallback parse regex \b([A-D])\b (run_exp.py) can match a capital article 'A' at the start of a sentence, inflating or deflating per-model correctness. This follows the registered rule and affects both routers equally, but it adds noise to the labels.
The selected k=30 is at the upper edge of the kNN grid, consistent with the router mostly predicting the majority class (1.5B).

Neither router beats the best single model on OOD (kNN 0.700 = best single; MLP 0.693), and the oracle is 0.847. There is no routing gain to 'retain', so the retention question the registration poses cannot be addressed.
opus.reason: The code implements the registered protocol closely. The only substantive change is dropping 6 non-4-option ARC items, which the registered fixed A-D prompt requires and which is reported. The numbers come from real local generations and are scored consistently, with no leakage between ARC train/ID and the CSQA test, and best-single is chosen on train. However, the registered 16-token budget cripples the 3B model, so both routers degenerate into near-constant predictors of the 1.5B model and differ on only a handful of items. The resulting +0.67-point difference has a CI spanning both zero and the 0.02 threshold, so the experiment neither supports nor meaningfully refutes the hypothesis. This is a valid but largely uninformative null.

departures: run_exp.py filters ARC before the seed-0 shuffle, requiring exactly four choices, normalized labels in A–D order, and a valid A–D key. The registration specifies shuffling the ARC train-plus-validation pool without this filter. The pool falls from 1,418 to 1,412 items; changing the permutation population can change both sampled splits, router training, and the reported difference. This is result-relevant despite its format-matching motivation.

Potential departure in run_exp.py: the discriminative subset is defined by disagreement of binary correctness, using C.sum(1) % 3 != 0, rather than disagreement of parsed answers. It therefore excludes all-wrong examples even when model answers differ; the displayed generations for ACTAAP_2015_7_8 provide one such example. The registration's phrase 'do not all agree' is ambiguous, and its all-wrong labeling rule is unspecified. Under an answer-disagreement interpretation, this changes training membership and could change the result; under a correctness-disagreement interpretation, it is consistent.

run_exp.py assigns all-wrong training items to 0.5B if the full-training fallback is used, a rule not stated in the registration. That fallback was not used because 255 discriminative items were retained, so this rule did not affect the reported value.
outputs/generations.jsonl is an additional diagnostic artifact beyond the registered raw outputs. It does not affect the experiment or statistic.
problems: run_exp.py changes the registered ARC sampling population before shuffling. No comparison with the unfiltered registered sampling procedure is available to quantify its effect.

outputs/metrics.json reports substantial parse failures under the registered 16-token budget, especially for 3B: 224/400 training, 79/150 ID, and 96/300 OOD examples. Displayed generations support the concern that reasoning is frequently truncated before an answer. This limits interpretation of model capability and routing transfer, although it is a registered design limitation rather than an implementation departure.

The registered parser implemented in run_exp.py can treat an option mentioned during reasoning as an answer. For example, the displayed 3B generation for ef818f9e31e79d450268b888fb3e88ac begins analyzing options and mentions 'A. Military base'; the fallback parser accepts that A without an explicit final answer.

outputs/metrics.json shows near-constant routing to 1.5B: 292/300 OOD items for kNN and 297/300 for MLP, with neither selecting 3B. kNN merely matches the train-selected single-model baseline at 70%, while MLP scores 69.33%; neither demonstrates positive OOD routing gain. The oracle reaches 84.67%, so complementary correct answers exist, but these routers do not exploit them effectively.

The paired bootstrap interval is approximately [-1.00, +2.33] percentage points. It includes both zero and advantages exceeding the registered two-point threshold, so the observed event failure establishes neither equivalence nor exclusion of the hypothesized population effect. One training seed and 300 OOD queries provide limited precision.

The registered CSQA transformation excludes gold-E questions and removes the E distractor. The result consequently concerns this modified four-option subset, not unrestricted CommonsenseQA or cross-domain routing generally.
sol.reason: The fresh evaluation completed successfully and reported kNN at 210/300 versus MLP at 208/300, giving +0.00667 and correctly marking the registered event false. The displayed code supports a genuine, paired computation from local model generations, with training-only tuning and baseline selection and no apparent test leakage or hard-coded result. Fidelity is unfaithful because the additional ARC filter changes the population before seeded sampling and could change the reported value. Research value is limited by severe answer-format failures and nearly constant routing, while the confidence interval leaves both no advantage and an advantage above two points plausible.

departures: run_exp.py drops ARC-Challenge items without exactly four choices, and items whose labels are not exactly A-D or whose gold is not A-D after 1-4 normalization, before the seed-0 shuffle (1418 to 1412). The registration only specifies shuffling train+validation and normalizing keys. This exclusion is required to apply the fixed A-D prompt; it can change which items enter the 400/150 split and thus the trained routers and the OOD difference, but only six items were removed and the label-order check removed none beyond those six.

run_exp.py wraps every prompt in the Instruct chat template (apply_chat_template, add_generation_prompt=True). The registration does not specify chat formatting. That is the standard interface for the named Instruct models and is an open choice; versus a raw prompt it could change generations and the statistic.

run_exp.py's unused fallback would label all-wrong items as 0.5B if the discriminative set were under 200. The registration does not specify that label. The path was not taken (255 kept), so it did not change this result.
problems: Registered max_new_tokens=16 truncates answers, especially 3B: outputs/metrics.json parse_failures are 224/400 train, 79/150 ID, and 96/300 OOD, and outputs/generations.jsonl shows 3B cut off in 'To determine...' reasoning. 3B then scores below 0.5B, so the pool does not have the intended cost-quality order.

Both routers collapse to 1.5B (outputs/metrics.json): OOD kNN 292/300 and MLP 297/300, with zero routes to 3B, and 3B is the train label on only 13/255. The OOD gap is 2/300 items and does not measure transferable routing.

There is no in-distribution routing gain to transfer: ID kNN 0.647 and MLP 0.667 versus best-single 0.667, while oracle is 0.793 ID and 0.847 OOD (outputs/metrics.json). k=30 is the top of the grid and CV accuracy rises monotonically with k, consistent with majority-class collapse.

The 2000-resample 95% interval [-0.010, 0.023] in outputs/metrics.json includes 0 and still reaches just above 0.02, so this single run neither supports the registered event nor precisely rules a 2-point gap out.
grok.reason: The code follows the registered splits, models, greedy 16-token decoding, parser, cheapest-correct labels, shared MiniLM embeddings, CV-tuned kNN and MLP, and the OOD difference; the fresh run reproduced 0.0067, so the event did not occur. Dropping six non-4-option ARC items is required by the fixed A-D prompt, and the Instruct chat template is an unspecified but standard choice, so neither makes this a different experiment. The value is valid: it comes from real generations, train and test are disjoint, best-single is chosen on train, and 0.700 versus 0.693 is exactly 210 versus 208 correct out of 300. The null is uninformative about cross-domain transfer because truncation makes 3B unusable and both routers send almost everything to 1.5B, leaving a two-item gap whose interval includes zero.

registration.title: Persona-shuffle control for user-conditioned routing gain
registration.seed_connection: Seed reports personalized routers beat agnostic routers on persona judge but rankings flip on real Slack users, raising judge-artifact concerns. This directly tests persona-specificity with a shuffle control using the same judge-then-route construction with neutral candidates to avoid trivial style alignment.
registration.hypothesis: A persona-conditioned kNN router predicts persona-judge preferences better with true personas than with shuffled personas by more than 5 points, proving gain is user-specific.
registration.contribution: Adds the missing shuffle control for persona-conditioned routing with a small local judge and neutral candidates: same router with true versus shuffled persona inputs on fixed judge labels plus query-only baseline. Prior personalized-judge work studies reliability but not routing, and seed reports persona gains without this control.

closest_work.difference: Shows LLM-as-personalized-judge has only 60 to 72 percent agreement and persona sparsity, but does not test routing or whether router gains survive persona shuffling.
Builds synthetic personalized preferences for reward modeling and tests transfer to real users, but does not evaluate user-conditioned versus shuffled routing decisions.

inputs: HuggingFace dataset allenai/ai2_arc config ARC-Challenge and tau/commonsense_qa fallback allenai/commonsense_qa for question stems splits train plus validation
HuggingFace models Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for neutral candidates, Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as persona judge
HuggingFace embedding sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
Python libraries datasets, transformers, torch, accelerate, sentence-transformers, scikit-learn, numpy
registration.method: Do not use APIs. Implement locally with transformers. 1) Load ARC and CSQA pools, shuffle each seed 0, take 150 ARC plus 150 CSQA total 300. Assign true personas stratified 50-50 seed 0 with 150 concise and 150 detailed, texts are You are a busy user who prefers concise direct answers with no extra explanation and You are a curious learner who prefers detailed explanatory answers with reasoning. Split into 180 train with 90 per persona and 120 test with 60 per persona disjoint stratified. Each item keeps question plus options text. 2) Generate neutral responses with 0.5B and 3B Instruct using same prompt Answer the following multiple-choice question plus State your chosen letter and explain your reasoning plus Question plus Options, greedy max 128 tokens float16 batch 8, no style instruction. 3) Judge each query once with 1.5B Instruct greedy max 16 using prompt You are simulating the following user persona plus persona plus As this persona evaluate which assistant response you would personally prefer plus User Question plus Assistant 1 plus Assistant 2 with neutral responses in randomized order per query seed 0 plus Output ONLY one of 1 2 Tie. Parse first 1 or 2 or Tie case-insensitive, failures as Tie. Map to preferred model, keep Ties as tie. 4) Exclude ties from router training and agreement denominator, report tie rate. Train persona-kNN embedding Persona plus persona plus Query plus question-options with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 normalized, KNeighbors n_neighbors 15 cosine, on non-tie train to judge-preferred labels. Train query-only kNN baseline embedding Query only same k and labels. Predict test twice for persona-kNN with true persona strings and shuffled persona strings from random permutation seed 1. Agreement is fraction matching true-persona judge labels on non-tie test.

event.description: Persona-conditioned kNN agreement with judge exceeds shuffled-persona agreement by more than 5 points
event.statistic: agree_correct_persona_minus_shuffled

evaluation.procedure: Compute agreement of persona-kNN with true-persona judge labels on non-tie test when router sees true vs shuffled personas. Statistic is true minus shuffled. Write outputs/scores.jsonl with one JSON per test query holding id question true and shuffled persona responses judge raw and parsed preference predictions in both conditions and baseline. Write outputs/metrics.json holding train test sizes non-tie counts tie rate win rates per persona fraction shuffled differing agnostic query-only agreement both conditioned agreements difference and bootstrap interval from 2000 resamples.
evaluation.controls: Judge labels fixed from true personas. Response order randomized per query and recorded. Tie rate and per-persona win rates as manipulation checks. Query-only kNN without persona as context. Fixed seeds.

registration.full_scale_study: If event occurs, run larger personalization study with 10 plus diverse personas, more candidates, certainty-filtered judging and human validation to determine which user encodings transfer beyond the judge.

agent.reason: Persona text dominates MiniLM similarity so true-vs-shuffled predictions will diverge, and even weak 1.5B judge persona sensitivity should produce a 5-point swing, though high tie rates and verbosity bias add noise.

outcome.executor_notes:
I implemented the registered experiment as written, running locally with transformers and no API calls. The candidates were Qwen2.5-0.5B and 3B-Instruct, the persona judge was Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and the routers were kNN classifiers (k=15, cosine) over all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings. The query pool was 150 ARC-Challenge plus 150 CommonsenseQA questions, each drawn from train+validation after a seed-0 shuffle. Personas were assigned 150/150 with seed 0. The split was 180 train / 120 test, stratified by persona (90/60 per persona). Answer order for the judge was randomised per query (seed 0) and recorded. Judge output was parsed as the first "1", "2" or "Tie" (case-insensitive), and parse failures counted as Tie. Ties were excluded from router training and from the agreement denominators. Shuffled test personas came from a seed-1 permutation over all 120 test items. The bootstrap uses 2000 paired resamples of the non-tie test items.

Small implementation choices I made:
- Prompts were sent as a single chat user turn, with left padding and fp16 greedy decoding at batch 8.
- Answer options were written as "A. text B. text".
- Persona stratification was done by persona only, not also by source dataset.
- I added some diagnostic outputs beyond those registered: the judge's position bias, candidate letter accuracy, agreement on the subset where the shuffle actually changed the persona, and a file of train judgements (outputs/train_judgments.jsonl).

Result from my test run (one repetition): the statistic agree_correct_persona_minus_shuffled was -0.026, with a bootstrap 95% CI of [-0.094, 0.043]. Agreement was 0.538 with true personas, 0.564 with shuffled personas and 0.496 for the query-only baseline. The training majority label matched 0.504 of the non-tie test items. The registered event (a gap greater than 0.05) did not occur.

Manipulation checks:
- Tie rate was 2%.
- The 3B model's win rate was 0.43 under the concise persona and 0.50 under the detailed persona. That is only a small persona effect in the judge labels.
- The judge picked position 1 only 34% of the time, which suggests a position bias.
- The shuffle changed the persona on 52% of non-tie test items and changed 15% of predictions.

My interpretation, not shown directly by these results: the 1.5B judge's labels seem to carry little persona-specific signal, so this run cannot show a user-specific routing gain. The confidence interval is wide, and a non-significant difference does not prove the gain is absent.
